Section 6-103(B)(5) requires an Analysis for Erosion, Sedimentation and Flooding if any Solar Panels or accessory facility is located within the 100-year floodplain, including a preliminary report addressing potential for wind erosion, water erosion, sedimentation and flooding, with a final report required if there are modifications to locations prior to construction. Section 6-105(A)(8)(d) mandates that "Erosion and sedimentation control measures that ensure that disturbed areas and soil stockpiles are stabilized during construction shall be implemented. Disturbed areas shall be revegetated in accordance with landowner agreements." These requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities defined as "an electricity generating facility ... whose main purpose is to supply electricity to off-site customer(s) with equal to or greater than 100 kilowatts in total nameplate capacity," which fits the typical definition of utility-scale solar energy systems.
section: Section 6-103      Conditional Use Development Permit Application Requirements for a Wind or Solar Energy Facility

summary: Setback from inhabited structures including: residence, school, hospital, church or public library is 500 feet for Solar Energy Facilities. Other setbacks include 70 feet from above-ground public electric power lines or communication lines, 70 feet from existing public road or highway or railroad, and 70 feet from all other property lines. (Section 6-105(B)(3)(b))
section: Section 6-105 Standards Applicable to Wind or Solar Energy Facility

summary: The following setbacks shall apply to each Solar Panel comprising the Solar Energy Facility: Setback from above-ground public electric power lines or communication lines: 70 feet. (Measured from the outer boundary of the public utility right-of-way or easement [or from existing power line or telephone line]). Other setback options include for wind energy facilities: 1.1 times system height from above-ground public electric power lines or communication lines; setbacks from existing public road or highway or railroad; setbacks from inhabited structures; and setbacks from all other property lines.
section: Section 6-105              Standards Applicable to Wind or Solar Energy Facility

summary: For Large Solar Energy Systems, a decommissioning plan must be submitted and approved as part of the application, addressing "the removal of all equipment and restoration of the site upon cessation of use." Additionally, the application must provide "a plan for site rehabilitation after the use is terminated." The Board of County Commissioners may require financial security "to secure the execution of the site rehabilitation plan conforming to best management practices." Other standards for Large Solar Energy Systems include compliance with setbacks, height limits (not exceeding 20 feet), screening from adjacent residential uses and public rights-of-way, impacts to wildlife and traffic, and operational standards to prevent nuisances. Small Solar Energy Systems have separate standards, including lower height limits and setback requirements, but decommissioning requirements are not explicitly stated for them. If a solar energy system is not operated for 12 months, it is considered abandoned and must be removed within 90 days of notice.

Section 5.2.20 C)4 requires that "All solar energy systems shall be designed and located to prevent glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and roadways and to not pose a safety hazard to motorists or pedestrians." Section 5.2.20 H) states that large solar energy systems "shall be operated so that it does not emit heat, glare, radiation, or fumes that substantially interfere with the existing use of adjoining properties or which constitutes a public nuisance or hazard." These provisions explicitly impose glare restrictions on large solar energy systems. Other related standards include setbacks, height limits, screening, decommissioning plans, and operational requirements, but these do not specifically address glare.

The maximum height of any structure associated with a large solar energy system shall not exceed 20 feet, as measured from the natural grade at the base of the structure to its highest point. Other related height limits include small solar energy systems with a maximum height of 15 feet, roof-mounted small systems not extending more than 5 feet above the highest roof point, and ground-mounted solar panels not exceeding 25 feet in height. However, for large solar energy systems specifically, the 20 feet maximum height applies.

Large solar energy systems shall be screened from adjacent residential uses and public rights-of-way to the extent practicable through the use of landscaping, berms, fencing, or other screening methods (5.2.20 D) 2) c)). Additionally, all ground-mounted systems and other energy system appurtenances shall be screened from views at grade to the best extent possible, without compromising the solar energy system’s access to the sun (5.2.20 M)).

Large Solar Energy System is listed as a conditional use (marked 'C') in the districts RUR, AF, AR, UR, RM, CI, IM, and BC, indicating that it requires approval such as a conditional use permit. It is permitted as a use (marked 'A') in districts B, RC, and R. The ordinance states: 'Large Solar Energy System, C in RUR, AF, AR, UR, RM, CI, IM, BC; A in B, RC, R' and refers to standard 5.2.20 which outlines application requirements including site plan submittal, impacts to wildlife, traffic, separation distances, site rehabilitation, financial security, sound standards, operations, lighting, dimensional standards, and screening. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this determination as per instructions.

The total area of the ground mounted small solar energy system cannot exceed fifty percent of the lot’s net area. This applies to Small Solar Energy Facilities defined as facilities developed for supplying or distributing electrical energy to users/customers. Other related coverage limits include: for accessory solar energy systems designed to supply power to the principal use on the lot, ground mounted systems cannot exceed ten percent of the lot’s net area; and the ground mounted system may exceed five acres if sized for the principal use. The unit is expressed as a percentage of the lot’s net area.
section: Accessory Solar and Small Solar Facilities

summary: A Small Solar Energy Facility application must include an agreement that addresses decommissioning and abandonment of the facility. The agreement must at a minimum provide for reuse or dismantlement of the facility at the owner’s expense. Disturbed areas shall be reestablished to historic drainage patterns and ground cover.

A ground mounted small solar energy facility in which all components together disturb an area of five (5) or fewer acres requires review and approval through the Public Site Plan review process. Additionally, the total area of the ground mounted solar energy system cannot exceed fifty percent of the lot’s net area. The most restrictive maximum lot size is 5 acres of disturbance. Units are expressed in acres.

A small solar energy facility "must be designed to minimize site disturbances." "Reestablishment of all disturbed areas, including the construction access, shall maintain the historic drainage patterns and permeable ground cover and must be done to minimize environmental impacts." "Temporary and permanent erosion control measures shall be used as necessary to minimize erosion of the site." These requirements apply to ground mounted small solar energy facilities disturbing five (5) or fewer acres, which require review and approval through the Public Site Plan review process prior to building permit application. Other conditions include setbacks matching minimum building setbacks, total area not exceeding fifty percent of the lot’s net area, underground power lines except near transmission connections, and inclusion of transmission facilities in the project proposal. Building mounted small solar energy facilities meeting certain height and mounting standards are allowed by right.

Section G.3.M. requires a Decommissioning Plan describing the decommissioning and final land reclamation plan to be followed after the anticipated useful life, abandonment, or termination of the project, including evidence of proposed commitments with affected parties that ensure proper final reclamation of the solar energy project. The plan should address revegetation and road repair activities, as well as the applicant’s ability to honor this provision in the event of insolvency. A bond, an irrevocable letter of credit, or cash shall be required for the decommissioning of any solar energy facilities. The amount shall be determined from a third party decommissioning evaluation made prior to construction and every five years throughout the project life at the expense of the applicant.
section: G. Standards for Regulation of the Construction and Operation of Solar Power Facilities

summary: Under Section G.2.3.a (Safety/Access), "An appropriate security/livestock fence (height and material to be established through the use by special review process) shall be placed around the perimeter of the solar power plant and maintained by the facility operator." This fencing requirement applies specifically to large scale solar facilities as indicated by the section heading "DESIGN STANDARDS FOR LARGE SCALE SOLAR FACILITIES." Other options and conditions include: Small Scale Solar Development does not require permitting; Medium Scale Solar Development requires a building permit and must meet manufacturers’ standards, with a 15 foot fire separation if panels are ground-mounted; Large Scale Solar Facilities are subject to setbacks, safety/access including fencing, noise limitations, visual appearance standards, underground electrical interconnections, fire protection, and other requirements as part of the Use by Special Review process.
section: G. Standards for Regulation of the Construction and Operation of Solar Power Facilities

summary: Under Section G, 2.B.5.d, the ordinance states: 'No solar power plant shall produce glare that would constitute a nuisance to occupants of neighboring properties or persons traveling neighboring public roads.' This glare restriction applies specifically to Large Scale Solar Facilities, as indicated by the section heading 'DESIGN STANDARDS FOR LARGE SCALE SOLAR FACILITIES.' Other related design standards for large scale solar facilities include setbacks, safety/access, noise limitations, visual appearance, electrical interconnections, fire protection, and lighting requirements.
section: Section G, 2.B. Design Standards for Large Scale Solar Facilities

summary: No operating solar power plant shall produce noise that exceeds any of the following limitations: 50 dBA at the property line of any neighboring residentially-zoned lot; 45 dBA at any existing neighboring residence between the hours of nine p.m. and seven a.m.; 60 dBA at the property lines of the project boundary, unless the owner of the affected property and the planning commission agree to a higher noise level. The most restrictive limit is 45 dBA during nighttime hours. Units are A-weighted decibels (dBA).

Large solar facilities shall be set back from all property lines, and public road rights-of-way at least one hundred feet. Setbacks from an occupied structure of a non-participating landowner shall be negotiable through public hearings and the permitting process but may not be within one thousand feet (1,000 feet) of an occupied structure unless written consent is given by the non-participating landowner and any other affected parties. Setbacks within a participating landowner’s rights shall be negotiated between the participating landowner and the developer.
section: G. Standards for Regulation of the Construction and Operation of Solar Power Facilities, 2. Regulations and Design Standards for Solar Power Facilities, B. DESIGN STANDARDS FOR LARGE SCALE SOLAR FACILITIES, 2. Setbacks

summary: Large solar facilities shall be set back from all property lines, and public road rights-of-way at least one hundred feet. (Section G.2.a) Setbacks from an occupied structure of a non-participating landowner shall be negotiable but may not be within one thousand feet unless written consent is given. Screening may be required between public roadways and residences. (Section G.2.b, G.2.d)
section: G. Standards for Regulation of the Construction and Operation of Solar Power Facilities, 2. Setbacks

summary: Under Section G.2.d, "Screening of the solar facility may be required through the review process between public roadways and residences with appropriate landscaping or screening materials." This applies to all large scale solar facilities (greater than 2 MWDC) and is part of the minimum regulations and design standards they must comply with. No other explicit vegetative buffer or screening requirements are detailed in the text provided.
section: G. Standards for Regulation of the Construction and Operation of Solar Power Facilities

summary: Under Section G.2.3 Safety/Access, "appropriate warning signage shall be placed at the entrance and perimeter of the solar power plant project." This signage requirement applies to all large scale solar facilities, which are defined as "a system with a nameplate rating of greater than two megawatts, Direct Current (2 MWDC) generation capacity providing power to one or more users." Other relevant requirements for large scale solar facilities include setbacks, security fencing, noise limitations, visual appearance standards, underground electrical interconnections, fire protection, and the use by special review development process.
section: G. Standards for Regulation of the Construction and Operation of Solar Power Facilities

summary: The ordinance requires Large Scale Solar Facilities to include "dust and erosion control" in their site and development plans (Section G.3.C). Siting considerations must avoid "visual areas of erodible slopes and soils, where concerns for water quality, landslide, severe erosion, or high storm runoff potential have been identified" (Section G.4.B). Additionally, the Land Use Board/Commissioners may require an "analysis of impacts to historic, cultural and archaeological resources, soil erosion (water and wind), flora, and water quality and water supply in the area" when there is reason to believe adverse impacts may occur (Section G.4.G). These requirements apply as part of the Use by Special Review development process for all large scale solar facilities (Section G.2.A).
section: G. Standards for Regulation of the Construction and Operation of Solar Power Facilities

summary: Setbacks from an occupied structure of a non-participating landowner shall be negotiable through public hearings and the permitting process but may not be within one thousand feet (1,000 feet) of an occupied structure unless written consent is given by the non-participating landowner and any other affected parties. Other options include setbacks within a participating landowner’s rights, which shall be negotiated between the participating landowner and the developer.
section: G. Standards for Regulation of the Construction and Operation of Solar Power Facilities, 2. Regulations and Design Standards for Solar Power Facilities, B. DESIGN STANDARDS FOR LARGE SCALE SOLAR FACILITIES, 2. Setbacks

summary: Section G.4.E Visual Impacts, Appearance, and Scenic Viewsheds requires that projects within a sensitive viewshed, or that propose structures taller than thirty feet, must provide a viewshed analysis of the project, including visual simulations from no less than four vantage points that together provide a view from all sides of the project. More visually sensitive proposals may require analysis from significantly more vantage points. The Land Board/Commissioners may also require a Zone of Theoretical Visibility/Zone of Visual Impact (ZVI) Analysis, which is a 360-degree computer analysis to map lands within a defined radius that would likely see an object. When a dispute arises on whether a location is in a sensitive viewshed, the Board has final determination. Significant visual impacts that cannot be adequately mitigated are grounds for denial.
section: Section G.4.E Visual Impacts, Appearance, and Scenic Viewsheds

summary: Section 1-103(A)(7) requires the Applicant to provide a detailed Decommissioning Plan explaining how the project will be deconstructed and disposed of upon abandonment or end of its useful life, including the method and manner of site reclamation and the proposed financial guarantee to secure the decommissioning obligation. Section 1-105(B)(8) states: "The obligation to perform decommissioning will be financially secured in a form and manner approved by the Logan County Board of Commissioners, in its sole discretion. The decommissioning obligation will be secured by a letter of credit, bond or cash deposit, in an amount based on a certified estimate prepared by a professional engineer hired by the Applicant. The decommissioning plan, obligation and financial guarantee will be incorporated into an enforceable Development Agreement." These requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities defined as electricity generating facilities with equal to or greater than 100 kilowatts in total nameplate capacity, whose main purpose is to supply electricity to off-site customer(s).
section: Section 1-103 Special Use Permit Application Requirements for a Solar Energy Facility and Section 1-105 Standards Applicable to Solar Energy Facility

summary: Fencing, or other barriers acceptable to the County, shall be installed to prevent unauthorized access to the Solar Energy Facility substations. This requirement applies to Solar Energy Facilities defined as electricity generating facilities with equal to or greater than 100 kilowatts in total nameplate capacity, whose main purpose is to supply electricity to off-site customer(s).
section: Section 1-105 Standards Applicable to Solar Energy Facility

summary: The ordinance states: 'Setback from all other property lines. 1. Measured from the outer boundary of the public utility right-of-way or easement [or from existing power line or telephone line]. 2. Measured from the outer boundary of the public road/highway right-of-way or railroad right-of-way.' The minimum setback from property lines is 70 feet. Other setbacks include 300 feet from inhabited structures and a case-by-case setback from Section Lines (parcels). Scenic resource setbacks require a minimum 1/4 mile distance from designated scenic highways or roadways. The setback from Section Lines is reviewed on a case-by-case basis due to county right-of-way considerations.

The ordinance specifies a minimum setback of 70 feet from existing public roads, highways, or railroads, measured from the outer boundary of the railroad right-of-way. This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined by the text (equal to or greater than 100 kilowatts and intended to supply electricity off-site). Other setbacks mentioned include 70 feet from above-ground public electric power lines or communication lines, 300 feet from inhabited structures such as residences, schools, hospitals, churches, or public libraries, and a scenic resources setback of 1/4 mile from designated scenic highways or roadways.
section: Section 1-105 B. Site and Facility Development Standards

summary: Setback from existing public road or highway or railroad is 70 feet. Additionally, there is a scenic resources setback requiring solar panels to be setback a minimum 1/4 mile from any highway designated as a scenic highway or roadway by the Logan County Comprehensive Plan or by the state. Also, setbacks from section line rights-of-way (30 feet on each side) are reviewed on a case-by-case basis to avoid conflicts with current or future county road plans.

The ordinance requires a Water and/or Erosion Control Plan as part of the Pre-Construction Materials, including a preliminary plan showing existing and proposed grading and a description of practices to prevent erosion and run-off during construction, with a final Drainage and Erosion Control Plan required prior to commencement of construction if there are any modifications. Additionally, "Erosion and Sedimentation Control. Erosion and sedimentation control measures that ensure that disturbed areas and soil stockpiles are stabilized during construction shall be implemented. Disturbed areas shall be revegetated in accordance with landowner agreements." These requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities defined as electricity generating facilities with equal to or greater than 100 kilowatts in total nameplate capacity, intended to supply electricity to off-site customers. Other related requirements include an analysis for erosion, sedimentation, and flooding if any solar panels or accessory facilities are located within the 100-year floodplain, and compliance with applicable County, State, and Federal regulations for drainage and storm-water run-off, including obtaining a Construction Stormwater Discharge Permit if applicable.

Solar Energy Facilities (defined as electricity generating facilities with equal to or greater than 100 kilowatts capacity intended to supply off-site customers) require a Special Use Permit. Section 3.1 states: 'Agricultural Zone Solar Energy Facilities Use by Special Permit (P)'. Additionally, 'Solar Energy Facilities shall require a Special Use Permit issued, prior to construction, by the Board of County Commissioners upon the recommendations of the County Planning Commission.' No other districts are mentioned for such facilities outside of overlay districts.
section: Section 3.1 - Use Schedules for Zoning Districts

summary: The ordinance states a fixed setback distance of 300 feet from inhabited structures including residence, school, hospital, church or public library, unless appropriate easements are secured. Other setback distances mentioned include 70 feet from above-ground public electric power lines or communication lines, 70 feet from existing public road or highway or railroad, and 70 feet from all other property lines. The relevant text is: 'Setback from inhabited structures including: residence, school, hospital, church or public library, unless appropriate easements are secured. 300 feet.'

The ordinance specifies a minimum setback of 70 feet from above-ground public electric power lines or communication lines for utility-scale solar energy systems. This is stated as: 'Setback from above-ground public electric power lines or communication lines. 70 feet'. It also references measurement from the outer boundary of the public utility right-of-way or easement (or from existing power line or telephone line). Other setbacks mentioned in the ordinance pertain to roads, inhabited structures, and property lines, but these are not relevant to setbacks from overhead electrical transmission lines or utility easements.

Section 4-835 Decommissioning Requirements for Solar Collector Facilities states: (A)(1) If a solar collector facility ceases to perform its originally intended function for more than 12 consecutive months unless for the purpose of repowering the facility or as explicitly agreed to in writing by the County Planning Department, the permit holder and/or property owner shall remove the facility, mount and associated equipment and facilities by no later than 270 days after the end of the 12-month period. (A)(2) If permit holder and/or property owner notifies the County of the termination of operations, decommissioning shall be completed no less than 180 days from the date of the notice. (A)(3) Upon removal, the property shall be restored to the condition prior to development or as agreed in writing by the County Planning Department and landowner. (B) The decommissioning plan shall include contact information, a detailed removal plan including removal of structures, debris and cabling to depths agreed or 24 inches, a cost estimate prepared by a professional engineer or contractor, and roles and responsibilities of involved parties. (C) The decommissioning cost minus salvage value shall be secured by cash, surety bond or irrevocable letter of credit at 50% before construction and 50% prior to the twelfth anniversary of construction commencement. (D) If decommissioning does not proceed per plan, the County may enter the property to perform abandonment and decommissioning measures. These requirements apply to solar collector facilities more than 20 acres as indicated in the use table and throughout the text.
section: 4-835 Decommissioning Requirements for Solar Collector Facilities

summary: Section 4-825(D)(16)(d) states: 'The panels shall be located so as to minimize glare visible from an abutting property.' Additionally, 4-825(D)(16) requires that 'Construction and operation of the solar collector facility shall not significantly increase existing glare, dust, or noise at surrounding properties.' These requirements apply to principal ground-mounted solar collectors, which include Solar Collector Facilities more than 20 acres. Other related standards in 4-825(D) include setbacks, maximum height, and scenic resource setbacks, but these do not specifically address glare. The glare restrictions are explicit and mandatory for large-scale solar collector facilities.

The maximum height of the solar panels shall not exceed 30 feet in height or 35 feet in height for agrivoltaics when oriented at maximum tilt. This applies to principal ground-mounted solar collectors, which would typically include large-scale commercial solar collector facilities over 20 acres.

The ordinance distinguishes solar collector facilities by size, explicitly stating 'Solar collector facilities more than 20 acres' are allowed only as a Special Use (SU) in certain zone districts and 'Solar collector facilities, 20 acres or less' are allowed as a Conditional Use (CU) or Not Permitted (NP) in others. This establishes a minimum lot size of more than 20 acres for the larger solar collector facilities category. The units for this minimum size are acres, a standard area measurement.

Setback from all other property lines 70 feet. The setback requirement from property lines, which are not section lines, may be waived for property lines that are located within the project boundary, as shown on the site plan/map required in Sec. 4-820(A). Under no circumstances may a waiver under this subsection be granted for setback requirements from property lines that are located outside the project boundary. Setback from the section lines: The County has established right-of-ways (ROWS) that are located 30 feet on each side of section lines. Placement of solar panels within this ROW will be reviewed by the County on a case-by-case basis. Scenic Resources Setback: Solar panels shall be set back a minimum ¼ mile from any highway designated as scenic, but this is not a property line setback. Other setbacks mentioned (e.g., from inhabited buildings, roads, transmission lines) are excluded as they do not pertain to property lines or parcels.

Setback from existing public road or highway or railroad: 70 feet. This setback applies to principal ground-mounted solar collector facilities, which include solar collector facilities more than 20 acres. The setbacks in this subsection shall govern over any setbacks established in these Zoning Regulations. Other setbacks listed include: 70 feet from above-ground public utility power lines or communication lines; 500 feet from inhabited buildings including residence, school, hospital, church or public library; and 70 feet from all other property lines.

Minimum Setback: Setback from existing public road or highway or railroad 70 feet. Additionally, setback from the section lines includes a 30-foot right-of-way on each side, subject to county review and possible waiver. There is also a scenic resource setback of ¼ mile from any highway designated as scenic by the Morgan County Comprehensive Plan or the state, which may be reduced by the Board under certain conditions.

Section 4-820(I) requires the applicant to provide a "Water and/or Wind Erosion Control Plan" showing existing and proposed grading for the solar collector site, accompanied by a description of practices to prevent erosion and run-off during construction. If there are modifications, a final drainage and erosion control plan must be provided prior to construction. Section 4-825(12) mandates that "Erosion and sedimentation control measures that ensure that disturbed areas and soil stockpiles are stabilized during construction shall be implemented." Disturbed areas must be revegetated in accordance with landowner agreements. These requirements apply to solar collector facilities more than 20 acres as defined in the text. Other related requirements include a geotechnical report (4-820(J)) and drainage/storm-water run-off management (4-825(13)), but the explicit soil, erosion, and sediment control measures are in 4-820(I) and 4-825(12).
section: 4-820 Submittal Requirements and 4-825 Solar Collector Facility Standards

summary: The setback from inhabited buildings including: residence, school, hospital, church or public library is 500 feet. This setback may be reduced if appropriate screening through landscape or an opaque fence is installed, or upon submittal to the County of a waiver or informed consent signed by the owner of the inhabited structure agreeing to the lesser setback. Other setbacks mentioned include 70 feet from above-ground public utility power lines or communication lines, 70 feet from existing public road or highway or railroad, and 70 feet from all other property lines, but these do not pertain to occupied dwellings or similar structures.

Minimum Setback: Setback from above-ground public utility power lines or communication lines 70 feet. (4-825(D)(1)) The setbacks in this subsection shall govern over any setbacks established in these Zoning Regulations. Overhead transmission lines are permissible from the project substation to the point of electrical interconnection. (4-825(D)(17))

Section 4-820(C)(4) requires a Narrative and Impact Analysis including: "a description of baseline conditions and the impacts that the proposed solar collector may cause; a description of how the applicant will mitigate impacts; and documentation that applicable standards will be satisfied." This is part of the submittal requirements for solar collectors, which apply to facilities more than 20 acres (noted as Special Use in the use table). The Impact Analysis is explicitly required as part of the application and constitutes a visual impact assessment. Other submittal requirements include site plans, drawings, utility interconnection, decommissioning plans, and various technical reports, but only the Impact Analysis explicitly addresses assessment of impacts. The regulations apply to solar collector facilities more than 20 acres, which require a Special Use permit (SU).

The Phillips County Board of County Commissioners enacted a six-month temporary moratorium on processing applications for utility-scale solar energy systems and battery energy storage systems located wholly or partially within Phillips County. The moratorium applies to "utility-scale solar energy system" defined as "an electricity generating facility consisting of ground-mounted solar arrays and associated control or conversion electronics, occupying more than 5 acres and used to produce utility power to off-site customers." The moratorium "shall end on March 30, 2026, unless terminated or extended by a resolution of the Board." It applies broadly without conditions or exceptions based on compliance, location subsets, prior approvals, or other conditions. The moratorium took effect on the date of adoption, September 30, 2025, and is currently in effect as of December 6, 2025.

Solar Energy Facilities on properties over 5 acres shall require a 1041 permit, in addition to a Special Use Permit. Prior to beginning commercial operations, Prowers County and the Applicant must formulate a Decommissioning Plan to ensure that the Solar Energy Facility is properly decommissioned. The Decommissioning Plan shall include: (1) Provisions describing the triggering events for decommissioning; if landowner agreements do not describe the schedule, decommissioning shall be completed within 18 months of filing a Notice of Termination of Operations with Prowers County. (2) Provisions for removal of structures, debris, and cabling, including those below the soil surface. (3) Provisions for restoration of soil and vegetation. (4) Applicant must provide a guarantee of financial security (Financial Assurance) within the first ten years of the project, in the form of cash or surety bond, negotiable with the Board of County Commissioners. The Financial Assurance is based on an independent cost estimate updated every five years after year 10, accounting for salvage values. The Financial Assurance may be released when the site is returned to its original or acceptable condition. Other options include Solar Energy Facilities for non-commercial uses as a Use by Right, and commercial use on properties under 5 acres as a Use by Special Review, but these do not explicitly mention decommissioning requirements.

The Solar Energy Facilities shall be enclosed with a security fence as approved pursuant to a fencing plan submitted to the Prowers County Land Use Administrator. Appropriate signage shall be placed upon such fencing that warns the public of the high voltage therein. This fencing requirement applies to Solar Energy Facilities, which includes commercial facilities on properties over 5 acres that require a 1041 permit in addition to a Special Use Permit.

Noise levels when measured at the property line of any adjacent landowner shall not exceed 50 decibels from 7 am to 7 pm, and shall not exceed 45 decibels from 7 pm to 7 am. Noise provisions may be waived by signing a waiver that sets forth the applicable noise provision(s) and the proposed changes. Noise shall be measured by an internal study and does not require a third-party noise study. The units are standard noise measurement units (decibels), assumed as dBA.

Setbacks for Commercial Solar Energy Facilities on properties over 5 acres require panels to be set back no less than 50 feet from a public right of way. Other setback distances include no less than 300 feet from the residence of a participating landowner (unless waived to 100 feet), no less than 100 feet from a non-occupied structure, and no less than 500 feet from the residence of a non-participating landowner. However, only the 50 feet setback from a public right of way directly pertains to roads.

The ordinance requires that for Solar Energy Facilities on properties over 5 acres, which require a 1041 permit and a Special Use Permit, the Applicant must provide a WATER AND/OR SOIL EROSION CONTROL PLAN including a preliminary plan showing existing and proposed grading and a description of practices to prevent erosion and run-off during construction, with a final plan required prior to construction if modifications occur. Additionally, if any solar collector or accessory facility is located within the 100-year floodplain, the Application must include an ANALYSIS FOR EROSION, SEDIMENTATION AND FLOODING addressing potential soil erosion, water erosion, sedimentation, and flooding, with a final report required prior to construction if there are modifications. These requirements are part of the Special Use Review Application process for commercial solar energy facilities on properties over 5 acres. Other related requirements include compliance with Prowers County Zoning Regulations and 1041 Regulations, submission of various fees, and additional reports such as a Geotechnical Report. The ordinance also includes provisions for septic systems, water supply, setbacks, noise, road use agreements, fencing, FAA compliance, fire protection, wildlife habitat considerations, waste management, property damage responsibility, maintenance, and decommissioning plans.

No less than 500 feet from the residence of a non-participating landowner to the panel. Other related provisions include a maximum Project Area of no more than 5,000 acres for Utility-Scale Solar Facilities (no size limit in P-1). The coverage limit is expressed as a percentage of the Project Area, not as an absolute area value.
section: F. Minimum Development and Performance Standards

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Utility-Scale Solar Facilities. Section I 'Decommissioning and Reclamation' states: 'Solar facilities that have reached the end of their useful life or have not been in active and continuous service for a period of six (6) months, shall be decommissioned at the Solar Facility owner’s or operator’s expense, except if the project is being repowered or a force majeure event has or is occurring requiring longer repairs; however, the County may require evidentiary support that a longer repair period is necessary.' The owner/operator must notify the Zoning Administrator in writing of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Decommissioning must comply with the approved Decommissioning Plan, which may be amended by the BOCC. It includes removal of all above and below-ground structures and restoration of the Project Area to pre-development conditions, including grading and re-seeding/replanting within 12 months of removal. Exceptions to site restoration require written landowner requests and BOCC approval. Hazardous materials must be disposed of according to federal and state law. The County controls the release of funds upon compliance and may approve partial release as portions of the plan are performed. If the owner/operator fails to remove the installation timely, the County may collect financial security and remove the installation. Additionally, application requirements (E.13) require a detailed Decommissioning and Reclamation Plan certified by a licensed design professional, including cost estimates without salvage value, financial security (cash escrow, surety bond, or other security), third-party review, and periodic updates every five years with adjustments to the security amount if costs change by more than 10%. Alternative financial securities may be approved by the County. These requirements apply to utility-scale solar facilities as indicated by references to substations and battery storage as part of such facilities.

Security fencing requirements for Solar Facilities include that they "shall be enclosed by security fencing not less than six (6) feet in height." Heights greater than six feet "may require a building permit from the Pueblo Regional Building Department and zoning authorization from Pueblo County." The fencing "shall be placed around sections of the facilities, including PV pods, to provide openings between the sections and pods to allow for the movement of migratory animals and other wildlife." Additionally, security fencing "shall be placed on the interior of the Buffer Zone to be significantly screened from public view." Maintenance is required: "Fencing must be maintained in a good and functional condition" and failure to maintain "may result in a show cause hearing" or "revocation of the permit." This fencing requirement applies to Utility-Scale Solar Facilities as described in the ordinance. Other screening methods such as landscaping, berming, and visually solid fencing (at least 75% visually solid) are mentioned but fencing "shall not be the primary method" for screening. The ordinance also includes setback requirements for fencing: minimum setbacks of 50 feet from commercial/industrial parcels and 150 feet from other parcels, and a 500-foot setback from dwellings.
section: F. Minimum Development and Performance Standards

summary: The ordinance explicitly restricts glare for Utility-Scale Solar Facilities by stating: 'No glare shall be discernible beyond the outer boundaries of parcel.' This is found under section F. Minimum Development and Performance Standards, item 18. The ordinance also includes other related performance standards such as setbacks, height limits, screening, and lighting requirements, but the specific glare restriction is clearly stated as above.
section: F. Minimum Development and Performance Standards

summary: The maximum height of the lowest edge of the photovoltaic panels shall be 10 feet and the maximum height of the highest edge of the photovoltaic panels shall be 20 feet as measured from the finished grade. The maximum height of all other structures associated with the Solar Facility shall be 45 feet as measured from the finished grade at the base of the structure to its highest point, including appurtenances, with the exception of substations and electrical power transmission lines. The Board of County Commissioners may approve a greater height based upon the demonstration of a significant need and where the impacts of increased height are mitigated. Units are feet.

The maximum Project Area for a Utility-Scale Solar Facility shall be no more than 2,500 acres (with a note that 5,000 acres is also mentioned but 2,500 is the more restrictive value). The text states: 'The minimum Project Area of a Utility-Scale Solar Facility shall be more than 10 acres, and the maximum Project Area shall be no more than 2,5005,000 acres (no size limit in P-1). Requests for higher acreage projects may be submitted at the time of application if there is a clear justification based on location or other factors.' The units for this maximum size are acres.
section: 17.168.050 Solar Facilities, F. Minimum Development and Performance Standards

summary: The minimum Project Area of a Utility-Scale Solar Facility shall be more than 10 acres, and the maximum Project Area shall be no more than 5,000 acres (no size limit in P-1). Other scale categories include Medium-Scale Solar Facility with a minimum area of one (1) acre and maximum area of ten (10) acres. The units for these size requirements are expressed in acres.
section: 17.168.050 Solar Facilities, F. Minimum Development and Performance Standards

summary: The minimum setback of structures and uses associated with the Solar Facility to exterior parcel lines or the Official Street Line shall be based on the zoning district of the adjacent parcel as indicated: 50 feet from commercial and industrial zoned parcels, or 150 feet from all other parcels (unless located within the P-1 District).
section: F. Minimum Development and Performance Standards, 3. Setbacks, a. Project Boundary Setbacks

summary: The ordinance requires a Buffer Zone within the Project Area "reserved for open space, landscaping, or berming," located between the Project Boundary or Official Street Line and the required Project Boundary Setback to mitigate effects on surrounding properties and the community at large. Screening and buffering "shall be used to mitigate adverse visual impacts and to provide for compatibility between dissimilar adjoining uses." Screening must "substantially block any view of material, equipment, or stored vehicles from any point located on a street or adjoining property adjacent to the site." Methods include: (a) Existing Screening such as vegetation or topography; (b) Landscaping with "evergreen trees that are 5-6 ft. in height at time of planting and deciduous trees that are 5-6 ft. in height at time of planting," planted in no less than three rows and spaced 15 ft. on center; (c) Berming with "3:1 side slope to rise ratio, 4-6 ft. above the adjacent grade, with a 3 ft. wide top" and sculpted edges; (d) Fencing that is "at least 75 percent visually solid" and may be combined with other methods but not used as the primary method. Ground cover "shall be native vegetation," and security fencing "shall be placed on the interior of the Buffer Zone to be significantly screened from public view." Wildlife corridors must be identified and shown on plans. A final Screening and Vegetation Plan must be submitted for approval, including native species, pollinators, plant density, and maintenance requirements. Only EPA approved herbicides may be used with restrictions near groundwater wells. A revegetation bond is required to cover landscaping and erosion control. These requirements apply to Utility-Scale Solar Facilities subject to the 1041 Permit process, including those with substations and battery storage.

The ordinance explicitly requires soil, erosion, and sediment control for Utility-Scale Solar Facilities. It mandates submission and approval of a final Grading Plan that "limits grading to the greatest extent practicable by avoiding steep slopes and laying out arrays parallel to landforms," includes "locations and amount of topsoil to be stripped and stockpiled onsite," and ensures "an earthwork balance achieved on-site with no import or export of soil." It also requires "installation of all stormwater and erosion and sediment control infrastructure at the outset of the project" with a limit that "no more than 50 percent of the land disturbance areas... shall be disturbed without soil stabilization at any one time," where stabilization means "application of seed and straw to disturbed areas." An Erosion and Sediment Control Plan and a Stormwater Management Plan must be submitted, reviewed by a third party, and approved by the County, with bonds or other securities posted for construction and post-construction phases. Compliance with Pueblo County and Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment stormwater permits is also required. These requirements apply to large scale solar facilities, including utility-scale projects, as indicated by references to "Utility-Scale Solar Facilities" and "large scale solar facility (i.e., medium-scale and utility-scale solar project)" throughout the text.

Setbacks from Dwellings. To minimize adverse impacts upon surrounding nearby residential uses, the minimum setback of structures and uses associated with the Solar Facility, including fencing, PV panels, parking areas, and outdoor storage, but not including landscaping and berming, shall be not less than 500 feet from the nearest dwelling existing at the time the Solar Facility was approved by the County to the nearest Solar Facility structure (typically the fencing). Other setback options include Project Boundary Setbacks of 50 feet from commercial and industrial zoned parcels, or 150 feet from all other parcels (unless located within the P-1 District), but these relate to parcel lines, not dwellings.
section: F. Minimum Development and Performance Standards

summary: Section E.5 Visual Impact Analysis requires "a visual impact analysis demonstrating project siting and proposed mitigation, if necessary, so that the solar facility minimizes impact on the visual character of the surrounding area." The applicant must provide "accurate, to scale, photographic simulations showing the relationship of the solar facility and its associated amenities and development to its surroundings," including views from property lines and roadways as deemed necessary by the County. The number and perspectives of simulations "shall may be established by the Zoning Administrator after the pre-application meeting." This requirement is "not applicable in P-1 and may be waived by the Zoning Administrator for Medium-scale solar facilities." These provisions apply to large scale solar facilities, including utility-scale projects, as defined in the ordinance.

A Decommissioning/Reclamation Plan shall be submitted with the application and address the following: decommissioning shall commence after six (6) months of the facility having equipment removed, disconnected from power, or loss of lease and be completed within twelve (12) months; all non-utility owned equipment, conduits, structures, fencing, and foundations shall be removed to a depth of at least three (3) feet below grade; property shall be restored to a condition reasonably similar to its condition prior to development; the developer or owner is responsible for decommissioning; valid surety is required within ten (10) years of commercial operation, equal to the estimated cost of decommissioning plus 150%, updated every five (5) years; engineered cost estimates must include all costs associated with removal, reclamation, revegetation, and administrative costs; land disturbed shall be reseeded or revegetated to a condition reasonably similar to its condition prior to development within one (1) calendar year, with a possible six-month extension. These requirements apply to both Community-Scale and Utility-Scale Solar Facilities. Other options or conditions include retaining fences, graveled areas, and access roads if a landowner agreement is presented in writing.

summary: The facility shall be enclosed with a security fence approved pursuant to a fencing plan. Appropriate signage shall be placed upon the fencing that warns the public of the high voltage. All fencing shall comply with the wildlife fencing requirements outlined in Section 3.36.D.23.h, which includes specifications such as: white wire for visibility, wire placement on the domestic animal side, smooth wire or rounded rail on top, fence height of 42 inches or less, specific wire spacing, posts at minimum 16 feet apart, gates or removable sections where animals cross, and visual markers on top of the fence. summary: Ground-mounted solar collectors shall not exceed twenty-five (25) feet in height, measured from the lowest grade below each solar collector to the highest extent of the solar collector rotation. This height limitation applies to both Community-Scale and Utility-Scale Solar Energy Facilities as indicated in Section 3.36.D.4.

summary: The sound pressure level of the solar energy system and all ancillary equipment shall not exceed the residential standard of 55 dBA at the property line of an adjoining non-participating lot. This standard applies to both Community-Scale and Utility-Scale Solar Energy Facilities as indicated in Section 3.36.D.17.
section: 3.36. Standards for Community-, and Utility- Scale Solar Energy Systems

summary: Section 3.36.D.8 Screening requires that "Screening and buffering shall mitigate any adverse visual and audible impacts to adjacent developments. Screening is required to minimize the impacts of solar energy system from any point located on an adjacent right-of-way." It further states that "Vegetation or other screening techniques, such as fencing, may be used to effectively screen the area. All fencing shall comply with the wildlife fencing requirements outlined in Section 3.36.D.21.g." Additionally, Section 3.36.D.6.b.iii provides that the residential setback requirement for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems "may be reduced by up to fifty (50) percent if appropriate screening through landscaping, if an opaque fence is installed, or upon submittal of a waiver or informed consent signed by the affected landowner agreeing to the lesser setback. If landscaping or opaque fencing is substituted for setback, a landscaping plan or fencing plan shall be submitted and approved through the review process." These requirements apply to Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance.
section: 3.36. Standards for Community-, and Utility- Scale Solar Energy Systems

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Key provisions include: land disturbance or clearing shall be limited to what is minimally necessary (3.36.D.2.b); a dust mitigation plan is required with practices such as limiting area of disturbance, stabilizing roads and stripped areas, increasing watering during high winds, and revegetating disturbed areas (3.36.D.9); ground cover and vegetation preservation and management must maximize pre-construction vegetation, seed disturbed land with native prairie grasses and forbs, use deep-rooted vegetative cover to reduce maintenance, and maintain vegetation throughout the permit duration (3.36.D.11); erosion and sedimentation control measures must stabilize disturbed areas and soil stockpiles during construction, retain and reuse topsoil on-site, contour topsoil stockpiles for vegetative cover, and revegetate all disturbed areas within one growing season (3.36.D.12); stormwater and water quality standards require infiltration, soil bulk density limits, minimizing grading, and post-construction soil decompaction if needed (3.36.D.13); solar collectors must be arranged to allow runoff passage and vegetation growth beneath and between arrays (3.36.D.14); and a Decommissioning/Reclamation Plan must include soil stabilization, revegetation to pre-development conditions, soil testing before and after operation, and completion of revegetation within one calendar year of removal (3.36.D.26). These requirements apply to Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems subject to Special Use Permit approval (3.36.C.2).
section: 3.36. Standards for Community-, and Utility- Scale Solar Energy Systems

summary: For Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems: The improved area must be at least one hundred (100) feet from existing residential buildings. The residential setback requirement may be reduced by up to fifty (50) percent if appropriate screening through landscaping, if an opaque fence is installed, or upon submittal of a waiver or informed consent signed by the affected landowner agreeing to the lesser setback. If landscaping or opaque fencing is substituted for setback, a landscaping plan or fencing plan shall be submitted and approved through the review process. In no case will the setback be reduced to less than that required by the underlying zone district for properties that are not part of the improved area.
section: 3.36. Standards for Community-, and Utility- Scale Solar Energy Systems

summary: Section 3.36.D.5 states: 'Visual Impacts: In order to minimize the potential visual impacts of the Solar Energy System, certain activities should be minimized or avoided, detailed below. A site plan and visual impacts statement shall be included in the application to determine compliance with these standards.' This applies to both Community-Scale and Utility-Scale Solar Energy Facilities, with Utility-Scale defined as 'renewable energy systems that are large in scale and primarily serve the energy demands off-site from the facility, either as retail or wholesale' and 'are those systems that are up to 20 acres or larger in size.' The review process for Utility-Scale Solar Systems requires Planning Commission and BCC review for a Special Use Permit Approval and compliance with the requirements in 3.36.D. Other related requirements include setbacks, screening, dust mitigation, and wildlife considerations, but the explicit visual impact assessment requirement is the submission of a visual impacts statement with the application.
section: 3.36. Standards for Community-, and Utility- Scale Solar Energy Systems

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires a "Drainage and Erosion Control Plan" that "identifies existing and proposed drainage patterns and the methods for controlling erosion during construction and operation of the Facility" (Section 6.2.24). It also includes "Surface Disturbance Standards" with the purpose "to minimize negative impacts to surface activities and surface conditions" (Section 8.5). Under reclamation requirements (Section 8.5.6), the ordinance mandates a "Re-vegetation Plan" and specifies that "roads should be designed and constructed to allow for successful interim and eventual final reclamation," including salvaging and re-spreading topsoil and applying mulch or other sediment control to stabilize soils (Section 8.5.6.5). Additionally, drainage must be maintained to avoid erosion on primitive roads (Section 8.5.6.6). The ordinance also notes that mitigation for water quality impacts "may include an erosion control plan required under this Section" (Section 6.2.21.2). These requirements apply to Utility-Scale Solar Energy Facilities, defined as installations rated to produce more than 5 MW of electricity, which require permits under this Article.
section: XXII.6. Application Submittal Requirements for a Solar Energy Facility Permit; XXII.8. Performance Standards for All Solar Energy Facilities; XXII.8.5. Surface Disturbance Standards

summary: The ordinance requires that any potentially polluting activity associated with the solar energy facility may be located a minimum of 1000 feet from the normal high water mark of any water body. Non-polluting activities must be located a minimum of 150 feet from the normal high water mark. Additionally, facilities shall not be sited in an area of wetlands under the jurisdiction of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers or within a floodway of a stream or river as shown on Flood Insurance Rate Maps or as determined by a licensed professional engineer.

The ordinance requires a Decommissioning and Restoration Plan for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, defined as solar arrays occupying thirty (30) acres or more. The plan must be updated every five (5) years or more frequently and include: the responsible party; timeline and process for decommissioning and site reclamation; restoration to a condition similar to or better than prior to development; removal or conversion of all components including those above and below ground; site restoration of soil and vegetation; a monitoring plan for a minimum of three (3) years post-decommissioning; cost estimates for decommissioning and restoration updated every five (5) years; and a process for updating the plan. The Large-Scale Solar Development must be decommissioned and the site restored consistent with the approved plan. Additionally, financial security guarantees are required to ensure performance of the permit, including decommissioning, removal, and reclamation. Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems have similar but somewhat less detailed decommissioning plan requirements, and financial security may be required if deemed necessary. Small-Scale systems are not subject to these decommissioning requirements.

The ordinance explicitly requires fencing for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Section 6-203 B.III requires applicants to provide information on "Structures, fencing, equipment, and other improvements related to the facility." Section 6-204 C.IV mandates that the Large-Scale Solar Development "must be protected by fencing or other barriers to prevent unauthorized access." Additionally, Section 6-204 K.III specifies that proposed fencing "shall be wildlife-friendly to the maximum extent possible," following best practices such as the Colorado Department of Transportation Deer Fence, Gate, and Game Ramps Standard Plan NO. M-607-4 or substantially similar designs. It also requires minimizing fenced area footprints, regular inspection for trapped wildlife, installation of wildlife permeable fencing, and construction of unfenced wildlife passageways. These requirements apply to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems defined as solar arrays occupying thirty (30) acres or more of land. Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems have similar but scaled requirements, including fencing and wildlife-friendly fencing per Section 6-206 J.III. The ordinance distinguishes between Large-Scale, Medium-Scale, Microgrid Medium-Scale, and Small-Scale Solar Energy Systems, with fencing requirements explicitly detailed for Large-Scale and Medium-Scale systems but not for Small-Scale systems.
section: 6-204 Review Criteria for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems

summary: Section 6-203 N requires a "Glare, Glint and Lighting Impact Assessment" for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, including mapping and description of potential glare impacts on highways, scenic byways, public roads, trails, scenic vistas, airplane landing strips, and adjacent residential lots, and a description of proposed techniques to mitigate impacts of glare, glint, and lighting. Section 6-204 P sets review criteria stating: "The glare and glint from the Large-Scale Solar Development will not unreasonably interfere with the use and enjoyment of existing highways, designated scenic byways, public roads, trails, driveways, scenic vistas, unique land formations, recreational sites, airplane landing strips, and adjacent residential lots, nor result in a risk to public health, safety, welfare, or the environment." It also requires that glare and glint "will not create an unreasonable attractive nuisance for birds, wildlife, or persons." These requirements apply specifically to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, defined as solar arrays occupying thirty (30) acres or more of land. Other solar system scales (Medium-Scale and Small-Scale) have similar but separate provisions with different acreage and capacity thresholds and review criteria.
section: 6-203 N. Glare, Glint, and Lighting Impact Assessment; 6-204 P. Glare and Glint

summary: Large-Scale Solar Energy System: A Solar Energy System consisting of solar arrays occupying thirty (30) acres or more of land. The acreage calculation shall include the total area within the fenced or enclosed exterior boundary of the Solar Energy System and shall not include setbacks from property lines. Other scale definitions include Medium-Scale Solar Energy System occupying more than one-half (1/2) acre and less than thirty (30) acres, and Small-Scale Solar Energy System occupying no more than one-half (1/2) acre. The minimum lot size for Large-Scale systems is thus 30 acres or more.

Section 6-204 O. Noise, Dust, Fumes, Vibration, and Odor states: 'Sound emissions shall be less than fifty decibels (50 dB) at all property lines.' This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, defined as systems occupying thirty (30) acres or more. For Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems, a similar restriction is found in Section 6-206 M.II, also stating sound emissions shall be less than fifty decibels (50 dB) at all property lines. The units are expressed as decibels (dB), which is the standard unit for noise levels.
section: 6-204 Review Criteria for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems

summary: Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted only in the following zone districts: Forestry, Agriculture and Open (F), Heavy Commercial (HC), Low Intensity Industrial (I), Public (PUB), and West End (WE). Notably, "large-scale facilities would not be allowed in the Wright’s Messa zone districts." Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems may be permitted in additional districts including Wright’s Mesa Light Industrial (WMLI) and Wright’s Mesa Rural Agriculture (WMRA), which may require rezoning from Wright’s Mesa (WM). Microgrid Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems may be permitted in even more districts. Small-Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted in all zone districts as accessory uses. The text explicitly states that large-scale facilities are not allowed in Wright’s Mesa zone districts, indicating an unconditional prohibition there.

Fencing or other enclosures, solar panels, equipment, and structures shall be set back a minimum of two-hundred (200) feet from all property lines and one quarter (¼) mile from a Colorado designated Scenic Byway. Setbacks may be increased or decreased during the review and evaluation of the application. This setback applies to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, defined as solar arrays occupying thirty (30) acres or more of land. Setbacks to Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems are a minimum of 50 feet from all property lines.

Section 6-204 D. Signage: "All signage must comply with the LUC, Article 5, Section 5-704, Sign Requirements. The operator of the Large-Scale Solar Development shall post and maintain in legible condition warning signs at all entrances identifying emergency contact information." This requirement applies explicitly to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, defined as systems "consisting of solar arrays occupying thirty (30) acres or more of land." Other scale categories include Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems and Small-Scale Solar Energy Systems, with similar but separate provisions. The signage requirement is part of the review criteria for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems and is distinct from other application materials and review standards.
section: 6-204 Review Criteria for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires a "Grading, Erosion, and Sediment Control Plan" as part of the application materials for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems (Section 6-203 K). This plan must include measures to avoid soil disturbance, minimize erosion, control sediment, drainage facilities, construction schedules, cost estimates, and relevant permits. The review criteria (Section 6-204 M) mandate that "Erosion and sedimentation control measures will be implemented in conformance with the approved Grading, Erosion, and Sediment Control Plan to prevent erosion and sediment runoff and ensure that disturbed areas and soil stockpiles are stabilized." Similar requirements apply to Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems (Sections 6-205 H and 6-206 K). Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems are defined as those "consisting of solar arrays occupying thirty (30) acres or more of land." The permit application and review process for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems includes these soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements. Other related plans required include a Stormwater Management Plan (6-203 H), Revegetation and Weed Management Plan (6-203 L), and Decommissioning and Restoration Plan (6-203 AA).

summary: Section 6-203 O requires the applicant for a Large-Scale Solar Energy System to submit a "Visual Quality Impact Assessment" including: "Map and description of the existing scenic rural landscape within one (1) mile of the outer perimeter of the Large-Scale Solar Development," "at least four (4) visual renderings of the proposed development from key vantage points," and a "Description of the direct, indirect, and cumulative impacts of the Large-Scale Solar Development on the visual quality of the scenic rural landscape within one (1) mile." It also requires a "Description of proposed techniques that will be used to mitigate impacts to the visual quality of the scenic rural landscape within one (1) mile of the outside perimeter of the Large-Scale Solar Development such as proposed visual buffering, natural topography, plantings, earth berms, or fencing." Section 6-204 R sets the review criterion that the Large-Scale Solar Development "will not cause a significant adverse impact to the visual quality of the scenic rural landscape within one (1) mile of the Large-Scale Solar Development, including without limitation views from adjacent lots, towns, highways, designated scenic byways, public roads, trails, recreational sites, scenic vistas, and unique land formations." These requirements apply specifically to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, defined as "solar arrays occupying thirty (30) acres or more of land." Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems have similar but adjusted requirements in Sections 6-205 L and 6-206 P, which require visual quality impact assessments and review criteria for impacts to "nearby roads and properties."
section: Section 6-203 O. Visual Quality Impact Assessment and Section 6-204 R. Visual Quality

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires a Decommissioning Plan for Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems, including: anticipated life of the project; an estimate of decommissioning costs certified by a Professional Engineer and updated every five years after year fifteen; financial security provisions; triggering events for decommissioning after eighteen months of continuous non-operation; provisions for removal of structures, debris, and cabling down to twenty-four inches below soil surface; restoration of soil and vegetation; and County rights to review, reconsider, and access the site to ensure compliance. Financial security must be provided before permit issuance, equal to decommissioning costs, unless waived by the Board if the landowner agreement ensures decommissioning compliance and consents to waiver. Failure to decommission in compliance is a violation subject to enforcement, and the County may enter the property to complete decommissioning if necessary. Removal of discontinued Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems is required if the system ceases to perform its intended function for more than eighteen consecutive months, with removal and site restoration completed within ninety days after the 18-month period. These requirements are found in Section 13-105(A)(1)(k), 13-105(B)(4), and 13-105(D)(g). Other categories such as Residential Solar Energy Systems and Distributed Solar Energy Systems have separate standards and removal requirements but do not apply to Utility Scale systems as defined.

Section 13-105(D)(1) states: "Fencing or other barriers acceptable to the County shall be installed to prevent unauthorized access to solar collectors and equipment." This fencing requirement applies specifically to Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems "occupying more than 30 acres and that will be used to produce utility power to off-site customers." Other related requirements for Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems include setbacks, maximum system height, visual impacts, fire protection, location restrictions, certification, and removal of discontinued systems, but fencing is explicitly mandated only under the safety and security subsection.
section: 13-105: Utility Wind and Solar Requirements and Standards

summary: The Utility Scale Solar Energy System "shall not have an adverse visual impact on the natural features or character of the surrounding area and shall be located to minimize glare on adjacent properties and roadways." This is stated in Section 13-105(D)(1)(c). Other related requirements include setbacks (minimum setback complying with Industrial/Commercial Setbacks and a scenic resource setback of ¼ mile from designated scenic highways or roadways), maximum system height (panels may exceed the roofline by up to five feet), safety and security measures, location restrictions, certification requirements, and removal of discontinued systems.

The Utility Scale Solar Energy System shall be setback a minimum of ¼ mile (1320 feet) from any highway eligible or designated to be a scenic highway or roadway by the Sedgwick County Land Use Regulations or by the state. This scenic resource protection setback requirement may be reduced if the Board determines that the characteristics of the surrounding property eliminate or substantially reduce considerations of scenic value. Alternatively, Utility Scale solar collection panels and equipment shall comply with the Industrial/Commercial Setbacks, which include a front setback of 30 feet from the road right-of-way (ROW).
section: 13-105: Utility Wind and Solar Requirements and Standards

summary: Section 13-105(A)(1)(g) requires a Geotechnical Report that includes: 'Soils engineering and engineering geologic characteristics of the site based upon on-site sampling and testing,' 'Slope stability analysis,' and 'Grading criteria for ground preparation, cuts and fills, and soil compaction.' The Decommissioning Plan in Section 13-105(A)(1)(k) includes provisions for 'restoration of the soil and vegetation' and 'site restored' after removal of discontinued Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems. These requirements explicitly address soil, erosion, and sediment control for Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems. Other related requirements include setbacks, maximum system height, visual impacts, safety and security, location restrictions, certification, and removal of discontinued systems, but these do not explicitly address soil, erosion, or sediment control.

The Utility Scale Solar Energy System "shall not have an adverse visual impact on the natural features or character of the surrounding area and shall be located to minimize glare on adjacent properties and roadways." This requirement is found in Section 13-105(D)(1)(c). Additionally, the ordinance includes setback requirements, maximum system height, safety and security measures, location restrictions, certification requirements, and removal of discontinued systems for Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems. Setbacks include a minimum setback complying with Industrial/Commercial Setbacks, a scenic resource setback of at least ¼ mile from scenic highways or roadways (which may be reduced by the Board), and provisions for waiver or reduction of setbacks upon demonstration that the reduction is necessary and will not harm public health, safety, welfare, or the environment.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Solar Power Production Facilities (SPPF) / Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems. It requires "proof that the financial security will be in effect before construction operations commence" in the form of "a surety bond, letter of credit, or cash, in a form acceptable to the County." The security amount "shall be the average of at least two independent demolition/removal quotes" and "shall be equal to no less than 100% of the estimated cost of decommissioning the entire SPPF," updated every two years at 1.5 times CPI. The applicant must demonstrate no adverse effect on neighboring properties by providing aerials, graphic renderings, and/or pictures demonstrating sight lines. These requirements apply as conditions for granting conditional use permits in the A-1, I-1, and I-2 districts. Other uses listed in these districts include telecommunications structures, landfills, recovered material processing facilities, composting facilities, junk yards (which must be "completely screened from view by a solid opaque wall, or existing natural screen at least eight (8) feet in height"), explosives plants, and public or private utility generation facilities including power plants and substations.
section: 7.1.9 CONDITIONAL USES IN A-1 DISTRICT; 7.12.8 CONDITIONAL USES IN I-1 DISTRICT; 7.13.8 CONDITIONAL USES IN I-2 DISTRICT

summary: Solar power generation facilities are allowed as a primary use in the A-1, I-1 and I-2 districts, with the granting of a conditional use permit. Sections 7.12.8 and 7.13.8 specify that in the I-1 and I-2 districts, solar power generation facilities are permitted only with the grant of a conditional use permit under the requirements of Article XVI. Conditions include sound barriers for noise mitigation, screening and fencing with a minimum 8-foot opaque fence plus shrubbery, trees or an earthen berm, and demonstration that the proposal will not have an adverse effect on neighboring properties by providing aerials, graphic renderings, or pictures. Other solar power uses, such as panels on a residential or other primary structure, are allowed as accessory uses and are not included here. Solar overlay districts are excluded per instructions.
section: 7.12.8 CONDITIONAL USES IN I-1 DISTRICT and 7.13.8 CONDITIONAL USES IN I-2 DISTRICT

summary: Solar power generation facilities not accessory to a residential structure require a conditional use permit in the A-1, I-1, and I-2 districts. The applicant shall demonstrate that the proposal will not have an adverse effect on neighboring properties by providing aerials of the site, graphic renderings of the project, and/or pictures from the site of surrounding parcels demonstrating sight lines. Appropriate vegetated buffers and/or plantings may also be required to help limit the visual impact of the site. Sound barriers, screening with a minimum 8-foot opaque fence plus shrubbery, trees or an earthen berm, and fencing to restrict unauthorized access are also required. These requirements are found under 7.1.9 CONDITIONAL USES IN A-1 DISTRICT (BB), 7.12.8 CONDITIONAL USES IN I-1 DISTRICT (B), and 7.13.8 CONDITIONAL USES IN I-2 DISTRICT (G). Other uses listed in these sections include telecommunications structures, landfills, recovered material processing facilities, composting facilities, junk yards, explosives plants, public or private utility generation facilities, wind power generation facilities, and public utility service structures, each with their own conditions.
