summary: An application for a solar farm permit shall be accompanied by a decommissioning and restoration plan prepared by a professional engineer duly licensed by the State of Georgia. The decommissioning plan shall include, at a minimum: a description of the anticipated life of the solar farm project; the parties responsible for the decommissioning and restoration; defined conditions upon which decommissioning will be initiated (e.g., end of lease, condition of a potential public safety hazard, etc.); the estimated decommissioning and restoration costs and timeframe for completion of activities; the amount by which such costs were reduced due to the recyclable value of any materials; the method for ensuring that funds will be available for decommissioning and restoration of the real property; removal of all non-utility owned equipment, conduits, structures, fencing, roads and foundations (and/or a written waiver signed by the property owner releasing the solar farm developer from this requirement or a portion thereof); restoration of the property to a condition prior to development of the solar project (and/or a written waiver signed by the property owner releasing the solar farm developer from this requirement or a portion thereof); and a signed statement from the party responsible for completing the decommissioning activities acknowledging such responsibility. Any solar farm that has not been in use for a period of 180 consecutive days for its original purpose as approved by the Bleckley County Building Department shall be deemed abandoned and shall not be authorized to recommence operations until a new application and inspection have been completed. No later than 90 days after abandonment or closure, the owners and operators of a solar farm shall remove the solar energy system, its equipment and parcels, and any appurtenant structures. No later than 120 days after abandonment or closure, the owners or operators of any such solar farm shall provide written documentation acceptable to the county’s building department office demonstrating that the solar panels and related equipment were properly disposed of in accordance with federal, state, and local laws and regulations. An application for a solar farm permit shall be accompanied by a copy of the solar power facility agreement between the land owner and the grantee and a copy of the financial assurances (surety or performance bond) delivered to the land owner and filed with the clerk of superior court. If the financial assurances required by Georgia law do not meet the requirements of 0.C.G.A. 46-3-67 (3)(B) and 0.C.G.A. 46-3-69.1(a)(1), a building permit will not be granted.

All solar farms shall be fenced in using a chain link fence with a height of at least six (6) feet, as measured from the finished grade of the fencing perimeter, with anti-climb devices with three (3) barbed wire line arms. Fencing shall be covered by a non-transparent dark colored material. Brightly colored signs no smaller than one foot by two feet shall be posted on the fence every 100 feet warning of danger and high voltage.

The following minimum setback distances shall be required for all system components for a solar farm project (exclusive of fencing and vegetative screening): 3. 100 feet from all property boundaries, with the exception of property boundaries adjoining parcels that are a part of a single solar farm project, as shown on the site plan. These property boundaries shall not be subject to this setback requirement. In such excepted case, a written waiver approved by the county and signed by the property owner(s) of all adjoining parcels included in the project shall be required. Other setback distances include 150 feet from all dwelling units (unless waived) and 100 feet from all public right-of-way frontages, but these do not pertain to property lines or parcels.

The ordinance requires a minimum setback distance of one hundred (100) feet from all public right-of-way frontages for all system components of a solar farm project (exclusive of fencing and vegetative screening). Other setback distances include 150 feet from all dwelling units and 100 feet from all property boundaries, but these do not pertain to roads. The relevant text states: 'The following minimum setback distances shall be required for all system components for a solar farm project (exclusive of fencing and vegetative screening): 2. One hundred (100) feet from all public right-of-way frontages;' This applies specifically to solar farms defined as large-scale systems designed to supply electricity directly to the utility grid, typically occupying many acres.

The ordinance requires that "Abutting residential properties shall be visually screened year-round from any solar farms to the reasonable satisfaction of the county through any one of a combination of planting or existing evergreen vegetative screening or privacy fencing, all of which shall be at least six (6) feet in height." The company is responsible to "maintain vegetative screening year-round for the length of the project." Additionally, "All solar farms shall be fenced in using a chain link fence with a height of at least six (6) feet... Fencing shall be covered by a non-transparent dark colored material." These requirements apply to solar farms defined as "a large-scale solar energy system that is designed to supply electricity directly to the utility grid, typically occupying many acres of land."

The ordinance requires that "brightly colored signs no smaller than one foot by two feet shall be posted on the fence every 100 feet warning of danger and high voltage." It also mandates that "the names of the manufacturers, installers, facility owners, and facility operators, and their addresses and phone numbers shall be posted on the required fencing at each entrance of a solar farm." Additionally, if a solar farm permit is revoked, "the solar farm shall post a sign at each entrance to the solar farm no smaller than one foot by two feet stating: 'This solar farm’s operations have ceased due to noncompliance with the Bleckley County Code of Ordinances. For more information, contact the Bleckley County Building Department.'" The ordinance prohibits solar farms from being "used to display permanent or temporary advertising, including signage, streamers, pennants, spinners, reflectors, banners, or similar materials," but allows "the manufacturers and equipment information, warning, or indication of ownership" on equipment.

The ordinance requires that "any disturbed land shall be stabilized by a permanent seeding of perennial vegetation such as grass or other dense surface cover that will protect the soil surface from erosion, prevent sediment and runoff at the site from reaching downstream areas, and enhance the aesthetics of the site." It is recommended that "a slow-growing, vegetative cover be utilized so that general maintenance of the growth can be kept to a minimum." Additionally, the application for a solar farm permit "shall be accompanied by a comprehensive site plan for the solar farm, which shall include, but not be limited to: Soil erosion and sediment control; Grading; Vegetation clearing and planting and mitigation or screening with vegetation, structures, or fences." These requirements apply to all solar farms or photovoltaic solar energy production facilities located in the county, installed and constructed after the effective date of the ordinance. The ordinance defines a solar farm as "a large-scale solar energy system that is designed to supply electricity directly to the utility grid, typically occupying many acres of land."

The following minimum setback distances shall be required for all system components for a solar farm project (exclusive of fencing and vegetative screening): 1. 150 feet from all dwelling units, except where the owner of a dwelling unit agrees to lessen such distance by executing a signed written waiver of this requirement. Power inverters and other sound-producing equipment shall be sited no less than 150 feet from any dwelling unit in place at the time of construction or installation.

The ordinance requires that "an application for a solar farm permit shall be accompanied by a comprehensive site plan for the solar farm, which shall include, but not be limited to: ... Landscape and visual buffer plans; ... Vegetation clearing and planting and mitigation or screening with vegetation, structures, or fences; ... Exterior lighting and any screening." The comprehensive site plan "must be approved in writing by the Bleckley County Building Department before a solar farm may receive a permit or commence operations." These requirements explicitly impose visual impact assessment elements that a solar farm developer must address. No alternative options or conditions for visual impact assessment are provided in the text.

summary: Section 1444(e) requires "screened chain-link or pressure treated lumber security fencing" with a minimum height of 6 feet and a maximum height of 8 feet around the perimeter of the facility inside the required setbacks, and it shall be regularly maintained. Section 1444(d) states "The buffer width shall be 2.0 times the minimum required with an approved fence, wall or berm."

Section 1444: Solar electric power generation includes glare restrictions such as: (j) The developer shall be able to graphically demonstrate ... that proposed solar collection devices ... shall be designed and located to avoid glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard. (k) Textured glass and/or anti-reflective coating shall be used on solar panels to minimize glare.

Section 1444(f) states: 'All mechanical equipment (including arrays and panels) and outdoor lighting fixtures shall be limited to a height of 15 feet.' This applies to solar electric power generation facilities that provide energy to electric power transmission or distribution systems, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. No other maximum height values are provided for these systems.

Section 1444(c) states: 'Minimum lot size is 10.0 acres.' This applies to solar electric power generation facilities described as non-residential establishments producing electric energy for transmission or distribution systems, which are typical utility-scale solar energy systems.

Inverters, transformers and similar noise producing equipment (not including arrays or panels) shall be placed a minimum of 75 feet away from properties abutting adjacent residential properties (Section 1444(b)). Other setbacks include 500 feet from any residence (Section 1444(a)), but this applies to buildings, not property lines. Security fencing is required around the perimeter of the facility inside the required setbacks (Section 1444(e)).

Section 1444(d) requires that 'The buffer width shall be 2.0 times the minimum required with an approved fence, wall or berm.' Section 1444(e) requires 'Screened chain-link or pressure treated lumber security fencing will be required at a minimum height of 6 feet, but not at a greater height than 8 feet around the perimeter of the facility inside the required setbacks, and it shall be regularly maintained.' These requirements apply to solar electric power generation facilities that provide electric energy to transmission or distribution systems.

The developer of any solar collection device or combination of devices shall provide the following documentation to the Administrative Official before any land development begins: ... 6) Submission of a site plan that meets the requirements of the county soil erosion and sedimentation ordinance, and a drainage plan approved by the county engineer.

In the AG-5 district, 'Solar Electric Power Generation' is permitted as a conditional use 'upon approval by the board of commissioners pursuant to section 413.' No other districts or conditions for utility-scale solar energy systems were mentioned in the provided text.

Buildings or structures shall be 500 feet from any residence. Inverters, transformers and similar noise producing equipment (not including arrays or panels) shall be placed a minimum of 75 feet away from properties abutting adjacent residential properties. The 500 feet setback applies to buildings or structures, which is the most restrictive setback distance directly pertaining to occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, and/or residences for utility-scale solar electric power generation systems.

The solar energy facility shall be fully screened from adjoining properties and adjacent roads by installation of a earthen berm which shall have a minimum height of eight (8) feet and evergreen buffer within 300 feet of the solar energy system. Equipment shall also be screened fenced with opaque screening to restrict unauthorized access for added security. Screening shall consist of a minimum of eight-foot opaque fence (color chosen by staff) around the perimeter of the solar energy facility with the addition of shrubbery, or trees.

Solar components must have a UL listing and must be designed with anti-reflective coating(s). The developer shall graphically demonstrate to the Candler County Board of Commissioners through the use of renderings, photographs or similar credible media that the proposed solar collection device or combination of devices shall be designed and located to avoid glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard. Screening, using fencing and/or vegetative buffers, shall be provided along all sides that do not collect energy to limit the visual impact of the site and minimize glare issues. Panels are to be located and situated so that glare does not create a distraction or nuisance to traffic or adjacent residential properties. An engineer or qualified consultant statement that glint and glare will not be offensive to residents and traffic must be submitted. Other site considerations include lot size minimums, screening requirements, setbacks, height limitations, storm water and sedimentation control, wetlands and stream buffer considerations, underground interconnection lines, noise level limitations, airport interference restrictions, and other conditions as deemed appropriate by the Board of Commissioners.

Freestanding solar panels that are ground-mounted shall not exceed 10 feet in height above the ground. No structure shall exceed a height greater than 25 feet, except for existing poles and overhead wiring. This is measured from the finished grade at the base of the structure to its highest point.

The minimum lot size required for a solar collection facility shall be ten (10) acres. This excludes any proposed solar collection facility to be installed on an existing or a proposed building. (ARTICLE THREE, section 3.1(a))
section:
ARTICLE THREE
        SOLAR COLLECTION SYSTEMS (COMMERCIAL AND UTILITY SCALE)

summary: The ordinance states: 'Inverter noise shall not exceed 30 decibels at the property line.' This applies explicitly to Commercial and Utility Scale Solar Collection Systems as described in ARTICLE THREE, section 3.1(i). The unit for noise level is assumed to be dBA, the standard unit for noise measurement.

A minimum building setback of 250 feet measured from the nearest point of the property line of the parcel upon which the solar collection system is to be located to any appurtenant components and structures of the solar collection facility if adjacent to residential properties. Other options include a minimum building setback of 100 feet if adjacent to non-residential properties, and a minimum setback of 65 feet from public rights-of-way for ground-mounted systems.

A minimum setback of 65 feet from public right-of-ways is required for ground-mounted systems. This excludes any proposed solar collection facility to be installed on an existing or a proposed building. Other setbacks mentioned include 250 feet from property lines adjacent to residential properties and 100 feet from property lines adjacent to non-residential properties, but these do not pertain to roads.

The solar energy facility shall be fully screened from adjoining properties and adjacent roads by installation of a earthen berm which shall have a minimum height of eight (8) feet and evergreen buffer within 300 feet of the solar energy system. The evergreen buffer shall consist of two (2) rows capable of reaching a height of fifty (50) feet, with at least 75 percent opacity at the time of planting. Screening shall consist of a minimum of eight-foot opaque fence (color chosen by staff) around the perimeter of the solar energy facility with the addition of shrubbery, or trees. Landscaping and buffers must be routinely maintained on a quarterly basis for the duration of the operation of the solar collection facility so as to maintain its original designed appearance. A berm shall be defined as an earthen mound or embankment designed to provide visual interest, screen views, reduce noise or fulfill other such purposes. Additionally, an evergreen buffer of 50' shall be required and maintained to limit the visual impact of the project/site from adjoining residential properties. The specific type of vegetation will be common for the area and be of a height at maturity to obscure the fence. In the event any portion of the buffer dies or is destroyed, it shall be replaced using comparable species and height of the existing buffer.

A sign shall be placed at every entry and exit gate of the collection facility which contains a 24-hour telephone number of personnel to contact by citizens or emergency personnel in the event of an emergency. The subject sign shall be 4 ft by 8 ft in size.
section: ARTICLE FOUR SOLAR COLLECTION SYSTEMS (RESIDENTIAL SOLAR SYSTEMS) 4.1 SITE CONSIDERATIONS (b) Warning Signage

summary: All solar collection systems shall comply with storm water and erosion and sedimentation control plan requirements in accordance with Georgia Department of Natural Resources Environmental Protection Division (DNR-EPD) general construction storm water National Pollution Discharge and Elimination System (NPDES) permit requirements. This applies to Commercial and Utility Scale Solar Collection Systems as defined in ARTICLE THREE, which includes systems on lots of at least ten (10) acres and excludes those installed on existing or proposed buildings. Other site considerations include lot size, glint and glare, screening, setbacks, height limitations, wetlands and stream buffer considerations, interconnection lines, noise level limitations, airport considerations, and other conditions deemed appropriate by the Candler County Board of Commissioners.

The ordinance requires a decommissioning plan for the anticipated service life of the facility or if the facility is abandoned or has reached its life expectancy (c)(11)(c). It mandates removal of any solar collection device not operated for 12 continuous months and considered abandoned, with a duty on the owner to remove it, and authorizes the governing authority to remove and place a lien if not removed within 12 months of notice (c)(12). Within 90 days of the Commercial Operation Date, the owner must provide a bond, letter of credit, or guaranty (Restoration Security) equal to the estimated costs of decommissioning and restoration less salvage value, with a process to resolve disputes over the amount by hiring an independent engineer (c)(13).

Unless 24-hour security guards or video surveillance is provided at the installation, the solar energy facility shall be enclosed by a security fence no less than 6 feet nor greater than 8 feet in height. Access gates and equipment cabinets must be locked when not in use.

The solar energy system components shall be designed with an antireflective coating or at least shall not produce glare that would constitute a nuisance to occupants of neighboring properties, aircraft, or persons traveling on adjacent or nearby roads. If lighting is required, it shall be activated by motion sensors, fully shielded and downcast type where the light does not spill onto any adjacent property or into the night sky.
section: Sec. 4-37 Solar energy systems, (c)(8) Glare and Lighting

summary: Freestanding solar panels or solar arrays shall not exceed 25 feet in height as measured from the grade at the base of the structure to the highest point. Mounted solar panels or solar arrays shall not exceed eight feet above the apex of the structure on which it is mounted or the maximum height for buildings in the zoning district in which it is located. The most restrictive maximum height is 25 feet for freestanding panels or arrays.
section: Sec. 4-37 Solar energy systems, (c) Solar energy facility or solar farm, (5) Height

summary: The ordinance states: 'Inverter noise shall not exceed 40dBA, measured at the property line.' This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for a Solar Energy Facility or Solar Farm. No other noise level restrictions are provided for these systems in the text.

A solar energy facility and its appurtenant components and structures shall be set back a minimum of 100 feet from all property lines of adjacent property owners; 500 feet from habitable residential use dwelling or neighboring/adjacent properties zoned RS2 and PRD. Setback requirements may be reduced if agreed to in writing by the adjacent property owner.

The ordinance requires that a Solar Energy Facility or Solar Farm "may be screened from adjoining properties, except for those adjoining properties that are also a party to the Solar Farm." Additionally, "All adjacent roads shall be screened using the natural topography or by installation of a vegetative buffer capable of reaching a height of 6 feet within five years of planting."

The text states that a Solar Energy Facility or Solar Farm (NAICS 221114) is allowed as a Special Use (SU) in the RR, RD, RM, and OI zoning districts, and allowed by right (A) in the HC and I districts. Section 4-37(c) details that "In districts where permitted as a principal use, a 'solar energy facility' or 'solar farm'... shall be subject to the following regulations" including site plan review, development permits, setbacks, height limits, security, and other operational standards. The table uses 'SU' to indicate Special Use approval is required, and 'A' to indicate allowed by right. Other districts either do not allow this use or are not mentioned. Solar overlay districts are excluded as per instructions.

A solar energy facility and its appurtenant components and structures shall be set back a minimum of 500 feet from habitable residential use dwelling or neighboring/adjacent properties zoned RS2 and PRD. Setback requirements may be reduced if agreed to in writing by the adjacent property owner. Other setback mentioned is 100 feet from all property lines of adjacent property owners, but this does not pertain to occupied dwellings or residences.

Freestanding solar panels located on the ground shall not exceed 20 feet in height above the ground. This applies to solar farms, which are utility-scale solar energy systems, as indicated by the requirement that solar farms be located on parcels greater than five acres. The height restriction is explicitly stated as '20 feet'.

The ordinance states: 'Solar farms shall be located on parcels greater than five acres.' This is a minimum parcel size requirement specifically for solar farms, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit of measurement is acres.

Freestanding solar panels shall meet a minimum setback of 25 feet from all property boundaries; the front setback shall be based upon the road category. Additionally, a 20-foot undisturbed, vegetated buffer shall be provided along the perimeter of the installation area.

Solar farms shall be located on parcels greater than five acres. A 20-foot undisturbed, vegetated buffer shall be provided along the perimeter of the installation area. The vegetated buffer must contain evergreen species.

Solar Farm (NAICS 221114) is designated as a special use (S) in the RA district according to Sec. 121-74: 'Solar Farm Change from A (allowed) to S (special use) in RA'. Additionally, Sec. 121-75 states: '(3) Solar farms shall be located on parcels greater than five acres.' and includes conditions such as height limits, setbacks, and vegetated buffers. No other districts are mentioned for special use of solar farms on parcels greater than five acres. No solar overlay districts are included.

summary: Section D.8 states: 'Unless otherwise approved by the Planning Division of Decatur County, Georgia, decommissioning shall begin no later than 12 months after a ground mounted solar energy system has ceased to generate electricity or thermal energy.' It further clarifies that 'temporary cessation of electricity generation for a period of less than 12 months would not trigger any decommissioning requirements.' The system 'shall be decommissioned in accordance with the most recent decommissioning plan for that solar energy system that has been submitted to the Planning Department.' Section E.1.f requires a decommissioning plan with the permit application that includes 'the applicant’s calculation of the estimated amount, if any (the  "Net Removal Cost" ), by which the cost of removing the Solar Energy System at the end of its useful life exceeds the salvage value of the solar energy system at the end of its useful life.' Section E.4 requires that 'prior to the issuance of any building permit for the solar energy system by the Planning Division, the applicant shall present evidence that security in the amount of the net removal cost specified in the decommissioning plan will be in place,' which may be a surety bond, letter of credit, parent/corporate guarantee, or other financial instrument. These requirements apply to 'any new solar energy system to be constructed or installed after the effective date of this ordinance within the jurisdiction of Decatur County, Georgia.'

The footprint of a solar energy facility shall be enclosed by a security fence no less than six feet nor no greater than eight feet in height. This requirement applies to all ground mounted solar energy systems. The ordinance also includes other requirements such as setbacks, placement restrictions, installation requirements, lighting, noise limits, interconnection procedures, and decommissioning plans, but the explicit fencing requirement is stated in section D.7.

Section D.3.b states: 'Excluding any overhead lines, substations, or switchyards, no ground mounted solar energy system shall exceed 25 feet in height as measured from the grade at the base of a structure to the highest point of that structure.' This is the explicit maximum height restriction for ground mounted solar energy systems, which would typically include utility-scale solar energy systems. No other height limits are provided that are more restrictive.

The ordinance states: 'Inverter noise shall be no greater than 40 dBA, as measured from a receptor’s residential structure on a non-participating parcel.' This applies to ground mounted solar energy systems, which are utility-scale systems. The unit 'dBA' is the standard unit for noise level measurement.

The footprint shall be set back a minimum of 15 feet from all property lines and 100 feet from any residential structure located on a non-participating parcel. The 15 feet setback applies directly to property lines, including non-participating property lines. The 100 feet setback applies to residential structures on non-participating parcels, which are not equivalent to property lines unless explicitly stated.

summary: The footprint shall be set back a minimum of 100 feet from any residential structure located on a non-participating parcel. This applies to all ground mounted solar energy systems. Other setbacks include 15 feet from all property lines, but that is not specific to non-participating occupied dwellings.

Section 4(d) states: 'Unless otherwise approved by the Board of Commissioners, decommissioning shall begin no later than 12 months after a Ground Mounted SES has ceased to generate electricity or thermal energy: 1. for a Ground Mounted SES allowed without a permit, within 6 months of the beginning of decommissioning, the SES and all structures associated with it shall be removed, all materials shall be recycled or otherwise reused to the extent reasonably practicable, and the property shall be returned to its condition prior to the installation of the SES or to some other condition reasonably appropriate for the designated land use; and 2. for a Ground Mounted SES allowed with a permit, the SES shall be decommissioned in accordance with the most recent decommissioning plan approved by the Board of Commissioners.' Section 5A(b)(4) requires that a Special Use Permit application include 'a decommissioning plan that contains the following: a. the name, address, telephone number, and e-mail address of the person(s) or entity(ies) responsible for implementing the decommissioning plan; b. a statement of conditions that require the decommissioning plan to be implemented; c. as part of decommissioning, a removal plan that identifies all structures, components, and non-utility owned equipment that shall be removed; d. as part of decommissioning, a plan for recycling or otherwise reusing all materials to the extent reasonably practicable; e. as part of decommissioning, a restoration plan to return the property to its condition prior to the installation of the SES or to some other condition reasonably appropriate for the designated land use after the SES is removed; and f. a timeline to complete decommissioning.' These requirements apply to Large Scale Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems as they fall under Ground Mounted SESs and require permits.

summary: Section 4B(b) requires that a Large Scale SES shall have, to the extent reasonably practicable, a visual buffer of natural vegetation, plantings, earth berms, and minimum fencing six (6) feet high that provides a reasonable visual and lighting screen to reduce the view of the SES from adjacent lots (including those lots located across a public right-of-way). The existing natural tree growth and natural land forms along the SES perimeter may create a sufficient buffer and shall be preserved when reasonably practicable. Any visual buffer must be established and maintained in accordance with the most recent visual buffer plan approved by the Board of Commissioners. For comparison, Intermediate Scale SESs have a similar requirement for a visual buffer including minimum fencing six (6) feet high in residential or agricultural districts, while general Ground Mounted SESs have no explicit fencing requirement stated.

summary: A Large Scale SES shall comply with the following setback requirements: the Large Scale SES shall be located no closer than the lesser of (a) 100 feet from any property line. section: Section 4B. – Specific Requirements for Large Scale Solar Energy Systems

summary: A Large Scale SES shall be located no closer than the lesser of (a) 100 feet from any public right-of-way. Other setback requirements include no closer than the lesser of (a) 100 feet from any property line and no closer than 100 feet from any residential dwelling unit on an adjacent lot.

summary: A Large Scale SES shall have, to the extent reasonably practicable, a visual buffer of natural vegetation, plantings, earth berms, and minimum fencing six (6) feet high that provides a reasonable visual and lighting screen to reduce the view of the SES from adjacent lots (including those lots located across a public right-of-way). summary: A Large Scale SES shall display signs (a) stating the risks that may result from contact with a Large Scale SES, (b) identifying the owner or operator of the Large Scale SES, and (c) providing a 24-hour emergency contact phone number; and (2) may have signs that contain educational information about the Large Scale SES. For comparison, an Intermediate Scale SES shall display signs with similar requirements and must comply with applicable zoning district advertisement rules. summary: Solar energy production facilities shall be fenced in using a minimum of three (3) strand barbwire fencing with danger, high voltage warning type signs attached to said fencing no less than every one hundred (100) feet. This applies to Photovoltaic Solar Energy Production Facilities with an area of use not exceeding one hundred (100) acres on site. Additional conditions include adherence to setback and height requirements, visual screening of abutting residential properties through plantings, existing vegetation or fencing (not to exceed eight (8) feet in height), posting of manufacturer's or installer's identification, facility owner's name and contact information, and appropriate warning signage on or near the panels and on the required fencing, underground electrical interconnection and distribution lines within the project boundary (except for power lines that leave the project or are within the substation), limited lighting to the minimum necessary, submission of Professional Engineer drawings, and provisions for abandonment and removal of the facility if not in use for 180 days. The Planning and Zoning Board may waive or add conditions as deemed necessary for public safety and welfare.

The ordinance states: 'Area of use may not exceed one hundred (100) acres on site with no aggregation of solar collection panels on adjacent properties which exceeds one hundred (100) acres.' summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Category 4 Solar Farms. These requirements apply to Category 4 Solar Farms, which are defined as "a ground-mounted Solar Energy System, where the footprint of the system is greater than 7 acres" and "generally utility-scale facilities for the collection and distribution of solar energy" (b)(19). CSES or USSES to be built on more than one parcel, and parcels are abutting, a zero side or rear setback shall be permitted to the property line in common with the abutting parcel(s). Solar panels shall be at least two hundred (200) feet from a residence that is not part of the CSES or USSES project area.

summary: Solar panels shall be eighty (80) feet from State rights-of-way and sixty (60) feet from County rights-of-way. summary: The ordinance requires that "A landscape buffer may be required to be installed and maintained during the life of the operation" for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems (USSES), with the Board of Adjustments determining screening requirements based on "adjacent or nearby surrounding land uses and topography." Additionally, "Ground around and under solar arrays and in project site buffer areas shall be planted and maintained in perennial vegetated cover or hay and pasture planting" with standards including planting native grasses and wildflowers, and maintenance practices consistent with recommendations from qualified natural resource professionals. The ordinance also specifies that "Blooming shrubs may be used in the buffer areas as appropriate for visual screening." These requirements apply as part of the Conditional Use Permit process for USSES. Other related requirements include setbacks, fencing, lighting, signage, utility connections, and ground cover and weed control plans, but only the landscape buffer and vegetative cover provisions explicitly address vegetative buffer and screening.
section: Community Solar Energy System (CSES) and Utility-Scale Solar Energy System (USSES)

summary: All CSES or USSES shall provide the following at all locked entrances: (a) a visible "High Voltage" warning sign, (b) name(s) and phone number(s) for the electric utility provider, (c) name(s) and phone number(s) for the site operator, (d) the facility's 911 address, (e) a lock box with keys as needed.

The ordinance requires that "the applicant agrees to conduct all roadwork and other site development work in compliance with a National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit as required by the Iowa Department of Natural Resources and comply with requirements as detailed by local jurisdictional authorities during the plan submittal." It further mandates that "If subject to NPDES requirements, the applicant must submit the permit for review and comment, and an erosion and sediment control plan before beginning construction." The plan must include "general 'best management practices' for temporary erosion and sediment control (both during and after construction), and permanent drainage and erosion control measures to prevent both damage to local roads/adjacent areas and sediment-laden runoff into waterways." These requirements apply specifically to Community Solar Energy Systems (CSES) and Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems (USSES) as part of the Conditional Use Permit process. Other related requirements include a grading plan showing all proposed changes to the landscape, and a stormwater management plan for pollutant removal and runoff management. The ordinance also includes detailed decommissioning requirements related to site restoration, including grading, top-soiling, re-seeding, and weed control according to USDA NRCS or technical recommendations.

Community Solar Energy Systems and Solar Farm Energy Systems are allowed in zoning districts A-1, Agricultural, C-1 Commercial, and I-1 Limited Industrial as a Conditional Use. An approved Conditional Use permit from the Allamakee County Board of Adjustments is required before any construction can commence. Other solar system types such as Personal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) and Solar Thermal Energy Systems (STES) are considered accessory uses and have different permitting requirements. Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) Systems are not permitted under this ordinance.

Solar panels shall be at least two hundred (200) feet from a residence that is not part of the CSES or USSES project area. Other setback options include 100 feet from a residence that is part of the project area, zero side or rear setback between abutting parcels within the project, and the Board of Adjustment may reduce property line setbacks with a written waiver.
section: General Requirements, Community Solar Energy System (CSES) and Utility-Scale Solar Energy System (USSES)

summary: The setbacks shall be a minimum of one hundred (100) feet from a residence that is a part of the CSES or USSES project area. Other setback distances mentioned include 200 feet from a residence not part of the project area, 100 feet from property lines, and various setbacks from roads and scenic byways, but these do not pertain to participating residences.

Section 8.14.16 Abandonment states a utility-scale solar energy system is deemed abandoned if discontinued for 180 consecutive days or if the owner notifies Boone County of discontinuation. The owner then has 270 days (the  "decommissioning period" ) to either reactivate or remove all above-ground and below-ground system facilities and structures. An extension of up to 90 days may be granted at the Zoning Administrator's discretion. Failure to comply allows Boone County to remove the system and assess costs against the owner. Alternatively, the owner may submit a plan for  "banking"  the system for future reactivation, updated every 180 days for up to 2 years, after which the system must be reactivated or removed. Section 8.14.17 Decommissioning Plan requires each utility-scale solar energy system to have a decommissioning plan submitted with the conditional use permit application, outlining the means and cost of removal at end of life or abandonment. Cost estimates must be by a competent party. The plan must identify financial resources to pay for decommissioning, and the applicant must maintain a financial assurance mechanism (performance bond or other security) at 130% of the total decommissioning cost for the life of the facility. The financial assurance must be fully funded before a zoning permit is issued and updated every 5 years with cost estimate adjustments. The County has sole discretion over the financial assurance mechanism.

Physical access to the utility-scale solar energy system shall be restricted by fencing or walls in accordance with the National Electrical Code. Razor wire is discouraged. All fencing or wall details shall be provided as part of a conditional use permit application. Except as provided in subsection (4), a conditional use permit shall not be issued for a proposed utility-scale solar energy system when the fence or wall surrounding the system would be located within two (2) miles of: a. The fence or wall surrounding any existing utility-scale solar energy system; or b. The proposed location of the fence or wall surrounding any future utility-scale solar energy system for which a conditional use permit has previously been issued. The limitation on the location of utility-scale solar energy systems contained in subsection (3) shall not apply to the construction of additional solar generating capacity by the holder of an existing conditional use permit for a utility-scale solar energy system, but a separate conditional use permit shall be obtained prior to such construction, the total combined horizontal surface area of all structures contained within the new construction and the existing utility-scale solar energy system shall not exceed one thousand (1,000) acres in size as required in section 8.14.02(2), and the fence or wall surrounding the additional solar generating capacity shall not extend within two (2) miles of the fence or wall surrounding any other existing utility-scale solar energy system or the proposed location of the fence or wall surrounding any future utility-scale solar energy system for which a conditional use permit has previously been issued.
Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be designed to minimize glare on adjacent property and roadways.

The combined horizontal surface area of all structures contained within a single utility-scale solar energy system, excluding transmission lines and collection lines, shall not exceed one thousand (1,000) acres in size. This is the maximum lot size restriction explicitly stated for utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit of measurement is acres, which is a standard area unit.

A conditional use permit shall not be issued for a proposed utility-scale solar energy system when the fence or wall surrounding the system would be located within two (2) miles of: a. The fence or wall surrounding any existing utility-scale solar energy system; or b. The proposed location of the fence or wall surrounding any future utility-scale solar energy system for which a conditional use permit has previously been issued. This separation requirement applies to the entire utility-scale solar energy system, measured from the fence or wall surrounding the system. The limitation does not apply to additional solar generating capacity by the holder of an existing conditional use permit, provided the total combined horizontal surface area does not exceed 1,000 acres and the new fence or wall does not extend within two (2) miles of any other existing or permitted utility-scale solar energy system.
Utility-scale solar energy systems are prohibited in the County except as a permitted conditional use in the following districts: Agricultural Districts; Commercial Districts; Industrial Districts.

Above-ground structures other than fences in a utility-scale solar energy system shall adhere to the following minimum setbacks; provided, however, that participating and non-participating landowners may sign a waiver consenting to placement within the minimum setback, in which case the solar energy system must instead comply with the principal structure setbacks in the zoning district in which the system is located: a. Seventy-five (75) feet from property lines, except where the property lines nearest to the utility-scale solar energy system define and separate properties belonging to two or more participating landowners. Other setback options include: b. Six hundred (600) feet from dwelling units; c. Fifty (50) feet from right-of-way lines, including future right-of-way lines if known at the time of application; d. One hundred fifty (150) feet from wildlife management areas and state recreation areas; e. One hundred fifty (150) feet from cemeteries.

Above-ground structures other than fences in a utility-scale solar energy system shall adhere to the following minimum setbacks; provided, however, that participating and non-participating landowners may sign a waiver consenting to placement within the minimum setback, in which case the solar energy system must instead comply with the principal structure setbacks in the zoning district in which the system is located: d. One hundred fifty (150) feet from wildlife management areas and state recreation areas.

Above-ground structures other than fences in a utility-scale solar energy system shall adhere to the following minimum setbacks; provided, however, that participating and non-participating landowners may sign a waiver consenting to placement within the minimum setback, in which case the solar energy system must instead comply with the principal structure setbacks in the zoning district in which the system is located: c. Fifty (50) feet from right-of-way lines, including future right-of-way lines if known at the time of application. Other setbacks include 75 feet from property lines, 600 feet from dwelling units, 150 feet from wildlife management areas and state recreation areas, and 150 feet from cemeteries.

Section 8.14.12 Screening and Planting requires that "Any new, installed, vegetative screening may be located within the setbacks required under section 8.14.05. Trees shall be a minimum of four (4) feet in height when planted. Installed screening shall be maintained or replaced as necessary for the life of the project." Section 8.14.11 Landscape Plan mandates "The applicant shall provide a landscape plan, which shall be submitted concurrent with the conditional use permit application," prepared by a licensed professional, preserving "Existing forestation, foliage, and native flora within, near, and surrounding the project shall be preserved insofar as is practical," and landscaping "may be required to address or mitigate visual impacts." Section 8.14.10(3) states "Any required buffers and landscaping shall be maintained as appropriate to maintain the health of the vegetation." These requirements apply to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance.

Section 8.14.07(1) states: 'A utility-scale solar energy system shall not be used to display advertising, including signage, streamers, pennants, spinners, reflectors, ribbons, tinsel, balloons, flags, banners, or similar materials.' This is the explicit signage requirement for utility-scale solar energy systems in the ordinance.
Utility-scale solar energy systems are prohibited in the County except as a permitted conditional use in the following districts: Agricultural Districts; Commercial Districts; Industrial Districts.

Above-ground structures other than fences in a utility-scale solar energy system shall adhere to the following minimum setbacks; provided, however, that participating and non-participating landowners may sign a waiver consenting to placement within the minimum setback, in which case the solar energy system must instead comply with the principal structure setbacks in the zoning district in which the system is located: b. Six hundred (600) feet from dwelling units. Other setback options include: a. Seventy-five (75) feet from property lines, except where the property lines nearest to the utility-scale solar energy system define and separate properties belonging to two or more participating landowners; c. Fifty (50) feet from right-of-way lines, including future right-of-way lines if known at the time of application; d. One hundred fifty (150) feet from wildlife management areas and state recreation areas; e. One hundred fifty (150) feet from cemeteries.

The application for a solar garden or utility scale solar installation larger than 50 kW "shall include... 5. Decommissioning plan." For solar system installations producing 50 kW or greater, "following a continuous 1-year period in which no electricity is generated, or if substantial action on the project is discontinued for a period of 1 year, the permit holder will have 1 year to complete decommissioning of the utility scale solar installation." "Decommissioning shall be completed in accordance with the approved decommissioning plan." The plan must describe: "the anticipated life of the utility scale solar installation; the anticipated manner in which the project will be decommissioned; the anticipated site restoration actions; the estimated decommissioning costs in current dollars; and the method for ensuring that funds will be available for decommissioning and restoration." Other requirements for solar installations over 50 kW include a security fence, certificate of insurance, and an irrevocable letter of credit, bond, or cash escrow to cover removal costs. Small solar energy facilities (50 kW or less) have different permitting and setback requirements and do not have explicit decommissioning requirements stated here.

A security fence must be installed along all exterior sides of the solar energy installations larger than 50 kW and be equipped with a minimum of one gate and locking mechanism on the primary access side. Security fences, gates and warning signs must be maintained in good condition until the utility scale solar installation is dismantled and removed from the site.

For solar farm/garden or utility scale solar installations larger than 50 kW, the ordinance requires that "All solar panels must be constructed to minimize glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and must not interfere with traffic, including air traffic, or create a safety hazard." Additionally, "For solar farms located within 1,000 feet of an airport or within approach zones of an airport, the applicant must complete and provide the results of the Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT) for the Airport Traffic Control Tower cab and final approach paths." Other requirements for these installations include site plan submission, A-2 zoning classification, Board of Supervisors approval, setbacks, screening, utility connections, grading plan, fencing/security, insurance, and decommissioning plans. Small solar energy facilities (50 kW or less) have different permitting and setback requirements and do not have explicit glare restrictions stated here.
section: 5-3-11.00 to 5-3-11.05 ARTICLE XI SOLAR ENERGY STANDARDS

summary: The ordinance states: 'Ground or pole mounted solar energy systems shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt.' This height restriction applies to active solar energy systems, which includes solar farm/garden or utility scale solar installations larger than 50 kW. Other height limits mentioned include building or roof-mounted systems which shall not exceed the maximum allowed height in any zoning district and shall not exceed ten (10) feet above roof height, but these apply to smaller or accessory systems. The 15 feet limit is the most restrictive explicit maximum height for ground-mounted systems relevant to larger solar installations. The units are feet as explicitly stated.

Large solar energy facilities (50 kW or greater) may only be permitted as a Principal Permitted Use in areas that are zoned  "A-2 Agricultural Limited District,"  upon approval by the Board of Supervisors after recommendation of the County Planning and Zoning Commission. Small solar energy facilities (50 kW or less) may be permitted in any zoning district as either a principal or accessory use. Concentrating solar power (CSP) systems or plants that use mirrors to concentrate the energy from the sun to drive traditional steam turbines or engines to create electricity shall be prohibited. A site plan shall be submitted and reviewed prior to the approval of a solar farm/garden or utility scale solar installations larger than 50 kW, and shall require A-2 zoning classification and approval by the Bremer County Board of Supervisors following review and recommendation of the County Planning and Zoning Commission.

Setbacks for all structures (including solar arrays) must adhere to the minimum accessory setback standards for the zoning district where the project is located; greater setbacks may be recommended absent a solar access easement agreement. Active solar energy systems must meet the accessory structure setback for the zoning district and primary land use associated with the lot on which the system is located, except that it may be located in a required front yard when meeting a minimum 10-foot setback from all property lines.
section: 5-3-11.03 and 5-3-11.04 Solar Energy Standards and Regulatory Requirements

Other requirements include submission of a site plan, grading plan, glare minimization, and compliance with local, state, and federal regulations.

For solar farm/garden or utility scale solar installations larger than 50 kW, "Warning signs, or manufacturer's, operator’s or installer’s identification signage, may be displayed." Security fences, gates and warning signs must be maintained in good condition until the utility scale solar installation is dismantled and removed from the site." Other requirements for these installations include site plan submission, setbacks, screening, utility connections, grading plan, glare minimization, aviation protection, compliance with regulations, appurtenant structures, flood hazard regulations, insurance, and decommissioning plans.

A grading plan shall be submitted for solar farm/garden or projects over 50 kW and shall include all proposed changes to the landscape of the site (e.g., clearing, grading, topographic changes, drainage, tree removal, etc.). Large solar energy facilities (50 kW or greater) may only be permitted as a Principal Permitted Use in areas zoned 'A-2' Agricultural Limited District, upon approval by the Board of Supervisors after recommendation of the County Planning and Zoning Commission. Setbacks, screening, utility connections, and other requirements also apply. Decommissioning and site reclamation plans are required, describing site restoration actions and ensuring funds for decommissioning and restoration. Other requirements include height limits, setbacks, plan approval, compliance with building and electric codes, utility notification, fencing/security, insurance, and financial assurance for removal costs.

Large solar energy facilities (50 kW or greater) may only be permitted as a Principal Permitted Use in areas that are zoned  "A-2" Agricultural Limited District, upon approval by the Board of Supervisors after recommendation of the County Planning and Zoning Commission. A site plan shall be submitted and reviewed prior to the approval of a solar farm/garden or utility scale solar installations larger than 50 kW, and shall require A-2 zoning classification and approval by the Bremer County Board of Supervisors following review and recommendation of the County Planning and Zoning Commission. Small solar energy facilities (50 kW or less) may be permitted in any zoning district as either a principal or accessory use, with various conditions including building permits or special exception approval depending on compliance with setback, height, and power output requirements. Concentrating solar power (CSP) systems are prohibited.

A site plan shall be submitted and reviewed prior to the approval of a solar farm/garden or utility scale solar installations larger than 50 kW, and shall require A-2 zoning classification and approval by the Bremer County Board of Supervisors following review and recommendation of the County Planning and Zoning Commission. The application shall include the following information on the site plan or in narrative form: number, location and spacing of solar panels/arrays; planned location of underground or overhead electric lines; project development timeline; interconnection agreement; and decommissioning plan. Screening (landscape buffer) may be required and will be determined by the Board of Adjustment based on adjacent or nearby land uses and topography. A grading plan shall be submitted for projects over 50 kW and include all proposed changes to the landscape of the site. Setbacks must adhere to minimum accessory setback standards. These requirements apply to large solar energy facilities (50 kW or greater) which may only be permitted as a Principal Permitted Use in A-2 Agricultural Limited District upon approval. Small solar energy facilities (50 kW or less) have different permitting conditions, including allowance in any zoning district and may only require a building permit if accessory and meeting certain standards.
section: 5-3-11.00 to 5-3-11.05 ARTICLE XI SOLAR ENERGY STANDARDS

summary: The ordinance requires that for solar system installations producing 50 kW or greater, the application must include a decommissioning plan describing the anticipated life, manner of decommissioning, site restoration actions, estimated decommissioning costs, and the method for ensuring funds will be available for decommissioning and restoration. If no electricity is generated for a continuous 1-year period or if substantial action on the project is discontinued for 1 year, the permit holder has 1 year to complete decommissioning in accordance with the approved plan. The landowner or tenant must notify the County when the project is discontinued. Additionally, for solar energy installations over 50 kW, the County requires an irrevocable line of credit, bond, or cash escrow held in trust to recover removal costs, with the amount set by the Board of Adjustment prior to Special exception approval. Other requirements include special exception permits, site plan submission, setbacks, screening, fencing/security, insurance, and compliance with various codes and regulations.

A security fence must be installed along all exterior sides of the solar energy installations larger than 50 kW and be equipped with a minimum of one gate and locking mechanism on the primary access side. Security fences, gates and warning signs must be maintained in good condition until the utility scale solar installation is dismantled and removed from the site.

Section 5.E states: 'All solar panels must be constructed to minimize glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and must not interfere with traffic, including air traffic, or create a safety hazard.' Section 5.F requires that 'For solar farms located within 1,000 feet of an airport or within approach zones of an airport, the applicant must complete and provide the results of the Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT) for the Airport Traffic Control Tower cab and final approach paths.' Other relevant conditions include setbacks, screening, utility connections, grading plans, and compliance with local, state, and federal regulations, but these do not specifically address glare.

Large Solar Farms (50 kW or greater) may only be constructed in areas zoned 'M' Manufacturing District upon approval of a Special exception by the Board of Adjustment after recommendation of the County Planning and Zoning Commission and a Resolution from the Buchanan County Board of Supervisors. The text states, 'Large solar energy facilities (50 kW or greater) may only be constructed in areas that are zoned  "M"  Manufacturing District...' and 'Large Solar Farms (50 kW or greater) may only be constructed in areas that possess 55 CSR or lower to be considered for rezoning, land use change, and also acquire a special exception permit.' Small solar energy facilities (50 kW or less) may be constructed in any zoning district as either a principal or accessory use. Additionally, 'Concentrating solar power (CSP) systems or plants that use mirrors to concentrate the energy from the sun to drive traditional steam turbines or engines to create electricity shall be prohibited.' No other districts are explicitly named as unconditionally prohibiting Large Solar Farms.

Active solar energy systems must meet the accessory structure setback for the zoning district and primary land use associated with the lot on which the system is located, except that it may be located in a required front yard when meeting a minimum 10-foot setback from all property lines. section: 4. Regulatory Requirements, B. Set Back and 5. Site and Structure Requirements, A. Setback

summary: Section 5.B. Screening: "A landscape buffer may be required to be installed and maintained during the life of the operation. Determination of screening requirements will be made by the Board of Adjustment as part of the review and approval process and will be based on adjacent or nearby surrounding land uses and topography." This applies to Large Solar Farms / Utility Scale Solar Installations (50 kW or greater). Other relevant requirements include: "Setbacks for all structures (including solar arrays) must adhere to the minimum accessory setback standards for the zoning district" (5.A.), and a security fence must be installed for installations larger than 50 kW (5.K.). Additionally, a site plan and special exception permit are required for installations larger than 50 kW (4.M. and 4.N.).

Section 5, item J states: 'Warning signs, or manufacturer’s, operator’s or installer’s identification signage, may be displayed.' Item K requires: 'A security fence must be installed along all exterior sides of the solar energy installations larger than 50 kW and be equipped with a minimum of one gate and locking mechanism on the primary access side. Security fences, gates and warning signs must be maintained in good condition until the utility scale solar installation is dismantled and removed from the site.' These signage requirements apply specifically to Large Solar Farms / Utility Scale Solar Installations (50 kW or greater).

Large Solar Farms (50 kW or greater) may only be constructed in areas zoned  "M"  Manufacturing District upon approval of a Special exception by the Board of Adjustment after recommendation of the County Planning and Zoning Commission and a Resolution from the Buchanan County Board of Supervisors. Additionally, solar farms or utility scale solar installations larger than 50 kW require submission and review of a site plan and approval of a Special exception permit. Small solar energy facilities (50 kW or less) may be constructed in any zoning district as either a principal or accessory use and generally do not require special exception approval unless they do not meet height or power requirements. Solar energy systems on historic buildings require a special exception permit. Concentrating solar power systems are prohibited.

Section 4.M requires that "A site plan shall be submitted and reviewed prior to the approval of a solar farm/garden or utility scale solar installations larger than 50 kW, and shall require approval of a Special exception permit." Section 5.B states "A landscape buffer may be required to be installed and maintained during the life of the operation. Determination of screening requirements will be made by the Board of Adjustment as part of the review and approval process and will be based on adjacent or nearby surrounding land uses and topography." Section 5.D requires "A grading plan shall be submitted for solar farm/garden or projects over 50 kW and shall include all proposed changes to the landscape of the site (e.g., clearing, grading, topographic changes, drainage, tree removal, etc.)." These requirements collectively establish visual impact assessment obligations for Large Solar Farms / Utility Scale Solar Installations (50 kW or greater).

Section 7 'Discontinuation and Decommissioning' states: 'A Large Solar Energy Facility shall be considered a discontinued use after a six (6) consecutive month period without operation OR following a one (1) year period in which the Solar Energy Facility has generated less than two thousand (2,000) kilowatt-hours (kWh), unless a plan is developed and approved by the Butler County Board of Supervisors outlining the steps and schedule for returning the facility to service; or upon revocation of the Large Solar Energy Facility permit. Once declared to be a discontinued use by the Butler County Board of Supervisors, the component(s) shall be subject to removal pursuant to this section.' It requires that 'All Large Solar Energy Facilities shall be removed to a depth of six (6) feet below finished grade... within one-hundred-eighty (180) days of the discontinuation of use.' Each project must have 'a decommissioning plan, developed by the applicant and approved by the Butler County Board of Supervisors' including: 'a description of the project components and a sequence and description of the activities required to remove the same... restoration of the land to its original state... within one hundred-eighty (180) days of decommissioning'; 'a report prepared by a qualified third-party... setting forth the procedures and estimated net costs associated with the removal'; and 'Cash, an irrevocable letter of credit, or performance bond... in an amount no less than the total estimated net removal/restoration costs.' The report must be updated every three years and upon any proposed transfer of the permit, with financial security adjusted accordingly. 'No transfer/assignment of any Solar Energy Facility permit shall be effective without corresponding transfer/assignment of the obligations and financial security required under the decommissioning plan.'

Section 6.D states: 'Glare minimization. All solar panels must be constructed to minimize glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and must not interfere with traffic, including air traffic, or create a safety hazard.' Section 6.E requires that 'For solar farms located within 1,000 feet of an airport or within approach zones of an airport, the applicant must complete and provide the results of the Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT) for the Airport Traffic Control Tower cab and final approach paths.' These glare restrictions apply to Large Solar Energy Facilities (50 kW or greater) as defined in the ordinance. Other relevant conditions include that large solar energy facilities require Special Exception approval, must meet height and setback requirements, and comply with various local, state, and federal regulations.

Section 5.A states: 'Ground or pole mounted solar energy systems shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt.' This is the maximum structure height explicitly enacted for Large Solar Energy Facilities (50 kW or greater). Other height limits mentioned include 'Building or roof-mounted solar energy systems shall not exceed the maximum allowed height in any zoning district, and shall not exceed ten (10) feet above roof height,' but these apply to roof-mounted systems and smaller installations. The 15 feet limit applies specifically to ground or pole mounted systems typical of large solar facilities.

Large solar energy facilities (50 kW or greater) may only be constructed in areas that are zoned  "A-2"  Agricultural Limited District, upon approval of a Special exception by the Board of Adjustment. Small solar energy facilities (50 kW or less) may be constructed in any zoning district. The text states that solar energy installations are permitted accessory uses in all zoning classifications subject to certain requirements, but large commercial solar installations are limited to the  "A-2"  district. Therefore, commercial solar installations are unconditionally prohibited in the  "A-1"  Agricultural District and all other districts not named. The ordinance distinguishes between small solar energy facilities, which have broader allowances, and large commercial solar energy facilities, which are restricted to  "A-2."

Active solar energy systems must meet the accessory structure setback for the zoning district and primary land use associated with the lot on which the system is located, except that it may be located in a required front yard when meeting a minimum 10-foot setback from all property lines. Ground-mounted solar energy systems may not extend into the required setback when oriented at minimum design tilt.

Section 6.A states: 'Screening. A landscape buffer may be required to be installed and maintained during the life of the operation. Determination of screening requirements will be made by the Board of Adjustment as part of the review and approval process and will be based on adjacent or nearby surrounding land uses and topography.' This screening requirement applies to Large Solar Energy Facilities (50 kW or greater) as defined in the ordinance. No other explicit vegetative buffer or screening requirements are detailed for large solar installations in the provided text.

Section 6.I. states: 'Warning signs, or manufacturer’s, operator’s or installer’s identification signage, may be displayed.' This applies to Large Solar Energy Facilities (50 kW or greater). Other related requirements include fencing/security in section 6.J. for installations larger than 50 kW, requiring a non-scalable security fence with gates and warning signs maintained until removal. The ordinance distinguishes between small (50 kW or less) and large (50 kW or greater) solar energy facilities, with large facilities requiring special exception approval and compliance with various regulatory and site requirements.

summary: The height of any solar array within an SFES shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet, measured from the highest point on a panel at maximum vertical tilt. summary: Article III, Section C ('Maintenance of Soil Health') requires that 'Top soils shall not be removed during development, except in any instance where necessary to remediate chemicals or hazardous substances from a prior use of the property.' summary: All USWECS, USSECS, and USBESS permit applications shall include a Decommissioning and Reclamation Plan that includes: the anticipated start and completion dates and manner of decommissioning; a description of which above-grade and below-grade improvements will be removed, retained, or restored; the projected decommissioning costs certified by an Iowa licensed engineer; and the method of ensuring funds will be available (e.g., surety bond, cash deposit). summary: The ordinance enacts a temporary moratorium on the installation of utility-scale solar energy projects in the unincorporated areas of Floyd County. Specifically, Section 3.1 states: 'The Floyd County Board of Adjustment shall not accept or approve any applications for conditional use permits or any other permits for the installation of utility-scale solar energy projects in the unincorporated areas of Floyd County from the effective date of this Resolution until such time as the Floyd County Zoning Ordinance is amended to provide regular procedure for the issuance of permits specifically for utility-scale energy projects or this moratorium is lifted, whichever occurs first.' The moratorium is effective immediately upon final passage, approval, and publication (Section 6.1). There is no fixed calendar expiration date; the moratorium expires only when the zoning ordinance is amended or the moratorium is lifted. The moratorium applies broadly to all permit applications for utility-scale solar energy projects in the unincorporated areas, without conditional exceptions based on location, prior approvals, or compliance.

summary: Section 16.14 Abandonment states that a utility-scale solar energy system is deemed abandoned if use is discontinued for 180 consecutive days or the owner notifies the county of discontinuation. Upon abandonment, the owner has 270 days (the 'decommissioning period') to either reactivate or remove all above-ground and below-ground facilities. An extension of up to 90 days may be granted at the Zoning Administrator's discretion. Failure to comply allows the county to remove the system and assess costs as a property tax. Alternatively, the owner may submit a plan for 'banking' the system for future reactivation, updated every 180 days for up to two years, after which the system must be reactivated or removed. Section 16.15 Decommissioning Plan requires each utility-scale solar energy system to have a decommissioning plan submitted with the conditional use permit application, outlining the anticipated means and cost of removal, with cost estimates by a competent party and identification of financial resources available for decommissioning and removal.

Physical access to the utility-scale solar energy system shall be restricted by fencing or walls in accordance with the National Electrical Code. Razor wire is discouraged. All fencing or wall details shall be provided as part of a conditional use permit application. The fence or wall surrounding the system must not be located within two (2) miles of the fence or wall surrounding any existing or future utility-scale solar energy system for which a conditional use permit has been issued, except for additional solar generating capacity by the holder of an existing conditional use permit, provided the total combined horizontal surface area does not exceed one thousand (1,000) acres. Emergency access information to the site shall be provided to the applicable emergency management personnel.

Section 16.8.6 states: "Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be designed to minimize glare on adjacent property and roadways." This is the explicit glare restriction applicable to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance. The definition of Utility-Scale Solar Energy System is provided in section 3.76, describing it as "an energy generation facility... primarily for use in locations other than where it is generated" and including systems such as solar plants, solar farms, or solar power plants. Other related standards include setbacks, fencing, landscaping, and design requirements, but these do not specifically address glare. No other explicit glare restrictions or conditions are provided in the ordinance.

Section 16.4 states: 'The combined horizontal surface area of all structures contained within a utility-scale solar energy system, excluding transmission lines and collection lines, shall not exceed one thousand (1,000) acres in size.' This is the explicit maximum lot size for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems. No other maximum size values are provided that are more restrictive.

Section 16.5 states: 'a conditional use permit shall not be issued for a proposed utility-scale solar energy system when the fence or wall surrounding the system would be located within two (2) miles of: (1) The fence or wall surrounding any existing utility-scale solar energy system; or (2) The proposed location of the fence or wall surrounding any future utility-scale solar energy system for which a conditional use permit has previously been issued.' (2) Setbacks. The buffer must use "trees, shrubs, grasses and forbs that are native to Iowa or where appropriate may include naturalized and non-invasive species or a combination thereof to provide a vegetation screen." Additionally, a Vegetation Mitigation Plan must be submitted, which includes planting "a perennial vegetated ground cover as identified in the Vegetation Mitigation Plan" under and around the solar array, with standards such as avoiding topsoil removal, maintaining vegetation for the full operational life, and annual reporting for five years. The ordinance requires that all Solar Energy Systems, Utility Scale (SESUS) provide at all locked entrances: (1) A visible  "High Voltage"  warning sign, (2) Name(s) and phone number(s) for the electric utility provider(s), (3) Name(s) and phone number(s) for the site operator(s), and (4) The facility’s 911 address and GPS coordinates. Additionally,  "Warning/No Trespassing"  signs, as well as contact information for emergency purposes, shall be posted within sight of all points of the security fence or no greater than one hundred fifty feet (150’) apart.

The ordinance explicitly requires that SESUS applicants comply with a National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit as required by the Iowa Department of Natural Resources and submit the permit along with an erosion and sediment control plan before the 'Commencement of Construction.' The plan must include 'best management practices' for temporary erosion and sediment control during and after construction and permanent drainage and erosion control measures. Additionally, the Agricultural Impact Mitigation Plan requires a soil analysis and describes best practices to protect and preserve topsoil, including avoidance of removal, segregation, stockpiling, replacement, grading minimization, compaction prevention, and decompaction. The Vegetation Mitigation Plan mandates planting and maintaining perennial vegetation to 'prevent erosion, manage runoff and build soil' and includes provisions for ground cover management and maintenance. The Decommissioning and Reclamation Plan includes provisions for restoration of soil, vegetation, and disturbed earth, with environmental monitoring addressing erosion and sediment control. These requirements apply specifically to Solar Energy Systems, Utility Scale (SESUS), defined as systems generating electricity primarily for sale to utilities or third-party commercial or industrial users.

The decommissioning standards require: "All structures, utility lines, and equipment associated with the SFES shall be removed, including the entirety of any such structures located below ground level," and the site must be "graded, reseeded, and otherwise restored to their condition prior to the establishment of the SFES." The financial security must cover "one-hundred thirty percent (130%) of the total cost estimate" and be renewed every three years, with the bond covering "no less than three (3) times the updated estimate for total cost." Abandonment is defined as ceasing operations for 365 consecutive days, triggering a requirement to dismantle and remove the system within 90 days unless reactivation evidence is provided. Failure to remove the system allows the Board to use the financial security to complete decommissioning and recover costs.
