summary: The ordinance specifies a setback of 50 feet from the nearest edge of a public road rights‐of‐way for Commercial Solar Energy Facilities (CSEFs). This is stated in Section VII.D.2: '50 feet from the nearest edge of a public road rights‐of‐way.' Other setback distances mentioned include 150 feet from occupied community buildings or dwellings on nonparticipating properties, and 50 feet to the nearest point on the property line of a nonparticipating property, but these do not pertain to roads.

The ordinance requires that "the entirety of the CSEF shall be enclosed within a living buffer of evergreen trees that must be planted and maintained during construction and will meet or exceed the height of the solar panels and all facility equipment, including fencing." Additionally, "an alternative buffer may also be considered. Earth berms or other topographical features and existing wooded areas may be accepted in lieu or in combination of the above requirements if they conceal the use from public view and are maintained." The equipment and structures must be "fully enclosed and secured by a woven wire or equivalent fence that allows ingress and egress by small animals with a minimum height of eight feet." These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance, which are devices "that (i) is ground installed and (ii) uses solar energy from the sun for generating electricity for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sale."

A 9-1-1 warning sign which conforms to the specifications of the Iroquois County Zoning Ordinance for size, color and reflectivity shall be placed and maintained by the facility owner at the entrance to each CSEF or supporting facility access road from a public road. A sign or posting no more than four square feet in area shall be placed and maintained in conjunction with, but in a subordinate position of, that same 9-1-1 sign, on all sides of the fenced CSEF or supporting facilities. The signs shall provide a toll-free telephone number, answered by a person 24 hours a day, seven days a week, for emergency calls and informational inquiries. A 9-1-1 compliant, visible warning sign concerning voltage must be affixed to fencing on all sides of the CSEF, including the base of all pad-mounted transformers and supporting facilities. Warning signs identifying underground wire locations shall be placed at all road crossings, creek, waterway, and ditch crossings, and at the exits of the CSEF and supporting facilities.

The ordinance requires a landscape plan "for review and approval by the Iroquois County Soil and Water Conservation District" which "shall also incorporate native grasses, flowers and plants which provide wildlife and pollinator habitat, soil erosion protection, and aid in strengthening the soil structure." It mandates that "CSEF inspections shall be conducted once the facility is planted/seeded and every three years thereafter" with costs invoiced to the facility owner. Additionally, "all drainage tiles shall be repaired or restored to same or better condition as to when the project began" with inspections for compliance. The Iroquois County Soil and Water Conservation District "shall verify that the landscape plan is being followed" during annual inspections. These requirements explicitly address soil, erosion, and sediment control for Commercial Solar Energy Facilities (CSEFs).

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Commercial Solar Energy Facilities (CSEF). It requires that "Applicant must formulate a Decommissioning Plan to ensure that the CSEF Project is properly decommissioned in accordance with the provisions of the AIMA and this Ordinance prior to the issuance of any Siting Approval Permit." The Decommissioning Plan "shall be binding upon the Applicant and its successors-in-interest and assigns, and shall apply to all participating parcels in the CSEF Project." Decommissioning "shall occur in accordance with the following conditions: Abandonment; Inactive construction for twelve (12) consecutive months; No electricity generated for twelve (12) consecutive months after initial generation or failure to pay Landowners for six (6) consecutive months; Dissolution or abandonment without transfer; or health and safety hazards." The CSEF Permittee "shall ensure that the CSEF Project is properly decommissioned within twelve (12) months of the end of the CSEF Project life." Financial Assurance is required to cover decommissioning costs, with the County having "immediate access to and may use the Financial Assurance for Decommissioning" upon abandonment, health and safety hazard, or failure to decommission. The Decommissioning and Site Reclamation Plan must include detailed methodology, cost estimates, work schedule, financial security, and provisions binding successors. The ordinance defines "Decommissioning" as "The removal of all above and below ground CSEF Project improvements from a participating property and the restoration of that property as provided in the AIMA."

A fence of not less than eight (8) feet in height shall enclose and secure the Commercial Solar Energy Facility except along any portion of the perimeter where the adjacent landowner has agreed to a differing height or otherwise waived fence height requirements. The County shall have authority to modify this requirement where the Applicant makes a showing that a fence of an alternative height is necessary (1) to comply with requirements or recommendations made by state agencies; (2) to comply with reasonable request from participating landowners and/or neighboring landowners; and/or (3) to meet public safety, aesthetic, or other reasonable interests supporting modification. In any circumstance, the fencing shall not be climbable. Fencing shall be resistant to collecting debris, and debris shall be removed and properly disposed of on an on-going basis as long as the fence is present. A fine of $50.00 per day will be assessed if, after a 30-day notification to remove debris, the debris has not been removed and properly disposed of.

Section 9, subsection C states: 'No component of a solar panel, cell or modules may exceed twenty (20) feet in height above the ground at full tilt.' This is the explicit maximum height limitation for Commercial Solar Energy Facility components. The unit is feet. No other height restrictions for CSEF components are provided that are more restrictive.

Setback distances shall be no less than: ... Boundary Lines of Nonparticipating Property: fifty (50) feet to the nearest point on the property line of the nonparticipating property. (Section 9.G.iv). Other setback options include: Occupied Community Buildings: 150 feet to the nearest point on the outside wall of the structure; Dwellings on Nonparticipating Properties: 150 feet to the nearest point on the outside wall of the structure; Boundary Lines of Participating Property: None; Public Road Rights-of-Way: 50 feet from the nearest edge of the public road right-of-way. Waivers of setbacks may be granted by written consent of the owner(s) of each affected nonparticipating property and must be recorded with the Recorder of Deeds of the County.

The CSEF Project shall be sited with a setback distance of no less than fifty (50) feet from the nearest edge of the public road right-of-way. This setback distance is measured from the nearest edge of any component of the CSEF Project unless waived by the written consent of the owner(s) of each affected nonparticipating property, with waivers recorded with the County Recorder of Deeds. Other setback distances include 150 feet from occupied community buildings and dwellings on nonparticipating properties, and 50 feet from boundary lines of nonparticipating property, but these do not pertain to roads.

summary: Section 9.D.1 requires the Applicant to include as a part of its Application a Vegetative Screening Plan which shall provide for a continuous line of native evergreen foliage and/or native shrubs and/or native trees and/or any existing wooded area and/or plantings of tall native grasses and other native flowering plants at and throughout the CSEF Project designed to screen the CSEF Project from the sight lines from neighboring roads or properties. The landscaping screen shall be located between the required fencing and the perimeter of the tax parcel(s) established by the County upon which the CSEF Project is located. An example of a compliant vegetative plan is attached hereto as Exhibit 1.

Signage regulations shall be consistent with ANSI standards. A reasonably visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations, and at all entrances to the CSEF Project.

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Commercial Solar Energy Facilities (CSEF). It requires the applicant to file a farmland drainage plan outlining how surface and subsurface drainage of farmland will be restored during and following construction or deconstruction of the CSEF, with all surface and subsurface damage to be repaired as soon as reasonably practicable (Section 8.D). The applicant must provide soil and geotechnical boring reports and follow guidelines for Conservation Practices Impact Mitigation submitted by the County Soil and Water Conservation District (Section 9.J). The CSEF Project owner must repair all waterways, drainage ditches, agricultural drainage systems, field tiles, or other infrastructure damaged during construction, maintenance, and operation phases in accordance with the Agricultural Impact Mitigation Agreement (AIMA), and compensate landowners for crop losses or other damages resulting from drainage system damage (Section 10.E). The Decommissioning Plan must include methodology and cost to restore all areas used for construction, operation, and access to a condition equivalent to the land prior to construction, including soil and vegetation restoration consistent with the AIMA (Section 12). These requirements are binding on the Applicant, Owner, Operator, and CSEF Permittee and apply to all participating parcels in the CSEF Project.

Setback distances shall be no less than: Dwellings on Nonparticipating Properties: one hundred fifty (150) feet to the nearest point on the outside wall of the structure. Other setback options include: Occupied Community Buildings: 150 feet; Boundary Lines of Participating Property: None; Boundary Lines of Nonparticipating Property: 50 feet; Public Road Rights-of-Way: 50 feet. Any waivers of setbacks shall run with the land and be recorded with the Recorder of Deeds of the County.

A decommissioning plan shall be required to ensure that facilities are properly removed after their useful life. Decommissioning of solar panels must occur in the event that they are not in use for 12 consecutive months. The operating company shall have six (6) months to complete the decommissioning plan or the county will take the necessary decommissioning steps. The plan shall include provisions for removal of all structures (including equipment, fencing and roads) and foundations, restoration of soil and vegetation and a plan ensuring financial resources will be available to fully decommission the site. Disposal of structure and/or foundation shall meet the provisions of any applicable Jefferson County ordinances and/or any regulations of the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency or the United States Environmental Protection Agency. The decommissioning security amount will be developed by a third party Illinois-licensed professional engineer which has been mutually agreed upon by the applicant and the Jefferson County Board and shall be required by the county in order to assure the proper decommissioning of the site. The third party Illinois-licensed professional engineer may account for the scrap and salvage value of the project in developing the proposed decommissioning security amount. In no instance shall the financial security be less than $1,000.00 per acre. This security financing should be in the form of an irrevocable letter of credit or bond. The decommissioning plan and financial security must be presented to and accepted by the Jefferson County Board prior to the start of construction for the facility. The applicant/owner will reevaluate the decommissioning cost and financial assurance at the end of years ten, twenty, and thirty, as applicable. The county shall have access to the financial assurance for the expressed purpose of completing decommissioning if decommissioning is not completed by the applicant within six (6) months of the end of the project life or facility abandonment. The county is granted the right of entry onto the site, pursuant to reasonable notice, to effect or complete decommissioning. The county is granted the right to seek injunctive relief to effectuate or complete decommissioning, as well as the county’s right to seek reimbursement from applicant or applicant successor for decommissioning costs in excess of the amount deposited in escrow and to file a lien against any real estate owned by the applicant or applicant’s successors, or in which they have an interest, for the amount of the excess, and to take all steps allowed by law to enforce said lien. Financial provisions shall not be so onerous as to make solar power projects unfeasible. An update to this decommissioning plan should be submitted to the county every three (3) years. In addition, any decommissioning plans signed by the party responsible for decommissioning and the landowner (if different) shall be submitted with the application. In the event that the State of Illinois enacts a law with regard to solar farms, such as AIMA legislation, the strictest requirements shall prevail. The county reserves the right to require reasonable additional information or components to the plan as the county deems necessary to ensure that an adequate proposal is in place to decommission the facility in its entirety and that adequate funds are available.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "The solar energy system shall be fully enclosed and secured by a fence with a minimum height of six feet." Additionally, "Keys shall be provided at locked entrances for access by appropriate emergency personnel." These fencing requirements apply to commercial solar farms as defined by the ordinance, which are solar farms "erected for commercial purposes" and not for personal use. The ordinance also mentions setbacks for equipment excluding fences, but does not provide alternative fencing options or conditions.

The ordinance states: 'Systems, equipment and structures shall not exceed 30 feet in height when ground mounted.' This height limit applies specifically to commercial solar farms. Excluded from this height requirement are electric transmission lines and utility poles.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'No commercial solar farm shall be erected on any lot less than five (5) acres in size.' This is the only minimum lot size restriction mentioned for commercial solar farms, and the unit is acres, a standard measure of area.

Noise levels measured at the property line shall not exceed 50 decibels when located adjacent to an existing residence or residential district. The unit is expressed as decibels, assumed to be dBA as the standard noise measurement unit.

Ground mounted solar energy systems as part of a solar farm shall have a setback for all equipment excluding fences a minimum of 100 feet on the front (entrance to solar energy farm) and 50 feet from all other property lines, with the exception of residential property lines, in which the solar energy system shall be setback 500 feet for existing residential properties, with the setback distances to be measured from the edge of the solar equipment of the solar farm to the property line of existing residential properties. For clarification, these setbacks do not apply to adjacent parcels included within the project site.

Ground mounted solar energy systems as part of a solar farm shall have a setback for all equipment excluding fences a minimum of 200 feet from the Right of Way centerline of State Highways and County Highways, and a setback a minimum of 100 feet from the Right of Way centerline of all other roads. The Jefferson County Commissioners may grant a variance to such setback requirement if the proposed or existing buffer is sufficient to screen the project from view from adjoining property or public rights-of-way, and if the owners of the adjoining properties agree to waiver these setback requirements. For clarification, these setbacks do not apply to adjacent parcels included within the project site. Other setback distances include 100 feet on the front (entrance to solar energy farm) and 50 feet from all other property lines, except 500 feet from existing residential property lines.

The ordinance requires that "The solar energy system shall be fully enclosed and secured by a fence with a minimum height of six feet." Additionally, "The lots on which the ground mounted solar energy systems are located shall be buffered/screened from residences and roadways by plantings, vegetation, earth berms, natural topographical features and other approved features." The applicant must "propose a landscaping plan, where necessary, to minimize the visibility of the project from adjacent residential structures and roadways," which shall include "the type(s) of vegetation to be planted, along with its approximate location." Other forms of screening/buffers may include "existing wooded areas."

An appropriate warning sign shall be provided at the entrance to the facility and along the perimeter to the solar farm project. The sign at the entrance to the facility shall include the facilities 911 address and two 24-hour emergency contact numbers in letters that are a minimum of 4 inches.

Ground mounted solar energy systems as part of a solar farm shall have a setback for all equipment excluding fences a minimum of 500 feet for existing residential properties, with the setback distances to be measured from the edge of the solar equipment of the solar farm to the property line of existing residential properties. Other setback distances include 100 feet on the front and 50 feet from all other property lines (except residential), but the 500 feet setback from residential properties is the most restrictive.

A decommissioning plan shall be required to ensure that CSEFs are properly removed after their useful life. Decommissioning of solar panels must occur in the event that they are not in use for 12 consecutive months. The owner/operator will have six months to complete the decommissioning plan after operation of a CSEF stops being operational, or the county will take the necessary decommission steps. The plan shall include provisions for removal of all structures (including equipment, fencing and roads) and foundations, restoration of soil and vegetation, and a plan ensuring financial resources will be available to fully decommission the site. The Jersey County Board may require the posting of a bond, letter of credit or establishment of an escrow account to ensure the proper decommissioning. The posting of a bond may be required prior to the issuance of a commercial solar energy facility permit for construction. Jersey County reserves the right to require additional information or components to the plan as the county deems necessary to ensure that an adequate proposal is in place to decommission the facility in its entirety and that adequate funds are available. The plan shall ensure financial resources equal to 125% of the entire cost of decommission, and approved by the Code Official and the state's attorney, in a surety performance bond that is readily convertible into cash at face value and that names Jersey County and its officials as the insured. This surety shall be retained by the county to cover the cost of the decommissioning requirements herein. Following initial submittal of the surety, the cost calculation shall be reviewed bi-annually, and adjusted accordingly based upon an updated estimate, excluding the salvage value, by an Illinois licensed engineer under seal; provided however, that any such periodic adjustment must be approved by the County Board. Failure to comply with any requirement of this section shall result in the immediate termination and revocation of all prior approvals and permits; further, the county shall be entitled to make immediate demand upon, and/or retain any proceeds of, the surety, which shall be used for decommissioning and/or removal of the solar energy facility, even if still operational.

Perimeter chain-linked fencing having a minimum height of six feet shall be installed, maintained, and secured around the boundary of the CSES. The fence shall contain appropriate warning signage that is posted such that it is clearly visible on the site. All gates to the fences of solar farms shall be at least six feet in height and shall additionally have at least three strands of barbed wire run above such six feet. All gates to the fences of all solar farms shall be equipped with locks and shall remain locked at all times except for those times when the owner and/or operator, or their respective agents, is/are using the gate for ingress and/or egress or is/are otherwise present and monitoring the solar farm(s). All gates to fences of all solar farms shall be constructed so as to substantially lessen the likelihood of entry into a solar farm by unauthorized individuals. The gates and barbed wire required hereunder shall be maintained in good condition. Failure to maintain the gates required hereunder shall constitute a violation of this chapter. The gate, barbed wire and lock requirements specified hereunder shall continue notwithstanding the fact that a solar farm is no longer operational and/or falls into disuse unless and until such solar farm is dismantled and removed from the parcel or parcels of land upon which it was constructed.

Section 151.05(K) states: "Solar collectors shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures, roadways or other areas accessible to the public. The applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation." This glare restriction applies to commercial solar energy facilities (CSEFs) defined as systems generating electricity for wholesale or retail sale. Other design standards in Section 151.05 include equipment compliance, height limits (not to exceed 20 feet), underground power lines, lighting requirements (shielded and downcast), noise compliance, fire safety coordination, signage, endangered species consultation, foundation certification, and agricultural impact mitigation, but these do not pertain to glare.

Section 151.05(E) states: 'Systems, equipment, and structures shall not exceed 20 feet in height above the ground at full tilt.' This height restriction applies to commercial solar energy systems (CSES) defined as systems generating electricity for wholesale or retail sale. The ordinance excludes electric transmission lines, utility poles, and other poles and equipment used in connecting a ground-mounted piece of equipment to an electric transmission line from this height requirement.

No CSES shall be erected in any lot less than 20 acres in size. This is an explicit minimum lot size requirement for commercial solar energy systems (CSES) intended for wholesale or retail sale of electricity. The unit 'acres' is a standard measure of land area.

The CSEF shall be sited as follows, with setback distances measured from the nearest edge of any component of the facility: (4) Boundary lines of nonparticipating property: 50 feet to the nearest point on the property line of the nonparticipating property. (3) Boundary lines of participating property: none. Other setback options include 150 feet from occupied community buildings and dwellings on nonparticipating properties and nonparticipating residences, but these relate to structures, not property lines.

Section 151.04(A)(5) states: 'Public road rights-of-way: 50 feet to the nearest edge of the public road right-of-way.' Other setback options include: 150 feet from occupied community buildings and dwellings on nonparticipating properties; 150 feet from nonparticipating residences; no setback from boundary lines of participating property; and 50 feet from boundary lines of nonparticipating property. Setback requirements for nonparticipating properties may be waived by written consent of the property owner.

Vegetative screening shall be provided for any part of the CSEF that is visible to nonparticipating residences. The landscaping screen shall be located between the required fencing and the property line of the participating parcel upon which the facility sits. The vegetative screening shall include a continuous line of native evergreen foliage and/or native shrubs and/or native trees and/or any existing wooded area and/or plantings of tall native grasses and other native flowering plants.

Section 151.05(M) requires that "A visible warning sign of 'high voltage' shall be posted at all points of site ingress and egress and along the perimeter fence of the facility, at a maximum of 300 feet apart." Additionally, "A sign that includes the facility's 911 address and a 24-hour emergency contact number shall be posted near all entrances to the facility." These signage requirements apply to commercial solar energy facilities (CSEFs) defined as systems "for generating electricity for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sale and not primarily for consumption on the property."

The CSEF shall be sited as follows, with setback distances measured from the nearest edge of any component of the facility: (1) Occupied community buildings and dwellings on nonparticipating properties: 150 feet to the outside wall of the structure. (2) Nonparticipating residences: 150 feet to the nearest point on the outside wall of the structure. Other options include: (3) Boundary lines of participating property: none. (4) Boundary lines of nonparticipating property: 50 feet to the nearest point on the property line of the nonparticipating property. (5) Public road rights-of-way: 50 feet to the nearest edge of the public road right-of-way. The setback requirements for nonparticipating properties may be waived by the written consent of the owner(s) of each affected nonparticipating property.

Section N. Decommissioning Plan requires that "A decommissioning plan must be submitted to ensure that the WECS project is properly decommissioned." The plan shall include: "a. Provisions describing the triggering events for decommissioning the WECS project; b. Provisions for the removal of structures, debris and cabling, including those below the soil surface; c. Provisions for the restoration of the soil and vegetation; d. An estimate of the decommissioning costs certified by a professional engineer; e. Financial assurance, secured by the owner or operator, for the purpose of adequately performing decommissioning, in an amount equal to the professional engineer's certified estimate of the decommissioning costs; f. Identification of and procedures for county access to financial assurances; g. A provision that the terms of the decommissioning plan shall be binding upon the owner or operator and any of their successors, assigns, or heirs; and h. A provision that the county shall have access to the site, pursuant to reasonable notice, to effect or complete decommissioning." These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance, which are "Any device or combination of devices that (i) is ground installed and (ii) uses solar energy from the sun for generating electricity for the primary purpose of or elements which rely on power obtained by harnessing the energy of the sun's rays, intended primarily to be sold to wholesale or retail markets sale and not primarily for consumption on the property in which the device or devices reside." The ordinance also states that "All commercial solar energy facilities shall fully comply with Public Act 102-1123 as amended and all other State and Federal laws, rules, and regulations that pertain to siting, construction, operating and maintaining the facility."

A fence of at least six (6) feet and not more than twenty-five (25) feet in height shall enclose and secure the Commercial Solar Energy Facility. This fencing requirement applies specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance. The ordinance also includes other requirements such as vegetative screening between the required fencing and the property line, lighting restrictions, setbacks, and special use permit procedures, but the explicit fencing mandate is: 'A fence of at least six (6) feet and not more than twenty-five (25) feet in height shall enclose and secure the Commercial Solar Energy Facility.'

Section F. Height states: 'No component of a solar panel, cell or modules may exceed twenty (20) feet in height above the ground at full tilt.' This is the explicit maximum structure height allowed for Commercial Solar Energy Facilities. The units are feet. Other height-related provisions include fencing height (minimum six (6) feet and maximum twenty-five (25) feet) which applies to fencing, not solar panels. No other maximum height restrictions for solar panels or components are provided.

The ordinance requires a Special Use permit for all commercial solar energy facilities, as stated: 'All commercial solar energy facilities shall fully comply with Public Act 102-1123...'. The use table shows commercial solar energy systems require a Special Use permit ('S') in the Agricultural (AG), Commercial (C), Manufacturing (M), and Industrial (I) districts. The zoning administrator notes that the State of Illinois Public Act 102-1123 mandates allowing commercial solar farms in Manufacturing, Industrial, and Agricultural districts with standardized setback requirements. No districts are identified where commercial solar energy facilities are permitted outright as a primary use without special conditions or approval. Overlay districts are assumed to be primary use districts but are not detailed in the text.

The Commercial Solar Energy Facility shall be sited as follows, with setback distances measured from the nearest edge of any component of the facility: d. Boundary Lines of Nonparticipating Property: fifty (50) feet to the nearest point on the property line of the nonparticipating property. Other setback options include: a. Occupied Community Buildings and Dwellings on Nonparticipating Properties: one hundred fifty (150) feet to the nearest point on the outside wall of the structure; b. Nonparticipating Residences: one hundred fifty (150) feet to the nearest point on the outside wall of the structure; c. Boundary Lines of Participating Property: None; e. Public Road Rights-of-Way: fifty (50) feet to the nearest edge of the public road right-of-way.

The Commercial Solar Energy Facility shall be sited with a setback from public road rights-of-way of fifty (50) feet measured to the nearest edge of the public road right-of-way. Other setback distances include 150 feet from Occupied Community Buildings and Dwellings on Nonparticipating Properties and Nonparticipating Residences, and 50 feet from boundary lines of Nonparticipating Property, but these do not pertain to roads.

The ordinance explicitly requires vegetative screening for Commercial Solar Energy Facilities: "A vegetative screen shall be provided for any part of the Commercial Solar Energy Facility that is visible to Non-participating Residence. The landscaping screen shall be located between the required fencing and the property line of the participating parcel upon which the facility sits. The vegetative screening shall include a continuous line of native evergreen foliage and/or native shrubs and/or native trees and/or any existing wooded area and/or plantings of tall native grasses and other native flowering plants." This requirement is part of the aesthetics and lighting standards. Other related requirements include fencing of at least six (6) feet and not more than twenty-five (25) feet in height, lighting that is shielded and downcast, and setbacks from occupied community buildings, nonparticipating residences, and property boundaries. The ordinance applies to commercial solar energy facilities requiring a special use permit and references compliance with Public Act 102-1123 and other state and federal laws.

The ordinance requires that commercial solar energy facilities submit a site plan showing "the location of any wetlands, flood plain, drainage structures including surface ditches and subsurface drainage lines" (Section C.3). A decommissioning plan must include "provisions for the restoration of the soil and vegetation" (Section N.1.c). Additionally, a structural engineer must certify that the design is within accepted professional standards "given local soil, subsurface and climate conditions" (Section D.1.b). The Agricultural Impact Mitigation Agreement (AIMA) is also required (Section C.6), which relates to agricultural and soil impacts. These requirements apply to commercial solar energy facilities requiring a special use permit, typically those with generating capacity around 1MW or more and intended for sale of electricity. No alternative options or conditions for soil, erosion, or sediment control requirements are provided in the text.

The use table (8-5A-6) shows commercial solar energy systems as a Special Use ('S') in the AG (Agricultural), Manufacturing (M), and Industrial (I) districts. Section 8-5B-54 states: 'This section governs the siting of commercial solar energy facilities and is applicable to all commercial solar energy facilities requiring a special use permit.' It further requires that 'No Commercial Solar Energy Facility or Substation governed by this Ordinance shall be constructed, erected, installed, or located within the county, unless prior siting approval has been obtained for each individual Commercial Solar Energy Facility or for a group of Commercial Solar Energy Facilities under a joint siting application pursuant to this Ordinance.' The zoning administrator confirms that 'we have to do to follow would be allow Commercial Wind and Solar Energy farms in the Manufacturing, Industrial, and Agricultural Districts' subject to special use approval. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this determination.
section: 8-5A-6: TABLE and 8-5B-54: SOLAR ENERGY FACILITY, COMMERCIAL

summary: The Commercial Solar Energy Facility shall be sited as follows, with setback distances measured from the nearest edge of any component of the facility: b. Nonparticipating Residences: one hundred fifty (150) feet to the nearest point on the outside wall of the structure. Other setback options include: a. Occupied Community Buildings and Dwellings on Nonparticipating Properties: 150 feet; c. Boundary Lines of Participating Property: None; d. Boundary Lines of Nonparticipating Property: 50 feet; e. Public Road Rights-of-Way: 50 feet.

The Applicant must formulate a Decommissioning and Site Reclamation Plan to ensure that the Commercial Solar Energy Facility is properly decommissioned. The Plan shall be binding upon the Applicant and its successors-in-interest and assigns and shall apply to all participating parcels. A signed Plan must be submitted prior to the granting of the Special Use Permit. The Applicant shall ensure decommissioning within twelve (12) months of the end of the Facility life, including removal of all physical material to a depth of sixty (60) inches beneath the soil surface and restoration in accordance with the Agricultural Impact Mitigation Agreement. The Plan shall be prepared by an independent Illinois Certified Professional Engineer and include: (1) methodology and cost to remove all above and below ground equipment; (2) provisions for removal; (3) methodology and cost to restore all areas to pre-construction condition; (4) work schedule and permit list; (5) methodology to manage hazardous materials; (6) submission of draft Financial Security (surety bond, irrevocable letter of credit, or cash escrow) naming the County as beneficiary; (7) Financial Security amount equal to total decommissioning and restoration cost minus salvage value, based on bids and certified estimates; (8) binding terms on Applicant and successors; (9) confirmation that decommissioning obligation is included in lease agreements; (10) provision allowing County to transfer materials to salvage firms; (11) identification of procedures for County to access Financial Assurances; (12) provision for County access to site with reasonable notice and retention of a portion of Decommission Security for one year post-decommissioning. summary: The ordinance requires that "a vegetative screen shall be provided and maintained (i.e., watered, trimmed and/or pruned, etc.) for any part of the Commercial Solar Energy Facility that is visible to a Non-participating Residence." The landscaping screen "shall be located between the required fencing and the property line of the participating parcel upon which the facility sits" and "shall include a continuous line of native evergreen foliage and/or native shrubs and/or native trees and/or any existing wooded area and/or plantings of tall native grasses and other native flowering plants." The Applicant "shall submit for County Board approval a landscape planting plan and landscape maintenance plan that conforms to any landscape and vegetation regulations adopted by the County (if any) or applicable State laws, as part of its CSEF Pre-Construction Submittal." The landscape plan must include: "(a) A map of homes within 300 feet of the proposed CSEF; (b) Locations and type of existing vegetation that provides screening of views of the proposed CSEF; (c) Locations of occupied buildings and residences within the CSEF project area and residential properties that have waived visual screening; (d) Topographic features that provide screening of the proposed CSEF; and (e) weed/grass control plan." The Applicant must maintain the fence, vegetative screening and adhere to the fence/landscape/grass/weed control plan during operation. The Applicant "may, but is not required to, install earth berms or similar structures for purposes of screening," which require County Engineer review and approval if proposed. Additionally, the Siting Approval Permit Application must include a site plan showing "the location of any wetlands, flood plain, drainage structures including surface ditches and subsurface drainage lines, underground mines, scenic and natural areas within one thousand five hundred (1,500) feet of the proposed Commercial Solar Energy Facility." These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities or Systems defined as projects of three (3) acres or more or with aggregate generating capacity in excess of 0.5 MW, which require a Siting Approval Permit under this Ordinance. Smaller or non-commercial systems are not subject to these requirements. No other explicit visual impact assessment requirements are detailed beyond these landscaping and site plan provisions.

Any Solar Energy System that requires a special use permit shall present a Decommissioning Plan as part of the application. The plan must include: provisions for the removal of above-ground structures, debris and underground foundations and cables; provisions for the restoration of the soil and vegetation; an estimate of the decommissioning costs certified by a Professional Engineer or other qualified professional reasonably acceptable to the County, updated every four years; Financial Assurance obtained by the Owner or Operator for adequately performing decommissioning, in an amount equal to the certified estimate; identification of and procedures for County access to Financial Assurances; a provision that the terms of the Decommissioning Plan shall be binding upon the Owner or Operator and any successors, assigns, or heirs; a provision that the County shall have access to the site, pursuant to reasonable notice, to effect or complete decommissioning; and a financial assurance instrument approved by the County States Attorney executed prior to construction. This applies explicitly to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities as defined in the text. Other solar energy systems not requiring a special use permit or defined as non-commercial are governed by different rules or are exempt from these decommissioning requirements.

A commercial solar energy facility shall have a perimeter that is enclosed by fencing having a height of at least 6 feet and no more than 25 feet. This fencing requirement is explicitly stated in Section 4.24, subsection 11. The text also includes setback distances for commercial solar energy facilities and other requirements such as coordination with local fire departments and decommissioning plans, but the fencing requirement is specifically: "A commercial solar energy facility shall have a perimeter that is enclosed by fencing having a height of at least 6 feet and no more than 25 feet."

No component of a solar panel shall have a height of more than 20 feet above ground when the solar energy facility’s arrays are at full tilt. This height restriction applies specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities as indicated in the section titled 'This section applies to "Commercial Solar Energy Facilities".' The fencing height around the facility is separately regulated to be at least 6 feet and no more than 25 feet, but this does not affect the maximum height of solar panels themselves.

The minimum setback for a commercial solar energy facility from the property line of nonparticipating property is 50 feet. There is no setback required from the boundary lines of participating property. Other setbacks mentioned include 150 feet from occupied community buildings and dwellings on nonparticipating properties (not property lines) and 50 feet from public road rights-of-way (excluded from consideration).

The minimum setback for a commercial solar energy facility from public road rights-of-way is 50 feet from the nearest edge of any component of the facility. Other setback distances include 150 feet from occupied community buildings and dwellings on nonparticipating properties, no setback from boundary lines of participating property, and 50 feet to the nearest point on the property line of nonparticipating property. These requirements may be waived with written consent of the affected nonparticipating property owner.

The ordinance defines a COMMERCIAL SOLAR ENERGY FACILITY as a ground-installed device generating electricity primarily for wholesale or retail sale. Access roads, fencing, groundcover, and landscaping may remain only if consistent with future use by agreement of the property owner. An abandoned COMMERCIAL SOLAR ENERGY FACILITY (defined as ceasing to generate electricity for 12 consecutive months or failure to pay rent) must be decommissioned and removed within 12 months (480 days in one place, 12 months in another), with an option to appeal for an extension. summary: The ordinance explicitly requires that "a managed vegetative buffer shall be present and maintained at all times around the perimeter of the exterior of the fencing and gate(s) which are required around the perimeter of all Solar Farm(s) and the setback area." It also mandates that "Ground-mount systems shall be maintained" with soils "planted to and maintained in perennial vegetation to prevent erosion, manage run off and build soil." Additionally, all Solar Farms must be fenced with a fence "at least six (6') feet in height but less than twenty-five (25’) feet," with gates also "at least six (6') feet in height" and locked when not in use. These fencing and gate requirements are intended to "substantially lessen the likelihood of entry into a Solar Farm by unauthorized individuals" and must be maintained in serviceable condition. The fencing and gates must remain even if the Solar Farm is no longer operational until properly decommissioned. These requirements apply to Solar Farms defined as "a commercial facility that converts sunlight into electricity... for the primary purpose of wholesale sales of generated electricity."

Solar farms are subject to the State of Illinois Storm Water Management regulations, erosion and sediment control provisions if adopted and NPDES permit requirements. Ground cover and buffer areas must be maintained with soils planted to and maintained in perennial vegetation to prevent erosion, manage run off and build soil, subject to the Illinois Noxious Weed Law (505 ILCS 100). The plan must include "submission of a draft form of Financial Security to the County in the form of cash escrow or surety bond" with the amount "equal to the total cost of all decommissioning, disposal, and restoration work minus any approved salvage value." The Financial Security is phased in over the first eleven years of operation, starting at 10% coverage on the first anniversary of Commercial Operation Date, 50% by the sixth anniversary, and 100% by the eleventh anniversary. The County has rights to access the Financial Security if the Applicant "fails to decommission the abandoned Commercial SEF in accordance with the Decommissioning and Site Reclamation Plan." The plan is binding on the Applicant and successors-in-interest. Decommissioning must occur "within twelve (12) months of the end of the Commercial SEF life" and includes removal of all physical materials to a depth of 60 inches beneath the soil surface and restoration "in accordance with the Agricultural Impact Mitigation Agreement." Provisions triggering decommissioning include failure to pay landowners for six consecutive months, abandonment without transfer, or disrepair causing health and safety issues. The County may require updated decommissioning plans every three years and holds rights to challenge salvage value assessments. The ordinance also requires restoration of soil and vegetation, repair of drainage and infrastructure, and allows the County to access the site to complete decommissioning if necessary. Failure to provide or maintain financial assurance is considered cessation of operation. These requirements apply specifically to Commercial SEFs as defined in the ordinance as facilities "that is ground installed and uses solar energy from the sun for generating electricity for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sale and not primarily for consumption on the property."

summary: Utility-scale solar energy systems, referred to as 'Solar Farm' or 'Solar Energy Systems, Commercial/Solar Farms,' 'shall be permitted... as a special use' in the A-1, A-C, and I-A districts. This is 'in accordance with the minimal regulations and design standards as set forth in Article X, I.' The fees listed in Article IV. A. 2. h. 'are not applicable to Solar Farm SUP applications,' but 'Special fees as set forth in Article X, I. apply.'

The Commercial Solar Energy Facility shall be sited as follows, with setback distances measured from the nearest edge of any component of the facility: (1) Occupied Community Buildings and Dwellings on Nonparticipating Properties: One hundred fifty (150) feet to the nearest point on the outside wall of the structure. (2) Nonparticipating Residences: one hundred fifty (150) feet to the nearest point on the outside wall of the structure. Other setback options include: (3) Boundary Lines of Participating Property: None; (4) Boundary Lines of Nonparticipating Property: fifty (50) feet to the nearest point on the property line of the nonparticipating property; (5) Public Road Rights-of-Way: fifty (50) feet the nearest edge of the public road right-of-way. The setback requirements for Nonparticipating properties may be waived by the property owner.

Prior to receiving any building permit for the Commercial Solar Energy Facility, the Applicant or Owner shall provide a Decommissioning Agreement and post the required Financial Assurances for the benefit of the County. The Decommissioning Agreement and Financial Assurances shall comply with 55 ILCS 5/5-12020. Periodically, and as required by the Agricultural Impact Mitigation Agreement, the Owner must update the Decommissioning Plan, cost estimations and provide update Financial Assurances to the benefit of the County.

summary: A fence of at least six (6) feet and not more than twenty-five (25) feet in height shall enclose and secure the Commercial Solar Energy Facility. The Commercial Solar Energy Facility is defined as any device or assembly of devices that is ground installed and uses solar energy from the sun for generating electricity for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sale and not primarily for consumption on the property.

The ordinance explicitly states under section 'C. Height': 'No component of a solar panel, cell or modules may exceed twenty (20) feet in height above the ground at full tilt.' This restriction applies to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities, defined as systems generating electricity for wholesale or retail sale. The unit of measurement is feet. No other maximum height values for utility-scale solar energy systems are provided.

The Commercial Solar Energy Facility shall be sited as follows, with setback distances measured from the nearest edge of any component of the facility: 'Boundary Lines of Nonparticipating Property: fifty (50) feet to the nearest point on the property line of the nonparticipating property.' Other setback options include: 150 feet from occupied community buildings and dwellings on nonparticipating properties, and 150 feet from nonparticipating residences, but these apply to structures, not property lines. No setback is required from boundary lines of participating property. The setback requirements for Nonparticipating properties may be waived by the written consent of the owner(s) of each affected Nonparticipating property.

The Commercial Solar Energy Facility shall be sited with a setback of fifty (50) feet from the nearest edge of the public road right-of-way. Other setback options include 150 feet from occupied community buildings and nonparticipating residences, and 50 feet from boundary lines of nonparticipating property. The setback from public road rights-of-way is specifically stated as fifty (50) feet. The setback requirements for nonparticipating properties may be waived by written consent of the property owner.

Vegetative Screening: A vegetative screen shall be provided for any part of the Commercial Solar Energy Facility that is visible to Non-participating Residence. The landscaping screen shall be located between the required fencing parallel to the property line of the participating parcel upon which the facility sits. The vegetative screening shall include a continuous line of native evergreen foliage and/or native shrubs and/or native trees and/or any existing wooded area and/or plantings of tall native grasses and other native flowering plants.

Under section D. Signage, the ordinance requires that "a reasonably visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations, and at all entrances to the Commercial Solar Energy Facility." This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities defined as "any device or assembly of devices that is ground installed and uses solar energy from the sun for generating electricity for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sale."

The ordinance requires the Applicant to provide soil and geotechnical boring reports to the County Engineer as part of its Commercial Solar Energy Facility Building Permit. The Applicant shall follow the guidelines for Conservation Practices Impact Mitigation submitted by the County Soil and Water Conservation District (or equivalent regulatory agency). The Applicant shall submit grading plans for the proposed Substations for review and comment by the County Soil and Water Conservation District prior to the issuance of any Commercial Solar Energy Facility Building Permit for the construction of said substations. Additionally, the Applicant, at its expense, will repair, in a prompt and timely manner, all waterways, drainage ditches, agricultural drainage systems, field tiles, or any other private and public infrastructure improvements damaged during construction, maintenance and operation phases of the Commercial Solar Energy Facility in accordance with the Agricultural Impact Mitigation Agreement.

summary: The Ordinance states: 'No Commercial Solar Energy Facility or Substation governed by this Ordinance shall be constructed, erected, installed, or located within the county, unless prior siting approval has been obtained for each individual Commercial Solar Energy Facility or for a group of Commercial Solar Energy Facilities under a joint siting application pursuant to this Ordinance.' The County Board may impose 'conditions, guarantees and restrictions' and has authority to revoke permits if conditions are not met or the project is abandoned. The text does not specify any zoning districts or abbreviations where utility-scale solar energy systems are permitted as special use or similar; rather, it establishes a county-wide permitting process applicable to all such facilities. No solar overlay districts are included in this determination.

summary: The Commercial Solar Energy Facility shall be sited as follows, with setback distances measured from the nearest edge of any component of the facility: a, Occupied Community Buildings and Dwellings on Nonparticipating Properties: one hundred fifty (150) feet to the nearest point on the outside wall of the structure. b. The setback requirements for Nonparticipating properties may be waived by the written consent of the owner(s) of each affected Nonparticipating property.

Section 40-5-36(K) requires the Developer to provide a decommissioning plan for the anticipated service life of the facility or in the event the facility is abandoned or had reached its life expectancy. If the solar farm is out of service or not producing electrical energy for a period of twelve (12) months, it will be deemed nonoperational and decommissioning and removal of that facility will commence according to the decommissioning plan as provided and approved. The plan must include removal within six (6) months of all solar collectors and components, foundations, pads, underground electrical wires, and hazardous materials. A cost estimate for decommissioning must be prepared by a professional engineer or contractor and must explicitly detail the cost before considering any projected salvage value. Financial assurance in the form of cash, surety bond, or irrevocable letter of credit must be provided before construction commences. The plan must also include a restoration plan for the site. The agreement between the applicant and the County must provide that financial resources for decommissioning shall be in the form of a Surety Bond or escrow account, with conditions for disbursement, County access to funds, right of entry, injunctive relief, and lien rights. Financial provisions shall not be so onerous as to make solar power projects unfeasible.

Section 40-5-36(C) requires that "Perimeter fencing having a height of six (6) to eight (8) feet shall be installed around the boundary of the solar farm." The fence must contain "appropriate warning signage that is posted such that it is clearly visible on the site." The applicant must submit "an acceptable weed/grass control plan for property inside and outside the fenced area for the entire property," and the Operating Company must adhere to this plan. Failure to comply results in "a fine of Five Hundred Dollars ($500.00) per week" until compliance is achieved. This applies to Commercial/Large Scale Solar Farms defined as "Ground Mount solar energy systems that are the primary use of the lot, designed for providing energy to off-site uses or export to the wholesale market."

Ground mount community solar energy systems must be less than five (5) acres in total size, and ground-mount solar developments covering more than five (5) acres shall be considered a solar farm. This implies that Commercial/Large Scale Solar Farms are those ground-mounted systems exceeding five acres in size, establishing a minimum area threshold of 5 acres for such systems.

summary: Section 40-5-36 (F) states: 'A minimum of fifty (50) feet must be maintained on all property lines.' This setback applies explicitly to Commercial/Large Scale Solar Farms (SES). Additionally, solar panels must be kept at least five hundred (500) feet from a residence not part of the Special Use Permit, but this is related to residences, not property lines or parcels, and thus not included here.

Perimeter fencing having a height of six (6) to eight (8) feet shall be installed around the boundary of the solar farm. The fence shall contain appropriate warning signage that is posted such that it is clearly visible on the site. The applicant shall maintain the fence and adhere to the weed/grass control plan. This signage requirement applies specifically to Commercial/Large Scale Solar Farms (SES) as defined as utility scale commercial facilities that convert sunlight to electricity for onsite or offsite use with the primary purpose of selling wholesale or retail generated electricity.

Section 40-5-36 (Commercial/Large Scale Solar Farm (SES)) requires: (C) Fencing and Weed/Grass Control: "The applicant shall submit an acceptable weed/grass control plan for property inside and outside the fenced area for the entire property. The Operating Company or Successor during the operation of the Solar Farm shall adhere to the weed/grass control plan." Also, (K) Decommissioning of the Solar Farm requires "a restoration plan shall be provided for the site with the application" and details removal of foundations and reclamation to a depth of four (4) feet below the surface of the ground. These provisions explicitly address soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Commercial/Large Scale Solar Farms. Other sections such as 40-5-33 (Ground Mount and Roof Mount Commercial/Residential Application (SES)) and 40-5-35 (Community Solar Gardens (SES)) do not explicitly enact soil, erosion, or sediment control requirements for Commercial/Large Scale Solar Farms.

Commercial/Large Scale Solar Farm (SES) "require a Special Use in the Agriculture Districts of the Randolph County Zoning Code." Community Solar Gardens that are ground mount and less than five acres "require a special use in all districts." Ground-mount solar developments covering more than five acres are considered solar farms and thus subject to the Commercial/Large Scale Solar Farm provisions. Ground Mount and Roof Mount (SES) are permitted as an accessory use by building permit in all zoning districts where there is a principal structure. Building Integrated Systems are permitted outright in all zoning districts.

For Commercial/Large Scale Solar Farms (SES), the ordinance states: 'Solar panels shall be kept at least five hundred (500) feet from a residence that is not part of the Special Use Permit.' Additionally, a minimum setback of fifty (50) feet must be maintained on all property lines, but this does not pertain to setbacks from occupied dwellings or residences.

A decommissioning plan shall be required to ensure that facilities are properly removed after their useful life. Decommissioning of solar panels must occur in the event that they are not in use for twelve (12) consecutive months. The operating company shall have six (6) months to complete the decommissioning plan, or the county will take the necessary decommissioning steps. The plan shall include provisions for removal of all structures (including equipment, fencing and roads) and foundations, restoration of soil and vegetation and a plan ensuring financial resources will be available to fully decommission the site. Disposal of structure and/or foundation shall meet the provisions of any applicable Richland County ordinances and/or any regulations of the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency or the United States Environmental Protection Agency. The decommissioning security amount will be developed by a third-party Illinois-licensed professional engineer which has been mutually agreed upon by the applicant and the Richland County Board and shall be required by the county in order to assure the proper decommissioning of the site. The third-party Illinois-licensed professional engineer may account for the scrap and salvage value of the project in developing the proposed decommissioning security amount. In no instance shall the financial security be less than $1,000.00 per acre. This security financing should be in the form of cash placed into an escrow account, a guaranty, an irrevocable letter of credit or bond. The decommissioning plan and financial security must be presented to and accepted by the Richland County Board prior to the start of construction for the facility. The applicant/owner will re-evaluate the decommissioning cost and financial assurance at the end of years ten, twenty, and thirty, as applicable. The reevaluation will be performed by a third-party licensed professional engineer. The reevaluation of the decommissioning cost and financial assurance will be mutually agreed upon by the applicant and the Richland County Board. All costs associated with the third-party Illinois-licensed professional engineer will be paid by the owner operator of the solar farm. The county shall have access to the financial assurance for the expressed purpose of completing decommissioning if decommissioning is not completed by the applicant within six (6) months of the end of project life or facility abandonment. The county is granted the right of entry onto the site, pursuant to reasonable notice, to effect or complete decommissioning. The county is granted the right to seek injunctive relief to effectuate or complete decommissioning, as well as the county’s right to seek reimbursement from applicant or applicant successor for decommissioning costs in excess of the amount deposited in escrow and to file a lien against any real estate owned by applicant or applicant’s successor, or in which they have an interest, for the amount of the excess, and to take all steps allowed by law to enforce said lien. An update to this decommissioning plan should be submitted to the county every three (3) years. In addition, any decommissioning plans signed by the party responsible for decommissioning and the landowner (if different) shall be submitted with the application. The county reserves the right to require additional information or components to the plan as the county deems necessary to ensure that an adequate proposal is in place to decommission the facility in its entirety and that adequate funds are available. Except as otherwise provided, the County shall not require standards for construction, decommissioning, or deconstruction of a Commercial solar energy facility or related financial assurances that are more restrictive than those included in the Illinois Department of Agriculture’s standard solar agricultural impact mitigation agreement, version 8.19.19, as applicable and in effect on December 31, 2022.

The ordinance applies only to solar farms that are erected for utility purposes and shall not apply to any solar power generated for on-premises use. The solar energy system shall be fully enclosed and secured by a fence with a minimum height of six feet and not more than 25 feet. Keys shall be provided at locked entrances for access by appropriate emergency personnel. The lots on which the ground mounted solar energy systems are located shall be buffered/screened from residences and roadways by plantings, vegetation, earth berms, natural topographical features, and other approved features. The applicant shall propose a landscaping plan, where necessary, to minimize the visibility of the project from adjacent residential structures and roadways.

summary: The ordinance explicitly states: 'Height. Systems, equipment and structures shall not exceed 25 feet in height when ground mounted.' This height restriction applies to commercial solar farms (utility-scale systems) and excludes electric transmission lines and utility poles.

The ordinance states: 'Minimum lot size. No commercial solar farm shall be erected on any lot less than five (5) acres in size.' This applies to commercial solar farms erected for utility purposes, i.e., utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit 'acres' is a standard area measurement.

Ground mounted solar energy systems as part of a solar farm shall have a setback for all equipment excluding fences a minimum of 50 feet on the front and 50 feet from all other property lines, with the exception of residential property lines, in which the solar energy system shall be setback 150 feet for existing residential properties, with the setback distances to be measured from the edge of the solar equipment of the solar farm to the property line of existing residential properties. Other options include a 50 feet setback from all other property lines (non-residential).

Ground mounted solar energy systems as part of a solar farm shall have a setback for all equipment including fences a minimum of 50 feet from the nearest edge of State Highways and County Highways, and a setback a minimum of 50 feet from the nearest edge of all other roads. The Richland County Board may grant a variance to such setback requirement if the proposed or existing buffer is sufficient to screen the project from view from adjoining property or public rights-of-way, and if the owners of the adjoining properties agree to waiver these setback requirements.

The ordinance requires that "the lots on which the ground mounted solar energy systems are located shall be buffered/screened from residences and roadways by plantings, vegetation, earth berms, natural topographical features, and other approved features." The applicant "shall propose a landscaping plan, where necessary, to minimize the visibility of the project from adjacent residential structures and roadways." The landscape plan must consider "the type(s) of vegetation to be planted, along with its approximate location." Other forms of screening/buffers may include, but are not limited to, existing wooded areas. Additionally, the solar energy system "shall be fully enclosed and secured by a fence with a minimum height of six feet and not more than 25 feet."

summary: An appropriate warning sign shall be provided at the entrance to the facility and along the perimeter to the solar farm project. The sign at the entrance to the facility shall include the facilities 911 address and two 24-hour emergency contact numbers in letters that are a minimum of 4 inches.

The ordinance explicitly requires that the "Applicant shall submit an erosion control plan." It applies to commercial solar farms defined as solar farms "erected for utility purposes" and not for on-premises use. Additionally, the project’s engineer must certify that the foundation and design of the solar panel is within accepted professional standards "given local soil and climate conditions." The ordinance also mandates compliance with "any applicable local, state and federal regulatory standards," including Illinois Public Act 099-0906 and the National Electric Code. These requirements are part of the application process for commercial solar farms and relate directly to soil and erosion control. No alternative options or conditions for soil, erosion, or sediment control plans are provided in the text.

Ground mounted solar energy systems as part of a solar farm shall be setback 150 feet for existing residential properties, with the setback distances to be measured from the edge of the solar equipment of the solar farm to the property line of existing residential properties. Other setbacks include a minimum of 50 feet on the front and 50 feet from all other property lines (except residential), and 50 feet from roads and highways. These setbacks apply only to commercial solar farms erected for utility purposes and not to on-premises use.

A plan for the decommissioning of the facility when it becomes obsolete shall accompany the application. This plan shall be in compliance with the standards and requirements set forth in Illinois Department of Agriculture’s standard solar farm agricultural impact mitigation agreement (AIMA), version 8.19.19 or its successor and identical to the facilities in the AIMA executed with the Illinois Department of Agriculture. A bond in the amount identified in the decommissioning plan minus the salvage value shall be filed with Rock Island County Zoning & Building Safety Department showing Rock Island County as the beneficiary prior to the issuance of a building permit for the project. This bond shall be updated at intervals as prescribed in the AIMA.

A commercial solar energy facility's entire perimeter shall be enclosed by a fence constructed of a type suitable for security purposes. The fence must be a minimum of 6 feet (6’) high but no more than twenty-five feet (25’) in height.

Section D.4 states: 'Vegetative screening provided along the outside perimeter of the fence at a suitable height and density to minimize the view of the facility from nonparticipating properties and public rights-of way may be added as a condition of the special use.' It also specifies that 'Earthen berms or similar structures shall not be required.' This screening requirement applies to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance. Other related development standards include fencing requirements (Section D.3: 'A commercial solar energy facilities entire perimeter shall be enclosed by a fence... minimum of 6 feet (6’) high but no more than twenty-five feet (25’) in height'), setbacks, height limits, lighting, ground cover, and stormwater management, but these do not pertain to vegetative buffer or screening.

summary: The ordinance requires that Commercial Solar Energy Facilities meet all requirements of the Rock Island County Stormwater Ordinance and obtain a grading & Drainage permit prior to any grading activities. Vegetative ground cover must be established on all commercial solar energy facilities, with a plan consistent with the Pollinator-Friendly Solar Site Act and guidelines from the Illinois Department of Natural Resources, including both short-term and long-term property management practices to protect pollinators. Alternative ground cover allowing agricultural use under or adjacent to panels may be permitted. Additionally, facility owners are authorized to cross or impact drainage systems without prior approval but must repair or pay for any damage caused by construction within a reasonable time after completion.

summary: A Commercial Solar Energy Facility is permitted as a special use in the Agricultural, Suburban Estates, and Industrial zoning districts. Specifically, it is added as a special use in AG-1, AG-2, SE-1, I-1, and I-2 districts. The text states: 'A Commercial Solar Energy Facility is permitted as a special use in the Agricultural, Suburban Estates and Industrial zoning districts and shall meet the requirements set forth in Section C Development Standards.' Additionally, the facility is added as a special use in Sections 10.3 (AG-1), 11.3 (AG-2), 12.3 (SE-1), 30.3 (I-1), and 31.3 (I-2). Other types of solar energy systems such as Solar Private are permitted accessory uses in any zoning district but are not considered commercial solar energy facilities.

Commercial solar energy facilities shall be setback a minimum distance of 150’ from the nearest point on the outside wall of the structure of an occupied community building or a dwelling on nonparticipating property. Other setback options include zero setback from the boundary line of participating property, 50-foot setback from the nearest edge of a public road right-of-way, and 50-foot setback from the nearest point on the property line of any nonparticipating property. These setback requirements may be waived subject to the written consent of the owner of each affected nonparticipating property.
