summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Commercial Solar Energy Facilities (CSEF). It requires the Applicant or CSEF Permittee to prepare a Decommissioning Plan "prior to the issuance of any Siting Approval Permit" that "shall be binding upon the Applicant and its successors-in-interest and assigns, and shall apply to all participating parcels in the CSEF Project." The Decommissioning Plan must comply with the Illinois Department of Agriculture’s Agricultural Impact Mitigation Agreement (AIMA) and include a detailed description of removal and restoration methods. Decommissioning must commence upon any of the following: "Abandonment," "Inactive construction, after the Commencement of Construction, for twelve (12) consecutive months," "If no electricity is generated by the CSEF Project for twelve (12) consecutive months after electricity is initially generated or the CSEF Permittee has not paid Landowners those amounts owed in accordance with their applicable agreements for a period of six (6) consecutive months after such payments were due and payable," "The CSEF Permittee or Owner dissolves or abandons the CSEF Project without first transferring the CSEF Project to a successor-in-interest or assign," or "If any part of the CSEF Project falls into disrepair or creates any other health and safety hazard as determined by applicable County, state, or federal officials." The CSEF Permittee must ensure decommissioning is completed within twelve (12) months of the end of the CSEF Project life. Financial Assurance is required and phased in over the first 11 years of operation to cover 100% of estimated decommissioning costs, with the County having immediate access to these funds upon abandonment, health and safety hazard, or failure to decommission. The County or participating property owners may draw upon the Financial Assurance if the Permittee fails to comply. These requirements apply to commercial solar energy facilities as defined, which include systems with total nameplate generating capacity measured in megawatts for commercial sale of electricity, consistent with facilities over 2 MW.

The ordinance explicitly requires that the Commercial Solar Energy Facility (CSEF) perimeter "shall be enclosed by fencing having a height of at least six (6) feet and no more than twenty-five (25) feet above natural grade level." It further allows "hazardous fencing such as barbed wire, electrically charged fencing or fencing with metal spikes." The Siting Approval Permit Application must include the "Location and type of the fencing enclosing the CSEF Project’s perimeter and verification that the fence shall be a minimum of six (6) feet and not more than twenty-five (25) feet in height." These requirements apply to CSEF projects as defined, which include facilities for the "primary purpose of production and/or delivery of commercial generating, producing, or delivering electricity from solar energy generation from the sun for wholesale or retail sale."

The ordinance explicitly states: 'Height. No component of a solar panel, cell or modules may exceed twenty (20) feet in height above the ground at full tilt.' This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities (CSEF) as defined, which include facilities for commercial sale of electricity and typically above 1 MW, thus covering systems over 2 MW. No other maximum height values are provided for CSEF projects. The unit of measurement is feet.

Setback distances shall be no less than: Boundary Lines of Nonparticipating Property: fifty (50) feet to the nearest point on the property line of the nonparticipating property. Other setback options include: Occupied Community Buildings: one hundred fifty (150) feet to the nearest point on the outside wall of the structure; Nonparticipating Residences: one hundred fifty (150) feet to the nearest point on the outside wall of the structure; Boundary Lines of Participating Property: None; Public Road Rights-of-Way: fifty (50) feet from the nearest edge of the public road right-of-way.

The CSEF Project shall be sited with setback distances measured from the nearest edge of any component of the CSEF Project. Setback distances shall be no less than fifty (50) feet from the nearest edge of the public road right-of-way. This setback can only be waived by written consent of the owner(s) of each affected nonparticipating property, with waivers recorded with the County Recorder of Deeds. Other setback distances include 150 feet from occupied community buildings and nonparticipating residences, and 50 feet from nonparticipating property lines, but these do not pertain to roads.

The ordinance explicitly requires vegetative screening for Commercial Solar Energy Facilities (CSEF) visible to Non-participating Residences. "A vegetative screen shall be provided for any part of the CSEF Project that is visible to Non-participating Residence." The landscaping screen "shall be located between the required fencing and the perimeter of the tax parcel(s) established by the County upon which the CSEF Project is located." The vegetative screening shall include "a continuous line of native evergreen foliage and/or native shrubs and/or native trees and/or any existing wooded area and/or plantings of tall native grasses and other native flowering plants." This requirement applies to CSEF Projects, which are defined as commercial solar energy conversion facilities intended for the production and delivery of electricity for wholesale or retail sale, typically above 1 MW. Other related requirements include fencing of at least six (6) feet and no more than twenty-five (25) feet in height, lighting restrictions, and underground burial of power and communication lines until reaching the property line or substation. These requirements are part of the design and installation standards that a developer must comply with when obtaining a Siting Approval Permit for a CSEF Project over 2 MW.

The ordinance requires that "a reasonably visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and Substations" (17.37.040 - Design and Installation, F. Warnings). Additionally, signage regulations "shall be consistent with ANSI standards" and a "reasonably visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations, and at all entrances to the CSEF Project" (17.37.050 - Operation, E. Signage). These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities (CSEF) as defined, which include facilities for the "primary purpose of production and/or delivery of commercial generating, producing, or delivering electricity from solar energy generation from the sun for wholesale or retail sale."

The ordinance applies to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities (CSEF) primarily for commercial generation and sale of electricity, including those over 2 MW. It requires the Applicant to submit "a farmland drainage plan with the County and any impacted drainage districts outlining how surface and subsurface drainage of farmland will be restored during and following construction or deconstruction of the CSEF." The plan "shall include the location of any potentially impacted drainage district facilities," "plans to repair any subsurface drainage affected during construction or deconstruction using procedures outlined in the AIMA," and "procedures for the repair and restoration of surface drainage affected during construction or deconstruction." All surface and subsurface damage "shall be repaired as soon as reasonably practicable." Additionally, the Applicant/Owner "will repair, in a prompt and timely manner, all waterways, drainage ditches, agricultural drainage systems, field tiles, or any other private and public infrastructure improvements damaged during construction, maintenance and operation phases of the CSEF Project in accordance with the AIMA." The Applicant/Owner "shall compensate landowners for crop losses or other agricultural damages resulting from damage to the drainage system caused by the construction of the CSEF." The Decommissioning Plan requires removal of all physical material and CSEF Project improvements and restoration of all soil and vegetation in accordance with the AIMA and this ordinance. These provisions explicitly enact soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for commercial solar projects over 2 MW. Section 2, subsection H requires the CSEF project owner/operator to submit a decommissioning plan as part of the building permit application. Lighting must be shielded and downcast to prevent light spill onto adjacent parcels. A decommissioning plan shall be required to ensure that facilities are properly removed after their useful life. Decommissioning of solar panels must occur in the event that they are not in use for 12 consecutive months. The operating company shall have six (6) months to complete the decommissioning plan or the county will take the necessary decommissioning steps. The plan shall include provisions for removal of all structures (including equipment, fencing and roads) and foundations, restoration of soil and vegetation and a plan ensuring financial resources will be available to fully decommission the site. Disposal of structure and/or foundation shall meet the provisions of any applicable White County ordinances and/or any regulations of the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency or the United States Environmental Protection Agency. The decommissioning security amount will be developed by a third party Illinois-licensed professional engineer which has been mutually agreed upon by the applicant and the White County Board and shall be required by the county in order to assure the proper decommissioning of the site. The third party Illinois-licensed professional engineer may account for the scrap and salvage value of the project in developing the proposed decommissioning security amount. In no instance shall the financial security be less than $1,000.00 per acre. This security financing should be in the form of a guaranty, an irrevocable letter of credit or bond. The decommissioning plan and financial security must be presented to and accepted by the White County Board prior to the start of construction for the facility. The applicant/owner will re-evaluate the decommissioning cost and financial assurance at the end of years ten, twenty, and thirty, as applicable. The reevaluation of the decommissioning cost and financial assurance will be mutually agreed upon by the applicant and the White County Board. All costs associated with the third party Illinois-licensed professional engineer will be paid by the owner operator of the solar farm. The county shall have access to the financial assurance for the expressed purpose of completing decommissioning if decommissioning is not completed by the applicant within six (6) months of the end of project life or facility abandonment. The county is granted the right of entry onto the site, pursuant to reasonable notice, to effect or complete decommissioning. The county is granted the right to seek injunctive relief to effectuate or complete decommissioning, as well as the county’s right to seek reimbursement from applicant or applicant successor for decommissioning costs in excess of the amount deposited in escrow and to file a lien against any real estate owned by applicant or applicant’s successor, or in which they have an interest, for the amount of the excess, and to take all steps allowed by law to enforce said lien. Financial provisions shall not be so onerous as to make solar power projects unfeasible. An update to this decommissioning plan should be submitted to the county every three (3) years. In addition, any decommissioning plans signed by the party responsible for decommissioning and the landowner (if different) shall be submitted with the application. In the event that the State of Illinois enacts a law with regard to solar farms, such as AIMA legislation, the strictest requirements shall prevail. For the avoidance of doubt, this provision shall not apply to any projects or properties that are otherwise grandfathered and/or exempted under such legislation. The county reserves the right to require reasonable additional information or components to the plan as the county deems necessary to ensure that an adequate proposal is in place to decommission the facility in its entirety and that adequate funds are available.

The ordinance regulates commercial solar energy facilities (solar farms) and explicitly requires that "The solar energy system shall be fully enclosed and secured by a fence with a minimum height of six feet and no more than 25 feet." Keys must be provided at locked entrances for access by appropriate emergency personnel. This fencing requirement applies to commercial solar farms as defined in the ordinance. Other related provisions include setbacks for all equipment excluding fences, screening through landscaping plans, and maintenance requirements such as weed/grass control and fence security with fines for violations.

The ordinance states: 'Height. Systems, equipment and structures shall not exceed 30 feet in height when ground mounted.' This applies to commercial solar energy facilities (solar farms) erected for commercial purposes. The unit is explicitly given as feet. No other maximum height values are provided for utility-scale solar energy systems.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'Minimum lot size. No commercial solar farm shall be erected on any lot less than five (5) acres in size.' This minimum lot size applies to commercial solar energy facilities (solar farms) intended for commercial purposes. The unit 'acres' is a standard measure of land area.

The ordinance states: 'Noise levels measured at the property line shall not exceed 50 decibels when located adjacent to an existing residence or residential district.' This applies to commercial solar energy facilities (solar farms) which are utility-scale systems. The unit is expressed as decibels, assumed to be dBA as the standard unit for noise measurement.

The ordinance requires that "The solar energy system shall be fully enclosed and secured by a fence with a minimum height of six feet and no more than 25 feet." Additionally, "The applicant shall propose a landscaping plan, where necessary, to minimize the visibility of the project from adjacent residential structures." The landscaping plan must consider "the type(s) of vegetation to be planted, along with its approximate location." Acceptable forms of screening include "Earth berms and other topographical features and existing wooded areas."

The ordinance requires that "an appropriate warning sign shall be provided at the entrance to the facility and along the perimeter to the solar farm project." The sign at the entrance must include "the facilities 911 address and two 24-hour emergency contact numbers in letters that are a minimum of 4 inches." This signage requirement applies to commercial solar energy facilities (solar farms) erected for commercial purposes, which are subject to the ordinance. No alternative signage options or conditions are provided.

The ordinance applies only to commercial solar energy facilities (also referred to as  "solar farms" ) erected for commercial purposes on lots of five (5) acres or more. It requires a special use permit recommended by the White County Board Solar Farm Subcommittee, stating: "At least one meeting with the White County Board Solar Farm Subcommittee is required for the recommendation of a solar farm special use permit." The ordinance outlines detailed application requirements and conditions but does not specify any particular zoning district names or abbreviations where such solar farms are permitted as a special use or similar. No solar overlay districts are included in this text.

summary: Section (e)(2)(k) states: 'A decommissioning plan shall be required to ensure that facilities are properly removed after their useful life. Decommissioning of solar panels must occur in the event they are not in use for 12 consecutive months. The plan shall include provisions for removal of all structures and foundations, restoration of soil and vegetation and a plan ensuring financial resources will be available to fully decommission the site. Disposal of structures and/or foundations shall meet the provisions of the Whiteside County Solid Waste Ordinance. Whiteside County may require the posting of a bond, letter of credit or the establishment of an escrow account to ensure proper decommissioning. In the event that the State of Illinois enacts a law with regard to the decommissioning of solar farms, the strictest requirements shall prevail.' This applies specifically to Solar Farms defined as 'Ground-mount solar energy arrays that are the primary use on the lot, designed for providing energy to off-site uses or export to the wholesale market.' Other related uses include Solar Gardens (less than five acres, providing retail power to multiple households or businesses) which are treated differently and are not subject to these decommissioning requirements explicitly.

All solar energy systems using a reflector to enhance solar production shall minimize glare from the reflector affecting adjacent or nearby properties. Measures to minimize glare include selective placement of the system, screening on the north side of the solar array, modifying the orientation of the system, reducing use of the reflector system, or other remedies that limit glare. For solar farms located within 500 feet of an airport or within approach zones of an airport, the applicant must complete and provide the results of the Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT) for the Airport Traffic Control Tower cab and final approach paths, consistent with the Interim Policy, FAA Review of Solar Energy Projects on Federally Obligated Airports, or most recent version adopted by the FAA. These requirements apply to solar farms defined as commercial facilities for wholesale sales of generated electricity and are the principal land use on the parcel. The same aviation protection requirement applies to solar gardens and solar farms. Other options to minimize glare include screening, orientation modification, or reducing reflector use.

Ground or pole-mounted solar energy systems shall not exceed 20 feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt. This applies to active solar energy systems, which include solar farms as defined as commercial facilities primarily for wholesale sales of electricity. Other height provisions include building or roof-mounted solar energy systems not exceeding the maximum allowed height in any zoning district, with solar energy systems other than building-integrated systems given an equivalent exception to height standards as building-mounted mechanical devices or equipment. The 20 feet limit is the most restrictive explicit height limit for ground-mounted systems, which would include solar farms.

A minimum setback of 50 feet must be maintained on all property lines for Solar Farms. Solar panels will be kept at least 500 feet from a residence that is not a part of the Special Use. For special use permits involving pole-mounted or ground-mounted active solar energy systems, a setback of one foot from the property line is required. Ground-mounted solar energy systems as accessory uses must meet the accessory structure setback for the zoning district and primary land use associated with the lot on which the system is located. Ground-mounted solar energy systems may not extend into the side-yard or rear setback when oriented at minimum design tilt, except as otherwise allowed for building mechanical systems.

Section (e)(2)(c) requires that "soils shall be planted to and maintained in perennial vegetation to prevent erosion, manage run off and build soil" for solar farms, constituting a vegetative buffer requirement. Section (d)(3) states that "Active solar energy systems shall be designed to conform to the county comprehensive plan and to blend into the architecture of the building or be screened from routine view from public right-of-ways other than alleys provide that screening shall not affect the operation of the system," which is a screening requirement. These requirements apply to Solar Farms defined as "a commercial facility that converts sunlight into electricity... for the primary purpose of wholesale sales of generated electricity. A solar farm is the principal land use for the parcel on which it is located."

Solar farms are subject to Whiteside County's Stormwater Management regulations, erosion and sediment control provisions if adopted and NPDES permit requirements. Top soils shall not be removed during development, unless part of a remediation effort. Soils shall be planted to and maintained in perennial vegetation to prevent erosion, manage run off and build soil. These requirements apply to ground-mount solar energy arrays that are the primary use on the lot, designed for providing energy to off-site uses or export to the wholesale market. Other standards include compliance with local, state and federal regulatory codes, burial of power and communication lines underground with some exemptions, site plan requirements, setbacks, aviation protection, agricultural protection, and decommissioning plans.

Solar farms are defined as ground-mount solar energy arrays that are the primary use on the lot, designed for providing energy to off-site uses or export to the wholesale market. They are permitted as special uses in agricultural districts, airport safety zones subject to additional conditions, and at the landfill. Ground-mount community solar energy systems less than five acres are special uses in all districts, while those over five acres are considered solar farms. The text also notes that solar farms should be added as a special use in the A-1 zone under Transportation and Utilities. Active solar energy systems that do not meet visibility standards require a special use permit as well.

Solar panels will be kept at least 500 feet from a residence that is not a part of the Special Use. Additionally, a minimum setback of 50 feet must be maintained on all property lines. This 500-foot setback specifically applies to Solar Farms, which are defined as ground-mount solar energy arrays that are the primary use on the lot, designed for providing energy to off-site uses or export to the wholesale market.

Section (F) Security barrier requires that "Solar energy systems that are part of a commercial solar energy facility must be enclosed by perimeter security fencing or other county-approved barrier with a minimum height of at least six feet and no more than 25 feet unless waived by written consent by each affected non-participating property owner in accordance with 55 ILCS 5/5-12020 Counties Code Section (e)." The use of barbed wire or razor wire that runs along the top of chain linked fences is permitted.

Section (D) Glare states: "Solar energy systems must be designed, constructed and sited to minimize glare or reflections on adjacent properties and roadways and to not interfere with traffic, including air traffic, or otherwise create a safety hazard." This applies to commercial solar energy facilities, which are defined as solar energy systems subject to special use approval in certain zoning districts. No other specific glare restriction options or conditions are provided in the text.

Ground-mounted solar energy systems may not exceed 20 feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt unless waived by written consent by each affected non-participating property owner in accordance with 55 ILCS 5/5-12020 Counties Code Section (e). Buildings are subject to the height limits of the subject zoning district. The unit for the height restriction is feet.

Solar energy systems, excluding fences, are subject to the following setbacks: (b) At least 50 feet from adjacent properties not included in the subject property as depicted in the site plan unless waived by written consent by each affected non-participating property owner in accordance with 55 ILCS 5/5-12020 Counties Code Section (e). Other setback options include: (a) At least 50 feet from the nearest edge of public right-of-way; (c) At least 150 feet from the nearest point of the outside wall of a dwelling unit or occupied community building on any property not part of the subject property; (e) Zero feet for side and rear yards on all properties that are adjacent and within the subject property.

Zero feet for side and rear yards on all properties that are adjacent and within the subject property. Other setback options include at least 50 feet from adjacent properties not included in the subject property and at least 50 feet from the nearest edge of public right-of-way, but these apply to non-participating properties.

Solar energy systems, excluding fences, are subject to the following setbacks: (a) At least 50 feet from the nearest edge of public right-of-way unless waived by written consent by each affected non-participating property owner in accordance with 55 ILCS 5/5-12020 Counties Code Section (e). Other setback options include 50 feet from adjacent properties not included in the subject property, 150 feet from the nearest point of the outside wall of a dwelling unit or occupied community building on any property not part of the subject property, zero feet for side and rear yards on all properties that are adjacent and within the subject property, and district requirements for existing structures of the subject property.

Perennial vegetative ground cover must be maintained or established in all areas of the solar energy systems. Perennial vegetative ground cover or farm crops must be maintained or established in required setbacks to prevent erosion and manage run-off. A Visual screening report must be submitted including locations and type of existing vegetation that provides screening of views of the facility, among other details.

Section (E) Soil and ground cover requires that 'Topsoils shall not be removed from the site during development unless the removal is expressly approved as part of the special use permit.' It mandates that 'Perennial vegetative ground cover must be maintained or established in all areas of the solar energy systems' and that 'Perennial vegetative ground cover or farm crops must be maintained or established in required setbacks to prevent erosion and manage run-off.' Stormwater calculations showing a net watershed benefit may be accepted in lieu of a stormwater management plan. A Preliminary Maintenance Plan must be approved and implemented during the term of the Special Use Permit. The use of earthen berms is permitted but not required. Section (K) Conservation Plan requires submission of a conservation plan reviewed by the Will/South Cook Soil & Water Conservation District addressing 'soils, plantings/vegetation, drainage, and maintenance,' with the district reserving the right to conduct inspections to assess soil erosion and sediment controls. These requirements apply to commercial solar energy facilities, which are utility-scale solar energy systems.

Prior to applying for a building permit, the SFES project owner/operator shall submit a decommissioning plan to the Woodford County Zoning Department. The plan shall include: a description of the plan to remove the SFES equipment and restore the land to its previous use upon the end of the project's life; provisions for removal of structures, debris, and associated equipment on the surface and to a level of not less than five (5) feet below the surface; provisions for restoration of soil and vegetation; an estimate of decommissioning costs certified by an independent professional engineer; no consideration of scrap value in decommissioning costs; a written financial plan to ensure funds will be available for decommissioning and land restoration; a provision that the terms of the decommissioning plan shall be binding upon the owner/operator and successors; a surety bond set at 110% of the estimated cost; and a new estimate of decommissioning costs every five (5) years with possible requirement for a new financial plan. Failure to provide an acceptable financial plan shall be considered a cessation of operations. Additionally, if any SFES has not been in operation and producing electricity for at least 180 consecutive days, it shall be removed. The Woodford County Zoning Administrator shall notify the owner to remove the system, and failure to do so will result in referral to the State's Attorney for enforcement.

Section 30-1200 C.3 states: "A fence of at least six (6) feet in height but no greater than eight (8) feet shall enclose the SFES." Other related requirements for SFES include height limits, setbacks, lighting, noise, underground wiring, outdoor storage, and annual reporting, but these do not pertain to fencing.

Other special requirements for SFES include height limits, setbacks, fencing, lighting, noise, underground wiring, outdoor storage, and various operational and reporting obligations.

Section 30-1200.C.1 states: 'Height. Shall not exceed eighteen (18) feet at maximum tilt of the solar panel(s).' This is the explicit maximum structure height allowed for Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES). The units are feet. Other height restrictions mentioned apply only to Personal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), such as ground mounted PSES height not greater than eighteen (18) feet and structure mounted PSES height not greater than the allowable height of any structure within the zoning district, which do not apply to SFES.

Noise levels measured at the property line shall not exceed fifty (50) decibels when located adjacent to an existing residence or residential district. The unit is expressed as decibels (dBA), the standard unit for noise level measurement.

(Section 30-1200 C.2) Other setback references include a 500 ft setback from residences not part of the Special Use, but that does not pertain to property lines or parcels.

For Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES), "solar panels will be kept at least 500 ft from a residence that is not part of the Special Use." This is found in Section 30-1200 C. Special Requirements, item 2). The ordinance also mentions a 50 feet setback from property lines, but that is not directly related to occupied dwellings or residences.

The ordinance requires that a project owner may not install or locate a Commercial Solar Energy System (CSE System) in unincorporated Allen County unless the project owner submits to the Plan Commission and the Commissioners a satisfactory decommissioning and site restoration plan, and posts a surety bond or equivalent security in an amount equal to 150% of the estimated cost of decommissioning the CSE System, as calculated by a third party licensed or registered engineer. The decommissioning plan must be approved to the satisfaction of relevant county offices and agencies. The bond amount must be reevaluated every three years and adjusted as necessary. The project owner must provide written notice of intent to decommission at least sixty days before discontinuation of commercial operation. After discontinuation, all structures, foundations, roads, gravel areas, and cables must be removed within one year, and the ground restored to a condition reasonably similar to pre-construction. If the project owner fails to remove assets within one year, the Plan Commission and Commissioners may engage contractors to remove assets, remediate the site, and recover costs. Project assets may remain if conforming with local regulations and with landowner consent. Additionally, if a CSE System does not generate electricity for six consecutive months, it is considered abandoned, triggering the same removal and remediation requirements. summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Commercial Solar Energy System - CSES-1. It mandates a Natural Resource Impact Report including "identification and analysis of (a) topography, geology, vegetation, soil types, water resources including wetlands..." and "potential mitigation measures such as open space, erosion control, and habitat replacement to reduce the identified impacts on the project area." It requires "Protection of Wetlands, Waterways, Flood Plains" by conducting "a thorough inventory of wetlands, waterways, and flood plains within and adjacent to the designated solar installation area," avoiding encroachment, and enforcing "sediment ponds or other appropriate techniques... to capture and divert water runoff away from these environmentally sensitive zones." A Drainage Plan approved by the Carroll County Drainage Board is required, including financial assurance for repair or replacement of damaged drains, ditches, and tiles, and ensuring that "any newly constructed access roads shall not impede the flow of water and will comply with the County drainage ordinance." The ordinance imposes liability for drainage damages for a period from construction to five years after decommissioning. It also prohibits construction of CSES-1 projects in floodplains, floodways, their fringes, or above aquifers. These requirements apply specifically to CSES-1 projects, which are defined as commercial solar energy systems intended primarily for off-site utility grid use and subject to industrial zoning and special exception approval. Other related provisions include well testing requirements and decommissioning plans that include soil and vegetation remediation. No other options or conditions for soil, erosion, or sediment control requirements are provided beyond these explicit mandates.

CSES-1 systems are allowed in zoning districts designated I(1) and I(2). After being zoned industrial, a special exception shall be applied for in regards to operation of a CSES-1. No Improvement Location Permits shall issue to any Applicant without the Area Plan Commission, or BZA granting preliminary and final approval at public hearings. No construction of a CSES shall commence before the issuance of an Improvement Location Permit by the Zoning Administrator. Other system types include CSES-2 (more than 1 acre up to 20 acres on one or more properties, electricity used primarily for on-site use) and CSES-3 (one acre or less and one landowner, electricity exclusively behind the meter generation for single property owner), but these are not described as requiring special use approval in the provided text.

summary: No solar panels may be located less than One Thousand (1,000) feet from any non-participating landowner property line. This setback applies to Commercial Solar Energy System - CSES-1 projects. Other setback distances mentioned include 12,000 feet from school corporation property lines, 2 miles from residential, commercial, industrial or artisan wells, and 100 feet from road rights-of-way, but these do not specifically address non-participating occupied dwellings. The ordinance does not specify a fixed setback distance directly from non-participating occupied dwellings, buildings, or structures, only from non-participating landowner property lines which include such dwellings.

The ordinance requires a Visual Impact Evaluation Report for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES-1) as part of the preliminary development plan approval. The report must be conducted by a third party approved by Carroll County and funded by the applicant or co-applicant. It must include: (a) a map depicting the dimensions of the proposed site, names and addresses of adjoining non-participating property owners, setbacks from each Distal Solar Panel and adjoining property lines, and locations of various community and environmental features; (b) a detailed description of the potential visibility of each Distal Solar Panel and the methodology used to evaluate visibility within the View Shed Areas; (c) View Shed Areas defined as a ½ mile radius from each Distal Solar Panel adjacent to the project boundary; (d) photographic simulations of the View Shed Area sufficient to capture general visibility of Distal Solar Panels; and (e) any mitigation measures proposed to minimize the visual impact of the project. This applies specifically to CSES-1, which are commercial solar energy systems primarily for off-site utility grid use. Other tiers (CSES-2 and CSES-3) have different definitions and requirements, but the visual impact assessment is explicitly required for CSES-1. The relevant text is found in Section 24.2(i)(6).

Section 524.01.K requires that "a decommissioning agreement must be approved and signed by the County Commissioners before a building permit is issued." The agreement must include "a description of implementing the decommissioning, a description of the work required, a cost estimate for decommissioning, a schedule for contributions to the decommissioning fund, and a demonstration of financial assurance." Financial assurance must be "in an amount at least equal to said demolition and removal contractor cost estimate, through the use of a bond, letter of credit or other security acceptable to the County," and is subject to review every five years. The CSES owner must notify the Planning Department immediately upon cessation or abandonment, which is presumed if "no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months." Decommissioning must start within ninety (90) days and be completed within one hundred and eighty (180) days, including removal of all solar related equipment and associated facilities. Failure to comply allows the municipality to complete decommissioning at the owner's expense. If a ground mounted CSES is removed, "any earth disturbance resulting from the removal must be graded and reseeded" in consultation with the property owner. Other related conditions include requirements for maintenance, noise limits, setbacks, fencing, and signage, but these do not pertain directly to decommissioning. The text also includes decommissioning requirements for Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES) in section 524.02.H, which require decommissioning to start within 90 days and be completed within 180 days if no electricity is generated for 12 months or if not maintained in good working order, but these apply only to ASES, not CSES.
All ground-mounted CSES shall be completely enclosed by a six (6) foot high fence. In areas abutting residential properties two (2) times a classification V buffer shall be provided.

Section 524.01 F states: 'Glare from a CSES is prohibited from being directed towards vehicular traffic and any habitable portion of an adjacent inhabited structure.' The applicant has the burden of proving that there is no glare produced on inhabited structures or in the roadway. All glare concerns shall be documented, and mitigation will be determined by the County Commissioners and consulted with the CSES Owner.

Section 524.01, subsection R states: 'Solar Panels shall not exceed 22’6"  in height. The height is determined from the ground to the top of the panel at any angle.' This is the explicit maximum structure height allowed for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES). No other maximum height values for CSES are provided. The units are feet, as indicated by the use of the symbol (') for feet and (" ) for inches.

The ordinance explicitly states in section 524.01, subsection H: 'CSES are a minimum 5 acres.' This sets a minimum lot, parcel, or tract size of 5 acres for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES). The unit 'acres' is clearly indicated as the area measurement for this minimum size.

Section 524.01, subsection G states: 'Noise from a CSES shall be no greater than sixty (60) decibels measured from nearest property line.' This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES). The unit is expressed as decibels, assumed to be dBA as the standard unit for noise measurement.

summary: A decommissioning plan shall be submitted for all CSES, outlining the removal of all equipment, structures, and restoration of the site to its pre-development condition. Decommissioning shall commence within twelve (12) months of cessation of operations and be completed within eighteen (18) months. The project owner shall provide a decommissioning plan for all parcels and easements related to the project prior to any commercial solar energy devices being installed. The decommissioning plan shall be approved by the County Commissioners and updated every five (5) years or if any operator or project owner changes. The plan must include: (1) Affidavit of Responsibility signed and recorded by property owners acknowledging ultimate responsibility for decommissioning costs; (2) Insurance requirements including commercial general liability and environmental liability insurance naming Clark County as additional insured; (3) Continuity of the decommissioning plan binding on successors; (4) Restoration of site to natural state including removal of all structures and foundations to a depth of forty-eight inches (48" ); (5) Estimated decommissioning costs calculated by a third-party engineer and agreed upon by the project owner and County Engineer; (6) Surety bond or equivalent security equal to 125% of the estimated decommissioning cost, required prior to issuance of building permits and maintained every five years or upon ownership changes; (7) Penalties for failure to comply including civil penalties and enforcement actions. Decommissioning must be completed within twelve (12) months of the project or component not producing energy, with possible extensions upon reasonable circumstances. Disposal of materials must comply with all local, state, and federal ordinances.

The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES). It requires that "SES shall be designed and located to minimize glare on adjacent properties and public rights-of-way." Additionally, for Commercial SES, "A glare study shall be provided by the project owner that shows the Commercial Solar Energy Facility is situated to eliminate concentrated glare on other parcels and rights-of-way." These requirements are part of the use and operational standards and procedures for Commercial Solar Energy Systems. Other related standards include setbacks, screening, height limits, fencing, noise and vibration limits, and decommissioning plans, but the glare restrictions specifically mandate design to minimize glare and submission of a glare study.

summary: All Commercial Solar Energy Systems shall be fully screened year-round, including across any street or right-of-way, from existing residential dwellings, existing residentially zoned parcels, or existing parcels platted for residential development unless the solar arrays are more than six hundred twenty-five (625) feet away or waived under written, recorded, mutual agreement of all effected property owner(s). Screening may include continuous vegetation, and/or berms that adequately screens the view of the solar panels and accessory equipment as outlined below (fencing is not a permitted screening material). The BZA shall have the discretion to reduce or waive the above screening standards when existing vegetation on the Commercial SES property is determined to provide an acceptable screen, and this vegetation will be maintained in a manner consistent with the intent of this section. All screening shall comply with all standards of the UDO. A landscape plan shall be submitted that identifies the type and extent of proposed buffer and screening. Vegetation or another type of buffer can be proposed if it fully screens the facility year-round and is approved as part of the special exception. Screening shall be consistent with the buffer yard standards of the UDO. Additional screening may be required if there is a clear community interest in maintaining a viewshed or to mitigate the impact on an adjacent parcel. Landscape material must consist of evergreen trees that are included on Indiana DNR’s current  "Tree Species Information"  list and are at least 5 ft tall at the time of planting and reach a mature height of at least fifteen (15) feet. All trees shall be arranged utilizing a triangular spacing pattern (staggered) with spacing that does not exceed ten (10) feet between centers unless approved by the Administrator based on anticipated tree width at maturity. The effectiveness of screening must be maintained at all times and as the plants mature.

Signage for SES shall be limited to identification, warning, and safety signs, and shall comply with the sign regulations of the zoning district. This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) as defined: "A solar energy system that is the principal use of a lot and is designed to provide energy primarily for sale to the grid or other off-site users." The ordinance also includes other development standards for CSES such as setbacks, screening, fencing, emergency response, noise and vibration, signal interference, decommissioning plans, and permits, but only the signage requirement explicitly addresses signage. No other specific signage options or conditions are provided beyond the limitation to identification, warning, and safety signs and compliance with zoning district sign regulations.

summary: Section 406.03 Abandonment and Decommissioning requires that a Commercial Solar facility is considered abandoned if it has not operated for twelve (12) months or 60 days past its projected life without updating its Decommissioning Plan and financial assurance. The ordinance also includes other requirements for CSES permit applications such as economic development agreements, site development plans, safety and security plans, screening and landscape management plans, decommissioning plans, and more, but the explicit fencing requirement is limited to the six-foot fencing around solar panel arrays.

Applications for CSES permit shall include the following: (k) Glint and glare study. This requirement applies specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES), which are defined as any area used by any property owner and/or entity and its contained industrial scale group for the conversion of photovoltaic solar energy into usable electricity or thermal power, primarily or solely for off-site utility grid use, including any SES covering an area greater than one contiguous acre. The glint and glare study must be submitted for review by the County Plan Director as part of the application for improvement location permit.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'No solar panel may exceed 25 feet in height at its highest extended rotation.' This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) solar panels as part of the site development plan requirements. The unit of measurement is feet. No other maximum height values for CSES are provided.

Commercial solar energy systems may be located in zoning districts designated A-1 and I-2. AUSES are considered an accessory use to the principal use and are allowed without any improvement location permit in all zoning districts; however, AUSES are not the same as CSES. The text states: 'Commercial solar energy systems may be located in zoning districts designated A-1 and I-2.'

Commercial solar energy systems may be located in zoning districts designated A-1 and I-2. By implication, CSES are unconditionally prohibited in all other zoning districts not listed. Residential Accessory Uses Solar Energy Systems (AUSES) are allowed in all zoning districts but are accessory uses, not commercial systems.
No solar panel may be located less than 25 feet from any non-participating adjacent property line, unless waived by the owner in writing.

A screening and landscape management plan shall be submitted with the application for improvement location permit. The screening plan must demonstrate the effort to mitigate visual impacts of CSES when panels or any associated CSES structures are located within 250 feet or less from existing residences or other principal structures on adjoining parcels, unless waived by the property owner in writing. When distance from these structures exceeds 250 feet, screening for visual impact mitigation does not apply. A combination of new and/or suitable existing vegetation, in combination with optional opaque fencing are encouraged for screening and buffer purposes. Unhealthy or dead specimens must be replaced within one year. All solar panel arrays for the CSES project must be surrounded by fencing no less than six feet in height.

The ordinance requires that the site development plan for a Commercial Solar Energy System (CSES) include "Identification, access, informational, and warning signs" (§ 155.04(E)(1)(d)(8)). Additionally, all CSES projects must provide the following warnings and safety information at each locked entrance: "A visible 'High Voltage' warning sign," "Name and phone number for the electric utility operator," "Name and phone number for the operator," and "Facility 911 address, GPS coordinates" (§ 155.04(K)(2)). These signage requirements are explicit and must be complied with by CSES developers.

The ordinance requires a 'landscape management plan' that 'shall demonstrate the proposed method to mitigate site erosion and soil degradation both during construction and permanently on-site once construction is complete,' including 'the expedient planting of grass or other crops that provide continuous living roots' and a plan to control invasive species and noxious weeds (§ 155.04(I)(2)). A 'drainage and stormwater pollution prevention plan' must be submitted and approved, ensuring 'drainage shall not impede the flow of water and shall comply with all county ordinances related to drainage and stormwater' (§ 155.04(G)). The 'decommissioning plan' must outline 'potential soil remediation, vegetative alterations, erosion mitigation' and include a cost estimate (§ 155.04(J)). These requirements apply explicitly to Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES), defined as systems 'primarily or solely for off-site utility grid use' and covering 'an area greater than one contiguous acre' (§ 155.02).

The ordinance states that 'Commercial solar energy systems may be located in zoning districts designated A-1 and I-2.' There is no mention that these locations require special use permits, approval by the zoning appeals board, or meeting certain conditions like completing a permitting process. The text only distinguishes Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) from Residential Accessory Uses Solar Energy Systems (AUSES), which are allowed without any improvement location permit in all zoning districts but are accessory uses limited to one contiguous acre. No other districts or special use conditions for CSES are mentioned.

No solar panel may be located less than 250 feet from an existing primary principal structure. This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) and includes occupied dwellings or residences. Additionally, no solar panel may be located less than 25 feet from any non-participating adjacent property line, unless waived by the owner in writing. The 250-foot setback is the most restrictive distance directly pertaining to setbacks from non-participating occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, and/or residences.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "a project operator may not install or locate a CSES project unless the project operator submits as part of the Development Plan the Decommissioning and Site Restoration Plan including the recycling of as much of the solar panels and other equipment as reasonably possible," and "posts a surety bond or equivalent means of surety acceptable to the Zoning Administrator, Plan Commission, County Commissioners, and County Attorney, including a bond or irrevocable letter of credit and also a liability insurance policy naming DeKalb County as an additional insured." The bond or letter of credit must be "equal to 125% 115% of the decommissioning costs included in the Development Plan as calculated by a third party licensed or registered engineer or professional." The bond must be updated every five years. The operator must maintain liability insurance with specified coverage amounts and provide proof annually. Upon intent to decommission, "all solar panels, structures, foundations, roads, gravel areas, cables and all product, materials or other items associated with the CSES project shall be removed," and "the ground shall be restored to a condition reasonably similar to its condition before the start of construction." Decommissioning must be completed within one year, with a possible six-month extension. The ordinance also defines abandonment as "three hundred and sixty‐five (365) days after the date on which the CSES last generated electricity," after which decommissioning must follow the same procedures. These requirements apply specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) as defined: "A solar energy system for the sole purpose of generating and selling large scale power."

Fences are permitted required around the perimeter of a CSES project area anywhere on a property and are not subject to setback requirements except as noted. Fences shall not encroach on an existing right-of-way line along roadways and shall only be placed in a drainage or utility easement with written permission. Opaque (privacy) fences shall not exceed six (6) feet in height. There is no height limit for transparent (chain link) fences. Razor wire fences are not permitted. Barbed wire is permitted. Transparent fences are permitted in the corner vision clearance. All other fences shall meet all vision clearance standards in Section 5.60: Vision Clearance; General. No fence shall block vision of an existing driveway at the intersection of the road it exits onto. This shall follow the Vision Clearance Standards, Section 5.59.

A CSES at no time shall create glare on any non‐participating property line, structure or right‐of‐way. All CSES using a reflector to enhance solar production shall minimize glare from the reflector affecting adjacent or nearby properties, including any public right‐of‐way. If the CSES project area is within any Airport Compatibility Overlay District, Glint and Glare Evaluation report shall be submitted with the Development Plan and approval from the Airport Board is required prior to Development Plan approval.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'No part of a solar panel or other equipment associated with the CSES shall exceed 15 feet in height when oriented at the maximum tilt height.' This is the maximum structure height allowed for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES). No other height restrictions for CSES are provided. The unit of measurement is feet.

Section O. Nuisance Prevention, subsection a states: 'a project owner may not install or locate a CSES unless the project owner demonstrates to the Zoning Administrator that the CSES will operate so the sound attributed with the CSES will not exceed an hourly average sound level of fifty (50) A-Weighted decibels, as modeled at the outer wall of an existing dwelling located on an adjacent nonparticipating property or no less than 150 feet from any non-participating property line that does not include a residence.' The unit is dBA, which is the standard unit for noise level measurement.

The Commercial Solar Energy Systems Overlay District is intended to establish standards for the safety and compatibility for the occupants of the land in the immediate vicinity of a Commercial Solar Energy System (Solar Farm) by setting development standards that supplement or supersede the underlying Zoning District. The permitted uses within the Commercial Solar Energy Systems Overlay District shall be those of the underlying zoning district with the addition of the following uses: Commercial Solar Energy System (CSES). The base zoning shall be any zoning district, with the exception of OP (Open Space and Parks). This overlay district does not regulate small scale, private solar panels on residential or agricultural land and/or structures that is not sold commercially to a utility but rather is used for personal energy consumption.

summary: The ordinance states: 'To qualify for the CSESO, the base zoning shall be any zoning district, with the exception of OP (Open Space and Parks).' The Commercial Solar Energy Systems Overlay District adds CSES as a permitted use in all underlying zoning districts except OP. summary: Setbacks from Non-Participating Land Owner for Single Family Residence: The CSES shall be at least 400 feet from the foundation of the primary structure of a non-participating, pre-existing residential dwelling, as measured at the foundation to the edge of the CSES panel, including across a roadway if applicable. Setbacks from Non-Participating Land Owner for a church, school or commercial business: The CSES shall be at least 200 feet from the foundation of the primary structure of a non-participating, pre-existing church, school or commercial business, as measured at the foundation to the edge of the CSES panel, including across a roadway if applicable. Setbacks may be reduced by half if a 30 foot wide landscape buffer is utilized and written acceptance is received by the adjacent non-participating property owner.

The ordinance explicitly requires a 'Visual Buffer, Vegetation/Landscape Plan & Setback Plan' as part of the Development Plan for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES). It mandates that 'existing natural woods on a participating land owner property shall remain in its natural state if abutting a non-participating land owner' and allows that 'other landscape buffering may be required that may include berms and landscape material during Development Plan Approval by the Plan Commission.' Setbacks from non-participating landowners may be reduced by half if a '30 foot wide landscape buffer is utilized and written acceptance is received by the adjacent non-participating property owner.' A Setback Plan must address 'the size and placement of required landscape buffers' between the CSES and adjacent non-participating properties. Additionally, CSES owners must plant and maintain native forbs and warm season grasses as described in the Development Plan. These requirements apply specifically to CSES as defined in the ordinance, which are large-scale systems for commercial sale of electricity.

A standard metal sign shall be posted on the fence gate at the entrance of the CSES Facility that includes the CSES Owner Name, Facility Name, Emergency Contact Phone Number and physical Site address.

The ordinance requires that no applicant shall construct, operate, locate or enlarge a Commercial Solar Energy System without first obtaining approval and fully complying with the provisions of this ordinance. Specifically, the Development Plan must include a "Storm Water & Erosion Control Plan as approved by the Soil Water Conservation District and Indiana Department of Environmental Management." This is listed under the required items that "shall not receive waivers" during the Development Plan approval process. Additionally, any damage to waterways, drains, or other drainage infrastructure caused by the CSES must be repaired to near original condition and approved by the DeKalb County Drainage Board.

The CSES shall be at least 400 feet from the foundation of the primary structure of a non-participating, pre-existing residential dwelling, as measured at the foundation to the edge of the CSES panel, including across a roadway if applicable. Other options include a 200 feet setback from non-participating, pre-existing church, school or commercial business, and setbacks may be reduced by half if a 30 foot wide landscape buffer is utilized and written acceptance is received by the adjacent non-participating property owner.
section: 3.13 Additional Development Standards, H. Setbacks, c. Non-Participating Land Owners

summary: Section 1930.E requires a decommissioning plan for SES-Cs, including "written assurance that SES-C will be properly decommissioned upon the expiration of its serviceable life or in the event of their discontinuance or abandonment," and "an estimate of the costs of decommissioning and removing the SES-C" by a qualified professional. Financial assurance must be provided via escrow or bond, with a 20% contingency, and verified by the Planning Director. Discontinuation and abandonment are defined, with removal required "within 365 days of the discontinuation or abandonment of the SES-C". Waste management and written notice procedures are also specified. Section 1930.F declares unsafe SES-Cs a public nuisance to be abated per the approved decommissioning plan. Other options include waiver requests for abandonment time extensions under certain conditions, and the County's right to remove the system and recover costs from escrow or bond funds.

All SES-Cs and their appurtenant structures shall be located, fenced or otherwise secured in a manner that prevents unauthorized access. SES-C sites must have a completely fenced perimeter that is wildlife-friendly and can include clearance at the bottom of six (6) inches or less. The fencing for the perimeter must be at least six (6) feet in height with locking gate access and be designed to be harmonious with the natural surroundings to the extent feasible. Alternative fencing can be requested as part of the Site Plan Review process if the site is either incorporating agrivoltaics, or if the applicant is proposing alternative fencing and/or other barriers—including those that are natural—that are determined to be equal to or better than the ordinance requirements and the intent of this Article.

All Solar Energy Systems using a reflector to enhance solar production shall minimize glare from the reflector affecting adjacent or nearby properties, and must adhere to Article 25, Section 2530 with respect to Glare.

The height of any SES-C ground-mounted solar equipment is limited to twenty (20) feet, as measured from the natural grade below each panel to the top of each panel at its maximum tilt in the vertical direction. This applies to Solar Energy Systems–Commercial (SES-C), which include Medium and Large Ground Mounted SES. Roof-mounted SES-As and Integrated Solar Energy Systems may exceed the maximum allowed building height of the building or structure in which it is located by up to three (3) feet in all zoning districts, but this does not apply to SES-C ground-mounted systems.

Section 1930.D.8 requires a Noise Evaluation Report for Solar Energy Systems–Commercial (SES-C), including Ground Mounted SES, Large. The report must include projected maximum noise levels and potential mitigation measures to minimize sound levels above 40 decibels and 55 decibels, where 40 decibels is considered an accepted noise level in a quiet rural setting and 55 decibels in a quiet urban area. The most restrictive maximum noise level allowed is 40 decibels (dBA).

Solar Energy Systems – Commercial (SES-Cs) are permitted in Industrial (I-1, I-2, I-3) and Community Business (B-2) zoning districts. For Solar Energy Systems—Commercial proposed in other zoning districts, a Conditional Use must be obtained first. This means SES-Cs are not allowed as a matter of right outside of I-1, I-2, I-3, and B-2 districts. The ordinance states: 'This Section applies to all Industrial (I-1, I-2, I-3) zoning districts and the Community Business zoning (B-2) district. For Solar Energy Systems—Commercial that are proposed to be located in other zoning districts, a Conditional Use must be obtained (first).' No districts are explicitly listed as unconditionally prohibiting SES-Cs without possibility of conditional use approval.

Any SES-C equipment, excluding perimeter fencing, poles, and wire necessary to connect the facility to an electric utility, must be setback at least one-hundred-and-fifty feet (150) feet from any property line of a non-participating landowner—unless a landscape bufferyard is placed between the SES-C equipment and the adjacent non-participating property line(s). If a landscape bufferyard is installed, then the setback may be reduced to seventy-five (75) feet.

summary: For participating properties, any SES-C equipment, excluding perimeter fencing, poles, and wire necessary to connect the facility to an electric utility, must be setback at least thirty (30) feet from primary structures and at least ten (10) feet from all other structure(s) on a participating landowner’s property that is part of the SES-C. Additionally, property line setbacks between separate parcels of different ownership—both or all of which are participating as part of an SES-C—may be waived upon agreement of the landowners. Otherwise, SES-C equipment must be setback at the same distance as a primary structure in the zoning district in which it is located—except for equipment creating objectionable sound levels, which must meet the 150-foot setback set forth for adjacent non-participating properties.
section: SECTION 1930 - Solar Energy Systems – Commercial (SES-Cs), Subsection C (Location)

summary: A SES-C "shall have, to the extent reasonably practicable, a visual buffer of natural vegetation, plantings, earth berms, and/or fencing that provides a reasonable visual and lighting screen to reduce the view of the SES-C from non-participating residential uses and structures on adjacent lots, including those lots located across a road right-of-way." Bufferyards "shall be required in accordance with Article 22 (Section 2270, Table 22.1) where applicable, depending on the proposed site, site layout, and adjacent uses, and will be determined during the Site Plan Review process." For street frontages where there are non-participating properties next to, or across from, a proposed SES-C, landscaping "shall also be required in accordance with Article 22, Sections 2240 and 2260." Any visual buffer must be "established and maintained in accordance with the most recent landscaping and bufferyard plan approved by the Technical Review Committee."

All Solar Energy Systems – Commercial (SES-Cs) and their appurtenant structures shall contain a standard metal road sign no larger than four (4) square feet in order to provide the name(s) of the owner(s) and operator(s) of the SES-C as well as emergency phone number(s) and the address of the site. This sign shall be visible from the access point of the site—but shall be located just outside of the road right-of-way, outside of the sight triangles in either direction—and shall not be lighted, unless lighting is required by applicable law, rule or regulation. A four (4) square-foot warning sign concerning voltage must also be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations in a conspicuous location. No other signage, including advertising, shall be permitted.

All Solar Energy Systems must meet the requirements of the Dearborn County Code of Ordinances regarding drainage and erosion control. Stormwater design and calculations must be done in accordance with Article 3, Section 325 of the Dearborn County Subdivision Control Ordinance. Additionally, an Erosion Control permit or Stormwater Construction Permit must also be obtained where applicable, and submitted as part of the Site Plan Review process. Applicants of all Solar Energy Systems – Commercial (SES-Cs) shall prepare a written statement acknowledging responsibility for addressing on-going road maintenance, drainage, erosion control, or dust issues identified by the Dearborn County Engineer, IDEM, or another applicable public agent during all phases of the construction process, and must address such issues in the prescribed time(s) and manner(s) set forth by the applicable governmental entity.

Other setback options include 200 feet from primary structures on non-participating properties, 150 feet from property lines of non-participating landowners (reducible to 75 feet with a landscape bufferyard), and zoning setbacks for participating properties equal to those for primary structures in the zoning district.

summary: Section 10(A)(4) requires a Decommission and Restoration Plan and Agreement to be submitted and approved by the Delaware County Commissioners. The plan must include "a reliable and detailed estimate of the costs of decommissioning prepared by a professional engineer or contractor," and "a performance bond or other approved method of providing appropriate surety for the cost of decommissioning." Decommissioning includes removal of all solar electric systems, buildings, cabling up to four feet deep, electrical components, security barriers, roads, foundations to a depth of four feet, pilings, and any other associated facilities, restoring the site to tillable agricultural use unless the landowner requests otherwise in writing and the request is approved. Solar farms that have reached the end of their useful life or have not been in active and continuous service for twelve (12) months must be removed within twelve (12) months at the owner’s or operator’s expense, except if the project is being repowered or a force majeure event requires longer repairs. If removal is not completed, the County may collect the surety and remove the installation. These requirements apply to "Solar Farms," defined as "a group of interconnected solar panels/arrays for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity."

Section 10(F) FENCING requires that facilities enclosed by security fencing shall have the fencing located on the interior of the buffer area. Solar farms that do not coincide with livestock shall use wildlife-permeable fence, fencing with larger holes than a traditional chain-link fence that allows for small- to medium-sized animals to move freely through the fence for at least ten (10) percent of the fence lines where the 10% shall be evenly distributed along each quarter mile section and at identified wildlife corridors. Substation locations identified on the site plans will be allowed to use traditional chain-link fencing around the entire structure. Fencing shall be maintained in good condition for the life of the solar farm operation.

Section 10(I) GLARE states: "Solar panel placement should be prioritized to minimize or negate any solar glare onto nearby properties or roadways, without unduly impacting the functionality or efficiency of the solar system. Exterior surfaces of the collectors and related surfaces shall have nonreflective finish." This applies to solar farms defined as "a group of interconnected solar panels/arrays for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity."

Section 10.B HEIGHT states: 'The height of the solar collector and any mounts shall not exceed 20 feet when oriented at maximum tilt.' This applies to solar farms defined as groups of interconnected solar panels/arrays for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity, including all related equipment and facilities. The unit 'feet' is explicitly used in the ordinance.

Section 10(J) NOISE states: 'Sound attributable to the solar farm shall not exceed an hourly average sound level of sixty (60) A-weighted decibels as modeled at the property line adjacent to a dwelling or residence zone.' This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for utility-scale solar energy systems (solar farms) as defined in the ordinance. The units are standard noise measurement units, dBA (A-weighted decibels). No other noise level restrictions are provided for solar farms in the text.

The ordinance explicitly permits 'Solar Farms' as a permitted use in the F FARMING ZONE and the IL LIMITED INDUSTRIAL ZONE. Specifically, ARTICLE XII F FARMING ZONE, Section 1 PERMITTED USES includes '21. Solar Farms. Solar farms are subject to the requirements set forth herein in Article XII, Section 10.' ARTICLE XXIII IL LIMITED INDUSTRIAL ZONE, Section 2 PERMITTED USES includes '32. Solar Farms. Solar farms are subject to the requirements set forth herein in Article XII, Section 10.' Article XII, Section 10 outlines requirements for solar farms but does not indicate special approvals or conditions beyond compliance, implying these are primary permitted uses. No other districts or overlay zones are mentioned in the text provided.

summary: A minimum fifty (50) foot setback, which includes a screening buffer and other native vegetation as described below, shall be maintained from the solar farm structures to any non-participating owner’s adjoining property line which is a perimeter boundary line for the project area. The setbacks set forth in items 2. and 3. above may be reduced by up to 50% with a written waiver from the property owner(s). Other setback options include a 50-foot setback from road right-of-way lines and setbacks from non-participating dwellings (250 feet and 100 feet), but these do not pertain to property lines.
section: Section 10. SOLAR FARM REQUIREMENTS, C SETBACKS

summary: A minimum fifty (50) foot setback shall be maintained from the solar farm structures to the road right-of-way line, existing or proposed, whichever is greater. This applies to solar farms defined as utility-scale systems. Other setbacks mentioned include 50 feet from non-participating adjoining property lines and 250 feet from non-participating dwellings, but these do not pertain to roads.

The ordinance requires that solar farms be "significantly screened from the viewshed of adjacent residential dwellings or commercial buildings by a buffer zone extending from the property line." A minimum 50-foot buffer zone "containing native plants including trees, shrubs and pollinators, shall be maintained." If existing vegetation is inadequate, "native plants shall be planted to create the visual screen." Existing wooded areas of an acre or more may not be removed, and large trees removed must be replaced at a 2 to 1 ratio. "Opaque architectural screening methods may be used to supplement other screening methods but shall not be the primary method." A landscape plan prepared by a professional landscape architect is required. The buffer zone requirement may be waived in whole or in part by the property owner. The ordinance also requires fencing to be located on the interior of the buffer area and specifies wildlife-permeable fencing for at least 10% of fence lines. These requirements apply to solar farms defined as "a group of interconnected solar panels/arrays for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity."

Each solar farm must include an informational sign, 1 per frontage, with the name of the facility owner and the phone number for a 24-hour emergency contact. The informational sign may not exceed 6 square feet.

The ordinance requires a "stormwater/erosion control permit" prior to permit issuance for solar farms. Section 10(G) GROUND COVER mandates: "Top soil shall not be removed during development, unless part of a remediation effort." and "Soil shall be planted and maintained in perennial vegetation to prevent erosion, manage run-off, and build soil." Section 10(N) GENERAL PROVISIONS, item 3 states: "Installation of solar farm facilities must not interfere with existing drainage tiles unless mitigation measures are taken such as reconstruction, repairs, replacing tile, installing additional drainage features, or re-routing." These requirements apply to solar farms defined as "a group of interconnected solar panels/arrays for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity."

The ordinance text permits Solar Farms as a permitted use in the Farming Zone (Article XII F) and the Limited Industrial Zone (Article XXIII IL), subject to requirements in Article XII, Section 10. There is no mention of Solar Farms being permitted as a special use or requiring approval by a zoning appeals board or similar conditional permitting process. The text states: 'Solar Farms. Solar farms are subject to the requirements set forth herein in Article XII, Section 10.' No other districts or special use conditions are referenced for utility-scale solar energy systems.

summary: A minimum two hundred fifty (250) foot setback shall be maintained from any non-participating dwelling to any solar farm structure, not including security fencing if applicable. A minimum one hundred (100) foot setback shall be maintained for all other dwellings. The setbacks set forth in items 2. and 3. above may be reduced by up to 50% with a written waiver from the property owner(s).

Applications for solar farms must include a concept plan and a site plan. The concept plan shall include "the location and nature of proposed buffers, including vegetative and constructed buffers and berms." The site plan must include "a separate landscape plan prepared by a professional landscape architect" and "an assessment form or score card from an approved source showing that the proposed landscape plan meets or exceeds accepted pollinator and habitat standards." A minimum 50-foot buffer zone containing native plants including trees, shrubs and pollinators shall be maintained. "If there is no existing vegetation or if the existing vegetation is inadequate to serve as a screen, native plants shall be planted to create the visual screen." Existing wooded areas of an acre or more may not be removed, and large trees removed must be replaced at a 2 to 1 ratio. "Opaque architectural screening methods may be used to supplement other screening methods but shall not be the primary method." The buffer zone requirement may be waived in whole or in part by the property owner. The ordinance also requires the concept plan and site plan to show points of ingress/egress and fencing location, which must be located on the interior of the buffer area. These requirements apply to solar farms defined as "a group of interconnected solar panels/arrays for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity."

Fencing shall be required surrounding the entire panel area. Fences shall be a minimum of 6 feet in height and located on the panel side of any required buffer. Ground-mounted solar arrays are permitted according to the following table: Up to 1,500 sq. ft. panel area; More than 1,500 sq. ft. panel area, less than 3,000 sq. ft.; More than 3,000 sq. ft. panel area; less than 10 acres fenced area; 10 acres fenced area or more requires Zone Map Change to A-E.

Other standard and special purpose districts reference solar energy systems but defer to Section 158.04(F), indicating that large systems are not permitted by-right outside the A-E overlay without rezoning or special approval.

These setbacks apply to ground-mounted solar energy farms with 10 acres fenced area or more, measured from the fence to the road centerline. The most restrictive setback from roads is 120 feet from a major road.
