summary: The A-E Alternative Energy Overlay (Section 158.04(F)) requires buffering and screening for ground-mounted solar energy systems, specifically stating: 'Buffering and screening is required as outlined in Article 158.06.' For systems with '10 acres fenced area or more,' a Zone Map Change to A-E is required. Fencing is also mandated: 'Fencing shall be required surrounding the entire panel area. Fences shall be a minimum of 6 feet in height and located on the panel side of any required buffer.' The overlay applies to alternative energy uses on land and includes standards for setbacks, noise, lighting, and signage. Other size thresholds for ground-mounted solar arrays include: up to 1,500 sq. ft. panel area permitted by-right; more than 1,500 sq. ft. but less than 3,000 sq. ft. panel area with conditions; and more than 3,000 sq. ft. but less than 10 acres fenced area with additional conditions. Only systems with 10 acres fenced area or more require the zone map change and are subject to the buffering and screening requirements.
section: 158.04(F) SPECIAL PURPOSE & OVERLAY DISTRICTS A-E Alternative Energy Overlay

summary: Ground-mounted solar arrays with 10 acres fenced area or more require a "Zone Map Change to A-E" (the Alternative Energy Overlay district) as stated: "10 acres fenced area or more Zone Map Change to A-E." The text specifies that building or roof-mounted solar arrays up to certain sizes are permitted by-right or with special use permits if placement standards are not met, but for large ground-mounted systems of 10 acres or more, rezoning is mandatory. No standard or special purpose districts (R-2, R-3, R-4, B-1, B-2, B-3, M-1, M-2, E-3, A-3, A-4) explicitly permit these large systems as special use or similar. The only option for such large systems is rezoning to the A-E overlay district.

Setbacks: Residential Building (between fence & non-participating residential building) 200’. Other setbacks include Residential Use or District (between fence and residential use or district boundary) 100’, Property line (between fence & non-participating property line) 50’, Major road (between fence and centerline) 120’, County Road (between fence and centerline) 75’. The 200 feet setback applies to non-participating residential buildings for ground-mounted solar energy farms with 10 acres fenced area or more, which require a Zone Map Change to A-E Alternative Energy Overlay.

This indicates a required setback of 100 feet between the fence of the solar energy farm and any body of water, which includes lakes, reservoirs, streams, rivers, and wetlands. Other setback distances mentioned include: Major road (120 feet), County Road (75 feet), Property line (50 feet), Residential Building (200 feet), Residential Use or District (100 feet), but these do not pertain to bodies of water.

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires SES-3 systems to submit and enter into a Decommissioning-Restoration Plan and Agreement with the County Commissioners prior to receiving an Improvement Location Permit. The owner/operator must give written notice of intent to abandon use at least 120 days prior to discontinuation of electrical production. An SES is considered abandoned after one year without energy production unless a Rehabilitation Plan is approved. The SES owner/operator must remove all physical material above and below ground, recycle panels, and restore the site to as near as practicable to the original condition within 365 days of discontinuation. Hazardous materials must be identified and handled according to law. A performance guarantee in the form of a bond or financial security equal to 150% of estimated decommissioning and restoration costs must be provided and updated every five years. The county may remove the SES if the owner/operator defaults, using funds from the surety. Written notice and a reasonable negotiation period (up to 60 days) are required before enforcement. Costs incurred by Fayette County for removal due to owner/operator failure must be paid by the owner/operator. These requirements apply specifically to SES-2 and SES-3 systems, which include systems "10 to 400 acres (not including required buffers) and/or greater than 16 MW/ac."
section: S. Decommissioning-Restoration Plan and Agreement (for SES-2 and SES-3)

summary: For security, all ground-mounted SES-2 and SES-3 shall be completely enclosed by a minimum six (6) foot high chain link fence with a locking gate accessed by a keypad or Knox box with key. The fence should be located at the setback distance. Any required landscaping or buffer may be outside the fence. A fence in an agriculture zone located on the property lines is the sole responsibility of the SES owner/operator. (Section I.13 Fence) Additionally, setbacks and separation distances from property lines or ROW to fencing are specified as 100' for SES-2 and 1320' for SES-3 (Section I.3.a).

The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for SES-3 systems under section I.6 "Color, Finish and Glare," which applies to SES-1, SES-2, and SES-3. It requires that "solar energy panels, regardless of how they are mounted, shall be oriented and/or screened year-round so that glare is directed away from adjacent properties and streets" to the extent reasonably possible. Additionally, the SES "shall be designed using such features as colors, materials, textures, screening, and landscaping to blend into their settings and avoid visual blight." The exterior surface of visible components "shall be non-reflective, neutral color like black, white, gray or another non-obtrusive color" with finishes that "shall be matte or non reflective." The property owner "has the burden of mitigating any glare produced so as not to have significant adverse impact on adjacent uses," with the Executive Director's determination being conclusive. These glare restrictions apply to SES-3, which are defined as systems "10 to 400 acres (not including required buffers) and/or greater than 16 MW/ac."
section: I. TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS, 6. Color, Finish and Glare

summary: The ordinance states: 'Ground-mounted SES shall not exceed 15 feet in height above the ground elevation surrounding the systems.' This applies to SES-2 and SES-3. Additionally, in residential zone districts, the maximum height is 10 feet, but since SES-3 typically involves larger commercial systems, the 15 feet limit is the most relevant and less restrictive for SES-3. The height restriction is explicitly for ground-mounted solar energy systems and is measured from the ground elevation surrounding the systems.

The ordinance defines SES-3 as systems occupying "10 to 400 acres (not including required buffers) and/or greater than 16 MW/ac" and explicitly states "No SES larger than 400 acres shall be permitted." It further clarifies that "Each SES-2 or SES-3 project, either singly or as a combination of contiguous parcels, shall not exceed 10 acres or 400 acres (not including required buffers)." The units for the maximum size are acres.

SES-3 is defined as systems occupying "10 to 400 acres (not including required buffers) and/or greater than 16 MW/ac" with a clear minimum size threshold of 10 acres. The ordinance states: "Each SES-2 or SES-3 project, either singly or as a combination of contiguous parcels, shall not exceed 10 acres or 400 acres (not including required buffers)." The units for this minimum size are acres, a standard area measurement. Other SES types have different size limits: SES-1 is 5 acres or less and/or less than 1 MW/ac; SES-2 is up to 10 acres maximum and less than 1 MW/ac (5 to 10 acres including buffers and/or more than 1 MW/ac and less than 15 MW/ac). No SES larger than 400 acres shall be permitted.

No operating SES shall produce noise that exceeds any of the following limitations except during construction or maintenance. Adequate setbacks, barriers, enclosures, use of quieter equipment, or other effective means of reducing noise shall be used to comply with these limitations: a. Fifty dBA, as measured at the property line of any adjacent residentially zoned lot; b. Forty-five dBA, as measured at any existing adjacent residence between the hours of nine p.m. and seven a.m.; and c. Sixty dBA, as measured at the property lines of the project boundary, unless the owner of the affected property agrees to a higher noise level, as follows: The owner of an adjacent property that would otherwise be protected by the sixty dBA noise limitations may voluntarily agree, by written waiver, to a higher noise level. Any such agreement must specifically state the noise standard being modified, the extent of the modification, and be in the form of a legally binding contract or easement between the landowner (including assignees in interest) and the solar energy system developer, effective for the life of the project. This waiver must be recorded and cross-referenced with the affected property (properties). The units for these noise levels are dBA.

The ordinance explicitly requires a 'three mile neutral zone' between each SES-3 project, which translates to 15,840 feet. Additionally, it specifies a '1320’ setback and separation distance from property line or ROW to fencing' for SES-3. The three-mile (15,840 feet) neutral zone is the most restrictive minimum separation distance between SES-3 projects. SES-3 is defined as systems covering 10 to 400 acres and/or greater than 16 MW/ac, representing large-scale commercial solar energy systems.

The ordinance requires a 1320' setback and separation distance from property line or ROW to fencing for SES-3 systems. Specifically, 'SES-3 - 1320' from any adjoining road or from the property line of a non-participating homeowner to the beginning of the project/fencing.' This setback applies to the entire SES including solar panels, racking, underground cabling, fencing, access roads/lanes, and other power equipment. Other options include SES-1 with setbacks equivalent to building setbacks (currently 50 feet) and SES-2 with 100' setback from property line or ROW to fencing.
section: I. TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS, 3. Ground-Mounted SES, a. Setback and Separation distance

summary: No SES-3 facility shall be sited within three miles of any FEMA/DNR floodplain, major named creek, and river, and any natural flowing spring well. (Section I.21 "Buffer from Water Sources (SES-3 only)") Additional related requirements include environmental impact analysis and cooperation with wildlife agencies (Section I.18 and II.K), and avoidance of placement within special flood hazard areas or regulated drainage easements without permission (Section I.3.d).

Setbacks are as follows: SES-3 - 1320' from any adjoining road or from the property line of a non-participating homeowner to the beginning of the project/fencing. Setbacks apply to the entire SES including solar panels, racking, underground cabling, fencing, access roads/lanes, and other power equipment. Other options include SES-2: 100' setback and separation distance from property line or ROW to fencing; SES-1: minimum yard setbacks equivalent to building setback in zoning district (50 ft currently).
section: II. Application for a SES, D. Safety, Design, and Installation Standards for SES-2 and SES-3 Zoning, 1. Setbacks and Siting of Facilities

summary: Signs shall comply with the Sign Standards provided in the Fayette County Code of Ordinances. Development Signs: An identification sign relating to a SES may be located on each side of the fenced facility area provided that there shall be no more than one (1) sign located on any side of the SES fenced facility area unless additional identification signs are required to provide reasonable notice to the general public. A sign shall be securely posted on each gate entry point clearly displaying an emergency telephone number(s) and other contact information. All ingress/egress roads to a SES shall have posted in a conspicuous location a 911 address road sign indicating the assigned address for that location. Warning signs shall comply with applicable laws. No portion of the SES shall contain or be used to display advertising. The manufacturer's name and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of the SES provided they comply with the prevailing sign regulations. All signage required or permitted by this Ordinance shall be made of materials and constructed in a manner to be durable and long lasting. The same shall be painted or made of material with a distinct, high contrast background and be weatherproof paint or other weatherproof material to promote safety and protect the public from hazards and/or potential hazards.

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for SES-3 systems. It requires "an erosion control plan shall be developed in accordance with protocol of the Natural Resources Conservation Services (NRCS), and any storm water quality management plan adopted by the applicable jurisdiction(s)." The area beneath the ground-mounted SES is considered pervious cover, and "Natural (pervious) ground covers are required beneath the solar arrays." For SES-3, "Damages, including but not limited to damming, cutting, removing, and blocking, to surface, subsurface drains, or any other drainage infrastructure... must be restored by the SES-3 owner to a condition that is equal to or better than the pre existing conditions within three (3) months after receipt of notice of such damage." The SES-3 owner is responsible for all expenses related to repairs and must post a surety bond payable to the Drainage Board. The SES-3 owner and operator must "fully comply with Indiana Code requirements regarding regulated drains except as otherwise approved by the Drainage Board." Additionally, prior to issuing an Improvement Location Permit, the applicant must provide a Drainage Agreement approved by the County Commissioners, which "must prescribe or reference provisions to address field tile damages and repairs thereof." The petitioner must post a surety bond to address drainage tile repair, replacement, or re-routing caused by construction activities or installation of the Project. The petitioner must comply with the reasonable direction of the County Surveyor regarding inspection and repair of drainage improvements. These requirements explicitly apply to SES-3 and impose planning, restoration, financial assurance, and regulatory compliance obligations related to soil, erosion, and sediment control.
section: II. Application for a SES, U. Erosion Control Plan, 20. Sub-surface and surface drains (regulated and non-regulated)- Applies to SES-3, T. Drainage Agreement, and Road Use and Maintenance Agreements

summary: The ordinance defines SES-3 as large solar energy systems between 10 to 400 acres and/or greater than 16 MW/ac. It states that "The SES-2,and 3 requires a Special Use Permit from the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA)." Minimum setbacks for SES-3 are "1320' from any adjoining road or from the property line of a non-participating homeowner to the beginning of the project/fencing." The text mentions A-1 Zoned Property (Farmland) with a condition that "No more than 10% of a SES-3 may be located on A-1 Farmland as designated" and requires a letter from NRCS or qualified source with the Improvement Location Permit. However, the ordinance does not explicitly list specific zoning district names or abbreviations where SES-3 is permitted as a special use. Other SES types include SES-1 (property/homeowner use, less than 1 MW/ac, 5 acres or less) and SES-2 (commercial use or sale, up to 10 acres and less than 1 MW/ac or 5 to 10 acres and/or more than 1 MW/ac and less than 15 MW/ac). Roof-mounted and wall-mounted SES-1 and SES-2 are permitted accessory uses in all zoning districts under certain conditions. Ground-mounted SES-3 have specific setback and height requirements but no explicit district permissions are listed.

SES-3 - 1320' from the property line of a non-participating homeowner to the beginning of the project/fencing. Setbacks apply to the entire SES including solar panels, racking, underground cabling, fencing, access roads/lanes, and other power equipment. Additionally, any inverter shall be a minimum of five hundred (500) feet from any dwelling. Other options include SES-2 with 100 feet setback and SES-1 with setbacks equivalent to the building setback in the zoning district (50 feet currently).
section: I. TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS, 2. Solar Energy Systems 2 and 3 (SES-2 and SES-3) Property use, Modification and Value, D. Safety, Design, and Installation Standards for SES-2 and SES-3 Zoning, 1. Setbacks and Siting of Facilities

summary: Setbacks are as follows: SES-3 - 1320' from any adjoining road or from the property line of a non-participating homeowner to the beginning of the project/fencing. Setbacks apply to the entire SES including solar panels, racking, underground cabling, fencing, access roads/lanes, and other power equipment. Additionally, the furthest horizontal extension of a SES-2 or 3 shall not be less than fifteen (15') feet from any above ground electrical transmission line, electrical distribution line or other above ground communication or transmission line. Poles carrying overhead wiring and underground wiring connecting SES components have no setback requirements from property lines if located within a recorded easement for such purpose.
section: 2. Safety, Design, and Installation Standards for SES-2 and SES-3 Zoning

summary: No SES-3 facility shall be sited within three miles of any FEMA/DNR floodplain, major named creek, and river, and any natural flowing spring well. Additionally, a wetland delineation and report shall be submitted on properties proposed for use as a SES within 3 miles of a wetland. Ground-mounted SES shall not be placed within any storm water conveyance system, regulated drain easement, special flood hazard area, or in any other manner that would alter or impede storm water runoff. These setbacks apply specifically to SES-3 systems, which are defined as 10 to 400 acres and/or greater than 16 MW/ac. No other numeric setback distances from lakes, reservoirs, streams, rivers, or wetlands are specified for SES-3.
section: I. TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS, 21. Buffer from Water Sources (SES-3 only)

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for SECS-1 (Tier 1) projects, defined as "Project covering greater than twenty (20) acres for production of electricity sold to utility transmission lines." Section 6a requires a "Decommissioning Agreement to ensure that the Project is properly decommissioned" prior to permit issuance, including "financial assurance that the Project facilities are properly decommissioned upon the end of the Project life or abandonment." Section 10a mandates that "the Applicant shall deliver to the Administrator a pro forma performance or surety bond, letter of credit or other form of financial assurance" called the "Decommissioning Security" securing performance of decommissioning obligations, with amounts scaling from 25% to 100% of Restoration Costs over time. The Decommissioning Agreement must include "removal and proper disposal of all physical material pertaining to the Project improvements to a depth of four (4) feet beneath the soil surface, and restoration of the area occupied by the Project improvements such that it is suitable for an equivalent land use to what existed immediately before construction." Section 10h states that a SECS or individual solar panel block is "presumed at the end of its useful life and/or abandoned if the SECS or the individual solar panel block generates no electricity for a continuing period of twelve (12) months" and such facilities "shall be subject to removal pursuant to the Decommissioning Agreement." Other tiers defined are SECS-2 (Tier 2) "Project covering more than one (1) acre and up to twenty (20) acres situated on one or more landowner’s property generating electricity used primarily for on-site use" and SECS-3 (Tier 3) "Project covering one acre or less and owned by one landowner generating electricity exclusively behind the meter for single property owner."

The ordinance defines SECS-1 (Tier 1) as a "Project covering greater than twenty (20) acres for production of electricity sold to utility transmission lines." It explicitly requires that "All solar panels for the Project must be fenced in with a fence not less than six (6) feet in height." Other tiers include SECS-2 (Tier 2) for projects "covering more than one (1) acre and up to twenty (20) acres situated on one or more landowner’s property generating electricity used primarily for on-site use," and SECS-3 (Tier 3) for projects "covering one acre or less and owned by one landowner generating electricity exclusively behind the meter for single property owner." The fencing requirement applies to the entire Project, which is measured from a permitted fence surrounding the total solar generation facilities including substations, energy storage, or electrical support buildings.

The ordinance requires for SECS-1 (Tier 1) projects, defined as projects covering greater than twenty (20) acres for production of electricity sold to utility transmission lines, that "A glint and glare study, which provides that the Project will minimize glint and glare, shall be submitted." This is found in Section 6(d). Other tiers include SECS-2 (Tier 2) - projects covering more than one (1) acre and up to twenty (20) acres generating electricity used primarily for on-site use, and SECS-3 (Tier 3) - projects covering one acre or less generating electricity exclusively behind the meter for a single property owner. The glare restriction applies explicitly to SECS-1 projects as part of the permit application requirements.

Section 9(d) states: 'No solar panel may exceed 25’ in height at its highest extended rotation.' This applies to SECS-1 (Tier 1) systems, which are defined as projects covering greater than twenty (20) acres for production of electricity sold to utility transmission lines. Other height or setback restrictions apply to solar panels generally, but this 25 feet limit is the explicit maximum height for solar panels. The unit is feet as indicated by the apostrophe (').

SECS projects are divided into three tiers: SECS-1 (Tier 1) — Project covering greater than twenty (20) acres for production of electricity sold to utility transmission lines; SECS-2 (Tier 2) - Project covering more than one (1) acre and up to twenty (20) acres situated on one or more landowner’s property generating electricity used primarily for on-site use; SECS-3 (Tier 3) — Project covering one acre or less and owned by one landowner generating electricity exclusively behind the meter for single property owner. Acreage for SECS is measured from a permitted fence surrounding the total solar generation facilities including any substations, energy storage or electrical support buildings.

No solar panel may be located less than twenty-five (25) feet on all sides from any Non-Participating landowner property line. This setback applies to SECS-1 (Tier 1) projects, which are defined as projects covering greater than twenty (20) acres for production of electricity sold to utility transmission lines. Other setback provisions include a 150 feet setback from the foundation of any existing residence of a Non-Participating landowner, but residences are not equivalent to property lines or parcels unless explicitly stated.

A screening plan shall be implemented which shall consist of opaque fencing, new vegetation, utilizing existing natural screening or a combination thereof. To the extent that solar panels are established more than 200 feet from the foundation of an existing residence of a Non-Participating landowner, this standard shall not apply. This applies to SECS projects including SECS-1 (Tier 1) defined as projects covering greater than twenty (20) acres for production of electricity sold to utility transmission lines.

Section 6(h) requires the Applicant to establish a twenty-four (24) hour toll-free phone number for the registering of complaints and concerns. This number shall be posted at every road intersection throughout the Project area before a Permit is issued and before any construction or earth moving can commence. Section 8(b) states: "A visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all pad mounted transformers and substations." These signage requirements apply to SECS projects, including SECS-1 (Tier 1), as the ordinance governs Tier 1 projects and the signage requirements are stated in the context of the overall SECS project standards. Other options or conditions related to signage are not provided in the ordinance.

The ordinance requires a Drainage Plan approved by the Gibson County Drainage Board "prior to the initiation of construction" for SECS-1 projects, including financial assurance for repair or replacement of damaged drains, ditches, and tiles. The Drainage Plan "shall state that any newly constructed access roads shall not impede the flow of water and will comply with all County ordinances related to drainage and the management of stormwater." Additionally, a Natural Resource Impact Report must be submitted, including "identification and analysis of... soil types," and within 120 days of project completion, the Applicant must submit "a site map detailing all ground disturbed through construction activity." SECS-1 (Tier 1) is defined as a "Project covering greater than twenty (20) acres for production of electricity sold to utility transmission lines." The ordinance also distinguishes SECS-2 (Tier 2) and SECS-3 (Tier 3) projects with different acreage and usage thresholds, but the soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements apply explicitly to SECS-1 projects as described.

No solar panel shall be located less than one hundred fifty (150) feet from the foundation of any existing residence of a Non-Participating landowner. Other setback options include no solar panel may be located less than twenty-five (25) feet on all sides from any Non-Participating landowner property line, but this pertains to property lines, not residences.

Section 153.719 SFES Decommissioning Plan Agreement requires that prior to receiving construction approval for the SFES project, the applicant, owner and/or operator must provide proof of a signed Decommissioning Plan Agreement between the Grant County Commissioners and the applicant, owner and/or operator. The Decommissioning Plan is to ensure that the SFES facilities are properly decommissioned upon the end of the project life or facility abandonment. The applicant, owner and/or operator’s obligations with respect to decommissioning shall include removal of all physical material pertaining to the project improvements to a depth of 48" beneath the soil surface, and restoration of the area occupied by the project improvements to the same or better condition that existed immediately before construction of such improvements. Prior to issuance of an Improvement Location Permit, the applicant, owner and/or operator shall provide a contractor/engineer cost estimate for demolition and removal of the SFES facility and will provide financial assurance, taking into consideration any salvage or recycling value, in an amount at least equal to said demolition and removal contractor cost estimate, through the use of a bond, letter of credit or other security acceptable to the Area Plan Commission, the cost of decommissioning the solar field(s) under the building permit, which security shall be released when said solar field(s) is properly decommissioned as determined by the Area Plan Commission. The Financial assurance shall automatically renew each year or have no expiration. The decommissioning plan and financial assurance will be updated by the Owner of the SFES Facility every five (5) years and adjusted as necessary to ensure sufficient funds are available to decommission the project over its life. In the event of abandonment by the owner and/or operator, the applicant will provide an affidavit to the Area Plan Executive Director representing that all easements for the solar field(s) shall contain terms that provide financial assurance, including access to the salvage or recycling value of the equipment, for the property owners to ensure that facilities are properly decommissioned within twelve (12) months of expiration or earlier termination of the project. The applicant, owner, and/or operator's failure to comply with, or make reasonable progress in getting into compliance with any of the above provisions shall constitute a default under this Ordinance. If the Owner or operator of the solar facility fails to remove the installation in accordance with the agreement or within the proposed date of decommissioning, the Area Plan Commission shall send forth a recommendation to the Commissioners for collection of the surety and with approval, direct the staff to hire a third party to enter the property to physically remove the installation.

All SFES systems equipment, panels and structures shall be fully enclosed and secured by a fence with a minimum height of 6 feet and must setback a minimum of 50 feet from any property line. Fences must be equipped with a minimum of one gate and locking mechanism on the primary access side. (Section 153.716 Fencing) This fencing requirement applies to all SFES systems, which includes Major Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES Major) as defined: "A commercial facility, on a parcel(s) of 10 acres or more that converts sunlight to electricity... with the primary purpose of selling wholesale or retail generated electricity." Other related requirements include setbacks, buffers, screening, and landscaping, but these do not replace or negate the explicit fencing requirement.

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Major Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES Major). It states: 'All Solar Panels must be constructed to minimize glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and must not interfere with traffic, including air traffic, or create a safety hazard.' This is found under the 'Glare minimization' provision in the Solar Farm Energy System (SFES) Site & Landscape Requirements. Other related provisions include setbacks, buffers, screening, noise limits, fencing, and lighting, but glare restrictions are specifically addressed only in this context.
section: 153.716 Solar Farm Energy System (SFES) Site & Landscape Requirements

summary: The ordinance explicitly states: 'The Height of the solar collector and any mounts shall not exceed 20’ when oriented at maximum tilt.' This applies to Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES), including Major SFES. The unit is feet as indicated by the use of the apostrophe (') symbol for feet. No other maximum height values for SFES Major are provided in the text.
section: 153.716 Solar Farm Energy System (SFES) Site & Landscape Requirements

summary: Major Solar Farm Energy System (SFES Major) is defined as a commercial facility on a parcel(s) of 10 acres or more that converts sunlight to electricity, with the primary purpose of selling wholesale or retail generated electricity. Minor Solar Farm Energy System (SFES Minor) applies to parcels from 1 acre up to 10 acres. Residential Solar Energy Systems (RSES) are only considered RSES if installed on one (1) acre or less. The minimum lot size for Major SFES is explicitly stated as 10 acres or more, with units in acres.

Sound attributable to the solar farm shall not exceed an hourly average sound level of sixty (60) A-weighted decibels as modeled at the property line adjacent to a dwelling or residence zone. This applies to Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES) designed for commercial energy production, including Major Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES Major). The unit 'dBA' refers to A-weighted decibels, a standard noise measurement unit.
section: 153.716 Solar Farm Energy System (SFES) Site & Landscape Requirements

summary: A minimum fifty (50) foot setback, which will include all screening, buffering, and other native vegetation, shall be maintained from the solar farm structures/equipment to any non-participating owner's adjoining property line which is a perimeter boundary line for the projected area. Setbacks will be measured from Solar Energy Equipment, including Substations, but do not include security fence or distribution poles/wires. Security fencing and distribution poles/wires may be located within the setbacks but may not be located in the right-of-way. Setbacks may be reduced with a written waiver agreement from all involved property owners per waiver agreement as defined in definitions. Setbacks from right-of-ways shall be maintained & not reduced, regardless of waiver.

A minimum fifty (50) foot setbacks shall be maintained from the solar farm structures/equipment to the road right-of-way line including all state & county roads. Setbacks may be reduced with a written waiver agreement from all involved property owners per waiver agreement as defined in definitions. Setbacks from right-of-ways shall be maintained & not reduced, regardless of waiver.

Section 153.716 requires a minimum 25’ wide buffer zone containing native plants including trees, shrubs, and pollinators along road frontage and perimeters adjacent to non-participating properties with residential dwellings. If existing vegetation is inadequate, native plants shall be planted to create the visual screen. Screening must be densely planted with blooming shrubs or trees at least four feet high at planting, forming a year-round dense screen at least six feet high. Earth berms may be incorporated as part of screening measures where appropriate. Emphasis is placed on screening around non-participating structures, both residential and commercial. Areas adjacent to non-participating property lines without structures are not required to be screened.
section: 153.716 Solar Farm Energy System (SFES) Site & Landscape Requirements

summary: Section 153.716 J. Signage states: "No signs other than appropriate warning signs, or standard manufacturer’s, operator's, or installer’s identification signage, shall be displayed." and "All Ingress/Egress roads to a SFES shall have posted an address road sign indicating the assigned address for that location." These signage requirements apply to Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES), which includes Major Solar Farm Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance as commercial facilities on parcels of 10 acres or more with the primary purpose of selling wholesale or retail generated electricity.
section: 153.716 Solar Farm Energy System (SFES) Site & Landscape Requirements

summary: Section 153.714.B.2 requires an "Approved Drainage Plan. A drainage plan for construction and operation must be approved by the Grant County Drainage Board prior to issuance of any permits." Section 153.714.B.3 requires "An Erosion Control Plan (Rule 5) must be approved by the Grant County Soil & Water Conservation District regarding IDEM Rule 5 requirements prior to issuance of any permits." These requirements apply to Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES) designed for commercial energy production, including Major Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES Major) defined as "a commercial facility, on a parcel(s) of 10 acres or more that converts sunlight to electricity... with the primary purpose of selling wholesale or retail generated electricity."

A minimum three hundred (300) foot setback shall be maintained from any non-participating dwelling to any solar farm structures/equipment, not including security fencing, if applicable. Other setback options include a minimum one hundred (100) foot setback from any participating dwelling. Setbacks are measured from Solar Energy Equipment, including Substations, but do not include security fence or distribution poles/wires. Setbacks may be reduced with a written waiver agreement from all involved property owners, except setbacks from right-of-ways which shall be maintained and not reduced.

The ordinance requires a Development Plan Application & Review for any Solar Farm Energy System (SFES) designed for commercial energy production, including Major SFES. The application must include a detailed site plan showing "the proposed Solar Development District location on the SFES showing the projected maximum extent boundaries of the site," "the location of all proposed SFES structures including substations," "property lines, including identification of adjoining properties," "location of all primary structures located in adjacent properties, within quarter (1/4) mile," and a "Topographic Map of the project site and the surrounding area which shall encompass an area at least a quarter (1/4) mile radius from the proposed project site with contours of not more than five (5) feet intervals." The ordinance also requires a "Landscape plan, prepared by a professional landscape architect, will provide an assessment form or score card to ensure that proposed landscape plan meets or exceeds accepted pollinator and habitat standards," including "Densely planted (or having equivalent natural growth) with blooming shrubs or trees at least four feet high at the time of planting, of a type that will form a year-round dense screen at least six feet high." Screening is emphasized around "Non-Participating Structures, both Residential & Commercial." The Area Plan Commission (APC) reviews the Development Plan and may request additional materials or testimony, holding a public hearing before making a recommendation to the County Commissioners. These requirements constitute explicit visual impact assessment requirements for Major SFES. Other options or conditions include minor revisions handled by the Executive Director, public hearings for major revisions, and possible variances through the Board of Zoning Appeals.
section: 153.712 Solar Farm Energy System (SFES) Development Plan Application & Review

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires a decommissioning agreement to be executed by the applicant and county executive (§ 156.047 (G)(1)). Prior to issuance of an improvement location permit, a decommissioning plan must be approved by the county executive, recorded with the county recorder, and cross-referenced to the deeds of all associated project parcels (§ 156.047 (K)(1)). The decommissioning plan is activated if the system has not generated power for 12 consecutive months at 80% capacity and must include: the useful life of the project; timeline for construction and operation; decommissioning cost estimate including salvage value; restoration and reclamation requirements such as restoration of preconstruction surface grade and soil profile, re-vegetation, and restoration of crops or forest resource land on leased property; and any other requirements determined by the county executive (§ 156.047 (K)(2)). Bonds or financial assurance may be required at the discretion of the county executive to cover decommissioning and other related costs (§ 156.047 (L)).

The setback requirements for a large-scale solar energy system project that is ground-mounted include: (3) A minimum of 150 feet from any adjoining property which is not owned by a person or an entity participating in the solar energy system project. Other setback options include: (1) A minimum setback of 100 feet as measured from any public right-of-way; (2) A minimum setback of 300 feet from any primary structure on property not owned by a participant. The 150 feet setback from adjoining property lines is the relevant fixed distance setback from property lines or parcels.

The setback requirements for a large-scale solar energy system project that is ground-mounted are as follows: (1) A minimum setback of 100 feet as measured from any public right-of-way as designated in the county's thoroughfare plan. Other setback requirements include 300 feet from any primary structure on property not owned by a participant and 150 feet from adjoining property not owned by a participant, but these do not pertain to roads.

Applicants for a large-scale solar energy system shall provide and execute a plan, subject to the approval of the Planning Director, to incorporate the elements in § 156.082 (F)(4) and the requirement that landscape buffers/screening shall be provided along all highways, roadways and along all property lines. Except for a property line with road frontage, adjoining parcel owners may opt out of the landscape buffer and screening requirement along a property line if all owners agree, there is a written legal agreement, the Board of Zoning Appeals approves the waiver as a variance, and the waiver agreement is properly recorded.

The ordinance requires review of 'Stormwater drainage, erosion, and sediment control requirements' as part of the development plan approval process for large-scale solar energy systems (§ 156.047 (H)(2)(f)(1)). It mandates an operations plan including 'Plans, if any, to remove soil and plans to restore soil' (§ 156.047 (G)(5)(d)). The decommissioning plan must include 'Restoration of the preconstruction surface grade and soil profile' and 'Restoring soil areas with re-vegetation' (§ 156.047 (K)(2)(d)). Other related requirements include setbacks, landscaping plans, decommissioning agreements, traffic management plans, and financial assurance measures, but these do not explicitly address soil, erosion, or sediment control.

The setback requirements for a large-scale solar energy system project that is ground-mounted include: 'A minimum setback of 300 feet from any primary structure on property not owned by a person or entity participating in the solar energy system project.' Other setback distances mentioned are 100 feet from any public right-of-way and 150 feet from any adjoining property not owned by a participant, but the 300 feet setback from primary structures is the most restrictive related to occupied dwellings, buildings, or structures.
section: § 156.047 SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS - LARGE SCALE (SES-OL), (D) Setbacks

summary: The ordinance adds a definition for Commercial Solar Energy Systems as those "primarily used or designed, to capture solar energy and to convert solar energy to electrical energy or thermal power and to supply electrical or thermal power to the electrical grid for off-site consumption or resale." It explicitly states that "Commercial Solar Energy Systems are not permitted in any District." The prohibition is effective "upon passage and publication at the earliest date provided by law." There are no conditions, exceptions, or expiration dates mentioned for this prohibition.

The ordinance defines a Large-Scale Solar Energy System as a commercial solar energy system with a project size greater than ten acres (§ 157.03). Additionally, the chapter applies to solar energy system installations that have a footprint over one acre in size, with a rated capacity over 200 kilowatts, and providing energy to be used off-site (§ 157.01). The minimum lot size specifically for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems is therefore greater than ten acres, with 'acres' as the unit of measurement.

The ordinance explicitly requires a Decommissioning – Restoration Agreement approved by the County Commissioners that includes: (1) an outline of the anticipated means, costs and method of payment of all costs in carrying out such Decommissioning-Restoration Plan and Agreement at the end of the SES life or the life of any part of a SES, upon becoming an abandoned use, or being declared a public nuisance; (2) a requirement that the SES owner or project operator shall give written notice of intent to abandon use of an SES facility 60 days prior to the discontinuation of electrical production to the County Commissioners and Plan Commission; (3) a requirement that the SES owner or project operator shall restore the land substantially to the same condition as prior to construction; (4) a requirement that the SES owner or project operator shall clear the site of all constructed features and modifications post-operation, including but not limited to solar panels, racks, inverters, piles, foundations, transformers, fencing, roads, utility poles, lines, and connections; (5) a requirement that the SES owner or project operator shall complete the decommissioning process within a 24-month timeframe; (6) prior to issuance of a permit to begin construction of an SES, the applicant must provide to the County a performance guarantee in the form of a (i) bond; (ii) irrevocable letter of credit and agreement, or (iii) cash to be held in escrow by the County Treasurer or a bank, in the amount of 125% of the estimated decommission and restoration cost, with estimates determined by a licensed engineer; (7) a financial guarantee for decommissioning is required to be in place no later than the commencement of construction of the SES; (8) the project developer or operator is responsible for covering all expenses related to the estimation, acquisition, and maintenance of the decommissioning financial assurance and performance guaranty; (9) security must be initially posted for a five-year term and must be subject to renewal every five years; (10) every three years a new engineer's estimate of probable cost of Decommissioning and Restoration shall be submitted to the County Commissioners for approval and the bond, cash deposit or letter of credit shall be adjusted accordingly; (11) written notices must be provided to the owner/operator for any failure to decommission with a reasonable cure period not to exceed 60 days before further remedies are pursued. These requirements apply to all SES requiring Development Plan approval in the Renewable Energy District, which includes utility-scale solar energy systems. No other options or alternative decommissioning provisions are provided in the text.

Section 2.3(J), subsection 22 (Fencing) states: 'Any substation shall be completely enclosed with perimeter fencing and locked gates that comply with state and federal regulations. A SES facility shall be surrounded by perimeter fencing with the appropriate accommodations for the protection of wildlife. The perimeter fence style shall be  "game style,"  with no barbed wire, unless otherwise required by the National Electrical Safety Code, or applicable fencing state or federal regulations. The minimum height requirement for perimeter fencing shall be eight (8) feet. The Plan Commission has the right to negotiate the minimum height and style during the review of a development plan.' These fencing requirements apply to Solar Energy Systems (SES) as defined in the ordinance, which includes utility-scale systems intended for electricity generation and sale. No other fencing options or conditions are provided beyond the possibility of Plan Commission negotiation and exceptions if required by applicable codes or regulations.

Section 20. Glare: a SES facility at no time shall create glare on any non-participating property line or right-of-way; and a SES facility at no time shall create glare that shall interfere with vehicular traffic, including air traffic. A professional study shall be presented to the Approving Agency as part of the Development Plan Application to demonstrate that the glare requirements are met.

Section 2.3(J), subsection 17 'Height Restrictions' states: 'No part of a solar panel or rack shall be over twelve (12) feet tall as measured from the natural grade level directly below the panel to the top of each panel at its maximum tilt in the vertical position.' Additionally, 'No part of a solar panel, rack, inverter or other equipment associated with an SES system shall be less than three (3) feet above the BFE (Base Flood Elevation) if within a 100-year-old flood plain.' The maximum height restriction applicable to utility-scale solar energy systems is 12 feet, measured from natural grade to the top of the panel at maximum tilt.

The Renewable Energy (RE) District is described as "Primarily For renewable energy facilities." The text states that "*Solar Energy Systems" are among "The following uses are permitted in a RE District." It also notes that "Solar Energy Systems or SES are a Permitted use only within the zoning districts shown as 'Permitted' in the relevant Permitted Use Tables or as otherwise specifically provided herein." Development Plan approval is required but this is a standard procedural step, not a special or conditional use approval. No other districts or overlay districts are explicitly named in the text as permitting utility-scale solar energy systems as a primary use.

summary: SES equipment must adhere to the following setback(s): iv) One Thousand (1,000) feet from a nonparticipating property line. Other setback options include: i) 1,000 feet from the nearest edge of the right-of-way of a federal, state, or county highway; ii) 1,000 feet from the nearest edge of the right-of-way from a collector road; iii) 1,000 feet from the nearest edge of the right-of-way from a local road; v) 1,000 feet from the nearest wellhead. Battery Energy Storage Systems must adhere to 1,000 feet from all property lines.

SES equipment must adhere to the following setback(s): One Thousand (1,000) feet from the nearest edge of the right-of-way of a federal, state, or county highway; One Thousand (1,000) feet from the nearest edge of the right-of-way from a collector road; One Thousand (1,000) feet from the nearest edge of the right-of-way from a local road.

Section 2.3(J), subsection 29 "Visual Buffer" explicitly requires that "A SES facility shall be separated by a landscape buffer from non-participating, pre-existing residences." The buffer "shall be installed on the SES facility, not on a non-participating property." The Development Plan must determine "the required height and species of plantings used for a landscape buffer," and "The use of native and pollinator-friendly plant species is required." A "Landscape Plan and Vegetation Management Plan shall be submitted as part of the Development Plan Application." Ground cover must be "planted, established, and maintained for the life of the solar project in perennial vegetated ground cover" with a diverse seed mix of naturalized and non-invasive species. The SES owner/operator must prepare a control plan for noxious species and maintain the buffer, including vegetation and obnoxious weeds. The SES owner/operator "shall substantially screen panels and racks from surrounding properties" and submit a landscaping plan showing plant numbers, types, and sizes for Plan Commission approval. All buffers requiring landscaping/screening "shall have 100% opacity year-round." These requirements apply to utility-scale SES in the Renewable Energy District requiring Development Plan approval. Other related requirements include fencing, setbacks, and maintenance plans, but the vegetative buffer and screening requirements are specifically detailed in subsection 29.
section: 2.3(J) Solar Energy System (SES) Standards, subsection 29 Visual Buffer

summary: Section 2.3(J), subsection 24 "Emergency Contact Signage" requires "a standard metal road sign [to] include the owner’s name, facility’s name, emergency contact phone number and the physical site address and shall be posted at the entrance to the facility in addition to all ingress/egress roads to the SES facility in a conspicuous location." The sign "shall be posted just outside of the public road right-of-way." Warning signs must comply with applicable laws.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "all SESs shall meet environmental performance requirements ... and follow tree preservation, habitat protection, and erosion control and stormwater management standards." An "erosion control plan shall be developed by an SES applicant, developed in accordance with the Natural Resources Conservation Services (NRCS), and any storm water quality management plan adopted by the County." Additionally, "an applicant for an SES shall conduct and present a soil identification study ... Use of prime farmlands for solar array placement and SESs is not permitted." Ground cover must be "planted, established, and maintained for the life of the solar project in perennial vegetated ground cover" with limitations on clearing natural vegetation and tree removal. SESs must submit an "operations and maintenance plan ... including measures for maintaining ... storm water controls." The ordinance also requires repair of damages to drainage infrastructure and submission of a drainage maintenance plan. For Development Plan approval, an "Erosion Control Plan" is explicitly required as supporting information. These requirements apply to Solar Energy Systems in the Renewable Energy District requiring Development Plan approval, indicating applicability to utility-scale solar energy systems.
section: Section 2.3 J. Solar Energy System (SES) Standards

summary: The Renewable Energy (RE) District is intended to regulate renewable energy facilities and includes Solar Energy Systems as a permitted use with specific development standards. All Solar Energy Systems (SES) require Development Plan approval before construction or operation. The text states: 'All Solar Energy Systems (SES’s) will require Development Plan approval' and 'No applicant shall construct, operate, locate, or enlarge a Solar Energy System (SES) or Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) within Huntington County without first obtaining Development Plan approval.' This indicates that utility-scale solar energy systems are permitted in the RE District subject to meeting conditions such as completing a permitting process. No other districts or overlay districts are mentioned as permitting utility-scale solar energy systems as a special use or similar.
section: Section 2.1 Zoning Districts and Overlay Districts; Section 2.3 J. Solar Energy System (SES) Standards

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires a 'Visual Buffer' for Solar Energy Systems (SES) facilities, stating: 'A SES facility shall be separated by a landscape buffer from non-participating, pre-existing residences.' The 'Development Plan will determine the required height and species of plantings used for a landscape buffer,' and 'Landscape Plan and Vegetation Management Plan shall be submitted as part of the Development Plan Application.' It further requires that 'All Buffers requiring landscaping/screening shall have 100% opacity year-round' and that the SES owner/operator 'shall substantially screen panels and racks from surrounding properties' with a landscaping plan submitted for approval. Additionally, 'Visual Buffer including landscaping plan (detailed plans)' is listed among the required supporting information before the Plan Commission may consider approval of a Development Plan. The Plan Commission must determine that the SES development 'is compatible with surrounding land uses' and 'will not interfere with the use and value of surrounding real estate' as part of the approval criteria. These provisions apply to SES as permitted uses in the Renewable Energy District and require Development Plan approval, indicating they apply to utility-scale solar energy systems intended for commercial electricity generation and sale. No other options or conditions for visual impact assessment are provided beyond these landscaping and buffer requirements.

Indiana law requires wind and commercial solar project owners to submit decommissioning and site restoration plans and post escalating financial security, reaching full coverage of estimated decommissioning costs by the twentieth year of operation. For solar facilities, owners must also provide advance notice of decommissioning, complete removal within one year, and restore the site to a condition reasonably similar to its preconstruction state.
Glare must be minimized on adjacent properties and roadways as well as not interfere with vehicular traffic, including air traffic

A decommissioning agreement must be executed by the applicant which stipulates that decommissioning of the entire facility will begin upon the occurrence of twelve (12) consecutive months of no power generation at the facility. Applicants must file a notice of intent to decommission detailing the means and timeline for completion. The agreement must include a description of implementing the decommissioning, a description of the work required, a cost estimate for decommissioning, a schedule for contributions to a decommissioning fund, and a demonstration of financial assurance. Salvage value shall be considered in determining decommissioning cost. The operator must secure and provide a performance bond or escrow deposit in an amount determined by a third-party engineering firm to ensure proper decommissioning and removal. Financial assurance must be in place prior to the issuance of an improvement location permit and re-evaluated every five (5) years. In the event of a force majeure causing 12 months of nonoperation, the applicant must demonstrate substantial operational status within 24 months or initiate decommissioning 18 months after the event. This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems and Battery Energy Storage Systems (CSES/BESS) as defined and regulated in the ordinance.

Fences are required around the perimeter of a CSES/BESS project area and are subject to setback requirements. Chain link fences shall have a minimum height limit of eight (8) feet. Razor wire and/or electric fences shall be prohibited. Fence weave is strongly recommended in chain link fencing where residences are in close proximity. This fence weave will be maintained by the solar owner. Fences shall not obstruct wildlife corridors. All ground-mounted electrical and control equipment for CSES shall be fenced and labeled or secured to prevent unauthorized access. The solar array and/or modules shall be designed and installed to prevent access by the public, and access to same shall be through a locked gate.

The height of any CSES/BESS ground mounted solar equipment is limited to twenty (20) feet. Height of solar panels shall be calculated when panels are in full tilt and measured from the surrounding natural grade. If a substation is required to connect the project to the electrical grid, the substation’s design, including height, will be in accordance with applicable electrical codes.

Battery energy storage systems shall be limited to a maximum of ten (10) acres in total area, as determined by calculating the area within the system’s perimeter security fencing. This standard shall not apply to the campus of the R M Schahfer Generating Station. Commercial solar energy systems shall have a minimum total area of ten (10) acres. Additionally, an earlier section requires a minimum two (2) acre lot for commercial solar energy systems, and limits the number of commercial solar energy systems per lot based on lot size (one system on lots 15 acres or less, up to two systems on lots more than 15 acres), but these do not specify maximum lot size. The maximum lot size restriction explicitly applies to BESS at 10 acres.

A commercial solar energy system shall have a maximum rated power level of five hundred kilowatts (500kW) (0.5 MW). Additionally, a lot with fifteen (15) acres or less shall be restricted to one (1) commercial solar energy system, and a lot with more than fifteen (15) acres may have up to two (2) commercial solar energy systems. Battery energy storage systems shall be limited to a maximum of ten (10) acres in total area. The maximum rated power limit is the most restrictive numerical value for system size. The units are megawatts (MW) as 500 kW equals 0.5 MW.

Commercial solar energy systems shall have a minimum total area of ten (10) acres. Battery energy storage systems shall be limited to a maximum of ten (10) acres in total area, as determined by calculating the area within the system’s perimeter security fencing. This standard shall not apply to the campus of the R M Schahfer Generating Station. An earlier section states a minimum two (2) acre lot for commercial solar energy systems, but the more detailed CSES/BESS standard of 10 acres is more restrictive and applicable here.

Noise from an operational CSES shall not exceed fifty (50) dBA, as measured at the property line of a CSES or BSES nonparticipating adjoining parcel on an hourly average basis (Leq) (one (1) hour). These limits may be waivable by any adjoining property owners consistent with the provisions of setback waivers. The unit 'dBA' refers to A-weighted decibels, a standard noise measurement unit.

Any BESS equipment, including security fencing, excluding poles, roads, and wires necessary to connect to facilities of the electric utility, must be set back a minimum distance of one thousand three hundred twenty feet (1,320) from the property line in accordance with the following standards: a. Shall be set back a minimum of one thousand (1,000) feet from any adjoining property line; and b. Shall be subject to an enhanced minimum setback distance of one thousand three hundred twenty (1,320) feet from the property line of any BESS nonparticipating adjoining parcel (Residential, Educational, and Religious Use). Enhanced minimum setbacks from the property line of any CSES nonparticipating adjoining parcel may be waived in writing by the owner of the adjoining nonparticipating property; however, the minimum one thousand (1,000) foot setback cannot be waived. For CSES equipment, enhanced minimum setbacks from each property line of a CSES nonparticipating adjoining parcel (residential, educational, and religious use) range from 300 feet (one side) up to 800 feet (all sides), with a minimum 300 feet setback that cannot be waived.

The standards for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) apply to the following zoning districts: A1, A2, A3, A4, I1, I2, HI, CO. Approvals required for a CSES/BESS are as follows: in all these districts, CSES are permitted with 'SE' (Special Exception), indicating that approval through a special use or similar permitting process is required. No other options or conditions are listed for these districts.

A commercial solar energy system shall be a minimum of fifty (50) feet from any above-ground utility line. Other setbacks from property lines for CSES equipment including wires necessary to connect to electric utility facilities range from 300 feet minimum to up to 800 feet depending on adjacency to nonparticipating parcels, but the only explicit fixed distance stated directly from overhead utility lines is 50 feet.
section: 20.50.950 CS-01 Commercial solar energy systems, G. Location Restrictions, 3. Setback from Utilities

summary: Section 219.10 Decommissioning states: 'Commercial Solar Farms shall have a decommissioning plan to remove all equipment and restore the site to its original condition when the system is no longer in use.' Section 219.13 SFES DECOMMISSIONING PLAN AGREEMENT requires that 'prior to receiving construction approval for the SFES project, the applicant, owner and/or operator must provide proof of a signed Decommissioning Plan Agreement between the County and the applicant, owner and/or operator.' The Decommissioning Plan shall include 'removal of all physical material pertaining to the project improvements to a depth of 48" beneath the soil surface, and restoration of the area occupied by the project improvements to the same or better condition that existed immediately before construction of such improvements.' It also requires financial assurance 'in an amount at least equal to said demolition and removal contractor cost estimate, through the use of a bond, letter of credit or other security acceptable to the County.' Failure to comply constitutes a default under the Ordinance with enforcement procedures outlined. These requirements apply explicitly to Commercial Solar Farms or Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES) designed for commercial energy production, not to smaller or personal solar energy systems.
section: 219.10 Decommissioning and 219.13 SFES DECOMMISSIONING PLAN AGREEMENT

summary: Section 219.10 SFES FENCING & LANDSCAPING PLAN requires that "All SFES systems equipment, panels and structures shall be fully enclosed and secured by a fence with a minimum height of 6 feet but no greater than 8 feet and must setback a minimum of 30 feet from any property line." Additionally, the SFES shall have a 25 feet wide buffer with a compact evergreen hedge or other green foliage along road frontage and adjacent single family dwellings. This fencing requirement applies specifically to Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES), defined as commercial facilities on parcels of five acres or more with the primary purpose of selling wholesale or retail generated electricity.

Section 219.8(H) states: 'The SFES shall be designed and located in order to prevent glare toward any inhabited buildings or adjacent properties as well as adjacent highways or right-of-ways.' Additionally, Section 219.11(B) requires that 'If, after construction of the SFES, the owner and/or operator receives a written complaint related to ... glare, the SFES owner and/or operator shall take reasonable steps to respond to minimize the complaint.' These provisions explicitly impose glare restrictions on Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES).

Section 219.8.G states: 'Height: Shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in maximum tilt of the solar panel(s).' This applies specifically to Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES), which are commercial facilities designed for wholesale or retail electricity generation. No other maximum height limits for SFES are provided. The units are feet as indicated in the text.

The ordinance defines a Solar Farm Energy System (SFES) as "a commercial facility, on a parcel(s) of five acres or more that converts sunlight to electricity..." and states that a "Solar Farm Energy System Project Area... consists of five acres of land or more." This establishes a minimum lot size of five acres for SFES projects. The units are explicitly given as acres. No other minimum lot size values for SFES are provided.

Noise levels for Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES) shall not exceed 50 decibels when measured from any primary structure. This standard shall supersede any noise standard as set forth in any other Article in the Zoning Ordinance. (Section 219.8, subsection I) The unit for noise level is assumed to be dBA, the standard unit for noise measurement. No other numerical noise limits for SFES are provided in the text.

The minimum setback distance for Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES) from non-participating property lines is 25 feet, measured from the edge of the equipment to the property line. This setback requirement may be waived in writing by participating landowners. Other setback distances include 150 feet from residential dwellings for non-participating landowners (waivable), 150 feet from churches, schools, businesses or public buildings (from property line), 25 feet from areas zoned Commercial, Rural Residential, and commercial recreational areas, 50 feet from road rights-of-way, and 50 feet for access driveways adjacent to non-participating landowner property lines. Fencing must also be set back a minimum of 30 feet from any property line. These requirements are found in Section 219.7 SFES SETBACKS and Section 219.10 SFES FENCING & LANDSCAPING PLAN.

The minimum setback distance for Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES) from nature preserves, parks, recreational uses including property owned by IDNR, Friends of the Limberlost, and public conservation lands is 25 feet from the property line, measured from the edge of the SFES to the nearest point of the land in question. Other SFES setbacks include 25 feet from property lines for non-participating landowners, 150 feet from residential dwellings for non-participating landowners, 150 feet from churches, schools, businesses or public buildings, 25 feet from commercial and recreational zoned areas, 50 feet from road right-of-way, and 50 feet for access driveways to non-participating landowner property lines.

The minimum setback distance for Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES) from a road right-of-way is 50 feet, measured from the edge of the equipment to the edge of the right-of-way. No part of a SFES shall be constructed in any setback, dedicated easement, or County road right-of-way without prior written authorization from the County. Other setback distances for SFES include 25 feet from property lines for non-participating landowners, 150 feet from residential dwellings for non-participating landowners, 150 feet from churches, schools, businesses or public buildings, 25 feet from areas zoned Commercial or Rural Residential, and 25 feet from nature preserves, parks, recreational use areas, and public conservation lands.

Section 219.10 SFES FENCING & LANDSCAPING PLAN requires that the SFES shall have a 25 feet wide buffer of which part shall be consisting of a compact evergreen hedge or other type of green foliage which shall be along the road frontage and perimeter of adjacent single family dwelling. Section 219.8.H states: "The SFES shall be designed and located in order to prevent glare toward any inhabited buildings or adjacent properties as well as adjacent highways or right-of-ways." Section 219.8.F requires: "If lighting is provided at the project, lighting shall be shielded and downcast such that the light does not spill on to the adjacent parcel and/or residence and/or primary structure." These requirements apply explicitly to Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES), defined as commercial facilities on parcels of five acres or more with the primary purpose of selling wholesale or retail generated electricity.

All SFESs shall provide the following at all locked entrances: 1. A visible  "High Voltage"  warning sign 2. Names and phone numbers for the electric utility provider 3. Names and phone numbers for the site operator 4. The facilities 911 address, GPS coordinates, and 5. A knox box with keys as needed. (Section 219.8.E Safety & Warnings)

Section 219.6.B.3 requires that "An Erosion Control Plan (Rule 5) must be approved by the Jay County Soil & Water Conservation District regarding IDEM Rule 5 requirements prior to issuance of any permits." Additionally, Section 219.6.B.2 requires "Approved Drainage Plan. A drainage plan for construction and operation must be approved by the Jay County Drainage Board prior to issuance of any permits." These requirements apply to Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES) as defined as "a commercial facility, on a parcel(s) of five acres or more that converts sunlight to electricity... with the primary purpose of selling wholesale or retail generated electricity."

summary: The minimum setback distance for Solar Farm Energy Systems (SFES) from residential dwellings (non-participating landowners) is 150 feet, measured from the edge of the equipment to the structure. The setback requirement may be waived in writing by participating landowners. Other setback distances include 25 feet from property lines for non-participating landowners, 150 feet from churches, schools, business or public buildings (measured from equipment to structure), 25 feet from commercial or rural residential zoned areas, 50 feet from road right-of-way, and 25 feet from nature preserves or parks. However, the 150 feet setback from non-participating residential dwellings is the most restrictive setback directly pertaining to occupied dwellings.

A maximum of four thousand (4,000) acres of Commercial SES projects can be approved as a Commercial SES use within all areas of Jefferson County, which shall include the planning jurisdiction of Jefferson County, Madison, and Hanover. Acreage within the fenced areas and tillable acreage and pasture land acreage outside the fenced areas which are taken out of production shall be counted as Commercial SES project cap acreage.

summary: Prior to receiving approval for a Commercial SECS under this Ordinance, the Board of Zoning Appeals and the applicant, County Commissioners, and owner and/or operator shall formulate a decommissioning plan approved and signed by the County Commissioners and the applicant, outlining the anticipated means and cost of removing the Commercial SECS at the end of its serviceable life or upon becoming a discontinued or abandoned use, to ensure that the Commercial SECS is properly decommissioned. Applicant for a Commercial SECS shall provide a bond, or other proof of financial responsibility that is of an amount determined by the County Commissioners to be sufficient to satisfy the decommissioning agreement requirements. Other proof of financial responsibility may be: (a) Cash advance to county to be released upon completion of decommissioning plan; or, (b) An arrangement whereby the county would have access to the funds in an escrow account or other type of account held by a bank, until the completion of the decommissioning plan. The bond, or other proof of financial responsibility, shall be released upon receipt of a certificate of inspection by the Director of the Planning and Zoning Department indicating that the Commercial SECS has been fully decommissioned in accordance with the decommissioning plan, with no unresolved issues related to the required decommissioning. A decommissioning plan shall include, at a minimum, language addressing: (i) Written assurance that the facilities will be properly decommissioned upon the end of the project life or in the event that the facility is abandoned; (ii) Contractor cost estimate for demolition and removal of the Commercial SECS facility including any offsetting effects of salvage value; (iii) Cost estimate adjustments derived from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Indexes (CPI) to protect against inflation. Discontinuation: All Commercial SECS shall be considered a discontinued use after six (6) consecutive months without energy production, unless a plan is developed and submitted to the Director outlining the steps and schedule for returning the Commercial SECS to service within six (6) consecutive months. Commercial SECS shall be subject to decommissioning upon ceasing energy production for more than twelve (12) consecutive months. Abandonment by the owner or operator: The applicant shall provide an affidavit to the Director representing that all easements for solar collection shall contain terms that provide financial assurance, including access to the salvage value of the equipment, for the property owners to ensure that facilities are properly decommissioned within one (1) year of expiration or earlier termination of the project. Removal: An SECS owner’s obligations shall include, at the SECS owner’s expense, removal of all physical material pertaining to the project improvements to no less than a depth of six (6) feet below ground level within three hundred sixty-five (365) days of the discontinuation or abandonment of the SECS, and restoration of the project area to as near as practicable the condition of the site immediately before construction of such SECS improvements, unless otherwise agreed to by the property owner and Johnson County at the time of the discontinuation or abandonment of the SECS. Written Notices: Prior to implementation of the existing procedures for the resolution of a decommissioning default(s), the Director shall first provide written notice to the owner and/or operator, setting forth the alleged default(s). Such written notice shall provide the owner and/or operator a reasonable time period not to exceed sixty (60) days, for good faith negotiations to resolve the alleged default(s). Costs Incurred by the County: If the County removes a SECS and appurtenant facilities, it may sell the salvage to defray the costs of removal. The permittee or grantor shall grant a license to Johnson County to enter the property to remove the SECS pursuant to the terms of an approved decommissioning plan.

For Commercial SECS, "Perimeter fencing for the site shall not include barbed wire or woven wire designs and shall preferably use wildlife-friendly fencing standards." Additionally, "The following notices shall be clearly visible and facing the public right-of-way on all facility perimeter fencing near the main entrance of the facility (which may be combined on one sign) if fenced: 'No Trespassing' signs, 'Danger' warning signs appropriate for electrical systems, and signage posting emergency telephone number(s)."

For Commercial SECS, "Ground or pole-mounted solar energy systems shall not exceed 25 feet in height as measured from the natural grade to the top of the panel or arrays when oriented at maximum tilt." Additionally, "Building and roof-mounted solar energy conversion system shall be measured together when determining the building or structure height and shall not cause the building or structure to exceed the maximum allowed height in the zoning district." The 25 feet limit applies specifically to ground or pole-mounted systems, while building/roof-mounted systems must comply with zoning district height limits.

The noise level of all SECS shall be no greater than fifty (50) decibels measured from the nearest property line. This level may only be exceeded during short-term events such as utility outages and/or severe windstorms. All other noise and vibration levels shall follow all county, state, and federal regulations. The unit for noise level is assumed to be dBA as standard for noise measurements.
