Setback distance for Commercial SECS shall be measured from the edge of the solar energy conversion system array, excluding security fencing, screening, or berm. All ground-mounted solar panels or arrays must be at least 150 (one-hundred fifty) feet from any property line of a non-participating landowner’s property line. Property line setbacks between separate parcels both of which are participating in the project may be waived upon agreement of the landowner(s). Other setback distances include: 200 feet from the property line if adjoined by property zoned residential or agricultural with a single family dwelling within 500 feet; 100 feet from the edge of any public right of way; no required setback from internal property lines within a multi-parcel project. The 150 feet setback from non-participating property lines is the most restrictive fixed distance directly pertaining to such setbacks.

All ground-mounted solar panels or arrays must be at least one hundred (100) feet from the edge of any public right of way. Setback distance for Commercial SECS shall be measured from the edge of the solar energy conversion system array, excluding security fencing, screening, or berm. Other setback distances include 150 feet from any property line of a non-participating landowner, 200 feet from property lines adjoining residential or certain agricultural properties, and 150 feet from existing participating dwelling units, but these do not pertain to roads.

Any Commercial SECS shall be required to meet the landscape standards as listed in Section 6-101-8(C)(2)(a). All Commercial SECS installation shall require a minimum Buffer Yard where the subject parcel abuts a parcel with a permitted residential use. Ground around and under solar panels and in project site buffer areas shall be planted, established, and maintained for the life of the solar project in perennial vegetated ground cover. To the maximum extent feasible and economical, perennial vegetation ground cover shall be based on a diverse seed mix of native species consistent with guidance specific to the local area based on guidance provided by the National Resources Conservation Service, Soil and Water Conservation District, or Conservation District. The site shall be planted and maintained to be free of all invasive species, as listed by the Indiana Invasive Species Council. No insecticide use is permitted on the site, except for limited exceptions. Perimeter fencing for the site shall not include barbed wire or woven wire designs and shall preferably use wildlife-friendly fencing standards. These requirements apply to Commercial SECS, defined as systems with a nameplate capacity of at least ten (10) megawatts and intended for selling electricity for use offsite.

Other requirements for Commercial SECS include setbacks, height limits, landscape buffers, lighting, ground covering plans, fencing, and decommissioning plans, but these do not pertain to signage. Commercial SECS are only permitted in Agricultural, Rural Residential, and Industrial Zones as special exceptions. "With the approval of a special exception, a review of an improvement location permit will be conducted administratively for Commercial SECS to ensure compliance to ordinances." The Director may require site plan approval from the Johnson County Technical Review Committee prior to permit issuance. Accessory SECS are permitted in all zoning districts without special exception. Off-grid solar energy conversion systems are exempt from these standards.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Commercial Solar Energy System Farms (CSES). It states: "Any (CSES) that is not operated for a continuous period of 6 months shall be considered abandoned." The owner must remove the system within 150 days of notice and "restore the site to its condition prior to location of the (CSES) (excluding replanting of original vegetation and trees), subject to reasonable wear and tear and shall stabilize soils through use of ground cover. All concrete and rebar must be removed from the soil." A decommissioning plan approved by the Kosciusko County Technical Committee is required, including: "The Physical removal of all solar energy systems, structures and equipment from the site; Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations; Stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion." The plan must also include a timeline not exceeding 150 days after discontinued operations, written assurance of proper decommissioning, cost estimates updated every five years, and financial assurance secured by a surety bond or similar instrument. Failure to remove an abandoned CSES within 150 days allows the County to pursue violations and remove the system using the surety funds. These requirements apply specifically to Commercial Solar Energy System Farms as defined: "A Solar Energy System facility and all associated components, whose primary purpose is to collect, store, convert, and distribute solar energy to utility companies."

summary: Section 3.30.5.4.W states: 'Screening & Buffering - Proper screening and buffering shall be installed to reduce the visual impact on adjacent properties as deemed necessary by the Kosciusko County Board of Zoning Appeals.' This is an explicit vegetative buffer and/or other screening requirement for Commercial Solar Energy System Farms (CSES).

A sign no more than 4 square feet in area displaying an address and telephone number for emergency calls and informational inquiries shall be posted at the entrance of the (CSES) access road. No (CSES) or site shall include an advertising sign.

The ordinance explicitly requires that Commercial Solar Energy System Farms (CSES) comply with soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements. Specifically, 'Solar Energy Systems shall meet the requirements of the Kosciusko County Stormwater & Erosion Control Ordinance' (3.30.4). For CSES, 'A detailed drainage plan compliant with the requirements of the Kosciusko County Stormwater Control Ordinance shall be submitted and approved of' and 'an erosion control plan showing how any disturbance will be controlled on site as required under the Kosciusko County Stormwater and Erosion Control Ordinance shall be submitted' (3.30.5.4.N). Additionally, 'All damages to waterways, drainage ditches, field tiles, or any other infrastructures caused by the construction or maintenance of the CSES, must be completely repaired to near original condition' (3.30.5.4.N.4). Upon decommissioning or abandonment, the owner must 'restore the site to its condition prior to location of the (CSES)... and shall stabilize soils through use of ground cover' (3.30.5.4.1.J.4) and 'Stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion' is required (3.30.8). Application requirements for CSES include submission of a drainage plan and an erosion control plan compliant with the Kosciusko County Stormwater and Erosion Control Ordinance and all other local, state, and federal regulations (3.30.5.4.B.1.A.11 and 3.30.5.4.B.2.A.11).

Commercial Solar Energy System (CSES) also known as Solar Farms "shall be permitted in those districts at listed on Table A of the Kosciusko County Zoning Ordinance or as approved by the Board of Zoning Appeals." All CSES "shall be subject to special exception approval and all requirements for special exception uses in Article 5, section 5.4." Large SES "shall be allowed in those districts either as a permitted use or exception use as listed on Table A of the ordinance." Specifically, in the Heavy Industrial  "I-3"  district, "Commercial Solar Energy System Farms" are listed under Exceptional Uses, indicating special use approval is required. Other districts such as Agricultural and Light Industrial  "I-2"  list Large Solar Energy Systems as permitted uses but do not explicitly mention CSES as special uses. Additional requirements include review and approval by the Kosciusko County Technical Review Committee, Improvement Location Permits, and possibly drainage review compliance.

Section 3.30.5.4.1.G requires that each Commercial Solar Energy System Farm (CSES) "shall, to the extent possible, use materials, and colors that will blend them into the natural setting and surrounding buildings." Section 3.30.5.4.1.W mandates that "Proper screening and buffering shall be installed to reduce the visual impact on adjacent properties as deemed necessary by the Kosciusko County Board of Zoning Appeals." The application requirements for special exception approval (3.30.5.4.2.A and B) require submission of detailed site plans and descriptions including "the proposed location of the Solar Energy System," "Primary Structures within one mile of any CSES," and other site features, which support assessment of visual impacts. Other relevant requirements include setbacks, lighting, and aesthetics provisions, but the explicit visual impact assessment requirements are primarily the use of blending materials/colors and screening/buffering as determined by the Board of Zoning Appeals.

The ordinance requires a decommissioning plan as part of the Site Development Plan, including "the anticipated life of the Facility; the anticipated Manner in which the project will be decommissioned; the anticipated site restoration actions; and the estimated decommissioning costs in current dollars." The plan must include a mechanism for posting a bond equal to "125% of the decommissioning costs included in the Site Development Plan," updated every five years. Restoration activities must include "restoration of the pre-construction surface grade and soil profile," "re-vegetation of restored soil areas," and removal of "all solar panels, structures, foundations, roads, gravel areas, cables, and all product, materials, or other items associated with the Facility project." A Facility is considered abandoned if it has not generated electricity for six months unless a rehabilitation plan is approved. Upon abandonment or closure, the Owner must submit a letter of intent for decommissioning at least sixty days prior, and decommissioning must be completed within one year, with a possible six-month extension. The County may intervene to remove the Facility and recover costs from the bond if the Owner fails to act. The bond shall be returned upon satisfactory decommissioning, but the County may recover costs from it. These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Facilities, which are utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance.

Section (J)(6)(h) requires that "A security fence must be installed along all exterior sides of the Facility and be equipped with a minimum of one gate and locking mechanism on the primary access side." The fence must be "a minimum of six (6) feet tall" and "Security fences, gates, and warning signs must be maintained in good condition until the utility scale solar installation is dismantled and removed from the site." This fencing requirement applies to Commercial Solar Facilities, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. No other fencing options or conditions are provided in the ordinance.

Section (J)(6)(d) requires that "All solar panels must be constructed to minimize glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and must not interfere with traffic, including air traffic, or create a safety hazard." The Plan Commission may require anti-reflective coatings in appropriate cases. This applies to Commercial Solar Facilities, which are defined as utility-scale solar energy systems subject to this ordinance.
No Facility shall be constructed or operated unless within a zone designated as A-1. Concentrating solar power facilities are prohibited.

Setbacks for all structures (including solar arrays) must adhere to the minimum principal setback standards for the A-1 zoning district. Additionally, solar panels shall be installed at least one hundred (100) feet from any non-participating property line.

Section (J)(6)(b) requires the applicant to submit a landscaping plan outlining proposed screening for the project, including existing vegetation, with emphasis on screening adjacent residences. Section (J)(7)(b) mandates that ground around and under solar arrays and in project site buffer areas shall be planted and maintained in perennial vegetated ground cover, meeting standards such as preventing erosion, managing runoff, building soil, and controlling invasive species and noxious weeds. These provisions apply to Commercial Solar Facilities and constitute explicit vegetative buffer and screening requirements.

Section (J)(6)(f) requires that "A sign shall be posted on each entry fence gate of the Facility that includes owner name, facility name, emergency contact phone number, physical street address, company spokesperson, or point of contact phone number." It also mandates that "All hazardous materials, public hazards, and potential hazards must be marked with signage." Section (J)(6)(g) further requires that "The Facility owner and/or operator shall maintain a phone number and identify a person responsible for the public to contact with inquiries and complaints throughout the life of the project and provide this number and name on all entry signs of the Facility." These signage requirements apply to Commercial Solar Facilities, which are utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance. Other related provisions include fencing and security requirements, but these do not pertain directly to signage.

Section (J)(7)(a) requires the Owner to conduct all roadwork and other site development work in compliance with a NPDES Permit as may be required by the Indiana Department of Natural Resources and comply with requirements as detailed by local jurisdictional authorities during the plan submittal. The Plan Commission may refer the Site Development Plan to the LaGrange County Soil & Water Conservation District for review and potentially further development of a sediment control plan. Section (J)(7)(b) mandates that ground around and under solar arrays and in project site buffer areas shall be planted and maintained in perennial vegetated ground cover, with standards including: (i) Topsoil shall not be removed during development, unless part of a remediation effort; (ii) Perennial vegetation shall be planted and maintained in a density sufficient to prevent erosion, manage runoff, and build soil; invasive species and noxious weeds must be controlled; (iii) Maintenance practices shall be consistent with recommendations made by qualified natural resource professionals. These provisions explicitly address soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for commercial solar facilities, which are utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance.

summary: A Decommissioning Plan must be submitted as part of the Special Use application for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. The plan must specify that after the system can no longer be used, it shall be removed by the applicant or any subsequent owner. It must demonstrate how removal of all infrastructure and remediation of soil and vegetation will return the parcel to its original state prior to construction, include an expected timeline, and a cost estimate accounting for inflation. Removal must be completed in accordance with the plan. The plan may be updated until final construction permitting and must be prepared, signed, and stamped by a Professional Engineer. If the system is not decommissioned after being considered abandoned (no electrical energy generation for 1 year), the municipality may remove the system, restore the property, and impose a lien to cover costs. Compliance with the Decommissioning Plan is a condition of the special use permit issuance. Other requirements for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems include a minimum of 5 acres, adherence to buffer yard standards, height restrictions, fencing, signage, and utility approval for grid-tied systems.

All Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems shall be enclosed by fencing on all sides (including the front yard). Fencing shall not exceed 8 feet in height without a variance. Warning signs with the owner’s contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing. Fencing must adhere to Section 6.25 of this ordinance for standards not specified in this section. Other requirements for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems include a Special Use permit, adherence to Buffer Yard Standards in Section 6.7, maximum height restrictions of the zoning district, and signage on the fencing displaying the facility name, address, and emergency contact information. Reasonable accessibility for emergency services vehicles is also required.

Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems "shall adhere to the Buffer Yard Standards in Section 6.7 of this ordinance." Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted with a Special Use. Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted with a Special Use. IC 8-1-42-18 requires a project owner to submit a decommissioning and site restoration plan and post a surety bond or equivalent security "in an amount equal to the estimated cost of decommissioning the CSE system" before installing or locating a CSE system. The bond must be posted in increments: 25% at full commercial operation start, 50% by the fifth anniversary, and 100% by the tenth anniversary, with periodic reevaluation and adjustment. The project owner must provide written notice of intent to decommission at least 60 days before discontinuation of commercial operation. After discontinuation, "all structures, foundations, roads, gravel areas, and cables associated with the project shall be removed to a depth of at least thirty-six (36) inches below grade" and "the ground shall be restored to a condition reasonably similar to its condition before the start of construction activities." If the project owner fails to remove assets within one year, the permit authority may remove them and recover costs. Assets may remain if conforming with local regulations and with landowner consent. IC 8-1-42-19 and IC 8-1-42-20 address presumed abandonment and removal obligations if the system fails to generate electricity for 18 months or after a force majeure event, with similar removal and cost recovery provisions.

A decommissioning plan, prepared by a professional engineer, shall indicate the method and payment of the anticipated cost of removing the commercial solar energy system at the end of their serviceable life or upon their becoming a discontinued or abandoned use to ensure that the commercial solar energy systems are properly decommissioned within one (1) year of discontinuance/abandonment. The decommissioning plan shall include, at a minimum, the following: (a) Assurance: The cost of removal and site restoration is the full responsibility of the applicant and/or owner/operator. Written assurance that the solar energy system will be properly decommissioned upon the expiration of its serviceable life or in the event of their discontinuance or abandonment. A cost estimate, prepared by a professional engineer or professional with suitable experience in the decommissioning of wind power devices, shall be accepted by the PC. An evergreen or irrevocable bond, parent company guarantee, irrevocable letter of credit, or cash escrow account shall be provided by the applicant/owner that is equal to the accepted cost estimate as allowed by Indiana Code. (b) Discontinuation: Any commercial solar energy system shall be considered abandoned and a discontinued use after six (6) months without energy production, unless a plan is developed by the owner or applicant and approved by the Administrator outlining the steps and a schedule for returning the commercial solar energy system to service. (c) Removal: An applicant’s obligations shall include removal of all physical material pertaining to the project improvements to no less than a depth of four (4) feet below ground level. Said work shall be completed within one (1) year of the discontinuation or abandonment of the commercial solar energy system. The restoration of the project area shall result in as near as practicable the condition of the site immediately before construction of such improvements. (d) Written Notices: Prior to implementing procedures to resolve any alleged failure to comply with the decommissioning plan, the appropriate jurisdictional body shall first provide written notice to the owner and/or operator, setting forth the alleged default(s). Such written notice shall provide the owner and/or operator a reasonable time period, not to exceed sixty (60) days, to resolve the alleged default(s). (e) Costs Incurred by the Jurisdiction: If the jurisdiction removes a commercial solar energy system and/or appurtenant facilities, it may sell the salvage to defray the costs of removal. Each permittee, by virtue of the issuance of its construction permit or inspection certificate, grants a license to the jurisdiction to enter the property and to remove all commercial solar energy systems and/or appurtenant facilities pursuant to the terms of its approved decommissioning plan.

If necessary, the Zoning Administrator may engage qualified contractors to enter the site, remove CSES project assets, sell assets removed, remediate the site, and initiate proceedings to recover costs of decommissioning. The bond may be released upon receipt of certificate of inspection by the Building Inspector, County Surveyor, County Highway Department and Zoning Administrator and any other department necessary indicating that decommissioning is complete with no unresolved issues related to the CSES Development. In the event of abandonment or natural disaster, similar decommissioning requirements apply, including removal within 1 year and County's ability to use the surety and right of entry to perform decommissioning.

Fencing Standards: 3.04 H Shall meet the minimum setback standards or set no closer than the minimum setback of the buffer area; whichever is greater and included in the Development Plan, Section 23. A. Fences, gates and warning signs must be maintained in good condition until the CSES is dismantled and removed from site and B. Installation shall be installed with a consideration to allowing a wildlife corridor as defined in the Noble County Comprehensive Plan and C. Must comply with the National Electric Code. Maintenance, Repair or Replacement of CSES 3.04 P, 10.04 A 3: Maintenance shall include, but not limited to, painting, structural repairs and integrity of security measures including fencing.

The ordinance explicitly restricts glare from Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) stating: 'CSES at no time shall create glare on any non-participating property line, structure or right-of-way. All CSES using a reflector to enhance solar production shall minimize glare from the reflector affecting adjacent or nearby properties, including any public right-of-way.' This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems defined as those 'to generate and sell solar power.'

Section 7 'Height Restrictions: 3.04 E' states: 'No part of a solar panel or other equipment associated with the CSES shall exceed fifteen (15) feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt height.' This is the explicit maximum height restriction for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) intended to generate and sell solar power. The units are feet as directly stated in the text.

The ordinance explicitly states a minimum parcel size of five (5) acres for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES), which are defined as systems 'to generate and sell solar power.' This is found in section 5.A: 'Minimum Parcel Size: 3.02 B shall be a minimum of five (5) acres in size.' The units are acres, a standard measure of land area. No other minimum lot size values for utility-scale solar systems are provided.
section: Commercial Solar Energy System Over Lay District (CSES-OD)

summary: The ordinance states: 'Unless otherwise allowed by IC 36-7-4-1109, a project owner may not install or locate a CSES in Noble County unless the project owner demonstrates in the Development Plan that the CSES will operate so the sound attributed with the CSES will not exceed an hourly average sound level of fifty (50) A-Weighted decibels as measured at the CSES fence.' The unit is clarified as A-Weighted decibels (dBA), which is the standard unit for noise measurement.

The Commercial Solar Energy System Overlay District (CSES-OD) is established "to generate and sell solar power." It applies to parcels with a minimum size of five acres and is shown on the official Zoning Map as a hatched or textured pattern noted as CSES-OD. The overlay district's land use restrictions and additional development standards apply to all structures and improvements associated with Commercial Solar Energy System (CSES) development, superseding the base zoning district's standards for those improvements. The overlay does not replace the base zoning regulations but adds restrictions, and in case of inconsistency, the more restrictive regulation applies. The text states that "Under no circumstances shall a planned development or rezoning of property change the applicability of the CSES-OD land use restrictions and additional development standards." This indicates that utility-scale solar energy systems are permitted as a primary use within the CSES-OD without special conditions or approvals beyond those established in the overlay district.
section: Commercial Solar Energy System Over Lay District (CSES-OD)

summary: The ordinance states: 'To qualify for a CSES-OD, the base zoning shall be in any district, with the exception of Open Space (OS)...' and 'Under no circumstances shall a planned development or rezoning of property change the applicability of the CSES’s land use restrictions and additional development standards.' This means utility-scale Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) are unconditionally prohibited in the Open Space (OS) district. The overlay district (CSES-OD) can apply to any other base zoning district, and the more restrictive regulations between the overlay and base zoning apply. No other districts are explicitly mentioned as prohibiting utility-scale solar energy systems.
section: Commercial Solar Energy System Over Lay District (CSES-OD)

summary: The CSES shall be at least three hundred (300) feet from a non-participating pre-existing residential dwelling, as measured at the closest point of the foundation to the CSES, including across any right-of-way, or fifty (50) feet from the property line, whichever is greater. Development setbacks shall be included in the Development Plan, Section 23. Other options include the 300 feet setback from a dwelling, but the 50 feet from the property line is the minimum fixed setback distance.

The ordinance requires a "Visual Buffer: 3.04 J" consisting of "a Berm, natural vegetation or evergreen plants to provide a reasonable visual buffer for non-participating preexisting dwelling(s), to cover the minimum required radius for the entire viewshed," which "must meet a minimum of 6’ in height at the time of installation, located between the property line and CSES fence on the participating landowner property." The buffer "may include more than one buffer material with a clear intent to buffer CSES" and must be "subject to approval by the Development Plan Committee." In the event of natural disaster or loss, "replacement of the buffer shall be completed within no more than 1 year from the date of the event," with possible extensions. Additionally, "Ground Vegetation: 3.04 K" requires a "conservation stewardship plan for the establishment and maintenance of ground vegetation for the life of the CSES," including "site preparation and maintenance practices designed to control invasive species and noxious weeds," all to be included in the Development Plan. The Development Plan must include "Visual Buffer & Vegetative ground cover" for review by the Development Plan Committee. These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Energy Systems defined as systems "to generate and sell solar power," indicating utility-scale systems.

Emergency Contact Signage: CSES shall be identified with a E911 location address assigned by the Noble County Plan Commission. A standard metal sign displaying the facility name, emergency contact information and physical site address shall be posted at the entrance of the facility, substation and any other location deemed necessary by the Zoning Administrator or DPC. The sign shall be posted in compliance with the current ordinance, set outside the road right-of-way. Property owner must report to the Zoning Administrator within sixty (60) days of a change of ownership of the CSES, including contact information and signage change(s) on site.

The ordinance requires that the Development Plan for a Commercial Solar Energy System (CSES) include a "Storm Water Erosion Control Ordinance" (Section 23, item D) to be reviewed by the Development Plan Committee. Additionally, under "Ground Vegetation" (3.04 K), the CSES property owner and project owner must have a conservation stewardship plan for the establishment and maintenance of ground vegetation for the life of the CSES, including "site preparation and maintenance practices designed to control invasive species and noxious weeds". Failure to maintain ground vegetation may result in cancellation of the improvement location permit and remediation costs. These requirements apply to CSES, defined as "A solar energy system for the purpose of generating and selling solar power, includes all components associated with the generation and transmission of electricity."

The CSES shall be at least three hundred (300) feet from a non-participating pre-existing residential dwelling, as measured at the closest point of the foundation to the CSES, including across any right-of-way, or fifty (50) feet from the property line, whichever is greater. Additionally, laydown and staging areas, employee parking, equipment trucks, and office sites must be located a minimum of five hundred (500) feet from any nonparticipating existing dwelling. The 300 feet setback is the primary fixed setback for the system itself, while the 500 feet setbacks apply to specific ancillary uses. Waivers from these setbacks may be granted via notarized statements from nonparticipating landowners.

The ordinance requires that all applicants for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) submit a complete Development Plan (section 23) for Plan Commission review no less than ninety (90) days prior to public hearing. The Development Plan must include a "Visual Buffer & Vegetative ground cover" (Section 23 F) and a Site Plan with proposed landscaping buffers (Definitions: Site Plan xii). Section 13 (3.04 J) mandates installation of a natural landscape buffer "to provide a reasonable visual buffer for non-participating preexisting dwelling(s), to cover the minimum required radius for the entire viewshed," with specific height and location requirements, subject to approval by the Development Plan Committee. The Findings of Fact (9.10 E 6) require that "the proposed development is compatible to the site and its surroundings." The Development Plan Committee reviews these items, and final approval is by the County Commissioners. Other Development Plan requirements include road usage, decommissioning, fire safety, waste management, and more, but the visual buffer is explicitly listed as a required element for review.

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires SECS-1 projects to submit a Decommissioning Plan as part of the Final Development Plan approval, which "shall include financial assurance that the project facilities are properly decommissioned upon the end of the project life or abandonment consistent with this Ordinance." The Decommissioning Plan must include "removal and proper disposal of all physical material pertaining to the project improvements to a depth of five (5) feet beneath the soil surface, and restoration of the area occupied by the project improvements such that it is suitable for an equivalent land use to what existed immediately before construction of such improvements." Financial assurance (Decommissioning Security) equal to 125% of the estimated cost of decommissioning must be provided before commercial operations begin and adjusted annually. The Decommissioning Plan and Security must be re-evaluated every five years. A SECS or individual solar panel is "presumed at the end of its useful life and/or abandoned if the SECS or the individual solar panel generates no electricity for a continuing period of twelve (12) months" and must be removed pursuant to the Decommissioning Plan. Additionally, Tier 1 projects must provide an agreement with adequate surety or bond to reimburse the County and other entities for expenses incurred in evaluating the project, continuing through completion of decommissioning and removal. Other tiers (SECS-2 and SECS-3) have different requirements, such as fewer hearings and less extensive application materials, but the decommissioning requirements described apply explicitly to SECS-1 projects, defined as "Greater than 20 acres" and "Electricity sold to utility transmission lines."

summary: All solar panels and accessory buildings for the project must be fenced in with a fence not less than 7 feet in height. This requirement is found in section 153.126.02 DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS, subsection D. SECS-1 systems are defined as "Greater than 20 acres" and involve "Electricity sold to utility transmission lines." Other tiers include SECS-2: "More than 1 acre up to 20 acres on one or more properties" with electricity used primarily for on-site use, and SECS-3: "One acre or less and one landowner" with electricity exclusively behind the meter generation for a single property owner.

Section 153.126.03 (D) states: 'No solar panel may exceed 25' in height at its highest extended rotation.' This applies generally to solar panels in the project, including SECS-1 systems. Additionally, section 153.126.03 (E) states: 'No Tier 3 SECS solar panel may exceed the height restriction in the underlying zoning district,' but this does not apply to SECS-1. Therefore, the maximum height for SECS-1 solar panels is 25 feet.

SECS-1 systems are defined as those with "Greater than 20 acres" of total acreage measured from a perimeter fence surrounding the total solar generation facilities, including substations, energy storage, or electrical support buildings. This minimum acreage applies explicitly to SECS-1, which are systems where electricity is sold to utility transmission lines. Other tiers include SECS-2 (More than 1 acre up to 20 acres on one or more properties, electricity used primarily for on-site use) and SECS-3 (One acre or less and one landowner, electricity exclusively behind the meter generation for single property owner). The units for the minimum lot size are acres.

At any Non-Participating Landowner's residential lot, public school, public library, or recreational area within one-quarter mile of the project boundaries, for a period of more than 10% out of every hour, the audible A-weighted sound pressure levels as a result of the sound emitted by the project shall not exceed either, the greater of 45 decibels or, 5 decibels above the Ambient Baseline Sound Pressure Level of the project. The Ambient Baseline Sound Pressure Level, if used, shall be determined by a baseline acoustic emissions study conducted by the County Area Plan Commission and funded by the Applicant. Measurement of sound and vibration levels shall be conducted adhering to best practices within the applicable industry and in compliance with all other applicable county, state and federal regulations. The units for noise level are dBA.

No solar panel may be located less than One Hundred (100) feet from any Non-Participating landowner property line. (153.126.03(B)) Other related setback provisions include: No part of the project shall be constructed in any required setback, dedicated public easement or dedicated public right-of-way without prior written authorization (153.126.03(A)); and any SECS project shall not have a boundary closer than one mile to any municipal boundary line (153.126.03(C)).

The ordinance requires a Drainage Plan approved by the Posey County Soil and Water Conservation District-District Technician for SECS-1 projects as part of the Final Development Plan approval. The Drainage Plan must include a form of financial assurance acceptable to the County for the repair or replacement of all damaged drains, ditches, and tiles (if in the public right of way). The Transportation Plan and the Drainage Plan shall state that any newly constructed access roads shall not impede the flow of water and will comply with the County drainage ordinance. SECS-1 is defined as projects greater than 20 acres with electricity sold to utility transmission lines. Other tiers include SECS-2 (more than 1 acre up to 20 acres, electricity used primarily for on-site use) and SECS-3 (one acre or less and one landowner, electricity exclusively behind the meter generation for single property owner), but the soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements are explicitly tied to the Drainage Plan in the Final Development Plan approval for SECS-1.

Section 153.124.02(F) requires the Applicant to submit a Visual Impact Evaluation Report evaluating the visual impact of all solar panels on properties within certain distances of the project. The report shall include: (1) a map depicting the dimensions of the proposed site, names and addresses of adjoining property owners not participating in the project, setbacks distance from each Distal Solar Panel and adjoining property lines, and various landmarks; (2) detailed description of the potential visibility of each Distal Solar Panel and the methodology used to evaluate visibility within the View Shed Areas; (3) View Shed Areas defined as a ½ mile radius from each Distal Solar Panel adjacent to the project boundary; (4) photographic simulations of the View Shed Area capturing the general visibility of Distal Solar Panels; and (5) any mitigation measures proposed to minimize the visual impact of the project. This applies to SECS-1 systems, which are defined as solar energy conversion systems greater than 20 acres with electricity sold to utility transmission lines. Other tiers include SECS-2 (more than 1 acre up to 20 acres, electricity used primarily for on-site use) and SECS-3 (one acre or less, electricity exclusively behind the meter for single property owner).

Section 7.4 Decommissioning Plan requires that "a signed and executed decommissioning plan must be submitted to the plan administrator prior to the beginning of construction of the CSES or the project’s building permit will be revoked by the building inspector." The plan must include "written assurance guaranteeing that the facilities will be properly decommissioned upon the project life or in the event that the facility is abandoned;" a "contractor cost estimate for demolition and removal of the WECS or CSES facility" by a competent party; and "financial assurance in an amount at least equal to the cost estimate of demolition and removal of the WECS or CSES facility, less the estimated value of the equipment and materials utilized by the facility at the time of decommissioning, through the use of a bond, escrow deposit, or other security acceptable to the County." The security will be released when "each tower or solar array and improvements are properly decommissioned as determined by the Pulaski County building inspector." The plan must be updated every five years. Upon discontinuation or abandonment, removal of all physical material must begin within one year. The decommissioning plan is binding on the owner/operator and successors. Additionally, Section 7.18.A.1 requires submission of a decommissioning plan as prescribed in Section 7.4 prior to issuance of any building permit for a CSES.

All ground-mounted electrical and control equipment for CSES shall be surrounded by a fence no shorter than six (6) feet to discourage unauthorized access, unless state and federal agency guidelines provide otherwise. Such fencing shall not include barbed wire but shall be permeable for wildlife passage. Alternative fencing can be used if the site is incorporating agrivoltaics and said fencing is approved by the plan administrator. The solar array and/or modules shall be designed and installed to discourage access by the public, and access to same shall be through a locked gate. "No Trespassing" signs shall be attached to any perimeter fence. "Danger" and "High Voltage" signs shall be posted at the height of five (5) feet at entrances and every 600 feet along the fencing. Annually, the owner/operator shall provide to the plan administrator a report assessing the conditions of the screening and fencing surrounding all CSES facilities, including any damaged portions in need of repair, repairs completed, and plans for necessary repairs to keep the project in compliance.
section: 7.14 Safety, Design, and Installation Standards for SES

summary: Section 7.15.A states: "All CSES shall be designed, and reflection angles oriented or otherwise screened, to avoid concentrated and prolonged glare into abutting structures and roadways." This is the explicit glare restriction applicable to Commercial Solar Energy Systems. Other related provisions include noise limits and screening requirements, but these do not specifically address glare. No other sections provide explicit glare restrictions for CSES.

Section 7.2 General Regulations, subsection B. Height states: 'Ground- and pole-mounted SES shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in height at maximum tilt.' This is the explicit maximum height restriction applicable to solar energy systems, including Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES). Other height restrictions mentioned apply to building- and roof-mounted SES, which must meet zoning district height restrictions pursuant to Section 3, but no specific numerical values are given for those. The 20 feet limit is the most restrictive explicit numerical height limit provided for CSES. The units are feet as stated in the ordinance.

Noise from a CSES shall not exceed 60 dBA measured from the nearest property line. This restriction is not expected to be met during project construction or short-term periods of maintenance, including groundskeeping (such as mowing), except between 7:00 p.m. and 7:00 a.m. This limit may be waived by any adjoining property owner in writing and recorded at the Pulaski County Courthouse. All other noise and vibration levels shall be in compliance with all state and federal regulations. The unit for noise level is dBA, a standard unit for measuring sound.

From any CSES component to a non-participating/non-included property line or any right-of-way: 150 feet. Other setback distances include 75 feet from either side of an internal ditch, and 1.1 times the total height of a communications tower from an inverter or converter, but these do not pertain to non-participating property lines. (Section 7.17 Commercial SES Setbacks, Table 7.3)

From any CSES component to a non-participating/non-included property line or any right-of-way: 150 feet. (Section 7.17 Commercial SES Setbacks, Table 7.3) The ordinance specifies a fixed setback distance of 150 feet from any right-of-way (road) for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES). Other setbacks in Table 7.3 include 75 feet from internal ditches and 1.1 times the total height of a communications tower from inverters or converters, but these do not pertain to roads or rights-of-way. Additionally, the furthest horizontal extension of a SES shall not extend into a required setback or be closer than 12 feet to any right-of-way easement for above-ground utilities, but this is not a direct road setback. Landscaping buffers are also required along road frontage outside perimeter fencing, unless waived, but no additional setback distances are specified.

Section 7.14.B.3 requires that "The planting of landscaping along the perimeter of the CSES shall be required on the outside of the perimeter fencing along road frontage and facing all habitable dwellings fit for human occupation on non-participating properties within a half (1/2) mile of a CSES." The landscape buffer "shall be designed by a horticulturalist with the goal of balancing ecological environmental practices with a desire to maintain compatibility with the exist rural landscape" and "shall be consistent with prudent ecological design considerations to co include any trees, shrubs, berms, or related landscaping designed to create a natural-looking, semi-opaque area (i.e., the buffer will not be required to block the view of the project completely, but be substantial enough to meet the plan administrator’s approval) that prevents direct visual line of sight between the developed area and neighboring properties and/or public areas and roadways." "Evergreens must be at least 6’ tall on average by the beginning of on-site energy production." The plan administrator "may require the developer/operator/owner to upgrade installed vegetation screening to satisfy such standards." Property owners may waive planting requirements unless the plantings are designed to provide screening between the CSES and a public roadway; such waiver must be recorded. Landscaping buffering "shall be maintained and/or replaced by owner/operator so that it shall continue its purpose to serve as a screening as described herein." Screening is not required along non-participating properties used for agricultural purposes that do not require screening for adjacent roads or dwelling units. Annual reports on screening conditions must be submitted to the plan administrator (Section 7.20.A.5.b).
section: 7.14 Safety, Design, and Installation Standards for SES

summary: All signs, other than the manufacturer’s or installer’s identification, appropriate warning (including safety and trespassing) signs, or owner identification on a solar panel array and/or modules, building, or other structure associated with the CSES, shall be prohibited, except as permitted below. No sign shall exceed sixteen (16) square feet in surface area or eight (8) feet in height. A sign not to exceed two (2) square feet in surface area may be placed upon any compartment containing electrical equipment. A sign may be located on each side of the total project area, provided that there are no more than four (4) such signs located on any one contiguous project site.

The ordinance requires a Drainage Agreement (DA) that must contain provisions addressing "responsible storm-water management practices during construction and operation" (7.18.A.2.b). It mandates submission of "Any stormwater quality-management plan required by IDEM and as outlined by the Pulaski County Drainage Board" (7.18.A.4). During construction, "Reasonable stormwater best-management practices as outlined by IDEM" must be demonstrated (7.19.A.2). Ground cover must be "covered with low-growing native perennials, with an emphasis on pollinators, for the purpose of erosion control" and maintained for the life of the CSES project, including compliance with USDA Farm Services Agency guidelines for plantings within setbacks to ditches (7.14.H). The Drainage Agreement and Road Use and Maintenance Agreement (RUMA) also address ditch, tile, and culvert damages and stormwater management. These requirements explicitly apply to Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES).

summary: The furthest horizontal extension of a WECS (including guy wires) or SES shall not extend into a required setback in the zoning district or be closer than twelve (12) feet to any primary structure, or right-of-way easement for any above-ground telephone, electrical transmission or distribution lines.

A decommissioning and site restoration plan shall be required to ensure that facilities are properly removed after their useful life. This plan should indicate the method and payment of the anticipated cost of removing the SES-C at the end of their serviceable life or upon becoming discontinued or abandoned use. A surety bond or an equivalent means of security acceptable to the Putnam County Commissioners must be posted incrementally: 25% at start of full commercial operation, 50% at the fifth anniversary, and 100% at the tenth anniversary. The project owner shall provide written notice to the County not later than sixty (60) days before discontinuation of commercial operation. After discontinuation, all structures, foundations, roads, gravel areas, and cables shall be removed to a depth of at least thirty-six (36) inches below grade, and the ground restored to a condition reasonably similar to its pre-construction state. If removal is not completed within one year, the County may remove and remediate the site and recover costs. Decommissioning must occur if the project does not produce power for eighteen (18) consecutive months, with possible extension upon petition. Abandonment is defined as no electricity generation for eighteen (18) consecutive months plus 540 days, triggering mandatory removal within one year. Force majeure events allow for a twelve (12) month period to resume operation before abandonment is declared. These requirements apply to Solar Energy System-Commercial (SES-C), which includes Medium and Large Ground Mounted SES (site size larger than two (2) acres, with Large being larger than twenty (20) acres).
section: § 155.135 Development Standards for Solar Energy System-Commercial

summary: All SES-C and their appurtenant structures shall be completely enclosed with fencing that is at least six (6) feet high. This fencing requirement applies to Solar Energy System-Commercial (SES-C), which includes Medium Ground Mounted SES and Large Ground Mounted SES. The relevant text states: 'Fencing: All SES-C and their appurtenant structures shall be completely enclosed with fencing that is at least six (6) feet high.' Other related requirements for SES-C include setbacks, screening, height limits, access, ground cover, and safety and security plans, but the explicit fencing requirement is as stated.
