The design of the buildings and related structures associated with the Solar Farm shall use materials, colors, textures, screening, and landscaping that, to the greatest extent possible, will blend the facilities to the natural setting and surrounding structures. Exception or variance may be permissible, depending on individual circumstances.

The perimeter fence for ground-mounted solar energy systems must be set back at least three hundred (300) feet from all non-participating residences with an approved vegetative buffer. Exception of variance may be permissible, depending on individual circumstances. The ordinance also mentions a 100 feet setback from non-participating property lines, but the 300 feet setback from non-participating residences is the more restrictive and directly applicable requirement.

Section 13.19.14 'Decommissioning-Restoration Plan and Agreement' requires a plan outlining the anticipated means, costs, and method of payment for decommissioning and restoration at the end of the C-SES life or if abandoned or declared a public nuisance. The C-SES applicant, owner, operator must submit written notice of intent to abandon at least 60 days prior to discontinuation of electrical production. A C-SES is considered abandoned after one year without energy production unless a Rehabilitation Plan is approved. Removal and restoration must occur within 180 days of discontinuation, including removal of all physical material above ground and improvements below ground to a depth of 50 inches, except underground wiring 48 inches or deeper may remain if disconnected. Hazardous materials must be identified and handled per law. A performance guarantee of 125% of estimated decommissioning and restoration cost is required, with cost re-estimated every five years and adjusted accordingly. Failure to negotiate costs or maintain the plan may result in the county declaring the C-SES a nuisance and requiring cessation of operation and completion of decommissioning at the operator's expense.

For security, all above ground C-SES equipment shall be completely enclosed by a minimum seven (7) foot high fence with locking gates accessible only by a key pad or Knox Box with key. Fencing shall be located around the entire perimeter of the project site meeting the required setbacks. Any high voltage substation or battery storage facility shall be safeguarded at minimum by an eight (8) foot high fence with at least two (2) strands of barbed wire at the top and locking gates accessible only by a key pad or Knox Box with key. Fencing shall meet the required setbacks. Solid Fencing or walls constructed of materials making a solid visual barrier shall not be permitted as a use by the solar project applicant, owner, operator for screening, fencing or gates. It shall be the sole responsibility of the C-SES applicant, owner, operator to maintain all fencing, post, and gates in order to remain free from rust, corrosion, sag.

Section 13.15 GLARE AND LIGHTING, C-SES states: 'To the extent reasonably possible, solar arrays, regardless of how they are mounted, shall be oriented and/or screened year-round so that glare is directed away from adjacent properties, structures and roadways.' It further requires that 'solar energy components shall remain the color or finish that was originally applied by the manufacturer provided the exterior surface of any visible components are non-reflective and non-obtrusive. Finishes shall be matte or non-reflective.' The 'C-SES applicant, owner, operator shall have the burden of mitigating any glare produced so as not to have significant adverse impact on adjacent uses.' The 'determination of the Wabash County Commissioners shall be conclusive relative to applicant’s compliance with this standard.' Other options or conditions related to glare are not provided in the text.

Section 13.17 states: 'Ground mounted C-SES arrays shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt.' This is the explicit maximum height limitation for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (C-SES). Other height restrictions mentioned in the text apply only to Non-Commercial Solar Energy Systems (NC-SES) and are therefore not applicable here. The unit 'feet' is used consistently in the ordinance for height measurements.

Section 13.6.3 states: 'The maximum number of aggregate acres for all C-SES located within Wabash County, including any area required for setbacks, screening, buffering, and fencing, shall be limited to two thousand (2,000.00) acres.' This is the only explicit maximum lot size limit for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (C-SES) in the text. The units are acres, an area measurement.

The ordinance explicitly states a minimum parcel size of 105 acres for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (C-SES) in the SPECIAL EXCEPTION SETBACKS section of Exhibit A, under 'SOLAR UNIT, COMMERCIAL BPS'. This is the only minimum lot size value given for C-SES. The units are clearly indicated as acres. No other minimum lot size values for C-SES are provided.

No part of an operating C-SES shall produce noise that exceeds any of the following limitations except during construction. A maximum of thirty-two decibels (32 dB) from the Project on the A weighted LEQ scale shall be permitted, as measured immediately outside the closest point of the nearest residential or business structure. Modeling to evaluate compliance with respect to this limit shall be conducted according to ISO 9613-2 which is the international standard for sound propagation. If monitoring is conducted, it should follow applicable American National Standard Institute (ANSI) methods. For monitoring, a sound level meter meeting ANSI Type 1 specifications shall be utilized.

The ordinance specifies fixed setback distances from non-participating property lines for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (C-SES). Setback Charts 13.7.2.f and 13.7.2.g list setbacks such as 100 feet from property lines and adjoining participating landowners. Section 13.8.5 states: 'All buffer strips, screening shall be constructed on the property of the solar project and, at planting, be no closer than one hundred (100) feet to the property line.' Other setback values include 105 feet in certain zoning districts, and 1320 feet from public facilities or parks, but the most restrictive standard setback from non-participating property lines is 100 feet.

Setback Charts 13.7.2.f and 13.7.2.g specify setbacks of 1320 feet from public facilities, parks, campgrounds, recreational, and outdoor facilities for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (C-SES). For example, Chart #13.7.2.f lists 1320 feet setback from Public Facilities, Parks, Camp Grounds, Recreational, Outdoor Facilities, and Chart #13.7.2.g lists 1320 feet setback for inverters, battery storage facilities, and substations from Residential Structure, Public Facilities, Parks, Camp Grounds, Recreational. Additionally, ground-mounted C-SES shall not be placed within floodplains, flowage easements, storm water conveyance systems, or other natural resource protection areas. Buffer strips and screening shall be no closer than 100 feet to the property line. Other setback distances include 100 feet from residential structures and 105 feet from certain roads, but the 1320 feet setback is the most restrictive for public conservation and natural resource protection areas.

The minimum setbacks for all equipment, buffering, fencing and access roads/lanes associated with the C-SES shall be as listed in Setback Chart 13.7.2.f. and 13.7.2.g. Setbacks shall be measured from the center of the road, or from the adjoining property line. Setbacks apply to solar arrays, racking, inverters, battery storage facilities, substations, accessory buildings, buffering, fence, access roads/lanes and any other power equipment or meteorological towers. Setback Chart 13.7.2.f shows setbacks of 105 feet from SEC CO RD, PRI CO RD, and ST RD. Setback Chart 13.7.2.g shows setbacks of 105 feet for inverter, battery storage facility, and substation from state roads. Other setback values include 100 feet and 1320 feet depending on zoning district and equipment type.

The ordinance explicitly enacts vegetative buffer and screening requirements for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (C-SES). Section 13.8 states: "Each non-participating residential or business land owner location within the project area may request and receive screening around the perimeter of his/her residential or business structure." It requires "a Visual Barrier as defined in Section 1.7" and that "All visual buffer strips are to be shown in a certified landscape plan." Landscaping/screening "shall be placed on all sides adjacent to C-SES equipment" and "A visual barrier may be composed of landscaping, landscaped berm, or combination thereof." The buffer strips "shall be constructed on the property of the solar project and, at planting, be no closer than one hundred (100) feet to the property line." Section 13.9 requires "A natural vegetative ground cover shall be maintained under and around all solar arrays" with "Only non-invasive species shall be used and native species are recommended." Section 13.10 mandates that "All buffer, screening, landscape, vegetation materials shall be installed and maintained according to accepted USDA Farm Bill Biologist or local Soil and Water Conservation District industry practices." The C-SES owner/operator is responsible for maintenance, including replacement of unhealthy or dead plants. These requirements apply specifically to C-SES as defined in Section 13.6.1 as "a utility-scale commercial facility that converts sunlight into electricity with the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity."

Signs shall comply with the following standards and any other reasonable submittals: An identification sign relating to a C-SES development may be located on all sides of the fenced project area, provided that there shall be no more than one (1) sign located per one hundred (100) yards of the C-SES fenced facility area; A sign shall be securely posted on each gate entry point clearly displaying: Emergency telephone number(s), Applicant, Owner, Operator contact information, Electric utility provider contact information, The site locations E-911 address and GPS coordinates; All ingress/egress lanes/drives for a C-SES project site shall have posted, in a conspicuous location, an E-911 Address sign indicating the assigned address for that ingress/egress location; Warning signs shall comply with applicable laws and be posted accordingly; No signage shall be permitted to be posted for non-related solar advertising purpose; All signage required or permitted by this Ordinance shall be made of materials and constructed in a manner to be durable and long lasting.

Section 13.19.15 requires a Drainage Agreement approved by the Wabash County Commissioners addressing field tile damages and repairs, damages or alterations to creeks, streams, ditches, channels, spillways, retention ponds, water courses within the proposed C-SES project area and thirteen hundred twenty (1320) feet beyond. An erosion control plan developed in accordance with the Natural Resources Conservation Services (NRCS) guidelines, IDEM Construction Stormwater General Permit (CSGP), and any storm water quality management plan adopted by the applicable jurisdiction(s) shall be submitted. The area beneath the ground mounted C-SES is considered pervious cover. Natural (pervious) ground covers are required beneath the solar arrays. The relocation or removal of top soil for construction purposes is prohibited.
section: 13.19.15. Drainage Agreement Plan and Erosion Control Plan

summary: 13.6.2 states: 'C-SES may be submitted as a Special Exception if designated by the letter  "S"  on the Chart of Designated Uses contained in Section 3.6.' Section 13.6.3 details that for any variance approved by the Board of Zoning Appeals to allow a C-SES in an A1 zoning district, conditions and restrictions shall be imposed. Setback Charts 13.7.2.f and 13.7.2.g specify that C-SES are permitted by Special Exception in zones A2, FRC, and I. Thus, C-SES require special use approval or variance conditions in these districts. Other districts mentioned for NC-SES (Al, A2, FRC, R1, R2, LR1, LR2, GBD, and I) are not explicitly linked to C-SES special use in the text provided.

The ordinance specifies fixed setback distances for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (C-SES) from non-participating occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, and/or residences. According to Setback Charts 13.7.2.f and 13.7.2.g, the minimum setback is generally 100 feet from residential outdoor facilities, public facilities, and adjoining participating landowner structures. For example, Chart 13.7.2.f states: 'Residential Outdoor Facilities, Parks, Camp Grounds, Recreational, Setback 100 FT.' The ordinance also notes that 'Each non-participating residential or business land owner location within the project area may request and receive screening around the perimeter of his/her residential or business structure' and that 'All buffer strips, screening shall be constructed on the property of the solar project and, at planting, be no closer than one hundred (100) feet to the property line.' No multiplier based on structure height is mentioned; setbacks are fixed distances.

Section 13.7.1 states that the furthest horizontal extension of a C-SES shall not be less than 15 feet from any above-ground telephone line, electrical transmission line, electrical distribution line or other above ground communication or transmission line. Section 13.7.2.b clarifies that poles carrying overhead wiring and underground wiring connecting C-SES components have no setback requirements from adjoining property lines if located within a recorded easement or right-of-way. Section 13.7.2.c prohibits ground-mounted C-SES from being placed within any legal easement or right-of-way, including utility easements, except with written permission. Section 13.13.1 requires transmission cables and lines outside fenced areas to be buried at least 48 inches underground with warning mesh, and 60 inches below flow lines in waterways. These burial depths are not setbacks but safety installation requirements. The 15 feet setback is the fixed distance setback from overhead lines.

Prior to receiving siting approval under this Ordinance, the County and the Applicant, Owner, and/or Operator must formulate a Decommissioning Plan to ensure that the CSECS Project is properly decommissioned. The Decommissioning Plan shall include: Decommissioning of solar panels must occur in the event they are not in use for 12 consecutive months. Assurance that the facilities are properly decommissioned upon the end of the project life or facility abandonment. Applicant’s obligations with respect to decommissioning shall include removal of all physical material pertaining to the project improvements to a depth of 48"  beneath the soil surface, and restoration of the area occupied by the project improvements to as near as practicable to the same condition that existed immediately before construction of such improvements. Prior to issuance of a building permit, the Applicant shall provide a contractor cost estimate for demolition and removal of the CSECS facility and will provide financial assurance in an amount at least equal to said demolition and removal contractor cost estimate, through the use of a bond, letter of credit or other security acceptable to the County, for the cost of decommissioning each array to be constructed under that building permit, which security shall be released when such array is properly decommissioned as determined by the Warren County Building Commissioner. In the event of abandonment by the owner or operator, the Applicant will provide an affidavit to the Warren County Building Commissioner representing that all easements for solar arrays shall contain terms that provide financial assurance, including access to the salvage value of the equipment, for the property owners to ensure that facilities are properly decommissioned within twelve (12) months of expiration or earlier termination of the project. Every five years after the start of construction, updated proof of acceptable financial assurance must be submitted to the Warren County Commissioners for review. If the owner fails to dismantle and/or remove the CSECS within the established timeframes, the County may complete the decommissioning at the owners’ expense. The Applicant’s, Owner’s, or Operator’s failure to materially comply with any of the above provisions shall constitute a default under this Ordinance.

All CSECS’s must provide security fencing around the CSECS Compound. Said fencing must provide limited and secured access to prevent entry by unauthorized personnel. Fencing and access gates shall be eight (8) feet tall as measured from the average grade below the fence to the tallest point of the fence. Razor wire is prohibited on all fences.  "No Trespassing"  signs shall be attached to any perimeter fence.
Glare from a CSECS is prohibited from being directed towards vehicular traffic and any habitable portion of an adjacent inhabited structure.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'The height of any CSECS ground mounted solar equipment is limited to twenty-five (25) feet, as measured from the highest natural grade below each solar panel.' This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS) regulated by the ordinance, which govern systems generating electricity to be sold to wholesale or retail markets, including those above 3 MW. No other maximum height values are provided for CSECS in the text.

Minimum property size for any CSECS shall be five (5) acres situated in either a single parcel or contiguous parcels. This applies to commercial solar projects as defined in the ordinance, which govern systems generating electricity for sale and above 3 MW capacity. The unit is explicitly stated as acres.

The ordinance requires a noise study and states that 'at no point within 200 feet of a primary residence may the sound pressure levels from a solar array exceed the following sound levels... Maximum Permitted Sound Level ... 45 decibels measured 200 feet from edge of any Primary Structure.' Sound levels shall be measured with equipment complying with American National Standards Institute (ANSI) standards. This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS) above 3 MW intended for electricity sale. No other numerical noise limits are provided.

CSECS Equipment must be set back a minimum of two hundred (200) feet from the property line of a primary dwelling unit located on a parcel adjoining the CSECS. CSECS inverters must be set back an additional three hundred (300) feet, for a total of five hundred (500) feet, from the property line of a primary dwelling unit adjoining the CSECS. Solar farms shall meet the minimum zoning setbacks for the zoning district in which located. These setbacks may be waived in writing by property owners adjacent to the CSECS.
County regulated drains, or right-of way to a solar panel must have a setback of seventy-five (75) feet measured from the center of the right-of-way.

The ordinance explicitly requires vegetative buffer and/or other screening for Commercial Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS) above 3 MW. Specifically, it states: 'The planting of evergreens or use of opaque fencing along the perimeter of the CSECS, including along road frontage, shall be required, as determined by the Board of Zoning Appeals.' This requirement is part of the DESIGN AND INSTALLATION standards for CSECS projects. The ordinance governs CSECS that generate electricity to be sold to wholesale or retail markets, with owners of CSECS with an aggregate generating capacity of 3MW or less needing a variance to this ordinance. Other related requirements include security fencing, setbacks, and application procedures, but the explicit vegetative buffer or screening requirement is limited to the planting of evergreens or opaque fencing as described.

The ordinance explicitly requires signage for Commercial Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS) including: ' "No Trespassing"  signs shall be attached to any perimeter fence,' ' "Danger"  and  "High Voltage"  signs shall be posted at the height of five (5) feet on or near arrays and on accessory structures,' and 'At the locked entrance to the facility, a sign showing the names and phone numbers of the electric utility provider, the site operator and an emergency contact, as well as the facility’s 911 address and GPS coordinates shall be provided. Additionally, a sign should be posted containing the name and phone number of a person for the public to contact with the inquiries and complaints throughout the life of the project.' These signage requirements apply to CSECS projects regulated by the ordinance, which governs systems generating electricity to be sold to wholesale or retail markets and generally above 3 MW, as owners of CSECSs with an aggregate generating capacity of 3MW or less must obtain a variance to this Ordinance.

Under Section IV.C (Application for Improvement Location Permit), the Applicant must provide "a revegetation plan for restoring areas temporarily disturbed during construction" and "an erosion control plan must be developed in consultation with the Warren County Soil and Water Conservation District." These requirements apply to CSECS projects that generate electricity to be sold to wholesale or retail markets and exceed 3 MW, as the Ordinance governs such projects and requires permits and plans for them.

value: ['All Warren County townships except R-1, R-2, R-3, and R-4 (Residential) zones']
summary: CSECS may be sited and operated in all Warren County townships. Prior to construction, the Applicant shall obtain approval for a Conditional Use Permit, also known as a Special Exception Permit, from the Warren County Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA) to permit a CSECS in any zone other than R-1, R-2, R-3 or R-4 (Residential) zoned land. Owners of CSECSs with an aggregate generating capacity of 3MW or less on their own property must obtain a variance to this Ordinance.

CSECS Equipment must be set back a minimum of two hundred (200) feet from the property line of a primary dwelling unit located on a parcel adjoining the CSECS. CSECS inverters must be set back an additional three hundred (300) feet, for a total of five hundred (500) feet, from the property line of a primary dwelling unit adjoining the CSECS. These setbacks may be waived in writing by property owners adjacent to the CSECS.

The SES Facility shall be completely Fenced in with perimeter fencing and locked gates that are at least six (6) feet in Height. This fencing requirement applies to Large Solar Energy Systems as specified in section 14-08 SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEM (SES) DEVELOPMENT PLAN. Other development requirements for Large SES include setbacks, height limits (no part of the solar panel may be over twenty-five (25) feet tall), noise setbacks, visual buffers, emergency contact signage, underground electric collection systems (with exceptions), drainage infrastructure repair, liability insurance, and required agreements before permit issuance.

Section 14-08 SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEM (SES) DEVELOPMENT PLAN requires a development plan for any Large Solar Energy System. Under Development Requirements, subsection (G) Glare states: 'An SES Facility at no time shall create glare on any non-participating property.' Other relevant requirements include setbacks, height limits, interference with reception, visual buffers, and fencing. The ordinance applies to Large Solar Energy Systems defined as those requiring an SES Development Plan and rezoning to the Power Plant Overlay District  "P-1."

The ordinance states: 'No part of the solar panel may be over twenty-five (25) feet tall as measured from the average ground level directly below the panel to the top of each panel at its maximum tilt in the vertical direction.' This height restriction applies specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems (SES).

The ordinance specifies that any noise-generating equipment (such as inverters) that create potentially objectionable sound levels during normal operation must meet setbacks from non-participating pre-existing residential dwellings based on measured sound levels. The minimum (most restrictive) noise level referenced is 35 dBA, considered an accepted noise level in a rural setting, measured at five feet from the equipment. The setback distances increase with higher noise levels, starting at 560 feet for noise exceeding 73 dBA up to 1580 feet for noise exceeding 82 dBA. The noise level is measured in dBA, with clarifications that it is measured at five feet from the equipment and calculated using the Inverse Square Law.

Large Solar Energy Systems require an SES Development Plan and must be rezoned to include the Power Plant Overlay District 'P-1' (14-08 SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEM (SES) DEVELOPMENT PLAN, section (B) Overlay District). Large Solar Energy Facility is permitted as a primary use in the P-1 district. In other districts, Large Solar Energy Facilities require a Special Exception (SE) or are not permitted. For example, in districts A-R, A-1, B-1, B-2, B-3, C-1, I-1, I-2, L-1, M-1, and M-2, Large Solar Energy Facility is allowed only by Special Exception. Medium and Small Solar Energy Facilities have different permissions, but these do not apply to Large Solar Energy Facilities. The ordinance states: 'All properties that are participating in the SES Development Plan shall be Rezoned to include the Power Plant Overlay District  "P-1." ' This indicates that P-1 is the primary use district for Large Solar Energy Facilities.

Large Solar Energy Facility is only permitted in the P-1 district (Power Plant Overlay District) with a Special Exception (SE). The text states: 'All properties that are participating in the SES Development Plan shall be Rezoned to include the Power Plant Overlay District  "P-1." ' The table shows Large Solar Energy Facility is marked 'SE' only in P-1 and not permitted or allowed by special exception in any other districts. Other solar energy system types (Medium, Small, Structure Mounted) have different permissions, but for Large Solar Energy Facility, only P-1 allows it by SE.

An SES Facility shall be at least two hundred (200) feet from a non-participating property line. Other related setbacks include: a 400 feet setback from a non-participating pre-existing residence, no setbacks from participating property lines, and exclusions for driveways, perimeter fencing, visual buffers, poles, and wires necessary to connect the facility. These setbacks apply to Large Solar Energy Facilities as defined by the requirement for an SES Development Plan.

Section 14-08 SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEM (SES) DEVELOPMENT PLAN requires a visual buffer to be installed between a non-participating pre-existing residence and the SES Facility. This visual buffer "can be comprised of natural vegetation or plantings to provide a reasonable visual buffer and lighting buffer for the non-participating pre-existing residences." The buffer "shall cover the entire viewshed from the non-participating pre-existing residence to the SES Facility," "must be a minimum of six (6) feet in Height when installed," and "must be designed to grow to be a minimum of twenty (20) feet in Height." Other requirements include setbacks, fencing, appearance, and equipment standards, but the explicit vegetative buffer requirement is in subsection (L) Visual Buffers.

Section 14-08 SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEM (SES) DEVELOPMENT PLAN requires that for any Large Solar Energy System, a standard metal Public Way Sign including the Owner of the SES Facility’s name, emergency contact phone number, and physical site address shall be posted at each entrance to the facility. The Sign shall be posted just outside of the Public Way Right-Of-Way and sight triangle. Other requirements in this section include development plan submission, public notice, setbacks, height limits, fencing, visual buffers, and liability insurance, but only subsection (M) explicitly addresses signage requirements.

Large Solar Energy Facility requires a Special Exception (SE) in districts A-1, R-1, and R-2 as indicated in the table under 'Large Solar Energy Facility'. Additionally, 'Any time a Large Solar Energy System is being developed, an SES Development Plan is required' and 'The Plan Commission will review any SES Development Plan or its modifications.' Properties participating in the SES Development Plan must be rezoned to include the Power Plant Overlay District 'P-1.' Setback requirements also apply, such as 'at least two hundred (200) feet from a non-participating property line' and 'at least four hundred (400) feet from a non-participating pre-existing residence.' Other solar energy facility types (Medium, Small, Structure Mounted) have different permitted uses and conditions, but these are not applicable to Large Solar Energy Facilities.

An SES Facility shall be at least four hundred (400) feet from a non-participating pre-existing residence. Other related setbacks include: 200 feet from a non-participating property line; no required setbacks from participating residences; and noise-generating equipment setbacks ranging from 560 to 1580 feet depending on sound level. Setbacks exclude driveways, perimeter fencing, visual buffers, poles, and wires necessary to connect the facility.

All CSE projects must provide security fencing around the outer edge of each CSE system compound in addition to any screening requirements stipulated in Subsection 7.17. B. 8 of this Chapter. Said fencing must provide limited and secured access to prevent entry by unauthorized personnel. Fencing and access gates shall be between six (6) and ten (10) feet tall as measured from the ground grade to the top of the fencing material (post excluded). Note: When a CSE system project area is divided into sections as a result of roads/streets, alleys, easements or similar restricted areas, each CSE system compound within each section is subject to the security fencing requirements of this subsection.

Subsection 7.16 A.14 requires "Certification from an independent, industry, design professional or licensed engineer that the proposed development will not create undue glare or reflection so as to create a traffic hazard or cause a nuisance to neighboring properties; this Certification must clearly delineate all steps taken to mitigate such circumstances." Subsection 7.17 B.15 states a CSE system "must be designed and constructed to: a. Minimize glare on adjacent properties and roadways; and, b. Not interfere with vehicular or air traffic." These provisions explicitly impose glare restrictions for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSE).
section: 7.16 APPLICATION REQUIREMENTS and 7.17 DISTRICT REGULATIONS AND PERFORMANCE STANDARDS

summary: All solar arrays along with their associated support structures must be ground based not to exceed twenty-five (25) feet in height when the panels are in full tilt and as measured from the surrounding average grade. (Section 7.17 B. 5.) This is the explicit maximum height limit for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSE).

Subsection 7.17 B. 3 states: 'Any CSE project must have a minimum project area of at least five (5) acres; a project area may consist of multiple parcels, either contiguous or separated only by a road or alley, of which individual parcels may be less than five (5) acres.' This is the explicit minimum lot size for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSE).

A CSE may not produce in excess of an hourly average sound level of fifty (50) A-weighted decibels as modeled at the closest outer wall of a dwelling located on any adjacent, Non-Participating property. The sound level maximum may be waived with the written consent of the Non-Participating property owner. The units are standard noise measurement units, dBA.

The Official Schedule of Uses in the White County Zoning Ordinance Appendix A lists Solar Energy System, Commercial (CSE) as permitted ("P") in the districts CFO, R-1, R-2, R-3, R-4, A-1, A-2, B-1, B-2, B-3, B-4, B-5, L-1, RR, I-1, I-2, and I-3. The designation "P" indicates that CSE is permitted as a primary use without special conditions or approvals. No overlay districts are mentioned in the provided text. Other uses such as Solar Energy System, Individual (ISE) are marked as "A" (likely accessory or conditional), but this does not apply to CSE.
section: APPENDIX A: OFFICIAL SCHEDULE OF USES

summary: No perimeter point of a CSE system compound may be closer to a project area property line than fifty (50) feet. This setback requirement may be waived with the written consent of the effected property owners; either Participating or Non-Participating property owners. Other setback distances mentioned include 40 feet from federal/state/county highway rights-of-way, 30 feet from collector road rights-of-way, and 10 feet from local road rights-of-way, but these relate to roads, not property lines. Setbacks from dwellings on non-participating properties are 150 feet with landscape buffer requirements, but dwellings are not equivalent to property lines.
section: 7.17 B. Size, Height, Setbacks and Other Developmental Standards – CSE

summary: A CSE system compound may be located no closer than forty (40) feet to the nearest edge of any federal interstate highway, federal highway, state highway or county highway right-of-way; thirty (30) feet to the nearest edge of any collector road right-of-way or ten (10) feet to the nearest edge of any local road right-of-way (these setbacks do not apply to the infrastructure required to distribute electricity to the electrical grid or an associated substation).

Subsection 7.17 B. 8 requires a landscape buffer if a CSE system compound is closer than 150 feet to a dwelling on a non-participating property, with the buffer waived if the compound is at least 250 feet away or with written consent of the non-participating owner. Subsection 7.17 B. 9 requires screening along any CSE project property line abutting a residential zoning district and along property lines across the road from residential districts, with waivers possible if the compound is at least 250 feet away or with written consent of affected property owners. Screening may be vegetative (preferred) or berm, with specifications for vegetative screening (minimum two rows, spacing no more than 25 feet apart, height of 6 feet within two years) and berms (maximum slope 3:1, height 6 to 10 feet, vegetated with ground cover). Subsection 7.17 B. 10 requires a vegetation plan including perennial vegetated ground cover over all land not paved or graveled, maintained for the life of the project, using non-invasive native or naturalized species. Incorporation of pollinator friendly seed mixes is encouraged but not required.

A CSE system compound may be no closer than one hundred-fifty (150) feet to the nearest point of the outer wall of a dwelling on a non-participating owner’s property, subject to installation of a landscape buffer as provided for in subsection 7.17. B. 8 (a) of this Chapter. The landscape buffer requirement of this subsection is hereby waived if the outer edge of the CSE system compound is at least two hundred fifty (250) feet away from the nearest point of the outer wall of the subject dwelling. The landscape buffer may be waived with the written consent of the non-participating property owner.

Section SECS-6 Decommissioning requires that a project operator submit a Decommissioning and site restoration plan as part of the Development Plan, including recycling of solar panels and equipment, posting a surety bond or equivalent surety acceptable to the Zoning Administrator, Plan Commission, County Commissioners, and County Attorney, and a liability insurance policy naming Whitley County as an additional insured. The surety must be equal to the decommissioning costs calculated by a third party engineer, updated every five years, and allow the County to recuperate costs if it participates in decommissioning. Upon change in operator or owner, the new party must agree to prior requirements and provide a new surety. The operator must provide written notice of intent to decommission at least 60 days before discontinuation. All solar panels, structures, foundations, roads, gravel areas, cables, and associated materials must be removed to a depth of 36 inches, and the ground restored to a condition reasonably similar to before construction. Decommissioning must be complete within 1 year, with a possible 6-month extension. Section SECS-7 Abandonment states a SECS is considered abandoned 540 days after last electricity generation, triggering required decommissioning and removal from the Overlay District.

Perimeter fencing may be installed. If perimeter fencing is installed, the following apply: 1. Razor wire and electric fences shall be prohibited. 2. Allowance shall be made for wildlife ingress and egress.

The ordinance explicitly states in SECS-5, subsection D: 'Maximum height. 1. Electrical generation equipment and structures: 25’ 2. Other structures: as permitted in the underlying zoning district.' The maximum height allowed for electrical generation equipment and structures in a Solar Energy Collection System (SECS) is 25 feet. The units are feet as indicated by the apostrophe (’). Other structures related to SECS are subject to the height limits of the underlying zoning district.

Sound attributed to the SECS shall not exceed an hourly average sound level of fifty (50) decibels at the wall of an existing dwelling located on an adjacent nonparticipating property. This is stated in SECS-5, subsection L, Nuisance prevention, item 1. The unit is interpreted as dBA, the standard unit for noise levels.

summary: The ordinance establishes a Solar Energy Collection Systems (SECS) Overlay District as a supplemental zone that "may be created over any of the following zoning districts: AG, Agricultural; AGP, Agricultural Production; IPM, Industrial Park/Manufacturing; IN, Intensive Use; PUD, Planned Unit Development." Within this overlay district, "Permitted Uses" include "SECS, Solar Photovoltaic System" and "SECS, Agrivoltaic System." The overlay district "does not regulate small scale, private solar panels" and "Permitted and Special Uses of the underlying zoning district shall continue in effect, except as may be modified by this Overlay District." The overlay district is intended to add design standards and restrictions but permits large-scale solar systems as a primary use within the overlay. Planned Unit Developments "shall not permit SECS except in conformance with this section." Prohibited uses include "SECS, Concentrated Solar Thermal Power."

summary: Any structure or equipment used for electricity generation or distribution in a SECS shall have the following minimum setbacks: 30’ from a side property line; 30’ from a rear property line. Setbacks do not apply to property lines between separate parcels that are participating in the SECS. Other setback options mentioned include 40’ from the right-of-way of an adjacent public or private road (excluded here as roads are not considered), and an additional 10 feet of setback is required on yards abutting residentially zoned properties or properties containing existing dwellings.
Any structure or equipment used for electricity generation or distribution in a SECS shall have the following minimum setbacks: 1. 40’ from the right-of-way of an adjacent public or private road

SECS-5.E. Buffering: A SECS shall be screened from existing dwellings and residential areas. Where a SECS is adjacent to property that contains an existing dwelling or property that is zoned RR, LR, MR, or MP, the developer or owner of the SECS is responsible for installing the buffer yard; the adjacent property owner shall not have to participate. An additional 10 feet of setback is required in addition to the required setback on the yard(s) abutting the residential property. One (1) deciduous canopy tree planted an average of 30 feet, or one (1) coniferous tree planted an average of 20 feet must be planted within 10 to 30 feet from the property line on the subject property. Deciduous trees must be at least 1.5"  caliper at planting; conifers must be at least 6’ in height. Trees must be properly maintained and replaced if dead, diseased, or damaged. Additional areas may be required to be buffered to screen the SECS from public roads, public buildings and properties, or other sensitive uses, as determined during Development Plan review, with the same standards applying. Other related requirements include ground cover planting and fencing standards.

Section SECS-5, subsection I (Emergency and fire safety) requires that "a sign shall be posted at the entrance(s) of the SECS that includes the SECS owner name, operator name, facility name, emergency contact phone number, physical site address, and gate number (if applicable)." This is the explicit signage requirement stated for Solar Energy Collection Systems (SECS). No other signage requirements are detailed in the provided text.

The ordinance requires a Development Plan approval prior to permits, which must include an Erosion Control Plan (SECS-2.B.7.c) and a Stormwater management plan (SECS-2.B.4). These requirements apply to Solar Energy Collection Systems (SECS) defined as systems supplying energy primarily for off-site or utility use, excluding small-scale private solar panels. summary: Any structure or equipment used for electricity generation or distribution in a SECS shall be separated from certain uses and structures, as follows: 1. 250’ to the wall of an off-site dwelling in existence at the time of Development Plan approval. The ordinance requires a Decommissioning Plan "providing for the removal of all above-ground equipment and restoration of the site upon cessation of operations" and a Decommissioning Funding Mechanism "including financial assurance acceptable to the County sufficient to cover the full cost of decommissioning the project at the end of the life of the project, discontinuation of the project or abandonment of the project." The project shall not occupy more than twelve (12) acres in total land area. summary: The project shall be located at least fifteen (15) miles from any other Solar Energy Conversion Project, whether existing or approved. This applies to Solar Energy Conversion Projects defined as facilities intended to generate electricity primarily for off-site sale or commercial distribution. Other setback requirements in the text apply to distances from airstrips (1 mile), roads and property lines (300 feet), and residences (1 mile with consent), but these do not pertain to separation between solar projects themselves.

The Brown County Zoning Regulation states: 'No land within the jurisdiction of the Brown County Zoning Regulation shall be used for a Solar Energy Conversion Project, except as specifically permitted under subsection (C).' Subsection (C) allows a Solar Energy Conversion Project up to twelve (12) acres as a conditional use upon recommendation of the Brown County Planning Commission following a duly noticed public hearing and approval by the Board of County Commissioners, provided conditions such as size limitation, separation requirement, and compliance with police-power regulations are met. There are no specific district names or abbreviations mentioned where Solar Energy Conversion Projects are unconditionally prohibited or allowed.

No project facilities shall be located closer than three hundred (300) feet from any adjacent property line. Other setback requirements include a one (1) mile setback from any existing public or private airstrip and a one mile setback from any existing inhabited dwelling without written consent, but these do not pertain to property lines or parcels.

No project facilities shall be located closer than three hundred (300) feet from any public road right-of-way. This setback applies to Commercial-Sized Solar Energy Conversion Projects defined as facilities intended to generate electricity primarily for off-site commercial sale or distribution.

Resolution No. 2025-20 requires that the operation of a Solar Energy Conversion Project include a "Stormwater Drainage Plan — prepared by a licensed professional engineer, demonstrating adequate drainage and erosion control." This applies to commercial-sized projects defined as facilities "primarily intended to generate electricity for off-site commercial sale, distribution, or wholesale supply." Other required plans include a Disaster Response Plan, a Decommissioning Plan, and a Decommissioning Funding Mechanism. The project must also meet setback requirements and fencing standards.

The Brown County Zoning Regulation prohibits use of land for a Solar Energy Conversion Project except as specifically permitted under subsection (C). A Solar Energy Conversion Project up to twelve (12) acres may be permitted as a conditional use upon recommendation of the Brown County Planning Commission following a duly noticed public hearing and upon approval by the Board of County Commissioners, provided all of the following conditions are met: (1) Size Limitation: The project shall not occupy more than twelve (12) acres in total land area; (2) Separation Requirement: The project shall be located at least fifteen (15) miles from any other Solar Energy Conversion Project, whether existing or approved; (3) Compliance: The project shall comply with all police-power regulations adopted by Brown County. No specific zoning districts or abbreviations are mentioned in the text for this conditional use allowance.

No project facilities shall be located within one mile of any existing inhabited dwelling without the written consent of the owner and resident at the time operation is commenced. Other setback requirements include: at least fifteen (15) miles from any other Solar Energy Conversion Project, and no closer than three hundred (300) feet from any public road right-of-way or any adjacent property line, but these do not pertain to occupied dwellings.

Section X titled "DECOMMISSIONING, RECLAMATION, OR ABANDONMENT" requires the Applicant to submit a Solar Facility Decommissioning and Reclamation Plan ("DR Plan") describing the manner in which the US Solar Facility will be decommissioned and reclaimed from the Project Area at the end of the Project useful life, the timeframe or termination of the CUP, or upon abandonment. The DR Plan shall include removal of all above ground components, foundation removal to four feet below ground level, road removal and soil decompaction, use of standard decommissioning practices including dismantling, repurposing, salvaging, recycling, or disposing of improvements, and restoration of the Project Site to pre-construction conditions to the extent feasible. A detailed cost estimate for decommission and reclamation must be prepared, including anticipated lifespan, cost details, and full estimated cost without regard to salvage value. The Applicant must submit documentation showing financial capability and provide an escrow account, surety bond, insurance policy, or other financial security approved by the Board to assure removal and restoration. The County may call upon these funds if the Operator fails to comply. Abandonment is defined as one year of no or nominal electrical production without a restoration plan. Restoration must be completed within 18 months after lifespan end or abandonment. Liability provisions ensure the conditional use holder remains liable for expenses beyond the financial security and for misuse of funds. These requirements explicitly apply to Utility-Scale Solar Facilities as defined in the ordinance.

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires an 'Abandonment, Decommissioning, and Reclamation Plan' for CSECS to ensure proper removal and site reclamation, including removal of all structures, foundations, underground wiring, and materials foreign to the site. It mandates annual reporting of power generated to verify production levels and provides a process for issuing a Notice of Abandonment with a 30-day response period. The plan must ensure the site is reclaimed to a useful, nonhazardous condition without delay, including regrading, seeding, and revegetation. Soil testing before and after decommissioning is required to evaluate contamination and develop remediation if needed. Concrete and other construction materials must be removed or disposed of in approved landfills. The operator has one year to complete decommissioning after a notice of abandonment. Additionally, a bond or other financial security equal to estimated decommissioning costs must be posted prior to commencement of use, with provisions for adjustment over the project's life and County rights to call the bond in case of operator default. These requirements apply specifically to Commercial/Utility Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS).

Properties containing CSECS may be enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access. Wildlife friendly fencing, such as a barb-wire fence with smooth wires for the top and bottom strings, or woven wire or other permeable fencing, shall be used where possible. Where wildlife friendly fencing is not utilized, additional wildlife corridors, including escape corridors, may be required in areas prone to grass fires or flooding. Critical electrical and communications equipment may be fenced with chain-link fence topped with barbed wire when such measures are deemed necessary to ensure public safety and provide additional security for the equipment. A 25-foot deep buffer area shall be provided and maintained along property lines between the systems and adjoining non-participating residential properties, or along the Site Area fencing for participating residential properties, for the purpose of screening the residential portion of the property. The buffer may include a combination of berms, fences, and/or vegetation and may occur within the required setbacks on the facility property. Perimeter fencing shall incorporate appropriate safety signage, at a minimum spacing of every 500 feet.

All solar panels must be constructed to minimize glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and must not interfere with traffic, including air traffic, or create a safety hazard as per any Local, State, and Federal laws and regulations. Examples of measures that can be utilized to limit glare include, but are not limited to: 1) Textured glass; 2) Anti-reflective coatings; 3) Screening; 4) Distance; or 5) Positioning units in a manner that reduces glare.

Solar panels shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet in height, measured when oriented at maximum tilt; exceptions include appurtenant enclosed structures which must comply with the height limit for the zoning district, and the Board of County Commissioners may approve modifications to allow greater height if necessary to accommodate slopes without grading or agrivoltaics, provided the height does not negatively impact nearby land uses or the character of the area.

The CSECS Site Area shall be limited to no more than 1,000 acres total, unless the Board of County Commissioners approves a modification from this standard based on site specific characteristics which are determined to aid in the preservation of rural character or natural features or to promote the shared agricultural use of the property. The size of the CSECS Site Area is measured as the cumulative total of the Solar Modules within the facility, with panels in their most horizontal position, excluding access drives, batteries, transformers, ancillary structures, or their required setbacks. Additionally, Limited Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (LSECS) are limited to no more than 20 contiguous acres total, but this smaller limit applies only to LSECS, not CSECS.

The operational noise generated from the solar installation equipment, including inverters, battery energy storage systems, components, and associated ancillary equipment shall not exceed a noise level of 60 decibels (60 dBA) as measured at the property line or 500 feet from an existing residence (building permit plans have been submitted or the residence is on-site at time of conditional use permit approval). Applicants must submit equipment and component manufacturer noise ratings to demonstrate compliance. Transformers, inverters, or other sound or vibration generating equipment must be placed so that low level recurring ambient noise does not exceed this limit. Construction noise shall be analyzed and mitigated separately.

A 25-foot deep buffer area shall be provided, and maintained, along property lines between the systems and adjoining non-participating residential properties, or along the Site Area fencing for participating residential properties, for the purpose of screening the residential portion of the property. The buffer may include a combination of berms, fences, and/or vegetation and may occur within the required setbacks on the facility property. Additional setbacks may be required to mitigate site specific issues or to provide for frontage roads, cross-access easements, commercial corridors, or other means of egress/ ingress. All structures shall be located in compliance with the setbacks required for that zoning district.

Facilities shall be located a minimum of 200 feet from historic trails that are identified on the County GIS map. Temporary construction barriers shall be installed along the perimeter of the drip-line of a protected stand of mature trees, or 200 feet from the historic trail, or at the boundary of other protected environmentally sensitive lands. The maximum protection limit of 40% of the property set in Section 12-314 is not applicable to the CSECS projects; rather the area designated for protection shall be determined with the review of each conditional use permit.

The ordinance requires that CSECS projects "utilize existing terrain, vegetation, and structures to screen the project from off-site view, to the extent possible. If this is not possible, additional screening may be required." Ground around and under solar panels and in designated buffer areas "shall be planted and maintained in perennial vegetated ground cover or agricultural plants that are managed to prevent erosion and runoff." A 25-foot deep buffer area "shall be provided, and maintained, along property lines between the systems and adjoining non-participating residential properties, or along the Site Area fencing for participating residential properties, for the purpose of screening the residential portion of the property." This buffer "may include a combination of berms, fences, and/or vegetation and may occur within the required setbacks on the facility property." A Landscaping Plan is required detailing "all proposed changes to the landscape of the site required to accommodate buffering or screening from adjacent properties," including installation, establishment, and maintenance of buffering or screening landscaping. Fencing must be wildlife-friendly where possible, with wildlife corridors as determined necessary. These requirements apply explicitly to Commercial/Utility Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS).

Section 12-306-49.05(l) requires that "Perimeter fencing shall incorporate appropriate safety signage, at a minimum spacing of every 500 feet." It also mandates that "Signage, including addresses for each fenced area, shall be provided as required by the Emergency 911 dispatch." Additionally, section 12-306-49.05(k)(3) states that "Signage for the battery energy storage system shall be in compliance with ANSI Z535 and shall include the following information: the type of technology associated with the battery energy storage system; any special hazards associated; the type of suppression system installed in the area of the battery energy storage system, and 24-hour emergency contact information." These signage requirements apply explicitly to Commercial/Utility Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS).

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Commercial/Utility Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS). It requires that "ground around and under solar panels/Arrays and in designated buffer areas shall be planted and maintained in perennial vegetated ground cover or agricultural plants that are managed to prevent erosion and runoff" (12-306-49.05(g)). It mandates preservation of existing topsoil during grading and construction, with topsoil "stockpiled on the site" and "redistributed uniformly on the surface of all areas to be vegetated" (12-306-49.05(h)). The application must include a "grading/vegetation removal plan which includes all proposed changes to the topography and vegetation on the site" (12-306-49.06(d)(6)) and a "stormwater management plan with supporting calculations" documenting runoff conveyance and possible detention (12-306-49.06(d)(7)). A "soil sampling plan" is required to characterize soil health and contamination before construction, after construction, prior to decommissioning, and following reclamation, with remediation plans if contamination occurs (12-306-49.06(d)(17)). Additionally, a "vegetation management and agrivoltaic plan" must be submitted outlining measures to "minimize erosion, maintain soil health, and accommodate the proposed agrivoltaic use" (12-306-49.06(d)(14)). The decommissioning/reclamation plan must ensure the site is reclaimed with "regrading, with a minimum of ground disturbance, seeding of the land after the removal of equipment, and revegetation of reclaimed soil areas" and soil testing to evaluate contamination and remediation (12-306-49.18). These requirements apply specifically to CSECS as defined in the ordinance, which includes systems "that convert solar energy into electricity for the primary purpose of storage and sales of generated electricity" and includes appurtenant facilities. The ordinance also provides options and conditions for grading limits, topsoil displacement, and soil removal, including allowances for modifications by the Board of County Commissioners under certain conditions.

summary: The solar panels/Array and appurtenant structures shall be located a minimum of 500 feet from any existing residence (building permit plans have been submitted or the residence is on-site at time of conditional use permit approval), as measured from the dwelling, unless a lesser setback is agreed to by the owner of the residence. Battery storage shall not be located within 500 feet of an existing residence (building permit plans have been submitted or the residence is on-site at time of conditional use permit approval). Written evidence of the setback agreements, including any additional landscaping, shall be provided to the Planning Office as part of the conditional use permit application and, with the approval of the conditional use permit, shall be filed with the Register of Deeds by Planning Staff, at applicant’s expense.

Section 12-306-49.04 states that "Key issues to be considered with the review of the application include, but are not limited to: 1) Visual impact;". Section 12-306-49.06 requires detailed application materials including "Landscaping Plan; A landscape plan detailing all proposed changes to the landscape of the site required to accommodate buffering or screening from adjacent properties" and "Vegetation Management and Agrivoltaic Plan; A vegetation management and agrivoltaic plan detailing all proposed changes to the vegetation of the site and outlining all proposed agrivoltaic uses". Section 12-306-49.05 d.2 requires the system to "Utilize existing terrain, vegetation, and structures to screen the project from off-site view, to the extent possible. If this is not possible, additional screening may be required". Section 12-306-49.05 j.5 requires "a 25-foot deep buffer area shall be provided, and maintained, along property lines between the systems and adjoining non-participating residential properties, or along the Site Area fencing for participating residential properties, for the purpose of screening the residential portion of the property." These provisions collectively establish explicit visual impact assessment requirements for Commercial/Utility Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS) as part of the conditional use permit application and review process.

Section 9.10.05, Site Development Standards, subsection 2.A states: 'Lot coverage: No more than one percent of the gross site area shall be occupied by enclosed buildings and structures.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for Commercial Solar Conversion Systems (CSCS). The unit is expressed as a percentage of the total land area. summary: Section 3, item 8 requires that "a 25-foot-deep buffer area shall be provided, and maintained, along property lines between the systems and adjoining residential properties for the purpose of screening the residential portion of the property." The buffer "may include a combination of berms, fences, and/or vegetation" and "shall screen ground level views and activity." Specific landscaping requirements include "a combination of evergreen trees that are 5-6 ft. in height at time of planting and deciduous trees, which may include fruit trees, that are 5-6 ft. in height at time of planting," with trees placed "on average at 25 ft. or less on center." Berms "shall generally be constructed with a 3:1 side slope to rise ratio, 4-6 ft. above the adjacent grade, with a 3 ft. wide top" and be seeded with native prairie grasses and forbs. Buffer fencing "shall be at least seventy-five (75) percent visually solid" but "shall not be the primary method" and "shall not include chain link fencing with slats." The Planning Commission may approve phased screening plans and existing vegetation, topography, buildings, or open space may be considered as part of the required screening. These requirements apply to Commercial/Utility Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS) as defined as systems "that convert solar energy into electricity for the primary purpose of storage or sales of generated electricity" and include appurtenant facilities. The buffer area is "designed to buffer the view of the facility from the road and any adjoining residences."

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Commercial/Utility Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS). Key provisions include: "Ground around and under solar panels/Arrays and in designated buffer areas shall be planted and maintained in perennial vegetated ground cover or agricultural plants that are managed to prevent erosion and runoff"; "All grading and construction activities shall preserve existing topsoil" with requirements to minimize displacement, stockpile, redistribute, and restrict removal except as required by KDHE; grading on prime farmland or farmland of statewide importance is limited to "not exceed 5% of the site area unless a modification is granted" and may be increased to "not to exceed 10%" on previously disturbed land; applicants must submit a "grading/vegetation removal plan" and a "stormwater management plan with supporting calculations"; during construction, "Temporary construction barriers and erosion protection control shall be installed"; a "vegetation management and/or agrivoltaic plan" must include measures to "minimize erosion, maintain soil health"; and a "soil sampling plan" is required to monitor soil health and contamination with remediation plans if needed. These requirements apply specifically to CSECS, defined as systems "that convert solar energy into electricity for the primary purpose of storage or sales of generated electricity" and include appurtenant facilities.

The ordinance states that "all RECS development, other than a small private use system, will require submittals to the Jackson County Planning Commission and Governing Body for the Development Plan approval and establishment of an overlay zone." Commercial Scale Systems are defined as "5 acres or more." No specific district names or abbreviations are provided for where Commercial Scale Systems are permitted as a special use or similar. Other options include small "home" RECS allowed by right upon certain findings by the Zoning Administrator, with detailed requirements listed for height, setbacks, and parcel size.

The solar panels and appurtenant structures shall be located a minimum of 1,000 feet from any existing residence, as measured from the dwelling, unless a lesser setback is agreed to by the owner of the residence. Buffering or screening landscaping, fencing, agricultural uses, and access drives may be within this 1000-foot setback. Additionally, if there are residential parcels of land within the Project Extent that are not owned by the Operator or under any other agreement with the Operator (Non-Participating Parcels), and if the same adjoin the Project Area on two sides of the property, or if more than 50% of the exterior property lines adjoin the Project Area, then all setbacks shall be increased by 50 feet along the property lines of the Project Area.

If this is not possible, additional screening may be required' (Section 3.3.D). Setbacks and buffering/screening requirements include a minimum 1,000-foot setback from residences, a 25-foot buffer area for screening with berms, fences, and vegetation designed to 'minimize land disturbance and to create a visual buffer' (Section 3.8). The applicant must submit detailed site plans showing existing and proposed conditions, including vegetation, topography, and screening plans (Section 4.2 and 4.3). A Landscaping Plan detailing buffering or screening landscaping and a Vegetation Management or Agrivoltaic Plan outlining vegetation changes and management are also required (Sections 4.6 and 4.7). Additional requirements include FAA approval if within one mile of airports, solar glare hazard analysis, environmental assessments, road use agreements, and obtaining a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) before construction.

No SES-U shall be placed such that concentrated solar glare casts onto adjacent properties or roadways. The applicant shall provide a Solar Glare Hazard Analysis utilizing the latest version of the Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT), or its equivalent, to evaluate the solar glare aviation hazard. The full report for each flight path and observation point, as well as the contact information, shall be submitted to the Zoning Administrator at least 30 days before the required public hearing for the Conditional Use Permit for the SES-U. Any applicable SES-U design changes (e.g., module tilt, module reflectivity, etc.) after initial submittal shall be rerun in the SGHAT tool and the new full report shall be sent without undue delay to the County for accurate records of the as-built system. The analysis shall provide an assessment of when and where glare will occur throughout the year. If solar glare is predicted, the applicant shall provide mitigation measures to address the impacts of solar glare. Mitigation measures may include and are not limited to textured glass, anti-reflective coatings, screening, distance, and angling of solar PV modules in a manner that reduces glare to surrounding land uses of non-participating property owners.

The SES-U infrastructure, such as solar collector panels, shall not exceed fifteen feet (15’) in height; provided, said height restriction shall not apply to substation facilities or transmission lines. All other structures shall have a maximum height of 35 feet. The height restriction of 15 feet applies specifically to solar collector panels, which are part of the SES-U infrastructure. The 35 feet maximum height applies to all other structures except substations and transmission lines.

All SES-U structures shall be setback from the project boundary lines and public rights-of-way at least forty (40) feet. Additional setbacks may be required to mitigate site specific issues or to provide for access, road or commercial corridors. No SES-U shall be located nearer than one (1) mile from the incorporated limits of any city in Marion County. In the event that an applicant desires to locate a SES-U within this one-mile buffer requirement, the application may only be approved if findings are made by the Board of County Commissioners that circumstances exist which are believed to necessitate the need for a deviation from this buffer requirement.

summary: The ordinance requires that "Applicant shall submit a Decommissioning Plan with the application for a CSEP Special Use." The Plan must describe "the manner in which the CSEP improvements will be dismantled and removed from the site within 18 months of the abandonment or the end of useful life of the CSEP or of such improvement and shall require the removal of all above-ground components of the CSEP." Foundations and access roads must be removed "to the satisfaction of the property owner(s)," and the site restored "as nearly as practical to its condition at the time the CSEP Special Use Permit was granted." The ordinance also requires a "bond for complying with Section J herein" (the financial agreement) to be approved before construction begins, which must be maintained until decommissioning is complete and any damages to public roads caused by decommissioning are paid. The ordinance further states that the CSEP is "deemed abandoned at the end of a one-year period" if it does not produce electricity and there is no plan to restore it, and the Governing Body may require decommissioning or undertake it using the bond proceeds. Transfer of the Special Use requires approval and the new holder must meet the decommissioning funding requirements. No other options or conditions for decommissioning are provided.

The ordinance requires that "The entire CSEP perimeter shall be enclosed with a security type fence and all gates to fences shall be equipped with locks and shall always remain locked except for those times when the owner and/or operator is using the gates for ingress or egress." summary: The ordinance explicitly requires a decommissioning/reclamation plan for Commercial/Utility-Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS). The plan must ensure "facilities are properly removed after their useful life," including removal of "all structures, foundations, and underground wiring," site reclamation with "regrading, with a minimum of ground disturbance, seeding of the land after the removal of equipment, and revegetation of reclaimed soil areas," and soil testing with remediation if needed. Decommissioning must occur "within a 6-month time frame" if the system "do[es] not produce electricity and have no demonstrated plan to restore to operating condition and before the end of the life span of the conditional use permit." The operator must submit "a report of power generated by the CSECS annually." Upon a "Notice of Abandonment," the operator has "one year to complete the decommissioning of the utility/commercial-scale solar installation and reclamation of the area." The plan must include "estimated decommissioning costs in current dollars and the method for ensuring that will be available for decommissioning and reclamation." The applicant must post "a bond, with the Saline County Clerk, establish an escrow account, or provide such other financial security deemed acceptable by the County, in an amount equal to the estimated decommissioning costs." The bond must be "posted prior to the commencement of the use" and "include a mechanism for adjustment over the life of the project," including annual inflation adjustments and recalculations every five years. The County may call the bond if the operator is in default. These requirements apply specifically to CSECS, defined as systems "commonly referred to as ‘solar farms’, that convert solar energy into electricity for the primary purpose of storage and sales of generated electricity," with site areas up to 640 contiguous acres. The ordinance also distinguishes other system types: Personal or Accessory Solar Energy Conversion Systems (for on-site use, exempt from CUP and these standards) and Limited Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (LSECS) (up to 20 contiguous acres, typically cooperative use, with some standards applying).
