summary: The ordinance requires that "the plans for a proposed Solar Farm shall include a decommissioning plan for the remediation of the area of the Solar Farm upon the cessation of operations of the Solar Farm." Cessation of operations for more than 365 consecutive days triggers the decommissioning plan and termination of the Solar Farm permit. The plan must provide for "the removal of the solar panels, ancillary structures, and other infrastructure" and restore the land to a condition "free from any and all environmental hazards and free of all equipment, components and other debris," except as desired by the lessor. It must also provide for remediation of environmental hazards as determined by EPA, DEQ, or the Acadia Parish Government. Additionally, "applicant shall provide a bond or other acceptable financial security, payable to the Parish, to ensure the proper decommissioning or other closure of the Solar Farm." The bond amount is required by La. R.S. 30:1154(A)(9)(a) and ensures compliance with the chapter and decommissioning costs.

The buffer zone shall include a setback of at least fifty (50) feet from any adjacent property line at the time of the application. Other setback distances mentioned include not less than one hundred (100) feet from the center of any adjacent public roadway and at least one hundred fifty (150) feet from any residence, but only the 50 feet setback from adjacent property lines directly pertains to property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, parcels, and/or subdivisions.

The buffer zone may include a setback of not less than one hundred (100) feet from the center of any adjacent public roadway. This applies to Solar Farms with a generation capacity of at least fifty (50) kilowatts (kW) direct current (dc) or more, which are not intended for a single residential dwelling or commercial property. Other buffer zone requirements include setbacks of at least one hundred fifty (150) feet from any residence and fifty (50) feet from any adjacent property line, but these do not pertain to roads.

Sec. [ 1 ]-7 - Buffer zones requires the plans for a proposed Solar Farm to include the provision of a buffer zone around the perimeter of the Solar Farm. The buffer zone may include a setback of not less than one hundred (100) feet from the center of any adjacent public roadway, at least one hundred fifty (150) feet from any residence, and fifty (50) feet from any adjacent property line at the time of the application. Each buffer zone shall include a stand of trees or native prairie grassland, between the operational area of the Solar Farm and the adjacent roadway or property owner which, at maturity, will screen the Solar Farm from view, the sufficiency of which is subject to review and approval as part of the plans. The buffer zone shall be maintained in such a manner so as to not present a nuisance as provided for otherwise in the Code of Ordinances. Maintenance thereof shall be subject to the enforcement provisions in regard to nuisances. Additionally, Sec. [ 1 ]-11 - Maintenance Plan requires the plans to include a schedule of maintenance of the Solar Farm and buffer zone including but not limited to grass cutting, shrubbery and tree maintenance, and general upkeep of the premises. Adherence to the maintenance plan is subject to periodic or random inspections by the Parish, with penalties for failure to comply.

The ordinance requires that "the plans for a proposed Solar Farm shall include a drainage plan" which "shall include a hydrologic and hydraulic (H&H) analysis to establish that the Solar Farm will not have any adverse impact on the Parish drainage system or adjacent property owners; alternatively, the drainage plan shall establish a plan for remediating any adverse impact on the Parish drainage system or adjacent property owners that may result from the construction of and the operation of the Solar Farm." The drainage plan must also include "an ongoing schedule of water sampling and testing of water runoff from the site of the Solar Farm, the schedule of which shall be (i) during the construction of the Solar Farm, not less than once every six (6) months and (ii) after the Solar Farm is placed in service, not less than once every five (5) year period." In the event of failure to satisfy the drainage plan requirements, the permittee must remediate deficiencies within 30 days or face fines. The Parish may enforce the drainage plan through existing ordinances. Other related requirements include submission of a site plan with a drainage study as part of the permit application, and plans must be approved by the Parish engineer. These requirements apply to Solar Farms defined as having a generation capacity of at least fifty (50) kilowatts (kW) direct current (dc) or more, which are not intended solely for a single residential dwelling or commercial property.

The ordinance states, 'all Solar Farms shall be and are hereby considered as an industrial activity under any such zoning ordinance, and will be assigned the zoning classification of [I-1 (Light Industrial)].' There is no mention of Solar Farms or utility-scale solar energy systems being permitted as a special use or requiring approval by a zoning appeals board or similar conditional permitting process.

The buffer zone shall include a setback of at least one hundred fifty (150) feet from any residence. This applies to Solar Farms defined as having a generation capacity of at least fifty (50) kilowatts (kW) direct current (dc) or more, which are commercial-scale systems. Other buffer zone setbacks mentioned include not less than one hundred (100) feet from the center of any adjacent public roadway and fifty (50) feet from any adjacent property line, but these do not pertain to occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, or residences.

Subsection O.23 requires submission of a decommissioning and final immovable property reclamation plan ("decommissioning plan") in compliance with state law as contained in RS 30:1154, subsection (c). In the absence of state law, the Zoning Commission/Parish Council may establish the requirements for a decommissioning plan, which will include a surety bond or other suitable security to guarantee the execution of the decommissioning plan.
section: 17-2038. - Solar energy farm facility standards for development

summary: A minimum eight-foot security fence shall be placed around the perimeter of the SEFF to prevent unauthorized access. Fencing shall be agricultural-style woven wire fencing, chain link, or an alternative providing an equal or better measure of security and safety, as approved under the conditional use permit. Perimeter barbed wire fencing is not required, unless state or federal codes or regulations require otherwise. The fencing shall encompass the perimeter of facility inside of the vegetative buffer required under subsection N. Lock boxes and keys to the facility shall be stored at locked entrances for emergency access. Entrances shall be equipped with lights for nighttime illumination.

Subsection O.21 requires submission of a vehicular glare analysis on the layout, mounting and movement of the solar panels and demonstration that the glare will be minimized and will not interfere with vehicular traffic. The glare analysis methodology shall be consistent with that described in Ho, C. K., Ghanbari, C. M., and Diver, R. B., 2011, Methodology to Assess Potential Glint and Glare Hazards, as published in the ASME Journal of Solar Engineering, Vol. 133, August 2011. Glare impacts must fall within the "Low Potential for After-image" region shown in Figure 2 of that publication. Subsection O.22 requires submission of an aviation glare analysis developed by a qualified third-party contractor showing any potential aviation glare hazards that would arise from the facility and their effect on local airports and/or flightpaths. The aviation analysis shall be performed in accordance with Federal Aviation Administration policy related to solar systems, published on May 11, 2021, at 86 FR 2580 I, as updated but subsequently issued policies in force at the time an application is submitted.
section: 17-2038. - Solar energy farm facility standards for development.

summary: All solar panel structures and supporting equipment shall be restricted to a maximum height of 16 feet. Medium and low voltage collection lines shall not exceed the height of more than eight feet above the ground. Meteorology (met) towers necessary for monitoring of the SEFF shall not exceed 50 feet in height. These height restrictions shall not apply to interconnection equipment (i.e., collector substation, switchyard, high voltage transmission lines) to ensure public safety and to ensure compliance with electrical safety codes and standards.
section: 17-2038. - Solar energy farm facility standards for development.

summary: Minimum lot size of the facility shall be 20 contiguous acres or greater. This applies to solar energy farm facilities (SEFFs) defined as power generating facilities constructed on immovable property for the purpose of producing photovoltaic electricity, solar heated fluids, or solar thermal electricity intended for distribution and sale through the power grid. The unit 'acres' is a standard measure of land area.
section: 17-2038. - Solar energy farm facility standards for development.

summary: The SEFF shall not exceed 50 A-weighted decibels (dBA) or five dBA over existing ambient levels, whichever is greater, as measured at the facility's immovable property boundary(s) while the facility is in operation. A noise analysis demonstrating compliance with this noise standard shall be provided with the application. The study shall be conducted in conformance with American National Standard ANSI/ASA S1.13-2020: Measurement of Sound Pressure Levels in Air (as supplemented and updated as an American National Standard) and shall be completed by an independent third party.
section: 17-2038. - Solar energy farm facility standards for development

summary: All solar panels, support structures, inverters, transformers, and mechanical equipment within the SEFF shall be setback at least the greater of: 1) Five hundred feet from any occupied residence or formal place of worship; 2) Five hundred feet from the boundary of any nearby area designated for residential neighborhood or employment (industrial/business park); 3) Five hundred feet from the perimeter boundary of the SEFF if the facility is permitted in a residential neighborhood or employment (industrial/business park) area; 4) One hundred feet from any adjacent property line; 5) All lease/property boundaries of a SEFF shall be a minimum of 300 feet from any public road right-of-way. The setback from adjacent property lines is 100 feet, which is the most restrictive fixed distance directly pertaining to property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, parcels, and/or subdivisions.

All lease/property boundaries of a SEFF shall be a minimum of 300 feet from any public road right-of-way to allow for commercial or residential corridor development. Other setback options include 500 feet from any occupied residence or formal place of worship; 500 feet from the boundary of any nearby area designated for residential neighborhood or employment (industrial/business park); 500 feet from the perimeter boundary of the SEFF if the facility is permitted in a residential neighborhood or employment (industrial/business park) area; and 100 feet from any adjacent property line.

Subsection N requires that prior to commencing construction of the SEFF, a perimeter landscaping buffer shall be planted (but with allowances for construction ingress and egress). The buffer shall be designed and certified by a registered landscape architect to create an opaque vegetative "hedge" within two years of commercial operation along all property lines that are oriented to public roads, highways and existing occupied residences within 500 feet of the SEFF boundary. The vegetative perimeter shall consist of trees, foliage, bamboo, etc. such that the facility equipment is concealed from public view. Vegetation shall be maintained for the duration of the SEFF's operation. The Zoning Commission/Parish Council may require visual screening with fabric or solid fencing where special circumstances related to adjacent occupied structures warrant such treatment.

summary: Subsection J states: 'One or more signs shall be affixed to the fence at the main entrance identifying the owner of the facility and emergency contact information.' This signage requirement applies to solar energy farm facilities (SEFFs), which are defined as 'Power generating facilities constructed on immovable property for the purpose of producing photovoltaic electricity, solar heated fluids, or solar thermal electricity intended for distribution and sale through the power grid.'

Renderings must illustrate the visual appearance of the facility from relevant public roads and from areas of existing occupied residential or commercial development. This visual impact assessment is part of the SEFF permit application requirements. summary: Section 122-177 explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for utility-scale solar energy systems, stating: 'Any Solar Farm that has reached the end of its useful life, ceases to generate power as set forth in Section 122-177(c) below, or has been abandoned shall be removed in accordance with the Decommissioning Plan.' Removal must commence within ninety (90) days and be completed within twelve (12) months after discontinued operations. The Decommissioning Plan must include: '(a) the anticipated life of the Facility, (b) the estimated decommissioning cost in current dollars, (c) how said estimate was determined, including how credit for salvage value was calculated, (d) the manner in which the Facility will be decommissioned, and (e) an acceptable performance guarantee to cover the cost of decommissioning.' Additionally, Section 122-171(q)(8) requires a performance guarantee in the form of a bond, letter of credit, or cash escrow, with a minimum amount of $500,000.00, to cover decommissioning costs. The ordinance also provides enforcement mechanisms if removal is not completed timely, including use of the performance guarantee and legal means. Abandonment is defined as failure to generate electricity for more than one (1) year without written consent of the Parish Engineer.

Section 122-171(e) requires "A minimum eight (8) foot security fence (height and material to be established through the Solar Farm Permit process) shall be placed around the entire perimeter of the Facility to deter individuals from entering the premises and all electrical control equipment shall be equipped with a lock to prevent access." Section 122-171(f) further requires signage on the fence, including "One or more signs shall be affixed to the fence at the main entrance identifying the owner (and operator if there is a separate operator) of the Facility and emergency contact information. Warning signage, including the identification of the owner or operator and emergency contact information, shall be placed every three hundred (300) feet around the security perimeter fence of the Facility." These fencing requirements apply specifically to utility-scale solar project facilities ("Solar Farms") as defined in the ordinance.
section: Sec. 122-171. Utility scale solar project facility development and design standards.

summary: Section 122-171(b) states: 'All photovoltaic panels located in a Facility with rotating panels shall be restricted to a maximum height of the torque tube to sixteen (16) feet measured from the ground to the top of the torque tube.' It also provides an alternative for non-rotating panels: 'Facilities that have non-rotating (fixed) photovoltaic panels shall be limited to a maximum photovoltaic panel height of eighteen (18) feet measured from the ground to the top of the photovoltaic panel.' The most restrictive maximum height is 16 feet for rotating panels. The units are feet.
section: Sec. 122-171. Utility scale solar project facility development and design standards.

summary: Section 122-171(a) states: 'Minimum Lot Size: A Facility shall not be constructed on aggregate parcels of immovable property that are less than twenty (20) contiguous acres in size.' This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for utility-scale solar energy systems (Utility Scale Solar Project Facility or Solar Farm) intended for offsite electricity generation and sale. The unit is expressed as acres, a standard area measurement.
section: Sec. 122-171. Utility scale solar project facility development and design standards.

summary: All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with a Facility (excluding perimeter security fencing) shall be set back a minimum of one hundred (100) feet from public roads and neighboring immovable property boundaries, unless the adjoining immovable property boundary is wooded with no residence on the immovable property, in which case the setback shall be no less than fifty (50) feet. Inverters, transformers, and mechanical equipment shall be set back a minimum of one hundred (100) feet from adjacent immovable property boundaries even if the adjacent boundary is wooded. If an adjoining section of immovable property has an existing occupied residence or formal place of worship, all photovoltaic solar panels and support structures, including inverters, transformers, and mechanical equipment, shall be set back a minimum of five hundred (500) feet from the occupied residence or formal place of worship. These requirements are not applicable to adjoining landowners participating in the development of the Facility.
section: Sec. 122-171. Utility scale solar project facility development and design standards.

summary: All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with a Facility (excluding perimeter security fencing) shall be set back a minimum of one hundred (100) feet from public roads and neighboring immovable property boundaries, unless the adjoining immovable property boundary is wooded with no residence on the immovable property, in which case the setback shall be no less than fifty (50) feet. Inverters, transformers, and mechanical equipment shall be set back a minimum of one hundred (100) feet from adjacent immovable property boundaries even if the adjacent boundary is wooded. If an adjoining section of immovable property has an existing occupied residence or formal place of worship (e.g., Church, Synagogue, Mosque, etc.) all photovoltaic solar panels and support structures, including inverters, transformers, and mechanical equipment, associated with a Facility shall be set back a minimum of five hundred (500) feet from the occupied residence or formal place of worship. These requirements are not applicable to adjoining landowners participating in the development of the Facility.
section: Sec. 122-171. Utility scale solar project facility development and design standards

summary: Section 122-171(k) requires that "A Facility shall install perimeter landscaping that creates an opaque vegetative/foliage 'hedge' along each Facility property boundary that is adjacent to public roads, highways, and existing occupied residences within five hundred (500) feet of the Facility's property boundary." The vegetative perimeter "shall consist of trees, foliage, bamboo, etc., such that the Facility equipment is concealed from view from the Facility boundaries." Landscaping "shall be maintained and in good condition for the life of the Facility," with all unhealthy (sixty (60) percent dead or greater) and dead material replaced within one (1) year or the next appropriate planting period. "Any preexisting natural barrier that creates such conditions shall be deemed sufficient." Roads internal to the Facility are not subject to vegetative requirements.
section: Sec. 122-171. Utility scale solar project facility development and design standards.

summary: Section 122-171(f) states: "One or more signs shall be affixed to the fence at the main entrance identifying the owner (and operator if there is a separate operator) of the Facility and emergency contact information. Warning signage, including the identification of the owner or operator and emergency contact information, shall be placed every three hundred (300) feet around the security perimeter fence of the Facility." This applies to utility scale solar project facilities ("Solar Farms") as defined in the ordinance. No alternative options or conditions for signage requirements are provided in the text.
section: Sec. 122-171. Utility scale solar project facility development and design standards.

summary: The ordinance requires a drainage plan that "ensures that watershed, runoff and/or drainage from the Facility area flows to the appropriate ditches/channels, as identified by the Parish Engineer, so as to be disbursed appropriately." The plan "shall demonstrate that no immovable property within a mile radius of the Facility will experience measurably adverse impacts from watershed, runoff and/or drainage from the Facility site." The drainage plan "shall be reviewed by the Parish Engineer and additional requirements regarding drainage may be imposed on the Facility." The application must also indicate if a storm water permit from the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality for construction, operation, or both is required. Additionally, during decommissioning, the ordinance requires to "Stabilize or revegetate the Solar Farm site as necessary to minimize erosion." The contour of the property "shall be returned to what it was at the inception of the project, or as similar as reasonably possible," except where the property owner consents to altered contour and permanent drainage structures are in place. The Parish Engineer may allow leaving landscaping or below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and vegetation disruption. These requirements apply to utility-scale solar energy systems defined as "a solar electric power generating facility constructed on immovable property for the purpose of producing photovoltaic electricity... The power generated is sold to power purchasers for distribution throughout the power grid."
section: Sec. 122-171. Utility scale solar project facility development and design standards

summary: If an adjoining section of immovable property has an existing occupied residence or formal place of worship (e.g., Church, Synagogue, Mosque, etc.) all photovoltaic solar panels and support structures, including inverters, transformers, and mechanical equipment, associated with a Facility shall be set back a minimum of five hundred (500) feet from the occupied residence or formal place of worship. Other setback options include: 100 feet from public roads and neighboring immovable property boundaries; 50 feet if the adjoining property boundary is wooded with no residence; and 100 feet for inverters, transformers, and mechanical equipment from adjacent property boundaries even if wooded. These requirements do not apply to adjoining landowners participating in the development of the Facility.
section: Sec. 122-171. Utility scale solar project facility development and design standards.

summary: The ordinance requires in the Solar Farm Permit application to "Demonstrate the visual impact of the proposed Solar Farm using photos or renditions of the Facility with consideration given to vegetative plantings and setback requirements." It also requires including "the Facility's landscaping plan demonstrating how the requirements of Section 122-171(k) herein will be met." This is found in Section 122-171(p)(8). The ordinance defines a Utility Scale Solar Project Facility as "a solar electric power generating facility constructed on immovable property for the purpose of producing photovoltaic electricity... The power generated is sold to power purchasers for distribution throughout the power grid." The visual impact assessment is part of the permit application process reviewed by the Parish Engineer, who may employ outside experts if needed. The permit process includes evaluation, approval or denial, and appeals. Other application requirements include facility description, permits, lease, economic impact, boundaries, site plan, wildlife, environmental and health safety standards, elevation, drainage, waste, wind, lighting, transportation, vegetative maintenance, public safety, sound, magnetic field, telecommunications interference, photovoltaic panel angles (glare analysis excluded here), aviation analysis, and decommissioning plan. The Parish Engineer must ensure the Facility will conform to all requirements before recommending permit issuance.
section: Sec. 122-171. Utility scale solar project facility development and design standards

summary: Section 26-99(f) Decommissioning explicitly requires that a Decommission Plan be submitted and approved with the Development Permit. The Plan must include: "An estimated cost of decommissioning, net of salvage value, prepared by a licensed professional engineer"; "Decommissioning shall include disposal of non-utility owned equipment, including but not limited to solar panels, buildings, electrical components, roads, fencing, any cabling and other underground components up to thirty-six (36) inches below grade"; "Restoration of the property to a condition reasonably similar to its condition before development of the Solar Energy Facility, unless a written agreement is reached with the land owner to leave the property in its current condition"; and "Remediation of any environmental hazards on the Facility Site as a result of the operation of the Solar Energy Facility." Decommissioning must begin within thirty (30) days after a Decommissioning Event, which includes abandonment (failure to operate for more than six (6) months without written consent) or end of occupancy (expiration or termination of right to occupy the Facility Site). The Facility Owner must post a surety bond at 125% of the estimated decommissioning cost (less salvage value) naming the Parish as beneficiary at least thirty (30) days prior to construction. Failure to initiate or complete decommissioning allows the Parish to take legal action including calling the bond or revoking permits. These requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities defined as renewable energy facilities designed to provide alternative power for wholesale or retail consumption, thus covering utility-scale solar energy systems.

Security fencing shall be required around the perimeter of any ground mounted Solar Energy Facility. The fencing shall be installed a minimum of twenty-five (25) feet from the property line of any adjacent, non-participating parcel or public street right-of-way. Fencing shall not be installed within any required Landscape Buffer zone, but may be installed in the required setback. Lock boxes and keys must be provided at locked entrances for emergency personnel and appropriate access. Appropriate emergency contact signage shall be placed at the entrance of the Solar Energy Facility and every two hundred (200) feet along the fencing. The fencing required hereunder shall be maintained in good condition. Failure to maintain the fencing required hereunder shall constitute a violation of this Division. The fencing requirements specified hereunder shall continue notwithstanding the fact that a Solar Energy Facility is no longer operational and/or falls into disuse unless and until the Solar Energy Facility is decommissioned. The Facility Owner shall take reasonable steps to design and install fencing in a manner as to allow wildlife corridors through and around the Facility Site where requested by the Director.

Section 26-99(d)(1)(k) requires a Glint and Glare Study that "demonstrates either that the panels will be sited, designed, and installed to eliminate glint and glare effects on roadway users, nearby residences, commercial areas, and other sensitive viewing locations, or that the applicant will use all reasonably available mitigation techniques to reduce glint and glare to the lowest achievable levels." The study "will assess and quantify potential glint and glare effects and address the potential health, safety, and visual impacts associated with glint and glare." This applies to Solar Energy Facilities defined as "a renewable energy facility designed to provide alternative power for either wholesale or retail consumption," including utility-scale systems. No other options or conditions for glare restrictions are provided in the text.

Section 26-99(c)(4) states: 'Solar panels shall not exceed a height of twenty-five (25) fifteen (15) feet.' The height of solar panels is measured relative to the average elevation of the proposed finished grade to the highest point of the panel or supporting structure, whichever is higher. Solar panels which track the sun’s movement shall be measured at their highest vertical position. The most restrictive maximum height is fifteen (15) feet.

The routine operation of a Solar Energy Facility shall not produce noise that exceeds sixty (60) dBA, as measured at the property lines of the Facility Site, unless the Owner and the Board agree to a higher noise level in the Development Permit. This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems defined as Solar Energy Facilities designed to provide alternative power for wholesale or retail consumption.

The Solar Energy Facility shall be set back a minimum of fifty (50) feet from the property line of any adjacent, non-participating parcel. The setback shall be measured from the edge of the solar panel or supporting structure, whichever is closest, to the property line from which the setback is being measured. Fencing and buffering shall be allowed in the Setback. Additionally, security fencing shall be installed a minimum of twenty-five (25) feet from the property line of any adjacent, non-participating parcel or public street right-of-way, but fencing is not itself a setback. A minimum twenty-five (25) foot-deep Landscape Buffer is also required from the property line of any adjacent, non-participating parcel or public street right-of-way, except in the I-2 (Heavy Industrial) zoning district where no Landscape Buffer is required.

A Solar Energy Facility shall have a minimum twenty-five (25) foot-deep Landscape Buffer measured from the property line of any adjacent, non-participating parcel or public street right-of-way that provides a year-round visual buffer. The Applicant shall provide a landscape plan stamped by a licensed landscape architect or landscape horticulturalist. Existing vegetation shall be preserved within the twenty-five (25) foot Landscape Buffer, where reasonably possible. In locations where gaps in existing vegetation exist, trees and shrubs must be added to provide for a year-round visual buffer substantially similar to a planted buffer. Landscape Buffer zones without existing trees or shrubs must be designed and planted to meet the following requirements: (i) In the A-1 (Agricultural) zoning district, to achieve an 80% opacity by year five (5), the buffer must have four (4) class  "A"  trees, three (3) class  "B"  trees, and a minimum of twenty-two (22) shrubs every fifty (50) feet; (ii) In the I-1 (Light Industrial) zoning district, to achieve a 60% opacity by year five (5), the buffer must have three (3) class  "A"  trees, two (2) class  "B"  trees, and a minimum of seventeen (17) shrubs every fifty (50) feet; (iii) In the I-2 (Heavy Industrial) zoning district, no Landscape Buffer is required; (iv) At least fifty (50) percent of all plants must be evergreen; (v) No more than thirty (30) percent of any one species may be used; (vi) All trees must be a minimum of six (6) feet in height at installation; (vii) All shrubs must be a minimum of eighteen (18) inches in height at installation; (viii) Vegetative planting must only use trees and shrubs as listed in Appendix in the Parish Code, or as approved by the Director. The Facility Owner must maintain the landscaping using good husbandry techniques, removing and replanting dead or diseased vegetation as soon as practicable. Plants or grasses on the Facility Site not part of the landscaping buffer must be maintained so as not to constitute a nuisance.

Section 26-99(c)(12) Signage requires that "Emergency information signage shall be posted and maintained at the entrance of the Solar Energy Facility, and shall include at a minimum the name and phone number of the Facility Owner." It also states that "Solar equipment shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or Operator, or other information required by applicable local, state or federal law, rule or regulation." Additionally, "All signs, flags, streamers or similar items, both temporary and permanent, are prohibited on solar equipment except as specified above."

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Solar Energy Facilities, which are defined as renewable energy facilities designed to provide alternative power for either wholesale or retail consumption. Relevant provisions include: (c)(7) Land clearing, soil erosion, and habitat impacts, which states that clearing of natural vegetation shall be limited to what is necessary for construction, operation and maintenance; floodplains, wetlands, and steep slopes shall be reasonably protected from clearing, grading, filling, or construction; and the facility shall be designed to preserve existing tree lines where reasonably possible. Additionally, (d)(1)(f) requires an operation and maintenance plan including measures for storm water controls, and (d)(2)(b) requires a drainage runoff management plan (RMP) as part of the Development Permit application. These requirements apply to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance. No alternative options or conditions for soil, erosion, or sediment control requirements are provided beyond these stated provisions.

Inverters and transformers shall be sited no less than three hundred (300) feet from any occupied dwelling unit. The routine operation of a Solar Energy Facility shall not produce noise that exceeds sixty (60) dBA, as measured at the property lines of the Facility Site, unless the Owner and the Board agree to a higher noise level in the Development Permit. The Solar Energy Facility shall be set back a minimum of fifty (50) feet from the property line of any adjacent, non-participating parcel, but this setback is from property lines, not specifically from occupied dwellings.

The ordinance requires a petition for a zoning exception and/or rezoning to include a Facility Site Plan with detailed components of the Solar Energy Facility and a conceptual landscape plan. It also mandates a Community Impact Assessment "prepared by one or more professionals acting within his or her competency" that "shall analyze in specific terms the probable impact of the Solar Energy Facility on the vicinity and community over time," including visual impacts as part of the overall assessment. Additionally, a minimum twenty-five (25) foot-deep Landscape Buffer providing a year-round visual buffer is required from adjacent, non-participating parcels or public street right-of-way, with specific planting requirements depending on zoning district. These requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities defined as "a renewable energy facility designed to provide alternative power for either wholesale or retail consumption," thus covering utility-scale systems. Other required application elements include a narrative, documentation of major system components, leases or servitude agreements if applicable, interconnection application documentation, operation and maintenance plan, Decommission Plan, Cultural Resources Review, and a Glint and Glare Study. The ordinance exempts off-grid solar panel systems not defined as Solar Energy Facilities and Solar Energy Facilities on government-owned land.

The ordinance requires a signed and notarized decommissioning plan to be submitted to the parish, including "Plan for decommissioning and hazard abatement to be taken if facility is deemed 'abandoned', suspension, or notice of retirement." It mandates "A five-year financial security deposit in the form of a performance bond, conventional letter(s) of credit, cash, or any combination thereof in the amount of one hundred percent of the estimated decommissioning cost," with reevaluation every three years. The plan must include "Complete removal of all non-utility-owned solar energy equipment conduits, structures, fencing, roads and foundations, including all buried components; and restoration of property to a condition prior to development of the solar power plant, unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads not be restored." It also requires remediation of environmental hazards as determined by EPA, state DEQ, or parish government. The timeframe for decommissioning is to "begin within 60-days of termination of site use, abandonment, or revocation of permit and be completed within 12 months unless otherwise extended by the parish council." The ordinance states that if the owner/operator abandons the facility or fails to complete decommissioning, "the parish reserves the right to access the site and perform the decommissioning necessary using the provided financial assurance," and to seek reimbursement for any shortfall. Additionally, the parish may use staff or independent consultants to review and enforce compliance, with costs paid by the owner/operator. The ordinance applies to solar power plants defined as "any use of land where a series of one or more solar energy systems are placed in an area on a parcel of land for the purpose of converting sunlight into electricity, photovoltaics (PV), for the primary purpose of whole or retail sales of generated electricity," with a minimum site size of 50 acres, confirming applicability to utility-scale solar energy systems.

Fencing and gates are required around the perimeter of all solar power plants. An eight-foot security fence must be placed around the perimeter of the solar power plant. Lock boxes and keys must be provided at locked entrances for emergency personnel access and appropriate access, including, but not limited to, the fire chief, and the sheriff. A 12-foot access servitude inside the fence is required for emergency access. Appropriate warning signage must be placed at the entrance and perimeter of the solar power plant project every 200 feet, and shall specify the owner, operator, and include emergency contact information. These requirements apply to solar power plants defined as any use of land where a series of one or more solar energy systems are placed in an area on a parcel of land for the purpose of converting sunlight into electricity, photovoltaics (PV), for the primary purpose of whole or retail sales of generated electricity.

The ordinance requires that "all applications submitted pursuant to this section for approval of any solar power plant permit must include a detailed map analysis highlighting all airport operation and/or designated flight paths within five nautical miles of the outermost proposed boundaries of any proposed solar power plant," and must include "a certified letter of a notice of intent to construct a solar power plant," "a full report of potential aviation glare hazards (AGH) arising from the proposed solar power plant" using the "Department of Energy’s Sandia National Laboratories recently developed glare hazard assessment tool (or any other assessment tool required or otherwise recommended by the FAA)," and "proof of said notice and full report being actually delivered not less than 90 days prior to the submission of any application for a solar power plant permit" to relevant airport and FAA authorities. Additionally, "changes in proposed solar power plant design, standards, or type of solar energy equipment, prior to any permit approved under this section, will require proof of re-delivery of an updated notice and full report." These requirements are intended to address "legitimate concerns regarding the possibility for solar power plants to cause a glare hazard for pilots and/or traffic controllers."
section: Sec. 120-1. Renewable energy power plants (solar energy)

summary: The ordinance explicitly states: 'Maximum height. The height of solar panels shall be measured from the highest natural grade below each solar panel to the top of that panel. Panel height shall not exceed 15 feet.' This applies to solar power plants defined as systems for whole or retail sales of electricity. Poles and wires necessary to connect to public electric utilities are exempt from this height restriction but remain subject to other parish ordinances.

The ordinance states under Design standards: 'No photovoltaic solar power plant will be erected on any site less than fifty (50) acres in size.' This is a minimum site size requirement for utility-scale solar power plants primarily for whole or retail sales of electricity. The unit is explicitly given as acres, a standard measure of land area.

The ordinance states: 'No operating solar power plant shall produce noise that exceeds in this subsection 60 dBA, as measured at the fence lines of the project boundary. Adequate setbacks must be provided to comply with these limitations.' This maximum noise level applies specifically to solar power plants defined as utility-scale systems intended for whole or retail sales of generated electricity. The unit 'dBA' is the standard unit for noise level measurement.
section: Sec. 120-1. Renewable energy power plants (solar energy)

summary: The ordinance defines a solar power plant as any use of land where solar energy systems convert sunlight into electricity for whole or retail sales. Such solar power plants must be located on industrial zoned property and comply with setbacks including a 50-foot vegetative buffer and a minimum distance of one-half mile from residential property lines, places of worship, or occupied structures, except where the property was zoned industrial as of the ordinance enactment date (then a 300-foot setback applies) or a written waiver is obtained. A valid permit and ongoing compliance are mandatory. Additionally, no photovoltaic solar power plant will be erected on any site less than fifty (50) acres in size. By assumption, solar overlay districts are also considered primary use districts for these systems.
section: Sec. 120-1. Renewable energy power plants (solar energy)

summary: Photovoltaic solar power plants must be located on industrial zoned property and be at least fifty (50) acres in size. The ordinance states: 'solar energy equipment must be located on industrial zoned property' and 'No photovoltaic solar power plant will be erected on any site less than fifty (50) acres in size.' It also requires setbacks of at least one-half (1/2) mile from residential property lines, places of worship, or occupied structures, except for properties zoned industrial as of the ordinance enactment date, which may adhere to a 300-foot setback per state law, or if a written waiver is obtained. No concentrated solar thermal power plants are allowed. The ordinance does not explicitly name or abbreviate any other zoning districts where photovoltaic solar power plants are prohibited, but by requiring location on industrial zoned property, it implicitly prohibits them in all other districts.
section: Sec. 120-1. Renewable energy power plants (solar energy)

summary: The ordinance requires a minimum setback of at least a 50-foot vegetative buffer from all project boundary lines which make up the site perimeter. Additionally, solar energy equipment must be located on industrial zoned property and be at least one-half (1/2) mile (2640 feet) from all existing residential property lines, places of worship, or occupied structures, except where: (1) any property zoned industrial as of the ordinance enactment date is exempt and may adhere to the minimum setback of 300 feet as proscribed by the State of Louisiana; or (2) a written waiver is executed by all residential property owners, places of worship, or occupied structures within a one-half (1/2) mile radius of the property boundary. The 50-foot vegetative buffer is a fixed setback from the project boundary lines (facility perimeter), while the one-half mile setback applies from residential property lines. The most restrictive setback directly pertaining to property lines is the one-half mile (2640 feet) setback from residential property lines for utility-scale solar energy equipment on industrial zoned property.
section: Sec. 120-1 Renewable energy power plants (solar energy), subsection (d)(4) Setbacks and screening

summary: The ordinance requires that "The solar power plant must be set back from all project boundary lines which make up the site perimeter with at least a 50-foot vegetative buffer." It further mandates that "Solar power plants must be constructed with evergreen vegetative screening." Landscape buffers must meet specific requirements: "Existing undisturbed vegetative buffers with six trees over 50 feet deep within every 100 feet of project boundary line shall not be required to install new plant material if the existing vegetation creates a continuous opaque visual barrier within 25 feet of the project boundary line." Where gaps exist, "shrubs must be added along the edge of the property line as required to create an opaque barrier" with shrubs reaching "a minimum of six feet within a three-year period." For buffer zones without any trees or shrubs, a new 45-foot deep landscape buffer must be installed with "six Class A trees, three Class B trees and 24 shrubs" per 50 feet of project buffer zone. Additional requirements include that "a minimum of 50 percent of all plants must be evergreen," "no more than 30 percent of any one species will be allowed," and specific minimum heights for trees and shrubs at installation. All landscaping "must be maintained and warrantied for the life of the facility," and "failure to continuously maintain the foregoing visual buffers will constitute a violation." A "Maintenance Plan shall be prepared and include a schedule of maintenance of the facility." These requirements apply to solar power plants defined as uses of land for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity, i.e., utility-scale solar energy systems.
section: Sec. 120-1. Renewable energy power plants (solar energy)

summary: The ordinance requires that "The developer must post a sign behind every public right-of-way adjacent to the development" with the following requirements: "Sign must be four feet by eight feet in size," "Sign must state the name and type of development," "Developer's name and phone number," "Date and time of the parish council meeting date," and "Meeting location address and time." Additionally, "Appropriate warning signage must be placed at the entrance and perimeter of the solar power plant project every 200 feet, and shall specify the owner, operator, and include emergency contact information." These signage requirements apply to solar power plants defined as "any use of land where a series of one or more solar energy systems are placed in an area on a parcel of land for the purpose of converting sunlight into electricity, photovoltaics (PV), for the primary purpose of whole or retail sales of generated electricity," which corresponds to utility-scale solar energy systems.

The ordinance requires submission of an elevation certificate and preliminary drainage plan; site and development plans must include drainageways, grading, vegetation removal, revegetation methods, dust and erosion control, floodplains or wetlands, and other relevant items. An environmental analysis must cover impacts to soil erosion (water and wind) and water quality. The drainage plan must follow the latest parish development drainage requirements, including retention ponds. A Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) is required as per EPA and Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality permits for construction activities, describing practices to reduce pollutants in stormwater discharges. Ground-mounted solar panels require little earth disturbance and developments must not unduly create land disturbance. The decommissioning plan must include final land reclamation and restoration of property to a condition prior to development, including revegetation and road repair activities. These requirements apply to solar power plants defined as "any use of land where a series of one or more solar energy systems are placed in an area on a parcel of land for the purpose of converting sunlight into electricity, photovoltaics (PV), for the primary purpose of whole or retail sales of generated electricity," with a minimum site size of fifty (50) acres.
section: Sec. 120-1. Renewable energy power plants (solar energy)

summary: Photovoltaic solar power plants (minimum 50 acres) are permitted on industrial zoned property, subject to conditions including setbacks: "The solar power plant must be set back from all project boundary lines which make up the site perimeter with at least a 50-foot vegetative buffer" and "solar energy equipment must be located on industrial zoned property and located at least one-half (1/2) mile from all existing residential property lines, places of worship, or occupied structures," except if the property was zoned industrial as of the ordinance enactment date (then a 300-foot setback applies) or if a written waiver is executed by affected neighbors. A valid permit for installation and ongoing compliance is mandatory. Additionally, "No photovoltaic solar power plant will be erected on any site less than fifty (50) acres in size."
section: Sec. 120-1. Renewable energy power plants (solar energy)

summary: Solar energy equipment must be located at least one-half (1/2) mile from all existing residential property lines, places of worship, or occupied structures, except: (1) Any property zoned industrial, as of the date this ordinance is enacted, shall be exempt from this requirement and solar power plants may adhere to the minimum setback of 300 feet as proscribed by the State of Louisiana; or (2) A written waiver is executed by all residential property owners, places of worship, or occupied structures within a one-half (1/2) mile radius of the boundary of the property to be developed. Additionally, power inverters, BESS, and other sound-producing equipment or solar energy equipment that produces a fire risk must be no less than one-half (1/2) mile from any existing residential property lines, places of worship, or occupied structures at the time of construction/installation.
section: Sec. 120-1. Renewable energy power plants (solar energy) - Design standards (4) Setbacks and screening

summary: The ordinance requires that "Visual impacts, appearance, and scenic viewsheds" be considered, noting that "Potential visual impacts may be caused by components of the project such as above-ground electrical lines, accessory structures, access roads, utility trenches and installations, and alteration of vegetation." It mandates that "More visually sensitive proposals may require analysis from significantly more vantage points, such as different distances and sensitive locations. A photo simulation is required." It further states that "Significant visual impacts that cannot be adequately mitigated are grounds for denial." Additionally, there are detailed landscaping and vegetative buffer requirements: "The solar power plant must be set back from all project boundary lines which make up the site perimeter with at least a 50-foot vegetative buffer," and "Solar power plants must be constructed with evergreen vegetative screening." The landscaping buffer must meet specific planting and maintenance standards, including certification by a licensed landscape architect or horticulturist. Lighting must be "limited to the minimum necessary and full cut-off lighting (e.g., dark sky compliant) may be required when determined necessary to mitigate visual impacts." These requirements apply to solar power plants defined as "any use of land where a series of one or more solar energy systems are placed in an area on a parcel of land for the purpose of converting sunlight into electricity, photovoltaics (PV), for the primary purpose of whole or retail sales of generated electricity," and with a minimum site size of 50 acres. Other options or conditions include exemptions from setback requirements for properties zoned industrial as of the ordinance date, or where written waivers are executed by affected residential property owners or places of worship within a half-mile radius. The ordinance also requires submission of detailed site plans, including visual representations and maps, as part of the application process.
section: Sec. 120-1. Renewable energy power plants (solar energy)

summary: Any project adjacent to any natural or navigable waterway an additional setback of 50-feet on each bank of the waterway, as determined from the high-water mark, shall be required. The banks on either side shall not be disturbed by the proposed activities except as expressly allowed by the parish or by permit.
section: (d) Design standards, (4) Setbacks and screening, c.

summary: Section 7.D-9 titled 'Decommissioning, Removal and Abandonment' requires that any Facility that has reached the end of its useful life or ceases to generate power must be decommissioned. Decommissioning shall consist of: 1) Physical removal of all solar energy systems, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines from the site including all buried cabling; 2) Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations; 3) Stabilize or revegetation of the Facility site as necessary to minimize erosion, with the contour of the immovable property returned to its original state unless the property owner consents otherwise; 4) Remediation of any environmental hazards remaining on the site, as determined by the EPA, LDEQ, or the Parish President. The Facility is considered abandoned if it fails to generate electricity for more than one (1) year without written consent of the Parish President. If the owner/operator fails to remove the installation within twelve (12) months of abandonment or proposed decommissioning, the Parish may use the performance guarantee and legal means to complete removal. summary: Section 15. DECOMMISSIONING, REMOVAL AND ABANDONMENT requires that "Any Facility that has reached the end of its useful life, ceases to generate power as set forth in Section 7(3), or has been abandoned, shall be removed in accordance with the Decommissioning Plan." Removal and decommissioning must commence within ninety (90) days of termination, abandonment, or permit revocation, and physical removal must be completed "no more than eighteen (18) months after its final day of power generation." The owner, developer, and/or operator must notify the Permit Office by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and provide detailed removal and decommissioning plans. Decommissioning includes: (a) physical removal of all solar energy systems, structures, equipment, security barriers, and transmission lines; (b) disposal of all solid and hazardous waste per regulations; (c) stabilization or revegetation of the land to native vegetation within a one-mile radius, with some exceptions; and (d) remediation of environmental hazards as determined by EPA, LDEQ, or the Permit Office. The Facility is considered abandoned if it fails to generate electricity for more than one (1) year after issuance of the Operating Permit without written consent of the Permit Office. If removal is not completed within eighteen (18) months, the Parish may use the performance guarantee to complete decommissioning. The Decommissioning Plan must be submitted as part of the Building Permit Application (Section 7(27)) and include estimated costs, method of decommissioning, and a performance guarantee (Section 7(30)) in the form of a bond, letter of credit, or cash escrow, with a minimum amount of $500,000.00. The performance guarantee must list the immovable property owner as primary beneficiary and the Jury as secondary beneficiary, and it may not be amended or revoked without consent. The amount is reviewed every five years and adjusted for inflation and salvage value. The guarantee is released after satisfactory removal. The power generated is sold to power purchasers for distribution throughout the power grid."

summary: Section 3.11.3.2 requires 'Landscaping or architectural screening shall be provided to reduce the visual impact of installations and specifically to protect nearby receptors from danger, harm, or nuisance that may result from reflective solar glare of photovoltaic panels.' Any ground-mounted solar energy system that has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned shall be removed. The owner or operator shall remove all structures associated with the solar energy system within one year of the cessation of said use. The owner or operator shall notify the Building Department by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Decommissioning shall consist of: a. Physical removal of all medium-scale and large-scale ground-mounted solar energy installations, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines from the site; b. Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations; c. Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion. The Planning Board may impose a condition requiring the owner/operator to post a bond or other financial surety acceptable to the Town in an amount sufficient to cover the cost of removal and disposal of the solar energy system.

Section 6.7.4(2) requires that for ground-mounted installations requiring a special permit, reasonable efforts shall be made to minimize visual impacts by preserving natural vegetation, screening abutting properties, or other appropriate measures. Section 6.7.3(3) states that landscaping that visually buffers the solar energy system from adjacent properties, including, but not limited to, walls and fences, shall be properly maintained. These requirements apply to Medium-Scale and Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Other related standards include minimizing visual impacts, lighting restrictions, emergency vehicle clearance for solar carports, and maintenance and decommissioning requirements.

These requirements are part of the special permit standards for Medium-Scale and Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Plants "shall be maintained and replaced as necessary by the owner of the CSPI for the life of the CSPI."
