A sign shall be erected identifying the owner and providing a twenty-four-hour emergency contact phone number of the CSPI owner or operator. CSPIs shall not display any advertising. Any sign must comply with § 145-22.

The ordinance requires that "CSPI stormwater controls must comply with all Belchertown stormwater regulations and requirements, Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection requirements and guidelines, and USEPA requirements." It mandates that "the applicant must provide a proposed method for mounting the array that responds to existing water and soil conditions, with particular attention to high water tables and/or bedrock." Land clearing and soil erosion controls include that "clearing of natural vegetation shall be limited to what is necessary for the construction, operation, and maintenance of the CSPI," and "existing root structures and topsoil shall be maintained to the maximum extent practicable and provide for a minimum of six inches of topsoil on all exposed areas." Upon removal, "stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion" is required, and "any site that was deforested for the CSPI ... shall be restored to encourage native tree growth." The ordinance applies to commercial solar photovoltaic installations with a minimum 250 kW rated nameplate capacity and up to 15 acres fenced array area, with prohibitions on installations greater than 15 acres fenced array area, forest clearing greater than five acres, and on slopes exceeding 8% (with some waivers).

The bylaw applies to large-scale (minimum 250 kW rated nameplate capacity) commercial solar photovoltaic installations constructed after the effective date. Any such installation over parking lots or on existing structures is allowed as of right with site plan approval in all zoning districts. Any commercial solar photovoltaic installation not specified as as-of-right requires a special permit in all zoning districts from the Planning Board, with site plan approval but no second public hearing required. Installations greater than 15 acres fenced array area, requiring forest clearing over five acres, on slopes of 8% or greater (with possible waiver up to 12%), on parcels with inadequate frontage, or within the 500-year FEMA floodplain are not permitted.

For all CSPI, the setback from any developed residential property shall be at least 500 feet, from CSPI fence line to adjacent property line. Other setbacks include front setback depth of at least 150 feet, side setback depth of at least 75 feet, and rear setback depth of at least 75 feet.

Section F(2) requires that "A CSPI shall be designed to minimize its visibility, including preserving natural vegetation to the maximum extent possible, blending in equipment with the surroundings, adding vegetative buffers to provide an effective visual barrier from adjacent roads and driveways, and to screen abutting dwellings." It further mandates that "A diversity of plant species native to New England shall be used for any screens and vegetative erosion controls" and that "Plants shall be maintained and replaced as necessary by the owner of the CSPI for the life of the CSPI." Additionally, section D(1) requires site plan approval with detailed plans including "existing conditions plan with property lines and physical features," "proposed changes to the landscape of the site," and "off-site features including structures, water bodies, wetlands, riverfront areas, roads, buffers, slopes, aquifers, wellhead protection areas, and utility connections within 1,500 feet," which supports visual impact assessment as part of the approval process.

The applicant for a large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation shall provide a form of surety, either through escrow account, bond or otherwise, to cover the cost of removal in the event the Town must remove the installation and remediate the landscape, in an amount and form determined to be reasonable by the Planning Board, but in no event to exceed more than 125% of the cost of removal and compliance with the additional requirements set forth herein, as determined by the applicant. Such surety will not be required for municipally- or state-owned facilities. The applicant shall submit a fully inclusive estimate of the costs associated with removal, prepared by a qualified engineer. The amount shall include a mechanism for calculating increased removal costs due to inflation.

Installations shall be surrounded by security fencing of at least eight feet or other suitable barrier approved by the Planning Board, including locked gates to prevent unauthorized access. Electrical equipment shall be locked where possible. A Knox box approved by the Fire Chief shall be provided and installed at a location on site approved by the Fire Chief and contain keys and contact information for access to the facility in the event of an emergency.

The ordinance defines a Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installation as "A solar photovoltaic system on a parcel of at least 20 acres that is structurally mounted on the ground and is not roof-mounted, and has a minimum nameplate capacity of 250 kW DC." This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for such installations. No other minimum lot size values are provided for large-scale systems. The unit for this minimum lot size is acres.

For large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations, front, side and rear setbacks shall be as follows: Front yard depth shall be at least 20 feet; provided, however, that where the lot abuts a Residential District, the front yard shall not be less than 100 feet. Side yard shall have a depth at least 10 feet; provided, however, that where the lot abuts a Residential District, the side yard shall not be less than 100 feet. Rear yard depth shall be at least 20 feet; provided, however, that where the lot abuts a Residential District, the rear yard shall not be less than 100 feet.

Signs on such installations shall comply with the Town's Sign Bylaw. The following signs shall be required: (1) Those necessary to identify the owner, provide a twenty-four-hour emergency contact phone number, and warn of any danger. (2) Educational signs providing information about the facility and the benefits of renewable energy. (3) Installations shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the facility.

For large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations, setbacks from Residential Districts (which include occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, and/or residences) are as follows: front yard setback shall not be less than 100 feet where the lot abuts a Residential District (otherwise at least 20 feet); side yard setback shall not be less than 100 feet where the lot abuts a Residential District (otherwise at least 10 feet); rear yard setback shall not be less than 100 feet where the lot abuts a Residential District (otherwise at least 20 feet).

Section 7.3.6 Decommissioning states: 'Decommissioning shall consist of: 1. Physical removal of all medium-scale and large-scale ground-mounted solar energy installations, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines from the site. 2. Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state and federal waste disposal regulations. 3. Stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion.' Section 7.3.5 Removal requires: 'Any ground-mounted solar energy system which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned shall be removed. The owner or operator shall remove all structures associated with the solar energy system within one year of the cessation of said use.' Section 7.3.7 Financial Security provides that 'The Planning Board may impose a condition requiring the owner/operator to post a bond or other financial surety acceptable to the Town in an amount sufficient to cover the cost of removal and disposal of the solar energy system.' These requirements apply to large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems, defined as having more than 25,000 square feet of solar panel area, including solar carport systems.

Ground-mounted solar energy systems "shall be screened from view from public ways and abutting properties to the extent feasible by landscaping, fencing, or other means." For large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems ("those with a rated capacity of 250 kW or greater" or "having more than 25,000 square feet of solar panel area"), the Planning Board "may impose reasonable conditions to minimize adverse impacts on the neighborhood, including but not limited to screening, setbacks, and maintenance requirements." Additionally, for medium-scale and large-scale systems, "reasonable efforts, as determined by the Planning Board, shall be made to minimize visual impacts by preserving natural vegetation, screening abutting properties, or other appropriate measures."

Section 7.3.4, Standards; Medium-Scale and Large-Scale Systems, item 5 states: 'Signs affixed to or associated with ground-mounted solar energy installations shall comply with Section 6.2. A sign consistent with Section 6.2 shall be required to identify the owner and provide an up-to-date 24-hour emergency contact phone number.' This applies to large-scale systems defined as having more than 25,000 square feet of solar panel area, including solar carport systems. Other related requirements include compliance with all applicable local, state and federal laws, maintenance in good condition, underground utility connections where feasible, and reasonable efforts to minimize visual impacts through screening and landscaping.

Section 7.3.4 Standards; Medium-Scale and Large-Scale Systems, item 12 states: 'The land area being disturbed for the installation of large-scale ground-mounted solar installations shall be landscaped to minimize surface water run-off and soil erosion.' Section 7.3.6 Decommissioning requires: 'Stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion.' These provisions explicitly address soil and erosion control for large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems (defined as having more than 25,000 square feet of solar panel area). Other standards include compliance with all applicable laws, minimizing visual impacts, underground utility connections where feasible, limited clearing of natural vegetation, and dimensional requirements. Large-scale systems require site plan review and may have conditions imposed to minimize neighborhood impacts.

Large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems (those with a rated capacity of 250 kW or greater) require site plan review and approval by the Planning Board (7.3.7.1). The Planning Board may impose reasonable conditions to minimize adverse impacts on the neighborhood, including but not limited to screening, setbacks, and maintenance requirements (7.3.7.2). For ground-mounted installations, reasonable efforts shall be made to minimize visual impacts by preserving natural vegetation, screening abutting properties, or other appropriate measures, as determined by the Planning Board (7.3.4.2). Large-scale systems shall not be located within the required front yard setback and shall comply with all other dimensional requirements of the district (7.3.7.3 and 7.3.4.8).

Section K of § 300-135 requires that any large-scale ground-mounted solar energy system which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned shall be removed within 150 days after discontinued operations. The owner or manager must notify the Planning Department by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Decommissioning shall consist of physical removal of all systems, structures, equipment, security barriers, and appurtenant structures; disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with regulations; and stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion. The Planning Board may allow leaving landscaping or designated below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and disruption. Abandonment is defined as failure to operate for more than one year without written consent of the Planning Board. The City may remove abandoned systems after a court order and charge the property owner. Owners must provide financial surety covering removal costs, not exceeding 125% of estimated costs, except municipal-owned facilities. Indemnification of the City from liabilities is also required. These requirements apply specifically to large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance.

§ 300-135H(7) Design and performance standards - Visual impacts and glare: "The solar energy system, including all accessories and appurtenant structures shall be designed to minimize visual impacts... Reasonable efforts shall be made to design solar energy systems to prevent reflected solar radiation or glare from becoming a public nuisance or hazard to adjacent buildings, roadways, or properties. Such efforts may include, but not be limited to, deliberate placement and arrangement, anti-reflective materials, solar glare modeling, and screening in addition to required landscaping."

The height of any structure associated with a large-scale ground-mounted solar energy system shall not exceed 20 feet. The height of any solar panel from ground level shall not exceed 20 feet. (§ 300-135 E(3)) This is the explicit maximum height restriction for large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems. Other height limits mentioned in the text apply only to small-scale or roof-mounted systems and are therefore not applicable here.

Setbacks for large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems are fixed distances. Where lots abut residential districts, setbacks from the lot line(s) adjacent to the residential parcel shall be 50 feet. In districts requiring a special permit, setbacks are: front yard not less than 75 feet, side yard at least 50 feet, and rear yard not less than 50 feet. (See § 300-135 E.(1)(b)[1] and (c))

Section F requires that "Landscaping shall be provided and maintained on the site to screen the solar energy system, the accessory facilities, and appurtenant structures" with specific requirements for screening adjacent to residential districts or uses, including a "continuous screen of planting of vertical habit not less than three feet in width and six feet in height," with at least 75% evergreens. In lieu of continuous planting, "a solid brick, stone, or wood fence of a design approved by the Planning Board, or a planted earthen berm of a design approved by the Planning Board" may be used with plantings amounting to no less than 20% of the planting requirement. Section E(2) states that "Structures shall be screened from view by vegetation and/or joined or clustered to avoid adverse visual impacts." Section H(7)(a) requires that the system "shall be designed to minimize visual impacts... adding vegetative buffers to provide an effective visual barrier from adjacent roads and screen abutting residential properties." These requirements apply explicitly to large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance.

Signs on large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems shall comply with the City of Beverly Sign Ordinance and all other applicable requirements from Beverly's Code of Ordinances. A sign shall be required to identify only the owner or manager and provide a twenty-four-hour emergency contact phone number.

Section § 300-135I(2) requires that the facility "shall be designed to minimize impacts to environmentally sensitive land." It mandates that "The clearing of natural vegetation shall be limited to what is necessary for the construction, operation, and maintenance of the large-scale ground-mounted solar energy system." It also states "Topsoil will not be removed from the site" and "Clear cutting of forest shall not exceed five acres." Additionally, "The facility design shall minimize the use of concrete and other impervious materials to the maximum extent possible." Furthermore, § 300-135K(1)(c) requires "Stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion" after removal or decommissioning. These requirements explicitly address soil, erosion, and sediment control for large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems. Other related provisions include submission of a Stormwater Management Report and Checklist prior to building permit issuance (§ 300-135C(3)) and inclusion of stormwater and vegetation controls in the operations and maintenance plan (§ 300-135C(5)(a)).

The ordinance states that "Use restrictions for large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems are established in Article VII, District Regulations." It specifies that "The Planning Board shall be the granting authority for any special permit for a large-scale ground-mounted solar energy system" (§ 300-135B(2)) and that "In districts where large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems require a special permit, setback requirements shall be as follows..." (§ 300-135E(1)(c)). It also distinguishes that in districts where these systems are "permitted by right," the underlying zoning setback requirements apply (§ 300-135E(1)(b)). However, the text does not explicitly name or abbreviate any specific districts where large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems are permitted as a special use or require a special permit. Other options mentioned include by-right districts and solar overlay districts, but the latter are excluded from this analysis per instructions.

Setback requirements for large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems are fixed distances. In districts where such systems require a special permit, the front yard setback shall not be less than 75 feet, side yard setbacks shall be at least 50 feet, and rear yard setbacks shall be at least 50 feet. Additionally, where lots abut residential districts, setbacks from the lot line(s) adjacent to the residential parcel shall be 50 feet. (§ 300-135 E(1)(b) and (c))

Large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems require site plan review by the Planning Board prior to construction, installation, or modification (§ 300-135 D(1)). The applicant must provide a site plan showing proposed changes to the landscape, including screening vegetation or structures, and a visual rendering if requested by a property owner from whose lot the installation can be seen (§ 300-135 D(3)(a)[2], F(2)). The system shall be designed to minimize visual impacts by preserving natural vegetation, blending equipment with surroundings, and adding vegetative buffers to provide an effective visual barrier from adjacent roads and screen abutting residential properties (§ 300-135 H(7)(a)). Landscaping requirements include continuous screening planting of vertical habit not less than three feet in width and six feet in height, with at least 75% evergreens, or alternatively, a solid fence or planted earthen berm approved by the Planning Board (§ 300-135 F(3)(a)). Reasonable efforts must be made to prevent glare, but glare restrictions are not considered part of visual impact assessment (§ 300-135 H(7)(b)).

Section 2.5.8.4.5 states that all structures and panels and all associated equipment and fencing including COMMERCIAL SOLAR PHOTOVOLTAIC RENEWAL ENERGY INSTALLATIONS "may not exceed 50% of the total lot area." This is the explicit maximum land coverage limit for commercial solar installations of 250 kW or larger. The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the total lot area, not as a specific area value.

Section 2.5.8.6 Abandonment and Removal requires that any COMMERCIAL SOLAR PHOTOVOLTAIC RENEWABLE ENERGY INSTALLATION of 250 kW or larger that has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned "shall be removed". The owner or operator must physically remove the installation no more than 150 days after discontinued operations and notify the Special Permit and Site Plan Approval Granting Authorities by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Decommissioning shall consist of: 1) Physical removal of all installation structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines; 2) Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with regulations; 3) Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion, with possible allowance to leave landscaping or below-grade foundations. Section 2.5.8.7.1 Financial Surety requires proponents to provide a non-cancellable surety bond or other approved surety to cover removal costs, "in an amount and form determined to be reasonable" but not exceeding 150% of removal costs, including inflation adjustments. The surety must be secured before issuance of any building permits. Abandonment is defined as failure to operate for more than one year without written consent, and the town may remove the installation if the owner fails to do so within 150 days of abandonment or proposed decommissioning date.

Section 2.5.8.3.1 states: 'A COMMERCIAL SOLAR PHOTOVOLTAIC RENEWABLE ENERGY INSTALLATION may be permitted on a lot, which contains an area of not less than four (4) acres and meets the setbacks and maximum lot coverage under Other Uses of the Dimensional Regulations Section 2.3.5.' This is the explicit minimum lot size for Commercial Solar Photovoltaic Renewable Energy Installations of 250 kW or larger. No other minimum lot size values are provided for this category.

The Town of Bourne has established a Solar Photovoltaic Overlay District (SPOD) "as superimposed over any other districts" to promote large-scale, ground-mounted solar photovoltaic systems. The Use Regulation Schedule states that Solar Photovoltaic Systems Ground-Mounted are generally not permitted in base districts (R-40, R-80, V-B, B-1, B-2, B-3, B-4, GD) except in the SPOD, where they are permitted as indicated by footnote 13: "Except 'Yes' in the Solar Photovoltaic Overlay District, as permitted under the provisions of Section 3470." Section 3474 defines SPS as "a large-scale solar photovoltaic system that is structurally mounted on the ground, not roof-mounted, and has a nameplate capacity of at least 250 kW direct current (DC)." Thus, the SPOD is the only district explicitly permitting large-scale SPS as a primary use without special conditions or approvals beyond those in the overlay provisions.

SPS are subject to the front, side and rear yard setbacks as set forth in the underlying zoning district(s), however a fifty (50) foot setback is required when adjacent to conservation lands or residentially zoned or used lands.

Section 3479 states: 'SPS are subject to the front, side and rear yard setbacks as set forth in the underlying zoning district(s), however a fifty (50) foot setback is required when adjacent to conservation lands or residentially zoned or used lands.' This setback applies to large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic systems (250 kW or larger) as defined in section 3472. No other numeric setback distances from public conservation lands, natural resource protection areas, or preservation areas are provided.

Section 3480 Design Standards requires that all accessory structures, including equipment shelters, storage facilities, transformers, and substations, "shall be architecturally compatible with each other," "multiple accessory structures shall be clustered to the greatest extent feasible," and "views of such structures to residential properties and roadways shall be screened with landscaping." This screening requirement applies to large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic systems as defined in Section 3472 (250 kW or larger).

Signs on SPS are restricted as provided in Section 3200 for the underlying district. A sign shall be required to identify the owner and provide a twenty-four-hour emergency contact phone number. SPS shall not be used for displaying any advertising.

The ordinance applies to large-scale (250 kW or larger), ground-mounted solar photovoltaic systems (§3472). It requires a site plan including proposed changes to landscape, grading, vegetation clearing and planting (§3475(2)(A)(2)). An operation and maintenance plan must include a stormwater management plan (§3477). Land clearing and soil erosion are limited to what is necessary for construction, operation, and maintenance, and must comply with applicable laws (§3482(b)). Upon decommissioning, stabilization or revegetation of the site is required to minimize erosion (§3484(1)(c)).

Large-scale, ground-mounted Solar Photovoltaic Systems (SPS) with a nameplate capacity of at least 250 kW DC are only permitted in the Solar Photovoltaic Overlay District (SPOD) as stated: "Except 'Yes' in the Solar Photovoltaic Overlay District, as permitted under the provisions of Section 3470." The use regulation schedule shows 'No' or 'SPR' (Site Plan Review) for SPS in underlying districts R-40, R-80, V-B, B-1, B-2, B-3, B-4, GD, with footnotes clarifying that permission is granted only within the SPOD. The SPOD is "superimposed over any other districts" and provides "expedited project plan review and design standards for large-scale, ground-mounted solar photovoltaic systems."

Section 3479 states: 'SPS are subject to the front, side and rear yard setbacks as set forth in the underlying zoning district(s), however a fifty (50) foot setback is required when adjacent to ... residentially zoned or used lands.' This setback applies to large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic systems (250 kW or larger). No other specific setback distances from occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, or residences are provided. The underlying district setbacks also apply but are not numerically specified here.

Section 3475(1) requires that large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic systems of 250 kW or larger undergo Site Plan Review (SPR) by the Planning Board before approval. The project proponent must submit a site plan prepared by a registered professional engineer that includes: 'Proposed changes to the landscape of the site, grading, vegetation clearing and planting, exterior lighting, screening vegetation or structures' and 'Drawings of the SPS ... showing the proposed layout of the system and any potential shading from nearby structures' (3475(2)A2 and A3). Section 3480(c) requires accessory structures to be 'architecturally compatible' and 'views of such structures to residential properties and roadways shall be screened with landscaping' to avoid adverse visual impacts. These requirements explicitly establish visual impact assessment standards for large-scale (250 kW or larger) ground-mounted solar photovoltaic systems. Other requirements include documentation of site control (§3476), operation and maintenance plan (§3477), utility notification (§3478), dimensional requirements (§3479), and financial surety for decommissioning (§3484), but these do not explicitly pertain to visual impact assessment.

Any large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation which has reached the end of its useful life shall be removed. The owner or operator shall physically remove the installation no more than 150 days after the date of discontinued operations due to the installation reaching the end of its useful life. The owner or operator shall notify the Planning Board by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Decommissioning shall consist of: (a) Physical removal of all large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines from the site. (b) Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations. (c) Stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion. The Planning Board may allow the owner or operator to leave landscaping or designated below-grade foundations in order to minimize erosion and disruption to vegetation.

For large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations, front, side and rear setbacks shall be as follows: Front yard depth shall be not less than 25 feet in the Industrial (I) and Municipal Refuse (MRD) Districts and not less than 50 feet in other districts; Side yard depth shall be not less than 15 feet in the Industrial (I) and Municipal Refuse (MRD) Districts and not less than 50 feet in other districts; Rear yard depth shall be not less than 25 feet in the Industrial (I) and Municipal Refuse (MRD) Districts and not less than 50 feet in other districts. The most restrictive setback distance is 50 feet.

summary: Signs on large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations shall comply with Article VI of this bylaw. A sign consistent with Article VI shall be required to identify the owner and provide a twenty-four-hour emergency contact phone number. Solar photovoltaic installations shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the solar photovoltaic installation.

Large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations with 250 kW or larger of rated nameplate capacity shall undergo site plan review by the Planning Board, prior to construction, installation or modification. summary: Any ground-mounted solar energy system which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned (i.e., when it fails to operate for more than one year without the written consent of the Planning Board) shall be removed. The owner or operator shall physically remove the installation within 150 days of abandonment or the proposed date of decommissioning. The owner or operator shall notify the Planning Board by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. The Abandonment & Decommissioning Plan shall include a detailed description of how all of the following will be addressed: physical removal of all structures, disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with regulations, stabilization or re-vegetation of the site, and financial surety for decommissioning through escrow account, bond or other form of surety approved by the Planning Board, not to exceed 125 percent of the cost of removal. Such surety will not be required for municipal or state-owned facilities. The project proponent shall submit a fully inclusive estimate of the costs associated with removal, prepared by a qualified engineer. The amount shall include a mechanism for calculating increased removal costs due to inflation. All legal documents required to enable the Town to exercise its rights and responsibilities under the plan to decommission the site, enter the property and physically remove the installation must be provided. Additionally, for large-scale solar energy systems, a performance bond for the total amount of the contracted cost of construction is required prior to the start of work.

Noise generated by ground-mounted solar energy systems and associated equipment and machinery shall conform to applicable state and local noise regulations, including the DEP's Division of Air Quality noise regulations, 310 CMR 7.10. A source of sound will be considered in violation if it increases the broadband sound level by more than 10 dB(A) above ambient, or produces a 'pure tone' condition when an octave band center frequency sound pressure level exceeds the two adjacent center frequency sound pressure levels by three decibels or more. These criteria are measured both at the property line and at the nearest inhabited residence. 'Ambient' is defined as the background A-weighted sound level that is exceeded 90% of the time measured during equipment hours, unless established by other means with the consent of the DEP. The units for the noise level are dBA.

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for large-scale solar photovoltaic installations. Section E(13) states: 'A large-scale solar photovoltaic installation shall be deemed abandoned when the large-scale solar photovoltaic installation has not been in operation for a period of 12 months.' After 12 months of nonoperation, the Building Inspector notifies the owner/operator, who has 30 days to rebut. If deemed abandoned, 'The owner/operator of the large-scale solar photovoltaic installation shall remove the installation and restore the site within 180 days of the date of the written notification of abandonment.' If the owner/operator fails, 'the Town shall have the right... to enter onto the proposed site and physically remove the large-scale solar photovoltaic installation and restore the site at the sole expense of the owner/operator.' Additionally, Section E(9) requires financial surety: 'Prior to construction, applicants... shall provide a form of surety to cover the cost of removal and restoration of the site in the event the site is abandoned... in no instance shall the amount exceed 125% of the estimated cost of removal.' The cost estimate must be prepared by a registered professional engineer and updated every five years. These requirements apply specifically to large-scale solar photovoltaic installations, defined as 'a ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation that occupies 1/32 of an acre or more or occupies less than 1/32 of an acre and generates electricity for the purpose of off-site use.' The ordinance also includes similar but separate abandonment and removal provisions for small-scale solar photovoltaic installations, which are not applicable here.

A large-scale solar photovoltaic installation "shall be secured with a seven-foot-high fence constructed to prevent unauthorized persons from accessing the large-scale solar photovoltaic installation." This fencing requirement is part of the design requirements for large-scale solar photovoltaic installations, which also include height limits, setbacks, lighting restrictions, screening with dense native vegetation, vegetation clearing limits, habitat fragmentation avoidance, signage with emergency contact numbers, emergency access, underground utilities, and maximum lot coverage. The large-scale installations are defined as ground-mounted installations that occupy 1/32 of an acre or more or generate electricity for off-site use, and require a special permit from the Selectboard. Other requirements include operation and maintenance plans, proof of liability insurance, financial surety for removal and restoration, and detailed site plan submissions. Small-scale solar photovoltaic installations have different requirements and do not have explicit fencing mandates.

A large-scale solar photovoltaic installation shall not exceed 20 feet in overall height. This applies to large-scale solar photovoltaic installations defined as ground-mounted installations that occupy 1/32 of an acre or more or generate electricity for off-site use. The relevant text states: 'A large-scale solar photovoltaic installation shall not exceed 20 feet in overall height.' No other maximum height values for large-scale installations are provided.

For ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations, front, side and rear setbacks shall be as follows: Front yard: The front yard depth shall be at least 50 feet. Side yard: Each side yard shall have a depth at least 50 feet. Rear yard: The rear yard depth shall be at least 50 feet. (§ 310-8.11 H.(1)) Additionally, large-scale solar photovoltaic installations shall comply with the setback requirements set forth in §§ 150-5.6 and 150-5.7 (§ 150-8.11 E.(10)(b)).

The ordinance requires that "large-scale solar photovoltaic installations shall be screened year-round with dense native vegetation from all adjoining properties and public and private ways, to the fullest extent possible as determined by the special permit granting authority." This screening is a vegetative buffer requirement applicable to large-scale installations, defined as those "that occupy 1/32 of an acre or more or occupy less than 1/32 of an acre and generate electricity for the purpose of off-site use." Additionally, the ordinance includes other design requirements for large-scale installations such as height limits (not to exceed 20 feet), setbacks per §§ 150-5.6 and 150-5.7, lighting restrictions (only manually operated emergency lights when personnel are on-site), vegetation clearing limited to necessary areas, clustering to avoid habitat fragmentation, security fencing, signage, emergency access, underground utilities (except at grid connection), and maximum lot coverage requirements. The special permit granting authority may waive compliance with some or all of these design requirements.

Signs on large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations shall comply with a municipality's sign bylaw. A sign consistent with a municipality's sign bylaw shall be required to identify the owner and provide a twenty-four-hour emergency contact phone number. Solar photovoltaic installations shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the solar photovoltaic installation. For large-scale solar photovoltaic installations, the owner/operator shall install signs as determined by the special permit granting authority in order to protect public safety and shall include emergency contact number(s). The operation and maintenance plan (OMP) for large-scale installations shall specify signage measures. Other design requirements for large-scale installations include height limits, setbacks, lighting restrictions, screening, security measures, emergency access, underground utilities, and maximum lot coverage. The special permit granting authority may waive compliance with some or all of these design requirements.

The ordinance requires that applications for large-scale solar photovoltaic installations include "Engineering controls at the site and on the access road to control erosion and sedimentation both during construction and after construction as a permanent measure," which "shall conform to the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection's Stormwater Policy." This requirement is found in subsection E(11)(l). The ordinance defines a large-scale solar photovoltaic installation as "A ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation that occupies 1/32 of an acre or more or occupies less than 1/32 of an acre and generates electricity for the purpose of off-site use." Other relevant provisions include operation and maintenance plans that specify "stormwater control measures" (E(7)(c)) and limitations on vegetation clearing to what is necessary for construction, operation, maintenance, modification, and removal (E(10)(e)).

The ordinance states that "A large-scale solar photovoltaic installation may only be constructed or modified after the issuance of a special permit from the special permit granting authority in accordance with this section, Article 6, Special Permits, and § 150-4.8, Table of Use Regulations." The special permit granting authority is the Selectboard, with the Planning Board providing a recommendation. However, the text does not explicitly list any zoning district names or abbreviations where large-scale solar photovoltaic installations are permitted as special use or require special permit approval. The referenced § 150-4.8, Table of Use Regulations, presumably contains this information but is not included in the provided text. For comparison, small-scale solar photovoltaic installations are allowed as a primary or accessory use in all zoning districts except certain height restrictions in the U-C, A-R, and R-30 Zone Districts, with some uses requiring special permits from the Zoning Board of Appeals. Large-scale installations require a special permit from the Selectboard regardless of district, but specific districts are not named.

The ordinance requires large-scale solar photovoltaic installations (defined as ground-mounted installations occupying 1/32 of an acre or more or generating electricity for off-site use) to obtain a special permit from the Selectboard (E(1), E(2)). The Planning Board reviews and recommends on the application (E(3)). Applications must include detailed site plans with information such as property lines, elevation contours, outlines of existing and proposed structures, proposed changes to the site including landscaping and vegetation for screening, and detailed layout of the installation and fencing (E(11)). The large-scale installations "shall be screened year-round with dense native vegetation from all adjoining properties and public and private ways, to the fullest extent possible as determined by the special permit granting authority" (E(10)(d)). The owner/operator must submit an operation and maintenance plan including vegetation and vegetation screening (E(7)(h)). The special permit granting authority may impose site-specific requirements related to these matters (E(7)). These provisions explicitly establish visual impact assessment requirements through the special permit and site plan review process. Other design requirements include height limits, setbacks, lighting restrictions, and screening (E(10)).

Any GMSP installation that has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned shall be removed by the owner or operator no more than 150 days after discontinued operations. The owner/operator must notify the SPRA by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and removal plans. Decommissioning includes physical removal of all structures, equipment, security barriers, and transmission lines unless the property owner requests otherwise; disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with regulations; and stabilization or re-vegetation of the site to minimize erosion. The SPRA may allow leaving landscaping or designated below-grade foundations and conduit to minimize erosion and disruption. Abandonment is defined as failure to operate or discontinuation of operations for more than one year without written consent of the SPRA. If removal is not completed within 150 days of abandonment or proposed decommissioning, the Town may remove the installation. Additionally, applicants must provide financial surety acceptable to the Town to cover decommissioning costs and site restoration, including bonds or other security that survive the financial viability of the owner/operator. The financial surety must cover decommissioning and insurance coverage, with specific bond amounts required prior to construction and before lease expiration.

The GMSP installation shall be enclosed by suitable fencing, access gates and/or other barriers to prevent unauthorized access and shall contain closed circuit cameras and motion detectors for security if required by the SPRA. (Section F.4) The fencing requirement applies to ground-mounted solar photovoltaic systems with a minimum nameplate capacity of 250 kW DC and a minimum area of one acre. Other related requirements include mitigation of glare by fencing, vegetation or other means as reasonably required by the SPRA (Section F.3).

Glare shall be mitigated at the applicant's expense by the placement of fencing, vegetation or other means as reasonably required by the SPRA. This applies to ground-mounted solar photovoltaic (GMSP) installations defined as having a minimum nameplate capacity of 250 kW DC and a minimum area of one acre. The SPRA is the Cohasset Planning Board. The relevant text is: 'Glare shall be mitigated at the applicant's expense by the placement of fencing, vegetation or other means as reasonably required by the SPRA.'

The maximum height from grade to the top of the ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation shall not exceed 15 feet for each individual solar panel. This applies to ground-mounted solar photovoltaic (GMSP) installations with a minimum nameplate capacity of 250 kW DC and a minimum area of one acre, which are utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in the text.

Each sight line shall include all intervening trees, buildings, and other applicable objects and be illustrated in color photographs of existing conditions with the proposed installation superimposed on the photographs. Additionally, "The solar installation shall be screened from view of the street and neighboring parcels, in order to protect the rural character of the town" (Section 4.9.4.4), and "All appurtenant structures... shall be shaded from view from public ways and neighboring properties" using indigenous vegetation approved during site plan review (Section 4.9.3.8). These requirements apply to large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations defined as systems with a minimum nameplate capacity of 250 kW DC (Section 7.0 Definitions).

Section 51.8 Removal Requirements mandates that "At least thirty (30) days prior to the date of discontinued operations, the owner of the solar photovoltaic installation shall notify the Building Inspector by certified mail of any proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal." A system "not used for twelve (12) successive months, or that has reached the end of its useful life, shall be deemed discontinued, and shall be removed by the owner." The owner must "dismantle and physically remove the solar photovoltaic installation within ninety (90) days from the date of discontinued operations," including "physical removal of all large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines," "disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state and federal waste disposal regulations," and "stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion." Section 51.9 Performance Guarantee requires the Planning Board to "require surety, either in the form of a bond or other security, in an amount sufficient to assure satisfactory removal of the system," with a cost estimate including a 25% contingency fee, reviewed every five years. The Planning Board may claim the surety and remove the facility if the owner fails to remove it within the 90-day period. These requirements apply specifically to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installations defined as systems "structurally mounted on the ground and... with a minimum nameplate capacity of 250 kW DC."

Other design standards include dimensional requirements, height limits, fencing, screening, lighting, signage, and network interconnections, but only item 8 directly addresses glare.

Section 51.6, item 9 states: "No signs shall be erected on the solar photovoltaic installation except signs identifying the owner, the operator, the manufacturer, an emergency telephone number, safety signage, and warning signage. Special placards and signs shall be installed on all combiner boxes, inverters, transformers, disconnects, and panel feed breakers. This shall include the following placards: WARNING – SOLAR INVERTER OUTPUT DISCONNECT DO NOT RELOCATE THIS DEVICE AC Disconnects located at: (i.e. Rear of maintenance shed). summary: The installation shall be located at least one hundred (100) feet from existing residences. Section 3.13.6.7 (e) states: 'Maximum Lot Coverage: 50%.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installations, which are defined as systems with a minimum nameplate capacity of 250kW DC. The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the lot area. No other maximum land coverage values are provided for these installations in the text.

Section 3.13.6.12 (a) requires the owner or operator to "physically remove the installation no more than 150 days after the date of discontinued operations" and to "notify the Planning Board by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal." Decommissioning shall consist of: "Physical removal of all solar photovoltaic installations, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines from the site," "Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste shall be in accordance with local, state, and federal regulations," and "Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion." The Planning Board may allow leaving some vegetation or below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and disruption. Section 3.13.6.12 (b) states that the installation is considered abandoned if it "fails to operate or its operations are discontinued for more than one year without the written consent of the Planning Board" or if it is deemed a hazard and not corrected within six months. The Town may enter and remove abandoned or hazardous installations after six months if not removed by the owner. Section 3.13.6.13 requires proponents to provide "a form of surety, either through escrow account, bond or otherwise, to cover the cost of removal" in an amount determined reasonable by the Planning Board, including a cost estimate prepared by a qualified engineer and a mechanism for inflation adjustment. Surety is not required for municipally or state-owned systems but may be required for privately-owned systems on municipal land.

Section 3.13.6.8(e) states: 'A security fence shall be installed along or proximate to the perimeter of the system and shall be maintained for the lifetime of the system.' Additionally, Section 3.13.6.8(d) notes that 'Methods such as the use of landscaping, natural features and fencing may be utilized' to screen appurtenant structures. These fencing requirements apply explicitly to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installations, which are defined as systems with a minimum nameplate capacity of 250kW DC and ground-mounted. No alternative fencing options or exceptions are provided in the text.

Section 3.13.6.7(g) states: 'Height shall be determined by each individual panel measured to the grade level beneath that panel and shall not exceed 25 feet.' This maximum height restriction explicitly applies to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installations, defined as systems with a minimum nameplate capacity of 250kW DC, ground-mounted and not roof-mounted. No other height values for Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installations are provided in the text.

Section 3.13.6.7(a) states: 'Minimum Lot Area: 20 acres;' which explicitly sets a minimum lot size of 20 acres for Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installations. This minimum lot size applies specifically to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installations as defined in the bylaw (minimum nameplate capacity of 250kW DC and ground-mounted). No other minimum lot size values are provided for this category.

summary: The ordinance applies to ground-mounted solar energy facilities with name plate capacity of 250kw or greater. It requires that "The solar panels shall be positioned in such a way that there is no possibility of glare on a residence or public way at any time during the day." Large facilities may be sited "As of Right" on a specific Town-owned parcel with a solar array footprint not to exceed five acres, or by "Special Permit" with a footprint not to exceed ten acres. The total number of large facilities is limited to six concurrently. Siting requirements include either that the location "cannot reasonably be seen from a residence or public way during all seasons of the year" or that it is "so distant from a residence or public way, and/or so obscured by topography, tree lines, and/or vegetation, that the visual impact of the facility is rendered negligible."

The ordinance states: 'No facility may have a solar panel ( "solar array" ) footprint greater than five acres, excluding the buffer zone area.' This applies to a facility with name plate capacity of 250kw or greater sited  "As of Right"  on one selected Town-owned parcel. Another option is for facilities with name plate capacity of 250kw or greater sited by  "Special Permit,"  which may have a solar array footprint not to exceed ten acres. The most restrictive maximum footprint is five acres. Units are explicitly given as acres.

One (1) facility with name plate capacity of 250kw or greater, the solar array footprint not to exceed five acres, may be sited 'As of Right' on one selected parcel of Town-owned land described as approximately 12.6 acres. Other facilities with name plate capacity of 250kw or greater, with solar array footprint not to exceed ten acres, may be sited by 'Special Permit.' The text explicitly states the 12.6 acres parcel for 'As of Right' siting as the minimum lot size. The ten-acre footprint limit applies to the solar array size, not the parcel size. Thus, the minimum parcel size for 'As of Right' large facilities is 12.6 acres, and larger parcels would be required for special permit facilities up to ten acres footprint.

All facilities shall have front, side and rear yard setbacks of at least 50 feet for any fencing that is required by the Planning Board. Fencing shall be required to fully enclose the facility. Solar arrays and related equipment shall have front, side and rear yard setbacks of a minimum of 100 feet. In the event a front, side or rear lot line abuts one or more residences, the setback for that lot line shall be a minimum of 200 feet. Setback from a public way shall be at least 200 feet. A 50 foot minimum setback shall apply when the abutting parcel has the same owner and the same proposed use as that for the proposed facility. The Planning Board may allow a lesser setback along a property line, where, in its judgment, the proposed facility is not likely to negatively affect an existing or permitted land use on the abutting property. The Planning Board may require a greater setback along a property line, where in its judgment the proposed facility is likely to negatively affect an existing or permitted land use on the abutting property.

summary: Setback from a public way shall be at least 200 feet. This applies to all facilities including Large Facilities (250 kW or greater). summary: Where the front, side or rear yard faces and/or abuts one or more residences or a public way, a landscape architectural plan will be required. The plan’s object shall be to minimize to the greatest extent reasonable the visual impact of the facility. The plan shall show how, through the use of mature plantings, vegetation, berms, fencing, land contouring, and strategic placement of the solar panels and appurtenant structures, the facility will be screened from view from facing residences and public ways during all seasons of the year. Appurtenant structures shall be subject to the vegetative screening requirements to avoid adverse impacts. For siting large facilities (250kw or greater, up to ten acres footprint), one of the following conditions must be met: (a) the location cannot reasonably be seen from a residence or public way during all seasons due to topography, tree lines, and/or vegetation; or (b) the location is so distant and/or obscured by topography, tree lines, and/or vegetation that the visual impact is negligible, as determined by the Planning Board.

The solar energy facility shall comply with the regulations for signs in Section 3 of this Bylaw. A sign shall be provided to identify the owner and operator and provide a 24-hour emergency contact telephone number. A solar energy facility shall not display any advertising, except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer, owner and operator of the solar energy facility.

The ordinance requires that for Large Facilities (250 kW or greater), the applicant must submit an operation and maintenance plan including "storm water controls" (Section 8, C.3). Removal requirements include "Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to return the site to its original state, and minimize erosion" (Section 8, G.2.a). Site plans must show "grading, vegetation clearing and planting" (Section 8, C.2.a). These requirements apply to facilities with name plate capacity of 250 kW or greater, sited by special permit with solar array footprints not to exceed ten acres. Other siting options include: (1) one facility 250 kW or greater sited "As of Right" on a Town-owned parcel with footprint not to exceed five acres; (2) facilities less than 250 kW sited by special permit. All large facilities must meet additional dimensional requirements and siting conditions related to visibility and setbacks.

The entire Town of New Braintree is designated as the Agricultural and Rural - Residential District. Large solar energy facilities with name plate capacity of 250kw or greater, and solar array footprint not to exceed ten acres, may be sited by  "Special Permit."  The Planning Board shall be the Special Permit Granting Authority. One facility with name plate capacity of 250kw or greater for municipal government purposes may be sited  "As of Right"  on one selected Town-owned parcel. Facilities with name plate capacity of less than 250kw may also be sited by  "Special Permit."  All large facilities must meet dimensional and siting requirements, including visual impact conditions determined by the Planning Board.
section: SECTION 2 - ESTABLISHMENT OF A ZONING DISTRICT AND USE REGULATIONS; SECTION 8 –SOLAR ENERGY FACILITIES (NON-RESIDENTIAL)

summary: Large Facilities (250kw or greater, solar array footprint not to exceed ten acres) require a special permit and must undergo site plan review including a public hearing. Required plans must include "views of the site from residences and public ways from which the facility would be visible, and the proposed installation with the planned screening for the facility in place." Siting requirements mandate that "the location of the facility, due to topography, tree lines, and/or vegetation, cannot reasonably be seen from a residence or public way during all seasons of the year" or "the location of the facility is so distant from a residence or public way, and/or so obscured by topography, tree lines, and/or vegetation, that the visual impact of the facility is rendered negligible, as determined by the Planning Board, during all seasons of the year." Other options include siting one facility 250kw or greater "As of Right" on a specific Town-owned parcel with a footprint not to exceed five acres. Facilities under 250kw also require a special permit but are subject to different setback and screening requirements.

Section 8.9.6.13 'Abandonment & Removal' states: 'A large-scale solar photovoltaic installation shall be deemed abandoned when the large-scale solar photovoltaic installation has not been in operation for a period of twelve (12) months.' After 12 months of non-operation, the Building Inspector provides written notification, and the owner/operator has 30 days to rebut the presumption of abandonment. If not rebutted, the installation is deemed abandoned, and the owner/operator 'shall remove the large-scale solar photovoltaic installation and restore the site within one-hundred eighty (180) days of the date of the written notification of abandonment.' If removal is not done within 180 days, 'the Town shall have the right... to enter onto the proposed site and physically remove the large-scale solar photovoltaic installation and restore the site at the sole expense of the owner/operator.' Additionally, Section 8.9.6.7 'Financial Surety' requires applicants to provide surety prior to construction 'to cover the cost of removal and restoration of the site in the event the site is abandoned,' with the amount determined by the Special Permit Granting Authority but not exceeding 125% of the estimated removal cost. The surety must be updated every five years and renewed at least 90 days before expiration. These provisions explicitly impose decommissioning requirements for large-scale solar photovoltaic installations. Other related provisions include maintenance obligations under an Operation and Maintenance Plan (8.9.6.5) and insurance requirements (8.9.6.6).

Section 8.9.6.8.H states: 'A large-scale solar photovoltaic installation shall be secured with a seven foot (7’) high fence constructed to prevent unauthorized persons from accessing the large-scale solar photovoltaic installation.' Other design requirements for large-scale installations include height limits (not to exceed twenty feet), setbacks (not closer than forty feet to the street line or twenty-five feet from side or rear lot lines), lighting restrictions, screening with dense native vegetation, vegetation clearing limitations, habitat fragmentation avoidance, invasive species prevention, signage requirements, emergency access, emergency response plan, and underground utilities except at the property boundary.

Section 8.9.6.8.A states: 'A large-scale solar photovoltaic installation shall not exceed twenty feet (20’) in overall height.' This is the explicit maximum height restriction for large-scale solar photovoltaic installations, which are defined as ground-mounted installations occupying one eighth (1/8th) of an acre or more or those generating electricity for off-site use. Other height restrictions mentioned include a 20 feet limit for small-scale solar photovoltaic installations (Section 8.9.5.2.A), but these apply only to smaller or on-site use systems and are not relevant here. The units for the height restriction are feet, as clarified in parentheses.

A large-scale solar photovoltaic installation shall not be placed closer than forty feet (40’) to the street line or twenty-five feet (25’) from side or rear lot lines. These setbacks apply explicitly to large-scale systems as defined in the text (occupying one eighth of an acre or more or generating electricity for off-site use).

A large-scale solar photovoltaic installation shall not be placed closer than forty feet (40’) to the street line. Other setback requirements include twenty-five feet (25’) from side or rear lot lines, but only the forty feet (40’) from the street line pertains to roads.

Large-scale solar photovoltaic installations "shall be screened year-round with dense native vegetation from all adjoining properties and public and private ways" (8.9.6.8.D). The Operation and Maintenance Plan (OMP) submitted with the Special Permit application must specify maintenance of "Vegetation and vegetation screening" (8.9.6.5.H). Other design requirements include height limits, setbacks, lighting restrictions, security fencing, signage, emergency access, and underground utilities (8.9.6.8). Screening is mandatory and not subject to waiver, unlike the small-scale installations where screening "may be waived by the Special Permit Granting Authority" (8.9.5.2.C).

The owner/operator shall install signs at a large-scale solar photovoltaic installation as determined by the Special Permit Granting Authority for public safety and shall include emergency contact number(s) (Section 8.9.6.8 I). Additionally, the Operation and Maintenance Plan (OMP) submitted with the Special Permit application shall describe signage (Section 8.9.6.5 E). Other requirements for large-scale solar photovoltaic installations include height limits, setbacks, lighting restrictions, screening, vegetation clearing, habitat fragmentation prevention, security measures (7-foot fence), emergency access, emergency response plan, and underground utilities (Section 8.9.6.8).

The ordinance requires that applications for large-scale solar photovoltaic installations include "Proposed changes to the site, including grading, cut and fill, landscaping, native vegetation for screening and vegetation to be removed or altered" (8.9.6.10.K) and "Engineering controls at the site and on the access road to control erosion and sedimentation both during construction and after construction as a permanent measure," which must conform to the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection’s Stormwater Policy (8.9.6.10.L). These provisions explicitly impose soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements. Other relevant requirements include maintaining the site according to an Operation and Maintenance Plan (OMP) (8.9.6.5) that covers stormwater control measures, vegetation and vegetation screening, and site access. The OMP must be reviewed and approved by local authorities. The ordinance also includes design requirements limiting vegetation clearing to what is necessary and preventing invasive species introduction during construction or removal (8.9.6.8.E and 8.9.6.8.G).

Large-scale solar photovoltaic installations are allowed only after the issuance of a Special Permit from the Special Permit Granting Authority in accordance with Section 8.9 and Section 8.3  "Special Permit Granting Authority."  (8.9.6.1) The ordinance details extensive requirements for the Special Permit application, including ownership proof, utility approval, operation and maintenance plans, liability insurance, financial surety, design requirements, and findings required by the Special Permit Granting Authority. Other solar photovoltaic installations such as roof or building-mounted installations are allowed by right after a building permit (8.9.4.1), and small-scale ground-mounted installations may be allowed by right after a building permit (8.9.5.1) subject to design requirements (8.9.5.2). The text does not specify any particular zoning districts or abbreviations where large-scale solar installations are permitted as a special use or require a special permit.

The ordinance requires that before granting a Special Permit for a large-scale solar photovoltaic installation, the Special Permit Granting Authority shall find that the proposed installation "is not detrimental to important scenic views or vistas in the Town" (Section 8.9.6.9.D). Applications must include detailed site plans with elevation contour lines, outlines of structures, and proposed landscaping and vegetation for screening (Section 8.9.6.10.K). Additionally, "A View Shed Analysis regarding the proposed large-scale solar photovoltaic installation and its relation to surrounding properties may be required upon request by the Special Permit Granting Authority" (Section 8.9.6.11.A). These requirements apply specifically to large-scale solar photovoltaic installations defined as ground-mounted installations occupying one eighth (1/8th) of an acre or more or those generating electricity for off-site use (Section 8.9.3.3).

Any large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned or discontinued shall be removed within 150 days after the date of discontinued operations. The owner or operator must notify the site plan review authority by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Decommissioning shall consist of physical removal of all installations, disposal of waste according to regulations, stabilization or revegetation of the site, and acquiring all required permits. The installation is considered abandoned if it fails to operate for more than one year without written consent. If the owner fails to remove the installation, the Town may enter the property and remove it. Proponents must provide financial surety covering removal costs, not exceeding 125% of the estimated cost, except for municipally or state-owned facilities.
For large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations, front, side and rear setbacks shall be at least 100 feet from a residential property line.

Signs on large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations shall comply with § 310-6.9. A sign consistent with the requirements of § 310-6.9 shall be required to identify the owner and provide a twenty-four-hour emergency contact phone number. Solar photovoltaic installations shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the solar photovoltaic installation.

The ordinance requires an operation and maintenance plan that "shall include measures for maintaining safe access to the installation, stormwater controls" (§ 310-13.5). It limits clearing of natural vegetation "to what is necessary for the construction, operation and maintenance of the large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation or otherwise prescribed by applicable laws, regulations, and bylaws" (§ 310-13.9B). Upon decommissioning, "stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion" is required (§ 310-13.11A(3)). These requirements apply explicitly to large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations with 250 kW or larger capacity.

summary: Section 14.13 Removal, decommissioning, and abandonment requires that any commercial-scale ground-mounted solar energy system which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned shall be removed. The site owner and/or facility operator must notify the City by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. The system must be physically removed no more than six months after discontinued operations. Decommissioning includes: (1) Physical removal of all solar photovoltaic installations, including structures, equipment, security barriers, and transmission lines; (2) Disconnection of utility connections to the satisfaction of the North Adams Fire Department and the City's Wiring Inspector; (3) Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local and state regulations; and (4) Stabilization or revegetation of the site to minimize erosion, with possible allowance to leave landscaping or below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and disruption. Abandonment is defined as ceasing to operate for more than 12 months without written consent of the Planning Board. The City may remove abandoned systems and charge the property owner. Additionally, Section 14.11 Financial surety requires applicants to provide surety to cover removal and restoration costs, with the amount determined by the Planning Board but not exceeding 125% of removal costs, including inflation. All subsequent owners/operators must maintain this surety until removal is complete.

Section 14.8.3 states: "The entire perimeter of the commercial-scale solar energy system shall be fenced and gated for security to a height of six feet or higher as required by the National Electrical Code. Use of razor wire is not permitted." This fencing requirement applies specifically to commercial-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems. No alternative fencing options or conditions are provided in the text.

Noise generated by commercial-scale ground-mounted solar electric installations and associated equipment and machinery shall conform to applicable state and local noise regulations, including the DEP's Division of Air Quality noise regulations, 310 CMR 7.10. A source of sound will be considered in violation if the source: (a) Increases the broadband sound level by more than 10 dB(A) above ambient; or (b) Produces a pure tone condition, when an octave band center frequency sound pressure level exceeds the two adjacent center frequency sound pressure levels by three decibels or more. Said criteria are measured both at the property line and at the nearest inhabited residence. 'Ambient' is defined as the background, A-weighted sound level that is exceeded 90% of the time that the sound levels are measured, without the equipment in operation, unless established by other means with the consent of the DEP.

Wetland protections include prohibitions on ground alterations within 100 feet of wetlands, with limited exceptions. Upon decommissioning, "restoration of the site, including stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion" is required. For large-scale solar facilities (typically greater than five acres), the ordinance requires a minimum of 100 feet of vegetation buffer with 50 feet being undisturbed closest to the residential property, and the other 50 feet being allowed to be selectively cleared (6.10.5.2.1.5.c). The ordinance requires site plan review approval by the Plympton Planning Board for large scale ground mounted solar facilities (defined as occupying more than or equal to 40,000 square feet). Other options include setbacks for Small-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations: Property line setback: 50 feet; Front street setback: 100 feet. Required setback areas shall not be counted toward an Installation’s total acreage.

Minimum setbacks for Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations shall be: a. Front street setback: 500 feet (as required for Forest Conservation District). Other setback options include property line setback of 100 feet for Large-Scale installations, and smaller setbacks for Small-Scale installations which are not applicable here.

Section 8.10-5.D Visual Impacts requires to "Minimize visual impacts including preserving natural vegetation to the maximum extent possible, blending in equipment with the surroundings, and adding vegetative buffers to provide an effective visual barrier from adjacent roads and driveways, and to screen abutting residential dwellings." It further states, "If deemed necessary by the Planning Board, the depth of the vegetative screen shall be 30 feet and will be composed of native trees and shrubs staggered for height and density that shall be properly maintained." Additionally, "Landscaping shall be maintained and replaced as necessary by the owner/operator." These requirements apply to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations as defined in the bylaw. No alternative screening methods or waivers are explicitly detailed beyond the Planning Board's discretion to deem the vegetative screen necessary.

Section 8.10-5 B. Signage requires that "Sufficient signage shall be provided to identify the owner of the facility and provide a 24-hour emergency contact phone number." Additionally, "Signage at the perimeter warning pedestrians is allowable." Installations "shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of such Installation." These requirements apply to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations as part of the general Installations regulated under this bylaw.

Section 8.10-6 B "Land Clearing, Soil Erosion and Land Impacts" requires that "clearing of natural vegetation shall be limited to what is necessary for the construction, operation and maintenance of the Installation." It prohibits "grading that substantially disturbs the existing soil profile and structure" and mandates that "sites shall be selected where construction may be accomplished without such earth work." It also requires that "the limits of the work shown on the approved site plan shall be surveyed and clearly marked by a Professional Land Surveyor" prior to site disturbance. Installations must be "installed on water permeable surfaces" and locating installations on original, pre development grades in excess of 15% is prohibited, except for areas used exclusively for shade management. An environmental monitor may be designated to inspect the site during construction and after significant weather events for erosion and stormwater impacts. Section 8.10-6 D "Wetlands" prohibits "ground alterations, such as stump removal, excavation, filling, and grading, or the installation of drainage facilities, access driveways, or solar panels, within 100 feet of any wetlands or hydrologic features subject to the jurisdiction of the Shutesbury Conservation Commission" and requires compliance with the Shutesbury Wetlands Bylaw. Section 8.10-4 C6 "Mitigation of Stormwater" requires that "stormwater runoff from the property during construction and during operation shall not significantly increase from the volume or frequency prior to development, nor shall the pattern of stormwater distribution be significantly altered ... to protect water recharge, existing wells and prevent flooding or erosion." Stormwater management systems should use "natural designs including Low Impact Design (LID) and Best Management Practices (BMPs) as outlined in the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook" and be consistent with Massachusetts DEP stormwater standards. Section 8.10-8 B3 on removal requires "restoration of the site to its natural preexisting condition, including stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion." These requirements apply to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations, defined as installations occupying more than 1.5 acres of land.

For Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations, ground alterations such as stump removal, excavation, filling, grading, or the installation of drainage facilities, access driveways, or solar panels, are prohibited within 100 feet of any wetlands or hydrologic features subject to the jurisdiction of the Shutesbury Conservation Commission and must be in compliance with the Shutesbury Wetlands Bylaw. The Planning Board may impose additional conditions to control stormwater runoff that might negatively impact wetlands or hydrologic features even if the work area is outside the Conservation Commission’s jurisdiction.

summary: Any Photovoltaic Generating Installation which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned (i.e. when it fails to operate for more than one year without the written consent of the Planning Board) shall be removed. The owner or operator shall physically remove the installation within 150 days of abandonment or the proposed date of decommissioning. The owner or operator shall notify the Planning Board by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. The Abandonment & Decommissioning Plan shall include: physical removal of all structures; equipment, building, security barriers and transmission lines from the site, including any materials used to limit vegetation; disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations; stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion, with possible allowance to leave landscaping or designated below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and disruption; description of financial surety for decommissioning, with surety not to exceed 125 percent of the cost of removal, and subject to Planning Board approval and review; and all legal documents required to enable the Town to exercise its rights and responsibilities under the plan to decommission the site, enter the property and physically remove the installation. Surety is not required for municipal or state-owned facilities. Additionally, ownership changes require the successor to assume all obligations including the Decommissioning Plan and provide evidence of required decommissioning security.
