summary: Maximum Height of Structures - Residential Districts: 10 feet; Non-Residential Districts: 15 feet. The most restrictive maximum height allowed for Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installation is 10 feet in Residential Districts. This applies to Solar Electric Generating Facilities and appurtenant structures.

Noise generated by Photovoltaic Generating Installations and associated equipment and machinery shall conform to applicable state and local noise regulations, including the DEP's Division of Air Quality noise regulations, 310 CMR 7.10. A source of sound will be considered in violation if the source: (a) Increases the broadband sound level by more than 10 dB(A) above ambient, or (b) Produces a "pure tone" condition, when an octave band center frequency sound pressure level exceeds the two (2) adjacent center frequency sound pressure levels by three (3) decibels or more. Said criteria are measured both at the property line and at the nearest inhabited residence. "Ambient" is defined as the background A-weighted sound level that is exceeded 90% of the time measured during equipment hours, unless established by other means with the consent of the DEP.

The solar installation and all appurtenant structures shall have a setback from front property lines and public ways of at least 200 feet, and a setback from side, and rear property lines and public ways of at least 100 feet. If the solar installation abuts an open field, farm, or pasture it shall have a setback from front, side, and rear property lines and public ways of at least 300 feet. This may be reduced at the discretion of the Planning Board if sufficient natural vegetation exists in the setback area, but to not less than 100 feet. No facilities are permitted between the front of the principal building and the front lot line. Side and Rear yard setbacks for Medium/Intermediate/Large Scale installations are the same as required for the underlying district.

The solar installation and all appurtenant structures shall have a setback from front property lines and public ways of at least 200 feet. Other options include a setback from side and rear property lines and public ways of at least 100 feet, and if the solar installation abuts an open field, farm, or pasture, the setback from front, side, and rear property lines and public ways is at least 300 feet, which may be reduced by the Planning Board to not less than 100 feet if sufficient natural vegetation exists.

Section G.3 Visual Impact Mitigation requires that "all structures shall be shielded from view by a substantial sight-impervious vegetative screen" with "a depth of the vegetative screen shall be 30 feet and shall be composed of native or naturalized trees and shrubs staggered for height and density." The landscaping "shall be properly maintained and replaced as necessary by the owner/operator of the solar energy system." Vegetative screening "shall reach a mature form to effectively screen the installation within five years of installation" and "the mature height of the vegetated screening shall be such that the installation’s structures are not apparent to a person upon any public road and viewing the installation from a height of 10 feet." Planting "shall be completed prior to final approval of the photovoltaic installation by the Building Inspector." Additionally, the Planning Board may require screening using "methods such as landscaping, natural features, and opaque fencing" to shield structures from view to avoid adverse visual impacts. The text also notes that "whenever reasonable, structures should be screened from view by vegetation and/or joined or clustered to avoid adverse visual impacts."

Solar Electric Generating Facilities "shall not be used for displaying any advertising signage except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the solar electric installation." Signs "shall comply with Spencer's sign bylaw." A sign "shall be required to identify the owner, operator and interconnected utility and provide a 24-hour emergency contact phone number."

The ordinance requires that the Abandonment & Decommissioning Plan include "Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion." The design "shall minimize the use of concrete and other impervious materials to the greatest extent possible, to minimize erosion and transport of sediment," and a permit under the Spencer Erosion and Sediment Control for Stormwater Management is required. Projects must be designed to "minimize... soil erosion," and installations shall not occur on slopes greater than 15% to minimize erosion. No topsoil shall be removed; it must be stockpiled and protected against erosion until respread, and earthworks must limit soil export to 1000 cubic yards per acre. These requirements apply to Photovoltaic Generating Installations, including Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installations.

Section 6.28.5 Discontinuance states: 'A commercial solar photovoltaic installation shall be deemed to have been discontinued if it has not been in service for a continuous 24-month period. Upon receipt of a Notice of Discontinuance from the Building Inspector, the owner shall have the right to respond to the Notice within 30 days of receipt. The Building Inspector shall withdraw the Notice of Discontinuance and notify the owner that the Notice has been withdrawn if the owner provides information that demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Building Inspector that the commercial solar photovoltaic installation has not been discontinued. If the commercial solar photovoltaic installation is determined to be discontinued, the owner shall remove the installation, including all structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines, and stabilize or re-vegetate the site as necessary to minimize erosion and sedimentation, at the owner’s sole expense within three months of receipt of the Notice of Discontinuance. Failure to remove the installation and stabilize the site within said time period may subject the owner to enforcement pursuant to Section 8.1.'

Section 6.28.3(b) requires that a commercial solar photovoltaic installation including security fences surrounding the installation shall be set back from all property lines by a distance of not less than two hundred (200) feet. Section 6.28.3(d) states that "Landscaping, natural features and fencing may be utilized to mitigate such visual impacts."

The height of any or all structures comprising the commercial solar photovoltaic installation shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet above the pre-existing natural grade underlying each particular structure. The height of any or all structures may be increased to twenty (20) feet above the pre-existing natural grade upon the applicant’s demonstration to the Board of Selectmen of an economic necessity.

Section 6.28.3(a) states: 'A commercial solar photovoltaic installation may be erected, upon the issuance of a special permit by the Board of Selectmen, on a lot containing a minimum of fifteen (15) acres.' The unit for this minimum lot size is acres.
A commercial solar photovoltaic installation including security fences surrounding the installation shall be set back from all property lines by a distance of not less than two hundred (200) feet.

Section 6.28.3(d) requires that "the visual impact of the commercial solar photovoltaic installation, including all accessory structures and appurtenances, shall be mitigated." It states that "whenever reasonable, structures shall be shielded by vegetation from view; and shall be joined and clustered to avoid adverse visual impacts. Landscaping, natural features and fencing may be utilized to mitigate such visual impacts." Additionally, Section 6.28.4(e) provides that "Such conditions may also include additional screening of the facility." It further allows the applicant to be required to "replace up to 100% of any and all trees with a caliper of six (6) inches or over that are removed in order to facilitate construction of the commercial solar photovoltaic installation."

Section 29.5(A) states: 'Twenty Percent (20%) of a parcel’s total square footage may be used for a solar facility.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for Large Scale Solar Photovoltaic Energy Systems, which are defined as solar facilities with a total rated nameplate capacity of 100kW/0.1 MW or greater. No other maximum land coverage values are provided for large scale systems. The unit is expressed as a percentage of the parcel's total area.

Section 29.10 DISCONTINUANCE, DECOMMISSIONING, ABANDONMENT and REMOVAL requires that "Any solar energy facility that has reached the end of its useful life or has been discontinued, decommissioned, or abandoned... shall be removed." The owner or operator must "physically remove the facility within one hundred fifty (150) days after the date of discontinued or abandoned operations or decommissioning" and notify the Planning Board by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations or decommissioning and submit plans for removal. Removal includes "Physical removal of all of the equipment from the site, including, but not limited to, the solar arrays, structures, equipment, security barriers, and electrical transmission lines" and "Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion." The Planning Board may allow leaving landscaping or below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and disruption. Section 29.11 ABANDONMENT states that a facility is considered abandoned if it "fails to operate or operations are discontinued for more than one year without the written consent of the Planning Board." If removal is not done within 150 days of abandonment, the Town may enter the property and remove the facility. Section 29.12 FINANCIAL SURETY requires the applicant to provide "a form of surety, either through a cash deposit, bond or otherwise, in an amount determined by the Planning Board to cover the cost of removal and site restoration" prior to operation, with an estimate prepared by a qualified engineer including an escalator for inflation. This surety is not required for municipal facilities.

When a proposed project abuts a property in residential use, the minimum width of the buffer area shall be 200’ (measured from the proposed solar project to the property line of the property in residential use) and this distance shall supersede the 100’ setback. In all other cases buffering/shielding shall occur within the stated setback amount.

Ground-mounted solar energy facilities including appurtenant structures shall have a setback from front, side and rear property lines and public ways of at least One Hundred Feet (100’) in Special Use District and Industrial Districts. Section 29.5 B. Buffering: "The visual impact of large scale solar photovoltaic facilities including all appurtenant structures shall be mitigated. Structures shall be buffered/shielded from view and/or joined and clustered to avoid adverse visual impacts as deemed necessary by the Planning Board using landscaping and natural features as appropriate to accomplish the mitigation." Applicants for large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems shall provide a form of surety (decommissioning security), either through escrow account, bond, letter of credit, or other mechanism acceptable to the Planning Board, to cover the cost of removal of all solar energy system facilities in the event the Town must remove the facilities and restore the property, to the extent feasible, to its original condition. The decommissioning security shall be in an amount and form determined to be reasonable by the Planning Board, but in no event to exceed more than 150% of the estimated cost of removal and compliance with the additional requirements set forth herein. Applicants shall submit a fully inclusive estimate of the costs associated with removal, prepared by a qualified engineer, which estimate may be peer reviewed by a consultant selected by the Planning Board at the applicant's expense. The amount shall include a mechanism for calculating increased removal costs due to inflation over a period of 30 years. The decommissioning security shall be provided at completion of construction of the solar energy system (bonding date) and will be required before any electricity generated by the solar energy system is exported to the local electrical grid for sale to third parties. From and after the bonding date, the amount of decommissioning security may be reviewed at the Planning Board's direction every five years. In the event such review indicates the net decommissioning costs have increased since the bonding date, then the amount of the decommissioning security will be increased consistent with such revised estimate. The revised estimate will be obtained from a reputable, independent contractor selected by the owner of the solar energy system and may be peer reviewed by a consultant chosen by the Planning Board at the owner's expense. Additionally, a solar energy system shall be deemed to have been discontinued if it has not been in service for a continuous twelve-month period without the written consent of the Planning Board. If the solar energy system is determined to be discontinued, the owner shall remove the system, including all structures, buildings, equipment, appurtenances, security barriers, and transmission lines, and stabilize or revegetate the site as necessary to minimize erosion and sedimentation, at the owner's sole expense, within six months of receipt of the notice of discontinuance. Should the owner fail to remove the system and stabilize the site within said time period, the Town shall then have the option to enforce against the decommissioning security and/or may subject the owner to action pursuant to Section 1340, Violations and penalties.

Section 4841(e) states: 'All security fences surrounding a ground-mounted solar energy system shall be set back from property lines a distance equal to the setback requirement applicable to buildings within the zoning district in which the system is located.' Other relevant provisions include that ground-mounted solar energy systems require site plan review under Section 6300 prior to erection (4841(a)), may obtain minor site plan approval at the Planning Board's discretion (4841(b)), and that visual impact shall be mitigated using methods such as 'landscaping, natural features, and fencing' (4841(f)).

Section 4841(f) requires that "The visual impact of a ground-mounted solar energy system, including all accessory structures, buildings, equipment, and appurtenances, shall be mitigated." It further states that "structures shall be shielded from view by vegetation and/or joined and clustered to avoid adverse visual impacts." Methods such as "landscaping, natural features, and fencing shall be utilized." Other relevant provisions include setback, yard, buffer, and screening requirements applicable in the zoning district (4841(c)), and security fences must be set back from property lines equal to building setbacks (4841(e)).

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for ground-mounted solar energy systems, which are typically utility-scale. Key provisions include: "The clearing of existing vegetation on the subject property shall be limited to what is necessary as deemed by the Planning Board for the construction, operation, and maintenance of a ground-mounted solar energy system or otherwise prescribed by applicable laws, regulations, and bylaws" (4841(h)); "The entire square footage for the arrays of a Ground-Mounted Solar Energy System shall count toward the area of disturbance and impervious area square footage calculations" (4841(i)); upon discontinuance, "the owner shall remove the system... and stabilize or revegetate the site as necessary to minimize erosion and sedimentation" (4860); and the Zoning Board of Appeals must ensure "Environmental features of the site and surrounding areas are protected and the surrounding area will be protected from the proposed use by provision of adequate surface water drainage" (4870(d)(iii)). These requirements apply to ground-mounted systems subject to site plan review and special permits, indicating applicability to larger-scale systems. Other provisions address setbacks, visual impact mitigation, underground utility placement, security fencing, emergency response plans, and decommissioning security but do not explicitly address soil, erosion, or sediment control.

Section K, Abandonment or Decommissioning, requires removal of any Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installation and/or Battery Energy Storage Facility that has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned. The owner or operator must physically remove the installation within 150 days of abandonment or the proposed date of decommissioning. Removal includes physical removal of all installations, disposal of solid and hazardous waste in accordance with regulations, stabilization or re-vegetation of the site, and restoration of prime agricultural land if applicable. The Town may enter and remove the installation if the owner fails to do so, with costs charged as a tax lien. Financial surety covering removal costs must be provided by proponents, not exceeding 125 percent of the estimated removal cost. Other options and conditions include: Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations in the C-2 Zoning District occupying four acres or less are allowed by-right and subject to Site Plan Review; installations occupying more than four acres require a Special Permit and must meet the requirements of this section.

The ordinance states: 'No component of a Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installation shall exceed 15 feet.' This applies to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations, including those occupying more than four acres in the Commercial-2 (C-2) Zoning District. Other related provisions include setback requirements and special permit conditions depending on the size and presence of accessory battery storage, but the height limit of 15 feet is the explicit maximum for all such installations. The unit 'feet' is used as the standard measurement for height.

summary: Any large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned consistent with Section 3.12.2 of this bylaw shall be removed. The owner or operator shall physically remove the installation no more than 150 days after the date of discontinued operations. Decommissioning shall consist of: (a) Physical removal of all large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines from the site. summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Utility-Scale Solar Facilities, defined as large-scale solar arrays over 15MW. Key provisions include: removal requirements stating that "Any solar installation that is discontinued or abandoned shall be removed in compliance with the requirements of the Building Inspector" and must be removed within 180 days; notice requirements to the Town of Ware officials prior to ownership changes and if the facility is out of service for at least one year; abandonment criteria where the facility is considered abandoned if it fails to operate for more than one year, triggering removal by the Town if the owner fails to act; decommissioning consisting of "Physical removal from the site of the solar arrays, structures, equipment, security barriers, and electrical transmission lines" and "Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion"; and financial surety requirements where the applicant must provide surety prior to operation, including a cost estimate prepared by a qualified engineer, maintained for the lifespan of the facility. Salvage value for solar panels is excluded from decommissioning cost calculations. These requirements apply to large solar energy facilities and utility-scale solar facilities as defined in the ordinance.

The ordinance applies to Utility-Scale Solar Facilities defined as large scale solar arrays over 15MW in total size. It explicitly requires that "solar PV modules shall be positioned in such a way that there is minimal or no level of glare on a residence or public way at any time during the day." Additionally, "No solar energy facility shall produce glare that would constitute a nuisance to the public." This is found in the submission requirements under item o). Other relevant conditions include limits on the number of large scale solar arrays (no more than fourteen total, and only one utility-scale solar facility over 15MW), visibility requirements ("Utility-scale solar facility shall be minimally visible from public ways"), setbacks, buffers, and other design and operational standards. Exemptions include solar facilities for agriculture, one and two family dwellings, and solar parking canopies (which require site plan review but are exempt from this section).

The ordinance states: 'The acreage of a single large-scale solar array site may not exceed 40 acres.' This is the explicit maximum lot size for large-scale solar arrays, which includes utility-scale solar facilities as defined (e.g., large scale solar arrays over 15MW). Additionally, 'A single large-scale solar array site may not cross property boundaries which have separate ownership,' effectively limiting the tract to one parcel. No other maximum lot size values are provided for utility-scale solar facilities.

No more than one (1) utility-scale solar facility shall be permitted within the Town of Ware. Such facility shall be identified as a large scale solar array over 15MW in total size (§4.8.3 C.3.b.1). Additionally, no more than fourteen (14) total large scale solar arrays shall be permitted within the Town (§4.8.3 C.3.a). The acreage of a single large-scale solar array site may not exceed 40 acres (§4.8.3 C.3.c). A single large-scale solar array site may not cross property boundaries which have separate ownership (§4.8.3 C.3.d). The 15 MW value is the explicit system size threshold defining a utility-scale solar facility.

Decommissioning includes "Physical removal of all below-grade foundations, mounting structures, supports, solar energy structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines from the site," "Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations," and "Stabilization and re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion." The Wareham Zoning By-Law Section 590 enacts glare restrictions for Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installations (250 kW to 5,000 kW DC). Design standards mandate "earthen berms and landscape plantings will be required according to Article 10: Landscaping," with "all vegetative screening... designed with plants that include a diversity of native species, including deciduous and evergreen plants." A "mix of native species including evergreen and deciduous trees, as well as native bushes and plants to be used as ground cover sufficient to maintain soil integrity and minimize soil erosion must be established and maintained for the life of the project." The Special Permit Granting Authority (SPGA) will consider "the quality of the landscape plan and the methods used to provide a visual buffer and noise barrier between the PV array and the residences around it." Setbacks "shall not be used for any purpose other than natural vegetation or other screening required by the reviewing board." All appurtenant structures "shall be screened from the view of public rights-of-ways and persons not on the parcel, in all residential districts." Maintenance includes "painting, structural repairs, and integrity of security measures and planting and maintaining healthy native plants for vegetative visual screening." Screening methods such as "dense natural vegetated plantings of native plants, earthen berms and/or increased setbacks will be required, depending upon site specific conditions" to prevent glare and noise impacts. There shall be no signs, except announcement signs, no trespassing signs or any signs required to warn of danger. A sign is required that identifies the owner and operator with an emergency telephone number where the owner and operator can be reached on a twenty-four hour basis.

The Wareham Zoning By-Law Section 590 explicitly requires Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installations (minimum Rated Nameplate Capacity of 250 kW DC and up to 5,000 kW DC) to comply with soil, erosion, and sediment control measures. These include: a stormwater management plan detailing existing environmental and hydrological conditions, proposed alterations, drainage components, and measures for detention, retention, or infiltration of water to protect water quality and prevent flooding (Section 593.5). Design standards prohibit significant regrading and require any soil removal to be approved and consistent with Earth Removal Regulations; no removal of all field soils; minimal disturbance with displaced soils returned to affected areas; landscaping with native species to maintain soil integrity and minimize erosion; use of minimal soil impact mounting methods; soil penetrations for foundations or trenching done with minimal disturbance and soils recovered; and addressing existing soil and water resource concerns to avoid negative impacts such as erosion or runoff (Section 595.1). After decommissioning, stabilization and re-vegetation of the site are required to minimize erosion (Section 596.1). These requirements apply as conditions for Special Permit and Site Plan Review for Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installations. summary: The Wareham Zoning By-Law requires that all Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installations (250 kW to 5,000 kW DC) obtain a Special Permit and Site Plan Review. Applications must include a "Landscape plan including sizes, types and numbers of plantings and details," "Proposed changes to the landscape of the project area grading, vegetation clearing and planting, exterior lighting, screening vegetation or structures," and a "Line of Sight study to determine visual impact from all directions" with the goal that "all panels and equipment associated with the Solar Photovoltaic Installation should be invisible to any residential home in Wareham, as well as from any public or private road." The study and plans are to be conducted by a party mutually agreed upon by the Special Permit Granting Authority (SPGA) and the prospective developer. Design standards require vegetative screening, earthen berms, setbacks, and fencing designed to blend into the landscape to minimize visual impact. The SPGA may impose conditions related to screening, lighting, noise, fences, and modification of exterior appearance to safeguard the neighborhood. Other siting options include: Small-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Photovoltaic Installations (under 250 kW DC) and roof-mounted systems are permitted as-of-right; Large-Scale installations over 5,000 kW DC are prohibited; Large-Scale installations between 250 kW and 5,000 kW DC require Special Permit and Site Plan Review in specified zoning districts.

The ordinance explicitly requires that any large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation (minimum nameplate capacity of 250kW DC) which has reached the end of its useful life or has been discontinued "shall be removed" within 150 days after discontinued operations. Decommissioning shall consist of: (a) physical removal of all installations, structures, equipment, security barriers, and transmission lines; (b) disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with regulations; and (c) stabilization or re-vegetation of the site to minimize erosion, with possible allowance to leave landscaping or below-grade foundations. The owner or operator must notify the Planning Board and Building Commissioner by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Discontinuance is defined as failure to operate for more than one year without written consent of the Planning Board. If removal is not completed within 150 days, the Town may take enforcement action. Additionally, owners or operators must provide financial surety (escrow, bond, or otherwise) to cover removal and restoration costs, not exceeding 125% of the prevailing wage cost, with periodic updates required. This surety is not required for municipally- or state-owned facilities. The decommissioning plan must be included in the special permit application. Other related requirements include maintenance, emergency services coordination, and design standards, but these do not replace the explicit decommissioning requirements.

Abandonment or decommissioning requires that any LSGMSPI which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned shall be removed within 150 days after discontinued operations. Accessory structures to LSGMSPI shall not exceed 15 feet in height (§ 235-10.7). The most restrictive maximum height for the arrays themselves is 10 feet, with accessory structures allowed up to 15 feet. Units are explicitly stated as feet.

LSGMSPI is defined as a solar photovoltaic system that is a principal use on a site of at least 8.5 acres in common ownership. This sets a minimum site size requirement of 8.5 acres for large-scale ground-mounted solar installations. The unit 'acres' is explicitly stated as the area measurement.

summary: Large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation (LSGMSPI) is permitted (P7) in the C2 District provided the parcel contains at least 75% degraded or previously disturbed land, is held in common ownership as of the date of this amendment, and is subject to LSGMSPI site plan review by the Planning Board to assure compliance with the C2 District objectives contained in § 235-3.2, and as provided in § 235-10.3 of this bylaw. In other districts (CD, R1, R2, NSP, C), the use is marked as 'O', which implies permitted by right or outright without the special use conditions noted for C2.

LSGMSPI with 250 kW or larger of rated nameplate capacity shall require LSGMSPI site plan review by the Planning Board prior to issuance of a building permit (§ 235-10.3). The site plan review includes submission of a site plan showing "proposed changes to the natural vegetation and landscaping present at the site, as well as proposed grading, vegetation clearing and planting, exterior lighting, screening vegetation or structures" (§ 235-10.3C(1)(c)). Design standards require that the LSGMSPI "shall be designed to minimize visual impact; the maximum amount of natural vegetation shall be preserved; details of construction and finish shall blend with the surroundings; additional screening shall be employed where practical and particularly to screen surrounding property" (§ 235-10.8B). These provisions collectively constitute visual impact assessment requirements for LSGMSPI systems. Other related requirements include fencing, lighting, signage, and height limits, but these are design standards rather than assessment requirements.

Section M states: 'Any large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned shall be removed. The owner or operator shall physically remove the installation no more than 150 days after the date of discontinued operations or abandonment.' Decommissioning shall consist of: '(1) Physical removal of all large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations, structures, equipment, security barriers, and transmission lines from the site. (2) Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations. (3) Stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion.' The Planning Board may allow leaving landscaping or designated below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and disruption. Section N provides that if the owner/operator fails to remove the installation within 150 days, 'the Town may enter the property and physically remove the installation.' Section O requires a 'performance guarantee, in the form of an escrow account, bond or tripartite agreement, to cover the cost of removal' unless the facility is municipal- or state-owned.

The ordinance defines a large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation as "a solar photovoltaic system on a parcel, or set of contiguous parcels in common ownership on the effective date of this section, of at least 20 acres that is structurally mounted on the ground and is not roof-mounted, and has a minimum nameplate capacity of 250 kW DC." This 20-acre minimum parcel size is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for such installations.

Large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations "may proceed in all districts without the need for a special permit, variance, zoning amendment, waiver, or other discretionary approval." Such installations are subject only to site plan review by the Planning Board pursuant to § 255-13.5 and additional requirements in § 255-10.2D and E. Overlay districts are assumed to be primary use districts for utility-scale solar energy systems.

For large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations, front, side, and rear setbacks shall be as follows; provided, however, that by special permit the Planning Board may authorize a smaller front, side or rear yard setback: (1) Front yard. The front yard depth shall be at least 300 feet. (2) Side yard. Each side yard shall have a depth at least 300 feet. (3) Rear yard. The rear yard depth shall be at least 300 feet.

summary: Section 3.28.15 Discontinuance and Decommissioning requires removal of the solar energy facility no more than 150 days after discontinued operations, including physical removal of all ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations, stabilization or re-vegetation of the site, and disposal of all solid and hazardous waste. Section 3.28.16 Abandonment defines abandonment conditions and authorizes the Town to remove abandoned installations and charge the property owner. Section 3.28.17 Financial Surety mandates submission of a decommissioning plan with cost estimates prepared by a professional engineer, and requires the applicant to furnish security in the form of a cash deposit to secure orderly decommissioning, held by the Town Treasurer pursuant to M.G.L. c. 44, § 53 ½. The surety is kept in place until decommissioning is complete, and funds may be used by the Town to remove abandoned facilities. These requirements apply to Large-Scale Solar Energy Facilities defined as having a nameplate capacity of 250kw or greater and a solar array footprint greater than one acre.

All facilities shall have front, side and rear yard setbacks of at least 50 feet for any fencing that is required by the Zoning Board of Appeals. Fencing shall be required to fully enclose the facility. (Section 3.28.10.A.1) This applies to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Facilities, defined as commercial solar photovoltaic systems with a minimum nameplate output capacity of greater than 250 kw DC. The fencing requirement is part of the dimensional and density requirements for ground-mounted solar energy facilities. Other setback requirements include: solar arrays and related equipment must have setbacks of a minimum of 100 feet; if abutting residences, setbacks must be at least 200 feet; setback from a public way must be at least 200 feet; and a 50-foot minimum setback applies when the abutting parcel has the same owner and use. The Zoning Board of Appeals may allow lesser or require greater setbacks based on potential impacts.

Section 3.28.12.B.2 states: "The solar panels shall be positioned in such a way that there is no possibility of glare on a residence or public way at any time during the day." This glare restriction applies to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Facilities, which are defined as commercial solar photovoltaic systems with a minimum nameplate output capacity of greater than 250 kw DC. Other relevant provisions include the requirement for a "glare analysis and proposed mitigation, if any, to minimize the impact of glare on affected properties" as part of the site plan review (3.28.8.A.14).

Solar Energy Facilities with nameplate capacity of 250 kW or greater shall be sited by Special Permit only in the RR, RN and G zoning districts. One Solar Energy Facility with nameplate capacity of 250 kW or greater for municipal government purposes is allowed "As of Right" on one selected parcel of Town-owned land. The bylaw does not explicitly prohibit these facilities in any district unconditionally. Other solar energy systems with less than 250 kW capacity also require a Special Permit. Ground-mounted Solar Energy Facilities are allowed in all districts if the energy is primarily for on-premise use and conforms to yard requirements, but those used primarily off-premises require a Special Permit in all districts.

Setbacks for Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Facilities are fixed distances from property lines, lot lines, and facility perimeters. Specifically, "Solar arrays and related equipment shall have front, side and rear yard setbacks of a minimum of 100 feet." However, "If a front, side or rear lot line abuts one or more residences, the setback for that lot line shall be a minimum of 200 feet." Other setback distances include "front, side and rear yard setbacks of at least 50 feet for any fencing that is required" and "Setback from a public way shall be at least 200 feet." Additionally, "A 50-foot minimum setback shall apply when the abutting parcel has the same owner and the same proposed use as that for the proposed facility." The Zoning Board of Appeals may allow lesser or require greater setbacks based on potential impacts.

Setback from a public way shall be at least 200 feet. Other setback requirements include: fencing must have at least a 50-foot setback; solar arrays and related equipment must have front, side, and rear yard setbacks of a minimum of 100 feet; if a lot line abuts one or more residences, the setback for that lot line shall be a minimum of 200 feet; a 50-foot minimum setback applies when the abutting parcel has the same owner and use as the proposed facility. The 200-foot setback from public ways applies specifically to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Facilities, defined as commercial solar photovoltaic systems with a nameplate capacity greater than 250 kW DC.

Section 3.28.10.B.3 requires that "Whenever reasonable, structures shall be screened from view by vegetation approved by the Permit Granting Authority and/or joined or clustered to avoid adverse visual impacts on the neighborhood, abutting properties, and public ways." Section 3.28.10.E (Screening) mandates that "Where the front, side or rear yard faces and/or abuts one or more residences or a public way, a landscape architectural plan will be required" to "minimize to the greatest extent reasonable the visual impact of the Solar Energy Facility" using "mature plantings, vegetation, berms, fencing, land contouring, and strategic placement of the solar panels and appurtenant structures." For battery storage, which is considered an appurtenant structure, Section 3.28.10.B.4.j requires buffering "with vegetative plantings, berms, sound walls, or other measures if, in the opinion of the Special Permit Granting Authority, buffering is necessary to protect farmland, open space, and viewsheds." These requirements apply to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Facilities defined as commercial solar photovoltaic systems with a nameplate capacity of 250 kW or greater and a solar array footprint greater than one acre.

Signs shall comply with Section 5.3 of the West Brookfield Zoning Bylaws (Signs). The following signs shall be required: a) Those necessary to identify the owner, provide a 24-hour emergency contact phone number, and warnings of any danger; and b) Educational signs providing information about solar photovoltaic panels and the benefits of renewable energy. Signs for solar photovoltaic installations shall not exceed sixteen (16) square feet in area and shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the solar photovoltaic installation.

Section 3.28.10.H Land Clearing, Soil Erosion and Habitat Impacts requires that clearing of natural vegetation shall be limited to what is necessary for the construction, operation and maintenance of the ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation or otherwise prescribed by applicable laws, regulations, and bylaws. The installation design shall minimize fragmentation of open space areas and avoid permanently protected open space when feasible. The installation shall be located in such a manner that it does not have significant negative impacts on rare species in the vicinity. Section 3.28.10.I Environmental Impacts requires that proposed structures shall minimize tree, vegetation, and soil removal; minimize grade changes; and that limitations as to cutting trees, removing vegetation, land clearing and prevention of soil erosion shall be included as conditions in the Special Permit. Upon decommissioning, Section 3.28.15.B.2 requires stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to return the site to its original state and minimize erosion. These requirements apply to Large-Scale Solar Energy Facilities defined as having a nameplate capacity of 250kw or greater and a solar array footprint greater than one acre.

summary: Solar Energy Facilities with nameplate capacity of 250 kW or greater shall be sited by Special Permit. The Zoning Board of Appeals shall be the Special Permit Granting Authority for a ground-mounted Solar Energy Facility. Specifically, Solar Energy Facilities are permitted as follows: A. One (1) Solar Energy Facility with nameplate capacity of 250kw or greater for municipal government purposes, sited 'As of Right' on one selected parcel of Town-owned land. B. Solar Energy Facilities with nameplate capacity of 250kw or greater shall be sited by Special Permit. C. Solar Energy Facilities with name plate capacity of less than 250kw shall be sited by Special Permit. The bylaw states that Solar Energy Facilities shall be permitted by Special Permit only in the RR, RN and G zoning districts.

The ordinance requires that if a front, side or rear lot line abuts one or more residences, the setback for that lot line shall be a minimum of 200 feet. Other setback options include: 100 feet minimum front, side and rear yard setbacks for solar arrays and related equipment; 50 feet minimum setbacks for fencing enclosing the facility; 50 feet minimum setback when the abutting parcel has the same owner and use as the proposed facility. The Zoning Board of Appeals may allow lesser or greater setbacks based on potential impacts. (See Sections 3.28.10.A.1-7)

Section 3.28.8 requires site plan review including submission of a site plan showing "views of the site from residences and public ways from which the facility would be visible," and "the proposed installation with the planned screening for the facility in place." Section 3.28.10.E mandates "a landscape architectural plan" to "minimize to the greatest extent reasonable the visual impact of the Solar Energy Facility" using "mature plantings, vegetation, berms, fencing, land contouring, and strategic placement of the solar panels and appurtenant structures." Section 3.28.D requires that "one of the following conditions must be met: a) The location of the facility... cannot reasonably be seen from a residence or public way during all seasons of the year; or b) The location... is so distant from a residence or public way, and/or so obscured by topography, tree lines, and/or vegetation, that the visual impact... is rendered negligible, as determined by the Zoning Board of Appeals, during all seasons of the year." These requirements apply to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Facilities defined as "a commercial solar photovoltaic system... with a minimum nameplate output capacity of greater than 250 kw DC."

Section 8.3.9 Removal Requirements: "Any LGSPI which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned consistent with Section 5.G.10. of this bylaw shall be removed. The owner or operator shall physically remove the installation no more than 150 days after the date of discontinued operations. The owner or operator shall notify the Site Plan Review Authority by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Decommissioning shall consist of: a. Physical removal of all solar energy systems, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines from the site. b. Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations. c. Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion. The Site Plan Review Authority may allow the owner or operator to leave landscaping or designated below-grade foundations in order to minimize erosion and disruption to vegetation." Section 8.3.10 Abandonment: "Absent notice of a proposed date of decommissioning or written notice of extenuating circumstances, the large-scale ground-mounted solar energy system shall be considered abandoned when it fails to operate for more than one year without the written consent of the Site Plan Review Authority. If the owner or operator of the solar energy system fails to remove the installation in accordance with the requirements of this section within 150 days of abandonment or the proposed date of decommissioning, the town retains the right, after the receipt of an appropriate court order, to enter and remove an abandoned, hazardous, or decommissioned large-scale ground-mounted solar energy system." Section 8.3.11 Surety: "Proponents of any LGSPI shall provide a form of surety... to cover the cost of installation removal and stabilization of the site in the event the LSPGI has reached the end of its useful life or been abandoned... in an amount and form determined to be reasonable by the Planning Board, but in no event to exceed more than 125 percent of the cost of removal and compliance with the additional requirements set forth herein... The project proponent shall submit a fully inclusive estimate of the costs associated with removal, prepared by a qualified engineer... This surety will be due and payable at the issuance of the building permit... The financial surety shall be maintained by the proponent for the lifespan of the facility... The town shall have the right but not the obligation to remove the facility."

Section 8.3.5 states: 'All LGSPI and Appurtenant Structures shall conform with the Table of Dimensional Control below.' The table specifies a maximum height of 15 feet for PV Arrays and 35 feet for Appurtenant Structures. The most restrictive maximum structure height allowed for LGSPI is therefore 15 feet. Units are explicitly given as feet in the table header: 'Maximum height in feet (5.4)'.

Signs on LGSPI shall comply with Section 6.4. of the Zoning Bylaw. A sign consistent with the Zoning Bylaw shall be required to identify the Owner and provide a 24-hour emergency contact phone number. Reasonable identification of the manufacturer or Operator of the solar photovoltaic installation may be provided. Solar photovoltaic installations shall not be used for displaying any advertising.

The ordinance states that "A LGSPI may be constructed as of right on any Lot that any portion of is located within one thousand (1,000) feet of necessary supportive infrastructure... so long as that Lot is not a High Conservation Value parcel..." and "A LGSPI may only be constructed on a Lot shown to have adequate physical and legal access... as determined by the Planning Board." There is no mention of any districts where LGSPI are permitted only as a special use or require approval by the zoning appeals board or similar conditional processes. The text does not identify any zoning districts with special use or conditional approval requirements for LGSPI outside of solar overlay districts, which are excluded from consideration.

Ground-mounted solar energy generation systems at any scale shall not exceed 15 feet above the ground as measured under each panel module, except the overall height of tracking-type systems may exceed 20 feet for transient conditions when dumping snow.

Section 171-28.5 K. Abandonment or Decommissioning requires that any large-scale ground-mounted solar electric installation which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned shall be removed within 150 days. Decommissioning shall consist of: (a) Physical removal of all installations, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines; (b) Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with regulations; (c) Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary. The installation is considered abandoned if it fails to operate for more than one year without written consent. Proponents must provide financial surety covering removal costs, not exceeding 125% of the estimated cost. The surety may be in the form of escrow, bond, or other approved form. These requirements apply to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations defined as having a minimum nameplate capacity greater than 10 kW AC, occupying up to 10 acres with possible increases under certain conditions. Smaller installations (10 kW AC or less) that are accessory to existing uses are exempt from this section but must comply with other local, state, and federal requirements. Larger installations (>500 kW AC or occupying more than 2 acres) require a Special Permit and Site Plan Review in addition to these requirements.

The height of any structure associated with a Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installation shall not exceed 25 feet. [Amended height 5-9-2013 ATM, Art. 21]. This applies to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations greater than 10 kW AC, up to 10 acres with possible increases by special permit up to 15 acres. The ordinance explicitly states this maximum height restriction in section G.(3) Height of Structures. Other related dimensional requirements include setbacks of 100 feet for front, side, and rear yards, and size limits of 10 acres with possible increases of 2.5 acres each under certain conditions. The units for height are feet.

The size of the Solar Electric Generating Facility including required setbacks shall not exceed 10 acres, except that where the Special Permit Granting Authority determines it appropriate, the maximum size of the facility may be increased by (a) an additional 2 ½ acres if the Facility is sited on glacial till and sandy soil that is not heavily forested; and (b) an additional 2 ½ acres if the Facility is sited in a location where it is not visible from any existing residence. The units are expressed in acres as an area value.

summary: Noise generated by Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations and associated equipment and machinery shall conform to applicable state and local noise regulations, including the DEP’s Division of Air Quality noise regulations, 310 CMR 7.10. A source of sound will be considered in violation if it increases the broadband sound level by more than 10 dB(A) above ambient; or produces a  "pure tone"  condition, when an octave band center frequency sound pressure level exceeds the two (2) adjacent center frequency sound pressure levels by three (3) decibels or more. Said criteria are measured both at the property line and at the nearest inhabited residence.  "Ambient"  is defined as the background A-weighted sound level that is exceeded 90% of the time measured during equipment hours, unless established by other means with the consent of the DEP. Noise generated shall further comply with Section 171-15 B (1) of the Town of Whately bylaws.

Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations greater than 500 kWAC or occupying more than 2 acres are not allowed (N) in the Agriculture/Residential 1 district. In contrast, such installations require a Special Permit (SP) and Site Plan Review in the Agriculture/Residential 2, Commercial, Commercial-Industrial, and Industrial Zoning Districts. Specifically, the text states: 'Ground Mounted Solar Power Generating Facilities greater than 500 kWAC or occupying more than 2 acres that meet the requirements of Section 171-28.5' are marked 'N' in Agriculture/Residential 1 and 'SP' in the other districts. Additionally, installations greater than 10 kWAC up to 500 kWAC that occupy no more than 2 acres are allowed by right (Y*) in Agriculture/Residential 2, Commercial, Commercial-Industrial, and Industrial districts but not in Agriculture/Residential 1. The purpose of the bylaw is to facilitate Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations while addressing public safety and minimizing environmental impacts.

Setbacks for Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations, front, side and rear setbacks shall be as follows: (a) Front yard: The front yard depth shall not be less than 100 feet. (b) Side yard: Each side yard shall have a depth of at least 100 feet. (c) Rear yard: The rear yard depth shall not be less than 100 feet. The required setback areas should not be included in the 2 acre maximum calculation for By-Right solar electric installations (see Section 171-28.5 A.). Other setback options mentioned include setbacks for Large-Scale Battery Storage systems, which require no less than 500 feet from any abutting plot in the AR1 or AR2 Districts and no less than 200 feet from any well for lots not served by public water, but these do not apply to the general solar installation setbacks.
section: 171-28.5 G. Dimension, Size and Height Requirements

summary: All facilities must be located at least 100 feet from any wetland or Priority Habitat Area as delineated in accordance with the Massachusetts Endangered Species Act regulations at 321CMR 10.00 or successor regulation. Priority Habitat Areas are natural resource protection areas. No explicit numeric setback is given for public conservation lands or preservation areas. The ordinance also includes a Resource Replacement Fee for agricultural or forest land removed from production but this is not a setback. The relevant text is from Section 171-28.5 I.(2): 'All facilities must be located at least 100 feet from any wetland or Priority Habitat Area as delineated in accordance with the Massachusetts Endangered Species Act regulations at 321CMR 10.00 or successor regulation.'

Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations "shall be screened from view by a minimum fifteen (15) foot wide buffer zone with staggered and grouped planting of shrubs and small trees. Such plantings shall use native plants and a mix of deciduous and evergreen species and may be located within the setback area. Such plantings must be a minimum of five (5) feet high at the time of installation and any plant that is damaged or dies shall be replaced on an annual basis each Spring or Fall." This applies to installations greater than 10 kW AC, up to 10 acres, with possible increases of an additional 2 ½ acres if sited on glacial till and sandy soil that is not heavily forested, and an additional 2 ½ acres if the facility is not visible from any existing residence. Installations larger than 500 kW AC or occupying more than 2 acres require a Special Permit and Site Plan Review. All such installations are subject to the requirements of Section 171-28.5 and Site Plan Review under Section 171-17.

Signs on Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations shall comply with Whately’s sign bylaw, Section 171-14. A sign consistent with Whately’s sign bylaw shall be required to identify the owner and provide a 24-hour emergency contact phone number. Solar electric installations shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the solar electric installation.

The ordinance applies to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations greater than 10 kW AC and up to 10 acres, with possible increases by 2.5 acres under certain conditions. It explicitly requires that "clearing of natural vegetation shall be limited to what is necessary for the construction, operation and maintenance" and that installations "shall not occur on any slopes greater than 15% in order to minimize erosion." Upon decommissioning, "stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion" is required. Site plans must show "proposed changes to the landscape of the site, grading, vegetation clearing and planting." An operation and maintenance plan must include "storm water and vegetation controls." Other relevant requirements include limitations on herbicide use, alternatives such as mowing or grazing for vegetation control, and minimizing removal of existing trees. The ordinance also details site plan review, setbacks, and other design standards but these are not directly soil, erosion, or sediment control requirements. The ordinance distinguishes between installations: those greater than 10 kW AC up to 500 kW AC occupying no more than 2 acres are allowed by right but subject to site plan review and this section's requirements; installations larger than 500 kW AC or occupying more than 2 acres require a special permit and site plan review. Smaller installations (10 kW AC or less) that are accessory to existing uses are exempt from this section but must comply with other applicable requirements.

Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations which require a Special Permit and Site Plan Review in accordance with the Zoning Bylaws of the Town of Whately in addition to meeting the requirements of this section are as follows: (a) an installation larger than 500 kWAC; or (b) an installation occupying more than 2 acres of land on one or more adjacent parcels in common ownership (including those separated by a roadway) in the Agricultural Residential 2, Commercial, Commercial-Industrial or Industrial Zoning Districts. Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations greater than 10 kWAC up to 500 kWAC that occupy no more than 2 acres of land proposed to be constructed in the Agricultural/Residential District 2, Commercial, Commercial-Industrial, or Industrial Zoning Districts are allowed by right but are subject to Site Plan Review. Ground Mounted Solar Power Generating Facilities greater than 10 kWAC up to 500 kWAC that occupy no more than 2 acres and meet the requirements of Section 171-28.5 are allowed by right in Agriculture/ Residential 1, Agriculture/ Residential 2, Commercial, Commercial-Industrial, and Industrial districts. Ground Mounted Solar Power Generating Facilities greater than 500 kWAC or occupying more than 2 acres that meet the requirements of Section 171-28.5 require a Special Permit (SP) in Agriculture/ Residential 2, Commercial, Commercial-Industrial, and Industrial districts.

Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations greater than 10 kWAC up to 500 kWAC that occupy no more than 2 acres are allowed by right but are subject to Site Plan Review (see Section 171-17) and the requirements of Section 171-28.5. Installations larger than 500 kWAC or occupying more than 2 acres require a Special Permit and Site Plan Review. Site Plan Review requires submission of a site plan showing "proposed changes to the landscape of the site, grading, vegetation clearing and planting, exterior lighting, screening vegetation or structures including their height" and "locations of local or National Historic Districts, Priority Heritage Landscapes, and Scenic Roads and Scenic Views identified on the Scenic Resources and Unique Environments Map." Screening requirements mandate a "minimum fifteen (15) foot wide buffer zone with staggered and grouped planting of shrubs and small trees" using native plants, with plants "a minimum of five (5) feet high at the time of installation" and replacement of any damaged or dead plants annually. The purpose of the bylaw is to "minimize impacts on environmental, scenic, natural and historic resources."

All facilities must be located at least 100 feet from any wetland or Priority Habitat Area as delineated in accordance with the Massachusetts Endangered Species Act regulations at 321CMR 10.00 or successor regulation. This setback applies to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Electric Installations greater than 10 kW AC. No other explicit setbacks from lakes, reservoirs, streams, or rivers are specified for such installations.

summary: The maximum lot coverage for Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems shall be twenty-five percent (25%) when located in residential zoning districts and fifty percent (50%) when located in commercial or industrial (non-residential) zoning districts. For the purpose of this section, lot coverage shall be measured as the total aggregate area of land covered by buildings, structures, associated equipment including solar panels and all land contained within the perimeter security fence and calculated as a percentage of the total area of the lot.

Section 10.7.13 Decommissioning requires that any Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy System that has reached the end of its useful life or discontinued operations shall be decommissioned by the owner or operator no later than 180 days after discontinued operations. Decommissioning must include: (1) physical removal of all components including solar panels, structures, foundations, equipment, security barriers, and electrical transmission lines; (2) disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with regulations; and (3) restoration of the site to its natural pre-existing condition, with possible allowance by the Planning Board to leave landscaping, below-grade foundations, and access roads to minimize erosion and disruption. The owner/operator must provide at least 30 days prior notice to the Planning Board and Building Commissioner of the proposed shutdown and removal schedule. Systems inactive for 90 consecutive days without written consent are considered abandoned. If the owner/operator fails to remove the system, the Town may remove it at the owner's expense, with costs drawn from performance surety or charged as a tax lien. Prior to construction, the owner/manager must provide a performance surety to cover decommissioning costs, including an escalator for inflation but excluding salvage value. The surety must be maintained for the system's lifespan and may be increased as needed. Performance surety is not required for municipal or state-owned facilities.

Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems "shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing." The perimeter fence "shall be an eight-foot tall vinyl-coated chain link fence colored dark green or black and designed with a texture pattern or fabric screen, if deemed necessary, to blend into the background and minimize the visual impact on nearby properties and abutting roadways" and "shall be installed with a bottom gap of no less than six (6) inches) between the ground and the bottom of the fence to minimize impacts on wildlife movement." The fencing is required to "prevent unauthorized persons from accessing the Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy System." Additionally, setbacks are measured from the "perimeter fence enclosing the solar array," with specific minimum distances for front, side, and rear yards. Lot coverage calculations include "all land contained within the perimeter security fence."

Section 10.7.7(F) states: "Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems shall be designed to prevent concentrated solar radiation or reflected glare from becoming a public nuisance or hazard to nearby buildings, roadways or properties." This is the explicit glare restriction applicable to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems. Other related provisions include visual impact assessments, screening, and setback requirements to minimize visual impacts, but these do not specifically address glare. The Planning Board may impose conditions such as greater setbacks, modification of exterior appearance, screening, and additional design and siting modifications to mitigate adverse impacts.
The height of the solar panels in a Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy System shall not exceed twelve (12) feet in height above finished grade.

The minimum lot size for Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems shall be five (5) acres as stated in section 10.7.6(A). This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for such systems. Other dimensional requirements include minimum lot frontage of 200 feet and various setback distances, but these do not affect the minimum lot size. The unit 'acres' is a standard measure of land area.

Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems shall maintain a minimum setback distance measured from the respective property lot line to the perimeter fence enclosing the solar array as follows: The front yard setback distance shall be at least 150 feet; The side yard setback distance shall be at least 100 feet; The rear yard setback distance shall be at least 100 feet; and Where the side yard or rear yard abuts an existing residence the setback distance shall be a minimum of 200 feet. The Planning Board may authorize a reduction or require a greater setback based on site conditions and potential impacts.

The ordinance requires that a Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy System "shall be screened from the view of all abutting properties zoned for residential use by an undisturbed buffer strip of natural vegetation which shall be located along the outer perimeter of the parcel and which shall be a minimum of fifty (50) feet wide extending into the required front, side or rear yard measured from the property boundary." If existing natural vegetation is insufficient, "the Planning Board may require the applicant to plant additional landscaping within the buffer strip to better screen the use from abutting property." Further, the system "shall be sited and designed in a manner that effectively screens the solar array and appurtenant structures from the year-round view of adjacent roadways and abutting residential properties to the maximum extent that is reasonable and practical including but not limited to: preserving natural vegetation to the maximum extent possible; blending in equipment with the surroundings; and installing additional plant landscaping, opaque fencing, earthen berms and land contouring in the vegetative buffer strip as well as the portion of the setback area located outside the buffer strip if required to provide an effective visual barrier." Additional plantings must be "a minimum of six (6) feet in height at planting and staggered to better screen the solar arrays from view" and "shall be maintained and replaced if unhealthy by the owner or operator of the Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy System for the life of the installation." Appurtenant structures "shall be screened from view by vegetation and/or joined or clustered to avoid adverse visual impacts." The Planning Board may alter or waive screening requirements if they "determine that the strict adherence to such requirements would prove ineffective or unnecessary or serve no meaningful purpose for the site."

summary: A sign shall be erected at the gated entrance to identify the owner or manager and provide a 24-hour emergency contact phone number. All signage shall comply with section 12 of the Wilbraham Zoning By-Law.

The ordinance requires that applicants submit site plans showing "engineering controls at the site and on the access road to control erosion and sedimentation both during construction and after construction as a permanent measure" conforming to state, federal, and local stormwater regulations (10.7.5(F)(7)). Best Management Practices (BMP) must be used for controlling and managing stormwater runoff and drainage in compliance with all applicable regulations, including construction phasing to mitigate erosion and sedimentation (10.7.7(H)). Vegetation clearing is limited to what is necessary and any land disturbance is subject to stormwater management criteria and all applicable laws (10.7.7(C)(1)). Upon decommissioning, the site must be restored to its natural pre-existing condition, including stabilization or re-vegetation to minimize erosion (10.7.13(A)(3)). These requirements apply explicitly to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems.

summary: Municipal Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems owned, operated by, or developed for and on behalf of the Town of Wilbraham are allowed as-of-right in all zoning districts with site plan approval from the Planning Board. Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems with a footprint size less than 10,000 square feet that are accessory structures do not need to comply with this section but require a building permit and must comply with section 3.9.1.3 of the Wilbraham Zoning By-Law as applicable.
section: D. Municipal Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems

summary: Where the side yard or rear yard abuts an existing residence the setback distance shall be a minimum of 200 feet. Other setback distances include: front yard setback of at least 150 feet; side yard setback of at least 100 feet; rear yard setback of at least 100 feet. The Planning Board may authorize reductions or require greater setbacks based on potential impacts as evidenced by a visual impact assessment.

Section 10.7.5(I) requires applicants to "Provide a Visual Impact Assessment study of the Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy System which shall describe the visible components of the proposed project, evaluate the potential visibility of the project within the defined study area, identify key views for visual assessment, assess the potential project visibility, illustrate the appearance of the proposed project, and identify potential mitigation measures to minimize visibility to abutters." The assessment "shall produce a map showing all areas within a one-mile radius of the proposed installation where the Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy System can be seen and where it cannot be seen." Methods include "viewshed analysis, field verification and visual simulation," and may include "renderings, line-of-sight studies and two or three dimensional visualizations such as photomontage, video montage and animation produced through Spatial Information Systems (SIS) and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) technology." Additionally, section 10.7.7(B)(1) states that "A Visual Impact Assessment shall be submitted for review per section 10.7.5(I) and taken into account when evaluating the design of the Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy System." These requirements apply explicitly to Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance.

summary: Section 9.30-12 Removal Requirements and Abandonment explicitly requires that "Any ground-mounted solar PV installation which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned consistent with Section 9.30-12.1 of this bylaw shall be removed." The owner or operator must "physically remove the installation no more than 150 days after the date of discontinued operations" and notify the Planning Board by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Decommissioning shall consist of: (a) Physical removal of all ground-mounted solar PV installations, structures, equipment, security barriers, and electrical lines from the site; (b) Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations; (c) Stabilization and re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion." Additionally, Section 9.30-13 Financial Surety requires the project proponent to provide "a form of surety, either through escrow account, bond or otherwise, to cover the cost of removal" with the amount not to exceed 125 percent of the cost of removal. These requirements apply to commercial ground-mounted solar PV installations larger than 20 acres in the SPOD, as defined and regulated in Section 9.30. Other relevant conditions include abandonment defined as failure to operate for more than one year without written waiver (9.30-12.1), and the town's right to remove the installation upon court order if the owner fails to comply within 150 days.

Section 9.30-5.1 states: "There shall be a fence built surrounding the solar array and ancillary equipment. The fence shall be knuckled selvage chain link fence unless determined otherwise by the Site Plan Approval Authority. The fence shall be at least six inches above the ground to allow for small species of wildlife crossing under the fence." This fencing requirement applies to commercial ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations larger than 20 acres in the Solar Photovoltaic Overlay District (SPOD).

Sound levels under normal operating conditions of the ground-mounted solar PV installation measured at the boundary of the lot on which the installation is sited shall not be more than 10 decibels greater than would otherwise exist in the absence of the facility. The unit is expressed as decibels, assumed to be dBA as the standard unit for noise measurement.

The Solar Photovoltaic Overlay District (SPOD) is delineated as a district to promote large-scale commercial ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations. According to Section 7.4.4, "In the SPOD commercial Solar Photovoltaic installations up to 20 acres in area are allowed as of right with Site Plan Review by the Planning Board." Installations larger than 20 acres require a special permit within the SPOD. The Use Table in Section 3.0 shows that ground-mounted commercial solar photovoltaic installations larger than 20 acres are not permitted in the base districts VR, VM, and RU without special permits. The SPOD is an overlay district that allows these large installations as a primary use, overriding the underlying district restrictions. Other districts (Village Residential - VR, Village Mixed - VM, Rural - RU) require special permits or do not permit such large installations.

Section 9.30-2 clarifies that commercial ground-mounted PV installations larger than 20 acres require a special permit only in the Solar Photovoltaic Overlay District (SPOD), implying they are not allowed unconditionally outside the SPOD. The SPOD is intended to allow large-scale commercial ground-mounted solar installations with additional regulations, while the underlying districts VR, VM, and RU prohibit such large installations unconditionally.

summary: The setbacks for ground-mounted solar PV installations, including appurtenant structures and parking areas, shall be at least 50 feet from any property boundary. The setback areas shall not be included in the calculation of the size of the ground-mounted solar PV installation. (Section 9.30-8.1) This applies to commercial ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations larger than 20 acres in the Solar Photovoltaic Overlay District (SPOD). No multiplier or variable setback based on height or other factors is mentioned.

Section 9.30-9.6 Visual Impact Mitigation requires that the plan for a ground-mounted solar PV installation be designed to maximize preservation of on-site and abutting natural and developed features. "Structures should be screened from view by vegetation and/or joined or clustered to avoid adverse visual impacts and be architecturally compatible with each other." Vegetation used for screening "shall be of locally adapted species native to New England, excluding cultivars." The vegetative screening "shall reach a mature form to effectively screen the installation within five years of installation." The mature height and depth of the vegetated screening must be such that the installation’s structures "are not apparent to a person upon any public road and viewing the installation from a height of ten feet." Planting of the vegetative screening "shall be completed prior to final approval of the PV installation by the Building Inspector."

Section 9.30-9.2 Signage requires that any signs on ground-mounted solar PV installations and property shall comply with Section 9.8 Sign Restrictions of this Zoning Bylaw. A sign shall be required to identify the owner and provide a 24-hour emergency contact phone number. Solar PV installations shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the installation.

The ordinance requires submission of an Operation and Maintenance Plan that includes "measures for maintaining safe access to the installation, stormwater and erosion controls," and a Stormwater Management Plan "with the stamp and signature of a Registered Professional Engineer" detailing topography, stormwater conveyances, flood plains, groundwater elevation, vegetation, drainage, recharge analysis, and soils information from test pits. Clearing of natural vegetation "shall be limited to that which is necessary" and "sufficient vegetation shall be maintained to minimize soil erosion and maintain adequate topsoil." Installations "shall be installed only upon water-permeable surfaces as approved during site plan review." Upon removal, "stabilization and re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion" is required, with possible allowance to leave landscaping or below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and disruption. These requirements apply to commercial ground-mounted solar PV installations 1.25 acres and larger, including those larger than 20 acres in the Solar Photovoltaic Overlay District (SPOD).
