summary: The Use Table in Section 3.0 shows that Ground-mounted Commercial Solar Photovoltaic Installations larger than 20 acres are marked 'N' (Not Permitted) in all base districts (VR, VM, RU). Section 9.30-2 states that commercial ground-mounted PV installations larger than 20 acres in the Solar Photovoltaic Overlay District (SPOD) require a special permit, but per instructions, overlay districts are excluded from consideration. Installations between 1.25 and 20 acres in the RU and VM districts require a special permit or site plan review. Therefore, outside of the SPOD, there are no districts where commercial ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installations larger than 20 acres are permitted as a special use or similar.

Section 9.30-4 Site Plan Review requires "pre- and post-construction color photorealistic visualizations of the existing site and proposed large-scale ground-mounted solar PV installation from at least four perspectives... including from the nearest residential structure and of the area(s) that are most publicly visible, with technical explanation of how visualization was produced." This applies to commercial ground-mounted solar PV installations 1.25 acres and larger, including those larger than 20 acres in the SPOD, which require a special permit. Additionally, Section 9.30-9.6 Visual Impact Mitigation mandates that "the plan for a ground-mounted solar PV installation shall be designed to maximize the preservation of on-site and abutting natural and developed features," with requirements for vegetation retention, screening, and architectural compatibility to avoid adverse visual impacts. These requirements are part of the site plan review and special permit process for large commercial installations in the SPOD.

Sections 6.11.15 through 6.11.18 explicitly enact decommissioning requirements for solar energy collection systems requiring site plan review under sections 6.11.2 c and d. Section 6.11.15 states: 'Any installation which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned as defined in section 6.11.17 of this bylaw shall be removed. The owner or operator shall physically remove the installation no more than 150 days after the date of discontinued operations. The owner or operator shall notify the Planning Board by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Decommissioning shall consist of: a. Physical removal of the solar collectors, appurtenant structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines from the site. b. Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations.' Section 6.11.16 requires 'Stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion,' with possible exceptions allowed by the Planning Board. Section 6.11.17 defines abandonment and authorizes town removal if the owner fails to remove the installation within 150 days. Section 6.11.18 requires operators to provide financial surety 'to cover the cost of removal of the system in the event the town must remove it and remediate the landscape,' with the amount determined by the Planning Board or an independent engineer. Other solar energy collection systems not requiring site plan review (e.g., smaller or accessory systems) are not subject to these decommissioning requirements.

Section 6.11.12 states: 'Solar energy collections systems shall be surrounded by a chain link or similar fence adequate to prevent entry by unauthorized persons.' This applies to systems requiring site plan review under sections 6.11.2 c and d, which include 'Ground mounted Solar Energy Collection Systems ... subject to the site plan review requirements' and 'Other Solar Energy Collection Systems ... allowed ... by special permit issued by the Planning Board and the site plan review requirements.' Other options include: (a) systems producing energy exclusively for use on the premises or generating electricity sold to the utility but where the site is a net purchaser of electricity, permitted as accessory use; (b) systems mounted on buildings allowed by right in all zones; and (c) ground-mounted systems allowed by right in certain zones but subject to site plan review and other requirements.

Section 6.11.12(a) states: 'If the noise level measured at any property line of the system in normal operation is more than 10 db greater than the reported pre construction noise level at the same location, sound deadening measures may be required as a condition of allowing further operation of the system.' This applies to systems requiring site plan review under sections 6.11.2 c and d, which typically include utility-scale solar energy systems. The units are given as 'db' in the text, which is interpreted as decibels (dB).

The ordinance requires "appropriate installation of wooded buffers to protect neighboring residential properties, and to restrict visual access to the adjacent properties"; if a wooded buffer would shade the collectors, "the Planning Board may allow substitution of a fence." Additionally, "appurtenant structures... should be shaded from view by vegetation and/or joined or clustered to avoid adverse visual impacts." These requirements apply to Solar Energy Collection Systems subject to site plan review under sections 6.11.2.c and 6.11.2.d, which include ground-mounted systems and other larger systems. Other options include substitution of a fence if shading is a concern, and clustering or joining appurtenant structures to minimize visual impact.

Section 6.11.12(b) requires that "Each installation shall have a sign showing the name and address of the operator thereof and a telephone number where a responsible representative of the operator may be reached at any time." This applies to systems requiring site plan review under sections 6.11.2(c) and 6.11.2(d), which include ground mounted Solar Energy Collection Systems and other Solar Energy Collection Systems allowed by special permit. Other options for Solar Energy Collection Systems include: (a) systems producing energy exclusively for use on the premises or generating electricity sold to the utility but where the site is a net purchaser of electricity, permitted by right as an accessory use; (b) systems mounted on buildings allowed by right in all zones; (c) ground mounted systems allowed by right in certain zones but subject to site plan review; and (d) other systems allowed by special permit and site plan review.

Sections 6.11.8, 6.11.9, and 6.11.16 explicitly address soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Solar Energy Collection Systems. Section 6.11.8 states, "A Low Impact Development Permit under article 31 of the general bylaws will be required for Solar Energy Collection Systems." Section 6.11.9 requires "an operation and maintenance plan ... which shall include measures for maintaining safe access to the installation, storm water controls, as well as general procedures for operational maintenance of the installation." Section 6.11.16 mandates "Stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion," allowing the Planning Board to permit leaving landscaping or designated below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and disruption to vegetation. These requirements apply to systems requiring site plan review under sections 6.11.2 c and d, which include ground-mounted systems and other solar energy collection systems allowed by special permit, typically covering utility-scale systems intended for offsite electricity generation or sale.

The ordinance states that 'Other Solar Energy Collection Systems are allowed in all zoning districts by special permit issued by the Planning Board and the site plan review requirements of article 12 and the requirements of section 6.11.5 through 6.11.18.' Other categories include: (a) systems producing energy for exclusive on-site use or net purchasers of electricity are permitted by right as accessory uses; (b) building-mounted systems are allowed by right in all zones; (c) ground-mounted systems are allowed by right in R40, R80, C1, C2, and I zones subject to site plan review and additional requirements.

Section 26.11 Abandonment or Decommissioning requires that any solar photovoltaic installation which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned shall be removed within 150 days after discontinued operations. The owner or operator must notify the Building Commissioner and City Council by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Decommissioning includes physical removal of all installations, disposal of waste according to regulations, and site stabilization or re-vegetation. The City Council may allow leaving landscaping or below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and disruption. Abandonment is defined as failure to operate for more than one year without written consent of the City Council. If removal is not done within 150 days of abandonment or decommissioning date, the City may remove the installation. Section 26.11.3 requires proponents of large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic projects to provide financial surety (escrow, bond, or otherwise) to cover removal costs, not exceeding 125% of the estimated cost, as determined by the City Council. Such surety is not required for municipally- or state-owned facilities. The estimate must be prepared by a qualified engineer and reviewed by the City Engineer, including a mechanism for inflation adjustments. Other solar energy system types mentioned include roof-mounted, small-scale, medium-scale, large-scale (defined as occupying more than 40,000 sq ft or about 250 kW DC or greater), solar carport/canopy, off-grid, and solar thermal systems, but decommissioning financial surety is specifically required for large-scale ground-mounted systems.

Security fencing shall be required around any medium-scale or large-scale ground mounted solar energy systems. Security fencing associated with ground mounted solar photovoltaic installations shall not be subject to the provisions of Section 5.3.2 of this Ordinance. (Section 26.3, item 5) The ordinance defines a large-scale solar energy system as "An Active Solar Energy System that occupies more than 40,000 square feet of surface area (equivalent to a rated nameplate capacity of about 250kW DC or greater)." Other options include small-scale (1,750 square feet or less, about 10 kW DC or less), medium-scale (more than 1,750 but less than 40,000 square feet, about 10 - 250 kW DC), and off-grid systems. The fencing requirement applies explicitly to medium-scale and large-scale ground-mounted systems.

summary: Except for a small residential accessory solar energy generating system, the Department of Planning & Zoning shall require a decommissioning plan if one is not otherwise required as a result of obtaining a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity from the Public Service Commission (Section 22-8.D.9). This applies to major solar energy generating systems. Other related requirements include planting plans, stormwater management, and restrictions on forest clearing, but these do not pertain directly to decommissioning. The ordinance also details options for planting plans and fee in lieu for mitigation, but the explicit decommissioning requirement is as stated.

The Department of Planning & Zoning shall restrict forest clearing within 300 feet beyond the landward boundary of tidal waters or tidal wetlands, or the edge of each bank of a tributary stream for a major solar energy generating system in the Resource Conservation Area (Section 22-8.E.2). Additionally, planting plans may include planting on-site within 300 feet beyond the landward boundary of tidal waters or tidal wetlands, or the edge of each bank of a tributary stream (Section 22-8.F.1.a.i). Other provisions prohibit major solar energy generating systems in habitat protection areas and require buffer protections but do not specify other fixed setback distances.

Section 22-8.D.3 requires the Department of Planning & Zoning to "require the following minimum standards for the Critical Area Buffer: measure and delineate the Buffer; prohibit access through the Critical Area Buffer unless no feasible alternative; authorize one point of access if necessary with disturbance replanted at a 2.5:1 ratio and a buffer management plan." For major solar energy generating systems, Section 22-8.D.6 mandates "on-site or off-site planting of 15 percent of the total project area in a Limited Development Area; and 20 percent of the total project area in a Resource Conservation Area." Section 22-8.F requires a planting plan for mitigation, including planting under solar panels or replanting cleared forest areas, with long-term maintenance and protection through conservation easements or restrictive covenants. Alternative mitigation options include off-site planting, wetland migration areas, nature-based practices, or fee in lieu payments as described in Section 22-8.F.1.b and 22-8.G. These requirements apply to major solar energy generating systems as defined in the ordinance.

The ordinance requires stormwater management in accordance with Environment Article, §§ 4-201-4-215, Annotated Code of Maryland, and COMAR 26.17.02 (Section 22-8.D.8). It prohibits major or minor solar energy generating systems on steep slopes or highly erodible soils (Section 22-8.C.5.b). It mandates minimizing clearing of forest and developed woodlands, limiting clearing to 20 percent in Limited Development Areas and 10 acres or 20 percent in Resource Conservation Areas (Section 22-8.D.4). It requires replacement of cleared forest and woodlands on an equal area basis (Section 22-8.D.5) and planting of 15 percent or 20 percent of the total project area in Limited Development Areas or Resource Conservation Areas respectively (Section 22-8.D.6). A planting plan is required for mitigation (Section 22-8.D.7 and 22-8.F). The planting plan options include on-site planting within 300 feet beyond tidal waters or wetlands, contiguous to forest interior dwelling bird habitat, or wildlife corridors; off-site planting under certain agreements; creation of wetland migration areas or nature-based practices; or fee in lieu (Section 22-8.F.1). The ordinance applies these requirements to major solar energy generating systems and distinguishes them from small residential accessory systems throughout the text.

A commercial, institutional, or industrial solar energy generating system may be permitted in accordance with Section 22-3.J in the Resource Conservation Area (22-4.H.8). The Department of Planning & Zoning may authorize a major solar energy generating system in the resource conservation area without growth allocation in accordance with this Article and COMAR 27.01.14 (22-8.C.1.b). The Department of Planning & Zoning may not authorize a major solar energy generating system in habitat protection areas, steep slopes, or highly erodible soils (22-8.C.5). The Department of Planning & Zoning shall apply multiple criteria including minimizing forest clearing, requiring planting plans, stormwater management, and decommissioning plans for major solar energy generating systems (22-8.D). The Department of Planning & Zoning shall also apply additional standards when authorizing a major solar energy generating system in the Resource Conservation Area, including restrictions on forest clearing within 300 feet of tidal waters and recording a Reservation of Resource Conservation Area Density Rights Agreement (22-8.E). Other areas mentioned include Intensely Developed Area and Limited Development Area, but the text does not explicitly state that major solar energy generating systems are permitted there as special use or similar. Small residential accessory solar energy generating systems have separate provisions and are excluded from this summary.

Setbacks shall not be required from inner parcel boundary lines where a solar energy system encompasses multiple parcels. Setback modifications may be granted by owners of residentially zoned parcels or existing residences with a setback modification agreement. Additional setbacks may be required to mitigate aesthetic, noise, safety, glare, or other significant impacts or to provide for designated road or utility corridors.

The ordinance explicitly requires visual screening for commercial solar energy systems to prevent negative significant impacts to the aesthetic and scenic quality of the project area/location. Specifically, "Where screening buffers are required, they shall be opaque within 3 years and shall consist of mixed vegetation including trees, shrubs, and ornamental grasses." Additionally, "Where appropriate, pollinator habitat may be used in lieu of screening buffers." These requirements apply to commercial solar energy systems, including large scale systems defined as those engineered to produce over two megawatts (2 MW) of power. Other related design standards include setbacks, height limits, fencing, lighting, and utility connections, but the explicit vegetative buffer and screening requirements are as stated above.

A SIGN, NOT TO EXCEED ONE (1) SQUARE FOOT, SHALL BE POSTED AT EACH ENTRANCE TO THE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEM TO IDENTIFY THE PROPERTY OWNER, THE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEM OWNER, AND 24-HOUR EMERGENCY CONTACT PHONE NUMBER, AND the manufacturers or installers identification and 24-hour emergency contact phone number. INFORMATION ON THE SIGN SHALL BE KEPT CURRENT. THE SIGN shall be provided along with appropriate warning signage and shall be posted at the site in a clearly visible manner. This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, including Large Scale systems defined as those engineered and designed to produce over two megawatts (2 MW) of power.

The ordinance requires that site and development plans for commercial solar energy systems include identification of "Dust and sediment and erosion control" and "Proposed stormwater management measures." These requirements apply to commercial solar energy systems, including large scale systems engineered to produce over two megawatts (2 MW) of power. Specifically, the text states: "AT THE TIME OF APPLICATION, A CONCEPT PLAN... identifying... Dust and sediment and erosion control; Proposed stormwater management measures;" and "BEFORE FINAL APPROVAL, A MAJOR SITE PLAN... identifying all items listed in (1)...". The ordinance defines commercial solar energy systems as "A NON-ACCESSORY COMMERCIAL FACILITY... for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity," with large scale systems producing over 2 MW. Other design standards and siting considerations are also detailed but do not explicitly address soil, erosion, or sediment control beyond these plan requirements.

Solar ENERGY SYSTEMS power-plant structures must be located at least TWO one-hundred feet from all residentially zoned PARCELStet and existing residences. Setback modifications may be granted by owners of residentially zoned parcels or existing residences with a setback modification agreement.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Principal ground-mounted solar energy generating systems in C-2, C-3, I-1, and I-2 Districts with no size limits. Key provisions include: "A decommissioning plan shall be submitted for review and approval by the Zoning Administrator as part of the site plan approval process." The operator must notify the Zoning Administrator if the system is out of production for more than six months, with abandonment defined at twelve months. The operator must either recommence production or initiate decommissioning, and notify the Zoning Administrator of decommissioning plans. The site must be restored to its original predevelopment condition within 12 months of discontinued operation or abandonment. Financial assurance equal to 125% of the anticipated removal and restoration costs must be provided and maintained. The county may remove the system and restore the site at the property owner's expense if requirements are not met. Restoration includes removal of all solar equipment, proper waste disposal, removal of concrete pads and access roads unless agreed otherwise, replacement of topsoil, site stabilization with vegetative cover, and prohibition of onsite burial of materials. Other options and conditions: In EC District, ground-mounted systems are limited to 25 acres or 50% of site gross area; accessory use systems have size limits based on roof area or electric consumption; roof-mounted systems have height and size limits; accessory use systems generating more than 200% of baseline energy are prohibited on properties with agricultural land preservation easements unless permitted. Setbacks, height limits, fencing, buffers, lighting, and access requirements also apply.

The solar energy generating system shall be enclosed by a security fence that is located between the landscaped buffer and the facility. The fence shall be a minimum of six feet in height and suitable to prevent unauthorized access. The fence shall be constructed to meet any applicable state and federal rule or standard addressing the physical security of the power system facilities. Fencing shall be constructed of quality materials and opaque in nature to assist in screening. The use of barbed wire is prohibited. These fencing requirements apply to all solar energy generating systems, including principal ground-mounted systems in C-2, C-3, I-1, and I-2 Districts with no size limits. Other site requirements include setbacks, height limits, buffer landscaping, lighting, access roads, and decommissioning plans, but fencing specifics are as stated above.

Glare must be mitigated away from adjoining properties and adjacent roads. All solar panels used shall utilize glare-mitigation technology. A glare hazard analysis, certified by the installer prior to installation, is required to assess the impacts of glare, and if applicable, a plan to mitigate any glare hazard with additional screening shall be provided. These requirements apply to principal and accessory use solar energy generating systems. In C-2, C-3, I-1, and I-2 Districts, there shall be no size limits for ground-mounted principal use solar energy generating systems. Other size limits apply in EC District (no more than 25 acres or 50% of site gross area), and accessory use systems have size limits based on district and usage, such as no larger than the aggregate roof area in commercial and industrial districts, or specific square footage limits in residential and conservation districts.

For Principal ground-mounted solar energy generating systems in the C-2, C-3, I-1, and I-2 Districts, there are no size limits (§158.153(D)(a)(i)). The maximum structure height allowed is explicitly stated as: 'No portion of a ground mounted system shall exceed a total height of 15 feet above grade' (§158.153(F)(b)(i)). This 15 feet height limit applies to all ground-mounted solar energy generating systems, including principal uses. Other height limits mentioned include 10 feet for ground-mounted accessory use systems (§158.153(C)(b) 'Height limits. Ground-mounted systems may not exceed a total height of ten feet above existing grade.'), but this applies only to accessory uses, not principal systems. The units for the height restriction are feet.

summary: A landscaped buffer shall be provided along all property lines or along the exterior of the solar array. The buffer must be designed to provide four-season visual screening of the solar facility and include multi-layered, staggered rows of major and minor trees and shrubs that are a mix of evergreen and deciduous vegetation, with an emphasis on species native to Carroll County. Buffers shall be a minimum of 35 feet wide. Planting units (PU) shall be generated at one PU per 10 linear feet of area to be screened. Major trees shall be a minimum of six feet in height with a minimum caliper of two inches at the time of planting. Evergreen trees shall be a minimum of six feet in height at installation. Minor trees shall be at least five feet in height and 1.5-inch caliper at installation. Shrubs shall be a minimum of 3-gallon container stock and at least 24 inches in height at installation. Buffer screening height shall be a minimum of 12 feet. Screening may be achieved with a berm, vegetation at the time of planting, or a combination of berm and vegetation. If forest or hedgerows exist where screening or buffering is required, it must be preserved to the maximum extent practicable and supplemented with new plantings where necessary to provide the required screening or buffering. Buffers shall be installed in accordance with best management practices to ensure growth and plant materials survival. All required buffers shall be preserved and maintained to effectively provide visual screening year-round. Dead or dying buffer materials shall be replaced with similar plant materials on an annual basis. The operator or property owner shall enter into a surety agreement with the county to provide adequate guaranty to the county in the form of an irrevocable letter of credit, or other security approved by the county. The guaranty shall ensure the establishment of the plantings in an amount determined by the county. The surety shall remain in place for a period of five years following installation. Additionally, fencing requirements include a security fence located between the landscaped buffer and the facility, a minimum of six feet in height, opaque in nature to assist in screening, and constructed to meet applicable state and federal physical security standards. The use of barbed wire is prohibited. These requirements apply to principal ground-mounted solar energy generating systems in C-2, C-3, I-1, and I-2 Districts with no size limits.

A sign, not to exceed four square feet, shall be clearly visible and posted at each entrance to the solar energy generating system site to identify the property owner, the solar energy generating system operator, and the twenty-four-hour emergency contact phone number. Information on the sign shall be kept current. Placards shall be posted to identify the location of the AC power supply emergency disconnects. All other signage required by the electrical, building, or fire code shall be posted as required. No other signage shall be permitted without approval from the Zoning Administrator. The site, fencing, or barriers shall not be used to display any advertisements. Applies to principal and accessory use solar energy generating systems.

The ordinance explicitly requires vegetative stabilization for all ground-mounted solar energy generating systems, including minimizing removal of topsoil, retaining topsoil on site, planting native grasses or pollinator-friendly habitat under and around solar panels, maintaining ground cover not to exceed 36 inches except for pollinator management, and establishing ground cover prior to panel installation (§158.153(F)(2)(e)). There are no size limits for principal ground-mounted solar energy generating systems in the C-2, C-3, I-1, and I-2 Districts (§158.153(D)(a)(i)). Additionally, all ground-mounted solar energy generating systems covering more than 5,000 square feet must comply with Chapter 155, including the site plan process (§158.153(E)(2)(c)). The decommissioning plan requires restoration of the site with replacement of topsoil and stabilization with vegetative cover (§158.153(F)(2)(l)). Other district-specific size limits include: EC District systems limited to 25 acres or 50% of site gross area; accessory use systems limited by roof area or specific square footage in Residential, Conservation, Agricultural, and Commercial/Industrial districts (§158.153(C)(a), (D)(a)).

§158.153(D)(a)(ii) states that in the EC District, ground-mounted systems "shall be no more than 25 acres or 50% of the site gross area, whichever is lesser." §158.081(H) clarifies that ground-mounted solar energy generating systems in the EC District "may be approved as part of or separate from the development plan, pending conditional use approval." For C-2, C-3, I-1, and I-2 Districts, the systems are permitted uses with no size limits and do not require special or conditional use approval. Other districts and conditions include: Agricultural and Conservation Districts where systems are prohibited or limited in size; Residential Districts with size limits; and EC District requiring conditional use approval with size limits.

Section 162, subsection 13.b states: 'SOLAR FACILITIES, INCLUDING BUT NOT LIMITED TO SOLAR PANELS, FENCED AREA, ACCESS DRIVES, POWER CONVERSION, ETC., SHALL NOT ENCOMPASS MORE THAN 25% OF THE SITE.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for Solar, Community Based systems up to 2 MW. No other maximum land coverage values are provided for this category.

Section 162 requires a DECOMMISSIONING PLAN for Solar, Community Based systems: "THE APPLICANT, operator, and landowner SHALL SUBMIT, AND HAVE APPROVED, A PLAN FOR DECOMMISSIONING AND REMOVAL OF NON-FUNCTIONING SYSTEMS AND TO RESTORE THE SITE TO ITS PREVIOUS CONDITION." A solar facility is presumed abandoned if "NO ELECTRICITY IS GENERATED BY SUCH SOLAR FACILITY FOR A PERIOD OF TWELVE (12) CONTINUOUS MONTHS." The plan must be accompanied by a cost estimate and a performance bond or other surety in the amount of two hundred (200) percent of the cost estimate. The surety must assure removal and restoration, be payable to Cecil County, be issued by a financial institution authorized in Maryland, and be executed prior to major site plan approval. The surety may not be canceled without proper notice and replacement security. Additional requirements include yearly soil testing and certification that soil conditions are restored prior to release of bonding. The generating capacity of community based solar facilities "shall not exceed two megawatts (2MW), as measured by the alternating current rating of the system’s inverter." Other use categories mentioned include Non-Solar Generating Facilities (Section 156) and Solar, Accessory (Section 163), but decommissioning requirements are explicitly detailed only for Solar, Community Based in Section 162.

Solar facilities shall be enclosed by a security fence that is located between the landscape buffer and the facility. The fence must be a minimum height of six (6) feet and suitable to prevent unauthorized access. The fence shall be constructed to meet any applicable State or Federal regulations and address the physical security of power system facilities. Fencing shall be designed and installed to allow for the passage of small wildlife. The fence shall not be used to display any signage except, as required by law. This applies to Solar, Community Based systems with generating capacity not exceeding two megawatts (2MW). Other use categories include Non-Solar Generating Facilities (not permitted in Business-General zoning), Solar, Accessory (permitted in various residential and business zones with conditions), and Solar, Utility (regulated by PSC and subject to CPCN).

Section 162 states: 'PANELS SHALL NOT EXCEED FIFTEEN (15) FEET IN HEIGHT.' This maximum height restriction applies specifically to Solar, Community Based systems with generating capacity not exceeding two megawatts (2MW). The unit of measurement for height is feet. No other height limits for Solar, Community Based systems are provided in the text.

Community based solar facilities shall have a generating capacity that does not exceed two megawatts (2MW), as measured by the alternating current rating of the system’s inverter. This is stated explicitly in Section 162, item 8. No provisions are given to bypass this limit through permitting. The text also includes other conditions such as minimum setbacks, height limits (15 feet), minimum parcel size (50 acres in certain zones), and site coverage limits (not more than 25% of the site), but these do not affect the maximum system size limit. The 2MW limit applies specifically to Solar, Community Based systems intended for offsite consumption and not regulated by the Public Service Commission.

Solar facilities shall be located at least one hundred (100) feet from all other property lines. Other setbacks mentioned include at least three hundred (300) feet from the edge of pavement or road right of way, whichever is greater, and three hundred (300) feet from dwellings on adjoining properties, but these do not pertain to property lines or parcels. The relevant setback for property lines is the 100 feet distance.

Solar facilities shall be located at least three hundred (300) feet from the edge of pavement or road right of way, whichever is greater. Other setbacks mentioned include 100 feet from all other property lines and 300 feet from dwellings on adjoining properties, but these do not pertain to roads.

Section (5) Decommissioning requires a decommissioning plan to be submitted and approved by the Department prior to the application for a building permit. The owner must notify the Department in writing of an intent to decommission at least 45 days in advance. Decommissioning must begin within three months if the system is damaged beyond repair or abandoned, and be completed within one year of the notice. The plan must include decommissioning cost estimates, removal of all above ground and underground structures, a plan for reclamation, salvage, recycling and disposal, restoration of the property to a similar or better condition, an approved bond or financial guaranty, and a copy of the lease if applicable. A decommissioning cost estimate must be prepared by a Maryland licensed engineer and updated every five years or upon change in lessee/lessor. Financial surety in the form of a performance bond or other guaranty must be maintained continuously until decommissioning is complete and approved. The Department will not issue a building permit until the plan, cost estimate, and bond are approved and effective. Failure to maintain the bond is a violation and may lead to revocation of special exceptions or certificates of occupancy. summary: The ordinance defines a Commercial or Industrial Solar Energy Generating System as "a facility of solar energy collectors with the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity with a generating capacity greater than 2 megawatts." The use of such systems "shall be 'not permitted' in all zoning districts," effectively enacting a ban. This prohibition was adopted on December 21, 2021, and applies universally without conditions or expiration. summary: Section F titled 'DECOMMISSION' explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Solar, Utility systems, including: 'A DECOMMISSIONING PLAN IS REQUIRED TO BE SUBMITTED AND APPROVED BY THE WICOMICO COUNTY PLANNING AND ZONING DEPARTMENT PRIOR TO THE APPLICATION FOR A BUILDING PERMIT.' The owner must 'NOTIFY THE COUNTY OF AN INTENT TO DECOMMISSION 45 DAYS PRIOR TO DECOMMISSION' and begin decommissioning within three months of damage or abandonment unless a continuing use plan is approved. Decommissioning must be completed within one year of filing intent or the system becomes a nuisance under Chapter 174. The plan must include 'DECOMMISSIONING COST ESTIMATES,' removal of all above and underground structures, reclamation and restoration of property, and an approved financial guaranty. The cost estimate must be updated every five years or upon ownership change, and a performance bond or other financial guaranty must remain continuously in effect until decommissioning is complete. Failure to maintain the bond may result in revocation of special exceptions or certificates of occupancy. These requirements apply to Solar, Utility defined as 'A SOLAR ENERGY FACILITY WITH A RATED CAPACITY OF MORE THAN 2 MEGAWATTS OF POWER AND IS CONNECTED TO THE ELECTRIC DISTRIBUTION GRID SERVING THE STATE, AND REQUIRES THE ISSUANCE OF A CERTIFICATE OF PUBLIC CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY FROM THE MARYLAND PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION.'

All structures related to the solar facility shall be set back a minimum of 75 feet from all property lines. This requirement does not include perimeter fencing from certain rights-of-way or utility lines. summary: The ordinance requires that "the site plan shall include a vegetative buffer for the visual screening of active portions of the solar facility. This includes all related structures and appurtenances." A vegetative buffer is not required if "sufficient vegetation is in place on or adjacent to the site as determined by the zoning administrator." The buffer must have "a minimum of three staggered rows of plant materials with ten-foot center spacing... the farthest row from the solar facility must consist of evergreen trees," with plant material "a minimum of at least one gallon stock, or approximately 18 inches when planted." Buffers must be installed "in accordance with best management practices" and "preserved and maintained so as to effectively provide visual screening," with dead or dying materials replaced annually. Additionally, "a vegetative ground cover shall be provided within the solar array," using native Maryland species and excluding invasive or noxious species. These requirements apply to Solar, Utility systems defined as having "a rated capacity of more than 2 megawatts of power and is connected to the electric distribution grid serving the state."

The ordinance defines Solar, Utility as a solar energy facility with a rated capacity of more than 2 megawatts connected to the electric distribution grid and requiring a certificate from the Maryland Public Service Commission. Solar, Utility systems "may be permitted in A-I, VC, TT, C-1, C-2, C-3, LB-1, I-1, and I-2 zoning districts, subject to approval by the Public Service Commission." There is no mention of Solar, Utility being permitted as a special use or requiring approval by the zoning appeals board. By contrast, Solar, Minor systems "may be permitted by special exception" in certain districts, and Solar, Accessory systems are permitted outright in various districts. Thus, Solar, Utility uses require approval by the Public Service Commission but not special use permits or zoning appeals board approval.

ALL STRUCTURES RELATED TO THE SOLAR FACILITY SHALL BE SET BACK A MINIMUM OF 75 FEET FROM ALL PROPERTY LINES. THIS REQUIREMENT DOES NOT INCLUDE PERIMETER FENCING FROM: (C) ANY OVERHEAD UTILITY LINES. SERVICE LINES OWNED BY A PRIVATE PROPERTY OWNER OF THE LAND ON WHICH THE SERVICE LINES SIT ARE EXEMPT FROM THE SETBACK;

Any ground-mounted solar energy system which has not produced any electricity for a period of twelve months or more or found to be unsafe by the Building Official shall be considered abandoned and, as such, shall be repaired or decommissioned and removed by the property owner. The decommissioning shall include the removal of the solar energy system and all equipment, electrical components, support structures, cabling, or any other part of the system that is at ground level or above. The property owner shall be responsible for completing the decommissioning within ninety days of abandonment. For utility scale solar energy systems, the Step I concept plan approval requires a written narrative outlining the need and benefits of the proposed facility, the anticipated life of the facility, and proposed measures and financial sureties for decommissioning the facility at the end of its useful life. Other classifications include Small (5 kW or less), Medium (greater than 5 kW but less than 200 kW), and Large (200 kW up to and including 2.5 MW) solar energy systems, with different zoning and permitting conditions, but the decommissioning requirements explicitly apply to ground-mounted systems including utility scale systems (rated capacity in excess of 2.5 MW).

A Utility Scale Solar Energy System has a capacity in excess of 2.5 MW and a minimum lot area of 50 acres. Utility scale solar energy systems may be located in the A-1, A-2, E-1, V-1, C-1, C-2, C-3, I-1 and I-2 Districts with a minimum lot area of fifty acres which in no case may be reduced by action of the Board of Zoning Appeals notwithstanding the provisions of § ZS 1-116(c)(4). Other classifications include Large Solar Energy Systems (200 kW to 2.5 MW) with minimum areas of 20 acres (in A-1, A-2, I-1, I-2 districts) or 30 acres (in E-1, V-1, C-1, C-2, C-3 districts). The minimum lot size is expressed in acres.

All large solar energy systems shall provide a vegetated buffer at least six feet in width if solar panels are located within five hundred feet of any property zoned or used for residential purposes, said buffer to be located within the required yard setback adjoining such residential use or zoning district. Utility scale solar energy systems are subject to a two-step approval process and major site plan review, during which the County Commissioners may impose any conditions they see fit to protect health, safety and welfare, but no explicit vegetative buffer or screening requirements are stated for utility scale systems.

A Utility Scale Solar Energy System has a capacity in excess of 2.5 MW and a minimum lot area of 50 acres. It is a permitted use, by special exception, in the A-1, A-2, E-1, V-1, C-1, C-2, C-3, I-1, and I-2 zoning districts. Other classifications include Large Solar Energy Systems (200 kW to 2.5 MW) which are permitted by special exception in the Agricultural (A-1, A-2) and Industrial (I-1, I-2) districts with a minimum of 20 acres, and in Estate (E-1), Village (V-1), Neighborhood Commercial (C-1), General Commercial (C-2), and Commercial Marine (C-3) districts with a minimum of 30 acres. Small and Medium Solar Energy Systems have different permitted uses, generally allowed in all zoning districts. The minimum lot area for Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems cannot be reduced by the Board of Zoning Appeals.

Utility scale solar energy systems have a rated capacity in excess of two and one-half megawatts and a minimum lot area of fifty acres. All approvals of utility scale solar energy systems shall be in accordance with a two-step approval process. Step I concept plan approval requires submission of a sketch plan, preliminary designation of sensitive areas, delineation of disturbed areas, a written narrative outlining the need and benefits, an operations and maintenance plan, description of system components, and other information as reasonably required. The Technical Review Committee, Planning Commission, and County Commissioners review the submission, may request additional information including studies or reports, and hold a public hearing. Step II requires master site plan approval processed as a major site plan. Large solar energy systems (200 kW to 2.5 MW) and small/medium systems have different zoning and setback requirements but do not have this two-step approval process. This two-step process explicitly constitutes a visual impact assessment for utility scale solar energy systems.

A decommissioning plan must be approved by the City and signed by the party responsible for decommissioning and the landowner (if different). Such plan must be filed in the Registry of Deeds prior to the first operation of the array. Decommissioning shall occur within 12 months of the facility ceasing to operate. Prior to the issuance of a building permit, the owner/lessee shall provide the Code Enforcement Officer a performance bond in an amount approved by the City Engineer to cover the cost of removal should the solar array be abandoned, all in a form approved by the City Solicitor. A solar array where the panels occupy up to and including 10,000 square feet of surface area is exempt from this standard. Abandonment will occur if the system does not function for 12 months or is damaged and not repaired within 12 months, among other conditions. Upon determination of abandonment, the responsible party must remove the facility and restore the site within one year of notice. Failure to remove leads to removal by the City at the landowner's expense, with unpaid costs charged as a lien against the property.

Solar array structures shall be constructed to minimize glare beyond the property line. Smaller solar arrays exempt from Planning Board review include: (1) Roof-mounted or building-integrated solar shingles, panels or canopies; (2) Freestanding solar panels occupying less than and including 2,000 square feet of surface area on a lot as an accessory structure primarily serving the power needs of the principal use; (3) Freestanding solar panels on a lot as a principal use whereby the panels occupy up to and including 5,000 square feet of surface area and primarily serving the power needs of abutting property owners.

The ordinance states under section D(4): 'Height: maximum 25 feet.' This maximum height applies to solar arrays generally allowed in all districts except those prohibited. The text distinguishes exemptions for smaller arrays (e.g., less than or equal to 2,000 or 5,000 square feet), but the 25-foot maximum height applies to larger freestanding solar arrays, including those larger than 10,000 square feet. The unit for this height restriction is feet.

All side and rear setbacks shall be planted with Buffer Yard Type D in the following districts: Urban Residence 1 (URD-1), Urban Residence 2 (URD-2), Low-Density Residential District (LDR), Multifamily and Service District, High-Density Residential (HDR), and Rural Residence and Agricultural District (RR&A). summary: Section 102-1100(b) states: "Solar panels are designed to absorb (not reflect) sunlight; and, as such, solar panels are generally less reflective than other varnished or glass exterior housing pieces. However, solar panel placement should be prioritized to minimize or negate any solar glare onto nearby properties or roadways to the maximum extent practical." It further provides that "the Planning Board has the authority to require any applicant that proposes to install a large-scale ground-mounted solar energy system in an area that could affect the safety of airport operations to conduct a solar glare gauge analysis study as an element of the application submitted to the Planning Board." The Planning Board shall consider the results of the glare analysis in rendering a decision to approve or deny an application and any conditions of approval. This glare restriction applies specifically to large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems. Other related standards in the ordinance address visual impact and buffering, operations and maintenance, emergency management, installation conditions, vegetation management, signage, removal, community donation, reactivation, and decommissioning, but these do not explicitly address glare.

summary: Commercial ground-mounted systems and all industrial systems, or a portion thereof, shall be decommissioned if they cease to generate electricity for a continuous period of 12 months. As part of permitting commercial ground-mounted systems and all industrial systems, the applicant shall submit a decommissioning plan to the Town with a cost estimate for the costs of decommissioning. The decommissioning plan shall include financial assurance, naming the Town as beneficiary, to cover the costs associated with decommissioning the abandoned solar energy system through the life span of the facility. The Planning Board shall not approve an application for a commercial ground-mounted system or industrial system until the applicant has submitted an executed decommissioning access agreement that authorizes the Town to enter onto the property for decommissioning activities. The financial assurance shall be maintained at 150% of the cost of decommissioning and site restoration for the life of the system. The Town may take action to secure posted decommissioning funds and complete decommissioning if the owner/operator fails to do so. A final decommissioning plan must be submitted at least six months before decommissioning begins, detailing removal methods, restoration, timelines, and costs. Additionally, industrial solar energy systems must be removed at the end of their useful life or abandonment consistent with the decommissioning plan. Two-year updates/revaluations require submission of updated financial ability evidence and updated engineer's cost estimate for decommissioning. The ordinance distinguishes between residential, commercial, and industrial systems, with decommissioning requirements applying explicitly to commercial ground-mounted and industrial systems.

All systems shall have a fence enclosing the solar energy system at a minimum of six feet high. Fences should be elevated by a minimum of five inches to allow for passage of small terrestrial animals and shall be solid lock game fencing or fencing which has been modified to provide larger openings periodically to allow medium animal passage. This fencing requirement is stated under additional standards for industrial solar energy systems, indicating it applies to Industrial Solar Energy System (Ground-Mounted).
section: § 144-9 Additional standards for industrial solar energy systems

summary: Industrial solar energy systems shall not exceed 25 feet in height when oriented at minimum tilt to the vertical. Other height limits mentioned are: Residential and commercial solar energy systems shall not exceed 12 feet in height when oriented at minimum tilt to the vertical (which may be waived by the Planning Board), and building-integrated and roof-mounted systems shall not increase the total building height above the maximum height allowed in Chapter 140, Site Plan Review. The unit for the industrial system height limit is feet.

Ground-mounted industrial solar energy systems shall occupy no more than a total of 125 project acres at any one time in the Town of Bethel, including all industrial solar energy systems in operation on the effective date of this chapter. Up to an additional 50 acres may be developed if the Planning Board finds that an application meets the incentive criteria. Additionally, a maximum of 50% of a parcel's area or of the total parcel area of all the parcels participating in a project may be covered by the solar energy system, with a possible increase to 75% coverage if a density bonus is granted. The units for the maximum lot size are acres.

summary: No solar energy system shall emit sound greater than 20 dB(A) at the property lines of the parcel where it is located. This applies to all solar energy systems, including industrial ground-mounted systems as defined in the chapter. The unit dBA is the standard unit for noise level measurement.

All ground-mounted solar energy systems shall be regulated by the dimensional setback regulations stipulated in Chapter 140, Site Plan Review; however, in no case shall any type of ground-mounted system be installed within 100 feet of the public way.

Ground-mounted solar projects developed along a roadway or adjacent to a residential use shall require buffering and screening. Natural features shall be maintained wherever possible to provide a buffer between the development and abutting use. When natural features such as topography, gullies, stands of trees, shrubbery, rock outcrops do not exist or are insufficient to provide a visual buffer, a planted buffer will need to be established. An evergreen buffer may be used to meet this requirement, provided that there is a row of two or more staggered plantings, at a maximum of five feet apart and planted a maximum of four feet on center, or alternative spacing as approved by the Planning Board based on the approved plant species and its typical growth size. The intent of the buffer is to provide a visual screen so that the panels are not visible for the next 30 years. Evergreens shall be a minimum of six feet high at the time of planting. Fencing may be used to meet this requirement and shall be located within the property line to allow access for maintenance from both sides without intruding upon abutting properties. Fence shall provide a solid visual screen and be of a solid, neutral color that blends in with the surroundings. All buffer areas shall be maintained in a neat, sanitary, and vigorous condition by the owner. Dead or damaged trees that have less than 50% of the typical leaf area for the species and size shall be replaced by the owner.

A sign shall be placed on the industrial solar energy system to identify the owner and provide a twenty-four-hour emergency contact phone number. This requirement is explicitly stated in § 144-9G under 'Additional standards for industrial solar energy systems.'
section: § 144-9 Additional standards for industrial solar energy systems

summary: The ordinance requires for Industrial Solar Energy System (Ground-Mounted) projects: submission of "an erosion control plan designed by a qualified professional that meets the standards of the Maine Erosion and Sediment Control Best Management Practices manual, current edition, or as replaced by MDEP" (§ 144-8B(2)); limitations on land clearing and soil erosion including that "clearing of natural vegetation shall be limited to what is necessary," "removal of mature trees shall be avoided to the extent possible," and "no prime agricultural soil or significant volume of topsoil shall be removed from the site" (§ 144-9D). Additionally, "any topsoil to be stripped shall be stockpiled on-site in such a way to ensure that there is no mixing with subsoils," and "stockpiled soil shall be seeded and mulched or otherwise stabilized within 14 days of placement," with stripped topsoil to be "spread evenly on disturbed areas prior to seeding" (§ 144-9D(1) and (2)). These requirements apply to ground-mounted systems, including industrial systems defined as "a system used primarily for the production of energy for the power grid" (§ 144-2B(3)). Other system types include Residential (energy produced at applicant's residence) and Commercial (energy produced at a business or leased space), with commercial ground-mounted systems also requiring site plan review (§ 144-2B(1) and (2)).

summary: All ground-mounted solar energy systems shall be set back from the high water mark of all rivers, streams and brooks a minimum of 25 feet. In areas regulated by shoreland zoning, the stricter setbacks shall apply.

The ordinance defines a large-scale solar farm as "a ground-mounted solar energy system, other than an accessory solar energy system, whose solar land area exceeds 2.5 acres or whose nameplate capacity is greater than 500 kW (DC)." Decommissioning requirements for permissible solar farms (which include large-scale solar farms interconnected with a line tap to a subtransmission line with a voltage of 46kv or less) include: "The owner or operator of record of a permissible solar farm shall, at its expense, be responsible for the decommissioning and removal of the permissible solar farm, in compliance with a decommissioning plan approved by the permitting authority, within twelve (12) months of the end of the manufacturer-identified useful life of the solar photovoltaic (PV) technology, or 90 days of the receipt of a notice to the owner or operator of record of a determination by the CEO that the permissible solar farm has been abandoned." Abandonment is defined as when "it ceases to generate electricity for a consecutive period of twelve (12) months." The permitting authority may extend the 12-month decommissioning deadline if the owner or operator demonstrates economic feasibility beyond the useful life. Additionally, the permitting authority may require a "performance guarantee in the form of an escrow account, irrevocable letter of credit, or other form satisfactory to the Town in an amount equal to the anticipated total cost of decommissioning." Other solar energy system categories mentioned include accessory solar energy systems (no site plan review required), local-scale solar farms (solar land area not exceeding 2.5 acres and capacity 500 kW or less, site plan review required), and solar microgrids (site plan review required).

The height of any ground-mounted solar photovoltaic (PV) panel associated with a permissible solar farm shall not exceed twenty-five (25) feet. This applies to large-scale solar farms as defined: a ground-mounted solar energy system, other than an accessory solar energy system, whose solar land area exceeds 2.5 acres or whose nameplate capacity is greater than 500 kW (DC). Other categories include local-scale solar farms (up to 2.5 acres and 500 kW) and accessory solar energy systems (up to 0.5 acres and 125 kW), but the 25 feet height limit specifically applies to permissible solar farms including large-scale solar farms. The unit 'feet' is used for the height measurement.

Large-scale solar farms must meet a minimum setback of 100 feet from any lot line. Other setback options include local-scale solar farms with a 50 feet setback from lot lines and solar microgrids with setbacks determined by the permitting authority. The ordinance states: 'Minimum Setbacks. Permissible solar farms and all structures shall meet the following minimum setbacks: Large-scale solar farm 100 feet from any lot line.'

Large-scale solar farm must have a minimum setback of 100 feet from any residence on an abutting lot. Other options include local-scale solar farm with 100 feet setback from residences on abutting lots and 50 feet from lot lines, and solar microgrid setbacks determined by the permitting authority. Specifically: 'Large-scale solar farm         100 feet                          100 feet' (setbacks from lot line and residence on abutting lot respectively).

Section 442.7 Decommissioning Plan requires the applicant to submit a plan for decommissioning the solar energy system, including: physical removal of all solar energy systems, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines; disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations; and stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion. The plan must be prepared by a Maine licensed Professional Engineer and include the anticipated life of the project, the anticipated present value cost of decommissioning, an explanation of the cost calculation, a physical plan for decommissioning, and a surety to cover the cost of decommissioning. The plan and cost estimate must be updated every five years. Section 442.7.13 requires a decommissioning surety guarantee in the form of a performance surety bond, irrevocable letter of credit, or other acceptable security, approved by the City Solicitor, in the amount of 120% of the estimated demolition cost. The surety must be adjusted every five years. Section 442.7.15 Removal requires removal of the system no more than 150 days after discontinued operations, with notification to the Code Enforcement Officer. Section 442.7.16 Abandonment states the system is considered abandoned if it fails to operate for more than one year without written consent, and the City may use the surety to remove abandoned systems. These requirements apply specifically to large-scale ground- or pole-mounted solar energy systems. Other solar energy systems such as building-integrated, roof-mounted, and small-scale ground- or pole-mounted systems have different standards and do not have explicit decommissioning requirements in this text.

The ordinance explicitly requires decommissioning for Industrial Solar Energy Systems (ISES) as follows: "Any Ground Mounted Solar Energy System that has reached the end of its useful life, ceases to generate power, or has been abandoned shall be removed pursuant to a plan approved by the Planning Board during the application process." Removal must be completed "no more than 180 days after the date of discontinued operations." Decommissioning includes "physical removal of all solar energy systems, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines from the site; disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with Local, State and Federal waste disposal regulations; and stabilization and re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion." A system is considered abandoned if it "fails to generate 10% or less permitted capacity of electricity for a continuous period of twelve (12) months without having first obtained the written consent of the Code Enforcement Officer." If removal is not completed within 180 days of abandonment or discontinuation, the Town may use the performance guarantee and legal means to remove the system.

Section 7.1 (Standards for Approval) states: "Fence - Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems shall be enclosed by a project-appropriate perimeter fence." This fencing requirement applies to Industrial Solar Energy Systems (ISES), defined as any SES with a total area projected over the ground equal to or greater than 2 acres (87,120 square feet) or that generates a nameplate capacity of 500 kW or greater. Other categories include Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) with area between 3,000 square feet and less than 2 acres or capacity between 31 kW and less than 500 kW, Residential-Business Solar Energy Systems (RBSES) with less than 3,000 square feet or less than 31 kW, and Private Residential Solar Energy Systems (PRSES) with less than 2,000 square feet and less than 21 kW. The fencing requirement is explicitly stated only for ground-mounted systems and applies to ISES and CSES. For RBSES and PRSES, fencing is not explicitly required but a fence providing visual screening may be allowed only if a vegetative screen is deemed impractical by the Planning Board.

Section 7.1 (Standards for Approval) states: "Glare - All SES shall be situated to eliminate concentrated glare onto nearby structures, public or private ways, or any otherwise non-SES associated property." This applies to Industrial Solar Energy Systems (ISES), defined in Section 4 as "Any SES with a total area projected over the ground equal to or greater than 2 acres (87,120 square feet) or that generates a nameplate capacity of 500 kW or greater." Other categories include Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) with area between 3,000 square feet and 2 acres or capacity between 31 kW and 500 kW, Residential-Business Solar Energy Systems (RBSES) with area less than 3,000 square feet or capacity less than 31 kW, and Private Residential Solar Energy Systems (PRSES) with area less than 2,000 square feet and capacity less than 21 kW. The glare restriction is explicitly stated for all SES, including ISES, CSES, RBSES, and roof-mounted systems, but the focus here is on ISES as defined by the ordinance.

Section 7.1.10 states: 'Any solar collector device shall be a maximum height of 15 feet when oriented at maximum tilt above the ground surface.' Industrial Solar Energy Systems (ISES) are defined as any SES with a total area projected over the ground equal to or greater than 2 acres (87,120 square feet) or that generates a nameplate capacity of 500 kW or greater. Other categories include Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) with area between 3,000 square feet and less than 2 acres, and Private Residential Solar Energy Systems (PRSES) with less than 2,000 square feet. The minimum lot size for ISES is explicitly stated as 2 acres (87,120 square feet).

Section 7.1 Noise standard for Industrial Solar Energy Systems (ISES) states: 'No noise generated by the SES or Solar Related Equipment shall be 10 decibels (dB) greater than the preconstruction / existing background level, nor generate a Pure Tone.' The background noise limit is based on the quietest period of the night, typically 3:00 a.m. The unit is expressed as decibels (dB), which is the standard unit for noise levels.

Section 7.1.10 states: 'Structures within a SES shall be set back a minimum of 200 feet from all lot lines.' This applies to Industrial Solar Energy Systems (ISES) as defined in Section 4 as any SES with a total area projected over the ground equal to or greater than 2 acres or that generates a nameplate capacity of 500 kW or greater. Other categories such as Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) and Residential-Business Solar Energy Systems (RBSES) have different setback requirements, e.g., RBSES require a minimum setback of 50 feet from side and rear property lines (Section 7.2.2), but these do not apply to ISES.

Section 7.1 Screening - Lots on which Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems are located shall utilize buffers / screening from roads and residences by plantings, berms, and natural topographical features. Ground mounted SES shall be screened from view to the greatest extent practical from any adjacent property that is residentially zoned or used for residential purposes, as well as from any public way. The screen shall consist of a vegetative barrier which provides a visual screen. In lieu of a vegetative screen, a fence that provides visual screening, and meets requirements of the controlling ordinance, may be allowed only if a vegetative screen is deemed impractical by the Planning Board.

Section 7.1 Signage - "A sign shall be required to identify the permit holder and provide a 24-hour emergency contact phone number. Solar energy systems shall not be used for displaying any advertising. A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on any fence surrounding the SES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards." This applies to Industrial Solar Energy Systems (ISES) defined as any SES with a total area projected over the ground equal to or greater than 2 acres or that generates a nameplate capacity of 500 kW or greater. Other categories include Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) with area between 3,000 square feet and 2 acres or capacity between 31 kW and 500 kW, Residential-Business Solar Energy Systems (RBSES) under 3,000 square feet or less than 31 kW, and Private Residential Solar Energy Systems (PRSES) under 2,000 square feet and less than 21 kW. Signage requirements for RBSES and PRSES only state that "Solar energy systems shall not be used for displaying any advertising" without further signage specifics.

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Industrial Solar Energy Systems (ISES). It requires an operations and maintenance plan that includes "stormwater controls" (Section 6.13), a "stormwater management plan, certified by a professional engineer," demonstrating stormwater infiltration equal to pre-development rates (Section 6.14), and prohibits placement of ground-mounted SES components within stormwater conveyance systems or in ways that impede stormwater runoff or impact adjacent water supplies (Section 7.1.4). Additionally, decommissioning and removal must include "stabilization and re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion" (Section 8.2.3), with allowance for leaving landscaping or foundations to minimize erosion and vegetation disruption. These requirements apply to ground-mounted SES, which includes ISES defined as systems with a total area projected over the ground equal to or greater than 2 acres or generating 500 kW or greater. Other SES categories include Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) with area between 3,000 square feet and 2 acres or capacity between 31 kW and 500 kW, Residential-Business Solar Energy Systems (RBSES) with less than 3,000 square feet or less than 31 kW, and Private Residential Solar Energy Systems (PRSES) with less than 2,000 square feet and less than 21 kW, but the soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements are explicitly detailed for ISES and CSES.
section: Section 6. Specific Application Requirements; Section 7. Standards for Approval; Section 8. Decommissioning and Removal

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires a Decommissioning Plan for any Commercial Solar Energy System (SES) up to 25 acres and greater than 500 kW. The plan must be developed by a qualified expert and approved by the Planning Board and CEO, adhering to the  "State of Maine Act to Ensure Decommissioning of Solar Energy Developments"  (S.P. 113-LD 802, § 1, 35-A M.R.S.A c 34-D). The plan shall include: (1) a description of the work required to physically remove all SES structures, equipment, security barriers, foundations, and transmission lines with a decommissioning schedule; (2) an estimate of the total cost including an itemized list of major expenses and environmental protection measures; (3) an inflation guard provision adjusting costs yearly based on CPI; (4) a performance bond or other financial assurance covering 110% of the inflation-adjusted cost, granting the Town access to funds if the Applicant fails obligations; (5) a disposal plan for all decommissioned equipment and facilities complying with waste regulations; and (6) a letter acknowledging and agreeing to decommissioning plan performance triggers. Triggers include abandonment (cessation of operation for more than 12 consecutive months), contamination beyond baseline levels without timely remediation, and court-ordered decommissioning for serious ordinance violations. The Applicant must provide annual reports on power output and soil/water contamination. Decommissioning must be completed according to the approved plan and schedule, with notification to the CEO. Financial assurances may be released only after satisfactory removal and Planning Board approval. The ordinance also requires deed registration of decommissioning requirements and proof of financial resources to fund decommissioning. Other relevant provisions include operational maintenance plans, emergency management coordination, and compliance with all relevant laws and standards.

Section 6 (Standards), item 13 states: "Fence - Commercial SESs shall be protected by a well-constructed perimeter security fence at least eight feet in height. Such fences shall be raised 6 (six) inches above the ground to allow for small wildlife passage and movement." This fencing requirement applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance, which includes systems up to 25 acres and greater than 500 kW. No other fencing options or conditions are provided in the text.

Section 6 (Standards), item 16 states: "Glare — Commercial SESs shall be situated and constructed in a way that eliminates concentrated glare visible from other properties, abutters, roadways, scenic areas, waterways, and waterbodies." This glare restriction applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems (SES) as defined in the ordinance, which includes systems up to 25 acres and greater than 500 kW. The ordinance defines Commercial SES as "a solar energy system where the primary purpose of the system is to generate income from the power produced for off-site consumption." The ordinance applies to all new Commercial SES projects, including structures, enlargements, and new land uses, and sets standards such as lot coverage, setbacks, equipment quality, fencing, signage, physical screening, noise, height restrictions, lighting, stormwater management, utility connections, emergency services, fire safety, electromagnetic emissions, ongoing maintenance, and decommissioning. The glare restriction is one among many standards the Planning Board uses to judge applications.

Commercial SES solar photovoltaic cells or arrays shall be subject to a maximum height of 15 feet above the ground surface when oriented at maximum tilt. Associated SES structures shall be subject to the maximum height regulations specified for principal and accessory buildings within the applicable zoning district. (Section 6, Standards, item 21, Height restrictions)

The ordinance explicitly states: 'Commercial SESs shall not cover more than 25 acres and shall not exceed 50% coverage of any lot.' This maximum lot size applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems greater than 500 kW and up to 25 acres. The units for this maximum lot size are acres. Additionally, application and permit fees are based on ground space definitions, with 'More than 2 acres but not more than 25 acres > 500 kw' as a category, reinforcing the relevance of the 25-acre maximum.

Any noise generated by the Commercial SES shall not be more than 10 decibels greater than the ambient noise level measured prior to construction, nor should it be a pure tone. The background noise measurement should be conducted during the quietest time of the night. This noise standard must be met at all property lines, public roads and right of ways, or any coastal or inland shoreline. The unit is expressed as decibels (dBA).
All Commercial SES structures shall be set back a minimum of 200 feet from all lot lines to mitigate visual and functional impacts.

Section 6, Standard 16 ('Physical Screening') requires that Commercial SESs have perimeter screening that ensures structures, equipment, and facilities are screened from view to the greatest extent practical from any adjacent properties, roads, public ways or waterways. The screen shall consist of plantings, berms, or natural topographic features that will provide a visual screen. If these methods are deemed impractical by the Planning Board, a fence may be used if it complies with other town ordinances.

Section 6. STANDARDS, item 14. Signage - "Clear and visible signage shall be installed which identifies the Commercial SES operator and provides a 24-hour emergency contact phone number. A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on any fence surrounding the Commercial SES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards. Signs should be posted at distances of every 25 ft. Commercial SESs shall not be used to display any advertising." This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems up to 25 acres and greater than 500 kW as regulated by the ordinance. No other signage options or conditions are provided.

The ordinance requires a "stormwater management system designed by a Maine Professional Engineer for both pre and post development conditions" to prevent negative impacts on water supplies or septic systems. It mandates that "any earth disturbance must be graded and reseeded, unless authorized for another use" and that "reseeding will be only with native species of this area, and no invasive species shall be used." Applicants must submit a "Soils and Groundwater Assessment, a Soils Management Plan, and a Soils Testing Plan from a qualified soils and water expert" including baseline testing before construction, annual testing during operation, and remediation plans if contamination occurs. The Decommissioning Plan must include "stabilization and re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion" and grading and reseeding of disturbed earth. These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Energy Systems up to 25 acres and greater than 500 kW, as defined in the ordinance.

summary: The ordinance requires that "All reasonable efforts, as determined by the Planning Board, shall be made to ensure that Commercial SESs are visually consistent with the character of the community and maintain scenic views identified by Jonesport Comprehensive Plan." It mandates "Physical Screening - Commercial SESs shall have perimeter screening that ensures structures, equipment, and facilities are screened from view to the greatest extent practical from any adjacent properties, roads, public ways or waterways." Additionally, "Setback — All Commercial SES structures shall be set back a minimum of 200 feet from all lot lines to mitigate visual and functional impacts." The Planning Board uses these standards to judge applications and may grant waivers per the Jonesport Land Use and Development Ordinance. The application submission requirements include a "Commercial SES design and equipment layout plan showing conformance to applicable industry standards" and a "site plan," which support visual impact assessment. These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Energy Systems up to 25 acres and greater than 500 kW, as indicated by the fee schedule and applicability sections. Other options or conditions include waivers granted under Section 8 of the Jonesport Land Use and Development Ordinance and the Planning Board's discretion in determining reasonable efforts and impracticality of screening methods.

The ordinance applies to Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems defined as systems that (a) are structurally mounted to the ground; (b) have a physical size based on total airspace projected over the ground that is greater than 20,000 square feet; and (c) that are not directly connected to a Residential Structure. Section 8. Decommissioning and Removal requires that any such system that has reached the end of its useful life, ceases to generate power or has been abandoned shall be removed pursuant to a plan approved by the Lisbon Planning Board during the application process. The owner or operator shall physically remove the installation no more than 180 days after the date of discontinued operations and notify the Code Enforcement Officer by certified mail. Decommissioning includes (1) physical removal of all solar energy systems, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines from the site; (2) disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with Local, State and Federal waste disposal regulations; and (3) stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion. The Code Enforcement Officer may allow leaving landscaping or designated below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and disruptions to vegetation. Systems are considered abandoned if they fail to generate electricity for more than one year without written consent of the Code Enforcement Officer. If removal is not completed within 180 days of abandonment or proposed decommissioning, the Town may use the performance guarantee and legal means to cause removal. Section 7 requires a performance guarantee of 150% of the estimated decommissioning cost before permit issuance, subject to review by the Code Enforcement Officer, which may be released upon satisfactory removal of the system and associated structures.

Section 6.B states that Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems "shall be protected by a perimeter fence designed to allow for passage of wildlife." Additionally, "One or more signs shall be affixed to the fence identifying the owner of the facility and 24-hour emergency contact information." A KnoxBox or other system agreed to by the Fire Chief providing emergency access inside the security gate shall be installed. Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems are defined in Section 4 as systems that (a) are structurally mounted to the ground; (b) have a physical size based on total airspace projected over the ground that is greater than 20,000 square feet; and (c) are not directly connected to a Residential Structure.
