summary: Section 5.A states: 'Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems in residential zoning districts shall not exceed twelve (12) feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt.' It also provides a less restrictive limit of 25 feet for Commercial, Industrial, and Diversified Development zoning districts. The units for these height limits are feet.

Section 5.B states: 'Minimum front setback shall be 50 feet, minimum side setback shall be 50 feet and minimum rear setback shall be 50 feet.' This applies to Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems defined as having a physical size greater than 20,000 square feet and not directly connected to a Residential Structure, i.e., utility-scale systems. No other setback distances or multipliers based on height or other factors are provided.

Minimum front setback shall be 50 feet for Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems greater than 20,000 square feet and not directly connected to a Residential Structure. This front setback applies to roads or rights-of-way. Other setbacks include minimum side setback of 50 feet and minimum rear setback of 50 feet. Additionally, lots with Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems shall be buffered from roads by plantings, berms, and natural topographical features, subject to Planning Board approval.

Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems are defined as systems "that are structurally mounted to the ground; (b) has a physical size based on total airspace projected over the ground that is greater than 20,000 square feet; and (c) that is not directly connected to a Residential Structure."

This signage requirement applies in conjunction with perimeter fencing designed to allow wildlife passage. No other signage options or conditions are provided in the ordinance.
section: Section 6. Screening, Security, Maintenance and Regulatory Compliance

summary: Section 8.B.(3) requires "stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion" as part of the decommissioning process for Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems. These systems are defined in Section 4 as "a solar energy system that is structurally mounted to the ground; has a physical size based on total airspace projected over the ground that is greater than 20,000 square feet; and that is not directly connected to a Residential Structure." The ordinance also allows the Code Enforcement Officer to "allow the owner or operator to leave landscaping or designated below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and disruptions to vegetation."

The Owner/Operator of any Solar Energy System shall, at their expense, be responsible for complete decommissioning of the project and site restoration within twelve (12) months after it ceases to generate electricity, or after its permit has been revoked. Decommissioning shall include the removal of all parts of the project (including foundations) in accordance with local, state and federal laws and regulations. A professional engineer shall produce a detailed cost estimate of the total decommissioning cost. No permit will be issued until decommissioning funds have been posted. Estimates shall be redone annually and at ownership transfer, with funds maintained accordingly. Decommissioning Funds may be in the form of a performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit or other financial assurance acceptable to the Town. If decommissioning is not completed timely, the Town may take necessary actions to secure funds and ensure completion. Facilities unused or out of service for more than eighteen (18) continuous months shall be considered abandoned and removed, with costs assessed as a lien against the property. If a detailed decommissioning plan is required by the Maine Department of Environmental Protection, a copy must be provided; otherwise, the above standards apply.

Solar Energy Systems shall be completely enclosed by a secure fence that consists of a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a locking gate. The fence should be constructed in such a way to allow for passage of small animals at its lowest point. A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the solar energy system informing individuals of potential voltage hazards. In lieu of a vegetative screen, a fence that provides visual screening and meets requirements of this ordinance may be used with Planning Board approval.

summary: Maine law requires solar developers of facilities with ground-mounted panels on three or more acres to submit a decommissioning plan with financial assurances, restoration of farmland, grading and revegetation of disturbed areas, and updates to financial assurances every five years following an initial review fifteen years after plan approval.

All applicants seeking approval of a Large-Scale Solar Array Energy System (LSAES) shall submit a decommissioning plan that meets the requirements set forth in 35-A M.R.S.A. §§ 3491 through 3496 and pertinent regulations by the Maine Department of Environmental Protection. The owner/operator must provide a financial guarantee (performance bond, surety bond, irrevocable letter of credit, or other acceptable form) to assure proper removal and remediation upon abandonment or termination of production. The Town of Mechanic Falls shall be named as a co-beneficiary of the financial guarantee. Failure to maintain the financial guarantee may result in suspension of production and notification to the Maine Public Utilities Commission. If an LSAES has failed to operate for more than one year, it must be decommissioned according to the approved plan or state requirements, including physical removal of all components, disposal of waste per regulations, and site stabilization and revegetation with native seed mixtures. If the owner/operator fails to decommission within one year, the Town may access the financial guarantee and conduct decommissioning. The deadline may be extended for up to one year if production cessation is temporary and certified. These requirements apply specifically to LSAES and medium-scale systems (MSAES) as well.

All ground-mounted MSAES and LSAES shall be completely enclosed by solid-lock game fences. Such fencing would start with eight-inch by twelve-inch openings at the bottom (ground) with progressively smaller openings at the top of the fence. This type of fencing meets the National Electric Code for human safety. Fences should be elevated by a minimum of five inches to allow for passage of small terrestrial animals. Five-inch or larger diameter wooden escape poles shall be placed in two or more corners of the perimeter fence as an alternative means for wildlife to escape the enclosed area. Fencing shall consist of a minimum eight-foot-high fence with a locking gate, or as designated by the permitting authority. For ground-mounted LSAES, fencing shall be a minimum of 20 feet from the property line inward, and there shall be an additional clear space of 20 feet to the solar panel from any fencing shielding any line-of-sight visibility from a home or roadway. In lieu of a vegetative screen, the Planning Board may permit use of a fence that provides screening and meets requirements of the controlling ordinance.

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires that "All MSAES and LSAES shall be situated to eliminate concentrated glare onto nearby structures or roadways" (§ 162-6(H)) and further states that "All MSAES and LSAES shall eliminate concentrated glare onto nearby structures or roadways. The Code Enforcement Officer may require additional plantings or screening to avoid glare" (§ 162-7(E)). These glare restrictions apply specifically to medium- and large-scale solar array energy systems, including LSAES, which are defined as solar arrays with total panel area in excess of 15,000 square feet.

The screen shall consist of a vegetative barrier which provides a visual screen. In lieu of a vegetative screen, the Planning Board may permit use of a fence that provides screening and meets requirements of the controlling ordinance. Additionally, LSAES shall have a thirty-foot vegetative buffer from the property line inward. Fencing shall be a minimum of 20 feet from the property line inward, and there shall be an additional clear space of 20 feet to the solar panel from any fencing shielding any line-of-sight visibility from a home or roadway.

section: § 162-6 Design and construction standards for all medium-scale solar array energy systems (MSAES) and large-scale solar array energy systems (LSAES)

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Large-Scale Solar Array Energy Systems (LSAES). It requires that ground-mounted LSAES "shall not be placed within any stormwater conveyance system, or in any other manner that would alter or impede stormwater runoff from collecting in a constructed stormwater conveyance system" (§ 162-6.K.(7)). The applicant must submit "a stormwater management plan, certified by a licensed engineer, that demonstrates stormwater from the MSAES or LSAES will infiltrate into the ground beneath the MSAES or LSAES at a rate equal to that of the infiltration rate prior to the placement of the system" (§ 162-6.K.(8)). If this infiltration rate cannot be achieved, that area may be considered impervious. Upon removal of any ground-mounted MSAES or LSAES, "any earth disturbance must be graded and reseeded with native seedings, wildflowers, and meadow grasses" (§ 162-7.F). Additionally, decommissioning requires "stabilization and revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion" using native seed mixtures (§ 162-8.F.(1)(c)).

summary: Inverters and transformers must be at least 200 feet from any residence (§ 162-6 K(12)). Additionally, there is a 20-foot clear space from fencing to solar panels to shield line-of-sight visibility from a home or roadway (§ 162-6 L), but the 200 feet distance for inverters and transformers is the most restrictive setback directly pertaining to occupied dwellings.

summary: Section 6(j) requires a decommissioning plan for any Medium-Scale or Large-Scale Ground-Mounted SES, including: 1) a description of the trigger for implementing the decommissioning plan with a rebuttable presumption if no electricity is generated for 12 months; 2) a description of the work required to physically remove all solar panels, associated foundations, buildings, cabling, electrical components, and any other associated facilities, with earth disturbed during decommissioning to be graded and re-seeded unless the landowner requests otherwise; 3) an estimate of the total cost of decommissioning less salvage value and itemization of major expenses; 4) demonstration of financial assurance for 100% of the total cost of decommissioning, less salvage value, via performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit, parental guarantee or other form acceptable to the Planning Board; 5) financial assurance must be in place prior to construction and include a provision granting the Town access to funds to perform decommissioning if the SES is abandoned or obligations are unmet; and 6) a waiver option for Medium-Scale SES that is an Accessory Structure. Section 7(a) states the owner or operator "shall be responsible for decommissioning and site restoration when the solar energy system has reached the end of its useful life, or is otherwise determined to be abandoned, unless an extension is granted by the Planning Board."

The Planning Board may require that a SES be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access. This applies to Medium-Scale and Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems. Reasonable efforts shall be made to minimize undue visual impacts by preserving native vegetation, screening abutting properties, or other appropriate measures, including height and setback requirements.
Structures within a SES shall be setback a minimum of 50 feet from the side and rear property lines and meet the front setback requirements for structures within the zoning district.

The ordinance requires that "reasonable efforts, as determined by the Planning Board, shall be made to minimize undue visual impacts by preserving native vegetation, screening abutting properties, or other appropriate measures, including height and setback requirements" for Large-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems. Additionally, "the Planning Board may require that a SES be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access." These provisions are found under the standards for approval for Medium-Scale and Large-Scale Ground-Mounted SES. Other related standards include setbacks, lot size and coverage, safety, and maintenance, but only the visual impact and fencing provisions explicitly address vegetative buffer and screening requirements.

Signage shall be required to identify the owner of the SES and provide a 24‐hour emergency contact phone number. This signage shall not be used for advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the SES. A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the SES, informing individuals of potential voltage hazards.

Section 7, Decommissioning and Abandonment, requires the owner or operator of the facility to "remove all non-utility owned equipment, conduits, structures, fencing, and foundations" and to "submit the results of Phase 1 ESA by a qualified professional to compare to the original Phase 1 ESA taken at the time of application." It also mandates revegetation of cleared areas unless otherwise requested and filling in all holes or depressions. All removal and decommissioning must occur within 12 months of the facility ceasing to operate. Abandonment is defined by conditions such as the land lease ending, system non-functioning for 12 months, or system damage not repaired. The Code Enforcement Officer must notify responsible parties to remove the facility within 365 days of notice. If the lessee or landowner fails to comply, the Town may remove the facility and recover costs from the performance guarantee. Section 6, Guarantee for Removal, requires a financial guarantee equal to 125% of the estimated removal cost, updated every five years, to ensure funds are available for decommissioning. The ordinance defines Industrial Solar Energy Systems (ISES) as systems "principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power, and supply electrical or thermal power, primarily or solely for off-site grid use," with no limit on rated nameplate capacity and up to 200 acres in surface area.

Section 8, General Standards for all Arrays, subsection 7 states: "Array placement must be designed to minimize or negate any solar glare onto nearby properties, or roadways." This glare restriction applies to all arrays, including Industrial Solar Energy Systems (ISES), which are defined in Section 4 as systems "principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power, and supply electrical or thermal power, primarily or solely for off-site grid use," with no limit on rated nameplate capacity and up to 200 acres in surface area. Other array types defined in Section 4 include Private Residential Solar Energy Systems (PRSES) and Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES), which have smaller size and capacity limits and are primarily for on-site use. Exempt arrays include roof-mounted residential systems below state minimum sizes, ground- or pole-mounted private use systems below state minimum sizes, building integrated solar, repair or replacement without enlargement, and commercial buildings using solar only for on-site operational purposes.
section: Section 8. General Standards for all Arrays

summary: Section 4, Permitted Arrays, subsection 3 states: 'Industrial Solar Energy Systems (ISES)... can be up to two hundred (200) acres in surface area, and there is no limit on the rated nameplate capacity of an ISES.' Other options include Private Residential Solar Energy Systems (PRSES) up to 2,000 square feet and Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) up to 20,000 square feet, but these apply to smaller, non-industrial systems. The unit for the maximum lot size for ISES is explicitly given as acres.

Section 8, General Standards for all Arrays, subsection 10 requires that "The boundaries of any nonexempt array that borders any road or any abutting residential dwelling lot shall consist of a vegetated buffer the width of the required setback along that border, in addition to any fence that may be erected, and existing vegetation should be used to satisfy these planting requirements where possible." Berms with vegetation are encouraged and the Planning Board may allow up to 25% reduction in buffer width where a berm is constructed. If no natural vegetation exists, "a plan by a licensed arborist shall be submitted to the Planning Board for approval" with indigenous conifers or evergreens and must be maintained to adequately screen the array. This applies to all nonexempt arrays, which includes Industrial Solar Energy Systems (ISES) as defined in Section 4. Other options include fencing and berms as components of the buffer. The ordinance also notes that "Arrays covering permanent parking lots and other hardscape areas approved by the Planning Board are encouraged" and in such cases, the Planning Board may waive the vegetated buffer requirement if the required setback is met.
section: Section 8. General Standards for all Arrays

summary: Section 5 states: 'Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems will not exceed 25 feet in height.' This applies to systems larger than 20,000 square feet and not directly connected to a residential structure, which are typical characteristics of utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit of measurement is feet.

Section 6 states: 'Subject to the approval of the Parkman Planning Board, the lots on which Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems are located may be required to install a buffer from roads and residences with a natural barrier.' This applies to Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems defined as systems greater than 20,000 square feet and not directly connected to a Residential Structure. The buffer is a natural barrier and is subject to Planning Board approval.
section: Section 6. Screening, Security, Maintenance and Regulatory Compliance

summary: Solar photovoltaic energy systems minimum setback shall be 30 feet from all property lines.

The Roxbury Solar Energy System Ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for medium- and large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems. Section 5(9) Removal states: "Solar energy systems that have reached the end of their useful life or have been abandoned consistent with this ordinance shall be removed. The owner or operator shall physically remove the installation no more than 200 days after the date of discontinued operations." Section 5(10) Abandonment provides that a system "shall be considered abandoned when it fails to operate for more than one year" and if not removed within 200 days, "the Town retains the right to use all available means to cause an abandoned, hazardous or decommissioned medium-scale or large-scale ground-mounted solar energy system to be removed." Section 7(b) Decommissioning Plan requires submission of a plan showing: "How physical removal of all solar energy systems, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines from the site will be accomplished," disposal of waste, site stabilization and re-vegetation, cost estimates, and financial assurance via a performance bond at 100% of estimated costs paid into escrow. The owner must provide annual updates to the cost estimate and adjust the financial guarantee accordingly. The performance guarantee must be provided prior to the issuance of a building permit/site plan review permit. Failure to maintain the guarantee can result in permit revocation. These requirements apply specifically to medium- and large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems, defined as systems with facility sizes greater than or equal to 43,560 square feet (1 acre) for medium-scale and 217,800 square feet (5 acres) for large-scale.
section: Section 5. Dimensional Standards; Section 7. Site Plan Review

summary: Section 5(6) states: "Fencing shall be installed as required by the NEC for ground-mounted solar energy systems in accordance with the size of the solar energy system. To allow for wildlife passage, fences should be elevated by a minimum of 5 inches." This fencing requirement applies to ground-mounted solar energy systems, which includes large-scale systems as defined in the ordinance. Other related standards for large-scale systems include setbacks, height limits, and safety reviews, but fencing specifics are only explicitly addressed in this provision.

summary: Section 7.16 Solar Energy – Utility-Scale requires a decommissioning plan to be submitted and approved prior to the issuance of a Special Use Permit. The plan must include: (1) the anticipated life of the project; (2) the manner of decommissioning including removal of above-grade and below-grade improvements; (3) estimated decommissioning costs excluding salvage value; and (4) financial assurance in the form of surety bond, irrevocable letter of credit, or cash deposit equal to 1.25 times the estimated costs, reviewed every three years and adjusted for inflation. Additionally, abandoned solar energy facilities not operated for twelve continuous months must be removed within 180 days of notice, including removal of foundations to a depth of five feet and site restoration. Failure to remove allows the Township to remove the facility at the owner's expense. The Planning Commission may grant extensions or require vegetative screening removal for agricultural access. These requirements apply to utility-scale solar energy systems designed to supply power primarily for off-site use and systems covering one acre or more. Other options include amending the decommissioning plan with Planning Commission approval or proceeding with the approved plan.

Section 7.16 Solar Energy – Utility-Scale explicitly requires that "The entire solar energy facility shall be enclosed by a fence at least six (6) feet in height." Additionally, it states: "Solar Energy Facilities may be secured with perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access. Fencing is not subject to setbacks. The Planning Commission may require wildlife-friendly fencing." This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems designed to supply energy primarily for off-site use. Other fencing options or conditions are not specified beyond the potential requirement for wildlife-friendly fencing by the Planning Commission.

Section 7.16 Solar Energy – Utility-Scale states: "Solar collection devices, or a combination of devices, shall be designed and located to avoid glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard. This may be accomplished by both the placement and angle of the collection devices as well as human-made or environmental barriers. Plans to reduce glare may be required in the initial materials submitted." This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems designed to supply power primarily for off-site use. Other related glare provisions exist in Section 7.15 for accessory solar energy systems, but those apply to systems designed primarily for on-site use and smaller scale, and thus are not relevant to utility-scale systems.

Section 7.16.C.2 states: 'The total height for all solar collection devices shall not exceed twenty-five (25) feet when oriented at maximum tilt.' This applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems designed to supply power primarily for off-site use. Other height limits mentioned in the text, such as fifteen (15) feet, apply to accessory or smaller scale systems and are not relevant here. The unit 'feet' is explicitly used in the ordinance.

The minimum lot size for a utility-scale solar energy system shall be twenty (20) acres. This is explicitly stated in Section 7.16 Solar Energy – Utility-Scale, subsection C.2.a: 'The minimum lot size for a utility-scale solar energy system shall be twenty (20) acres.' The units are acres, a standard area measurement. This minimum applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems designed to supply energy primarily for off-site use.

Section 7.16.C.8 states: 'The sound pressure level of a Solar Energy Facility and all ancillary solar equipment shall not exceed fifty-five (55) dBA (Leq (1 hour)) at the nearest outer wall of the nearest dwelling located on a participating lot.' It also states the noise 'shall not exceed fifty-five (55) dBA (Leq (1 hour)) at the nearest lot line located on an adjacent non-participating lot.' These are the explicit maximum noise levels for utility-scale solar energy systems designed to supply power primarily for off-site use. The units are decibels A-weighted (dBA), measured as an equivalent continuous sound level over one hour (Leq (1 hour)).

The setbacks of all solar collection devices and ancillary equipment shall be at least one hundred (100) feet from the road right-of-way and all lot lines of non-participating lots. Additionally, utility-scale solar energy systems shall be set back at least one hundred (100) feet from all property lines and public rights-of-way. There is also a 300-foot setback from residences and occupied community buildings on non-participating lots, but these are not equivalent to property lines. The setback is a fixed distance measured from the lot line to the nearest portion of the structure.

Section 7.16.E Repowering states: '1. In addition to repairing or replacing solar energy components to maintain the system, a Solar Energy Facility may at any time be repowered, without the need to apply for a new Special Use permit, by reconfiguring, renovating, or replacing the solar energy components to increase the power rating within the existing project footprint. 2. A proposal to change the project footprint of an existing Solar Energy Facility shall be considered a new application, subject to the Ordinance standards at the time of the request.' This means repowering is allowed without a new permit if power rating is increased within the existing footprint; however, any change to the project footprint requires a new application. No other repowering options or conditions are provided.

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be set back at least one hundred (100) feet from the road right-of-way and all lot lines of non-participating lots. This setback is a fixed distance and applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems designed to supply power primarily for off-site use. Other setback distances mentioned include three hundred (300) feet from all residences and occupied community buildings on non-participating lots, but these do not pertain to roads.

Section 7.16 Solar Energy – Utility-Scale explicitly requires screening: "The Planning Commission may require that solar devices be screened year-round from view from any existing adjacent non-participating lot line and the public right-of-way by use of a screening wall, evergreen vegetation, or other screening of similar effectiveness and quality, as determined by the Planning Commission." Screening "shall look as natural as possible through the use of varying plant materials of varying heights, if possible." It "shall be placed outside the perimeter fence" and "maintained throughout the life of the facility including replacing dead vegetation within six (6) months or at the earliest feasible time of year dependent on the weather." The Planning Commission may "reduce or waive screening requirements provided that any such adjustment is in keeping with the intent of the Ordinance."

Section 7.16 Solar Energy – Utility-Scale explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for utility-scale solar energy systems. It requires a drainage plan prepared by a registered civil engineer if more than 8,000 square feet of impervious surface will be located on the site, showing how stormwater runoff will be managed. If groundcover (such as conservation cover, pollinator habitat, forage cover, or agrivoltaics) is utilized, then a drainage plan is not required, but the Planning Commission may require soil stabilization through groundcover. Land disturbance or clearing shall be limited to what is minimally necessary, and topsoil distributed during site preparation (grading) shall be retained on site. Access drives shall be designed to minimize soil disturbance, water runoff, and soil compaction, with temporary use of geotextile fabrics and gravel permitted during construction but removed once the facility is in operation. Agricultural protection measures include ground mounting panels by screw, piling, or similar systems that do not require permanent mounting to minimize soil compaction, siting panels to avoid disturbance and compaction of farmland, maintaining drainage infrastructure, and siting to avoid isolating farm areas. These requirements apply to utility-scale solar energy systems designed to supply energy primarily for off-site use.

The text indicates that Solar Energy Facilities – Utility-Scale (§7.16) are permitted with a Special Use Permit ("S") in certain zoning districts as shown in the TABLE OF PERMITTED & SPECIAL USES under Utilities, Energy & Communications. The text also references other related uses such as Wind Energy Facilities & Anemometer Towers - Utility-Scale (§7.18) and Battery Energy Storage Systems (§7.19), which also require special use permits in some districts.

The setbacks of all solar collection devices and ancillary equipment shall be at least one hundred (100) feet from the road right-of-way and all lot lines of non-participating lots and shall be three hundred (300) feet from all residences and occupied community buildings on non-participating lots.

Under Section 7.16 Solar Energy – Utility-Scale, the ordinance requires that "Additional studies may be required by the Planning Commission if reasonably related to the standards of this ordinance as applied to the application site, including but not limited to: a. Visual Impact Assessment. A technical analysis by a third-party qualified professional of the visual impacts of the proposed project, including a description of the project, the existing visual landscape, and important scenic resources, plus visual simulations that show what the project will look like (including proposed landscape and other screening measures) a description of potential project impacts, and mitigation measures that would help to reduce the visual impacts created by the project and documented on the site plan." This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems designed to supply power primarily for off-site use. Other additional studies that may be required include Environmental Analysis, Stormwater Study, Glare Study, and Groundwater Study, each with specific conditions. No visual impact assessment requirements are explicitly stated for accessory solar energy systems or smaller systems.
The height of the solar energy system and any mounts must not exceed ten feet when oriented at maximum tilt.
Evergreen landscaping, sight obscuring fencing, or the combination of the two, must be provided to screen the racking (i.e., the framing below the panels) from view on all sides.

The ordinance states: 'the maximum lot coverage ratio for a Free-Standing Utility SES including solar panels shall be ten (10) percent.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for Free-Standing Utility SES. Other categories such as Free-Standing Small SES have different conditions (e.g., exceeding ten (10) percent of the total lot area requires a Special Use Permit), but these do not apply to Free-Standing Utility SES. The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the total lot area.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Free-Standing Utility SES in section 4, subsection (n) Decommissioning: "The applicant shall engage a certified professional engineer acceptable to the Township to estimate the total cost of decommissioning all structures in the facility in accordance with the requirements of this ordinance, including the reclamation to the original site conditions." It requires removal of all above and below ground materials and restoration of the ground to its original condition within sixty (60) days of removal. The owner/operator must give notice to the Township one (1) year in advance of decommissioning. Additionally, subsection (o) Security Bond requires posting a security bond "equal to two hundred (200) percent of the total estimated decommissioning, code enforcement, and reclamation costs" to ensure funds are available. Subsection (q) Abandonment and Removal states that if a SES ceases to perform its intended function for more than one hundred eighty (180) days, it is considered abandoned and must be removed within ninety (90) days unless an extension is granted. Failure to remove allows the Township to remove the SES and place a lien on the property. These requirements apply specifically to Free-Standing Utility SES, which are permitted as a special use in the Agricultural District and subject to various conditions including lot size, setbacks, height, screening, noise, safety, drainage, environmental impact, site plans, permits, maintenance, and complaint resolution. Other SES types such as Attached Small SES and Free-Standing Small SES have different conditions and do not have these decommissioning requirements explicitly stated.

Section 3.24, subsection 4(f) Safety / Access requires that "security fencing shall be installed around all electrical equipment related to the Free-Standing Utility SES including, but not limited to, transformers and transfer stations." Additionally, "appropriate warning signage shall be placed at the roadside and one sign at each entrance to the site, easily visible throughout four seasons." The signs must include warnings such as "Warning high voltage; participating landowner’s name, SES owner’s name, and operator’s name; at least one (1) emergency telephone number and web address; and unique identification such as address of SES that first responders can positively identify." The SES shall not be used to display advertising, but manufacturers’ equipment information, warning, or indication of ownership is allowed if compliant with Township sign regulations.

SES shall have a nonglare coating and be of neutral color; be placed and oriented such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto roadways and nearby properties; and the design and construction shall not produce light emissions, either direct or indirect (reflective) that would interfere with pilot vision and/or traffic control operations. Applicants have the burden of proving any glare produced does not cause annoyance, discomfort, or loss in visual performance and visibility. These glare restrictions apply to all SES, including Free-Standing Utility SES, which must comply with all General Regulations for All SES. Other SES categories include Attached Small SES (2-20 kW) and Free-Standing Small SES (2-20 kW), which have additional specific conditions but are not the focus here. The height of required lightning rods attached to the power switchyard or Free-Standing Utility SES related equipment shall not be subject to the twelve (12) foot height limitations; however, the height of lightning rods shall be limited to protect the equipment from lightning.

This is the only explicit minimum lot size requirement for Free-Standing Utility SES in the text. The units are acres, a standard area measurement.

The ordinance states: 'In addition to the maximum noise level of forty (40) dB(A) Lmax and fifty-five (55) db(C)/Lmax, noise abating structures in the form of a solid decorative masonry wall or evergreen tree berm, are required surrounding all inverters.' The most restrictive maximum noise level allowed for Free-Standing Utility SES is 40 dB(A) Lmax measured at the property line of any adjacent non-participating property/lot lines. The units are dBA, a standard noise measurement unit. Noise measurements must be done by a third-party qualified professional using a sound meter meeting ANSI S1.4 Type II specifications, with documentation provided to the Planning Commission within 60 days of commercial operation.

Section 3.24 SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS, subsection 4(d) requires "A berm of a height at least two (2) feet taller than the highest point of the SES is required to screen all Free-Standing Utility SES and accessory structures from view from adjacent properties and the road right-of-way." The berm "shall be planted with non-invasive plant species (grasses or similar natural vegetation) to minimize erosion on the slope. At least fifty (50) percent of plants must be native evergreen trees, which shall not be less than four (4) feet tall at the time of planting." Other options for screening include a decorative fence for smaller SES types, but these do not apply to Free-Standing Utility SES. This vegetative buffer and screening requirement is explicitly applicable to Free-Standing Utility SES as defined in the ordinance.

Section 4(f) requires that security fencing be installed around all electrical equipment related to the Free-Standing Utility SES. Appropriate warning signage shall be placed at the roadside and one sign at each entrance to the site, easily visible throughout four seasons. Signs shall uniquely identify each SES and contain at least the following: Warning high voltage; participating landowner’s name, SES owner’s name, and operator’s name; at least one emergency telephone number and web address; and unique identification such as address of SES that first responders can positively identify. The SES shall not be used to display advertising, including signage, streamers, pennants, spinners, reflectors, ribbons, tinsel, balloons, flags, banners or similar materials. Manufacturer’s equipment information, warning, or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of the system provided they comply with the prevailing Township sign regulations. Other SES categories mentioned include Attached Small SES (2-20 kW) and Free-Standing Small SES (2-20 kW), but signage requirements are only explicitly detailed for Free-Standing Utility SES.

Section 4(g) Drainage and Stormwater: Free-Standing Utility SES shall not increase stormwater runoff to adjacent properties. The application shall include a drainage plan prepared by a registered civil engineer showing how stormwater runoff shall be managed and demonstrating that runoff from the site shall not exceed the agricultural runoff rate or otherwise cause undue flood. Prior to construction of the SES, all existing drainage tile must be inspected by means of robotic camera and the imagery submitted to the Township to establish baseline condition of tile. Supports shall be constructed to preserve any drainage field tile and/or drainage system. Any damaged or inoperable tile shall be repaired prior to construction and such repairs shall be documented and a report submitted to the landowner and Township indicating the location, nature and satisfactory completion of such repairs. Section 4(j) Site Plans: Site plans shall include methods for dust and erosion control. These requirements explicitly address soil, erosion, and sediment control for Free-Standing Utility SES.

Free-Standing Utility Solar Energy Systems (SES) are permitted in the Agricultural District when authorized as a special use by the Planning Commission. The ordinance states: 'Free-Standing Utility as defined by Section 2.79 of this Ordinance are permitted in the Agricultural District when authorized as a special use by the Planning Commission.' The application for Special Use Permit requires extensive conditions including lot size (minimum 40 acres), setbacks (minimum 500 feet from lot lines and public road rights-of-way), height limits (not to exceed 12 feet), screening, noise abatement, safety measures, environmental impact assessments, site plans, additional permits, maintenance plans, decommissioning, security bonds, transfer or sale notifications, abandonment and removal procedures, and complaint resolution processes. Other types of solar energy systems such as Attached Small SES and Free-Standing Small SES are permitted in any zoning district but are limited to smaller scale uses (2-20 kW) and generally not for power sale, with some requiring special use permits if exceeding certain size thresholds (e.g., Free-Standing Small SES exceeding 10% of lot area). However, these smaller systems are not considered Free-Standing Utility SES and thus are excluded from this summary per instructions.

Section 4.44(G)(6) states: 'A decommissioning plan shall be submitted for approval by the Planning Commission, detailing the removal of all equipment and restoration of the site to its pre-development condition upon cessation of use.' Section 4.44(G)(7) requires: 'The applicant shall provide financial assurance, in a form acceptable to the Township, to ensure the proper decommissioning and removal of the solar energy system.' These requirements apply specifically to Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems, defined as 'a principal use of the lot, designed and intended to provide energy primarily to off-site uses or export to the wholesale electricity market.' Other related provisions include general standards for all Solar Energy Systems and specific standards for Small-Scale Solar Energy Systems, but decommissioning requirements are explicitly stated only for Utility-Scale systems.

For Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems, the ordinance requires: "A security fence at least 6 feet in height shall be installed around the perimeter of the solar energy system." Additionally, "A landscaped buffer shall be provided along all property lines abutting residential uses or public rights-of-way, consisting of evergreen trees or shrubs planted to provide a year-round visual screen." These requirements are found under the subsection titled 'Fencing and Screening.' Other related standards for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems include minimum lot size of 20 acres, setbacks of 100 feet from property lines and road rights-of-way, maximum height of 20 feet, access drives constructed to all-weather standards, a decommissioning plan, and financial assurance for removal and restoration. Small-Scale Solar Energy Systems have different requirements, including screening by fencing, landscaping, or other means in residential districts, but the explicit fencing mandate applies only to Utility-Scale systems as described.

Section 4.44(E)(2) states: 'All Solar Energy Systems shall be designed, constructed, and operated to prevent the misdirection and/or reflection of solar rays onto neighboring properties, public roads, and public rights-of-way.' This glare restriction applies to all Solar Energy Systems, including Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as 'a principal use of the lot, designed and intended to provide energy primarily to off-site uses or export to the wholesale electricity market.' Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted as a special land use in the RRAOS and I zoning districts, subject to requirements and Planning Commission approval. Other relevant standards for Utility-Scale systems include minimum lot size (20 acres), setbacks (100 feet), maximum height (20 feet), fencing and screening, access, decommissioning, and financial assurance. Small-Scale Solar Energy Systems have separate, more specific requirements including a glare provision that 'Solar panels shall be placed such that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways.'

Section 4.44(G)(3) states: 'The maximum height of any structure or equipment shall not exceed 20 feet.' This applies specifically to Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems, defined as systems that are a principal use of the lot and designed to provide energy primarily to off-site uses or export to the wholesale electricity market. Other height restrictions mentioned include a 15 feet maximum height for ground-mounted Small-Scale Solar Energy Systems, but these do not apply to Utility-Scale systems. The unit for the height restriction is feet.

The minimum lot size for a utility-scale solar energy system shall be 20 acres. This applies specifically to Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems defined as a principal use of the lot, designed and intended to provide energy primarily to off-site uses or export to the wholesale electricity market. The text states: 'The minimum lot size for a utility-scale solar energy system shall be 20 acres.' No other minimum lot size values for utility-scale systems are provided.

For Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems, "All equipment and structures shall be set back a minimum of 100 feet from all property lines and road rights-of-way." This setback applies specifically to property lines and is a fixed distance. Other related provisions include a minimum lot size of 20 acres and fencing and screening requirements, but no other setback distances from property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, parcels, or subdivisions are specified.

For Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems, all equipment and structures shall be set back a minimum of 100 feet from all property lines and road rights-of-way. This setback is a fixed distance and applies specifically to roads (rights-of-way). Additionally, a landscaped buffer shall be provided along all property lines abutting residential uses or public rights-of-way. No multiplier based on structure height is mentioned for setbacks from roads.

Section 4.44(G)(4)(b) requires "a landscaped buffer... consisting of evergreen trees or shrubs planted to provide a year-round visual screen" along all property lines abutting residential uses or public rights-of-way for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Additionally, Section 4.44(G)(4)(a) requires "a security fence at least 6 feet in height... around the perimeter of the solar energy system." These requirements apply to Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems defined as "a principal use of the lot, designed and intended to provide energy primarily to off-site uses or export to the wholesale electricity market." Other options for screening or buffers are not specified for Utility-Scale systems, but for Small-Scale Solar Energy Systems, Section 4.44(F)(3) requires screening "from view from adjacent properties by fencing, landscaping, or other means as approved by the Zoning Administrator" only in residential districts.

Solar Energy System – Utility Scale is marked as 'S' (Permitted by Special Use Permit) in the RRAOS and I districts. The table notes: 'P = Permitted by Right, S = Permitted by Special Use Permit, Blank = Prohibited.' Section 10.31, subsection 18 requires a commercial SES application to include a decommissioning and reclamation plan that shall address, at a minimum, the anticipated life of the project, the manner in which all structures and equipment shall be disassembled and removed from the participating parcels, and the manner in which the participating parcel shall be returned to its pre-existing state including revegetation. When a commercial SES is decommissioned, all items shall be removed from the subject property, including electrical components, structure foundation, or other associated components to a depth not less than ten (10) feet below the ground surface. Any material left more than ten (10) feet below the ground surface shall be documented and recorded upon a certified survey and recorded within the County Register of Deeds. Subsection 17 requires posting a performance guarantee equal to one hundred percent (100%) of the total estimated decommissioning and reclamation costs prior to permit issuance, with re-evaluation every five (5) years. Subsection F.12 requires a detailed decommissioning plan addressing the project’s estimated duration period, the manner in which all SES features shall be removed, and the manner in which the site shall be reclaimed to its former condition, including a financial security guaranteeing removal of the system, posted at the time of receiving a construction permit. The security shall be no less than the estimated cost of removal and may include inflationary adjustments. The estimate shall be prepared by the engineer for the developer and subject to Township approval. Other SES categories include Small SES (up to 1,000 sq ft, accessory use), Medium SES (1,001-10,000 sq ft, accessory use), and Large SES (more than 10,001 sq ft, permitted as accessory and principal uses, subject to special land use review).

Section 10.31(C)(8) states: "In the case of Medium SES and Large SES, a fence of a minimum eight (8) feet in height shall be erected to prevent access by the public to any solar panels and other facility equipment, with locked gates, and shall include 'danger' signage in both English and Spanish." This fencing requirement applies explicitly to Medium and Large Solar Energy Systems. Other related provisions include screening requirements for Medium and Large SES (C)(9), setback and height restrictions (C)(4), and various submittal and approval procedures for Large SES. The ordinance defines Large SES as systems occupying more than 10,001 square feet and typically intended for off-lot use or as a solar farm (A)(4).

Section 10.31(C)(3) states: 'SES collection panels shall be designed and placed such that concentrated solar radiation or solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties and public roads. The applicant shall submit documentation to verify compliance with this section.' Section 10.31(F)(11) requires: 'Provide a report prepared by a qualified person with documented training, certification and/or licensing in glare associated with SES including training in the use of computer software designed to assess glare potential, attesting to the glare and radiation impact on nearby properties and public roads and verifying compliance with this Section.' Large SES are defined as systems occupying more than 10,001 square feet and intended for use principally in association with multiple dwellings and/or businesses on a single lot and/or for use by off-lot properties and persons including in association with energy utility providers. Other SES categories include Small SES (up to 1,000 sq ft, typically for single residential units or businesses) and Medium SES (1,001-10,000 sq ft, typically for multiple dwellings/businesses on a single lot).

Ground-mounted panels that are part of a Large SES and exceed 10,001 square feet in area shall not exceed twelve (12) feet in height as measured from the ground below to the top of the panel when in its most vertical position. Other height limits include: Small SES panels not exceeding 12 feet, Medium SES panels (1,001-5,000 sq ft) not exceeding 12 feet, and Medium SES panels (5,001-10,000 sq ft) not exceeding 12 feet. The unit of measurement for height is feet.

Section 10.31, subsection C.10 states: 'Sound levels measured along a property line of a parcel adjacent to but not part of a commercial SES shall not exceed fifty-five (55) decibels on the dB(A) scale.' This maximum noise level applies to Large Solar Energy Systems (Large SES), which are described as commercial SES. No other numerical noise limits are provided for Large SES in the text.

summary: Section P. Abandonment: "Any large freestanding solar array that ceases to generate energy for more than 180 days, or which fails to have a power purchase agreement in place for more than 180 days, or which has does not have an in-force interconnection agreement, shall be deemed 'abandoned' under this Ordinance, and the Special Use permit shall be considered void." The process requires: "1. All equipment and structures must be removed from the site, including all foundations, wiring, and other below-grade aspects of the solar arrays... 2. The removal process must begin within 90 days... and must be completed within 365 days... 3. The Planning Commission shall require a performance bond... 4. If removal is not completed within 365 days, the Township shall remove the panels and assess costs against the bond. 5. Decommissioned material must be removed from the Township and disposed of in a State-approved landfill or other facility. 6. The site must be returned to a state where crop production is viable, with a remediation plan submitted with the original application." Other related conditions include the requirement for a power purchase agreement and interconnection agreement (Section O), and consequences for failure to maintain these agreements (Section P).

The outer boundaries of the large freestanding solar array shall be surrounded by fence at least six-feet-high with a self-locking gate. The fence shall not be subject to setback requirements, except where necessary to preserve wildlife corridors. The design of the fence must be approved by the Planning Commission, and no design other than the approved design shall be installed.
No large freestanding solar array shall produce glare that causes negative impacts on any adjacent lot (participating or non-participating), or causes a danger to motorists on any roadway.

The ordinance states: 'Freestanding solar panels shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet in height above the ground.' No other maximum height values are provided for large arrays specifically. The unit is explicitly given as feet.

summary: No Special Use permit shall be approved for a Solar Farm on land enrolled in the Michigan Farmland and Open Space Preservation Program (otherwise known as PA 116). Large Freestanding Solar Panel Arrays shall be permitted by Special Use in the A-1 and I-1 districts. Community Solar Gardens are permitted in all Zoning Districts. Small Freestanding Solar Panel Arrays are permitted accessory structures in all Zoning Districts.

All solar panels and other structures associated with the large freestanding solar array shall meet the following minimum setback requirements. From a lot line abutting a lot that is not participating in the solar project: 500 feet. From a lot line abutting a lot that is participating in the solar project: 10 feet. The purpose of this setback is to ensure there are corridors through the large freestanding solar array for the passage of wildlife. The Planning Commission may permit alternate wildlife corridors, in lieu of the 10 foot setback. From a public or private roadway: 500 feet.

From a lot line abutting a lot that is participating in the solar project: 10 feet. The purpose of this setback is to ensure there are corridors through the large freestanding solar array for the passage of wildlife. The Planning Commission may permit alternate wildlife corridors, in lieu of the 10 foot setback. Other setback options include 500 feet from a lot line abutting a non-participating lot and 500 feet from a public or private roadway.

All solar panels and other structures associated with the large freestanding solar array shall meet the following minimum setback requirements. From a public or private roadway: 500 feet. Other setback options include: from a lot line abutting a lot that is not participating in the solar project: 500 feet; from a lot line abutting a lot that is participating in the solar project: 10 feet. The purpose of the 10-foot setback is to ensure wildlife corridors. Screening requirements must be met along all public or private road frontages, with landscape screening allowed anywhere within the required setback.

Section 6.06.E requires that "Screening requirements must be met along all lot lines adjacent to non-participating parcels and along all public or private road frontages." When landscape screening is required, it "may be planted anywhere within the required setback," and must include "Evergreen trees, planted in a staggered double row designed to form a dense visual screen while still allowing for healthy development of the trees." The trees "must be at least 6 feet in height at the time of planting in all areas where the solar panels will be visible from a residence (in the opinion of the Planning Commission), and at least 4 feet in height at the time of planting in all other areas." The applicant must submit a description of the height and spread of each proposed evergreen species at maturity and an estimated timeline for maturity. The Planning Commission determines if the plantings constitute a "dense visual screen" and may require additional plantings or design changes. Existing trees shall be preserved unless the Planning Commission determines otherwise, and existing foliage on participating lots may count for screening if it provides a continuous screen from neighboring non-participating lots, with maintenance responsibilities on the solar array owners. Ground cover between panels must be "no mow" grass and other natural vegetation such as native grasses, grazing grasses, or pollinator habitat. All plantings must be maintained in sound health as a continuous screen, with dead or damaged plants replaced. This applies specifically to Large Freestanding Solar Panel Arrays as defined in the ordinance.

Section G. Drainage requires inspections of all drains, culverts, and stormwater infrastructure on participating and adjacent non-participating parcels prior to approval and construction, with repairs of any damage required by the solar farm owner/operator. Written confirmation from the County Drain Commissioner that stormwater drainage will not be impacted or that impacts will be mitigated is required before Special Use permit approval. Damage to underground drainage tiles or other stormwater infrastructure caused during installation or operation must be repaired within 30 days. Section E.2. Ground Cover mandates that between solar panels, the ground must be covered by  "no mow"  grass and other natural vegetation including native grasses, grazing grasses, or pollinator habitat. These requirements apply to Large Freestanding Solar Panel Arrays, defined as freestanding solar panel arrays larger than the footprint of the principal building or without a principal building, permitted by Special Use in the A-1 and I-1 districts.

Large Freestanding Solar Panel Arrays require a Special Use Permit in the A-1 and I-1 districts: 'Freestanding Solar Panel Arrays that are larger than the footprint of the principal building on the same lot, or which have no principal building on the same lot, shall be permitted by Special Use in the A-1 and I-1 districts.' Additionally, 'no Special Use permit shall be approved for a Solar Farm on land enrolled in the Michigan Farmland and Open Space Preservation Program (PA 116).' Other options include Small Freestanding Solar Panel Arrays, which are permitted accessory structures in all districts, and Community Solar Gardens, which are permitted uses in all districts but require Site Plan Approval by the Planning Commission and must meet requirements applicable to Large Freestanding Solar Panel Arrays.

For Large Freestanding Solar Panel Arrays, the ordinance requires a setback of 500 feet from a lot line abutting a lot that is not participating in the solar project. This setback is intended to protect adjacent properties, including occupied dwellings, buildings, and structures on non-participating lots. Other setback distances include 10 feet from a lot line abutting a participating lot and 500 feet from a public or private roadway, but these do not directly relate to occupied dwellings. The ordinance does not specify setbacks measured directly from buildings or residences, nor does it provide a multiplier based on structure height.

From a lot line abutting a lot that is participating in the solar project: 10 feet. The purpose of this setback is to ensure there are corridors through the large freestanding solar array for the passage of wildlife. The Planning Commission may permit alternate wildlife corridors, in lieu of the 10 foot setback. Other setback options include: 500 feet from a lot line abutting a lot that is not participating in the solar project, and 500 feet from a public or private roadway.

Section 14.41, subsection 15 'Abandonment and Decommissioning' requires that 'following the operational life of the project, or at the time the project becomes obsolete, uneconomic or an Abandoned Solar Energy System, as determined by the Zoning Administrator or any other expert or specialist to be designated by the Township to make such a determination, the applicant shall perform decommissioning and removal of the Large Solar Energy System and all its components.' The applicant must prepare 'a decommissioning plan prepared by a Professional Engineer licensed in the State of Michigan, and submit it to the Planning Commission for review as a part of the Special Use Permit.' The plan must include steps to '(a) Remove the system; (b) Dispose of or recycle its components; (c) Restore of the land to original conditions; and (d) An estimated cost schedule to meet the requirements.' The plan requires removal of 'all structures, equipment, conduit, fencing, roads and structure foundations, including any equipment, structures or materials below-grade, and removed offsite for disposal,' with 'no concrete, piping and other materials may be left in place.' The ground must be restored and revegetated 'within one hundred eighty (180) days of becoming an Abandoned Solar Energy System, or decommissioning, whichever occurs first.' Additionally, subsection 22 requires 'continuing security and a continuing escrow deposit' to ensure compliance with decommissioning and removal, including a financial guarantee 'in an amount determined by the Township to be reasonably sufficient to restore the property to its previous condition prior to construction and operation of the Large Solar Energy System.' Failure to maintain these securities constitutes a violation and may lead to enforcement or revocation of the special use permit.

A Large Solar Energy System shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access. Such fencing shall be eight (8) feet in height as measured from the natural grade of the fencing perimeter. Electric fencing is not permitted. The perimeter of Large Solar Energy Systems shall also be screened and buffered by buffer areas whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels. Unless screened and buffered at all times by natural forest vegetation meeting the minimum spacing and height requirements, a continuous evergreen vegetative buffer shall be installed and maintained at all times at the perimeter of all Large Solar Energy Systems. The evergreen or native vegetative buffer shall be composed of native or evergreen trees that at the time of planting shall be a minimum of four (4) feet in height, with shrubs being at least two (2) feet in height. The evergreen trees shall be spaced no more than fifteen (15) feet apart on center, native trees no more than thirty (30) feet apart, and shrubs no more than seven (7) feet apart. All unhealthy and dead material shall be replaced within six (6) months or the next appropriate planting period. All plant materials shall be installed between March 15 and November 15. If planting cannot occur during this period, a letter of credit, surety or guarantee equal to 1.5 times the cost of planting deficiencies must be provided to the Township. Failure to maintain the required buffer constitutes a violation and grounds for revocation of the special use permit.

Section 14.41, item 13 states: "All solar panels shall be placed such that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways (public or private) at any time of the day." This is a specific glare restriction that applies to Large Solar Energy Systems, defined as utility-scale systems with power output equal to or greater than one (1) megawatt, intended for sale, delivery, or consumption by more than one end user. Other related provisions include general regulations in Section 14.40 that address glare for all Solar Energy Systems, stating: "All Solar Energy Systems must be installed in a manner ensuring that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways." However, Section 14.40 primarily references Small Solar Energy Systems in many of its subsections, while Section 14.41 explicitly governs Large Solar Energy Systems as a special use with detailed requirements.

Maximum height of a Solar Array shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet. Other collection devices, components or buildings of the Large Solar Energy System shall not exceed thirty-five (35) feet, or the maximum building height permitted within the district in which that Solar Energy System is located, whichever is less, at any time or location on the property. The height shall be measured from the natural grade at the base of the Solar Array, device, component or building measured. The Planning Commission may waive or modify these height requirements for certain aspects of a Solar Energy System (such as structures associated with above-ground transmission lines) through the implementation of conditions when appropriate.

Section 14.41, item 6 states: 'A Large Solar Energy System shall be located on one (1) or more parcels with an aggregate area of Eighty (80) contiguous acres or smaller.' This is the explicit maximum lot size for Large Solar Energy Systems. Additionally, it states: 'The maximum amount of Township land developed as Large-Scale Solar Energy System Facilities shall not exceed fifty percent (50%) of the combined acreage of the Commercial and Industrial Districts within the Township.' However, the 80 acres limit is the direct maximum size for the system's location. The units are acres, a standard measure of land area.

Section 14.41, item 6 states: 'A Large Solar Energy System shall be located on one (1) or more parcels with an aggregate area of Eighty (80) contiguous acres or smaller.' This is the explicit minimum lot size for Large Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as utility-scale systems with power output equal to or greater than one (1) megawatt intended for sale or delivery to more than one end user. No other minimum lot size values are provided for Large Solar Energy Systems. The unit of measurement is acres, a standard area unit.

No component of any Large Solar Energy System shall emit noise exceeding fifty (50) dBA averaged over a one (1) hour period as measured at the outside perimeter of the project. The unit dBA refers to A-weighted decibels, a standard measure of noise level.

A minimum setback distance of one-hundred (100) feet from all property boundaries on the outside perimeter of the Large Solar Energy System shall be required for all buildings and Solar Arrays except for property boundaries where the applicable adjoining owner(s) agree to lessen or increase that setback distance by executing a signed written waiver of this requirement in recordable form, provided no such waiver shall act to permit less than the required minimum setback of the applicable zoning district.

summary: Section 14.41, subsection 9 requires that a Large Solar Energy System "shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access" with fencing "eight (8) feet in height" and prohibits electric fencing. The perimeter "shall also be screened and buffered by buffer areas whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels." If natural forest vegetation does not meet minimum spacing and height requirements or have a similar obscuring effect, "a continuous evergreen vegetative buffer shall be installed and maintained at all times at the perimeter of all Large Solar Energy Systems, including without limitation between such Large Solar Energy Systems and adjacent residential or agricultural areas and/or public highways or streets." The evergreen or native vegetative buffer must be composed of "native or evergreen trees that at the time of planting shall be a minimum of four (4) feet in height, with shrubs being at least two (2) feet in height." Spacing requirements are: evergreen trees no more than fifteen (15) feet apart on center, native trees no more than thirty (30) feet apart on center, and shrubs no more than seven (7) feet apart on center. Unhealthy or dead material (60% dead or greater) must be replaced within six (6) months or the next appropriate planting period. Plant materials must be installed between March 15 and November 15, or a financial guarantee must be provided to cover planting deficiencies. Failure to maintain the buffer is a violation and grounds for revocation of the special use permit. This applies specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems as defined (utility-scale, 1 MW+ systems for sale, delivery, or consumption by more than one end user).

Section 14.41, item 10 states: "No lettering, company insignia, advertising, graphics or other commercially-oriented inscriptions or designs shall be on any part of the Solar Arrays or other components of the Large Solar Energy System. This section does not prohibit signs reasonably necessary to inform the public of potential safety hazards associated with the Large Solar Energy System, nor does it prohibit any other signs that may be required by this Ordinance, the special use permit or other applicable law."

Section 14.41(2)(E)(i) requires "geotechnical report, prepared by a Professional Engineer licensed in the State of Michigan, demonstrating appropriate foundation designs and pavement designs based on findings of the geotechnical soil report. These geotechnical soil borings will also need to demonstrate the in-situ soil conditions prior to the proposed development." Section 14.41(2)(P) requires "a written description of measures to be taken to support the flow of rainwater throughout the Large Solar Energy System, including any measures to promote the growth of vegetation beneath the arrays and/or otherwise limit the impacts of storm water runoff. The measures shall be subject to the approval of the Eaton County Drain Commission." Section 14.41(15)(A)(iv) requires that "The ground must be restored to its original condition and the site shall be revegetated to blend with the existing surrounding vegetation within one hundred eighty (180) days of becoming an Abandoned Solar Energy System, or decommissioning, whichever occurs first." Section 14.41(15)(B) requires "geotechnical soil analysis shall be performed and a geotechnical soil report submitted demonstrating that the post-decommissioning soil conditions are reasonable to in-situ soil conditions prior to project development. The report shall be prepared by a Professional Engineer licensed in the State of Michigan. The Township may require that the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy (EGLE) verify the decommissioning soil analysis."

The District Use Table (Section 3.05) identifies Solar Energy System, Large as 'S' (uses permitted by Special Use Permit Approval) in the RC and R-1 districts. Article 8 (Section 8.02) and Article 9 (Section 9.02) specify that in the Commercial (C) and Industrial (I) districts, Solar Energy System, Large is permitted by Special Use Permit. summary: Section 14.41 requires that all applications for a Large Solar Energy System must be accompanied by detailed site plans, drawn to scale and certified by a registered engineer, displaying the location and height of all proposed Solar Arrays, buildings, structures, electrical tie lines and transmission lines, security fencing, and all above-ground structures and utilities (14.41(2)(E)). It also requires horizontal and vertical (elevation) scale drawings showing the location of proposed components (14.41(2)(F)) and land elevations for the Solar Array(s) location and their relationship to existing and proposed structures (14.41(2)(I)). Screening and buffering requirements mandate that the Large Solar Energy System "shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing" and "screened and buffered by buffer areas whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels" (14.41(9)). The evergreen or native vegetative buffer must meet specific height and spacing requirements (14.41(9)(A)-(C)). The Planning Commission may require "landscaping, walls, fences and other improvements that are reasonable in relation to and consistent with the nature of the applicable or adjacent zoning districts" as conditions of approval (14.41(18)). These requirements apply to Large Solar Energy Systems defined as "utility-scale solar energy system where the primary use of the land is to generate electric energy ... for the sale, delivery or consumption of the generated energy by more than one end user, and typically the power output ... is equal to or greater than one (1) megawatt" (Section 2.19). Glare restrictions are addressed separately and are not part of this visual impact assessment. No other options or alternative visual impact assessment procedures are provided in the ordinance.

Section 300.1151(J) Abandonment and Decommissioning requires that any solar farm that reaches its end of useful life shall be deemed abandoned and must be removed by the owner/operator. A performance bond or letter of credit sufficient to cover removal costs must be submitted prior to special land use issuance and adjusted every three years. If removal is not performed by the owner/operator, the Township may use the bond proceeds to remove the system. Decommissioning must be completed within one year after the end of useful life, with a possible extension of up to 15 months granted by the Planning Commission for good cause. Decommissioning includes removal of all panels, support structures, underground and aboveground equipment, berms, and foundations to allow reuse of the land for agricultural purposes. All decommissioning expenses are the responsibility of the owner/operator.

Section 300.1151(D)(5) requires that "A chain link security fence (minimum 6 feet in height) shall be installed and maintained around the entire perimeter of any solar farm." The ordinance defines a solar farm as "Land primarily designated or used for the purpose of producing solar or photovoltaic electricity... that comprise or occupy 10,000 square feet or more of panel area..." and includes systems where "The power generated is sold or transferred to electric companies or other third parties for distribution through a power grid." This fencing requirement applies specifically to solar farms and is part of the development and design standards. Other related requirements include securing all electrical equipment in enclosed structures or approved weatherproof cabinets and providing access gates with Knox Boxes for emergency services. No alternative fencing options or conditions are provided in the text.

Section 300.1151 D.3 states: 'All photovoltaic panels located on a solar farm shall be restricted to a maximum design height of 16 feet.' This applies specifically to solar farms defined as land primarily designated or used for producing solar electricity sold or transferred to electric companies or third parties, occupying 10,000 square feet or more of panel area. Other height restrictions mentioned include a 6-foot minimum height for security fencing and an 18-foot limit for light poles, but these do not apply to the solar panels themselves. The unit for the height restriction is feet.

The ordinance states: 'Solar farms shall only be permitted on lots where at least 20 acres can be dedicated to solar energy production.' This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for Solar Farms as defined in the ordinance. The unit is expressed in acres. No other minimum lot size values for Solar Farms are provided in the text.

The noise from a solar farm shall not exceed 55 decibels as measured at any property line. This applies specifically to Solar Farms as defined in the ordinance: "Solar Farm: Land primarily designated or used for the purpose of producing solar or photovoltaic electricity... The power generated is sold or transferred to electric companies or other third parties for distribution through a power grid..." The unit is expressed as decibels, and for the purposes of this extraction, the standard unit for noise is 'dBA'.

All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with solar farms (excluding perimeter security fencing) shall be a minimum of 20 feet from any side or rear property line. Other setbacks mentioned include a minimum of 50 feet from any road or highway right-of-way or easement, but this does not pertain to property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, parcels, or subdivisions.
section: 300.1151 SOLAR FARMS AND SOLAR PANELS, Subsection D.4. Setbacks

summary: Section 300.1151(C) states: "Modifications to an existing lawful solar farm (which existed as of the effective date of this Ordinance) that increases the area by more than 10% of the original footprint or changes the solar panel type shall be fully subject to this Ordinance." Section 300.1151(J) details abandonment and decommissioning requirements: "Any solar farm or part thereof that reaches its end of useful life... shall be deemed to be abandoned... It shall be the obligation of the solar farm owner or operator to remove the abandoned system." Decommissioning must be completed within one year after the end of useful life, with possible extensions not exceeding 15 months. Decommissioning includes removal of all panels, support structures, underground wires/cables, and foundations to allow land reuse for agricultural purposes. These provisions apply specifically to solar farms defined as systems producing electricity for sale and occupying 10,000 square feet or more of panel area.

All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with solar farms (excluding perimeter security fencing) shall be a minimum of 50 feet from any road or highway right-of-way or easement.

summary: A Large Solar Energy System shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access, unless waived by the Township.
