The perimeter of Large Solar Energy Systems shall also be screened and buffered by greenbelts whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels, subject to the following requirements: a) Unless screened and buffered at all times by natural forest vegetation meeting the minimum spacing and height requirements, and having a substantially similar obscuring effect of an evergreen vegetative buffer installed pursuant to this Section, a continuous evergreen vegetative buffer shall be installed and maintained at all times at the perimeter of all Large Solar Energy Systems, including without limitation between such Large Solar Energy Systems and adjacent residential or agricultural areas (where those areas exist outside the project area and abut such systems) and public or private highways, or streets. Any required screening and landscaping shall be placed outside the perimeter fencing. b) The evergreen or native vegetative buffer shall be composed of native or evergreen trees that at planting shall be a minimum of four (4) feet in height and shrubs two (2) feet in height. The evergreen trees shall be spaced no more than fifteen (15) feet apart on center (from the central trunk of one plant to the central trunk of the next plant), native trees shall be placed no more than thirty (30) feet apart on center and shrubs shall be spaced no more than seven (7) feet apart on center. All unhealthy (60 percent dead or greater) and dead material shall be replaced by the applicant within six (6) months, or the next appropriate planting period, whichever occurs first, but under no circumstances should the applicant allow unhealthy or dead material to remain in place for more than six (6) consecutive months. Failure to maintain the required evergreen vegetative buffer as required by this section shall constitute a violation of this Ordinance and sufficient grounds for revocation of any special use permit previously granted. c) Screening requirements may be reduced or waived provided that any such adjustment is in keeping with the intent of the Ordinance including agricultural preservation, minimizing negative impacts to drain tiles, buffering and screening of Large Solar Energy Systems to prevent aesthetic and visual impacts to adjacent residential uses, and reuse of the property. d) All plant materials shall be installed between March 15 and November 15. If the applicant is unable to plant during the first installation period at the time that final zoning approvals are provided by the Township, the applicant will provide the Township with a letter of credit, surety or corporate guarantee for an amount equal to one and a half (1.5) times the cost of any planting deficiencies that the Township shall hold until the next planting season. summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Large Solar Energy Systems. summary: Large freestanding solar farms are defined as utility scale commercial facilities for wholesale or retail sales of electricity off-site. They require approval by the Planning Commission, an electrical permit, and a building permit with a site plan prepared and stamped by an engineer. A minimum of 20 acres is required. Specific requirements include height restrictions (14 feet max), setbacks (15 feet from side/rear property lines, 30 feet from roads), security fencing, sound limits (65 dBA max), and compliance with local, state, and federal permits. Decommissioning is explicitly required: "Following the operational life of the project, the applicant shall perform decommissioning and removal of the large photovoltaic solar farm facilities and all its components." The applicant must "prepare a decommissioning plan and submit it to the Planning Commission for review and approval prior to issuance of the Special Land Use Permit." Other system types include Attached Systems (500W+), Small Freestanding Systems (500W to 10kW, for use only on the same parcel), and Medium Freestanding Systems (10kW+, not for resale, on parcels of two acres or more).

For Large Freestanding Systems (Solar Farms), the ordinance requires "A security fence (height and material to be established through the special land use permit process) shall be placed around the perimeter of the solar power plant and electrical equipment shall be locked." Electric fencing is not permitted. Additionally, "The Planning Commission may require fences or barriers as they deem necessary to provide screening for adjacent properties." Other system sizes have different requirements: Small Freestanding Systems (500W to 10kW) must meet setbacks and structural requirements but no explicit fencing is mentioned; Medium Freestanding Systems (10kW or more, but not for resale) may have fences or barriers required by the Planning Commission for screening; Attached Systems and Small Freestanding Systems have no explicit fencing requirements stated.

This applies specifically to Large Freestanding Systems (Solar Farms) defined as utility scale commercial facilities for wholesale or retail sales of electricity off-site. Other categories include Small Freestanding Systems (500W to 10kW) and Medium Freestanding Systems (10kW or more, but not for resale), which have different height restrictions (e.g., medium systems have a maximum top panel height of 14 feet, but this is not for resale). summary: The ordinance explicitly prohibits ground-mounted solar electric systems, including standard and pole mounted arrays, stating they "are not permitted." A decommissioning plan signed by the responsible party and the land owner (if different) addressing the following shall be submitted prior to approval of a Utility-Scale Solar Energy Collector system: (1) Defined conditions upon which decommission will be initiated (e.g., end of land lease, no power production for 12 months, abandonment, etc.); (2) Removal of utility-owned equipment and non-utility-owned equipment, which may include but not be limited to conduit, structures, fencing, solar panels, and foundations; (3) Restoration of property condition which existed prior to the development of the system; (4) Specification of the timeframe from completion of decommissioning activities; (5) Description of any agreement (i.e., lease) with landowner regarding decommissioning, if applicable; (6) Identity of the entity or individual responsible for decommissioning; (7) Plans for updating the decommissioning plan; (8) A performance guarantee shall be posted in the form of a bond, letter of credit, cash, or other form acceptable to the Township to ensure removal upon abandonment. The responsible party shall provide at least two cost estimates from qualified contractors for full removal and disposal of equipment, foundations, and structures associated with the system. These amounts will assist the Township when establishing the initial performance guarantee amount. The performance guarantee amount shall be valid throughout the lifetime of the system, and it shall be adjusted by the Township every five years based upon at least two new cost estimates from qualified contractors obtained by the responsible party. Bonds and letters of credit shall be extended on a regular basis with expiration dates never less than two years from the annual anniversary of Special Land Use approval. Additionally, a Solar Energy Collector system that ceases to produce energy on a continuous basis for 12 months will be considered abandoned unless the responsible party provides substantial evidence of intent to maintain and reinstate operation every six months after the 12 months of no energy production. The responsible party shall remove all equipment and facilities and restore the Lot to its condition prior to the development of the system within one year of abandonment.

Large Solar Energy Systems (Large SES) "shall comply with the site development standards of subsection (D) for Medium SES except as follows" (Section 7.29 E.2). Medium SES decommissioning requirements include: "a decommissioning and reclamation plan that shall address, at a minimum, the anticipated life of the project, the manner in which all structures and equipment shall be disassembled and removed from the lot, and the manner in which the lot shall be returned to its pre-existing state including revegetation" (Section 7.29 D.4.i). Additionally, "Prior to the issuance of a Medium SES permit, the applicant shall engage a licensed professional engineer to estimate the total cost of decommissioning..." and "shall post a performance guarantee... equal to one hundred percent (100%) of the total estimated decommissioning and reclamation costs" (Section 7.29 D.4.j). Large SES may provide power to multiple lots or the general utility network (Section 7.29 E.2.a). Other categories include Small SES (up to 800 sq. ft., serving a single residential unit or business) and Medium SES (800 to 10,000 sq. ft., accessory use serving the principal use of the lot), each with distinct provisions and no explicit decommissioning requirements stated for Small SES. Large SES are subject to special land use review and approval (Section 7.29 E.1).

Fencing of a minimum height of six (6) feet but not to exceed eight (8) feet shall be erected to prohibit access by the public to all portions of the SES facility. All SES facilities shall be within the fenced area and shall be set back a minimum distance of twenty-five (25) feet from such fence. Large Solar Energy Systems (Large SES) shall comply with the site development standards of Medium SES except as provided otherwise by this Section. Therefore, Large SES are subject to the fencing requirements applicable to Medium SES. Other provisions include setbacks, screening, and operational requirements for Medium and Large SES, but fencing is specifically mandated for Medium SES and by extension Large SES.

Large Solar Energy Systems (Large SES) "shall comply with the site development standards of subsection (D) for Medium SES except as follows." Medium SES glare restrictions include that "solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties and public roads so as to cause nuisance conditions," with required documentation and mitigation measures if glare occurs. Specifically, "If an SES subsequently results in nuisance glare conditions, effective mitigation measures shall be employed within thirty (30) days of notification by the Zoning Administrator." Additionally, the design must ensure glare "shall not produce glare, either direct or indirect (reflective), that can be expected to interfere with pilot vision and /or air traffic control operations." Other SES categories include Small SES, which have similar but distinct glare provisions, and Medium SES, which are accessory uses serving the principal use of the lot. Large SES may provide power to multiple lots or the general utility network and have additional setback and lot size requirements.

The ordinance states: 'No Large SES shall be established on a lot less than twenty (20) acres in area.' This is the explicit minimum lot size for Large Solar Energy Systems (Large SES). Other categories such as Small SES and Medium SES have minimum lot sizes of one (1) acre, but these do not apply to Large SES. The unit 'acres' is used to specify the area.

For Large Solar Energy Systems (Large SES), solar collection panels shall be setback from all property lines a minimum distance of one hundred fifty (150) feet. Additionally, no substation shall be located closer than one hundred fifty (150) feet to a property line of a lot not otherwise part of the Medium SES, except that in the case of a substation more than 30,000 sq. ft. in area, the minimum setback shall be increased to four hundred (400) feet.

summary: Large SES shall comply with the site development standards of subsection (D) for Medium SES except as follows: Screening of ground-mounted panels shall be provided as required for Small SES, according to subsection (C), except that in the case of ground mounted solar panel(s) located on a lot that is adjacent to a lot in an Agricultural or Residential District, where the panels are to be located within two hundred (200) feet of a shared lot line with such lot, a double-row of evergreen tree plantings shall be provided and positioned in relation to one another to provide the greatest degree of screening. In addition, evergreen trees shall be of a minimum height at the time of installation as the height of the proposed solar panels. All plant material shall be maintained in a healthy condition to provide the necessary screening, shall be permitted to grow according to its natural habit, and shall be replaced upon death or disease. For Small SES, screening consists of one (1) evergreen tree per twenty (20) linear feet of panel length spaced no greater than twenty-five (25) feet apart measured on-center, with trees a minimum height equal to fifty percent (50%) of the height of the panel(s). The Zoning Administrator may permit a maximum fifty percent (50%) reduction in the number and size of tree plantings under certain conditions. Other conditions for Small and Medium SES include setbacks, height limits, and operational provisions. Large SES must also meet minimum setbacks of one hundred fifty (150) feet from all property lines and minimum lot size of twenty (20) acres.

Large SES signage requirements: "Signs shall be located at the base of all ground mounted transformers and substations providing appropriate warning of high voltage and emergency contact information. Similar signs shall be posted at all facility and building entrances." Other relevant provisions for Large SES include: "Large SES shall comply with the site development standards of subsection (D) for Medium SES except as follows," and "A Large SES may provide electrical power to only the lot on which the SES is located, or to multiple lots including lots on which no portion of the SES is located, or to the general utility network or utility providers." Also, Large SES must be on lots "no less than twenty (20) acres in area" and solar collection panels must be "setback from all property lines a minimum distance of one hundred fifty (150) feet."

Large Solar Energy Systems (Large SES) "shall comply with the site development standards of subsection (D) for Medium SES except as follows" (Section E.2). Medium SES site development standards include: "No construction shall be initiated prior to the Zoning Administrator receiving approvals from county and state agencies having jurisdiction, as applicable, including ... Saginaw County Drain Commissioner approvals for runoff discharge and erosion control" (D.1.e); a maintenance plan that "demonstrates that the SES will be designed, constructed, and operated to minimize dust generation, including during construction," "delineates the manner how unpaved access roads will be treated and maintained for dust control," and includes "measures that will be employed to maintain and promote native vegetation while minimizing the proliferation of weeds during and following construction" (D.1.f); and a requirement that if a ground mounted Medium SES ceases operation or is abandoned, the applicant "shall repair and restore the system to good working order ... or otherwise remove the system in its entirety ... and restore the ground to its preconstruction state" (D.4.g). Other SES categories include Small SES (up to 800 sq. ft., typically for single residential or agricultural use) and Medium SES (800 to 10,000 sq. ft., typically for multiple dwellings or off-lot use), with their own provisions. Large SES are defined as systems occupying more than 10,000 sq. ft. and "typically intended to produce energy for use principally in association with multiple dwellings and/or businesses on a single lot ... and/or for use by off-lot properties and persons including in association with energy utility providers" (A.1.c).

Large Solar Energy Systems (Large SES) are "an authorized permitted use according to Tables 3-2 and 3-3" but "shall be subject to the special land use review and approval provisions of Article 15." In the provided zoning table, Large SES are marked as "S4" in the I-1 district, indicating special use approval is required. Other districts listed (B-1 and B-2) show "-4," indicating Large SES are not permitted there. The ordinance also distinguishes Small and Medium SES, which have different authorization and approval procedures, but these are not applicable to Large SES.

summary: Item 11 under 'Additional Special Use Criteria' requires the applicant to 'describe the decommissioning and final reclamation plan after the anticipated useful life or abandonment/termination of the project,' including 'proper removal of all equipment and restoration of the site within six (6) months of decommissioning or abandonment of the project.' It also mandates that applicants 'include a description of the financial security guaranteeing removal of the system which must be posted with the Township within fifteen (15) days after approval or before a building or construction permit is issued for the project.' The financial security options are: '1) a cash bond; or 2) an irrevocable bank letter of credit or a performance bond, in a form approved by the Township.' The amount must be 'no less than the estimated cost of removal and may include a provision for inflationary cost adjustments,' with the estimate prepared by the applicant's engineer and subject to Township approval. If the owner fails to remove or repair any defective, abandoned or terminated project, 'the Township... may pursue legal action to abate the violation by seeking to remove the project and recover any and all costs, including attorney fees.' These requirements apply to 'Solar Farms' defined as solar arrays 'for the primary purpose of the wholesale sales of generated electricity' and permitted by special use permit in the A-1 Agricultural District. Other provisions in the ordinance address site plan requirements, safety, setbacks, and other operational criteria but do not pertain directly to decommissioning.

A security fence (height and material to be proposed and reviewed/approved through the special land use permit process) shall be placed around the perimeter of the solar farm and electrical equipment. Knox boxes and keys shall be provided at locked entrances for emergency personnel access. This applies to solar farms defined as solar arrays composed of multiple solar panels on ground-mounted racks or poles which are not directly connected to or designed to serve the energy needs of the primary use, but rather for the primary purpose of the wholesale sales of generated electricity.

The ordinance defines Solar Farms as "a solar array composed of multiple solar panels on ground-mounted rack or poles which is not directly connected to or designed to serve the energy needs of the primary use, but rather for the primary purpose of the wholesale sales of generated electricity." It explicitly states that "Solar farm facilities shall be located or placed so that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed toward or onto nearby properties or roadways at any time of the day." This glare restriction applies to utility-scale solar energy systems (solar farms). Other relevant conditions include height restrictions (maximum 16 feet), setbacks, noise limits, landscaping, and special use permit requirements. The ordinance also details additional site plan and special use criteria for solar farms.

The ordinance states: 'All photovoltaic panels and support structures located in a solar farm shall be restricted to a maximum height of sixteen (16) feet when oriented at a maximum tilt.' This applies specifically to solar farms, defined as solar arrays primarily for wholesale sales of generated electricity, i.e., utility-scale solar energy systems. No other maximum height values for utility-scale systems are provided. The unit for this height restriction is feet.

The ordinance states: 'No solar farm facilities shall exceed sixty (60) dBA as measured at the property line.' This applies explicitly to solar farms, which are defined as solar arrays primarily for wholesale sales of electricity, thus utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit 'dBA' is the standard unit for noise level measurement.

All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with such facilities (excluding perimeter fencing) shall be setback a minimum of seventy-five (75) feet from a side or rear property line and a minimum of fifty (50) feet from any road right-of-way. All facilities shall also be setback at least to the limit of any established County drain right-of-way or easement unless special provisions are formally agreed to with the Saginaw County Public Works Commissioner.

All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with such facilities (excluding perimeter fencing) shall be setback a minimum of fifty (50) feet from any road right-of-way. Other setback requirements include seventy-five (75) feet from side or rear property lines, but these do not pertain to roads.

The ordinance requires that "The special land use application for a solar farm shall include a proposed landscaping and screening/buffering plan prepared by a licensed landscape architect." It further mandates that "The use of berms and evergreen plantings along property lines adjacent to residential land uses is required." Trees "shall be a minimum of four (4) feet tall at time of planting and be placed in two (2) rows twelve (12) feet apart," with spacing and staggered rows specified. "If Berms are being used berms shall be a minimum of ten (10) feet tall." These requirements apply to Solar Farms, defined as "a solar array composed of multiple solar panels on ground-mounted rack or poles which is not directly connected to or designed to serve the energy needs of the primary use, but rather for the primary purpose of the wholesale sales of generated electricity."

The ordinance requires as part of the additional site plan requirements for solar energy facilities: 'A site grading, erosion control and storm water drainage plan. The plans will be reviewed by the Township's engineering firm at the applicant's cost.' This applies to solar farms defined as 'a solar array composed of multiple solar panels on ground-mounted rack or poles which is not directly connected or designed to serve the energy needs of the primary use, but rather for the primary purpose of the wholesale sales of generated electricity.'

Solar Farms: Permitted by Special Use Permit in A-1 Agricultural District and meet requirements of this ordinance amendment. Solar Farms are defined as a solar array composed of multiple solar panels on ground-mounted rack or poles which is not directly connected to or designed to serve the energy needs of the primary use, but rather for the primary purpose of the wholesale sales of generated electricity.

Project design and layout will ensure any structures or other improved areas located within the fenced/improved area shall be located a minimum of one-hundred (100) feet from any residential structure, church, school, family or group child day-care home, and bed and breakfast establishments. Other setbacks mentioned include 75 feet from side or rear property lines and 50 feet from road right-of-way, but these do not pertain directly to occupied dwellings or residences.

The ordinance defines Solar Farms as "a solar array composed of multiple solar panels on ground-mounted rack or poles which is not directly connected to or designed to serve the energy needs of the primary use, but rather for the primary purpose of the wholesale sales of generated electricity." Solar Farms are "Permitted by Special Use Permit in A-1 Agricultural District and meet requirements of this ordinance amendment." Under Additional Special Use Criteria, the applicant must provide a "Visual Impacts: Graphically demonstrate the visual impact of the project using photos or renditions of the project with consideration given to setbacks and proposed landscaping." This requirement explicitly enacts a visual impact assessment for utility-scale solar energy systems. Other criteria include project description, environmental analysis, landscaping plans, noise, lighting, transportation, public safety, and more, but only the visual impact demonstration is relevant here.

Commercial solar energy generation facility projects shall include a decommissioning plan to ensure complete removal and site restoration upon the end of the project life or facility abandonment. The decommissioning plan shall include: a detailed plan for removal of any foundation, including concrete footings, pilings, support structures, and other appurtenances below grade; removal of all non-utility owned equipment, conduit, structures, fencing, roads, and equipment; and restoration of the land to conditions suitable for agricultural use. A detailed cost estimate of decommissioning, removal, and restoration costs prepared by a professional engineer, and identification of the financial resources to be used to accomplish decommissioning, subject to Township Engineer review and Planning Commission acceptance. The plan shall confirm that a performance guarantee for the accepted amount will be deposited with the Township, allowing the Township to fund completion if the owner fails to do so. Every five years, the Planning Commission may require an updated cost estimate and amended performance guarantee. All decommissioning, removal, and restoration activities must be completed within 180 calendar days after the end of project life or facility abandonment, unless an alternative schedule is authorized. Additionally, any commercial solar energy generation facility for which a special use permit has been rescinded or that is determined abandoned must be removed within 90 calendar days of a written removal order. Failure to remove allows the Township to remove the facility at the owner's expense, using any performance guarantee. Removal includes foundations, equipment, fencing, roads, and restoration of land to pre-development condition. Other options and conditions include location limitations, height and setback requirements, screening, fencing, protection of land and soils, natural features protection, on-site battery storage, and required permits and insurance.

summary: For a lot or contiguous tract of land exceeding 30.0 acres in gross lot area, a minimum setback of 200 feet shall be required between the facility and any road right-of-way or perimeter lot boundary. Other options include: for a lot or contiguous tract of land up to 30.0 acres, a minimum setback of 100 feet is required; where a facility is located on multiple contiguous lots not under single ownership or control, the tract shall be treated as a single lot for setback purposes.

For a lot or contiguous tract of land exceeding 30.0 acres in gross lot area, a minimum setback of 200 feet shall be required between the facility and any road right-of-way or perimeter lot boundary. For a lot or contiguous tract of land up to 30.0 acres in gross lot area, a minimum setback of 100 feet shall be required between the facility and any road right-of-way or perimeter lot boundary.

Section 11.39.F.4 requires that "adequate screening shall be provided" for commercial solar energy generation facilities to ensure they "do not impair the visual character of the Township’s rural environment or adversely impact adjacent uses or residents." The screening must be "located within the required perimeter setback area, unless the Planning Commission determines that an alternative location will provide for improved screening." At minimum, the screening shall include "a mix of evergreen and deciduous trees planted in staggered rows of sufficient width and density of plantings to provide immediately effective, year-round screening." Tree species and sizes "shall conform to the requirements of Section 11.10 (Landscaping and Screening), and shall be hardy, native to Michigan, suitable for soil conditions, and not attractive to deer." Use of arborvitae is prohibited. Existing vegetation and topography may be used for screening with Planning Commission approval. Berms are allowed only incidentally and must comply with Section 11.10D.4. The ordinance also includes other conditions for commercial solar energy generation facilities such as location limitations, height limitations, setbacks, perimeter fencing, land and soil protection, natural features protection, battery storage, decommissioning plans, and additional provisions related to permits and approvals.
section: Section 11.39 Solar Energy Facilities and Devices

summary: Section 11.39.F.6 requires that the commercial solar energy generation facility "shall be designed, constructed, and maintained in a manner that maximizes protection of the land and soils for future agricultural use," including: "a. The network of underground agricultural drainage tiles shall be protected during facility construction, and promptly repaired or replaced as necessary to maintain adequate drainage conditions on the lot and for surrounding land. b. Site grading for the facility shall be limited to the minimum necessary for ingress and egress of vehicles, to maintain surface water drainage, and to provide for any required buildings or transformer pads. Removal or stockpiling of topsoil from the site shall be prohibited. c. Use of the land within the perimeter of the facility for agricultural purposes shall be maintained to the maximum extent feasible. d. At a minimum, a dense mix of groundcover plantings designed to attract a variety of pollinator species... shall be required to be maintained on all areas of the lot encumbered by the facility that are not in agricultural use." Section 11.39.F.7 requires impacts on natural features including watercourses, wetlands, floodplains, steep slopes, groundwater recharge areas, and existing trees and woodlands to "conform to all applicable requirements of Section 11.05 (Natural Features Protection)." Other options or conditions in the ordinance relate to location limitations, height, setbacks, screening, fencing, decommissioning, and other operational standards, but these do not explicitly address soil, erosion, or sediment control.

Any principal use small solar energy collector system which has reached the end of its useful life or has not operated continuously for one year or longer shall be fully removed and the parcel owners shall be required to restore the site to its prior state. The owner/operator shall physically remove the installation no more than 150 days after the date of discontinued operations. The owner/operator shall notify the City directly or by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. If the owner/operator fails to remove the installation in accordance with the requirements of this section within 150 days of abandonment or the proposed date of decommissioning, the City may enter the property and physically remove all of the solar energy system and facilities and charge the cost back to the owner(s) of the lot. Removal shall include physical removal of all aboveground or underground solar energy systems, structures, equipment, security barriers, and transmission lines; disposal off-site of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations; and restoration and stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion. The applicant shall provide a financial guarantee in the form of monetary surety or security acceptable to the City Attorney, covering removal costs up to 125% of estimated costs, subject to review and approval by the Planning Commission and City Attorney, and adjusted by the Federal CPI every five years.

summary: Section 12.12.F.5.b requires a decommissioning plan signed by the responsible party and landowner prior to issuance of the zoning permit, including: "the anticipated life of the project; the estimated decommissioning costs net of salvage value in current dollars; the method of ensuring that funds will be available for decommissioning and restoration, to include but not limited to: Complete removal of all non-utility owned equipment, conduit, structures, fencing, roads, solar panels and foundations, and Complete restoration of property to condition prior to development of the Solar Energy Facility; the anticipated manner in which the project will be decommissioned and the site restored; a provision to give notice to the Township one year in advance of decommissioning; a surety bond to assure payment of the cost of decommissioning shall be required." summary: The ordinance requires that any structures or other improved areas located within the fence of a Solar Energy Facility shall be located at least 30 feet from the fence line (facility perimeter). Additionally, all fences and improved areas must comply with the applicable setback for the district in which the facility is located, implying setbacks from property or lot lines as per district regulations. A minimum 20-foot landscape buffer is also required around the facility. The relevant text states: 'All fences and improved areas located on the site shall comply with the applicable setback for the district in which it is located. Furthermore, any structures or other improved areas located within the fence shall be at located least 30 feet from a fence line.' Other setback references include a 130-foot setback from residential dwellings and similar structures, but these do not pertain to property lines or parcel boundaries.

All access roads and storage areas shall be established on a 30’ minimum easement to a public right of way, which shall be paved or graveled in a manner sufficient to provide a solid base at all times of the year. (Section 12.12.F.3.a.iv) This is the only explicit numeric setback distance from roads or rights-of-way for Solar Energy Facilities as defined (those primarily selling electricity off-site). No other numeric setback distances from roads are provided for the facilities themselves.

Section 12.12.F.3.a.v requires that "All solar energy facilities shall have a minimum landscape buffer of 20 feet. The buffer shall contain evergreen trees or bushes planted no more than 8 feet apart and at least 4’ tall at time of planting. The buffer shall obtain a height of 10 feet within 3 growing seasons. The trees or bushes may be trimmed but no lower than a height of 10 feet." Additionally, subsection 3.e states: "The design of solar energy facilities buffers shall use materials, colors, textures, screening and landscaping, that will blend the facility into the natural setting and existing environment." These requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities defined as "those facilities that primarily sell electricity to be used off site."

summary: The ordinance requires a Decommissioning Plan for Primary and Secondary Use Solar Energy Facilities to ensure proper decommissioning upon the end of the project life or facility abandonment. Decommissioning shall include removal of all structures (including transmission equipment and fencing) and debris to a depth of four (4) feet, restoration of the soil, and restoration of vegetation within six (6) months of the end of project life or facility abandonment. The plan must state how the facility will be decommissioned, the Professional Engineer's estimated cost of decommissioning, the financial resources to be used, and the escrow agent. The applicant must post a performance bond or equivalent financial instrument of at least $250,000 with a replenishment obligation. The Township has rights to access escrow funds and the site to complete decommissioning if not done by the applicant, seek injunctive relief, recover costs exceeding the bond, and file liens. This applies to Primary Use (SEF using over 50% of the parcel and devoted to off-site power generation) and Secondary Use (SEF using less than 50% of the parcel and not the primary use) solar energy facilities. Direct Use SEFs (designed for on-site energy demand) are not mentioned in the decommissioning requirements. Other conditions include restoration plans, maintenance plans, and compliance with setbacks, height limits, and biological resource protections.

This glare restriction applies to all Solar Energy Facilities (SEFs), which include utility-scale systems as defined in the ordinance. The ordinance defines SEFs as "an energy facility, an area of land, or a structural rooftop principally used to convert solar energy to electricity." The ordinance also distinguishes uses as Direct Use (on-site energy), Primary Use (over 50% of parcel, primarily for off-site use), and Secondary Use (less than 50% of parcel). The glare restriction applies generally to all SEFs regardless of use type.

Ground mounted solar energy systems are limited to fifteen (15) feet in height. Height restrictions will be measured from natural grade below each module in the event the site has topographic changes. Roof mounted solar energy systems are limited to five (5) feet above roof surface not to exceed the roof ridge. Primary and Secondary Use SEFs, which include utility-scale systems, must conform to the height limits of Table 3. The ordinance explicitly states: 'Ground mounted solar energy systems are limited to fifteen (15) feet in height.'

summary: Section 5.38.C.28 'Abandonment and Decommissioning' requires that following the operational life of the project, or at the time the project becomes obsolete, uneconomic or an Abandoned Solar Energy System, the applicant shall perform decommissioning and removal of the Solar Farm Energy System and all its components. The applicant must prepare a decommissioning plan, agreement, and bond for submittal to the Township Board for review prior to issuance of the special land use permit. All structures and facilities, including below-grade structures, must be removed offsite for disposal with no concrete, piping, or other materials left in place. Any Solar Array or combination of Photovoltaic Devices that become an Abandoned Solar Energy System shall be removed under the decommissioning plan. The ground must be restored to its original condition within six months of becoming an Abandoned Solar Energy System or decommissioning, whichever occurs first. In lieu of decommissioning, the Applicant or Operator may apply for repowering by submitting an application and site plan compliant with this Section.

A Solar Farm Energy System "shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access." Such fencing "shall be at least eight feet in height as measured from the natural grade of the fencing perimeter and the fence must include fabric screening or be of a solid material to conceal the sight of improvements within the fence from outside the fence." "Electric fencing is not permitted."

Section 5.38.C.3.15 states: 'All solar panels shall be placed such that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways.' Additionally, Section 5.38.C.3.x requires 'A solar glare study such as a glint and glare assessment that is prepared by a professional engineering firm or other qualified third-party expert that analyzes whether glare will be directed by the Solar Farm Energy System onto any nearby properties or roadways.' These glare restrictions apply specifically to Solar Farm Energy Systems, defined as 'A utility-scale solar energy system where the primary use of the land is to generate electric energy or other energy ... typically the power output of that system is equal to or greater than 1 megawatt.' Other options mentioned include Small Solar Energy Systems, which have separate provisions but are not the focus here.

Maximum height of a Solar Array shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet measured from the natural grade at the base of the Solar Array to the top of the system when oriented at maximum tilt. Other collection devices, components or buildings of the Solar Farm Energy System shall not exceed thirty-five (35) feet, or the maximum building height permitted within the district in which that Solar Energy System is located, whichever is less, at any time or location on the property. The height shall be measured from the natural grade at the base of the Solar Array, device, component or building measured. The Township Board may waive or modify these height requirements.

The ordinance states: 'A Solar Farm Energy System shall be located on one or more parcels with an aggregate area of 5 acres or greater.' This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for Solar Farm Energy Systems, which are defined as utility-scale systems typically 1 megawatt or greater intended for sale, delivery, or consumption by more than one end user. The unit of measurement for this minimum lot size is acres.

summary: Section 5.38.C.28 states: "Following the operational life of the project, or at the time the project becomes obsolete, uneconomic or an Abandoned Solar Energy System, as determined by the Township Engineer or any other expert or specialist to be designated by the Township to make such a determination, the applicant shall perform decommissioning and removal of the Solar Farm Energy System and all its components." It further provides that "In lieu of decommissioning, the Applicant or Operator may apply for repowering by submitting an application and site plan compliant with this Section." This means repowering is explicitly recognized as an alternative to decommissioning and requires compliance with the application and site plan requirements for Solar Farm Energy Systems. Other options include decommissioning and removal of all structures and facilities, restoring the ground to its original condition within six months, and removal of any Abandoned Solar Energy System under the decommissioning plan.

Section 5.38.C.13 Screening: "The Solar Farm Energy System perimeter shall be screened and buffered by installed evergreen vegetative plantings whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Solar Farm Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels," with requirements including: "a continuous evergreen vegetative buffer shall be installed and maintained at all times at the perimeter of all Solar Farm Energy Systems" unless natural forest vegetation meets spacing and height requirements and has a similar obscuring effect; "The evergreen or native vegetative buffer shall be at least 25 feet in width and composed of native or evergreen trees that at planting shall be a minimum of four (4) feet in height and shrubs two (2) feet in height"; spacing requirements for trees and shrubs; replacement of unhealthy or dead material within six (6) months or three (3) months depending on the material; planting between March 15 and October 15 or provision of a financial guarantee; and that "Failure to maintain the evergreen vegetative buffer as required by this subpart shall constitute a violation of this Ordinance and is ground for revocation of any permit previously granted." Additionally, Section 5.38.C.12 Security requires "perimeter security fencing" at least eight feet in height with "fabric screening or be of a solid material to conceal the sight of improvements within the fence from outside the fence."

The ordinance explicitly requires for Solar Farm Energy Systems: a "written description of measures to support the flow of rainwater throughout the Solar Farm Energy System, including any measures to promote the growth of vegetation beneath the arrays and/or otherwise limit the impacts of storm water runoff as compared to before construction" subject to approval by the Ingham County Drain Commissioner; a "Ground cover vegetation establishment and management plan, including invasive plant species and noxious weed control"; a prohibition on clear-cutting with the requirement that "Ground cover vegetation shall be maintained for the duration of the Solar Farm Energy System"; and upon decommissioning or abandonment, "The ground must be restored to its original condition within six months (6) of becoming an Abandoned Solar Energy System, or decommissioning, whichever occurs first." These requirements apply to Solar Farm Energy Systems defined as "utility-scale solar energy system where the primary use of the land is to generate electric energy ... for the sale, delivery or consumption of the generated energy by more than one end user, and typically the power output of that system is equal to or greater than 1 megawatt."

Solar Farm Energy Systems are listed as a Special Land Use in the A-1 District, requiring a Special Land Use Permit and site plan approval. The text states: 'All Solar Farm Energy Systems require a Special Land Use Permit and site plan approval.' Additionally, Solar Farm Energy Systems 'shall be permitted by special use permit in the Light Industrial (LI) district.' Other solar systems, specifically Small Solar Energy Systems, are permitted by right in the RC and A-1 Districts, but these do not apply to larger or commercial Solar Farm Energy Systems.

summary: Section 5.38.C.3.xxi requires "a visual impact analysis prepared by a third-party qualified professional that analyzes the visual impacts of the proposed project, including a description of the project, the existing visual landscape, and important scenic resources, plus visual simulations that show what the project will look like (including proposed landscape and other screening measures) after construction." This applies to Solar Farm Energy Systems, defined as "a utility-scale solar energy system where the primary use of the land is to generate electric energy or other energy by converting sunlight... for the sale, delivery or consumption of the generated energy by more than one end user, and typically the power output of that system is equal to or greater than 1 megawatt." The ordinance also requires detailed site plans and supporting materials, including an Environmental Impact Study, Ground Cover Program, and a Solar Glare study, among others, as part of the special land use permit application process for Solar Farm Energy Systems.

Section 14.7(2)(f) requires a decommissioning plan detailing how the SES facility will be decommissioned following the operational life of the project, including removal of all structures, concrete, piping, facilities, and other project materials above and below grade to be removed offsite for disposal. The plan must include a fully inclusive estimate of the costs associated with decommissioning and removal of structures, prepared by a qualified engineer, subject to Planning Commission approval. Section 14.7(3)(c) states that if the facility becomes abandoned, dangerous, obsolete, or not in compliance, the applicant must decommission the facility, remove all components (above and below ground), properly dispose of them, and return the land to its original state within one year. The Planning Commission may require a performance guarantee to ensure project completion and removal costs, which shall not exceed 125% of the cost of removal and compliance and must remain in effect during the entire time the SES facility exists. These requirements apply specifically to utility-scale SES as regulated in Article 14.

Section 14.7(3)(h) states: "The granting of a special use permit may be conditioned upon the SES not resulting in excessive glare on neighboring properties. The applicant shall take and shall continue to take (including implementing new technologies developed after the permit is issued) all reasonable steps to eliminate or significantly reduce any glare from the SES imposed on neighboring properties." Utility-scale SES are defined as systems that "1. Is primarily used for generating electricity for sale and distribution to an authorized public utility; 2. The total surface area of all solar collector surfaces exceeds 1,500 square feet; and/or 3. Is not an accessory use or structure." Utility-scale SES may be permitted only as a special exception use in the Agricultural District and are subject to requirements in Section 14.7, Article 20 (Site Plan Review) and Article 27 (Special Exception Uses).

Section 14.7(1)(a) states: 'Minimum project area shall be twenty (20) acres.' This minimum area applies to utility-scale SES, which are defined as systems primarily used for generating electricity for sale, exceeding 1,500 square feet of solar collector surface, or not accessory uses. Multiple parcels may be assembled but must be contiguous. The unit 'acres' is explicitly used to describe the minimum lot size.

When the system is adjacent to a residentially-zoned or used parcel, side and rear yard screening may be required as a condition of granting a special use permit. Where feasible, ancillary solar equipment shall be located inside of a building or be screened from public view. All ancillary solar equipment such as, but not limited to, water tanks, supports, batteries, and plumbing shall be screened to the maximum extent possible without compromising the effectiveness of the solar collectors.

Section 14.7(1)(a) states: "One sign not exceeding thirty-two (32) square feet in area shall be allowed identifying the owner of the system. This provision shall not prohibit necessary warning signs, e.g. high voltage, etc, or any other signs required under these regulations." This signage requirement applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems, which are defined as systems that "1. Is primarily used for generating electricity for sale and distribution to an authorized public utility; 2. The total surface area of all solar collector surfaces exceeds 1,500 square feet; and/or 3. Is not an accessory use or structure."

Utility-scale Solar Energy System may be permitted only as a special exception use in the Agricultural District and is subject to the requirements in Section 14.7, Article 20 (Site Plan Review) and Article 27 (Special Exception Uses). Section 5.3 states: 'Utility-scale Solar Energy System as regulated in Article 14' is added as a special land use allowed in the AG-Agricultural District. Other solar energy systems such as personal-scale SES are allowed as accessory uses in various districts but are not relevant to utility-scale systems. The ordinance specifies detailed site requirements for utility-scale SES in Section 14.7, including minimum project area, setbacks, signage, and utility interconnection requirements.

Section 14.7(2)(e) requires that an application for a special use permit for a utility-scale SES "shall be accompanied by... Sketch elevation of the premises accurately depicting the proposed SES installation and its relationship to all structures within three hundred (300) feet." Additionally, the application must include "Location and height of all buildings, structures, security fencing, and other above ground structures associated with the SES" and "Where feasible, ancillary solar equipment shall be located inside of a building or be screened from public view." The ordinance defines utility-scale SES as a solar system that meets one or more of the following: "1. Is primarily used for generating electricity for sale and distribution to an authorized public utility; 2. The total surface area of all solar collector surfaces exceeds 1,500 square feet; and/or 3. Is not an accessory use or structure." The application requirements are in addition to the special use permit requirements in Section 27.1 and site plan review in Article 20. Other application requirements include lot lines and dimensions, lighting details, setbacks, access roads, security measures, maintenance programs, glare studies, manufacturer instructions, engineering certifications, and a decommissioning plan. The Planning Commission may also require environmental assessments or impact studies. These requirements explicitly establish visual impact assessment elements for utility-scale SES.

Section 89 requires that Large Solar Energy Systems "meet all the requirements of Section 88 Medium Solar Energy Systems" and that "Potential impact on neighboring properties in terms of glare, stormwater runoff, property values, aesthetics, and screening shall be considered by the Planning Commission in determining whether the use is appropriate on the subject property." Section 88(K) states: "Solar panels shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways. Traffic safety shall be protected, and adjacent properties shall be protected from unreasonable glare and radiation. The applicant shall submit documentation to verify compliance with this section. When deemed appropriate, the Planning Commission may require a report from a registered civil engineer or other professional the Planning Commission finds to be qualified to address this issue." Large Solar Energy Systems are defined as "a utility-scale solar energy conversion system ... occupying more than five (5) acres of land, and that will be used to produce utility power to off-site customers." Other system sizes include Small (up to 0.09 acres, primarily on-site use) and Medium (0.10 to 5 acres, producing utility power to on-site and off-site customers), with their own respective sections and conditions. Large systems are treated as a Special Land Use in AG, B-2, B-1, ROS, and OS districts, and as a Principal Permitted Use in IND districts, subject to these standards.

The ordinance sets a maximum height of 20 feet for Large Solar Energy Systems, defined as systems over 5 acres used to produce utility power to off-site customers. This is stated in Sections 87, 88, and 89, with the text: 'Large2 Over 5 acres 20 feet PPU in IND; SLU in AG, B-1, ROS, OS.' Section 89 clarifies that Large Solar Energy Systems shall meet all requirements of Section 88, including the 20 feet maximum height. The units are explicitly given as feet. Other system sizes have the same 20 feet maximum height: Small (0-0.09 acres) and Medium (0.10-5 acres).

Large Solar Energy System is defined as a utility-scale solar energy conversion system occupying more than five (5) acres of land, used to produce utility power to off-site customers (Section 114). The minimum lot size for Large Solar Energy Systems is explicitly stated as 'over 5 acres' in the definitions and reiterated in the tables under Sections 87, 88, and 89. Other system size categories include Small (0-0.09 acres) and Medium (0.10 – 5 acres). The units for the minimum lot size are acres.

Section 88.H states: 'Ground-mounted solar facilities shall meet the front, rear, and side yard setback requirements of the zone in which they are located, with the following exception: In all zones abutting a residential district (including AG) or residential use, the setbacks shall be at least fifty (50) feet from all property lines adjoining said district(s) or use.' Section 88.E also requires equipment (excluding solar collection panels) to be not closer than five (5) feet from any property line, and Section 88.F requires a rear yard setback of five (5) feet for ground-mounted solar collection panels. However, the 50 feet setback is the most restrictive fixed distance directly pertaining to setbacks from property lines for Large Solar Energy Systems. Section 89.B requires Large Solar Energy Systems to meet all requirements of Section 88.

When a ground mounted solar panel is located adjacent to a residential or agricultural district or public right-of-way, a twenty-six (26) foot wide (minimum) greenbelt shall be constructed so as to provide a buffer between the panels and the adjacent residential/agricultural or public property. Planning Commission may waive or reduce the greenbelt requirement upon a determination that the solar panel is located more than two hundred (200) feet from an adjacent property zoned residential or agricultural or from any public right-of-way. Planning Commission may waive or reduce the greenbelt requirement if the adjacent residential or agricultural property is likely to remain undeveloped, or existing natural features to remain provide adequate screening. Large solar energy systems shall meet all the requirements of Section 88 Medium Solar Energy Systems.

Section 89 requires Large Solar Energy Systems to meet all the requirements of Section 88. Section 88(J) states: 'Any mechanical equipment used as part of the solar system shall be screened from view from any public street, residential district, or agricultural district by use of a masonry screen wall, evergreen vegetation or other screening of a similar effectiveness and quality, as determined by the Planning Commission.' Section 88(P) requires: 'When a ground mounted solar panel is located adjacent to a residential or agricultural district (i.e., properties zoned AG, R-l, R-2, RT, or ROS) or public right-of-way, a twenty-six (26) foot wide (minimum) greenbelt shall be constructed so as to provide a buffer between the panels and the adjacent residential/agricultural or public property.' The greenbelt must be planted as part of an approved site plan and maintained in a healthy, growing condition. Specific planting requirements include: a planting strip no less than twenty-six (26) feet in width; plant materials not closer than four (4) feet from the property line; a minimum of one (1) evergreen tree planted at twenty (20) foot intervals; and a minimum of three (3) intermediate shrubs placed between the spaced evergreen trees. The Planning Commission may waive or reduce the greenbelt requirement under certain conditions. Other system size categories include Small Solar Energy Systems (0-0.09 acres, subject to Section 87) and Medium Solar Energy Systems (0.10-5 acres, subject to Section 88), each with their own standards and screening requirements. Large Solar Energy Systems are defined as systems occupying more than five (5) acres and used to produce utility power to off-site customers.

Section 89 states that Large solar energy systems "shall meet all the requirements of Section 88 Medium Solar Energy Systems," which includes that "The application shall include a drainage plan prepared by a registered civil engineer showing how stormwater runoff will be managed and demonstrating that runoff from the site will not exceed the agricultural runoff rate or otherwise cause undue flooding." It also requires "stormwater quality protection measures" and "Any necessary permits from outside agencies for off-site discharge shall be provided." Section 88 applies to Medium solar energy systems and includes other conditions such as setbacks, height limits, screening, and greenbelt requirements. The system size categories are: Small (0-0.09 acres), Medium (0.10 – 5 acres), and Large (Over 5 acres). Large systems are a principal permitted use in IND districts and a special land use in AG, B-1, ROS, and OS districts. Systems up to 4,000 square feet require a sketch plan and building permit; systems over 4,000 square feet require site plan approval by the Planning Commission.

Section 88(H) states: 'In all zones abutting a residential district (including AG) or residential use, the setbacks shall be at least fifty (50) feet from all property lines adjoining said district(s) or use.' Additionally, Section 88(P) requires a twenty-six (26) foot wide (minimum) greenbelt buffer between ground-mounted solar panels and adjacent residential or agricultural districts or public right-of-way, which may be waived or reduced under certain conditions. Large Solar Energy Systems are treated as a Special Land Use in AG, B-2, B-1, ROS, and OS Districts and as a Principal Permitted Use in IND Districts, subject to these setback and screening standards.

summary: The ordinance states: 'No more than 20% of the total lot area may be covered by a Commercial Solar Energy System.' This applies specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems as defined in the text (ground mounted, located in Commercial/Industrial districts, requiring special use permits). Other solar energy system types, such as Ground Mounted Private Solar Energy Systems, also have a 20% maximum lot area coverage, but this response focuses only on Commercial Solar Energy Systems. The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the total lot area, not as a specific area value.

Section C.14 states: 'If a Commercial Solar Energy System is abandoned or otherwise nonoperational for a period of one (1) year, the property owner or the operator must notify the Township and must remove the system within six (6) months after the date of abandonment. Removal requires receipt of a demolition permit from the Building Official and full restoration of the site to the satisfaction of the Zoning Administrator. The site must be filled and covered with topsoil and restored to a state compatible with the surrounding vegetation.' Section C.15 requires: 'Financial security in the form of a security bond, escrow payment, or irrevocable letter of credit in an amount equal to 125% of the total estimated cost of decommissioning, code enforcement, and reclamation, which cost estimate must be approved by the Township.' These requirements apply specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are 'allowed in Commercial and Industrial zoning districts and require a special land use permit and site plan review.' Other solar energy system types such as Private Solar Energy Systems have separate provisions, including removal within three months after abandonment for roof or ground mounted private systems, but these do not apply to Commercial Solar Energy Systems. Additionally, Section D outlines provisions for Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more under PA 233, but these do not negate the decommissioning requirements stated in Section C.

Section 3.41.C.8 requires "Security fencing must be installed around all electrical equipment related to the Commercial Solar Energy System, including any transformers and transfer stations." Appropriate warning signs and emergency numbers must be posted. Section 3.41.C.5 states that "In lieu of a planting greenbelt, a decorative fence that meets the requirements of this ordinance to fences may be used if approved by the Planning Commission." Additionally, subsection D.b requires that for Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more, "Fencing for the Solar Energy Systems must comply with the latest version of the National Electric Code as November 29, 2024, or as subsequently amended." These fencing requirements apply specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance. Other options include greenbelt screening consisting of shrubbery, trees, or other non-invasive plant species to obscure the system from adjacent residences, with at least 50% evergreen trees at least six feet tall at planting.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems must not produce any glare that is visible to neighboring lots or to persons traveling on public or private roads. Additionally, no glare should interfere with aircraft and or any air trafficking opportunities. (Section 3.41.C.6 and 3.41.C.7) Other related requirements include greenbelt screening to obscure the system from adjacent residences, lighting limited to the minimum necessary for safe operation with illumination not extending beyond the lot perimeter, and setbacks and height restrictions. These glare restrictions apply specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems allowed in Commercial and Industrial zoning districts and requiring a special land use permit and site plan review.

The height of the Commercial Solar Energy System and any mounts, buildings, accessory structures, and related equipment must not exceed fifteen (15) feet when oriented at maximum tilt. Lightning rods may exceed fifteen (15) feet in height, but they must be limited to the height necessary to protect the Commercial Solar Energy System from lightning. For Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more under PA 233, solar panel components must not exceed a maximum height of 25 feet above ground when the arrays are at full tilt.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems must be located on parcels of land five (5) acres in size or larger. This is explicitly stated in Section C.2.b: 'Commercial Solar Energy Systems must be located on parcels of land five (5) acres in size or larger.' The units are acres, a standard measure of land area. No other minimum lot size values for Commercial Solar Energy Systems are provided in the text.

The noise generated by a Commercial Solar Energy System must not exceed the following limits: Forty (40) Dba L MAX, as measured at the property line of any neighboring residence or business. The Township may, in its sole discretion, allow a higher noise level only if the owner of the neighboring residence or business signs a waiver consenting to a specific higher noise level and the waiver is recorded with the County Register of Deeds. Additionally, for Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more under PA 233, the noise must not exceed 55 average hourly decibels as modeled at the nearest outer wall of the nearest dwelling located on an adjacent nonparticipating property. Decibel modeling shall use the A-weighted scale as designed by the American National Standards Institute.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems (including all solar panels, structures, and equipment) must be set back 50 feet from all lot lines and public road rights-of-way, 100 feet from residential lot lines. Township, at their sole discretion, may allow a lesser set-back only if approved by neighboring property owner and recorded with the county. Under PA 233 for Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more, setbacks must be measured from the nearest edge of the perimeter fencing of the facility, with a 50 feet setback from the nearest shared property line.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems (including all solar panels, structures, and equipment) must be set back 50 feet from all lot lines and public road rights-of-way, 100 feet from residential lot lines. Township, at their sole discretion, may allow a lesser set-back only if approved by neighboring property owner and recorded with the county. Under PA 233 for systems 50 MW or larger, the setback from public road right-of-way is also 50 feet measured from the nearest edge of the public road right-of-way.

Section 3.41, C.5 requires "Greenbelt screening is required around any Commercial Solar Energy System and around any equipment associated with the system to obscure, to the greatest extent possible, the Solar Energy System from any adjacent residences." The greenbelt "must consist of shrubbery, trees, or other non-invasive plant species that provide a visual screen." At least 50% of the plants must be "evergreen trees that are at least six feet tall at the time of planting." In lieu of a planting greenbelt, "a decorative fence that meets the requirements of this ordinance to fences may be used if approved by the Planning Commission."

Section 3.41, Commercial Solar Energy Systems, subsection C, item 8 requires that "appropriate warning signs must be posted at safe intervals at the entrance and around the perimeter of the Commercial Solar Energy System. Emergency numbers must be posted on site with an address." Other requirements for Commercial Solar Energy Systems include special land use permit and site plan review, ground mounted systems only, minimum parcel size of five acres, setbacks, height limits, greenbelt screening, lighting restrictions, noise limits, underground transmission lines, decommissioning plans, financial security, and annual reporting. Private Solar Energy Systems have different requirements and do not have explicit signage mandates in this text.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems require "Proof of environmental compliance, including compliance with ... Part 91, Soil Erosion and Sedimentation Control (MCL 324.9101 et. seq.) and any corresponding County ordinances." Additionally, applicants must provide "a written plan for maintaining the subject property, including a plan for maintaining and inspecting drain tiles and addressing stormwater management, which is subject to the Township’s review and approval." These requirements apply specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are "allowed in Commercial and Industrial zoning districts and require a special land use permit and site plan review." Other types of solar energy systems include Private Solar Energy Systems (such as Private BIVPs, Roof or Building Mounted Private Solar Energy Systems, and Ground Mounted Private Solar Energy Systems), which have different permit and location requirements but do not explicitly mention soil, erosion, or sediment control requirements.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems (Ground Mounted only) are permitted in Commercial and Industrial zoning districts and require a special land use permit and site plan review. The text states: 'Commercial Solar Energy System - All Commercial Solar Energy Systems (Ground Mounted only) - Commercial/Industrial - Required [special use permit].' Additionally, ground-mounted private solar energy systems require a special land use permit in Agricultural-Residential (A-R), Rural-Residential (R-R), Commercial, and Industrial districts, but these are not classified as utility-scale systems. Other options include Private Solar Energy Systems (BIVPs and Roof or Building Mounted) permitted in all districts without special use permits, and Ground Mounted Private Solar Energy Systems requiring special use permits in A-R, R-R, Commercial, and Industrial districts.

Under PA 233 provisions for Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more, the setback from occupied community buildings and dwellings on nonparticipating properties is 300 feet from the nearest point on the outer wall. Additionally, for Commercial Solar Energy Systems generally, the ordinance requires a 100-foot setback from residential lot lines, with the Township able to allow a lesser setback if approved by the neighboring property owner and recorded with the county. The 300 feet setback is the most restrictive value directly pertaining to setbacks from occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, and/or residences.
