summary: Section E. Decommissioning/Abandonment states: 'A SES shall be deemed abandoned if it is out of service for a continuous 12-month period.' A 'Notice of Abandonment' will be issued to the owner advising removal at the owner's expense within three months. Removal requires a demolition permit and includes 'removal of panels, non-utility owned equipment, conduit, structures, and foundations.' Upon removal of a ground array SES, 'the site shall be cleaned and restored to blend with the existing surrounding vegetation at the time of abandonment.' Failure to remove within three months may result in the Township Board designating a contractor to complete decommissioning with expenses charged to the violator and becoming a lien against the premises. These requirements apply to ground-mounted solar energy arrays and/or farms, which are permitted as special land use in certain zoning districts and must comply with height and setback restrictions as described in Section C.

Ground-mounted solar energy arrays and/or farms shall not exceed sixteen (16) feet in height, measured from the ground at the base of such equipment. This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems such as ground-mounted arrays and farms. Other provisions mention building-mounted solar collectors with height limits tied to building walls, but these apply to smaller or non-commercial systems. The 16 feet limit is the explicit maximum height restriction for utility-scale systems.

Ground-mounted solar energy arrays and/or farms shall be a permitted only as a special land use, upon approval by the Planning Commission, and only in the AG, FR-1, LDR, GC and IND zoning districts, in accordance with the provisions of this section. Zoning approval is required prior to application for a building permit. Building-mounted solar energy collectors shall be permitted in all zoning districts. Solar panels shall be permitted as a rooftop installation in any zoning district.

The ordinance requires a decommissioning and final reclamation plan for Solar Farms, including: 'The anticipated life of the project'; 'The anticipated present value cost of decommissioning which does not credit the value of any salvage materials or re-sale credits... prepared by a professional third-party engineer'; 'An updated anticipated cost of decommissioning every 3 years'; 'An explanation of the calculation of the cost of decommissioning and recycling'; 'The physical plan of decommissioning'; and 'An updated list of decommissioning contractors and recycling centers... All material removed, including panels, are to be recycled.' It also requires 'evidence of an agreement with the underlying property owner that ensures proper removal of all equipment and restoration of the site within six (6) months of decommissioning or abandonment of the project.' Financial security guaranteeing removal must be posted with the Township before permits are issued, in the form of '1) a cash bond; or 2) an irrevocable bank letter of credit or a performance bond, in form approved by the Township.' The amount must be 'no less than the estimated cost of removal' and may include inflation adjustments. The Township may pursue legal action to remove abandoned or defective projects and recover costs, including attorney fees, within thirty (30) days of the defect. These requirements apply specifically to Solar Farms as defined: 'a solar array compound of multiple solar panels on ground-mounted rack or poles... for the primary purpose of the wholesale sales of generated electricity.'

The ordinance requires that "a security fence eight (8) feet in height and material to be proposed reviewed/approved through the special land use permit process shall be placed around the perimeter of the solar farm and electrical equipment." It further specifies that "areas that host visible Solar Farm improvements (e.g., ground mounted solar panels) shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access," with fencing "eight (8) feet in height as measured from the natural grade of the fencing perimeter." The required fencing "cannot utilize barbed or razor wire" and "must be in between the required Solar Farm landscaping and Solar Farm improvements."
Solar farm facilities shall be located or placed so that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed toward or onto nearby properties or roadways at any time of the day.

All photovoltaic panels and support structures located in a solar farm shall be restricted to a maximum height of fourteen (14) feet when oriented at a maximum tilt. This applies specifically to Solar Farms, which are defined as solar arrays primarily for wholesale sales of generated electricity. The unit of measurement for this height restriction is feet.

The ordinance states: 'Maximum lot coverage to be either 25% of solar array of the parcel area or 100 acres, whichever is less.' This means the maximum lot size allowed for Solar Farms is limited to 100 acres or 25% of the parcel area, whichever is smaller. The unit for the maximum lot size is acres.

No solar farm facilities shall exceed forty (40) dBA Lmax as measured at the property line. Noise levels to be verified by a third-party testing company within 60 days from the completion of the project. The findings are to be posted with the Township within thirty (30) days of end of testing.

All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with such facilities (including perimeter fencing) shall be setback a minimum of three hundred fifty (350) feet from a side property line, one hundred fifty (150) feet from the rear and front property lines, and a minimum of one hundred (100) feet from any road right-of-way to fence line. The most restrictive setback from property lines is 350 feet from side property lines.

All facilities shall also be setback at least one hundred fifty (150) feet from any wetland, stream, river, or established County drain right-of-way or easement. Additionally, all setback areas adjoining County drains, streams, rivers and wetlands shall be seeded to grasses and pollinator plantings that deter runoff. This riparian buffer zone, or filter strip shall be designed to adhere to FAS/CREP guidelines.

All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with such facilities (including perimeter fencing) shall be setback a minimum of ... a minimum of one hundred (100) feet from any road right-of-way to fence line. Other setbacks include 350 feet from side property lines, 150 feet from rear and front property lines, and 350 feet from any structural building, but these do not pertain to roads.

The ordinance requires that "The perimeter of all visible Solar Farm improvements shall be screened and buffered by required installed evergreen or native vegetative plantings located outside of the required fencing whenever existing natural forest vegetation or berming does not otherwise continuously obscure Solar Farm improvements from adjacent parcels." It further specifies: "a continuous evergreen or native vegetative buffer shall be installed and maintained at all times at the perimeter of all Solar Farm improvements, including without limitation, between such Solar Farms and adjacent residential or agricultural areas and/or public highways." The evergreen buffer must be "composed of spruce or conifer trees that at planting shall be a minimum of six (6) feet in height," planted in "two staggered rows, spaced no more than fifteen (15) feet apart on center." Dead or unhealthy material must be replaced within six months. The buffer must be "25 feet in width." The Township may waive landscaping requirements if an applicant proposes "an adequate alternative method to screen the Solar Farm from adjacent properties and roadways or if a particular area of a Solar Farm does not require screening due to, among other things, no reasonable impacts from glare." Additionally, "All setback areas adjoining County drains, streams, rivers and wetlands shall be seeded to grasses and pollinator plantings that deter runoff."

The ordinance requires the applicant to submit "a site grading, erosion control and storm water drainage plan" as part of the site plan for each Solar Energy Facility, which "will be reviewed by the Township’s engineering firm at the applicant's cost." Additionally, "All setback areas adjoining County drains, streams, rivers and wetlands shall be seeded to grasses and pollinator plantings that deter runoff. This riparian buffer zone, or filter strip shall be designed to adhere to FAS/CREP guidelines." These requirements apply to Solar Farms defined as "a solar array compound of multiple solar panels on ground-mounted rack or poles which is not directly connected to or designed to serve the energy needs of the primary use, but rather for the primary purpose of the wholesale sales of generated electricity."

"Solar Farms: Permitted by Special use permit and meet requirements of this ordinance." The text indicates that solar farms (utility-scale solar energy systems) require a special use permit and must meet ordinance requirements, but does not specify any particular district names or abbreviations where this applies.

All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with such facilities (including perimeter fencing) shall be setback a minimum of three hundred fifty (350) feet from any structural building. Additionally, project design and layout will ensure any structures or other improved areas located within the fenced/improved area shall be located a minimum of one hundred (100) feet from any residential structure, church, school, family or group child day-care home, and bed and breakfast establishments. The 350 feet setback from structural buildings is the most restrictive setback directly pertaining to occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, and/or residences.

The ordinance requires that for Solar Farms, the applicant must "Graphically demonstrate the visual impact of the project using photos or renditions of the project with consideration given to setbacks and proposed landscaping." Solar Farms are defined as "a solar array compound of multiple solar panels on ground-mounted rack or poles which is not directly connected to or designed to serve the energy needs of the primary use, but rather for the primary purpose of the wholesale sales of generated electricity." This visual impact assessment is part of the "Additional Special Use Criteria" that must be addressed in the application for solar farm facilities. Other criteria include project description, traffic analysis, environmental analysis, waste, lighting, transportation plan, public safety, sound limitations, telecommunications interference, life of the project and final reclamation, insurance, emergency services, fee, complaint resolution, continuing compliance and enforcement escrow deposit, required fencing, concrete foundations, inspections, transferability, and remedies.

All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with such facilities (including perimeter fencing) shall be setback ... a minimum of one hundred fifty (150) feet from any wetland, stream, river, or established County drain right-of-way or easement. Additionally, all setback areas adjoining County drains, streams, rivers and wetlands shall be seeded to grasses and pollinator plantings that deter runoff. This riparian buffer zone, or filter strip shall be designed to adhere to FAS/CREP guidelines. Other setback distances mentioned in the ordinance pertain to property lines, structures, and roads, but these do not apply to lakes, reservoirs, streams, rivers, or wetlands.

The ordinance requires a "decommissioning and final reclamation plan after the anticipated useful life or abandonment/termination of the project," including "proper removal of all equipment and restoration of the site within six (6) months of decommissioning or abandonment of the project." It mandates that applicants "include a description of the financial security guaranteeing removal of the system which must be posted with the Township within fifteen (15) days after approval or before a building or construction permit is issued for the project." The financial security options are: "1) a cash bond; or 2) an irrevocable bank letter of credit or a performance bond, in a form approved by the Township." The amount must be "no less than the estimated cost of removal and may include a provision for inflationary cost adjustments," with the estimate prepared by the applicant's engineer and subject to Township approval. If the owner fails to remove or repair any defective, abandoned or terminated project, "the Township... may pursue legal action to abate the violation by seeking to remove the project and recover any and all costs, including attorney fees." These requirements apply to solar farms defined as "a solar array composed of multiple solar panels on ground-mounted rack or poles which is not directly connected to or designed to serve the energy needs of the primary use, but rather for the primary purpose of the wholesale sales of generated electricity."

A security fence (height and material to be proposed and reviewed/approved through the special land use permit process) shall be placed around the perimeter of the solar farm and electrical equipment. Knox boxes and keys shall be provided at locked entrances for emergency personnel access.

The ordinance defines Solar Farms as solar arrays composed of multiple solar panels on ground-mounted racks or poles which are not directly connected to or designed to serve the energy needs of the primary use, but rather for the primary purpose of the wholesale sales of generated electricity. It explicitly states: 'Solar farm facilities shall be located or placed so that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed toward or onto nearby properties or roadways at any time of the day.' This glare restriction applies to utility-scale solar energy systems (solar farms). Other relevant conditions include height restrictions (maximum height of sixteen (16) feet), setbacks, noise limits, landscaping, and special use permit requirements. The ordinance also includes detailed site plan and special use criteria for solar farms.

All photovoltaic panels and support structures located in a solar farm shall be restricted to a maximum height of sixteen (16) feet when oriented at a maximum tilt. This applies to solar farms defined as solar arrays composed of multiple solar panels on ground-mounted racks or poles intended for wholesale sales of generated electricity. The text also mentions light poles restricted to a maximum height of eighteen (18) feet, but this is not the primary structure height restriction for the solar panels themselves.

The ordinance states: 'Maximum Lot Size: Maximum lot size for a solar farm is 100 acres.' This applies to solar farms defined as solar arrays primarily for wholesale sales of electricity, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. No other maximum lot size values are provided for utility-scale systems.

The ordinance states: 'No solar farm facilities shall exceed sixty (60) dBA as measured at the property line.' This applies explicitly to solar farms defined as solar arrays for the primary purpose of wholesale sales of generated electricity, i.e., utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit 'dBA' refers to A-weighted decibels, a standard noise measurement unit.

Solar Farms are permitted by Special Use Permit in A-1 Agricultural District, B Commercial, and M Manufacturing districts and must meet the requirements of the ordinance amendment. No other districts are explicitly mentioned as permitting Solar Farms, implying that Solar Farms are not allowed or are prohibited in all other districts. The text does not explicitly name or list those other districts where Solar Farms are prohibited.

All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with such facilities (excluding perimeter fencing) shall be setback a minimum of seventy-five (75) feet from a side or rear property line and a minimum of fifty (50) feet from any road right-of-way. The setback from property lines is the more restrictive value applicable to utility-scale solar farms.

All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with such facilities (excluding perimeter fencing) shall be setback a minimum of fifty (50) feet from any road right-of-way. Other setbacks include seventy-five (75) feet from side or rear property lines and setbacks related to County drain right-of-way or easements, but these do not apply to roads.

The special land use application for a solar farm shall include a proposed landscaping and screening/buffering plan prepared by a licensed landscape architect. This plan will be reviewed through the special land use approval process to assure that the proposed facility is appropriately landscaped in relation to adjacent land uses and road rights-of-way. The use of berms and evergreen plantings along property lines adjacent to residential land uses is strongly encouraged. Trees shall be a minimum of four (4) feet tall at time of planting and shall remain in good condition for the life of the solar farm.

No portion of the Solar Energy Facility shall contain or be used to display advertising. The manufacturers’ name and equipment information or dedication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of the solar energy system provided they comply with the prevailing sign regulation.

The ordinance requires that the applicant submit a site plan including 'a site grading, erosion control and storm water drainage plan' for each Solar Energy Facility. This plan 'will be reviewed by the Township's engineering firm at the applicant's cost.' The ordinance applies to Solar Farms defined as 'a solar array composed of multiple solar panels on ground-mounted rack or poles which is not directly connected to or designed to serve the energy needs of the primary use, but rather for the primary purpose of the wholesale sales of generated electricity.' Additional requirements include compliance with local, state, and federal permits, and other special use criteria such as project description, environmental analysis, and decommissioning plans.

Section 1912 Utility-Scale Solar Energy Collectors and Systems explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements. It requires "A decommissioning plan shall be submitted as part of the special use application, detailing the removal of all equipment, structures, and foundations, and the restoration of the site to its pre-development condition." If the system is "inoperable or abandoned for a period of twelve (12) consecutive months," the owner must "remove the system, including all supporting equipment and structures, within ninety (90) days of notice from the Township." The Township "may require a performance guarantee to ensure the proper decommissioning and removal of the system." The plan must include: "Defined conditions upon which decommission will be initiated (e.g., end of land lease, no power production for twelve [12] months, abandonment, etc.), removal of utility-owned equipment and non-utility-owned equipment, restoration of property condition which existed prior to the development of the system, specification of the timeframe from completion of decommissioning activities, description of any agreement (i.e., lease) with landowner regarding decommissioning, identity of the entity or individual responsible for decommissioning, plans for updating the decommissioning plan, and a performance guarantee posted in the form of a bond or other form acceptable to the Township." These requirements apply specifically to utility-scale solar energy collectors and systems as defined: "A solar energy collector that is the principal use on a lot and is designed to primarily serve off-site uses." Other sections, such as Section 346, address small scale solar energy collectors and systems and include removal requirements for those systems if abandoned or inoperable for twelve months, but these apply only to small scale systems and not utility-scale systems.

summary: Large Solar Energy Systems are defined as systems "where the principal design, purpose or use of such system is to provide energy to off-site uses or the wholesale or retail sale of generated electricity to any person or entity." Decommissioning requirements include: removal of the system within six (6) months if abandoned (not in operation for one (1) year), with notification to the Township, obtaining a demolition permit, and site restoration to the satisfaction of the Zoning Administrator. The Township may pursue legal action to remove the system and recover costs if the owner fails to comply. Other options and conditions include: Small Solar Energy Systems (used exclusively for private purposes and not for commercial resale except surplus energy sales) are permitted by right in all districts and have separate removal requirements if abandoned, including removal within six (6) months and notification to the Township. Building permits and operation permits with renewals every five years are required for all system types.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Large Solar Energy Systems, defined as utility-scale systems with power output equal to or greater than 25 kW for sale, delivery, or consumption by more than one end user. Section 16.52(A)(1)(p) requires the applicant to prepare a decommissioning plan, agreement, and bond for submittal to the Planning Commission and Township Board prior to issuance of the special use permit. "Following the operational life of the project, or at the time the project becomes obsolete, uneconomic or an Abandoned Solar Energy System... the applicant shall perform decommissioning and removal of the Large Solar Energy System and all its components." All structures and facilities, including below-grade, must be removed offsite with no concrete, piping, or other materials left in place. The ground must be restored to its original condition within 170 days of becoming abandoned or decommissioned. Additionally, Section 16.52(A)(1)(cc) requires "non revocable security in the form of a cash deposit, letter of credit, or surety bond acceptable to the Township... to ensure full compliance with this section, including, but not limited to, decommissioning and restoration requirements." This security must equal 110 percent of the estimated cost of decommissioning and restoration, adjusted annually. The ordinance also includes continuing escrow deposits for enforcement costs. Small Solar Energy Systems have separate, less detailed removal requirements applying only to abandoned systems, which must be removed by the property owner within six months. The decommissioning requirements and financial securities apply specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems as defined.

A Large Solar Energy System "shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access." The site plan for Large Solar Energy Systems must include "Location and height of all proposed Solar Array(s), buildings, structures, electrical tie lines and transmission lines, security fencing, and all above-ground structures and utilities associated with the Large Solar Energy System." The ordinance also requires a "continuous evergreen vegetative buffer" at the perimeter unless natural forest vegetation provides similar screening. The fencing and buffer requirements apply specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems, defined as utility-scale systems with power output equal to or greater than 25 kW intended for sale, delivery, or consumption by more than one end user. Small Solar Energy Systems have separate fencing and screening requirements, but these do not apply to Large Solar Energy Systems.

Section 16.52(A)(n) states: 'All solar panels shall be placed such that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways.' This applies to Large Solar Energy Systems defined as 'A utility-scale solar energy system where the primary use of the land is to generate electric energy or other energy ... for the sale, delivery or consumption of the generated energy by more than one end user, and the power output of that system is equal to or greater than 25 kW.' Other relevant conditions for Large Solar Energy Systems include requirements for special use permits, site plan review, setbacks, height limits, screening, security fencing, noise emissions, lighting, abandonment and decommissioning, and continuing security and escrow deposits. Small Solar Energy Systems, defined as those primarily for personal consumption with generating capacity less than 25 kW, have separate accessory structure requirements and also must ensure that 'concentrated solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways.'

The ordinance states: 'Maximum height of a Solar Array shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet. The ordinance requires that a Large Solar Energy System "shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access." summary: Solar powered electricity generating sources and solar farms are special approval uses in a solar energy facility overlay zoning district (Section 15.18.04). All Solar Energy Facilities shall be considered any special use in a Solar Energy Overlay Zoning District, subject to the restrictions contained in the Ordinance (Section 15.18.07). The Planning Commission reviews all Solar Energy Facility land use applications in the Solar Energy overlay zoning district (Section 15.18.05). It is unlawful to operate or establish a Solar Energy Facility without site plan approval by the Delaware Township Planning Commission (Section 15.18.06). The Solar Energy Overlay Zoning District is defined by parcels identified in the Solar Overlay District map (Section 15.18.20). No other districts or abbreviations are mentioned for special use or similar permitting of utility-scale solar energy systems.

summary: The ordinance requires that all improved areas of utility-scale Solar Energy Facilities "shall maintain a 25 ft. set back from residential areas and adjacent properties." Additionally, for improved areas located in residential areas, there must be a minimum landscape buffer within 25 ft. The buffer shall contain evergreen trees or bushes planted no more than 8 ft. apart and at least 4 ft. tall at the time of planting, reaching a height of 10 ft. The setback is a fixed distance and applies to facilities that sell electricity offsite and are not small-scale systems.

Section 5.44, subsection (w) 'Abandonment and Decommissioning' requires that following the operational life of the project, the applicant or their successor shall perform decommissioning and removal of the solar energy system and all its components. Any system not operated for twelve (12) months or considered no longer useful shall be deemed abandoned and removed under the Decommissioning Plan. The Plan must be submitted for review and approval prior to permit issuance and include: removal of all structures and materials above and below grade; environmental verification by an independent company; restoration of original topography; drain tile repair; naming the responsible party; possible exemptions for certain items with Township permission; and completion of all work within three hundred sixty-five (365) days of abandonment or decommissioning. Additionally, subsection (v) 'Performance Guarantee' mandates posting a bond or cash escrow to ensure removal upon abandonment, covering reclamation and code enforcement costs, reviewed every three years, and maintained for the life of the project. Failure to maintain the guarantee may result in revocation of the special approval, cessation of operation, and removal orders. These requirements apply specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as a Special Approval Use in the Industrial zoning district only.

A Commercial Solar Energy System "shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access." The fencing "shall be secured to the ground to prevent underground access, as well as, six (6) feet in height consisting of galvanized mesh wire with wood posts (also known as deer fence or agricultural fence or some other fencing type as approved by the Planning Commission during the site plan review process)." "Electric fencing is not permitted." Failure to install or continuously maintain the required perimeter fencing "shall constitute a violation of this Ordinance and any Special Approval Use permit may be subject to revocation."

Section 5.44, subsection 4, paragraph q states: "Solar panels shall be placed such that solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways. Traffic safety shall be protected and adjacent properties shall be protected from unreasonable glare. The applicant shall submit documentation to verify compliance with this section. When deemed appropriate, the Planning Commission may require a report from a registered civil engineer or other professional the Planning Commission finds to be qualified to address this issue." This applies specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as a Special Approval Use in the Industrial zoning district only. Other types of solar energy collectors mentioned include building-mounted and ground-mounted systems with various size and use thresholds, but glare restrictions are explicitly stated only for Commercial Solar Energy Systems.

Section 5.44, subsection 4(f) states: 'Maximum height of a Solar Array, other collection device, components or buildings of the Commercial Solar Energy System, excluding substation and electrical transmission equipment, shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet at maximum tilt (as measured from the natural grade at the base of improvements) at any time or location on the property.' Substation and electrical transmission equipment have a separate maximum height of one hundred (100) feet. This 15 feet limit applies specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as special approval uses in the Industrial zoning district. Other height limits mentioned in the ordinance apply only to smaller or accessory solar energy collectors and are not relevant to Commercial Solar Energy Systems.

A Commercial Solar Energy System shall be located on one (1) or more parcels with an aggregate area of ten (10) acres or greater. This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for commercial solar projects. Other related provisions include: 'Large Accessory Use Solar Energy Collectors' up to 2 MW and occupying ten (10) acres or less, but these are accessory uses primarily for on-site needs and not commercial systems. The minimum lot size for commercial systems is thus 10 acres or greater.

No component of any Commercial Solar Energy System shall emit noise exceeding fifty (50) Dba Lmax as measured at the exterior property boundary or the existing ROW line. A sound barrier of a solid masonry wall or evergreen tree berm shall be constructed surrounding all inverters, no more than 20 feet from the inverter and no less than the height of the inverter.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems shall be a Special Approval Use in the Industrial zoning district only. This implies that Commercial Solar Energy Systems are unconditionally prohibited in all other zoning districts. Other solar energy systems include: Building-mounted solar energy collectors permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts; Small Accessory Use Energy Collectors (up to 100 KW) permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts; Large Accessory Use Solar Energy Collectors (up to 2 MW, 10 acres or less) permitted with special approval in agriculture, commercial, and industrial districts only.

Setbacks for Commercial Solar Energy Systems are listed in the table below. The Planning Commission may, if deemed in the interest of the health, safety, and welfare, require additional setbacks as part of a Special Approval Use approval. Front Setback 200 feet; Side Setback 100 feet; Rear Setback 100 feet; From Residential Districts or Sites Containing Residential Uses 300 feet; Setback from Residential structures 400 feet; Distance from Non-Residential structures 100 feet.

Section 5.44(m) Landscaping requires that "The perimeter of Commercial Solar Energy Systems shall also be screened and buffered by installed evergreen or native vegetative plantings whenever existing natural vegetation does not otherwise reasonably obscure the Commercial Solar Energy System," with specifications including "at least 20 feet wide," "native or evergreen trees that at planting shall be a minimum of four (4) feet in height and shrubs two (2) feet in height," and spacing requirements. It also mandates maintenance and replacement of unhealthy or dead material. Section 5.44(l) Screening/Security requires that "A Commercial Solar Energy System shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access," specifying fencing type, height, and installation requirements. These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Energy Systems defined as a Special Approval Use in the Industrial zoning district. Other options for smaller or accessory solar energy collectors are subject to different provisions and do not include these vegetative buffer or screening mandates.

Section 5.44(o) states: "No advertising or non-project related graphics shall be on any part of the solar arrays or other components of the Commercial Solar Energy System. This exclusion does not apply to entrance gate signage or notifications containing points of contact or any and all other information or warnings that may be required by Township or authorities having jurisdiction for electrical operations and the safety and welfare of the public." This is the explicit signage requirement for Commercial Solar Energy Systems. Other options or conditions for signage are not provided beyond this allowance for entrance gate signage and required safety notifications.

The ordinance requires for Commercial Solar Energy Systems: "detailed map of all surface water drainage ways" (4.b.5); "a comprehensive plan on how disruption to all drainage systems (surface and subsurface) will be avoided, minimized, or mitigated" (4.b.12); "Drain tiles on the site shall be protected during the life of the project and are subject to professional review" with repair requirements if non-functioning (4.t); "The property must be restored to its original topography" and drain tile must be in working order during decommissioning (4.w); and "Ground cover vegetation shall be installed and maintained for the duration of the operation until the site is decommissioned" with a required "Ground Cover Vegetation Establishment and Management Plan" including control of invasive species and fire prevention (4.n). Other options in the ordinance include Small Accessory Use Energy Collectors (up to 100 KW, primarily on-site use) and Large Accessory Use Solar Energy Collectors (up to 2 MW, 10 acres or less, primarily on-site use) with separate requirements, but these do not apply to Commercial Solar Energy Systems which are defined as Special Approval Use in the Industrial zoning district only.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems shall be a Special Approval Use in the Industrial zoning district only. The following requirements shall apply to all Commercial Solar Energy Systems: Height shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet at maximum tilt; lot size must be ten (10) acres or greater; setbacks include 200 feet front, 100 feet side and rear, 300 feet from residential districts or sites containing residential uses, 400 feet from residential structures, 100 feet from non-residential structures, and 80 feet from drain ditches. Other options include Small Accessory Use Energy Collectors (up to 100 KW) permitted as accessory use in all zoning districts, and Large Accessory Use Solar Energy Collectors (up to 2 MW and 10 acres or less) permitted as accessory use with special approval in agriculture, commercial, and industrial districts only.

All applications for a Commercial Solar Energy System use must be accompanied by detailed site plans, drawing to scale and dimensioned and certified by a registered engineer licensed in the State of Michigan, displaying the following information: (6) Location and height of all proposed solar array(s), buildings, structures, electrical tie lines and transmission lines, security fencing, and all above-ground structures, and utilities associated with the Commercial Solar Energy System. (7) Horizontal and vertical (elevation) to scale drawings with dimensions that show the location of the proposed solar array(s), buildings, structures, electrical tie lines and transmission lines, security fencing, and all above ground structures and utilities on the property. (10) Land elevations for the solar array(s) location and the relationship to the land elevations of all existing and proposed structures within the Commercial Solar Energy System at a minimum of one (1) foot contours. These requirements are part of the Special Approval Use application process for Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are permitted only in the Industrial zoning district. Other options for solar energy collectors include: Small Accessory Use Energy Collectors generating up to 100 KW primarily for on-site use, and Large Accessory Use Solar Energy Collectors generating up to 2 MW and occupying 10 acres or less, also primarily for on-site use, both subject to different requirements and not classified as Commercial Solar Energy Systems.

Setbacks for Commercial Solar Energy Systems include an 80 feet setback from drain ditches (from top of bank). Other setbacks listed are: Front Setback 200 feet, Side Setback 100 feet, Rear Setback 100 feet, From Residential Districts or Sites Containing Residential Uses 300 feet, Setback from Residential structures 400 feet, Distance from Non-Residential structures 100 feet. The ordinance states: 'No more than 20% of the total lot area may be covered by a Commercial Solar Energy System.' This applies generally to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, including those with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more. The units are expressed as a percentage of the total lot area, not an absolute area value. Additional provisions under PA 233 for systems 50 MW or more do not alter this maximum land coverage limit.

Section 434.C.12 states: 'If a Commercial Solar Energy System is abandoned or otherwise nonoperational for a period of one year, the property owner or the operator must notify the Township and must remove the system within six (6) months after the date of abandonment. Removal requires receipt of a demolition permit from the Building Official and full restoration of the site to the satisfaction of the Zoning Administrator. The site must be filled and covered with top soil and restored to a state compatible with the surrounding vegetation.' Section 434.C.13 requires: 'Financial security in the form of a security bond, escrow payment, or irrevocable letter of credit in an amount equal to 125% of the total estimated cost of decommissioning, code enforcement, and reclamation, which cost estimate must be approved by the Township.' The ordinance defines Commercial Solar Energy System as 'a Solar Energy System in which the principal design, purpose, or use is to provide energy to off-site uses or the wholesale or retail sale of generated electricity to any person or entity.' Additionally, the subsection 'Commercial Solar Energy Systems under PA 233' applies to systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more and states that these provisions control if in conflict with Section 434, but it does not add further decommissioning specifics. Other options and conditions include private solar energy systems with different requirements and smaller scale systems, which are not subject to these decommissioning rules.

For Commercial Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more, fencing must comply with the latest version of the National Electric Code as of November 29, 2024, or as subsequently amended. Additionally, security fencing must be installed around all electrical equipment related to the Commercial Solar Energy System, including transformers and transfer stations, with appropriate warning signs posted at safe intervals at the entrance and around the perimeter of the system. These requirements are part of the general provisions for Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which also include setbacks, height limits, screening, lighting, noise, underground transmission, and other operational and safety standards. The subsection titled 'Commercial Solar Energy Systems under PA 233' specifically applies to systems of 50 MW or more and controls over conflicting provisions. Other options and conditions include: Commercial Solar Energy Systems must be ground mounted, located on parcels of 20 acres or larger, not permitted on PA 116 enrolled properties, must meet 500-foot setbacks from lot lines and public roads (except shared lot lines), and have a maximum height of 15 feet (except lightning rods). Screening can be a greenbelt or a decorative fence at least 50% opaque if approved by the Planning Commission.

Section 434.A.3 states: 'Solar Energy Systems must be located or placed so that concentrated solar glare is not directed toward or onto nearby properties or roadways at any time of the day.' Section 434.C.6 states: 'The Commercial Solar Energy System must not produce any glare that is visible to neighboring lots or to persons traveling on public or private roads.' These provisions apply to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems 'in which the principal design, purpose, or use is to provide energy to off-site uses or the wholesale or retail sale of generated electricity to any person or entity.' Commercial Solar Energy Systems require a special land use permit and site plan review and must comply with various requirements including setbacks, height limits, screening, lighting, noise, underground transmission, and decommissioning. For Commercial Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more, additional provisions under PA 233 apply, but these do not explicitly address glare. Other options for solar energy systems include Private Solar Energy Systems (BIVPs, Roof or Building Mounted, Ground Mounted) with their own specific requirements.

For Commercial Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more, under the subsection 'B. Commercial Solar Energy Systems under PA 233,' the ordinance states: 'Solar panel components must not exceed a maximum height of 25 feet above ground when the arrays are at full tilt.' This is the most restrictive height limit explicitly provided for such large commercial systems. Other height limits mentioned include a 15 feet maximum height for Commercial Solar Energy Systems generally (not specifically for 50 MW+), and a 15 feet maximum height for Ground Mounted Private Solar Energy Systems. Lightning rods may exceed 15 feet but only as necessary for protection. The 25 feet limit applies specifically to systems 50 MW or more and is measured above ground level.

Section 434.C.2.b states: 'Commercial Solar Energy Systems must be located on parcels of land twenty (20) acres in size or larger.' This minimum lot size applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, including those with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more. The units are expressed in acres, which is a standard area measurement. No other minimum lot size values more restrictive than this are provided for such systems in the text.

Section 434.C.8 states: 'The noise generated by a Commercial Solar Energy System must not exceed the following limits: a. Forty (40) Dba Lmax, as measured at the property line of any adjacent R-1 (Residential) or B-1 (Business) zoned land... b. Forty (40) Dba Lmax, as measured at any neighboring residence... between 9:00 p.m. and 7:00 a.m. c. Forty (40) Dba Lmax, as measured at the lot lines of the project boundary.' For Commercial Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more (subject to PA 233 of 2023), the noise limit is '55 average hourly decibels as modeled at the nearest outer wall of the nearest dwelling located on an adjacent nonparticipating property' using the A-weighted scale. The most restrictive limit is 40 dBA Lmax. Units are expressed as dBA (A-weighted decibels).

Section 434.C.5 requires "Greenbelt screening is required around any Commercial Solar Energy System and around any equipment associated with the system to obscure, to the greatest extent possible, the Solar Energy System from any adjacent residences." The greenbelt "must consist of shrubbery, trees, or other non-invasive plant species that provide a visual screen. At least 50% of the plants must be evergreen trees that are at least six feet tall at the time of planting." In lieu of a planting greenbelt, "a decorative fence that is at least 50% opaque and that meets the requirements of this Ordinance applicable to fences may be used if approved by the Planning Commission."

Section 434.C.7 requires that "appropriate warning signs must be posted at safe intervals at the entrance and around the perimeter of the Commercial Solar Energy System." This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems "in which the principal design, purpose, or use is to provide energy to off-site uses or the wholesale or retail sale of generated electricity to any person or entity." Commercial Solar Energy Systems must be ground mounted, located on parcels of twenty (20) acres or larger, and require a special land use permit and site plan review. Other requirements include setbacks, height limits, screening, lighting, security fencing, noise limits, underground transmission, drain tile inspections, insurance, decommissioning, financial security, reporting, inspections, transferability, and remedies. The ordinance requires that Commercial Solar Energy Systems must provide "Proof of environmental compliance, including compliance with Part 91, Soil Erosion and Sedimentation Control (MCL 324.9101 et. seq.) and any corresponding County ordinances." This applies to all Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems "in which the principal design, purpose, or use is to provide energy to off-site uses or the wholesale or retail sale of generated electricity to any person or entity." Additionally, for Commercial Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more, the provisions under PA 233 of 2023 apply, which supersede conflicting provisions in Section 434. Other requirements for Commercial Solar Energy Systems include special land use permits, site plan review, minimum setbacks, height limits, screening, underground transmission lines, drain tile inspections, decommissioning plans, financial security, and compliance with all county, state, and federal permits. Private Solar Energy Systems and smaller systems have different requirements and are not subject to these soil, erosion, and sediment control provisions.

summary: Section 5.15, subsection 3, parts H and I explicitly require that if a large solar energy system ceases to operate or is abandoned for six (6) months or is deemed unsafe or not consistent with code, the Applicant shall repair and restore the system to good working order within a year or remove the system in its entirety, including removing posts, equipment, panels, foundations and other items so that the ground is restored to its preconstruction state. Additionally, any solar system not operated for a continuous period of six (6) months shall be considered abandoned and must be removed within ninety (90) days of receiving an abandonment notification from the Township. Failure to remove the system within ninety (90) days allows the Township to remove it at the owner's expense. The Planning Commission may require the applicant to post a bond equal to the reasonable cost of removal as a condition of Special Land Use approval.

A large solar energy system shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing with a minimum height of eight (8) feet to restrict unauthorized access. The material of such fence shall be established through the Site Plan approval process. All access gates shall be large enough to allow entry of emergency equipment (including firefighting equipment) and the perimeter fence be established at a minimum of thirty (30) feet from the solar energy panels. Lock boxes and keys meeting Township requirements shall be provided for emergency personnel access. Electric fencing is not permitted.

For Large Solar Energy Systems or Solar Farms, the ordinance explicitly requires that "Solar panels shall be placed such that solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways. Traffic safety shall be protected and adjacent properties shall be protected from glare exceeding twenty (20) percent of the incident sun intensity." The applicant must "submit documentation to verify compliance with this section." Additionally, "When deemed appropriate, the Planning Commission may require a report from a registered civil engineer or other professional the Planning Commission finds to be qualified to address this issue." This glare restriction is part of a broader set of regulations in Section 5.15, which also covers small and medium solar energy systems with similar but separately stated glare restrictions. For example, small and medium systems also have the same 20% incident sun intensity glare limit and documentation requirements, but the large systems are specifically addressed under subsection 3.E with additional Planning Commission oversight.

Section 5.15, subsection 3.C states: 'Solar energy system panels or collection devices shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in height, excluding substation and electrical transmission equipment (as measured from the natural grade at the base of improvements).' It further clarifies: 'The maximum height for all structures associated with the large solar energy system shall comply with the maximum height requirements for principal structures of the district in which they are located.' This is the explicit maximum height limit for Large Solar Energy Systems or Solar Farms. Other solar system categories (small and medium) also have a 20 feet height limit for ground-mounted panels, but the focus here is on large systems. The units are feet as explicitly stated.

Section 5.15, subsection 3, paragraph N states: 'No component of any large solar energy system shall emit noise exceeding sixty-five (65) dBA as measured at the exterior property boundary or the existing right-of-way line.' This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for Large Solar Energy Systems or Solar Farms. No other maximum noise levels for large systems are provided in the text.

For Large Solar Energy Systems or Solar Farms, "Solar energy system structures shall comply with the setback requirements of the district in which they are located, with the following exception: in all zones abutting residential districts (including agricultural) or residential uses, the setbacks shall be at least fifty (50) feet from all property lines adjoining said districts or uses." Additionally, "the perimeter fence be established at a minimum of thirty (30) feet from the solar energy panels" and "the perimeter of a large solar energy system shall be completely screened by a minimum twenty (20)-foot wide vegetative buffer." The 50 feet setback from property lines is the most restrictive fixed setback distance directly pertaining to property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, parcels, and/or subdivisions.

The ordinance requires that 'The perimeter of a large solar energy system shall be completely screened by a minimum twenty (20)-foot wide vegetative buffer' with 'Minimum planting requirements for buffers are one (1) deciduous tree, one (1) evergreen tree, and four (4) shrubs for each thirty (30) linear feet to be screened, rounded upward, or a combination of planting(s) as approved by the Planning Commission.' Plant materials must be installed between March 15 and November 15, with financial guarantees if planting is delayed. Unhealthy or dead material must be replaced within one year or the next planting period. Failure to maintain the buffer constitutes a violation and may lead to revocation of the Special Use Permit. The Planning Commission may waive or reduce the buffer requirement if 'the solar panels are not visible from an adjacent residential property or public road,' or if 'existing natural features such as trees provide adequate screening,' or if 'other conditions warrant a waiver or reduction in requirements.'

For Large Solar Energy Systems or Solar Farms, the ordinance requires that "The application shall include a drainage plan prepared by a registered civil engineer showing how stormwater runoff will be managed and demonstrating that runoff from the site will not exceed the agricultural runoff rate." It also mandates that if detergents are used to clean solar panels, details on the type, frequency, quantity of use, quantity and source of water, and stormwater quality protection measures be provided, along with any necessary permits for off-site discharge. Additionally, if the system ceases operation or is abandoned for six months or more, the applicant must "remove the system in its entirety" and restore the ground to its preconstruction state. These requirements are specific to large solar energy systems or solar farms as defined in the ordinance. Other system sizes (small and medium) have similar but distinct provisions, such as drainage plans for medium systems and impervious surface thresholds for small systems, but the explicit soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for large systems are as stated.

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Primary Use Solar Energy Facilities (SEFs). Section H.5 states: 'The SEF project must contain a Decommissioning Plan to ensure it is properly decommissioned upon the end of the project life or facility abandonment.' Decommissioning includes 'Removal of all structures (including transmission equipment and fencing) and debris to a depth of four (4) feet, restoration of the soil, and restoration of vegetation within twelve (12) months of the end of project life or facility abandonment.' The plan must include 'how the facility will be decommissioned, the Professional Engineer’s estimated cost of decommissioning, the financial resources to be used to accomplish decommissioning, and the type of surety to be provided prior to construction.' Surety requirements include posting 'a surety in a form acceptable to the Township, such as security bond, irrevocable letter of credit, escrow, or other form deemed acceptable by the Township equal to one-hundred fifty (150) percent of the total estimated decommissioning and reclamation costs, prior to issuance of a building permit.' The surety must be maintained and reviewed every five years, and the Township may access the surety and the site to complete decommissioning if the owner/operator fails to do so within twelve months of project end or abandonment. These requirements apply specifically to Primary Use SEFs, which are defined as 'a SEF that is devoted to solar electric power generation primarily for use off-site' and are subject to a Special Use Permit under Section H.1.

summary: Section 5.17 requires "A decommissioning plan, to outline steps for removal of the SES, is required." It also states that "If a SES ceases to perform its intended function for more than 12 consecutive months, the property owner must remove the collector, mount, and associated equipment and facilities no later than 60 days. The property must be restored to the condition prior to the development of the system." An exception is provided for inoperable BIPV materials that still perform another purpose, with additional requirements for licensed electrician disconnection and documentation. These requirements apply to principal-use SES, which may include larger, utility-scale systems, as opposed to accessory use SES which have separate standards.

Section 5.17.B.4 states: 'A principal-use SES must be secured with perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access, subject to Section 3.08: Fences.' This fencing requirement applies to principal-use SES, which are ground-mounted solar energy systems that are not accessory use. Other conditions in Section 5.17 include setback requirements, height limits, screening requirements in residential and mixed-use districts, building permit and engineering drawing requirements, and decommissioning plans. Accessory use SES must meet requirements of Section 0: Accessory Structures: Distributed Energy Systems and have location restrictions in residential and mixed-use districts.

Ground-mounted SES cannot exceed 15-feet in height at maximum tilt. Taller structures, not to exceed the maximum height of the underlying zoning district, may be considered by the Planning Commission as a Special Land Use. This applies to principal-use SES, which would typically include utility-scale systems intended for offsite electricity generation or sale.

Ground-mounted SES must be setback at least 8-feet from any side or rear lot line. This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems as described in Section 5.17.B.2. Other related provisions include that ground-mounted SES cannot be located closer than 10-feet to any principal building (not a property line setback), and principal-use SES may require landscaped screening from front lot and side rights-of-way but no additional setback distance is specified.

In residential and mixed-use zoning districts, principal-use Solar Energy Systems (SES) may be required by the Planning Commission to have a landscaped screen to screen from front lot and side rights-of-way. Accessory Use SES must be located in the rear or side yard unless they are screened, then they may be located in the front plane of the house. When located within the non-required front yards, a landscaped screen may be required by the Planning Commission to screen from front lot and side public rights-of-way. This applies to ground-mounted SES that are principal-use, which are typically utility-scale systems.

Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems (SES) are designated as a 'Special Land Use' (S) in the R-2 district, indicating they require special approval or a permitting process. In other districts, ground-mounted solar is 'Permitted Land Use' (P) in R-1, MXD-1, MXD-2, CBD, I-1, and I-2. Other types of solar energy systems such as Building Exterior Side-Mounted are 'Special Land Use' (S) only in R-2, and 'Permitted Land Use' (P) in MXD-1, MXD-2, CBD, I-1, and I-2. Building Integrated Solar (BIPV) and Rooftop Solar are permitted (P) in all listed districts. The text excludes solar overlay districts from consideration.

The total area of the commercial solar energy system shall be included in calculations to determine lot coverage and shall not exceed a maximum lot coverage of twenty-five (25%) percent regardless of the residing zoning district. This is explicitly stated in subsection (OO) 2(b). Other related provisions mention 15% lot coverage limits but only for on-site ground-mounted solar energy collectors as accessory uses, which do not apply to commercial solar energy systems. The unit is a percentage of total lot coverage.

Any commercial solar energy system that is not operated or found to be inoperable due to disrepair for a continuous period of six (6) months shall be considered abandoned. The Planning Commission shall provide written notice to the applicant/owner/operator of a hearing to determine if the system should be decommissioned. Within ninety (90) days of the hearing, if the system is deemed abandoned or inoperable, the owner/operator must obtain permits to remove all structures and equipment consistent with the approved decommissioning plan. Failure to obtain permits allows the township to remove the system at the owner's expense. Decommissioning includes removal of all equipment above and below ground, internal or perimeter access roads, and restoration of the site to its prior condition, including topography, vegetation, soils, drainage, and environmental features. Restoration must comply with erosion control and soil stabilization requirements and be completed within one year, with possible extensions. Prior to site plan approval, a decommissioning plan must be approved describing the expected duration, decommissioning methods, estimated cost by a Professional Engineer, and financial resources (bond or similar instrument) at 125% of estimated costs. The township reviews the adequacy of financial resources annually and may require additional deposits. The township has rights of entry, injunctive relief, and lien enforcement to ensure decommissioning. Other options include repair certified by a Licensed Professional Engineer to resume operation. The planting of native ground covers must be maintained on site during operation until decommissioning. The text also details setback and visual buffer requirements, lot size minimums, and height and lot coverage limits for commercial solar energy systems but these are not decommissioning requirements.

Section (OO) 2(a) states: 'Ground-mounted solar energy collectors shall not exceed 12 feet in height measured from the ground at the base of such equipment. The height of the ground-mounted solar energy collector shall be measured from ground level to the highest point of the solar panel.' This is the explicit maximum height restriction for Commercial Solar Energy Systems. Other height restrictions mentioned apply only to on-site roof-mounted or on-site ground-mounted solar energy collectors that are not commercial systems.

Commercial solar energy systems must be located on lots larger than 2 acres. This is explicitly stated in section (OO) point 3: 'Commercial solar energy systems must be located on lots larger than 2 acres.' The unit 'acres' is used as the area measurement for the minimum lot size.

When a commercial solar energy system is adjacent to a residential use, the system shall be set back at least three hundred (300) feet from the property line. In addition, commercial solar energy systems shall meet the required front, side, and rear setbacks for the RSA zoning district. If located on multiple contiguous parcels owned by the same property owner, some setback requirements may be waived by the Planning Commission during site plan review. Other setback references include 500 feet from any dwelling unit (not equivalent to property line) and 300 feet from any road right-of-way (not property line).

Commercial solar energy systems shall be setback at least three hundred (300) feet from any road right-of-way. A landscaped visual buffer shall be provided within the setback area that obscures the commercial solar energy system from view. In addition to the residential and street frontage setback requirements, commercial solar energy systems shall meet the required front, side, and rear setbacks for the RSA zoning district. Some setback requirements may be waived by the Planning Commission during site plan review if the system is located on a site with multiple contiguous parcels owned by the same property owner.

Section (OO) 4 Visual Buffer Requirements states: '(a) Residential Property: When a commercial solar energy system is adjacent to a residential use, the system shall be set back at least three hundred (300) feet from the property line and at least five hundred (500) feet from any dwelling unit. A landscaped visual buffer shall be provided within the setback area that obscures the commercial solar energy system from view. (b) Street Frontage: Commercial solar energy systems shall be setback at least three hundred (300) feet from any road right-of-way. A landscaped visual buffer shall be provided within the setback area that obscures the commercial solar energy system from view. (c) Visual Buffer: A required landscaped visual buffer, including a greenbelt and/or landscaped berm, that meets the minimum standards of Sec. 36-324 shall be installed to effectively screen the commercial solar energy system from view. The visual buffer shall be installed prior to the placement of solar collectors to the extent feasible and must be maintained by the property owner. The Planning Commission may require the installation of additional vegetation and other landscaping or visual screening in excess of the minimum requirements to screen residential districts and uses. The planting of native ground covers shall be maintained on site during the operation, until the site is decommissioned. (d) Setback: Required setback areas and visual buffers may be used for agricultural purposes or left in a natural state. In addition to the residential and street frontage setback requirements in this Section, commercial solar energy systems shall meet the required front, side, and rear setbacks for the RSA zoning district. If a commercial solar energy system is located on a site that includes multiple parcels owned by the same property owner that form a single contiguous site, some setback requirements may be waived by the Planning Commission during site plan review. (e) The Planning Commission may approve substitution of vegetation for an obscuring fence, wall, and other protective barriers as long as it meets requirements in Sec. 36-408. (f) The planting of native ground covers shall be maintained on site during the operation, until the site is decommissioned.' These requirements apply specifically to commercial solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance text.

Subsection (PP) Decommissioning requires that the site be restored to a condition that reflects the character of the site prior to installation of the commercial solar energy system including topography, vegetation, soils, drainage, and any unique environmental features. The restoration shall include re-grading, soil stabilization, and re-vegetation necessary to return the subject property to a stable condition consistent with conditions existing prior to establishment of the commercial solar energy system. The restoration process shall comply with all state, county, or local erosion control, soil stabilization, and/or runoff requirements or ordinances and shall be completed within one year. Extensions may be granted upon request to the Planning Commission prior to expiration of the one-year requirement for completed decommissioning.

When a commercial solar energy system is adjacent to a residential use, the system shall be set back at least five hundred (500) feet from any dwelling unit. Other related setbacks include at least three hundred (300) feet from the property line and from any road right-of-way, with a landscaped visual buffer required within the setback area. Additionally, commercial solar energy systems shall meet the required front, side, and rear setbacks for the RSA zoning district, with some setback waivers possible for contiguous parcels owned by the same property owner.

Commercial solar energy systems must provide a visual buffer when adjacent to residential use or street frontage, including setbacks of at least 300 feet from property lines and road right-of-ways, and 500 feet from any dwelling unit. A landscaped visual buffer, including a greenbelt and/or landscaped berm meeting Sec. 36-324 standards, shall be installed to effectively screen the system from view and maintained by the property owner. The visual buffer shall be installed prior to placement of solar collectors to the extent feasible. The Planning Commission may require additional vegetation or screening beyond minimum requirements and may approve substitution of vegetation for fences or walls per Sec. 36-408. Setback areas and visual buffers may be used for agricultural purposes or left natural. Some setback waivers may be granted by the Planning Commission during site plan review for contiguous parcels. These requirements apply to commercial solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance, which must also meet other conditions such as height limits, lot size, and lot coverage. Other options or conditions include: setbacks of 300 feet from property lines and road right-of-ways, 500 feet from dwellings; landscaped buffers per Sec. 36-324; Planning Commission discretion for additional screening or substitution with fences/walls; and possible setback waivers for contiguous parcels during site plan review.

On-site ground-mounted solar energy collectors shall be a minimum of 25 feet from all-natural features including water courses, wood lots, wetlands, and 100-year floodplains. Commercial solar energy systems must meet all requirements for solar energy collectors, including this setback.

For Level 3 Systems, defined as systems with a footprint of 5 acres or more, or that do not meet the requirements of a Level 1 or 2 system, "all mechanical equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum 6 foot high fence, with locking gate" when the system is not accessory to a residential living structure. Additionally, Level 3 Systems "shall be set back at least 100 feet from non-participating property boundaries, excluding any security fencing, poles and wires necessary to connect to facilities of the electrical grid." Level 1 Systems are roof mounted or building integrated with specific height and coverage limits, and Level 2 Systems are ground mounted or free standing small scale systems under five acres with requirements including year round screening along the back panel of the solar collection device(s).

Level 3 System — Defined as systems with a footprint of 5 acres or more, or that do not meet the requirements of a Level 1 or 2 system. Level 2 System is defined as ground mounted or free standing small scale systems (Under five (5) acres in size). The minimum lot size for Level 3 Systems is therefore 5 acres or more.

For Level 3 Systems (defined as systems with a footprint of 5 acres or more, or that do not meet the requirements of a Level 1 or 2 system), the system "shall be set back at least 100 feet from non-participating property boundaries, excluding any security fencing, poles and wires necessary to connect to facilities of the electrical grid." Other system levels have different conditions: Level 1 systems are roof mounted or building integrated with no specific setback from property lines mentioned; Level 2 systems are ground mounted or free standing small scale systems under five acres and must comply with setbacks for accessory structures in the district but no specific setback from non-participating property boundaries is stated.

Solar energy systems shall be subject to storm water management, erosion and sediment control best practices and shall obtain required permits from the Michigan Department of Environmental Quality, Michigan Department of Transportation and any other required governmental approvals. Level 3 System is defined as systems with a footprint of 5 acres or more, or that do not meet the requirements of a Level 1 or 2 system.
