Section 13.19(B) Solar Energy Facilities requires that "the applicant shall submit a decommissioning plan to ensure removal of the facility and restoration of the site upon cessation of use." Further, subsection 5 ABANDONMENT AND DECOMMISSIONING states: "A Solar Energy Facility that ceases to produce energy on a continuous basis for 12 months will be considered abandoned... It is the responsibility of the responsible party... to remove all equipment and facilities and completely restore the Parcel to its condition prior to development of the Solar Energy Facility." The Zoning Administrator must notify the responsible party to remove the facility within six (6) months of notice, and if they fail, the Planning Commission may remove the facility and recover costs. The decommissioning plan must include: "the anticipated life of the project; the estimated decommissioning costs net of salvage value in current dollars; the method of ensuring that funds will be available for decommissioning and restoration... including complete removal of all non-utility owned equipment, conduit, structures, fencing, roads, solar panels and foundations, and complete restoration of property to condition prior to development of the Solar Energy Facility; the anticipated manner in which the project will be decommissioned and the site restored; a provision to give notice to the Township one year in advance of decommissioning; a surety bond to assure payment of the cost of decommissioning... The security shall be a: 1) cash bond; 2) irrevocable bank letter of credit; or 3) performance bond in a form approved by the Township." These requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities defined as "an energy facility... principally used to convert solar energy to electricity... that primarily sell electricity to be used off site." Exempt Solar Energy systems (Section 13.19(A)) that do not primarily involve sale of electricity offsite are not subject to these decommissioning requirements.

Section 13.19(B)(3)(b) requires that "A Solar Energy Facility shall be surrounded by an eight (8) foot tall chain link fence. The fence shall securely enclose the whole improved area and shall be designed to restrict unauthorized access." This applies to Solar Energy Facilities defined as "An energy facility, an area of land, or a structural rooftop principally used to convert solar energy to electricity... that primarily sell electricity to be used off site." Additional fencing-related requirements include that "All fences and improved areas located on the site shall comply with the applicable setback for the district in which it is located" and "any structures or other improved areas located within the fence shall be located at least 30 feet from a fence line."

Solar Energy Facilities are permitted as a special land use in the AR Agricultural-Residential District and the I Industrial District, subject to requirements including: "The facility shall be designed and constructed to prevent glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and public rights-of-way." (Section 13.19(B)(3)(g)). Additionally, "The design and construction of Solar Energy Facilities shall not produce light emissions, either direct or indirect (reflective), that would interfere with pilot vision and/or traffic control operations as stated in section 3.2.2 of the 2011 AICUZ report." (Section 13.19(B)(3)(h)). For facilities within five nautical miles of an airport, notification and use of the Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT) is required to evaluate solar glare aviation hazard (Section 13.19(B)(4)(c)). Exempt Solar Energy systems (those primarily used on site and not for offsite sale) are subject to different provisions and do not have these glare restrictions (Section 13.19(A)).

Section 13.19(B)(3) states: 'The maximum height of any structure shall be fifteen (15) feet.' This applies specifically to Solar Energy Facilities, which are defined as facilities that primarily sell electricity off site. Other height limits mentioned, such as three (3) feet above roof for roof-mounted and fifteen (15) feet for ground-mounted solar energy systems, apply only to Exempt Solar Energy systems (non-commercial, on-site use) and are not relevant to Solar Energy Facilities.

Section 13.19(B)(1) states: 'Minimum lot size shall be twenty (20) acres.' This applies specifically to Solar Energy Facilities, which are defined as facilities that primarily sell electricity offsite. The unit 'acres' is explicitly used as the measure of area for the minimum lot size.

Solar energy facilities shall be set back a minimum of one hundred (100) feet from all property lines and road rights-of-way. Additionally, any structures or other improved areas located within the fence shall be located at least 30 feet from a fence line (facility perimeter). A minimum landscape buffer of 20 feet is required along all property lines abutting residentially zoned or used property. These setbacks apply to Solar Energy Facilities as defined in Section 13.19(B), which are commercial-scale systems primarily selling electricity off site.

Solar energy facilities shall be set back a minimum of one hundred (100) feet from all property lines and road rights-of-way. Additionally, all access roads and storage areas shall be established on a 30’ minimum easement to a public right of way, which shall be surfaced with a pavement having an asphalt or concrete binder or with compacted limestone or with compacted, crushed asphalt. The 100 feet setback is the primary fixed distance requirement from roads for Solar Energy Facilities, which are defined as facilities primarily selling electricity offsite.

Section 13.19(B)(3)(a)(v) requires a minimum landscape buffer of 20 feet containing evergreen trees or bushes planted no more than 8 feet apart and at least 4 feet tall at time of planting. The buffer shall obtain a height of 10 feet within 3 growing seasons. The trees or bushes may be trimmed but no lower than a height of 10 feet. Section 13.19(B)(3)(a)(vi) requires good husbandry techniques including proper pruning, fertilizer, and mulching to ensure vegetation maturity and density. Dead or diseased vegetation must be removed and replanted at the next appropriate planting time. Section 13.19(B)(3)(a)(e) states the design of Solar Energy Facility’s buffers shall use materials, colors, textures, screening and landscaping that will blend the facility into the natural setting and existing environment. Section 13.19(B)(3)(d) requires an eight (8) foot tall chain link fence to securely enclose the improved area. Section 13.19(B)(4) requires all mechanical equipment to be enclosed or screened from view from adjacent properties and public rights-of-way. These requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities defined as facilities that primarily sell electricity offsite and are permitted as a special land use in the AR Agricultural-Residential District and the I Industrial District. Other conditions include minimum lot size of twenty (20) acres, setbacks, maximum height, security fencing, glare prevention, decommissioning plans, and compliance with state and federal laws.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "The manufacturers or installer’s identification and appropriate warning sign shall be posted on or near the panels in a clearly visible manner; furthermore, an information sign shall be posted and maintained at the entrance(s), which shall list the name and phone number of the operator." This signage requirement applies specifically to Solar Energy Facilities, which are defined as facilities that "primarily sell electricity to be used off site." These facilities are permitted as a special land use in the AR Agricultural-Residential District and the I Industrial District, subject to various requirements including setbacks, fencing, landscaping, and compliance with state and federal laws. Other requirements include a security fence, landscape buffers, decommissioning plans, and notification procedures related to aviation. The signage requirement is part of the standards and requirements for Solar Energy Facilities under subsection B(3)(c).

Solar Energy Facilities shall only be allowed as a special land use in the AR Agricultural-Residential District and the I Industrial District, pursuant to Article 17 as to Special Land Use approvals and the following requirements: (Section 13.19 B.1). Exempt solar energy panels used primarily on site are permitted accessory uses in all zoning districts (Section 13.19 A). The ordinance includes detailed application, site plan, and operational requirements for Solar Energy Facilities, including insurance, certification, decommissioning plans, and complaint resolution processes. The special land use permit process involves Planning Commission review, public hearings, and site plan approval (Section 13.19 B.1.c).

Improved areas shall be located at least 300 feet from any existing residential dwellings, church, school, family or group child day-care homes, bed and breakfast establishments, rooming houses, residential facilities, and any other residence. The owner of a leased parcel may waive this requirement. In which case, written proof of this waiver must be provided to the Fremont Township Planning Commission prior to site plan approval. (Section 13.19(B)(3)(a)(iii)) Other setback requirements include a minimum of 30 feet from a fence line for structures or improved areas within the fence, and a 100 feet setback from all property lines and road rights-of-way, but these do not pertain to occupied dwellings or residences.

Section 13.19(B)(3)(e) requires that "The design of Solar Energy Facility’s buffers shall use materials, colors, textures, screening and landscaping, that will blend the facility into the natural setting and existing environment." Section 13.19(B)(2) requires submission of a site plan including "the location, height, and dimensions of all existing and proposed structures and fencing," "existing topography," and "all new infrastructure, both above and below ground, related to the project." These requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities defined as "An energy facility... principally used to convert solar energy to electricity... that primarily sell electricity to be used off site." The Planning Commission may impose additional conditions to protect public health, safety, and welfare (13.19(B)(3)(j) and (l)). The ordinance also requires a special land use permit and site plan review process (13.19(B)(1)(c)). Other provisions include setback, height, fencing, landscaping, and decommissioning requirements, but these do not explicitly constitute visual impact assessment requirements. Exempt Solar Energy systems (Section 13.19(A)) are not subject to these requirements.

The ordinance requires a decommissioning plan for utility-scale solar energy collector systems prior to approval. The plan must include: a. Defined conditions upon which decommission will be initiated (e.g., end of land lease, no power production for 12 months, abandonment, etc.). b. Removal of utility-owned equipment and non-utility-owned equipment, which may include but not be limited to conduit, structures, fencing, solar panels, and foundations. c. Restoration of property condition which existed prior to the development of the system. d. Specification of the timeframe from completion of decommissioning activities. e. Description of any agreement (i.e., lease) with landowner regarding decommissioning, if applicable. f. Identity of the entity or individual responsible for decommissioning. g. Plans for updating the decommissioning plan. h. A performance guarantee shall be posted in the form of a bond, letter of credit, cash, or other form acceptable to the township to ensure removal upon abandonment. The responsible party shall provide at least two cost estimates from qualified contractors for full removal and disposal of equipment, foundations, and structures associated with the system. The performance guarantee amount shall be valid throughout the lifetime of the system and adjusted every five years. Additionally, abandonment is defined as no energy production for 12 months without substantial evidence of intent to maintain operation, triggering removal of all equipment and restoration of the lot within one year.

summary: Section 7.9.F states: 'If a Utility-Scale Solar Facility ceases to be used for its intended purpose for a period of twelve (12) consecutive months, the owner shall remove the facility and all associated equipment and restore the site to its original condition.' Section 7.9.G adds: 'If a Solar Energy Facility owner or operator intends to abandon and, in fact, does abandon a Solar Energy Facility by not operating it for a continuous period of twelve (12) months, said Solar Energy Facility shall be considered abandoned, and the owner of such Solar Energy Facility shall remove the same within one hundred eighty (180) days of the receipt of a notice of abandonment by the City.' Failure to remove the facility within this period allows the City to remove it at the owner's expense. The decommissioning plan required at application (Section 7.9.C.23) must include: '(1) The anticipated life of the project. (2) The anticipated manner in which the project will be decommissioned, including a description of which above-grade and below-grade improvements will be removed, retained (e.g. access drive, fencing), or restored for viable reuse of the property consistent with the zoning district. Removal shall include removing equipment, foundations, and other items so that the ground is restored to its preconstruction state and is ready for development as another land use. (3) Performance Guarantee. The City may require a performance guarantee (pursuant to Section 9.5) at the time of approval equal to two (2) times the estimated decommissioning cost.' The City may require third-party cost estimates and periodic reviews every three years. The method of ensuring funds will be available must be provided (e.g., surety bond, irrevocable letter of credit, or cash deposit). A Solar Energy Facility owner may proceed with the approved decommissioning plan or amend it with Planning Commission approval. These requirements apply specifically to Utility-Scale Solar Facilities as defined in Section 7.9.B.1 as 'a solar energy system that is designed and intended to generate energy for sale or use off-site.'

Utility-Scale Solar Facilities "may be secured with perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access." Fencing is exempt from standards in Section 20.500 – 20.509 (Fences Ordinance). The Planning Commission may require wildlife-friendly fencing. Fencing detail must be included in the site plan application. This is stated in Section 7.9.B.9 and Section 7.9.C.13. Accessory solar panels have separate fencing/screening requirements under Section 7.8.F, which requires ground-mounted accessory solar panels to be screened by "a solid fence, wall, or landscaping, as approved by the Zoning Administrator." However, this applies only to accessory solar panels, not Utility-Scale Solar Facilities.

Utility-Scale Solar Facilities "shall be designed and located to avoid glare or reflection onto adjacent lots and adjacent roadways and shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard." Plans to reduce glare may be required in the initial materials submitted. This applies to solar energy systems "designed and intended to generate energy for sale or use off-site" and includes solar panels, mounting structures, inverters, transformers, and related equipment. The glare restriction is part of the development standards which also include setbacks, height limits, screening, lighting, noise, fencing, and other regulations. Accessory solar panels, which are primarily for on-site use, have separate glare restrictions under Section 7.8, but those are not applicable to Utility-Scale Solar Facilities. Additionally, accessory solar panels that produce 2 MW or more or cover more than half an acre may be required to comply with the Utility-Scale Solar Facilities standards.

Section 7.9.B.2 states: 'The total height for all solar collection devices shall not exceed twenty (20) feet when oriented at maximum tilt.' This applies specifically to Utility-Scale Solar Facilities, defined as solar energy systems designed to generate energy for sale or use off-site. Other height limits mentioned in the text, such as 15 feet for solar panels and mounting structures in Section 7.9.E.2, apply to different contexts or smaller systems and are not more restrictive for Utility-Scale Solar Facilities.

Accessory solar panels which provide power on-site but which cover more than one-half (1/2) acre of land or produce two (2) MW of power or more shall fall under Section 7.9 Utility-Scale Solar Facilities and shall only be allowed in the M-1 District. This sets a maximum system size threshold of two (2) MW for classification as a Utility-Scale Solar Facility. No other explicit maximum system size or total installation limit is provided for Utility-Scale Solar Facilities in Section 7.9.

Section 7.9.B.8 states: 'The sound pressure level of a solar energy facility and all ancillary solar equipment shall not exceed fifty-five (55) dBA (Leq (1 hour)) at the nearest outer wall of the nearest dwelling located on an adjacent non-participating lot.' This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for Utility-Scale Solar Facilities, which are defined as systems designed to generate energy for sale or use off-site. No other numerical noise limits for Utility-Scale Solar Facilities are provided in the text.

Utility-Scale Solar Facilities (Solar Energy Facilities §7.9) are only permitted in the M-1 district. The text states: 'Solar Energy Facilities §7.9 P' under M-1 only. Section 7.9 applies to Utility-Scale Solar Facilities and requires a Special Use permit. Section 7.8 clarifies that accessory solar panels producing 2 MW or more or covering more than one-half (1/2) acre fall under Section 7.9 and 'shall only be allowed in the M-1 District.' No other districts list Utility-Scale Solar Facilities as permitted or with a special use permit, indicating they are prohibited or not allowed in R-1, R-2, B-1, C-1, and C-2.

The setbacks of all solar collection devices and ancillary equipment shall be at least fifty (50) feet from the road right-of-way and all lot lines of non-participating lots. Additionally, fencing for solar energy facilities is exempt from setbacks. The ordinance states: 'The setbacks of all solar collection devices and ancillary equipment shall be at least fifty (50) feet from the road right-of-way and all lot lines of non-participating lots.'

Section 7.9.D Repowering states: "In addition to repairing or replacing solar energy components to maintain the system, a solar energy facility may at any time be repowered, without the need to apply for a new Special Use permit, by reconfiguring, renovating, or replacing the solar energy components to increase the power rating within the existing project footprint." It further provides that "A proposal to change the project footprint of an existing solar energy facility shall be considered a new application, subject to the Ordinance standards at the time of the request." This regulation applies specifically to Utility-Scale Solar Facilities, which are defined as facilities "designed and intended to generate energy for sale or use off-site."

Utility-Scale Solar Facilities shall have setbacks of all solar collection devices and ancillary equipment at least fifty (50) feet from the road right-of-way. This setback is a fixed distance and applies specifically to roads (rights-of-way). Additionally, setbacks must comply with the setback requirements for principal buildings in the zoning district, except that no part of the facility shall be located less than fifty (50) feet from any lot line. Other related provisions include a 300 feet setback from residences and occupied community buildings on non-participating lots, and screening requirements from the public right-of-way. The setback from roads is explicitly stated as fifty (50) feet and is not based on any multiplier of structure height.

Utility-Scale Solar Facilities shall be screened from view from adjacent lots and streets by a solid fence, wall, or landscaping, as approved by the Planning Commission. Screening shall look as natural as possible through the use of varying plant materials of varying heights, if possible. Screening shall be placed outside the perimeter fence. Natural vegetation may be counted toward screening requirements. Screening shall be maintained throughout the life of the facility including replacing dead vegetation within six (6) months or at the earliest feasible time of year dependent on the weather. The Planning Commission may reduce or waive screening requirements provided that any such adjustment is in keeping with the intent of the Ordinance.

Section 7.9.E.6 states: 'No signs or other advertising shall be permitted on any part of the facility, except for safety or hazard warnings.' This signage requirement applies to Utility-Scale Solar Facilities, which are defined as 'a solar energy system that is designed and intended to generate energy for sale or use off-site.' The ordinance also includes other development standards such as setbacks, height limits, screening, glare minimization, lighting restrictions, noise limits, fencing, and decommissioning plans, but only the signage requirement explicitly addresses signs. Accessory solar panels and smaller systems are regulated separately under Section 7.8 and do not have this signage provision.

Section 7.9 Utility-Scale Solar Facilities explicitly addresses soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements. It states: 'The Planning Commission may require soil stabilization through groundcover.' Additionally, 'If required by the Zoning Administrator, the application shall include a drainage plan showing how stormwater runoff will be managed.' If detergents are used to clean solar panels, details on detergent type, frequency, quantity, and stormwater quality protection measures must be provided, along with any necessary permits for off-site discharge. If groundcover such as conservation cover or pollinator habitat is utilized, then a drainage plan is not required. The application must also include 'plans for land clearing and/or grading required for the installation and operation of the system, and plans for ground cover establishment and management.' Furthermore, a 'drainage plan including a plan to control runoff during construction' is required. Other requirements in this section include site plan approval, fencing, setbacks, underground power lines, decommissioning plans, security deposits, maximum structure height of twenty feet, and obtaining all necessary permits before construction.

summary: Ground-mounted Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES), Solar Farms; i.e. ground mounted, shall be considered a Special Use in Agriculture Residential, Commercial Industrial, and all other Commercial zoning districts. Roof mounted CSES shall be considered a Permitted Use in those districts. Site Plan and Special Use applications shall be presented to and approved by the Planning Commission. Additional conditions include setbacks, fencing, decommissioning plans, bonding, and height limits. All necessary local, state, and federal permits must be obtained before starting construction.

Setbacks shall meet district requirements and be setback 100 feet from any non-leased residence. This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES), defined as solar energy systems designed and built to provide energy to the utility grid, for end use off, or away from, the property or parcels of property upon which the CSES is located. Roof mounted CSES shall be considered a Permitted Use and shall not extend beyond the peak of the roof. Ground mounted CSES (solar farms) are considered a Special Use and must comply with this 100-foot setback from any non-leased residence.

Decommissioning: A decommissioning plan signed by the party responsible for decommissioning and the landowner addressing the following shall be submitted prior to the issuance of the zoning permit, which shall include: the anticipated life of the project; the estimated decommissioning costs net of salvage value in current dollars; the method of ensuring that funds will be available for decommissioning and restoration, to include but not limited to: Complete removal of all non-utility owned equipment, conduit, structures, fencing, roads, solar panels and foundations, and Complete restoration of property to condition prior to development of the Solar Energy Facility; the anticipated manner in which the project will be decommissioned and the site restored; A provision to give notice to the Township one year in advance of decommissioning. A surety bond to assure payment of the cost of decommissioning shall be required. To ensure proper removal of the structure when it ceases to be used for a period of one (1) year or more, any application for a new solar energy facility shall include a description of the financial security guaranteeing removal of the solar energy facility which will be posted at the time of receiving a building permit for the facility. The security shall be a: 1) cash bond; 2) irrevocable bank letter of credit; or 3) performance bond in a form approved by the Township. The amount of such guarantee shall be no less than the estimated cost of removal and may include a provision for inflationary cost adjustments. The estimate shall be prepared by the engineer for the developer and shall be approved by the Township. Every five (5) years, the PC shall review and, if necessary, update the Decommissioning Bond. The applicant shall be responsible for the payment of any costs or attorney fees incurred by the Township in securing removal; and The timeframe for completion of decommissioning activities.

Solar Energy Facilities shall be surrounded by an eight (8) foot tall chain link fence. The fence shall be designed to restrict unauthorized access. All fences and improved areas located on the site shall comply with the applicable setback for the district in which it is located. Furthermore, any structures or other improved areas located within the fence shall be at located least 130 feet from property line.

Solar Energy Facilities shall have a minimum landscape buffer of 30 feet. A glare study to determine planting area is to be provided, followed up with an arborist recommendation. The buffer shall contain evergreen trees or bushes planted no more than 20 feet apart and at least 8 feet tall at time of planting. The buffer shall obtain a height of 10 feet within 3 growing seasons. The trees or bushes may be trimmed but no lower than a height of 10 feet.

Any structures or other improved areas located within the fence shall be at located least 130 feet from property line. All solar energy facilities shall have a minimum landscape buffer of 30 feet. The buffer shall contain evergreen trees or bushes planted no more than 20 feet apart and at least 8 feet tall at time of planting.

All solar energy facilities shall have a minimum landscape buffer of 30 feet. A glare study to determine planting area is to be provided, followed up with an arborist recommendation. The buffer shall contain evergreen trees or bushes planted no more than 20 feet apart and at least 8 feet tall at time of planting. The buffer shall obtain a height of 10 feet within 3 growing seasons. The trees or bushes may be trimmed but no lower than a height of 10 feet.

The ordinance requires that "the manufacturer’s or installer's identification and appropriate warning sign shall be posted on or near the panels in a clearly visible manner; furthermore, an information sign shall be posted and maintained at the entrance(s), which shall, at minimum, list the name and phone number of the operator." These requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities, which are allowed as a special land use in the AR, C, and I Districts. The ordinance also details application, site plan, location, security, decommissioning, and complaint resolution requirements for Solar Energy Facilities.

Solar Energy Facilities shall only be allowed as a special land use in the AR (Agricultural-Residential), C (Commercial) and I (Industrial) Districts, pursuant to Article XVII as to Special Land Use approvals and the following requirements. Exempt Solar Energy panels located on the premises of a farm, home, or business and which do not primarily involve the sale of electricity off the premises shall be exempt from the requirements of Subsection  "B"  and allowed as a permitted accessory use in all zoning districts, providing the electricity is primarily used on site.

A decommissioning plan must be submitted with the Special Use application, to be approved and kept on file by the Township. The decommissioning plan must include a bond of no less than ten (10%) percent of the construction costs of the array to be set aside for decommissioning by the Township, if necessary. This applies to solar panel arrays larger than the footprint of the Main Building on the same lot (or on a lot with no Main Building), including all solar arrays greater than ten (10) acres in area.

A glare study, completed by a qualified third-party professional, shall be submitted, and shall show that no glare will impact public roadways or residential dwellings. This applies to Solar Panel Arrays that are larger than the footprint of the Main Building on the same lot (or on a lot with no Main Building), which includes all solar arrays greater than ten (10) acres in area. Additionally, all solar arrays greater than ten (10) acres in area must include one or more of the following amongst the panels of the solar array: Crop cultivation; Livestock grazing, with the panels raised to allow an eight (8) foot clearance for the animals to pass underneath; Pollinator fields, including milkweed and other native plantings.

For Solar Panel Arrays larger than the footprint of the Main Building on the same lot (including those greater than ten (10) acres), ground solar panel arrays may not exceed twenty-five (25) feet in height. This is explicitly stated in Section 3.03(B)(3): 'Ground solar panel arrays may not exceed twenty-five (25) feet in height.' The units are feet. Other height restrictions mentioned include roof arrays and smaller ground arrays, but these apply to smaller or accessory systems and are not relevant to arrays greater than ten (10) acres.

Section 3.03(B) states that Solar Panel Arrays larger than the footprint of the Main Building shall be permitted by Special Land Use in the AG, RR, RP, C-1, C-2, and I-1 districts. The text does not list R-1, R-2, or R-3 among these districts, implying that large solar arrays are not allowed or are prohibited in these residential districts. Smaller solar panel arrays (smaller than the footprint of the Main Building) are permitted accessory structures in all zoning districts. Therefore, large solar arrays are allowed only by special use permit in AG, RR, RP, C-1, C-2, and I-1, and are effectively prohibited in R-1, R-2, and R-3.

Energy storage facilities must be setback at least one-hundred (100) feet from the nearest lot line. Solar panel arrays larger than the footprint of the Main Building must meet all required setbacks for a Main Building in the district they are located within, but no fixed numeric setback distance is specified for the arrays themselves. Ground-mounted arrays shall not be located in the required front yard.

Solar Panel Arrays that are larger than the footprint of the Main Building on the same lot (or on a lot with no Main Building) shall be permitted by Special Land Use in the AG, RR, RP, C-1, C-2, and I-1 districts, and shall be subject to the following standards. All arrays meeting the description in this Section and not explicitly exempted by the Michigan Right to Farm Act (Public Act 93 of 1981) shall be required to obtain a special use permit prior to construction. Standards include setbacks, height limits, submission of a plan for electrical grid connection, a glare study, and a decommissioning plan with a bond. Additionally, arrays greater than ten (10) acres must include crop cultivation, livestock grazing, or pollinator fields amongst the panels. Smaller solar panel arrays (smaller than the footprint of the Main Building) are permitted accessory structures in all zoning districts with other standards. Solar overlay districts as primary use are not included.

Ground mounted solar energy equipment shall not exceed a height of 16 feet from the ground measured to the highest point of the equipment. Ground mounted solar energy equipment larger than 500 square feet in area may be permitted in the Commercial Zoning Districts with special land use approval subject to site plan review and the general conditions for special land use approval or may be permitted within a Planned Unit Development. The 16 feet height limit applies generally to ground-mounted solar energy equipment, including those requiring special land use approval.

Ground mounted solar energy equipment larger than 500 square feet in area may be permitted in the Commercial Zoning Districts with special land use approval subject to site plan review and the general conditions for special land use approval or may be permitted within a Planned Unit Development. Ground mounted solar energy equipment shall not exceed a total of 500 square feet in surface area and not exceed a height of 16 feet from the ground measured to the highest point of the equipment when permitted without special approval. Solar energy equipment which provides electricity or heat only for the principal use on the lot is permitted as an accessory structure. Building mounted solar energy equipment is permitted subject to height and location restrictions.

The ordinance states: 'All commercial solar energy systems, as combined or aggregated, shall not cover more than ten percent (10%) of the total ground area in the Township.' This is the maximum land coverage allowed for utility-scale solar energy systems, which are defined as systems primarily used for generating electricity or heat for sale and/or distribution off-site. Other related coverage limits apply only to smaller scale or non-commercial systems, such as ground-mounted solar energy systems on agricultural, commercial, and industrial uses limited to 10,000 square feet, or residential uses limited to 1% of lot area up to 1,500 square feet, but these do not apply to utility-scale systems. The 10% coverage is expressed as a percentage of the total ground area in the Township.
section: Section 3.43 Solar Energy Systems, subsection B, part 1.d

summary: For Large Solar Energy Systems (no more than 2 ½ acres), the ordinance requires: obtaining a Special Use Permit, submitting a site plan approved by a State Certified Engineer, and approval from the Planning Commission. Installations must follow Grand Traverse County Building Codes. Specific requirements include: solar energy systems may not exceed five (5) feet above the existing roof surface; ground mounted solar panels shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in height in residential zones and must meet a 30-foot Greenbelt requirement; mechanical equipment must be screened from view. The applicant must submit documentation including a drainage plan and a yearly report showing power produced and sold. If the system ceases operation or is abandoned for six months or deemed unsafe or non-compliant, the owner must repair it within six months or remove it entirely at their expense within six months of notice. Removal includes posts, equipment, panels, foundations, and restoring the ground to its pre-constructed state. Additionally, the applicant must post a performance guarantee to cover removal costs in case of abandonment or failure to comply with laws. Other options include Small Solar Energy Systems (no more than 2,000 sq. ft.) and Medium Solar Energy Systems (no more than 1 acre), each with similar but distinct requirements and decommissioning provisions.

Section 3.43(B)(1)(t) Decommissioning: "A decommissioning plan shall be required and approved by the Planning Commission to ensure that the utility-scale solar energy system is properly removed after its useful life. Said plan must be filed with the Township Clerk prior to the commencement of construction of the LSES. The plan shall include provisions for removing all structures and foundations, restoring soil to a depth of 36 inches, and restoring vegetation, the timeframe for completion of decommissioning activities, estimated costs, and a plan ensuring financial resources will be available to decommission the site fully." "Any utility-scale solar energy system that has reached the end of its useful life or has not operated continuously for one (1) year or longer shall be fully removed. The parcel owners shall be required to restore the site to its prior state. The owner/operator shall physically remove the installation no more than one hundred and fifty (150) days after the date of discontinued operations." "If the owner/operator fails to remove the installation in accordance with the requirements of this Section within 150 days of abandonment or the proposed date of decommissioning, the Township may enter the property and physically remove all of the solar energy system and facilities and charge the cost back to the owner(s) of the lot." Section 3.43(B)(1)(u) Financial Guarantee: "The applicant for a utility-scale solar energy system shall provide the Township a form of monetary surety or security ... to cover the cost of removal ... The amount of the surety or security shall not exceed more than 125 percent of all costs of removal ... The surety or security shall be subject to review and approval by the Planning Commission and the Township Attorney and shall be a condition of special land use approval." Other relevant conditions include special land use approval, site plan requirements, setbacks, height limits, noise limits, screening, fencing, and maintenance obligations, all detailed in Section 3.43(B).

For the purpose of restricting unauthorized access to the site, the Planning Commission may require that the perimeter of a utility-scale solar energy system be fenced in with at least a six (6) foot-tall high fence. This fencing requirement is found in Section 3.43, subsection B, item l. Utility-scale solar energy systems are defined as systems primarily used for generating electricity or heat for sale and/or distribution off-site, with total solar collector surface area exceeding 1,500 square feet, or not considered an accessory use or structure by the Township Zoning Administrator. Other requirements for utility-scale solar energy systems include site plan approval, setbacks, height limits, noise limits, screening, glare and reflection controls, underground power lines, lighting, signage, road repair, inspections, operation and maintenance plans, emergency services cooperation, maintenance, decommissioning plans, financial guarantees, and joint responsibility of owners and landowners. Screening methods may include fencing among other options such as walls, berms, landscaping, and natural vegetation.

Large solar energy systems (no more than 2 ½ acres) must ensure that "Solar panels shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways. Traffic safety shall be protected and adjacent properties shall be protected from unreasonable glare and radiation." It is a requirement to submit a report from a state certified engineer to verify compliance. Other system sizes include Medium solar energy systems (no more than 1 acre) with similar glare restrictions and reporting requirements, and Small solar energy systems (no more than 2,000 sq. ft.) which also have glare restrictions but with less stringent reporting requirements.

The ordinance explicitly restricts glare for utility-scale solar energy systems as follows: "The exterior surfaces of utility-scale solar energy collectors shall generally be neutral in color and substantially non-reflective of light. A solar collector surface shall not be installed or located so that sunlight or glare is reflected into neighboring residences or adjacent streets." This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems defined as those primarily used for generating electricity or heat for sale and/or distribution off-site, with total collector surface area exceeding 1,500 square feet, or not considered an accessory use. Other relevant conditions for utility-scale systems include requirements for site plans, special land use approval, setbacks, height limits, noise limits, screening, location, obstruction, underground power lines, fencing, lighting, signage, road repair, inspections, operation and maintenance plans, emergency services cooperation, maintenance, decommissioning, financial guarantees, and joint responsibility with landowners. Smaller scale systems (small-scale solar energy systems) have separate glare restrictions: "The exterior surfaces of solar energy collectors shall generally be neutral in color and substantially non-reflective of light. Such collectors shall not be installed or located so that sunlight or glare is reflected into neighboring dwellings or onto adjacent roads."

For Large Solar Energy Systems, the ordinance states: 'In no instance shall ground mounted solar panels exceed twenty (20) feet in height in residential zones.' This is the explicit maximum height restriction for Large Solar Energy Systems. Other categories such as Small and Medium Solar Energy Systems have similar height limits of 20 feet for ground-mounted panels in residential zones, but the focus here is on Large Solar Energy Systems. The units for this height restriction are feet.

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall not exceed sixteen (16) feet in height, measured from the natural grade below the collector or equipment to the highest point at full tilt. (Section 3.43, subsection B, paragraph e). This is the explicit maximum height restriction for utility-scale solar energy systems, which are defined as systems primarily used for generating electricity or heat for sale and/or distribution off-site, or systems with total solar collector surface area exceeding 1,500 square feet, or not considered accessory uses. Other height limits mentioned apply only to small-scale or building-mounted solar energy systems, such as building-mounted solar energy collectors not exceeding building height maximums by more than three (3) feet, or ground-mounted solar energy collectors in agricultural, commercial, and industrial uses not exceeding sixteen (16) feet, but these are not for utility-scale systems. The unit for the height restriction is feet.

The ordinance defines a 'Large solar energy system' as a utility-scale solar energy conversion system occupying no more than 2 ½ acres of land, used to produce utility power to off-site customers. It further states that large solar energy systems 'may be installed and operated' on no more than 2 ½ acres in the A-1, A-2, and R2 districts. Other system sizes include Medium solar energy systems (no more than 1 acre) and Small solar energy systems (no more than 2,000 sq. ft.). The maximum lot size for large systems is explicitly given as 2 ½ acres, which is equivalent to 2.5 acres.

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be located on a lot at least five (5) acres in size. This is explicitly stated in Section 3.43, subsection B, part 1.c. The unit for this minimum lot size is acres, a standard measure of land area. Other lot size requirements mentioned in the text pertain to small-scale or ground-mounted solar energy systems but do not apply to utility-scale systems. For example, ground-mounted solar energy systems for agricultural, commercial, and industrial uses have a maximum collector panel size of 10,000 square feet and a minimum lot area of one (1) acre, but these apply to smaller scale systems, not utility-scale systems.

Noise emanating from the solar energy collector system shall not exceed 50 decibels (dBA) as measured from any property line. This applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in Section 3.43 subsection B. The text states: 'Noise. Noise emanating from the solar energy collector system shall not exceed 50 decibels (dBA) as measured from any property line.'
section: Section 3.43 Solar Energy Systems, subsection B Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems

summary: For Large Solar Energy Systems, excluding solar collection panels, solar energy system equipment may be installed within the required side and rear yard but shall not be closer than thirty (30) feet from any property line. Other system sizes have different setbacks: Medium systems also require 30 feet from any property line, while Small systems must not be closer than the setbacks from any property line (unspecified fixed distance).

All solar panels, buildings, and structures are required to be located at least 75 feet from any other non-participating property line or right-of-way line of any highway, road, or street. When the utility-scale solar energy system is proposed on multiple contiguous parcels, the setbacks shall be only required to be maintained along a property line where a participating parcel within the solar energy system is located contiguous to a non-participating parcel. The Planning Commission may require greater setbacks if it is determined that greater separation would better protect adjacent residents and property owners. (Other setback options include 125 feet from any occupied dwelling and its associated accessory structures, but this does not pertain to property lines.)
section: Section 3.43 B. Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems, item e. Setbacks

summary: For Large Solar Energy Systems (no more than 2 ½ acres) installed in A-1, A-2, and R2 districts, the ordinance requires a 30-foot Greenbelt and screening of any mechanical equipment from view from any public street, residential district, or agricultural district by use of a masonry screen wall, evergreen vegetation, or other screening of similar effectiveness and quality, as determined by the Planning Commission. The Planning Commission may waive some planting restrictions if existing natural features provide adequate natural screening. Similar screening and greenbelt requirements apply to Medium Solar Energy Systems (no more than 1 acre) and Small Solar Energy Systems (no more than 2,000 sq. ft.), with specific conditions such as setbacks and height limits. All systems require Special Use Permit approval, site plans, and compliance with building codes.

The ordinance states that "The Planning Commission may require a utility-scale solar energy system to be screened from adjoining residential properties or public rights-of-way." Screening methods "may include the use of material, colors, textures, screening walls, fencing, berms, landscaping, and/or natural vegetation that will blend the facility into the natural setting and existing environment." This applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in Section 3.43(B). Other related provisions include setbacks, height limits, fencing, and landscaping requirements, but only the screening provision explicitly mandates vegetative or other screening. The ordinance also distinguishes small-scale solar energy systems, which have different requirements and do not apply to utility-scale systems.

Signs are required as part of the utility-scale solar energy system to provide the public with general information about the facility's knowledge and safety. The Planning Commission shall determine the design, size, height, and location of said signs. Such signs shall only contain emergency contact numbers and information related to the utility-scale solar energy system, including the information required by Article 7 below. Other commercial speech is not permitted.

For Large Solar Energy Systems (no more than 2 ½ acres), the ordinance requires: 1) Obtain a Special Use Permit application/guidelines from the Zoning Administrator; 2) Submit a site plan, (approved by a State Certified Engineer) drawn to scale, showing existing and proposed structures, driveways, adjacent structures within 100 feet, and any other information requested by the Planning Commission; 3) Approval from the Planning Commission; 4) All installations must follow the Grand Traverse County Building Codes. Specific soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements include: "The applicant shall submit documentation to verify compliance with this section, the application shall include a drainage plan prepared by a registered civil engineer showing how storm water runoff will be managed and demonstrating that runoff from the site will not exceed the agricultural runoff rate or otherwise cause undue flooding. If detergents will be used to clean solar panels, details on the type of detergent, frequency and quantity of use, quantity and source of water, and storm water quality protection measures shall be provided. Any necessary permits from outside agencies for off-site discharge shall be provided." Additionally, upon removal, "Removal shall include removing posts, equipment, panels, foundations, and other items so that the ground is restored to its pre-constructed state and is ready for development as another use." Other system sizes include Medium Solar Energy Systems (no more than 1 acre) and Small Solar Energy Systems (no more than 2,000 sq. ft.), each with similar but distinct requirements and conditions.

Utility-scale solar energy systems are permitted as special land uses in the Agricultural District [A] ('Utility-scale solar energy systems as a principal use'), Rural Residential District [R-R] ('Utility-scale solar energy systems as a principal use'), and Industrial District [I] ('Utility-scale solar energy systems as a principal use'). Other solar energy system types such as small-scale solar energy systems are permitted as accessory uses in multiple districts, and commercial solar energy systems are listed as special land uses in the General Commercial District [C], but utility-scale systems specifically require special use approval in the three districts listed.

All Solar Panels, buildings, and structures are required to be located at least 125 feet from any occupied dwelling and its associated accessory structures. When the utility-scale solar energy system is proposed on multiple contiguous parcels, the setbacks shall be only required to be maintained along a property line where a participating parcel within the solar energy system is located contiguous to a non-participating parcel. The Planning Commission may require greater setbacks if it is determined that greater separation would better protect adjacent residents and property owners.

Large solar energy systems (no more than 2 ½ acres) require: 1) Obtain a Special Use Permit application/guidelines from the Zoning Administrator; 2) Submit a site plan, (approved by a State Certified Engineer) drawn to scale, showing existing and proposed structures, driveways, adjacent structures within 100 feet, and any other information requested by the Planning Commission necessary to determine compliance; 3) Approval from the Planning Commission; 4) All installations must follow the Grand Traverse County Building Codes. Additionally, solar panels must be placed to avoid directing concentrated solar radiation or solar glare onto nearby properties or roadways, with a required report from a state certified engineer. The applicant must submit documentation to verify compliance. Other options include Medium solar energy systems (no more than 1 acre) and Small solar energy systems (no more than 2,000 sq. ft.), each with their own specific requirements and district allowances.

Utility-scale solar energy systems require special land use approval by the Planning Commission and must meet additional standards including: "If there are existing or proposed utility-scale solar energy systems within 1 mile of another, the proposed new utility-scale solar energy system will not unreasonably visually dominate the area or horizon."; "The presence of the proposed utility-scale solar energy system shall not substantially change the aesthetic views and visual horizons of the area."; "The presence of the utility-scale solar energy system would not unreasonably distract drivers and vehicles traveling on adjacent or nearby roads."; and "The proposed utility-scale solar energy system will not change the essential character of the area or the neighborhood where the system would be located." These are part of the special land use approval standards in Section 3.43(B)(1)(b). Other requirements for utility-scale systems include site plan submission, setbacks, height limits, screening, fencing, lighting, signage, maintenance, decommissioning, financial guarantees, and inspections. Small-scale solar energy systems are regulated separately in Section 3.43(A) and do not have these visual impact assessment requirements.

SECTION 17.37 LARGE SOLAR SYSTEMS FOR UTILITY USE requires prior to construction permits, a financial surety bond for 150% of estimated decommissioning costs, updated every three years. A decommissioning plan must be provided prior to construction, requiring removal of all solar panels, electrical equipment, poles, piles, foundations and conduits (above and below ground up to a depth of four (4) feet), with access roads, fencing and other equipment allowed to remain only if consistent with future use. The plan must include an estimate of decommissioning costs and salvage value, certified by a professional, updated every five years, and be binding on the owner/operator and successors. If the system ceases operation or is abandoned for twelve (12) months or is deemed unsafe or non-compliant, the current landowner/operator shall repair and restore or remove the system entirely, restoring the ground to its preconstruction state. Other options for decommissioning requirements exist for Medium Solar Energy Systems (Section 17.36) and Medium and Large Solar Energy Systems requiring Special Land Use Approval (Section 15.47 referencing Sections 17.36 and 17.37), but only Section 17.37 explicitly details decommissioning for Large Solar Energy Systems intended for utility use.
section: SECTION 17.37 LARGE SOLAR SYSTEMS FOR UTILITY USE

summary: For Large Solar Energy Systems (SES) intended for utility use, the ordinance requires that "mechanical equipment, apparatus, and panels shall be enclosed by an eight (8’) foot standard chain link fencing (as determined by DNR requirements)." This fencing requirement is found in Section 17.37, which applies to utility grid solar energy systems designed to provide electricity to the electric utility grid. Other related fencing or screening requirements for smaller systems include: Medium Solar Energy Systems require panels to be "screened from residential districts and public rights of way by a greenbelt and/or six (6) foot high privacy fence," and Small Solar Energy Systems require mechanical equipment to be "screened from street and neighboring residences by fencing or landscaping." However, these apply to smaller or non-utility systems and not to Large Solar Energy Systems.
section: SECTION 17.37      LARGE SOLAR SYSTEMS FOR UTILITY USE

summary: Section 17.37 states: 'The SES shall not produce glare that would constitute a nuisance to occupants, neighboring properties, or persons traveling on neighboring roadways.' This applies to Large Solar Energy Systems defined as utility grid solar energy systems on parcels of at least twenty (20) acres. Other related sections include Section 17.36 for Medium Solar Energy Systems (1 to 5 acres) which requires 'documentation that glare will be eliminated, insofar as possible,' and Section 17.35 for Small Solar Energy Systems (less than 1 acre) which also requires 'documentation that glare will be eliminated, insofar as possible.' However, only Section 17.37 explicitly enacts a glare restriction for Large Solar Energy Systems.
section: SECTION 17.37      LARGE SOLAR SYSTEMS FOR UTILITY USE

summary: Section 17.37 states: 'The maximum ground-mounted panel height is twelve (12) feet measured from the grade to the top of the panel.' This applies specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems (utility grid solar energy systems or solar farms). For comparison, medium solar energy systems have a maximum ground-mounted panel height of ten (10) feet (Section 17.36), and small systems have a maximum ground-mounted panel height of eight (8) feet (Section 17.35). The units for the height restriction are feet.
section: SECTION 17.37      LARGE SOLAR SYSTEMS FOR UTILITY USE

summary: Section 17.37 states: 'The SES shall not be installed on combined parcels less than twenty (20) acres.' This is the minimum lot size for Large Solar Energy Systems (utility grid solar energy systems or solar farms). Other parcel size minimums mentioned are for smaller systems: Medium systems require parcels of at least ten (10) acres (Section 17.36), and Small systems require parcels of at least one (1) acre (Section 17.35). The units for the minimum lot size for Large Solar Energy Systems are acres.
section: SECTION 17.37      LARGE SOLAR SYSTEMS FOR UTILITY USE

summary: SECTION 17.37 LARGE SOLAR SYSTEMS FOR UTILITY USE states: 'SES shall not produce noise that exceeds 45 dBA Lmax as measured at the property lines.' This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for Large Solar Energy Systems intended for utility use. Other sections address small and medium systems but do not specify maximum noise levels. The unit 'dBA' refers to A-weighted decibels, a standard noise measurement unit.
section: SECTION 17.37 LARGE SOLAR SYSTEMS FOR UTILITY USE

summary: Large scale systems shall only be considered for utility purposes and are permitted in the I-U and I-1 District. Utility grid solar energy systems may be permitted as a special land use in I-A and AG/R Districts. All large solar systems shall be subject to, in compliance with, and provide the following: ... Since Large Solar Energy Systems are only permitted in these districts (some by special land use approval), it follows that they are unconditionally prohibited in all other zoning districts not listed here. The text does not explicitly name or abbreviate any districts where Large Solar Energy Systems are unconditionally prohibited; it only identifies the districts where they are allowed, implying prohibition elsewhere.
section: SECTION 17.37      LARGE SOLAR SYSTEMS FOR UTILITY USE

summary: The SES shall have a setback of: i. Four hundred (400) feet from the property line of any participating property. Other setbacks mentioned include 100 feet from any and all existing structures, but structures are not equivalent to property lines or parcels unless explicitly stated.
section: SECTION 17.37      LARGE SOLAR SYSTEMS FOR UTILITY USE

summary: For Large Solar Energy Systems (utility grid solar energy systems or solar farms), Section 17.37 requires that "Panels shall be screened from residential/agricultural districts and public rights-of-way by a greenbelt (consisting of three staggered rows of evergreen trees chosen from the list in Section 17.16.3.a, not less than 5 feet tall at time of planting, with 15 foot spacing between the trees in each row). The Planning Commission may require supplemental plantings of small evergreens and/or deciduous shrubs. Planting requirements may be reduced by the Planning Commission (but not eliminated) only when existing natural vegetation accomplishes a substantial portion of the screening requirement. The greenbelt must be seasonally maintained and dead trees must be replaced as soon as possible." Other solar system categories (small and medium) also have screening requirements, such as mechanical equipment being screened by fencing or landscaping, and panels being screened from residential districts and public rights of way by a greenbelt and/or six (6) foot high privacy fence, with possible waivers if natural vegetation accomplishes the same. However, these apply to smaller or different system types. The large system screening requirement is specific and detailed for utility-scale systems.
section: SECTION 17.37      LARGE SOLAR SYSTEMS FOR UTILITY USE

summary: For Large Solar Energy Systems (SES) under SECTION 17.37 LARGE SOLAR SYSTEMS FOR UTILITY USE, the ordinance states: 'No signage will be allowed except for that required to preserve public and employee safety, and that required by federal, state, county and township regulations. A sign shall be posted providing the name(s) of operator(s) and a phone number in case of an onsite emergency.' Other options and conditions for solar energy systems include Small Solar Energy Systems (Section 17.35) and Medium Solar Energy Systems (Section 17.36), but these sections do not explicitly mention signage requirements for large or utility-scale systems.
section: SECTION 17.37 LARGE SOLAR SYSTEMS FOR UTILITY USE

summary: The ordinance requires a decommissioning plan for Commercial Solar Energy Facilities (CSEF) to be submitted prior to the issuance of the development permit. The plan must include: defined conditions upon which decommissioning will be initiated (e.g., end of land lease, no power production for 12 months, abandonment), removal of all non-utility owned equipment, conduit, structures, fencing, roads, solar panels and foundations, restoration of property to condition prior to development of the CSEF, the time frame for completion of decommissioning activities, description of any agreement with landowner regarding decommissioning, the party currently responsible for decommissioning, and plans for updating the decommissioning plan. Additionally, a CSEF that ceases to produce energy on a continuous basis for 12 months will be considered abandoned unless the responsible party provides substantial evidence of intent to maintain and reinstate operation. Upon abandonment determination, the responsible party must remove the CSEF and restore the site within 360 days of notice. Failure to comply allows the zoning administrator to remove the facility and recover costs. These requirements apply specifically to CSEF defined as facilities that sell electricity to be used off-site.

CSEF shall be fenced completely as defined in definitions above. The perimeter fence shall be designed to restrict unauthorized access. If a wire fence is used, vegetation must be planted along the sides and adjoining a public road. Each owner, operator or maintainer of a CSEF who chooses to use vegetation with wire fence shall utilize good husbandry techniques including proper pruning, fertilizer, and mulching so that the vegetation will reach maturity as soon as practical and have maximum density in foliage. Dead or diseased vegetation shall be removed and replaced at the next appropriate planting time. Plants or grasses not part of landscaping shall be maintained by the facility operator not to exceed 10 inches in height.

summary: Section 7.31.C.9 states: 'A condition of every approval of a Commercial Solar Energy System shall be adequate provision for the removal of the system whenever it ceases to be used for one (1) year or more. In the event that a system has been abandoned (meaning not having been in operation for a period of one (1) year), the property owner and developer/applicant shall notify the Township and shall remove the system within one (1) year from the date of abandonment. Removal includes the proper receipt of a demolition permit from the Building Official and proper restoration of the site to the satisfaction of the Zoning Administrator. The site shall then be filled and covered with topsoil and restored to a state compatible with the surrounding vegetation.' Section 7.31.C.10 requires financial security guaranteeing removal, which must be posted within fifteen (15) days after approval or before a construction permit is issued, in the form of a cash bond, irrevocable bank letter of credit, or performance bond, with the amount no less than the estimated cost of removal. Section 7.31.C.11 provides that if the owner fails to remove the system, the Township may pursue legal action to abate the violation and recover costs including attorney fees. These requirements apply specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems intended to provide energy to off-site uses or for wholesale or retail sale of electricity, and are only allowed as a special use in Agricultural-Residential or Industrial Districts, subject to additional conditions such as minimum parcel size, setbacks, height limits, screening, and sound level limits.

Section 7.31.A.2 states: 'Solar Energy Systems shall be located or placed so that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed toward or onto nearby properties or roadways at any time of the day.' Commercial Solar Energy Systems are defined as systems 'where the principal design, purpose or use of such system is to provide energy to off-site uses or the wholesale or retail sale of generated electricity to any person or entity.' Commercial Solar Energy Systems are subject to special use approval and must be ground mounted, located on parcels no less than twenty (20) acres, set back 200 feet from non-participating property lines, not exceed 15 feet in height at maximum tilt, and be screened year-round from residential uses and public rights-of-way. Other requirements include sound limits, site plan submission, interconnection agreements, removal upon abandonment, financial security for removal, and repowering provisions.

The height of the Commercial Solar Energy System and any mounts shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet when oriented at maximum tilt. This is specified in Section 7.31, subsection C, item 4. Other height restrictions mentioned in the ordinance apply only to Private Solar Energy Systems, such as ground mounted private systems not exceeding fifteen (15) feet above the ground at maximum tilt, but these do not apply to Commercial Solar Energy Systems.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems shall be located on parcels of land no less than twenty (20) acres in size. This is explicitly stated in Section 7.31, subsection C, item 2. The unit 'acres' is used as the area measurement for the minimum lot size.

The sound pressure level of a solar energy facility and all ancillary solar equipment shall not exceed fifty-five (55) forty-five (45) dBA (Leq (1 hour)) at the property line of an adjacent non-participating lot. The most restrictive value is 45 dBA. This applies specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance.

summary: Commercial Solar Energy Systems "shall only be allowed in the Agricultural-Residential District or the Industrial District as a special use approved by the Planning Commission." This means they are not permitted in the Residential (R), Forest-Residential (F-R), or Commercial (C) districts. In contrast, Commercial Solar Energy Systems are allowed as a special use in the Agricultural-Residential District (A-R) and the Industrial District (I).
