section: Section 7.31. SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS, C. COMMERCIAL SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS

summary: Section 7.31, subsection C, item 12 states: "Repowering: In addition to repairing or replacing solar energy components to maintain the system, a solar energy facility may at any time be repowered, without the need to apply for a new Special Use permit, by reconfiguring, renovating, or replacing the solar energy components to increase the power rating within the existing project footprint. A proposal to change the project footprint of an existing solar energy facility shall be considered a new application, subject to the ordinance standards at the time of the request." This applies specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which "shall be ground mounted and are subject to the following requirements" including minimum parcel size, setbacks, height limits, screening, sound limits, site plan submission, interconnection agreements, removal upon abandonment, financial security for removal, and enforcement provisions. Other options for solar energy systems include Private Solar Energy Systems and Building Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPVs), which have separate requirements and are not subject to this repowering provision.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems shall be ground mounted and are subject to the following requirements: "Solar devices shall be screened year-round from view from any existing residential use and the public right-of-way by use of a screening wall, evergreen vegetation, or other screening of similar effectiveness and quality, as determined by the Planning Commission." Screening "shall be installed which screen the facility fully from view from the time of planting or installation" and "shall be maintained throughout the life of the facility including replacing dead vegetation within six (6) months or at the earliest feasible time of the year dependant on the weather."

Commercial Solar Energy Systems shall only be allowed in the Agricultural-Residential District or the Industrial District as a special use approved by the Planning Commission. The ordinance states: 'Commercial Solar Energy Systems shall only be allowed in the Agricultural-Residential District or the Industrial District as a special use approved by the Planning Commission.' Other solar energy systems such as Private Solar Energy Systems are permitted by right in all zoning districts, and roof or ground mounted private systems are considered accessory uses. The ordinance also details specific requirements for Commercial Solar Energy Systems including minimum parcel size, setbacks, height limits, screening, sound levels, site plan submission, interconnection agreements, removal conditions, and financial security for removal.

Section 6A.41 Solar Energy, Large Systems establishes standards for the siting, installation, operation, repair, decommissioning and removal of Large Solar Energy Systems. It requires that "the applicant shall perform decommissioning and removal of the Large Solar Energy System and all its components" when the project becomes obsolete, uneconomic or abandoned. A decommissioning plan "prepared by a Professional Engineer licensed in the State of Michigan" must be submitted for review as part of the Conditional Use Permit. The plan requires removal of "all structures, equipment, conduit, fencing, roads and structure foundations, including any equipment, structures or materials below-grade, and removed offsite for disposal" with no materials left in place. The ground must be restored to its original condition and revegetated within 180 days. A geotechnical soil report must be submitted demonstrating that post-decommissioning soil conditions are reasonable compared to pre-development conditions. Continuing security and escrow deposits are required to ensure compliance with decommissioning and removal obligations, including a financial guarantee to restore the property to its previous condition and an escrow deposit to cover enforcement costs. Failure to maintain these financial securities constitutes a material violation subject to enforcement and permit revocation. These requirements apply specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems, defined as utility-scale systems with power output equal to or greater than one (1) megawatt and intended for sale, delivery or consumption by more than one end user.

A Large Solar Energy System "shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access." The fencing "shall be at least seven (7) feet and no more than eight (8) feet in height as measured from the natural grade of the fencing perimeter." "Electric fencing is not permitted." The fencing system "shall have openings that allow wildlife to traverse over or through the fenced area." Additionally, "The perimeter of Large Solar Energy Systems shall also be screened and buffered by buffer areas whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels," with detailed requirements for evergreen or native vegetative buffers. These requirements are found in Section 6A.41, subsection M (Screening/Security).

Section 6A.41 Solar Energy, Large Systems includes the glare restriction: 'All solar panels shall be placed such that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways (public or private) at any time of the day.' This applies specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems, defined as utility-scale systems with power output equal to or greater than one (1) megawatt, intended for sale, delivery, or consumption by more than one end user. Other related provisions include requirements for site plans, environmental impact studies, setbacks, screening/security, height limits, and compliance with safety codes, but only subsection Q explicitly addresses glare. The ordinance also includes a similar glare provision for all Solar Energy Systems in Section 6A.39 G: 'All Solar Energy Systems must be installed in a manner ensuring that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways.' However, Section 6A.39 primarily addresses Small Solar Energy Systems and general solar system regulations, while Section 6A.41 specifically governs Large Solar Energy Systems as a conditional use.

Section 6A.41, subsection H states: 'Maximum height of a Solar Array shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet. Other collection devices, components or buildings of the Large Solar Energy System shall not exceed thirty-five (35) feet, or the maximum building height permitted within the district in which that Solar Energy System in located, whichever is less, at any time or location on the property.' The height is measured from the natural grade at the base of the Solar Array, device, component or building. The Planning Commission may waive or modify these height requirements for certain aspects of a Solar Energy System through conditions when appropriate.

Section 6A.41, subsection I states: 'A Large Solar Energy System shall be located on one (1) or more parcels with an aggregate area of Eighty (80) contiguous acres or smaller.' This explicitly sets a maximum aggregate lot size of 80 acres for Large Solar Energy Systems. The units are acres, a standard measure of land area.

Section 6A.41, subsection I states: 'A Large Solar Energy System shall be located on one (1) or more parcels with an aggregate area of Eighty (80) contiguous acres or smaller.' This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for Large Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as utility-scale systems typically with power output equal to or greater than one (1) megawatt. No other minimum lot size values are provided for Large Solar Energy Systems in the text. The unit of measurement is acres, a standard area unit.
No component of any Large Solar Energy System shall emit noise exceeding fifty (45) dBA averaged over a one (1) hour period as measured at the outside perimeter of the project.

A minimum setback distance of one-hundred (100) feet from all property boundaries on the outside perimeter of the Large Solar Energy System shall be required for all buildings and Solar Arrays except for property boundaries where the applicable adjoining owner(s) agree to lessen or increase that setback distance by executing a signed written waiver of this requirement in recordable form, provided no such waiver shall act to permit less than the required minimum setback of the applicable zoning district.
section: Section 6A.41 Solar Energy, Large Systems, subsection K. Setbacks

summary: Section 6A.41, subsection M (Screening/Security) requires that a Large Solar Energy System "shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access" with fencing "at least seven (7) feet and no more than eight (8) feet in height" and prohibits electric fencing. The perimeter "shall also be screened and buffered by buffer areas whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels." If natural forest vegetation does not meet the minimum spacing and height requirements, "a continuous evergreen vegetative buffer shall be installed and maintained at all times at the perimeter of all Large Solar Energy Systems, including without limitation between such Large Solar Energy Systems and adjacent residential or agricultural areas and/or public highways or streets." The evergreen or native vegetative buffer "shall be composed of native or evergreen trees that at the time of planting shall be a minimum of four (4) feet in height, with shrubs being at least two (2) feet in height." Spacing requirements are: evergreen trees no more than fifteen (15) feet apart on center, native trees no more than thirty (30) feet apart on center, and shrubs no more than seven (7) feet apart on center. Unhealthy or dead material must be replaced within six (6) months or the next appropriate planting period. Plantings must be installed between March 15 and October 15, or a financial guarantee must be provided. Failure to maintain the buffer constitutes a violation and grounds for revocation of the conditional use permit.

No lettering, company insignia, advertising, graphics or other commercially-oriented inscriptions or designs shall be on any part of the Solar Arrays or other components of the Large Solar Energy System. This section does not prohibit signs reasonably necessary to inform the public of potential safety hazards associated with the Large Solar Energy System, nor does it prohibit any other signs that may be required by this Ordinance, the conditional use permit or other applicable law.
section: Section 6A.41 Solar Energy, Large Systems, subsection N. Signage

summary: Section 6A.41(A)(5) requires a geotechnical report, prepared by a Professional Engineer licensed in the State of Michigan, demonstrating appropriate foundation designs and pavement designs based on findings of the geotechnical soil report, including in-situ soil conditions prior to development. Section 6A.41(C) requires "a written description of measures to be taken to support the flow of rainwater throughout the Large Solar Energy System, including any measures to promote the growth of vegetation beneath the arrays or otherwise limit the impacts of storm water runoff," subject to approval by the Eaton County Drain Commission. Section 6A.41(W) mandates that "geotechnical soil analysis shall be performed and a geotechnical soil report submitted demonstrating that the post-decommissioning soil conditions are reasonable to in-situ soil conditions prior to project development," prepared by a Professional Engineer licensed in Michigan, with possible verification by the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy (EGLE). These requirements explicitly address soil, erosion, and sediment control for Large Solar Energy Systems.

Section 6A.41 states that Large Solar Energy Systems are established as a conditional use, requiring standards for siting, installation, operation, repair, decommissioning, and removal. It references that the maximum amount of Township land developed as Large-Scale Solar Energy System Facilities shall not exceed fifty percent (50%) of the combined acreage of the Commercial and Industrial Districts within the Township, but does not explicitly state that these districts permit Large Solar Energy Systems as a special or conditional use. Section 6A.39 addresses Small Solar Energy Systems only and is not relevant to Large Solar Energy Systems. No solar overlay districts are mentioned.

Section 6A.41 Solar Energy, Large Systems requires that all applications for a Large Solar Energy System be accompanied by detailed site plans, including "horizontal and vertical (elevation) scale drawings with dimensions that show the location of the proposed Solar Array(s), buildings, structures, electrical tie lines and transmission lines, security fencing and all above ground structures and utilities on the property" and "land elevations for the Solar Array(s) location and the relationship to the land elevations of all existing and proposed structures within the Large Solar Energy System." Additionally, "The perimeter of Large Solar Energy Systems shall also be screened and buffered by buffer areas whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels," with options including a "continuous evergreen vegetative buffer" composed of native or evergreen trees and shrubs meeting specified height and spacing requirements. Failure to maintain the buffer is grounds for revocation of the conditional use permit. The Planning Commission may impose additional reasonable conditions including landscaping, walls, fences and other improvements consistent with the nature of the zoning districts. These requirements explicitly address visual impact assessment and mitigation for Large Solar Energy Systems.

Section 7.31.C.9 states: 'A condition of every approval of a Commercial Solar Energy System shall have an adequate provision for the removal of the system whenever it ceases to be used for one (1) year or more. In the event that a system has been abandoned (meaning not having been in operation for a period of one (1) year). Either the zoning administrator or the property owner and developer/applicant shall notify the Township that the SES is abandoned, and the property owner and developer/applicant shall remove the system within one (1) year from the date of abandonment. Removal includes the proper receipt of a demolition permit from the Building Official and proper restoration of the site to the satisfaction of the Zoning Administrator. The site shall then be filled and covered with topsoil and restored to a state compatible with the surrounding vegetation.' Section 7.31.C.10 requires financial security: 'applications shall include a description of the financial security guaranteeing removal of the system which must be posted with the Township within fifteen (15) days after approval or before a construction permit is issued for the facility. The financial security shall be a performance bond (surety bond), in a form approved by the Township. The amount of such guarantee shall be no less than 150% of the estimated cost of removal and may include a provision for inflationary cost adjustments.' The Planning Commission shall annually review and require adjustments if necessary. Section 7.31.C.11 provides enforcement: 'If the owner of the facility or the property owner fails to remove or repair the defective or abandoned Commercial Solar Energy System, the Township ... may pursue legal action to abate the violation by seeking to remove the Solar Energy System and recover any and all costs, including attorney fees.' Other options for solar energy systems (Private SES) have separate removal requirements, but these do not apply to Commercial SES.

The height of the Commercial Solar Energy System and any mounts shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet when oriented at maximum tilt. This is explicitly stated in Section 7.31, subsection C, item 3. The units are feet as indicated in the text. Other height restrictions mentioned apply only to Private Solar Energy Systems, such as ground mounted private systems not exceeding fifteen (15) feet and roof-mounted private systems not extending more than two (2) feet above the roof surface, but these do not apply to Commercial Solar Energy Systems.

The sound pressure level of a solar energy facility and all ancillary solar equipment shall not exceed forty-five (45) dBA (Leq (1 hour)) at the property line of an adjacent non-participating lot at 2 a.m. This restriction applies specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance.

summary: The Commercial Solar Energy System all Photovoltaic (PV) systems and support structures associated with such facilities (excluding perimeter fencing) shall be setback a minimum of forty (40) feet from a side or rear property line and a minimum of fifty (50) feet from any road right-of-way. summary: Commercial Solar Energy Systems shall be ground mounted and are subject to the following requirements: "Solar devices shall be screened year-round from view from any existing residential use and the public right-of-way by use of a screening wall of native shrubbery, trees, or other native, non-invasive plant species that provide a visual screen of effectiveness and quality, as determined by the Planning Commission. Commercial Solar Energy Systems shall only be allowed in the Agricultural-Residential District or the Industrial District as a special use approved by the Planning Commission. Section 1502 – Large Solar Energy Systems requires that "following the operational life of the project, or at the time the project becomes obsolete, uneconomic or an Abandoned Solar Energy System, as determined by the Township Engineer or any other expert or specialist to be designated by the Township to make such a determination, the applicant shall perform decommissioning and removal of the Large Solar Energy System and all its components." The applicant must "prepare a decommissioning plan and submit it to the Planning Commission for review prior to issuance of the special use permit." Additionally, subsection 22 requires "continuing security and a continuing escrow deposit prior to commencement of construction, which shall remain in effect until the Large Solar Energy System has been finally removed," including a "Continuing Restoration Security" and a "Continuing Compliance and Enforcement Escrow Deposit" to ensure compliance with decommissioning and removal obligations. Failure to maintain these securities constitutes a violation and may lead to enforcement actions or revocation of the special use permit.

Section 21.48.4.15 Abandonment or Decommissioning requires that any large-scale ground-mounted solar energy system which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned shall be removed within one hundred fifty (150) days after discontinued operations. The owner or operator must notify the Planning Commission or Zoning Administrator by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Decommissioning shall consist of: a) Physical removal of all solar energy systems, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines from the site; b) Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations; c) Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion. The Site Plan Review Authority may allow leaving landscaping or designated below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and disruption. Abandonment is defined as failure to operate for more than one (1) year without written consent. If removal is not completed within 150 days of abandonment or proposed decommissioning, the County may enter and remove the system after a court order and charge costs to the responsible party. Per Section 25.6, a performance guarantee may be required to cover removal costs. Other sections provide permit criteria and operational requirements but do not explicitly address decommissioning.

A Large Solar Energy System "shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access. Such fencing shall be 8 feet in height as measured from the natural grade of the fencing perimeter. Electric fencing is not permitted." Additionally, the perimeter "shall also be screened and buffered by buffer areas whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels," with detailed requirements for evergreen vegetative buffers. Other setback requirements include a minimum 60-foot front, side, and rear yard setback for all improved areas, and a minimum 25-foot setback from the associated perimeter fencing for solar panels, electrical inverters, storage buildings, and access roads (which may be reduced to 20 feet if an opaque fence is installed).

Solar Energy Facility (Utility-Scale)* (§7.35) is permitted with a Special Use Permit (S) in the Agricultural (A) and Forest/Recreational (FR) districts, indicating a conditional or secondary use status. In the Industrial (I) district, it is permitted by right (P), representing a primary use. It is not permitted in the R-1, R-2, or Commercial (C) districts. The ordinance uses the designations 'P = Permitted by right' and 'S = Permitted with a Special Use Permit' to distinguish primary from accessory or conditional uses.

summary: Utility-scale solar energy systems require a decommissioning plan to be submitted and approved prior to the issuance of a zoning permit, including provisions for removal of all equipment, structures, and foundations and restoration of the site to its pre-development condition. A performance guarantee must be provided to ensure proper decommissioning. Any solar energy system not operated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months shall be considered abandoned and must be removed within ninety (90) days of notice, including removal of all equipment, structures, and foundations to a depth of at least forty-eight (48" ) inches below grade and restoration of the site to its pre-development condition. Utility-scale solar energy systems are permitted only in Agricultural (AG) and Industrial (I) zoning districts as a Special Land Use, subject to requirements including minimum lot size of twenty (20) acres, setbacks, height limits, and screening. Other solar energy systems such as building-mounted and ground-mounted have different height, setback, and screening requirements but do not have explicit decommissioning requirements detailed here.

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be screened from adjacent properties and public rights-of-way by landscaping, fencing, or other screening methods approved by the Planning Commission. (Section 7.35 H.5) Other options for screening include landscaping or other screening methods, but fencing is explicitly mentioned as one of the approved methods. This requirement applies to utility-scale solar energy systems defined as "a solar energy system that is designed and intended to supply energy primarily into a utility grid for sale to the general public or for off-site consumption."

Solar collection devices, or combination of devices, shall be designed and located to avoid glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard. Glare intensity is considered an issue if it measures more than twenty (20%) percent of the incident sun intensity. Plans to reduce glare may be required in the initial materials submitted. This applies to Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems defined as systems designed and intended to supply energy primarily into a utility grid for sale to the general public or for off-site consumption. Other related provisions include setbacks, screening, height limits, and decommissioning plans, but these do not specifically address glare.

The maximum height of any structure associated with a utility-scale solar energy system shall not exceed twenty (20’) feet above grade. This is explicitly stated in Section 7.35, subsection H.4. Other height limits mentioned in the text apply to building-mounted solar energy systems (not exceeding maximum building height by more than 5 feet) and ground-mounted solar energy systems (not exceeding 15 feet above grade), which do not apply to utility-scale systems. The unit 'feet' is used consistently in the ordinance.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'Minimum lot size for a utility-scale solar energy system shall be twenty (20) acres.' This is a clear minimum lot size requirement for utility-scale solar energy systems, which are defined as systems designed and intended to supply energy primarily into a utility grid for sale to the general public or for off-site consumption. No other minimum lot size values are provided for utility-scale systems in the text.

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall comply with the following minimum setbacks: a. One hundred (100’) feet from any property line. (Section 7.35 H.3.a) Other setback values include two hundred (200’) feet from any residential dwelling unit on an adjacent property (H.3.b) and fifty (50’) feet from all property lines for solar collection devices and ancillary equipment (Section 7.35 A.4), but the 100 feet from property lines is the most directly applicable fixed setback for property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, parcels, and/or subdivisions.

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be screened from adjacent properties and public rights-of-way by landscaping, fencing, or other screening methods approved by the Planning Commission. Additionally, solar devices shall be screened from view from any residential district or use by use of a masonry screen wall, evergreen vegetation, or other screening of a similar effectiveness and quality, if determined as necessary by the Planning Commission. These screening requirements apply specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems designed to supply energy primarily into a utility grid for sale or off-site consumption. Other options for screening include masonry screen walls and evergreen vegetation, with the Planning Commission having discretion to approve other methods. The ordinance also includes setback and height requirements, but these are separate from screening.

Solar Energy Facility (Utility-Scale)* (§7.35) is permitted with a Special Use Permit (S) in the Agricultural District (A) and Forest/Recreational District (FR). In the Industrial District (I), it is permitted by right (P). It is not listed as permitted or special use in R-1, R-2, or Commercial (C) districts. The text uses the designations 'P = Permitted by right' and 'S = Permitted with a Special Use Permit' to indicate conditions.

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall comply with the following minimum setbacks: Two hundred (200’) feet from any residential dwelling unit on an adjacent property. Other setback options include one hundred (100’) feet from any property line, but this does not pertain to occupied dwellings.

summary: Section 7.30.C.3 states: 'No more than 20% of the total lot area may be covered by a Commercial Solar Energy System.' This applies to all Commercial Solar Energy Systems, including those with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more. The ordinance clarifies in subsection D that for Commercial Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more, the provisions in subsection C apply except where there is a conflict, and no different maximum land coverage is specified. Therefore, the maximum land coverage allowed is 20 percent of the total lot area.

Section 7.30.C.12 states: 'If a Commercial Solar Energy System is abandoned or otherwise nonoperational for a period of one year, the property owner or the operator must notify the Township and must remove the system within six (6) months after the date of abandonment. Removal requires receipt of a demolition permit from the Building Official and full restoration of the site to the satisfaction of the Zoning Administrator. The site must be filled and covered with top soil and restored to a state compatible with the surrounding vegetation.' Section 7.30.C.13 requires: 'Financial security in the form of a security bond, escrow payment, or irrevocable letter of credit in an amount equal to 125% of the total estimated cost of decommissioning, code enforcement, and reclamation, which cost estimate must be approved by the Township.' Section 7.30.D applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more and states that 'to the extent these provisions conflict with the provisions in subsection C above, the provisions below control as to such Commercial Solar Energy Systems.' However, subsection D does not explicitly alter decommissioning requirements but focuses on setbacks, fencing, height, noise, lighting, environmental regulations, and host community agreements. Therefore, the ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements including removal, site restoration, notification, and financial security for Commercial Solar Energy Systems, including those with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more.

Fencing for Commercial Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more must comply with the latest version of the National Electric Code as November 29, 2024, or as subsequently amended. This requirement is stated in subsection D, which applies to such systems under PA 233 of 2023. Additionally, subsection C (applying generally to Commercial Solar Energy Systems) requires that greenbelt screening is required around any Commercial Solar Energy System and around any equipment associated with the system to obscure, to the greatest extent possible, the Solar Energy System from any adjacent residences. The greenbelt must consist of shrubbery, trees, or other non-invasive plant species that provide a visual screen. In lieu of a planting greenbelt, a decorative fence that is at least 50% opaque and that meets the requirements of this Ordinance applicable to fences may be used if approved by the Planning Commission. Other fencing-related provisions include security fencing around all electrical equipment related to the Commercial Solar Energy System, including any transformers and transfer stations, with appropriate warning signs posted at safe intervals at the entrance and around the perimeter of the system. The subsection D fencing requirement supersedes subsection C to the extent of any conflict for systems 50 MW or larger. Other options and conditions include: greenbelt screening or decorative fencing (50% opaque) approved by the Planning Commission for general Commercial Solar Energy Systems; security fencing specifically around electrical equipment; and the PA 233 subsection D fencing requirement for 50 MW+ systems.

For a solar energy facility, all of the following: (ii) Fencing for the solar energy facility complies with the latest version of the National Electric Code as of November 29, 2024 or any applicable successor standard approved by the Michigan Public Service Commission as provided in MCL 460.1226(8)(a)(ii). This applies to solar energy facilities defined as systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more, intended for sale or use in locations other than solely the solar energy facility property.

The ordinance requires that "Solar Energy Systems must be located or placed so that concentrated solar glare is not directed toward or onto nearby properties or roadways at any time of the day." For Commercial Solar Energy Systems, "The Commercial Solar Energy System must not produce any glare that is visible to neighboring lots or to persons traveling on public or private roads." These glare restrictions apply to all Commercial Solar Energy Systems, including those with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more, as subsection D states that all provisions in subsection C that do not conflict remain in full force and effect. Other relevant provisions for Commercial Solar Energy Systems include requirements for setbacks, height limits, noise limits, lighting, screening, fencing, and decommissioning, among others.

For Commercial Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more under PA 233 of 2023, the ordinance states: 'Solar panel components must not exceed a maximum height of 25 feet above ground when the arrays are at full tilt.' This provision controls over the general Commercial Solar Energy System height limit of 15 feet in subsection C. The height restriction applies specifically to solar panel components and is measured above ground level.

summary: For a solar energy facility, all of the following: (iii) Solar panel components do not exceed a maximum height of 25 feet above ground when the arrays are at full tilt. Commercial Solar Energy Systems must be located on parcels of land twenty (20) acres in size or larger. This is stated explicitly in Section 7.30.C.2.b: 'Commercial Solar Energy Systems must be located on parcels of land twenty (20) acres in size or larger.' This minimum lot size applies specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems intended to provide energy to off-site uses or for wholesale or retail sale. The units are acres, a standard area measurement. Other related provisions include setback requirements, height limits, and special use permits, but no other minimum lot size values are given for these systems.

Section 7.30.D states: 'The Commercial Solar Energy System must not generate a maximum sound in excess of 55 average hourly decibels as modeled at the nearest outer wall of the nearest dwelling located on an adjacent nonparticipating property. Decibel modeling shall use the A-weighted scale as designed by the American National Standards Institute.' This applies specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more once PA 233 of 2023 is in effect. Other noise limits for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (not specifically 50 MW+) in Section 7.30.C.8 set a maximum of 40 dBA Lmax at property lines and neighboring residences during certain hours, but the 55 dBA limit in Section 7.30.D controls for 50 MW+ systems. The units are dBA, the standard A-weighted decibel scale.

The solar energy facility does not generate a maximum sound in excess of 55 average hourly decibels as modeled at the nearest outer wall of the nearest occupied community building or dwelling on nonparticipating properties. The noise level shall use the A-weighted scale as designed by the American National Standards Institute.

summary: Commercial Solar Energy Systems are allowed only in the Renewable Energy Overlay Area and "are not permitted on any properties enrolled in the PA 116 Farmland and Open Space Preservation Program." Other uses and districts include Private Solar Energy Systems permitted in all zoning districts (roof or building mounted) or in AG (Agricultural) district for ground mounted private systems, with various permit and special use requirements.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems (including all solar panels, structures, and equipment) must be set back 500 feet from all lot lines and public road rights-of-way. If a single Commercial Solar Energy System is located on more than one lot, then the lot-line setbacks of this subsection do not apply to the lot lines shared by those lots. Additionally, under PA 233 provisions for systems with 50 megawatts or more, setbacks must be measured from the nearest edge of the perimeter fencing of the facility, including 50 feet from the nearest shared property line of nonparticipating parties. This provision controls over the general commercial solar setback of 500 feet from public road rights-of-way stated in Section 7.30.C.2.d, which applies to commercial systems generally. The 500-foot setback applies to all commercial solar energy systems, but the 50-foot setback specifically applies to systems 50 MW or more once PA 233 is in effect.

For a solar energy facility, all of the following: (i) The following minimum setback requirements, with setback distances measured from the nearest edge of the perimeter fencing of the facility: Public road right-of-way 50 feet measured from the nearest edge of a public road right-of-way. Other setback options include 300 feet from occupied community buildings and dwellings on nonparticipating properties, and 50 feet from nonparticipating parties' shared property lines.

Section 7.30.C.5 states: 'Greenbelt screening is required around any Commercial Solar Energy System and around any equipment associated with the system to obscure, to the greatest extent possible, the Solar Energy System from any adjacent residences. The ordinance requires Commercial Solar Energy Systems to provide "proof of environmental compliance, including compliance with Part 91, Soil Erosion and Sedimentation Control (MCL 324.9101 et. seq.) and any corresponding County ordinances" as part of the application (Section 7.30.C.1.n). These requirements apply to all Commercial Solar Energy Systems requiring a special land use permit and site plan review. For Commercial Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more, subsection D states they must comply with "applicable state or federal environmental regulations" (Section 7.30.D.f). Other provisions for Commercial Solar Energy Systems include setbacks, height limits, noise limits, screening, underground transmission, decommissioning, and financial security. Private Solar Energy Systems have separate requirements and are not the focus here.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems are allowed only in the Renewable Energy Overlay Area and require a special land use permit and site plan review. "Commercial Solar Energy Systems are allowed only in the Renewable Energy Overlay Area (except they are not permitted on any properties enrolled in the PA 116 Farmland and Open Space Preservation Program) and require a special land use permit and site plan review." Additionally, for Commercial Solar Energy Systems with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more, "On or after November 29, 2024, once PA 233 of 2023 is in effect, the following provisions apply... Other options for solar energy systems include Private Solar Energy Systems permitted in all zoning districts (roof or building mounted) or in AG district (ground mounted with special use permit), but these do not apply to commercial systems of 50 MW or more.

The application to construct a solar energy facility (50 megawatts or more) is processed as a special land use subject to review by the Planning Commission and Township Board, with specific standards including setbacks, fencing, height limits, sound limits, and lighting requirements. Specifically, Section 4.7.C states: 'Subject to the specific provisions applicable to the special land use, the following uses may be allowed in the AG-F District: ... 9) Solar energy facilities.' This indicates solar energy facilities require special permit approval in the AG-F district. Section 702(l) Decommissioning requires the applicant of a solar farm to submit a decommissioning plan prior to project approval. The plan shall include: 1) the anticipated life of the project, 2) the estimated decommissioning costs net of salvage value in current dollars, 3) the method of ensuring that funds will be available for decommissioning and restoration, and 4) the anticipated manner in which the project will be decommissioned and the site restored. Any foundation shall be removed to a minimum depth of four (4) feet below grade, by the owner of the facility or its assigned. Following removal, the location of any solar farm foundation shall be identified on a map as such and recorded with the deed to the property with the Saginaw County Register of Deeds. Any access roads shall be removed, cleared, and graded by the owner of the large wind energy facility or its assigns, unless the property owner requests in writing a desire to maintain the access road. The Township will not be assumed to take ownership of any access road unless through official action of the Township Board. A performance bond or equivalent financial instrument shall be posted in an amount determined by the Township [to be utilized in the event the decommissioning plan needs to be enforced with the respect to the panel removal, site restoration, etc.]. The bond shall be in favor of Lakefield Township and may be provided jointly as a single instrument for multiple townships within a solar farm, provided that such single instrument shall be in an amount of at least $1 million/unit and shall contain a replenishment obligation. In the event of bankruptcy, there needs to be protection with a prepayment within three (3) years.

Section 702(f) states: 'A security fence (height and material to be established through the special use permit process) shall be placed around the perimeter of the solar power plant and electrical equipment shall be locked.' This fencing requirement applies specifically to large photovoltaic solar farm facilities, which are defined as facilities constructed on parcels of at least twenty (20) acres, with photovoltaic panels restricted to a height of fourteen (14) feet, and intended for large-scale solar energy generation. The ordinance also includes other provisions such as minimum lot size, height restrictions, setbacks, noise limits, landscaping, and special use criteria, but only the fencing requirement in subsection (f) explicitly mandates a security fence for large solar farms.

Section 702(c) states: 'All photovoltaic panels located in a solar farm shall be restricted to a height of fourteen (14) feet.' This applies explicitly to large photovoltaic solar farm facilities. Other height restrictions mentioned in the text apply only to smaller or residential systems and are not relevant for large solar farms.

Section 702(b) states: 'Large photovoltaic solar farm facilities shall not be constructed on parcels less than twenty (20) acres in size.' This is the explicit minimum lot size for large photovoltaic solar farm facilities. Other minimum parcel sizes mentioned, such as 15,000 square feet, apply only to smaller or accessory solar energy systems and are not relevant to large photovoltaic solar farm facilities. The unit 'acres' is used to specify the minimum lot size.

Section 702(g) states: 'No large photovoltaic solar farm facilities shall exceed forty-five (45) dBA as measured at the property line.' This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for large photovoltaic solar farm facilities, which are defined as large systems subject to reasonable conditions to protect public health, safety, and welfare. The unit 'dBA' refers to A-weighted decibels, a standard noise measurement unit.
All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with such facilities (excluding perimeter security fencing) shall be a minimum of ten (10) feet highway right-of-way.

Section 702(h) Landscaping requires large photovoltaic solar farm facilities to install perimeter landscaping equal to one (1) tree for each twenty-five (25) feet of road or highway frontage. Additionally, one (1) tree is required along the sides and rear of such developments equal to one (1) tree every twenty-five (25) feet of property line when abutting existing homes or developed parcels. Trees must be a minimum of four (4) feet tall when planted and remain in good condition for the life of the large photovoltaic solar farm. The Planning Commission may alter the landscaping requirement depending upon the location and existing plant material on the site.

The ordinance establishes regulations for large photovoltaic solar farm facilities, including minimum lot size, height restrictions, setbacks, safety, noise limits, landscaping, permitting, and decommissioning. Large photovoltaic solar farm facilities require a special use permit with detailed application criteria (Section 702(k)). The Planning Commission has authority to review dimensional and development requirements but "shall not have the authority to review or to allow large photovoltaic solar farm facilities within any other zoning district" (Section 702(O)), implying that such facilities are only permitted in certain unspecified districts. No specific district names or abbreviations where large photovoltaic solar farm facilities are permitted as special use or similar are provided in the text. The ordinance also separately addresses smaller or accessory solar energy systems allowed as accessory uses in all zoning districts (Chapter 7(C)), but these do not apply to large photovoltaic solar farm facilities.

Section 702(k)(3) requires that the Special Use application for large photovoltaic solar farm facilities include a visual impact review and demonstration "using photos or renditions of the project or similar projects with consideration given to tree plantings and setback requirements." Large photovoltaic solar farm facilities are defined as those on parcels of at least twenty (20) acres, with panels restricted to a height of fourteen (14) feet, and subject to other requirements such as setbacks, landscaping, noise limits, and special use criteria. The visual impact assessment is one of several topics to be addressed in the Special Use application, alongside project description, traffic analysis, wildlife impact, environmental analysis, waste, lighting, transportation, public safety, sound, and telecommunications interference.

Utility Scale Solar Energy Collectors may be permitted as a Special Land Use subject to Planning Commission approval. A decommissioning plan must be submitted prior to approval and include: "defined conditions upon which decommissioning and removal will be initiated (e.g., end of land lease, no power production for twelve [12] months, abandonment, etc.); removal of Utility Scale Solar Energy Collectors and associated equipment, including, structures, fencing, solar panels, foundations, and all non-natural screening; restoration of a Lot to the condition which existed prior to the development of the Utility Scale Solar Energy Collectors; specification of the timeframe to complete decommissioning activities; description of any agreement (such as a lease) with the landowner regarding decommissioning, if applicable; identity of the entity or individual responsible for decommissioning activities; plans for updating the decommissioning plan, as necessary; a performance guarantee posted in the form of a bond, letter of credit, cash, or other form acceptable to the Township to ensure removal of the Utility Scale Solar Energy Collectors upon abandonment." Additionally, "A Utility Scale Solar Energy Collector that ceases to produce energy on a continuous basis for twelve (12) months will be considered abandoned" and "shall decommission and remove all equipment and facilities and restore the Lot to its condition prior to the development of the system within one (1) year of abandonment."

summary: A decommissioning plan is required at the time of application. The plan shall include: i. The anticipated manner in which the project will be decommissioned, including a description of which above-grade and below-grade improvements will be removed, retained (e.g. access drive, fencing), or restored for viable reuse of the property consistent with the zoning district; ii. The projected decommissioning costs for removal of the solar farm (net of salvage value in current dollars) and soil stabilization, less the amount of the surety bond posted with the State of Michigan for decommissioning of panels installed on PA 116 lands; iii. The method of ensuring that funds will be available for site decommissioning and stabilization (in the form of surety bond, irrevocable letter of credit, or cash deposit). A review of the amount of the performance guarantee based on inflation, salvage value, and current removal costs shall be completed every 3 years, for the life of the project, and approved by the Township Board. A Solar Farm owner may at any time: i. Proceed with the decommissioning plan approved by the Planning Commission and remove the system as indicated in the most recent approved plan; or ii. Amend the decommissioning plan with the Planning Commission approval and proceed according to the revised plan. Other related regulations include design standards, setbacks, height limits, noise limits, visual appearance requirements, and safety/access provisions, but these do not specifically address glare. The ordinance distinguishes Large Solar Energy Facilities (Solar Farms) as 'a utility-scale commercial facility that converts sunlight into electricity, whether by photovoltaics (PV) or various experimental solar technologies, for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity' (Section 20.01.78.25.a). The 30 feet setback from lot lines is the fixed setback distance, while the 100 feet setback applies to certain residential zoning districts and residences, which are not equivalent to property or lot lines unless explicitly stated.

Other design standards for Large Solar Energy Facilities include minimum lot size, maximum height, setbacks, safety/access, noise limits, visual appearance, lighting, glare control, and vegetative ground cover for erosion control. The ordinance also distinguishes Small Solar Energy Facilities, which have separate requirements and do not include these screening mandates.

This signage requirement applies specifically to Large Solar Energy Facilities (Solar Farms), which are defined as "A utility-scale commercial facility that converts sunlight into electricity, whether by photovoltaics (PV) or various experimental solar technologies, for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity." Other provisions in the ordinance address design standards, location, setbacks, safety/access, noise, visual appearance, and permits, but only this subsection explicitly mandates signage. Small Solar Energy Facilities have separate provisions and restrictions, including that they "shall not be used to display advertising, including signage," but this does not apply to Large Solar Energy Facilities.

If installed, perimeter fencing shall meet the Zoning District requirements per Section 54.706 and require a fence permit. Wildlife-friendly fencing materials and with openings to allow passage for small animals should be used where appropriate. Barbed wire is prohibited. Fencing is not subject to setbacks but shall not encroach past the property lines.

summary: A Ground-mounted SES shall not exceed 20 feet measured from the average grade across the supports to the top of the system when oriented at maximum tilt (tallest, most vertical position of a solar array). This applies specifically to Ground-Mounted SES ≥ 20 kW (0.02 MW) to < 2 MW – Principal Use. Other height limits mentioned for different uses or accessory systems include 10 feet or 16 feet under certain proximity conditions to residential uses, but these do not apply to principal-use systems in the specified capacity range.

summary: Setback distance shall be measured from all of the property lines to the closest point of the solar array at minimum tilt (lowest, least vertical position of a solar array) or any SES components as follows: A Ground-mounted SES shall follow the zoning district setback distance for primary buildings or structures; however, the SES must be at least 10-ft from the front property line. A Ground-mounted SES is not subject to the side or rear property line setbacks for common property lines of two or more participating lots; however, the side and rear setbacks will apply to the overall property lines for the site.

For Ground-Mounted SES ≥ 20 kW (0.02 MW) to < 2 MW – Principal Use, "this type of principal-use SES may at any time be repowered by reconfiguring, renovating, or replacing the SES to increase the power rating within the existing project footprint." Additionally, "A proposal to change the project footprint of an existing SES shall be considered a new application, subject to the Land Development Code standards in effect at the time of the application." Other relevant conditions include application requirements, height limits (not to exceed 20 feet at maximum tilt), location and setbacks, fencing, landscaping/screening, ground cover, land clearing, access drives, signage, sound requirements, and decommissioning plans as detailed in subsection 6.F.2.

summary: For Ground-Mounted SES ≥ 20 kW (0.02 MW) to < 2 MW – Principal Use, the ordinance requires screening of the SES from the view of surrounding streets "to the maximum extent feasible without compromising the ability to effectively use solar collectors, by use of vegetation fences and or walls as permitted in the zoning district per Section 54.706." Landscaping must consist of "trees and shrubs as approved in Section 54.1004, and existing vegetation may be used for screening." Berms of natural material up to three (3) feet above grade may be used in addition to vegetation, provided runoff does not create ponding or flow to adjacent properties. Screening shall achieve "an opacity of approximately 80 percent of the SES up to either six (6) feet above grade or 60 percent of the maximum tilt (vertical) height of the solar array(s), whichever is more." Where buffer/greenbelt screening is required along side and rear yard property lines per Section 54.1003(D), these are only required where an adjoining, non-participating lot has an existing residential or public use. The Planning Commission or Zoning Administrator may waive some screening and/or landscaping requirements or require substitute screening consisting of native deciduous trees planted ≥ 30 feet on center and native conifer trees planted ≥ 15 feet on center along existing, non-participating residential uses.

summary: For Ground-mounted SES (SES ≥20 kW (0.02 MW) to < 2MW) - Principal Use, the ordinance requires: 'An SES shall include the installation of perennial ground cover vegetation maintained for the duration of operation until the site is decommissioned. The applicant shall include a ground cover vegetation establishment and management plan as part of the site plan.' Land disturbance or clearing 'shall be limited to what is minimally necessary for the installation and operation of the SES and to ensure all-season access.' 'Topsoil disturbed during site preparation (grading) on the property shall be retained on site unless a higher authority requires removal due to contamination.' New access drives 'shall be designed to minimize the extent of soil disturbance, water runoff, and soil compaction on the premises.' Additionally, 'Decommissioning must commence when the soil is dry to prevent soil compaction and be complete within 18 months after abandonment.' These requirements explicitly address soil, erosion, and sediment control for principal-use ground-mounted solar energy systems in the specified size range.

summary: The ordinance states that Ground-Mounted SES ≥20 kW (0.02 MW) to < 2 MW are subject to both permitted use and special land use provisions depending on the zoning district, as indicated by repeated references to Section 54.1403 for Special Land Use if the zoning district requires it. Applications must include a site plan and other documentation, and a building permit may be required. The text specifies conditions such as height limits (not to exceed 20 feet), location and setbacks (e.g., side or rear yard in residential districts, minimum setbacks from property lines), fencing, landscaping/screening, ground cover, land clearing, access drives, signage, sound, repowering, and decommissioning requirements. However, the ordinance does not explicitly list or name any specific zoning districts or their abbreviations where these systems are permitted as special use or require approval by a zoning appeals board or similar authority. The determination of whether the use is permitted or special use depends on the zoning district regulations and Section 54.1403, which are not detailed in the provided text. Other options in the ordinance include Ground-Mounted SES <20 kW as accessory use with specific height and setback requirements, and roof-mounted or building-integrated SES with their own permitting and setback rules.

Off-site systems may cover 65 percent of the land including the area encompassing the panels and equipment. Additionally, if ground cover is done using native plants which attract and promote pollination, a 10 percent increase in land cover is permitted.

Removal of solar panels is required when solar panels are no longer producing power for more than 12 months. Requirements for removal to be provided at the time of special use application include: defined conditions upon which decommissioning will be initiated (i.e., end of land lease, no power production for 12 months, etc.); removal of all non-utility owned equipment, conduit, structures, fencing, roads, and building foundations to a depth of five feet below grade; restoration of property to the condition prior to development of the Solar Energy System; the timeframe for completion of decommissioning activities; description of any agreement (e.g., lease) with the landowner regarding decommissioning; provisions for updating the decommissioning plan; a statement signed by the owner or operator that they take full responsibility for re-claiming the site in accordance with the decommissioning plan and special land use permit upon cessation of use; a Mecosta Township Building and Zoning inspector shall conduct a final inspection to confirm that the Solar Energy System has been decommissioned consistent with the provisions of the decommissioning plan; any property that is no longer producing power and has not gone through the decommissioning process will be considered in violation of the Mecosta Township Zoning Ordinance. Off-site energy systems (Solar Farms) are permitted by special land use approval in the A, AF, and AG Districts and must meet additional requirements such as ground cover, land coverage limits, and fencing.

For Off-Site Solar Energy Systems (Solar Farms), the ordinance states: 'Fencing is required to meet the National Electrical Code.' This applies to systems 'that provide energy intended primarily for off-site uses.' Other regulations for Off-Site Solar Energy Systems include: 'Off-site energy systems are permitted by special land use approval in the A, AF, and AG Districts,' 'Ground cover shall be required after installation to prevent erosion of the land,' and 'Off-site systems may cover 65 percent of the land including the area encompassing the panels and equipment.'

For Off-Site Solar Energy Systems (Solar Farms), the ordinance requires that "Ground cover shall be required after installation to prevent erosion of the land." Additionally, if native plants are used for ground cover that attract and promote pollination, "a 10 percent increase in land cover is permitted." Other relevant conditions include that off-site systems "may cover 65 percent of the land including the area encompassing the panels and equipment," and "Fencing is required to meet the National Electrical Code." Removal requirements include restoration of property to the condition prior to development of the Solar Energy System. The ordinance distinguishes between On-Site Solar Energy Systems (attached or ground-mounted for primarily on-site use), Detached Solar Energy Systems (ground-mounted but smaller scale), and Off-Site Solar Energy Systems (Solar Farms) which provide energy primarily for off-site use and require special land use approval in certain districts.

Off-site energy systems are permitted by special land use approval in the A, AF, and AG Districts. On-site solar energy systems shall be permitted as an accessory structure in all zoning districts. Detached solar energy systems shall not be located in the front yard without special land use approval from the Planning Commission, subject to general conditions and a showing that solar exposure is insufficient in other yards or would require removal of attractive trees or vegetation.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Solar Energy Facility (Utility Scale/Commercial) systems. Section 3, subsections 31, 32, and 33 address decommissioning: 31. Abandonment - "Any freestanding solar energy collection site, unit or device which is not used for six (6) continuous months shall be deemed to be abandoned." The applicant/permit holder must dismantle the site and return it to its original state, or the Township will do so at the owner/applicant’s expense. 32. Performance Guarantee - "The Planning Commission may require an owner to deposit funds in escrow with the Township or provide an insurance bond... to assure the removal of the solar renewable energy facility." This financial security must be maintained by successor owners. 33. Decommissioning Plan - "A decommissioning plan is required at the time of application," including the manner of decommissioning, projected costs (net of salvage value), and method of ensuring funds availability (surety bond, letter of credit, or cash deposit). The plan is reviewed every five years and may be amended with Planning Commission approval. These requirements apply specifically to commercial solar renewable energy facilities as defined in the ordinance.

Section 9, item 7: "Setback distances shall be from the adjacent lot line or road right-of-way line to the proposed perimeter fencing around the solar energy facility." Item 11(a): "A security fence shall be placed around the perimeter of a commercial solar renewable energy system and the electrical equipment shall be locked. The fence shall be located between the solar array, wind turbine, or battery system and the landscaping buffer. The fence shall meet the minimum requirements of the National Electrical Code requirements. If deemed appropriate, the Planning Commission can require specific fencing as needed." Item 12: "Solar Renewable Energy Facilities may be secured with perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access. Fencing is not subject to setbacks in subsection 7."

Section 3, Ordinance T.4 (Reflection/Glare) states: "Solar collection devices, Wind Turbine Generators, or any combination of devices, shall be designed and located to avoid glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard." It further specifies: "Glare intensity is considered an issue if it measures more than twenty (20) percent of the incident sun intensity." Additionally, "Plans to reduce glare may be required in the initial materials submitted." This applies to commercial solar renewable energy facilities defined as Solar Energy Facility (Utility Scale/Commercial), which are "designed to capture and utilize the energy of the sun to generate electrical power to be used primarily off-site."

summary: The ordinance explicitly states in Section 9, subsection T, item 13: 'Solar collection devices shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt (measured from the ground at the base of the equipment).' This is the maximum structure height allowed for Solar Energy Facility (Utility Scale/Commercial). Other height restrictions mentioned apply only to accessory solar energy panels, which are not commercial scale systems.

summary: Commercial solar renewable energy system facilities shall not exceed 50 dBA Leq (1-hour) measured at the project boundary. As part of the application, and prior to installation, the applicant shall provide noise modeling study and analysis that will demonstrate the solar renewable energy system will not exceed the maximum permitted noise levels. Site plans shall include modeled sound isolines extending from the sound source to the property line to demonstrate compliance with this standard. Post construction, the applicant and/or owner will conduct sound monitoring to ensure the project complies with the zoning ordinance standards.

All solar energy facilities shall have the following setbacks. Setback distances shall be from the adjacent lot line or road right-of-way line to the proposed perimeter fencing around the solar energy facility. b. Nonparticipating property line: 50 feet. Other setbacks include: a. Road right-of-way: 50 feet; c. Nonparticipating Dwelling: 300 feet from the closest side and rear walls of a dwelling unit on an adjoining property; d. No solar energy system shall be placed between the closest point of a dwelling unit and the road right-of-way line on the same lot as the dwelling unit and the adjacent lots extending the width of the setback area defined above; e. Internal Property Lines: A solar energy facility is not subject to property line setback requirements for common property lines of two or more participating parcels, except road right-of-way setbacks shall apply.

summary: Section 3, item 30 "Repowering" states: "a solar renewable energy facility may at any time be repowered, without the need to apply for a new Special Land Use permit, by reconfiguring, renovating, or replacing the solar renewable energy components to increase the power rating within the existing project footprint." It further provides: "a proposal to change the project footprint of an existing solar renewable energy facility shall be considered a new application, subject to the ordinance standards at the time of the request." Also, "the Applicant/Owner would not need to apply for a new permit if they are performing routine maintenance, as described in the provided maintenance plan." These provisions apply specifically to commercial solar renewable energy facilities as defined in the ordinance.

All solar energy facilities shall have the following setbacks. Setback distances shall be from the adjacent lot line or road right-of-way line to the proposed perimeter fencing around the solar energy facility. a. Road right-of-way: 50 feet. Other setbacks include 50 feet from nonparticipating property line and 300 feet from nonparticipating dwelling. No solar energy system shall be placed between the closest point of a dwelling unit and the road right-of-way line on the same lot as the dwelling unit and the adjacent lots extending the width of the setback area defined above. Internal property lines between participating parcels are exempt from property line setbacks except road right-of-way setbacks shall apply.

summary: Section 9, subsection T.6 Screening requires that "Solar, wind and battery devices shall be screened year-round from view from any existing residential use and the public right-of-way by use of a screening wall, evergreen vegetation, or other screening of similar effectiveness and quality, as determined by the Planning Commission." Screening "shall be installed which screens the facility fully from view from the time of planting or installation" and "shall be maintained throughout the life of the facility including replacing dead vegetation within six (6) months or at the earliest feasible time of year dependent on the weather."

summary: Section 9, item 11 (Signage and Security) requires that "the applicant, operator, and/or owner is required to place an identification placard on site of the solar renewable energy facility with their company name, address, a contact name, and a contact phone number for the life of the project." It also mandates that "the manufacturers or installer's identification and appropriate warning sign shall be posted on or near the panels unit in a clearly visible manner; furthermore, an information sign shall be posted and maintained at the entrance(s), which shall list the name and phone number of the operator." Additionally, "No portion of the solar renewable energy system shall contain or be used to display advertising. The manufacturers’ name and equipment information or dedication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of the solar energy system."

The ordinance explicitly requires for commercial solar renewable energy facilities: submission of "A site grading, erosion control and storm water drainage plan" (Section 9, item 9.6) reviewed by the Township’s engineering firm at the applicant’s cost; design of new access roads to "minimize the extent of soil disturbance, water runoff, and soil compaction" with permitted use of geotextile fabrics and gravel for temporary roads (item 23); a maintenance plan that "demonstrates the SES renewable energy system will be designed, constructed, and operated to minimize dust generation" and treatment of unpaved access roads to prevent excessive dust (items 25.b and 25.c); and compliance with Part 91 Soil Erosion and Sedimentation Control (MCL 324.9101 et seq.) of the Michigan Natural Resources and Environmental Protection Act (item 19.a). These requirements apply to Solar Energy Facility (Utility Scale/Commercial) as defined: "A facility designed to capture and utilize the energy of the sun to generate electrical power to be used primarily off-site."

Commercial solar renewable energy facilities shall be limited and subject to obtaining a special land use permit from the Planning Commission in A-R zoning districts. Accessory solar energy panels are allowed as a permitted accessory use in all zoning districts but are distinct from utility-scale commercial facilities. The ordinance states: 'Commercial solar renewable energy facilities shall be limited and subject to obtaining a special land use permit from the Planning Commission in A-R zoning districts.'

All solar energy facilities shall have the following setbacks. Setback distances shall be from the adjacent lot line or road right-of-way line to the proposed perimeter fencing around the solar energy facility. c. Nonparticipating Dwelling: 300 feet from the closest side and rear walls of a dwelling unit on an adjoining property. Other setback options include: a. Road right-of-way: 50 feet; b. Nonparticipating property line: 50 feet; d. No solar energy system shall be placed between the closest point of a dwelling unit and the road right-of-way line on the same lot as the dwelling unit and the adjacent lots extending the width of the setback area defined above; e. Internal Property Lines: A solar energy facility is not subject to property line setback requirements for common property lines of two or more participating parcels, except road right-of-way setbacks shall apply.
