summary: Section 9, item 10.d requires the applicant to "Review and demonstrate the visual impact of the proposed project from a minimum of 5 viewpoints at the time of commercial operation, projected after five years and ten years post construction. The visual simulations shall use photos or renditions of the project with consideration given to tree plantings and setback requirements." This is part of the "Additional Special Land Use Criteria" for commercial solar renewable energy facilities. Other related requirements include submitting a site plan with detailed project boundaries, structures, roads, topography, water bodies, grading, setbacks, infrastructure, construction areas, and a landscape/screening plan. Screening requirements (item 6) mandate that solar, wind, and battery devices "shall be screened year-round from view from any existing residential use and the public right-of-way" by walls, vegetation, or similar means. Glare restrictions (item 4) are noted but excluded from this assessment. The ordinance applies to Solar Energy Facility (Utility Scale/Commercial) defined as "a facility designed to capture and utilize the energy of the sun to generate electrical power to be used primarily off-site."

Section O - Abandonment and Decommissioning requires the applicant to perform decommissioning and removal of the Large Solar Energy System and all its components following the operational life of the project. The applicant must prepare a decommissioning plan and submit it to the Planning Commission for review and approval prior to issuance of the Special Approval Use. All structures, concrete, piping, facilities, and other project related materials above grade and any structures up to forty-two (42) inches below-grade shall be removed offsite for disposal. Any Solar Array not operated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months shall be considered abandoned and removed under the decommissioning plan. The ground must be restored to its original topography within three hundred sixty-five (365) days of abandonment or decommissioning, including bringing soil to its pre-development composition to ensure agricultural use in AG1 or AG2 districts or to pre-development conditions in I1 and I2 districts. Soil tests are required before development and prior to decommissioning. The applicant must obtain a surety bond for reclamation in an amount determined by the Township as a condition of site plan approval, which remains in place for the length of leases/contracts. Section V - Continuing Security requires posting decommissioning security prior to construction, kept in full force and irrevocable during the entire time the Large Solar Energy System exists or is in place. Failure to maintain this security constitutes a material violation subject to enforcement actions. Other sections related to maintenance, inspections, and removal timelines are also included but the primary decommissioning requirements are in Sections O and V.

A Large Solar Energy System shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing (such as chain link) to restrict unauthorized access in accordance with Federal guidelines. Such fencing shall be either seven (7) feet in height or at least six (6) feet in height with a one (1) foot extension arm consisting of a minimum of three strands of barbed-wire placed above the fencing and slanting outward as measured from the natural grade of the fencing perimeter. Electric fencing is not permitted.

Maximum height of a Solar Array, other collection device, components or buildings of the Large Solar Energy System, excluding substation and electrical transmission equipment, shall not exceed twenty (20) feet (as measured from the natural grade at the base of improvements) at any time or location on the property. Substation and electrical transmission equipment shall not exceed one hundred (100) feet.

No component of any Large Solar Energy System shall emit noise exceeding sixty-five (65) dBA as measured at the exterior property boundary or the existing ROW line. This limitation does not apply to construction, decommissioning or repairs to the Large Solar Energy System.

Large Solar Energy Systems shall be permitted only in the AG-1, AG-2, I-1, and I-2 districts. By implication, Large Solar Energy Systems are prohibited in all other districts. The text states: 'Solar Array(s) shall be permitted only in the AG-1, AG-2, I-1, and I-2 districts.' Electric substations, collector lines, and interconnection transmission or distribution lines affiliated with Large Solar Energy Systems are permitted as accessory uses in any zoning district. The table of permitted uses shows Large Solar Energy System use marked as 'S' (Special Approval Use) only in AG-1, AG-2, I-1, and I-2 districts, and no allowance in other districts.

A minimum setback distance of fifty (50) feet from all property boundaries on the outside perimeter of the Large Solar Energy System ... shall be required for all buildings and Solar Arrays, provided that a setback of seventy-five (75) feet shall be required adjacent to any residential structure.

A minimum setback distance of fifty (50) feet from all existing public roads and railroad rights-of-way shall be required for all buildings and Solar Arrays of a Large Solar Energy System, provided that a setback of seventy-five (75) feet shall be required adjacent to any residential structure.

The ordinance requires that "The perimeter of Large Solar Energy Systems shall also be screened and buffered by installed evergreen or native vegetative plantings whenever existing natural vegetation does not otherwise reasonably obscure the Large Solar Energy System from adjacent residential structures." The buffer must be composed of "native or evergreen trees that at planting shall be a minimum of four (4) feet in height and shrubs two (2) feet in height." Evergreen trees must be spaced no more than fifteen (15) feet apart, native trees no more than thirty (30) feet apart, and shrubs no more than seven (7) feet apart. Unhealthy or dead material (sixty (60) percent dead or greater) must be replaced within one (1) year or the next appropriate planting period. Plant materials must be installed between March 15 and November 15, or the applicant must provide a financial guarantee for planting deficiencies. Failure to install or maintain the vegetative buffer constitutes a violation and may lead to revocation of the Special Approval Use. Additionally, the Large Solar Energy System must be "completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing (such as chain link)" with specific height and barbed-wire requirements, but electric fencing is not permitted.

No advertising or non-project related graphics shall be on any part of the Solar Arrays or other components of the Large Solar Energy System. This exclusion does not apply to entrance gate signage or notifications containing points of contact or any and all other information that may be required by authorities having jurisdiction for electrical operations and the safety and welfare of the public.

Following the operational life of the project, the applicant shall perform decommissioning and removal of the Large Solar Energy System and all its components. The ground must be restored to its original topography within three hundred sixty-five (365) days of abandonment or decommissioning. Restoration shall also include bringing soil to its pre-development composition to ensure agricultural use upon restoration in AG1 or AG2 districts or to pre-development conditions in I1 and I2 districts. Soil tests shall be required as a part of the Decommissioning Plan both before development and prior to decommissioning. Soil shall be brought back to pre-development state within three hundred sixty-five (365) days of abandonment or decommissioning.

Large Solar Energy Systems are permitted as a Special Approval Use in the AG-1, AG-2, I-1, and I-2 districts. The ordinance states: 'Solar Array(s) shall be permitted only in the AG-1, AG-2, I-1, and I-2 districts.' Applications must be accompanied by detailed site plans and comply with the Special Approval Use requirements, including an escrow deposit of $15,000 to cover review costs. The process includes compliance with the National Electric Safety Code and state construction codes. The text specifies: 'All applications for a Large Solar Energy System use must be accompanied by detailed site plans... as required by the Special Approval Use requirements of the Milan Township Zoning Ordinance.' Other uses such as electric substations and transmission lines affiliated with the Large Solar Energy System are permitted as Accessory Uses in any zoning district. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this summary per instructions.

A minimum setback distance of fifty (50) feet from all property boundaries on the outside perimeter of the Large Solar Energy System and existing public roads and railroad rights-of-way shall be required for all buildings and Solar Arrays, provided that a setback of seventy-five (75) feet shall be required adjacent to any residential structure.

summary: Section 40-4.5.E (Abandonment) states: 'Any freestanding solar collection site or device which is not used for six (6) months shall be deemed to be abandoned. The applicant/permit holder will be so notified in writing by Millen Township and requested to dismantle the site and return it to its original state. If there are mitigating circumstances as to why the site has not been used, the applicant/permit holder may contact Millen Township and request a three-month extension. If a site has been deemed abandoned and no request for an extension is received, the applicant/permit holder will again be notified and dismantle the site and return it to its original state. If the applicant/permit holder does not do this, Millen Township will have the removal and restoration done at the applicant/permit holder's expense. Removal shall include removing posts, equipment, panels, foundations and other items so the site is restored to its preconstruction state and is ready for development as another land use.' Other provisions in Section 40-4.5 address reflection/glare, impervious surface/stormwater, screening, and setbacks but do not relate to decommissioning.

The ordinance requires that solar collection devices "shall be designed and located to avoid glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and shall not interfere with traffic or create a traffic hazard." Glare intensity is considered an issue if it measures more than 20% of the incident sun intensity. "Plans to reduce glare may be required in the initial materials submitted."
section: Article XXXIV, Section 3.5-AG-3.53 and Article 4.0, 40-4.5 Solar Energy Facility (Utility-Scale)

summary: The setbacks of all solar collection devices and ancillary equipment shall be at least 50 feet from all property lines.

Section 40-4.5.C states: 'Solar devices shall be screened from view from any public street or residential district by use of a masonry screen wall, evergreen vegetation or other screening of a similar effectiveness or quality, as determined by the Millen Township Zoning Board.' This screening requirement applies to utility-scale solar energy facilities as defined in the ordinance. Other options for screening include masonry screen walls or other screening methods deemed similarly effective by the Zoning Board.

Utility-scale solar energy systems are defined as 'Solar Energy Facilities (Utility Scale)' and are added as a 'special exception use' in the Agricultural District (AG). The ordinance states: 'That the Millen Township Zoning Ordinance Section 3.5-AG-3.53 (Agricultural District) is hereby amended to add the following as a special exception use: 16. Solar Energy Facilities (Utility Scale)'. No other districts or overlay districts are mentioned in the text for special use or similar permitting of utility-scale solar energy systems.
section: Section 3.5: Additions to the Millen Township Zoning Ordinance

summary: Section C.10 requires a decommissioning and final reclamation plan after the anticipated useful life or abandonment/termination of the project. This includes supplying evidence of an agreement with the underlying property owner that ensures proper removal of all equipment and restoration of the site within six (6) months of decommissioning or abandonment of the project. To ensure proper removal, a bond, letter of credit or cash surety shall be: a) in an amount approved by the Township to be no less than the estimated cost of removal and shall include a provision for inflationary cost adjustments; b) based on an estimate prepared by the engineer for the applicant, subject to approval of the Township, and provided to the Township prior to the issuance of a zoning permit; c) used in the event the owner of the project or the underlying property owner fails to remove or repair any defective, abandoned or terminated project. The Township may pursue legal action to abate the violation by seeking to remove the project and recover any and all costs, including attorney fees.

Section 117.1624 B.5 requires that "A security fence (height and material to be proposed and reviewed/approved through the special zoning permit approval process) shall be placed around the perimeter of the solar energy farm and electrical equipment." This applies to solar energy farms, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. Additionally, emergency key box and keys must be provided at locked entrances for security personnel access.

Solar energy farm facilities "shall be located or placed so that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed toward or onto nearby properties or properties within line of sight or rights-of-way at any time of the day." Support structures "shall be of a single, non-reflective matte finish that is consistent throughout the project."

All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures located in a solar energy farm shall be restricted to a maximum height of sixteen (16) feet when orientated at maximum tilt. This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems defined as solar energy farms. The unit of measurement is feet.

Section B.6 states: 'No solar energy farm shall exceed sixty (60) decibels as measured at the property line.' This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for utility-scale solar energy systems defined as solar energy farms. The unit is assumed to be dBA, the standard unit for noise levels.

All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with such facilities (excluding perimeter fencing) shall be set back a minimum of fifty (50) feet from all property lines. If the right-of-way exists as an easement, the fifty (50) foot setback shall be measured from the edge of the easement. Solar panels shall be kept at least two hundred (200) feet from an existing residential dwelling, measured to the nearest point on the residential structure. Any additional setback requirements in this Ordinance that exceed this requirement shall be adhered to.

The ordinance requires a landscape plan for solar energy farms that includes a "twenty-five (25) foot wide landscape buffer" consisting of "two (2) rows of staggered evergreen trees that at planting shall be a minimum of four (4) feet in height," or "six (6) feet at the time of planting" if adjacent to residential dwellings or districts. The trees "shall be spaced no more than fifteen (15) feet apart on center." The buffer must also include "native grasses, wildflowers, or plants which will provide wildlife and pollinator habitat, soil erosion protection, and/or aid in strengthening the soil structure." This buffer is required if solar panels are located "within two hundred (200) feet of a public road right-of-way or a property that allows for a residential use." Existing topographical features and wooded areas may be accepted in lieu of or in combination with the buffer by Planning Commission approval. Plantings must be installed between April 1st and September 15th, or by May 1st the following year if construction begins after August 15th. A financial guarantee of "one and one-half (1.5) times the cost of the required plantings" is required, and the plantings must be "continuously maintained in a healthy condition" with dead evergreens replaced.

These signage requirements apply specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities (CSEF), defined as solar energy facilities "the design, purpose and use of which, is to provide energy for the use of the premises where the system is located or the sale of generated energy to any person or entity."

Commercial Solar Energy Facilities shall only be allowed as a special approval use in the Agricultural Residential District. No Commercial Solar Energy Facility shall be located, constructed, erected, or altered in Moore Township until the owner/operator has obtained a special approval use permit. An Exempt Solar Energy Facility is a permitted use in all zoning districts, but this does not apply to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities.

Every CSEF shall meet the following setback requirements measured from the closest of the solar panels: Participating property owners 300 feet set back from any dwelling (household). Other setback options include 500 feet from any road right-of-way and 1000 feet from any non-participating parcel, but these do not pertain to participating occupied dwellings.

The applicant shall submit a decommissioning plan to ensure that facilities are properly removed after their useful life. The plan shall include provisions for removal of all structures and foundations, restoration of soil and vegetation, and a plan ensuring financial resources will be available to fully decommission the site, net of any salvage value. The Planning Commission may require the posting of a bond, letter of credit or the establishment of an escrow account to ensure decommissioning, or proof with such financial security required under any agreement with the lessor or owner of the parcels upon which the Solar Energy System will be located. Any part or all of the Solar Energy System and related equipment which is abandoned or not used for 180 days or more shall be removed within 180 days of the ceasing of operations, unless a time extension is granted in writing by the Zoning Administrator. A one-time extension, of up to six months, may be permitted by the Zoning Administrator if he or she determines that the operator of the facility is taking active steps to ensure its removal. Any further extensions must be granted by the Township Board.

The ordinance requires that "all mechanical equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum six (6) foot high fence with a self-locking gate." Additionally, "a six foot chain link fence shall be constructed and maintained around the entire perimeter area of the Solar Energy System." These requirements apply to Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as renewable energy systems that generate electricity from sunlight and consist of one or more PV systems and other appurtenant structures within the site boundaries. The ordinance also includes other standards such as setbacks, height limits, signage, and compliance with regulatory approvals, but the fencing requirements are specifically stated as above.

Solar Energy Systems shall be constructed and operated in compliance with all Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) guidelines and regulations, including glint glare in the siting and design of the solar facility, including impacts to adjacent residences and street rights-of-way. Impacts from above the guideline thresholds will be mitigated by screening from view with berms, vegetation or privacy fencing.

The ordinance states: 'Solar Energy Systems shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in height. The height of the systems will be measured from the highest natural grade below each solar panel.' This applies to Solar Energy Systems located in the Natural Resources District or the Industrial District and approved as special land uses. No other maximum height values are provided.

Utility-scale Solar Energy Systems shall be located only in the Natural Resources District or the Industrial District, and shall be approved only as a special land use in accordance with the procedures set forth in Chapter 11, Special Land Uses. The text states, 'Solar Energy Systems shall be located only in the Natural Resources District or the Industrial District,' which implies that such systems are prohibited in all other districts not named. The ordinance does not specify the names or abbreviations of any other districts where these systems are prohibited.

Solar Energy Systems shall be set back a minimum of one hundred (100) feet from non-Participating Property boundaries, excluding any security fencing, poles, and wires necessary to connect to facilities of the electric utility.

The ordinance requires "a clearly-visible warning sign concerning voltage" to be placed at the base of all pad mounted transformers and substations within Solar Energy Systems. It also mandates that "all mechanical equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum six (6) foot high fence with a self-locking gate." These requirements apply to Solar Energy Systems defined as renewable energy systems generating electricity from sunlight, subject to special land use approval in the Natural Resources or Industrial Districts. Other standards include setbacks, height limits, FAA compliance, fencing, and potential landscaping or screening conditions imposed by the Planning Commission.

The ordinance requires that the site plan for Solar Energy Systems include "proposed erosion and sediment control measures." It also states that Solar Energy Systems "are subject to stormwater management and erosion and sediment control best practices and NPDES permit requirements, and shall obtain required permits from the Michigan Department of Environmental Quality, Michigan Department of Transportation and other required governmental approvals." Solar Energy Systems must be located only in the Natural Resources District or the Industrial District and are approved only as a special land use in accordance with Chapter 11, Special Land Uses, and subject to review under Chapter 12, Site Plan Review.

Utility-scale Solar Energy Systems shall be located only in the Natural Resources District or the Industrial District, and shall be approved only as a special land use in accordance with the procedures set forth in Chapter 11, Special Land Uses. They shall be subject to review and approval under Chapter 12, Site Plan Review. Section 5.3(j) and Section 9.3(n) explicitly list Solar Energy Systems as special land uses in the Natural Resources District and Industrial District, respectively.

Solar Energy Systems shall be set back a minimum of one hundred (100) feet from non-Participating Property boundaries, excluding any security fencing, poles, and wires necessary to connect to facilities of the electric utility.

Section 7.10.D.5 'Abandonment or Decommissioning' requires that any utility-scale solar energy system which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned shall be removed and the site restored to its original condition. The owner/operator must physically remove the installation no more than one-hundred and fifty (150) days after discontinued operations and notify the Township and Planning Commission by certified mail. The system is considered abandoned if it fails to operate for more than one year without notice. If removal is not completed within 150 days of abandonment, Morton Township may enter the property and remove the installation. Decommissioning consists of physical removal of all systems, disposal of waste according to regulations, and site stabilization or re-vegetation. Additionally, Section 7.10.D.7 requires the applicant to provide financial surety to cover removal costs, not exceeding 125 percent of the estimated cost, including inflation adjustments. Utility-Scale SES is defined as systems primarily used for generating electricity for sale, exceeding 1,500 square feet of solar collector surface, or not accessory uses.

Section D.2.g states: 'Solar panels shall be placed such that concentrated radiation or solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways. When deemed appropriate, the Planning Commission may require a report from a registered civil engineer or other professional to address this issue.' This applies to utility-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems, which are defined as systems that 'meet one or more of the following: i. Is primarily used for generating electricity for sale and distribution to an authorized public utility; ii. The total surface area of all Solar Collector Surfaces exceeds 1,500 square feet; and/or iii. Is not an accessory use or structure.'

Minimum lot area for a utility-scale solar energy system shall be five (5) acres. This applies specifically to utility-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems as stated in Section 7.10.D.2.c. The unit 'acres' is explicitly used to describe the minimum lot size.

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be set back at least fifty (50) feet from the road right-of-way line. Each side yard shall be at least twenty-five (25) feet, but where utility-scale solar energy systems abut a residentially-zoned (including A-2) or used lot, the side yard shall not be less than fifty (50) feet. The rear yard shall be at least twenty-five (25) feet, but where utility-scale solar energy systems abut a residentially-zoned (including A-2) or used lot, the rear yard shall not be less than fifty (50) feet.

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be set back at least fifty (50) feet from the road right-of-way line. This applies to ground-mounted utility-scale SES as defined by the ordinance. Other setback requirements include side yards of at least twenty-five (25) feet (or fifty (50) feet if abutting residentially-zoned or used lots) and rear yards of at least twenty-five (25) feet (or fifty (50) feet if abutting residentially-zoned or used lots), but these do not pertain to roads.

Section D.2.g states: 'When a utility-scale solar energy system is adjacent to a residentially-zoned or used lot, side and rear yard screening may be required as determined by the Planning Commission to address specific site needs at the time of site plan review.' Section D.6 requires that 'ancillary solar equipment ... shall be screened to the maximum extent possible without compromising the effectiveness of the solar collectors.' These are the explicit screening requirements for Utility-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems. Other related standards include setbacks, height, lighting, signage, utility connections, and special use permit requirements, but these do not explicitly mandate vegetative buffers or screening.

Section D.2.e states: 'Signs shall comply with the requirements described in Section 7.3. Further, utility-scale solar energy system installations shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the solar energy system.' This applies to Utility-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems primarily used for generating electricity for sale and distribution to an authorized public utility, having a total surface area of all Solar Collector Surfaces exceeding 1,500 square feet, and/or not an accessory use or structure. Other related standards for utility-scale systems include setbacks, height, lighting, utility connections, screening, and special use permit requirements, but these do not pertain to signage.

Section 7.10.D.4.b requires an Operation and Maintenance Plan that "shall include measures for maintaining safe access to the installation, storm water controls, as well as general procedures of operational maintenance of the installation." Section 7.10.D.5.c.iii mandates "Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion" as part of decommissioning. These provisions explicitly address erosion and sediment control requirements for Utility-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems. Other related requirements include special land use approval, setbacks, height limits, minimum lot area, lighting, signage, utility connections, screening, site control, emergency services cooperation, maintenance, site clearing limited to necessary vegetation removal, ancillary equipment screening, and financial surety for removal costs.

Utility-scale SES shall be permitted as a special use in all districts, subject to the following standards: "Prior to the construction of a utility-scale solar system, an application for a special use permit must be filed and approved by the Planning Commission." The Planning Commission reviews the special use based on this Section and Section 5.19. Additional requirements include compliance with local, state, and federal requirements, obtaining all applicable permits, and approval by the authorized utility company for interconnected generators. Standards for ground-mounted utility-scale SES include setbacks, height conforming to district standards, minimum lot area of five acres, lighting, signage, underground utility connections, and possible screening when adjacent to residentially-zoned or used lots. Other types of solar energy systems mentioned are Personal-Scale SES, which are permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts with specific standards and permit requirements, and Building-Mounted SES, which are subject to additional standards. The ordinance does not specify particular district names or abbreviations for utility-scale SES special use approval, only that it applies in all districts.

For Utility-Scale Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems, when abutting a residentially-zoned (including A-2) or used lot, the side yard setback shall not be less than fifty (50) feet and the rear yard setback shall not be less than fifty (50) feet. Other setback options include a front yard setback of at least fifty (50) feet from the road right-of-way line, and side and rear yards of at least twenty-five (25) feet when not abutting residentially-zoned or used lots.

Section 7.10.D.2.g states: "When a utility-scale solar energy system is adjacent to a residentially-zoned or used lot, side and rear yard screening may be required as determined by the Planning Commission to address specific site needs at the time of site plan review." It further provides that "When deemed appropriate, the Planning Commission may require a report from a registered civil engineer or other professional to address this issue." This constitutes an explicit visual impact assessment requirement for utility-scale ground-mounted SES. Other related standards include setbacks, height, minimum lot area, lighting, signage, utility connections, and ancillary equipment screening, but these do not explicitly require visual impact assessments. The ordinance distinguishes utility-scale SES as those "primarily used for generating electricity for sale and distribution to an authorized public utility;" or with "total surface area of all Solar Collector Surfaces exceeds 1,500 square feet;" or "is not an accessory use or structure."

Section 18.53.I requires that prior to site plan approval, a Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy System shall have a plan approved by the Township Planning Commission for decommissioning the site. The Decommissioning Plan must include the expected duration of the project, how the improvements will be decommissioned, a Professional Engineer's estimated cost of decommissioning, the financial resources to be used, and the surety bond holder or similar financial instrument. The financial resources must be 125 percent of the estimated removal and restoration cost, with annual reviews and replenishment obligations. Section 18.53.J states that any Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy System not operated or found inoperable for six months shall be considered abandoned and must be decommissioned within 90 days of a Planning Commission hearing. Decommissioning includes removal of all equipment up to four feet in depth and site restoration consistent with prior conditions. The township has rights to enter the site, seek injunctive relief, and recover costs if decommissioning is not completed. Other options and conditions include requirements for Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Collector Systems and Building-Mounted Solar Energy Collector Systems, but decommissioning requirements are explicitly detailed only for Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy Collector Systems.

Section 18.53.H.4.q states: "For the purpose of restricting unauthorized access to the site, the Planning Commission may require that the perimeter of a Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy Collector System be fenced in with at least a six (6) foot high fence." This fencing requirement applies specifically to Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy Collector Systems. Other requirements for these systems include location on lots of at least twenty (20) acres, height not exceeding 12 feet, setbacks from wetlands and property lines, screening if the system negatively impacts views from adjacent residential properties, noise limits, and infrastructure requirements. The Planning Commission has discretion to require fencing to restrict unauthorized access, but it is not an absolute mandate in every case.

Section 18.53.H.4.g states that the exterior surfaces and structural components of a Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy Collector System "shall be generally neutral in color and substantially non-reflective of light." It further provides that "a solar collector surface shall not be installed or located so that sunlight or glare is reflected into neighboring residences or onto adjacent streets." Other relevant requirements for Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy Collector Systems include location on lots of at least twenty (20) acres, height not exceeding 12 feet, setbacks from wetlands and property lines, screening if the system negatively impacts views from adjacent residential properties, and compliance with site plan review and special land use permits. Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Collector Systems (non-commercial) and Building-Mounted Solar Energy Collector Systems have separate provisions and requirements.

Section 18.53.H.4.b states: 'Ground-mounted Commercial Solar Energy Collector Systems shall not exceed 12 feet in height measured from the ground at the base of such equipment. The height of the ground-mounted Commercial Solar Energy Collector System shall be measured from ground level to the highest point of the solar panel.' This is the explicit maximum height restriction for Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy Collector Systems. Other related height restrictions include a 12 feet maximum for non-commercial ground-mounted systems (Section 18.53.G.5) and a 5 feet maximum projection above roof height for building-mounted systems (Section 18.53.D.4), but these apply to different system types. The unit for the height restriction is feet.

Section 18.53.H.4.a states: 'A Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy Collector System shall be located on a lot, lots, parcel or parcels, of at least twenty (20) acres.' This is the explicit minimum lot size for commercial ground-mounted solar systems. Other related minimum lot size restrictions apply only to non-commercial systems, such as 'No Ground-Mounted Non-Commercial Solar Energy Collector System will be allowed on a parcel of land less than one (1) acre in size.' The unit for the commercial system minimum lot size is acres.

Section 18.53.H.4.m states: 'Noise emanating from a Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy Collector System shall not exceed 50 decibels (dBA) as measured from any property line.' The Township Planning Commission may reduce this maximum noise level to protect adjacent residents and property owners. This is the only explicit maximum noise level restriction for Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy Collector Systems in the provided text.

Section 18.53.H.4.d states: 'A Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy System shall be located at least one mile from all other Commercial Solar Energy Systems, whether located in Mt. Morris Township or an adjacent jurisdiction.' One mile equals 5,280 feet. This is the explicit minimum required separation distance with other existing or planned commercial solar energy conversion systems. Other setback requirements include 60 feet from property lines and 100 feet from residential districts, but these do not pertain to separation between commercial solar systems.

Section 18.53.H.4.r requires that the applicant for a special use permit for a Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy Collector System "shall submit a plan for the operation and maintenance of the Commercial Solar Collector Energy System, which shall include measures for maintaining safe access to the installation, storm water controls, as well as general procedures of operational maintenance of the installation, as applicable." Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy Collector Systems are permitted in the (RA) Rural Agricultural District, (M-1) Light Industrial District, and (M-2) Heavy Industrial District. The ordinance also distinguishes between Building-Mounted Solar Energy Collector Systems, Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Collector Systems, and Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy Collector Systems, with different permitting and locational requirements for each.

Section 58-507 Decommissioning/Abandonment requires that a SES shall be deemed abandoned if it is out of service for a continuous 12 month period. A  "Notice of Abandonment"  will be issued to the owner advising them that the SES shall be removed at the owner’s expense within three months of the date of notice. Removal shall require a demolition permit, and the demolition will consist of removal of panels, non-utility owned equipment, conduit, structures, and foundations. Upon removal of a ground array SES, the site shall be cleaned and restored to blend with the existing surrounding vegetation at the time of abandonment. Failure by the owner(s) to complete removal within the three months’ time period may result in the Township Board designating a contractor to complete decommissioning with all the expenses thereof charged to the violator and to become a lien against the premises.

Sec. 58-505(b) states: 'Ground-mounted solar energy collectors shall not exceed sixteen (16) feet in height, measured from the ground at the base of such equipment.' This is the explicit maximum height restriction applicable to ground-mounted solar energy systems, which typically include utility-scale solar energy systems. Other height-related provisions apply only to building-mounted or wall-mounted solar energy collectors and do not specify numerical height limits for utility-scale systems. The unit of measurement is feet.

summary: Solar farms shall be considered a Special Land use and allowed in the Agricultural and Light Industrial zones. The property owner or agent must apply for a Special Land Use permit applying the standards in this Ordinance and under Article 13-Special Land Use Approval Requirements, Section 1300 (General Requirements and Procedures) and the Michigan Zoning Enabling Act, (MZEA), Public Act 110 of 2006.

Section K.12 requires that "any application for approval of a new photovoltaic solar farm shall include a description of the financial security guaranteeing removal of the system which must be posted at the time of receiving a construction permit for the facility." The security shall be one of the following: "1) a cash bond; 2) an irrevocable bank letter of credit; or 3) a performance bond in a form approved by the Township." The amount must be "no less than the estimated cost of removal and may include a provision for inflationary cost adjustments." The estimate is "prepared by the engineer for the developer and shall be subject to approval by the Township." If the property owner fails to remove or repair the defective or abandoned system, "the Township may pursue legal action to have the system removed and assess its cost to the tax roll." The applicant is responsible for "the payment of any costs and attorney fees incurred by the Township in securing removal of the structure."

A security fence (height and material to be established through the special use permit process) shall be placed around the perimeter of the solar power plant and electrical equipment shall be locked. Knox box and keys shall be provided at locked entrances for emergency personnel access.

Section C. Height Restrictions states: 'All photovoltaic panels located in a solar farm shall be restricted to a height of fourteen (14) feet.' This applies explicitly to large photovoltaic solar farm facilities. Other height-related restrictions include lighting poles restricted to eighteen (18) feet in height, but this does not pertain to the solar panels themselves. The unit for the maximum height is feet.

Large photovoltaic solar farm facilities shall not be constructed on parcels less than twenty (20) acres in size. The Planning Commission may consider a joint application of adjacent properties for reduction to the minimum lot size of 20 acres if all owners agree and other conditions are met. The minimum lot size is explicitly stated as twenty (20) acres, which is an area measurement.

Section G states: 'No large photovoltaic solar farm facilities shall exceed sixty-five (65) dBA as measured at the property line.' This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for large photovoltaic solar farm facilities, with units clarified as dBA (decibels A-weighted). No other noise level restrictions for large photovoltaic solar farm facilities are provided in the text.

All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with such facilities (excluding perimeter security fencing) shall be a minimum of ten (10) feet from a side or rear property line. Other setback mentioned is twenty (20) feet from any road or highway right-of-way, which is not applicable here.

All photovoltaic solar panels and support structures associated with such facilities (excluding perimeter security fencing) shall be a minimum of twenty (20) feet from any road or highway right-of-way. Other setback requirements include ten (10) feet from side or rear property lines, but these do not pertain to roads.

Large photovoltaic solar farm facilities shall be required to install perimeter landscaping equal to one (1) tree for each twenty-five (25) feet of road or highway frontage. The equivalent of one (1) tree shall be required along the sides and rear of such developments equal to one (1) tree every twenty-five (25) feet of property line when abutting existing homes or developed parcels. The Planning Commission may alter the landscaping requirement depending upon the location and existing plant material on the site. Trees shall be a minimum of four (4) feet tall when planted and remain in good condition for the life of the large photovoltaic solar farm.

Solar farms shall be considered a Special Land use and allowed in the Agricultural and Light Industrial zones. The property owner or agent must apply for a Special Land Use permit applying the standards in this Ordinance and under Article 13-Special Land Use Approval Requirements, Section 1300 (General Requirements and Procedures) and the Michigan Zoning Enabling Act, (MZEA), Public Act 110 of 2006.

Section K.3 requires that the Special Use application for large photovoltaic solar farm facilities include a visual impact review and demonstration using photos or renditions of the project or similar projects, with consideration given to tree plantings and setback requirements. This is part of the Additional Special Use Criteria that must be addressed. The ordinance also includes other criteria such as project description, traffic analysis, wildlife impact, environmental analysis, waste, lighting, transportation plan, public safety, sound limitations, telecommunications interference, and life of the project and final reclamation. The Planning Commission reviews these criteria as part of the Special Land Use permit process.

Section 21.09 ABANDONMENT AND DECOMMISSIONING PLAN requires that a decommissioning plan "signed by the party responsible for decommissioning and the landowner (if different)" be submitted prior to permit issuance. The plan must address: "Defined conditions upon which decommissioning will be initiated (i.e. end of land lease, no power production for 12 months, abandonment etc.)"; "Removal of all non-utility owned equipment, conduit, structures, fencing, roads, solar panels and foundations"; "Restoration of property to condition prior to development of the SEF"; "The timeframe for completion of decommissioning activities"; "Description of any agreement (e.g. lease) with landowner regarding decommissioning"; "The party currently responsible for decommissioning"; and "Plans for updating this decommissioning plan." Additionally, abandonment is defined as a SEF that "ceases to produce energy on a continuous basis for 12 months" and upon determination of abandonment, the responsible party must remove the SEF and restore the site within 360 days of notice. Failure to comply allows the Zoning Administrator to remove the SEF and recover costs. These requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities defined as those that "sell electricity to be used off site."

Section 21.06 Security states: 'Solar energy facilities shall be fenced completely as defined in Section Three above. The perimeter fence shall be designed to restrict unauthorized access. If a wire fence is used, vegetation above must be planted along the sides and adjoining a public road.' The definition of 'Fence' in Section 21.03 is: 'A continuous barrier extending from the surface of the ground to a uniform height of not less than six (6) feet from the ground at any given point, constructed of dirt, wood, stone, steel, or other metal, or any substance of a similar nature and strength.' Additionally, if an opaque fence is installed, setbacks from public roads may be reduced (Section 21.05 B), and a planted buffer may not be required (Section 21.05 F). These requirements apply to solar energy facilities defined as those that sell electricity to be used off site.

All improved areas, including disposal areas, shall be at least 25 feet from a fence line. In the event that an opaque fence is installed the setback may be reduced to 20 feet. Improved areas shall be 100 feet from a residence or church, measured from the property line in a residential area (R-1).

All improved areas, including disposal areas, shall be at least 60 feet from a public road and 25 feet from a fence line. In the event that an opaque fence is installed the setback may be reduced to 20 feet. All access roads and storage areas shall be established on a 30’ minimum easement to a public right of way.

Section 21.05(F) requires all solar energy facilities located in a residential area to have a minimum landscape buffer of 25 feet containing evergreen trees or bushes planted no more than 8 feet apart and at least 4’ tall at time of planting. The buffer shall obtain a height of 10 feet within 3 growing seasons. The trees or bushes may be trimmed but no lower than a height of 10 feet. A buffer area will not be required between a solar energy facility and an industrial, agriculture, timber or commercial use. A planted buffer will not be required if an opaque fence is installed. Section 21.06(A) requires solar energy facilities to be fenced completely, and if a wire fence is used, vegetation must be planted along the sides adjoining a public road. Section 21.07(C) states that the design of solar energy facilities buffers shall use materials, colors, textures, screening and landscaping that will blend the facility into the natural setting and existing environment.

Section 21.07(A) requires that "The manufacturers or installer’s identification and appropriate warning sign shall be posted on or near the panels in a clearly visible manner." Section 21.07(J) requires "An information sign shall be posted and maintained at the entrance(s) which lists the name and phone number of the operator." These signage requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities defined as "those facilities that sell electricity to be used off site."

Improved areas shall be at least 50 feet from any residence or church, measured from the principal building in a non-residential area (AR-1 and C-1). Improved areas shall be 100 feet from a residence or church, measured from the property line in a residential area (R-1).

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems under Section 6C.19.D.3.s. It states: "Any utility-scale solar energy system which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned consistent with this section of the Zoning Ordinance shall be removed and parcel owners shall be required to restore the site to a substantially similar condition as predevelopment." The owner or operator must "physically remove the installation no more than 150 days after the date of discontinued operations" and notify the Township by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. If the system remains nonfunctional for 18 months, it is considered abandoned. The Township may remove the installation at the owner's expense if not removed within 150 days. Decommissioning includes: "Physical removal of all utility-scale solar energy systems, structures, equipment, security barriers, concrete, and transmission lines (including underground lines) from the site," "Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state and federal waste disposal regulations," and "Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion." Prior to construction, a decommissioning agreement and financial assurance (bond, parent company guarantee, or irrevocable letter of credit, excluding cash) must be prepared and approved by the Township Board. The financial assurance amount "shall not credit salvage value" and must be periodically updated (e.g., every five years) to account for changing costs. Other related requirements include restoration of agricultural drainage infrastructure and inclusion of restoration costs in the decommissioning security. No alternative options or conditions for decommissioning are provided beyond these requirements.

Fencing for the utility-scale solar energy system shall comply with the latest version of the National Electric Code or any applicable successor standard approved by the Planning Commission. Areas that host visible utility-scale solar energy system components shall be completely enclosed by a perimeter security fence to restrict unauthorized access. Such fencing shall be eight (8) feet in height as measured from the natural grade of the fencing perimeter and the fencing must utilize fabric screening or other acceptable methods to the Township to screen the utility-scale solar energy system from visibility. Additionally, a utility-scale solar energy system shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access.

Under Section D.3.g, the ordinance states: "All solar panels shall be placed such that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways." Applicants must provide a pre-construction and post-construction glare study to the Township demonstrating compliance and may be required to utilize operational controls on a utility-scale solar energy system (e.g., tilting of panels at certain times) to ensure such compliance.
section: Section 6C.19 Solar Energy Systems, D. UTILITY-SCALE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS, 3. Operation Requirements

summary: Under Section 6C.19.D.3.c, the ordinance states: 'Solar panel components shall not exceed a maximum height of 18 feet above ground when the arrays are at full tilt.' This is the explicit maximum height limitation for utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit 'feet' is used as the standard measurement for height in this context.

No utility-scale solar energy systems shall cause noise in excess of forty-five (45) dBA (using Leq-10 minute or other acceptable scale to the Township, but not Lmax) as measured at the property line of a non-participating parcel. Applicants must provide a pre-construction and post-construction sound study to the Township demonstrating compliance with this standard.
section: Section 6C.19 Solar Energy Systems, D. UTILITY-SCALE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS, 3. Operation Requirements, d. Noise

summary: Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be permitted as a special land use in the A-1 and C-1 zoning districts subject to the following standards. Utility-scale solar energy systems are exempt from all lot coverage requirements in this Zoning Ordinance. Utility-scale solar energy systems are subject to the requirements for special land use permitting and approval under this Zoning Ordinance in addition to the regulations in this section. Small Solar Energy Systems shall be permitted as accessory uses in all Zoning Districts, subject to the requirements of this Ordinance.

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be subject to the following setback requirements, which shall be measured from required fencing. No setbacks shall apply between participating properties hosting the same project. Setback Description: Nonparticipating Properties. Setback Requirement: 300 feet measured from the nearest shared property line.
section: Section 6C.19 Solar Energy Systems, D. UTILITY-SCALE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS, 3. Operation Requirements, a. Setbacks

summary: The ordinance defines Repowering as "Replacing significant project components such as solar arrays with the intent of extending the project’s useful life in lieu of decommissioning the project." It explicitly requires that "The owner or operator must apply for and be granted a new special land use permit and site plan under the Zoning Ordinance prior to repowering the project." This applies to Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems, which are "solar energy system[s] intended to distribute electricity via a utility or to off-site customers." The repowering requirement is found under the subsection titled "Application Consistency and Repowering," which states: "Any project must be constructed, operated, and maintained consistent with this Section and its zoning approval unless the owner or operator obtains a new zoning approval from the Township to alter the approved project."

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be subject to the following setback requirements, which shall be measured from required fencing. Setback Description: Public road right-of-way. Setback Requirement: 100 feet measured from the nearest edge of a public road right-of-way. Other setback options include 400 feet from buildings regularly occupied by humans on nonparticipating properties and 300 feet from nonparticipating property lines, but these do not pertain to roads.
section: D. UTILITY-SCALE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS. 3. Operation Requirements. a. Setbacks.

summary: The ordinance requires that a utility-scale solar energy system "shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access" and that the fencing "must utilize fabric screening or other acceptable methods to the Township to screen the utility-scale solar energy system from visibility." Furthermore, "unless screened and buffered at all times by natural forest vegetation meeting the minimum spacing and height requirements, and having a substantially similar obscuring effect of an evergreen vegetative buffer installed pursuant to this section, a continuous evergreen vegetative buffer shall be installed and maintained at all times at the perimeter of all utility-scale solar energy systems, including without limitation between such utility-scale solar energy system and adjacent residential or agricultural areas and/or public highways or streets." The evergreen or native vegetative buffer "shall be composed of native or evergreen trees that at planting shall be a minimum of four feet in height and shrubs two feet in height," with specific spacing requirements: "evergreen trees shall be spaced no more than 15 feet apart on center," "native trees shall be placed no more than 30 feet apart on center," and "shrubs shall be spaced no more than seven feet apart on center." Dead or unhealthy material must be replaced within six months. Planting must occur between March 15 and November 15, or a financial guarantee must be provided. The landscaping requirements can be waived "in instances where screening may be unnecessary such as in between two participating properties, in between two vacant farm fields, or in other similar situations." The Township may also accept "reasonable alternative plantings" if they provide the same or greater screening effect.

The ordinance requires utility-scale solar energy system applicants to submit an approved stormwater management plan and a drain tile maintenance plan to preserve agricultural drainage and manage stormwater. Applicants must ensure modifications do not adversely impact neighboring agricultural drainage infrastructure and must restore all public and private drainage systems (including agricultural drain tile) at decommissioning to allow drainage consistent with pre-construction conditions, including conditions that provide for agricultural uses of properties. Any erosion or flooding caused by construction or operation is the responsibility of the owner or operator. Decommissioning shall include stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion.

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be permitted as a special land use in the A-1 and C-1 zoning districts subject to the following standards. Utility-scale solar energy systems are subject to the requirements for special land use permitting and approval under this Zoning Ordinance in addition to the regulations in this section. Small Solar Energy Systems shall be permitted as accessory uses in all Zoning Districts, subject to the requirements of this Ordinance, and require zoning compliance and building permits, with possible Site Plan Approval if adverse impacts are found.

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be subject to the following setback requirements, which shall be measured from required fencing. No setbacks shall apply between participating properties hosting the same project. Setback Description: Buildings regularly occupied by humans on nonparticipating properties. Setback Requirement: 400 feet from the nearest point on the outer wall. Other setback options include: 100 feet from public road right-of-way and 300 feet from nonparticipating property lines, but these do not pertain to occupied dwellings.
section: D. UTILITY-SCALE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS, 3. Operation Requirements, a. Setbacks

summary: The ordinance requires that all applications for a utility-scale solar energy system include a "Visual Analysis. Renderings of the proposed project that show the Township how the proposed project will look from various vantage points from roadways and non-participating properties." This is part of the submission requirements for special land use permitting. Other submission requirements include detailed site plans certified by a registered engineer, project description, environmental impact studies, public health and safety information, alternative locations analysis, consultations with state and federal agencies, agricultural lands analysis, interference mitigation plans, drainage reports, fire and emergency response plans, decommissioning bond and plan, as-built files, material safety data sheets, community impacts analysis, and more. The visual analysis is one among many detailed studies and plans required for approval.

Section 1319.L requires that "A decommissioning plan must be submitted with the conditional use permit application." The plan must include: "1. Description of the manner in which the facility will be decommissioned, including which above and below ground improvements will be removed or retained and how the land will be restored with 18 months after operations cease or are abandoned." "2. The projected cost of decommissioning the facility net of salvage value in current dollars." "3. The method of ensuring funds are available for decommissioning (surety bond, irrevocable letter of credit, or cash deposit at applicant’s option)." Section 1319.M states: "A decommissioning agreement between the applicant and the Township Board must be a condition to the effectiveness of a conditional use permit and must include provisions specifying the form of decommissioning security, requiring review of the decommissioning security amount no less than every five (5) years, taking into account inflation, changes in salvage value, and then-current labor and equipment rates, and determining cessation of operations or abandonment." These requirements apply to "transmission-connected solar energy facility," defined as "A photovoltaic system for generating electricity for transmission to the electric grid."

Section 1319(F) states: 'Notwithstanding Section 902, the facility shall be enclosed by a perimeter fence not less than 7 feet in height to restrict unauthorized access. Perimeter fencing may be located within the required setback from non-participating property lines. Barbed wire is not permitted unless required by the National Electric Code.' This fencing requirement applies to transmission-connected solar energy facilities, which are defined as 'a photovoltaic system for generating electricity for transmission to the electric grid' and thus constitute utility-scale solar energy systems.

summary: Section 1319, subsection H states: 'Lighting shall be limited to where required for safety and security and shall be shielded to prevent glare or spillover on to adjacent non-participating parcels.' This glare restriction applies to transmission-connected solar energy facilities, defined as 'a photovoltaic system for generating electricity for transmission to the electric grid.'

The ordinance explicitly states: 'The maximum height of a solar array shall not exceed 25 feet as measured from grade to the top of the PV Panel in its most upright position; substations and transmission lines are not subject to the maximum height limitation.' This applies to transmission-connected solar energy facilities, which are utility-scale systems generating electricity for transmission to the electric grid.

Inverter sound pressure levels shall not exceed 55 dBA (Leq 1-hour) at a non-participating property line. The site plan must include modeled sound isolines extending from the sound source to demonstrate compliance with this standard. This applies to transmission-connected solar energy facilities, defined as photovoltaic systems for generating electricity for transmission to the electric grid.

All solar arrays, inverters, and any operations and maintenance shelter shall be setback 50 feet from the property line of a non-participating parcel. Access drives, security fencing and transmission lines are permitted within a setback required from a non-participating property line. Additionally, perimeter fencing may be located within the required setback from non-participating property lines. Note that no setback is required from common participating parcel property lines.

All solar arrays, inverters, and any operations and maintenance shelter shall be setback 50 feet from the edge of a road right-of-way (edge of right-of-way being 33 feet from the center line of the right-of-way) irrespective of the existence of any common participating property lines. Access drives, security fencing and transmission lines are permitted within a setback required from a non-participating property line.
section: Section 3. Conditional Use Permit Standards. Article XIII: Conditional Use Permits, Section 1319 Transmission-Connected Solar Energy Facility

summary: The ordinance requires that "existing vegetation along a non-participating property line shall be retained to the extent feasible between the facility and adjacent non-participating parcels" (Section 1319(J)) and that "the facility shall be enclosed by a perimeter fence not less than 7 feet in height to restrict unauthorized access" (Section 1319(F)). Barbed wire fencing is not permitted unless required by the National Electric Code. These requirements apply to "transmission-connected solar energy facilities" defined as "a photovoltaic system for generating electricity for transmission to the electric grid."

summary: Section 3, subsection O states: 'In addition to any signage allowed by Article X, a sign may be attached to the security fencing at each access drive entrance identifying the name of the owner/operator, location, and emergency contact information.' This signage requirement applies to transmission-connected solar energy facilities, which are defined as 'a photovoltaic system for generating electricity for transmission to the electric grid' and are subject to various conditional use permit standards.
