summary: Section 1319.G requires that access drives "shall be designed to minimize the extent of soil disturbance and soil compaction outside the access drive lane, and to maintain surface water flows." Section 1319.K mandates that "a groundcover vegetation management plan must be submitted with the site plan" and "must provide for ground cover under and around solar arrays unless a state agency requires otherwise." These requirements apply to "transmission-connected solar energy facilities," defined as "a photovoltaic system for generating electricity for transmission to the electric grid."

The ordinance states: 'Section 313 RP-Resource Product District, subparagraph C, Conditional Uses Authorized by Permit is amended to add the following additional land use: 20. Transmission-connected solar energy facility (221114) subject to the requirements of Section 1319.' This indicates that utility-scale solar energy systems classified as transmission-connected solar energy facilities are permitted as conditional uses requiring a permit in the RP district. No other districts or conditions are mentioned in the provided text. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this summary as per instructions.

All solar arrays shall be setback 100 feet from any existing single-family dwelling unit on a non-participating parcel. Other setback requirements include 50 feet from the property line of a non-participating parcel for all solar arrays, inverters, and any operations and maintenance shelter, but this applies to property lines, not dwellings.

Section 300.509.3.14 states: "If a Large Solar Energy System is abandoned or otherwise nonoperational for a period of one year, the property owner or the operator must notify the Township and must remove the system within six months after the date of abandonment. The Planning Commission may extend this six-month period upon good cause shown. Removal requires receipt of a demolition permit from the Building Official and full restoration of the site to the satisfaction of the Zoning Administrator. Decommissioning requires removing all structures, fencing, equipment foundations, footings, and debris to a depth of four feet and restoring the soil and vegetation to the condition they were in before construction of the Large Solar Energy System. The requirements of this subsection also apply to a Large Solar Energy System that is never fully completed or operational if construction has been halted for a period of one year." Section 300.509.3.15 requires "the applicant must post a financial security in the form of a surety bond with MDARD or post financial security in the form of a surety bond, escrow payment, or irrevocable letter of credit in an amount equal to 125% of the total estimated cost of decommissioning, code enforcement, and reclamation, which cost estimate must be approved by the Township." The operator and Township will review this amount every two years. The Township may draw from the financial security to decommission the Solar Farm and pay associated costs if the applicant/operator fails to timely decommission. Other options and conditions include the Planning Commission's ability to extend removal deadlines upon good cause, and the requirement for a demolition permit and site restoration to the satisfaction of the Zoning Administrator.

Section 300.509.3(8) states: 'The applicant or operator must install a seven (7) foot wildlife (woven wire) fence around the perimeter of the Large Solar Energy System, which must enclose all electrical equipment related to the Large Solar Energy System, including any transformers and transfer stations. Appropriate warning signs must be posted at safe intervals at the entrance and around the perimeter of the Large Solar Energy System, which must include emergency contact information and emergency shutdown procedures.' This fencing requirement applies specifically to Large Scale Utility Energy Systems 50 megawatts or more. Other types of solar energy systems have different requirements or no explicit fencing mandates, such as Ground Mounted Small Solar Energy Systems which may use a decorative fence that is 50% opaque if approved by the Planning Commission, but this applies only to smaller systems.

Section 300.509.1(3) requires that "Solar Energy Systems must be located or placed so that concentrated solar glare is not directed toward or onto nearby properties or roadways at any time of the day." For Large Solar Energy Systems (including Large Scale Utility Energy Systems 50+ megawatts), Section 300.509.3(7) states: "The Large Solar Energy System must not produce any glare that is visible to neighboring lots or to persons traveling on public or private roads." Other options and conditions for solar energy systems include Small Solar Energy Systems such as Private BIPVs, Roof or Building Mounted Small Solar Energy Systems, and Ground Mounted Small Solar Energy Systems, each with their own permit and location requirements. For example, Roof or Building Mounted Small Solar Energy Systems must also ensure that "concentrated solar glare is not directed toward or onto nearby properties or roadways at any time of the day." Large Solar Energy Systems require special land use permits, site plan review, and must meet various application, location, screening, lighting, noise, and decommissioning requirements.

The ordinance states: 'The height of the solar equipment on their mounts and oriented at maximum tilt measured from the natural grade at the base of the component must not exceed 15 feet.' This applies specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems 50 megawatts or more. Lightning rods may exceed 15 feet but only to the height necessary for lightning protection. This is the explicit maximum height restriction for such large systems.

Section 300.509.3.2.b states: 'Large Solar Energy Systems must be located on parcels of land 15 acres in size or larger.' This is the explicit minimum lot size for Large Scale Utility Energy Systems 50 megawatts or more. Other related restrictions include a limit of 1% total acreage of the township for such systems, 1 mile separation between systems, and setback requirements, but these do not affect the minimum parcel size. The unit 'acres' is used as the standard area measurement.

The noise generated by a Large Solar Energy System must not exceed the following limit: The solar energy facility does not generate a maximum sound in excess of 45 average hourly decibels as modeled at the nearest outer wall of the nearest dwelling located on an adjacent nonparticipating property. This is the explicit maximum noise level requirement for Large Scale Utility Energy Systems 50 megawatts or more. The unit is expressed as dBA, the standard unit for noise measurement.

There must be 1 mile of separation between Large Solar Energy System as measured from the fenced in area of the Solar Energy System. Additional setbacks include 350 feet from all parcel lines and 200 feet from all public road rights-of-way. Setbacks for participating parcels vary by parcel type, including 20 feet from adjoining parcels with solar arrays operated by a different company. These requirements apply to Large Scale Utility Energy Systems 50 megawatts or more.

Non-Participating Parcel Setbacks for Large Solar Energy Systems (including all solar panels, structures, and equipment) must be set back 350 feet from all parcel lines and 200 feet from all public road rights-of-way. Participating parcel setbacks vary by parcel type, including 20 feet for adjoining agricultural parcels (vacant or improved), 150 feet for residential parcels, 60 feet for commercial parcels, 20 feet for industrial parcels, and 20 feet for adjoining parcels with solar arrays operated by different companies. Additionally, there must be 1 mile of separation between Large Solar Energy Systems as measured from the fenced-in area of the Solar Energy System.

Participating Parcel Setbacks for Large Solar Energy systems: Proof of being a participating parcel must be in writing and included with the application. Setbacks for participating parcels are presented in the table below and are dependent on parcel type. Parcel Type Minimum Setback allowed for Participating parcel: Adjoining agricultural parcel (vacant) 20’; Adjoining agricultural parcel (improved) 20’ from parcel line or 150’ from dwelling; Residential parcel (improved or vacant) 150’; Commercial parcel (improved or vacant) 60’; Industrial parcel (improved or vacant) 20’; Adjoining parcel with solar array operated by different company 20’ Nature Corridor.
section: 300.509 Solar Energy Systems, subsection 3. Large Solar Energy System, part 2.g

summary: Non-Participating Parcel Setbacks for Large Solar Energy Systems (including all solar panels, structures, and equipment) must be set back 350 feet from all parcel lines and 200 feet from all public road rights-of-way. Additionally, all LSES shall have a minimum landscape buffer of 25 feet along any road or adjacent to a residential use, consisting of grass ground cover and rows of evergreen plantings to form a visual barrier. The Large Solar Energy System must not produce any glare visible to persons traveling on public or private roads.

Large Solar Energy Systems shall include a landscaping and screening buffering plan. The plan will be reviewed through the approval process to assure that the proposed Large Solar Energy System is appropriately landscaped in relation to adjacent land uses and road rights-of-ways. Evergreen plantings and/or berms shall be used to mitigate views of the Large Solar Energy System from road rights-of-ways and from residential structures to the extent possible. For residential structures, visual mitigation is required within 1,300 feet from the Large Solar Energy System during all times of the year. Exceptions to landscaping requirement may be granted by the planning commission on a case-by-case basis. Requirements include: (a) The applicant shall submit landscape plan detailing all proposed changes to the landscape of the site, including temporary or permanent roads or driveways, grading, vegetation clearing, and planting. (b) All LSES shall have a minimum landscape buffer of 25 feet along any road or adjacent to a residential use, which shall consist of grass ground cover and (2) rows of closely-spaced, staggered evergreen plantings, planted no more than twelve (12) feet on center, front to back and side to side, which can reasonably be expected to form a visual barrier that is at least eight (8) feet above ground level within three (3) years of planting. The minimum height at time of planting shall be no less than six (6) feet in height with a diameter of no less than four (4) feet at its base and a species of evergreen that produces dense growth capable of producing a complete visual barrier. The landscape buffer shall be installed outside of SEF fence line extending towards the road or residential use. (c) Land clearing of natural vegetation shall be limited to that which is necessary for the construction, operation, and maintenance of the LSES pursuant to practices of best management of natural areas or good husbandry of the land or forest other prescribed by applicable laws, regulations, and bylaws. (d) Each owner, operator or maintainer of a solar energy facility shall maintain the landscape buffer so that the vegetation will reach maturity as soon as practical and will have maximum density in foliage. Dead or diseased landscaping shall be removed and must be replanted at the next appropriate planting time. The buffer zone may be utilized for agricultural use. (e) Applicant must provide detailed maintenance plan for the proposed solar energy system and surrounding area, including provisions that will be employed to maintain and promote native vegetation while minimizing the proliferation of invasive vegetation during and following construction. (f) Applicant must provide a plan for meeting or exceeding pollinator standards throughout the lifetime of the facility, as established by the  "Michigan Pollinator Habitat Planning Scorecard for Solar Sites"  developed by the Michigan State University Department of Entomology in effect on the effective date of the amendatory act that added this section or any applicable successor standards approved by the commission as reasonable and consistent with the purposes of this subdivision. Seed mix used to establish pollinator plantings shall not include invasive species as identified by the Midwest Invasive Species Information Network, led by researchers at the Michigan State University Department of Entomology and supporting regional partners. (g) Wherever screening is adjacent to a residence and/or non-participating lot, the Planning Commission may require additional screening methods consistent with industry standards or complaints submitted pursuant Section 19.

Section 300.509.3(8) states: 'The Large Solar Energy System must not display any signs, logos, advertising, graphics, lettering, or commercial inscriptions on the solar arrays or any part of the Large Solar Energy System. The Solar Farm may only post the warning signs required under this Ordinance and signs at each entrance to the Large Solar Energy System, subject to all Township sign regulations.' Additionally, Section 300.509.3(8) requires 'appropriate warning signs must be posted at safe intervals at the entrance and around the perimeter of the Large Solar Energy System, which must include emergency contact information and emergency shutdown procedures.' Other types of solar energy systems have different requirements or no signage requirements explicitly stated, such as Small Solar Energy Systems and Ground Mounted Small Solar Energy Systems, which are regulated differently and do not have explicit signage requirements in this text.

Large Scale Utility Energy Systems 50+ megawatts must obtain a certificate from the Michigan Public Service Commission and require a special land use permit and site plan review. The applicant must provide "a plan for managing erosion and sediment control," "a written plan and schedule for maintaining the subject property, including a plan for maintaining and inspecting drain tiles and addressing stormwater management," and "proof of environmental compliance, including compliance with Part 91, Soil Erosion and Sedimentation Control (MCL 324.9101 et. seq.) and any corresponding County ordinances." Other requirements include landscaping and screening buffering plans, setbacks, height limits, underground transmission lines, decommissioning plans, financial security, and annual reporting. Small Solar Energy Systems have different requirements based on type and size, such as Ground Mounted Small Solar Energy Systems requiring a special use permit if greater than 2600 sq ft and including drainage management plans if over 2,000 sq ft. Large Solar Energy Systems are only allowed on properties enrolled in the PA 116 Farmland and Open Space Preservation Program and must meet various setback and acreage limitations.

Large Solar Energy Systems are permitted in the AR District only by special use permit, as stated in Section 300.305, subsection 'O': 'Large Solar Energy Systems subject to special use, see Section 300.509 and application and special use regulations therein.' Section 509.1 specifies: 'All Large Solar Energy System (Ground Mounted only) AR Required.' Section 509.3 further requires that Large Solar Energy Systems are only allowed on properties enrolled in the PA 116 Farmland and Open Space Preservation Program and require a special land use permit and site plan review. Other solar energy system types include Small Solar Energy Systems, which are permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts with varying conditions, such as size limits and permit requirements, but these do not apply to Large Solar Energy Systems.

Participating Parcel Setbacks for Large Solar Energy systems: Proof of being a participating parcel must be in writing and included with the application. Setbacks for participating parcels are presented in the table below and are dependent on parcel type. Residential parcel (improved or vacant) requires a 150’ setback. Other options include: Adjoining agricultural parcel (vacant) 20’; Adjoining agricultural parcel (improved) 20’ from parcel line or 150’ from dwelling; Commercial parcel (improved or vacant) 60’; Industrial parcel (improved or vacant) 20’; Adjoining parcel with solar array operated by different company 20’ Nature Corridor.
section: 300.509.3.2.g Participating Parcel Setbacks for Large Solar Energy systems

summary: The ordinance requires that Large Solar Energy Systems (50 megawatts or more) obtain a special land use permit and site plan review. The applicant must provide "a site plan that includes all proposed structures and the location of all equipment, transformers, and substations, as well as all setbacks, panel sizes and locations, and the location of property lines, signage, fences, greenbelts and screening..." and "scaled drawings depicting the location, height, elevation, and size of all components." Additionally, the applicant must submit "current photographs of the subject property" and "a graphical demonstration (preferably computer-generated) of the Large Solar Energy System as completed." The ordinance also mandates a "landscaping and screening buffering plan" to assure appropriate landscaping in relation to adjacent land uses and road rights-of-ways, including "evergreen plantings and/or berms shall be used to mitigate views of the Large Solar Energy System from road rights-of-ways and from residential structures to the extent possible" with visual mitigation required within 1,300 feet from the Large Solar Energy System during all times of the year. Other types of solar energy systems include Small Solar Energy Systems (private BIPVs, roof or building mounted, ground mounted) with various permit and size requirements, and Large Solar Energy Systems (ground mounted only) requiring special use permits on properties enrolled in the PA 116 Farmland and Open Space Preservation Program.

Large Freestanding Solar Panel Arrays are subject to decommissioning and removal requirements if they cease to actively produce power for 180 days or more. Removal must include obtaining a demolition permit, restoring the site to original condition, and removing all components to at least six feet below grade within 365 days of non-operation. A financial security guarantee of 125% of demolition quotes must be provided before construction, updated every two years, and held by the Township. Failure to maintain this security or to decommission timely may result in enforcement actions, including use of the security funds by the Township. Other options include small freestanding solar panel arrays, which are smaller than the principal building footprint and have different standards, and rooftop or wall-mounted arrays, which must comply with building codes but do not have decommissioning requirements stated here.

They "may not exceed 25 feet in height." "All structures associated with the solar array must be screened to a height of 8 feet by a screening wall or screen of evergreen trees." Alternatively, "A berm with landscaping may be substituted for this requirement, provided that the berm and landscaping provide adequate screening, in the opinion of the Planning Commission." Other requirements include energy storage setbacks, grid connection plans, and decommissioning provisions.

section: SECTION 5.42: Solar Energy System (Small or Large)

summary: Large freestanding solar panel arrays may not exceed 25 feet in height. This applies to freestanding solar panel arrays that are larger than the footprint of the principal building on the same lot, or which are the principal use of land, permitted by Special Use in the AR and M-1 districts. section: SECTION 5.42: Solar Energy System (Small or Large)

summary: Large freestanding solar panel arrays shall not be permitted on lots under 40 acres in area. This is the minimum lot size requirement explicitly stated for Large Freestanding Solar Panel Arrays. The text specifies 'lots under 40 acres in area,' indicating the unit is acres. Other conditions include setbacks, height limits, and special use permit requirements, but these do not affect the minimum lot size.

summary: Large Freestanding Solar Panel Arrays are permitted by Special Use in the AR and M-1 districts. They must not be located on lots under 40 acres in area and must meet minimum setbacks: Front 50 feet, Side 20 feet, Rear 50 feet. Other types of solar panel arrays include Rooftop or Wall-Mounted Solar Panel Arrays, which must comply with Building Code and height/setback limits; Small Freestanding Solar Panel Arrays, which are permitted accessory structures in all districts with conditions such as not being in the front yard, meeting lot coverage and setback requirements, and not exceeding 15 feet in height.

Section 8.4(q) states: 'Following the operational life of the project, or at the time the project becomes obsolete, uneconomical or an Abandoned Solar Energy System, as determined by the Township Engineer or any other expert or specialist to be designated by the Township to make such a determination, the applicant shall perform decommissioning and removal of the Large Solar Energy System and all its components.' It requires a 'decommissioning plan prepared by a professional engineer' and a 'decommissioning agreement with the Township Board ... that establishes a financial instrument ... such as a surety bond to ensure decommissioning of the project.' The plan must include removal of all structures and facilities, including below-grade components up to six feet, with no concrete, piping or other materials left above six feet below ground. The ground must be restored to its original condition within 365 days of becoming an Abandoned Solar Energy System or decommissioning, whichever occurs first. If decommissioning is not completed within 365 days, the Township Board may complete it and charge the applicant. Section 8.4(y) requires 'continuing security' in the form of a cash deposit, letter of credit, or surety bond to ensure compliance and restoration, with possible annual escalators. The financial security must be kept in full force and effect during the entire time the Large Solar Energy System exists or is in place. Failure to maintain this security is a material violation. These requirements apply specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems as defined in Section 7.0(b): 'A utility-scale energy system ... for the sale, delivery, or consumption of the generated energy by more than one end user, and typically the power output ... equal to or greater than 1 megawatt.'

Section 8.4 (j) Screening/Security: "A Large Solar Energy System shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access and that contains fabric screening (or other cover mechanism on the fence) to screen the Large Solar Energy System. Such fencing shall be eight (8) feet in height as measured from the natural grade of the fencing perimeter and must include fabric screening obscuring the Large Solar Energy System and be kept (including the fabric) at all-times in good-repair. Electric fencing or barbed wire fencing is not permitted unless required by law." Additionally, "Unless this requirement has been waived or modified by the Township Board, the perimeter of the Large Solar Energy System shall also be screened and buffered by installing evergreen vegetative plantings (greenbelts) whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System's entire perimeter from adjacent parcels," with detailed spacing and maintenance requirements for the vegetative buffer. The evergreen vegetative buffer requirement may be waived or modified if all adjoining landowners consent in writing. These fencing and screening requirements apply specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance.

The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Large Solar Energy Systems. Section 8.2(d) states no Solar Energy System shall be installed in a way that causes "excessive production of ... glare." Section 8.2(g) requires that "concentrated solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways." Section 8.4(n) mandates that "all solar panels in a Large Solar Energy System shall be placed such that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways." It also requires a "pre-construction and post-construction glare and glint or comparable study to confirm this standard is met." The Township may require "operational controls (e.g., panel movements) during operation of the Large Solar Energy System to ensure that no glare is cast onto nearby properties or roadways regardless of screening installed by an applicant." These requirements apply to Large Solar Energy Systems, defined as "a utility-scale energy system ... for the sale, delivery, or consumption of the generated energy by more than one end user, and typically the power output of that system is equal to or greater than 1 megawatt."

Section 8.4(g) states: 'Maximum height of a Solar Array shall not exceed twenty (20) feet. Other collection devices, components or structures associated with the Solar Array shall not exceed thirty-five (35) feet at any time or location on the property.' The height is measured from the natural grade at the base of the Solar Array, device, component, or building. The Township Board may waive or modify these height requirements for certain aspects of a Large Solar Energy System when appropriate.

A Large Solar Energy System shall be located on one or more parcels with an aggregate area of twenty (20) acres or greater. This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for Large Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance. The unit is expressed in acres as an area value. This requirement is found in section 8.4(h) 'Lot Size'.

The sound pressure level generated by a Large Solar Energy System shall not exceed 45dB(A) Leq over a one (1) hour period as measured at any Non-Participating Property line. Applicants must provide the Township a pre-construction and post-construction sound study report to confirm this standard is met.

A minimum setback distance of two hundred (200) feet from all property boundaries on the outside perimeter of the Large Solar Energy System (i.e., lands where a person developing a Large Solar Energy System does not have land rights to construct the Large Solar Energy System) shall be required for all buildings and Solar Arrays, except for property boundaries where the applicable adjoining owner(s) agree to reduce that setback distance by executing a signed written waiver of this requirement.

The ordinance explicitly regulates repowering of a Large Solar Energy System by requiring that "Should a person desire to make changes to a Large Solar Energy System in the Township (e.g., expand a project) or 'repower' (i.e., in lieu of decommissioning replace project components to extend the life of a Large Solar Energy System) such a system, they must submit a new SESP application under this Ordinance, but may refer to previously submitted information to fulfill application requirements if applicable." This means repowering is treated as a modification requiring a new permit application. Other options for changes include expansion of the project, which also requires a new SESP application. The ordinance does not provide alternative procedures for repowering aside from submitting a new permit application.

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires that a Large Solar Energy System "shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access and that contains fabric screening (or other cover mechanism on the fence) to screen the Large Solar Energy System." The evergreen or native vegetative buffer must be composed of native or evergreen trees at least four (4) feet in height and shrubs two (2) feet in height, with specific spacing requirements: evergreen trees no more than fifteen (15) feet apart, native trees no more than thirty (30) feet apart, and shrubs no more than seven (7) feet apart. Unhealthy or dead material must be replaced within six (6) months or the next appropriate planting period. Plantings must occur between March 15 and November 15, or a financial guarantee must be provided until planting occurs. The continuous evergreen vegetative buffer requirement may be waived or modified if all adjoining landowners consent in writing. Electric fencing or barbed wire fencing is not permitted unless required by law.

Required stormwater control measures shall be subject to the approval of the Ionia County Drain Commissioner or other entity as applicable, and evidence of such approval shall be submitted to the Township Clerk. Section 8.4(o) states: 'Applicants must provide evidence that its measures to limit the impacts of stormwater runoff and water quality from the SES are approved by the Ionia County Drain Commissioner. Upon project decommissioning, the applicant shall restore all private drainage infrastructure in accordance with Participating Property owner leases or easement agreements as well as restore all private drainage infrastructure in a manner to allow future agricultural activities on any lands utilized for the Large Solar Energy System which were previously used for agricultural activities prior to hosting Large Solar Energy System activities.'

The ordinance requires that all applications for a Solar Energy System Permit (SESP) for a Large Solar Energy System "must be accompanied by detailed Survey Drawing, drawn to scale and dimensioned and certified by a registered engineer licensed in the State of Michigan" with information "sufficient to enable the Township to ascertain compliance with this Ordinance." This includes "location and height of proposed Solar Array(s), buildings, structures, electrical tie lines and transmission lines, security fencing, and all above-ground structures and utilities" (8.4(c)(10), (18)), "location of all existing vegetation and the location, type, and size of all proposed landscaping, and the location, height, and type of existing and proposed fences and walls" (8.4(c)(13)), and "areas of aesthetic or historical importance" (8.4(c)(23)(ix)). The ordinance also mandates screening and buffering: "A Large Solar Energy System shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing ... that contains fabric screening ... to screen the Large Solar Energy System" and "the perimeter ... shall also be screened and buffered by installing evergreen vegetative plantings ... whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System's entire perimeter" (8.4(j)). The Township Board may impose additional reasonable conditions on approval related to these standards (8.4(s)). These requirements explicitly constitute visual impact assessment requirements for Large Solar Energy Systems. No other options or alternative methods for visual impact assessment are provided in the ordinance.

Section 16B.05.F requires that "A decommissioning plan signed by the responsible party and the land owner (if different) addressing the following shall be submitted prior to approval of a utility-scale solar energy collector system." The plan must include: "1. Defined conditions upon which decommission will be initiated (e.g., end of land lease, no power production for twelve [12] months, abandonment, etc.) 2. Removal of utility-owned equipment and non-utility-owned equipment, which may include but not be limited to conduit, structures, fencing, solar panels, and foundations. 3. Restoration of property condition which existed prior to the development of the system. 4. Specification of the timeframe from completion of decommissioning activities. 5. Description of any agreement (i.e., lease) with landowner regarding decommissioning, if applicable. 6. Identity of the entity or individual responsible for decommissioning. 7. Plans for updating the decommissioning plan. 8. A performance guarantee shall be posted in the form of a bond, letter of credit, cash, or other form acceptable to the Township to ensure removal upon abandonment." The performance guarantee amount is based on at least two cost estimates from qualified contractors and must be valid throughout the system's lifetime, with bonds or letters of credit extended regularly. Additionally, Section 16B.04.H states that "A solar energy collector system that ceases to produce energy on a continuous basis for twelve (12) months will be considered abandoned" unless evidence of intent to maintain is provided, and the responsible party "shall remove all equipment and facilities and restore the lot to its condition prior to the development of the system within one (1) year of abandonment." These requirements apply specifically to utility-scale solar energy collector systems as defined in the ordinance, which are "large-scale facility of solar energy collectors with the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity."

summary: The ordinance requires that for Commercial Solar Energy Collector (Solar Farm) systems, the applicant must submit a decommissioning plan that provides for the removal of all equipment and restoration of the site to its original condition upon cessation of use (Section 13.19(F)(1)(f)). Additionally, a decommissioning plan is required to ensure facilities are properly removed after their useful life or if not in use for twelve (12) consecutive months. The plan must include removal of all structures, foundations, electrical equipment, internal or perimeter access roads, restoration of soil and vegetation, and a financial guarantee in the form of a letter of credit, cash deposit, or bond equal to one-hundred twenty-five percent (125%) of the costs to meet the decommissioning requirements (Section 13.19(G)(11)). Other requirements for commercial solar energy collectors include setbacks, screening with a financial guarantee for landscaping, vegetation management, burial of power and communication lines (with exceptions), site restoration plan, fire department review, and access drive requirements. These requirements apply to utility-scale facilities with the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity, permitted in the AR - Agriculture-Residential District subject to Special Land Use Approval.

Section 13.19(F)(1)(d) states that the solar farm "shall be screened from view from adjacent properties and public roads by fencing, landscaping, or other suitable means." Section 13.19(B)(3) defines screening as including "fencing, wall, evergreen vegetation, berm or combination thereof." For Commercial Solar Energy Collectors, Section 13.19(E)(3) requires that they "shall be screened from residential dwelling units and/or other land uses required by the Planning Commission," with the screening zone showing the location of "fences/landscape buffers." Thus, fencing is explicitly required or allowed as part of screening for commercial solar farms. Other screening options include landscaping, walls, evergreen vegetation, berms, or combinations thereof.

Section 13.19(G)(12) requires that if the project is within two (2) miles of an airport, the applicant must complete and provide the results of the Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT) for the Airport Traffic Control Tower final approach paths, consistent with the Interim Policy, FAA Review of Solar Energy Projects on Federally Obligated Airports, or successor policy. The applicant must also complete the Air Space Case Analysis (Form 7460) and provide the results. Additionally, Section 13.19(C)(3) states: "Solar energy collectors and racking shall be dull or dark in color, non-glossy, and substantially non-reflective of light. This shall not create a nuisance to adjacent dwelling units." These are explicit glare-related restrictions applicable to Commercial Solar Energy Collectors (Solar Farms).

Section 13.19(F)(1)(c) states: 'The maximum height of any structure shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet above grade.' This applies specifically to solar farms defined as utility-scale facilities designed to provide electricity to the electric grid, i.e., Commercial Solar Energy Collector (Solar Farm). Other height limits mentioned include 10 feet for ground-mounted solar energy systems as accessory uses and 3 feet above roof for building-mounted systems, but these apply to smaller or non-commercial systems. The 15 feet limit is the most restrictive for commercial solar farms. The units are feet as explicitly stated.

Section 13.19(F)(1)(a) states: 'Minimum lot size shall be twenty (20) acres.' This applies specifically to solar farms defined as utility-scale facilities designed to provide electricity to the electric grid, i.e., Commercial Solar Energy Collector (Solar Farm). No other minimum lot size values for commercial solar farms are provided in the text. The unit 'acres' is explicitly used to describe the minimum lot size.

The use of a utility-scale facility for solar energy collectors with the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity shall be permitted in the AR - Agriculture-Residential District subject to Special Land Use Approval. No other districts are mentioned as permitting commercial solar energy collectors, implying prohibition in all other districts. The ordinance states: 'Commercial Solar Energy Collector: The use of a utility-scale facility for solar energy collectors with the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity shall be permitted in the AR - Agriculture-Residential District subject to Special Land Use Approval.' Other uses such as private use solar energy collectors (building-mounted or ground-mounted) are permitted in all zoning districts with permits, but these do not apply to commercial utility-scale systems.

Section 13.19(E)(3) states: 'Commercial solar energy collectors shall be screened from residential dwelling units and/or other land uses required by the Planning Commission. The screening zone shall show the location of fences/landscape buffers and residential dwelling units on contiguous lots. The screening must meet the definition of screening in Section 13.19(B) of this Zoning Ordinance.' Section 13.19(B)(3) defines screening as: 'Solar energy collector screening shall be a minimum of 80% opaque and installed on the front and on all sides or rear of a solar energy collector visible from a public right-of-way. Screening shall consist of fencing, wall, evergreen vegetation, berm or combination thereof. Plant material used for screening shall be a minimum of twenty-four (24" ) inches tall and of a size, quantity and spacing to achieve a fifty (50%) percent year-round opacity at the time of planting.' Additionally, Section 13.19(F)(d) requires that 'the solar farm shall be screened from view from adjacent properties and public roads by fencing, landscaping, or other suitable means.' The ordinance also requires a financial guarantee to ensure landscaping requirements are met. These requirements apply explicitly to Commercial Solar Energy Collectors (Solar Farms) defined as 'a utility-scale facility of solar energy collectors with the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity.'

Section 13.19(C)(4) states: 'The installation of any solar panel (private or commercial) shall not negatively impact adjacent properties with additional or excessive storm water runoff and/or drainage.' Section 13.19(E)(4) requires: 'Vegetation requirements and management shall meet requirements of this Section 13.19 related to the clearing of existing vegetation and establishment of vegetated ground cover. Additional requirements may apply as required by the Planning Commission: a. Restrictions on tree clearing, the removal of mature trees, or mitigation for cleared trees may be required by the Planning Commission. Such restrictions shall be designed to protect neighboring properties from nuisance (audio, visual or otherwise), decline in property value, and to protect the health, safety and welfare of the surrounding community. b. Vegetation ground cover shall be maintained in good condition on the entire site during the operation until the site is decommissioned.' These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Energy Collector (Solar Farm) systems, defined as 'a utility-scale facility of solar energy collectors with the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity.'

The use of a utility-scale facility for solar energy collectors with the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity shall be permitted in the AR - Agriculture-Residential District subject to Special Land Use Approval with the following requirements: compliance with building-mounted or ground-mounted system requirements, setbacks of minimum 200 feet from residential dwelling units not on the property, screening from residential units as required by the Planning Commission, vegetation management, burial of power and communication lines unless exceptions apply, a site restoration plan, fire department review and approval, and drive requirements for emergency vehicle access. Other uses such as solar energy collectors for private use (building-mounted or ground-mounted) are permitted in all zoning districts with a zoning permit, but these do not apply to commercial utility-scale facilities. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this summary per instructions.

Setback requirements for solar farms must meet the minimum building setback requirements for the zoning district it is in, but will be a minimum of two-hundred (200’) feet from a residential dwelling unit not located on the property. The setback shall be measured to the nearest solar array or other structure within the solar farm, excluding security fencing, screening, or berm.

Section G. SITE PLAN REVIEW REQUIREMENTS FOR COMMERCIAL SOLAR ENERGY COLLECTION SYSTEMS requires "an analysis of the potential visual impacts from the project including solar panels, roads, and fencing along with measures to avoid, minimize, or mitigate the visual effects." It further states that "A plan may be required showing vegetative screening or buffering of the system from those items to mitigate for visual impacts in accordance with this Zoning Ordinance." This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Collector (Solar Farm) defined as "A utility-scale facility of solar energy collectors with the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity." Other requirements for commercial solar farms include setbacks, screening and financial guarantees, vegetation management, power communication line burial, site restoration plan, fire department review, and drive requirements.

Commercial SES facilities considered under this Section must contain a Decommissioning Plan acceptable to the Planning Commission to ensure that structures and appurtenances are properly decommissioned upon the end of their operational life, inoperability or improvement abandonment. A Decommissioning Plan shall be submitted for review and approval detailing the expected duration of the project, how the improvements will be decommissioned, a Professional Engineer’s estimated cost of decommissioning, the financial resources to be used to accomplish decommissioning, and the surety bond holder with which the financial resources shall be deposited. Any commercial SES that is not operated or found to be inoperable due to disrepair for a continuous period of six (6) months shall be considered abandoned. If abandoned, the Planning Commission shall provide written notice to the applicant/owner/operator of a hearing to determine if the commercial SES should be decommissioned. Within ninety (90) days of the hearing where the Planning Commission has determined that a commercial SES is abandoned or inoperable, the owner/operator shall obtain a demolition permit to remove any commercial SES. Failure to obtain a demolition permit within the 90-day period shall be grounds for the Township to remove the commercial SES at the Owner’s expense. Decommissioning shall include removal of all equipment associated with the commercial SES including all materials above and below ground, and site restoration to a condition reflecting the specific character of the site, including road repair, hazardous waste cleanup, re-grading, soil stabilization, and re-vegetation. The restoration process shall comply with all state, county, or local erosion control, soil stabilization and/or runoff requirements and be completed within one (1) year, with possible extensions granted by the Planning Commission. The decommissioning plan must include an agreement that financial resources for decommissioning shall be in the form of a surety bond with a replenishment obligation, amounting to 125% of the estimated removal and restoration cost, with annual reviews by the Planning Commission. The Township has rights to access surety bond funds, enter the site, seek injunctive relief, and file liens to enforce decommissioning. Other options or conditions include repair certification by a Professional Engineer prior to resumption of operation if the system is repaired after being inoperable. These requirements apply specifically to Commercial SES as defined in the ordinance as any SES facility and accessory structures designated and built to exclusively provide electricity to the electric utility’s power grid and not accessory to any other use.

A commercial SES facility shall erect fencing to secure the site. In addition, the site shall be required to install a greenbelt, buffer strip, and/or a berm consistent with the standards of Section 6.2.13. The Planning Commission may increase the requirements of Section 6.2.13 upon finding that the proposed landscaping will not adequately screen the commercial SES from adjacent properties or the roadway.

Section 14.34, subsection 3.J states: 'SES facilities shall be located or placed so that concentrated solar glare shall not directed toward or onto nearby properties or roadways at any time of the day.' This glare restriction applies to all private and commercial SES. Commercial SES are defined as 'Any SES facility and accessory structures, including fencing, or use that is designated and built to exclusively provide electricity to the electric utility’s power grid and is not accessory to any other use.' Commercial SES require a conditional use permit and final site plan approval. Other relevant standards include setbacks, height limits, noise levels, and lighting restrictions. Private SES are permitted by-right up to 20 kW and are accessory to a principal use. Commercial SES are permitted in specific zoning districts (A-1, A-2, M-1, M-2) with additional requirements such as fencing, greenbelt, buffer strip, or berm for visual screening.

All PV systems and support structures associated with such facilities shall be restricted to a maximum height of fourteen (14) feet when oriented at maximum tilt, except for rooftop and building mounted solar systems which rely upon Section 5.6.1 of the Ordinance for height permitting standards. This height restriction applies to both private and commercial SES.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'Commercial SES shall not exceed a total area of one-hundred sixty (160) acres. The commercial SES area shall be calculated based on the total area located within the perimeter fencing for the site.' This is the maximum lot size restriction for Commercial SES. No other maximum lot size values are provided for Commercial SES in the text.

The noise generated from a SES shall not exceed forty (40) dB(A) at the exterior of any habitable structure, also measured at the closest property line to the SES. This sound pressure level may be exceeded during short-term events such as utility shortages, or severe wind storm. If the ambient sound pressure level exceeds forty (40) dB(A), the standard shall be the ambient dB(A) plus five (5) dB(A). This applies to both private and commercial SES unless otherwise specifically noted.
There shall be a minimum distance of one (1) mile between each commercial SES. This buffer shall also apply to commercial SES located in adjacent local units of government.

All SES that are not rooftop or building-mounted shall be setback a minimum of fifty (50) feet from a side or rear property line. Additionally, commercial SES setbacks include a minimum of five hundred (500) feet from any dwelling unit and from any residential zoning district, but these do not pertain to property lines or parcels. For multiple parcel sites, required property line setbacks may be waived by the Planning Commission if no adverse impacts occur. The most restrictive fixed setback directly pertaining to property lines is fifty (50) feet.

All SES that are not rooftop or building-mounted shall be setback a minimum of fifty (50) feet from any road right-of-way. This applies to both private and commercial SES. Additionally, commercial SES must comply with other setback requirements such as 500 feet from dwelling units and residential zoning districts, and 25 feet from wetlands or sensitive environmental areas, but these do not pertain to roads.

Section 14.34, subsection 4.D states: 'A commercial SES facility shall erect fencing to secure the site. In addition, the site shall be required to install a greenbelt, buffer strip, and/or a berm consistent with the standards of Section 6.2.13. The Planning Commission may increase the requirements of Section 6.2.13 upon finding that the proposed landscaping will not adequately screen the commercial SES from adjacent properties or the roadway.' This explicitly requires vegetative buffer and/or other screening for Commercial SES. The options for screening include a greenbelt, buffer strip, and/or berm, with the possibility of increased requirements by the Planning Commission if needed.

The ordinance requires that decommissioning of commercial SES include removal of all equipment and restoration of the site to a condition reflecting the specific character of the site including topography, vegetation, soils, drainage, and any unique environmental features. The restoration shall include: road repair and hazardous waste cleanup, if any, all re-grading, soil stabilization, and re-vegetation necessary to return the subject property to a stable condition consistent with conditions existing prior to establishment of the solar energy system. The restoration process shall comply with all state, county, or local erosion control, soil stabilization and/or runoff requirements or ordinances and shall be completed within one (1) year. Extensions may be granted upon request to the Planning Commission prior to that expiration of the one (1) year requirement for completed decommissioning.

Commercial SES are permitted by issuance of a conditional use permit and approval of a final site plan by the Planning Commission in the A-1, A-2, M-1 and M-2 districts. An application for conditional use permit and final site plan shall contain information required pursuant to ARTICLE 9: CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT APPROVAL, ARTICLE 8: SITE PLAN APPROVAL and other information as required in this section and in this Ordinance. Private SES that are accessory to one or more principal structures are permitted by-right subject to receiving a zoning permit and may produce up to twenty (20) kilowatts (kW) of energy per hour. Except where noted, it is unlawful to construct, erect, install, use or locate a SES unless a special use permit, final site plan and/or zoning permit have been approved pursuant to this Ordinance.

All commercial SES shall be setback a minimum of five hundred (500) feet from any dwelling unit. Other setback requirements include 500 feet from any residential zoning district and 25 feet from wetlands or sensitive environmental areas, but these do not pertain directly to occupied dwellings. The ordinance states: '1. Dwelling Units. All commercial SES shall be setback a minimum of five hundred (500) feet from any dwelling unit.'

Section 14.34.4.C requires that Commercial SES "Graphically demonstrate the visual impact of the project using photos or renditions of the project with consideration given to setbacks and proposed landscaping." This visual impact assessment is part of the additional standards for Commercial SES, which also include requirements for project description, traffic analysis, visual screening, environmental analysis, setbacks, maximum area, buffer distances, lighting, transportation plan, public safety, sound limitations, telecommunications interference, and decommissioning plans. Commercial SES are permitted by conditional use permit and final site plan approval, which must contain information required pursuant to ARTICLE 9: CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT APPROVAL, ARTICLE 8: SITE PLAN APPROVAL, and other information as required in this section and in this Ordinance.

All commercial SES shall be set back a minimum of twenty-five (25) feet from any wetlands or other sensitive environmental areas. Other setback requirements for commercial SES include: 500 feet from any dwelling unit and 500 feet from any residential zoning district (R-1 through R-5).

summary: The ordinance requires that "the applicant shall prepare a Decommissioning Plan and submit it to the Planning Commission for review prior to issuance of the Conditional Land Use Permit." The plan mandates that "all structures and facilities shall be removed, including any structures below-grade, and removed offsite for disposal. No concrete, piping and other materials may be left in place." Furthermore, "The ground must be restored to its original condition within 180 days of becoming an Abandoned Solar Energy System, or decommissioning, whichever occurs first." The ordinance also requires "continuing security and a continuing escrow deposit prior to commencement of construction, which shall remain in effect until the Large Solar Energy System has been finally removed." The financial security must be "in an amount determined by the Township to be reasonably sufficient to restore the property to its previous condition prior to construction and operation of the Large Solar Energy System" and "shall be kept in full force and effect during the entire time that the Large Solar Energy System exists or is in place." These requirements apply specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems, defined as "a utility-scale solar energy system where the primary use of the land is to generate electric energy or other energy ... for the sale, delivery, or consumption of the generated energy by more than one end user, and typically the power output of that system is equal to or greater than 1 megawatt."

A Large Solar Energy System "shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access." The fencing "shall be eight feet in height as measured from the natural grade of the fencing perimeter and the fence must include fabric screening or be of a solid material to conceal the sight of improvements within the fence from outside the fence." "Electric fencing is not permitted." The perimeter shall also be "screened and buffered by installed evergreen vegetative plantings whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels," with detailed requirements for the buffer's width, plant types, spacing, and maintenance. This fencing and screening requirement applies specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems, defined as "a utility-scale solar energy system where the primary use of the land is to generate electric energy ... for the sale, delivery, or consumption of the generated energy by more than one end user, and typically the power output of that system is equal to or greater than 1 megawatt."

The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Large Solar Energy Systems, requiring that "all solar panels shall be placed such that harmful solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways." Within one year of construction, the owner or operator must submit "a post-construction glare study prepared by a third-party engineer or other qualified professional demonstrating that the project, as constructed, complies with such glare requirements." Additionally, "a Solar Energy System shall have a non-glare coating and be of a neutral color. Solar panels shall be finished with non-reflective coatings. Exposed frames and components shall have a non-reflective surface." These requirements apply specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems, defined as "a utility-scale solar energy system where the primary use of the land is to generate electric energy or other energy... and typically the power output of that system is equal to or greater than 1 megawatt."

Maximum height of a Solar Array shall not exceed eighteen (18) feet measured from the finished grade at the base of such equipment to the fully elevated highest point of the improvement. Other collection devices, components, or buildings of the Large Solar Energy System shall not exceed thirty-five (35) feet, or the maximum building height permitted within the zoning district in which the Large Solar Energy System is located, whichever is less. The height shall be measured from the natural grade at the base of the Solar Array, device, component or building measured. The Township Board may waive or modify these height requirements for certain aspects of a Solar Energy System (such as structures associated with above-ground transmission lines) through the implementation of conditions when appropriate.

The ordinance states: 'A Large Solar Energy System shall be located on one or more parcels with an aggregate area of 10 acres or greater.' This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for Large Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as utility-scale solar energy systems typically with power output equal to or greater than 1 megawatt and intended for sale, delivery, or consumption by more than one end user. No other minimum lot size values are provided for Large Solar Energy Systems in the text. The unit 'acres' is explicitly used to describe this minimum lot size.

No component of any Large Solar Energy System shall emit noise exceeding forty-five (45) dBA (measured Leq one hour) as measured at the outside perimeter of the project. This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for Large Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as utility-scale solar energy systems with power output equal to or greater than 1 megawatt, intended for sale, delivery, or consumption by more than one end user. The unit dBA refers to A-weighted decibels, a standard unit for measuring noise levels.

The ordinance states that 'Large Solar Energy Systems may only be located within the following lands within the Township’s Utility Solar Overlay Zoning District' and that this district is the designated location for such systems. It further clarifies that 'All Large Solar Energy Systems require a Conditional Land Use Permit and site plan approval.' The AG-1 Agricultural Zoning District previously allowed Large Solar Energy Systems as a Conditional Land Use, but this has been removed, and such systems may only be constructed, operated, and maintained within the Utility Solar Overlay Zoning District (which may include lands of the AG-1 Zoning District). The Utility Solar Overlay Zoning District is an overlay district and thus is by assumption a primary use district for utility-scale solar energy systems, although use is conditional.

section: SECTION 2. AMENDMENT TO ZONING ORDINANCE ARTICLE VIII, SECTION 8.19

summary: A minimum setback distance of 150 feet from all property boundaries on the outside perimeter of the Large Solar Energy System shall be required for all buildings and Solar Arrays except for property boundaries where the applicable adjoining owner(s) agree to lessen or increase that setback distance by executing a signed written waiver of this requirement in recordable form, provided no such waiver shall act to permit less than the required minimum setback of the applicable zoning district.

An owner or operator may only  "repower"  a Large Solar Energy System (replace substantial components of the land use in lieu of decommissioning the project) by submitting a new Conditional Land Use Permit application and site plan and having such requests approved by the Township.

The ordinance explicitly requires that Large Solar Energy Systems be "completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access" with fencing that "must include fabric screening or be of a solid material to conceal the sight of improvements within the fence from outside the fence." Additionally, "the perimeter of Large Solar Energy Systems shall also be screened and buffered by installed evergreen vegetative plantings whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels." The evergreen or native vegetative buffer "shall be at least 25 feet in width and composed of native or evergreen trees that at planting shall be a minimum of six (6) feet in height and shrubs two (2) feet in height," with spacing and maintenance requirements detailed, including replacement of unhealthy or dead material within six months. If natural forest vegetation already provides continuous screening with similar obscuring effect, the buffer may not be required. The ordinance also prohibits clearing of a 25-foot natural screening buffer near properties not consenting to development without authorization. These requirements apply to Large Solar Energy Systems defined as utility-scale systems with power output equal to or greater than 1 megawatt and intended for sale, delivery, or consumption by more than one end user.

Signage: No lettering, company insignia, advertising, graphics or other commercially-oriented inscriptions or designs shall be on any part of the Solar Arrays or other components of the Large Solar Energy System unless otherwise permitted by this Ordinance. This section does not prohibit signs reasonably necessary to inform the public of potential safety hazards associated with the Large Solar Energy System, nor does it prohibit any other signs that may be required by this Ordinance, the Conditional Land Use Permit, or other applicable law. One sign must be located at each entrance (e.g., gate) of a Large Solar Energy System and such sign must be easily visible throughout all four seasons. Large Solar Energy System entrance signs shall be two feet by four feet and placed in the road right of way. The entrance signs shall contain at least the following: Warning High Voltage, Large Solar Energy System owner/operator name, an emergency telephone number, a website address of the Large Solar Energy System owner/operator, and the physical street address of Large Solar Energy System.

The ordinance requires "a written study describing measures to be taken to manage stormwater runoff throughout the Large Solar Energy System, including any measures to promote the growth of vegetation beneath the arrays and/or otherwise limit the impacts of storm water runoff to avoid unreasonably increasing such runoff as compared to before construction of any improvements." Such stormwater runoff measures must be approved by the Jackson County Drain Commissioner and Parma Township. Additionally, upon decommissioning or abandonment, "The ground must be restored to its original condition within 180 days of becoming an Abandoned Solar Energy System, or decommissioning, whichever occurs first." These requirements apply to Large Solar Energy Systems defined as "utility-scale solar energy system where the primary use of the land is to generate electric energy or other energy ... for the sale, delivery, or consumption of the generated energy by more than one end user, and typically the power output of that system is equal to or greater than 1 megawatt."

Large Solar Energy Systems may only be located within the Township’s Utility Solar Overlay Zoning District as depicted on the map. All Large Solar Energy Systems require a Conditional Land Use Permit and site plan approval. Large Solar Energy Systems were removed as a Conditional Land Use in the AG-1 Agricultural Zoning District and may only be constructed, operated, and maintained within the Utility Solar Overlay Zoning District (which may include lands of the AG-1 Zoning District).

summary: All applications for a Large Solar Energy System must be accompanied by a "visual impact analysis prepared by a third-party qualified professional that analyzes the visual impacts of the proposed project, including a description of the project, the existing visual landscape, and important scenic resources, plus visual simulations that show what the project will look like (including proposed landscape and other screening measures) after construction." This is required as part of the Conditional Land Use Permit and site plan approval process for Large Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as utility-scale solar energy systems with power output equal to or greater than 1 megawatt intended for sale, delivery, or consumption by more than one end user. Other requirements include detailed site plans, environmental impact studies, and various operational and safety standards, but the visual impact analysis is the explicit visual impact assessment requirement.

Large Solar Energy Systems shall also be setback at least 150 feet from all lakes, rivers, streams, or wetland unless such a requirement is waived by the Township Board due to a finding of no unreasonable impacts to such bodies of water due to the Large Solar Energy System.

Section 6.38.2 Commercial Solar Installations requires a decommissioning plan to be submitted as part of the special land use application, detailing the removal of solar panels, equipment, and restoration of the site upon cessation of use. Decommissioning shall include removal of all structures (including transmission equipment and fencing) and debris to a depth of four feet, restoration of the soil, and restoration of vegetation within 12 months of the end of project life or facility abandonment. The plan must state how the facility will be decommissioned, the professional engineer's estimated cost of decommissioning, the financial resources to be used, and the type of surety to be provided prior to construction. The owner/operator may be required to post a surety equal to 150 percent of the total estimated decommissioning and reclamation costs prior to issuance of a building permit, with periodic reviews and adjustments. Failure to maintain the surety can lead to revocation of the special land use permit and order for removal and reclamation. These requirements apply specifically to commercial solar installations permitted as a special land use in AG and I zoning districts. Personal solar installations have separate abandonment removal requirements but do not have a detailed decommissioning plan or surety requirements.

Section 6.38.2 Commercial Solar Installations requires that ground-mounted commercial solar installations "shall be enclosed by a fence, barrier, barbwire, or other appropriate means as determined by National Electric Code (NEC), as amended." Fences or barriers "shall work to incorporate wildlife friendly design, when identified as appropriate." This fencing requirement applies when lighting is required for site access or safety. Additionally, commercial solar installations "shall be screened from view from adjacent properties and public rights-of-way by landscaping, fencing, or other approved methods." The Planning Commission may evaluate screening and buffering requirements on a site-by-site basis and may excuse buffer areas if an opaque fence is installed. Other options for screening include landscaping or existing topography/vegetation. The fencing or barrier is part of the broader screening and buffering standards for commercial solar installations.

Section 6.38.2 Commercial Solar Installations states: 'Solar panels and equipment shall be located to minimize glare onto adjacent properties and public rights-of-way.' This applies to commercial solar energy systems, including solar farms and utility-scale solar energy facilities, permitted as a special land use in the AG and I zoning districts. Other relevant standards include height limits (maximum 15 feet), setback requirements, screening, and maintenance. Personal solar installations (6.38.1) also have glare restrictions but apply only to systems for personal use, not commercial installations.

The maximum height of any solar panel or related equipment for Commercial Solar Installations shall not exceed 15 feet. Additionally, it is stated that facilities shall conform to 16 feet height, but the more restrictive 15 feet limit applies. This restriction is explicitly for commercial solar energy systems including solar farms and utility-scale solar energy facilities. Units are given in feet.

The minimum lot size for a commercial solar installation shall be 10 acres. This is explicitly stated in section 6.38.2, subsection C, item 2: 'The minimum lot size for a commercial solar installation shall be 10 acres.' No other minimum lot size values for commercial solar installations are provided. The unit 'acres' is the standard area measurement used.

Lot coverage for ground mounted structures shall be limited by the 75 feet setbacks. The buffer may be reduced if the decision-making body determines that there is a substantial screen such as existing topography or landscaping vegetation and/or an operational management plan and/or an agricultural operation easement is provided. The Planning Commission has the authority to either increase or decrease the buffer requirements based on site conditions.

Commercial solar installations "shall be screened from view from adjacent properties and public rights-of-way by landscaping, fencing, or other approved methods." A landscaping plan must be submitted as part of the special land use application. The Planning Commission may evaluate screening and buffering requirements on a site-by-site basis and may excuse buffer requirements if there is "existing natural vegetation or lack of impact due to adjoining land uses, such as but not limited to crop productions, wood lots, etc." A buffer area may not be required between a solar energy facility and an industrial or commercial use. A planted buffer may not be required if an opaque fence is installed. The Planning Commission has authority to increase or decrease buffer requirements based on site conditions.

Section 6.38.2.G states that for commercial use solar installations, "the following requirements shall apply for soil stabilization, erosion control, and ground water management: 1. To the extent feasible and compatible with the climate and pre-project landscaping of the property, the site shall be restored with native vegetation. The re-vegetation plans shall be reviewed and approved by the Township. 2. A stormwater management plan showing existing and proposed grading and drainage demonstrating the project is in compliance with applicable stormwater regulations shall be submitted to the Zoning Administrator prior to the start of actual construction on the approved site or sites. 3. A maintenance plan shall be submitted for the continuing maintenance of the commercial solar installation, which may include, but not be limited to, planned maintenance of vegetation or ground cover, equipment maintenance, and plans for cleaning of solar panels if required, prior to issuance of a building permit. 4. After construction is completed, as-built surveys for the project must be prepared by a licensed professional surveyor or other approved qualified professional and shall be submitted to the reviewing agency's engineer for review and record keeping. The surveys shall show that the as-built conditions are substantially the same as those submitted for building permit." Other related provisions include grading minimization (6.38.2.D), protection of high value biological resources (6.38.2.F), and screening and buffering evaluated through the special use permit process (6.38.2.G.5).

A Large Solar Energy System "shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access." No component of any Large Solar Energy System shall emit noise exceeding a sound pressure level of 50 dB(A) as measured at the outside perimeter of the project. This sound pressure level shall not be exceeded for more than 6 minutes (L 10) in any hour of the day. The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems.
