summary: The ordinance adds a new Paragraph 37 entitled 'Solar Energy Systems' under Section 18 'Special Exception Uses' Subsection C. It defines Commercial solar energy systems as those where the principal design, purpose or use is to provide energy to off-site uses or the wholesale or retail sale of generated electricity. For commercial systems that are the principal use of the property, they 'shall be required to have a minimum of 20 acres and the front-yard setback shall be not less than 100 feet from any abutting property line and the road right-of-way' and 'shall only be permitted within the "A-1", "AB", "D-1", "E" or "RP" zoning districts.' Other conditions include a maximum height of 15 feet, screening by a 6-foot opaque fence or landscape screening, and location in side or rear yards for private systems. The ordinance also distinguishes: (a) Private solar energy system mounted to roof or building or utilizing building integrated photovoltaics permitted in all districts; (b) Private ground-mounted accessory use or commercial solar energy systems permitted in all districts; and (c) Commercial solar energy systems that are the principal use of the property permitted only in specified districts. Additional requirements include site plan submission, color and glare restrictions, abandonment removal, and possible financial guarantees. The ordinance does not explicitly mention signage but includes fencing and screening requirements that regulate system visibility and safety.
section: Part 300 "Zoning" Section 18 "Special Exception Uses" Subsection C "List of uses with specific conditions" Paragraph 37 "Solar Energy Systems"

summary: Commercial systems that are the principal use of the property shall be required to have a minimum of 20 acres and the front-yard setback shall be not less than 100 feet from any abutting property line and the road right-of-way. They shall only be permitted within the "A-1", "AB", "D-1", "E" or "RP" zoning districts. These systems are subject to special exception use review and approval, including conditions such as height limits (not to exceed 15 feet), screening requirements, and setback rules. Other solar energy systems include: (a) Private solar energy system mounted to roof or building or utilizing building integrated photovoltaics permitted in all districts; (b) Private ground-mounted accessory use or commercial solar energy systems permitted in all districts; and (c) Commercial solar energy systems that are the principal use of the property permitted only in the specified districts with special exception use approval.
section: SECTION 6 AMENDMENT TO PART 300 "ZONING" SECTION 18 "SPECIAL EXCEPTION USES"

summary: The ordinance requires that commercial ground-mounted solar energy systems that are the principal use of the property and have a minimum of 20 acres must submit a site plan complying with Section 18.A of the zoning ordinance. The system installation must be generally neutral in color and substantially non-reflective of light. The maximum height shall not exceed 15 feet, and the base must be screened by no less than a 6-foot opaque fence or landscape screening. The front-yard setback shall be not less than 100 feet from any abutting property line and the road right-of-way. These systems are only permitted within the "A-1", "AB", "D-1", "E" or "RP" zoning districts. Other options include: (a) Private solar energy system mounted to roof or building or utilizing building integrated photovoltaics permitted in all districts; (b) Private ground-mounted accessory use or commercial solar energy systems permitted in all districts; (c) Commercial solar energy systems that are the principal use of the property permitted in A-1, AB, D-1, E, RP districts. Additional conditions include compliance with height and setback requirements for roof or building mounted systems, submission of certification for structural integrity, and potential requirements for financial guarantees for removal if abandoned. The Planning Commission may require additional information as part of the review.
section: Part 300 "Zoning" Section 18 "Special Exception Uses" Subsection C "List of uses with specific conditions" Paragraph 37 "Solar Energy Systems"

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires a decommissioning plan for Solar Farms, defined as "a solar energy system which is the principal use of a parcel and which is designed and constructed to produce electrical energy for sale back into an electrical energy grid system and is not consumed on site." The applicant must submit a decommissioning plan addressing: "conditions upon which decommissioning will be initiated (i.e., end of land lease, no power production for nine months, obsolete equipment and similar circumstances), removal of all non-utility owned equipment, conduit, structures, fencing, roads, and building foundations to a depth of three feet below grade, restoration of property to the condition prior to development of the solar farm including measures to ensure that soils are not contaminated during decommissioning, the timeframe for completion of decommissioning activities, an engineer’s cost estimate for all aspects of the decommissioning plan, description of any agreement with the landowner regarding decommissioning, provisions for updating the decommissioning plan, and a statement signed by the owner or operator that they take full responsibility for reclaiming the site." The Planning Commission may require a financial guarantee to cover decommissioning costs. Additionally, a "Removal Cost Guarantee" requires the applicant/owner/operator to provide financial security in the form of a cash deposit or performance bond approved by the Township Board, based on independent demolition quotes plus 20%, updated every five years. Failure to maintain this security is a material violation subject to enforcement, fines, revocation of permits, and removal of solar facilities. The landowner is liable if the operator defaults, and the Township may remove the structures at the owner's expense, including legal action to recover costs. These requirements are specific to Solar Farms allowed only in AG-Agricultural and I-Industrial zoning districts, with minimum lot size of 20 acres and subject to Special Use Permit approval.

For Solar Farms, the ordinance requires: "A security fence shall be placed and maintained around the perimeter of the solar farm with a locked gate." The "height and material of the fence shall be as approved by the Planning Commission depending upon the location of the facility." Solar Farms are defined as "a solar energy system which is the principal use of a parcel and which is designed and constructed to produce electrical energy for sale back into an electrical energy grid system and is not consumed on site." Other requirements for Solar Farms include minimum lot size of 20 acres, setbacks, landscaping, decommissioning plans, and maintenance records, but these do not pertain to fencing. No other fencing options or conditions are provided.

For Solar Farms, the ordinance states: 'A ground mounted SES shall not exceed a height of 20 feet above natural grade. The height shall be measured from the highest point of the panel when oriented at its maximum tilt to the ground immediately below the panel.' Other height limits in the ordinance include 10 feet for Level 1 Onsite Ground Mounted SES and 14 feet for Level 2 Onsite Ground Mounted SES, but these apply to smaller or accessory systems, not Solar Farms. The unit of measurement is feet.
section: 4.7 — Solar Energy Systems (SES), Subsection G. Solar Farms

summary: The ordinance states: 'The minimum lot size for a solar farm shall be 20 acres.' This applies specifically to Solar Farms defined as 'a solar energy system which is the principal use of a parcel and which is designed and constructed to produce electrical energy for sale back into an electrical energy grid system and is not consumed on site.' No other minimum lot size values for Solar Farms are provided. The unit 'acres' is explicitly used as the area measurement.

The noise emitted from any SES shall not exceed 55 decibels at any property line for the lot on which the SES is located. This applies to all Solar Energy Systems, including Solar Farms, which are defined as a solar energy system designed and constructed to produce electrical energy for sale back into an electrical energy grid system and is not consumed on site. The unit for noise level is assumed to be dBA, the standard unit for noise measurement.

Solar farms are only allowed in the AG-Agricultural and I-Industrial zoning districts subject to review and approval of a Special Use Permit by the Planning Commission in accordance with the requirements and procedures of Chapters 7 and 8 herein and also the following requirements. By implication, solar farms are unconditionally prohibited in all other zoning districts not named AG or I. Other types of solar energy systems such as Level 1 and Level 2 Onsite Ground Mounted SES are allowed in all zoning districts as accessory uses, subject to various size, setback, height, and approval requirements. Roof and wall mounted SES are permitted accessory uses in all zoning districts subject to review and approval by the Township Building Official.

Solar panels shall be setback a minimum of 50 feet from all road right-of-way or easement boundary lines and 10 feet from all other lot lines except solar panels shall not be placed closer than 100 feet from the lot line of another parcel containing a dwelling unit. (Section 4.7.G.5.e)

summary: For Solar Farms, the ordinance requires that "Plantings shall be installed around the perimeter of the parcel or parcels containing the solar farm. One deciduous or conifer tree for every 25 feet of property line length is required." The Planning Commission may modify the landscaping requirement "depending upon the location of existing plant material on the site or if additional plantings are needed to buffer existing land uses." Trees "shall be a minimum of four (4) feet tall when planted and remain in good condition for the life of the project." Additionally, the application must include "a landscaping plan illustrating the number, size, type and spacing of trees proposed to screen the solar farm from nearby roadways." These requirements are found under subsection G.5.d and G.3.k. No other screening or vegetative buffer options or conditions are provided for Solar Farms in the ordinance.

The ordinance explicitly requires for Solar Farms a decommissioning plan that includes 'Restoration of property to the condition prior to development of the solar farm including measures to ensure that soils are not contaminated during decommissioning.' It also mandates that 'The portion of the premises on which the array of collector panel structures is located shall not be paved with asphalt or any other surface material that is impervious to rainwater.' Additionally, a financial guarantee for removal and site restoration is required to ensure proper site reclamation. These requirements apply to Solar Farms defined as 'a solar energy system which is the principal use of a parcel and which is designed and constructed to produce electrical energy for sale back into an electrical energy grid system and is not consumed on site.' The ordinance distinguishes Solar Farms from Level 1 and Level 2 Onsite Ground Mounted SES, which have different size, setback, and height limits and accessory use status, but the soil and erosion control requirements are specifically detailed for Solar Farms under the decommissioning and site restoration provisions.

Solar farms are only allowed in the AG-Agricultural and I-Industrial zoning districts subject to review and approval of a Special Use Permit by the Planning Commission in accordance with the requirements and procedures of Chapters 7 and 8 herein and also the following requirements. Level 1 Onsite Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems are allowed in all zoning districts as a permitted accessory use subject to review and approval by the Building Official. Level 2 Onsite Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems are allowed in all zoning districts as an accessory use subject to review and approval of a Special Use Permit by the Planning Commission. Roof and wall mounted SES are a permitted accessory use in all zoning districts and are subject to review and approval by the Township Building Official.

For Solar Farms, "solar panels shall not be placed closer than 100 feet from the lot line of another parcel containing a dwelling unit." Other setback requirements for Solar Farms include a minimum of 50 feet from all road right-of-way or easement boundary lines and 10 feet from all other lot lines, but the 100 feet setback from parcels with dwellings is the most restrictive setback related to occupied dwellings.
section: 4.7 — Solar Energy Systems (SES), Subsection G.5.e Additional Requirements for Solar Farms

summary: Under Section G.3.e, the applicant for a Solar Farm must provide "Information on the visual impact of the proposed solar farm using photos or computer-generated images of the project on the site to demonstrate the appearance of the project from off site." Solar Farms are defined as "a solar energy system which is the principal use of a parcel and which is designed and constructed to produce electrical energy for sale back into an electrical energy grid system and is not consumed on site." Additional application requirements include proof of lease or ownership, panel type and hazardous chemicals, manufacturer details, expected energy output, maintenance schedule, decommissioning plan, security and landscaping plans, and other information as required by the Planning Commission. The Planning Commission may waive or modify some requirements if deemed unnecessary for proper review.

All Commercial SECS or WECS shall submit with their special land use application a decommissioning and final reclamation plan after the anticipated useful life or abandonment/termination of the project. This includes supplying evidence of an agreement with the underlying property owner that ensures proper removal of all equipment and restoration of the site within six (6) months of decommissioning or abandonment of the project. To ensure proper removal of the project upon abandonment/termination, a bond, letter of credit or cash surety shall be: (1) In an amount approved by the City Council to be no less than the estimated cost of removal and may include a provision for inflationary cost adjustments; (2) Based on an estimate prepared by the engineer for the applicant, subject to approval of the City Council; (3) Provided to the City prior to the issuance of a zoning permit; (4) Used in the event the owner of the project or the underlying property owner fails to remove or repair any defective, abandoned or terminated project. The City, in addition to any other remedy under this Ordinance, may pursue legal action to abate the violation by seeking to remove the project and recover any and all costs, including attorney fees.

Section 7.24.4(A) states: 'A security fence (height and material to be proposed and reviewed/approved through the special land use approval process) shall be placed around the perimeter of Ground Mounted Commercial SECS and electrical equipment.' This fencing requirement applies explicitly to Commercial Solar Energy Conversion Systems (SECS) with a rated capacity of 10 kW or more. Other related standards include height, placement, coverage, and visibility requirements for Ground Mounted Commercial SECS (7.24.3(A)), but fencing is specifically mandated only in 7.24.4(A).
section: 7.24.4 Solar Energy Conversion System Approval Standards

summary: Section 7.24.4.B (Visual Impact) states: 'SECS shall be located or placed so that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed toward or onto nearby properties or rights-of-way at any time of the day.' This applies to all Solar Energy Conversion Systems, including Commercial SECS with a rated capacity of 10 kW or more. Other related standards include: Ground Mounted Commercial SECS must be setback 50 feet from property lines and 200 feet from residential zones, have a maximum height of 16 feet, and be screened with an 8-foot vegetated screen; Roof or Building Mounted Commercial SECS must not exceed maximum allowed height and be designed to blend into architecture or be screened from routine public view. Additional standards cover safety, noise, electromagnetic interference, lighting, signage, feeder lines, and compliance with construction and interconnection codes.
section: 7.24.4 Solar Energy Conversion System Approval Standards

summary: The maximum height of a Ground Mounted Commercial SECS shall be sixteen (16) feet above grade at maximum tilt. This applies specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Conversion Systems (SECS) with a rated capacity of 10 kW or more. Other related height restrictions include roof-mounted commercial SECS, which shall not exceed the maximum allowed height in any zoning district and are considered mechanical devices for height measurement purposes. Ground Mounted Personal SECS (rated capacity no more than 10 kW) have different height limits tied to accessory structures, but these do not apply to commercial systems.

Section 7.24.4.C states: 'All SECS shall have a maximum noise production rating of fifty (50) dBA and shall conform to this standard under normal operating conditions as measured at any property line.' This applies to all Solar Energy Conversion Systems, including Commercial SECS with a rated capacity of 10 kW or more, such as Ground Mounted Commercial SECS. The unit for noise level is dBA, a standard unit for measuring sound levels.
section: 7.24.4 Solar Energy Conversion System Approval Standards

summary: Ground Mounted Commercial SECS shall be setback a minimum of fifty (50) feet from all property lines and public rights-of-way, and two hundred (200) feet from any residential zoning district or use. The most restrictive setback is two hundred (200) feet from any residential zoning district or use.

Ground Mounted Commercial SECS shall be setback a minimum of fifty (50) feet from all public rights-of-way. This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Conversion Systems (SECS) with a rated capacity of 10 kW or more. Other setback requirements include two hundred (200) feet from any residential zoning district or use, but that is unrelated to roads.

Ground Mounted Commercial SECS with a rated capacity of 10 kW or more "shall be screened on all sides with a vegetated screen or green belt at a minimum height of eight (8) feet." This is found in section 7.24.3.A.4. Other related standards for Ground Mounted Commercial SECS include: maximum height of sixteen (16) feet above grade at maximum tilt (7.24.3.A.1), setbacks of fifty (50) feet from all property lines and public rights-of-way and two hundred (200) feet from any residential zoning district or use (7.24.3.A.2), and no limit on the number of such systems on a property (7.24.3.A.5).

A Commercial SECS operator is required to provide a single posting, not to exceed four (4) square feet, at the entrance of a Commercial SECS prohibiting trespassing, warning of high voltage, and providing the emergency contact information for the operator. This signage requirement applies to Commercial Solar Energy Conversion Systems (SECS) with a rated capacity of 10 kW or more. Other related standards for Commercial SECS include height limits, setbacks, screening, and security fencing, but these do not pertain to signage.
section: 7.24.4 Solar Energy Conversion System Approval Standards

Section 17.115, subsection H states: 'Any ground-mounted solar photovoltaic installation which ceases to operate, has been abandoned, or is in disrepair, as determined by the Zoning Administrator or Building Inspector, shall be removed. Unless otherwise approved by the Township, decommissioning shall begin no later than six (6) months after the solar project has ceased to generate electricity. All panels and structures associated with the project shall be completely removed. All reasonable effort shall be made to reuse or recycle solar components following the regulations and guidelines established by the Federal Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA), and any other state or local rules that may be currently applicable. The property shall be returned to its condition prior to the installation of the project or to some other condition, as approved by the Township.' Subsection I further details decommissioning requirements including removal of all equipment, disposal of waste, site stabilization, restoration, and financial security requirements: 'Prior to construction, Rives Township requires a detailed decommissioning plan with documented decommissioning costs and salvage value projections... The financial security shall be in the form of a surety bond... with specified funding milestones... An update of the decommissioning plan costs shall be performed every five (5) years... In the event of bankruptcy or similar financial default of the Solar Energy System owner, the property owner of the project site shall bear the decommissioning costs.' These requirements apply to Large Solar Energy Systems defined as 'A utility-scale commercial facility, occupying an area of more than one acre... used for the purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity to off-site customers.'
section: SECTION 17.115 – LARGE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS OFF-SITE UTILITY USE; REQUIREMENTS

summary: Section 17.115, subsection J (Safety/Security) requires that the site of a Large Solar Energy System be secured by a fence along all exterior sides of the facility that is a minimum of eight (8) feet in height with a gate and locking mechanism that will allow for emergency access at all times. The fencing shall consist of wildlife-friendly, durable materials which shall be approved by the Planning Commission. The fencing must be located between the required landscape greenbelt and all photovoltaic solar devices and support structures associated with the facility, and shall comply with all federal, state, and local regulations, including MI-DNR Wildlife Conservation Order 2.11.
section: SECTION 17.115 – LARGE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS OFF-SITE UTILITY USE; REQUIREMENTS

summary: Section 17.113, subsection N states: 'No Solar Energy System shall produce glare that would constitute a nuisance to occupants of neighboring properties or to persons traveling neighboring roads. Upon written notice to the owners of the Solar Energy System from Township Supervisor, that glare from the Solar Energy System is causing a nuisance to neighboring residents, or to persons traveling neighboring roads, the owner of the Solar Energy System shall have a reasonable time (not to exceed six (6) months) from the date of such notice to remediate such glare.' This glare restriction applies to all Solar Energy Systems, including Large Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance. No other specific glare restrictions or alternative conditions are provided for Large Solar Energy Systems.
section: SECTION 17.113 – SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS – GENERAL REQUIREMENTS

summary: The maximum height for Solar PV panels and associated racking for Large Solar Energy Systems is limited to 15 feet when measured at maximum tilt. All other buildings/accessory structures must meet the height requirements of the underlying zoning district. This is stated in SECTION 17.115 – LARGE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS OFF-SITE UTILITY USE; REQUIREMENTS, subsection G. Other height limits mentioned include 8 feet maximum height for ground mounted Solar Energy Systems in residential or agricultural districts (smaller systems) and 16 feet maximum height for ground mounted Commercial Solar Energy Systems (not explicitly defined as Large Solar Energy Systems). The unit for the height restriction is feet.
section: SECTION 17.115 – LARGE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS OFF-SITE UTILITY USE; REQUIREMENTS

summary: Section 17.115, subsection C states: 'A Large Solar Energy System shall not be installed on a parcel less than ten (10) acres.' This is the explicit minimum lot size for Large Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as utility-scale commercial facilities occupying more than one acre and intended for wholesale or retail sales of electricity to off-site customers. The unit is expressed in acres. Smaller systems, such as Small Solar Energy Systems, have a different minimum parcel size of one (1) acre for ground-mounted panels, but this applies only to smaller, non-commercial systems.
section: SECTION 17.115 – LARGE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS OFF-SITE UTILITY USE; REQUIREMENTS

summary: No operating Solar Energy System shall produce noise that exceeds Fifty-Five (55) dB(A), as measured at the property line of any neighboring lot with the facility at full capacity or production. Adequate setbacks shall be provided to comply with this requirement. The unit dB(A) is expressed as dBA in standard noise measurement terms.
section: SECTION 17.113 – SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS – GENERAL REQUIREMENTS

summary: Section 17.115(F) requires the Large Solar Energy System applicant to submit a Visual Impact Assessment Plan signed off by a Professional Engineer in Landscape. The greenbelt/visual screening plan "shall be consistent with the Township Master Plan’s intent to protect the rural character of the Township and include, at a minimum, 2-4 staggered rows of evergreen trees, 5-8 feet high, intermixed with intermediate sized shrubs, 25% of trees or shrubs must be natural to the area, within a total depth of approximately 25 feet." Alternative screening plans may be considered by the Planning Commission to mitigate visual impact. The Planning Commission may require more extensive visual screening in some areas to protect rural character. Section 17.115(D) states that "Fencing, greenbelts, roads, landscaping and crop production may be developed within the setback area." Section 17.115(J) requires the site to be secured by a fence "a minimum of eight (8) feet in height" located between the required landscape greenbelt and all photovoltaic solar devices and support structures. These requirements apply to Large Solar Energy Systems defined as "a utility-scale commercial facility, occupying an area of more than one acre, with multiple ground-mounted solar arrays... used for the purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity to off-site customers."
section: SECTION 17.115 – LARGE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS OFF-SITE UTILITY USE; REQUIREMENTS

summary: SECTION 17.115 – LARGE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS OFF-SITE UTILITY USE; REQUIREMENTS: "A sign shall be posted and maintained at the entrance(s) which lists the name and phone number of the owner or operator, and public contact information for inquiries. The Solar Energy Facility owner or operator shall respond to the public’s inquiries promptly." This signage requirement applies specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems, defined as "A utility-scale commercial facility, occupying an area of more than one acre, with multiple ground-mounted solar arrays and their associated control or conversion electronics, that converts sunlight into electricity by photovoltaics and will be used for the purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity to off-site customers." Other requirements for Large Solar Energy Systems include dual use land management practices, setback requirements, installation standards, screening, height limits, decommissioning, safety/security fencing, emergency services cooperation, transportation plans, complaint resolution processes, escrow deposits for enforcement, transfer of ownership notifications, and additional special approval criteria.
section: SECTION 17.115 – LARGE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS OFF-SITE UTILITY USE; REQUIREMENTS

summary: Section 17.113(M) states: 'Drainage, including stormwater, soil erosion and sediment control, and snowmelt runoff shall be managed in a manner consistent with all applicable federal, state, county, and local regulations. All drainage infrastructures on-site, including drain tile and ditches, shall be maintained during the operation of the Solar Energy System, and shall not impact setback/buffer areas or neighboring properties.' Additionally, Section 17.115(I)(3) requires as part of decommissioning: 'Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion. The Township may allow the applicant to leave certain portions of the landscaping inplace in order to minimize erosion and disruption to vegetation.' These requirements apply to Large Solar Energy Systems defined as 'A utility-scale commercial facility, occupying an area of more than one acre, with multiple ground-mounted solar arrays and their associated control or conversion electronics, that converts sunlight into electricity by photovoltaics and will be used for the purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity to off-site customers.'
section: SECTION 17.113 – SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS – GENERAL REQUIREMENTS

summary: For Large Solar Energy Systems, all ground mounted solar arrays shall be set back a distance of 1.5 times their structure height from all buildings or the setbacks of the underlying zoning district, whichever is greater. Other multipliers mentioned include 2.0 times the structure height for ground-mounted Solar Energy Systems in residential or Agricultural districts, but this applies to smaller or on-site systems, not Large Solar Energy Systems.
section: SECTION 17.114 – LARGE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS ON-SITE UTILITY USE; REQUIREMENTS

summary: Large Solar Energy System is defined as "A utility-scale commercial facility, occupying an area of more than one acre, with multiple ground-mounted solar arrays and their associated control or conversion electronics, that converts sunlight into electricity by photovoltaics and will be used for the purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity to off-site customers." Such systems require "Zoning Compliance Permit, Building Permit, Public Hearing, Special Approval and Site Plan, and Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment Review." Specifically, under SECTION 17.115 – LARGE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS OFF-SITE UTILITY USE; REQUIREMENTS, subsection R.6 states: "Visual Impact Assessment: To preserve the 'Rural Character' of the township, a Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment (LVIA) is required. The LVIA shall be submitted to the Planning Commission for review prior to the Site Plan Review or the issuance of a Special Approval Permit. The assessment shall include, but not be limited to: i. Identify, evaluate, and describe the existing landscape characteristics of the site and its surroundings. ii. Identify affected residents and consider their reaction to the type of changes proposed. iii. Identify and evaluate any impacts of the development and the extent they affect the viewshed. iv. Establish and describe mitigation measures appropriate for the proposed development, including zone of theoretical visibility maps and an accurate visual representation of the proposed development."
section: SECTION 17.115 – LARGE SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS OFF-SITE UTILITY USE; REQUIREMENTS

summary: Section 32-289(E) states: 'Any Freestanding solar collection site or device which is not used for six (6) months shall be deemed to be abandoned. The applicant/permit holder will be so notified in writing by the municipality and requested to dismantle the site and return it to its original state. ... If the applicant/permit holder does not do this, the municipality will have the removal and restoration done at the owner/applicant’s expense. Removal shall include removing posts, equipment, panels, foundations, and other items so that the ground is restored to its preconstruction state and is ready for development as another land use.' Other subsections address reflection/glare, impervious surface/stormwater, screening, and setbacks but do not impose decommissioning requirements.

Solar Energy Facilities (Utility-Scale) shall be designed and located to avoid glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard. Glare intensity is considered an issue if it measures more than twenty (20) percent of the incident sun intensity. Plans to reduce glare may be required in the initial materials submitted.
The setbacks of all solar collection devices and ancillary equipment shall be at least fifty (50) feet from all property lines.

Section 32-289(C) requires that solar devices "shall be screened from view from any public street or residential district by use of a masonry screen wall, evergreen vegetation, or other screening of a similar effectiveness and quality, as determined by the Planning Commission." The options for screening include masonry screen walls, evergreen vegetation, or other similarly effective screening methods.

If more than eight thousand (8,000) square feet of impervious surface will be located on the site, the application shall include a drainage plan prepared by a registered civil engineer showing how stormwater runoff will be managed. If detergents will be used to clean solar panels, details on the type of detergent, frequency and quantity of use, and stormwater quality protection measures shall be provided. Any necessary permits from outside agencies for off-site discharge shall be provided.

Utility-scale solar energy systems, referred to as Solar Energy Facilities (Utility-Scale), are permitted with a Special Use Permit (marked 'S*') in the I-1 district and other districts referenced on pages 16 and 17. The notation 'S*' indicates that these systems require approval as a special use and are subject to supplemental development regulations (§32-289). No districts are listed as permitting these systems by right (R). Solar overlay districts are excluded from this determination.

Section 14.29.C.16 requires that "following the operational life of the project, or at the time the project becomes obsolete, uneconomic or an Abandoned Solar Energy System, as determined by the Township Engineer or any other expert or specialist to be designated by the Township to make such a determination, the applicant shall perform decommissioning and removal of the Large Solar Energy System and all of its components." The applicant must "prepare a decommissioning plan and submit it to the Planning Commission for review prior to the issuance of the Conditional Land Use Permit." The plan requires that "all structures and facilities shall be removed, including any structures below-grade, and removed offsite for disposal. No concrete, piping or other materials may be left in place." Additionally, "the ground must be restored to its original condition within 180 days of becoming an Abandoned Solar Energy System, or decommissioning, whichever occurs first." Section 14.29.C.23 mandates that the applicant "shall be required to post continuing security and a continuing escrow deposit prior to commencement of construction, which shall remain in effect until the Large Solar Energy System has been finally removed." The financial security must be "reasonably sufficient to restore the property to its previous condition prior to construction and operation of the Large Solar Energy System" and remain "in full force and effect during the entire time that the Large Solar Energy System exists or is in place." Failure to maintain this security is a "material and significant violation" subject to enforcement and revocation of the Special Use Permit.

A Large Solar Energy System "shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access." Such fencing "shall be eight (8) feet in height as measured from the natural grade of the fencing perimeter." "Electric fencing is not permitted." The perimeter "shall also be screened and buffered by installed evergreen vegetative plantings whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels." The evergreen or native vegetative buffer must meet specific height and spacing requirements, and unhealthy or dead material must be replaced within six months or the next planting period. Failure to maintain the buffer is grounds for revocation of the Special Use Permit. The fencing and screening requirements are part of the special use permit application and site plan requirements for Large Solar Energy Systems, which must include "security fencing" details on the site plan.

Section 14.29.C.14 states: "All solar panels shall be placed such that concentrated solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways." This glare restriction explicitly applies to Large Solar Energy Systems, defined as utility scale systems with power output equal to or greater than 1 megawatt, intended for sale, delivery, or consumption by more than one end user. The ordinance also includes other requirements for Large Solar Energy Systems such as site plan details, height limits, setbacks, screening, noise limits, lighting, underground transmission lines, abandonment and decommissioning, safety, and maintenance, but the specific glare restriction is only found in subsection 14.29.C.14.

Maximum height of a Solar Array shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet. Other collection devices, components or buildings of the Large Solar Energy System shall not exceed thirty-five (35) feet, or the maximum building height permitted within the district in which that Solar Energy System is located, whichever is less, at any time or location on the property. The height shall be measured from the natural grade at the base of the Solar Array, device, component, or building measured. The Township Board may waive or modify these height requirements for certain aspects of a Solar Energy System (such as structures associated with above-ground transmission lines) through implementation of conditions when appropriate.

A Large Solar Energy System shall be located on one or more parcels with an aggregate area of 10 acres or greater. This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for Solar Energy System, Large as defined in the ordinance. The unit 'acres' is used to specify the area. No other minimum lot size values for Large Solar Energy Systems are provided in the text.

Section 14.29, subsection C, item 12 states: 'No component of any Large Solar Energy System shall emit noise exceeding 45 dba as measured at the outside perimeter of the project.' This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for Solar Energy System, Large. No other numerical noise limits for Large Solar Energy Systems are provided. The unit 'dBA' refers to A-weighted decibels, a standard unit for measuring noise levels.

A minimum setback distance of forty (40) feet from all property boundaries on the outside perimeter of the Large Solar Energy System shall be required for all buildings and Solar Arrays except for property boundaries where the applicable adjoining owner(s) agree to lessen or increase that setback distance by executing a signed written waiver of this requirement in recordable form, provided no such waiver shall act to permit less than the required minimum setback of the applicable zoning district.
section: 14.29 SOLAR ENERGY, C. Large Solar Energy Systems, 8. Setbacks

summary: A Large Solar Energy System shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access. Such fencing shall be eight (8) feet in height as measured from the natural grade of the fencing perimeter. Electric fencing is not permitted. The perimeter of Large Solar Energy Systems shall also be screened and buffered by installed evergreen vegetative plantings whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels, subject to the following requirements: (a) Unless screened and buffered at all times by natural forest vegetation meeting the minimum spacing and height requirements, and having a substantially similar obscuring effect of an evergreen vegetative buffer installed pursuant to this Section, a continuous evergreen vegetative buffer shall be installed and maintained at all times at the perimeter of the Large Solar Energy Systems, including without limitation between such Large Solar Energy Systems and adjacent residential or agricultural areas and/or public highways or streets. (b) The evergreen or native vegetative buffer shall be composed of native or evergreen trees that at planting shall be a minimum of four (4) feet in height and shrubs two (2) feet in height. The evergreen trees shall be spaced no more than fifteen (15) feet apart on center, deciduous trees no more than thirty (30) feet apart on center, and shrubs no more than seven (7) feet apart on center. All unhealthy (60 percent dead or greater) and dead material shall be replaced by the applicant within six (6) months, or the next planting period, whichever occurs first. Failure to maintain the required evergreen vegetative buffer shall constitute a violation and grounds for revocation of any Special Use Permit previously granted. (c) All plant materials shall be installed between March 15 and November 15. If planting cannot occur during this period, the applicant must provide a financial guarantee equal to 1.5 times the cost of any planting deficiencies until the next planting season. After all plantings have occurred, the financial guarantee shall be returned.

No lettering, company insignia, advertising, graphics or other commercially-oriented inscriptions or designs shall be on any part of the Solar Arrays or other components of the Large Solar Energy System. This section does not prohibit signs reasonably necessary to inform the public of potential safety hazards associated with the Large Solar Energy System, nor does it prohibit any other signs that may be required by this Ordinance, the Special Use Permit or other applicable law.
section: SECTION 14.29 SOLAR ENERGY, C. Large Solar Energy Systems, 11. Signage

summary: For Large Solar Energy Systems, the ordinance requires an environmental impact study including review of "Unique farmlands or soils" and "Effects on floodplains and wetlands" (C.2.o.8-9). It also mandates "A written description of measures to be taken to support the flow of rainwater throughout the Large Solar Energy System, including any measures to promote the growth of vegetation beneath the arrays and/or otherwise limit the impacts of storm water runoff," subject to approval by the Roscommon County Drain Commission (C.2.p). Additionally, a detailed site plan certified by a registered engineer must be submitted (C.2), and a continuing restoration security in an amount "reasonably sufficient to restore the property to its previous condition prior to construction and operation of the Large Solar Energy System" is required (C.23.A). These provisions explicitly address soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Large Solar Energy Systems. Other requirements include site plan details, setbacks, screening, maintenance, and decommissioning, but these do not explicitly address soil, erosion, or sediment control.

Solar Energy System, Large is permitted as a special use or similar in the following districts: Commercial District (C) under 'USES PERMITTED BY SPECIAL USE PERMIT' (SECTION 7.3, J), Commercial Mixed Use/Industrial District (C/I) under 'SPECIAL USES' (SECTION 10.2, J), and Agriculture District (A) under 'SPECIAL USES' (SECTION 11.3, S). Solar Energy System, Large is not listed as a permitted use by right in any district. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this analysis.
section: ARTICLE VII SECTION 7.3; ARTICLE X SECTION 10.2; ARTICLE XI SECTION 11.3

summary: All applications for a Large Solar Energy System must be accompanied by detailed site plans, drawn to scale and dimensioned and certified by a registered engineer, displaying horizontal and vertical (elevation) scale drawings with dimensions that show the location and height of the proposed Solar Array(s), buildings, structures, electrical tie lines and transmission lines, security fencing, and all above ground structures and utilities (Section 14.29.C.2.e-f). The ordinance requires screening and buffering by installed evergreen vegetative plantings whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels (Section 14.29.C.10). The evergreen or native vegetative buffer must meet specific height and spacing requirements, and failure to maintain it constitutes a violation (Section 14.29.C.10.a-c). These requirements serve as a visual impact assessment for Large Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as utility scale systems typically equal to or greater than 1 megawatt intended for sale, delivery, or consumption by more than one end user (Section 14.29.A.4).

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for utility-scale solar energy systems defined as 'Solar Farms' (solar panel energy systems designed and intended to provide electricity to off-site customers or the electric grid). Section V, Item 36, subsection H ('Removal') requires: 'A documented decommissioning plan shall be provided and shall: a. State the anticipated life of the project; b. Describe estimated decommissioning costs in current dollars and provide that this figure will be updated every fifth (5th) year after commercial operation of the utility-scale solar panel energy system; c. Be signed by the party responsible for decommissioning and the landowner (if different); d. Define the conditions upon which decommissioning will be initiated (e.g.; end of land lease, no power production for 12 months, etc.); e. State that all equipment, conduit, structures, fencing, roads, and foundations will be removed by the end of the decommissioning period; f. Require property to be restored to the condition it was in prior to the development of the solar farm; g. Describe the timeframe for completion of decommissioning activities; h. Describe any agreement (e.g., lease) with the landowner regarding decommissioning; i. State the party currently responsible for decommissioning; and j. Describe any plans or circumstances requiring an update of the decommissioning plan.' Additionally, 'Decommissioning shall be completed within 12 months of determination by the Zoning Administrator that the solar farm is no longer being maintained in an operable state of good repair, unless the current responsible party with ownership interest in the facility provides substantial evidence to the Zoning Administrator of the intent to maintain and reinstate operation of the farm.' A financial security instrument 'equal to the cost of decommissioning' is also required and must be adjusted to reflect updated cost estimates. These requirements apply specifically to solar farms as defined and regulated under the ordinance.
section: SECTION V AMENDMENT TO ARTICLE 20, STANDARDS REQUIRED OF SPECIAL LAND USES, BY ADDING ITEM 36 - SOLAR FARMS

summary: The ordinance defines a 'Solar Farm' as a solar panel energy system designed and intended to provide electricity to off-site customers or the electric grid. Under Item 36.D of Section V, it explicitly requires that 'Solar panels shall be placed and arranged such that reflected solar radiation or glare shall not be directed onto adjacent buildings, properties, or roadways.' Additionally, 'The exterior surfaces of solar panels and associated structures/equipment shall be generally neutral in color and substantially non-reflective of light.' These glare restrictions apply specifically to solar farms, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. Other relevant conditions include setback requirements, height limits, underground power transmission lines, FAA glare guidelines, and buffering requirements. The ordinance also includes provisions for energy storage systems, permits, and decommissioning plans for solar farms.
section: SECTION V AMENDMENT TO ARTICLE 20, STANDARDS REQUIRED OF SPECIAL LAND USES, BY ADDING ITEM 36 - SOLAR FARMS

summary: Section V, Item 36.F states: 'Screening shall be provided along the perimeter of a solar farm, including along the adjacent road right-of-way, in accordance with the buffer zone requirements of Section 18.6. Buffering should be at a height to obstruct the view at ground level but not inhibit solar production caused by shading. Required buffering is not intended to screen every part of the solar farm.' This applies to solar farms defined as 'a solar panel energy system designed and intended to provide electricity to off-site customers or the electric grid.'
section: SECTION V AMENDMENT TO ARTICLE 20, STANDARDS REQUIRED OF SPECIAL LAND USES, BY ADDING ITEM 36 - SOLAR FARMS

summary: The ordinance states that 'Solar farms shall be allowed as a Special Land Use in the I-R Restricted Industrial District as the principal use on a lot.' It further details that solar farms must conform to special land use standards including setbacks, height limits, buffering, permitting, and decommissioning requirements. Other solar panel uses, such as building-mounted solar panels, are permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts subject to administrative review, but these do not apply to utility-scale solar energy systems intended to provide electricity to off-site customers or the electric grid. No other districts are mentioned as permitting utility-scale solar energy systems as a special use or similar conditional approval.
section: Article 20, Standards Required of Special Land Uses, Item 36. Solar Farms

summary: §153.628(B)(12) Decommissioning: A decommissioning plan is required at the time of application that is in recordable form to be recorded with the county register of deeds. The plan must include: (a) A description of which above-grade and below-grade improvements will be removed, retained, or restored; (b) The anticipated life of the project, estimated decommissioning costs net of salvage value in current dollars, method of ensuring funds are available, and anticipated manner of decommissioning and site restoration; (c) The City may require surety (escrow, bond, or otherwise) to cover removal costs, not exceeding 125% of removal cost; (d) Surety not required for municipally or state-owned systems; (e) Review of performance guarantee every 5 years; (f) Decommissioning must commence when soil is dry and be complete within 18 months after abandonment; abandonment is triggered if no electricity is produced for 12 consecutive months. Principal-Use Solar Power Systems include SMALL SCALE (up to 2 MW DC) and LARGE SCALE (more than 2 MW DC) systems intended for off-site use. Other site plan requirements include height, setbacks, fencing, screening, ground cover, lot coverage, land clearing, access drives, wiring, lighting, and repowering provisions.

§153.628(B)(4) states: "Fencing: Principal-Use SES shall be secured with perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access. Fencing shall be subject to height, setbacks, and other applicable regulations contained in section 153.086 for the zone it is located in." Principal-Use Solar Energy Systems include SMALL SCALE systems (SES generating up to and including 2 MW DC) and LARGE SCALE systems (SES generating more than 2 MW DC). Other related requirements for Principal-Use SES include height limits, setbacks, screening/landscaping, ground cover, access drives, wiring, lighting, decommissioning, and repowering, but fencing is specifically mandated to restrict unauthorized access.

§153.628(B)(1) states: 'Height: Total height shall not exceed 20 feet measured from the ground to the top of the system when oriented at maximum tilt.' This maximum height applies to Principal-Use Solar Power Systems, which include Large Scale Principal-Use Solar Energy Systems. Other related provisions include setback distances and fencing requirements, but the 20 feet height limit is the explicit maximum structure height. The unit of measurement is feet.

Large Scale Ground-Mounted SES setback distance are as follows: (i) 50 feet from the property line of a non-participating lot. (ii) 100 feet from any existing dwelling unit on a non-participating lot. A Ground-Mounted SES is not subject to property line setbacks for common property lines of two or more participating lots, except road right-of-way setbacks shall apply. Small Scale Ground-Mounted SES shall follow the setback distance for primary buildings or structures for the district in which it is sited.

§153.628(B)(13) Repowering: In addition to repairing or replacing SES components to maintain the system, a principal-use SES may at any time be repowered, without the need to apply for a new site plan, by reconfiguring, renovating, or replacing the SES to increase the power rating within the existing project footprint. Repowering may require an application for an electrical permit as determined by the Electrical Inspector or this Code. Principal-Use Solar Power Systems include LARGE SCALE systems (SES generating more than 2 MW DC). Other options include: (14) A proposal to change the project footprint of an existing SES shall be considered a new application, subject to the ordinance standards at the time of the request.

§153.628(B)(5) Screening/Landscaping: Principal-Use SES shall be designed to follow the screening and/or landscaping standards for the zoning district of the project site. Any required screening and landscaping shall be placed outside the perimeter fencing. In districts that call for screening or landscaping along rear or side property lines, these shall only be required where an adjoining non-participating lot has an existing residential or public use. When current zoning district screening and landscaping standards are determined to be inadequate based on a legitimate community purpose consistent with local government planning documents, the Chief Inspector or Planning Commission may require substitute screening consisting of native deciduous trees planted 30 feet on center, and native evergreen trees planted 15 feet on center along existing non-participating residential uses. The Planning Commission may reduce or waive screening requirements provided that any such adjustment is in keeping with the intent of the ordinance and is appropriately documented (e.g. abutting participating lots; existing vegetation). Screening/landscaping detail shall be submitted as part of the site plan that identifies the type and extent of screening for a Small Principal-Use SES, which may include plantings, strategic use of berms, and/or fencing.

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control-related requirements for Large Scale Principal-Use Solar Energy Systems under §153.628. It requires that "Land disturbance or clearing shall be limited to what is minimally necessary for the installation and operation of the system and to ensure sufficient all-season access to the solar resource given the topography of the land. Topsoil distributed during site preparation (grading) on the property shall be retained on site." It also mandates that "New access drives within the SES shall be designed to minimize the extent of soil disturbance, water runoff, and soil compaction on the premises. Access drives should consist of six inches of stone mix or gravel. The use of geotextile fabrics and gravel placed on the surface of the existing soil for temporary roadways during the construction of the SES is permitted, provided that the geotextile fabrics and gravel are removed once the SES is in operation." Additionally, "Principal-Use SES shall include the installation of perennial ground cover vegetation, i.e. Pennsylvania Sedge, Bearberry, Canada Anemone, etc., maintained for the duration of operation until the site is decommissioned." Sites with majority impervious surface or those included in a brownfield plan are exempt from installing ground cover but must comply with on-site storm water requirements and include a land management plan.

§ 153.628 PRINCIPAL-USE SOLAR POWER SYSTEMS states: 'LARGE SCALE PRINCIPAL-USE SES is a permitted use by special use in M-1, M-2, and M-3, zoning districts.' Other related uses include SMALL SCALE PRINCIPAL-USE SES, which is permitted by special use in R1-A, B-1, B1-A, B-2, M-1, M-2, and M-3 zoning districts. The ordinance requires approval of the City Planning Commission in accordance with processing procedures in § 153.562 for special use permits. Additionally, § 153.347 includes 'Small scale and Large scale principal-use solar energy systems, subject to standards established in §153.628' as permitted uses after special approval.

Large Scale Ground-Mounted SES setback distance are as follows: (ii) 100 feet from any existing dwelling unit on a non-participating lot. Other options include: (i) 50 feet from the property line of a non-participating lot; (a) Small Scale Ground-Mounted SES shall follow the setback distance for primary buildings or structures for the district in which it is sited.

§153.628 PRINCIPAL-USE SOLAR POWER SYSTEMS requires Principal-Use Solar Power Systems, including LARGE SCALE systems (SES generating more than 2 MW DC), to be subject to site plan review and Special Use Permit application. Site Plans must include a detailed site plan with height (not exceeding 20 feet), setbacks (50 feet from non-participating lot property line and 100 feet from any existing dwelling on a non-participating lot for Large Scale SES), fencing, and screening/landscaping standards. Screening and landscaping must be placed outside perimeter fencing and may be adjusted by the Planning Commission based on community purpose. Ground cover vegetation and other design elements are also required to protect public health, safety, and welfare. Other options include SMALL SCALE PRINCIPAL-USE SES permitted by special use in various zoning districts, with setback distances following primary building setbacks. The ordinance also covers accessory and roof-mounted systems separately (§153.627) and defines Principal-Use Solar Energy System as "a commercial, ground-mounted solar energy system that converts sunlight into electricity for the primary purpose of off-site use through the electrical grid or export to the wholesale market," including both small scale (up to 2 MW DC) and large scale (more than 2 MW DC) systems (§153.626).

Section 2222.M states: 'At the time an application is submitted for a Level 2 or Level 3 SES, as required by Section 2222.5, a decommissioning plan shall be submitted as follows: i. Defined conditions upon which decommissioning will be initiated (i.e., end of land lease, no power production for twelve (12) months, etc.); ii. Removal of all non-utility owned equipment, conduit, structures, fencing, roads, and building foundations to a depth of three (3) feet below grade; iii. Restoration of property to the condition prior to development of the SES; iv. The timeframe for completion of decommissioning activities; v. An engineer’s cost estimate for all aspects of the decommissioning plan; vi. Description of any agreement (e.g., lease) with the landowner regarding decommissioning; vii. Provisions for updating the decommissioning plan; viii. The decommissioning of any electrical equipment/components shall be executed by a licensed electrical contractor; ix. A statement signed by the owner or operator that they take full responsibility for reclaiming the site in accordance with the decommissioning plan and the Special Land Use Permit upon cessation of use; x. Saginaw Charter Township may mandate that the owner or operator provide a financial guarantee to cover the costs of decommissioning the site; xi. The decommissioning plan shall be recorded with the Saginaw County Register of Deeds; xii. The Saginaw Charter Township Electrical Inspector shall conduct a final inspection to confirm that the SES has been decommissioned consistent with the provisions of the decommissioning plan; xiii. Saginaw Charter Township may require a performance bond or other financial guarantee to ensure removal of the approved solar energy system upon the terms identified in M.i above.' Level 3 Solar Energy Systems are defined as those systems that exceed the parameters stipulated for Level 1 and Level 2 Solar Energy Systems. Level 1 systems generally provide energy primarily for on-site uses and have size limits; Level 2 systems may provide energy for on-site and/or off-site uses and have larger size limits depending on zoning district. The decommissioning requirements apply specifically to Level 2 and Level 3 SES, which are permitted by special use permit in certain zoning districts.

Section 2222.6.F states: "The design and construction of solar energy systems shall not produce light emissions, either direct or indirect (reflective), that would emit unreasonable glare or negatively impact adjacent properties. All panels shall have tempered, non-reflective surfaces." This glare restriction applies to all Solar Energy Systems regulated under this section, including Level 3 Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as "those systems that exceed the parameters stipulated for Level 1 and Level 2 Solar Energy Systems." Level 1 systems generally provide energy primarily for on-site uses with size limits, Level 2 systems may provide energy for on-site and/or off-site uses with larger size limits depending on zoning districts, and Level 3 systems exceed these parameters. Additionally, applicants for Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3 SES over twenty thousand (20,000) square feet must comply with Federal Aviation Administration siting requirements due to potential glare hazards for pilots.

Ground mounted solar energy collectors in other districts shall not exceed seventeen (17) feet in height as measured from ground level to the top of the solar collectors when oriented at maximum tilt. Rooftop mounted SES shall not project more than five (5) feet above the highest point of the roof, but, in any event, shall not exceed the maximum building height for the zoning district in which it is located. Roof-mounted SES shall not project beyond the eaves of the roof. These height limits apply generally to all solar energy systems, including Level 3 Solar Energy Systems. The units for height are feet.

On a residentially-zoned or residentially-utilized parcel, ground-mounted SES shall have a minimum setback of five feet from the rear property line and eight feet from the side property line. In all other zoning districts ground mounted SES shall not be located in the required front, side or rear yard. (Section 2222.6.B) The ordinance does not specify numeric setbacks for non-residential districts but requires compliance with the required yard setbacks established by the zoning district. Level 3 Solar Energy Systems are those exceeding Level 1 and Level 2 parameters and are subject to these setback requirements.
section: Sec. 2222. – Solar Energy Systems (SES), 6. General Regulations, B. Setbacks

summary: Section 2222.6.I states: 'Buffer zones around the perimeter of an SES shall be required in accordance with bufferyard requirements outlined in Section 303.4 herein as they pertain to the zoning district in which they are located. The Planning Commission may require additional bufferyard and screening requirements as necessary.' This applies to all SES, including Level 3 Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as 'those systems that exceed the parameters stipulated for Level 1 and Level 2 Solar Energy Systems.' Level 1 systems generally provide energy primarily for on-site uses with size limits; Level 2 systems may provide energy for on-site and/or off-site uses and have larger area limits depending on zoning districts; Level 3 systems exceed these parameters. Therefore, Level 3 SES must comply with the buffer zone and screening requirements as part of the standards in Section 2222.

Level 3 Solar Energy Systems are "subject to the standards contained in section 2222 and issuance of a special use permit" in the A-2, CB-1, and M-1 zoning districts. The ordinance states: "Amend Chapter 9, A-2, Agricultural Districts, Section 904. Uses permitted by special use permit to add: 21. Level 2 and Level 3 solar energy systems, subject to the standards contained in section 2222." Similarly, for CB-1: "Level 2 and Level 3 solar energy systems, subject to the standards contained in section 2222 and issuance of a special use permit." For M-1: "Level 2 and Level 3 solar energy systems, subject to the standards contained in section 2222." The table in Section 2222(5) confirms Level 3 SES are "S" (permitted by Special Land Use Permit) in these districts. Other levels and districts have different conditions: Level 1 SES are generally permitted under special conditions (P) in many districts; Level 2 SES are permitted by special use permit (S) in several commercial and agricultural districts but not Level 3 except in the three districts above. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this summary as requested.

The ordinance requires that utility-scale SES be set back at least six hundred (600) feet from road right-of-way lines and all noncontiguous development area parcel property lines. Where a utility-scale SES is located adjacent to agriculturally or residentially zoned or used lot, side and rear yard screening may be required as determined by the Planning Commission. Solar panels shall be placed such that concentrated radiation or solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways. When deemed appropriate, the Planning Commission may require a report from a registered civil engineer or other professional to address this issue.

summary: Utility-scale SES shall be set back at least six hundred (600) feet from road right-of-way lines and all noncontiguous development area parcel property lines.

summary: Where a utility-scale SES is located adjacent to a agriculturally or residentially zoned or used lot, side and rear yard screening may be required as determined by the Planning Commission to address specific site needs at the time of site plan review. Screening is not mandatory in all cases but is subject to the Planning Commission's discretion. Additionally, solar panels must be placed such that concentrated radiation or solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways. The Planning Commission may require a report from a registered civil engineer or other professional to address this issue when deemed appropriate.
section: Section 11.09.D.2.g. of Article 11, Special Development Standards, Section 11.09 Solar Energy Systems

summary: The ordinance requires that for Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems (USSES), the applicant must prepare a decommissioning plan including: (A) the anticipated life of the project; (B) the estimated decommissioning costs, net of salvage value, in current dollars; (C) the manner in which the project will be decommissioned and removed and the site restored; and (D) the method of insuring that funds will be available for decommissioning, removal, and site restoration. Additionally, the owner/operator must provide security to the township to insure complete decommissioning, removal, and site restoration. The security can be provided by (A) a cash bond posted with the Township; (B) an irrevocable letter of credit in favor of the township from a bank or other financial institution approved by the Township; or (C) a surety bond issued in favor of the Township issued by a surety approved by the Township. The security must remain in effect until the system is decommissioned and removed and the site restored, and the amount must not be less than the estimated cost of decommissioning, removal, and restoration, including a reasonable inflation factor. The security is to be provided after approval of a special use permit but before issuance of the permit. If the owner/operator fails to decommission and remove the system and restore the site within the time limits set forth, the Township may use the funds to perform these actions and refund any unused funds to the owner/operator.
section: Section 6.52(f)(7) and (8) Decommissioning Plan and Decommissioning, Removal and Restoration Security

summary: Section 6.52(d)(2) states: 'Solar Energy Systems shall be located and constructed in a manner which does not cause glare onto any other property or roadway at any time.' This glare restriction applies to all Solar Energy Systems, including Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems (USSES), which are defined as systems 'the principal design, purpose, or use of which is to provide energy for consumption off the site where the system is located or the sale of generated electricity to any person or entity.'

Section 6.52(f)(4) states: 'No solar panels shall exceed 20 feet in height above the ground at maximum tilt.' This maximum height restriction applies specifically to Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems (USSES), defined as systems intended to provide energy for consumption off the site or for sale. Other height restrictions mentioned include ground mounted personal scale solar systems limited to 20 feet, but those apply only to smaller, non-commercial systems. The unit 'feet' is explicitly used in the ordinance.

The ordinance states: 'No Utility Scale Solar Energy System shall be located on a parcel of land less than 5 acres in size.' This is the explicit minimum parcel size requirement for USSES. The unit 'acres' is a standard measure of land area. Other related provisions include setbacks and height limits, but these do not specify minimum lot sizes. The minimum parcel size applies specifically to Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems, defined as systems intended to provide energy for consumption off-site or for sale.

All Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems shall be set back at least 25 feet from the nearest property line. The setback from the center line of a right of way on an abutting street shall be 108 feet on paved or unpaved local roads and 150 feet on state highways or primary roads.

All Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems shall be set back at least 25 feet from the nearest property line. The setback from the center line of a right of way on an abutting street shall be 108 feet on paved or unpaved local roads and 150 feet on state highways or primary roads.

Section 6.52(f)(5) states: 'When a Utility Scale Solar Energy System is adjacent to a residentially zoned or used lot, side and rear yard screening may be required as determined by the Planning Commission to address specific site needs at the time of the site plan review.' The ordinance does not explicitly require vegetative buffers but mandates screening as determined by the Planning Commission. Additionally, lighting must be 'of a fully shielded and downcast type where light does not spill onto the adjacent parcel or the night sky.'
section: Section 6.52(f) Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems

summary: Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems shall be allowed as a special land use in the agricultural/residential, commercial, and industrial districts. Other solar systems such as Personal Scale Solar Energy Systems (PSSES) are permitted land uses in all zoning districts with specific requirements based on system type, including height limits and setback requirements in Agricultural Residential, Commercial, Industrial, and Lakefront Residential Districts.

Section 11.04, subsection LL, item 19 ('Decommissioning') states: 'Any utility-scale solar energy system which has reached the end of its useful life or has not operated continuously for one year or more shall be removed and parcel owners shall be required to restore the site. The owner/operator shall physically remove the installation no more than one hundred and fifty (150) days after the date of discontinued operations.' The owner/operator must notify the Township of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. If the owner/operator fails to remove the installation within 150 days, the Township may enter the property and physically remove it. Removal includes 'Physical removal of all aboveground or underground utility-scale solar energy systems, structures, equipment, security barriers, and transmission lines from the site,' 'Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations,' and 'Stabilization or re-vegetation.' Additionally, a financial guarantee is required to cover the cost of removal through 'a form of surety, either through account, letter of credit, bond, or other instrument acceptable to the Township.'

Utility scale solar energy systems shall not exceed sixteen (16) feet in height, measured from the natural grade below the unit to the highest point at full tilt. The Planning Commission may approve a higher elevation where animal grazing is permitted under the solar collector surface. This height restriction applies specifically to Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance.

The ordinance states: 'Utility scale solar energy systems shall be located on a lot of at least ten (10) acres.' This is the explicit minimum lot size for Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems. The unit is acres, a standard measure of land area. No other minimum lot size values for utility scale systems are provided.

Utility scale solar energy systems shall be located at least 50 feet from all property lines. The Township may require larger setbacks if it is determined that greater separation would better protect adjacent residents and property owners.
