Additionally, for accessory buildings including battery storage and inverters, 'Inverters and battery storage buildings must be set back at least 1,000 feet from the lot line of a non-participating lot.' The 300 feet setback applies generally to Solar Farm structures from non-participating lot lines, while the 1,000 feet setback applies specifically to inverters and battery storage buildings.
section: F. Setback and G. Accessory Buildings, including Battery Storage and Inverters

summary: There shall be a 50 ft. setback requirement from the lot line of a neighboring participating parcel. Additionally, inverters and battery storage buildings must be set back at least 200 feet from the lot line of a participating lot. These setbacks apply to all structures that are accessory to a Solar Farm and supersede all other setback requirements in this Zoning Ordinance.
section: F. Setback and G. Accessory Buildings, including Battery Storage and Inverters

summary: From wetland delineated by the State of Michigan, regardless of whether the wetland is regulated by the State of Michigan: 200 feet. (Section II, F. Setback, item 3) The ordinance does not specify any fixed setback distances from public conservation lands or preservation areas. No multipliers based on structure height are mentioned for setbacks from these areas. Other setbacks mentioned (e.g., 300 feet from lot lines of non-participating lots or road rights-of-way) are not applicable as they relate to property lines and roads.

The ordinance states: 'From a public or private road right-of-way line: 300 feet.' This setback applies to all structures accessory to a Solar Farm and supersedes all other setback requirements in the Zoning Ordinance. Additionally, there is a landscaping buffer requirement of 25 feet along any road adjacent to a Solar Farm, but this is separate from the setback distance.

Section II, subsection H ('Landscaping and Buffering') requires that 'Solar farms must have a landscape buffer of 25 feet along any road or adjacent to a residential use. The buffer shall be located outside of any perimeter fencing associated with the land use. The buffer shall contain a mix of native deciduous and evergreen plant material and be at least five (5) feet in height at the time of installation.' The Planning Commission may allow the use of existing vegetation to serve as a landscape buffer or modify these landscaping requirements at the applicant's request. Vegetation used as a buffer must be maintained with good husbandry techniques to reach maturity with maximum foliage density, and dead or diseased vegetation must be removed and replanted at the next appropriate planting season. Existing trees within the required setback area shall be preserved to the greatest extent possible, and the Planning Commission may modify or waive the buffer requirements if existing foliage provides sufficient screening. Additionally, fencing around the Solar Farm and accessory equipment must be 'provided with evergreen landscaping that is sufficient to buffer the equipment from view of adjacent streets and lots.'
section: SECTION II, H. Landscaping and Buffering

summary: Each Solar Farm shall have one sign per lot, located at the roadside and easily visible throughout all four seasons. Signs shall be at least two to six square feet in area. Additional signage on and around the solar panels is recommended. All signage shall meet the requirements of Section. The sign shall contain at minimum the following: 1. Warning High Voltage. 2. Participating Landowner’s name, Solar Farm owner’s name, and Operator’s name. 3. Emergency telephone numbers and web address (list more than one number if needed). 4. Signs shall be placed on the perimeter fence at the fence entrance gate. 5. Unique identification such as address of the Solar Farm.

The ordinance explicitly requires Solar Farm applicants to provide "A plan for managing erosion and sediment control" (Section II, B.3.vii) as part of the Conditional Use Permit application. Additionally, applicants must provide "Proof of environmental compliance, including compliance with Part 91, Soil Erosion and Sedimentation Control (MCL 324.9101 et. seq.) and any corresponding County ordinances" (Section II, B.3.xxiii). These requirements apply to Solar Farms defined as "A utility-scale commercial facility that converts sunlight into electricity... for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electric power off-site."
section: SECTION II AMENDMENT TO SECTION 9.17 OF THE TUSCOLA TOWNSHIP ZONING ORDINANCE

summary: Solar Farms are allowed only in the AG (Agricultural) zoning district and require a conditional land use permit and site plan review. An application for a Conditional Use permit shall be filed with the Township pursuant to Section 3.23 as to Conditional Use approvals. In addition to all requirements for a conditional use permit under Section 3.23 of the Zoning Ordinance and site plan review and approval under Article 12 of the Zoning Ordinance, Solar Farms are also subject to the requirements of this Section. Small Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted in all zoning districts without Conditional Use Approval and are approved by the Zoning Administrator, but this does not apply to Solar Farms.
section: SECTION II AMENDMENT TO SECTION 9.17 OF THE TUSCOLA TOWNSHIP ZONING ORDINANCE

summary: The ordinance requires Solar Farm applicants to submit a Conditional Use Permit application including a "graphical demonstration (preferably computer-generated) of the Solar Farm as completed" showing "the completed Solar Farm on the proposed site as seen from four (4) separate angles" and "a real-time, visual model of the Solar Farm showing the direction and intensity of glare during daylight hours over the course of a 24-hour period" for each season. Additionally, applicants must provide a site plan with "all proposed structures and the location of all equipment, transformers, and substations, as well as all setbacks, panel sizes and locations, and the location of property lines, signage, fences, greenbelts and screening, drain tiles, easements, floodplains, bodies of water, lighting, proposed access routes, land elevations, structures on adjacent parcels, and road rights-of-way." A detailed landscaping plan prepared by a licensed professional is also required to ensure appropriate landscaping and buffering to minimize off-site visual impacts. These requirements are part of the Conditional Use Permit process for Solar Farms, defined as "a utility-scale commercial facility that converts sunlight into electricity... for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electric power off-site."
section: SECTION II - AMENDMENT TO SECTION 9.17 OF THE TUSCOLA TOWNSHIP ZONING ORDINANCE

summary: From wetland delineated by the State of Michigan, regardless of whether the wetland is regulated by the State of Michigan: 200 feet. Other setbacks include 300 feet from a lot line abutting a non-participating lot and 300 feet from a public or private road right-of-way line, but these are not related to lakes, reservoirs, streams, or rivers. No fixed setback distances are specified for lakes, reservoirs, streams, or rivers.

Large SES are classified as special land uses and are authorized in the Agricultural Residential District only. By implication, Large SES are prohibited in all other districts. Small SES are authorized accessory structures in all districts, and Medium SES are authorized permitted uses in all districts.

Large SES shall comply with the site development standards of subsection (D) for Medium SES. Medium SES ground-mounted solar collection panels "shall be setback from all property lines the same distance as required for the principal building on the property. Such setback shall be a minimum of fifty (50) feet where the respective yard is adjacent to property in an Agricultural or Residential District." No multiplier based on height or other factors is mentioned. Other setback distances mentioned in the text apply only to Small or Medium SES or relate to structures, not property lines.

Large SES are classified as special land uses and are authorized in the Agricultural Residential District only. They "shall comply with the site development standards of subsection (D) for Medium SES, and shall be subject to the special land use approval standards." By contrast, Small SES are authorized accessory structures in all districts with Zoning Administrator approval, and Medium SES are authorized permitted uses in all districts subject to Planning Commission approval. Self-Contained Solar Energy Systems are permitted in all districts without a zoning permit.

Section 13.14.00(D)(5) "Abandonment or Decommissioning" states: "Any utility-scale solar energy system which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned consistent with this Section of the Zoning Ordinance shall be removed and parcel owners shall be required to restore the site to its original condition. The owner/operator shall physically remove the installation in no more than 150 days after the date of the discontinued operations. The owner/operator shall notify the Township and the Planning Commission by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal." It further provides that "Absent notice of a proposed date of decommissioning or written notice of extenuating circumstances, the utility-scale SES shall be considered abandoned when it fails to operate for more than one year." Decommissioning includes: "Physical removal of all utility-scale solar energy systems, structures, equipment, security barriers, and transmission lines from the site; Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations; Stabilization and re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion." Additionally, Section 13.14.00(D)(7) "Financial Security" requires the applicant to provide "a form of surety, either through an escrow account, bond, or otherwise, to cover the cost of removal... in an amount and form determined reasonable by the Planning Commission, but in no event to exceed more than 125 percent of the cost of removal and compliance with the additional requirements set forth herein." The ordinance defines Utility-Scale SES as systems that meet one or more of the following: "i. Is primarily used for generating electricity for sale and distribution to an authorized public utility; ii. The total surface area of all Solar Collector Surfaces exceeds 1,500 square feet; and/or iii. Is not an accessory use or structure."

The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Under Section 13.14.00(D)(2)(g), it states: "Solar panels shall be placed such that concentrated radiation or solar glare shall not be directed onto nearby property or roadway(s)." Additionally, under Section 13.14.00(E)(f), for building-mounted SES, it requires that the system "shall be located to minimize glare on adjacent properties and roadways." These provisions apply to utility-scale systems defined as those "primarily used for generating electricity for sale and distribution to an authorized public utility;" or where "the total surface area of all Solar Collector Surfaces exceeds 1,500 square feet;" and/or "is not an accessory use or structure."

The ordinance states: 'Minimum Lot Area: Minimum lot area for a utility-scale solar energy system shall be five acres.' This applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined by the ordinance, which includes systems primarily used for generating electricity for sale, systems with solar collector surfaces exceeding 1,500 square feet, or those not accessory uses or structures. The unit 'acres' is a standard measure of land area.
section: 13.14.00 SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS, D. Standards for Utility-Scale SES, 2. Standards for Ground-Mounted Utility Scale SES

summary: Utility-scale solar energy systems shall have side yard and rear yard setbacks of at least 50 feet, but where they abut a residentially-zoned (including AR) or used lot, the side yard and rear yard setbacks shall not be less than 100 feet. (Section 13.14.00(D)(2)(a)(ii) and (iii)) Other setback options include a 50 feet side and rear yard setback when not abutting residentially-zoned or used lots.
section: 13.14.00 SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS, D. Standards for Utility-Scale SES, 2. Standards for Ground-Mounted Utility Scale SES, a. Setbacks

summary: Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be set back at least 150 feet from the center of the road. Other setbacks include side yards of at least 50 feet (or 100 feet if abutting residentially-zoned or used lots) and rear yards of at least 50 feet (or 100 feet if abutting residentially-zoned or used lots).

When utility-scale solar energy systems abut a residentially-zoned (including AR) or used lot, side and rear yard screening may be required as determined by the Planning Commission to address specific site needs at the time of the site plan review. Ancillary solar equipment such as water tanks, supports, batteries, and plumbing shall be screened to the maximum extent possible without compromising the effectiveness of the solar collectors. Screening is discretionary ('may be required') and is subject to Planning Commission determination during site plan review.

Section 13.14.00(D)(2)(e) states: "Signage: Signs shall comply with the requirements in the Washington Township Zoning Ordinance. Further, utility-scale solar energy system installations shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the solar energy system." This is the explicit signage requirement for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Other related standards for Utility-Scale SES include setbacks, height, minimum lot area, lighting, utility connections, screening, and special land use permit requirements, but these do not pertain to signage.

The ordinance requires that for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems, "Clearing of natural vegetation shall be limited to what is necessary for the construction, operation, and maintenance of the installation." Additionally, upon decommissioning, "Stabilization and re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion" must be performed. These provisions explicitly address soil disturbance, erosion, and sediment control. Other related requirements include site plan and special land use permit approval, setbacks, height limits, screening, underground utility connections, operation and maintenance plans including storm water controls, and financial security for removal costs.

Utility-scale SES shall be permitted as a use permitted after special approval in the AR - Agricultural Residential District and I - Industrial District, subject to the following standards: Prior to the construction of a utility-scale solar energy system, a site plan and an application for special land use permit must be filed and approved by the Planning Commission. The Planning Commission shall review the site plan based on the provisions of this Section as well as the standards of Article XVI and the special land use permit based on the provisions of this Section as well as the standards of Article XVII. The construction and operation of all utility-scale solar energy systems shall be compliant with all applicable local, state, and federal requirements. No utility-scale solar energy system shall be constructed, installed, or modified without first obtaining all applicable permits. Applications must be accompanied by fees for site plan review and special land use permit, and an escrow account to cover Township costs. Other standards include setbacks, height, minimum lot area, lighting, signage, utility connections, screening, and additional special land use permit requirements such as site control, operation and maintenance plan, emergency services cooperation, maintenance, site clearing, safety manuals, abandonment or decommissioning procedures, ancillary solar equipment screening, and financial security. Other types of SES such as Personal-Scale SES are permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts with different standards and permitting requirements.

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall have side and rear yard setbacks of at least 100 feet where they abut a residentially-zoned (including AR) or used lot. Other setback distances include 50 feet for side and rear yards generally, and 150 feet from the center of the road for front yards. The ordinance states: 'ii. Each side yard shall be at least 50 feet. Where utility-scale solar energy systems abut a residentially-zoned (including AR) or used lot, the side yard shall not be less than 100 feet.' and 'iii. The rear yard shall be at least 50 feet. Where utility-scale solar energy systems abut a residentially-zoned (including AR) or used lot, the rear yard shall not be less than 100 feet.' No fixed setback distance is specified directly from occupied dwellings, buildings, or structures; setbacks are tied to adjacency to residentially-zoned or used lots.

summary: Section 11.26.G Restoration Plan: "A restoration plan is required and shall describe the decommissioning of the commercial/utility photovoltaic solar facility and final restoration conditions of the land within twelve (12) months of abandonment or end of project useful life, including evidence of proposed commitments to the owners of leased lots. The plan shall be filed at the time of application. The restoration plan shall be prepared by a professional engineer or registered landscape architect. All restoration operations shall be performed in accordance with the restoration plan. The restoration plan must be approved by the Waterloo Township Board as part of the permit approval process. The restoration plan shall be totally completed within 12 months of the termination of the solar operation." Section 11.26.F Surety Bond: "The financial security shall be in an amount determined by the Township to be reasonably sufficient to restore the property to its previous condition prior to construction and operation of the solar facility... kept in full force and effect during the entire time that the solar facility exists or is in place, and such financial security shall be irrevocable and non-cancelable." Section 11.26.H Forfeiture of Decommissioning Escrow Account: "The bond is forfeited in the event the operator does not comply with their restoration plan within twelve (12) months of one of the following three conditions: a. Termination of the lease b. Failure to complete the project c. Inactivity for twelve (12) months." These requirements apply explicitly to Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems as defined in Section 11.26.B.1.
section: Section 11.26 Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems

summary: Section 11.26.D.3 requires that "Seven (7) foot fencing is required around the entire facility. Additional fencing is required around the Power Switchyard and shall be at least twelve (12) feet in height." This fencing requirement applies specifically to Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems. Additional related provisions include: Knox boxes and keys for emergency access at locked entrances, warning signage at the entrance and perimeter, and a minimum 33 feet unobstructed access around the facility located internal to any fencing. Screening requirements include landscape buffers and rows of trees to block views from public roads. These requirements are part of the site and development standards for Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems.
section: Section 11.26 Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems

summary: Section 11.26 Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems includes a specific glare restriction: "All Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems shall be designed such that they do not produce glare that would constitute a nuisance to occupants of neighboring properties or to persons traveling neighboring roads." Furthermore, "Upon written notice ... that glare from the Solar Energy System is causing a nuisance ... the owner ... shall have a reasonable time (not to exceed sixty (60) days) ... to remediate such glare." This applies to systems defined as Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems, i.e., those providing energy to off-site uses or for wholesale/retail sale of electricity. Other related provisions include setback requirements, screening, and operational standards, but the explicit glare restriction is found in subsection D.6 and A.9 of Section 11.26.
section: Section 11.26 Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems

summary: The maximum height of solar panels is 25 feet. This takes into account the rotation of panels to maximize exposure to sunlight throughout the day. The height of the ‘power switchyard’—the structure needed to connect the solar energy facility to electric transmission lines—is limited to the height needed to tie into the electric transmission lines. All other buildings/accessory structures must meet the height requirements of the underlying zoning district.
section: Section 11.26 Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems

summary: No operating Solar Energy System shall produce noise that exceeds Forty-Five (45) dBA, as measured at the property line of any neighboring lot. Adequate setbacks and screening shall be provided to comply with this requirement. This applies specifically to Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems as defined in Section 11.26. The unit for noise level is dBA, a standard unit for measuring sound levels.
section: Section 11.26 Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems

summary: Table 9-2 shows that Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems are prohibited (marked with  "–" ) in the RNF, R-1, R-2, R-3, and R-4 districts. They are permitted as a Special Land Use (S) in Public Conservation (PC), Agricultural-1 (A-1), and Agricultural-2 (A-2) zones. Table 9-3 shows they are permitted as a Special Land Use (S) in Commercial (C-1, C-2) and Industrial (I-1) districts. The ordinance states:  "Commercial/Utility Solar Energy Systems are permitted in the Public Conservation and Agricultural Zones as a Special Land Use provided that they are approved according to the provisions of Article 11.02 and 11.26."  Private solar energy systems are permitted as an accessory use in all districts, but this does not apply to commercial/utility systems. The text also notes that  "No land use shall be established on a lot or parcel except in conformance with Tables 9-2 and 9-3."
section: Section 9.05 Permitted Uses in Zoning Districts

summary: Any component of the Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy System, including but not limited to the solar array, energy storage system, or any accessory buildings or ancillary equipment shall be located at least fifty (50) feet from any adjacent parcel property lines. (Section 11.26.D.1) The ordinance also requires a 300 feet setback from habitable structures, but habitable structures are not equivalent to property or parcel lines unless explicitly stated.
section: Section 11.26 Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems

summary: Section 11.26.D.5 Screening requires: a minimum landscape buffer of 20 feet around accessory mechanical buildings and substations not included within the solar array footprint, with evergreen trees or bushes planted no more than 8 feet apart and at least 4 feet tall at planting, expected to grow to 10 feet within 3 growing seasons; trees may be trimmed but no lower than 10 feet. Additional visual screening may be required to protect adjacent residential property. Also, two rows of staggered trees must block the view of the facility from any public road, with trees at least 6 feet tall at planting, expected to grow to 10 feet within 3 years, deer resistant, and replaced within 90 days if they die. Access requires a minimum of 33 feet unobstructed access around the entire facility located internal to any fencing. These requirements apply explicitly to Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance as systems intended to provide energy to off-site uses or for wholesale or retail sale of electricity. No other screening or vegetative buffer options or conditions are provided in the text for these systems.
section: Section 11.26 Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems

summary: Section 11.26.D.4 requires that "appropriate warning signage shall be placed at the entrance and perimeter of the Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems." It also mandates that "the facility operator’s emergency contact information and appropriate warning sign shall be posted on or near the panels in a clearly visible manner." Additionally, Section 11.26.D.19 states that "the operator must install a sign containing the phone number to the Waterloo Township offices that is visible from the road for residents to use to call in case of a complaint or an emergency." These are the explicit signage requirements for Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems. No other signage options or conditions are provided in the text.
section: Section 11.26 Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems

summary: Section 11.26.A.8 requires that "Drainage, including stormwater, soil erosion and sediment control, and snowmelt runoff shall be managed in a manner consistent with all applicable federal, state, and local regulations." Additionally, Section 11.26.D.13 states that "The construction and maintenance of the commercial/utility photovoltaic solar facility shall not adversely affect the natural and existing drainage of the site or adjacent properties. Stormwater collection systems shall be installed as necessary to prevent erosion and any and all runoff onto neighboring parcels. Any erosion or flooding of property as a result of the construction or operations of a solar facility is the responsibility of the developer/owner of the structures." These provisions explicitly impose soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements on Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems developers. No other options or conditions for soil, erosion, or sediment control requirements are provided in the text.
section: Section 11.26 Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems

summary: Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems are permitted as a Special Land Use in the Public Conservation and Agricultural Zones, as stated: "Commercial/Utility Solar Energy Systems are permitted in the Public Conservation and Agricultural Zones as a Special Land Use provided that they are approved according to the provisions of Article 11.02 and 11.26." Table 9-2 shows these systems as Special Land Uses (S) in PC, A-1, and A-2 districts, and Table 9-3 shows them as Special Land Uses in C-1, C-2, and I-1 districts. The text further specifies that "Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems are only permitted in the Public Conservation and Agricultural Zones as a Special Land Use provided that they are approved according to the general provisions of Article 11.02 and the specific provisions of this Section, 11.26." The detailed Section 11.26 outlines the application, site, and development standards, and the requirement for a Special Land Use Permit. Other uses such as onsite solar energy systems are permitted by right in all districts, and private solar energy systems are accessory uses permitted in all districts. Commercial/utility wind energy systems are prohibited in all districts.

summary: Any component of the Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy System, including but not limited to the solar array, energy storage system, or any accessory buildings or ancillary equipment shall be located at least fifty (50) feet from any adjacent parcel property lines and three hundred (300) feet from any habitable structures on the project site or any adjacent parcels.
section: Section 11.26 Commercial/Utility Photovoltaic Solar Energy Systems, Article 11: Standards for Special Land Uses, D. The following site and development standards shall apply

summary: The ordinance applies to any Large Solar Energy System (SES-L) with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more. Fencing for the SES-L must comply with the latest version of the National Electric Code as of November 29, 2024, or as subsequently amended. Other provisions include setbacks measured from the nearest edge of the perimeter fencing, height limits of 25 feet for solar panel components, noise limits of 55 average hourly decibels at the nearest dwelling on adjacent nonparticipating property, dark sky-friendly lighting, compliance with applicable state or federal environmental regulations, and a host community agreement requiring a payment of $2,000 per megawatt of nameplate capacity to the Township. These provisions apply only if PA 233 of 2023 is in effect and do not apply to SES-L systems with less than 50 megawatts.
section: Section 1. Addition of New Subsection J(22) to Ordinance No. 2022-1, as amended.

summary: Section C states: 'Solar panel components must not exceed a maximum height of 25 feet above ground when the arrays are at full tilt.' This applies explicitly to Large Solar Energy Systems (SES-L) with a nameplate capacity of 50 megawatts or more. No other maximum height values are provided for SES-L in the text. The unit 'feet' is used as the standard measurement for height.

The SES-L must not generate a maximum sound in excess of 55 average hourly decibels as modeled at the nearest outer wall of the nearest dwelling located on an adjacent nonparticipating property. Decibel modeling shall use the A-weighted scale as designed by the American National Standards Institute.
section: Section 1. Addition of New Subsection J(22) to Ordinance No. 2022-1, as amended.

summary: An SES-L must comply with the following minimum setback requirements, with setback distances measured from the nearest edge of the perimeter fencing of the facility: 50 feet measured from the nearest shared property line of nonparticipating parties. Other setback distances include 300 feet from occupied community buildings and dwellings on nonparticipating properties (not property lines) and 50 feet from the nearest edge of a public road right-of-way.

summary: An SES-L must comply with the following minimum setback requirements, with setback distances measured from the nearest edge of the perimeter fencing of the facility: Public road right-of-way 50 feet measured from the nearest edge of a public road right-of-way. Other setback options include 300 feet from occupied community buildings and dwellings on nonparticipating properties, and 50 feet measured from the nearest shared property line of nonparticipating parties.

An SES-L must comply with the following minimum setback requirements, with setback distances measured from the nearest edge of the perimeter fencing of the facility: Occupied community buildings and dwellings on nonparticipating properties - 300 feet from the nearest point on the outer wall. Other setbacks include 50 feet from public road right-of-way and 50 feet from the nearest shared property line with nonparticipating parties, but these do not pertain to occupied dwellings or structures.

summary: The Weare Township Board has adopted a limited moratorium on issuing zoning permits and authorizing building permits for large scale or industrial scale solar energy development for a period of six to nine months. "Any applications made for solar development shall be held in abeyance until such ordinance is adopted and effective or by December 31, 2025." The moratorium "shall not apply to wind generation-based operations." The ordinance "is effective the day after publication" and was adopted in May 2025. As of December 3, 2025, the moratorium remains in effect and will expire no later than December 31, 2025.

summary: Large Solar Energy Systems may be used as accessory structures within the dedicated open space of Planned Unit Development Districts (PUD) and Open Space Preservation Communities, provided that: (1) the system is primarily and predominantly used for generating electricity for use within the PUD or Open Space Preservation Community (such that any sale and distribution of excess available energy to a public utility or other third party shall be incidental and immaterial in amount); (2) the system complies with all applicable requirements in this Zoning Ordinance; and (3) the land hosting the system is conserved through a permanent conservation easement. Other districts allow Large Solar Energy Systems as a permitted or special use but not explicitly as accessory or secondary uses. For example, Section 12.115 states Large Solar Energy Systems are allowed as a Permitted Use only within the Commercial District, the Office District and the Industrial District and as a Special Use only within the Agriculture District, the Agribusiness District and the Public Land District. Small Solar Energy Systems are permitted as accessory uses in every zoning district but are not relevant here as they are not Large Solar Energy Systems.

summary: Section 12.115.C(17) requires a Decommissioning Plan (including decommissioning and removal procedures, schedules and projected costs) pursuant to which all above-grade and below-grade structures and improvements shall be decommissioned and removed offsite for disposal at the end of the Large Solar Energy System’s useful life, with no concrete, piping and other materials left in place, and pursuant to which the site shall be fully restored to a clean, safe condition comparable to (or better than) the site’s condition as it existed prior to installation of the Solar Energy System. Section 12.115.J mandates that following the operational life of the project, or at the time the project becomes an Abandoned Solar Energy System, the applicant shall perform decommissioning and removal of the Large Solar Energy System and all its components in accordance with the Decommissioning Plan approved by the Township as part of the approved site plan. All structures and improvements must be removed and the ground must be restored to its original condition and topography within 180 days of becoming an Abandoned Solar Energy System, or decommissioning, whichever occurs first. If removal and restoration are not completed within this time, the Township may remove or secure removal and draw on the security described in Section 12.115.K. Section 12.115.K requires the applicant to deposit security of a performance guarantee to ensure full compliance with this Ordinance and any conditions of approval, covering removal of the facility when abandoned, no longer in use, or in violation of the Ordinance. The security must be irrevocable and non-cancelable during the entire time the Large Solar Energy System exists or is in place.

Section 12.115.D.9 states: "A Large Solar Energy System shall be completely enclosed by perimeter security fencing to restrict unauthorized access. Such fencing shall be eight (8) feet in height as measured from the natural grade of the fencing perimeter. Electric perimeter security fencing is not permitted." This fencing requirement applies specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance.

Section 12.115.D.(15) states: "All solar panels shall be placed such that they do not negatively impact nearby properties or roads, including without limitation due to glare or heat concentration." This glare restriction explicitly applies to Large Solar Energy Systems as defined in Section 12.115. The ordinance also includes other requirements for Large Solar Energy Systems such as height limits, setbacks, perimeter screening, vegetation requirements, security fencing, compliance with building and safety codes, and decommissioning plans, but these do not specifically address glare. Smaller or non-commercial systems (Small Solar Energy Systems) have separate provisions, but the glare restrictions cited here pertain specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems.

Maximum height of a Solar Array shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet. Other collection devices, components or buildings of the Large Solar Energy System shall not exceed thirty-five (35) feet, or the maximum building height permitted within the zoning district in which that Solar Energy System is located, whichever is less. The height shall be measured from the natural grade at the base of the Solar Array, device, component or building measured.

A Large Solar Energy System shall be located on one or more parcels with an aggregate area of: (i) 10 acres or greater (if located in the Commercial (C), Office (O) or Industrial (I) zoning district), or (ii) 20 acres or greater (if located in any other zoning district). The units for these minimum lot sizes are acres.

Section 12.115.D.(7) Perimeter Screening requires that "The perimeter of Large Solar Energy Systems shall be screened and buffered by installed evergreen vegetative plantings whenever existing natural forest vegetation does not otherwise continuously obscure the Large Solar Energy System’s entire perimeter from adjacent parcels." The vegetative buffer must "maintain a minimum opacity of at least eighty percent (80%), and a mature height of not less than the greater of (x) eight (8) feet or (y) sixty percent (60%) of the height of the Ground Mounted Solar Energy System when oriented to maximum tilt." The opacity standard is measured by observation of any two (2) square yard area of landscape screen between one (1) foot above the established grade and the top or highest point of the required screen, based on growth over three (3) years. The applicant must agree in writing to install additional plantings if the landscaping has not screened the view as required after three years. The buffer must be composed of native or evergreen trees meeting height, spacing, and other requirements set forth in Section 13.75.C. Unhealthy or dead plant material (60% dead or greater) must be replaced within six (6) months or by the next appropriate planting period. Failure to maintain the buffer is grounds for revocation of any Special Use Permit. Plantings must be installed between April 1 and November 1, or the applicant must provide a financial guarantee equal to 1.5 times the cost of planting deficiencies. Additionally, Section 12.115.D.(8) requires "installation and maintenance of native perennial prairie vegetation mix of low-growing, flowering herbaceous plants and grasses underneath and surrounding all components of the Large Solar Energy System" to reduce erosion and provide habitat. This vegetation requirement may also be secured by a financial surety. These requirements apply explicitly to Large Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance.

Section 12.115.C.(23) requires "a written description of measures to be taken to support the flow of rainwater throughout the Large Solar Energy System, including any measures to promote the growth of vegetation beneath the arrays and/or otherwise limit the impacts of storm water runoff." Section 12.115 states: 'Large Solar Energy Systems shall be allowed as a Permitted Use only within the Commercial District, the Office District and the Industrial District and as a Special Use only within the Agriculture District, the Agribusiness District and the Public Land District, subject to the regulations and requirements of this Section and, if applicable, the general Special Use procedures, standards and criteria of Article 10 of this Ordinance.' Section 5. Abandonment and Decommissioning requires the applicant to prepare a decommissioning plan and submit it to the Planning Commission for review and approval prior to issuance of the Special Land Use Permit. The plan must state how the large photovoltaic solar farm facilities will be decommissioned, provide the estimated cost of decommissioning, the financial resources to be used, and the escrow agent with which the resources will be deposited. Any large photovoltaic solar farm facilities that are not operated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months shall be considered abandoned and shall be removed under the decommissioning plan. All structures, concrete, piping, facilities, and other project related materials above-grade and below-grade shall be removed offsite for disposal. All access roads or driveways shall be removed, cleared, and graded by the applicant, unless the property owner(s) request, in writing, a desire to maintain any access road or driveways. The ground must be restored to its original topography or mutually agreed variation within three hundred sixty-five (365) days of abandonment or decommissioning. The plan must include an agreement that prior to permit issuance, the applicant shall furnish a Professional Engineer’s estimate of decommissioning and a performance guarantee of at least 125% of the estimated cost in the form of a surety bond or cash deposit. The Township reserves the right to adjust the guarantee every two years. The Township may access escrow funds to complete decommissioning if the applicant fails to do so within 365 days of project end or abandonment, and is granted rights of entry and to seek injunctive relief and reimbursement for costs exceeding escrow amounts. Financial provisions shall not exceed reasonable anticipated decommissioning costs.

section: Subsection 14.07(VV) Commercial Solar Energy Facilities Conversion systems

summary: A commercial solar energy facility conversion system, or any part thereof, must be fully decommissioned within 180 calendar days of abandonment. There is a rebuttable presumption that a commercial solar energy facility is abandoned if it ceases to be operationally functional for a period of one year or more. Decommissioning requires the complete removal and disposal of all commercial solar energy facility conversion system components, including but not limited to, buildings, structures, equipment to include photovoltaic and thermal panels, transformers, and inverters; signage; fences; collection lines, wires, conduits, and cables; and underground infrastructure. The removal of screening vegetation is not required. Within one growing season, the lots previously comprising the commercial solar energy facility conversion system must be planted with perennials that will stabilize the soil and prevent soil erosion. The Township may draw upon the decommissioning financial security posted pursuant to this subsection and complete the decommissioning if the decommissioning is not timely completed. To ensure the proper and timely decommissioning, the property owner must maintain financial security from the issuance of the special land use permit through the completion of the commercial solar energy facility’s final decommissioning. The security must be in the form of 1) a noncancellable surety bond on terms and from a financial institution acceptable to the Township naming the Township as the sole beneficiary or 2) an irrevocable letter of credit on terms and from a financial institution acceptable to the Township naming the Township as the sole beneficiary. The amount of security will be determined by the Township Board on a case-by-case basis and will reasonably approximate 1.25 x the cost of decommissioning that portion of the commercial solar energy facility on the property in question. Such security amount will not include salvage values. The applicant will provide the Township with an initial decommissioning estimate at the time of application. The security will be reviewed every five years by the Township Board. If requested, the property owner will provide the Township Board with a then-current decommissioning estimate. Any increase or modification to the security must be provided to the Township within 30 calendar days of request. Required financial security must be filed with the Township Clerk following approval of the special land use, but prior to the issuance of any special land use permit or commencement of the approved use.

summary: Section 329.4(f) Decommissioning requires the permit holder to maintain a performance guarantee in the form of a surety bond or irrevocable letter of credit naming the Township as sole obligee or beneficiary. The security amount is determined by the Planning Commission to reasonably approximate the cost of decommissioning the CSES and excludes salvage values. The security is reviewed every five years and must be updated within 30 days of request. Financial security must be filed after permit approval but before issuance and construction or operation. A CSES must be fully decommissioned within one year of abandonment, which includes complete removal of all components such as structures, equipment, signage, fences, and lines, and the parcel must be planted with perennials to stabilize soil within one growing season. The Township may draw upon the security if the permit holder fails to comply. Other related requirements include insurance maintenance from permit issuance through final decommissioning and penalties for violations. The decommissioning plan must demonstrate compliance with these requirements as part of the special land use application. The ordinance distinguishes CSES as systems whose principal purpose is to provide off-site energy for wholesale or retail trade. Private Solar Energy Systems (PSES) have separate decommissioning requirements but are not considered CSES.

If the CSES must be enclosed by fencing, it must meet the minimum requirements of the NEC and NESC as amended. The security gate must be approved by the Wright Township Fire Department for emergency access. Additionally, the site plan for a CSES must depict fences; greenbelts, vegetation and screening. Greenbelt screening is required around the perimeter of the CSES and along any public rights-of-way and should obscure the CSES and its fencing to the greatest extent feasible. Screening may be comprised of fencing, greenery, or a combination thereof. The fencing and screening requirements are specific to CSES and distinct from those for Private Solar Energy Systems (PSES), which require screening that may include fencing but apply only to non-commercial systems.

The ordinance explicitly requires that 'All Solar Arrays must be placed in such a manner as to prevent solar glares from being directed onto nearby properties or roadways' (329.4(d)(10)). Additionally, a 'Glare impact study and glare map' must be included as part of the CSES special land use application (329.4(c)(9)). These requirements apply specifically to Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES), defined as systems whose principal purpose is to provide off-site energy for wholesale or retail trade. The ordinance also distinguishes CSES from Private Solar Energy Systems (PSES), which have separate glare restrictions and lower thresholds. The CSES glare restrictions are part of a broader set of standards for approval, including structural height limits, setback requirements, noise emissions, lighting, and environmental impact studies.

The ordinance explicitly states in subsection 329.4(d)(1) that ground-mounted Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) "may not exceed a height of twenty (20) feet when measured from the ground to the top of the panel when oriented at maximum tilt." This is the only maximum height restriction provided for CSES. For comparison, Private Solar Energy Systems (PSES) have a different height limit of ten (10) feet, but that does not apply to CSES.

The noise pressure level generated by a CSES must dissipate to 50 dB(A) Leq (1-min) as measured at the perimeter of the lot upon which it is located and any public rights-of-way or private roads. This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES). For comparison, the text also mentions a 40 dB(A) Leq (1-min) limit for Private Solar Energy Systems (PSES), but that does not apply to CSES. The units are expressed as dBA, which is the standard unit for noise measurement.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) are only permitted as Special Land Use within the  "I"  Industrial district. By implication, CSES are prohibited in all other zoning districts. The text states: 'CSES are only permitted as Special Land Use within the  "I"  Industrial district.' and 'CSES are subject to the requirements of the zoning district in which they are located.' No other districts are named for CSES use. Private Solar Energy Systems (PSES) are permitted as accessory uses in any zoning district, but this does not apply to CSES.

All above-ground structures and equipment including Solar Arrays, Transformers, and Inverters must meet the Industrial District setbacks for buildings except in the case where the subject property is adjacent to any other zoning district. In that case, the setback shall be one-hundred (100) feet to the non-industrial-zoned adjacent parcel line. If a CSES is located on more than one Parcel, the setbacks do not apply to the parcel lines shared by those Parcels. Setback requirements do not apply to roof-mounted CSES on buildings that existed prior to May 16, 2023, perimeter fencing, and greenbelt screening.

Greenbelt screening is required around the perimeter of the CSES and along any public rights-of-way. The Greenbelt screening should obscure the CSES and its fencing to the greatest extent feasible. All Greenbelt screening must be properly maintained. The following are minimum Greenbelt screening requirements: (i) Greenbelt must consist of evergreen trees planted at no more than 15 feet apart measured from the centerline of the tree trunk; (ii) Evergreens must be a minimum of 4 feet in height when planted; (iii) All evergreens must be planted between March 15 and November 15. If Applicant requests a final certificate of occupancy from the Township and the Applicant is unable to plant during the installation period, the Applicant must provide the Township with a letter of credit, surety or performance guarantee for an amount equal to one and one-half (1.5) times the cost of any planting deficiencies that the Township will hold until the next planting season. Existing vegetation must be maintained to the greatest extent possible.

The ordinance requires an environmental and ecological impact study and mitigation plan that must address erosion and sediment control (329.4(c)(10)). It mandates proof of environmental compliance including Part 91 – Soil Erosion and Sedimentation Control (329.4(c)(11)). Native, perennial ground cover must be present where available to stabilize soil and prevent sedimentation runoff, with exceptions granted by the Planning Commission in writing (329.4(d)(6)). Upon decommissioning, the parcel must be planted with perennials to stabilize soil and prevent erosion within one growing season (329.4(f)(4)).

Sec. 329.4(a) states that 'CSES are only permitted as Special Land Use within the  "I"  Industrial district.' Additionally, Sec. 1202(w) lists 'Commercial Solar Energy Systems in accordance with Section 328 of this Ordinance' as a special use. Other uses mentioned include Private Solar Energy Systems (PSES), which are permitted as accessory uses in any zoning district with a zoning permit, but these do not apply to CSES. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this consideration.

The ordinance requires as part of a CSES special land use application: "Scaled renderings depicting the three typical views of the CSES, including one view from the public right-of-way" and "The site plan must depict the following: The size, height, and location of all proposed structures and equipment...; Parcel lines; Fences; greenbelts, vegetation and screening; Land elevations; All structures within 300 feet of a Solar Array...depicting its size, height, and location." These requirements explicitly constitute visual impact assessment requirements for Commercial Solar Energy Systems. Other application requirements include project description, noise impact study, glare impact study, environmental and ecological impact studies, proof of environmental compliance, transportation plan, and decommissioning plan, but these do not explicitly address visual impact assessment. The ordinance also mandates greenbelt screening to obscure the CSES and its fencing to the greatest extent feasible, but this is a standard and not an assessment requirement.

Section 807.6.B states: 'Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems and Fields are a permitted accessory use in the following districts: R-1 through R-4, I-T, L-K, and I-C.' The ordinance requires Planning Commission approval and site plan review for ground-mounted systems. Solar overlay districts are not included as accessory uses per instructions.

The unit for the maximum height is feet.

Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy Systems and Fields are permitted as a special use in the R-1 through R-4 Districts and any Industrial only, subject to the approval of the Planning Commission under Article 9. Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems and Fields are a permitted accessory use in the following districts: R-1 through R-4, I-T, L-K, and I-C. The special use may include terms and conditions in addition to those stated in this subsection.

Section 18.05 Decommissioning Plan requires the owner/operator to submit a decommissioning plan for all solar energy systems to ensure proper removal of equipment and/or facilities upon the end of the project life or after their useful life. The plan must include removal of all structures and foundations, electrical transmission components, restoration of soil and vegetation, and a financial assurance plan. The owner/operator of CSES and/or Solar Farm shall provide a current-day decommissioning cost estimate and post a bond, letter of credit, or establish an escrow account with an inflationary escalator, at a minimum of $1400.00 per acre, to ensure proper decommissioning. Other types of solar energy systems regulated include Rooftop or Architecturally-Integrated Solar Energy Systems (not regulated by this section), Ground-Mount Solar Energy Systems (accessory use, height limit 15 feet, building permit required), Community Solar Energy Systems (CSES) requiring an Interim Use Permit valid for five years, and Solar Farms (principal use, Conditional Use Permit required, minimum 5 acres, prohibited in certain zones, subject to setback, height, and coverage limitations). Solar Farms with capacity 50 megawatts or more fall under Minnesota Public Utilities Commission jurisdiction and are not subject to county review.

Section 18.02.D.4 states that 'All Solar Farm components must meet the setback, height and coverage limitations for the zoning district in which the system is located.' The only explicit numerical height limit given in the text is for ground-mount solar energy systems (accessory to the principal use), which 'shall not exceed 15 feet' in height (Section 18.02.B.3). Since no other specific numerical height limit is provided for Solar Farms under 50 megawatts, the 15 feet limit is the most restrictive explicit numerical value related to height. The units for this height restriction are feet.

Solar Farms shall be located on parcels of land no less than five acres in size. This is explicitly stated in Section 18.02.D.2: 'Solar Farms shall be located on parcels of land no less than five acres in size.' Additionally, Section 18.03.A requires a Conditional Use Permit for Solar Farms on contiguous or aggregate site areas larger than 5 acres. The unit 'acres' is the standard area measurement used.

summary: The County prohibits Solar Farms within the following zoning district of Shoreland, designated wetland areas, and within 600 feet of areas designated or formally protected from development by Federal, State, or County Agencies as wildlife habitat, wildlife management areas or designated as National Wild and Scenic land or corridor. Solar Farms are ground-mount solar energy arrays which are the principal use on the property, designed for providing energy to off-site users or export to the wholesale market, and require a Conditional Use Permit (CUP) in all other zones. The classification list shows Solar Farms as conditionally permitted ('C') in all listed zoning districts: FR (Farm Residential), R (Residential), C (Commercial), M (Manufacturing), P (Public), and O (Open).

The County prohibits Solar Farms within 600 feet of areas designated or formally protected from development by Federal, State, or County Agencies as wildlife habitat, wildlife management areas or designated as National Wild and Scenic land or corridor; this applies to Solar Farms under 50 megawatts which require a Conditional Use Permit. Other related provisions include prohibitions within Shoreland and designated wetland areas, but the 600 feet setback specifically applies to protected natural resource areas.

Section 18.03(C) requires that "Landscaping and buffer screening visible from adjacent residential properties and public rights-of-way shall be submitted to minimize the visual impact of the above grade site improvements" for Community Solar Energy Systems and Solar Farms. A waiver is possible if existing vegetation or topography provides screening. The Planning Commission may impose further vegetative screening details. Section 18.04(9) requires a "Landscape Plan, including required screening of site perimeter and/or perimeter security fencing" as part of the Conditional Use Permit application for Solar Farms. The ordinance applies to solar energy systems producing less than 50 megawatts (Section 18.01). Solar Farms are defined as "Ground-mount solar energy arrays which are the principal use on the property, that are designed for providing energy to off-site users or export to the wholesale market" and require a Conditional Use Permit (Section 18.02.D). Other types of solar systems include Rooftop or Architecturally-Integrated Systems (not regulated by this Section), Ground-Mount Systems accessory to the principal use, and Community Solar Energy Systems (CSES) which require an Interim Use Permit and have their own standards.

Solar Farms: Ground-mount solar energy arrays which are the principal use on the property, that are designed for providing energy to off-site users or export to the wholesale market shall be a permitted use in all zones excluding those defined in d(3). A Conditional Use Permit (CUP) will be required for Solar Farms. The Appendix A – Classification List shows Solar Energy System-Solar Farm as 'C' (Conditional Use Permit required) in all listed districts: Farm Residential, Residential, Commercial, Manufacturing, Public, and Open. Other types of solar energy systems include Rooftop or other Architecturally-Integrated Solar Energy Systems (permitted accessory uses in all districts, no building permit required), Ground-Mount Solar Energy Systems (permitted accessory uses in all districts with building permit and accessory use standards), and Community Solar Energy Systems (CSES) which require an Interim Use Permit (IUP) and are allowed as principal or accessory permitted uses in all districts except prohibited zones.

The ordinance requires a Conditional Use Permit (CUP) for Solar Farms under 50 megawatts, which includes submission of landscaping and buffer screening visible from adjacent residential properties and public rights-of-way to minimize visual impact (18.03 C). The CUP application must be accompanied by horizontal and vertical elevation drawings showing solar arrays, fencing, landscape plans including required screening of site perimeter and/or perimeter security fencing, and other site features (18.04). Solar Farms are defined as ground-mount solar energy arrays designed for providing energy to off-site users or export to the wholesale market, located on parcels no less than five acres, and prohibited in certain zoning districts (18.02 D). Other solar energy system types include Rooftop or Architecturally-Integrated Systems (not regulated by this section), Ground-Mount Systems accessory to the principal use (regulated with building permits and dimensional standards), and Community Solar Energy Systems (CSES) requiring an Interim Use Permit (IUP) and subject to similar but distinct regulations (18.02 A-C, 18.03 A). Solar Farms with capacity 50 megawatts or more fall under Minnesota Public Utilities Commission jurisdiction and are not subject to County review (18.01, 18.03 B).

A decommissioning plan shall be required to ensure that facilities are properly removed after their useful life. Decommissioning of solar panels must occur in the event they are not in use for 12 consecutive months. The plan shall include provisions for removal of all structures and foundations, restoration of soil and vegetation and a plan ensuring financial resources will be available to fully decommission the site. Disposal of structures and/or foundations shall meet all applicable rules and regulations to proper disposal. To ensure proper decommissioning, the applicant shall provide a financial surety by posting a bond, letter of credit or the establishment of an escrow account at a rate of $25,000 per MW or fraction thereof for Community Solar Farms and at a rate of $500 per acre for Private Solar Gardens. Any financial surety arrangement shall be approved by the County Attorney’s Office as to form and issuing bank. The issuing bank must be an FDIC insured bank. The issuing bank must be available in its entirety to fulfill the obligations of Developer under the Agreement. Any letter of credit to the County shall contain language requiring its automatic renewal prior to December 31 of each calendar year, unless cancellation of the letter of credit is specifically approved in writing by the County.

Section 9.20.2.1(G)(4) states: 'Applicant shall provide mitigation of glare issues, failure to mitigate will be a violation of the IUP.' Additionally, screening to mitigate potential glare concerns is required when there is less than 1,000 feet of separation from residential dwellings, consisting of 'earth mounds or berms; neutral colored fences; or landscaping used in combination or singularly so as to block direct visual access and to mitigate potential glare concerns.' The landscaping must be '80 percent opaque at the time of maturity' with 'healthy plant materials at least 6 feet in height at the time of planting' or 'at least 2 staggered rows of evergreen trees placed no more than 8 feet apart.' Screening fences must be maintained in good condition, with dead plantings replaced within the current or next growing season.

summary: Private solar gardens or community solar farms shall be screened from residential dwelling units as follows when there is less than 1,000 feet of separation between the solar array and residential dwelling: Screening shall consist of earth mounds or berms; neutral colored fences; or landscaping used in combination or singularly so as to block direct visual access and to mitigate potential glare concerns. The use of berming and landscaping shall be 80 percent opaque at the time of maturity. Planting screens shall consist of healthy plant materials at least 6 feet in height at the time of planting. Or planting screens shall include at least 2 staggered rows of evergreen trees placed no more than 8 feet apart. Screening fences that are in disrepair shall be repaired. Planting screens shall be maintained in a neat and healthy condition with plantings that have died being replaced within the current or next growing season. Applicant shall provide mitigation of glare issues, failure to mitigate will be a violation of the IUP.

The ordinance requires Community Solar Farms to obtain an Interim Use Permit (IUP), which is a form of special use approval. Relevant excerpts include: "The interim use permit shall expire at the same time the solar energy farm lease expires... The IUP may be extended following the same process as establishment of the original IUP." The Planning Commission is involved in granting exemptions and approvals, such as for foundation certification, removal of windbreaks, and permit extensions. The text details extensive performance standards and application requirements for Community Solar Farms, including setbacks, maximum height, screening, and decommissioning plans. However, the ordinance does not specify any particular zoning district names or abbreviations where Community Solar Farms are permitted as a special use or similar. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this analysis as per instructions.

Community Solar Farms must be located a minimum of 300 feet from a residential dwelling unit not located on the property. Setbacks shall be measured to the nearest solar array or other structure within the community solar farm, excluding security fencing, screening or berm. This is stated as: 'Private solar garden and community solar farms must meet the minimum principal building setback for the zoning district and be located a minimum of 300 feet from a residential dwelling unit not located on the property. Setbacks shall be measured to the nearest solar array or other structure within the private solar garden or community solar farm, excluding security fencing, screening or berm.'

Large solar energy systems shall meet or exceed the following setbacks: The setback distance from the outermost edge of a solar array to the nearest wall or portion of a dwelling, including an attached garage, is 750 feet in Agriculture, Conservation, Rural Residence, or Rural Townsite Districts. In Highway Business, General Business, Light Industry, or Heavy Industry Districts, the setback is 200 feet. The setback does not apply to a dwelling owned by the applicant.

The ordinance requires that for Commercial Solar Energy Systems (Solar Gardens and Solar Farms), the owner/operator shall submit a decommissioning plan to ensure proper removal of equipment and facilities upon the end of project life or after their useful life. The owner/operator shall decommission the solar panels if not in use for twelve (12) consecutive months. The plan must include provisions for removal of all structures and foundations, removal of all electrical transmission components, restoration of soil and vegetation or installation and continuation of beneficial habitat standards, and compliance with the Carlton County Solid Waste Ordinance. Additionally, the owner/operator must provide a current-day decommissioning cost estimate and post a bond, letter of credit, or establish an escrow account with an inflationary escalator, in an amount determined by the County Board, to ensure proper decommissioning. These requirements apply to Solar Gardens and Solar Farms, which are commercial SES allowed as conditional or interim uses in specified zoning districts. Non-commercial SES and smaller systems are regulated differently and do not have these decommissioning requirements explicitly stated.

Section 7.31, B.2.h. requires that at time of application for an Administrative Permit or Interim Use Permit, the project developer of all ground-mounted commercial solar energy systems shall submit a decommissioning plan for approval. The plan must ensure removal of all structures and foundations, electrical transmission components, restoration of soil and vegetation, and include a financial surety "ensuring financial resources will be available to fully decommission and restore the site." The plan must include an industry engineer’s estimate of the decommissioning cost, with financial surety equal to or greater than 125% of the approved surety. The plan must also include inflationary or financial surety review and adjustment provisions. Failure to maintain financial surety or update the plan can result in revocation or nullification of permits. Additionally, the permit holder must provide annual notification certifying compliance and a minimum 90-day notice of intent to decommission. Commercial solar energy systems require either an Administrative Permit (for site area footprint less than 10 acres) or an Interim Use Permit (for 10 acres or larger), with the decommissioning plan submitted at application. The ordinance applies to systems generating less than 50 megawatts, with larger systems referred to the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission.

Per Section 7.31, D.3.f.i, "Perimeter fence and landscape improvements shall be installed prior to all other above grade site improvements and confirmed compliant by County inspection." Additionally, Section 7.31, E.4.b requires "All commercial solar projects shall include the development, installation, and maintenance of a performance-based landscape plan wind row style plantings placed outside the fenced perimeter." Section 7.31, E.4.b.iii reiterates that "Perimeter fence and landscape improvements shall be installed prior to all other above grade site improvements and confirmed compliant by County inspection." Commercial Solar Energy Systems under 50 megawatts require either an Administrative Solar Permit (for projects less than 10 acres) or an Interim Use Permit (for projects 10 acres or larger), as determined by site footprint and/or the Zoning Administrator (Section 7.31, B.2.b).

Commercial solar energy systems shall be located on parcels of land no less than five (5) acres in size. Projects with a site area footprint less than ten (10) acres require an Administrative Solar Permit, while projects with a site area footprint greater than ten (10) acres require an Interim Use Permit. The site area footprint is the total area of the solar array enclosed by the security perimeter and may include contiguous parcels. The minimum lot size is explicitly stated as five acres, which is the most restrictive minimum parcel size for commercial solar energy systems under 50 megawatts.

summary: The required minimum setback from roadways for all project elements of Commercial Solar Energy Systems under 50 megawatts are fixed distances. Specifically, 135 feet from the centerline of State and County Roads for the first commercial solar energy system on any single parcel and 735 feet from the centerline of State and County Roads for any additional commercial solar energy system on the same parcel. Additionally, 135 feet from the centerline of all other public roads. Other setbacks include 75 feet from all non-right of way property lines or 275 feet from any dwelling, whichever is greater.

Section 7.31, E.4 requires that "Existing forestation, foliage, and native fauna within, near and surrounding the project area shall be preserved insofar as is practical." It mandates that "The permit holder shall establish and maintain an approved landscaped vegetative visual buffer on-site in the manner prescribed below so as to limit undue impact to potentially affected abutting/nearby properties." The screening must be "a performance-based landscape plan wind row style plantings placed outside the fenced perimeter and consisting of suitable native shrubbery and trees." Trees and/or shrubs "shall be a minimum of six (6) feet tall when planted and shall reach project-affiliated fence height and leaf-on conditions seventy-five (75) percent opacity screening by the end of year three (3) of the project." A "site specific performance based landscape plan designed by Minnesota-licensed landscape architect or Minnesota-certified arborist shall be submitted verifying that the above-stipulated height and opacity goals will be achieved by the end of year three (3) of the project." Alternatively, "the planting of two (2) staggered rows of six (6) foot tall coniferous trees coupled with site specific earthen berm construction may be proposed to meet the seventy-five (75) percent opacity screening requirement." Financial surety "in an amount sufficient to guarantee that the planting heights and seventy-five (75) percent opacity screening goals are achieved by the end of year three (3) shall be provided prior to building permit approval." Also, "All new, installed vegetative screening shall be established outside of the security fence, and shall maintain a minimum twenty (20) foot setback from all property lines." These requirements apply to commercial solar energy systems defined as "Systems designed to supply energy for off-site users on the distribution grid or for export to the wholesale market via connection to the electric transmission grid (i.e. community 'solar gardens' or 'solar farms' and other commercial systems generating less than fifty (50) megawatts)" and are enforced through Administrative or Interim Use Permits depending on site footprint size. Other relevant provisions include that "Perimeter fence and landscape improvements shall be installed prior to all other above grade site improvements and confirmed compliant by County inspection."

Section 7.31, C.2 states: 'The permit holder shall implement those MPCA-recommended erosion and sediment control which are deemed by the Department to be applicable. If applicable, the permit holder shall obtain an NPDES Permit and provide the Department with the Storm Water Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) submitted to the MPCA as part of the (NPDES) permit application. Those erosion and sedimentation control measures determined to be necessary shall be installed or implemented prior to construction and maintained in accordance with the SWPPP.' This applies to all solar energy systems generating less than fifty (50) megawatts of power as per Section 7.31, A.3. Other relevant requirements include Administrative Permits for projects less than ten (10) acres and Interim Use Permits for projects with site area footprint greater than ten (10) acres, with specific submittal and performance standards detailed in Sections 7.31, D and F.

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts visual impact assessment requirements for Commercial Solar Energy Systems under 50 megawatts. It requires a landscape plan "specifically tailored and emphasized as it pertains to the view from the adjacent home(s). Opacity levels must be met, and the level of overall landscape treatment shall be commensurate with the project setback." (Section 7.31, D.3.d). Additionally, under Administrative Permit Performance Standards, "Existing forestation, foliage, and native fauna within, near and surrounding the project area shall be preserved insofar as is practical" and "All commercial solar projects shall include the development, installation, and maintenance of a performance-based landscape plan wind row style plantings placed outside the fenced perimeter and consisting of suitable native shrubbery and trees" with "seventy-five (75) percent opacity screening by the end of year three (3) of the project" verified by a licensed landscape architect or certified arborist (Section 7.31, E.4). The screening must be maintained for the life of the project and guaranteed by financial surety. The community meeting prior to permit application must include presentation of the landscaping and screening plan and a report addressing community concerns and mitigation measures, which is used to establish conditions of approval (Section 7.31, D.2). Site plan submittal requirements include detailed elevation drawings and landscaping plans showing screening of the site perimeter and fencing (Section 7.31, D.3.g). Other permit requirements include Administrative Permits for projects under 10 acres and Interim Use Permits for projects 10 acres or larger, with similar submittal and performance standards (Sections 7.31, D and F).

A decommissioning plan is required to ensure that facilities are properly removed after their useful life. A solar farm shall be considered abandoned after 12 consecutive months without energy production, unless a plan is submitted outlining the steps and schedule for returning the solar farm to service. The decommissioning plan shall include provisions for removal of all structures and foundations, restoration of soil and vegetation, and assurances that financial resources will be available to fully decommission the site. Structures in solar farms shall not exceed 15 feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt. Solar Farms (5 acres and larger) must have "Vegetative screening such as coniferous trees a minimum of 6’ in height or an alternative approved by the Zoning Administrator, installed around the perimeter of the Solar Farm at the time the Solar Farm is installed." A decommissioning plan shall be required to ensure that facilities are properly removed after their useful life. The plan shall include provisions for removal of all structures, foundations, electrical equipment and internal or perimeter access roads, restoration of soil and vegetation and a plan ensuring financial resources will be available to fully decommission the site. Disposal of structures and/or foundations shall meet applicable local, state and federal regulations. The applicant shall submit a financial guarantee in the form of a letter of credit, cash deposit or bond in favor of the County equal to one hundred twenty-five (125) percent of the costs to meet the requirements of the decommissioning plan. Solar farms shall be screened from residential dwelling units and/or other land uses as required by the Board. A security fence shall encompass all components of a Utility Scale Solar Installation (USSI) or a Utility Scale Battery Energy Storage System (USBESS), featuring at least one gate with a locking mechanism on the primary access side.
