summary: Section 30.8 Decommissioning explicitly requires the project owner of a SEOD to provide financial security phased over the first eleven (11) years of solar power generation to cover estimated costs of decommissioning and site reclamation, with amounts starting at twenty (20) percent by the first anniversary, fifty (50) percent by the sixth anniversary, and one hundred and twenty (120) percent by the eleventh anniversary. The security must be in an acceptable form such as a letter of credit, cash escrow, or performance bond, and must be maintained until all decommissioning and site reclamation is completed and paid for. The project owner must commence reclamation within 90 days of abandonment, defined as no electricity production for nine (9) continuous months without a viable restoration plan, with possible extensions granted by the County Commission. The County may initiate reclamation if the owner fails to act, following notice and a hearing. Additionally, all underground equipment and foundations must be removed to a depth of at least four feet to allow for future land use. These requirements apply specifically to utility scale solar projects within a SEOD. Other related provisions include the requirement for a final decommissioning and reclamation plan as part of the building permit application (30.9.4.6) and the County Commission's authority to remove the overlay district if the project is abandoned (30.10.3).

Section 30.7.1.1 states: "Glare from photovoltaic panels should not exceed the levels predicted as part of the glare study. Any additional glare that was not predicted as part of the glare study should be remediated." This applies as a requirement for utility scale solar projects within a designated Solar Energy Overlay District (SEOD).

Section 30.6.5.3 states: 'Height shall be determined by the top of the panel at its maximum tilt measured from grade at the base. Height of the solar structures must not exceed 25 feet.' This applies directly to solar structures within a Solar Energy Overlay District (SEOD) for utility scale solar projects. No other maximum height values are provided for utility scale solar within the SEOD.

Section 30.2.1.2 states: 'Area within each SEOD cannot exceed a total of more than 640 acres except as allowed in Section 30.2.2.5.' Section 30.2.2.5 allows additional land above 640 acres if a minimum of one (1) percent of the total area is dedicated for wildlife pollinators, with a formula provided for calculating the total allowable area based on the percent of land for pollinators. The maximum area is expressed in acres.

Section 30.2.1.1 states: 'Minimum Area. Area within each SEOD must be a minimum of 20 acres.' Additional dimensional requirements include a minimum width of 150 feet and minimum depth of 250 feet (Section 30.2.2.2), but the minimum lot size is explicitly given as 20 acres. The Solar Energy Overlay District (SEOD) is established to "permit utility scale solar energy production by photovoltaic (PV) solar cells and associated support facilities." The SEOD "may be requested in Agriculture or Industrial zoning districts." The SEOD requires a minimum area of 20 acres and a maximum area of 640 acres, with specific design and setback requirements. Battery or power storage facilities require separate Conditional Use Permits, but the utility-scale solar energy production itself is permitted as a primary use within the SEOD. No other districts are explicitly mentioned as permitting utility-scale solar energy systems as a primary use without special conditions or approval.

Section 30.6.5.1 states: "Buffers. Vegetative screening, when required, must include a mixture of deciduous and evergreen trees capable of screening panels within five (5) years of project completion." Section 729.7.14 DECOMMISSIONING requires removal of all solar and solar related equipment within six (6) months of discontinuation or abandonment, with removal and restoration completed no later than twelve (12) months after commencement. The unit of measurement is feet.

The plan must include removal of all structures, foundations, underground wiring, and foreign materials; site reclamation with regrading, seeding, and revegetation; soil testing before and after decommissioning with remediation if needed; and disposal of materials in accordance with local, State, and Federal regulations. The operator must submit annual power generation reports, respond to a Notice of Abandonment within 30 days, and complete decommissioning within one year of such notice. Financial assurance is required via a bond or escrow equal to estimated decommissioning costs, with provisions for cost adjustments and County rights to call the bond in case of non-compliance. Other system types mentioned include Personal or Accessory Solar Energy Conversion Systems (for on-site use, not sale) and Limited Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (LSECS) limited to 20 contiguous acres, which are not subject to these decommissioning standards.

Properties containing CSECS shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access. Wildlife friendly fencing, such as a barb-wire fence with smooth wires for the top and bottom strings, or woven wire or other permeable fencing, shall be used where possible. Where wildlife friendly fencing is not utilized, additional wildlife corridors, including escape corridors, may be required in areas prone to grass fires or flooding. Critical electrical and communications equipment may be fenced with chain-link fence topped with barbed wire when such measures are deemed necessary to ensure public safety and provide additional security for the equipment. Wildlife corridors shall be provided as determined necessary by wildlife biologists or other specialists. Unless waived by the property owner, a 25-foot deep buffer area shall be provided and maintained along property lines between the systems and adjoining non-participating residential properties, or along the Site Area fencing for participating residential properties, for the purpose of screening the residential portion of the property. The buffer area may include berms, fences, and/or vegetation and may occur within the required setbacks on the facility property.

All solar panels must be constructed to minimize glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and must not interfere with traffic, including air traffic, or create a safety hazard as per any local, State, and Federal laws and regulations. Examples of measures that can be utilized to limit glare, include, but are not limited to: textured glass; anti-reflective coatings; screening; distance; or positioning units in a manner that reduces glare.

The CSECS Site Area shall be limited to no more than one thousand (1,000) acres total, unless the BZA approves a modification from this standard based on site specific characteristics. This size limit applies to Commercial/Utility Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS) and is measured as the cumulative total of the Solar Modules within the facility, with panels in their most horizontal position. The most restrictive value is 50 dBA between dusk and dawn.

The ordinance states that 'CSECS Site Areas shall be spaced at least one thousand three hundred twenty (1,320) feet from one another.' The term 'Site Area' is defined as the footprint of the solar facility including the various Solar Modules within the facility, measured with the panels as horizontal as possible, excluding access drives, batteries, transformers, ancillary structures, or their required setbacks. This minimum separation distance applies to full Commercial/Utility Scale Solar Energy Conversion System (CSECS) installations (i.e., full farms or utility-size installations), not just individual components. A minimum setback of 100 feet shall be required for all structures located on the subject property measured from the subject property lines to the structure in question. The solar panels/array and appurtenant structures shall be located a minimum of five hundred (500) feet from the property line of any residentially zoned property; a minimum of three hundred (300) feet from the property line of any adjacent agricultural, commercial or industrially zoned property; and a minimum of one thousand (1,000) from the property line of any school or church. Unless waived by the property owner, a 25-foot deep buffer area shall be provided, and maintained, along property lines between the systems and adjoining non-participating residential properties, or along the Site Area fencing for participating residential properties, for the purpose of screening the residential portion of the property. The ordinance explicitly requires vegetative buffer and screening for Commercial/Utility Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS). This buffer may include "a combination of berms, fences, and/or vegetation and may occur within the required setbacks on the facility property" and is designed to "buffer the view of the facility from the residence and the residential portion of the property." The ordinance also requires a Landscaping Plan detailing "all proposed changes to the landscape of the site required to accommodate buffering or screening from adjacent properties," including species lists and management schedules (F.4.m). Other options for screening include landscaping, fencing, or other appropriate means as determined by the Board of Zoning Adjustment (BZA) (Section 400.661, F.3).

The ordinance explicitly requires signage for Commercial/Utility Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS). Per Section E.12, "Perimeter fencing shall incorporate appropriate safety signage, at a minimum spacing of every five hundred (500) feet." Additionally, "Signage, including addresses for each fenced area, shall be provided as required by the Emergency 911 dispatch." For battery energy storage systems associated with CSECS, signage must comply with ANSI Z535 and include "the type of technology associated with the battery energy storage system; any special hazards associated; the type of suppression system installed in the area of the battery energy storage system, and 24-hour emergency contact information." Also, "disconnect and other emergency management information shall be clearly displayed on a light reflective surface," and "a clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations." The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Commercial/Utility Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS). It requires that "ground around and under solar panels/arrays and in designated buffer areas shall be planted and maintained in perennial vegetated ground cover or agricultural plants that are managed to prevent erosion and runoff" (E.7). It mandates preservation of existing topsoil during grading and construction, with topsoil to be "stockpiled on the site" and "redistributed uniformly on the surface of all areas to be vegetated" (E.8). The application must include a "grading/vegetation removal plan which includes all proposed changes to the topography and vegetation on the site" (F.4.f), a "stormwater management plan with supporting calculations" documenting runoff conveyance (F.4.g), and a "Vegetation Management and Agrivoltaic Plan" detailing vegetation installation and maintenance to "minimize erosion, maintain soil health" (F.4.n). A "Soil Sampling Plan" is required to characterize soil health and contamination before, during, and after construction and decommissioning, with remediation plans if degradation occurs (F.4.q). The "Abandonment, Decommissioning, And Reclamation Plan" must ensure site reclamation with "regrading, with a minimum of ground disturbance, seeding of the land after the removal of equipment, and revegetation of reclaimed soil areas" (F.4.r). These requirements apply specifically to CSECS as defined: "Solar Energy Conversion Systems... that convert solar energy into electricity for the primary purpose of storage and sales of generated electricity" (C.3).

The solar panels/array and appurtenant structures shall be located a minimum of one thousand (1,000) feet from any existing residence (building permit plans have been submitted or the residence is on-site at time of Special Use Permit approval) as measured from the dwelling, unless a lesser setback is agreed to by the owner of the residence and approved by the County Commission; other setback options include 500 feet from the property line of any residentially zoned property, 300 feet from the property line of any adjacent agricultural, commercial or industrially zoned property, and 1,000 feet from the property line of any school or church. Battery storage shall not be located within one thousand (1,000) feet of an existing residence. A 25-foot deep buffer area shall be provided and maintained along property lines between the systems and adjoining non-participating residential properties for screening purposes.

The ordinance requires that applications for Commercial/Utility Scale Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS) include "elevation drawings or renderings of the proposed SECS" (Section G.2), a "landscaping plan detailing all proposed changes to the landscape of the site required to accommodate buffering or screening from adjacent properties" including "installation, establishment, and maintenance of buffering or screening landscaping" (Section F.4.m), and a "vegetation management and agrivoltaic plan detailing all proposed changes to the vegetation of the site and outlining all proposed agrivoltaic uses" (Section F.4.n). The system must "utilize existing terrain, vegetation, and structures to screen the project from off-site view, to the extent possible" and if not possible, "additional screening may be required" (Section E.4.b). A "25-foot deep buffer area shall be provided, and maintained, along property lines between the systems and adjoining non-participating residential properties... for the purpose of screening the residential portion of the property" (Section E.10.e). These requirements are part of the Special Use Permit application process and are intended to "minimize the impact of the system on nearby properties" (Section B.2.c.(2)). Other related requirements include setbacks, fencing, and lighting standards, but these are not explicitly described as visual impact assessment requirements. The ordinance also allows the Board of Zoning Adjustment (BZA) to require "any other information deemed necessary" to evaluate the application (Section G.4), which could include further visual impact assessments.

Large Accessory Solar Energy Systems (LASES) "shall be permitted by Special Use Permit only in all Zoning Districts" (13.6-2 A) and "shall require both a special use permit and a building permit" (13.6-2 B). The ordinance does not specify particular district names or abbreviations for LASES accessory use, but rather allows them in all zoning districts subject to special use permit approval. Other options include Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES) with a maximum power rating of not more than 30 kW, which "shall be permitted as a use by right in all zoning districts" (13.5-2 A) and require only a building permit (13.5-2 B). Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) are prohibited if intended to generate power for off-site use or if rated capacity exceeds 100 kW (13.7-1 and 13.7-2). Section 13.6-14 Decommissioning requires that "The LASES owner is required to notify Clinton County Zoning Office immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation." The system "shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months." The owner "shall then have twelve (12) months in which to dismantle and remove the LASES including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations and other associated facilities from the property." The owner "shall also restore the land to its original condition, including forestry plantings of the same type/variety and density as the original." If the owner fails to comply, "Clinton County may complete the decommissioning and land restoration at the owner’s expense." Once the LASES use is discontinued, the special use permit "shall become null and void and all rights thereunder shall terminate."

Section 422.L states: 'The owner or operator of a utility scale solar energy project shall remove all equipment and restore the site to its original condition within twelve (12) months of the cessation of operations. A decommissioning plan shall be submitted as part of the conditional use application.' Further, Section 422.12 requires: 'Decommissioning must begin within one year of when the solar project ceased to generate electricity or thermal energy and shall be completed no later than one year from start.' The plan must include: (A) conditions for initiation; (B) removal of all non-utility owned equipment, conduits, structures, fencing, roads and foundations; (C) restoration of the property to pre-development condition; (D) an estimate of decommissioning costs and security to ensure funds availability, with reevaluation every five years. These requirements apply to utility scale solar energy projects defined as systems intended primarily to provide electricity to the electric utility grid for sale, and solar projects generating 1 MW or more or with a footprint greater than ½ acre. Other conditions include location, setbacks, fencing, height, screening, noise, lighting, emergency response plans, and abandonment rules, but these do not pertain directly to decommissioning.

The entire perimeter of the utility scale solar energy project shall be enclosed by a security fence at least six (6) feet in height. Additionally, all solar projects shall be completely enclosed with a minimum of 10-foot-high security fencing, which is measured from the finished grade of the fencing perimeter. Evergreen vegetative screening or a privacy fence must be installed so as to obscure the solar project from adjacent parcels, with vegetative screening at maturity exceeding 15 feet tall.

Section 422.06 states: 'No mirrored or reflective surface shall be allowed. All solar panels shall be treated or constructed with anti-reflective materials.' Section 422.08 requires site plan review to include 'approval of glare control.' These requirements apply to utility scale solar projects defined as systems 'intended to primarily provide electricity to the electric utility grid for sale to wholesale or retail customers.' Other related conditions include setbacks (300 feet from dwelling units, 100 feet from public right-of-way and property boundaries), fencing (minimum 10-foot-high security fencing with vegetative screening exceeding 15 feet), height limits (not to exceed 18 feet), underground transmission, and decommissioning plans. Lighting must be shielded and directed downward to minimize glare and light trespass (Section J).

The solar project shall not exceed 18 feet in height from the highest finished grade below each solar panel to the top of that panel and must not exceed the screening height. The minimum lot size for a utility scale solar energy project shall be twenty (20) acres. This applies to utility scale solar energy projects defined as systems intended primarily to provide electricity to the electric utility grid for sale. The text also references solar projects generating 1 MW or more or requiring an acreage footprint greater than one half (½) acre, but the explicit minimum lot size requirement stated is 20 acres. Other dimensional requirements such as setbacks and height are provided but do not specify smaller minimum lot sizes. The unit 'acres' is used as the standard area measurement.

Noise generated by the utility scale solar energy project shall not exceed fifty (50) decibels as measured at the property line. Additionally, a 'performance guarantee' in the form of surety equal to 125% of the estimated decommissioning cost must be provided prior to permit issuance. The surety must be reviewed every five years and adjusted accordingly. If the SEF ceases to produce energy for 12 months, it is considered abandoned unless evidence of intent to maintain operation is provided. Upon abandonment, the responsible party must remove the SEF and restore the site within 365 days of notice, or the county may remove the SEF using the performance guarantee funds and take legal action to recover costs.

The buffer shall obtain a height of ten feet within three growing seasons. The trees or bushes may be trimmed but no lower than a height of ten feet. § 155.06(A) states that a planted buffer must be planted along the sides adjoining a public road. These requirements apply to solar energy facilities defined as those that sell electricity to be used off site.

Section 46-43(e) requires a decommissioning plan as part of the Conditional Use Permit application for Level 2 and 3 SESs. The plan must be prepared by a third party engineer, signed by the party responsible for decommissioning and all landowners, and include: a description of any agreement with landowners, identification of responsible parties, type of solar panels and components, and an estimated cost for removal including grading and re-seeding. The plan must be recorded prior to permit issuance. Performance security equal to one and a quarter times the estimated cost must be provided before construction. The plan and cost must be updated every 5 years or upon ownership changes. The responsible party has 12 months to complete decommissioning if no energy is generated for 12 continuous months. The performance security may be drawn if the responsible party fails to decommission. The landowner is ultimately responsible if the responsible party fails. Section 46-43(f) states that a Level 2 or 3 SES that ceases energy production for 12 months is considered abandoned unless substantial evidence of intent to maintain operation is provided. The Planning Director may enforce removal and decommissioning, including use of performance security and judicial proceedings. Other options and conditions include: the decommissioning plan must be prepared by a third party engineer not associated with the site plan engineer; performance security can be a bond, cash escrow, or irrevocable letter of credit; the letter of credit must be issued by a federally chartered bank with a branch in northeastern North Carolina; failure to maintain performance security can lead to permit revocation; SES components will not be accepted at county solid waste or recycling facilities.

The major SEPGS owner is responsible for decommissioning and reclamation "to its condition prior to commencement of activities on the site, including all costs associated therewith." The decommissioning plan must include steps such as disconnecting from the power grid, removing all non-utility owned equipment and foundations to a depth of at least three feet below grade, removing graveled areas, fences and access roads unless the property owner agrees in writing for them to remain, restoring the property to a condition reasonably comparable to that which existed prior to development, and post-decommissioning inspections and monitoring by licensed professionals. The ordinance also requires periodic review and updating of the decommissioning plan and financial assurance every five years or upon change of ownership. Failure to comply results in revocation of permits and use of financial assurance funds by the county to complete decommissioning. Other related requirements include insurance, inspections, and maintenance until decommissioning is complete.

Section 4.D states: 'A six (6) foot high fence shall be installed for all major SEPGS ground mounted systems to protect from damage and vandalism, prevent trespassing, and provide for safety and security. No fencing is required for a minor SEPGS.' Additionally, Section 6.C.13 requires: 'Security fencing, a minimum of six (6) feet in height, shall be provided along the entire perimeter of the major SEPGS.' These provisions explicitly impose fencing requirements for major SEPGS. No other fencing options or conditions are provided for major SEPGS.

Section 4 Site Standards, subsection C states: 'A ground or pole mounted SEPGS shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in height as measured from grade at base of the racking and module structures to its highest point.' This height restriction applies to SEPGS generally, including Major SEPGS. No other height limits more restrictive than 20 feet are provided for Major SEPGS.

A letter of certification from a North Carolina licensed engineer indicating that inverter noise shall not exceed the lower of 3 dBA Leq (1 HR) above preconstruction background or 40 Leq (1 HR) dBA, measured at any property line during output that exceeds 95% of rated capacity from the facility. The units for noise level are dBA.
section: Section 6 Approval Requirements for Major SEPGS

summary: With respect to a major SEPGS, all structures and fencing associated with a major SEPGS shall meet a minimum front, rear, and side property line setback of 250 feet. A major SEPGS shall also meet the buffer requirements set out in Section 10.3.E, which requires a 100-foot wide buffer yard around the entire perimeter of the major SEPGS. Minor SEPGS setbacks differ and are based on accessory structure setbacks or structure setbacks if integrated, but these do not apply to major SEPGS.

Section 4.E requires that "The entire perimeter of a major SEPGS shall be screened from the adjacent properties by a one hundred (100) foot wide buffer yard. The buffer yard shall be a continuous vegetative screen buffer designed by a North Carolina licensed landscape architect or contractor and approved by the Zoning Administrator that provides a visual buffer of at least 80% opacity to a height of 10 feet within four (4) growing seasons." Additionally, Section 4.D mandates "A six (6) foot high fence shall be installed for all major SEPGS ground mounted systems to protect from damage and vandalism, prevent trespassing, and provide for safety and security." These requirements apply explicitly to major SEPGS. Minor SEPGS have different or no such requirements, e.g., no fencing is required for minor SEPGS. The buffer and fencing requirements are part of the site standards that major SEPGS must meet prior to approval.

Section 6.C.2(a) requires final site plans to include the "size and location of signs." Section 6.C.16 mandates "a sign stating the major SEPGS’s owner’s contact information including name, address and phone number shall be located at the entrance of the major SEPGS. Typical warning signs at the entrance shall also be required." Section 5.E states that "signage must be maintained in good condition until the major SEPGS is decommissioned, dismantled and removed from the site." These signage requirements apply explicitly to major SEPGS. No other signage options or conditions are provided in the text.
section: Section 6 Approval Requirements for Major SEPGS

summary: An erosion and sedimentation control plan shall be prepared by a North Carolina licensed engineer and shall meet the storm water requirements of the NC Department of Environmental Quality ('NCDEQ') and shall provide for ongoing monitoring of storm water runoff. Upon decommissioning, the property shall be restored to a condition reasonably comparable to that which existed prior to development of the major SEPGS, including the replacement of topsoil removed or eroded and revegetating any cleared or damaged areas with native vegetation unless the landowner requests otherwise in writing. The decommissioning plan must include these restoration requirements and be prepared by a North Carolina licensed third party professional engineer. Post-decommissioning monitoring shall be conducted for at least three years, including groundwater, vegetation health, density and vigor, and overall landscape stability. These requirements apply explicitly to major SEPGS, which are defined as SEPGS that do not meet the standards of a minor SEPGS and require a Special Use Permit.
section: Section 6 Approval Requirements for Major SEPGS

summary: The ordinance states that 'A major SEPGS and related facilities are allowed only with the approval of a Special Use Permit by the Board of Adjustment pursuant to Article V.' It further requires that 'The SEPGS shall meet the site standards and approval requirements of this Article prior to approval of the Special Use Permit.' Additionally, 'A Special Use Permit approved by the Board of Adjustment is required before a zoning compliance can be issued for construction of a major SEPGS.' In contrast, 'A minor SEPGS and related facilities are allowed in all zoning districts by right, provided the provisions of Section 4 of this Article are met.' No specific district names or abbreviations are mentioned for major SEPGS special use approval.
section: Article XII. – Solar Power Generation Systems Section 1. General

summary: SECTION 8.103, J. DECOMMISSIONING PLAN requires that the application include decommissioning plans describing the anticipated life of the solar farm, estimated decommissioning costs, funding methods, and the manner of decommissioning and site restoration. Following a continuous six-month period with no electricity generation, the permit holder has six months to complete decommissioning, which includes removal of solar panels, buildings, cabling, electrical components, and other associated facilities below grade. Prior to permit issuance, a performance guarantee must be provided, amounting to one and one-quarter the estimated decommissioning cost minus salvage value, or $50,000, whichever is greater. The performance guarantee may be a surety or performance bond, a certified check, or a no-contest irrevocable bank letter of credit, each with specific conditions. The landowner or tenant must notify the county when the site is abandoned.

Section 8.103.F.2 requires that "A security fence equipped with a gate and a locking mechanism must be installed at a minimum height of eight feet along all exterior sides of the solar farm." Additionally, Section 8.103.B states that "All structures and security fencing must meet a 100-foot front setback measured from the edge of the rights-of-way and 50-foot side and rear setbacks." Section 8.103.C requires a landscape buffer/screen along all exterior sides of the security fence, with options including: (1) on-site mature vegetation at a minimum height of ten feet and depth of 75 feet; (2) a single row of evergreens combined with mature vegetation, installed at five feet height achieving opaqueness and ten feet height in five years; (3) a double row of off-set evergreens, installed at five feet height achieving opaqueness and ten feet height in five years; or (4) a berm combined with evergreen vegetation installed at five feet height achieving opaqueness and ten feet height in five years. These requirements apply to the Solar Collector Facility defined as a commercial solar photovoltaic facility whose primary purpose is to generate power to sell for commercial gain.

Section 8.103 F.1 requires that "All solar panels must be constructed to minimize glare or reflection onto abutting properties and abutting roadways and must not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard." This applies to solar photovoltaic facilities whose primary purpose is to generate power to sell for commercial gain. Other relevant provisions include setbacks, screening options (such as on-site mature vegetation, single or double rows of evergreens, or berm combined with vegetation), topography considerations for screening, maintenance requirements, safety standards including fencing and signage, erosion control, nuisance control, change of ownership notification, decommissioning plans, and supplemental requirements for permits and utility approvals.

All structures and security fencing must meet a 100-foot front setback measured from the edge of the rights-of-way and 50-foot side and rear setbacks. Additionally, inverters shall be located a minimum 150 feet from any property line or public right-of-way. The most restrictive setback directly pertaining to property lines is the 150 feet for inverters, but the general facility setback is 100 feet front and 50 feet side and rear.
All structures and security fencing must meet a 100-foot front setback measured from the edge of the rights-of-way. Side and rear setbacks are 50 feet but are not related to roads.

A landscape buffer/screen shall be provided along all exterior sides of the security fence and must consist of: 1. On-site mature vegetation at a minimum height of ten feet and depth of 75 feet between the security fence and abutting property including rights-of-way; or 2. A single row of evergreens in combination with mature vegetation, installed at a height of five feet achieving opaqueness and a minimum height of ten feet in five years; or 3. A double row of off-set evergreens, installed at a height of five feet achieving opaqueness and a minimum height of ten feet in five years; or 4. A berm combined with evergreen vegetation installed at a height of five feet achieving opaqueness and a minimum height of ten feet in five years. Where visibility of the solar farm is increased due to topography, the landscape buffer/screen must be planted on-site in an area that lessens the view of the solar farm from off-site areas. Where visibility is decreased due to topography, the landscape buffer/screen may be reduced. The location of screening shall be determined by the Administrator. Landscape buffer/screens, ground cover, security fences, gates, and warning signs must be maintained in good condition until the solar farm is dismantled and removed from the site.

Section 8.103 F.3 requires "A warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the main gate to include the name of the solar farm operator and a local phone number for the solar farm operator in case of an emergency." Additionally, Section 8.103 E states that "Landscape buffer/screens, ground cover, security fences, gates, and warning signs must be maintained in good condition until the solar farm is dismantled and removed from the site."
Erosion control measures must be installed at construction entrances in order to minimize off-site soil damage. Existing grass must be maintained in perpetuity sufficient to prevent erosion.

New solar facilities of 2 MW or greater must submit a decommissioning plan prepared by a qualified engineer that includes a detailed procedure, cost estimate, financial assurance, removal of all components, proper waste disposal, recycling where practicable, and restoration of the property, with landowners and local governments able to impose stricter requirements.

The ordinance requires that the application for a commercial Solar Power Generation Facility include decommissioning plans describing the anticipated life, estimated decommissioning cost, method for ensuring funds, and the manner of decommissioning and site restoration, which means returning the site to its original condition. Following a continuous 6 month period with no electricity generation, the permit holder has 6 months to complete decommissioning, including removal of solar panels, buildings, cabling, electrical components, and other facilities. Prior to issuance of a zoning permit, the applicant must provide a performance guarantee equal to 1.25 times the estimated decommissioning cost minus salvage value or $50,000, whichever is greater. The performance guarantee may be: 1) a surety or performance bond that renews automatically with a 60-day notice prior to cancellation, approved by the Planning Director, and from a certified company; 2) a certified check deposited with the county finance director in an interest-bearing account; or 3) a no-contest irrevocable bank letter of credit valid for 12 months and renewed annually. The full amount must remain in effect until decommissioning and site restoration are complete. The landowner or tenant must notify the County when the site is abandoned.
section: 13-1 REMOVAL OF THE SOLAR FARM EQUIPMENT AND RESTORATION

summary: The ordinance requires that for Solar Power Generation Facilities for commercial power generation only: (a) all structures and security fencing must meet a 100 foot front setback and a 50 foot side and rear setback; (b) a landscape buffer/screen along all exterior sides of the security fence must consist of a double row or off-set evergreens installed at a height of 5 feet achieving opaqueness and a minimum height of 10 feet in 5 years; (f) a security fence equipped with a gate and a locking mechanism must be installed at a minimum height of six (6) feet topped with one foot of barbed wire along all exterior sides of the solar farm; (g) landscape buffer/screens, ground cover, security fences, gates and warning signs must be maintained in good condition until the solar farm is dismantled and removed from the site. The ordinance also details performance guarantees for decommissioning, which include options such as a surety or performance bond, a certified check, or a no-contest irrevocable bank letter of credit, with specific conditions for each.

All solar panels must be constructed to minimize glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and must not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard. This applies to Solar Power Generation Facilities for commercial power generation only. Other restrictions include setbacks, landscape buffers, underground power transmission lines, security fencing, and decommissioning plans. Performance guarantees can be in the form of a surety or performance bond, a certified check, or a no-contest irrevocable bank letter of credit, with specific conditions for each.

All structures and security fencing must meet a 100 foot front setback measured from the edge of the rights of way and a 50 foot side and rear setback; these setbacks apply to Solar Power Generation Facilities for commercial power generation only.

For commercial power generation solar power facilities, all structures and security fencing must meet a 100 foot front setback measured from the edge of the rights of way. Additionally, there is a 50 foot side and rear setback, but the front setback from rights-of-way (roads) is 100 feet.

For Solar Power Generation Facilities for commercial power generation only, the ordinance requires: 'a landscape buffer / screen along all exterior sides of the security fence must consist of a double row or off-set evergreens, absent mature vegetation, installed at a height of 5 feet achieving opaqueness and a minimum height of 10 feet in 5 years.' Additional requirements include setbacks, minimizing glare, underground power lines, security fencing, and maintenance of landscape buffers/screens until dismantling. Performance guarantees for decommissioning are also required, with options including surety bonds, certified checks, or irrevocable bank letters of credit.

The Agricultural-Residential District (AR) permits "Solar Power Generation Facilities for commercial power generation only" as a permitted use with specific conditions, including setbacks, landscape buffers, glare minimization, utility authorization, underground power lines, security fencing, maintenance, decommissioning plans, and performance guarantees. There is no mention of these facilities being permitted only as a special use or requiring approval by a zoning appeals board or similar special permitting process. No other districts or special use provisions for utility-scale solar energy systems are mentioned in the provided text.

A decommissioning plan shall be submitted as part of the application for a ground-mounted solar electricity system. The plan shall include: the anticipated life of the project; the estimated decommissioning cost in current dollars; the method of ensuring that funds will be available for decommissioning and restoration; the manner in which the project will be decommissioned and the site restored. Decommissioning shall include the removal of all equipment, structures, fencing, and foundations to a depth of at least three (3) feet below grade, and the restoration of the site to its pre-development condition, including the replacement of topsoil and re-vegetation. The decommissioning plan shall be updated every five (5) years and submitted to the Zoning Administrator for review and approval. If the system ceases to operate for a continuous period of twelve (12) months, it shall be deemed abandoned and removed in accordance with the approved decommissioning plan. The County may require the posting of a bond, letter of credit, or other financial assurance to ensure proper decommissioning. Additional requirements in certain zoning districts include: defined conditions for decommissioning initiation; removal of all non-utility owned equipment, conduit, structures, fencing, roads and foundations; restoration to pre-development conditions; completion timeframe not exceeding eighteen (18) months; estimated costs and funding methods; agreements with landowners; responsible party identification; and plan updates. Evidence of recording the decommissioning plan with the Register of Deeds is required prior to final electrical inspection. Failure to comply constitutes a zoning violation.
section: SECTION 9.13: INDUSTRIAL, TRANSPORTATION, UTILITY, AND WAREHOUSING ADDITIONAL REQUIRED STANDARDS

summary: Ground-mounted solar electricity systems (also referred to as solar farms or solar energy facilities) "shall be enclosed by a security fence not less than six (6) feet in height." These systems must comply with all applicable laws and industry standards, and the height of the system including appurtenant structures "shall not exceed twenty (20) feet." Additional requirements include setbacks, signage, lighting, and decommissioning plans. Security fencing, poles, and wires necessary to connect to electric utility facilities are not subject to setback requirements. The fencing requirement is explicitly stated in Section 9.13.K.2.f. Other relevant provisions include decommissioning requirements that include removal of fencing and restoration of the site.
section: SECTION 9.13: INDUSTRIAL, TRANSPORTATION, UTILITY, AND WAREHOUSING ADDITIONAL REQUIRED STANDARDS

summary: Ground-mounted solar electricity systems "shall be designed, constructed, and operated to prevent the misdirection and/or reflection of solar rays onto neighboring properties, public roads, and rights-of-way." In certain zoning districts (Rural Agriculture, Light Industrial, Heavy Industrial), proof of delivery of a glint/glare study to specified agencies (including airports and military installations) is required at least thirty (30) days before the technical review committee meeting. The system "will not reflect light of such intensity or directed in such manner as to impair pilot visibility or otherwise interfere with the safe operation of overhead aircraft."
section: SECTION 9.13: INDUSTRIAL, TRANSPORTATION, UTILITY, AND WAREHOUSING ADDITIONAL REQUIRED STANDARDS

summary: The height of ground-mounted solar electricity systems, including all appurtenant structures, shall not exceed twenty (20) feet, as measured from the average finished grade at the base of the structure to its highest point. Additionally, the height of the system as measured from the highest natural grade below each solar panel may not exceed twenty (20) feet. Any utility poles or antennas constructed for the project are excluded from this limitation.
section: SECTION 9.13: INDUSTRIAL, TRANSPORTATION, UTILITY, AND WAREHOUSING ADDITIONAL REQUIRED STANDARDS

summary: Ground mounted equipment must be setback thirty (30) feet from all public and private streets rights-of-way, fifteen (15) feet from side lot lines and twenty-five (25) feet from rear property lines. In no case shall any component of a ground-mounted solar electricity system be located within fifty (50) feet of any property line abutting a residentially zoned or used property. The most restrictive setback directly pertaining to property or lot lines is fifteen (15) feet from side lot lines. Security fencing, poles, and wires necessary to connect to facilities of the electric utility are not subject to these setbacks.
section: SECTION 9.13: INDUSTRIAL, TRANSPORTATION, UTILITY, AND WAREHOUSING ADDITIONAL REQUIRED STANDARDS

summary: Ground mounted equipment must be setback thirty (30) feet from all public and private streets rights-of-way. Security fencing, poles, and wires necessary to connect to facilities of the electric utility are not subject to these setbacks.
section: K. SOLAR ELECTRCITY SYSTEM, GROUND MOUNTED, 2. Requirements

summary: The ordinance requires a Type D buffer in accordance with Article 10 Section 10.8 (Buffering) along all property lines abutting residentially zoned or used property. Additionally, in the Rural Agriculture (RA), Light Industrial (L-IN), and Heavy Industrial (H-IN) Zoning Districts, Table 10-1 (Buffer Yard Requirements) applies except where the site abuts a residential use or residential zoning district, in which case a Type C buffer is required.
section: SECTION 9.13: INDUSTRIAL, TRANSPORTATION, UTILITY, AND WAREHOUSING ADDITIONAL REQUIRED STANDARDS

summary: Signage shall be limited to no trespassing signs, warning signs, and signs that provide 24-hour emergency contact information. All signage shall comply with Article 12 (Sign Regulations). A warning sign concerning voltage and including the name and telephone number of the system operator must be placed at the facility’s main gate or entry point.
section: SECTION 9.13: INDUSTRIAL, TRANSPORTATION, UTILITY, AND WAREHOUSING ADDITIONAL REQUIRED STANDARDS, K. SOLAR ELECTRICITY SYSTEM, GROUND MOUNTED

summary: Ground-mounted solar electricity systems are permitted in several districts, but in the Rural Agriculture (RA), Light Industrial (L-IN), and Heavy Industrial (H-IN) districts, "the following additional requirement standards shall apply," including proof of delivery of written notice to specified military and airport authorities, submission of a decommissioning plan, setbacks (e.g., 30 feet from streets, 100 feet from residential dwellings), height limits (not to exceed 20 feet), buffer yard requirements, lighting controls, and other conditions. These requirements imply a permitting or review process. The text states: "The intent of the Onslow County Planning and Development Department is that the site plans for Ground Mounted Solar Electricity Systems be thoroughly reviewed by all the applicable agencies during the review process." No districts are explicitly listed as special use or requiring zoning appeals board approval, but these conditions indicate a conditional approval process. Other districts show a permitted use ("P") without these additional conditions. Solar overlay districts are not included in this analysis.

Ground-mounted equipment must be set back one hundred (100) feet from any residential dwelling unit in existence at the time the application was submitted. Other setback options include complying with the minimum setback requirements for principal structures in the zoning district, and no component of the system being located within fifty (50) feet of any property line abutting residentially zoned or used property. However, the 100 feet setback from residential dwelling units is the most restrictive and directly applicable setback from occupied dwellings.
section: SECTION 9.13: INDUSTRIAL, TRANSPORTATION, UTILITY, AND WAREHOUSING ADDITIONAL REQUIRED STANDARDS, K. SOLAR ELECTRICITY SYSTEM, GROUND MOUNTED

summary: Section IX titled 'ABANDONMENT AND DECOMMISSIONING PLAN' requires that a Solar Energy Facility that ceases to produce energy for 12 months will be considered abandoned unless evidence of intent to maintain operation is provided. The responsible party must remove all equipment and restore the parcel within 360 days of notice. A decommissioning plan must be submitted prior to permit issuance, addressing conditions for decommissioning, removal of all non-utility owned equipment, restoration of property, timeframe for completion, responsible party, and a surety equal to 125% of estimated decommissioning costs. The surety is reviewed annually and must be approved by the County. Failure to comply results in termination of permits and use of the surety for decommissioning. These requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities, defined as energy facilities principally used to convert solar energy to electricity, excluding rooftop installations and those with an Improved Area less than or equal to 10 acres.
section: SECTION IX ABANDONMENT AND DECOMMISSIONING PLAN

summary: Solar energy facilities shall be fenced completely by a continuous barrier extending from the surface of the ground to a uniform height of not less than 6 feet from the ground at any given point, constructed of dirt, wood, stone, steel, or other metal, or any substance of a similar nature and strength. The perimeter fence shall be designed to restrict unauthorized access.
section: SECTION VI ENCLOSURE FENCING AND SECURITY

summary: Section VII.F states that the design and construction of Solar Energy Facilities "shall not produce light emissions, either direct or indirect (reflective), that would interfere with pilot vision and/or traffic control operations as stated in the most recent AICUZ report, as well as low level military training routes as then utilized by any branch of the US Department of Defense." Section X.D requires that if requested, the proponent of the Solar Energy Facility "shall use the latest version of the Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT), per its user's manual to evaluate the solar glare aviation hazard" for airports within 5 nautical miles, with specific reporting requirements to airport managers, FAA Airport District offices, or military officials depending on the airport type. The SGHAT analysis must be provided at least 30 days prior to site plan approval, and any design changes must be rerun in the SGHAT tool and reported accordingly. These provisions apply to Solar Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance, which generally excludes small or rooftop systems and includes larger commercial-scale facilities.
section: SECTION VII SUPPLEMENTAL REGULATIONS and SECTION X AVIATION NOTIFICATION

summary: Improved Areas shall be at least 100 feet from any contiguous property line not associated with a Solar Energy Facility. Other related setbacks include 25 feet from the fence line and 30-foot minimum easement for access roads and storage areas. These setbacks apply to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined by the ordinance (Improved Area greater than 10 acres).

All Improved Areas shall be at least 100 feet from a public road and 25 feet from the fence line. All access roads and storage areas shall be established on a 30-foot minimum easement to a public right-of-way.

All Solar Energy Facilities shall have a minimum landscape buffer containing evergreen vegetation screening where existing buffers do not obscure solar energy system perimeters from dwelling units on adjacent parcels. At maturity required vegetative screening shall not be less than 15 feet tall regardless of line of sight. An optional earthen berm may be used in conjunction with planted vegetation provided all of the following are met: The combined height of the berm and planted vegetation shall be at least 15 feet and provide approximately 75% opacity within one year of planting; The slope of the berm shall be stabilized with vegetation and no steeper than 3:1; The height of the berm shall be a minimum of 6 feet, with a level or rounded area on top of the berm; The berm shall be constructed of compacted earth; When berms are planned to be installed within required buffers, storm drainage plans submitted with an application shall be designed to anticipate a 100-year storm event; When visible from an adjoining residential use (including across a street) the berm shall be composed of view-obscuring vegetation in combination with a berm designed to obscure views to a height of 15 feet from the ground, except for mechanical equipment which shall be screened to the height of the equipment plus six inches; Prior to issuance of the first certificate of compliance, berms shall be planted to ensure coverage by live plant material within 3 to 5 years.

Section VII.A requires that "The manufacturers or installer's identification and appropriate warning sign shall be posted on or near the panels in a clearly visible manner." Additionally, Section VII.J states "An information sign shall be posted and maintained at the entrance(s) which lists the name and phone number of the operator." These signage requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities, which are defined as energy facilities "principally used to convert solar energy to electricity" and exclude smaller rooftop or less than or equal to 10 acres facilities, indicating applicability to utility-scale solar energy systems.

A decommissioning plan shall be required as part of the Major Special Use Permit application. This plan shall be prepared by a third party engineer and must be signed off by the party responsible for decommissioning and all landowners of property included in the project. The plan must address: agreements with landowners, responsible party identification, panel and material specifications, removal costs down to 36 inches below grade, and grading and re-seeding costs. The plan must be recorded in the Pasquotank County Registry of Deeds prior to building permit issuance and updated every 5 years or upon ownership change. The owner must provide a bond, cash escrow, or irrevocable letter of credit equal to 1.25 times the estimated decommissioning cost, with specific conditions for letters of credit. Solar farms have 12 months to complete decommissioning if no electricity is generated for 12 continuous months, excluding force majeure delays. The bond may be drawn if the responsible party fails to decommission as required.

All structures and security fencing shall meet the following setbacks: 150’ front property line setback; 50’ side and rear property line setback; 150’ setback from adjacent residential property lines or residential zoning districts; 100’ minimum setback from adjacent water bodies, wetlands, or any other additional setback required by the Army Corps of Engineers or CAMA; ½ mile setback from Highway 17, Future I-87 and Halstead Boulevard Extended. All exterior sides of the security fence shall be screened with a landscape buffer that meets one of the following criteria: 1) Existing on-site mature vegetation at a minimum height of ten (10) feet and depth of fifty (50) feet; 2) A single row of evergreens in combination with mature vegetation, installed at a height of five (5) feet achieving opaqueness and a minimum height of ten (10) feet in five years; 3) A double row of off-set evergreens absent existing mature vegetation, installed at a height of five (5) feet achieving opaqueness and a minimum height of ten (10) feet in five years; 4) A berm combined with evergreen vegetation installed at a height of five (5) feet achieving opaqueness and a minimum height of ten (10) feet in five years.

Solar collectors "shall be configured to avoid glare and heat transference to adjacent properties." Solar energy components "must be designed with anti-reflective coating(s)." These requirements apply to solar farms up to 1,500 acres. Additionally, solar farms must meet setbacks, height limits, and landscaping buffers as detailed in the ordinance. Landscape buffer options include: (1) existing on-site mature vegetation at a minimum height of ten (10) feet and depth of fifty (50) feet; (2) a single row of evergreens combined with mature vegetation installed at five (5) feet achieving opaqueness and ten (10) feet height in five years; (3) a double row of off-set evergreens installed at five (5) feet achieving opaqueness and ten (10) feet height in five years; or (4) a berm combined with evergreen vegetation installed at five (5) feet achieving opaqueness and ten (10) feet height in five years.

Section 9.03-26(c) states: 'Structures shall not exceed twenty-five (25) feet in height, as measured from grade at the base of the structure to its highest point.' This maximum height applies explicitly to Solar Farms up to 1,500 acres. No other height restrictions for Solar Farms are provided in the text.

No solar farm shall exceed a maximum of 1,500 acres. The size of a solar farm shall be calculated based on the parcel size(s) where the development is located. This is the explicit maximum lot, parcel, or tract size allowed for solar farms. The unit of measurement is acres, which is a standard area unit.

Solar farms shall observe a minimum separation of one mile from any other solar farm that has received a Use Permit approval. This separation shall be measured from the closest points of the property lines where solar farms are located and proposed.

Solar Energy Facilities shall only be permitted in areas zoned Rural Agriculture (RA). The ordinance states: 'Solar Energy Facilities shall only be permitted in areas zoned Rural Agriculture (RA).' Additionally, the ordinance requires that Solar Energy Facilities obtain a Zoning Permit and comply with other applicable laws. There is also a limitation that 'the percentage of land permitted for all Solar Energy Facilities be more than five (5) percent of the total land in Yadkin County.' No other districts are mentioned as permitting utility-scale solar energy systems as a primary use. By assumption, any solar overlay districts would also be considered primary use districts, though none are specified in the provided text.

Solar Energy Facilities shall only be permitted in areas zoned Rural Agriculture (RA). By implication, utility-scale solar energy systems are unconditionally prohibited in all other zoning districts besides Rural Agriculture (RA).

The fence which secures the SEFs improved areas shall be at least twenty-five (25) feet along all property lines not on a public roadway. summary: The fence which secures the SEFs improved areas shall be setback at least one hundred twenty five (125) feet from the center of all public roadways, with the exception of divided US Highways and Interstates where it shall be at least fifty (50) feet from the edge of the right of way. summary: Section V(3) Vegetative Buffer requires that "a vegetative buffer shall be installed in front of the fence within the required setback of the SEF for the entire perimeter of the SEF." The buffer "shall consist of a row of evergreen bushes, planted no more than eight (8) feet apart, which are at least six (6) feet tall at the time of planting, which will reach at maturity a minimum height of fifteen (15) feet within three (3) years of planting." The bushes "may be trimmed, but to no lower than a height of fifteen (15) feet," must "provide full screening from two (2) feet above ground level to the required fifteen (15) foot height," and "must grow to a minimum of eight (8) feet in width at the base, or the spacing between bushes must be reduced." The buffer "must be maintained, including keeping vegetation healthy, neat and orderly in appearance, and free of litter and debris." Existing adequate vegetative screening may be used with Planning Board approval. Additionally, Section V(2) requires fencing around the entire perimeter of the SEF, with specific height and material requirements, and Section V(9) states that "the height of solar panels shall not exceed the height of the required vegetative buffer."

SEFs must meet all requirements of the State of North Carolina and the Federal government, including but not limited to: Storm water Permit from the NC Dept. of Environmental Quality; Erosion and Sedimentation Control Permit from the NC Dept. of Environmental Quality. Soil with adequate vegetative cover must be maintained under and around the panels in order to reduce runoff and erosion. Native grasses and wildflowers are encouraged to be used as ground cover for the SEF.

Solar Energy Facilities shall only be permitted in areas zoned Rural Agriculture (RA). They must obtain a Zoning Permit from the Central Permitting Office prior to applying for Building Permits, in accordance with the procedures outlined in this Ordinance. The Ordinance applies to all areas of Yakin County except lands within municipalities unless requested otherwise. Additionally, the percentage of land permitted for all Solar Energy Facilities shall not exceed five (5) percent of the total land in Yadkin County.

SEFs shall be separated by a minimum distance of three hundred (300) feet from all residential, commercial, and institutional buildings, with the exception of accessory buildings such as storage sheds. Such minimum setbacks for a SEF shall be measured from the required fence of the facility. The fence which secures the SEFs improved areas shall be setback at least one hundred twenty five (125) feet from the center of all public roadways, with the exception of divided US Highways and Interstates where it shall be at least fifty (50) feet from the edge of the right of way. The fence shall be at least twenty-five (25) feet along all property lines not on a public roadway. Solar arrays and other equipment shall be setback at least twenty-five (25) feet from the interior fence line of the SEF. The property owner of an affected building may waive all or any portion of the separation requirements except the fence setbacks from roadways and property lines.

summary: The ordinance defines a Solar Energy Conversion Facility (Solar Farm) as generating 15kW direct current or more. It requires that fencing, gates, locks, and vegetative buffers "shall be maintained" even "notwithstanding the fact that the solar farm is no longer operational" and "until the solar farm is dismantled and removed from the parcel of land upon which it was constructed." Additionally, a reclamation bond is required for some allowed uses and many conditional use permits, including a bond for "one hundred fifty (150%) percent of a licensed engineer’s estimate of the cost to remove all above ground structures and all underground structures... re-grade the site so it has a predevelopment appearance, and re-seed the site with native grasses and vegetation." The bond must be presented before construction and may be waived if it duplicates a state-required bond. Other bonds include construction bonds and violation bonds with specific conditions.

summary: All solar farms shall be fenced around the exterior with a fence that shall be at least 6 feet in height and shall have at least three strands of barbed wire run above the six feet. The fencing shall be constructed to substantially lessen the likelihood of unauthorized entry to the solar farm. The fence shall be maintained in good order. Failure to maintain the fencing shall constitute a violation of this ordinance. The fence requirements shall continue notwithstanding the fact that the solar farm is no longer operational. The fencing requirement remains until the solar farm is dismantled and removed from the parcel of land upon which it was constructed. All gates in the fences of the solar farm shall be at least 6 feet in height with at least three strands of barbed wire run above the six feet. All gates shall be equipped with locks and shall remain locked at all times except for those times the owner, operator, or their agents are accessing the property and are present in the solar farm. The gates shall be constructed to substantially lessen the likelihood of unauthorized entry to the solar farm. The gates and locks shall be maintained in good order. Failure to maintain the gates shall constitute a violation of this ordinance. The gate requirements shall continue notwithstanding the fact that the solar farm is no longer operational. The requirement remains until the solar farm is dismantled and removed from the parcel of land upon which it was constructed.

All photovoltaic panels shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures, roadways or airfields. The applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation.

Every solar farm shall be setback at least 100 feet from all property lines of the parcel upon which the solar farm is located. All setbacks shall be measured from the exterior of the vegetative buffer. Other setback distances mentioned include 200 feet from the centerline of any public road and 100 feet from the high water mark of any lake and the stream banks of any navigable stream, but these do not pertain to property lines or parcels.

Every solar farm shall be setback at least 200 feet from the centerline of any public road. All setbacks shall be measured from the exterior of the vegetative buffer. Other setbacks include at least 100 feet from all property lines and 100 feet from the high water mark of any lake and the stream banks of any navigable stream.

Section 7.1.3(5) requires that "a continuous evergreen vegetative buffer shall be maintained at all times around the exterior perimeter of the fencing." The buffer "shall be composed of evergreen trees or shrubs which at planting shall be a minimum of 4 feet in height and which shall be maintained at maturity at a height of not less than six feet." The vegetative buffer "shall be carefully planted and maintained in good condition" and "failure to maintain the vegetative buffer shall constitute a violation of this ordinance." The buffer requirements "shall continue notwithstanding the fact that the solar farm is no longer operational" and remain "until the solar farm is dismantled and removed from the parcel of land upon which it was constructed." Other screening-related requirements include fencing at least 6 feet in height with three strands of barbed wire, gates with locks, and setbacks measured from the exterior of the vegetative buffer. These requirements apply to "solar farms" defined as facilities generating 15kW direct current or more. No other vegetative buffer or screening options or conditions are provided.

The ordinance lists 'Solar Energy Conversion Facilities' as a conditional use under section 5.1.3(22) in the Agricultural District, indicating that utility-scale solar energy systems require special approval or a permitting process in this district. No other districts or conditions were provided in the text. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this summary as per instructions.

Every solar farm shall be measured at least 100 feet from the high water mark of any lake and the stream banks of any navigable stream. All setbacks shall be measured from the exterior of the vegetative buffer. Other setbacks include 100 feet from all property lines and 200 feet from the centerline of any public road, but these do not pertain to lakes, reservoirs, streams, rivers, or wetlands.

The ordinance requires a Complete Decommissioning Plan as part of the Utility-Scale solar energy system application, which "must contain the following information that provides for the removal and reclamation of the facility or site(s) within 9 months": removal of all solar energy system components, foundations, underground electric wires to a depth of four feet, restoring the site to its original, pre-construction condition unless otherwise agreed in writing by the landowner, proper disposal of hazardous materials, and removal of access roads unless the landowner requests to keep them. Additionally, within nine (9) months of termination or abandonment, the permittees or current owners/operators must dismantle and remove all solar panels, support structures, cables, foundations, buildings, ancillary equipment, surface road materials (unless requested otherwise), and restore the site to substantially the same physical condition as before construction, including grading, topsoiling, and seeding. The applicant or current owner must provide "proof of financial surety for decommissioning" at 125% of estimated removal and restoration costs before construction can begin, with annual reviews and updates. If the State enacts decommissioning laws, the strictest requirements will prevail. Abandonment is defined as ceasing to produce energy for 12 months, triggering potential removal actions by the county using the financial surety. These requirements apply to Utility-Scale SES, defined as systems primarily for commercial sale, with manufacturer rating >20 kW, collector surface >1,000 sq ft, not accessory use, or occupying >2 acres.

summary: Any security or perimeter fence placed at a Utility-scale solar energy system will be constructed from metal chain-link material, will be a minimum of six (6) feet in height and not exceed eight (8) feet in height. Electric fencing will not be permitted.

For ground-mounted Utility-scale solar energy systems, the maximum height allowed is twenty (20) feet above ground. For building-mounted Utility-scale solar energy systems, the solar energy systems mounted on the roof will not project more than five (5) feet above the highest point of the roof and will not exceed the maximum building height limitation for the zoning jurisdiction. These height limits apply explicitly to Utility-Scale SES as defined in the ordinance.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'Minimum lot area for a Utility-scale solar energy system will be twenty (20) acres.' This is the minimum lot size requirement for Utility-Scale SES, which are defined as systems primarily used for commercial sale and distribution of electricity, having a manufacturer rating greater than 20 KW, exceeding 1,000 square feet of solar collector surface, not accessory uses, or occupying an area larger than 2 acres. The unit for this minimum lot size is acres.

No Utility-scale solar energy system shall exceed forty-five (45) dBA as measured at the property line. This is the explicit maximum noise level restriction for Utility-Scale SES. The unit dBA refers to A-weighted decibels, a standard measure of sound pressure level. This restriction is found under section 6.17.4, item 10, titled 'Sound Pressure Level'.

Utility-scale solar energy systems will be set back at least one hundred fifty (150) feet from the adjacent non-participating property line. Other setback options include 150 feet from all public roads, highway rights-of-way and section lines, and 500 feet from any building or structure.

Utility-scale solar energy systems will be set back at least one hundred fifty (150) feet from all public roads, highway rights-of-way and section lines. Setbacks will be measured from the road right-of-way.

The ordinance explicitly requires vegetative buffer and screening for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Under section 6.17.4.A.13 Landscaping, it mandates: 'Soils will be planted to, and maintained in, perennial vegetation using approved NRCS seeds to prevent erosion, manage runoff and build soil.' Dead or diseased vegetation must be removed and replanted until established, and established vegetation must be maintained or replanted if unable to be maintained. No land assets (topsoil, trees, lumber) may be removed without written landowner approval. Additionally, section 6.17.5 requires that 'ancillary solar equipment ... will be screened from public view ... to the maximum extent possible without compromising the effectiveness of the solar collectors.' Also, section 6.17.6.D.5 requires that applications include a 'Description of the screening to be provided for ground or building-mounted solar energy equipment.' These requirements apply specifically to Utility-Scale SES, defined as systems primarily used for commercial sale, greater than 20 KW, over 1,000 square feet of collector surface, not accessory, or occupying more than 2 acres.

Signs will comply with the requirements described In the Bowman County Zoning Ordinance (see Section 6.12). Further, Utility-scale solar energy system installations will not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the solar energy system. An information sign will be posted and maintained at the entrance(s), which lists the name and phone number of the operator. Warning Signage: Signs warning of the high voltage associated with the solar farm will be posted at every entrance to the facility and at the base of all pads mounted transformers and substations. A sign that provides emergency contact information, such as phone number, will be posted near the entrance and at any operations and/or maintenance buildings.

The ordinance explicitly requires that for Utility-scale solar energy systems, "Topsoil’s will not be removed during development, unless part of a remediation effort. Soils will be planted to, and maintained in, perennial vegetation using approved NRCS seeds to prevent erosion, manage runoff and build soil." A "Watershed Assessment must be completed and approved by the Bowman Slope Soil Conservation District, and paid for by the developer, prior to the start of construction." Additionally, "Each owner, operator, or maintainer of a solar energy system to which this Ordinance applies must regulate and control erosion and sediment runoff. If the topography of the site indicates this may be a problem, it is required that dikes be installed to control runoff. A plan for runoff, containment and reclamation, along with dike-engineered blueprints, if required, must be included with the Conditional Use Permit application." The application must also include a "Storm Water Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP): Watershed Assessment Plan for drainage disposal and erosion control approved by the Bowman/Slope Soil Conservation District Office, all costs of which will be incurred by the applicant." These requirements apply specifically to Utility-Scale SES, which are defined as systems primarily used for commercial sale, with manufacturer rating over 20 KW, surface area over 1,000 square feet, not accessory use, or occupying more than 2 acres.

All applications for Utility-scale solar energy systems will be required to submit both a Conditional Use Permit as well as an Alternate Energy Construction Permit and have them approved prior to the start of any construction. Utility-scale solar energy systems will be located outside of city limits and the Extra-Territorial Area (ETA), which extends from organized cities located in Bowman County, out to one (1) mile. No specific district names or abbreviations are provided for where these systems are permitted as a special use or similar.

Utility-scale solar energy systems will be set back at least five hundred (500) feet from any building or structure. This applies to non-participating occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, and/or residences. Other setback requirements include 150 feet from public roads and adjacent non-participating property lines, but these do not pertain to buildings or structures.

In the Agricultural District, 'Solar Energy Conversion Facility' is listed under Conditional Uses, which require an application for a conditional use permit, a hearing before the Planning and Zoning Commission, and approval by the Divide County Board of County Commissioners. The text states: 'Conditional Uses – The following uses require an application for a conditional use permit, a hearing before the Planning and Zoning Commission, and approval by the Divide County Board of County Commissioners. 47) Solar Energy Conversion Facility.' Prohibited uses include all uses not specifically listed as permitted or conditional. No other districts or overlay districts are mentioned for accessory or secondary use of utility-scale solar energy systems.

All solar farms shall be fenced around the exterior with a fence that shall be at least 6 feet in height and shall have at least three strands of barbed wire run above the six feet. The fencing shall be constructed to substantially lessen the likelihood of unauthorized entry to the solar farm. The fence shall be maintained in good order. Failure to maintain the fencing shall constitute a violation of this ordinance. The fence requirements shall continue notwithstanding the fact that the solar farm is no longer operational. The fencing requirement remains until the solar farm is dismantled and removed from the parcel of land upon which it was constructed. Gates in the fences of the solar farm shall be at least 6 feet in height with at least three strands of barbed wire run above the six feet, equipped with locks, and remain locked at all times except when accessed by the owner, operator, or their agents. Gates and locks must be maintained in good order, with failure to maintain constituting a violation. These requirements continue until the solar farm is dismantled and removed.

Section 7.13.3(f)(i) states: 'All photovoltaic panels shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures, roadways or airfields. The applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation.' This glare restriction applies to Solar Energy Conversion Facilities (Solar Farms) generating 15 kW direct current or more. Other regulations for solar farms include fencing, gates and locks, setbacks, noxious weed control, vegetative buffers, and light and heat trespass, but only the light and heat trespass subsection explicitly addresses glare. The ordinance defines a solar farm as a facility generating 15 kW DC or more and distinguishes it from smaller solar collectors for individual residential, agricultural, or commercial buildings.

Every solar farm shall be setback at least 100 feet from all property lines of the parcel upon which the solar farm is located. All setbacks shall be measured from the exterior of the fencing and gates. Other setback distances mentioned relate to roads and water bodies but do not pertain to non-participating property lines.
