summary: Section 7.13.3(e) requires that "A continuous evergreen vegetative buffer shall be maintained at all times around the exterior perimeter of the fencing." The buffer "shall be composed of evergreen trees or shrubs which at planting shall be a minimum of 4 feet in height and which shall be maintained at maturity at a height of not less than six feet." The vegetative buffer "shall be carefully planted and maintained in good condition. Failure to maintain the vegetative buffer shall constitute a violation of this ordinance." This requirement "shall continue notwithstanding the fact that the solar farm is no longer operational" until the solar farm is dismantled and removed. Other related requirements for solar farms include fencing at least 6 feet in height with barbed wire, locked gates, setbacks from property lines and roads, and noxious weed control, but these do not pertain to vegetative buffer or screening.

In the Agricultural District, a 'Solar Energy Conversion Facility' is listed under 'Conditional Uses' which 'require an application for a conditional use permit, a hearing before the Planning and Zoning Commission, and approval by the Divide County Board of County Commissioners.' All other uses not specifically listed as permitted or conditional are prohibited.

Every solar farm shall be setback at least 100 feet from the high water mark of any lake and the stream banks of any navigable stream. Other setbacks include 100 feet from all property lines, 165 feet from the centerline of any township road, 200 feet from any county road, and 250 feet from any state or federal highway, but these do not pertain to lakes, reservoirs, streams, rivers, or wetlands.

Section 4-18-5 Site Decommissioning and Restoration requires that "Within one (1) year of termination or abandonment of leases or Easements for a Solar Energy System in McKenzie County, the permittee shall, at its expense, fully remove all Solar Energy System structures and components from the site. This includes all associated above ground and below ground infrastructure., which must be placed in a landfill approved for disposal of such materials. Any Easements of record must be released." Additionally, "Areas disturbed by the construction or decommissioning of a Solar Energy System shall be restored to their original condition and shall be graded, top-soiled, and reseeded according to Natural Resource Conservation (NRCS) recommendations or similar best practices, unless the landowner requests in writing that access roads or other Development be retained."

Section 4-18-3(F)(2) requires "a minimum 6-foot security fence shall enclose all electrical and mechanical components of the Solar Energy System." The fence must be maintained by the owner/operator, and lock boxes and keys must be stored at locked entrances for emergency personnel access. This fencing requirement applies to Solar Energy Systems regulated under Section 4-18, which governs larger, commercial-scale ground-mounted systems. Other related provisions include public safety plans, firebreaks, and signage requirements. Section 4-17 addresses Accessory Solar Energy Systems, including small ground-mounted systems, but does not include fencing requirements.

Section 4-18-3(A) states: 'A ground-mounted Solar Energy System shall not extend more than 20 feet above grade when solar arrays are oriented at maximum tilt.' This applies to commercial-scale or larger solar energy systems. For smaller, accessory ground-mounted systems, Section 4-17-4(A) limits height to 15 feet, but this applies only to small accessory systems. The units for the height restriction are feet.

Table 4-5. Solar Facility Setback Standards specifies a setback distance of 500 feet from Property Lines (Non-Participating) for Solar Energy Systems. The text states: 'Property Lines (Non-Participating) 2 500 feet' with a footnote that setbacks from property lines for non-participating properties may be reduced with written permission from the affected landowner. Other setback distances listed include 50 feet for Occupied Buildings (Participating), 1,000 feet for Occupied Buildings (Non-Participating), 250 feet for Federal, State, and County Roads, 150 feet for Township Roads, and 133 feet for Section Lines, but these do not pertain to property lines or parcels. Section 4-18-3(C) clarifies that setbacks are measured as the horizontal distance between the nearest solar array or other structural component integral to Solar Energy System operation and the roadway centerline, but the 500 feet applies specifically to non-participating property lines.
section: Sec. 4-18 Solar Energy System, 4-18-3 Development Standards, Table 4-5. Solar Facility Setback Standards

summary: Setbacks shall be measured as the horizontal distance between the nearest solar array or other structural component integral to Solar Energy System operation and the roadway centerline. All Setbacks may be reduced by up to 50 percent if solar arrays are fully screened from the Setback point of measurement, so long as Development satisfies the Agricultural District (AG) Setback requirements and McKenzie County’s general roadway Setback standards. Table 4-5 specifies setbacks from roads as follows: Federal, State, and County Roads - 250 feet; Township Roads - 150 feet; Section Lines - 133 feet. The 250 feet setback from Federal, State, and County roads is the most restrictive value.

Section 4-18-2(G) requires applicants to prepare a visual impact assessment for the proposed Solar Energy System and states that "the Board of County Commissioners may require vegetative screening or buffering in accordance with Section 2-12 of this Ordinance" to mitigate visual impacts. Section 4-18-3(E)(3) mandates that "Grassland/grazing vegetation shall be installed and maintained for the duration of use," with a seeding and maintenance plan submitted prior to issuance of the building permit. These requirements apply to Solar Energy Systems generally, including ground-mounted systems intended for offsite electricity generation or sale. Other related provisions include minimizing tree removal and replacing removed trees on a 1:1 ratio within one year, and maintaining a clear firebreak area around the site perimeter. No other explicit vegetative buffer or screening options or conditions are detailed in the provided text.

Signs identifying the Solar Energy System owner, operator, and emergency contact information shall be affixed at all entrances to the facility. Warning signs, including contact information, shall be displayed at intervals of 500 feet along the perimeter of the facility. This applies to Solar Energy Systems as described in Section 4-18, which includes ground-mounted systems with specified height, setback, and public safety standards.

Section 4-18 requires that "Grassland/grazing vegetation shall be installed and maintained for the duration of use" with a "seeding plan and maintenance plan shall be submitted prior to issuance of the building permit." The owner/operator must allow the McKenzie County Soil Conservation District to conduct site visits to verify that ground cover is properly maintained. Additionally, "Areas disturbed by the construction or decommissioning of a Solar Energy System shall be restored to their original condition and shall be graded, top-soiled, and reseeded according to Natural Resource Conservation (NRCS) recommendations or similar best practices." These requirements apply to ground-mounted Solar Energy Systems regulated under Section 4-18, which are commercial-scale systems. Other related provisions include construction and maintenance standards for roads and power lines, but these do not explicitly address soil, erosion, or sediment control. Section 4-17 addresses Accessory Solar Energy Systems, including small ground-mounted systems, but does not include explicit soil, erosion, or sediment control requirements.

Table 4-5. Solar Facility Setback Standards specifies a setback distance of 1,000 feet from Occupied Buildings (Non-Participating). The footnote clarifies that setbacks from occupied buildings for non-participating properties may be reduced with written permission from the affected landowner. Other setback options include 50 feet for Occupied Buildings (Participating) and various distances for property lines and roads, but these do not apply to non-participating occupied buildings.

Table 4-5 specifies a setback distance of 50 feet from occupied buildings (participating) for Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems. Other options include 1,000 feet for occupied buildings (non-participating), which may be reduced with written permission from the affected landowner. The setback is a fixed distance and does not vary by structure height.

Applicants shall prepare a visual impact assessment for the proposed SES. The visual impact assessment must analyze the potential visual impacts of solar panels and fencing from non-participating properties. To mitigate visual impacts, the Board of County Commissioners may require vegetative screening or buffering in accordance with Section 2-12 of this Ordinance.

Turbine setback from an unimproved section line or other public right of way is two hundred (200) feet, and one and one half (1.5) times the height of the turbine plus seventy-five (75) feet from state, county, or township maintained roadways, unless another setback applies or a site specific variance is granted.
section: 6.5.11 WIND and SOLAR ENERGY FACILITIES GENERAL PROVISIONS

summary: Turbine(s) and any electrical power transmission lines from NDPSC permitted wind or solar facility, turbines, whether they are within the county or intrastate, and whether they were installed for existing energy sources, or new or upgraded energy sources, shall be setback at least one (1) mile beyond the ordinary high water mark of the Missouri River, Lake Sakakawea, and Lake Audubon. However, this setback does not apply to power lines that must cross one of these water bodies.
section: 6.5.11 WIND and SOLAR ENERGY FACILITIES GENERAL PROVISIONS

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Prior to operation, the Permittee must file "the estimated decommissioning cost, in current dollars at the time of filing, for the proposed facility and a comprehensive decommissioning plan" (14a). The Decommissioning Plan must comply with NDCC 49-02-27 and NDAC 69-09-09 and include provisions for removal of "all Solar Energy System components, aboveground improvements, and outside storage," removal of "foundations, pads and underground electric wires removed to a depth of four feet," restoring the site to its "original, pre-construction, condition, unless authorized in writing by the Board of Commissioners," proper disposal of hazardous materials, removal of access roads unless the landowner requests otherwise, and conditions for on-site buildings (14b). Bonding requirements include submission of a bond upon Conditional Use Permit approval and prior to construction, and within one year of termination or abandonment, the Permittee must dismantle and remove all solar panels, cables, foundations, roads, and restore the site to substantially the same physical condition as before construction, unless prior written arrangement with the landowner exists (14c). The surety must be "one hundred twenty-five (125) percent of the estimated removal and restoration costs less the salvage value of the equipment" and must be maintained annually or upon ownership transfer (4b.iv-v, 4b.vi). These requirements apply to Utility-Scale SES defined as systems "primarily used for generating electricity for commercial sale and distribution on the electrical grid" or with a "manufacturer’s rating of greater than 20 Kilowatts (KW)" (2ff).

Any security or perimeter fence placed at a Utility-scale Solar Energy System will be constructed from metal chain-link material, will be a minimum of six (6) feet in height and not exceed eight (8) feet in height. All fencing is to be maintained by the Permittee. Electric fencing will not be permitted.

The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems (SES) under section 7(b)(ii): "The Permittee shall make every reasonable effort, including landscape design, to minimize the effects of Glare and or reflective light on any neighboring occupied dwelling or roadways. Upon receipt of a verified complaint, the Land Use Administrator may request a glare and reflection study be prepared at the expense of the Permittee by a registered professional engineer... If it is determined that glare or reflective light exists the Permittee shall implement and maintain all necessary remedial measures." This applies specifically to Utility-Scale SES as indicated by the section heading "STANDARDS FOR UTILITY-SCALE SES." Other related standards in this section include height limits, electrical interconnections, fencing, lighting, sound pressure levels, road repairs, and signage requirements.

Utility-scale ground-mounted Solar Energy Systems will have a maximum height of twenty (20) feet above ground. This is explicitly stated in section 7) STANDARDS FOR UTILITY-SCALE SES, subsection b) Design, item (iii). For building-mounted utility-scale systems, the height shall not project more than five (5) feet above the highest point of the roof and shall not exceed the maximum building height limitation for the zoning jurisdiction. The units for the maximum height are feet.

Section 7(b)(ix) states: 'No Utility-scale Solar Energy System shall exceed sixty-five (65) dBA as measured at the property line.' This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for Utility-Scale SES. The unit dBA refers to A-weighted decibels, a standard unit for measuring noise levels.

Utility-scale Solar Energy Systems will be set back at least two hundred fifty (250) feet from the adjacent non-participating property line. Permittee may build within the Adjacent Non-Participating Property Lines setback if written consent is obtained from the owner of the adjacent non-participating property. Other setbacks mentioned include 250 feet from the center line of any public roadway, highway, or railroad right-of-way; 50 feet from any unoccupied building or structure; 2,500 feet from occupied dwellings or commercial buildings; and 5,280 feet from shooting ranges, but these do not pertain to non-participating property lines.

All SES structure including fencing shall be two hundred fifty (250) feet from the center line of any public roadway, highway (whether improved or not), or railroad right-of-way. Other setbacks include: 250 feet from adjacent non-participating property lines, 2,500 feet from occupied dwellings or commercial buildings, 50 feet from unoccupied buildings, and 5,280 feet from shooting ranges. These apply to Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance.

All SES structure including fencing shall be two hundred fifty (250) feet from the center line of any public roadway, highway (whether improved or not), or railroad right-of-way. Other setbacks include 100 feet from above ground communication and electrical line easements, 250 feet from adjacent non-participating property lines (with possible waiver), 2,500 feet from occupied dwellings or commercial buildings (unless negotiated), 50 feet from unoccupied buildings (unless negotiated), and 5,280 feet from shooting ranges. The 250 feet setback from roads applies to Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems as indicated by the context and fee sections referring to utility scale systems.

Utility-scale Solar Energy System installations will not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the Solar Energy System. Signs warning of the high voltage associated with Solar Energy System will be posted at every entrance to the facility and at the base of all pad mounted transformers and substations. A sign providing emergency contact information, such as phone number, will be posted near the entrance and at any operations and/or maintenance buildings. Signs shall be current and maintained by the operator of the solar energy facility.

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems. It requires that "topsoil will not be removed during development, unless part of a remediation effort," and that "soils will be planted to, and maintained in, perennial vegetation using approved NRCS seeds to prevent erosion, manage runoff and build soils." Dead or diseased vegetation "will be removed and must be replanted at the next appropriate planting time until such time that it is considered established." Additionally, "Each owner, operator, or maintainer of a Solar Energy System to which this Ordinance applies must regulate and control erosion and sediment runoff." If topography indicates potential problems, "Dikes be installed to control runoff," with a plan and engineered blueprints included in the Conditional Use Permit application, and dikes must meet state requirements. A "Drainage Disposal Plan" and "Watershed Assessment Plan for drainage disposal and erosion control approved by the Mercer County Soil Conservation District" must be completed and paid for by the Permittee prior to construction. Upon decommissioning, "Areas disturbed by the construction of the Solar Energy System and decommissioning activities must be graded, top soiled and seeded according to the Natural Resources Conservation Services Technical Guide recommendations and other agency recommendation," with an established stand required within three years or re-seeding by the Permittee. These requirements apply to Utility-Scale SES as defined (e.g., systems primarily for commercial sale or rated above 20 kW).

Utility-scale Solar Energy Systems must be set back a horizontal distance of not less than two thousand five hundred (2,500) feet from any occupied dwelling, commercial building or publicly used structure or facility, unless otherwise negotiated with the landowner of the structure. Other setbacks include 250 feet from adjacent non-participating property lines (with possible written consent to build within setback), and 50 feet from any unoccupied building or structure unless otherwise negotiated.

All SES structures including fencing shall be located one hundred (100) feet from the centerline of any above ground communication and / or electrical line easement rights-of-way on the project site. Additionally, a general setback of two hundred fifty (250) feet from utilities is mentioned, but the 100 feet setback from above ground electrical line easements is the most specific and directly applicable to overhead electrical lines.

A solar farm shall be decommissioned in the event it is not in use for 12 consecutive months. Structures and foundations shall be disposed in compliance with state law. The application shall include provisions for removal of all structures and foundations and restoration of soil and vegetative resources. Provide a letter of credit as stipulated in Section 6.12. The letter of credit shall be in place to ensure site restoration. The letter of credit shall be the sum equal to the total cost of reclamation as estimated by a North Dakota licensed engineer. The estimate provided by a North Dakota licensed engineer shall be verified by the Board of County Commissioners or designee.

Section 5.7.4 Development and Operating Standards, subsection G states: 'Perimeter fencing shall conform with the fencing requirements of Section 4.3 of this Code.' This fencing requirement explicitly applies to Solar Energy Facilities, Utility-scale (Solar Farm) as defined in the ordinance. No other fencing options or conditions are provided in the text.

Section 5.7.4 Development and Operating Standards, subsection C.4 states: 'All solar energy systems using a reflector shall minimize glare affecting adjacent or nearby properties.' This glare restriction applies to utility-scale solar farms as defined: 'A utility-scale, ground-mounted solar energy system that produces and distributes electricity for wholesale' with a minimum project size of five (5) acres and is the principal use on the parcel(s). Other development and operating standards include height limits (not to exceed fifteen (15) feet), setbacks from roads and dwellings, screening requirements, ground cover, foundation certification, power line burial, and fencing, but these do not pertain to glare. The glare restriction is the only explicit glare-related requirement for utility-scale solar energy facilities in the text.

Section 5.7.4 Development and Operating Standards, subsection A. Height states: 'Ground-mounted solar energy systems shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt.' This maximum height applies explicitly to utility-scale solar farms as defined in the ordinance.

A large-scale solar energy system has a minimum project size of five (5) acres and is the principal use on the parcel(s) on which it is located. This applies specifically to Solar Energy Facilities, Utility-scale (Solar Farm) that produce and distribute electricity for wholesale.

Utility-scale solar energy facilities (solar farms) are permitted as a conditional use only in the Agriculture (Ag) and Industrial (In) districts, as stated: 'Solar farms are permitted as a conditional use in the Agriculture (Ag) District and the Industrial (In) District.' The Table 3.1 shows 'c' (conditional use) for utility-scale solar energy facilities in Ag and In districts, and no designation (implying prohibition) in Residential (Res), Rural Residential (R-Res), Commercial (Co), and Recreation (Rec) districts. Small solar energy facilities are permitted in all districts, but utility-scale systems are not allowed outside Ag and In districts.

Setbacks from state Highways and County Roads: 250 feet from roadway centerline. Setbacks from Other Roads: 150 feet from roadway centerline. These setback distances apply specifically to solar farms, which are defined as utility-scale solar energy systems producing and distributing electricity for wholesale, with a minimum project size of five acres and being the principal use on the parcel(s).

All solar farms shall be fully screened from existing dwellings. Screening shall not be required along property lines within the same zoning district, except where the adjoining lot contains an existing dwelling. Mountrail County may require perimeter screening if it determines that there is a clear community interest in maintaining a viewshed.

Section 5.7.4.D Ground Cover requires that "appropriate ground cover shall be installed to mitigate stormwater impacts and facilitate site restoration following decommission of the use. Grassland/grazing vegetation is required ground cover." Additionally, Section 5.7.6.B.6 requires the project narrative to include "all grading, drainage, and erosion control measures that are planned for the site." These provisions explicitly address soil, erosion, and sediment control for utility-scale solar energy facilities (solar farms).

Solar Energy Facility, Utility-scale (Solar Farm) is defined as a utility-scale, ground-mounted solar energy system that produces and distributes electricity for wholesale, with a minimum project size of five (5) acres and is the principal use on the parcel(s). According to Table 3.1 and sections 3.5.2 and 3.9.2, it is a conditional use in the Agriculture (Ag) and Industrial (In) Districts. Section 5.7.2 states: 'Solar farms are permitted as a conditional use in the Agriculture (Ag) District and the Industrial (In) District where such systems present few land use conflicts with current and future land use patterns.' Other districts such as Residential, Rural Residential, Commercial, and Recreation do not list utility-scale solar facilities as permitted or conditional uses. Small solar energy facilities are permitted uses in multiple districts but are excluded from this summary as they are not utility-scale.

Setbacks from Existing Dwellings: 150 feet. Other setback options include 250 feet from state Highways and County Roads, 150 feet from other roads, and minimum yard setbacks compliant with district setback requirements. This applies to Solar Energy Facilities, Utility-scale (Solar Farm) as defined: a utility-scale, ground-mounted solar energy system that produces and distributes electricity for wholesale with a minimum project size of five (5) acres and is the principal use on the parcel(s).

Solar facility owners in North Dakota must submit a decommissioning plan with proof of financial assurance before receiving a certificate of operation, and they are responsible for all decommissioning costs. The plan must detail dismantling procedures, site restoration, anticipated impacts on natural resources, and cost estimates, with updates required every five years and financial assurance provided for both new and existing facilities.

Commercial solar energy systems (Solar Energy Projects) require a decommissioning plan submitted with the conditional use permit application to ensure proper removal after their useful life (6.9.4.1). Decommissioning must occur if the project does not produce power for twelve (12) consecutive months, with an option for the owner to petition for an extension upon showing reasonable circumstances (6.9.4.2). The plan must include removal of all structures and foundations to a depth of 48 inches, restoration of soil and vegetation, and assurances of financial resources for full decommissioning (6.9.4.3). The Township may require financial surety such as a bond, letter of credit, or parent guarantee to ensure proper decommissioning (6.9.4.4). If the responsible party fails to decommission, the Township may take necessary action, including forfeiture of performance bonds or assessing costs against the land, and has rights of ingress and egress to complete decommissioning and restore the property (6.9.5.1).

Solar Energy Projects shall be enclosed by security fencing not less than 6 feet in height (6.9.8.a). Commercial solar energy systems shall be screened from adjacent residential uses by landscaping or fencing as determined by the Zoning Commission (6.9.4.e). Additionally, for commercial uses of solar panels, a fence must be erected that completely surrounds the solar panels, must be at least ten (10) feet tall, and must be two hundred (200) feet from the center of township road, two hundred (200) feet from adjacent properties (not part of the Project), and two hundred fifty (250) feet from state and federal right-of-way/easements (6.9.3.2 and 6.9.3.3).
section: 6.9 Solar Energy Systems and 6.9 Solar Energy Project

summary: Section 6.9.7 Height states: 'Ground mounted solar energy systems shall not exceed 20 feet in height as measured from the natural grade at the base of the system to its highest point.' This applies to commercial solar energy projects as defined in the ordinance. No other maximum height values more restrictive than 20 feet are provided for commercial solar energy systems. The unit of measurement is feet.

Solar Energy Projects shall be set back a minimum of 100 feet from all property lines. Additionally, the surrounding fence for commercial solar panels must be at least 200 feet from adjacent properties (not part of the Project).

The surrounding fence must be two hundred (200) feet from the center of township road for commercial solar panel projects. Additionally, Solar Energy Projects shall be set back a minimum of 100 feet from all public road rights-of-way. The 200 feet fence setback is more restrictive. Other related setbacks include 100 feet from property lines and 250 feet from state and federal right-of-way/easements.

Commercial solar energy systems shall be screened from adjacent residential uses by landscaping or fencing as determined by the Zoning Commission (6.9.4.e). Solar Energy Projects shall be enclosed by security fencing not less than 6 feet in height (6.9.8.a). A vegetative buffer or other screening may be required by the Township to minimize visual impacts (6.9.8.b). Additionally, for commercial solar panel projects, a fence must be erected that completely surrounds the solar panels and be at least ten (10) feet tall, with the fence set back two hundred (200) feet from the center of township roads, two hundred (200) feet from adjacent properties not part of the project, and two hundred fifty (250) feet from state and federal right-of-way/easements (6.9.3.2 and 6.9.3.3).
section: 6.9 Solar Energy Systems / Solar Energy Projects

summary: Section 6.9.10 Signage states: 'No advertising or promotional signage is allowed on Solar Energy Projects except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator, emergency contact information, and appropriate warning signs.' This applies to Solar Energy Projects defined as commercial facilities for wholesale electricity sales. Other related provisions include fencing and screening (6.9.8), lighting (6.9.9), and decommissioning (6.9.11), but these do not address signage. The ordinance distinguishes between non-commercial and commercial solar energy systems, with commercial systems requiring conditional use permits and specific operational standards.

In the A-1 Agricultural District, a Solar Energy Project is a conditionally permitted use (5.1.3.16) subject to provisions of Section 6.9. For commercial solar energy projects, a conditional use permit must be obtained (6.9.3.1). Additional requirements include erecting a fence at least ten (10) feet tall surrounding the panels (6.9.3.2), setback distances from roads and properties (6.9.3.3), grass planting and inspection prior to installation (6.9.3.4), weed control (6.9.3.5), a minimum distance of one-half mile from any primary residential structure unless waived (6.9.3.6), burying all power lines (6.9.3.7), and ensuring installation does not impede drainage (6.9.3.8). No other districts or overlay districts were mentioned for commercial solar energy projects as special or conditional uses.
section: 5.1.3.16 Solar Energy Project Subject to Provisions of Section 6.9

summary: Panels cannot be constructed closer than one-half mile (1/2 mile) from any primary residential structure. Such residential setback distance may be waived with written consent of impacted property owners. Other setback distances mentioned include 100 feet from property lines and 200 feet from adjacent properties for fencing, but these do not specifically pertain to occupied dwellings or residences.

The surrounding fence must be ... two hundred fifty (250) feet from state and federal right-of-way/easements. (6.9.3.3) These easements typically include utility easements and transmission lines. Additionally, all power lines servicing the Project must be buried and cannot be exposed. (6.9.3.7) Other setback distances mentioned include 200 feet from township roads and adjacent properties, but these do not pertain to overhead electrical transmission lines or utility easements.

All solar panel or photovoltaic systems 25 kW or more shall not be installed or constructed without a Conditional Use Permit and a Zoning Permit. "Decommissioning: All systems when they are no longer generating power and will no longer be used shall follow a decommissioning plan that has been agreed to upon by Adams County, the electric utility, and the owner/developer." The decommissioning plan "shall include provisions for removal of all structures and foundations, restoration of soil and vegetation and a plan ensuring financial resources will be available to fully decommission the site." Adams County "reserves the right to require the posting of a bond, letter of credit or the establishment of an escrow account to ensure proper decommissioning." Systems less than 25 kW require only a Zoning Permit. Concentrated Solar Power systems are prohibited.

A Decommissioning Plan for installed facilities and infrastructure must be submitted to the Planning Commission at the time of permit application. The plan must include: (a) the manner in which the facility will be decommissioned; (b) a decommissioning schedule; (c) a detailed estimate of the cost of decommissioning a solar generation facility by a professional engineer licensed in the state of Nebraska that shall at a minimum include dismantling and removal of all towers, turbine generators, transformers, overhead cables and debris; removal of underground cables to a depth forty eight (48) inches; removal of foundations, buildings, and ancillary equipment to a minimum depth of forty-eight (48) inches below grade; site restoration and reclamation to the approximate original topography; repairs and reconstruction from damage to public roads, culverts and natural drainage ways; removal, clearing, and grading of all access roads unless otherwise agreed; the current salvageable value of the facility; and all expenses related to decommissioning shall be the responsibility of the solar generation facility owner. A decommissioning performance surety bond is required for all approved special use permits granted for the installation of Commercial Solar Farms / Facilities. The bond must be transferable upon sale of the facilities and may not be refunded until decommissioning has been satisfactorily completed or transferred to the Brown County Planning Commission. The Commission determines the bond amount based on estimated costs submitted by the owner and other factors, and reviews the bond amount every 5 years. Penalties apply for failure to submit the bond. Surety bonds and certificates of deposit have specific requirements and conditions. The Commission may forfeit bonds to complete decommissioning if necessary, and owners remain liable for costs exceeding bond amounts.
The height of the solar collector and any mounts within an established solar farm shall not exceed thirty (30) feet when oriented at maximum tilt.

Solar farms shall require a minimum setback of fifty (50) feet from all adjacent property lines. (Section 6.63(2)) This setback applies to Solar Farms as defined in the ordinance (utility-scale solar energy conversion systems intended for the sale of electricity). No other setback distances from lot lines, facility perimeters, parcels, or subdivisions are specified.

A Decommissioning Plan for installed facilities and infrastructure must be submitted to the Planning Commission at the time of permit application. The plan must include site restoration and reclamation to the approximate original topography that existed prior to the construction of the facility with grading, topsoil re-spread over the disturbed areas at a depth similar to that in existence prior to the disturbance, and reseeding to achieve the same utility of native vegetation of the surrounding area to prevent adverse hydrological effects, unless the Commission approves a signed request by the applicable landowner identifying surface features to remain. This explicitly addresses soil and erosion control requirements for Solar Farms. Other requirements include dismantling and removal of equipment, removal of underground cables and foundations to a minimum depth of forty-eight (48) inches below grade, repairs to public roads and drainage ways, removal or retention of access roads based on agreement, and financial responsibility for all decommissioning expenses by the solar generation facility owner.

Solar Farms shall be permitted in the  "AG"  Agriculture District as a Special Permitted use. Solar energy conversion systems of up to 100 kW, excluding solar farms, shall be permitted in all zoning districts. Solar energy conversion systems above 100 kW, excluding solar farms, may be allowable as a Special Permitted use.

A Decommissioning Plan for installed facilities and infrastructure must be submitted to the Planning Commission at the time of permit application. The plan must include: the manner in which the facility will be decommissioned; a decommissioning schedule; a detailed estimate of the cost of decommissioning a solar generation facility by a professional engineer licensed in Nebraska, including dismantling and removal of equipment, removal of underground cables to 48 inches, removal of foundations to 120 inches below grade, site restoration and reclamation to approximate original topography with grading, topsoil, reseeding, repairs to public roads and drainage, removal or retention of access roads per agreement, salvageable value of the facility, and all expenses related to decommissioning. Copy of as-built plans certified by a professional engineer must be included. The Commission or Board of Supervisors may reject a plan if it does not provide for decommissioning as defined or adequately describe costs. A decommissioning performance surety bond is required for all approved conditional use permits for Commercial Solar Farms/Facilities, must be transferable upon sale, and may not be refunded until decommissioning is satisfactorily completed or transferred to Burt County. The bond amount is based on estimated costs to the Commission/Board to perform decommissioning, including costs from public contracting requirements, management after abandonment, and salvage value. The bond must be submitted within specified deadlines, with penalties for late submission. Bond amounts are reviewed every five years and may be adjusted. Surety bonds have specific requirements including limits on amounts, registration, and cancellation notices. Upon abandonment concurrent with bond cancellation, the bond is forfeited and the site decommissioned. The Board of Supervisors or Commission may forfeit bonds and recover costs exceeding bond amounts. Appeals follow established Burt County Zoning Regulations procedures. These requirements apply explicitly to utility-scale solar energy conversion systems or 'solar facilities' intended for sale of electricity to utilities, industries, and/or businesses.

Solar panel placement should be prioritized to minimize or negate any glare onto nearby properties or roadways, without unduly impacting the functionality or efficiency of the solar energy conversion system. Electric solar energy system components must have a UL listing and must be designed with anti-reflective coating(s). These requirements apply to both personal scale solar energy conversion systems and Solar Facilities (Solar Farms), which are utility-scale systems intended for the sale of electricity to utilities, industries, and/or businesses.

The height of the solar collector and any mounts within an established solar farm shall not exceed twenty (25) feet when oriented at maximum tilt. This is explicitly stated in Section 6.15, part C.1) of the Burt County Zoning Regulations. Other height limits mentioned apply only to smaller or personal scale solar energy conversion systems (e.g., 15 feet for non-solar farm systems). The unit for this maximum height is feet.

The ordinance states: 'Solar energy conversion systems, excluding solar facilities, shall be permitted in all zoning districts as a permitted use.' It distinguishes utility-scale solar energy conversion systems, or 'solar facilities', intended for the sale of electricity to utilities, industries, and/or businesses, but does not specify any districts where these are prohibited or banned unconditionally.

Setbacks for Solar Panels must be 83’ from the property line or 200’ from the exterior wall of a non-participating residence, whichever is greater. The non-participating would be able to sign a waiver to reduce the setbacks.

The ordinance explicitly addresses repowering in Section I. Bond Deadline, subsection 4), stating: "If a solar generation facility is repurposed, as determined by the Commission (or Board of Supervisors) in consultation with the owner, any existing bond must be maintained, or a new bond acquired and submitted." This is a specific regulatory requirement tied to repowering of solar generation facilities (solar farms). Other options or conditions include: submission of a bond payable to Burt County conditioned on faithful decommissioning (Section I. Bond Deadline, subsections 1-3), penalties for failure to submit bond (Section J), and adjustment of bond amount every five years (Section K). The ordinance also includes detailed decommissioning plan requirements, decommissioning bond requirements, and surety bond conditions, but these do not specifically address repowering.

The ordinance requires a Decommissioning Plan for Solar Facilities (Solar Farms) that must include: "Site restoration and reclamation to the approximate original topography that existed prior to the construction of the facility with grading, topsoil, re-spread over the disturbed areas at a depth similar to that in existence prior to the disturbance, and reseeding that achieves the same utility of native vegetation of the surrounding areas to prevent adverse hydrological effects, unless the Commission/Board of Supervisors approves a signed request by the applicable landowner, identifying the surface features the land owner prefers to remain in place and a valid reason the landowner prefers those features to remain." The plan must also include removal of underground cables, foundations, buildings, and ancillary equipment to specified depths, and repairs to damage to public roads, culverts, and natural drainage ways. A decommissioning performance surety bond is required to ensure these reclamation activities. The bond amount is based on estimated costs to the Commission/Board of Supervisors to perform decommissioning and reclamation work, including site restoration. Failure to submit the bond may result in penalties and forfeiture. These requirements explicitly address soil disturbance, erosion control, and sediment management for commercial-scale Solar Facilities. No other explicit soil, erosion, or sediment control requirements are detailed.

Setbacks for Solar Panels must be 83’ from the property line or 200’ from the exterior wall of a non-participating residence, whichever is greater. The non-participating would be able to sign a waiver to reduce the setbacks.
section: Section 6.15 Solar Energy Conversion Systems, Exhibit B, C. Solar Facilities (Solar Farm), 3) Installation and Design, d.

summary: Each application shall have a decommissioning plan (removal of equipment/improvements and restoration of lands) that is reviewed and approved by the County prior to beginning operations. The decommissioning plan shall provide the following: 1) A plan outlining the means, procedure, and costs of removing the Large Solar Farm, including, but not limited to, the solar panels and collectors, electrical wiring/cabling, fencing, and any related supporting infrastructure completely. 2) At the expense of the permittee, a cost estimate for the decommissioning of the Large Solar Farm and any estimated resale and salvage value shall be prepared by a professional engineer. The permittee shall provide to the County a revised and updated decommissioning cost estimate every five years from the date of approval to cover the cost of meeting this obligation. The decommissioning cost estimate shall explicitly detail the cost, any estimated resale and salvage values, shall account for inflation, cost and value changes, and advances in decommissioning technologies and approaches. 3) The estimated decommissioning cost, less any resale and salvage value, shall be guaranteed in one of the following forms: (i) surety bond in the amount of 110% of anticipated decommissioning costs, or (ii) cash to be held in escrow by the County at a bank. The owner of the Large Solar Farm shall provide the decommissioning cost guaranty no later than the end of the 2nd year of operation of each phase, and shall maintain the financial security thereafter for as long as the Large Solar Farm is in existence or upon discontinuance, decommissioning, or abandonment of the Large Solar Farm. Such financial security shall be updated every five years to cover the costs associated with the updated decommissioning cost estimates. 4) For purposes of this Section, discontinuance, decommissioning, or abandonment shall mean the Large Solar Farm has produced no energy for 12 consecutive months. The owner or operator shall have 12 months to complete decommissioning of the Large Solar Farm. If the owner or operator of the Large Solar Farm fails to remove the installation in accordance with the requirements of this permit or within 12 months following discontinuance, decommissioning, or abandonment, the County may collect the bond or other financial security and the County or a hired third party may enter the property to physically remove the installation. Other solar conversion systems (Individual, Neighborhood, Commercial) also have decommissioning requirements but with different timelines and conditions, e.g., Commercial Solar Conversion Systems require removal within 90 days of abandonment (defined as one year without energy production), Neighborhood Solar Conversion Systems require a decommissioning plan with removal if not in use for 12 consecutive months, and Individual Solar Conversion Systems require removal within six months of ceasing operation.

Section 8.18.05 Commercial Solar Conversion Systems states: "I. Fencing: Due the unique security requirements of this land use, and to facilitate the educational value of seeing this land use, fencing up to eight feet in height is permitted provided the fencing material is predominantly open." This fencing requirement applies to commercial solar farms, which are described as fixed-panel photovoltaic solar farms or CSCS consisting of ground-mounted solar panels capturing energy from the sun and converting it to electricity. The Large Solar Farms section (8.18.06) does not explicitly mention fencing requirements, so the fencing provision in the commercial solar farm section is the explicit fencing requirement applicable to Large Solar Farms. No other fencing options or conditions are provided for Large Solar Farms.

The ordinance states: 'The average height of the solar panel arrays shall not exceed 15 feet.' This applies specifically to Large Solar Farms as defined in Section 8.18.06. No other maximum height values for Large Solar Farms are provided. The units are feet.

No electrical substation owned or operated by an electric supplier to support the generation, transmission or distribution of electricity for a Large Solar Farm shall be located as to cause an exceedance of the following noise level standards: 1) From the hours of 10 pm to 7 am: 50 dBA maximum 10-minute LAeq (most restrictive); 2) From the hours of 7 am to 10 pm: 60 dBA maximum 10-minute LAeq. Noise levels shall be measured at the closest exterior wall of any dwelling unit located on the property that submitted the noise complaint.

Large Solar Farm setback requirements from non-participating properties are: Non-Participating Property with a Dwelling 2,640 feet (1/2 mile); Non-Participating Property without a Dwelling 2,640 feet (1/2 mile). Other setback options include Participating Property with or without a Dwelling at 0 feet, County roads at 1,320 feet (1/4 mile), and State and Federal highways at 1,980 feet (3/8 mile).

The Large Solar Farm shall meet the following setback requirements: Participating Property with a Dwelling 0 feet; Participating Property without a Dwelling 0 feet. Other options include Non-Participating Property with a Dwelling 2,640 feet (1/2 mile), Non-Participating Property without a Dwelling 2,640 feet (1/2 mile), County roads 1,320 feet (1/4 mile), and State and Federal highways 1,980 feet (3/8 mile).

Repowering: If any SCS is no longer operating for purposes of Repowering, replacement, or maintenance, Decommissioning provisions will not apply for up to six months. However, an SCS that is not operating or is operating at a substantially reduced capacity for more than six months will be considered abandoned and Decommissioning provisions will apply. Repowering does not require a new Conditional Use permit or permit amendment if the footprint of the SCS is the same or reduced. Any increase in the footprint of the facility will require a permit amendment.
section: 8.18.02 General Provisions Applying to ISCS, NSCS, and/or CSCS

summary: The Large Solar Farm shall meet the following setback requirements: County roads 1,320 feet (1/4 mile), State and Federal highways 1,980 feet (3/8 mile). Other setback options include: Non-Participating Property with a Dwelling 2,640 feet (1/2 mile), Non-Participating Property without a Dwelling 2,640 feet (1/2 mile), Participating Property with a Dwelling 0 feet, Participating Property without a Dwelling 0 feet.

For Large Solar Farms, signage requirements are explicitly stated: "Signage shall conform to Article 7 of this Resolution as well as any sign limitations of the zoning districts." This applies specifically to Large Solar Farms as defined in Section 8.18.06. Other related solar system types such as Commercial Solar Conversion Systems (CSCS) have a general signage requirement stating "Signage shall conform to the Cherry County Sign Regulations," but this is distinct from the Large Solar Farm section. No other specific signage requirements are detailed for Large Solar Farms beyond this conformity to existing sign regulations.

Section 8.18.06 Large Solar Farms explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements including: 'No large solar farms shall be located within areas considered environmentally sensitive (soils, wetlands, high water table, etc.); especially areas designated as being in the Valentine Soil Association.'; 'No large solar farms shall be located in any canyon within the county.'; 'No large solar farms shall be located in areas considered to contain moderate to high soil erodibility specifically within areas dominated by Valentine soils.'; 'Large solar farms shall not remove more than 20% of any land from production considered to be areas are prime farmland, Farmland of statewide importance, Prime farmland if drained, and Prime farmland if irrigated.'; and 'Stormwater Management: Large solar farms with fixed panel solar arrays shall submit and maintain all additional runoff on the project site; however, in no case shall the drainage basin be built on undisturbed land.' Additionally, the decommissioning plan must include 'restoration of soil and vegetation' and financial assurances to ensure proper decommissioning. Other conditions include setbacks, fire department access, signage, road agreements, and electrical requirements.

value: ['CCAG – Cattle Country Agricultural District', 'NRCAG – Niobrara River Corridor Agricultural District']
summary: No solar panel, neighborhood solar or solar farm shall be installed or constructed within the zoning jurisdiction of Cherry County unless a Conditional Use Permit has been issued. Large Solar Farms may be allowed in the CCAG and NRCAG Districts under the following conditions: use photovoltaic cells, avoid environmentally sensitive areas, meet setback requirements, and comply with other regulations. The Conditional Use Permit process involves review by the Planning Commission and approval by the County Board as described in Sections 4.08.03 and 4.09.03. Other districts either do not permit Large Solar Farms or are not mentioned for this use type. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this summary per instructions.

The Large Solar Farm shall meet the following setback requirements: Non-Participating Property with a Dwelling 2,640 feet (1/2 mile); Non-Participating Property without a Dwelling 2,640 feet (1/2 mile); Participating Property with a Dwelling 0 feet; Participating Property without a Dwelling 0 feet.

Section 8.23.05 B (i) states: 'Lot coverage: No more than one percent of the gross site area shall be occupied by enclosed buildings and structures.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for Commercial Solar Conversion Systems (CSCS). The unit is expressed as a percentage of the total site area, not as a specific area measurement.

Section 8.23.05.C.(x) requires "A decommissioning plan shall be required to ensure that facilities are properly removed after their useful life. Decommissioning of solar panels must occur in the event they are not in use for 12 consecutive months. The plan shall include provisions for removal of all structures and foundations, restoration of soil and vegetation and a plan ensuring financial resources will be available to fully decommission the site." Additionally, "Cuming County reserves the right to require the posting of a bond, letter of credit or the establishment of an escrow account to ensure proper decommissioning." Section 8.23.05.E states "A CSCS shall be considered abandoned after one year without energy production. The solar equipment owner shall remove all SCS equipment and appurtenances within 90 days of abandonment." Other solar conversion systems have different decommissioning provisions: Section 8.23.02.D requires "All systems when they are no longer generating power and will no longer be used shall follow a decommissioning plan that has been agreed to upfront by Cuming County, the electric utility, and the owner/developer." Section 8.23.04.D requires for Neighborhood Solar Conversion Systems "A decommissioning plan shall be required to ensure that facilities are properly removed after their useful life... Cuming County may require the posting of a bond, letter of credit or the establishment of an escrow account to ensure proper decommissioning." summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Commercial Solar Conversion Systems (CSCS). It requires the use of a rammed post construction technique that "allows for minimal disturbance to the existing ground and grading of the site." Stormwater management provisions state that "Solar PV panel arrays shall be considered pervious" and the property "shall be designed to absorb or detain specific runoff." The decommissioning plan must include "restoration of soil and vegetation and site restoration and reclamation to the approximate original topography that existed prior to the construction of the facility with grading, topsoil respread over the disturbed areas at a depth similar to that in existence prior to the disturbance, and reseeding to achieve the same utility of native vegetation of the surrounding area to prevent adverse hydrological effects." These requirements apply specifically to CSCS, defined as "a series of solar panels and equipment connected together in order to commercially supply the converted energy to a community and/or power grid."

Section 6.90 Discontinuation and Decommissioning requires a cash escrow account before permit approval to guarantee removal and restoration upon discontinuation, decommissioning or abandonment of the facilities. The escrow must be funded at minimum 10% increments annually until fully funded by year 10, with 3% annual funding thereafter and 5-year cost reviews. A CSECS is considered discontinued after one year without energy production unless a plan is submitted to return to service. All CSECS and accessory facilities must be removed four feet below ground within 90 days of discontinuation, extendable by the Zoning Administrator. Each CSECS must have a decommissioning and restoration plan detailing means and costs of removal, with cost estimates reviewed and updated every 5 years. Additionally, section 6.86.A.11 requires each Class 4 CSECS application to include a decommissioning plan outlining means, procedure and costs of removing all related support infrastructure, with removal within one year of discontinuance. Other classes have similar but distinct requirements: Class 1 requires a plan stating all equipment will be removed upon discontinuance; Class 2 and Class 3 require a decommissioning plan with means, procedure and costs of removal, and removal within one year of discontinuance.

For Class 4 - Commercial Solar Energy Conversion System (CSECS) (> 2 MW), the ordinance explicitly requires that "any CSECS facility shall be equipped with anti-climbing devices if applicable. Tower climbing apparatus shall not be located within fifteen (15) feet of the ground and site shall be enclosed with a locked protective fence at least eight (8) feet high around the site." Additionally, visual screening for adjacent non-participating public park uses and school uses may include "Fences, walls, berming, vegetation or some combination thereof to provide visual screening." Fencing, walls or berming may supplement other screening methods but shall not account for over fifty percent (50%) of the screening. Acceptable fence materials include masonry, stone and wood, but exclude chain link fences (with or without slats) unless approved by the Zoning Administrator. Visual screening is not required along the property line adjacent to a Participating property. The decommissioning plan must state that "all equipment, support structures, electrical equipment and fences will be removed upon discontinuance of the system’s operation within one (1) year." Other options for visual screening include walls, berming (with side slopes not exceeding 3:1 and erosion protection), and vegetation (at least four trees every 100 linear feet with specific tree type and height requirements).

summary: Section 6.76 requires a Decommissioning Plan for installed facilities and infrastructure to be submitted at the time of permit application, including: (a) the manner in which the facility will be decommissioned; (b) a decommissioning schedule; and (c) a detailed estimate of the cost of decommissioning a solar generation facility by a professional engineer licensed in Nebraska. The estimate must include dismantling and removal of all equipment, removal of underground cables to 48 inches, removal of foundations to 120 inches below grade, site restoration to original topography, repairs to public roads and drainage, removal of access roads unless otherwise agreed, salvageable value, and all expenses related to decommissioning. Section 6.77 mandates a decommissioning performance surety bond for all approved special use permits for Commercial Solar Farms/Facilities, which must be transferable upon sale and may not be refunded until decommissioning is satisfactorily completed or transferred to the Loup County Nebraska Planning Commission. Additional sections (6.78 to 6.714) detail bond amount determination, deadlines, penalties for failure to submit bonds, bond adjustments, surety bond requirements, certificates of deposit, and effects of forfeiture. These requirements apply specifically to Solar Farms as defined as "an area of land designated use for the sole purpose of deploying photovoltaic power and generating electric energy."

summary: Section 603.C Site Development Standards states: 'No more than five percent of the gross site area shall be occupied by enclosed buildings.' This is the only explicit maximum land coverage-related limit provided for utility-scale solar farms. No other explicit maximum land coverage percentage or area limit for the solar panels or arrays themselves is provided.

A decommissioning plan shall be required to ensure that facilities are properly removed after their useful life. Decommissioning of solar panels must occur in the event they are not in use for 12 consecutive months. The plan shall include provisions for removal of all structures and foundations, restoration of soil and vegetation and a plan ensuring financial resources will be available to decommission the site. The Board may require the posting of a bond, letter of credit or the establishment of an escrow account to ensure proper decommissioning. A solar farm shall be considered abandoned after one year without energy production. The property owner shall remove all solar farm equipment and appurtenances within 90 days of abandonment.

Section 603.C, item 7 states: "Fencing: Due to the unique security requirements of this land use, and to facilitate the educational value of seeing this land use, fencing up to eight (8) feet in height is permitted provided the fencing material is predominantly open as defined in Appendix A." This fencing requirement applies specifically to ground-mounted photovoltaic solar farms, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. Other related standards in Section 603.C include lot coverage limits, setbacks, height restrictions, landscaping buffer, signage, burial of customer-owned power lines, and compliance with state and federal codes.

The ordinance states: 'The average height of the solar panel arrays shall not exceed 20 feet.' This applies specifically to ground-mounted photovoltaic solar farms, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit of measurement is feet.

Setbacks shall be applied as 83’ from center of the road, 15 ‘ side and 25’ rear property lines. A thirty-foot side and rear setback shall apply only to the setback area measured from a lot line that abuts a residential use or residential zoning district. The most restrictive setback from property lines for utility-scale solar farms is 15 feet from side property lines.

summary: Section 41.6.3 DECOMMISSIONING requires that "all Solar Energy Conversion Systems shall comply with the decommissioning terms set out below." These include: (A) "The Facility Owner shall have six (6) months to complete decommissioning of the System if no electricity is generated for a continuous period of six (6) months unless otherwise extended by the County Board or other jurisdiction with zoning authority." (B) "Decommissioning shall include removal of solar arrays, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, and any other associated facilities down to thirty-six (36) inches below grade." (C) "Disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded, unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored." (D) "A development agreement, prepared by the County, must be signed and part of the special use permit application to address decommissioning responsibilities and filed with the Register of Deeds." For Solar Energy Conversion Systems requiring a special use permit, this development agreement must be signed by the developer, applicant, or other appropriate party prior to the public meeting at which the County Board will address the special use permit application, and filed with the Sarpy County Register of Deeds. Section 41.6.2 details that a Solar Energy Conversion System utilized as a primary use for a property may be allowed with an approved special use permit, which is valid for a maximum of 20 years and may be renewed. The special use permit application must include "Decommissioning plans that describe the anticipated life of the solar power project, the estimated decommissioning costs in current dollars, the method for ensuring that funds will be available for decommissioning and restoration, and the anticipated manner in which the solar power project will be decommissioned and the site restored."

Section 41.6.2.3 INSTALLATION AND DESIGN states: "11. Security Fencing. All boundary line fencing shall be located entirely upon the property of the Solar Energy Conversion System. Fences shall consist of open fencing such as chain link or barbed wire. Fences shall not exceed eight (8) feet in height." Additionally, "12. Screening. A berm (2:1 maximum slope with supplemental plant materials including trees, shrubs, and groundcovers) and/or a continuous evergreen vegetative buffer shall be provided and maintained at all times around the perimeter of the fencing that faces (a.) public road right-of-way, b.) an existing residence or farmstead not on the subject parcel, or c.) residentially zoned or platted property. The evergreen vegetative buffer shall be composed of evergreen trees or shrubs of a type which at time of planting shall be a minimum of six (6) feet in height and which shall be maintained at maturity at a height of eight (8) feet in height to screen the fence." These requirements apply to ground mounted Solar Energy Conversion Systems as a primary use requiring a special use permit. Other fencing options or conditions are not provided for these systems in the text.

Section 41.6.1(B)(2) requires that "the design, construction, operation and maintenance of any Solar Energy Conversion System shall prevent the misdirection and/or reflection, glare or glint of solar rays onto neighboring properties, businesses, public roads, public parks and other public facilities in excess of that which already exist." For Solar Energy Conversion Systems as a primary use requiring a special use permit, Section 41.6.2.2(H) mandates a "Glare study required or provide verification of FAA approval." These glare restrictions apply to Solar Energy Conversion Systems as a primary use under a special use permit. Other related requirements include site plans, decommissioning plans, and design criteria, but the explicit glare restrictions are limited to the prevention of glare and the requirement of a glare study or FAA approval verification.

summary: Section 9.14.05 B (II) states: 'Lot coverage: No more than five percent of the gross site area shall be occupied by enclosed buildings and structures.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for Commercial Solar Conversion Systems (CSCS), defined as systems generating more than 5 MW and covering more than 40 acres. The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the gross site area. Other related provisions include setbacks, height limits, and fencing, but these do not specify maximum land coverage.

Section 9.14.05 (C)(VIII) and (IX) require a cost estimate for decommissioning and a decommissioning plan that includes removal of all structures and foundations, restoration of soil and vegetation, and financial resources to fully decommission the site. Section 9.14.05 (E) states: "A CSCS shall be considered abandoned after 12 consecutive months without energy production; provided, however, that a CSCS shall not be considered abandoned if the energy is not being produced as a result of maintenance, repairs, or replacement of the CSCS system. The CSCS owner shall remove all SCS equipment and appurtenances within 180 days of abandonment." Other solar conversion system types (Individual and Neighborhood) have separate decommissioning provisions with different thresholds and requirements.

Section 9.14.05 Commercial Solar Conversion Systems (CSCS) states: "Due the unique security requirements of this land use, to ensure public safety, and to facilitate the educational value of seeing this land use, fencing up to eight feet in height is permitted, provided the fencing material is predominantly open. For security and safety purposes, chain-link fence or similar is required." Other solar conversion system types have different provisions: Individual Solar Conversion Systems (ISCS) and Neighborhood Solar Conversion Systems (NSCS) have no explicit fencing requirements except NSCS which states "A ground mounted NSCS shall be protected with fencing and/or bollards." (IV)) This applies specifically to Commercial Solar Conversion Systems (CSCS) defined as systems generating more than 5 MW and larger than 40 acres, connected to the electrical grid for utility distribution. Other solar system types such as Individual Solar Conversion Systems (ISCS) and Neighborhood Solar Conversion Systems (NSCS) have different provisions but do not specify maximum height limits for CSCS. Commercial Solar Conversion Systems (CSCS) are permitted uses, with an approved Conditional Use Permit, only in the A-1 (Agricultural), TA-1 (Transitional Agricultural), I-1 (Light Industrial), and I-2 (General Industrial) zone districts. The text does not explicitly list any districts where CSCS are unconditionally prohibited, but by omission, all other districts are implicitly excluded from permitting CSCS. Other solar system types such as Neighborhood Solar Conversion Systems (NSCS) are also permitted in the same districts with a Conditional Use Permit.

The required setbacks shall meet or exceed the required setbacks for the zoning district in which the CSCS is located. A 30-foot side and rear setback shall apply only to the setback area measured from a lot line that abuts a residential use or residential zoning district. The side and/or rear setback shall be eliminated where the CSCS does not abut a residential use or residential zoning district, or the CSCS and the residential use or residential district are separated by a public right-of-way and/or where the CSCS project is located on adjacent or contiguous parcels.

Section 9.14.02 General Provisions states: 'G. Repowering: If any SCS is no longer operating for purposes of repowering, replacement, or maintenance, decommissioning provisions will not apply for up to 12 months. However, an SCS that is not operating or is operating at a substantially reduced capacity for more than 12 months will be considered abandoned and decommissioning provisions will apply.' and 'H. Repowering does not require a new permit or permit amendment if the footprint of the SCS is the same or reduced. Any increase in the footprint of the facility will require a permit amendment.' These provisions apply to all solar conversion systems (SCS), including Commercial Solar Conversion Systems (CSCS) as defined in the ordinance. Other options or conditions include that decommissioning provisions apply if the system is abandoned (not operating for more than 12 months) and that permit amendments are required only if the footprint increases during repowering.

CSCS shall provide visual screening only along a lot line that abuts a residential use or residential zoning district. The screen shall only be required if the closest exterior wall of a dwelling on the adjacent property is within 300 feet of the CSCS. Screening is not required where the CSCS does not abut a residential use or residential zoning district, or the two districts are separated by a public right-of-way. There are no requirements for screening from public streets.

All CSCS operations shall have, located at key access points, signage stating specific language as outlined by the electric utility or owner. Signage shall conform to the Saunders County Sign Regulations. (Section 9.14.05.B.VII) Other solar conversion systems have different provisions: Neighborhood Solar Conversion Systems (NSCS) require signage at key access points with language outlined by the electric utility and must conform to Saunders County Sign Regulations (9.14.04.B.XI). Individual Solar Conversion Systems (ISCS) and smaller systems do not have explicit signage requirements stated in the provided text.

Section 9.14.05(A) states that CSCS are "constructed with techniques that support the flow of rainwater between each module, the growth of vegetation beneath the arrays, limit the impacts of stormwater runoff, and allow for minimal disturbance to the existing ground and grading of the site." Section 9.14.05(B)(VI) requires that "CSCS shall be considered pervious and the property shall be designed to absorb or detain specific runoff." The impervious cover calculation includes support posts, roads, parking areas, and buildings. Other solar conversion system types include Individual Solar Conversion Systems (ISCS) requiring a Zoning Permit, Neighborhood Solar Conversion Systems (NSCS) generating between 500 kW and 5 MW with specific neighborhood distribution and easement requirements, and CSCS defined as systems generating more than 5 MW on more than 40 acres with a one-way connection to the power grid.

Commercial Solar Conversion Systems (CSCS) generating more than 5 mega-watts (MW) of capacity, and with a Project Area larger than 40 contiguous, or non-contiguous, acres, are "permitted uses, with an approved Conditional Use Permit, in the A-1 (Agricultural), TA-1 (Transitional Agricultural), I-1 (Light Industrial), I-2 (General Industrial) zone districts." Other solar system types such as Neighborhood Solar Conversion Systems (NSCS) generating between 500 kW and 5 MW are also permitted with a Conditional Use Permit but are considered separately.

For Commercial Solar Conversion Systems (CSCS), 'A 30-foot side and rear setback shall apply only to the setback area measured from a lot line that abuts a residential use or residential zoning district.' The setback is eliminated where the CSCS does not abut a residential use or residential zoning district, or where separated by a public right-of-way and/or where the CSCS project is located on adjacent or contiguous parcels. The required setbacks shall meet or exceed the required setbacks for the zoning district in which the CSCS is located.

summary: Section 42.13 DISCONTINUATION AND DECOMMISSIONING PLAN requires that "a gross estimate for the decommissioning costs of this approved Solar Facility, including any estimated resale and salvage value, shall be prepared by a Nebraska licensed professional engineer." The plan must include "the means, procedure, and costs of removing Solar Facility components." The estimated cost must be guaranteed by financial security such as "surety bond; a letter of credit from a financial institution reasonably acceptable to the County which shall be irrevocable unless replaced with cash or other form of security reasonably acceptable to County." The operator must maintain this security "for as long as the Solar Facility is in existence, or upon discontinuance, decommissioning, and/or abandonment." Discontinuance is defined as "the Solar Facility... has ceased energy production for twelve (12) consecutive months," after which the operator has twelve (12) months to complete decommissioning. Failure to remove the installation allows the County to "collect the financial security and... enter the property to physically remove the installation." Decommissioning costs include "all costs associated with the dismantlement, recycling, and safe disposal of facility components and site reclamation activities." Solar Facility components include "solar panels and collectors; battery energy storage systems; substations; switchyards, generators, transmission lines, and electrical wiring; cabling; conduit; racking; facility roads and fencing; and any other related supporting infrastructure to a minimum depth of three (3) feet." Disturbed earth "shall be graded and re-seeded, unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored." Other sections such as 42.07 (Class 2) require a decommissioning plan for Commercial Solar Energy Conversion Systems, but the detailed financial assurance and removal requirements are explicitly stated in Section 42.13, which applies to all Solar Facilities including Class 3 USECS.

Section 42.07 requires that "Reasonable measures shall be taken to mitigate specific adverse visual impacts such as potential glint or reflections which affect residences within or immediately adjacent to the project area." Section 42.10.I mandates "A pre-construction noise and glare study shall be conducted; and shall include all property within one (1) mile (5,280 ft) of the site. Projections of any glare on a structure shall include the extent and duration of the glare on the existing structure." This study must be submitted to the Scotts Bluff County Planning Department for review at the time of the application. These requirements apply to both Class 2 and Class 3 solar projects. For Class 3 - Utility Solar Energy Conversion System (USECS), Section 42.08 outlines general site and design standards but does not explicitly restate glare restrictions beyond the application requirements. Therefore, glare restrictions for USECS are explicitly enacted through the application requirements and the mitigation measures referenced in the Class 2 standards, which are applicable to Class 3 as well. Other options include visual screening methods such as "Fences, walls, berming, and vegetation or some combination thereof to provide visual screening" (Section 42.08.2) and minimizing electromagnetic interference (Section 42.08.3).

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires that all Commercial Solar Conversion Systems (CSCS) no longer generating power must follow a decommissioning plan agreed to upfront by the Thayer County Board, the electric utility, and the owner/developer (10.04.03(5)). A decommissioning plan is a submittal requirement for CSCS (10.04.06(3)(I)). A CSCS is considered abandoned after one year without energy production, and the solar equipment owner must remove all SCS equipment and appurtenances within one year of abandonment (10.04.06(5)(A)). Section 10.04.07 details the Solar Facility Decommissioning Plan requirements, including that each CSCS shall have a plan outlining the anticipated means and cost of removal, including removal of above-ground structures within one year, removal of underground cables and foundations to a depth of 48 inches unless waived by the landowner, site restoration, and repair of public roads if damaged. Financial assurances must be provided via a Standby Letter of Credit (SBLC) prior to construction, with specific requirements for the SBLC's terms and review. Failure to submit an acceptable SBLC results in revocation of the conditional use permit. The plan must be prepared or approved by a professional engineer licensed in Nebraska. These requirements apply specifically to CSCS as defined: "a series of solar panels and equipment connected together in order to commercially supply the converted energy to a community and/or power grid."
