summary: A Fifty (50) foot setback shall be provided from all property lines or road/access easements. This applies specifically to Commercial Solar Conversion Systems (CSCS) as stated in the Site Development Standards. No other setback distances or multipliers based on height are mentioned for roads.

The ordinance requires that Commercial Solar Conversion Systems (CSCS) use a rammed post construction technique that "allows for minimal disturbance to the existing ground and grading of the site." Fixed panel solar arrays "shall be considered pervious and the property shall be designed to absorb or detain specific runoff." The Decommissioning Plan must include "site restoration and reclamation to the approximate original topography that existed prior to the construction of the facility with grading, topsoil respread over the disturbed areas at a depth similar to that in existence prior to the disturbance, and reseeding to achieve the same utility of native vegetation of the surrounding area to prevent adverse hydrological effects." These requirements explicitly address soil disturbance minimization, stormwater runoff management, and site reclamation for CSCS projects.

A Decommissioning Plan for installed facilities and infrastructure must be submitted to the Planning Commission at the time of permit application. The plan must include: (a) the manner in which the facility will be decommissioned; (b) a decommissioning schedule; (c) a detailed estimate of the cost of decommissioning a solar generation facility by a professional engineer licensed in the state of Nebraska that shall at a minimum include dismantling and removal of all towers, turbine generators, transformers, overhead cables and debris; removal of underground cables to a depth forty eight (48) inches; removal of foundations, buildings, and ancillary equipment to a minimum depth of one hundred twenty (120) inches below grade; site restoration and reclamation to the approximate original topography; repairs and reconstruction from damage to public roads, culverts and natural drainage ways; removal, clearing, and grading of all access roads unless otherwise agreed; the current salvageable value of the facility; and all expenses related to decommissioning shall be the responsibility of the solar generation facility owner. A copy of as-built plans certified by a professional engineer must also be included. A decommissioning performance surety bond is required for all approved special use permits granted for the installation of Commercial Solar Farms / Facilities. The bond must be transferable upon sale of the facilities and may not be refunded until decommissioning has been satisfactorily completed or transferred to the Thomas County Nebraska Planning Commission. The bond amount is based on estimated costs to the Commission to perform decommissioning and reclamation work, including costs from public contracting requirements, management, operation, and maintenance upon abandonment, and considers the character and nature of the site and salvage value. The owner must submit the bond within specified deadlines, with penalties for failure to do so. The bond amount is reviewed every 5 years and may be adjusted. Surety bonds and certificates of deposit are subject to specific requirements. The Commission may forfeit bonds if necessary and recover costs exceeding the bond amount from the owner.

The height of the solar collector and any mounts within an established solar farm shall not exceed 20 feet when oriented at maximum tilt. A solar farm shall be considered abandoned after one year without energy production. The property owner shall remove all solar farm equipment and appurtenances within 90 days of abandonment.

summary: Section 1507.A.7 requires that Class 4 CSECS "shall provide visual screening for adjacent non-participating, public park uses and school uses: Fences, walls, berming, vegetation or some combination thereof to provide visual screening shall be used. Fencing, walls or berming may be used to supplement other screening methods, but shall not account for over fifty percent (50%) of the screening." Vegetative screening must be provided "at a rate of at least ten (10) trees every one hundred (100) linear feet. Of the ten (10) trees every one hundred (100) linear feet, at least one (1) shall be a deciduous shade tree and three (3) shall be evergreen or ornamental trees." Additional requirements include that "at least two-thirds (2/3), but no more than three quarters (3/4) of the total ornamental/evergreen trees along the property line shall be made up of evergreen trees," "each tree shall have a minimum mature height of fifteen (15) feet," and "seedlings are not acceptable and are not to be used for screening purposes." Visual screening is not required along the property line adjacent to a Participating property. Other screening options include fences or walls made of masonry, stone, or wood (excluding chain link fences), and berming with side slopes not exceeding 3:1 and erosion protection. These requirements apply specifically to Class 4 – Large Scale Commercial Solar Energy Conversion Systems (CSECS) as defined by having a rated capacity greater than five (5) megawatts and supplying electricity to off-site customers.

summary: Any Ground-Mounted Solar Energy System which has been abandoned or is no longer operational shall be removed. The owner and/or operator shall physically remove the installation no more than 365 days after the date of discontinued operations and plans for the removal. A Commitment of Deconstruction shall be included in the plan for when the system is no longer in use. The Planning Board reserves the right to require a posting of a bond for the removal of an unused facility. The Planning Board has the authority to ask for more information and seek outside expertise if, in the opinion of the Planning Board, it is necessary. The permit-granting authority may require the applicant for a large-scale solar facility to provide a form a surety, either through escrow account, bond, or otherwise, to cover the cost of removal in the event the Town must remove the facility. The amount and form, as determined by the permit-granting authority, is to be reasonable and shall not exceed more than 125% of the cost of removal. Such surety will not be required for municipally or state-owned facilities. The applicant shall submit a fully inclusive estimate of the costs associated with removal, prepared by a qualified engineer. The amount shall include a mechanism for Cost of Living Adjustment.

The maximum height of any Ground-Mounted Solar Energy System shall not exceed 20 feet off the ground. Roof-Mounted Solar Energy Systems shall be considered exempt for height requirements. This applies to Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems as they are included in Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems. (Section 148-6, subsection B)

Utility (Ground) solar energy systems are prohibited (marked 'N') in R-1 and VCB districts. Other districts have the following conditions: Rural (CUP), GB (CUP), LI (CUP), and GI (CUP), where CUP means Conditional Use Permit. The ordinance applies to systems intended for provision of power for the owner/operator, community, or for selling power as a utility. The note clarifies Y = Yes; N = No; CUP = Conditional Use Permit.

The ordinance requires that Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems provide adequate screening to ensure adjacent property values are not adversely impacted, including but not limited to glare from the solar panels. Screening may be provided by maintaining existing vegetation or through the installation of site-specific evergreen landscaping, suitable fencing, or a combination thereof, and must be maintained during the operative lifetime of the Solar Energy System Conditional Use Permit (§148-6(G)). A detailed screening plan may be required by the Planning Board or Historic District Commission to address neighborhood sensitivities and mitigate visual impacts. Additionally, all Community- and Utility-Scale solar energy generation facilities must provide a landscape plan indicating proposed screening vegetation or other structures (§148-8(E)). Appurtenant structures should be screened from view by vegetation and/or joined or clustered to avoid adverse visual impacts whenever reasonable (§148-8(H)).

The ordinance requires that Commercial Solar Collection Systems (CSCS), which include large commercial, industrial, utility, and generation station solar systems, submit a Decommissioning Plan. This plan must ensure decommissioning and site restoration within twelve (12) months after the system is deemed unsafe, abandoned, or at the end of its useful life (defined as no electricity generated and sent to the power grid for a continuous period of twelve (12) months). The Restoration Plan must include removal of all items in outdoor storage, removal of on-site roads and open-work areas to preconstruction conditions (except for approved retained roads), re-grading and re-vegetation to return the property to its preconstruction condition, and implementation of a post-decommissioning stormwater runoff plan. Additionally, financial assurance in the form of a bond, cash, or other security is required to cover the cost of decommissioning and site reclamation, which must remain in effect during the entire life of the CSCS and until decommissioning is complete. The Town may use these funds to remove the system and restore the site if the applicant fails to do so. These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Collection Systems, which include Solar Power Generation Stations defined as any Solar Collection System over 30 MW in nameplate capacity requiring approval by the New Hampshire Site Evaluation Committee. Other solar system types mentioned include Residential Solar Energy Systems (primarily for on-site use, up to 15 kW), Small Commercial Solar (up to 1 MW and less than 5 acres), Large Commercial Solar (1 MW to 5 MW and 5 to 25 acres), Industrial Solar (25 to 50 acres), Utility Solar (over 50 acres and less than 30 MW), and Primary Agriculture Solar (up to 1 MW or over 5 acres with preserved agricultural use).

Mitigation may include angle of panels, details on the anti-reflective nature of the panel coating or any additional specific screening to minimize resulting impacts." This applies to Commercial Solar Collection Systems, which include Large Commercial, Industrial, Utility, and Generation Station systems, typically defined as Solar Power Generation Stations (e.g., systems over 30 MW nameplate capacity requiring NH Site Evaluation Committee approval).

The ordinance defines a SOLAR POWER GENERATION STATION as any Solar Collection System that is over 30 MW in nameplate capacity and requires approval by the New Hampshire Site Evaluation Committee. It explicitly states: 'In no case shall a Solar Power Generation Station exceed 150 acres.' Other related categories include INDUSTRIAL SOLAR (25 to 50 acres), LARGE COMMERCIAL SOLAR (5 to 25 acres), SMALL COMMERCIAL SOLAR (less than 5 acres), and UTILITY SOLAR (over 50 acres but less than 30 MW). The ordinance defines a SOLAR POWER GENERATION STATION as any Solar Collection System that is over 30 MW in nameplate capacity; and such systems also require approval by the New Hampshire Site Evaluation Committee. In no case shall a Solar Power Generation Station exceed 150 acres. Other categories include SMALL COMMERCIAL SOLAR (up to 1 MW and less than 5 acres), LARGE COMMERCIAL SOLAR (between 1 MW and 5 MW and between 5 and 25 acres), INDUSTRIAL SOLAR (between 25 and 50 acres), and UTILITY SOLAR (over 50 acres and less than 30 MW). The units for the maximum project size are in MW for capacity and acres for land coverage, with the 30 MW capacity being the key threshold for Solar Power Generation Stations.

The ordinance explicitly requires that Commercial Solar Collection Systems (CSCS), which include large commercial, industrial, utility, and generation station solar systems, "shall be screened from abutting residential properties and public ways to the extent practicable" (§229-135 C). Additionally, all applications must submit "a detailed buffering plan demonstrating how the proposed Ground Mounted solar installation will be incorporated into the local landscape so that effective screening is provided along public ways and from abutting views." The ordinance explicitly requires soil, erosion, and sediment control measures for Commercial Solar Collection Systems, including Solar Power Generation Stations. These apply to large commercial, industrial, utility, and Solar Power Generation Stations (over 30 MW), which require Planning Board site plan approval and compliance with these standards.

summary: Section 3.13.8 Abandonment requires that "At such time that a commercial or agriculture (primary) solar energy system is scheduled to be abandoned or discontinued, the applicant will notify the building inspector by certified U.S. mail of the proposed date of abandonment or discontinuation of operations." The owner "shall physically remove the solar energy system within 90 days from the date of abandonment or discontinuation of use," including "removal of all above-grade components" and "restoration of the location of the solar energy system to its natural condition." If the system is out-of-service for a continuous 12-month period without notice, the building inspector may issue a Notice of Abandonment, and the owner must remove the system within 90 days of receipt. Failure to remove may result in legal action. Section 3.13.9 Bonding and Security Insurance requires the Planning Board to "set the form and amount of security that represents the cost for removal and disposal of such abandoned facilities" and to require proof of liability insurance prior to construction. Additionally, Section 3.13.6(e)(15) states that "The Planning Board, at the time of review, may require the applicant to file a decommissioning plan and post a decommissioning security" based on estimated removal and restoration costs. These requirements apply explicitly to commercial solar energy systems as defined in Section 3.13.3(c).

Section 3.13.5(c) states: 'Solar energy systems shall be sited in a manner that will minimize impact due to glare on neighboring or adjacent uses.' Section 3.13.6(e)(5) requires 'A glare analysis, prepared by the manufacturer or qualified engineer, detailing potential glare onto abutting structures and roadways estimating the interaction of sun to panel angle, time of year and visibility locations.' The Planning Board may require 'reasonable mitigation' including 'angle of panels, details on the anti-reflective nature of the panel coating or any additional specific screening to minimize resulting impacts.' These requirements apply to commercial solar energy systems as defined in 3.13.3(c) and are part of the Conditional Use Permit application process.

Solar energy systems shall be landscaped with a buffer of plant materials that effectively screens the view of the solar system compound from adjacent streets and residential property. The standard buffer shall consist of a landscaped strip at least ten (10) feet wide outside the perimeter of the compound. Additionally, all solar energy systems, including the panels, shall comply with building setback requirements in accordance with the Dimensional and Density Requirements, Section IV, as applicable, unless modified elsewhere in this Ordinance. For tracking systems, the setback shall be measured from the point and time where the array is closest to the lot line. No portion of a system may cross into the setback.

Section 3.13.5(h) states: 'Solar energy systems shall be landscaped with a buffer of plant materials that effectively screens the view of the solar system compound from adjacent streets and residential property. The standard buffer shall consist of a landscaped strip at least ten (10) feet wide outside the perimeter of the compound. Natural vegetation is preferred.' It further provides that 'In locations where the visual impact of the system would be minimal, the landscaping requirement may be reduced or waived entirely.' Additionally, 'Existing mature tree growth and natural landforms on the site shall be preserved to the maximum extent possible.' Section 3.13.5(l) requires that 'All applications shall include a plan demonstrating how the proposed ground-mounted solar installation will be incorporated into the local landscape so that effective screening is provided along public ways and from abutting views. Section 3.13.5(d) states: 'All signs are prohibited, except for manufacturer identification, contact information for the owner/operator, or proper warning signs.' This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems as defined in 3.13.3(c) as 'a use of land that consists of one or more free-standing, ground-mounted, solar energy systems regardless of rated nameplate capacity and solar land coverage that is designed primarily to serve off-site uses.' Post construction requirements include "restoration of those areas of soil compaction to natural conditions" and plantings of "native species" to maintain a healthy habitat that can "attenuate stormwater on the site." Additionally, Section 3.13.6(d)(7) requires a Conditional Use Permit application to include "a plan demonstrating effective stormwater infiltration along with erosion control measures and soil stabilization." Section 3.13.6(d)(7) also requires "a plan detailing erosion control measures that will be adhered to during construction" with Best Management Practices for erosion control. These requirements apply to commercial solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance, which are "one or more free-standing, ground-mounted, solar energy systems regardless of rated nameplate capacity and solar land coverage that is designed primarily to serve off-site uses."

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires that "it is the responsibility of the applicant to minimize, where possible, the visual impacts for surrounding neighbors and the community" (3.13.5(f)). All applications must include "a plan demonstrating how the proposed ground-mounted solar installation will be incorporated into the local landscape so that effective screening is provided along public ways and from abutting views" (3.13.5(l)). For Conditional Use Permits, applicants must submit "a detailed landscape plan showing all systems visually screened via preservation of existing vegetation or use of landscaped screening" (3.13.6(d)(8)) and "demonstrate through site planning and proposed mitigation that the solar energy system’s visual impacts will be minimized for surrounding neighbors and the community" (3.13.6(f)(14)). The owner or operator of large-scale ground-mounted solar energy system shall submit a decommissioning plan to the Community Development Department as part of their application for a solar energy system conditional use permit to ensure the proper removal of the system and associated equipment upon the end of the project life or after their useful life. The owner or operator shall decommission the solar panels in the event they are not in use for 12 consecutive months. The plan shall include provisions for the removal of all structures, foundations, and electrical transmission components (including below grade components), and the restoration of soil and vegetation within 6-months of abandonment. The Planning Board may require that the owner or operator post a bond, letter of credit, or establish an escrow account, including an inflationary escalator, in an amount deemed acceptable by the Community Development Director, to ensure proper decommissioning.

Perimeter and/or security fencing shall have a maximum height of 8-ft for medium-scale and large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems requiring a conditional use permit. Large-scale systems are defined as occupying 1-acre or more of solar footprint and must be located on parcels no less than 5-acres in size. These systems shall not exceed 15-ft in height and require a minimum setback distance of 50-ft from all exterior property lines and existing public rights-of-way. The visual impact of fencing and associated equipment shall be mitigated through preservation of existing vegetation and/or installation of a visual buffer approved by the Planning Board.

The ordinance requires that large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems "shall be designed and/or sited to minimize the adverse impacts of glint or glare on adjacent properties or roadways." Large-scale systems are defined as those occupying 1-acre or more of solar footprint and require a conditional use permit from the Planning Board. Additional relevant standards include: systems must be located on parcels no less than 5-acres; solar footprint shall not exceed 20 contiguous acres; height shall not exceed 15-ft; a minimum setback of 50-ft from exterior property lines and public rights-of-way is required; and visual impacts must be mitigated through preservation or installation of visual buffers. The Planning Board may impose conditions to minimize adverse effects, including glare. Other scale categories (small-scale and medium-scale) have different definitions and permit requirements, but the explicit glare restriction is stated for medium- and large-scale systems under the conditional use permit review criteria.

The height of ground-mounted solar energy systems shall not exceed 15-ft, as measured from the ground to the highest point of the system, when oriented at maximum design tilt. This applies to large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems defined as occupying 1-acre or more of solar footprint. Other scale categories (small-scale and medium-scale) also have a 15-ft height limit, but this response focuses on large-scale systems. Roof-mounted solar energy systems may exceed maximum building height by up to 8-ft, but this does not apply to large-scale ground-mounted systems. The unit 'ft' refers to feet.

The solar footprint of large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems shall not exceed 20 contiguous acres. Large-scale systems are defined as those occupying 1-acre or more of solar footprint. Additionally, large-scale systems must be located on parcels no less than 5 acres in size (minimum parcel size). The maximum size limit is specifically on the solar footprint, not the entire parcel. These provisions are found in Section 8.3.7.D.2.b and reiterated in Article 16.2 Review Criteria (A and B).

summary: Medium-scale and large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems shall be sited in a manner to reasonably minimize the view of the system from surrounding properties and public rights of way. The visual impact of medium-scale and large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems, associated equipment, and any extensive or imposing perimeter fencing on adjacent parcels and public rights-of-way shall be mitigated through the preservation of existing vegetation and/or through the installation of a visual buffer approved by the Planning Board. If landscaping is used to provide a visual buffer, it shall: 1. Provide year-round screening of the ground-mounted solar energy system and associated equipment; 2. Be composed of native plant species; and, 3. Be maintained for the full term that the ground-mounted solar energy system is located on the site. The conditional use permit application shall include a landscape plan that includes the location of existing vegetation to be preserved; details on the location, dimensions, and composition of any visual buffers on site; and information on the proposed location, number, type and size (at planting and maturity) of any replacement or proposed vegetation and ground cover on the site. These requirements apply to large-scale systems defined as occupying 1-acre or more of solar footprint and requiring a conditional use permit unless located in the Industrial District.

Owners of solar facilities over 30 MW must submit a decommissioning plan with financial assurances, obtain necessary permits, complete removal of project components, restore the site through grading and revegetation, and ensure safe disposal of hazardous materials as part of their certificate application to the site evaluation committee.

Fencing shall be installed as required by the National Electric Code or Utility. Additional security or fencing may be required if the location of the system presents a safety concern for abutting land uses. This applies to Enterprise Solar Energy Systems including Shared/Community Solar Energy Systems, which are permitted in the Business and Commercial Districts subject to Planning Board review and a Conditional Use Permit (CUP). Enterprise Solar Energy Systems shall adhere to Section 190-5.11D(2)(a)[1-6] and all applicable buffer requirements set forth in Section 190-2.2(I). Other system types include Single-Family or Duplex Residential Solar Energy Systems, which must be screened from adjacent properties by fencing or a combination of evergreen and deciduous plantings, and Multiunit Residential or Nonresidential Solar Energy Systems, which require Planning Board review and CUP and must be sited to minimize clearing and provide screening. Roof- or Building-Mounted Systems are permitted with building permits and must comply with building and fire codes but do not have explicit fencing requirements stated.

Enterprise Solar Energy Systems are permitted in the Business and Commercial Districts "not to exceed 5 MW AC of Rated Nameplate Capacity" (§ 190-5.11D(2)(d)). These systems "shall constitute Freestanding Solar Energy Systems and shall adhere to Section 190-5.11D(2)(a)[1-6]" and require Planning Board review and a Conditional Use Permit (CUP). The 5 MW AC limit is explicit and no provision allows bypassing this maximum via permit. Other system types and conditions include: Roof- or Building-Mounted Systems permitted with building permit; Freestanding Single-Family or Duplex Residential Systems permitted with building permit and height limits; Multiunit Residential or Nonresidential Systems subject to CUP and Planning Board review; and Shared/Community Solar Systems may be included within Enterprise Solar Energy Systems. The unit for the maximum project size is megawatts (MW), specifically AC rated capacity.

All Freestanding Solar Energy Systems, except Single-Family or Duplex Residential Solar Energy Systems, "shall be located to minimize visual impacts to abutting properties and the road" by preserving "existing vegetation, topography or structures to screen the freestanding system from abutting properties and roads." If existing vegetation or other site characteristics cannot be preserved or do not exist to adequately screen the system, "additional landscape screening shall be provided." Enterprise Solar Energy Systems "shall adhere to Section 190-5.11D(2)(a)[1-6]" and "shall further adhere to all applicable buffer requirements set forth in Section 190-2.2(I)." The Conditional Use Permit application requires a "Landscaping Plan showing the location, height and spacing of existing vegetation to be preserved, and areas where new planting will be required," with buffer areas containing "sufficient existing vegetation, as approved by the Planning Board or be planted with evergreen type plantings of such height, spacing and arrangement as, in the judgment of the Planning Board, will effectively screen the solar energy system from neighboring areas." Other system types have different or additional conditions: Single-Family or Duplex Residential systems must be "screened from adjacent properties by fencing or a combination of evergreen and deciduous plantings," Multiunit Residential or Nonresidential systems must be "located in the rear of the property between the building and rear property line when feasible" and "adhere to all applicable buffer requirements set forth in Section 190-2.2I," and all systems must comply with setback, soil disturbance, and other environmental protections.

Enterprise Solar Energy Systems (up to 5 MW AC) are permitted in the Business and Commercial Districts subject to Planning Board review and a Conditional Use Permit. These systems "shall adhere to Section 190-5.11D(2)(a)[1-6]" which includes requirements that the location "shall be selected and prepared to minimize soil disturbance and grading," "systems shall not be sited in a manner that disturbs wetlands," and "any runoff created by the photovoltaic cells shall be mitigated using best engineering practices." Additionally, "all disturbed soils on the site will be properly stabilized and revegetated" and "stormwater will be properly managed on the site." The ordinance also notes that systems on previously disturbed commercial or industrial properties may be approved if they meet these standards and minimize clearing vegetation or soil disturbance beyond what is necessary. Other system types and their conditions include: Single-Family or Duplex Residential Solar Energy Systems (onsite accessory use) with specific siting, height, and stabilization requirements; Multiunit Residential or Nonresidential Solar Energy Systems subject to Planning Board review and CUP with similar soil disturbance and stabilization requirements; and Shared/Community Solar Energy Systems included under Multiunit Residential or Nonresidential and Enterprise categories. All Freestanding Solar Energy Systems are considered structures and must comply with setback and impervious coverage requirements.

Enterprise Solar Energy Systems (up to 5 MW AC) are permitted in the Business and Commercial Districts subject to Planning Board review as a Nonresidential development and a Conditional Use Permit (CUP), and require a building permit. They shall adhere to Section 190-5.11D(2)(a)[1-6], which includes: compliance with building setback requirements, minimizing soil disturbance and grading, avoiding wetlands and flood zones, and minimizing visual impacts to abutting properties and roads by preserving existing vegetation, topography, or structures for screening or providing additional landscape screening if needed. The systems must also adhere to all applicable buffer requirements set forth in Section 190-2.2(I). The CUP application requires submission of a landscaping plan showing existing vegetation to be preserved and new plantings to effectively screen the system from neighboring areas. Other system types include Roof- or Building-Mounted Systems permitted with building permits, Freestanding Single-Family or Duplex Residential Systems permitted with building permits and specific siting and screening requirements, and Multiunit Residential or Nonresidential Systems subject to Planning Board review and CUP with similar siting and screening standards. Glare restrictions are not considered part of visual impact assessment here.

The ordinance includes decommissioning requirements under section (f) Abandonment and Decommissioning: 'The owner of a solar system shall remove panels, ground-mounted structures, anchors, underground utility lines, equipment shelters, security fencing, and other facilities from the site within one hundred and twenty (120) days of discontinuance or abandonment of the system. The site must be restored and left in a stable, noneroding, litter-free, and attractive condition.' Additionally, 'a decommissioning bond for Multiunit Residential or Nonresidential Solar Energy Systems, and Commercial Solar Energy Systems, shall be provided for in a form, and an amount that is acceptable to the Planning Board, equal to the estimated cost of removal of the approved facilities.' Other categories of solar energy systems addressed in the ordinance include Municipal Solar Energy Systems (exempt from land use regulations), Roof- or Building-Mounted Systems (permitted on all buildings with certain conditions), Freestanding Solar Energy Systems divided into Single-Family or Duplex Residential (onsite accessory use), Multiunit Residential or Nonresidential (onsite accessory use), and Commercial Solar Energy Systems (a principal use permitted in certain districts subject to Planning Board Site Plan Review and other conditions).

Freestanding Solar Energy Systems (Ground-Mounted) must be located to minimize visual impacts to abutting properties and the road. To the greatest extent possible, sites shall be designed to preserve and take advantage of existing vegetation, topography or structures to screen the freestanding system from abutting properties and roads. If existing vegetation or other site characteristics cannot be preserved or do not exist to adequately screen the system, additional landscape screening shall be provided. Commercial Solar Energy Systems, defined as a principal use designed to generate energy for use off site, are permitted in certain districts subject to Planning Board Site Plan Review and must minimize clearing and provide proper stabilization and revegetation. Other categories include: Roof- or Building-Mounted Systems, which must minimize visual impacts if extending above the roofline; Single-Family or Duplex Residential Solar Energy Systems, which must provide screening to minimize adverse visual impacts; and Multiunit Residential or Nonresidential Solar Energy Systems, which must provide screening to minimize adverse visual impacts and may not be sited in front of a building unless adequately screened.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems – a principal use - are permitted in the Rural, Commercial-Industrial, Business Office or Industrial District, subject to Planning Board Site Plan Review, issuance of a building permit, and the following: Systems shall be sited to minimize the need for clearing of forest and site grading and all disturbed soils shall be properly stabilized and revegetated. Other categories include: Municipal Solar Energy Systems (exempt from land use regulations), Roof- or Building-Mounted Systems (permitted on all buildings with building permit and compliance with building and fire codes), Freestanding Solar Energy Systems (Ground-Mounted) with general standards including compliance with state and local codes, setback requirements, impervious surface rules, underground wiring to the maximum extent practical, visual impact minimization, and anti-reflective coatings. Subcategories of Freestanding Systems include Single-Family or Duplex Residential Systems (onsite accessory use with requirements to minimize clearing and stabilize disturbed soils), Multiunit Residential or Nonresidential Systems (onsite accessory use with similar soil stabilization and siting requirements), and Commercial Solar Energy Systems as described above.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems – a principal use - are permitted in the Rural, Commercial-Industrial, Business Office or Industrial District, subject to Planning Board Site Plan Review, issuance of a building permit, and the following: systems shall be sited to minimize the need for clearing of forest and site grading and all disturbed soils shall be properly stabilized and revegetated; on site lighting shall be minimal and limited to access and safety requirements only, all lighting shall be downcast and shielded from abutting properties; emergency response requirements including site access, fire department guidance, safety procedures, and contact information must be provided and posted. Other categories include: Municipal Solar Energy Systems exempt from land use regulations; Roof- or Building-Mounted Systems permitted in all districts with building permit and compliance with codes; Freestanding Solar Energy Systems as accessory uses permitted in all districts with conditions and permits, including Single-Family or Duplex Residential and Multiunit Residential or Nonresidential systems with site plan review and building permits.

Section 15B.7 Abandonment and Decommissioning explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Industrial Systems. It requires the owner or operator of an SCS other than a Residential System to give not less than [one] month’s prior written notice to the Town of its intent to cease operation (15B.7.1). The Ground Mounted portions of an abandoned or decommissioned SCS that are above grade shall be removed in accordance with applicable State, Federal and local rules, and the site shall be restored to its natural state within six months (15B.7.2). Applications for Large Commercial or Industrial Systems must include a plan addressing decommissioning and removal of equipment as required by 15B.7.2, and the owner or operator shall post a bond or other surety covering the full cost of removal if not properly and timely removed (15B.7.3). Other system types mentioned include Residential Systems, which are exempt from these requirements, and Large Commercial Systems, which share similar decommissioning obligations as Industrial Systems.

Section 15B.5.5 states: 'The location and composition of any fencing required by applicable code or the utility, provided that the Ground Mounted portion of an SCS with a Rated Capacity greater than 100kW AC shall be fenced. The Planning Board may, in addition, require additional security or fencing if the location of the SCS presents a safety concern for abutting land uses.' This fencing requirement applies to Industrial Systems, which are defined as any SCS intended to (1) reduce on-site consumption of utility power, (2) generate power for sale to customers, or (3) produce energy strictly for distribution to the power grid, with (a) a Rated Capacity of 30 MW AC or less and (b) 100 acres or less Solar Land Coverage.

Section 15B.5.7 Lighting and Glare requires "an assessment of potential glare onto abutting structures and roadways, based on different sun to panel angles, seasons, and visibility locations" for Agricultural, Large Commercial and Industrial Systems. The Planning Board may require "reasonable mitigation of potentially significant glare, including, without limitation, adjustment of the angle of panels, anti-reflective panel coatings, or additional specific screening."

No Ground Mounted portion of an SCS shall exceed 30 feet in height, provided that it shall be no more than 20 feet in height at the permitted building perimeter on the lot. This applies to Industrial Systems as they are a subset of Solar Collection Systems (SCS). The most restrictive maximum height is 20 feet at the permitted building perimeter. Units are feet.

Section 15B.2.3 defines an Industrial System as any Solar Collection System with (b) 100 acres or less Solar Land Coverage. Other system types have different maximum Solar Land Coverage limits: Agricultural System (five acres or less), Large Commercial System (20 acres or less), Residential System (1000 square feet or less), Shared System (one acre or less), and Small Commercial System (500 square feet or less). The unit for the maximum lot size for Industrial Systems is explicitly given as acres.

The ordinance defines an Industrial System as any Solar Collection System intended to (1) reduce on-site consumption of utility power, (2) generate power for sale to customers, or (3) produce energy strictly for distribution to the power grid, with (a) a Rated Capacity of 30 MW AC or less and (b) 100 acres or less Solar Land Coverage. Other system types include Agricultural System (1 MW AC or less, 5 acres or less), Large Commercial System (5 MW AC or less, 20 acres or less), Residential System (12 kW AC or less, 1000 square feet or less), Shared System (100 kW AC or less, 1 acre or less), and Small Commercial System (12 kW AC or less, 500 square feet or less). The Rated Capacity is defined as the maximum rated AC output of an SCS based on its design output.

The ordinance states: 'Solar Collection Systems complying with this ordinance shall be permitted in the following districts:' followed by a table where 'X' marks indicate prohibition. Utility-scale solar energy systems are unconditionally prohibited in the Downtown Commercial district (marked 'X' in most rows) and in the Industrial district for most system types except the Industrial district itself. Other districts such as Residential, Residential/Agricultural, Commercial, and Office Park/Research and Office Park have mixed permissions ('P') and prohibitions ('X') depending on the system type. For example, Residential district allows solar systems in some rows but prohibits in others. The table uses 'P' for permitted and 'X' for prohibited.

Section 15B.5.4 requires "A buffering plan demonstrating how the Ground Mounted portion of an SCS will be effectively screened from public ways and neighboring views, including, without limitation, (a) the location, height and spacing of existing vegetation to be preserved: (b) areas of new planting and the type thereof; and (c) how existing or manufactured topography will be used to reduce visual impact." Additionally, Section 15B.5.7 requires for Agricultural, Large Commercial and Industrial Systems "an assessment of potential glare onto abutting structures and roadways... The Planning Board may require reasonable mitigation of potentially significant glare, including, without limitation, adjustment of the angle of panels, anti-reflective panel coatings, or additional specific screening."

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Industrial Systems under Section 15B.6. It states: 'The Ground Mounted portions of Solar Collection Systems shall be installed in accordance with best management practices for erosion, sedimentation and runoff control during all site preparation, installation and post-installation restoration phases.' For Type 2 solar energy systems, the applicant must provide a "site-specific visual mitigation and buffering plan prepared by a New York State licensed landscape architect" (§ 130-80G(2)(m)). The Planning Board and Zoning Board of Appeals "shall provide for enhanced screening and buffering for Type 2 solar energy systems that are placed adjacent to residential zoning districts, areas containing residential uses or abut a public road." Maintenance of "visual mitigation, buffering and screening elements, including the replacement as needed of any plantings during the life of the solar energy system" is required (§ 130-80G(2)(g)[3]). These requirements explicitly enact vegetative buffer and screening obligations for Type 2 solar energy systems. Other related requirements include a property operation and maintenance plan, clearing, grading, stormwater and erosion control plans, tree surveys, glare analysis, and decommissioning plans, but these do not replace or negate the explicit vegetative buffer and screening mandates.

For Type 2 solar energy systems, the applicant "shall place a four-foot-by-eight-foot sign at the proposed entrance to the site upon which a Type 2 solar energy system is to be constructed." The sign "shall remain erected until all conditions of approvals have been fully satisfied and a certificate of compliance has been issued." The sign "shall indicate that an application for a Type 2 solar energy system is pending with the Town of Avon Planning Board and Zoning Board of Appeals." It must also include "the address and tax map number of the property(s) to be developed, name and contact information of the applicant as well as a synopsis of the proposed solar energy system improvements, including the approximate size of area to be covered by panels and proposed nameplate capacity."

For Type 2 solar energy systems, the applicant "shall submit an engineered stormwater and erosion control plan to the Town's consulting engineer for its review and approval, which shall demonstrate that post-development runoff, storm drainage and erosion will not be negatively impacted by placement of the Type 2 solar energy system on the site." Additionally, the applicant and any successor permit holder, owner or operator "shall be required to maintain all drainage improvements and shall implement necessary changes or improvements, should the originally approved and installed improvements fail to perform as intended." If drainage problems occur, the applicant must "engineer and implement a revised drainage plan and/or infrastructure or facilities at its own cost" and comply with timelines for remediation or face revocation of approvals and decommissioning. These requirements are explicitly for Type 2 solar energy systems, defined as "A ground-mounted solar energy system intended to produce energy for off-site sale to and consumption by one or more customers."

Type 2 solar energy systems are permitted only in Agricultural Districts (A) and are subject to the requirements set forth in this section, including site plan approval pursuant to § 130-45E, and are allowed only after the issuance of a special use permit pursuant to § 130-35. Other types of solar energy systems such as commercial building-mounted and commercial roof-mounted solar energy systems are allowed in multiple districts but also require special use permits and site plan approval. Smaller or accessory systems (Type 1) are allowed in all zoning districts except Planned Unit Development and Planned Development Districts, often with fewer restrictions.

For Type 2 solar energy systems, which are defined as "A ground-mounted solar energy system intended to produce energy for off-site sale to and consumption by one or more customers," the ordinance requires a "site-specific visual mitigation and buffering plan prepared by a New York State licensed landscape architect that is appropriate to the scale of the solar energy system and is sensitive to the proximity of impacted property owners." The plan "shall contain a variety of landscaping measures that soften and minimize the visual impact associated with the development" and "shall include a mixture of plant species, sizes/heights, deciduous and evergreen trees and/or shrubs" with enhanced screening for systems adjacent to residential zoning districts or public roads. Additionally, the applicant must provide a "viewshed/line-of-sight analysis, prepared by a New York State licensed landscape architect with scaled color visual renderings overlayed on actual photographs to demonstrate the adequacy of proposed buffering, screening and mitigation at the completion of construction of the solar energy system, and similar visual renderings of the projected maturation of the buffering/screening during all four seasons at five years and 10 years after completion." Solar carports shall be considered abandoned after 12 consecutive months without electrical energy generation. All above-ground and below-ground equipment, structures, and foundations must be removed from the property at the owner and/or operators’ expense no later than 90 days after deemed abandoned. A decommissioning plan signed by the owner and/or operator shall be submitted by the applicant, including the anticipated life, all associated removal costs, removal methods, and restoration methods required, prior to issuance of a special exception use permit. The decommissioning plan shall state that the site shall be restored to its previous condition, including surface grade, soil, vegetation, or pavement, within six months of the removal. As part of the decommissioning plan, the applicant shall be required to post with the Town, as a condition precedent to receiving all necessary approvals, a performance bond approved by the Town Board of no less than 125% of the estimated removal costs. The applicant shall acknowledge that should the removal not occur in accordance with the plan, the bond shall be forfeited to the Town, which shall then utilize the funds to undertake or complete the decommissioning plan. The bond shall remain in effect until restoration of the property, as set forth in the decommissioning plan, is completed.

Solar carports, defined as ground-mounted solar energy systems that cover parking facilities, are permitted in specified business, industrial, and residential zones and must be installed by a qualified solar installer. Specifically, solar carports "shall be designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare within airport approach zones, adjacent street rights-of-way, or any habitable or occupiable buildings on adjacent properties." Additionally, solar carports must be connected to the utility grid and provide a "proof of concept letter" from the local utility company acknowledging interconnection to sell electricity. Other conditions include restrictions on location (e.g., not permitted in certain residential zones or sensitive areas), height limits (maximum 20 feet), minimum clearances, landscaping buffers, and prohibition of battery energy storage systems on site.

Under § 213-576.C.(7) Signs, "No signage or graphic content shall be displayed on solar carport structures except for the manufacturer’s badge, safety information, and equipment specification information, along with yellow caution signs on structure bases and minimum clearance height." Solar carports must be "connected to the utility grid and shall provide a 'proof of concept letter' from the local utility company acknowledging the solar energy production facility will be interconnected to the utility grid in order to sell electricity to the public utility entity."

The ordinance requires that all solar carports shall be a minimum of 25 feet away from the nearest building or structure and there shall be a minimum side yard and rear yard setback of 25 feet from residential properties. summary: Section 8(c)(x) requires that "A visual screen of the large-scale solar system from residential uses shall be accomplished, to the extent practicable, by the use of berms, landscaping, or other means, as determined by the Town Board." Additionally, section 8(c)(v) mandates that "All large scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access," with fencing height and type determined by the Town Board. The ordinance also limits removal of existing vegetation "to the extent necessary for the construction and maintenance of the solar installation" (8(c)(viii)).

All large scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing. The height and type of fencing shall be determined by the Town Board and must meet the minimum requirements of the Building Code.

Section 8(b)(v) requires "A stormwater, erosion, and slope analysis of the land shall be required to be assessed by a New York State licensed professional engineer for the site and any road used to access the site." The applicant must "comply with the State Pollutant Discharge Elimination System guidelines." A "SWPPP (Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan) shall be prepared, if determined to be required, and all local stormwater regulations shall be complied with." Additionally, Section 8(c)(viii) states "The removal of existing vegetation shall be limited to the extent necessary for the construction and maintenance of the solar installation." Section 8(c)(ix) requires "Vehicular paths must be designed to minimize the extent of impervious materials and soil compaction." These requirements apply specifically to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, defined as systems "used primarily to convert solar energy into electricity for off-site consumption or sale and/or systems that have the capacity to produce more than 25 kW per hour of energy."

Large Scale Solar Systems are permitted by the issuance of a special use permit by the Town Board within the Agricultural (A) District, subject to the requirements set forth in this section. Every application for a Large-Scale System within the Town of Boston shall be made to the Town Board and shall be approved by a majority vote thereof. Prior to Town Board review, the application may be referred to the Planning Board for site plan review, report, and recommendation. The Town Board shall hold a public hearing before granting the special use permit. The ordinance details application requirements, special use permit standards, and conditions including minimum lot area, maximum height, setbacks, fencing, underground electrical lines, open space preservation, vegetation removal limits, vehicular path design, and visual screening. Other solar energy systems such as small-scale or accessory systems are permitted in other districts or as accessory uses but do not require special use permits. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this summary per instructions.

For Large Scale Solar Energy Systems, the ordinance requires that the system "Must be located at least 250 feet from any building or structure, unless said building is used for the actual operation of the large-scale solar energy system." Other setback distances mentioned include 500 feet from property lines bordering a residential district, 100 feet from all property lines, 200 feet from any public road or railroad, and 750 feet from any school or public park, but these do not pertain directly to occupied dwellings, buildings, or structures.

Section 8(b)(vi) requires that "A visual assessment analysis of the impact of the facility on the community shall be prepared if requested by the Planning Board or Town Board" as part of the Special Use Permit application for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems are defined as "Solar energy systems located on land in the Town of Boston used primarily to convert solar energy into electricity for off-site consumption or sale and/or systems that have the capacity to produce more than 25 kW per hour of energy." The visual assessment is conditional upon a request by the Planning Board or Town Board, not an automatic requirement. Other application requirements include verification of utility notification, blueprints, stormwater and erosion analysis, equipment specifications, operation and maintenance plan, and a decommissioning plan. Small-scale and building-integrated systems are exempt from SEQRA and do not have this visual assessment requirement.

A Large-Scale Solar Energy System that is ground mounted shall not exceed 70 percent of the lot on which it is installed. The surface area covered by Solar Panels shall be included in total lot coverage. This is found in Section (5) C. 3. For comparison, ground-mounted Solar Energy Systems primarily for onsite use are also limited to 70 percent lot coverage, but the 70 percent limit specifically applies to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems as a maximum land coverage restriction.

summary: A Large-Scale Solar Energy System that is ground-mounted shall not exceed eighty percent (80%) coverage of the lot on which it is installed. Other coverage limits mentioned apply only to smaller or residential systems, such as a 10% lot coverage limit for ground-mounted systems on residential properties.

Section 41 requires a Decommissioning Plan as part of the special use permit application for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. The plan "must specify that after Large-Scale Solar Energy System has not used the electrical energy produced at that site for a twelve (12) month period and can no longer be used, it shall be removed by the applicant and any subsequent owner." It must "demonstrate how the removal of all infrastructure and the remediation of soil and vegetation shall be conducted to return the parcel to its original state prior to construction," include "an expected timeline for execution," and provide "a cost estimate detailing the projected cost of executing the Decommissioning Plan" prepared by a Professional Engineer or Contractor. Section 46 states that "Solar Energy Systems are considered abandoned after twelve (12) consecutive months of discontinued use to generate electrical energy at that site and all equipment above grade and to a depth of four (4) feet below grade shall be removed from the site." The soil must be "recompacted to a depth of two (2) feet, regraded and reseeded to resemble its original state" within one year of cessation. Applications for a six-month extension may be requested. Financial assurance is required: "The applicant and his successors and assigns shall continuously maintain a bond or fund in the amount of the decommissioning costs... payable to the Town for the removal and restoration of the non-functional or inoperable device." This assurance must be in place "before the commencement of construction" and is reviewed every two years. It may be in the form of "a letter of credit, a bond, escrow account, a parent guarantee or other form approved by the Town." A special permit application will not be processed without proof of deposit. These requirements apply explicitly to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems as defined in Section 40: "A Solar Energy System that is ground-mounted and produces more than one hundred ten percent (110%) of energy used onsite and developed primarily for the purpose of offsite sale or consumption."

No solar energy production facility shall be located in certain sensitive areas unless a special permit is granted by the Town Board.

All applications for a solar energy production facility shall be accompanied by a decommissioning plan to be implemented upon abandonment, or cessation of activity, or in conjunction with removal of the solar energy production facility or structure. Prior to issuance of a building permit, the owner or operator shall post a performance bond or other suitable guarantee in a face amount of not less than 150% of the estimated cost to ensure removal of the facility or structure in accordance with the decommissioning plan. If the applicant ceases operation for 12 months or begins but does not complete construction within 12 months after final site plan approval, a decommissioning plan must ensure site restoration including removal of equipment, restoration of surface grade and soil, and revegetation with native seed mixes. If construction is not completed within 18 months, the Town may require completion or implementation of the decommissioning plan within 180 days. Upon cessation of activity for one year, the owner/operator must restore operation to 80% capacity or implement the decommissioning plan within 180 days. Failure to comply allows the Town to restore the site at the owner's expense, with costs assessed as a lien and tax on the property.

All mechanical equipment of a principal solar energy production facility, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight-foot-high anchored mini-mesh chain-link fence with two-foot tip out and a self-locking gate. Said fence shall contain five-inch-high by sixteen-inch-wide grade-level cutouts every 75 feet to permit small animals to move freely into and out of the site. Landscape screening shall be provided in accordance with the landscaping provisions of this chapter. This fencing requirement applies to solar energy production facilities as principal uses with a minimum lot area of five acres and maximum height of 20 feet for freestanding solar panels. Other requirements include a minimum twenty-five-foot perimeter buffer and a minimum 100-foot setback from any residential dwelling or zone.

All solar energy production facilities shall be designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare toward any inhabited buildings on adjacent properties as well as adjacent street rights-of-way (§ 85-813B(4)(f)). This applies to solar energy production facilities permitted as principal uses with a minimum lot area of five acres and height restrictions not exceeding 20 feet (§ 85-813B(1), (2)). Other special permit criteria include buffer and setback restrictions, design standards, fencing, proof of utility interconnection, debris removal, lighting standards, fire access, stormwater management, and soil/material removal (§ 85-813B).

The maximum height for freestanding solar panels located on the ground or attached to a framework located on the ground shall not exceed 20 feet in height above the ground. This applies to solar energy production facilities, which are utility-scale systems intended for electricity generation and sale, as indicated by the special permit criteria in § 85-813 B(2).

The minimum lot area for a solar energy production facility shall be five acres (§ 85-813B(1)). This applies to solar energy production facilities intended for offsite electricity generation or sale. The unit 'acres' is explicitly stated as the area measurement.

No specific zoning districts are unconditionally prohibited for utility-scale solar energy systems. However, solar energy production facilities "shall not be located in the areas listed in Subsection A(2) below unless a special permit is granted by the Town Board." These areas include: "One-hundred-year flood hazard zones considered a V or AE Zone on the FEMA Flood Maps," "Historic and/or culturally significant resources, in an historic district, or historic district transition zone," "Within 100 feet landward of a tidal or freshwater wetlands," "Adjacent to, or within, the control zone of any airport, subject to approval by the Federal Aviation Administration," and "Within the Manorville Farm Protection Area or Eastport Farm Protection Area." A minimum twenty-five-foot perimeter buffer, consisting of natural and undisturbed vegetation, supplemented with evergreen plantings in accordance with Town standards, as needed, shall be provided around all mechanical equipment and solar panel arrays to provide screening from adjacent residential properties and Town, county and state roads. Additionally, a minimum setback for a solar energy production facility and equipment used in conjunction with the solar energy production facility shall be located at least 100 feet from any residential dwelling or zone. The 25-foot perimeter buffer is the most directly applicable fixed setback distance related to the facility perimeter.

A minimum twenty-five-foot perimeter buffer, consisting of natural and undisturbed vegetation, supplemented with evergreen plantings in accordance with Town standards, as needed, shall be provided around all mechanical equipment and solar panel arrays to provide screening from adjacent residential properties and Town, county and state roads (§ 85-813B(3)(a)). Additionally, all solar energy production facilities shall be designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare toward adjacent street rights-of-way (§ 85-813B(3)(f)).

§ 85-813B(3)(a) requires "a minimum twenty-five-foot perimeter buffer, consisting of natural and undisturbed vegetation, supplemented with evergreen plantings in accordance with Town standards, as needed," around all mechanical equipment and solar panel arrays to provide screening from adjacent residential properties and Town, county and state roads. The ordinance requires that "ground cover under, between, and adjacent to the rows of solar panels shall be required and shall consist of low-maintenance, native, non-fertilizer-dependent grasses and wildflowers" to "reduce erosion, runoff of stormwater." Roadways "shall not be constructed of impervious materials and shall be designed to minimize the extent of roadways constructed and soil compaction." Additionally, "all stormwater and drainage shall be contained on site in accordance with the Town's green landscaping and design standards." These requirements apply to solar energy production facilities, which must have a minimum lot area of five acres and are subject to special permit criteria. Other conditions include height restrictions, buffer and setback requirements, design standards limiting clearing, fencing, and decommissioning plans, but these do not directly address soil, erosion, or sediment control.

A solar energy production facility may be permitted as a principal use or accessory use in any L Industrial 1, L Industrial 2, J Business 2, J Business 5 and J Business 4 District when authorized by special permit from the Board of Appeals subject to the requirements of §§ 85-813B and 85-57 of this chapter. No solar energy production facility shall be located in the areas listed in Subsection A(2) below unless a special permit is granted by the Town Board. Said uses shall be subject to the criteria as set forth in Article VI, § 85-68. Areas of potential sensitivity include flood hazard zones, historic districts, wetlands, airport control zones, and farm protection areas. Solar energy collection systems as accessory uses are permitted in additional districts but are not considered utility-scale systems.

A minimum setback for a solar energy production facility and equipment used in conjunction with the solar energy production facility shall be located at least 100 feet from any residential dwelling or zone (§ 85-813B(3)(b)). Additionally, a minimum twenty-five-foot perimeter buffer shall be provided around all mechanical equipment and solar panel arrays to provide screening from adjacent residential properties (§ 85-813B(3)(a)). These requirements apply to utility-scale solar energy production facilities, which must have a minimum lot area of five acres (§ 85-813B(1)) and are subject to special permit criteria.

No solar energy production facility shall be located within 100 feet landward of a tidal or freshwater wetlands unless a special permit is granted by the Town Board (§ 85-813 A(2)(c)). This setback applies to utility-scale solar energy production facilities permitted as principal or accessory uses in specified industrial and business districts. Other areas of potential sensitivity listed include 100-year flood hazard zones, historic resources, airport control zones, and farm protection areas, but these do not specify setback distances from lakes, reservoirs, streams, or rivers.

The ordinance explicitly requires a decommissioning plan for major solar energy systems, which must be included in the site plan application (§ 173-5(A)(19)). The plan must ensure site restoration, including removal of all above-ground equipment, restoration of soil and vegetation, a timeline for decommissioning, estimated costs with contingency, and financial surety (§ 173-5(A)(19)(a)-(l)). The operator must provide a letter of credit, performance bond, or other security covering 150% of the estimated decommissioning cost, certified by a licensed professional engineer (§ 173-6(A)). The surety remains in effect until the decommissioning plan is fully implemented and any road damage repaired (§ 173-6(B)-(C)). The permit is valid for 24 months with possible extensions, and if construction is not completed or the system ceases operation, the Village may require implementation of the decommissioning plan within 150 days (§ 173-7(A)-(B)). Failure to implement allows the Village to perform decommissioning and recover costs from the operator, owner, or financial security (§ 173-7(C)). The decommissioning plan and agreement must be recorded as an irrevocable deed restriction benefiting the Village (§ 173-5(D)(4)).

Removal must be completed in accordance with the decommissioning plan and agreement. If not decommissioned after abandonment, the Town may remove the system and impose a lien to cover costs. Systems are considered abandoned if not maintained, a safety risk, or after one year without electrical generation or storage, with possible six-month extensions reviewed by the Planning Board. If the system ceases to perform for more than 12 consecutive months, the owner must remove it within 90 days and restore the site within one year. Failure to comply results in enforcement action. The applicant may be required to provide financial sureties, including a bond amounting to 110% of removal and restoration costs, updated for inflation and changes every five years, in a form acceptable to the Town Attorney.

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for commercial solar projects under § 165-104.7O. It requires "the submission of an acceptable decommissioning plan and decommissioning bond/security subject to review by the Town's consulting attorneys and engineers and approved by the Town of Cazenovia." Decommissioning events triggering removal include: a) if construction and installation are not completed within 18 months of commencement; b) if the solar energy facility ceases to be used for its intended purpose for 12 consecutive months; c) at the time of decommissioning, complete removal of the project within 90 days thereafter (except for certain access roads or buried conduit); d) upon the end of the project's operation; e) if the applicant seeks dissolution or bankruptcy; or f) failure to maintain adequate decommissioning securities. The plan must include "complete removal of above-ground and below-ground equipment, fencing, structures, and foundations," "restoration of the surface grade and soil," replanting of trees, herbaceous revegetation with native seed mixes, and address the lifespan and disposal of solar storage batteries if applicable. The applicant must file and record the plan against the property. The bond/security must be from a highly rated company, be no less than 150% of the removal and restoration cost, cover the projected life plus two years, and be renewed regularly. The bond covers removal, restoration, and replacement of screening plantings. These requirements apply specifically to commercial solar projects, which are defined and regulated in the same article and are typically 1 MW and above projects.
section: § 165-104.7O Decommissioning and removal of commercial solar project facilities

summary: Commercial solar projects shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access, with "HIGH VOLTAGE" placards affixed every 50 feet, and as otherwise approved by the Planning Board. Style and type of fence shall be approved by the Planning Board as part of the site plan. Fence height shall be established at a minimum of seven feet, subject to Planning Board approval. Proposed fencing shall be designed to allow periodic low level gaps (no greater than 12 inches from ground level) to accommodate wildlife movement for smaller species.

The height of the solar panel array shall not exceed 12 feet at its highest tilt measured from the ground and including any base or supporting materials. However, the Planning Board may consider heights in excess of 12 feet in circumstances when active agricultural uses are proposed for the life of the lease, but in no case shall panel height exceed 20 feet. This restriction applies specifically to commercial solar projects of one megawatt (1 MW) and above.

The ordinance requires a minimum lot area of 50 contiguous acres under single ownership (when such parcel is not bisected by a public road) for commercial solar projects. This is explicitly stated in § 165-104.7C(2): 'Minimum lot area: 50 contiguous acres under single ownership (when such parcel is not bisected by a public road).' Other related requirements include minimum street frontage of 300 feet and various setback distances, but the minimum lot size is specifically 50 acres.

The ordinance states in § 165-104.7 Commercial solar projects, subsection F(1)(y): "In no instance shall noise exceed 50 dB as measured from the subject parcel's property line." This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for commercial solar projects of one megawatt (1 MW) and above. The text uses 'dB' as the unit for noise level, which is the standard unit for sound measurement. No other noise level values or units are provided for commercial solar projects in the text.

Specifically, § 165-104.7E(1)(g) states: "Screening, including plantings, berms, and other screening methods, may be required to mitigate any unavoidable impacts. Such plantings and screening shall be continuously maintained and replaced if dead, dying, or falling into disrepair." summary: Ground-Mounted Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted as principal and accessory uses through the issuance of a Conditional Permit within Agriculture and Industrial Zoning Districts, subject to the requirements set forth in this section. Specifically, 'Ground-Mounted Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted as principal and accessory uses through the issuance of a Conditional Permit within Agriculture and Industrial Zoning Districts.' Additionally, systems producing electricity primarily for active farming uses under 110% of farm use are exempt from the Conditional Permit requirement. Other uses such as Building-Mounted Solar Energy Systems are permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts when attached to lawfully permitted buildings, and Ground-Mounted Small-Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted as principal and accessory structures in all zoning districts. However, Ground-Mounted Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems are limited to Agriculture and Industrial districts for accessory use status.

Section K (Abandonment and Decommissioning) requires that at the time of submittal of the application for a Conditional Permit for a Ground-Mounted Large-Scale Solar Energy System, the Solar Energy Applicant shall submit and agree to the performance of a decommissioning plan that includes the removal of the Solar Energy System and all associated equipment, driveways, structures, buildings, equipment sheds, lighting, utilities, fencing, and gates. If such System becomes technologically obsolete or ceases to perform its originally intended function for more than six (6) consecutive months, the Town may require its removal in accordance with the decommissioning plan. The Town shall provide the Solar Energy System Owner thirty (30) days prior written notice of a request for decommissioning. Upon removal, the land shall be restored to its previous condition. Additionally, at the time of obtaining a building permit, the Solar Energy Applicant may be required to provide a financial security bond or other form of financial security acceptable to the Town for removal and property restoration, with the Town as obligee. The Town Board may adjust the bond amount upon amendment of the Conditional Permit. If the system is not decommissioned after being considered abandoned, the Town may remove the system and restore the property and impose a lien to recover costs. Other Solar Energy Systems (not Ground-Mounted Large-Scale) are considered abandoned after 6 consecutive months without generation and must be removed, with possible extensions granted by the Town Board for good cause.

Ground-Mounted Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems "shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access." Warning signs with the owner’s name and emergency contact information "shall be placed on any access point to the system and on the perimeter of the fencing." The fencing and the system "shall be further screened by any landscaping or decorative fencing needed to avoid adverse aesthetic impacts as approved by the Town Planning Board." This fencing requirement is specific to Ground-Mounted Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Other types of solar energy systems, such as Building-Mounted Solar Energy Systems and Ground-Mounted Small-Scale Solar Energy Systems, do not have explicit fencing requirements stated in the ordinance. The ordinance also allows for motion-activated or staff-activated security lighting around the equipment area and may require a locked gate at the intersection of the access way and a public road, provided the gate is located entirely upon the lot and not on the public right-of-way.

Additionally, these systems "shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access" and "further screened by any landscaping or decorative fencing needed to avoid adverse aesthetic impacts as approved by the Town Planning Board." These requirements are part of the Conditional Use Design and Installation Standards that apply to Ground-Mounted Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, which are permitted through a Conditional Permit in Agriculture and Industrial Zoning Districts. summary: Section I. Signage and/or Graphic Content requires that "No signage or graphic content may be displayed on the solar PV system except the manufacturer’s badge, safety information and equipment specification information" within an area no more than thirty-six (36) square inches. "Disconnect and other emergency shutoff information will be clearly displayed on a light reflective surface." "24 hour emergency contact information will be clearly displayed." Additionally, "Systems and sites may not be used for displaying advertising except for reasonable identification of the owner/operator and shall comply with all signage restrictions." Other options and conditions in the ordinance include distinctions between Building-Mounted Solar Energy Systems, Ground-Mounted Small-Scale Solar Energy Systems, and Ground-Mounted Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, with the latter requiring a Conditional Permit and subject to various location, height, setback, and design standards, but the signage requirements explicitly apply to the systems generally and are detailed in section I.

Ground-Mounted Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted as principal and accessory uses through the issuance of a Conditional Permit within Agriculture and Industrial Zoning Districts, subject to the requirements set forth in this section. "Ground-Mounted Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems that produce electricity or thermal energy primarily for active farming or agricultural uses, where the generation is less than one hundred and ten percent (110%) of the farm use, shall be exempt from the requirement to obtain a Conditional Permit." They shall not be located in certain sensitive areas unless approved by the Town Planning Board in conjunction with the Conditional Permit approval process. The Conditional Permit requires demonstration that the system "conforms to all federal and state laws," "is designed and constructed in a manner which minimizes visual impact," "complies with all other requirements of the Town of Cortlandville Zoning Law," "conforms to all adopted plans of the Town of Cortlandville," "complies with a fifty-foot (50) front yard, rear yard, and side yard setback," "does not exceed twenty (20) feet in height," and "has a solar collector surface area... that does not exceed twice the maximum lot coverage as permitted in the underlying zoning district." Other solar energy systems such as Building-Mounted Solar Energy Systems are permitted as accessory uses in all districts without a Conditional Permit (except in certain height increase cases), and Ground-Mounted Small-Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted as principal and accessory structures in all zoning districts and are generally exempt from Conditional Permit requirements except in specified sensitive areas.

The ordinance requires that Ground-Mounted Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems "shall have the least visual effect practical on the environment, as determined by the Town Planning Board." The Planning Board may require "line-of-sight drawings, detailed elevation maps, visual simulations, before and after renderings, and alternate designs to more clearly identify adverse impacts for the purpose of their mitigation." These requirements are part of the Conditional Use Design and Installation Standards. Additionally, no Conditional Permit shall be granted unless the applicant "is designed and constructed in a manner which minimizes visual impact to the extent practical." Other options and conditions include exemptions from Conditional Permits for systems producing less than 110% of farm use energy, and location restrictions such as avoidance of prime farmland soils, environmental sensitivity areas, and slopes greater than 15% unless mitigated.
