summary: Utility-scale solar energy systems are subject to decommissioning requirements under § 137-25.2.1H(3). The applicant and property owner must agree in writing to remove the solar energy system and all associated equipment and structures if the system ceases to be used for its intended purpose for 12 consecutive months, with removal to be completed within six months thereafter. A decommissioning plan must be submitted as part of the application, specifying removal procedures, site remediation, a timeline (no greater than six months after cessation), and a cost estimate prepared by a professional engineer or contractor. Compliance with the approved decommissioning plan is a condition of the special permit. Additionally, the applicant must provide security acceptable to the Town to cover removal and restoration costs, which is subject to reevaluation every five years. Owners and operators are jointly and severally liable for costs exceeding the security, and the Town may place a lien on the property to recover costs. These requirements apply specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems, defined as "A solar energy system that produces energy primarily for the purpose of off-site sale or consumption." Other solar energy systems such as large-scale and small-scale systems have removal requirements if unused for 12 consecutive months, but with different timelines (three months) and no detailed decommissioning plan or security requirements.

For Utility-scale solar energy systems, the ordinance requires that "The entire solar energy system shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing at a height of at least seven feet in order to restrict unauthorized access. There shall be a six-inch gap at the bottom of the fencing to allow small wildlife access to and from the site." Additionally, the maximum height of fencing is set at eight feet. These requirements are found under § 137-25.2.1H(1)(c) and (a)(7). Other related conditions include dimensional requirements such as setbacks and height limits, special permit use in RA and I zoning districts, and screening requirements to mitigate visual impact.

Utility-scale solar energy systems are permitted as a special permit use in the RA (Residence/Agriculture) and I (Industrial) Zoning Districts and must comply with special conditions and safeguards. Specifically, "Solar panels and equipment shall be designed and sited so as to not reflect glare onto other properties, public roads or private roads or rights-of-way, and shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard." Other requirements include dimensional setbacks, maximum heights, screening, underground power lines, fencing, and decommissioning plans. Large-scale solar energy systems (over 12 kW serving buildings on the lot and adjacent lots) and small-scale solar energy systems (up to 12 kW serving only the building(s) on the lot) have separate provisions but do not explicitly mention glare restrictions.

The ordinance states in § 137-25.2.1H(1)(a) that the maximum height of solar collectors for a utility-scale solar energy system is 12 feet. It also specifies a building height limit of 35 feet, but the more restrictive maximum height for solar collectors is 12 feet. These height limits apply specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems, defined as systems producing energy primarily for off-site sale or consumption. The units for these height restrictions are feet.

The total area of the solar energy system shall not exceed 20 acres. This applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems, which are defined as systems that produce energy primarily for off-site sale or consumption. The relevant text states: 'The total area of the solar energy system shall not exceed 20 acres.' This is found in § 137-25.2.1H(1)(b).

The ordinance requires a front yard setback measured to the visible structural component of the solar energy system nearest to the fronting street(s) with distances of 100 feet from Town and County highways and 150 feet from State highways. The side yard setback is 75 feet from each side lot line, and the rear yard setback is 75 feet from the rear lot line. Specifically: Front yard setback: Town highway: 100 feet; County highway: 100 feet; State highway: 150 feet. Side yard setback (each): 75 feet. Rear yard setback: 75 feet.

Other solar energy system categories such as large-scale and small-scale solar energy systems have different siting, screening, and setback requirements but do not explicitly include signage requirements in the provided text.

Utility-scale solar energy systems are permitted as a special permit use in the RA (Residence/Agriculture) and I (Industrial) Zoning Districts and must comply with special conditions including setbacks, height limits, fencing, and screening. A Large-Scale Solar Energy System that is ground-mounted shall not exceed fifty percent (50%) of the lot on which it is installed. section: SECTION 823      SOLAR ENERGY, subsection D. Approval Standards for Large-Scale Solar Systems as a Special Use, item 3.e

summary: A Decommissioning Plan shall be submitted as part of the application for a Large-Scale Solar Energy System special use permit. The plan must specify that after the system can no longer be used, it shall be removed by the applicant or any subsequent owner, including removal of all infrastructure and remediation of soil and vegetation to return the parcel to its original state prior to construction. The plan shall include an expected timeline and a cost estimate prepared by a Professional Engineer or Contractor, considering inflation. Removal must be completed in accordance with the plan. If the system is abandoned (no electrical generation for six months), the municipality may remove it and impose a lien to cover costs. Appendix 2 specifies a maximum height of 20 feet for Tier 3 systems in Business and Agricultural/Residential districts. Tier 3 systems are not allowed in Residential districts. The height of systems will be measured from the highest natural grade below each solar panel.
section: IV. F. Permitting requirements for Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems

summary: Appendix 1 specifies minimum lot size requirements for Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems: 'Business ≥ 5 acres*' and 'Agricultural / Residential ≥ 5 acres*'. Residential districts do not allow Tier 3 systems ('--: Not Allowed'). The asterisk clarifies that 'Where a Solar Energy System is proposed to be constructed on more than one contiguous participating property, the minimum lot size requirement may be satisfied by aggregating the lot sizes of all participating properties.' The units for the minimum lot size are acres.

Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems are permitted only in Agricultural-Residential (A-R) and Business (B) Districts and only following the issuance of a Tier 3 Solar Special Use Permit and the approval of a site plan pursuant to the site plan application requirements. The Lot Size Requirements table shows Residential district as '--' meaning 'Not Allowed' for Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems. Similarly, the Height Requirements table shows Residential district as '--' for Tier 3 systems, confirming they are not allowed there. Tier 1 and Tier 2 systems have broader permissions, including all zoning districts or Agricultural-Residential districts, but Tier 3 systems are restricted to A-R and B districts only.

The Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems shall meet the following setback requirements: Setbacks from adjacent non-participating residential property lines shall be a minimum of 100 feet. Other setback options include 250 feet from adjacent non-participating residences, 50 feet from adjacent non-participating non-residential property lines, and exemptions for contiguous participating parcels. Fencing, access roads and landscaping may occur within the setback.

The Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems shall meet the following setback requirements: Setbacks from a state roads or highways shall be a minimum of 100 feet from the edge of the right of way. Setbacks from County or Town roads shall be a minimum of 70 feet from the edge of the right of way.

Section 413(F)(4)(o) Screening and Visibility requires that "Solar Energy Systems smaller than 10 acres shall have views minimized from adjacent properties to the extent reasonably practicable using architectural features, earth berms, landscaping, or other screening methods that will harmonize with the character of the property and surrounding area." For "Solar Energy Systems larger than 10 acres," the applicant must "conduct a visual assessment" and "submit a screening & landscaping plan to show adequate screening measures through landscaping, grading, or other means so that views of Solar Panels and Solar Energy Equipment shall be minimized as reasonably practicable from public roadways and adjacent non-participating properties." The plan must specify "locations, elevations, height, plant species, and/or materials" and include "a minimum of 2 evergreen tree species native to New York or naturalized and non-invasive, at least 6 feet tall at time of planting, plus 4 supplemental native or naturalized and non-invasive shrub species." Existing vegetation may be used to satisfy all or part of the requirement. Plant survivorship and visual screening performance standards are also specified. Additionally, Section 413(F)(4)(p)(ii) requires a "vegetation management plan to maintain the landscape screening and native perennial vegetation plantings for the life of the Solar Energy System." Fencing requirements are in Section 413(F)(4)(m). These requirements apply explicitly to Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems not included in Tier 1 or Tier 2 and typically involve larger, commercial-scale installations.

Section 413(F)(4)(e) states: "No signage or graphic content shall be displayed on the Solar Energy Systems except the manufacturer’s name, equipment specification information, safety information, and 24-hour emergency contact information. Said information shall be depicted within an area no more than 8 square feet." Additionally, "As required by National Electric Code (NEC), disconnect and other emergency shutoff information shall be clearly displayed on a light reflective surface. A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations." These signage requirements apply specifically to Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems, which are permitted only in Agricultural-Residential (AR) and Business (B) Districts following issuance of a Tier 3 Solar Special Use Permit and site plan approval. Other tiers have different permitting and design requirements but do not include explicit signage rules as detailed here.

Section 413(F)(2)(k) requires that applications for Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems include "Erosion and sediment control and storm water management plans prepared to New York State Department of Environmental Conservation standards, if applicable, and to such standards as may be established by the Planning Board." The decommissioning plan in Section 413(F)(2)(m) must ensure site restoration including: "disturbed soils must be have subsoils buried and covered by at least 6 inches of native topsoil that is free of large rocks typical of subsoil," and "all soil disturbed during decommissioning will be stabilized within two weeks with a perennial grass stabilization mix applied using standard NYSDEC erosion and sediment control methods and seeding rates applicable for the season, soil type, and slope." These requirements apply specifically to Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems not included in Tier 1 or Tier 2 and require a Tier 3 Solar Special Use Permit and site plan approval. Other tiers have different permitting and exemption conditions, e.g., Tier 1 systems are permitted in all zoning districts and exempt from site plan review, Tier 2 systems are permitted as accessory structures and also exempt from site plan review, and On-Farm Solar Energy Systems have separate conditions.

Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems are permitted only in Agricultural-Residential (A-R) and Business (B) Districts and only following the issuance of a Tier 3 Solar Special Use Permit and the approval of a site plan pursuant to the site plan application requirements set forth in Section 808 and in this Sub-Section. Tier 1 Solar Energy Systems shall be permitted in all zoning districts and Tier 1 and Roof-Mounted or Building Integrated On-Farm Solar Energy Systems shall be permitted in Agricultural-Residential (A-R) Districts, exempt from site plan review. Tier 2 Solar Energy Systems shall be permitted in all zoning districts as accessory structures and Ground-Mounted On-Farm Solar Energy Systems shall be permitted in Agricultural-Residential (A-R) Districts, also exempt from site plan review. For Tier 3, minimum lot size requirements are ≥ 5 acres in Business and Agricultural-Residential districts, and height limits are 20 feet in these districts.

The Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems shall meet the following setback requirements: 1) Setbacks from adjacent non-participating residences shall be a minimum of 250 feet. Other setback options include: 2) Setbacks from adjacent non-participating residential property lines shall be a minimum of 100 feet; 3) Setbacks from state roads or highways shall be a minimum of 100 feet from the edge of the right of way; 4) Setbacks from County or Town roads shall be a minimum of 70 feet from the edge of the right of way; 5) Setbacks from adjacent non-participating non-residential property lines shall be a minimum of 50 feet. Property line and residence setback requirements do not apply to contiguous participating parcels. Fencing, access roads and landscaping may occur within the setback.

For Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems with an area exceeding ten (10) acres, the application must include a visual impact assessment and screening and landscaping plan meeting the standards of Section 413(F)(4)(o)(ii). The visual assessment must include a line-of-sight profile analysis and, depending on the scope and potential significance of the visual impacts, additional impact analyses such as a digital viewshed report. The screening and landscaping plan must show adequate screening measures to minimize views of Solar Panels and Solar Energy Equipment from public roadways and adjacent non-participating properties. For systems smaller than 10 acres, views must be minimized from adjacent properties to the extent reasonably practicable using architectural features, earth berms, landscaping, or other screening methods. These requirements apply only to Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems not included in Tier 1 or Tier 2, and are permitted only in Agricultural-Residential (AR) and Business (B) Districts following issuance of a Tier 3 Solar Special Use Permit and site plan approval.

Freestanding and ground-mounted solar energy systems "shall be screened when possible and practicable through the use of architectural features, earth berms, landscaping, or other screening which will harmonize the character of the property and the surrounding area." This applies to systems that are not attached to existing structures and are subject to site plan review and additional requirements under § 265-65. Other options for solar energy systems include rooftop-mounted systems permitted as of right (§ 265-63 A), building-mounted systems requiring site plan review (§ 265-63 B), and solar thermal systems permitted as of right (§ 265-63 D).
section: § 265-65 Additional requirements for freestanding and ground-mounted systems

summary: The total surface area of all ground-mounted and freestanding solar collectors, including solar photovoltaic cells, panels, and arrays, shall not exceed 80% of the total parcel area. This is the maximum land coverage allowed for commercial solar energy production systems as defined in the ordinance.

Any commercial solar energy production system that is not operated for a continuous period of 24 months shall be deemed abandoned. The owner must remove all components within 90 days of such abandonment or be in violation. The Town may recover removal costs through a surety bond or escrow. All applications must include a decommissioning plan with provisions for restoration of surface grade and soil, restoration with native seed mixes or suitable plant species, retention of access roads, fences, gates or buildings as required, and disposal of solid and hazardous wastes according to regulations. The Zoning Board of Appeals may require a surety bond, escrow account, or other form of surety to cover decommissioning costs, except for municipal or state-owned facilities. The applicant must submit a full cost estimate prepared by a professional engineer. These requirements apply to commercial solar energy production systems defined as systems designed to provide electricity for on-site or off-site use pursuant to a power purchase agreement.

All mechanical equipment of a commercial solar energy system, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, is completely enclosed by a minimum eight-foot-high fence with self-locking gate. This fencing requirement applies to commercial solar energy production systems as defined in the ordinance. Other related requirements include: the system must be on a parcel of not less than five acres; ground-mounted panels shall not exceed eight feet in height unless special circumstances exist; total surface area of solar collectors shall not exceed 80% of the parcel; installation of a vegetated perimeter buffer for year-round screening; prevention of reflective glare; underground placement of utility lines where feasible; visible warning signs on transformers and substations; and various site plan and decommissioning requirements.

All solar energy production systems are designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare toward any habitable buildings as well as streets and rights-of-way. This applies to commercial solar energy production systems defined as systems designed to provide electricity for on-site or off-site use pursuant to a power purchase agreement. Additional requirements include height limits, fencing, vegetated perimeter buffers, and visual impact minimization measures.

The ordinance states: 'All ground-mounted panels shall not exceed the height of eight feet unless the applicant can demonstrate special circumstances exist which warrant exceeding the eight feet height requirement.' This height restriction applies specifically to commercial solar energy production systems. The primary reason for the height restriction is to limit visibility of the structures from neighboring properties.

The commercial solar energy system shall be on a parcel of not less than five acres. This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for commercial solar energy production systems as defined in the ordinance. The unit 'acres' is a standard measure of land area. No other minimum lot size values are provided for commercial solar energy production systems in the text.

The ordinance requires the installation of a vegetated perimeter buffer to provide year-round screening of the system from adjacent properties (§146-79B(5)). Additionally, reasonable efforts must be made to minimize visual impacts by preserving natural vegetation, screening abutting properties, or other appropriate measures (§146-79B(14)). These requirements apply to commercial solar energy production systems, defined as systems designed to provide electricity for on-site or off-site use pursuant to a power purchase agreement. Other related requirements include height limits for ground-mounted panels, fencing of mechanical equipment, and site plan review criteria.

The ordinance requires the installation of a clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations for commercial solar energy production systems. This is stated in subsection B(8): 'The installation of a clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations.' No other signage requirements are explicitly detailed for commercial solar energy production systems in the provided text.

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for commercial solar energy production systems. It states that 'Clearing of natural vegetation shall be limited to what is necessary for the construction, operation and maintenance of ground-mounted solar energy systems or as otherwise prescribed by applicable laws, regulations, and bylaws/ordinances.' Additionally, the decommissioning plan must include 'Restoration of the surface grade and soil after removal of aboveground structures and equipment' and 'Restoration of soil areas with native seed mixes, and/or plant species suitable to the area, which shall not include any invasive species.' These requirements apply to commercial solar energy production systems as defined in the ordinance.

Under § 146-79(B)(14), "Reasonable efforts, as determined by the Zoning Board of Appeals, shall be made to minimize visual impacts by preserving natural vegetation, screening abutting properties, or other appropriate measures." The commercial solar energy production system requires a special use permit and site plan review, with the applicant providing documents including proposed changes to the landscape (§ 146-79(B)(11)) and project site features (§ 146-79(B)(10)). The Zoning Board of Appeals may waive or modify criteria if no detriment to public health, safety and welfare is found (§ 146-79(B)(23)).

The ordinance states: 'The total surface area of said solar energy system on a lot shall not exceed 800 square feet per acre in all zones.' This applies specifically to Large utility-scale solar energy systems, which are defined as systems that are ground mounted and produce energy for off-site consumption or sale. No other maximum system size per unit area values are provided for these systems.

All large utility-scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs with the owner's contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing. Other conditions for large utility-scale solar energy systems include setbacks, maximum height, adherence to codes, prevention of misdirection/reflection of solar rays, nonreflective structures, buried or existing overhead transmission lines, limited artificial lighting, possible berm or landscape screening, and surface area limits.

The design, construction, operation, and maintenance of a utility-scale solar energy system shall prevent the misdirection and/or reflection of solar rays onto neighboring properties, public roads, and public parks in excess of that which already exists (§ 118A-10(F)). Additionally, all structures and devices used to support solar collectors shall be nonreflective and/or painted a subtle or earth-tone color (§ 118A-10(G)). These glare restrictions apply specifically to Large utility-scale solar energy systems, which are defined as any solar energy system that is ground mounted and produces energy for the primary purpose of off-site consumption or sale (§ 118A-4). Other conditions for Large utility-scale solar energy systems include setbacks, maximum height, compliance with codes, impact on habitats, transmission line requirements, lighting restrictions, fencing, signage, screening, and surface area limits (§ 118A-10).

The height of a utility-scale solar energy system shall not exceed 15 feet above grade when oriented at maximum tilt. This applies specifically to Large utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in the text. The relevant provision is found in § 118A-10, subsection B. No other maximum height values for Large utility-scale solar energy systems are provided; other height limits mentioned apply only to smaller or non-commercial systems.

The location of said solar energy system shall be placed no closer than two times the standard setback requirements for an accessory building/structure of the zoning district in which it is located. Additionally, from schools or public parks: a minimum of 750 feet from all property lot lines bordering a school or public park. (Other options include setbacks from public roads and railroads at 150 feet, but these do not pertain to property lines or lot lines.)

Large utility-scale solar energy systems shall be placed no closer than 150 feet from any railroad (measured from the road right-of-way or property line). This setback is in addition to the setback requirements of the underlying district. Other setbacks include no closer than two times the standard setback requirements for an accessory building/structure of the zoning district and a minimum of 750 feet from all property lot lines bordering a school or public park.

For Large utility-scale solar energy systems, the ordinance requires a minimum setback of 150 feet from any public road (measured from the road right-of-way or property line). This is in addition to the setback requirements of the underlying district and a requirement that the system be placed no closer than two times the standard setback requirements for an accessory building/structure of the zoning district. Other setbacks include a minimum of 750 feet from all property lot lines bordering a school or public park.

Large utility-scale solar energy systems "shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access" and "A berm, landscape screen, or other opaque enclosure, or any combination thereof acceptable to the Town capable of screening the site, may be required along any property line that abuts an existing residence." (§ 118A-10 M). Other conditions include setbacks, height limits, nonreflective structures, buried transmission lines, limited artificial lighting, and signage regulations.

All large utility-scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs with the owner's contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing. Any signage used to advertise the solar energy facility shall be in accordance with the Town's signage regulations. (See § 118A-10, subsections K and L.)

Large utility-scale solar energy systems are not a permitted use except by special use permit and shall only be considered in Commercial (C3) and Industrial (I) Zones (§ 118A-5 C, § 118A-10). Ground-mounted solar energy systems are not a permitted use except by special use permit (§ 118A-5 B, § 118A-9). Rooftop-mounted and building-mounted solar energy systems that produce electricity on site for on-site consumption are permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts (§ 118A-5 A, § 118A-7 A, § 118A-8 A). Any inconsistent provisions allowing solar energy systems in other districts are superseded (§ 118A-5 D).

The enclosed or fenced in area of a Large-Scale Solar Energy System shall not exceed 60% of the lot on which it is installed. This is the explicit maximum land coverage restriction for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. No other maximum land coverage values are provided for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. The unit is expressed as a percentage of the lot area.
section: 6. Approval Standards for Large-Scale Solar Systems for a Solar Permit, C. Solar Permit Standards, 4) Lot Coverage

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires a Decommissioning Plan for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, which must be submitted with the Solar Permit application (Section 6.B.7). The plan must include: an estimate of the operational life, identification of the party responsible for decommissioning, description of any agreement with the landowner, a schedule for decommissioning and site restoration, a certified and sealed cost estimate prepared by a qualified engineer, and a financial plan ensuring resources for full decommissioning (Section 7.E.1). Financial surety equal to 125% of the decommissioning cost must be filed prior to building permit issuance and updated every two years (Section 7.E.1.f). A Large-Scale Solar Energy System is deemed abandoned if it fails to generate at least 25% of projected electricity for one year or if construction is not completed within 18 months of the first building permit (Section 7.B). Upon abandonment, the system must be removed within one year in accordance with the approved decommissioning plan (Section 7.C). Removal includes physical removal of all equipment and restoration of the site (Section 7.D). The Town may enforce removal and draw on financial surety if the owner/operator fails to comply (Section 7.F). Annual reports on system capacity and production must be submitted, and failure to do so is a violation (Section 7.E.3).

All Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs with the emergency contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing as required in the judgment of the Planning Board. The type of fencing shall be approved by the Planning Board and shall be a maximum of 8 feet and a minimum of 6 feet in height. (Section 6.C.6) Other related requirements include setbacks for fencing and enclosures: "Any Solar Energy Equipment and any related fencing or other enclosures of a Large-Scale Solar Energy System shall be setback at least thirty (30) feet from the side and back lines of the property owner’s lot and at least one hundred twenty five (125) feet from the centerline of any road bordering on such lot." (Section 6.C.2) Additionally, screening by landscaping may be required to avoid adverse aesthetic impacts (Section 6.C.7).

summary: Section 6.C.1 states: 'Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in height unless a variance is approved by the Planning Board pursuant to the standards set forth in Section 3.1 of the Site Plan Review Law or any successor provisions.' This is the explicit maximum height restriction for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Other height restrictions mentioned apply only to Building-Mounted or Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems that are not Large-Scale. The units for this height restriction are feet.

summary: The ordinance states: 'Large-Scale Energy Systems shall be located on lots with a minimum lot size of 5 acres.' This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems that feed electricity directly into the grid, are ground mounted, and larger than 4,000 square feet in total area. No other minimum lot size values are provided for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems in the text.
section: 6. Approval Standards for Large-Scale Solar Systems for a Solar Permit

summary: Any Solar Energy Equipment and any related fencing or other enclosures of a Large-Scale Solar Energy System shall be setback at least thirty (30) feet from the side and back lines of the property owner’s lot and at least one hundred twenty five (125) feet from the centerline of any road bordering on such lot. In the event the property has no road frontage or is a flag lot, the setback shall be at least thirty (30) feet from all sides of the lot. Other setback options include 125 feet from road centerline and 30 feet from all sides if no road frontage or flag lot.
section: 6. Approval Standards for Large-Scale Solar Systems for a Solar Permit, C. Solar Permit Standards

summary: Any Solar Energy Equipment and any related fencing or other enclosures of a Large-Scale Solar Energy System shall be setback at least one hundred twenty five (125) feet from the centerline of any road bordering on such lot. In the event the property has no road frontage or is a flag lot, the setback shall be at least thirty (30) feet from all sides of the lot. Other setback options include: for non-Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, setbacks are at least fifty (50) feet from the centerline of any road bordering the lot, and twenty (20) feet from all sides if no road frontage or a flag lot.

Section 6.C.6 requires that "All Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access." Section 6.C.7 states that "The Planning Board may require screening by landscaping to avoid adverse aesthetic impacts." These provisions explicitly enact fencing and potential vegetative screening requirements for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems that feed electricity directly into the grid and are larger than 4,000 square feet. No other specific vegetative buffer or screening requirements are detailed, but the Planning Board has discretion to impose landscaping screening to mitigate aesthetic impacts.

Warning signs with the emergency contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing as required in the judgment of the Planning Board." This is the explicit signage requirement for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. No other signage requirements are detailed in the text for such systems.

summary: Upon decommissioning and removal of a Large-Scale Solar Energy System, the ordinance requires: "Restoration of the ground surface and soil; Stabilization and revegetation of the site with native seed mixes and/or plant species (excluding invasive species) to minimize erosion." Additionally, Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems shall not be located "On slopes of greater than fifteen percent (15%), unless the applicant can demonstrate through engineering studies and to the satisfaction of the Planning Board that the proposed development will cause no adverse environmental impact that will not be satisfactorily mitigated."
section: 7. Abandonment and Decommissioning, D. Decommissioning and Removal

summary: The ordinance requires that applications for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems include site plans signed by a registered professional engineer and allows the Planning Board to require screening by landscaping to avoid adverse aesthetic impacts. The Planning Board may employ consultants to examine the application and related documentation, including "visual analysis," to verify the applicant’s conclusions. The Solar Permit application process includes a site plan review pursuant to the Site Plan Review Law, and the Planning Board may impose conditions on approval to enforce standards or discharge obligations under SEQRA. Specifically, Section 6.B.2 requires "Site Plans showing the layout of the Solar Energy System signed by a registered professional engineer licensed in the State of New York." Section 6.C.7 states, "The Planning Board may require screening by landscaping to avoid adverse aesthetic impacts." Section 6.E provides that "The Planning Board, at the expense of the applicant, may employ its own consultant(s) to examine the application and related documentation and make recommendations as to whether the criteria for granting the Solar Permit has been met, including, but not limited to, whether the applicant’s conclusions regarding safety analysis, visual analysis, structural inspection, and storm water management aspects are valid and supported by generally accepted and reliable engineering and technical data and standards." The ordinance does not specify a particular format for a visual impact assessment report but clearly includes visual impact assessment as part of the Planning Board’s review and approval process for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems.
section: 6. Approval Standards for Large-Scale Solar Systems for a Solar Permit

summary: All ground-mounted utility-scale solar energy systems and associated accessory structures and equipment shall not exceed a maximum lot coverage of 20% impervious lot coverage. For the purposes of this section, lot coverage shall be defined as the area measured from the outer edge(s) of the arrays, inverters, batteries, storage cells and all other mechanical equipment used to create solar energy along with all associated buildings and structures.

Section (p) Abandonment and decommissioning requires that "abandoned utility-scale solar energy systems" be removed pursuant to a decommissioning plan. A system is deemed abandoned if it "fails to generate and transmit electricity at a rate of more than 10% of its rated capacity over a continuous period of one year" or "is not completed and functioning within two years of being issued final site plan and special use permit approval." The system owner and/or landowner must "physically remove all components of the system within one year of abandonment" in accordance with an approved decommissioning plan. The plan must include: "an estimate of the anticipated operational life," "a schedule showing the time frame over which decommissioning will occur," "identification of the party responsible for decommissioning," "a cost estimate prepared by a qualified professional engineer," "a financial plan to ensure that financial resources will be available," removal of equipment and foundations, proper disposal of waste, restoration of surface grade and soil, and revegetation with native seed mixes. Financial surety in the form of an irrevocable letter of credit or other security is required and must be maintained throughout the life of the system, with updates every three years. The Town may remove the system and draw on the surety if the owner fails to comply. Annual reports on system capacity and electricity generated must be submitted. Removal permits must be obtained prior to decommissioning or removal. Costs incurred by the Town for removal not covered by surety become a lien and tax on the property. This applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance.
section: § 123-16. Renewable Energy Systems, (p) Abandonment and decommissioning

summary: All utility-scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing which shall be located on the interior of the required vegetative buffer. The Planning Board shall have the right to decide on the type and height of fencing based on the location and screening needs. The fence shall be wildlife friendly and shall have five-inch by twelve-inch openings at ground level spaced no more than 100 feet apart to allow unencumbered travel by small animals.

All solar panels shall have anti-reflective coating(s). Solar panels shall be placed and arranged such that reflected solar radiation or glare shall not be directed onto adjacent buildings, properties or roadways. A minimum 20-foot buffer, consisting of natural vegetation, shall be provided around all mechanical equipment, associated structures, and solar panel arrays to provide screening to adjacent properties and to minimize glare on adjacent properties and roadways. Non-invasive plant species and pollinator-friendly and wildlife-friendly native plants, shrubs, trees, grasses and wildflowers must be used in the vegetative buffer. Existing trees and vegetation may be maintained within such buffer areas except where dead, diseased or as necessary for development or to promote healthy growth, and such trees and vegetation may supplement or satisfy landscaping requirements as applicable. If existing trees and vegetation are disturbed, new plantings shall be provided for the buffer. The buffer shall be maintained for the life of the facility. When a utility-scale solar energy system site adjoins property zoned for residential use, an increase in the required vegetated buffer may be required between the residential lot and site improvements associated with the system. The additional buffer area shall be planted with a mixture of evergreen and deciduous plantings at a height so as to provide, as much as practicable, a visual screen of the ground-mounted system from residential uses. The species type, location and planted height of such landscaping shall be subject to the approval of the Planning Board.

The ordinance states: 'Ground-mounted utility-scale solar energy system arrays shall not exceed [15 feet] in height when oriented to maximum tilt.' This is the explicit maximum height restriction for utility-scale solar energy systems. Other height restrictions mentioned apply only to small-scale systems, such as 'small-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems shall not exceed a height of 12 feet' and rooftop-mounted small-scale systems with different limits. The 15 feet limit applies specifically to utility-scale systems, which are defined and regulated separately in the text.

The ordinance states: 'Ground-mounted utility-scale solar energy systems shall be located on lots with a minimum lot size of 10 acres.' This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for utility-scale solar energy systems. No other minimum lot size values for utility-scale systems are provided. The unit 'acres' is used as the standard area measurement.

summary: Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be allowed in the following Zoning Districts: Heavy Industrial (HI) District and R-40 Residential District west of US Rt. 9W. No utility-scale solar energy system shall be permitted east of US Rt. 9W.

Ground-mounted utility-scale solar energy systems, including all arrays, associated structures and equipment shall be located at least 100 feet from all lot lines. The Planning Board reserves the right to require additional setbacks to adequately buffer adjoining uses and public property.

Section (9)(f) requires "a minimum 20-foot buffer, consisting of natural vegetation, shall be provided around all mechanical equipment, associated structures, and solar panel arrays to provide screening to adjacent properties and to minimize glare on adjacent properties and roadways." The buffer must use "Non-invasive plant species and pollinator-friendly and wildlife-friendly native plants, shrubs, trees, grasses and wildflowers." Existing vegetation may be maintained or supplemented with new plantings. When adjoining residentially zoned property, "an increase in the required vegetated buffer may be required" with "a mixture of evergreen and deciduous plantings at a height so as to provide, as much as practicable, a visual screen of the ground-mounted system from residential uses," subject to Planning Board approval. The Planning Board may require visual assessment analysis including photo simulations. Additionally, fencing "shall be located on the interior of the required vegetative buffer" and be "wildlife friendly." These requirements apply specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance.

All electrical and control equipment shall be labeled. Solar equipment shall not be used for displaying any advertising. All signs, flags, streamers or similar items, both temporary and permanent, are prohibited on solar equipment, except: [1] Manufacturer’s/installer’s identification and/or facility name; [2] Appropriate warning signs and placards; [3] Signs that may be required by a federal agency; and [4] Signs that provide a 24 hour emergency contact phone number.

Utility-scale solar energy systems must be located on sites with "proper drainage and provisions for stormwater control" (§ 123-16 (9)(a)[1]). Existing on-site vegetation "shall be preserved to the maximum extent practicable" (§ 123-16 (9)(a)[5]), and "clear-cutting of all trees in a single continuous area exceeding 20,000 square feet" is prohibited (§ 123-16 (9)(a)[6]). Non-invasive, pollinator-friendly, low-maintenance vegetative groundcover is required under and beneath solar panels (§ 123-16 (9)(g)[1]), and the project area "will be seeded promptly following completion of construction in such a manner as to reduce invasive weed growth and sediment" (§ 123-16 (9)(g)[2]). The use of herbicides and pesticides is "strongly discouraged" (§ 123-16 (9)(g)[3]).
