Applicants seeking to install solar energy farms shall be required to: Conduct a visual assessment of the visual impacts of the solar energy farm on public roadways and adjacent properties. At a minimum, a line-of-sight profile analysis shall be provided. Depending upon the scope and potential significance of the visual impacts, additional impact analyses, including for example a digital viewshed report, shall be required to submitted by the applicant. Submit a screening and landscaping plan to show adequate measures to screen through landscaping, grading, fencing or other means so that views of solar panels and solar energy equipment shall be minimized as reasonably practical from public roadways and adjacent properties to the extent feasible. The screening and landscaping plan shall specify the locations, elevations, height, plant species, and/or materials that will comprise the structures, landscaping, and/or grading used to screen and/or mitigate any adverse aesthetic effects of the system. The landscaped screening shall be comprised of a minimum of one evergreen tree, at least six feet high at time of planting, plus two supplemental shrubs at the reasonable discretion of the Planning Zoning Commission, all planted within each 10 linear feet of the solar energy farm. Existing vegetation may be used to satisfy all or a portion of the required landscaped screening. The screening and landscaping plan shall specify the locations, elevations, height, plant species, and/or materials that will comprise the structures, landscaping, and/or grading used to screening and/or mitigate any adverse aesthetic effects of the system, following the applicable rules and standards established by the Town Landscape Guide. These requirements apply to large-scale solar farms permitted through conditional use permits in Highway Commercial, Research, Development and Technology, Riverfront Recreation/Commercial and Airport Districts, subject to site plan approval. The Planning and Zoning Commission may impose conditions on approval to enforce these standards or discharge obligations under SEQRA.
section: § 270-24.1. Overlay zoning districts. D. Solar Energy Farm Overlay District.

summary: The Town of Gorham enacts a moratorium that "shall prohibit the review, approval, creation, establishment, placement, relocation, construction, reconstruction, enlargement, modification or erection of any solar farm anywhere within the Town." A "solar farm" is defined as "a solar collection system intended to provide energy for use off site, for example intended to provide electricity to be sold back to the local electric utility company." The moratorium "shall be in effect for a period of one (1) year from the effective date of this Local Law" and may expire earlier if the Town Board enacts a resolution indicating the moratorium is no longer needed. It applies unconditionally to all zoning districts and all real property within the Town. Exceptions include that the Planning Board may review and approve existing special use permits for solar farms only if no modifications are requested. The moratorium prohibits issuance of building permits, certificates of occupancy, and variances related to solar farms. The moratorium "shall take effect immediately upon filing with the New York Department of State." The exact effective date is not provided, so it is unknown if the moratorium has expired as of November 29, 2025.

If a wind or solar energy system ceases to perform its originally intended function for more than 12 consecutive months or construction is not completed within 18 months of final site plan approval, the property owner shall remove the tower, collector, mount and/or associated equipment and facilities by no later than 90 calendar days after the end of the period noted and shall restore the property to its original condition unless good cause is shown for an extension of up to 45 additional days. The developer shall post a decommissioning cash bond with the Town in an amount equal to 150% of the decommissioning and reclamation costs for the entire system, including removal of footings at the Town Engineer's discretion. The bond must remain valid until decommissioning obligations are met and be reviewed every five years. Decommissioning is expected to follow general requirements including removal of all non-utility-owned equipment, conduits, structures, and foundations to at least three feet below grade; removal of fencing unless requested to remain; restoration of land to pre-construction condition with adequate topsoil; and environmentally responsible disposal or recycling of materials. Alternatively, the Town may require a decommissioning bond or other security in lieu of a cash bond for solar energy systems constructed on existing commercial rooftops, parking structures, brownfields, superfund sites, contaminated sites, or solid waste landfills, with removal of subsurface materials not required in such cases. Additionally, a decommissioning plan must be submitted as part of site plan and special permit applications, identifying the anticipated life of the project, method and process for removal, site restoration, and cost estimates. The responsible party for decommissioning is the property owner unless otherwise specified. Extensions for initiating decommissioning may be granted by the Town Board for up to two additional six-month periods upon demonstration of specific and unique conditions.

All wind and solar energy system installations must be securely fenced. Fencing may be chain-link or other suitable fence acceptable to the Planning Board and consistent with this chapter (§ 97-55F(9)). All fencing greater than four feet in height shall be located 80 feet from all property lines. Fencing shall provide security protection for the facility and may also provide screening of the facility for visual protection of neighboring properties. Fencing shall satisfy all NEC requirements as needed and may be a maximum of eight feet in height, unless otherwise required by the NEC (§ 97-55F(12)(d)).
section: § 97-55F General requirements for all accessory and principal wind, solar and photovoltaic energy systems

summary: All solar and wind energy systems shall be designed and located in order to prevent any unabated reflective glare toward any inhabited buildings on adjacent properties as well as adjacent roadways with sufficient studies submitted to confirm this has been mitigated to the extent practicable (§ 97-55F(6)). The solar collectors shall be located so that any glare is directed away from any adjoining property or street or is otherwise mitigated to extent practicable. Failure to adequately mitigate glare will be reason for rejection of an application for a building permit or site plan approval (§ 97-55F(17)(a)).

A minimum lot size of 10 acres is required for large-scale wind, solar and photovoltaic energy systems as permitted principal uses/structures (§ 97-55 E.(1)). This minimum lot size applies specifically to large-scale systems that would typically be defined as Major Solar Collection System or Solar Farm. Other lot size references in the text pertain to accessory or smaller systems and are not applicable to major systems.

For large-scale wind, solar and photovoltaic energy systems as permitted principal uses/structures, the minimum distance between any portion of a solar or photovoltaic energy facility and a street shall be 100 feet and the minimum distance from any other property line shall be 100 feet (§ 97-55E(2)). For accessory solar energy systems on farms, the minimum distance between any portion of a solar energy facility and a street property line shall be 100 feet, and the minimum distance from any other property line shall be 100 feet, unless a greater setback is required by the Department of Agriculture or any other outside agency (§ 97-55D(3)(a)). Other setback options include 40 feet from side and rear property lines on residential lots or 50 feet on nonresidential lots for ground-mounted or freestanding solar collectors as accessory uses/structures (§ 97-55C(2)(d)), but these apply to smaller or accessory systems. Fencing greater than four feet in height must be located 80 feet from all property lines (§ 97-55F(12)(d)).

The minimum distance between any portion of a solar energy facility and a street property line shall be 100 feet. This applies to large-scale solar energy systems as permitted principal uses/structures (§ 97-55E(2)) and accessory solar energy systems on farms (§ 97-55D(3)(a)). Both sections specify a 100-foot setback from streets (roads or rights-of-way). The ordinance distinguishes this from setbacks to other property lines, which also have a 100-foot minimum but are separate requirements. No height-based multiplier or variable setback distance is specified for road setbacks.

Section 97-55F(12) requires "landscaped vegetative screening... between any ground-mounted solar collectors or any ground-mounted equipment for any energy system and adjacent properties and streets". The purpose is "to obscure or substantially buffer the view of the solar energy system year-round." The screening must include "a minimum of one evergreen tree, at least six feet high at time of planting, plus two supplemental shrubs, all planted within each 10 linear feet of the area to be screened or such other equivalent and appropriate landscape solution as is acceptable to the Planning Board." Existing vegetation may be used to satisfy the requirement. Additionally, fencing requirements are specified, including that "all fencing greater than four feet in height shall be located 80 feet from all property lines" and "may also provide screening of the facility for visual protection of neighboring properties." These requirements apply in the context of large-scale solar energy systems, which are defined as principal uses requiring major site plan approval and special permits (§ 97-55E and § 97-55G(2)(b)).

Wind and solar energy systems and any associated structures shall not be used for displaying any advertising or signage, except for reasonable identification of the operator of the system and appropriate warning signs, with phone numbers for ESO/emergency contacts all not to exceed, in aggregate, four square feet in area per 100 lineal feet of running perimeter. All signs shall be affixed to equipment unless otherwise authorized by the approving authority (Building Inspector or Planning Board). The installation of a clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers, substations and battery storage facilities.
section: § 97-55F General requirements for all accessory and principal wind, solar and photovoltaic energy systems

summary: Site plan applications for wind, solar or photovoltaic energy systems must include "measures for containing drainage onsite and erosion and sediment control" and all grading must comply with Town Code Chapter 53 (§ 97-55G(3)(o)). Upon decommissioning, the land must be restored to its original condition, including "an adequate layer of topsoil where existing topsoil has been removed or eroded" (§ 97-55F(13)(c)). Ground areas beneath solar panels "shall be planted with a seed mixture of native, noninvasive shade tolerant grasses in order to prevent soil erosion" (§ 97-55F(17)(c)). These requirements apply to large-scale solar energy systems, including Major Solar Collection Systems or Solar Farms, which require site plan and special permit approval (§ 97-55E, § 97-55G(2)(b)).

The ordinance states that "the development of large-scale wind, solar and photovoltaic energy systems shall be a principal use in all zoning districts, subject to major site plan approval by the Planning Board and a special permit from the Town Board." No specific district names or abbreviations are provided. Other options discussed include small or accessory solar energy systems permitted as accessory uses/structures in all zoning districts with various size, height, and setback limitations, and subject to zoning permits or site plan approval depending on compliance. Farms have additional provisions and limitations. Rooftop installations are not permitted for principal use systems.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Major Solar Collection Systems. Prior to removal, a demolition permit must be obtained. The owner/operator must post a surety bond "in an amount and form acceptable to the Town for the purposes of removal in the event the Major Solar Collection System is abandoned," equal to "one hundred twenty-five percent (125%) of the projected cost of removal of the Solar Energy System and restoration of the property with an escalator of two percent (2%) annually for the life of the Solar Energy System." A Decommissioning Plan must be included with the application, specifying removal responsibilities, infrastructure removal, soil and vegetation remediation, waste disposal, an expected timeline "within the 365-day period set forth below," and a cost estimate. A Major Solar Collection System is deemed abandoned after "it has ceased operating for a continuous one (1) year period." Upon cessation of operations for one year, the Town may notify the owner/operator to implement the Decommissioning Plan, with 180 days to restore operation to 80% capacity or begin decommissioning. Failure to comply allows the Town to use the surety or proceed with removal and assess costs against the property. Other options and conditions include: Minor or Accessory Solar Collection Systems have separate decommissioning requirements requiring removal within 90 days after 12 months of non-operation, with Town removal and cost assessment if the owner fails to remove. The ordinance also details special use permit requirements, site plan review, and operational standards for Major Solar Systems.

Fencing may be provided around all equipment and solar collectors to provide screening from adjacent residential properties and roads. Fencing shall not be barbed wire. When fencing will enclose the perimeter of the site or facility, wildlife friendly fencing that allows the passage of small mammals and reptiles and is designed to minimize wildlife injury and death due to entanglement or strangulation shall be used on sites having a solar facility footprint greater than five (5) acres. Exceptions can be made by the Planning Board for sites that have limited surrounding wildlife habitat. All mechanical equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be enclosed by a minimum six-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "Solar collectors and other facilities shall be designed and located in order to minimize reflective glare and/or glint toward any inhabited buildings on adjacent properties and roads." This applies to Major Solar Systems, which are defined as systems "principally used to capture solar energy and convert it to electrical energy to transfer to the public electric grid" and include "one or more freestanding GROUND-MOUNTED or ROOF-MOUNTED solar collector devices." The glare restriction is part of the design standards for Major Solar Systems, which also include height and setback restrictions, fencing requirements, minimizing removal of vegetation, prohibiting removal of prime agricultural soil, underground placement of utility lines where feasible, and other safety and operational requirements.

The maximum height for freestanding solar panels located on the ground or attached to a framework located on the ground shall not exceed 20 feet in height above the ground. This applies specifically to Major Solar Systems as defined in the text. The relevant text states: 'The maximum height for freestanding solar panels located on the ground or attached to a framework located on the ground shall not exceed 20 feet in height above the ground.'
The minimum setback from property lines shall be 25 feet, unless adjacent to residential neighbor. The setback for residential neighbors shall be 100 feet.
section: E: MAJOR SOLAR SYSTEMS, 2. A Major Solar System may be permitted when authorized by site plan review and special use permit from the Town Planning Board subject to the following terms and conditions: a. Height and setback restrictions

summary: For Major Solar Systems, fencing may be provided around all equipment and solar collectors to provide screening from adjacent residential properties and roads. Fencing shall not be barbed wire and must be wildlife friendly on sites greater than five (5) acres, with exceptions by the Planning Board. For ground-mounted and freestanding solar collectors in minor systems, if the side or rear yard is visible from adjacent properties and roads, a solid fence, berm, or vegetative screening that conforms to local requirements may be installed to minimize visual impact. No explicit vegetative buffer requirement is mandated for Major Solar Systems.

A sign not to exceed twelve square feet shall be displayed on or near the main access point and shall list the facility name, owner and phone number. A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations not to exceed four (4) square feet.

Major Solar Systems must minimize the displacement of prime soils that are in active agricultural production and removal of any prime agricultural soil from the subject parcel is prohibited. The site plan must depict the location and extent of prime soils, soils of statewide importance, current agricultural uses, diversions, ditches, and tile drainage. A plan for clearing and/or grading the site and Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) must be included. The Decommissioning Plan must demonstrate how the removal of all infrastructures and the remediation of soil and vegetation shall be conducted to return the parcel to its original state prior to construction, including decompaction of soils to a depth of 18 to 24 inches, regrading, and reseeding the site. These requirements apply to Major Solar Collection Systems permitted through special use permit and site plan review in Commercial and Rural zoning districts. Other conditions include height and setback restrictions, fencing requirements, underground utility placement, glare minimization, safety measures, and decommissioning bonding and plans.

Major Solar Systems are permitted through the issuance of a special use permit in Commercial and Rural zoning districts and site plan review in accordance with this chapter. A Major Solar System may be permitted when authorized by site plan review and special use permit from the Town Planning Board subject to terms and conditions including height and setback restrictions, design standards, and safety requirements. Other uses mentioned include minor systems permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts, but these do not apply to Major Solar Systems.
For Major Solar Systems, the minimum setback from property lines shall be 25 feet, unless adjacent to a residential neighbor. The setback for residential neighbors shall be 100 feet.
section: E: MAJOR SOLAR SYSTEMS, 2. A Major Solar System may be permitted when authorized by site plan review and special use permit from the Town Planning Board subject to the following terms and conditions: a. Height and setback restrictions

summary: Major Solar Systems are permitted through the issuance of a special use permit in Commercial and Rural zoning districts and site plan review in accordance with this chapter. The site plan shall depict the location and extent of prime soils, current agricultural uses, and include a cross section of any subsurface foundations. A plan for clearing and/or grading the site and Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) must be included. Roadways shall be designed to minimize extent and soil compaction, and on-site utility and transmission lines shall, to the extent feasible, be placed underground. Solar collectors and other facilities shall be designed and located in order to minimize reflective glare and/or glint toward inhabited buildings and roads. The Decommissioning Plan shall include photographs or archival color images of the proposed site plan area to adequately portray the entire property for future reference when soil and vegetation remediation occurs. Site plan approval is required, and blueprints signed by a Professional Engineer or Registered Architect showing the layout of the system must be submitted. These requirements constitute explicit visual impact assessment requirements for Major Solar Collection Systems that a developer must abide by.

The ordinance states: 'The total coverage on a lot, including freestanding solar panels, shall not exceed 80%.' This applies to Major Solar Systems or Solar Farms as defined in the text. The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the lot area. No other maximum land coverage values are provided for Major Solar Systems.

For Major Solar Systems or Solar Farms, "All mechanical equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be enclosed by a minimum six-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate and provided with landscape screening." This fencing requirement is part of the design standards under section E.2.c.vii. Other conditions for Major Solar Systems include: total coverage not exceeding 80%, maximum height of 20 feet, minimum setback of 25 feet (unless adjacent to residential neighbor), landscaped buffer for screening, minimizing removal of trees and prime agricultural soil, underground placement of utility lines where feasible, minimizing glare and glint, and signage requirements.

Under section E.2.c.vi, the ordinance states that 'Solar collectors and other facilities shall be designed and located in order to minimize reflective glare and/or glint toward any inhabited buildings on adjacent properties and roads.' This glare restriction applies specifically to Major Solar Systems or Solar Farms, which are defined as systems 'principally used to capture solar energy and convert it to electrical energy to transfer to the public electric grid in order to sell electricity to or receive a credit from a public utility entity.' Major Solar Systems require a special use permit and site plan review and must meet criteria including coverage limits, height and setback restrictions, landscape buffering, design standards to minimize glare, and other conditions. Other options mentioned include Minor or Accessory Solar Collection Systems and Collective Solar installations, but glare restrictions are explicitly detailed only for Major Solar Systems.

The maximum height for freestanding solar panels located on the ground or attached to a framework located on the ground shall not exceed 20 feet in height above the ground. This applies specifically to Major Solar Systems as defined in the ordinance. (Section E.2.b.i) No other height restrictions for Major Solar Systems are provided.

The minimum lot size required is five acres in the M-1 and M-2 Districts, twenty-five acres in the R-1A District, and fifteen acres in the R1-B, R1-C, and R1-D Districts. These values represent the minimum lot, parcel, or tract size allowed for Major Solar Systems, which include Major Solar Collection Systems or Solar Farms, as explicitly stated in the ordinance. The units for these minimum lot sizes are acres.

The minimum setback from property lines shall be 25 feet, unless adjacent to residential neighbor. (Section E.2.b.ii) This applies to Major Solar Systems or Solar Farms as defined: "An area of land or other area used for a solar collection system principally used to capture solar energy and convert it to electrical energy to transfer to the public electric grid in order to sell electricity to or receive a credit from a public utility entity." Other conditions include maximum height of 20 feet and coverage limits, but no other setback distances from property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, parcels, or subdivisions are specified.

For Major Solar Systems, the ordinance requires 'A landscaped buffer of trees, shrubs or bushes shall be provided around all equipment and solar collectors to provide screening from adjacent residential properties and roads.' Additionally, 'All mechanical equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be enclosed by a minimum six-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate and provided with landscape screening.' These requirements are found under the terms and conditions for Major Solar Systems, which are permitted through special use permit and site plan review in specified zoning districts. Other conditions include maximum height of 20 feet, minimum setbacks, coverage limits, design standards to minimize tree removal and glare, underground utilities where feasible, and signage requirements.

Section E.2.d) Signs requires that "A sign not to exceed eight square feet shall be displayed on or near the main access point and shall list the facility name, owner and phone number." Additionally, "A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations not to exceed four square feet." These signage requirements apply specifically to Major Solar Systems or Solar Farms. Other conditions for Major Solar Systems include special use permit and site plan review, minimum lot sizes, height and setback restrictions, landscaped buffers, design standards to minimize glare and protect agricultural soils, underground utilities where feasible, fencing and screening of mechanical equipment, and prevention of obstruction of solar access to adjacent properties.

Major Solar Systems are permitted through the issuance of a special use permit and site plan review in accordance with this Chapter in the M-1, M-2, R1-A, R1-B, R1-C, and R1-D Districts. The minimum lot size required is five acres in the M-1 and M-2 Districts, twenty-five acres in the R-1A District, and fifteen acres in the R1-B, R1-C, and R1-D Districts. Major Solar Systems must meet criteria including total coverage not exceeding 80%, height restrictions (maximum 20 feet), minimum setbacks (25 feet), landscaped buffers, design standards to minimize environmental impact, and signage requirements. Other solar systems such as minor roof-mounted or ground-mounted systems are permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts but are not considered Major Solar Systems.

Major Solar Systems are permitted through the issuance of a special use permit and site plan review (Section E.1). Design standards require that "Solar collectors and other facilities shall be designed and located in order to minimize reflective glare and/or glint toward any inhabited buildings on adjacent properties and roads" and that "A landscaped buffer of trees, shrubs or bushes shall be provided around all equipment and solar collectors to provide screening from adjacent residential properties and roads" (Section E.2.c.vi and E.2.b.iii). Additionally, "All mechanical equipment... shall be enclosed by a minimum six-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate and provided with landscape screening" (Section E.2.c.vii). Site plan approval and special use permit require submission of a site plan and blueprints signed by a Professional Engineer or Registered Architect (Section F.1.d and F.1.e). These provisions explicitly enact visual impact assessment requirements for Major Solar Collection Systems or Solar Farms. Other conditions include lot size minimums, height and setback restrictions, and operational requirements, but these do not explicitly address visual impact assessment.

Section D(3)(i) Decommissioning requires that Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems "that have been abandoned and/or not producing electricity for a period of six (6) months, or as deemed acceptable by the Building Inspector, shall be removed at the owner and/or operator’s expense." A decommissioning plan must be submitted addressing "the cost of removing the Solar Energy System," "the time required to decommission and remove the Solar Energy System and any ancillary structures," and "the time required to repair any damage caused to the property by the installation and removal of the Solar Energy System." Security in the form of "cash, letter of credit, bond or other form of security reasonably acceptable to the Town Attorney" must be provided in an amount equal to "125% of the cost of removal of the Tier 3 Solar Energy System and restoration of the property with an escalator of 2% annually for the life of the Solar Energy System." In case of default, the security may be forfeited to the Town. Other Tier classifications (Tier 1 and Tier 2) are defined and regulated differently, with Tier 3 systems permitted as principal uses in certain industrial districts and subject to site plan approval and special use permits.

Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems are permitted as a principal permitted use in the General Industrial (IG) zoning district and in the Flexible Office Industrial zoning district upon issuance of a special use permit and site plan approval. Regarding glare, the ordinance explicitly requires that "All Solar panels shall have anti-reflective coating(s)." Other Tier 3 requirements include setbacks of 100’ from the zoning district boundary and 25’ from any property line internal to the district, undergrounding of on-site utility lines to the extent feasible, limited signage, lighting limited to safety and operational purposes, screening from public view, and decommissioning plans with security deposits. Tier 1 systems include Roof-Mounted and Building-Integrated Solar Energy Systems with specific mounting and height requirements and anti-reflective coatings. Tier 2 systems include Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems up to 25 kW AC with anti-reflective coatings and screening requirements.

Tier 3 systems shall be setback 100’ from the zoning district boundary, and 25’ from any property line internal to the district. The setback from property lines internal to the district is 25 feet, which is the most restrictive value directly pertaining to setbacks from property lines. Other setback mentioned is 100 feet from the zoning district boundary.

Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems are subject to screening requirements under section (H) Screening and Visibility: 'Solar installations shall be screened from public view with existing vegetation, topographic features, landscaping in accordance with the Town of Greece Landscape Guidelines for Development, or other means deemed suitable by the Planning Board and/or Board of Zoning Appeals.' Additionally, Tier 3 systems 'may be subject to an assessment of the visual impacts on public roadways and adjacent properties including but not limited to a line of sight profile or viewshed analysis.' Other relevant provisions include setbacks, underground utility requirements, signage restrictions, anti-reflective coating for panels, lighting limitations, and decommissioning plans with security deposits.

For Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems, signage requirements are explicitly stated: 'No signage or graphic content shall be displayed on the Solar Energy Systems except the manufacturers name, equipment specification information, safety information and 24-hour emergency contact information. Said information shall be depicted within an area no more than eight (8) square feet.' Additionally, 'As required by National Electric Code (NEC), disconnect and other emergency shutoff information shall be clearly displayed on a light reflective surface. A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations.' Other provisions for Tier 3 systems include permitted use in certain zoning districts, setbacks, underground utility requirements, anti-reflective coating for panels, lighting limitations, screening and visibility requirements, and decommissioning plans with security deposits. Tier 1 and Tier 2 systems have different permitting and installation requirements but do not have explicit signage requirements detailed here.

Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems are permitted as follows: (a) As a principal permitted use in the General Industrial (IG) zoning district, and subject site plan approval pursuant to the provisions of § 211-60; (b) In the Flexible Office Industrial zoning district, upon issuance of a special use permit by the Board of Zoning Appeals pursuant to the provisions of § 211-60A, and subject site plan approval pursuant to the provisions of § 211-60. The Light Industrial (IL) district does not list Tier 3 systems as permitted or special use, only Tier 2. Therefore, only FOI requires a special use permit for Tier 3 systems, while IG permits Tier 3 as a principal use with site plan approval.

Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems are permitted as a principal use in the General Industrial (IG) zoning district and in the Flexible Office Industrial zoning district with special use permit and site plan approval. They must have setbacks of 100’ from zoning district boundaries and 25’ from internal property lines. All on-site utility lines shall be placed underground to the extent feasible. Signage is limited to manufacturer and safety information within eight (8) square feet. Lighting is limited to safety and operational purposes and must be shielded and downcast. Screening from public view is required using vegetation, topography, landscaping, or other means. Importantly, Tier 3 systems "may be subject to an assessment of the visual impacts on public roadways and adjacent properties including but not limited to a line of sight profile or viewshed analysis."

This ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for commercial solar PV systems, defined as large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems with a rated capacity of 200 kW or more. It requires that abandoned commercial solar PV systems be removed pursuant to a decommissioning plan (§ 205-49A). A system is deemed abandoned if it fails to generate more than 10% of its rated capacity over a continuous period of one year or if construction is not completed within 18 months of the first building permit (§ 205-49B). Upon abandonment, the system must be decommissioned and removed within one year (§ 205-49B(2)). Decommissioning includes physical removal of all equipment and restoration of the site (§ 205-49C). Applications must include a decommissioning plan with an estimate of operational life, responsible party, schedule, cost estimate, and financial plan (§ 205-49E(1)). Financial surety must be filed prior to building permit issuance and every three years thereafter (§ 205-49E(2)). Annual reports on system operation and ownership changes are required (§ 205-49E(3)). The Town may decommission and remove abandoned systems and recover costs from the financial surety or property lien (§ 205-49F). Other solar PV systems not meeting the 200 kW threshold or not classified as commercial are not subject to these decommissioning requirements.

Fences not exceeding eight feet in height, including open-weave chain-link fences and solid fences, shall be permitted for the purpose of screening or enclosing a large-scale ground-mounted solar PV system, provided said system is classified as a principal use for the property on which it is located. Large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems are defined as those with a system capacity greater than 12 kW or generating more than 110% of the kWh's of electricity consumed over the previous twelve-month period by the land use(s) existing on the lot where the system is located. Commercial solar PV systems are large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems with a rated capacity of 200 kW or more. Other options and conditions include: small-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems (limited to 12 kW and generating no more than 110% of the kWh's consumed on the lot) which have different setback and height standards; building-mounted and building-integrated solar PV systems which have specific height and setback requirements but no explicit fencing requirements; and large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems classified as accessory use which are prohibited in front yards and have setback requirements but no explicit fencing provisions. The fencing requirement applies only to large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems classified as a principal use, which aligns with commercial solar PV systems.

Large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems, which are commercial solar PV systems, may not exceed 12 feet in height (§ 205-48C(2)(e)). Building-mounted solar PV systems have height limits such as not exceeding the highest point of the roof on sloped roofs or extending no more than five feet above the roof on flat roofs (§ 205-47B(4) and § 205-48D), but the most restrictive maximum height for commercial systems is 12 feet. The unit for height is feet.

The maximum lot size for large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems, which are commercial solar PV systems, is explicitly stated as 150 acres. Specifically, § 205-48C(2)(f) states: 'The minimum lot size for large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems shall be 20 acres and the maximum lot size shall be 150 acres.' This applies to systems requiring a special use permit and site plan approval, typically commercial in nature. Other related conditions include minimum lot size of 20 acres, lot coverage limits, setbacks, and prohibitions in certain zoning districts.

The minimum lot size for large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems shall be 20 acres (§ 205-48C(2)(f)). This applies to large-scale systems which are typically commercial solar PV systems. Other related conditions include maximum lot size of 150 acres and lot coverage requirements. The text explicitly states 'The minimum lot size for large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems shall be 20 acres.'

No large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems shall be permitted in the Conservation or Commercial Mixed-Use Zoning District (§ 205-48C(2)(j)). Large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems are permitted in the Rural Residential District upon obtaining a special use permit and site plan approval from the Planning Board (§ 205-48C(2)(a)). By-right solar PV systems generating at least 80% of electricity for the land use on the same lot and limited to 12 kW capacity are permitted in any zoning district (§ 205-47A). Systems exceeding these limits or providing electricity off-site require a special use permit (§ 205-48A).

Large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems are subject to the following setbacks: 100 feet front, 150 feet sides, 50 feet rear. No part of a ground-mounted system shall extend into the required yards and/or setbacks due to a tracking system or a short-term or seasonal adjustment in the location, position or orientation of solar-PV-related equipment or parts. If a large-scale ground-mounted solar PV system is located on a lot that adjoins a residential lot, the minimum setback area shall be planted with a mixture of evergreen and deciduous plantings to provide a visual screen. Other setback values include 100 feet front and 50 feet rear.
section: § 205-48 Facilities requiring special use permit, C(2)(b)

summary: For large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems (commercial solar PV systems), if located on a lot adjoining a residential lot, "the minimum setback area, shall be planted with a mixture of evergreen and deciduous plantings at a height so as to provide, as much as practicable, a visual screen of the ground-mounted system from residential uses." The species type, location and planted height of such landscaping shall be subject to the approval of the Planning Board. Additionally, "fences not exceeding eight feet in height, including open-weave chain-link fences and solid fences, shall be permitted for the purpose of screening or enclosing a large-scale ground-mounted solar PV system, provided said system is classified as a principal use for the property on which it is located." These requirements apply to large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems requiring a special use permit and site plan approval. Other options and conditions include: small-scale ground-mounted systems have different setback and height standards (§ 205-48C(1)); building-mounted and building-integrated systems have height and setback standards but no explicit vegetative buffer or screening requirements (§ 205-47 and § 205-48D); and commercial solar PV systems are defined as large-scale ground-mounted systems with rated capacity of 200 kW or more (§ 205-49).

The ordinance applies to large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems with a rated capacity of 200 kW or more, defined as commercial solar PV systems. Upon abandonment, these systems must be decommissioned and removed, including "restoration of the ground surface and soil" and "stabilization and revegetation of the site with native seed mixes and/or plant species (excluding invasive species) to minimize erosion." A decommissioning plan must be submitted with applications, addressing site restoration and financial surety to cover removal costs. The Planning Board may permit leaving certain improvements in place if not detrimental. Failure to remove abandoned systems allows the Town to remove them and recover costs from financial surety or property liens. Other options include extensions of abandonment time if a viable plan is presented, and annual reporting requirements. These requirements are found in the decommissioning and removal provisions for commercial solar PV systems.

All large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems are permitted in the Rural Residential District upon obtaining a special use permit and site plan approval from the Planning Board (§ 205-48B(2)(a)). The ordinance sets specific standards including setbacks (100 feet front, 150 feet sides, 50 feet rear), height limits (may not exceed 12 feet), minimum lot size (20 acres), maximum lot size (150 acres), and lot coverage (20%, no more than 30 acres). Large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems are prohibited in the Conservation or Commercial Mixed-Use Zoning District (§ 205-48C(2)(j)). Other solar PV systems, such as by-right systems, are limited to smaller capacities (12 kW) and accessory uses, while systems exceeding these limits or providing electricity off-site require special use permits (§ 205-47 and § 205-48A).

Section 697.2 Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems explicitly requires decommissioning plans that include: "plans for the removal of all system components, whether above ground or underground." If construction is not completed within 18 months, the Town may require implementation of the decommissioning plan within 180 days. Upon cessation of activity for one year, the owner/operator must either restore operation to 80% capacity or implement the decommissioning plan within 180 days. Failure to comply allows the Town to restore the site and recover costs, which become a lien on the property. These provisions apply specifically to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems defined as systems producing more than 20MW for offsite sale or consumption. Additionally, Section 697.1 requires a decommissioning plan for Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems with detailed provisions including removal of structures, debris, cabling, restoration of soil and vegetation, timetable, cost estimates, financial assurance, and Town access rights. The Large-Scale requirements build upon these Medium-Scale provisions with added enforcement and abandonment triggers.

All Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs with the up-to-date owner’s contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing. The type of fencing shall be approved by the Town Planning Board. Solar equipment shall not be used for displaying any advertising. All application and standards requirements for Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems shall also apply to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems.
section: Section 697.1 Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems and Section 697.2 Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems

summary: All solar collectors and related equipment shall be surfaced, designed, and coated with anti-reflective materials and shall be sited to minimize glare reflected onto adjacent residences and roadways. All application and standards requirements for Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems also apply to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Additionally, all applicants for Medium-Scale and Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems shall conduct a glare analysis to prevent unwanted visual impacts to air control towers and airplane pilots. Proof of written submission of the project plan to the Airfield and Airport are required by the applicant.

Section 586 states: 'Ground – or pole-mounted solar energy systems shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt.' Section 697.2 (Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems) specifies that all application and standards requirements for Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems apply to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, including the height limit. Therefore, the maximum structure height allowed for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems is 20 feet measured from the highest natural grade below each solar panel to its maximum potential height.

Section 697.2.E states: 'Large-Scale Energy Systems shall not collectively occupy more than a total of Five Hundred (500) acres in the Town of Greig. For purposes of this provision,  "total acreage"  shall be calculated based on physical infrastructure. Meaning, allotted acreage within the Town shall be calculated by physical system occupancy, not tax parcel acreage. Additionally, the parcels participating in a Large-Scale Solar Facility must each have a minimum tax parcel acreage of at least twenty (20) acres.' This is the maximum lot size restriction explicitly given for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. The units are acres, and the acreage is based on physical system occupancy rather than tax parcel size.

The parcels participating in a Large-Scale Solar Facility must each have a minimum tax parcel acreage of at least twenty (20) acres. This is explicitly stated in Section 697.2 Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, subsection E: 'Additionally, the parcels participating in a Large-Scale Solar Facility must each have a minimum tax parcel acreage of at least twenty (20) acres.' The units are acres, which is an area measurement. For context, Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems also require a minimum tax parcel acreage of twenty (20) acres.

Enclosure fence shall be located at least 250’ from the side or rear of non-participating property lot lines. Other setback distances include 250’ from the property line of any State Road and 150’ from the property line of any County or Town Road, but these relate to roads, not non-participating property lines.
section: Section 697.1 Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems, L. The following standards shall be required

summary: Solar Energy Systems shall avoid designated wetlands as defined by the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation and/or any Federal Agency to the extent practicable. Impacts that cannot be practicably avoided may be properly permitted or allowed by the applicable regulatory authority. The Town Planning Board shall determine the potential impact on important bird areas, as identified by the New York Audubon Society, other recognized habitats such as any nearby New York State wildlife management areas, and any locally recognized priority habitat areas such as those set aside for bats and any areas considered "sensitive," which may include but not be limited to areas such as bird conservation areas or areas covered under mitigation for species such as grassland birds; and at least 500 feet from state-identified and/or federally-identified wetlands. No Solar Energy System shall be installed on Critical Environmental Areas (CEAs) as defined by the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation. The ordinance does not specify a fixed numeric setback distance from other public conservation lands or preservation areas beyond wetlands, but requires avoidance of CEAs and consultation with environmental agencies.

Section 697.2 Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems requires that "All Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems shall be adequately screened with a combination of vegetative buffers, earth berms, or landscaping from all streets and adjacent residential uses to the extent practicable." It further mandates "Appropriate landscaping and/or site design features, including both the maintenance of existing natural vegetation and the introduction of new plantings consisting of a naturally appearing blend of deciduous and coniferous species, shall be required to help screen the facility and accessory structures from roads, neighboring residences, and other uses." These provisions explicitly impose vegetative buffer and screening requirements for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Other options for screening include earth berms and landscaping, and existing trees may be used to satisfy screening and tree planting requirements.

The ordinance explicitly requires that for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, "The manufacturer or installer’s identification, contact information, and appropriate signage shall be posted at the site and clearly visible. All emergency contact information shall be displayed and updated within 15 days of any changes." This signage requirement is found in Section 697.2(N). Additionally, all Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems must comply with all requirements of Section 586 and Section 697.1 (Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems), which include various application, screening, fencing, and operational standards, but these sections do not explicitly mention signage requirements. The ordinance also details fencing and warning signs for Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems in Section 697.1(M), but this applies specifically to Medium-Scale systems. Therefore, the explicit signage requirement for Large-Scale systems is limited to posting identification and emergency contact information visibly on site.

Section 697.1 requires clearing and grading plans that include methods to stockpile, reduce erosion of topsoil, and reuse all topsoil from the site. If one (1) acre or more of land is to be disturbed, the applicant shall submit a preliminary Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan consistent with NYS DEC or local MS4 requirements. Clearing and/or grading activities are subject to review by the Town Planning Board and shall not commence until the issuance of the Special Use Permit Approval. Section 697.2 states that all application and standards requirements for Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems set forth above shall also apply to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Additionally, Section 697.2(O) requires that following construction of a Large-Scale Solar Energy System, all disturbed areas where the soil has been exposed shall be reseeded with grass and/or planted with low-level vegetation capable of preventing soil erosion and airborne dust. Pollinator-friendly vegetation is preferred.

Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted in the Solar Energy Systems Overlay District through the issuance of a Zoning Permit and a Special Use Permit, in which the Town Planning Board will review each application concurrently, subject to the requirements set forth in this Law. All procedures including, but not limited to, sketch plan review, public hearing, and time frames pursuant to the zoning law shall be met. All application and standards requirements for Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems set forth above shall also apply to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems are also permitted within the Solar Energy System Overlay District, subject to receiving a zoning permit and Special Use Permit from the Town of Greig Planning Board. The text does not mention any other districts or abbreviations where Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted as special use or similar.

Solar Panels shall be placed at least 350’ from an occupied residence not involved in the project. (Section 697.1 L(d)) Additional related setbacks include enclosure fences located at least 250’ from the side or rear of non-participating property lot lines (L(c)). These setbacks apply to Medium-Scale and Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems, with all application and standards requirements for Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems also applying to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems (Section 697.2).

Section 697.1 requires "Photo simulations shall be included showing the proposed Medium-Scale Solar Energy System in relation to the building/site along with elevation views and dimensions, and photo simulations of the proposed Medium-Scale Solar Energy System, solar collectors, and other components." The Town Planning Board "may require photo simulations to be provided from specific roads or other public areas that may be impacted" and "may require an applicant to submit a viewshed analysis that meets the procedures identified within the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation’s SEQRA publication entitled 'Assessing and Mitigating Environmental Impacts.'" Section 697.2 states that "All application and standards requirements for Medium-Scale Solar Energy Systems set forth above shall also apply to Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems." Additionally, Section 697.2 requires that "All Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems shall be adequately screened with a combination of vegetative buffers, earth berms, or landscaping from all streets and adjacent residential uses to the extent practicable."

Solar Energy Systems shall avoid designated wetlands as defined by the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation and/or any Federal Agency to the extent practicable. Impacts that cannot be practicably avoided may be properly permitted or allowed by the applicable regulatory authority. The Town Planning Board shall determine the potential impact on important bird areas, as identified by the New York Audubon Society, other recognized habitats such as any nearby New York State wildlife management areas, and any locally recognized priority habitat areas such as those set aside for bats and any areas considered "sensitive," which may include but not be limited to areas such as bird conservation areas or areas covered under mitigation for species such as grassland birds; and at least 500 feet from state-identified and/or federally-identified wetlands.

Section 5, subsection H ('Abandonment and Decommissioning (Tier 3)') requires that 'Any Tier 3 solar generation facilities which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned consistent with this ordinance shall be removed' within 150 days after discontinued operations. The owner must notify the code enforcement officer by certified mail of the proposed removal date and plans. Removal includes 'Physical removal of all solar generation facilities, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines from the site,' 'Disposal of all solids and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations,' and 'Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion.' The ordinance defines abandonment as failure to operate for more than one year without written consent. The Town may remove abandoned facilities and impose a lien to cover costs. A decommissioning plan must be submitted with the application, specifying removal procedures and timelines. An estimate of decommissioning costs prepared by a qualified engineer and financial surety of 125% of projected costs (with 2% annual escalation) must be provided to ensure funds for decommissioning. These requirements apply explicitly to Tier 3 solar generation facilities, defined as those with 'a total surface area of 2,000 square feet or greater or with an energy capacity of 25 kW or greater' or those including battery storage systems unless accessory to Tier 1 or 2 facilities. Other tiers (Tier 1 and Tier 2) have different application and design requirements but no explicit decommissioning mandates are stated for them.

Section 5, subsection F (Battery Storage System (Tier 3)) states: 'All mechanical equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be enclosed by a minimum six-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate.' This fencing requirement applies specifically to battery storage systems associated with Tier 3 solar generation facilities. Additionally, 'All other relevant design standards that are applicable to the battery and storage system (e.g., screening, safety, set-back, signage, etc.) are to be met as part of site plan approval for the battery and storage system.' No other explicit fencing requirements for Tier 3 solar generation facilities are provided. Other options or conditions related to fencing are not mentioned for Tier 3 facilities beyond battery storage enclosures.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'Free standing ground mounted systems shall not exceed 20 feet in total height from the existing grade.' This applies to Tier 3 solar generation facilities, which are defined as solar generation facilities with a total surface area of 2,000 square feet or greater or with an energy capacity of 25 kW or greater, or those including battery storage systems not accessory to Tier 1 or Tier 2. The unit for this height restriction is feet. Other tiers have similar height restrictions (e.g., Tier 2 ground-mounted systems also limited to 20 feet), but this 20 feet limit is the most restrictive and directly applies to Tier 3 facilities.
section: Section 5. Requirements, Part D. Design Standards (Tier 3)

summary: The minimum setback from the property boundary with residential structures for all Tier 3 solar generation facility components (buildings, structures, and facilities) shall be 250 feet for the front, rear, and side yards of the lot or lots on which the system is proposed. Other setback distances include 200 feet from the front yard and 100 feet from all side and rear lot lines, and 200 feet from the boundary with adjoining lots (excluding residential structures).

Tier 3 community solar generation facilities "shall be fully screened so that they do not detract from the scenic values, scenic viewshed, rural character, or visual qualities of Hadley’s landscape and character." They "shall be screened as necessary with plantings of evergreen and deciduous plantings at a height so as to provide a visual screen of the ground mounted system from residential uses and scenic viewsheds." The "species, type, location, and planted height of such landscaping shall be subject to the approval of the planning board." Additionally, "appropriate landscaping and/or site design features, including berms, the maintenance of existing natural vegetation and the introduction of new plantings consisting of a naturally appearing blend of deciduous and coniferous species, shall be required to screen the Tier 3 community solar generation facility and its accessory structures from scenic roadways, scenic overlay areas, park lands, historic properties, and neighboring residences." These requirements apply to Tier 3 solar generation facilities defined as those with "a total surface area of 2,000 square feet or greater or with an energy capacity of 25 kW or greater."

The ordinance requires that Tier 3 solar generation facilities ("Solar generation facilities with a total surface area of 2,000 square feet or greater or with an energy capacity of 25 kW or greater") submit site plans including "Proposed changes to the landscape of the site, grading, vegetation clearing and planting" and limit "Clearing of natural vegetation ... to what is necessary for the construction, operation, and maintenance of solar generation facility or otherwise prescribed by applicable laws and regulations." The decommissioning plan must "demonstrate how the removal of all infrastructure and the remediation of soil and vegetation shall be conducted to return the parcel to its original state prior to construction" and include "Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion." The operation and maintenance plan must include "measures for maintaining safe access to the installation, stormwater controls, as well as general procedures for operational maintenance of the installation." The Town may require an operation and maintenance bond to ensure "proper operation and maintenance of all stormwater management, site civil and landscaping elements" and may use these funds to address "deficiencies related to erosion and sediment control." These requirements apply specifically to Tier 3 facilities, which are defined as those with 25 kW or greater capacity or 2,000 square feet or greater surface area. Tier 1 and 2 facilities have different, less detailed requirements and do not explicitly mention soil, erosion, or sediment control.

The minimum setback from the property boundary with residential structures for all Tier 3 solar generation facility components (buildings, structures, and facilities) shall be 250 feet for the front, rear, and side yards of the lot or lots on which the system is proposed. Other setback options mentioned include 200 feet from front yard and 100 feet from side and rear lot lines for protection of neighbors, and 200 feet from adjoining lots excluding residential structures, but the 250 feet setback specifically applies to residential structures.

Under Section 5, Part C (Tier 3 Solar Generation Facilities), "at the applicant's expense, the applicant shall provide the planning board with a visual impact assessment, including appropriate simulations and photography assessing the visibility from key viewpoints." The assessment "shall include proposed elevations, taking into account surrounding topography and including visual representation of the required visual mitigation for all season screening." Tier 3 facilities "shall be fully screened so that they do not detract from the scenic values, scenic viewshed, rural character, or visual qualities of Hadley’s landscape and character." The ordinance also requires "appropriate landscaping and/or site design features, including berms, the maintenance of existing natural vegetation and the introduction of new plantings consisting of a naturally appearing blend of deciduous and coniferous species, shall be required to screen the Tier 3 community solar generation facility and its accessory structures from scenic roadways, scenic overlay areas, park lands, historic properties, and neighboring residences." Other tiers (Tier 1 and 2) require building permits and encourage landscape screening but do not explicitly mandate a visual impact assessment. Tier 3 facilities must also submit a site plan and undergo site plan review after Adirondack Park Agency approval.

Section 4.4 Decommissioning states: "Prior to removal of a Major Solar Collection System, a demolition permit for removal activities shall be obtained from the Town of Hammond." It requires a "Decommissioning Bond" where "the owner or operator of the Solar Energy System shall post a surety in an amount and form acceptable to the Town for the purposes of removal in the event the Major Solar Collection System is abandoned." The surety must be "125% of the projected cost (not including salvage value) of removal of the Solar Energy System and restoration of the property with an escalator of 2% annually for the life of the Solar Energy System." The "Decommissioning Plan" must be included with the application and specify removal responsibilities, ownership changes, removal of all infrastructure, soil and vegetation remediation, waste disposal compliance, timeline, and cost estimates. Section 4.5 Abandonment and Removal provides that a Major Solar Collection System "shall be deemed to be abandoned after it has ceased operating for a continuous one (1) year period." Upon notice, the owner/operator has 180 days to restore operation to 80% capacity or implement the Decommissioning Plan. Failure to comply allows the Town to use the surety or proceed with removal and assess costs against the property as a lien and tax. Other options include extensions of up to 180 days reviewed by the Town Board and possible waiver or deferral of removal if deemed in the Town's best interest. These requirements apply specifically to Major Solar Collection Systems, defined as systems "principally used to capture solar energy and convert it to electrical energy to transfer to the public electric grid but also may be for on-site use and is intended to be used for any purpose, other than private, or residential, or agricultural use, including community based systems" and "which generate more than 110% of the energy demand for onsite use."

Section 4.2.1.3 requires that "Fencing shall be provided around all equipment and solar collectors to provide screening from adjacent residential properties and roads." The fencing "shall not be topped with barbed wire." For sites with a solar facility footprint greater than 5 acres, "wildlife friendly fencing that allows the passage of small mammals and reptiles and is designed to minimize wildlife injury and death due to entanglement or strangulation shall be used." Exceptions to this wildlife-friendly fencing can be made by the Planning Board for sites with limited surrounding wildlife habitat and/or designed to accommodate small livestock grazing. Additionally, section 4.2.2.7 mandates that "All mechanical equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be enclosed by a minimum six-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate."

Section 4.2.2.6 states: "Solar collectors and other facilities shall be designed and located in order to minimize reflective glare and/or glint toward any inhabited buildings on adjacent properties and roads." This applies to Major Solar Systems, which require a special permit and site plan review (Section 4). Major Solar Systems are defined as systems "principally used to capture solar energy and convert it to electrical energy to transfer to the public electric grid but also may be for on-site use and is intended to be used for any purpose, other than private, or residential, or agricultural use, including community based systems." Other relevant conditions for Major Solar Systems include height and setback restrictions (max height 20 feet, setbacks 25 feet or 100 feet adjacent to residential neighbors), fencing requirements, design standards to minimize environmental impact, and decommissioning plans. Minor or Accessory Solar Collection Systems have separate provisions and do not have the same glare restrictions explicitly stated.

The maximum height for freestanding solar panels located on the ground or attached to a framework located on the ground shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in height above the ground. This restriction applies specifically to Major Solar Systems, which require a special permit and site plan review. (Section 4.2.1.1) No other height values for Major Solar Collection Systems are provided.

The ordinance explicitly prohibits 'large scale solar' in the 'S Shoreline District' under section 2.1.1.1, which states: 'Industrial, large scale solar, large scale wind, chemical manufacturing, kennels and animal hospitals.' Other districts such as the 'R-A Residential-Agricultural District' list 'Solar Energy Facilities' under 'Uses Requiring Special Permit,' indicating conditional allowance rather than prohibition. The ordinance also includes provisions for minor solar systems, such as roof-mounted and ground-mounted solar collectors, with specific requirements, but these do not apply to utility-scale or large scale solar energy systems.
The minimum setback from property lines shall be twenty-five (25) feet, unless adjacent to residential neighbor. The setback when adjacent to residential neighbors shall be 100 feet.

Section 4.2.1.3 states: "Fencing shall be provided around all equipment and solar collectors to provide screening from adjacent residential properties and roads. Fencing shall not be topped with barbed wire. When fencing will enclose the perimeter of the site or facility, wildlife friendly fencing that allows the passage of small mammals and reptiles and is designed to minimize wildlife injury and death due to entanglement or strangulation shall be used on sites having a solar facility footprint greater than 5 acres. Exceptions can be made by the Planning Board for sites that have limited surrounding wildlife habitat and/or are designed to accommodate small livestock grazing." There is no explicit requirement for vegetative buffers. The ordinance requires fencing as a screening method for Major Solar Collection Systems but does not mandate vegetative buffers or other screening types explicitly.

Section 4.2.3 Signs requires that "A sign not to exceed twelve (12) square feet shall be displayed on or near the main access point and shall list the facility name, owner and phone number." Additionally, "A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations not to exceed four (4) square feet." These signage requirements apply specifically to Major Solar Systems, which are permitted through special permit and site plan review as described in section 4. Major Solar Systems must also meet other criteria including height and setback restrictions, fencing, design standards, safety, decommissioning, and abandonment provisions.

Major Solar Systems must minimize the displacement of prime soils in active agricultural production. The site plan shall include a plan for clearing and/or grading the site and a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP). The Decommissioning Plan must demonstrate how soil and vegetation remediation will return the parcel to its original state, including decompaction of soils to a depth of 18 to 24 inches, regrading, and reseeding with native plants excluding invasive species. The site plan must depict prime soils, soils of statewide importance, agricultural uses, diversions, ditches, and tile drainage. Additionally, if the array uses at-grade ballast footers, the underlayment should include crushed stone atop monofilament woven geotextile fabric for easy removal upon decommissioning.

In the R-A Residential-Agricultural District, 'Solar Energy Facilities' are listed under 'Uses Requiring Special Permit (See Article V),' indicating that utility-scale solar energy systems require a special permit. In contrast, the S Shoreline District explicitly prohibits 'Industrial, large scale solar, large scale wind, chemical manufacturing, kennels and animal hospitals.' Other provisions discuss general requirements for solar energy systems but do not specify additional districts where utility-scale solar systems are permitted as special use. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this consideration.
The minimum setback from property lines shall be twenty-five (25) feet, unless adjacent to residential neighbor. The setback when adjacent to residential neighbors shall be 100 feet.

Section § 150-48(H) states: 'The following requirements shall be met for decommissioning: (1) Solar farms and solar power plants which have not been in active and continuous service for a period of one year shall be removed at the owner's or operator's expense. (2) The site shall be restored to as natural a condition as possible within six months of the removal.' This applies explicitly to solar farms and solar power plants, defined as 'Energy generation facility or area of land principally used to convert solar energy to electricity, whether by photovoltaics, concentrating solar thermal devices or various experimental solar technologies, with the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of electricity.'
section: § 150-48 Solar farms and solar power plants

summary: Solar farms and solar power plants shall be permitted in all zoning districts as an electric-generating use subject to special use permit review and approval by the Town Board, subject to the following supplementary regulations: A. Solar farms and solar power plants shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access at a height of 8 1/2 feet. B. The following requirements shall be met for decommissioning: (1) Solar farms and solar power plants which have not been in active and continuous service for a period of one year shall be removed at the owner's or operator's expense. summary: Large Scale Solar Systems are permitted by special use permit in the Agricultural (A) District. The decommissioning plan must include: notification to the Town Board if the facility remains  "not used"  for 180 days; removal of all infrastructure including concrete to a depth of four (4) feet; remediation of soil and vegetation back to its original state unless otherwise permitted; a cost estimate prepared by a Professional Engineer, Registered Architect, or licensed contractor that accounts for inflation; and a form of surety (escrow, bond, or equivalent) established prior to construction start covering a minimum of 125 percent of the estimated decommissioning cost. Other requirements for Large-Scale Systems include adherence to height and setback requirements, minimum lot size, fencing, underground electrical lines, limited vegetation removal, annual mowing, and road bonding.
