All large-scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing. The height and type of fencing shall be determined by the special use permit process.

Large scale systems shall be located on lots with a minimum lot size that is large enough to accommodate the proposed system and still meet the required setback requirements for the zoning district. In general, facilities and equipment shall be greater than 100 feet from any property line, 300 feet from a roadway, and 500 feet from an occupied dwelling. (Only the 100 feet from any property line is relevant here.) Additionally, large scale solar energy systems shall adhere to the height and setback requirements of the underlying zoning district, with additional restrictions possible during the special use permit process.
section: SECTION 614 SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS, E. Solar as Principal Use, 3. Special Use Permit Standards

summary: Large scale systems shall be located on lots with a minimum lot size that is large enough to accommodate the proposed system and still meet the required setback requirements for the zoning district. In general, facilities and equipment shall be greater than 100 feet from any property line, 300 feet from a roadway, and 500 feet from an occupied dwelling.

All large-scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing. The height and type of fencing shall be determined by the special use permit process.

Large-Scale Systems (defined as solar energy systems with capacity of 60 KW or more for off-site consumption or sale) require submission of an Erosion and Sedimentation Control Plan for construction activities and a stormwater Management Plan meeting NYSDEC standards. Post construction runoff must be limited to 100% of the 2-year, 25-year, and 50-year storms, with a preference for infiltration over detention barriers. These requirements are part of the Special Use Permit Application Requirements for Large-Scale Systems. Other options include Small-Scale Systems (less than 60 KW, for on-site consumption) and Building-Integrated Photovoltaic systems, which are exempt from SEQRA and do not have these specific soil, erosion, or sediment control requirements. The ordinance also includes requirements for landscaping plans, vegetation clearing descriptions, and maintenance plans.

Large Scale Solar Systems are permitted by the issuance of a special use permit by the Town Board within the Agricultural (A) District, subject to the requirements set forth in this section. Every application for a Large-Scale System within the Town of Harmony shall be made to the Town Board and shall be approved by a majority vote thereof. Prior to Town Board review of the application, it may refer said application to the Zoning Board of Appeals for site plan review, report, and recommendation for approval or disapproval. The Town Board shall hold a public hearing upon ten (10) days notice duly posted and published and published in the official newspaper of the Town and on the Town bulletin board, before granting the special use permit. Other districts mention solar systems only as accessory uses or small-scale systems, or do not explicitly permit large-scale systems as special use.

Large scale systems shall be located on lots with a minimum lot size that is large enough to accommodate the proposed system and still meet the required setback requirements for the zoning district. In general, facilities and equipment shall be greater than 100 feet from any property line, 300 feet from a roadway, and 500 feet from an occupied dwelling.
section: SECTION 614 SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS, E. Solar as Principal Use, 3. Special Use Permit Standards

summary: A Tier 3 Solar Energy System shall not exceed 50% of the lot on which it is installed. If a landowner owns more than one contiguous lot, lot coverage may increase to 80% of the lot area, as long as the total area of coverage does not exceed 50% of all contiguously owned lots. Where a Tier 3 Solar Energy System is not the principal use of the site, the lot coverage may not exceed 50%, which shall also include all principal and accessory uses on the lot. The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the lot area, not as a specific area value.

All Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems shall submit a Decommissioning Plan along with the Building Permit application. The Decommissioning Plan shall consist of: documentation of termination of the lease (if applicable); removal of all operator owned equipment, concrete, conduits, structures, fencing driveways and foundations; removal of any hazardous wastes from the site in accordance with local, County State and Federal waste disposal requirements; restoration to the property to the condition that existed prior to the installation of the Solar Energy System; restoration landscaping plan; timeframe for the completion of decommissioning activities; and identification of the party responsible for decommissioning. Upon cessation of electricity generation on a continuous basis for 12 months, the Town may notify and instruct the owner/operator to implement the Decommissioning Plan, which must be completed within 120 days of notification. If the owner/operator fails to comply, the Town may utilize a security deposit (bond) of no less than 125% of the cost of removal with a 2% annual escalator to remove the system and restore the site. The security remains in effect until restoration is complete.

All mechanical equipment, including any structure for storage batteries, shall be enclosed by a seven-foot high fence, with a self-locking gate to prevent unauthorized access. This fencing requirement applies to Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems, which include systems producing 25 MW or greater. Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems are permitted as a Special Exception Use on parcels containing twenty-five (25) acres or greater, subject to various safeguards and conditions including site plan approval, special exception use approval, screening by vegetated buffers, height limits, environmental assessments, underground utility lines, and signage restrictions.

A Tier 3 Solar Energy System shall not exceed 15 feet in height for a ground-mounted solar array and 20 feet for a solar canopy above a parking lot. The most restrictive maximum height is 15 feet for ground-mounted arrays. This applies specifically to Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems, which include systems producing 25 MW or greater. [§ 206-6 C (8)]

A Tier 3 Solar Energy System shall be permitted as a Special Exception Use in the SB-100, SB-35, SB-1, SB-0, R-1 and R-2 zoning districts only on parcels containing twenty-five (25) acres or greater in land area. This minimum lot size applies to Tier 3 systems, which include large-scale or community solar facilities with significant off-site energy use or capacity. The unit for this minimum lot size is acres.

A Tier 3 Solar Energy System shall not encroach into the 100-foot special Purchase buffer. Additionally, all sides of a Tier 3 Solar Energy System shall be screened by a vegetated buffer ... and shall be a minimum of 25 feet wide. A Tier 3 Solar Energy System shall not be located in a front, side or rear yard setback. The 100-foot special Purchase buffer is the most restrictive fixed distance setback mentioned. Other setback-related requirements include not locating within front, side, or rear yard setbacks (variable by zoning district) and a 25-foot wide vegetated screening buffer around the facility perimeter.

All sides of a Tier 3 Solar Energy System shall be screened by a vegetated buffer. The height of the vegetated screening to the south shall be equal to the height of the solar panels, solar canopies and associated equipment, to allow for proper solar exposure, but also suitable to screen the facility from public view. Screening on the sides when solar exposure is unnecessary, shall be of a height deemed adequate in the judgement of the Planning Board to suitably screen the facility from surrounding properties. Screening can consist of landscaping, berms, architectural features or other screening methods, and shall be a minimum of 25 feet wide. Additionally, Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems in R-1 or R-2 Zones must be screened so as to not be visible from other private or public properties or roadways. Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems producing 25 MW or greater shall obtain a permit at the state level through the siting process administered through the Office of Renewable Energy Siting.

For Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems producing 25 MW or greater, signage requirements are explicitly stated: "No signage or graphic content shall be located so as to be visible from off-site or any public view." Permissible signage includes "manufactures name, equipment specification information, safety information and twenty-four-hour emergency contact information" only "on the interior of the site, in a location that is not visible from a public vantage point." Additionally, "As required by National Electric Code (NEC), disconnect and other emergency shutoff information shall be clearly displayed on a light reflective surface. A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations." Other Tier classifications (Tier 1 and Tier 2) do not have explicit signage requirements detailed in the provided text.

A Tier 3 Solar Energy System shall comply with the Stormwater Management and Erosion and Sediment Control requirements of Chapter 130 of the Town Code. Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems are defined as "Solar Energy Systems that are not included in the list for Tier 1 and Tier 2, or any Community Solar Facility where 75% or greater percent of the energy generated at the site is utilized off-site." Tier 1 systems include Roof-Mounted and Building-Integrated Solar Energy Systems, permitted with building permits and exempt from site plan review. Tier 2 systems are ground-mounted systems up to 950 square feet for on-site consumption, also permitted with building permits and exempt from site plan and architectural review. Tier 3 systems are permitted as a Special Exception Use on parcels 25 acres or greater, require site plan approval, special exception use approval, and for systems producing 25 MW or greater, a state-level permit through the Office of Renewable Energy Siting. Additional Tier 3 requirements include vegetated screening, height limits, environmental and visual assessments, carbon sequestration assessment, underground utilities, pervious surfaces with native vegetation, and maintenance driveway design to minimize site disturbance.

Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems are permitted as a Special Exception Use in the SB-100, SB-35, SB-1, SB-0, R-1 and R-2 zoning districts only on parcels containing twenty-five (25) acres or greater in land area, subject to safeguards and conditions. "A Tier 3 Solar Energy System shall be permitted pursuant to the issuance of Site Plan Approval by the Planning Board in accordance with § 235-71 of the Town Code, and the issuance of Special Exception Use Approval by the Planning Board and reviewed by the Town Board in accordance with Chapter 235 Article V of the Town Code." Other tiers include Tier 1, permitted in all zoning districts and exempt from site plan and Architectural Review Board approval but limited to on-site energy consumption; and Tier 2, permitted as an accessory use in all zoning districts, exempt from site plan and Architectural Review Board approval, limited to small-scale ground-mounted systems not exceeding 950 square feet and 15 feet in height, and only installed in side or rear yards.

A Visual Impact Assessment shall be submitted with every application for a Tier 3 Solar Energy System (§ 206-6 C (11)). Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems are defined as "Solar Energy Systems that are not included in the list for Tier 1 and Tier 2, or any Community Solar Facility where 75% or greater percent of the energy generated at the site is utilized off-site" (§ 206-3 C). Tier 3 systems are permitted as a Special Exception Use on parcels 25 acres or greater and subject to safeguards including site plan approval and special exception use approval (§ 206-6 C). Other tiers include Tier 1 (Roof-Mounted and Building-Integrated Solar Energy Systems, generally for on-site consumption and exempt from site plan and Architectural Review Board approval) and Tier 2 (Ground-Mounted systems up to 950 square feet for on-site consumption, also exempt from site plan and Architectural Review Board approval) (§ 206-6 A and B). The Visual Impact Assessment is defined as "the assessment of changes to a site or landscape resulting from the installation of a Solar Energy System as viewed from surrounding properties, adjacent roadways, or public viewpoints" and "shall consist of photographs, elevations, renderings and photo-simulations to adequately depict the comparison of existing conditions to the proposed developed condition" (§ 206-3).

The Town of Hartland Local Law No. 1 of 2024 imposes a "temporary town-wide moratorium on the approval and installation of Large Scale Solar Energy Systems, Utility Scale Solar Energy Systems and Battery Energy Storage Systems" for a period of 180 days from the effective date, with provision for two additional 90-day extensions. During this moratorium, "the Town Board, the Planning Board, the Zoning Board of Appeals, the Building Department and the Zoning Administrator shall not permit, accept, process, interpret, deliberate upon, decide or approve any application for the installation of any Large Scale Solar Energy Systems, Utility Scale Energy Systems and Battery Energy Storage Systems." The moratorium applies town-wide and to all currently pending and future applications without conditional exceptions or geographic limitations. The moratorium "shall take effect upon its adoption and filing with the Secretary of State." The exact effective date is not specified in the text provided, so it cannot be determined if the moratorium has expired as of December 13, 2025.

The total surface area of all ground-mounted and freestanding solar collectors, including solar Voltaic cells, panels and arrays, shall not exceed 80% of the total parcel area. This is the maximum land coverage allowed for Major Solar Collection Systems (Solar Farms). Other related conditions include parcel size minimums and height limits, but these do not affect the maximum land coverage percentage. The 80% limit is expressed as a percentage of the total parcel area.
section: ARTICLE VI, Section 34, D. Major Solar Collection System

summary: Section 34.D Major Solar Collection System requires an operation and maintenance plan which shall include measures for maintaining safe access to the installation, storm water controls, as well as general procedural operational maintenance of the installation. Additional minimum requirements include: solar farms of less than 26 kW on parcels of not less than five acres, otherwise a minimum of ten acres is required; ground-mounted panels shall not exceed ten feet in height; all mechanical equipment including battery or storage cell structures must be enclosed by a minimum eight-foot high fence with a self-locking gate; total surface area of all ground-mounted and freestanding solar collectors shall not exceed 80% of the total parcel area; installation of a vegetated perimeter buffer to provide year-round screening of the system from adjacent properties; and case-by-case examination of the proposed location by the Town Board/Planning Board to ensure no detriment to residents, business or traffic. These requirements apply to Major Solar Collection Systems defined as ground-mounted accessory systems with a total surface area greater than 2,000 square feet, principally used to capture solar energy and convert it to electrical energy to transfer to the public electric grid in order to sell electricity to or receive a credit from a public utility entity, but also may be for on-site use.

For Major Solar Collection Systems (Solar Farms), the ordinance requires that "All mechanical equipment on a Solar Farm, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, are completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence; with a Self-locking gate." Other conditions include: Solar Farms of less than 26 kW must be on a parcel of not less than five (5) acres, otherwise a minimum of ten (10) acre parcel is required; ground-mounted panels shall not exceed ten (10) feet in height; total surface area of all ground-mounted and freestanding solar collectors shall not exceed 80% of the total parcel area; installation of a vegetated perimeter buffer to provide year-round screening; and case-by-case examination by the Town Board/Planning Board to ensure no detriment to residents, business or traffic.

Section 34.C.5 states that solar collectors and other facilities "shall be designed and located to minimize reflective glare toward any inhabited buildings on adjacent properties and roads." Section 34.D.1.h requires "Information on reflectivity/glare of solar panels and identify impacts to adjacent properties" as part of the application for Major Solar Collection Systems. Other conditions for Major Solar Collection Systems include: parcels must be at least five acres for systems under 26 kW or ten acres otherwise; ground-mounted panels shall not exceed ten feet in height; mechanical equipment must be enclosed by an eight-foot fence with a self-locking gate; total surface area of solar collectors shall not exceed 80% of the parcel area; installation of a vegetated perimeter buffer for year-round screening; and case-by-case examination by the Town Board/Planning Board to ensure no detriment to residents, businesses, or traffic.

The ordinance states: 'All ground-mounted parcels shall not exceed ten (10) feet in height.' This is the maximum structure height allowed for Major Solar Collection Systems (Solar Farms). The units are feet. Other related conditions include: 'All mechanical equipment on a Solar Farm, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, are completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence;' and 'The total surface area of all ground-mounted and freestanding solar collectors shall not exceed 80% of the total parcel area.'

summary: The ordinance states: 'Solar Farms of less than 26 (kW) shall be on a parcel of not less than five (5) acres, otherwise a minimum of ten (10) acres parcel shall be required.' section: Section 34. Solar Energy Systems, D. Major Solar Collection System

summary: Section 34, Part D, Minimum Requirements for Major Solar Collection Systems states: 'The installation of a vegetated perimeter buffer to provide year-round screening of the system from adjacent properties.' Other conditions include: Solar Farms less than 26 kW must be on parcels of not less than five acres; otherwise, a minimum of ten acres is required. Ground-mounted panels shall not exceed ten feet in height. All mechanical equipment must be enclosed by an eight-foot high fence with a self-locking gate. The total surface area of ground-mounted solar collectors shall not exceed 80% of the parcel area. The Town Board/Planning Board will examine the proposed location on a case-by-case basis to ensure no detriment to residents, businesses, or traffic.

Section 34.D.1 requires application information for Major Solar Collection Systems including "Blueprints or drawings of the solar photovoltaic installation signed by a licensed Professional Engineer showing the proposed layout of the system," and "Confirmation prepared and signed by a licensed professional engineer that the solar farm complies with all applicable Federal and State standards." Section 34.D.2.c mandates that "All mechanical equipment on a Solar Farm, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, are completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence; with a Self-locking gate." While signage is not separately itemized, these requirements imply the need for safety and identification signage as part of compliance and operational safety measures. Other conditions include parcel size minimums, height limits, surface area limits, vegetated perimeter buffers, and case-by-case location review by the Town Board/Planning Board.

Major Solar Collection Systems are permitted in all districts subject to conditions including submission of an operation and maintenance plan which "shall include measures for maintaining safe access to the installation, storm water controls, as well as general procedural operational maintenance of the installation." Additional requirements include: parcel size minimums (less than 26 kW on parcels not less than 5 acres, otherwise minimum 10 acres), ground-mounted panels not exceeding 10 feet in height, mechanical equipment enclosed by an 8-foot fence with self-locking gate, total solar collector area not exceeding 80% of parcel area, and installation of a vegetated perimeter buffer for year-round screening. The Town Board/Planning Board will review locations on a case-by-case basis to ensure no detriment to residents or businesses.

Major Solar Collection Systems (Solar Farms) are permitted in all districts in the Town of Hartsville subject to conditions including detailed application requirements and compliance with standards. The text states: 'Major Solar Collection systems are permitted in all districts in the Town of Hartsville subject to the following conditions...' and 'In any district requiring a Special Use Permit for a Solar Farm, the development shall conform to the following standards...' However, the text does not specify or list the names or abbreviations of any districts where a Special Use Permit or similar approval is required. Other options and conditions include requirements for minor ground-mounted and freestanding solar systems permitted in all districts with building permits and special permits required for systems 10 feet or more in height, as well as design and installation standards.

Large scale solar systems, when added to other structures not associated with solar systems are limited to 50 percent maximum lot coverage. The surface area covered by solar panels shall be included in total lot coverage. It is understood that the area below the panels is pervious, however lot coverage requirements are in accordance with maximizing solar system usage while maintaining appropriate open space to retain the character of the underlying zoning district.

Solar Energy Systems are considered abandoned after twelve months without electrical energy generation and must be removed from the property. Applications for six-month extensions will be reviewed by the Planning Board. The site shall be restored to the natural condition within twelve (12) months of removal. A decommissioning plan shall be submitted as part of the initial application for Ground Mounted and Large Scale Solar Energy Systems and compliance with this plan shall be made a condition of Special Use Permit approval. The Decommissioning Plan must specify that after the Solar Energy System is inoperable or abandoned, the applicant or subsequent owner shall remove all equipment; illustrate the removal of all infrastructure and a property plan for the remediation of soil/vegetation to its original state; include an expected timeline for execution; and include a cost estimate detailing the project cost of the Decommissioning Plan prepared by a licensed professional engineer or certified contractor. If the system is not decommissioned, the municipality may remove the system and restore the property and impose a lien on the property to cover these costs. The applicant shall be required to provide sureties, including a bond covering the expense of removal and remediation, as agreed upon between the Town and the applicant.

Large scale solar systems. The type of fencing shall be determined by the Town Planning Board. Fencing is in addition to required site screening.

All solar collectors shall be installed so as to prevent glare and heat that is perceptible beyond said subject property’s lines. Particular attention shall be paid to panel orientation with regard to airport runway locations, and airplane flyover/ approach patterns in order to minimize potential glare impact on pilots. This applies to Ground Mounted/ Free Standing Solar Systems and Large Scale Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as ground mounted and producing energy primarily for off-site sale or consumption. Large Scale Solar Energy Systems are allowed in the AR-40 District through the issuance of a Special-Use permit subject to requirements including Site Plan approval. Other conditions include setbacks, height limits, lot size, lot coverage, fencing, screening, signage, noise, access and parking, and decommissioning plans.

Large scale solar systems shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt. This is explicitly stated under § 150-62.F.3.b. The text defines Solar System - Large Scale as a solar energy system that is ground mounted and produces energy primarily for the purpose of off-site sale or consumption. No other maximum height values for large scale solar systems are provided, making 15 feet the most restrictive limit. The unit 'feet' is used consistently in the ordinance.

The ordinance states: 'Lot size. Lot minimum is five (5) acres in area.' This minimum lot size applies specifically to Large Scale Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as ground-mounted systems producing energy primarily for off-site sale or consumption. The unit of measurement is acres, an area value. No other minimum lot size values for Large Scale Solar Systems are provided.

Minimum setback for solar structures and solar equipment shall be 100’ (feet) from the legal lot line. Any ancillary structure and equipment shall comply with all minimum setbacks for principal structures in accordance with Town of Henderson Zoning Law. All setback requirements of the underlying zoning district shall be enforced. Ground-mounted solar systems shall be installed in side or rear yard beyond set-back requirements. The site plan shall include all lot line setback dimensions. These requirements apply specifically to Large Scale Solar Energy Systems, defined as ground mounted and producing energy primarily for off-site sale or consumption.

Large scale solar systems "shall have the least visual effect practical on the environment, as determined by the Town Planning Board." "Reasonable efforts shall be made to minimize visual impacts by preserving natural vegetation, and providing landscape screening to abutting residential properties, public roads, and from public sites known to include important views and vistas." "No more than fifteen (15) percent of the total existing brush, trees, and other screening vegetation on a parcel of a property may be removed in order to accommodate a solar farm." "Appurtenant structures: inverters, batteries, equipment shelters, storage facilities, transformers, shall be screened." These requirements are in addition to fencing requirements and other design standards for large scale solar systems. Screening is site-specific and determined by the Planning Board based on topography, adjacent structures, and roadways.

Exceptions include: Manufacturers or installers identification; appropriate warning signs and place cards; signs that may be required by a Federal agency; and any signs that provide 24-hour emergency contact phone numbers to caution of dangers.
section: ARTICLE XI SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS REGULATIONS - § 150-62. F. Ground Mounted/ Free Standing Solar Systems - Large Scale Solar Energy Systems

summary: Large Scale Solar Energy Systems are allowed in the AR-40 District through the issuance of a Special-Use permit subject to the requirements set forth in this section and granted by the Town Planning Board. Requirements of this section, including Site Plan approval are prerequisites. Ground Mounted Solar Systems are a permitted accessory use in AR-40 zoning district. A Special Use Permit must be granted for ground mounted units in all remaining zoning districts. Schedule II notes that Large Scale (Offsite Energy) solar systems are subject to the underlying district (UD) regulations. The key defines SUP as Special Use Permit required and SP as Site Plan Review required.

Large-scale solar energy systems require the submission of a decommissioning plan and associated bond/escrow account prior to permit issuance. The plan must specify removal of the system after it can no longer be used, remediation of soil and vegetation to return the parcel to its original state, an expected timeline, and a cost estimate prepared by a professional engineer or contractor. Removal must be completed in accordance with the plan. If the system is not decommissioned within 90 days after being considered abandoned, the municipality may remove the system using bond proceeds and impose a lien for costs exceeding the bond. Additionally, all solar energy systems must be decommissioned upon abandonment. If no timeline is established, decommissioning must occur no later than six months after abandonment, with a possible single six-month extension granted by the Town Board for good cause. Failure to decommission may result in Town removal and cost recovery through liens. These requirements are explicitly for large-scale solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance.

summary: The ordinance requires that "a decommissioning plan shall be submitted as part of the application" for solar farms and solar power plants, specifying that "after the solar farm or solar power plant is no longer in use, it shall be removed by the applicant or any subsequent owner." The plan must "demonstrate how the removal of all infrastructure, and the remediation of soil and vegetation, shall be conducted to return the parcel to its original state prior to construction," include "an expected time line for execution," and provide "a cost estimate detailing the projected cost of executing the decommissioning plan" prepared by a professional engineer or contractor. The Zoning Board of Appeals must establish "the amount of such surety to be established by the applicant," which "must be in place prior to building permit issuance." The surety may be in the form of escrowed funds, bonds, or otherwise, to ensure the Town can remove the infrastructure and restore the site if the applicant fails to comply. Additionally, "Solar energy systems and equipment are considered abandoned after one year without electrical energy generation and must be removed from the property no later than 90 days after the end of the twelve-month period." These requirements apply specifically to solar farms and solar power plants, which require a special permit and site plan approval. Other solar energy systems, such as rooftop, building-mounted, freestanding, and ground-mounted systems with rated capacity of 25kW or less, have different permitting and siting requirements but do not have explicit decommissioning requirements stated here.

All solar farms and solar power plants shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs with the owner's contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing. The type of fencing shall be determined by the Planning Board. summary: Applications shall include a decommissioning plan to ensure the site will be restored to a useful nonhazardous condition immediately. The site developer shall provide financial surety acceptable to the Town that is equal to 20% (20 percent) of the project installation cost prior to permits being issued for any solar project. The bond shall be in place for the life of the facility and accessible to the Town to fund the de-commissioning of the facility in the event it is abandoned. If construction of the facility is started but not completed and functioning within 18 (eighteen) months of the issuance of the Special Use Permit approval, the Town may notify the operator and/or the owner to complete construction and installation of the facility within 180 (one hundred eighty) days. If the owner and/or operator fails to perform, the Town may notify the owner and/or operator to implement the decommissioning plan. Upon cessation of activity of a constructed facility for a period of 1 (one) year, the Town may require the owner and/or operator of the facility to implement the decommissioning plan. Within 180 (one hundred eighty) days of notice being served, the owner and/or operator can either restore operation equal to 80% (eighty percent) of approved capacity, or implement the decommissioning plan. If the owner and/or operator fails to fully implement the decommissioning plan within the required time period, the Town may, at its discretion, provide for the restoration of the site in accordance with the decommissioning plan and may recover incurred expenses directly from the defaulted owner and/or operator or through use of the approved financial surety. summary: Section E(3) requires a decommissioning plan to be submitted as part of the application for a utility-scale solar energy system special permit. The applicant must also provide security "in a form acceptable to the Town Attorney and Planning Board and in the amount sufficient to pay for the cost and expenses of removal of the solar energy system and related equipment and structures and restoration of the site." If the security is insufficient, the owner/operator and property owner are jointly and severally liable, and the Town may assess costs as a lien on the property. For utility-scale solar energy systems, the ordinance requires that "The entire solar energy system shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing at a height of at least seven feet to restrict unauthorized access. Additionally, the maximum height of fencing is set at 8 feet under the dimensional requirements. It also states that the solar energy system and related equipment shall not be located within the minimum required front, side and rear yards for the district in which the system is situated. The front yard setback is listed as 'nan' (not a number), indicating no fixed numeric value is provided for front yard setbacks from property lines. summary: The following dimensional requirements shall apply to a utility-scale solar energy system: Town highway setback is 100 feet, County highway setback is 125 feet, and State highway setback is 150 feet. The most restrictive setback from roads is 150 feet from a State highway.

Other conditions for utility-scale systems include dimensional requirements (e.g., lot width 250 feet, maximum solar collector height 12 feet), maximum area of 25 acres, setbacks from property lines, perimeter fencing, underground power lines unless impracticable, and screening to "screen the solar energy system and fencing from residential properties, public roads, private roads and private rights-of-way to the maximum extent practicable." Additional requirements include equipment specifications, operation and maintenance plans, decommissioning plans, emergency action plans, and compliance with various codes and safety standards.

Section Q titled 'Decommissioning' requires that all site plan applications for solar farms be accompanied by a Decommissioning Plan to be implemented upon abandonment, cessation of activity for 12 consecutive months, or removal of the structure. The Plan must explain removal of all above ground material and remediation of soil and vegetation to return the parcel to its original state prior to construction, with a timeline not exceeding one year. The site must be restored to as natural a condition as possible within six months of removal. Prior to issuance of permits, the owner/operator must execute a Decommissioning Agreement secured by a performance bond or other guarantee of not less than 150% of estimated costs, subject to periodic review every five years. The Town may remove the system and impose a lien if removal does not occur per the Plan. Alternatively, the Town Board may permit a Decommissioning Agreement in lieu of a bond, allowing the Town to remove the system and recover costs, which become a lien and tax on the property, binding subsequent owners. This provision does not preclude other legal actions and holds the owner/operator liable for legal expenses. These requirements apply to solar farms defined as electric generating uses on parcels of at least ten acres.

Solar farms shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing, eight feet in height and set back at a sufficient distance from all components of the solar installation to restrict unauthorized access or other safety hazard. The type of perimeter fencing shall be subject to approval by the Planning Board.

Other relevant conditions include minimum parcel size of ten (10) acres, maximum size of 30 acres including fencing, maximum average panel height of 12 feet, perimeter fencing requirements, setback requirements, and decommissioning plans. The Planning Board may require additional documentation such as a viewshed analysis. No solar farm shall be permitted on federal or state wetlands, ecologically sensitive land, or prime agricultural land removed from production.

The ordinance states: 'The average height of the solar panel arrays shall not exceed 12 feet.' This applies to solar farms defined as electric generating uses subject to special permit and site plan review, consistent with utility-scale solar energy systems intended for offsite electricity generation or sale. No other maximum height values are provided for utility-scale solar systems in the text. The unit 'feet' is explicitly used in the ordinance.

The ordinance states: 'No Solar farm shall be larger than 30 acres, including fencing.' This is the maximum lot size allowed for utility-scale solar energy systems defined as solar farms. Additionally, the parcel must be a minimum of ten (10) acres. The units for this maximum size are acres.

The parcel on which a solar farm is sited shall be a minimum of ten (10) acres. This minimum lot size applies specifically to solar farms defined as 'electric generating' uses subject to special permit and site plan review. The unit of measurement for this minimum lot size is acres. Other related restrictions include a maximum solar farm size of 30 acres and setback requirements, but these do not affect the minimum lot size.

No part of any structure shall be closer than 100 feet to any property line or to any public road. However, the Planning Board shall have the authority to impose greater setbacks as it determines necessary to preserve the rural character and scenic qualities of the surrounding community or to mitigate adverse visual impacts of the solar farm facility. Solar farms shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing, eight feet in height and set back at a sufficient distance from all components of the solar installation to restrict unauthorized access or other safety hazard. The type of perimeter fencing shall be subject to approval by the Planning Board.

No part of any structure shall be closer than 100 feet to any property line or to any public road. The ordinance requires that "appropriate landscaping and/or screening materials may be required to help screen the solar power plant and accessory structures from scenic roadways, park lands, historic properties and neighboring residences." This applies to solar farms defined as utility-scale solar energy systems. Other relevant provisions include perimeter fencing requirements (§130-8.G), setbacks (§130-8.F), and restrictions on tree cutting and site disturbance (§130-8.C).

The ordinance requires that "The manufacturer’s or installer's identification and appropriate warning signage and emergency contact information shall be posted at the site and clearly visible." Other conditions for solar farms include minimum parcel size of ten (10) acres, maximum size of 30 acres including fencing, perimeter fencing eight feet in height, setbacks of at least 100 feet from property lines or public roads, and various environmental and operational requirements.

The ordinance defines Solar Farms as an  "electric generating"  use subject to special permit and site plan review. It requires the applicant to submit, among other things, "Erosion and sediment control and storm water management plans prepared to New York State Department of Environmental Conservation standards, if applicable, and to such standards as may be established by the Planning Board." Additional requirements include a soil map, property operation and maintenance plan, and a decommissioning plan. Solar farms must be on parcels of at least ten (10) acres and no larger than 30 acres. They are prohibited on federal or state wetlands, ecologically sensitive land, land under conservation or agricultural easements precluding solar farms, and land that would remove prime agricultural land from production. Site disturbance caused by grading, tree removal, or other work cannot exceed one acre. The Planning Board may impose additional standards as necessary.

Solar farms shall be permitted in the Greenbelt District as an  "electric generating"  use subject to special permit and site plan review and approval by the Planning Board. No Solar farm shall be permitted on federal or state wetlands, ecologically sensitive land or water resources, land subject to conservation or agricultural easements precluding construction, or to remove prime agricultural land or farmland of statewide importance from potential agricultural production. Agricultural uses may be carried out within the fenced perimeter of a solar farm.

The ordinance requires that for solar farms, the applicant must submit detailed information including "proposed changes to the landscape of the site, grading, vegetation clearing and planting, exterior lighting, and screening vegetation or structures" and "drawings showing the location and size of all proposed towers or utility lines." Additionally, "the Planning Board may require an applicant to submit a viewshed analysis meeting the procedures identified within the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation’s SEQRA publication entitled 'Assessing and Mitigating Visual Impacts'." This viewshed analysis is an explicit visual impact assessment requirement. Other submission requirements include soil maps, property lines, electrical diagrams, operation and maintenance plans, erosion and sediment control plans, blueprints, equipment specifications, clearing descriptions, and other documentation deemed necessary by the Planning Board.

Large-scale ground-mounted photovoltaic systems are permitted as an accessory use in Planned Development Zones; principal use only if the individual Planned Development Zone specifically allows it as a permitted principal use (G.(2)(c)[1][b]). The Large-Scale Photovoltaic Solar Energy System Overlay District allows principal and accessory uses but is excluded from this response as a primary use district. Other zones allow medium-scale systems as accessory uses (e.g., Medium Density Residential, High Density Residential, Mobile Home Park, Multiple Residence, Conservation, Neighborhood Commercial, Community Commercial, and Planned Development Zones) or principal and accessory uses for medium-scale in Agricultural, Low Density Residential, Light Industrial, Industrial, and Office Park Commercial Zones, but these do not apply to large-scale systems. Small-scale systems are permitted as principal and accessory uses in all zones. The ordinance states: 'Solar energy systems are permitted in all Town zones, including Planned Development Zones, subject to the requirements described below' (§ 270-219.1 B.(2)).

The ordinance explicitly requires a decommissioning plan for large-scale ground-mounted photovoltaic solar energy systems as part of the site plan application. The plan must specify events requiring decommissioning, including "the Town notifies the owner and operator to implement the decommissioning plan," "lack of production for six continuous months (or for 12 of any 18 months)," "lack of a current permit," "failure to maintain any required decommissioning bond or other security," and "a violation of any site plan conditions or permit conditions that continues more than 30 days after the Town provides written notice." The plan must also specify "the timeline and means and methods for removal and disposition of all solar panels, battery energy storage systems, electrical appurtenances, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines within 180 days of the date decommissioning is required," and include "disposal of all solid and hazardous wastes in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations." Security is required in the form of "a bond, letter of credit or other form of security or undertaking" equal to "125% of the cost of facility removal and restoration of the site," with updates every three years. Enforcement includes Town removal and cost recovery, including liens against the property. Other scale categories (small-scale and medium-scale) are defined but do not have decommissioning requirements or security obligations. Small-scale systems have a footprint of 2,000 square feet or less and medium-scale systems have a footprint between 2,000 and 7,000 square feet, with different permitted uses and setback requirements, but no decommissioning mandates are specified for these categories.

For large-scale ground-mounted photovoltaic solar energy systems (defined as having a solar facility footprint greater than 7,000 square feet up to 35 acres), fencing requirements include: "Chain-link, barbed, razor, and concertina wires, electrically charged wire, railroad ties, concrete masonry units, scrap metal, tarped, and cloth fences are not permitted as fencing." When fencing encloses the perimeter of a site with a solar facility footprint greater than three acres, "wildlife-friendly fencing that allows the passage of small mammals and reptiles and is designed to minimize wildlife injury and death due to entanglement or strangulation shall be used." Mechanical equipment and energy storage system components "shall be enclosed by a seven-foot-high fence, or the height required by the National Electrical Code if it requires more than seven feet, with a self-locking gate to prevent unauthorized access." Other scale categories include small-scale (footprint 2,000 sq ft or less) and medium-scale (footprint more than 2,000 sq ft up to 7,000 sq ft) systems, with fencing restrictions only explicitly stated for medium-scale and large-scale systems, where certain fencing materials are prohibited.

For large-scale ground-mounted photovoltaic solar energy systems (defined as having a total solar facility footprint greater than 7,000 square feet up to a maximum of 35 acres), the ordinance requires that "Photovoltaic solar energy systems and other facilities shall be designed and located in order to minimize reflective glare toward roads or any habitable or occupiable building on adjacent properties." Other size categories include small-scale systems (footprint of 2,000 square feet or less) and medium-scale systems (footprint more than 2,000 square feet up to and including 7,000 square feet), with their own respective standards. For medium-scale systems, glare minimization is also required: "Photovoltaic solar energy systems and other facilities shall be designed and located in order to minimize reflective glare toward roads or any habitable or occupiable building on adjacent properties." Small-scale systems do not have explicit glare restrictions mentioned. Additionally, rooftop and building-mounted photovoltaic solar energy systems must have "antireflective coating(s)" on all solar panels but are not subject to the large-scale ground-mounted system glare standards.

The maximum height for all ground-mounted systems is 20 feet when the system is oriented at maximum tilt. For farms in the Agricultural and Low Density Residential Zones that utilize agrivoltaic farming, the Planning Board may approve a greater height if it finds a greater height is necessary to accommodate continued or new agricultural activity. This applies to large-scale ground-mounted photovoltaic systems as defined by a footprint greater than 7,000 square feet up to a maximum of 35 acres. The height limit is explicitly stated in subsection F(1) and applies to all ground-mounted photovoltaic systems, including large-scale systems.

Large-scale ground-mounted photovoltaic systems have a total solar facility footprint greater than 7,000 square feet up to a maximum of 35 acres. Other size categories include small-scale systems (2,000 square feet or less) and medium-scale systems (more than 2,000 square feet up to and including 7,000 square feet). The maximum size for large-scale systems is explicitly stated as 35 acres.

summary: Large-scale photovoltaic solar energy systems are permitted as principal and accessory uses in the Large-Scale Photovoltaic Solar Energy System Overlay District, which is superimposed on underlying (base) zones. In Planned Development Zones, large-scale systems are permitted as accessory uses and as principal uses only if the individual Planned Development Zone specifically allows it as a permitted principal use. Other scale categories (small and medium) have different permissions and conditions. For example, medium-scale systems are principal and accessory uses in Agricultural, Low Density Residential, Light Industrial, Industrial, and Office Park Commercial Zones, but large-scale systems are not permitted as principal uses in these base zones without the overlay. Site plan review and additional documentation are required for large-scale systems.

For large-scale ground-mounted photovoltaic solar energy systems (defined as having a total solar facility footprint greater than 7,000 square feet up to a maximum of 35 acres), the setback measured from the lot line to the closest part of the photovoltaic solar energy system is a seventy-five feet minimum from all lot lines. Roads, landscaping and fencing may occur within the setback. The Planning Board may consider a solar facility project that is comprised of several lots to be treated as a single lot for purposes of applying setback standards. Other setback options for smaller systems include: small-scale systems require ten feet minimum from side and rear yard lot lines and a front lot line setback equal to the maximum required front yard in the zone (or 50 feet in certain zones); medium-scale systems require sixty feet minimum from lot lines abutting non-commercial/industrial zones, thirty feet minimum from lot lines abutting commercial/industrial zones, and front lot line setbacks similar to small-scale but with some zone exceptions.

For large-scale ground-mounted photovoltaic solar energy systems (footprint greater than 7,000 square feet up to 35 acres), the ordinance requires that "practicable efforts shall be made to minimize visual impacts by preserving natural vegetation and providing dense landscape year-round screening to abutting residential properties and roads," with the condition that "the screening should minimize shading of photovoltaic solar energy systems." This is found under the design standards subsection G(5)(e). Other design standards include fencing restrictions, glare minimization, road design, lighting, signage, utility connections, noise considerations, and possible freestanding ballast or racking systems. The ordinance also divides ground-mounted photovoltaic systems into small-scale (≤2,000 sq ft), medium-scale (>2,000 to 7,000 sq ft), and large-scale (>7,000 sq ft to 35 acres) categories, each with different permitted uses, setback requirements, lot coverage rules, and site plan review requirements.

For large-scale ground-mounted photovoltaic solar energy systems, "All signage shall comply with the Town's Sign Law (Ithaca Town Code Chapter 270, Article XXIX). A sign shall be displayed on or near the main access point identifying the owner and providing a twenty-four-hour emergency contact phone number." Large-scale systems are defined as those with a total solar facility footprint greater than 7,000 square feet up to a maximum of 35 acres. Other size categories include small-scale (2,000 square feet or less) and medium-scale (more than 2,000 up to 7,000 square feet), with different use, setback, lot coverage, site plan review, and design standards, but signage requirements are explicitly stated only for large-scale systems.

The ordinance explicitly requires soil, erosion, and sediment control measures for large-scale ground-mounted photovoltaic solar energy systems (defined as having a footprint greater than 7,000 square feet up to 35 acres). The decommissioning plan must "specify the means and methods to minimize disruption to field drains and soils; remediate drains and soils; and avoid or minimize erosion, including stabilization and revegetation of any sites with native seed mixes, excluding any invasive species." Construction standards include: "All topsoil from agricultural areas used for vehicle and equipment traffic, parking, and equipment laydown and storage areas shall be stripped and stockpiled," and "All surface or subsurface drainage structures damaged during construction shall be repaired or replaced to as close to original condition as possible." A monitoring and remediation period of no less than two years is required, with seasonal inspections to address "topsoil thickness, relative content of rock and large stones, trench settling, crop production, drainage and repair of severed subsurface drain lines, fences, and any other conditions." An environmental monitor (EM) with agricultural expertise must oversee construction and restoration on prime farmland or farmland of statewide importance. These requirements are part of the site plan review process for large-scale systems. Other size categories include small-scale (footprint 2,000 sq ft or less) and medium-scale (footprint more than 2,000 sq ft up to 7,000 sq ft) systems, which have different setback, use, and site plan review requirements but do not have these detailed soil and erosion control provisions explicitly stated.

Large-scale ground-mounted photovoltaic systems are permitted as accessory uses in Planned Development Zones; principal use only if the individual Planned Development Zone specifically allows it as a permitted principal use. Site plan review is required prior to construction, installation or modification. The ordinance states: '[c] Large-scale photovoltaic solar energy system standards: (1) Permitted use: [b] Accessory use in Planned Development Zones; principal use only if the individual Planned Development Zone specifically allows it as a permitted principal use.' Other scale categories include small-scale and medium-scale systems with different permitted uses and site plan requirements, but these do not apply to large-scale systems. The Large-Scale Photovoltaic Solar Energy System Overlay District is also mentioned as allowing principal and accessory uses but is excluded per instructions.

For large-scale ground-mounted photovoltaic solar energy systems (defined as having a total solar facility footprint greater than 7,000 square feet up to a maximum of 35 acres), site plan review is required prior to construction, installation or modification. As part of the site plan application, a "Visual assessment of the visual impacts of the photovoltaic solar energy system" must be submitted. This assessment shall include: line-of-sight profile analysis; the locations, elevations, height, plant species, and/or materials that will comprise the structures, landscaping, and/or grading used to screen and/or mitigate any adverse aesthetic effects of the system; visual simulations, including photographic images, depicting the maximum height of the proposed system components taken from the perspectives of the public right-of-way and of any properties situated in closest proximity; before and after renderings; and possible impacts to any important/scenic views listed in the Tompkins County or Town of Ithaca Scenic Resources Inventories. Other size categories include small-scale (footprint of 2,000 square feet or less) and medium-scale (footprint more than 2,000 up to 7,000 square feet) systems, which have different setback, use, and site plan review requirements, but do not explicitly require visual impact assessments. Glare restrictions are addressed separately and are not part of the visual impact assessment requirements.

A decommissioning plan shall be submitted as part of the application for a special use permit for large-scale solar energy systems (§ 160-158(B)(5)(a)). The plan must specify that after the system can no longer be used or ceases to be used, it shall be removed by the applicant or any subsequent owner, including removal of all infrastructure and remediation of soil and vegetation to return the parcel to its original state prior to construction. The plan shall include an expected timeline and a cost estimate prepared by a professional engineer or contractor, accounting for inflation. Removal must be completed in accordance with the plan. If the system is considered abandoned (defined as one year without electrical energy generation and metered use, § 160-159), and not decommissioned, the municipality may remove the system and restore the property, charging the owner for costs plus a 10% service charge (§ 160-158(B)(5)(b)). Applications for extensions of abandonment are reviewed by the Town Planning Board for a period of two years (§ 160-159).

These requirements apply to solar farms of minimum 15 contiguous acres and 2 MW and above. Other conditions for solar farms include minimum lot area, setbacks, screening, emergency/safety measures, prohibition in certain districts, and compliance with various codes and plans. The Planning Board may impose additional conditions to minimize adverse effects and protect health, safety, and welfare.

The ordinance explicitly states in § 134-52.9 Solar farms, subsection F(1)(m): 'The average height of the solar panel array shall not exceed 15 feet measured from the ground and including any base or supporting materials.' This is the maximum structure height allowed for solar farms defined as having a minimum of 15 contiguous acres and 2 MW and above. No other more restrictive height limits for solar farms are provided in the text. The units are feet as specified in the ordinance.

The ordinance explicitly states a minimum lot area of 15 contiguous acres for solar farms in § 134-52.9 C (1). This minimum lot size applies specifically to solar farms, which are defined and regulated separately in this section. The text states: 'Minimum lot area: 15 contiguous acres.' The following lot area and yard regulations shall apply to solar farms: Minimum front yard setback to fence: 250 feet. Minimum rear yard setback to fence: 100 feet. Also, additional setbacks may be required by the Planning Board in order to provide for the public's safety, health and welfare.

The ordinance explicitly requires screening and vegetative buffers for solar farms (minimum 15 contiguous acres, 2 MW and above). Screening methods include "plantings, berms, and other screening methods" which "may be required to mitigate any impacts" and "shall be continuously maintained and replaced if dead, dying, or falling into disrepair." A landscape plan must show "proposed screening and fencing" and a berm or landscape screen "capable of screening the site, shall be provided along any property line" with evergreen trees planted in double rows. Additionally, for projects on agricultural lands, applicants must "develop, implement, and maintain native vegetation to the extent practicable pursuant to a vegetation management plan" using "native perennial vegetation and foraging habitat beneficial to game birds, songbirds, and pollinators." The Planning Board may require screening "as may be necessary to ensure compatibility with surrounding uses and to protect the natural, historic and scenic resources of the Town."

The ordinance requires that for solar farms, "The manufacturer's or installer's identification and appropriate warning signage shall be posted at the site and be clearly visible." Additionally, "Solar energy systems shall be marked in order to provide emergency responders with appropriate warning and guidance with respect to isolating the electric systems. Materials used for marking shall be weather-resistant. The marking shall be placed adjacent to the main service disconnect location clearly visible from the location where the lever is operated." Furthermore, "Only signage used to identify the location of the solar farm as well as perimeter warning signs shall be allowed and such signage shall otherwise comply with the Town's sign regulations and requirements or as otherwise approved by the Planning Board."

The ordinance explicitly requires for solar farms (minimum 15 contiguous acres, 2 MW and above) a site plan including "existing vegetation and proposed clearing and grading of all sites involved," with clearing and grading activities subject to Planning Board review and requiring written authorization from the Town's Code Enforcement Officer. It mandates submission of "a plan for clearing and/or grading of the site and a stormwater pollution prevention plan (SWPPP) for the site," which must be filed and recorded and include security approved by the Town's Consulting Engineer. Post-construction, "all disturbed areas where soil has been exposed shall be reseeded with grass and/or planted with low-level vegetation capable of preventing soil erosion and airborne dust and demonstrating established growth," with maintenance provisions included in the operations and maintenance plan. For projects on agricultural lands, detailed soil preservation and erosion control measures are required, including preservation of drainage and erosion control structures, topsoil stripping and stockpiling, restoration requirements such as soil decompaction, regrading, seeding, repair of drainage structures, and a monitoring and remediation period of no less than two years. These requirements are part of the conditions for site plan approval and ongoing operation of solar farms.

§ 134-52.9(A) states: 'Subject to the issuance of site plan approval and a special use permit and other requirements as set forth herein, solar farms shall not be a permitted use in any zoning district other than the Agricultural District (AG); Agricultural/Residential District (AR); Planned Development District (PD) and the Industrial/Manufacturing District (IM) within the Town.' § 134-52.9(B) prohibits solar farms in Residential Districts (RA, RB, RC, RM), Business/Commercial Districts (BN, BG, BR), Conservation/Outdoor Recreation District (CR), and Major Highway District (HY). Other solar energy systems such as building-integrated, rooftop-mounted, and ground-mounted systems are permitted as accessory uses or with building permits but are not classified as solar farms.

The ordinance explicitly requires a visual impact analysis as part of the full environmental assessment form for solar farms (§ 134-52.9, F(1)(r)). Photographic simulations must be included showing the proposed solar farm from neighboring properties and other vantage points selected by the Planning Board. The Planning Board must make specific determinations that the solar farm "will not impair any scenic viewshed" (§ 134-52.9, C(7)) and must "avoid areas that substantially contribute to and are important to the scenic quality of the landscape" (§ 134-52.9, C(8)). The Planning Board may require screening, including plantings, berms, and other methods to mitigate impacts (§ 134-52.9, C(r)). The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems in § 220-98, Subsections N, O, and P. It requires "a cash deposit, bond or other form of security... in an amount sufficient to ensure the good-faith performance of the terms and conditions of the permit... and shall also provide for the removal of the solar energy system and restoration of the lot subsequent to removal." The security amount is "125% of the cost of removal of the solar energy system and restoration of the property with an escalator of 2% annually for the life of the solar energy system," reduced by estimated salvage value. Upon default, the Town may forfeit the security to remove the system and restore the property. If the system ceases electricity generation for 12 months, the Town may notify the owner/operator to implement the decommissioning plan within 360 days. Failure to comply allows the Town to use the security for removal and restoration. The decommissioning plan must address "the cost of removing the solar energy system," "the time required to decommission and remove the solar energy system and any ancillary structures," and "the time required to repair any damage caused to the property." The site must be restored "to as natural a condition as possible within six months of the removal of all equipment, structures and foundations," including "restoration of the surface grade and soil after removal of all equipment and revegetation of restored soil areas with native seed mixes."

summary: All ground-mounted solar energy systems shall be dismantled and removed immediately from a lot where the permit or approval has been revoked or the system has been deemed inoperative or abandoned for more than 365 days, at the cost of the solar energy system owner. Tier 2 solar energy systems shall have glare restrictions requiring that "All solar panels shall have antireflective coating(s)." They are permitted as accessory structures in all zoning districts, with site plan approval required for commercial or industrial business use, but exempt for farm operations. Other tiers include Tier 1 systems (roof-mounted or building-integrated) which also require antireflective coatings on solar panels, and Tier 3 systems which are prohibited. The 15 feet limit is the most restrictive and applies generally and specifically to farm operations within certain districts. Units are explicitly stated as feet.

Tier 2 solar energy systems, defined as ground-mounted systems that generate no more than 110% of the electricity consumed on-site or on multiple properties owned by the same entity, are permitted as accessory structures in all zoning districts, subject to site plan approval for commercial or industrial uses producing energy principally for on-site use. Systems for farm operations are exempt from site plan review but must meet setback, height, and glare requirements. Tier 1 systems (roof-mounted and building-integrated) are permitted outright in all zoning districts. Tier 3 systems, which include systems not classified as Tier 1 or Tier 2, are prohibited in all zoning districts. The ordinance took effect immediately upon filing with the Secretary of State of New York and is currently in force.

Tier 2 solar energy systems shall be located in the side or rear yard of a property. All Tier 2 solar energy systems shall be screened so that the view of such systems is minimized from adjacent properties to the extent reasonably practicable. Evergreen tree plantings may be required to screen portions of the site from nearby residential property, public roads, and from public sites known to contain important views or vistas, such as gateway entrances to the Town. (Section 150-166(B)(1)(e)) Tier 2 solar energy systems are ground-mounted solar energy systems that generate no more than 110% of the electricity consumed on the site or more than one site or piece of property within the jurisdictional limits of the Town of Livonia owned by the same person, entity, farm or business over the previous 12 months. Tier 2 systems may be developed, operated and maintained by a third party by lease agreement or power purchase agreement but shall not produce power in excess of the 110% total consumption. Tier 2 systems are permitted as accessory structures in all zoning districts, with site plan approval required for those built or modified for commercial or industrial business use, while other Tier 2 systems including farm operations are exempt from site plan approval. Screening requirements apply to all Tier 2 systems. Other requirements for Tier 2 systems include setbacks, location restrictions (side or rear yard, no front yard unless 200 feet from road and concealed), height limits (maximum 15 feet), and glare reduction (antireflective coatings).

The ordinance requires that "Solar Energy Systems that have been abandoned and/or not producing electricity for 1 year shall be removed at the owner and/or operators’ expense, which at the owner’s option, paid by the owner or from any security that was required as part of the permit by the Town." For Tier 1 and Tier 2 systems, failure to remove after 1 year results in removal by the Town and reimbursement of expenses, with unpaid expenses re-levied on taxes. For Tier 3 systems, a decommissioning plan must be submitted addressing removal costs, time for decommissioning, and site repair, with a security bond of 125% of removal cost plus 2% annual escalator. The ordinance states that "Any solar energy system Tier 1,2,3 or4" requires decommissioning and bonding agreements approved before permit issuance. summary: Any site containing a utility-scale solar energy system shall contain fencing or other device acceptable to the Town, enclosing all solar energy system components that present safety hazards, subject to animal migration mitigation design. The ordinance explicitly requires that "The design, construction, operation, and maintenance of a utility-scale solar energy system shall prevent the misdirection and/or reflection of solar rays onto neighboring properties, public roads, and public parks to the extent practicable." The height of a utility-scale solar energy system shall not exceed 15 feet when oriented at maximum tilt. This is explicitly stated in § 200-204 Special use permit criteria, subsection D. Section 200-204(P) requires "Screening of a permanent nature, such as a berm, landscape screen, other opaque enclosure, or a combination thereof, capable of fully enclosing the solar energy system, such that it will significantly diminish sight lines from all adjacent property." It mandates "Vegetative screening consisting of two staggered rows of evergreen trees, minimum of seven feet tall when planted, spaced no farther than 10 feet apart" and "one row of shrubs/bushes, with an expected growth height of at least 10 feet tall, at least three feet tall when planted, placed no farther than 10 feet apart." The Planning Board may require "additional screening, including but not limited to opaque fencing materials and or additional vegetative plantings" to protect sight lines. All vegetation must be "exclusively of vegetation native to the Western New York Region chosen to promote the habitats of native wildlife and pollinators." Screening plans must be "drafted and endorsed by licensed engineer or other competent professional" and include images of screening at installation and at 2, 5, and 10 years after installation. Temporary screening during construction is also required to "significantly diminish sight lines from all adjacent roadways and any residential dwellings on adjacent properties." These requirements apply specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in the article. Other conditions in section 200-204 include setbacks, height limits, fencing requirements, and decommissioning plans, but the vegetative buffer and screening requirements are detailed in subsection P.

Applicants for a special use permit to place, construct, and/or make a major modification to a utility-scale solar energy system must submit "Documentation of the clearing, grading, stormwater and erosion control plans" (§ 200-203.B.(3)). Before the Town of Lockport issues a clearing, grading, stormwater or building permit for a utility-scale solar energy system, "the applicant shall submit a stormwater and erosion control plan to the Town Engineer and Stormwater Management Officer for their review and approval" (§ 200-203.T.(1)). The plan "shall minimize the potential adverse impacts on wetlands and Class I and II streams and the banks and vegetation along those streams and wetlands and minimize erosion or sedimentation" (§ 200-203.T.(2)). These requirements apply specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in the article.

summary: The ordinance requires a "Decommissioning and removal plan" to be submitted as part of the application for Large-scale solar energy systems, which "shall specify that after the solar energy system ceases operation for its intended purpose, the system shall be removed" by the applicant or subsequent owners. The plan must include "how the removal of the solar energy system and all related equipment and structures shall be conducted and how the remediation of soil and vegetation shall be conducted to return the property to substantially its condition prior to construction," a timeline for execution, and a cost estimate prepared by a professional engineer or contractor. The removal and restoration must occur "no greater than six (6) months after the solar energy system ceases, for twelve (12) consecutive months, to be used for its intended purpose." Additionally, the applicant must provide "security in a form acceptable to the Town’s attorney and Planning Board and in an amount sufficient to pay for the costs and expenses of removal of the solar energy system and related equipment and structures and the restoration of the site," which is subject to re-evaluation every five years. If the security does not cover costs, the owner and operator are "jointly and severally, and corporately and personally, liable" and the Town may place a lien on the property. These requirements apply specifically to Large-scale solar energy systems permitted as a special permit use, subject to site plan approval and other conditions listed in the ordinance.

summary: All Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems "shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing at a height of at least seven (7) feet to prevent unauthorized access." There "shall be a six inch gap at the bottom of the fencing to allow small wildlife access to and from the site." "Warning signs with the owner’s contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing." Additionally, the "maximum height of fencing" is set at "8 feet." These requirements are part of the special use permit conditions for Large-scale solar energy systems, which are permitted as a special permit use in all zoning districts except the Ridge and Valley Protection (RVP) district. Other conditions include lot width, setbacks, building height, decommissioning plans, security, screening, and maintenance requirements.

Among the special use permit requirements, solar panels and equipment "shall be designed and sited so as to not reflect glare onto other properties, public roads or private roads or right-of-ways, and shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard." Other conditions include equipment specifications, operation and maintenance plans, decommissioning and removal plans with security, ownership change notifications, dimensional requirements, fencing, screening, and aesthetic considerations.

The ordinance states under subsection H.(2)(h) that the maximum height of solar collectors for large-scale solar energy systems is 16 feet, and the building height limit is 35 feet. These height limits apply specifically to large-scale solar energy systems, defined as ground-mounted systems producing energy primarily for offsite sale or consumption. The total area to be occupied by the solar energy system shall not exceed twenty (20) acres. This is the maximum lot size explicitly stated for Large-scale solar energy systems, which are defined as ground-mounted systems producing energy primarily for offsite sale or consumption. summary: The ordinance permits accessory freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems in all zoning districts as accessory structures subject to site plan approval and conditions (§ 250-36F). It states: "Accessory freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems are permitted in all zoning districts as an accessory structure subject to the following conditions." Solar facilities and solar power plants as primary uses are also permitted in all zoning districts with site plan and special use permit approval (§ 250-36G). Rooftop and building-mounted solar power systems are permitted in all zoning districts without Planning Board approval unless deemed necessary (§ 250-36C). Freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems accessory to single-family and two-family residences are permitted in all zoning districts with conditions and kilowatt limits (§ 250-36E). The text does not specify or list any particular zoning district names or abbreviations for these uses, only referring generally to "all zoning districts."

Notwithstanding bulk table requirements to the contrary, developmental coverage of a lot with a solar facility or solar power plant shall not exceed 85%. This coverage limit is expressed as a percentage of the lot's developmental coverage, not as a specific area value. This applies specifically to solar facilities or solar power plants, which are defined as energy generation facilities primarily for wholesale or retail sales of electricity.
