summary: § 250-38 Decommissioning requires that if a freestanding solar power system, ground-mounted solar power system, solar facility or solar power plant has been out of active and continuous service for a period of one year, it shall be removed from the premises to a place of safe and legal disposal, including any and all structures and accessory structures. The site shall be restored to as natural a condition as possible. Such removal shall be completed within 18 months of the cessation of active and continuous use. A permit for demolition is required under Chapter 94 of the Town Code. If the owner fails to remove the system, the Town may serve a notice of demand to remove, and if noncompliance continues, the Town Supervisor may authorize removal and recover costs by assessment and lien on the property. Additionally, § 250-36G(1)(c) requires a written narrative describing the eventual decommissioning of the solar facility or solar power plant, including the anticipated life, estimated decommissioning costs, and method for insuring funds will be available for decommissioning and restoration of the site. These requirements apply specifically to solar facilities and solar power plants, which are defined as energy generation facilities with the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of electricity.

The solar facility or solar power plant installation shall be enclosed by a fence consistent with NYSERDA regulations. Planning Board may require a greater height in fencing depending on individual conditions. Other related fencing requirements include: freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems shall be enclosed by a continuous fence (or fence with privacy slats) consistent with NYS and federal requirements (§ 250-36E(5)); accessory freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems shall be enclosed by a fence consistent with NYSERDA regulations (§ 250-36F(4)).

Solar facility and solar power plant panels and equipment shall be surfaced, designed and sited so as not to reflect glare onto adjacent properties and roadways (§ 250-36 G(12)). Solar facilities and solar power plants require site plan and special use permit approval, must be on lots of at least 10 acres, have a maximum height of 15 feet for freestanding or ground-mounted collectors, and be enclosed by a fence consistent with NYSERDA regulations (§ 250-36 G). Additional general glare restriction states all solar energy power systems and equipment shall be surfaced, designed and sited so as not to reflect glare onto adjacent properties and roadways (§ 250-36 I).

The height of the freestanding or ground-mounted solar collectors and any mounts shall not exceed 15 feet when oriented at maximum tilt (§ 250-36 G(10)). This applies specifically to solar facilities and solar power plants, which are defined as energy generation facilities primarily for wholesale or retail sales of electricity. Other related height limits include 10 feet for freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems accessory to single-family and two-family residences (§ 250-36 E(7) and F(6)), and rooftop and building-mounted solar power systems must not exceed the maximum permitted building height in the zoning district (§ 250-36 C(2)). The unit for the maximum height is feet.

The ordinance states: 'A solar facility or solar power plant shall only be permitted on lots with a minimum size of 10 acres.' This is found in § 250-36 G(8). Other minimum lot sizes mentioned for smaller or accessory solar power systems include 80,000 square feet for freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems accessory to single family and two-family residences (§ 250-36 E(2)), but these do not apply to solar facilities or solar power plants as defined. The unit for the minimum lot size for solar facilities or solar power plants is explicitly given as acres.

All solar facility or solar power plant equipment and installations shall be subject to a minimum setback of 100 feet plus the setback minimum from all property lines required in the zoning district. The Planning Board may require increased setbacks as it deems necessary based on the surrounding conditions. (§ 250-36 G (7)) Other setback provisions exist for smaller or accessory freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems, such as a 15-foot setback from property lines (§ 250-36 E(4) and F(2)), but these apply to smaller or accessory systems, not commercial-scale solar facilities or power plants.

Solar facilities and solar power plants "shall be screened when possible and practicable from adjoining lots and street rights of way through the use of architectural features, earth berms, landscaping, or other screening which will harmonize with the character of the property and surrounding area." Additional screening may be required as part of the Planning Board approval (§ 250-36(G)(6)). Other related provisions include: freestanding or ground-mounted solar power systems requiring fencing and possible additional screening if Planning Board approval is needed (§ 250-36(E)(5), (10); § 250-36(F)(4), (5), (10)).

For solar facilities and solar power plants, the ordinance requires that "The manufacturer's or installer's identification and appropriate warning signage shall be posted at the site and clearly visible." This is stated in § 250-36.G.(5). Other conditions for solar facilities and solar power plants include site plan and special use permit approval (§ 250-36.G.(1)), compliance with environmental review (§ 250-36.G.(2)), fencing (§ 250-36.G.(11)), screening (§ 250-36.G.(6)), setbacks (§ 250-36.G.(7)), minimum lot size (§ 250-36.G.(8)), height limits (§ 250-36.G.(10)), and undergrounding of power lines (§ 250-36.G.(13)). For smaller or accessory freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems, different permitting, setback, height, and screening requirements apply (§ 250-36.E and § 250-36.F), but signage requirements are not explicitly mentioned for these categories.

The installation of a solar facility or solar power plant "shall be considered a land development activity for the purposes of Article XII, Stormwater Management, of the Code of the Town of Mount Hope." The site "shall comply with all current standards for New York State stormwater regulations." This requirement is explicitly stated in § 250-36G(3). Other related provisions include freestanding or ground-mounted solar power systems accessory to approved site plans, which "shall be considered a land development activity for purposes of Article XII, Stormwater Management," and must comply with New York State stormwater regulations (§ 250-36F(8)).

Solar facilities and solar power plants "shall be permitted as structures in all zoning districts subject to the following conditions: Site plan and special use permit approval granted by the Town of Mount Hope Planning Board is required under Article XI herein." Other solar energy systems such as rooftop and building-mounted systems are permitted in all zoning districts with building permits and limited Planning Board review (§ 250-36 C). Freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems accessory to single-family and two-family residences are permitted as accessory structures with building permits and size, setback, and height restrictions (§ 250-36 E). Larger freestanding or ground-mounted systems exceeding 30 kilowatts require site plan approval and special use permits (§ 250-36 E(10)). Accessory freestanding and ground-mounted systems require site plan approval and may require special use permits if exceeding certain kilowatt thresholds (§ 250-36 F). Solar facilities and solar power plants require site plan and special use permit approval in all zoning districts, with additional conditions including minimum lot size of 10 acres, setbacks, height limits, screening, and compliance with environmental and stormwater regulations (§ 250-36 G).

The ordinance states: 'A Tier 3 solar energy system shall not exceed 50% of the lot on which it is installed.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for Tier 3 solar energy systems, expressed as a percentage of the lot area. No other maximum land coverage values for Tier 3 systems are provided.

section: § 224A-8 Permitting requirements for Tier 3 solar energy systems

summary: For Tier 3 solar energy systems, the ordinance explicitly requires that "All solar panels shall have anti-reflective coating(s)." Tier 3 systems are defined as "all solar energy systems that are not included in the list for Tier 1 and Tier 2 solar energy systems, or any community solar facility where 75% or greater percent of the energy generated at the site is utilized off-site." section: § 224A-8 Permitting requirements for Tier 3 solar energy systems

summary: The total coverage of a lot with freestanding solar panels cannot exceed 60% lot coverage. "Lot coverage" is defined as the area measured from the outer edge(s) of the arrays, inverters, batteries, storage cells and all other mechanical equipment used to create, store or transfer solar energy, exclusive of fencing and roadways.

All applications for a SEPF shall be accompanied by a decommissioning plan to be implemented upon abandonment, or cessation of activity, or in conjunction with removal of the SEPF. Prior to issuance of a building permit, the owner or operator of the facility or structure shall post a letter of credit or other suitable financial guarantee, as determined by the Town, in a face amount of not less than 120% of the estimated cost of complete decommissioning and removal to ensure proper, safe removal of the facility and related structures. The plan shall include removal of aboveground and below-ground equipment, structures and foundations, restoration of the surface grade and soil, revegetation with native seed mixes, soil tests showing no contamination, a reasonable time frame for site restoration, and proper and lawful disposal of solar panels. The plan must be implemented without delay if the applicant ceases operation for 18 months, begins but does not complete construction within 18 months after final special permit approval, or the special permit expires or is not renewed. The Town may notify the applicant to implement the decommissioning plan under these conditions, with specified time frames for completion. If the applicant fails to implement the plan, the Town may restore the site at its own expense and recover costs from the financial guarantee and the applicant, with unpaid costs becoming a lien and tax on the property.

All solar panels shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight-foot-high fence that is of a type that is consistent with the surrounding neighborhood and the use of the property, as reasonably determined by the Town Planning Board. All mechanical equipment of a SEPF, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight-foot-high anchored mini-mesh chain-link fence with two-foot tip out and a self-locking gate. All such fences shall contain five-inch-high by sixteen-inch-wide grade-level cutouts every 75 feet to permit small animals to move freely into and out of the site. Landscape screening shall be provided in accordance with the landscaping provisions of this chapter.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "All SEPF shall be designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare toward any inhabited buildings on adjacent properties as well as adjacent street rights-of-way." This applies to commercial SEPFs, which are defined as "A SEPF that primarily produces energy for off-site sale or consumption, or any SEPF that has a capacity of 200 kilowatts or more." The glare restriction is found under design standards for commercial SEPFs. Other related requirements include minimum lot area, maximum lot coverage, height and setback restrictions, buffer and setback restrictions, fencing, and various design and operational standards, but the specific glare restriction is limited to preventing reflective glare toward adjacent inhabited buildings and street rights-of-way.

The maximum height for freestanding solar panels located on the ground or attached to a framework located on the ground shall not exceed 25 feet in height above the ground at their highest tilted position. This applies specifically to commercial SEPFs as defined in the ordinance. For comparison, noncommercial SEPFs have a maximum height of 20 feet, but that does not apply to commercial SEPFs.
The minimum lot area for a commercial SEPF shall be five acres, or six acres for every megawatt of capacity, whichever is more. The units are acres, which is a standard area measurement.

A minimum 150-foot setback from residential, agricultural, and sensitive site property lines, a 100-foot setback from the center of adjacent Town, county and state roads, and a minimum seventy-five-foot setback from all other adjacent property lines, shall be maintained. ("No commercial SEPF shall be located on a sensitive site. A minimum 150-foot setback from residential, and agricultural and sensitive site property lines, a 100-foot setback from the center of adjacent Town, county and state roads, and a minimum seventy-five-foot setback from all other adjacent property lines, shall be maintained.")

No commercial SEPF shall be located on a sensitive site. A minimum 150-foot setback from residential, and agricultural and sensitive site property lines, a 100-foot setback from the center of adjacent Town, county and state roads, and a minimum seventy-five-foot setback from all other adjacent property lines, shall be maintained.

A minimum 100-foot setback from the center of adjacent Town, county and state roads shall be maintained for commercial SEPFs. Other setback options include a 150-foot setback from residential, agricultural and sensitive site property lines, and a 75-foot setback from all other adjacent property lines.

A buffer of natural and undisturbed vegetation, supplemented with evergreen plantings which shall be at least 10 feet in height and no less than eight feet apart, shall be provided around all SEPF equipment to provide screening from such adjacent roads and parcels. Visibility of the SEPF equipment from any adjacent property or road shall be at least 50% screened by such vegetative screening. Landscape screening shall be provided in accordance with the landscaping provisions of this chapter. Additionally, all solar panels shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight-foot-high fence consistent with the surrounding neighborhood, and all mechanical equipment shall be enclosed by a minimum eight-foot-high anchored mini-mesh chain-link fence with specific features. These requirements apply to commercial SEPFs, defined as SEPFs that primarily produce energy for off-site sale or consumption, or any SEPF that has a capacity of 200 kilowatts or more.

A sign not to exceed 2.25 square feet shall be attached to a fence adjacent to the main access gate and shall list the facility name, owner and phone number. A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations. An emergency telephone number shall be posted at any SEPF building and on the applicants' website, if any, so that the appropriate people may be contacted should any SEPF need immediate attention.
section: § 113-15 Requirements for commercial SEPFs, subsection F. Signs

summary: The ordinance requires for commercial SEPF permit applications: "Plans to prevent the erosion of soil both during and after construction, excessive runoff, and flooding of other properties, as applicable. There should be preconstruction and post-construction drainage calculations for the site completed by a certified engineer. From this, the engineer must show how there will be no increase in runoff from the site." Additionally, the design standards include "A storm drainage and grading plan for analysis of proposed handling of surface water runoff and erosion control, including, where applicable, under state or federal requirements, a stormwater notice of intent and a stormwater pollution prevention plan." These requirements apply to commercial SEPFs, defined as those "that primarily produces energy for off-site sale or consumption, or any SEPF that has a capacity of 200 kilowatts or more."

§ 113-14 requires "Photography assessing the visibility from key viewpoints, existing tree lines, and proposed elevations. Pictures shall be digitally enhanced to simulate the appearance of the as-built aboveground site facilities as they would appear from distances within a three-mile radius of such SEPF." It also requires a "Preliminary report prepared by applicant describing... Proposed mitigation measures for visual impacts and other environmental impacts of each SEPF." § 113-15 E requires "The applicant shall submit a map plan which depicts and includes... A buffer of natural and undisturbed vegetation, supplemented with evergreen plantings... to provide screening from such adjacent roads and parcels." Height and setback restrictions (§ 113-15 C and D) also apply to commercial SEPFs to mitigate visual impact. These requirements apply to commercial SEPFs defined as "A SEPF that primarily produces energy for off-site sale or consumption, or any SEPF that has a capacity of 200 kilowatts or more."
section: § 113-14 SEPF permit applications requirements and § 113-15 Requirements for commercial SEPFs

summary: No commercial SEPF shall be located on a sensitive site. A minimum 150-foot setback from residential, and agricultural and sensitive site property lines, a 100-foot setback from the center of adjacent Town, county and state roads, and a minimum seventy-five-foot setback from all other adjacent property lines, shall be maintained. Sensitive sites include water bodies defined by water's edge at the time a SEPF permit application is submitted; Hunt's Pond, Great Brook, Millbrook, Unadilla River.

The ordinance defines a LARGE-SCALE SOLAR COLLECTION SYSTEM or SOLAR FARM as an area of land or other area, on property consisting of 10 acres or more, used for a solar collection system principally used to capture solar energy and convert it to electrical energy for interconnection to the utility grid under New York State regulations for remote net-metering and/or community distributed generation (CDG or community solar). The minimum lot size is explicitly stated as 10 acres or more.
section: 60-410L(2)(b){4} LARGE-SCALE SOLAR COLLECTION SYSTEM or SOLAR FARM

summary: A decommissioning plan shall be submitted as part of the application for large-scale solar energy systems and must specify that after the solar energy system is no longer producing power for a period of 12 months, it shall be removed by the property owner within 90 days of notification from the Town requiring removal. The plan shall demonstrate the existing conditions on the site before construction, the plan for removal including disposal or recycling of components, and restoration of soil and vegetation to return the parcel to its original state. All aboveground and below-ground equipment, structures and/or foundations must be removed. The plan shall include an expected timeline for removal and a cost estimate prepared by a professional engineer or contractor, taking inflation into account. Prior to issuance of a building permit, the property owner or operator must post a performance bond or other suitable guarantee in the face amount of the estimated cost of decommissioning, including inflation over the anticipated life of the array. The cost estimate and bond shall be reviewed and adjusted at five-year intervals. The bond or security shall be used by the Town to perform necessary decommissioning work in case of default and shall remain in full force until removal and restoration are complete. Proof of maintenance of the bond must be submitted annually. These requirements apply to large-scale solar energy systems, which are permitted in the Solar Overlay District upon granting of a special use permit and site plan approval by the Planning Board, with a nameplate capacity not exceeding 5 megawatts alternating current.

All large-scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access. The type of fencing shall be determined by the Planning Board as part of site plan review. Additionally, all mechanical equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum six-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate, and provided with landscape screening.

Large-scale solar energy systems, including community solar energy systems, are subject to regulations under Section 205-18, Paragraph O. These systems are permitted in the Solar Overlay District upon granting of a special use permit and site plan approval. They must not exceed a nameplate capacity of 5 megawatts alternating current and adhere to height and setback requirements. Specifically, "Solar panels and equipment shall be surfaced, designed and sited in order to prevent reflective glare onto any inhabited buildings on adjacent properties as well as roadways." Additional requirements include fencing, signage, landscaping, underground utility lines where practicable, and decommissioning plans. The special use permit application must include equipment specifications, operation and maintenance plans, and performance bonds. The Planning Board may impose conditions to enforce these standards or comply with SEQRA.

The ordinance states: 'No parcel shall include one or more large scale solar energy systems that, in the aggregate, exceed a nameplate capacity of 5 megawatts alternating current.' This is an explicit maximum project size limit for large-scale solar energy systems. The unit is specified as megawatts alternating current (MW AC). There are no other numerical size limits provided for large-scale systems in the text.

No component of any large scale solar energy system may be located within 75 feet of the front lot line or 35 feet of any side or rear lot line. These setbacks are in addition to adhering to the otherwise applicable height and setback requirements of the underlying zoning district.
section: SECTION 2, Paragraph D of Section 205-18, Subparagraph (2)(a)[4]

summary: Large-scale solar energy systems (up to 5 MW) are subject to special use permit and site plan approval. Screening requirements include: 'As determined necessary by the Planning Board, a landscaped buffer shall be provided around all equipment and solar energy systems to provide screening from neighboring residences and roadways.' Additionally, 'Any buildings, inverters, transformers and/or substations and accessory structures shall, to the extent reasonably possible, use materials, colors, and textures that will blend the facility into the existing environment and/or be screened from view.' Mechanical equipment must be 'completely enclosed by a minimum six-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate, and provided with landscape screening.' Fencing type is determined by the Planning Board. These requirements are part of the design standards under the special use permit and site plan standards for large-scale solar energy systems in the Solar Overlay District.

The ordinance requires that for large-scale solar energy systems, "the owner or operator of the solar energy system must have identification and contact information and appropriate warning signage posted at the entrance to the solar energy system and be clearly visible. Signage shall list the facility name, owner or operator and phone number." Additionally, "a clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all inverters, transformers and/or substations and in such other locations as the Planning Board determines is necessary." These requirements are found in Section 205-18, Paragraph O, Subparagraph (2)(c). Other related conditions include fencing, setback, and design requirements, but these do not pertain to signage. No other signage options or conditions are specified.

Large-scale solar energy systems, which term includes community solar energy systems, are permitted in the Solar Overlay District upon the granting of a special use permit and subject to site plan approval by the Planning Board (§ 205-18(D)(1)(a)). The text states: 'Large-scale solar energy systems are permitted in the Solar Overlay District upon the granting of a special use permit and subject to site plan approval by the Planning Board.' No other districts (RA-5, RA-2, RA-1, C, C-Rec, C-R, C-I, FZ-O) are indicated as permitting these systems as special use or otherwise. The Solar Overlay District is described as supplementing and being in addition to uses permitted or allowed by special permit in the underlying zoning districts (§ 205-5(A)).

Large-scale solar energy systems are permitted in the Solar Overlay District upon the granting of a special use permit and subject to site plan approval by the Planning Board (§ 205-18(D)(1)(a)). The Planning Board review includes standards such as: use of materials, colors, and textures that will blend the facility into the existing environment and/or be screened from view (§ 205-18(D)(2)(d)[1]); landscaped buffers around equipment and solar energy systems to provide screening from neighboring residences and roadways as determined necessary (§ 205-18(D)(2)(d)[3]); and placing on-site utility and transmission lines underground if visible and unable to be adequately screened (§ 205-18(D)(2)(d)[5]). The Solar Overlay District aims to minimize interference with existing viewsheds to the extent practicable (§ 205-4(B)(7)(g)). These requirements constitute explicit visual impact assessment requirements for large-scale solar energy systems up to 5 MW. Other conditions include site plan requirements, special use permit application materials, decommissioning plans, performance bonds, and inspection reports, but these do not specifically address visual impact assessment.

The total surface area of all ground-mounted and freestanding solar collectors, including solar voltaic cells, panels and arrays, shall not exceed 80% of the total parcel area. This is the maximum land coverage allowed for Solar Energy Farms exceeding six (6) acres. The unit is expressed as a percentage of the total parcel area.
section: §100-5.8 D Solar Energy Farm Site Requirements

summary: All applications for a solar farm shall be accompanied by a Decommissioning Plan to be implemented upon abandonment (2 years without annual site renewal) and/or in conjunction with removal of the facility. The owner or operator shall physically remove the installation no more than 150 days after the date of discontinued operations and notify the Land Use Officer by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Physical removal includes all ground-mounted solar collectors, structures, equipment, security barriers and transmission lines. Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste must comply with local, state, and federal regulations. The site must be stabilized or re-vegetated as necessary to minimize erosion, with possible allowance by the Town Board to leave landscaping or designated below-grade foundations. The solar farm is considered abandoned if it fails to operate for more than two years without written consent of the Town Board. If removal is not completed within 150 days of abandonment or proposed decommissioning, the Town may enter the property and remove the installation. Additionally, the applicant must provide an estimate of decommissioning costs prepared by a qualified engineer and establish financial surety (escrowed funds, bonds, or otherwise) to ensure funds are available for removal and restoration. These requirements apply to Solar Energy Farms defined as systems exceeding six (6) acres whose primary use is to capture solar energy and convert it to electrical energy to transfer to the public electric grid for sale or credit.

All mechanical equipment on a Solar Farm, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, are completely enclosed by a minimum 8’ high fence with a self-locking gate. This applies to Solar Energy Farms defined as systems exceeding six (6) acres whose primary use is to capture solar energy and convert it to electrical energy to transfer to the public electric grid. The fencing requirement is part of the Solar Energy Farm Site Requirements. Other standards include accessibility with two points of entry/exit at least 100 feet apart, setbacks of 50 feet from property lines (200 feet if abutting residential uses), and restrictions on signage limited to announcement signs such as  "no trespassing"  or danger warnings. The ordinance also requires annual site plan review renewal, local emergency services training, and decommissioning plans.

The ordinance states that "All solar energy production systems are designed and located in order to minimize reflective glare toward any habitable buildings, as well as streets and rights-of-way." This applies to Solar Energy Farms defined as systems exceeding six (6) acres whose primary use is to capture solar energy and convert it to electrical energy to transfer to the public electric grid. Other relevant conditions include setbacks, fencing, site plan review, and annual renewal requirements, but the explicit glare restriction is focused on minimizing reflective glare toward habitable buildings and public ways.

The Solar Energy Farm shall be at least six (6) acres in size. This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for Solar Energy Farms as defined in the ordinance. The unit 'acres' is used to specify the area. No other minimum lot size values are provided for Solar Energy Farms exceeding six acres.
section: §100-5.8 D. Solar Energy Farm Site Requirements

summary: All solar energy system components shall have a 50 foot setback, unless abutting residential uses. Whereby it shall be located a minimum of 200’ from property lines.

There shall be no signs except announcement signs, such as 'no trespassing signs or any signs required to warn of danger'. A sign is required that identifies the owner and operator with an emergency telephone number where the owner and operator can be reached on a 24-hour basis.

The ordinance states: 'The total surface area of all ground-mounted and freestanding solar collectors shall not exceed 1,000 square feet in area or 5% of the area of the lot on which they are located, whichever is less.' This means the maximum allowed system size per unit area is 5% of the lot area, which is the most restrictive limit compared to the absolute 1,000 square feet cap.

The height of the solar collector and any mounts shall not exceed the height of the principal structure or 20 feet, whichever is less, when oriented at maximum tilt. This applies to ground-mounted and freestanding solar collectors permitted by special permit (§ 331-25 D.(2)). Other height-related provisions include roof-mounted solar collectors extending no more than three feet above the roof surface (§ 331-25 A.(2)) and various height exceptions for rooftop collectors in different districts (§ 331-25 E), but these do not apply to ground-mounted systems covering 1,000 square feet or more. The units for the height restriction are feet.

Ground-mounted solar energy collectors not extending closer than six feet to any side lot line or 10 feet to a rear lot line. Other setback options include a minimum of five feet from all property lines (§ 331-25 A(3)), but the six feet side lot line setback is more restrictive. The rear lot line setback is 10 feet.

Ground-mounted and freestanding solar collectors are permitted by special permit to the Planning Board as accessory structures in all zoning districts, subject to requirements including that "Solar collectors shall be screened from neighboring properties and the public right-of-way, as appropriate." Systems covering 1,000 square feet or more require Planning Board approval (§ 331-25 A). Additional conditions include setbacks, height limits, location in side or rear yards, and removal of abandoned systems. Screening is explicitly required under § 331-25 D(7).

Ground-mounted and freestanding solar collectors are permitted by special permit to the Planning Board as accessory structures in all zoning districts, subject to requirements including setback, height, area limits, and obtaining a building permit. Rooftop and building-mounted solar energy collectors are allowed as a permitted accessory use in all zoning districts without special permit but with building permit requirements and height restrictions. The ordinance does not specify particular district names or abbreviations for utility-scale solar energy systems or similar large-scale systems requiring special use approval.

Fencing and other security features shall integrate wildlife corridors and make other accommodations to minimize impacts on local wildlife. If fencing is included in the design, the fence shall be a box wire fence with wood posts, or a similar, farm-style fencing. Chain link fencing is not permitted.

The ordinance requires that any project approval for a Large-Scale Solar project "include a plan for screening to minimize potential visual impacts associated with the Large-Scale Solar project from adjoining public roads, nearby residences and important viewsheds." The screening plan "shall include landscaping design with coniferous trees (evergreens), shrubs and Native Perennial Vegetation for screening purposes arranged to form a natural appearance and continuous solid screening," with a default design of "two (2) rows of coniferous trees, eight (8) feet on center, in staggered rows." The Planning Board may also allow "other screening methods" to maintain the character of the property and viewsheds. Additionally, the plan may "consider the use of optional earth berms in conjunction with a double row of staggered coniferous trees, shrubs, and Native Perennial Vegetation landscaping when topography and/or landscaping alone cannot screen more than 50% of the Large-Scale Solar facility from nearby residences, structures, important viewsheds, public parks and roads." The plan must "ensure the continued growth and survival of trees, shrubs, and other Native Perennial Vegetation landscaping for screening" and include a replacement plan for any vegetation that dies or fails to thrive, secured by a "three (3) year letter of credit." Existing trees and vegetation on property lines and adjacent roadways "shall be maintained to the greatest extent possible."

Section 190-58(H)(4)(a)(xv) SCREENING AND VISIBILITY requires a line-of-sight analysis and photosimulation to assess impacts from neighboring residential properties, adjoining public roads, and important viewsheds determined by the Planning Board. Viewshed assessment must consider screening/visibility from structures, residences, important viewsheds, and public places. The project approval must include a screening plan to minimize visual impacts, including landscaping with coniferous trees, shrubs, and Native Perennial Vegetation arranged to form natural continuous solid screening. Optional earth berms may be used with double rows of staggered coniferous trees and shrubs when topography or landscaping alone cannot screen more than 50% of the facility from nearby residences, structures, viewsheds, parks, and roads. The plan must ensure continued growth and survival of screening vegetation with a replacement plan and a three-year letter of credit to satisfy conditions. Existing trees and vegetation on property lines and adjacent roadways must be maintained to the greatest extent possible.

The ordinance states: 'Notwithstanding bulk table requirements to the contrary, developmental coverage of a lot with a solar farm or solar power plant shall not exceed 85%.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for solar farms or solar power plants. The unit is expressed as a percentage of the lot's developmental coverage. Other related conditions include minimum lot size of 10 acres, minimum 15-foot setbacks from property lines, and height limits of 15 feet for freestanding or ground-mounted solar collectors. These other conditions do not specify maximum land coverage but pertain to setbacks, height, and lot size.

If a freestanding solar power system, ground-mounted solar power system, solar farm or solar power plant has been out of active and continuous service for a period of one year, it shall be removed from the premises to a place of safe and legal disposal. Any and all structures and accessory structures shall also be removed. The site shall be restored to as natural a condition as possible. Such removal shall be completed within 18 months of the cessation of active and continuous use. A permit for the demolition of the system shall be required under § 107-04 of the Town Code. If the owner fails to remove the system, the Town may serve a notice of demand to remove and may perform the work at the owner's expense, with costs constituting a lien on the property. Additionally, as part of the Planning Board application for solar farms or solar power plants, a written narrative describing the eventual decommissioning, including anticipated life, estimated costs, and funding methods, must be submitted. These requirements apply specifically to solar farms and solar power plants as defined as "Energy generation facility or area of land whose principal use is allowed by special permit issued by the Planning Board to convert solar energy to electricity, whether by photovoltaics, concentrating solar thermal devices or various experimental solar technologies, with the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of electricity."

The ordinance requires that solar farm or solar power plant installations "shall be enclosed by a minimum six-foot solid fence (or fence with privacy slats). Planning Board may require a greater height in fencing depending on individual conditions." This fencing requirement is found in subsection E(6)(k). Other related conditions for solar farms or solar power plants include site plan and special use permit approval by the Planning Board (E(6)(a)), minimum lot size of 10 acres (E(6)(h)), a minimum fifteen-foot setback from all property lines (E(6)(g)), and screening from adjoining lots and street rights-of-way through architectural features, earth berms, landscaping, or other means (E(6)(f)). The Planning Board can require additional screening and/or fencing for solar installations requiring special use permit approval (E(4)(j) and E(5)(j)).

Solar farm and solar power plant panels and equipment shall be surfaced, designed and sited so as not to reflect glare onto adjacent properties and roadways. (E)(6)(l). Solar farms and solar power plants require site plan and special use permit approval by the Town of New Windsor Planning Board (E)(6)(a). They must comply with State Environmental Quality Review Act and may be reviewed by the Port Authority for New York and New Jersey to ensure no reflection interferes with Stewart Airport operations (E)(6)(b). They must be screened when possible and practicable from adjoining lots and street rights-of-way (E)(6)(f), have a minimum fifteen-foot setback from all property lines (E)(6)(g), be located on lots with a minimum size of 10 acres (E)(6)(h), have developmental coverage not exceeding 85% (E)(6)(i), and have freestanding or ground-mounted solar collectors not exceeding 15 feet in height (E)(6)(j). The installation must be enclosed by a minimum six-foot solid fence (E)(6)(k). Additionally, all solar energy power systems and equipment shall be surfaced, designed and sited so as not to reflect glare onto adjacent properties and roadways (E)(8).

The height of the freestanding or ground-mounted solar collectors and any mounts shall not exceed 15 feet when oriented at maximum tilt. This applies specifically to solar farms or solar power plants, defined as energy generation facilities with the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of electricity. Other height limits mentioned include 10 feet for freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems accessory to single family and two-family residences, and 15 feet for ground-mounted solar energy power systems generally. Roof-mounted solar energy power systems shall not exceed the maximum permitted building height for the zoning district. The 15 feet limit for solar farms or solar power plants is the most restrictive applicable to commercial-scale systems. Units are explicitly stated as feet.

The ordinance states: 'A solar farm or solar power plant shall only be permitted on lots with a minimum size of 10 acres.' This is the explicit minimum lot size for solar farms or solar power plants. Other minimum lot sizes mentioned apply only to smaller or accessory freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems, such as a minimum lot size of 80,000 square feet for freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems accessory to single family and two-family residences, which do not qualify as solar farms or solar power plants. The unit 'acres' is the standard area measurement used for this minimum lot size.

All solar farm or solar power plant equipment and installations shall be subject to a minimum fifteen-foot setback from all property lines. The Planning Board may require increased setbacks as it deems necessary based on the surrounding conditions. (Section E(6)(g)) Other setback provisions for smaller or accessory freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems also specify a fifteen-foot setback from the property line, but these apply to non-commercial or accessory systems, not solar farms or solar power plants.

The ordinance requires that solar farms or solar power plants "shall be screened when possible and practicable from adjoining lots and street rights-of-way through the use of architectural features, earth berms, landscaping, or other screening which will harmonize with the character of the property and surrounding area." Additional screening may be required as part of the Planning Board approval. Other related requirements include: site plan and special use permit approval (§ 300-86 and § 300-87), a minimum fifteen-foot setback from all property lines, enclosure by a minimum six-foot solid fence (or fence with privacy slats), height not to exceed 15 feet at maximum tilt, and that panels and equipment "shall be surfaced, designed and sited so as not to reflect glare onto adjacent properties and roadways."

Solar farms and solar power plants shall be permitted as structures in all zoning districts subject to site plan and special use permit approval granted by the Town of New Windsor Planning Board under §§ 300-86 and 300-87 of the Town Code. Applicants must submit a written narrative describing construction, operation, maintenance, manufacturer's specifications, and decommissioning plans. Compliance with the State Environmental Quality Review Act is required. Any solar farm or solar power plant proposed in the AP Zoning District must also be reviewed and approved by the Port Authority for New York and New Jersey to ensure no interference with Stewart Airport operations. Other solar energy systems such as rooftop, building-mounted, freestanding, and ground-mounted systems have different permitting requirements and limitations, including size, location, and whether they require Planning Board approval or special use permits based on kilowatt production thresholds.

Solar farms and solar power plants require site plan and special use permit approval by the Town of New Windsor Planning Board (§ 300-28.1 E.(6)(a)). Applicants must submit a written narrative describing construction, operation, maintenance, and decommissioning plans, along with manufacturer's specifications. Compliance with the State Environmental Quality Review Act is required, including submission of a Full Environmental Assessment Form (E.(6)(b)). The solar farm or power plant "shall be screened when possible and practicable from adjoining lots and street rights-of-way through the use of architectural features, earth berms, landscaping, or other screening which will harmonize with the character of the property and surrounding area" (E.(6)(f)). Additional screening may be required as part of Planning Board approval. The Planning Board may also require increased setbacks and additional screening/fencing to mitigate visual impact (E.(6)(g), E.(6)(j)). Other solar energy power systems such as freestanding and ground-mounted systems under certain thresholds may require less or no Planning Board approval unless exceeding specified kilowatt limits (E.(4) and E.(5)).

Applicants for major renewable energy facilities in New York must submit a Final Decommissioning and Site Restoration Plan with proof of letters of credit, updated every five years, and a summary of local decommissioning laws, while addressing safety, environmental impacts, aesthetics, salvage, recycling, future site uses, and the facility’s useful life. For facilities on non-owned land or prime soils, the plan must include a decommissioning agreement with the landowner, funding and bonds, and assurance that structures will be removed and soils restored for agricultural use.

The fencing "shall be a minimum of seven feet in height as prescribed by the Code; this supersedes any other zoning requirement for fence heights." (§ 245-85(H)(2) and § 245-86(O)) Additionally, the fencing or enclosure must be "acceptable to the Town (and meeting State and National Code standards) enclosing all solar energy system components that present safety hazards." Other options include "another type of enclosure acceptable to the Town" and the style of fencing "shall fit into the character of the area and be approved by the Town Board."

The ordinance explicitly requires that the design, construction, operation, and maintenance of a large-scale or utility-scale solar energy system "shall prevent the misdirection and/or reflection of solar rays onto neighboring properties, public roads, and public parks in excess of that which already exists." A "glare study to Town requirements must be submitted to illustrate this," and the Town may hire an independent consultant to review and verify this study at the cost of the applicant. Additionally, for Tier 3 or 4 solar energy projects near the Niagara Falls Air Reserve Station and Niagara Falls International Airport, a glare impact analysis is required, including use of the Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT) to predict potential glare. These requirements apply specifically to Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems (Tier 4).

The height of a utility-scale solar energy system shall not exceed 15 feet when oriented at maximum tilt (§ 245-86 E). This is the explicit maximum height restriction for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems (Tier 4). Other height restrictions mentioned in the text apply only to smaller systems, such as Tier 2 ground-mounted systems, which have maximum heights of 12 feet in certain residential districts and 15 feet in other districts, but these do not apply to Tier 4 systems. The unit 'feet' is used consistently in the ordinance.

The Tier 3 or 4 project shall not result in any adverse noise impacts on any surrounding homes or other sensitive receptors (use of NYSDEC regulations concerning noise). Specifically, the project must be shown to not generate noise at 45 dBA or above at any nonparticipating property line.

The minimum required separation distance for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems (Tier 4) from other solar energy systems on participating properties is 50 feet from any property lot line, plus any screening required by the Planning Board. If the property line separates two parcels leased or purchased for panels, the 50-foot setback does not apply. Other setbacks include 200 feet from any nonparticipating property lot line, 300 feet from buildings on nonparticipating properties, and 500 feet from public roads. These distances are measured from the fence surrounding all panels and equipment (§ 245-86(D)).

Tier 4: Utility-scale solar energy systems shall not be considered a permitted use unless shown to meet the requirements of a special permit and are subject to site plan review and approval within the A, B-1, B-2, LI, PID, HI, SW, and PL districts. These systems shall not be located adjacent to properties in Residential districts (R-1, R-2, R-3/R-4, and Cluster Residential). Tier 3 and Tier 4 systems are not allowed in the R-1, R-2, R-3/R-4, and Cluster Residential zoning districts. Other tiers include Tier 1 (rooftop-mounted systems permitted with building permit) and Tier 2 (ground-mounted systems permitted with site plan approval and building permit). Tier 3 systems require a special permit and are allowed in certain districts with restrictions.
section: § 245-83 Permits and approvals required and applicable zoning districts.

summary: Any large-scale or utility-scale solar energy system shall adhere to the following setbacks (this setback distance shall be measured from the fence that surrounds all panels and equipment): (1) From any nonparticipating property lot line: a minimum of 200 feet from any property lot line, plus appropriate screening. Other setback options include: (2) From any participating property lot line: a minimum of 50 feet from any property lot line, plus any screening required by the Planning Board (if necessary). If the property line separates two parcels that are being leased or purchased to have panels placed on them, the fifty-foot setback does not apply.

From any participating property lot line: a minimum of 50 feet from any property lot line, plus any screening required by the Planning Board (if necessary). summary: Any large-scale or utility-scale solar energy system shall adhere to the following setbacks (this setback distance shall be measured from the fence that surrounds all panels and equipment): From public roads: (a) A minimum of 500 feet from any public road (measured from the fence to the road right-of-way or property line); and, (b) Where the lot line abuts a public right-of-way, the setbacks specified above shall be measured from such right-of-way line.

The ordinance explicitly requires vegetative buffer and screening for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems (Tier 4). It mandates "a berm, landscape screen, or other opaque enclosure, or any combination thereof acceptable to the Town capable of screening the site, shall be provided along any property line that abuts an important community resource, an existing residence or any property zoned other than LI, PID, HI, or SW." Additionally, "Solar energy systems shall have views minimized from adjacent properties using architectural features, earthen berms, landscaping, or other screening methods that will harmonize with the character of the property and surrounding area." The screening and landscaping plan must "specify the locations, elevations, height, plant species, and/or materials that will comprise the structures, landscaping, and/or grading used to screen and/or mitigate any adverse aesthetic effects of the system." The plan requires "evergreen/coniferous trees (planted at recommended spacing for the type of tree), at least eight feet to 10 feet high at the time of planting," plus "supplemental shrubs (deer resistant) placed in between the evergreen trees at the reasonable discretion of the Town Board." Plantings are typically "within 10 linear feet of the solar energy system fencing or as directed by the Planning Board to achieve maximum screening." Existing vegetation on participating properties may be used to satisfy screening requirements. All plantings must have a "ten-year guarantee and must be replaced if dead or diseased." Berms may be used but must not interfere with drainage and must be properly designed. Landscape plans must be completed by a NYS registered landscape architect. Furthermore, for large-scale or utility-scale solar energy systems, "a berm, landscape screen, or other opaque enclosure, or any combination thereof acceptable to the Town capable of screening the site may be required along any property line that abuts an existing residence."

Any signage shall be in accordance with the Town's signage regulations and meet the following: (1) No signage or graphic content shall be displayed on the solar energy systems except the manufacturer's name, equipment specification information, safety information, and twenty-four-hour emergency contact information. Said information shall be depicted within an area no more than eight square feet. (2) As required by National Electric Code (NEC), disconnect and other emergency shutoff information shall be clearly displayed on a light reflective surface. A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers, invertors, and substations.

For Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems (Tier 4), the ordinance requires that "before the Town of Niagara shall issue a clearing, grading, storm water or building permit for a large-scale or utility-scale solar energy system, the applicant shall submit a storm water and erosion control plan to the Town of Niagara for its review and approval;" and that "the plan shall minimize the potential adverse impacts on wetlands and Class I and II streams and the banks and vegetation along those streams and wetlands and minimize erosion or sedimentation." Other options for solar energy systems include Tier 1 (building-integrated, building-mounted, rooftop-mounted systems), Tier 2 (ground-mounted systems primarily for on-site use, with specific size and setback limits), and Tier 3 (large-scale systems less than 30 acres designed primarily to supply energy to the utility grid). Tier 3 and Tier 4 systems require special permits, site plan review, and additional criteria such as setbacks, screening, decommissioning plans, and compliance with various codes and regulations.

Utility-scale solar energy systems (Tier 4) shall not be considered a permitted use unless shown to meet the requirements (and one is issued) of a special permit pursuant to this article and Article IX of the Town of Niagara Zoning Code, and subject to site plan review by the Planning Board, approval by Town Board, and requiring issuance of a building permit within the A, B-1, B-2, LI, PID, HI, SW, and PL districts. These Tier 4 systems are also limited per the following: To further reduce potential impacts, a Tier 4 system shall not be located on a property adjacent (including across the street) to a property in a district zoned Residential (R-1, R-2, R-3/R-4, and Cluster Residential). Other tiers include: Tier 1 (rooftop-mounted, building-mounted and building-integrated solar energy systems) permitted upon issuance of building permit; Tier 2 (ground-mounted solar energy systems) permitted through site plan approval by Town of Niagara Board and building permit; Tier 3 (large-scale solar energy systems) require special permit, site plan review by Town Board, and building permit within the same districts as Tier 4, with adjacency restrictions to residential districts. Tier 3 and Tier 4 systems are not allowed in the R-1, R-2, R-3/R-4, and Cluster Residential zoning districts.

summary: Applications for large-scale and utility-scale Tier 3 and 4 solar energy systems shall meet the following additional criteria: "Photo simulations shall be included showing the proposed solar energy system in relation to the building/site along with elevation views and dimensions, and manufacturer's specs and photos of the proposed solar energy system, solar collectors, and all other components. These photo simulations must include before and after simulations from locations where the solar energy system will be viewed from off-site locations as determined by the Planning Board." Further, "Solar energy systems shall be required to: (a) Conduct a visual assessment of the visual impacts of the solar energy system on public roadways and adjacent properties and as directed by the Planning Board. As required previously, this analysis must consider conditions at day one of operation and when the landscaping has matured. At a minimum, a line-of-sight profile analysis shall be provided, but photo-simulations are required for all areas that will have a view of the project site. Depending upon the scope and potential significance of the visual impacts, additional impact analyses, including, for example, a digital view shed report, may be required to be submitted by the applicant. The Town may hire an independent consultant, at the cost of the applicant, to review and/or conduct their own visual assessment." These requirements apply to Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems (Tier 4) which are defined as "Any solar energy system that is 30 acres or more in size (as measured by the fenced in area), that cumulatively on a lot is designed and intended to supply energy primarily into a utility grid for sale to the general public or does not meet the definition of a Tier 1, Tier 2 or Tier 3 solar energy system." The visual impact assessment is part of the special permit application process required for Tier 4 systems, which also includes site plan review and approval by the Town Board and Planning Board.

All applications for a solar farm shall be accompanied by a decommissioning plan to be implemented upon abandonment, or cessation of activity, or in conjunction with removal of the facility, prior to issuance of a building permit. The decommissioning plan must ensure the site will be restored to a useful, nonhazardous condition without delay, including removal of aboveground and belowground equipment, structures and foundations; restoration of the surface grade and soil; revegetation with native seed mixes; and a time frame for completion. If construction is not completed within 18 months, the Town may require implementation of the decommissioning plan. Upon cessation of activity for six months, the Town may notify the owner/operator to restore operation to 80% capacity or implement the plan within 180 days. Failure to comply allows the Town to restore the site and recover costs, which become a lien on the property. The site developer must purchase a bond equal to the project installation and decommissioning costs prior to permits being issued, which shall be in place for the life of the facility and used to fund decommissioning if abandoned.

The glare restriction is part of the design standards for major systems or solar farms.

This limit applies specifically to major solar collection systems or solar farms, which are defined as systems principally used to capture solar energy and convert it to electrical energy to transfer to the public electric grid in order to sell electricity to or receive a credit from a public utility entity.

The landscape screening shall be comprised of evergreen species, eight feet in height at time of planting, spaced five feet apart, within 10 linear feet of the solar energy system. Post planting maintenance is required and trees must be healthy and growing two years after installation. Acceptance of suitable evergreens is at the reasonable discretion of the Planning Board. Property shall be maintained on a monthly basis including mowing to prevent overgrowth. Additionally, all mechanical equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be enclosed by a minimum eight-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate, provided with landscape screening.

It also mandates that "Roadways within the site shall not be constructed of impervious materials and shall be designed to minimize the extent of roadways constructed and soil compaction." Additionally, the decommissioning plan must include "Restoration of the surface grade and soil after removal of equipment" and "Revegetation of restored soil areas with native seed mixes, excluding any invasive species." These requirements apply to major solar collection systems or solar farms as defined in the ordinance. Other related conditions include site plan approval, height and setback restrictions, landscaped buffers, underground utility placement, and bonding for decommissioning, but these do not explicitly address soil, erosion, or sediment control.

summary: A major system or solar farm may be permitted in the B-A-R, I-A-R, I-B-A-R, I-2-B-A-R, and A-R districts in the Town when authorized by site plan approval from the Planning Board subject to the following terms and conditions. "A major system or solar farm shall be constructed pursuant to site plan approval from the Town Planning Board and must meet the criteria set forth below and obtain all other necessary approvals." The Town limits the total cumulative installed capacity of major solar systems or farms within the Town to 16 MW, processed on a first come basis with no preference given to any one location, property owner, or developer. Other uses such as rooftop and building-mounted solar collectors are permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts, and ground-mounted solar collectors are permitted as accessory structures with size and location restrictions, but these apply to minor systems and are excluded from this summary.

summary: Major Solar Collection Systems or Solar Farms require site plan approval from the Town Planning Board (§ 194-59(B)). The site plan must meet criteria including a landscaped buffer around all equipment and solar collectors to provide screening from adjacent residential properties and roads, with evergreen species eight feet in height at planting, spaced five feet apart, within 10 linear feet of the solar energy system (§ 194-59(D)(2)(c)). Solar collectors and other facilities must be designed and located to prevent reflective glare toward inhabited buildings on adjacent properties and roads (§ 194-59(D)(3)(c)). Other conditions include height and setback restrictions, underground placement of utility lines where feasible, and review of site and stormwater management plans prior to final site plan approval (§ 194-59(D)(2), (3)(b), (3)(g)).
section: § 194-59 Solar collectors and installations for major systems or solar farms.

summary: Areas of potential sensitivity include 'Within 100 feet landward of a freshwater (DEC) wetland' for Major Solar Collection Systems or Solar Farms as stated in § 194-59 C(2). No other explicit setbacks from lakes, reservoirs, streams, or rivers are mentioned for major systems or solar farms in the text provided.
section: § 194-59 Solar collectors and installations for major systems or solar farms

summary: The total surface area of any major solar system, together with all accessory structures, aisles, alleyways, walkways, roads, and parking areas, shall not occupy more than 80% of the lot. This is the only explicit maximum land coverage restriction for major solar systems mentioned in the text. The unit is expressed as a percentage of the lot area.

All major solar systems shall provide a decommissioning plan to be implemented upon abandonment, cessation of activity, or in conjunction with removal of the facility. The plan must ensure the site will be restored to a useful, nonhazardous condition without delay, including removal of aboveground and below-ground equipment, restoration of surface grade and soil, revegetation with native seed mixes, and a time frame for completion. Upon failure to complete construction within 18 months or cessation of solar production for 12 months, the Town may serve written notice requiring site restoration per the decommissioning plan, with the owner/operator required to repair the system within 30 days or complete decommissioning within the specified time. Additionally, the Town may require financial security to ensure funds for code violation cure or removal of abandoned or decommissioned systems.

All electrical equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be enclosed by a minimum six-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate and provided with landscape screening. This fencing requirement applies to major solar systems, which are defined as any ground-mounted solar system with a total surface area greater than 2,000 square feet. Other requirements for major solar systems include setbacks, height limits, underground utility lines, noise limits, signage, operation and maintenance plans, financial security, and decommissioning plans.

Solar systems shall be designed and located in order to minimize reflective glare toward any adjacent properties, roads, and inhabited buildings. This applies to all solar systems, including major solar systems as defined as any ground-mounted solar system with a total surface area greater than 2,000 square feet.

The maximum height for any major solar system shall not exceed 20 feet in height above the mean grade of the ground upon which it sits. This is stated explicitly in § 175-5 C (2). Other height restrictions mentioned apply only to minor solar systems, such as ground-mounted minor solar systems not exceeding 20 feet and roof-mounted minor solar systems not exceeding six feet, but these do not apply to major solar systems.

No major solar system shall produce noise in excess of 60 decibels, as measured at each nearest property line. This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for major solar systems. The unit 'decibels' is interpreted as 'dBA' for standard noise measurement.

The minimum setback for any major solar system shall be 200 feet from the centerline of any public or private right-of-way. No major solar project shall be located within 500 feet of Owasco Lake or Skaneateles Lake. This setback applies specifically to major solar systems, defined as ground-mounted solar systems with a total surface area greater than 2,000 square feet. Other setback options include 75 feet from the centerline of any public or private right-of-way for minor solar systems, which are smaller or non-commercial systems.

For major solar systems, removal of trees and other existing vegetation shall be minimized and offset with planting elsewhere on the property. Based on site specific conditions, including topography, adjacent structures, and roadways, a landscaped buffer may be required to provide screening from adjacent residential properties and roads. Additionally, all electrical equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be enclosed by a minimum six-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate and provided with landscape screening.

A sign not to exceed eight square feet shall be displayed on or near the main access point and shall list the facility name, owner and phone number. A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations. Solar collection systems shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the system.

For major solar systems, the ordinance requires that 'Removal of trees and other existing vegetation shall be minimized, and offset with planting elsewhere on the property.' Roadways must be 'constructed of materials appropriate to the site and shall be designed to minimize the extent of roadways constructed and soil compaction.' The decommissioning plan must include 'Restoration of the surface grade and soil after removal of equipment' and 'Revegetation of restored soil areas with native seed mixes, excluding any invasive species.' These requirements are found in § 175-5(C)(4), (5), and (12). Other conditions for major solar systems include setbacks, height limits, maximum lot coverage, underground utility lines, fencing, noise limits, signage, operation and maintenance plans, financial security, and decommissioning timelines.

No major solar project shall be located within 500 feet of Owasco Lake or Skaneateles Lake. This is the setback distance specifically for major solar systems, defined as ground-mounted solar systems with a total surface area greater than 2,000 square feet. Other setback requirements include a minimum setback of 200 feet from the centerline of any public or private right-of-way, but that is unrelated to lakes, reservoirs, streams, rivers, or wetlands.

§ 212-7D requires a decommissioning plan to be submitted as part of the special permit application for utility-scale solar energy systems, specifying removal after the system is no longer in use, how removal and restoration will be conducted, a timeline, and a cost estimate prepared by a professional engineer or qualified contractor. § 212-7E mandates a removal and restoration bond equal to 150% of the estimated cost, with annual proof and updates every five years. § 212-9F requires all solar energy systems to be dismantled and removed immediately when deemed inoperative or abandoned for more than 365 days, at the owner's cost, with the Town authorized to remove the system and place a tax lien if the owner fails to do so.

Any site containing a utility-scale solar energy system shall contain fencing or other device acceptable to the Town enclosing all solar energy system components (§ 212-8N). The special permit application must include proposed fencing and/or screening for the project (location, extent, and details) (§ 212-7C(3)). The operations and maintenance plan shall include replacement of any fencing or screening vegetation (§ 212-7F).
section: § 212-7 Special permit requirements and § 212-8 Special permit criteria

summary: The ordinance explicitly restricts glare for utility-scale solar energy systems by requiring that "The design, construction, operation and maintenance of a utility-scale solar energy system shall prevent the misdirection and/or reflection of solar rays onto neighboring properties, public roads and public parks in excess of that which already exists." (§ 212-8(H)). This applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems defined as those "designed and intended to supply energy exceeding 50 kw primarily into a utility grid for sale to the general public or to any utility." Other related provisions include that all structures and devices used to support solar collectors "shall be nonreflective and/or painted in a subtle or earth tone color" (§ 212-8(I)), and similar glare prevention language is found in § 212-6(B)(1)(i) and § 212-6(G) but these apply to ground-mounted solar energy systems not meeting the utility-scale definition or more generally to all solar energy systems. Utility-scale systems are allowed only by special permit in the R-A District with specific setbacks, height limits, and other criteria detailed in § 212-8. The glare restriction in § 212-8(H) is a clear, enforceable requirement for utility-scale systems.

The height of a utility-scale energy system shall not exceed 20 feet when oriented at maximum tilt (§ 212-8D). This is the maximum overall height restriction explicitly stated for utility-scale solar energy systems, which are defined as systems designed to supply energy exceeding 50 kw primarily into a utility grid for sale to the general public or to any utility. Other height restrictions mentioned in the text apply only to smaller or non-utility-scale systems, such as ground-mounted solar energy systems (not utility-grade) which shall not exceed 15 feet when oriented at maximum tilt (§ 212-6B(1)(f)), and rooftop-mounted and building-mounted solar energy systems which shall not be more than three feet higher than the finished roof (§ 212-6A). The unit for the maximum height is feet.

The minimum lot area for utility-scale solar energy systems is explicitly stated as 25 acres. This is found in § 212-8 Special permit criteria, subsection A: 'Minimum lot area: The minimum lot area shall be 25 acres.' This applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in the chapter.

Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be allowed only by special permit and only in the R-A (Residence-Agricultural) District in accordance with the criteria established in this chapter, after SEQRA review and concurrent site plan approval by the Town Planning Board and upon issuance of a building permit (§ 212-5 F). Other solar energy systems are permitted as follows: Residential solar energy systems up to 12 kw in all zoning districts; residential systems exceeding 12 kw but less than 25 kw with variance and site plan approval; commercial solar energy systems up to 25 kw in all commercial zoning districts; commercial systems exceeding 25 kw but less than 100 kw with variance and site plan approval; rooftop-mounted and building-mounted solar energy systems in all zoning districts; ground-mounted solar energy systems on lots of two or more acres in all zoning districts; and ground-mounted solar energy systems on lots less than two acres with site plan approval and possible variance (§ 212-5 A-E).

Any utility-scale solar energy system shall adhere to the following setbacks: (1) A minimum of 300 feet from all property lot lines. (2) From all buildings or structures: a minimum of 300 feet from any inhabited building or structure, except for buildings and structures located on the proposed project lot. (3) From any public roadway, park, playground or school: a minimum of 300 feet from any public roadway, park, playground or school.

Any utility-scale solar energy system shall adhere to the following setbacks: From any public roadway, park, playground or school: a minimum of 300 feet from any public roadway, park, playground or school. Other setback options include a 200 feet setback from any roadway or right-of-way for ground-mounted solar energy systems that are not utility-grade systems (§ 212-6 B(1)(d)). The design, construction, operation and maintenance of the system shall prevent misdirection and/or reflection of solar rays onto public roads and rights-of-way in excess of that which already exists (§ 212-6 B(i), § 212-8 H). Site plans must include location of access roads (§ 212-7 C(4)) and screening may be required along property lines abutting roadways (§ 212-8 O).

The ordinance explicitly requires screening for utility-scale solar energy systems. Section 212-8(O) states: "A berm, landscape screen or other opaque enclosure, or any combination thereof acceptable to the Town capable of screening the site may be required along any property line that abuts an existing roadway or residence." Additionally, Section 212-7C(3) requires the special permit application to include "Proposed fencing and/or screening for said project (location, extent, and details)." These provisions impose vegetative buffer and/or other screening requirements that a utility-scale solar energy system developer must abide by.

No advertising signs shall be permitted on the solar energy system. Signage shall be included which provides twenty-four-hour emergency contact phone numbers to the owner of the system and in accordance with state or federal law.

Applicants for a special permit to place, construct, or make a major modification to a utility-scale solar energy system must submit "documentation of the clearing, grading, stormwater and erosion control plans" (§ 212-7B(3)). Before issuing a building permit for a utility-scale solar energy system, "the applicant shall submit a stormwater and erosion control plan to the Town Planning Board for its review and approval" (§ 212-8S). The plan must "minimize the potential adverse impacts on wetlands and Class I and Class II streams and the banks and vegetation along those streams and wetlands and minimize erosion or sedimentation."
section: § 212-7 Special permit requirements and § 212-8 Special permit criteria

summary: Utility-scale solar energy systems shall be allowed only by special permit and only in the R-A (Residence-Agricultural) District in accordance with the criteria established in this chapter, after SEQRA review and concurrent site plan approval by the Town Planning Board and upon issuance of a building permit. Other solar energy systems have different conditions: Residential solar energy systems up to 12 kw are permitted in all zoning districts with a building permit; residential systems exceeding 12 kw but less than 25 kw require a variance and site plan approval. Commercial solar energy systems up to 25 kw are permitted in all commercial zoning districts with a building permit; those exceeding 25 kw but less than 100 kw require a variance and site plan approval. Rooftop and building-mounted systems are allowed in all zoning districts with a building permit. Ground-mounted systems on lots of two or more acres are allowed in all zoning districts with a building permit; on lots less than two acres, they require site plan approval and a building permit. The Town Planning Board may allow variances during site plan review for these smaller ground-mounted systems.

Any utility-scale solar energy system shall adhere to the following setbacks: From all buildings or structures: a minimum of 300 feet from any inhabited building or structure, except for buildings and structures located on the proposed project lot. Other setback options mentioned include 300 feet from all property lot lines and 300 feet from any public roadway, park, playground or school, but these do not pertain to occupied dwellings or structures.

Applications for a special permit to place, construct, or to make a major modification to a utility-scale solar energy system shall include "A completed full environmental assessment form (EAF) under the State Environmental Quality Review Act (SEQRA) which shall fully describe the proposed system, its location, purpose and potential environmental impact." Additionally, "A visual site assessment may also be requested subject to the discretion of the Planning Board." Utility-scale solar energy systems are defined as "Any solar energy system that is designed and intended to supply energy exceeding 50 kw primarily into a utility grid for sale to the general public or to any utility" and are allowed only by special permit (§ 212-5F). The special permit application process includes submission of detailed plans and environmental assessments, and the Planning Board has discretion to require a visual site assessment. Other solar energy systems (residential, commercial, ground-mounted under certain thresholds) have different permitting and site plan approval requirements but do not explicitly require visual impact assessments.
