Other sections address roof-mounted and ground-mounted solar energy systems primarily for onsite use, which require building permits and sometimes site plan approval, but these do not apply to large-scale solar energy systems as defined.
section: § 145-84 Large-scale solar systems as permitted use.

summary: Large-scale solar energy systems shall have a minimum yard/setback of 40 feet for the front, each side and rear. (§ 145-84 B(1)) This setback applies generally as a minimum yard/setback and is not expressed as a variable or dependent on other factors such as structure height.
section: § 145-84 Large-scale solar systems as permitted use

summary: For Class B Solar Energy Systems with a Nameplate Capacity of over 1 MW AC, a decommissioning plan shall be submitted by the applicant and shall address: (1) The time required to decommission and remove the Solar Energy System and any ancillary structures; (2) The time required to repair any damage caused to the property by the installation and removal of the Solar Energy System; (3) The cost of decommissioning and removing the Solar Energy System, as well as all necessary site remediation or restoration; (4) The provision of a decommissioning security, which shall be a cash, bond, or other form of security in an amount sufficient to ensure removal and restoration, set at 115% of the cost of removal and site restoration, revisited every five years and reduced by estimated salvage value. Upon cessation of electricity generation for 12 months, the Town may notify the owner/operator to implement the decommissioning plan, which must be completed within 12 months of notification. If the owner/operator fails to comply, the Town may use the bond/security for removal and site restoration. Other related provisions include permit time frames and enforcement measures. These requirements explicitly apply to Class B Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance.

For all Class B Solar Energy Systems with a Nameplate Capacity of up to 5 MW AC, all mechanical equipment shall be enclosed by a seven-foot-high fence, as required by NEC, with a self-locking gate to prevent unauthorized access. Class B Solar Energy Systems are defined as those intended to produce energy for off-site sale to and consumption by one or more customers and are a commercial use subject to site plan approval and grant of a special use permit. These fencing requirements are part of the site plan standards for Class B Solar Energy Systems. Other requirements for Class B systems include site plan approval, special use permits in certain districts, and adherence to standards established for Class A Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems, but fencing is specifically mandated as described.

All Class B Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems shall be permitted, subject to site plan approval in all zoning districts, except that they shall be prohibited in the Ridgeline Protection District and shall be permitted in the Scenic Overlay District subject to grant of a special use permit as specified below and site plan approval.

Class B Solar Energy Systems "shall have views minimized from adjacent properties to the extent reasonably practicable using architectural features, earth berms, landscaping, or other screening methods that will harmonize with the character of the property and surrounding area." Additionally, "applicants will need to propose mitigation measures with their plans that include an equal number of new trees to be planted that are proposed to be removed or removal of invasives and replacement with native plantings" if more than 10 trees are removed. Owners shall also "utilize and maintain native perennial vegetation to provide foraging habitat for pollinators in all appropriate areas within the Facility Area" and "use integrated pest management practices to refrain from/limit pesticide use (including herbicides) for long-term operation and site maintenance."

Class B Solar Energy Systems shall be permitted, subject to site plan approval in all zoning districts, except that they shall be prohibited in the Ridgeline Protection District and shall be permitted in the Scenic Overlay District subject to grant of a special use permit as specified below and site plan approval.

Class B Solar Energy Systems are "a commercial use subject to site plan approval and grant of a special use permit." They "shall adhere to the standards and requirements established for Class A Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems set forth herein, and in addition to (or in some cases amended by) the following requirements:" including site plan standards where "Class B Solar Energy Systems shall have views minimized from adjacent properties to the extent reasonably practicable using architectural features, earth berms, landscaping, or other screening methods that will harmonize with the character of the property and surrounding area." Applications must include "proposed changes to the landscape of the site, including site grading, vegetation clearing and planting, the removal of any large trees, access roads, exterior lighting, signage, fencing, landscaping, and screening vegetation or structures." Class B systems are "permitted, subject to site plan approval in all zoning districts, except that they shall be prohibited in the Ridgeline Protection District and shall be permitted in the Scenic Overlay District subject to grant of a special use permit as specified below and site plan approval." The special use permit standards of Town Code §§ 175-61 to 175-64 apply. Class A systems are "intended to produce energy for on-site consumption" and are accessory uses, with specific design requirements, while Class B systems are for "off-site sale to and consumption by one or more customers."

A large-scale solar energy system that is ground mounted shall not exceed 50% of the lot on which it is installed. The surface area covered by solar panels shall be included in the total lot coverage. This is stated explicitly in § 110-80C(3). No other maximum land coverage values for large-scale solar energy systems are provided in the text.
section: § 110-80 Approval standards for large-scale solar systems as special uses

summary: A decommissioning plan shall be submitted as part of the application for a large-scale solar energy system special use permit (§ 110-80B(7)). The plan must specify removal of the system after 12 months of abandonment, including removal of all infrastructure and remediation of soil and vegetation to return the parcel to its original state within six months. A cost estimate prepared by a licensed professional engineer or contractor must be included. If not decommissioned, the municipality may remove the system and impose a lien for costs (§ 110-80B(7), § 110-80B(8)). Under § 110-84, the property owner must notify the Town Board of discontinued operations and remove the system within 150 days. Decommissioning includes physical removal of all installations, disposal of waste per regulations, and site stabilization or revegetation. The Town may remove abandoned systems after 90 days of abandonment and recover costs by lien (§ 110-84). The property owner must provide an easement for Town access for inspections and removal (§ 110-84D).

summary: All large-scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing at least six feet in height to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs shall be posted in a visible area and shall be two feet by two feet in size, and the owner's contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing. The fencing and the system shall be further screened by appropriate landscaping acceptable to the Planning Board to avoid adverse aesthetic impacts.

summary: All solar energy systems shall be designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare from impacting roadways and contiguous properties to the maximum extent practicable (§ 110-83D). Additionally, solar energy systems designed for subdivision use shall comply with the requirement that "All solar energy systems shall be designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare to the maximum extent practicable" (§ 110-81C(13)). These provisions apply explicitly to large-scale solar energy systems, which are defined as ground-mounted systems producing energy primarily for off-site use, sale or consumption.
section: § 110-83 Safety standards applicable to all solar energy systems: monitoring and maintenance

summary: Large-scale solar energy systems shall have a maximum height of 12 feet, measured at maximum vertical tilt angle (§ 110-80C(1)). This applies to systems permitted as special uses in RS-1, RR-1.5, AG-1.5, GB-80, and M-3 zoning districts. Additionally, solar energy systems designed for subdivision use, which can be large-scale, have a maximum height of 12 feet above ground at maximum vertical tilt angle (§ 110-81C(2)).
section: § 110-80 Approval standards for large-scale solar systems as special uses

summary: Large-scale energy systems shall be located on lots with a minimum lot size of one acre (§ 110-80 C.(2)). This applies specifically to large-scale solar energy systems defined as ground-mounted systems producing energy primarily for off-site use, sale, or consumption. The unit 'acre' is a standard area measurement.
section: § 110-80 Approval standards for large-scale solar systems as special uses

summary: Large-scale solar energy systems are permitted through the issuance of a special use permit within the RS-1, RR-1.5, AG-1.5, GB-80, and M-3 Zoning Districts, subject to requirements including site plan approval. Large-scale solar energy systems are an excluded or nonpermitted use in the HR-1, BD-40, and BD-60 Zoning Districts. Additionally, large-scale solar energy systems shall not be permitted to be constructed on areas of prime farmland and/or soils of statewide significance as designated by the United States Department of Agriculture.
section: § 110-80 Approval standards for large-scale solar systems as special uses.

summary: Large-scale solar energy systems shall be no less than 50 feet off all property boundaries (§ 110-80C(1)). For solar energy systems designed for subdivision use, the minimum setback shall be at least 35 feet from all lot lines of parcels associated with the subdivision and 50 feet from all perimeter lot lines of contiguous parcels not a part of the subdivision (§ 110-81C(3)). The 50 feet setback from property boundaries is the most restrictive fixed distance value directly pertaining to setbacks for large-scale solar energy systems.
section: § 110-80 Approval standards for large-scale solar systems as special uses and § 110-81 Solar energy system designed for subdivision use

summary: Large-scale solar energy systems must be enclosed by fencing at least six feet in height and "further screened by appropriate landscaping acceptable to the Planning Board to avoid adverse aesthetic impacts." A minimum twenty-five-foot perimeter buffer, "consisting of natural and undisturbed vegetation, supplemented with evergreen plantings in accordance with Town standards, as needed," shall be provided around all mechanical equipment and solar panel arrays to provide screening from adjacent properties and roads. Existing on-site vegetation designated to be utilized as screening "shall be preserved to the maximum extent possible and shall be diligently maintained to protect its vitality." Site plans must provide for the preservation of natural vegetation in large unbroken blocks. Protective natural screening and/or solid panel fencing, with a minimum height of six feet, is required surrounding ground-mounted apparatus or along neighboring property boundaries. Solid panel fencing cannot be translucent. These requirements apply to large-scale solar energy systems and solar energy systems designed for subdivision use, which are ground-mounted and produce energy primarily for off-site use, sale, or consumption.
section: § 110-80 Approval standards for large-scale solar systems as special uses

summary: All large-scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing at least six feet in height to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs shall be posted in a visible area and shall be two feet by two feet in size, and the owner's contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing (§ 110-80C(4)). For solar energy systems designed for subdivision use, a sign no greater than two feet indicating the name of the facility owner(s) and a twenty-four-hour emergency telephone number shall be posted. In addition, a "No Trespassing" sign or other warning signs shall be posted. All signage shall be maintained in legible condition and contain accurate information. A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations. No signage of any kind shall be allowed to be attached to solar panels or support structures, except any required safety warnings (§ 110-81C(14)).

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires compliance with stormwater regulations and the State Pollution Discharge Elimination System guidelines (SPDES), including preparation of a stormwater pollution prevention plan (SWPPP) if determined necessary, and a stormwater, erosion, and slope analysis by a New York State licensed professional engineer (§ 110-80B(6)). For solar energy systems designed for subdivision use, a land-grading and vegetation-clearing plan must be prepared limiting clear-cutting to the equipment compound, emergency access roadway, and area required for solar access (§ 110-81C(7)), and a stormwater, erosion, and slope analysis with compliance to SPDES and local stormwater regulations is required (§ 110-81C(10)). During decommissioning, "stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion" is mandated (§ 110-84B(3)). These requirements apply explicitly to large-scale solar energy systems, defined as "a solar energy system that is ground mounted and produces energy primarily for the purpose of off-site use, sale or consumption."
section: § 110-80 Approval standards for large-scale solar systems as special uses

summary: Large-scale solar energy systems are permitted through the issuance of a special use permit within the RS-1, RR-1.5, AG-1.5, GB-80, and M-3 Zoning Districts, subject to the requirements set forth in this section, including site plan approval. Large-scale solar energy systems are an excluded or nonpermitted use in the HR-1, BD-40, and BD-60 Zoning Districts. Special use permit standards include height and setback requirements: no less than 50 feet off all property boundaries and a maximum height of 12 feet. These requirements pertain to the RS-1, RR-1.5, AG-1.5, GB-80, and M-3 districts, where such systems are a permitted special use.
section: § 110-80 Approval standards for large-scale solar systems as special uses.

summary: The ordinance requires that large-scale solar energy systems obtain a special use permit and site plan approval (§ 110-80). Applications must include fencing and "further screened by appropriate landscaping acceptable to the Planning Board to avoid adverse aesthetic impacts" (§ 110-80B(5), § 110-80C(4)). The Planning Board may impose conditions to enforce standards or discharge SEQRA obligations (§ 110-80B(8)). For solar energy systems designed for subdivision use, a minimum twenty-five-foot perimeter buffer with natural vegetation and evergreen plantings must be provided to screen mechanical equipment and solar panel arrays from adjacent properties and roads (§ 110-81C(4)). Increased consideration for mitigating visual impact is required where the system abuts residential uses, including increased setbacks and visual screening (§ 110-81C(5)). These requirements constitute explicit visual impact assessment elements as part of the approval process for large-scale solar energy systems. Other options include site plan review and special permit review for subdivision use systems (§ 110-78D), and compliance with local site plan requirements as applicable (§ 110-80B(7)).
section: § 110-80 Approval standards for large-scale solar systems as special uses

summary: For Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems located on Prime Farmland or Farmland of Statewide Importance, the system shall not exceed 50% of the area of such farmland on the parcel. Additionally, lot coverage of the Solar Energy System shall not exceed the maximum lot coverage requirement of the underlying zoning district, which is a separate, unspecified limit. The 50% limit is the only explicit numerical maximum land coverage value given for Tier 3 systems, expressed as a percentage of the farmland area.

summary: Section 6, subsection H ('Decommissioning') states: 'Solar Energy Systems that have been abandoned and/or not producing electricity for a period of 1 year shall be removed at the Owner and/or Operators expense, which at the Owner’s option may come from any security made with the Town as set forth in Section 10(b) herein.' It requires 'A decommissioning plan (see Appendix 4) signed by the owner and/or operator of the Solar Energy System' addressing removal cost, responsible party, time required for decommissioning and site repair. It mandates 'The deposit, executions, or filing with the Town Clerk of cash, bond, or other form of security reasonably acceptable to the Town attorney and/or engineer, shall be in an amount sufficient to ensure the good faith performance of the terms and conditions of the permit issued pursuant hereto and to provide for the removal and restorations of the site subsequent to removal.' Section 8 states: 'Upon cessation of electricity generation of a Solar Energy System on a continuous basis for 12 months, the Town may notify and instruct the owner and/or operator of the Solar Energy System to implement the decommissioning plan. The decommissioning plan must be completed within 360 days of notification.' It further provides that if the owner/operator fails to comply, 'the Town may, at its discretion, utilize the bond and/or security for the removal of the Solar Energy System and restoration of the site in accordance with the decommissioning plan.' These requirements apply specifically to Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems not included in Tier 1 or Tier 2, typically larger or for offsite electricity generation or sale.
section: 6. Permitting requirements for Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems

summary: Section 6, subsection 5 states: 'All mechanical equipment, including any structure for storage batteries, shall be enclosed by a fence, as required by NEC, with a self-locking gate to prevent unauthorized access. The fencing shall be compliant with Town Zoning Ordinance Regulations for the underlying district.' This fencing requirement applies specifically to Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems not included in Tier 1 or Tier 2 categories and are subject to Special Use Permit review. Other requirements for Tier 3 systems include underground utility lines (except main service connection and interconnection equipment), vehicular path design, signage restrictions, anti-reflective coating on panels, limited lighting, tree-cutting minimization, decommissioning plans, lot size, setbacks, height, lot coverage, screening and visibility measures, public environmental benefit contributions, agricultural resource protections, and ownership change conditions.

summary: Section 6, Permitting requirements for Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems, states: 'All Solar Panels shall have anti-reflective coating(s).' This is the explicit glare restriction for Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems. Other tiers have similar glare requirements: Section 4.B.2 requires Roof-Mounted Solar Energy Systems to have anti-reflective coatings, and Section 5.A requires Tier 2 Solar Energy Systems to have anti-reflective coatings. Tier 1 systems are not explicitly mentioned with respect to glare restrictions.
section: 6. Permitting requirements for Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems

summary: Section 6, part 6) Screening and Visibility requires Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems to: i. Conduct a visual assessment of the visual impacts of the Solar Energy System on public roadways and adjacent properties, including at minimum a line-of-sight profile analysis; ii. Submit a screening & landscaping plan to show adequate measures to screen through landscaping, grading, or other means so that views of Solar Panels and Solar Energy Equipment shall be minimized as reasonably practical from public roadways and adjacent properties to the extent feasible; iii. The screening & landscaping plan shall specify the locations, elevations, height, plant species, and/or materials that will comprise the structures, landscaping, and/or grading used to screen and/or mitigate any adverse aesthetic effects of the system.
section: 6. Permitting requirements for Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems

summary: Section 6, part C (Signage) states: 'No signage or graphic content shall be displayed on the Solar Energy Systems except the manufacturer’s name, equipment specification information, safety information, and 24-hour emergency contact information. Said signage must comply with the Town of Plattsburgh regulations for signs in the underlying district.' Additionally, 'As required by National Electric Code (NEC), disconnect and other emergency shutoff information shall be clearly displayed on a light reflective surface. A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations.' These requirements apply specifically to Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems not included in Tier 1 (Roof-Mounted and Building-Integrated) or Tier 2 (Ground-Mounted up to 25 kW AC and generating no more than 110% of onsite consumption).
section: 6. Permitting requirements for Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems

summary: All Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems are subject to Site Plan/Special Use Permit review and permitted only through the issuance of a Special Use Permit within the R2, MH, and A1 zoning districts, and subject to site plan/special use permit application requirements set forth in this Section. Other tiers such as Tier 2 Solar Energy Systems are permitted in all zoning districts as accessory structures and exempt from site plan review, subject to conditions like setbacks, height, screening, and lot size. Roof-Mounted and Building-Integrated Solar Energy Systems have separate design and permitting requirements. The special use permit standards for Tier 3 include lot size, setbacks, height, lot coverage, fencing, screening, public environmental benefit contributions, agricultural resource protections, and ownership change conditions.

summary: Section 6, part 6) Screening and Visibility requires Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems to "conduct a visual assessment of the visual impacts of the Solar Energy System on public roadways and adjacent properties. At a minimum, a line-of-sight profile analysis shall be provided. Depending upon the scope and potential significance of the visual impacts, additional impact analyses, including for example, a digital view-shed report, may be required to be submitted by the applicant." This is in addition to submitting a screening & landscaping plan to minimize views of Solar Panels and Solar Energy Equipment from public roadways and adjacent properties. Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems are defined as systems not included in Tier 1 (Roof-Mounted and Building-Integrated) or Tier 2 (Ground-Mounted up to 25 kW AC and generating no more than 110% of onsite consumption).

summary: All applications for commercial solar energy systems shall be accompanied by a decommissioning plan to be implemented upon abandonment, or cessation of activity, or in conjunction with removal of the structure. Prior to issuance of a building permit, the owner or operator shall post a performance bond or other suitable guarantee in a face amount of not less than 150% of the estimated cost, as determined by the Town Engineer, to ensure removal of the solar energy system in accordance with the decommissioning plan. If the applicant ceases operation for 18 months or does not complete construction within 18 months after final site plan approval, a decommissioning plan must be submitted to restore the site to a useful, nonhazardous condition, including removal of equipment, restoration of surface grade and soil, revegetation with native seed mixes, and a timeframe for completion. The Town may require implementation of the decommissioning plan and may recover costs as a lien on the property if the owner/operator fails to comply. Commercial solar energy systems are strictly prohibited in residential and conservation zoning districts except as provided in Subsection F, which permits them on parcels of minimum 25 acres with a footprint not exceeding 10% of the parcel or seven acres, whichever is lesser, subject to Planning Board approval and compliance with Subsection D requirements. Therefore, these decommissioning requirements apply to commercial solar energy systems in residential/conservation districts meeting these criteria.

All commercial solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs with the owner's contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing. The height and type of fencing shall be determined by the Planning Board during the site plan process. All mechanical equipment of a commercial system, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum six-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate and provided with landscape screening. For commercial solar energy systems in residential/conservation zoning districts with a minimum of 25 acres and a footprint not exceeding 10% of the parcel or seven acres, the footprint includes the perimeter fence. These systems must meet the requirements of Subsection D and are subject to Planning Board site plan approval. The Planning Board may impose additional restrictions and setback requirements. Screening with perimeter plantings is also required to minimize visual impact, and fencing may be required if landscape buffers are inadequate.

Commercial solar energy systems in residential/conservation zoning districts are permitted subject to Planning Board site plan approval if the parcel is a minimum of 25 acres and the footprint does not exceed 10% of the parcel or seven acres, whichever is lesser. Such systems "shall meet the requirements of Subsection D above." Subsection E(4)(i)[6] requires that "All commercial solar energy system facilities shall be designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare toward any inhabited building and adjacent properties as well as public roads." Additional requirements include height and setback adherence, fencing, screening, and utility notification. Commercial solar energy systems are otherwise prohibited in residential and conservation districts except as provided in Subsection F. Subsection D applies to private/residential use systems and includes glare minimization for roof-mounted systems by requiring panels to be "constructed of a material designed to minimize glare."

The maximum height for ground-mounted commercial solar energy systems shall not exceed 12 feet in height above the ground measured from the ground under the solar panel to the highest point of the solar panel or racking, whichever is greater. This applies to commercial solar energy systems, including those permitted in residential/conservation districts with minimum 25-acre parcel and maximum 7-acre footprint, as they must meet the requirements of Subsection D and E. Other height restrictions mentioned include roof-mounted private/residential systems and ground-mounted private/residential systems, but these do not apply to commercial systems. The unit of measurement is feet.

Subsection F(1) states: 'The parcel on which the solar energy system shall be placed has an acreage/size of a minimum of 25 acres.' Additionally, Subsection F(2) limits the footprint of the solar energy system, including the perimeter fence, to not exceed 10% of the parcel or seven acres, whichever is lesser. The minimum lot size is explicitly given as 25 acres, which is the most restrictive minimum lot size for commercial solar energy systems in residential/conservation zoning districts.

Commercial solar energy systems "will be permitted, subject to site plan approval by the Planning Board," in the following zoning districts: Mixed Use Commercial (MC), Office Industrial (OI), Quarry (Q) and Pleasant Valley Hamlet (H-PV). Additionally, commercial solar energy systems are designated as a permitted use in the Hamlet of Pleasant Valley (H-PV) pursuant to Subsection G, also subject to site plan approval. Commercial solar energy systems are strictly prohibited in all residential and conservation zoning districts except as provided under special conditions in Subsection F, which requires Planning Board approval and additional criteria. Ground-mounted solar energy systems on farms that are not on-farm equipment are regulated under these commercial provisions. Site plan approval is the only stated condition for these commercial and industrial districts, indicating these are permitted primary uses.

Commercial solar energy systems are strictly prohibited in all residential and conservation zoning districts in the Town, except as provided in Subsection F below. Subsection E states: 'commercial solar energy systems are strictly prohibited in all residential and conservation zoning districts in the Town, except as provided in Subsection F below.' Commercial solar energy systems will be permitted, subject to site plan approval by the Planning Board, in the following zoning districts: Mixed Use Commercial (MC), Office Industrial (OI), Quarry (Q) and Pleasant Valley Hamlet (H-PV). Subsection F allows commercial solar energy systems in residential and conservation districts subject to Planning Board approval and meeting specific criteria.

In zoning districts which have a minimum lot size of 3.5 acres, a minimum setback of 100 feet from any property line is required (Subsection D(2)(b)). Commercial solar energy systems in residential/conservation districts with minimum 25-acre parcels and maximum 7-acre footprints must meet the requirements of Subsection D and adhere to the height and setback requirements of the underlying zoning district (Subsections F(4) and E(1)). Additionally, the solar energy system shall be placed towards the interior of the parcel and not visible from any public roadway or adjoining parcel (Subsection F(3)). The Planning Board may impose additional setback requirements at its discretion during site plan review to minimize visual impact and protect neighborhood character (Subsections E(1) and F(6)).

Commercial solar energy systems in residential and conservation districts are permitted subject to Planning Board site plan approval if the parcel is a minimum of 25 acres and the footprint does not exceed 10% of the parcel or seven acres, whichever is lesser. The system "shall be placed so that the system is located towards the interior of the parcel and is not visible from any public roadway or from any residence on the adjoining parcel" and "shall meet the requirements of Subsection D above." Subsection E(4)(i) and (ii) require that "a ground-mounted commercial solar energy system shall be screened with perimeter planting, to consist of evergreen plantings, having a minimum height of four feet at the time of installation, and shall be set back as determined by the Planning Board in a manner to minimize the visual impact of the commercial solar energy system upon neighboring properties, public roads and public areas." Additionally, "a landscape buffer shall be provided around all equipment and solar panels to provide screening from adjacent properties and roads." The Planning Board may require fencing combined with plantings for adequate screening. Other conditions include height and setback requirements, fencing to prevent unauthorized access, and compliance with safety regulations. Commercial solar energy systems are otherwise prohibited in residential and conservation districts except as provided in this subsection.

Commercial solar energy systems are strictly prohibited in all residential and conservation zoning districts except as provided in Subsection F. Subsection F allows commercial solar energy systems in residential and conservation districts subject to Planning Board site plan approval, provided the parcel has a minimum of 25 acres and the footprint does not exceed 10% of the parcel or seven acres, whichever is lesser. These systems must meet the requirements of Subsection D and be sited to avoid visibility from public roadways or adjoining residences. Signage requirements for commercial solar energy systems (Subsection E(5)) include: a sign not to exceed eight square feet attached to the fence adjacent to the main access gate listing the facility name, owner, and phone number; and a clearly visible warning sign at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations, marked 'Danger,' listing all voltages present. Other options include commercial solar energy systems permitted in Mixed Use Commercial (MC), Office Industrial (OI), Quarry (Q), and Pleasant Valley Hamlet (H-PV) districts, subject to site plan approval and similar signage and fencing requirements.

Commercial solar energy systems are strictly prohibited in all residential and conservation zoning districts in the Town, except as provided in Subsection F. Commercial solar energy systems will be permitted, subject to site plan approval by the Planning Board, in the following zoning districts: Mixed Use Commercial (MC), Office Industrial (OI), Quarry (Q) and Pleasant Valley Hamlet (H-PV). Such commercial solar energy systems shall be subject to following requirements. Commercial solar energy systems in residential and conservation districts may be permitted subject to Planning Board approval with additional criteria. Commercial solar energy systems designed for placement over parking lots in the Hamlet of Pleasant Valley require Planning Board site plan approval and must meet certain conditions. Ground-mounted solar energy systems on farms not considered on-farm equipment are regulated under these provisions as commercial solar energy systems.

Commercial solar energy systems may be permitted in residential and conservation districts, subject to Planning Board site plan approval, if the parcel is a minimum of 25 acres and the footprint does not exceed 10% of the parcel or seven acres, whichever is lesser. The system must be placed towards the interior of the parcel and not visible from any public roadway or adjoining residence. The system shall meet the requirements of Subsection D (which includes screening and siting requirements). The Planning Board may restrict size or siting to protect environmental resources, including scenic views or neighborhood character. Additionally, all commercial solar energy systems require site plan approval by the Planning Board and must adhere to design standards including screening with perimeter plantings to minimize visual impact on neighboring properties, public roads, and public areas, with the Planning Board having authority over viewshed and screening requirements. Other options include commercial solar energy systems being strictly prohibited in residential and conservation districts except as provided in Subsection F, and permitted in Mixed Use Commercial, Office Industrial, Quarry, and Pleasant Valley Hamlet districts subject to site plan approval and similar requirements.
A large-scale solar energy system that is ground-mounted shall not exceed 85% of the lot on which it is installed. The surface area covered by solar panels shall be included in total lot coverage.

A decommissioning plan shall be submitted as part of the application for a Planned Development District (PDD) for large-scale solar energy systems. The plan must specify that after the system can no longer be used and/or is abandoned, it shall be expeditiously removed by the applicant or any subsequent owner, including removal of all infrastructure and remediation of soil and vegetation to return the parcel to its original state prior to construction. The plan shall include an expected timeline and a cost estimate prepared by a professional engineer or licensed contractor. Removal must be completed in accordance with the plan. If not decommissioned after being considered abandoned (defined as six months without electrical energy generation), the municipality may remove the system and impose a lien to cover costs. Responsibility for compliance and costs lies solely with the property owner, and any deed of conveyance must contain an express covenant that this responsibility runs with the land. Applications for extensions of abandonment periods may be granted for six months at a time by the Planning Board. Enforcement may include recovery of costs incurred in enforcement and discharge of the owner's responsibilities under the decommissioning plan. Other options include the Town Board's discretion to waive some requirements for large-scale systems harmonious with land uses, and site security and other conditions imposed as part of PDD approval.
section: § 187-7 Approval standards for large-scale systems; § 187-8 Abandonment and decommissioning

summary: For large-scale solar energy systems, "the property owner [is responsible] to ensure that the site is secure from trespass and that adequate warnings are posted along the perimeter of the lot." "If circumstances require, the Town Board, upon the recommendation of the Planning Board, may require the site to be enclosed by fencing. Such fencing shall at all times be properly maintained by the property owner."

Large-Scale Energy Systems shall be located on lots with the minimum lot size required for a Planned Development District. As set forth in § 150-61 of the Code, the minimum lot size shall be 10 contiguous acres. This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for large-scale solar energy systems intended primarily for off-site sale or consumption.

Large-scale solar energy systems are permitted only through the establishment of a Planned Development District (PDD) by the Town Board. The text states: 'Large-scale solar energy systems are permitted through the establishment of a Planned Development District (PDD) by the Town Board.' This implies that outside of a PDD, large-scale solar energy systems are effectively prohibited. The districts mentioned where smaller ground-mounted solar energy systems are allowed as accessory structures include Hamlet (H), Residential (R), Rural Residential 1 (RR-1), and Rural Residential 2 (RR-2), but these permissions apply to systems that use electricity primarily on site and do not override the requirement for PDD approval for large-scale systems.

Large-scale solar energy systems are permitted through the establishment of a Planned Development District (PDD) by the Town Board with input from the Town Planning Board in accordance with the terms and procedures set forth in Articles VIII, IX and XV of Chapter 150 of the Code of the Town of Poestenkill. Other solar energy systems such as roof-mounted and ground-mounted systems that use electricity primarily on site are permitted as accessory uses or structures in all zoning districts, with certain conditions (e.g., ground-mounted systems in RR-2 require a special use permit if sited in the front yard). However, these smaller or primarily on-site systems are not considered large-scale and thus are not included as special use districts for large-scale systems.

The Town of Pompey Local Law No. 1 of 2015 adds § 165-16.2 entitled  "Solar Energy Conversion Systems"  which explicitly prohibits "Commercial energy generation for sale off-site." The law allows solar energy conversion systems only if "such generated energy is used primarily by the principal user of the property where the SCS is located," with only ancillary sale of excess energy that produces no net revenue. This prohibition applies broadly and unconditionally to all solar energy conversion systems in the Town, without exceptions based on location, prior approvals, or other conditions. There is no expiration date for this prohibition. The law is effective upon filing with the Secretary of State. Other provisions regulate system size, location, and permitting but do not alter the prohibition on commercial off-site sales.

The location of free standing SCS shall be at least 25 feet from any property line. Additionally, minimum setbacks for freestanding SCS in applicable districts include side and rear setbacks of 25 feet, and a front setback of 200 feet if located in the front yard. Other options include front setback only allowed if minimum 200 feet, side setback 25 feet, rear setback 25 feet. These setbacks apply to freestanding solar collection systems in districts where commercial-scale systems would be permitted.

Additionally, the location of freestanding SCS shall be at least 25 feet from any public road right-of-way. The 200-foot front setback is the most restrictive value. summary: The location of free standing SCS shall be at least 25 feet from any overhead utility wires, unless otherwise approved by the utility company. summary: Notwithstanding bulk table requirements to the contrary, developmental coverage of a lot with a solar facility or solar power plant shall not exceed 85%. This is found in § 535-41(G)(9). The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the lot's developmental coverage, not as a specific area value.

§ 535-43 Decommissioning requires that if a solar facility or solar power plant has been out of active and continuous service for a period of one (1) year, it shall be removed from the premises to a place of safe and legal disposal. Any and all structures and accessory structures shall also be removed. The site shall be restored to as natural a condition as possible. Such removal shall be completed within eighteen (18) months of the cessation of active and continuous use. A permit for the demolition of the system shall be required. If the owner fails to remove the system, the City may serve a notice of demand to remove and may perform the work at the owner's expense, which shall constitute a lien on the property. Other related decommissioning provisions include: (A) If a solar energy power system ceases to perform its originally intended function for more than twelve (12) consecutive months, the property owner shall remove the power system, mount and associated equipment no later than ninety (90) days after the end of the 12 month period; (C) enforcement procedures if the owner fails to comply with removal requirements.

The solar facility or solar power plant installation shall be enclosed by a fence consistent with NYSERDA regulations. Planning Board may require a greater height in fencing depending on individual conditions (§ 535-41(G)(11)). Other related fencing requirements include: freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems as accessory structures must be enclosed by a continuous fence (or fence with privacy slats) consistent with NYS and Federal requirements (§ 535-41(E)(5)); accessory freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems shall be enclosed by a fence consistent with NYSERDA regulations (§ 535-41(F)(4)).

Solar facility and solar power plant panels and equipment shall be surfaced, designed and sited so as not to reflect glare onto adjacent properties and roadways (§ 535-41(G)(12)). Solar Facilities and Solar Power Plants require site plan and special use permit approval (§ 535-41(G)(1)) and must comply with various conditions including setbacks, fencing, height limits, and screening. Other solar power systems such as rooftop, building-mounted, freestanding, and ground-mounted systems have different permitting and installation requirements but do not explicitly mention glare restrictions.

The height of the freestanding or ground-mounted solar collectors and any mounts shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet when oriented at maximum tilt. This applies specifically to Solar Facilities and Solar Power Plants as defined in the ordinance. Other related height limits include: freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems as accessory structures to single family and two-family residences shall not exceed ten (10) feet in height (§ 535-41(E)(7)), and accessory freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems shall not exceed ten (10) feet in height (§ 535-41(F)(6)). Rooftop and building-mounted solar power systems shall not exceed the maximum permitted building height in the zoning district (§ 535-41(C)(2)). The units for the Solar Facility or Solar Power Plant height restriction are feet.

The ordinance states: 'A solar facility or solar power plant shall only be permitted on lots with a minimum size of 10 acres.' This is the explicit minimum lot size for Solar Facilities or Solar Power Plants. Other minimum lot sizes mentioned in the text, such as 80,000 square feet for freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems accessory to residences, do not apply to Solar Facilities or Solar Power Plants. The unit 'acres' is used as the standard area measurement for this minimum lot size.

All solar facility or solar power plant equipment and installations shall be subject to a minimum setback of 100 feet plus the setback minimum from all property lines required in the zoning district. The Planning Board may require increased setbacks as it deems necessary based on the surrounding conditions. (§ 535-41(G)(7)) This applies to commercial-scale solar facilities or power plants. Other setback provisions for smaller or accessory freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems specify a 15-foot setback from the property line, but these apply to smaller or accessory systems, not Solar Facilities or Solar Power Plants.

Solar Facilities and Solar Power Plants "shall be screened when possible and practicable from adjoining lots and street rights of way through the use of architectural features, earth berms, landscaping, or other screening which will harmonize with the character of the property and surrounding area." Additional screening may be required as part of the Planning Board approval (§ 535-41(G)(6)). Other related conditions include site plan and special use permit approval (§ 535-41(G)(1)), minimum setbacks (§ 535-41(G)(7)), minimum lot size (§ 535-41(G)(8)), maximum developmental coverage (§ 535-41(G)(9)), height limits (§ 535-41(G)(10)), fencing requirements (§ 535-41(G)(11)), glare reduction (§ 535-41(G)(12)), and underground power lines where practicable (§ 535-41(G)(13)).

The ordinance explicitly requires that for Solar Facilities and Solar Power Plants, "The manufacturer’s or installer’s identification and appropriate warning signage shall be posted at the site and clearly visible." This is stated in § 535-41(G)(5). Other options and conditions for solar energy power systems include: Rooftop and building-mounted solar power systems require building permits but no signage requirements are mentioned (§ 535-41(C)); Freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems under 30 kilowatts require building permits and have setback, fencing, and height limits but no signage requirements (§ 535-41(E)); Larger freestanding or ground-mounted systems require site plan and special use permit approval and may require additional screening or fencing (§ 535-41(E)(10)); Accessory freestanding and ground-mounted systems require site plan approval and fencing consistent with NYSERDA regulations but no explicit signage requirements (§ 535-41(F)).

Section G states: 'Solar Facilities and Solar Power Plants shall be permitted as structures in all zoning districts subject to the following conditions: (1) Site plan and special use permit approval granted by the City of Port Jervis Planning Board is required under Article XV herein.' This means that these large-scale solar systems require Planning Board approval and a special use permit in all zoning districts. Other solar system types and their conditions include: rooftop and building-mounted solar power systems permitted in all zoning districts without Planning Board approval unless deemed necessary by the Code Enforcement Officer; freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems permitted as accessory structures to single and two-family residences with kilowatt limits and possible Planning Board approval if exceeding those limits; and accessory freestanding and ground-mounted solar power systems requiring site plan approval and possibly special use permits if exceeding certain kilowatt thresholds.

Section 306-34.10 Abandonment and removal explicitly requires that all applications for a ground-mounted or primary use solar PV system that requires a special use permit shall be accompanied by a decommissioning plan to be implemented upon abandonment, or cessation of activity, or in conjunction with removal of the facility, prior to issuance of a building permit. The decommissioning plan must ensure the site will be restored to a useful, nonhazardous condition without delay, including physical removal of all aboveground and below-ground equipment, disposal of waste, restoration of ground surface and soil, and stabilization and revegetation of the site. A system may be deemed abandoned if construction is not completed within 18 months, if the facility is not functioning within 18 months of final site plan approval, or if the facility ceases all activity for one year or fails to generate more than 10% of its rated capacity over 12 months. The Town may notify the owner/operator to implement the decommissioning plan, and if they fail to do so within 180 days, the Town may restore the site and recover costs. The Planning Board may permit leaving certain improvements in place upon petition. Special use permit conditions include a licensed engineer's estimate of operational life, identification of the party responsible for decommissioning, description of any decommissioning agreement, a decommissioning schedule, a cost estimate, and annual reporting by the system owner. Failure to perform decommissioning may lead to permit revocation and Town enforcement. These requirements apply to "any permitted system classified as a principal use and all ground-mounted permitted systems," which includes large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems as defined in § 306-34.7.

Fences not exceeding six feet in height, including open-weave chain-link fences and solid fences, shall be permitted for the purpose of screening or enclosing a permitted system, regardless of the district in which the system is located. Large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems require a special use permit and site plan approval and are classified as permitted systems. Other solar PV systems requiring a special use permit include: building-mounted and building-integrated systems greater than 25 kW or generating more than 110% of on-site consumption; systems generating and distributing energy to the public-utility power grid or off-site locations; systems mounted on freestanding structures not constituting the principal use; and any system not eligible to be permitted by right.

summary: All solar panels shall have antireflective coatings (§ 306-34.8C). summary: In residential and residential-agricultural districts, large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems must meet setbacks of not less than 25 feet from any public highway right-of-way or utility easement, and natural vegetation shall be preserved within this buffer zone and, where possible, augmented with additional plantings. The plantings are intended to provide a visual screen of the permitted system from residential uses, with the species type, location and planned height subject to the approval of the Planning Board and to the extent possible shall consist of native plantings (§ 306-34.8J(2)(a) and (b)). Other relevant standards for permitted systems include requirements on minimum lot size, underground utility connections, antireflective coatings on panels, fences for screening or enclosure, height limits, maintenance using native pollinator-friendly plantings, sign restrictions, front yard location prohibitions, and compliance with applicable codes (§ 306-34.8).

All signs, flags, streamers or similar items, both temporary and permanent, are prohibited on solar equipment except: a) the manufacturer's or installer's identification; b) appropriate warning signs and placards; c) signs that may be required by a federal, state or local agency or any potential first responders; and d) signs that provide a twenty-four-hour emergency contact phone number and warn of any danger" (§ 306-34.8(G)). Other permitted systems requiring a special use permit include: (2) building-mounted and building-integrated solar PV systems with capacity greater than 25 kW or generating more than 110% of on-site consumption; (3) systems generating and distributing energy to the public-utility power grid or off-site locations; (4) systems mounted on freestanding structures not part of the principal building; and (5) any solar PV system not eligible to be permitted by right (§ 306-34.7(A)).

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires soil, erosion, and sediment control measures for large-scale ground-mounted solar PV systems, especially on agricultural lands. Key requirements include: maintaining all existing drainage and erosion control structures such as diversions, ditches, and tile lines or taking appropriate measures to maintain their design and effectiveness; installing culverts and water bars to maintain natural drainage patterns; stripping and separately stockpiling all topsoil areas used for vehicle and equipment traffic, parking, and equipment lay-down and storage; limiting vehicle and equipment traffic to designated work areas; restoring soil by decompacting to a depth of 18 inches, removing rocks, replacing topsoil to original depth, regrading access roads, restoring original surface drainage patterns, seeding restored areas with landowner-specified seed mix, repairing damaged drainage structures, and postponing restoration until favorable soil conditions exist; providing a monitoring and remediation period of no less than 365 days; and mitigating any topsoil deficiency and trench settling with imported topsoil consistent with site quality. Additionally, excess concrete must not be buried or left on active agricultural areas, and all permits for disposal must be obtained. These requirements apply as part of site plan approval for projects on lands currently used or suitable for agricultural operations, particularly for projects of at least 20 acres where an environmental monitor must be hired. The ordinance also includes decommissioning plan requirements that mandate restoration of the ground surface and soil, and stabilization and revegetation of the site with native seed mixes to minimize erosion upon abandonment or removal of the system.

By contrast, smaller or building-integrated systems generating electricity solely for on-site use are permitted by right (§ 306-34.6), and other solar PV systems exceeding certain thresholds or generating for off-site use also require special use permits (§ 306-34.7 A).

Any authorized aboveground utility lines shall be affixed to utility poles tall enough to provide 20 feet of clearance from the lowest electrical and/or utility line to the final grade (§ 306-34.8.B). For agricultural lands, aboveground interconnect cables and transmission lines must be located outside agricultural field boundaries, with poles providing 20 feet of clearance (§ 306-34.8.J.(3)(b)[17]).

summary: Section 6.A.1 states: 'Major Solar Collection Systems shall not exceed ten (10%) coverage of the total lot.' For comparison, Minor Solar Collection Systems have a maximum coverage of 10% as well, but this applies only to smaller or non-commercial systems. section: 6. MAJOR SOLAR COLLECTION SYSTEMS OR SOLAR FARMS

summary: All applications for a Major Solar Collection System or Solar Farm "shall be accompanied by a decommissioning plan that shall be implemented upon abandonment, or cessation of activity, or in conjunction with removal of the facility." The plan "shall be designed to ensure the proper removal of solar energy systems at the termination of their use" and "must specify that after the solar energy system is no longer used, it shall be removed by the applicant or any subsequent real property owner." Additionally, "Any solar energy systems which has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned consistent with this chapter shall be removed" within 150 days after discontinued operations, with notification to the Town Board. The system is considered abandoned if it "fails to operate for more than one year without the written consent of the Town Board." The Town may remove abandoned systems and impose a lien to cover costs. The applicant must provide "an estimate prepared by a qualified engineer, setting forth the costs associated with decommissioning" and "financial surety... prior to the issuance of the building permit" to ensure funds are available for decommissioning. These requirements apply specifically to Major Solar Collection Systems or Solar Farms. For Minor Solar Collection Systems, a similar decommissioning plan is required prior to permit issuance, but the text distinguishes the two categories and their permitting processes.

Section 6.A.11 states: 'All equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be screened and fenced from adjacent properties to restrict unauthorized access.' This fencing requirement applies explicitly to Major Solar Collection Systems or Solar Farms. Other related provisions include setback requirements, height limits, screening methods such as landscape or vegetative screening, fencing, earth berms, or other methods (6.A.19), and the requirement for Site Plan Review and a Special Use Permit (6.A.20).
section: 6. MAJOR SOLAR COLLECTION SYSTEMS OR SOLAR FARMS

summary: Section 6.A.8 states: "Solar Collection Systems and solar panels shall be placed and arranged such that reflected solar radiation, light or glare shall not be directed onto adjacent buildings, properties or roadways." This glare restriction explicitly applies to Major Solar Collection Systems or Solar Farms. Other related design standards for Major Solar Collection Systems or Solar Farms include: not exceeding ten (10%) coverage of the total lot; a maximum structural height of fifteen (15) feet; a minimum setback of five hundred (500) feet to all property boundaries (which may be waived if glare, visual impact, or line of sight obstruction is minimized by topography, terrain, or vegetation); ground mounting plans reviewed and approved by a New York State Engineer; installation in side or rear yards with a five hundred (500) foot setback preferred; certification by a New York State Building Inspector or licensed engineer; restrictions on advertising and illumination; screening and fencing requirements; prohibitions on creating shadows or preventing sunlight on adjacent properties; and requirements for stormwater management, removal of inactive systems, site restoration, and use of natural screening or landscaping. All Major Solar Collection Systems require Site Plan Review and a Special Use Permit.

This is the explicit maximum structure height for Major Solar Collection Systems or Solar Farms. For comparison, Minor Solar Collection Systems have a similar 15 feet height limit (Section 5.A.3), but the focus here is on Major systems. The units are explicitly given as feet.

summary: The design of the Solar Farm shall adhere to a minimum of five hundred (500) feet of setback to all property boundaries. If the proposed solar farm components can be incorporated into existing topography, terrain or vegetative covering that minimizes off site glare, visual impact or line of site obstruction, it shall be utilized, and the Planning Board may consider waiving this set back requirement. The Solar Energy System and equipment shall be installed in a side or rear yard whenever possible and shall have at minimum a five hundred (500) foot setback. In the event it is not possible to install a Solar Energy System in either the rear or side yards on any given parcel, the system may be installed in a front yard with a minimum five hundred (500) foot setback from the front property line, and subject to Site Plan Review.

Where no natural or existing site conditions are available, "the use of landscape or vegetative screening, fencing, earth berms, or other methods shall be incorporated into the site plan." Additionally, "All equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be screened and fenced from adjacent properties to restrict unauthorized access." These requirements are explicitly stated in subsections 6.A.11, 6.A.18, and 6.A.19. The ordinance also provides that the Planning Board may consider waiving setback requirements if the solar farm components can be incorporated into existing topography, terrain or vegetative covering that minimizes off site glare, visual impact or line of site obstruction (6.A.3).

summary: Section 6.A.14 requires that "Storm water and snowmelt runoff and erosion control shall be managed in a manner consistent with all applicable federal, state, and local regulations and shall not drain onto or impact neighboring properties." Additionally, section 7.A.1.c mandates "Stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion" as part of decommissioning. These provisions explicitly address erosion and sediment control requirements for Major Solar Collection Systems or Solar Farms. Other related requirements include setbacks, height limits, ground mounting plans, screening, fencing, and decommissioning plans, but these do not specifically address soil, erosion, or sediment control.

summary: The proposed amendment allows solar energy systems on roofs of buildings up to 4 feet in height, measured from the maximum height limit or the finished roof level, whichever is higher. Taller systems above 4 feet are allowed if set back at least 6 feet from the street wall, cover no more than 25% of the roof area, and are limited to 6 feet in R1 through R5 districts, 15 feet in R6 through R10 districts, and 6 feet when located on bulkheads or other obstructions. On roofs with slope greater than 20 degrees, systems are limited to 18 inches in height measured perpendicular to the roof surface. The most restrictive maximum height for utility-scale solar energy systems is therefore 15 feet. Units are feet.

All applications for solar farms shall be accompanied by a decommissioning plan to be implemented upon abandonment, or cessation of activity, or in conjunction with the removal of the structure, which shall be reviewed and approved by the Town Board. Solar farms and solar power plants which have not been in active and continuous service for a period of one year shall be removed at the owners' or operators' expense within six months of the date of expiration of the one-year period. All aboveground and below-ground equipment, conduits, structures, fencing and foundations shall be removed from the site to a depth of at least three feet below grade. The site shall be restored to as natural a condition as possible within six months of the removal of all equipment, structures and foundations, including restoration of surface grade and revegetation with native seed mixes. The Planning Board shall require the posting of a removal bond of the solar farm's and solar power plant's equipment. In lieu of a removal bond, the Town Board may permit the owner/operator to enter into a decommissioning agreement with the Town, allowing the Town to remove structures and recover costs if decommissioning is not completed within specified timeframes. Costs incurred by the Town may be assessed as a lien and tax on the property or collected by other legal means, with the owner/operator liable for legal expenses in such proceedings.

Solar farms shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access at a height consistent with the current fence code. However, the Planning Board shall have the discretion to vary or eliminate this requirement where the Planning Board has determined that safety and security at the site will be assured by alternate methods.

Solar farms (minimum land area of five acres) must have panels and equipment "surfaced, designed, and sited so as not to reflect glare onto adjacent properties, facilities, and roadways." Other requirements include perimeter fencing, signage, blending materials, landscaping/screening, height limits (average height not to exceed 12 feet, with Planning Board discretion to permit higher), underground power lines where practicable, and a decommissioning plan with specific removal and restoration conditions.

The average height of the solar panel arrays shall not exceed 12 feet. However, the Planning Board shall have the discretion to permit the solar panel arrays to exceed the height limitation of 12 feet to the extent necessary, as determined by the Planning Board, to achieve the intended purpose of the solar collectors. Such determination shall be made in consideration of the design of the solar collectors and the subject property's natural and proposed characteristics, including, but not limited to, topography, existing and proposed vegetative buffers, and proximity to residential and/or commercial uses.

The ordinance states: 'Solar farms shall require a minimum land area of five acres.' This is the explicit minimum lot size for utility-scale solar energy systems defined as solar farms. No other minimum lot size values are provided.

Solar farms shall require a minimum land area of five acres. Appropriate landscaping and/or screening materials may be required to help screen the solar farm and accessory structures from major roads and neighboring residences pursuant to Article 8 of Chapter 179. The Planning Board has discretion to vary or eliminate perimeter fencing requirements and to permit solar panel arrays to exceed the height limitation of 12 feet considering factors including existing and proposed vegetative buffers.

Solar farms shall require a minimum land area of five acres. The manufacturer's and installer's identification and appropriate warning signage and emergency contact information shall be posted at the site and clearly visible.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "If any Commercial/Industrial Solar Energy Conversion System remains non-functional or inoperative for a continuous period of 180 days, the applicant shall, without any further action by the Town, remove said system at its own expense" (Section E.1). An application must include "a decommissioning and site restoration plan" that provides for "removal from the Project Parcels and lawful disposal or disposition of all Commercial/Industrial Solar Energy Conversion Systems and other structures, hazardous materials, electrical facilities, and all foundations to a depth of not less than 60 inches below grade" and "restoration of the project parcels to farmland of similar condition to that which existed before construction" (Section F.1). The plan must include "the estimated decommissioning cost in current dollars," "the method of ensuring that funds will be available for decommissioning and restoration," and "financial security to secure completion of decommissioning" with a fund maintained at no less than 125% of the estimated cost (Section F.3, F.4). The permit holder must provide "written non-revocable authorization" for the Town to access the parcels and implement the plan if the permit holder fails to do so (Section F.5). If the permittee fails to remove the system and restore the site within 180 days of non-function or permit revocation, the Town may use the decommissioning fund to do so and charge the permit holder for any shortfall (Section F.6). Other options or conditions include the Town's ability to order a remedial action plan if good faith efforts to restore operation are demonstrated (Section E.1), and revocation of the permit with removal required within 180 days (Section H.2.3).
section: Section 10.27 – Commercial Solar Energy Conversion Systems

summary: Section 10.27 – Commercial Solar Energy Conversion Systems, subsection D, item 16 states: "Fencing is required to prevent unauthorized access. summary: Section G(3) states: 'The following requirements shall be met for decommissioning: (a) Major solar collection systems which have not been in active and continuous service for a period of months shall be removed at the owners' or operators' expense. summary: The ordinance explicitly requires a decommissioning agreement and financial surety for Tier 3 and larger solar energy systems, including Tier 4 systems. "A proposed decommissioning agreement shall be provided by the applicant and approved by the Town Board. No building permit shall be issued for a solar energy system until the decommissioning agreement has been executed and financial surety provided." The decommissioning plan must include: removal of all physical facilities, site restoration including decompaction and revegetation, cost estimates based on prevailing wages, no salvage value attributed, and a schedule for removal and restoration. Financial surety must be "150% of the estimated cost of removal of the solar energy system and restoration of the property," with an annual escalator and periodic review every five years. The Town may draw on the financial surety to implement decommissioning if the owner defaults, and any excess costs may be assessed against the property. These requirements apply to Tier 3 and larger systems, which includes Tier 4 systems (ground-mounted solar energy systems with a nameplate capacity of up to 25 MW AC).

Where fencing is required per this article or section 110.31 of NEC code and as revised, it shall encompass all solar collectors, electrical and control equipment, substations, batteries, and shall be labeled and secured to prevent unauthorized access. Such equipment shall be enclosed with a seven foot high fence or per most current NEC requirements. Fencing shall have a self-locking gate to prevent unauthorized access and shall be wildlife permeable/friendly by including one way wildlife gates every 1,000 linear feet of perimeter fencing (minimum of two). Fixed-knot woven wire or other wildlife friendly fencing and mixed used fencing is preferred and shall include areas which allow small-to-medium sized animals (e.g., turtles, raccoons, birds, etc.) to easily pass through. Fencing shall be located inside any landscaping buffer area required by this article. Barbed wire fencing is prohibited. These fencing requirements apply to Tier 4 solar energy systems as they are subject to all applicable requirements listed under § 270-224.2. Other options or conditions for fencing are not specified beyond these requirements.

All solar collectors shall have anti-reflective coating(s) to reduce glare to the maximum extent practicable. All solar collectors and related equipment shall be placed and arranged such that reflected solar radiation or glare shall not be directed onto adjacent properties or public roadways. Panels shall not reflect more than 2% of incoming sunlight. Tier 3 and larger systems shall submit glare studies prepared by an independent third-party vendor demonstrating that any glare or heat to be produced by the solar project does not have a significant adverse impact on neighboring properties or roadways. The study shall include a statement of projected glare impact certified by a qualified specialist or Professional Engineer and a post-construction glare monitoring plan requiring annual certification for at least two years after operation. These requirements apply to Tier 4 solar energy systems, which are defined as ground-mounted solar energy systems not included under Tier 1, 2, or 3 with a nameplate capacity of up to 25 MW AC.

summary: Landscaping buffer areas shall be required between the facility area and adjacent property lines to screen the view of Tier 2 and larger systems. Buffer widths shall be as follows: Tier 2: 25 feet (may be increased to 100 feet by the Code Enforcement officer; may be altered or waived by the Planning Commission for carport or canopy systems in parking lots); Tier 3: 50 feet (may be increased to 100 feet by the Planning Commission); Tier 4: 200 feet (may be reduced to 100 feet or other reasonable width by the Planning Commission if located in zones I-1 or I-2). Buffers shall use existing vegetation to the fullest extent practicable. If existing vegetation does not provide the desired screening or buffer width, it shall be supplemented with new landscaping to form a continuous hedge at least eight feet in height at planting and maintained for the life of the project. Berms, solid fencing, and opaque enclosures are the least desirable method of screening but may be proposed where landscaping is not practical. New landscaping shall be species native to the region and selected by a registered landscape architect. All landscaping and screening methods shall be maintained and replaced as necessary during the life of the project. Fencing shall be located inside any landscaping buffer area required by this article.

Warning signage shall be placed on solar equipment to the extent appropriate. All signs, streamers, or similar items, both temporary and permanent, are prohibited on solar equipment except the following, which must be posted at all points of facility area ingress/egress and any substation fencing: (1) Manufacturers or installer's identification; (2) Appropriate warning signs and placards; (3) Signs that may be required by a federal or state agency; (4) Signs that provide a twenty-four-hour emergency contact phone number and warn of any danger and signs that direct fire department and hazmat to emergency safety protocols within an area of no more than eight square feet; (5) As required by the NEC, disconnect and emergency shut off information shall be clearly displayed on a light-reflective surface; (6) A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations; (7) No advertising signage is permitted. Additionally, for Tier 4 systems, upon submission of an application, the applicant shall conspicuously post signage on the frontage of participating properties at all roads abutting the proposed project and at the proposed entryways/exits to the project. Signage must be of sufficient size to contain the name of the proposed project, the application number, a rough concept map of the project, and contact information for the developer as well as a proposed project website address. Signage shall be sized and placed at a safe distance from the public roadway as to not interfere with sight distance on the roadway or any adjacent driveways.

All engineering documents, including site plan and stormwater pollution prevention plan, shall be signed and sealed by a New York State-licensed professional engineer. The solar energy system shall comply with all requirements of Chapter 270, Article XXVI, Erosion and Sediment Control, of Town Code, and applicable New York State laws. The site shall be designed to avoid adverse changes to drainage, runoff, and overall site hydrology. Site disturbance, including grading, soil removal, excavation, and soil compaction, shall be minimized to the greatest extent practical. Performance guarantees shall cover stormwater management and erosion and sediment control facilities in the amount of 50% of the installed cost. The decommissioning plan shall include restoration of the property to its pre-installed condition, including grading and vegetative stabilization to eliminate any negative impacts to surrounding properties, following NYS Department of Agriculture and Markets Guidelines for Solar Energy Projects — Construction Mitigation for Agricultural Lands. These requirements apply to Tier 4 solar energy systems as incorporated by reference in the Tier 4 permitting requirements.

summary: For Tier 4 solar energy systems, the ordinance requires "A GIS viewshed analysis of the zone of visual impact (ZVI) prepared by an independent third-party vendor defined as the area from which the proposed undertaking may be visible within a 0.5 mile buffer around solar fields covering four to 39 acres in size, a one-mile buffer around solar fields covering 40 to 60 acres, a three-mile buffer for solar fields covering 61 to 80 acres, and a four-mile buffer for solar fields covering 81 to 100 acres." The analysis must be "based upon bare-earth topography only (do not factor in vegetation)" with forested lands assigned a height of 30 feet unless otherwise disputed. It must be "presented as an orthorectified aerial base map with the buffer boundary and project area indicated and ZVA highlighted." Additionally, "A visual analysis shall be provided from all property owners immediately adjacent to the proposed solar energy system. The analysis shall be for each season and from the building face at eye level from grade." The visual analysis will "quantify the severity of the visual impact." A "balloon study which provides aerial viewshed maps, model-massing, and photorealistic simulations shall be performed if deemed necessary by the Planning Commission." All required tests must comply with "specific balloon test performance criteria and simulation guidelines of the National Park Service and the Bureau of Land Management." summary: Section 10.K 'Abandonment or Decommissioning' requires that unsafe, inoperable, and/or abandoned Tier 3 Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems, and by extension Tier 4 Industrial-Scale Solar Energy Systems (which must meet Tier 3 requirements plus additional ones), shall be removed by the owner within six months of a determination that the systems are unsafe, inoperable, abandoned, or the Special Use Permit has expired or been revoked. A solar energy system is deemed abandoned when it fails to produce energy (50% or more of its total capacity) for at least one year. The site must be restored to its preexisting condition or as determined in the Decommissioning Plan within six months of removal. A Decommissioning Plan must be submitted as part of the Special Use Permit application, specifying removal procedures, restoration, timeline (not greater than 1 year), and a cost estimate prepared by a Professional Engineer or qualified Contractor. The plan must include standards from the NYS Department of Agriculture and Markets for agricultural lands. Additionally, a security deposit, bond, or other form of security equal to 125% of the cost of removal and restoration (with a 2% annual escalator) must be filed with the Town Clerk and renewed every five years. Failure to maintain this bond can result in revocation of the Special Use Permit. In the event of default, the security is forfeited to the Town to complete decommissioning. These requirements apply explicitly to Tier 3 and Tier 4 systems. Other tiers (Tier 1 and Tier 2) have different or no decommissioning requirements detailed here.
