summary: The ordinance explicitly requires for Tier 4 Industrial-Scale Solar Energy Systems: "A berm, landscape screen, or other opaque enclosure, or any combination thereof acceptable to the Town capable of screening the site, shall be provided along any property line that abuts an important community resource, an existing residence or any property zoned other than Business, Light Industrial or General Industrial." The landscaping plan must specify "locations, elevations, height, plant species, and/or materials" and include "evergreen/coniferous trees (planted at recommended spacing for the type of tree), at least 8-10 feet high at the time of planting... plus supplemental shrubs placed in between the evergreen trees at the reasonable discretion of the Town Planning Board." Existing vegetation on participating properties may be used to satisfy screening requirements. summary: Section J states: 'All Solar Panels and equipment shall be designed and sited so as to not reflect glare onto other properties, public or private roads, rights-of-way, or aircrafts in flight; and shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard.' This glare restriction applies to all Solar Energy Systems and equipment installed or modified after the effective date of this section (per B). Other relevant provisions include setback, height, and screening requirements for Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems (M), and mounting and structural requirements for Roof-mounted Solar Energy Systems (L), but these do not explicitly address glare.

The height of ground-mounted Solar Collectors and mounts shall not exceed twelve (12) feet when oriented at a maximum tilt. This applies to Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems, which may include utility-scale systems connected to the utility grid. The unit of measurement is feet. Other height-related provisions apply only to roof-mounted systems or smaller-scale systems and do not specify a maximum height for utility-scale systems.

The required rear yard and side yard setback for a Ground-Mounted Solar Energy System shall be at least fifty (50) feet from the property line. This applies to ground-mounted systems which are typically utility-scale. Other relevant provisions include that ground-mounted systems shall not be placed in a front yard and must not be sited within any required buffer area. Roof-mounted systems have setbacks from roof perimeters but those do not pertain to property or lot lines.

Ground-Mounted Solar Energy System equipment "shall be substantially screened from view from adjoining and neighboring properties and public and private roadways" using "architectural features, earth berms, landscaping or other screening which will harmonize with the character of the property and surrounding area." If landscape screening is proposed, "a landscape design, signed and stamped by a licensed landscape architect shall be submitted with all solar system site plan applications." Such screening "shall be designed and installed so as not to substantially interfere with normal operation of the Solar Collectors." Other relevant provisions include that ground-mounted systems require site plan review except on certain residential lots, must be set back at least 50 feet from property lines, and must not exceed 12 feet in height. Roof-mounted systems have different requirements and are not subject to site plan review. Screening requirements are explicitly stated only for ground-mounted systems.

All applications for large-scale solar energy systems shall be accompanied by a decommissioning plan to be implemented upon abandonment and/or in conjunction with removal of the system. The decommissioning plan shall include: an estimate of the anticipated operational life of the system; identification of the party(ies) responsible for decommissioning; a copy or description of any agreement with the landowner regarding decommissioning; a schedule showing the time frame over which decommissioning will occur and for completion of site restoration work; a cost estimate prepared by a qualified professional engineer estimating the full cost of decommissioning and removal of the large-scale solar energy system; and a financial plan to ensure that financial resources will be available to fully decommission the site. All responsible parties shall enter into a decommissioning agreement with the Town reflecting the decommissioning plan agreed to by the parties and the time frame for completion. The party(ies) responsible for decommissioning must provide a bond or approved letter of credit or other financial surety in an amount sufficient to fully cover the cost of decommissioning and implement the decommissioning plan. The bond or surety shall remain in effect throughout the life of the system and be renewed periodically. A large-scale solar energy system shall be deemed abandoned if it fails to generate and transmit electricity at a rate of more than 50% of its rated capacity over a continuous period of one year, or if construction is not completed within 18 months of issuance of the first solar permit. Upon abandonment, the owner and landowner are jointly and severally responsible to remove all components within one year in accordance with the approved decommissioning plan. Removal includes physical removal of all equipment and structures, disposal of waste, restoration of the ground surface and soil, and stabilization and revegetation of the site. The Town may remove the system if the owner fails to do so and recover costs from the financial surety or assess a lien on the property. Other options include extensions of abandonment time by the Planning Board upon presentation of a viable plan. These requirements apply specifically to large-scale solar energy systems designed to generate energy for sale or off-site use.

The Planning Board shall determine the extent to which a ground-mounted large scale solar energy system requires fencing, landscaping, and screening, including the type, height, and size of the fence. Generally, agricultural open-weave chain-link fences and solid fences shall be permitted for the purpose of screening or enclosing a large-scale solar energy system. (§ 161-6.A(4)(a)[3])

Large-scale solar energy systems shall be designed, installed and maintained in accordance with applicable codes, standards and manufacturer's specifications (§ 161-6B(4)(a)). The Planning Board shall determine the extent to which a ground-mounted large scale solar energy system requires landscaping, screening, a fence, and the type, height and size of the fence to be in general accordance with NYSERN guidelines (§ 161-6B(4)(a)[3]). Large-scale solar energy systems shall be located and designed to minimize glare and adverse visual impacts on neighboring properties and public rights-of-way (§ 161-6B(4)(a)). The ordinance also includes height limits (not to exceed 20 feet) and screening requirements to mitigate visual impacts (§ 161-6B(4)(a)[4]).

The ordinance states that for building-mounted large-scale solar energy systems installed on a flat roof, 'the highest point of the system shall not extend more than five feet above the height of the roof' (§ 161-6B(4)(b)[2]). This is the most restrictive explicit numerical height limit given. Other height limits include a general maximum of 20 feet for large-scale solar energy systems (§ 161-6B(4)(a)[4]) and for sloped roofs, the system cannot exceed the highest point of the roof (§ 161-6B(4)(b)[1]). The units for these height restrictions are feet.

Large-scale solar energy systems shall be located on lots with a minimum lot area of five acres. This is explicitly stated in § 161-6 Large-scale solar energy systems, subsection B(1): 'Large-scale solar energy systems shall be located on lots with a minimum lot area of five acres.' The unit 'acres' is the standard unit of area used here. No other minimum lot size values for large-scale solar energy systems are provided that are more restrictive.

The ordinance states: 'No large-scale solar energy systems shall be permitted in any residential districts.' Large-scale solar energy systems require a special use permit and site plan approval and may be classified as either a principal use or an accessory use depending on their purpose and location. Principal use includes systems providing electricity to off-site users, while accessory use includes systems generating electricity primarily for consumption on the same lot. Small-scale solar energy systems are permitted in all zoning districts with various conditions and permits required.

Ground-mounted large-scale solar energy systems are subject to a 50-foot setback from all property lines in commercial, industrial and planned unit development districts. No part of a large-scale ground-mounted system shall extend into the required setbacks. (§ 161-6.A(4)(a)[1]) Other setback references include compliance with minimum setback requirements for principal buildings in the Industrial (I) Zoning District (§ 161-6.B(2)), but the explicit fixed setback distance is 50 feet.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "The Planning Board shall determine the extent to which a ground-mounted large scale solar energy system requires landscaping, screening, a fence, and the type, height and size of the fence to be in general accordance with NYSERN guidelines." It further states that "Generally, agricultural open-weave chain-link fences and solid fences shall be permitted for the purpose of screening or enclosing a large-scale solar energy system." These requirements apply to large-scale solar energy systems defined as those "designed primarily to generate electricity for resale" or for off-site use or sale. No other specific vegetative buffer or screening requirements are detailed beyond the Planning Board's discretion to require landscaping, screening, and fencing.

A safety sign shall be attached to the fence at the main gate of any ground-mounted or freestanding large-scale solar energy system that contains a warning about high voltage and the Broome County Emergency Services telephone number. Any sign for a large-scale solar energy system classified as a principal use shall adhere to the sign requirements for the zoning district in which it is located. A solar energy system shall not be used to display permanent or temporary advertising, including signage, streamers, pennants, spinners, reflectors, banners or similar materials. (§ 161-6A(4)(a)[5])

The ordinance requires that for large-scale solar energy systems, if a stormwater pollution prevention plan (SWPPP), a wetland delineation, or a logging/site clearing permit, or a construction phasing plan is required, those items shall be submitted to the Town Planning Board as part of any application being reviewed by the Planning Board (§ 161-6A(2)(g)). Upon decommissioning and removal, "restoration of the ground surface and soil to previous site conditions" and "stabilization and revegetation of the site with native seed mixes and/or plant species (excluding invasive species) to minimize erosion" are required (§ 161-6B(4)(a)(3) and (4)). These provisions explicitly address soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements that large-scale solar energy system developers must abide by.

All large-scale solar energy systems require a special use permit and site plan approval from the Town Planning Board (§ 161-6 A(1)). No large-scale solar energy systems shall be permitted in any residential districts. Large-scale solar energy systems must conform to the area, yard, and bulk requirements of the zoning district in which the system is located, unless modified by other provisions (§ 161-6 A(3)(a)[2]). The text does not explicitly list or name any specific zoning districts or their abbreviations where large-scale solar energy systems are permitted. Other options include classification as either a principal use or accessory use: (a) Principal use: systems providing electricity to off-site users; (b) Accessory use: systems generating electricity for primary consumption on the same lot (§ 161-6 A(3)).

Large-scale solar energy systems require a special use permit and site plan approval (§ 161-6A(1)). Applications must include blueprints, plans or design drawings signed by a professional engineer or registered architect (§ 161-6A(2)(b)). The Planning Board "shall determine the extent to which a ground-mounted large scale solar energy system requires landscaping, screening, a fence, and the type, height and size of the fence to be in general accordance with NYSERN guidelines" (§ 161-6A(4)(a)[3]). Screening and fencing are required "to the extent practicable" (§ 161-4B(6) and § 161-6B(4)). The Planning Board also reviews setbacks, height, and utility connections as part of the standards (§ 161-6A(4)). The special use permit conditions include requirements for decommissioning plans, financial surety, and reporting, but do not explicitly mention additional visual impact assessment beyond screening and landscaping (§ 161-6A(5)).

All applications for large-scale solar system shall be accompanied by a decommissioning plan to be implemented upon abandonment, or cessation of activity, or in conjunction with removal of the structure. Prior to issuance of a building permit, the owner or operator shall post a performance bond or other suitable guarantee in a face amount of not less than 150% of the estimated cost, as determined by the Town Engineer, to ensure removal of the solar energy system or facility or structure in accordance with the decommissioning plan. The plan must include removal of above- and below-ground equipment, structures and foundations; restoration of the surface grade and soil after removal of equipment; revegetation of restored soil areas with native seed mixes, excluding any invasive species; and a time frame for the completion of site restoration work. If the system ceases operation for 18 months or construction is not completed within 18 months, the applicant must submit a decommissioning plan. The Town may require implementation of the plan if the owner/operator fails to complete construction or restore operation equal to 80% of approved capacity within specified timeframes. If the owner/operator fails to implement the plan within 180 days of notice, the Town may restore the site and recover costs as a lien on the property.

All large-scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs with the owner's contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing. The height and type of fencing shall be determined by the special use permit process. Additionally, all mechanical equipment of a large-scale solar system, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum six-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate.

Section G(15) explicitly requires that "All large-scale solar system facilities shall be designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare toward any inhabited buildings on adjacent properties as well as adjacent street rights-of-way." Large-scale solar systems are defined as "Solar energy systems located on land to convert solar energy into electricity for off-site energy consumption." Other relevant provisions for large-scale solar systems include height and setback requirements (G(1)), fencing and warning signs (G(2)), lighting restrictions (G(12)), landscape screening (G(17)), and decommissioning plans (G(20)).

The maximum height for ground-mounted solar systems shall not exceed 15 feet in height above the ground. This applies specifically to large-scale solar systems defined as solar energy systems located on land to convert solar energy into electricity for off-site energy consumption. The text states: 'The maximum height for ground-mounted solar systems shall not exceed 15 feet in height above the ground.'

A decommissioning plan shall be required to ensure that facilities are properly removed after their useful life. The site plan shall include provisions for removal of all supporting structures and foundations, restoration of soil and vegetation and a plan ensuring financial resources will be available to fully decommission the site. The Town may require the posting of a bond, a letter of credit or the establishment of an escrow account to ensure proper decommissioning. Ground-mounted solar energy systems shall not exceed 15 feet in height. This applies to solar farms, which are defined as ground-mounted solar energy systems that are principal uses, including those with rated capacity of 200 kW or greater on lots of 20 acres or more. Specifically, subsection A(2) states 'Ground-mounted solar energy systems shall not exceed 15 feet in height,' and subsection C(5) reiterates 'The height of the solar collector and any mounts shall not exceed 15 feet above the ground.' Subsection E(1) clarifies that solar farms with rated capacity of 200 kW or greater are only permitted on lots containing 20 acres or more, linking the height restriction to such large-scale solar farms. Solar farms having a rated capacity of 200 kW or greater are only permitted on lots containing 20 acres or more. This is stated explicitly in subsection E(1): 'solar farms having a rated capacity of 200 kW or greater are only permitted on lots containing 20 acres or more.' The units are acres, which is a standard area measurement. Other related conditions include that solar farms are a principal use allowed in certain districts subject to special use permit and site plan approval, and that ground-mounted solar energy systems located on a lot with another principal use are considered solar farms if they exceed certain surface area limits. However, these do not affect the minimum lot size requirement for solar farms with rated capacity of 200 kW or greater.

Ground-mounted solar energy systems "shall be screened from adjacent properties and roadways to the extent practicable." Specifically, "where a ground-mounted solar energy system is located within 100 feet of an adjacent property in a residential district or a street, it shall be screened by existing vegetation or topography or through the use of architectural features, earth berms, landscaping, or other screening which will harmonize with the character of the property and surrounding area. The buffer shall comply with the requirements of § 240-25B." For solar farms, "solar farms having a rated capacity of 200 kW or greater are only permitted on lots containing 20 acres or more." The Planning Board has discretion to modify screening height to prevent shading and may reduce setbacks with conditions. Other options for screening include existing vegetation, topography, architectural features, earth berms, landscaping, or other screening. The ordinance also requires setbacks and limits on surface area and impervious cover for solar farms.

A solar farm is a principal use allowed in the R-40/80, R-80, RA-3, RA-5, AI, CC and COP Districts subject to special use permit and site plan approval (§ 240-57 B(1)). Solar farms having a rated capacity of 200 kW or greater are only permitted on lots containing 20 acres or more (§ 240-57 E(1)). Additionally, site plan approval is required for all solar farms (§ 240-57 B(2)). Other conditions include that a ground-mounted solar energy system that is the sole use on a lot is considered a solar farm regardless of size (§ 240-57 B(3)), and solar farms on lots with another principal use are only permitted in the same districts (§ 240-57 B(5)). Accessory ground-mounted solar energy systems have different conditions and limitations (§ 240-57 A and D), but these do not apply to large solar farms as principal uses.

A large-scale solar energy system that is ground mounted shall not exceed 50% of the lot on which it is installed. The entire surface area of the solar panels shall be included in the total area regardless of the method by which the panels are supported or attached to the ground, or the angle at which they are placed. This is found in §134.6(4)(c). Other related provisions include a maximum of 1,000 square feet for freestanding and ground-mounted solar energy systems without a special use permit (applicable to smaller systems), but the 50% lot coverage limit explicitly applies to large-scale solar energy systems as defined (greater than 1,000 square feet and greater than 25kW for off-site sale or consumption).

A decommissioning plan shall be submitted as part of the application for a large-scale solar energy system special use permit (§134.6(h)). The plan must demonstrate how removal of all infrastructure both above and below ground and remediation of soil and vegetation will return the parcel to its prior condition (§134.6(h)(2)). It must include an expected timeline (§134.6(h)(3)) and a cost estimate prepared by a professional engineer, accounting for inflation (§134.6(h)(4)). A decommissioning performance surety bond equal to the decommissioning and reclamation costs must be issued to the Town and remain in effect for as long as the system exists, with a 20-year bond required and renewal after 15 years (§134.6(h)(4)). Removal must be completed in accordance with the plan (§134.6(h)(5)). If the system is abandoned or not decommissioned after being declared abandoned, the Town may remove the system and impose a lien to cover costs (§134.6(h)(1) and (6)). Other relevant conditions include that large-scale systems are ground-mounted, greater than 1,000 square feet and 25kW, permitted through special use permits in Industrial and Agricultural zones (§134.6(A)(B)(1)), and must meet setback, height, lot coverage, security, drainage, easement, and screening requirements (§134.6(4)).

All large-scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access, unless the Planning Board determines that fencing will cause environmental or ecological problems, or that such fencing is unnecessary. If the Planning Board makes such a determination, then the applicant must provide for other means, acceptable to the Planning Board, to prevent access to circuit conductors and other electrical components of the system. Warning signs with the property owner's contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the property and of the solar energy system at locations acceptable to the Planning Board. Any fencing installed shall be acceptable to the Planning Board and shall include screening of said fencing as required by the Planning Board.

summary: Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted through the issuance of a Special Use Permit within all residential districts subject to the requirements set forth in this Section, including site plan approval. Applications shall be reviewed by the Commissioner of Public Works and referred to the Town Board for review and action, which can include approval, approval with conditions, or denial. The Town Board shall refer site plan approval to the Planning Board prior to granting any Special Use Permit. In commercial districts, Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems are permitted under the site plan review process of the Planning Board. Front setbacks shall comply with the underlying zoning district. Additionally, Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems must adhere to height and setback requirements, be located on lots with a minimum size of 5 acres, and ground-mounted systems shall not exceed 20% lot coverage. A Large-Scale Solar Energy System is permitted as a primary structure in any commercially zoned property, while the Town Board considers issuance of a Special Use Permit in residential districts.
section: 6.) Approval Standards for Large -Scale Solar Energy Systems as a Special Use

summary: Section G 'Abandonment and decommissioning' applies to large-scale solar energy systems and requires that abandoned systems be removed pursuant to an approved decommissioning plan. The plan must be implemented upon abandonment, cessation of activity, or removal of the system and include: removal of all components including fencing, infrastructure, foundations, and supports to a depth of 48 inches; restoration of grade, soil, and vegetation; identification of responsible parties; a timeline for removal no longer than 180 days; a cost estimate approved by the Town's engineer; periodic reevaluation of decommissioning costs; and provisions allowing the Town to remove the system and claim against surety or impose liens if the owner fails to comply. Large-scale solar energy systems are deemed abandoned if construction is not completed within 12 months of final approvals or if the system fails to generate more than 10% of rated capacity over 12 months. Notice and appeal procedures are provided, and the Town may collect surety funds or assess liens to cover removal costs. These requirements are conditions of special use permit, site plan, and building permit approval.

The proposed large-scale solar energy project "shall be enclosed by fencing to prevent unauthorized access," unless the Planning Board determines that fencing will cause environmental or ecological problems or is unnecessary. In such cases, the applicant must provide other acceptable means to secure and prevent access. "All solar energy equipment, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be enclosed by a minimum six-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate."

All solar energy systems shall be designed and located to prevent reflective glare toward any inhabited building or adjacent property (§ 140-96.1 D.(3)). This glare restriction applies to all solar energy systems installed or modified after the effective date of the section (§ 140-96.1 B). Large-scale solar energy systems are regulated as a special use requiring a special use permit and site plan approval in certain zoning districts (§ 140-96.1 D.(2) and E). The ordinance includes detailed requirements for large-scale solar energy systems, including decommissioning plans, fencing, signage, and screening to mitigate adverse aesthetic impacts (§ 140-96.1 D, E, and H).

The ordinance requires that "Ground-mounted solar energy systems shall be screened from view of neighboring properties or the public right-of-way to the greatest extent practicable" (§ 140-96.1 D(4)). For large-scale solar energy systems, "The solar energy system shall be adequately screened to mitigate avoid adverse aesthetic impacts" (§ 140-96.1 E(8)). Additionally, "Removal of trees and other existing vegetation shall be minimized or offset with plantings elsewhere on the property, to maximize buffering and stormwater management as provided for herein" (§ 140-96.1 E(9)). These requirements apply in the context of large-scale solar energy systems permitted as a special use with site plan approval. Other provisions include fencing and signage requirements, but these are separate from vegetative buffer or screening mandates.

Section E(5) requires warning signs not exceeding eight square feet with the facility's name, the applicant/operator's and property owner's name and telephone numbers, and emergency contact information, placed on the entrance and perimeter of the property and the solar energy system at locations acceptable to the Planning Board. A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations. These signage requirements are in addition to and separate from any applicable sign regulations set forth in § 140-129. Other requirements for large-scale solar energy systems include fencing, site plan approval, decommissioning plans, and operational reporting, but these do not pertain to signage.

The ordinance applies to large-scale solar energy systems, which "may be permitted upon issuance of a special use permit and site plan approval" (§ 140-96.1 D). It requires a "soil erosion/drainage plan showing existing and finished grades and stormwater management plan approved by the Town Engineer" (§ 140-96.1 E(11)). For systems on prime agricultural land, detailed soil and erosion control measures include: hiring an environmental monitor; locating access roads to minimize agricultural impact; installing culverts and waterbars to maintain natural drainage; stripping and stockpiling topsoil separately; burying electric cables with minimum cover depths; protecting and repairing drainage and erosion control structures; removing excess subsoil, rock, and construction debris; and restoring soil compaction and contours with specified decompaction and seeding practices (§ 140-96.1 D(2)(e) and (f)). Restoration includes a monitoring and remediation period of no less than two years. Other solar energy systems are categorized as roof-mounted or small-scale, with different standards and exemptions, but these soil and erosion controls explicitly apply to large-scale systems as defined.

Large-scale solar energy systems may be permitted upon issuance of a special use permit and site plan approval in the following zoning districts: AG Agricultural, SM-AG Surface Mining-Agricultural, and M-1 General Industrial. Other solar energy systems include roof-mounted solar energy systems, which are permitted as an accessory use in all zoning districts and are exempt from site plan review or special use permit review; and small-scale solar energy systems, which are permitted as accessory structures in AG Agricultural, R-1 Low Density Residential, R-2 Medium-Density Residential, M-1 General Industrial, and SM-AG Surface Mining-Agricultural districts and are also exempt from site plan review or special use permit review.

Large-scale solar energy systems require site plan approval from the Planning Board, including submission of blueprints, equipment specifications, and a soil erosion/drainage plan. Specifically, the solar energy system "shall be adequately screened to mitigate avoid adverse aesthetic impacts" (§ 140-96.1 E(8)). Large-scale solar systems are permitted as a special use upon issuance of a special use permit and site plan approval (§ 140-96.1 D). The special use permit application must include various plans such as operation and maintenance, decommissioning, and construction schedule. Screening and mitigation of adverse aesthetic impacts are explicitly required as part of the site plan approval. Other requirements include fencing, signage, underground utility placement, and surety bonds. The Planning Board may waive certain requirements if deemed unnecessary. The ordinance applies to large-scale solar energy systems in specified zoning districts and excludes smaller or roof-mounted systems from these visual impact assessment requirements.
No solar energy systems shall be located within 100 feet of a freshwater wetland. This setback applies to large-scale solar energy systems as regulated by the ordinance. (Section H(1)(c))

Section 550.1.h requires that "a decommissioning plan shall be submitted as part of the application" for large scale solar energy systems, specifying that "after the large scale solar energy system can no longer be used, it shall be removed and disposed of by the applicant or any subsequent owner in a lawful and environmentally proper manner." The plan must include removal of all infrastructure and remediation of soil and vegetation to return the parcel to its original state, along with an expected timeline and a cost estimate prepared by a professional engineer or contractor. Section 550.1.i states that "the applicant may be required to provide financial sureties" including a bond "in an amount determined by the Town Board to cover the expense of removal of the system and remediation of the landscape." The bond must be 110% of the removal and restoration cost and updated periodically. Section 560 details abandonment and removal, stating that if a system "ceases to perform its originally intended function for more than twelve (12) consecutive months," the property owner must remove it within 90 days. Failure to comply results in enforcement action, and the Town may remove the system and impose a lien if not decommissioned, to the extent not covered by any surety/bond under Section 550.1.i.
section: Section 550. Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems and Section 560. Abandonment and Removal

summary: All large scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing with a self-locking gate to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs with the owner’s contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing. The fencing and the system may be required to be screened by landscaping as needed to avoid adverse aesthetic impacts. This is found in Section 550.2.c. Other requirements for large scale solar energy systems include lot size minimums, setbacks, signage, lighting, access roads, tree-cutting minimization, vegetation maintenance, and prime farmland considerations as detailed in Section 550.

Section 530.5 states: 'All solar collectors and related equipment shall be surfaced, designed and sited to minimize glare on adjacent properties and roadways.' This applies to all solar energy systems, including Large Scale Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems 'intended to supply energy principally into a utility grid for the purpose of off-site sale or consumption' or those with 'a total ground surface area of greater than 10,000 square feet.' Additional design requirements for Large Scale Solar Energy Systems are found in Section 550, but glare restrictions are specifically detailed in Section 530.5. Other relevant provisions include anti-reflective coatings on all solar panels (Section 530.4) and design standards to minimize sight obstructions and light migration (Section 530.6).

Large scale solar energy systems shall be located on lots with a minimum size of 10 acres. This is explicitly stated in Section 550, subsection 2(a): 'Lot Size. Large scale solar energy systems shall be located on lots with a minimum size of 10 acres.' The unit 'acres' is used as the standard area measurement. No other minimum lot size values for large scale solar energy systems are provided in the text.

Section 230 states: 'Solar Energy System, Large Scale               N            S            S               S' where 'N = Not allowed in this district.' This means Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems are unconditionally prohibited in the A District. In contrast, they require special use review ('S') in B, C, and D Districts. Other relevant provisions include Section 360 which prohibits 'Large battery energy storage systems' in the Water Supply Protection Overlay Zone but does not prohibit large-scale solar energy systems. Section 550 outlines review and design requirements for Large-Scale Solar Energy Systems but does not prohibit them in any district other than as noted in Section 230.

All large scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing with a self-locking gate to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs with the owner’s contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing. The fencing and the system may be required to be screened by landscaping as needed to avoid adverse aesthetic impacts.

Large scale solar energy systems shall be enclosed by fencing with a self-locking gate to prevent unauthorized access. Warning signs with the owner’s contact information shall be placed on the entrance and perimeter of the fencing. Signage shall include and be limited to: the manufacturer’s name, equipment specific information, safety information, and 24-hour emergency contact information within an area no more than eight square feet; disconnect and other emergency shutoff information shall be clearly displayed on a light reflective surface; a clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations.

Section 230 states: 'Solar Energy System, Large Scale               N            S            S               S' where 'S = Zoning permit required following special use review by the Town Board.' This means large-scale solar energy systems are not allowed in A District, but require special use approval in B, C, and D Districts. Small scale solar energy systems require a zoning permit (P) in all districts. Section 550 further details that 'Compliance with this plan shall be made a condition of the issuance of special use permit approval under this Section,' confirming the special use permit process for large-scale solar energy systems.

Section 550.1.g states: 'The Town Board may require that photo simulations included showing the proposed large scale solar energy system in relation to the site along with elevation views and dimensions, and manufacturer’s specifications and photos of the proposed Large scale solar energy system, solar collectors, and all other components. The Town Board may require photo simulations to be provided from specific roads or other public areas that may be impacted.' This is a visual impact assessment requirement for Large Scale Solar Energy Systems, defined as systems intended to supply energy principally into a utility grid for off-site sale or with a total ground surface area greater than 10,000 square feet. Other review requirements for large scale solar energy systems include financial deposits, legal consent if leased, professional engineer-signed plans, equipment specifications, operation and maintenance plans, wildlife identification, decommissioning plans, and sureties/bonds for removal costs, but these do not explicitly address visual impact assessment. The ordinance distinguishes Large Scale Solar Energy Systems from Small Scale Solar Energy Systems, which have separate design and siting requirements.

The ordinance explicitly requires a decommissioning plan for Commercial Solar Energy Systems as part of the application, which must "ensure that the site of the Commercial Solar Energy System will be restored to a natural, useful, non-hazardous condition (preferably the site’s original condition prior to construction) including removal of all above-and below-ground equipment, structures and foundations; disposal of all solid and hazardous waste; restoration of the surface grade and soil after removal of equipment, and re-vegetation of restored soil areas with any landscaping and grading approved under the decommissioning plan; and the plan shall include a timeframe for the completion of the site restoration work." The plan must be implemented upon abandonment and/or removal of the facility, with a permit required for removal activities. The ordinance defines abandonment conditions and requires removal and restoration within 180 days, including removal of all infrastructure, proper disposal of waste, restoration of soil and re-vegetation. The Town may remove the system and restore the site at the owner's expense if the owner fails to comply. Financial sureties are required in the form of security deposits and bonds to cover removal and restoration costs, with amounts determined by the Town Board in consultation with engineers. The bond must be at least the cost estimate prepared by a licensed professional and include an annual escalator. The bonding company becomes responsible if the owner fails to decommission. These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Energy Systems permitted up to a maximum coverage of twenty (20) acres per parcel.

The ordinance explicitly requires that the Site Plan for a Commercial Solar Energy System "shall include fencing of not less than seven feet (7 ft) in height, as currently set forth in the version of the National Electric Code that is current as of the date of application." This fencing requirement applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems permitted in Rural Development/ Agricultural/ Residential/ Hamlet Districts, which require a Special Use Permit and Site Plan review. The maximum coverage of a Commercial Solar Energy System on a parcel is twenty (20) acres, with specific coverage percentages depending on parcel size. Other requirements include setbacks, height limits, noise restrictions, signage, surveillance, and decommissioning plans, but fencing is specifically mandated as described.

Section 8, Subsection 2(D) states: 'All Solar Collectors shall be installed so as to prevent any glare and heat that is perceptible beyond subject property’s lot lines as determined by a glare study conducted prior to submission of the applications and documented as part of the application.' This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are permitted in Rural Development/ Agricultural/ Residential/ Hamlet Districts and require a Special Use Permit and Site Plan review. Other relevant conditions include minimum setbacks of 100 feet from lot lines, maximum height of 12 feet for Solar Collectors, and maximum coverage of 20 acres depending on parcel size.

Section 8, Subsection 2(E) states: 'All Solar Collectors shall have a maximum height of twelve feet (12 ft) from ground elevation. Any applicant wishing to have a Solar Collector with a greater height must first petition for and secure a Variance from the Zoning Board of Appeals.' This applies directly to Commercial Solar Energy Systems. Other height-related provisions include that all buildings and accessory structures, other than the actual Solar Collector, must comply with height limitations in the Zoning Law, but no specific numerical values are given for those. The units are explicitly given as feet.

A Commercial Solar Energy System shall only cover a particular parcel with a maximum coverage of twenty (20) acres. For lots consisting of three (3) acres to ten (10) acres, the maximum total coverage shall be one-third (33 1/3%) of the entire parcel; for lots consisting of ten (10) acres to twenty (20) acres, the maximum total coverage shall be two-fifths (40%) of the entire parcel; for lots consisting of twenty (20) acres to thirty (30) acres, the maximum total coverage shall be one half (50%) of the entire parcel; and for any parcel thirty (30) acres and more, the maximum total coverage shall be twenty (20) acres. The units for these maximum lot sizes are expressed in acres.

The ordinance states: 'A Commercial Solar Energy System, inclusive of buildings and accessory structures, shall only cover a particular parcel as set forth herein, with a maximum coverage of a parcel being twenty (20) acres: For lots consisting of three (3) acres to ten (10) acres, the maximum total coverage shall be one-third (33 1/3%) of the entire parcel; For lots consisting of ten (10) acres to twenty (20) acres, the maximum total coverage shall be two-fifths (40%) of the entire parcel; For lots consisting of twenty (20) acres to thirty (30) acres, the maximum total coverage shall be one half (50%) of the entire parcel; and For any parcel thirty (30) acres and more, the maximum total coverage shall be twenty (20) acres.' The minimum lot size is thus explicitly given as 3 acres, with units in acres.

All Solar Collectors shall be installed at least one hundred feet (100ft) from any lot line, and must be located in compliance with DEC and Federal Flood Plain regulations and specifications as they pertain to waterways, waterbodies, and designated wetlands. All buildings and accessory structures associated with Commercial Solar Energy Systems shall be a minimum of one hundred feet (100 ft) from any lot line. (Section 8, Subsection 2, items C and H). Other coverage limits include maximum parcel coverage of twenty (20) acres with percentage limits based on parcel size.

Section 8, Subsection 3(A)(iv) requires "Proposed landscaping, screening, and/or earth berming to minimize the potential visual impacts associated with the Commercial Solar Energy System and its accessory buildings, structures, and/or equipment." If deemed inadequate by the Planning Board, "additional landscaping, screening and/or earth berming may be required to mitigate visual and aesthetic impacts." The landscaping plan must be supervised by the Building Inspector/Code Enforcement Officer and supported by the Town Engineer. Additionally, "Any associated structure shall be screened, placed underground, depressed, earth bermed, or sited below the ridgeline to the greatest extent feasible, particularly in areas of high visibility." Where feasible, "all utilities serving the site shall be underground." These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Energy Systems permitted in Rural Development/Agricultural/Residential/Hamlet Districts with a maximum coverage of twenty (20) acres per parcel.

Each Commercial Solar Energy System shall have signage clearly readable from outside the site carrying emergency phone numbers and other useful contact information (Section 8, Subsection 2(L)). All signage pertaining to the Commercial Solar Energy System shall be indicated on the Site Plan and shall be in conformance with the sign requirements in the Zoning Law (Section 8, Subsection 3(A)(i)). Within five (5) days of filing an application for a Commercial Solar Energy System, the Applicant shall post a sign on the lot that is the subject of the application. The sign shall satisfy local zoning requirements and the following criteria: it should be visible to the public, located not less than fifteen feet (15 ft) and not more than thirty feet (30 ft) from the edge of pavement of the nearest road providing access to the property (with discretion for other locations), be in a standard format, color, font and style determined by the Building Inspector, and state that an application has been filed, provide the telephone number of the Building Department/Code Enforcement Office, and the Town website for further information. The sign shall remain installed until all public hearings are completed, with provisions for reinstallation if additional hearings are required (Section 8, Subsection 3(E)).

Section 8 states: 'Commercial Solar Energy Systems are permitted in Rural Development/ Agricultural/ Residential/ Hamlet Districts in the Town subject to the conditions set forth in Subsection 2 below.' All Commercial Solar Energy Systems require issuance of Special Use Permit and are subject to Site Plan review approval by the Planning Board as set forth in the Zoning Law. A Building Permit shall be required for installation of all Commercial Solar Energy Systems, and issued only after a Special Use Permit has first been issued by the Planning Board. Other conditions include setbacks, height limits, coverage limits (up to 20 acres), and compliance with various codes and standards.

All applications for Commercial Solar Energy Systems shall include a professionally prepared Site Plan containing a Visual Environmental Assessment Form (Visual EAF), landscaping plan, and visual assessment report, including appropriate modeling and photography assessing the visibility from key points identified in the Visual EAF, existing tree lines, surrounding topography, and proposed elevation. Proposed landscaping, screening, and/or earth berming to minimize the potential visual impacts associated with the Commercial Solar Energy System and its accessory buildings, structures, and/or equipment must be included. If deemed inadequate by the Planning Board, additional landscaping, screening and/or earth berming may be required to mitigate visual and aesthetic impacts. Any associated structure shall be screened, placed underground, depressed, earth bermed, or sited below the ridgeline to the greatest extent feasible, particularly in areas of high visibility. The Site Plan shall also include a lighting plan and other detailed siting considerations. These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Energy Systems permitted in Rural Development/ Agricultural/ Residential/ Hamlet Districts with a maximum coverage of twenty (20) acres per parcel.

A Decommissioning Plan to ensure the proper removal of utility-scale solar energy systems must be submitted as part of the special use permit application. The plan must specify that after the utility-scale solar energy system is no longer in use, it shall be removed by the applicant or any subsequent owner. It must identify the anticipated life of the project, demonstrate how removal of all infrastructure and restoration shall be conducted to return the parcel to its original state prior to construction, include an expected timeline for execution, and a cost estimate for decommissioning prepared by a Professional Engineer or qualified Contractor. Cost estimates shall take inflation into consideration and be revised every five (5) years during operation of the system and include any salvage value. Removal must comply with standards including removal of all structures and foundations, restoration of disturbed ground surfaces, and removal of electrical systems. A bond or other approved security equal to 150% of the construction estimate must be provided to cover removal and restoration costs. These requirements apply specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems, defined as systems designed and intended to supply energy primarily into a utility grid for sale to the general public, and permitted only by Special Permit and Site Plan approval in specified districts. Other solar energy systems such as rooftop-mounted, building-mounted, and ground-mounted systems have different permitting and size limitations but do not have these decommissioning requirements explicitly stated.

Under the Special permit criteria for utility-scale solar energy systems, "Any site containing a utility-scale solar energy system shall contain fencing or other device acceptable to the Town enclosing all solar energy system components that prevent safety hazards." Other related requirements include setbacks, height limits, screening, and security bonds, but the explicit fencing requirement is stated in criterion N.

The ordinance explicitly restricts glare for utility-scale solar energy systems by requiring that "The design, construction, operation, and maintenance of a utility-scale solar energy system shall prevent the misdirection and/or reflection of solar rays onto neighboring properties, public roads, and public parks in excess of that which already exists." This is found under the special permit criteria for utility-scale solar energy systems. Other relevant conditions for utility-scale systems include setbacks, maximum height (not to exceed twenty (20) feet at maximum tilt), location restrictions, and requirements for non-reflective structures. Utility-scale solar energy systems are defined as those "designed and intended to supply energy primarily into a utility grid for sale to the general public" and are permitted only by Special Permit and Site Plan approval in specified districts.

The height of a utility-scale solar energy system shall not exceed twenty (20) feet when oriented at maximum tilt. This is specified in the special permit criteria section. Other height limits mentioned in the text apply only to smaller or non-utility-scale systems, such as ground-mounted solar energy systems not classified as utility grade, which have height limits of twelve (12) feet in certain residential districts and fifteen (15) feet in agricultural, commercial, and industrial districts. The unit for the maximum height is feet.

The minimum lot area for utility-scale solar energy systems is explicitly stated as two (2) acres in the special permit criteria section: 'Minimum lot area: The minimum lot area shall be two (2) acres.' This applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems defined as those designed primarily to supply energy into a utility grid for sale to the general public. Other lot size conditions mentioned in the text apply to smaller or non-utility-scale systems and are not relevant here.

Any utility-scale solar energy system shall adhere to the following setbacks: (1) From any residential (R-W, R-1, R2 or R-3), business (RNB, R-C, or C-1), or Planned Unit Development (PUD) use district: A minimum one hundred (100) feet from all property lot lines bordering these use districts (and any screening that is required). (2) From any industrial (M-1, M-2) use district: A minimum of fifty (50) feet from all property lines bordering an industrial (M-1, M-2) use district. (3) From any property lot lines: A minimum of fifty (50) feet from any property lot line, plus appropriate screening.

Any utility-scale solar energy system shall adhere to the following setbacks: From public roads: (a) A minimum of one hundred (100) feet from any public road (measured from the road right-of-way or property line); and, (b) Where the lot line abuts a public right-of-way, the setbacks specified above shall be measured from such right-of-way line. Other setback options include: (1) 100 feet from all property lot lines bordering residential, business, or Planned Unit Development use districts; (2) 50 feet from all property lines bordering industrial use districts; (3) 50 feet from any property lot line plus appropriate screening; (4) 250 feet from any inhabited building or structure except those on the project lot.

The ordinance explicitly requires screening for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Under the Special permit criteria, subsection O states: 'A berm, landscape screen, or other opaque enclosure, or any combination thereof acceptable to the Town capable of screening the site may be required along any property line that abuts an existing residence.' Additionally, the special permit application must include 'Proposed fencing and/or screening for said project.' These are the explicit vegetative buffer and/or screening requirements for utility-scale solar energy systems.

Utility-scale solar energy systems are permitted only by Special Permit and Site Plan approval in certain districts (§ 200-XX Applicability D and § 200-XX General regulations D). Regarding signage, the ordinance states: 'Any signage used to advertise the solar energy facility shall be in accordance with the Town’s signage regulations' (§ 200-XX Special permit criteria M). Other requirements for utility-scale systems include setbacks, height limits, fencing, lighting, and compliance with all applicable laws. Signage requirements are explicitly limited to compliance with the Town’s general signage regulations.

Before the Town of Wheatfield shall issue a clearing, grading, storm water or building permit for a utility-scale solar energy system, the applicant shall submit a storm water and Erosion Control Plan to the Town of Wheatfield for its review and approval; and the Plan shall minimize the potential adverse impacts on wetlands and Class I and II streams and the banks and vegetation along those streams and wetlands and minimize erosion or sedimentation. This is found under the special permit criteria for utility-scale solar energy systems. Other requirements for utility-scale solar energy systems include special permit and site plan approval, SEQRA review, submission of detailed site plans including clearing and grading, a decommissioning plan with restoration of disturbed ground surfaces including topsoil and seeding, and bonding to cover removal and restoration costs.

Utility-scale solar energy systems are only permitted in an Agricultural-Residential District (A-R), Rural Residential District (R-R) or all Industrial districts (M-1, M-2) by Special Permit and Site Plan approval (§ 200-XX Applicability D). The systems require a Special Permit by the Town of Wheatfield Planning Board, SEQRA review, concurrent site plan approval, and issuance of a building permit (§ 200-XX General regulations D). Other solar energy systems such as rooftop-mounted and building-mounted systems are permitted in all districts by building permit, and ground-mounted systems are permitted as accessory structures with size limitations and site plan approval in various districts (§ 200-XX Applicability A-C).

Any utility-scale solar energy system shall adhere to the following setbacks: From buildings or structures: (a) A minimum of two hundred and fifty (250) feet from any inhabited building or structure, except for buildings and structures located on the proposed project lot. Other setback options include: (1) From any residential (R-W, R-1, R2 or R-3), business (RNB, R-C, or C-1), or Planned Unit Development (PUD) use district: A minimum one hundred (100) feet from all property lot lines bordering these use districts; (2) From any industrial (M-1, M-2) use district: A minimum of fifty (50) feet from all property lines bordering an industrial use district; (3) From any property lot lines: A minimum of fifty (50) feet from any property lot line, plus appropriate screening; (5) From public roads: A minimum of one hundred (100) feet from any public road. However, only the 250 feet setback from inhabited buildings or structures directly relates to occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, and/or residences for utility-scale solar energy systems.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Tier 4 Solar Energy Systems (less than 25 MW). Tier 4 systems require a special use permit and are subject to the special Tier 3 permit application requirements, including submission of a Decommissioning Plan [see Appendix 4] signed by the owner and/or operator. Upon cessation of electricity generation for 6 months, the Town may notify and instruct the owner/operator to implement the decommissioning plan, which must be completed within 12 months. Failure to comply allows the Town to utilize the bond and/or security for removal and site restoration. Appendix 4 details the decommissioning plan, including conditions triggering decommissioning, removal and restoration requirements, timelines, cost estimates, and security requirements. The decommissioning security shall be 115% of the cost of removal and site restoration and updated every 3 years. Tier 4 Solar Energy Systems located on Active Agricultural Lands shall be decommissioned in accordance with the NYS Department of Agriculture and Markets’  "Guidelines for Solar Energy Projects - Construction Mitigation for Agricultural Lands."

The ordinance requires that applications for Solar Energy Systems include "Information indicating that the glare factor of the installation meets current industry standards used to minimize glare" (Section 1.4.2.3) and that "Reasonable measures to minimize glare as viewed from adjacent properties and roads shall be taken" (Section 1.4.2.8). For Tier 4 Solar Energy Systems specifically, under Special Use Permit Standards, "All Solar Panels shall have anti-reflective coating(s)" (Section 1.8.D.4). These glare restrictions apply to Tier 4 Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as "Solar Energy Systems which are not included under Tier 1, Tier 2, or Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems but which are less than 25 megawatts (MW)" (Section 1.2.27.D). Other tiers have similar or related glare provisions, such as Tier 1 and Tier 3 also requiring anti-reflective coatings on solar panels.
section: 1.4 General Regulations and 1.8 Planning Board Requirements for Tier 4 Solar Energy Systems

summary: Appendix 3, Table 3.1: Height Requirements states that for Tier 3 & 4 Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Systems, the maximum height is 20 feet for Commercial / Business, Industrial, and Agricultural parcels. Residential parcels are marked as '—' (Not Allowed) for Tier 3 & 4 Ground-Mounted systems. The height of systems will be measured from the highest natural grade below each Solar Panel.

The minimum lot size requirements for Tier 4 Solar Energy Systems are specified in Appendix 1, Table 1.1: Lot Size Requirements. The smallest minimum lot size allowed is 2 acres for Residential parcels. Other minimum lot sizes include 5 acres for Commercial/Business parcels and 10 acres for Agricultural parcels. Industrial parcels are marked as Not Applicable (N/A). The units for these minimum lot sizes are expressed in acres.

Appendix 2, Table 2.2 states for Tier 4 Solar Energy Systems: Residential —: Not Allowed. Appendix 3, Table 3.1 also shows Residential Tier 3 & 4 Ground-Mounted systems as —: Not Allowed. Other districts such as Commercial / Business, Industrial, and Agricultural have specific setback and lot size requirements but are not unconditionally prohibited. For example, Commercial / Business, Industrial, and Agricultural require 50' setbacks and minimum lot sizes (≥ 5 acres for Commercial / Business, N/A for Industrial, and ≥ 10 acres for Agricultural).

Appendix 2, Table 2.2 specifies that Tier 4 Solar Energy Systems shall meet all applicable parcel line and other setback requirements, including a setback of 250 feet from Non-Participating Occupied Residences for Commercial / Business, Industrial, and Agricultural parcels. Residential parcels do not allow Tier 4 systems (indicated by '—'). Fencing, collection lines, access roads and landscaping may occur within the setback.

Section 1.8 states that "All Tier 4 Solar Energy Systems are permitted through the issuance of a Whitehall Solar Tier 4 Special Use Permit" and are "subject to the Special Tier 3 permit application requirements established for Tier 3 Solar Energy Systems in Section 1.9, in addition to (or in some cases amended by) the following requirements." Section 1.7.C.12 (Special Tier 3 Permit Standards) requires that "Solar Energy Systems smaller than 10 acres shall have views minimized from adjacent properties to the extent reasonably practicable using architectural features, earth berms, landscaping, or other screening methods that will harmonize with the character of the property and surrounding area." For systems larger than 10 acres, applicants must "submit a screening & landscaping plan to show adequate measures to screen through landscaping, grading, or other means so that views of Solar Panels and Solar Energy Equipment shall be minimized as reasonably practical from public roadways and adjacent properties." Removal includes "removal of all apparatuses, supports, and or other hardware" and "returning the property to a graded, seeded and/or landscaped state similar to its condition prior to the construction/installation." The application process requires "a maintenance schedule as well as a dismantling plan that outlines how the Solar Energy System including all equipment and components thereof will be dismantled at the end of their use and/or upon abandonment." summary: Small solar (self-generation) is defined as solar panels and associated facilities with a single interconnection to the electrical grid and designed for, or capable of, operations at an aggregate capacity of less than 50 megawatts, and that produces electricity exclusively for consumption on the property on which it is generated. Solar panels are permitted without a zoning permit provided they are attached to the roof of a building, do not exceed 120% of the average yearly personal or property use, and do not exceed the maximum height permitted in the applicable zoning district. Ground-mounted solar panels are permitted with a zoning permit provided they do not exceed the total square footage of roof area existing on permitted buildings on the parcel and/or do not exceed 120% of the average yearly personal or property use, and do not exceed the maximum height permitted in the applicable zoning district.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "All ground-mounted solar collector/panel/module systems shall be installed so there is minimum glare, optimally no glare, onto/into adjacent properties or towards the road right-of-way." Utility Scale Renewable Energy Generation Facilities are defined as "an energy generation facility or area of land principally used to convert solar and/or wind energy to electricity for resale at a profit" with a capacity of 0.1 MW to 49.99 MW. These facilities are "not permitted in the Township in any District." Other options include Private Use Renewable Energy Generation Facilities (max. 125% of use) permitted in all districts, Community Solar and/or Wind Facilities (under 50 MW) which are also not permitted, and roof and ground mounted solar collector systems permitted in all Residential, Agricultural, Commercial, and Industrial Zoning Districts. The glare restriction applies generally to ground-mounted solar collector systems and thus applies to utility scale facilities if permitted.

Utility Scale Renewable Energy Generation Facility — (under 50 megawatts) Are not permitted in the Township in any District. Such a facility is not permitted in any District in Taylor Creek Township. (Section C, item 3 and Section G). The ordinance applies universally across all districts without exception or specific district names/abbreviations given. Other solar energy systems such as Roof and Ground Mounted Solar Collector Systems and Private Use Renewable Energy Generation Facilities are permitted in all Residential, Agricultural, Commercial, and Industrial Zoning Districts, subject to various requirements and limitations.
section: SECTION C - PERMITTED USE and SECTION G - REGULATIONS FOR UTILITY SCALE RENEWABLE ENERGY GENERATION FACILITY, COMMUNITY SOLAR FACILITY

summary: In Agriculture, Commercial, and Industrial Zoned Districts, a ground-mounted solar collector system shall have a minimum set back distance of one-thousand (1000) feet from all property lines. Other setback distances mentioned include forty (40) feet from side and rear property lines in Residential Zoned Districts, but the 1000 feet applies to Utility Scale Renewable Energy Generation Facilities in the relevant zones. The ordinance states: 'In Agriculture, Commercial, and Industrial Zoned Districts, a ground-mounted solar collector system shall have a minimum set back distance of one-thousand (1000) feet from all property lines.'
section: SECTION F - REGULATIONS FOR ROOF MOUNTED & GROUND MOUNTED SOLAR COLLECTOR SYSTEMS

summary: The ordinance explicitly states that a Utility Scale Renewable Energy Generation Facility (0.1 MW to under 50 MW) "Are not permitted in the Township in any District." (SECTION C - PERMITTED USE, item 3 and SECTION G). No districts are listed where such facilities are allowed as a special use or with conditional approval. Other solar energy systems such as Roof and Ground Mounted Solar Collector Systems and Private Use Renewable Energy Generation Facilities are permitted in all Residential, Agricultural, Commercial, and Industrial Zoning Districts, subject to permitting requirements. However, utility scale facilities designed to commercially provide electricity to the electric utility grid are prohibited outright. Community Solar and/or Wind Facilities under 50 MW are also not permitted in any district. The ordinance requires zoning permits and site plans for smaller solar systems but does not provide any allowance for utility scale systems.

summary: Section (e)(6) states: 'If the solar energy system is not completed within the stated time period, the facility owner or operator or the landowner shall be required, at his or their expense, to complete decommissioning of the site within 180 days without exception.' Section (g) details abandonment requirements: '(1) At such a time a solar energy system is scheduled to be abandoned or operation is to be discontinued, the applicant will notify the Building Official and Planning Department of the proposed date of abandonment or discontinuation of use.' '(2) Upon abandonment or discontinuation of use, the owner shall physically remove the solar energy system within 180 days from the date of abandonment or discontinuation of use. This period may be extended sixty (60) days at the request of the owner but only upon the approval of the Building Official.' '(3) In the event that an applicant fails to give such notice, the system shall be considered abandoned or discontinued if the system is out-of-service for a continuous six-month period.' '(4) If the owner fails to respond to the Notice of Abandonment or if after review by the Building Official it is determined that the solar energy system has been abandoned or use discontinued, the owner of the solar energy system shall remove the system at the owner's sole expense within sixty (60) days of receipt of the Notice of Abandonment.' These requirements apply to solar energy systems including ground-mounted systems permitted by right in Industrial (I) Zones and conditional uses in Business (B) Zones, which would typically include utility-scale solar energy systems.

All related mechanical equipment, other than the actual photoelectric panels, shall be fully buffered from the adjacent properties by fencing and/or by evergreen plantings as prescribed by city ordinance and must be maintained and effective through the life of the system. Buffering shall permit work access to panel and shall conform to Chapter 1131. This applies to ground-mounted solar panels which shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet in height above the adjacent grade. Ground-mounted solar energy systems are permitted by right in Industrial (I) Zones and are conditional uses in residential and Business (B) Zones with specific location and setback requirements.

Ground-mounted solar panels located on the ground or attached to a framework located on the ground shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet in height above the adjacent grade. This applies to ground-mounted solar energy systems, which are permitted by right in Industrial (I) Zones. Roof-mounted solar systems have different height limits (e.g., 18 inches above pitched roofs, 5 feet above flat roofs) but these generally apply to smaller or accessory systems. The 15 feet limit is the most restrictive explicit maximum height for utility-scale solar energy systems. Units are feet as explicitly stated.

Section (e)(10)(B) requires that "All related mechanical equipment, other than the actual photoelectric panels shall be fully buffered from the adjacent properties by fencing and/or by evergreen plantings as prescribed by city ordinance and must be maintained and effective through the life of the system. Buffering shall permit work access to panel and shall conform to Chapter 1131." Ground-mounted solar panels are addressed in (e)(10), with height limits and location rules depending on zoning districts. Ground-mounted solar energy systems are permitted by right in Industrial (I) Zones, conditional in Residential and Business (B) Zones with specific yard restrictions. Screening requirements apply to related mechanical equipment, not explicitly to the panels themselves.

Section (e)(2) 'Appearance and Signage' states: 'The factory or original equipment manufacturer identification and/or logo are permitted. Required signage and emergency services disconnect placard shall be appropriate warning signs (Danger-High Voltage or Caution-Electrical Shock Hazard or any other recognized safety precaution signage) installed at the base of the solar array.' This signage requirement applies generally to solar energy systems, including utility-scale systems. Other related provisions include lighting restrictions, construction and electrical code compliance, and buffering requirements for ground-mounted systems, but these do not explicitly address signage.
