summary: Ground-mounted solar energy systems are conditional uses in Residential (R) and Business (B) zones, requiring "full compliance with this Zoning Code and approval from the Board of Building and Zoning Appeals." Specifically, "No ground installations are permitted by right" in these zones. In contrast, ground-mounted solar energy systems "shall be permitted by right in all Industrial (I) Zones." Roof-mounted solar energy systems are permitted in all zoning districts subject to design review and other requirements. The ordinance states: "Solar energy systems shall be considered a permitted use in any zoning district, subject to the requirements of any other applicable chapter of this Code."

The total coverage of a lot with solar energy collection systems cannot exceed 50% of the lot size for Commercial Distribution Solar Energy Systems. This is explicitly stated in Section 7.33, subsection (f)(6): 'The total coverage of a lot with solar energy collection systems cannot exceed 50% of the lot size.' For comparison, Private Use Solar Energy Systems have a maximum coverage of 25% of the lot size, but this does not apply to commercial systems. The unit is expressed as a percentage of the total lot size.

Section 7.33(g) states: 'Any commercial distribution solar energy system which has reached the end of its useful life, has been abandoned or is in disrepair shall be repaired or removed. The owner or operator has the responsibility to repair or remove the solar energy system within one year of the date it becomes inoperable.' This decommissioning requirement applies specifically to Commercial Distribution Solar Energy Systems. Other options include Section 7.32(f) for Private Use Solar Energy Systems, which has similar language but applies only to private use systems, not commercial distribution systems.
section: Section 7.33 Commercial Alternative Energy Zoning Regulations

summary: Section 7.33(f)(5) states: 'Freestanding solar panels located on the ground or attached to a framework located on the ground shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in height.' Additionally, section 7.33(f)(7) states: 'Roof-mounted solar panels installed on a building or structure with a sloped roof shall not project vertically more than the height requirements for the zoning district in which they are located.' The most restrictive explicit numerical limit is 20 feet for freestanding panels. Units are feet as stated in the text.
section: Section 7.33 Commercial Alternative Energy Zoning Regulations

summary: For Commercial Distribution Solar Energy Systems, the ordinance requires as part of the Site Plan requirements: 'Location size and type of required signage.' This is explicitly stated in Section 7.33, subsection d.(3). Other site plan requirements include property lines, setbacks, utility lines, easements, structures, sewage treatment systems, elevation, tree locations, manufacturer's specifications, scaled drawings, documentation of major system components, and contact information for installers and project proponents. Additionally, commercial systems must comply with safety markings including clearly marked means of shutting down the system, but specific signage details beyond the site plan submission are not provided.
section: Section 7.33 Commercial Alternative Energy Zoning Regulations

summary: Small Solar Facilities shall comply with the 60% maximum lot coverage requirement for non-residential districts. This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for Small Solar Facilities (less than 50 megawatts). Other coverage limits mentioned include Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems, which have maximum sizes of 300 square feet in Residential Districts and 600 square feet in Commercial and Industrial Districts, but these apply to smaller or non-commercial systems and are not the most restrictive for Small Solar Facilities. The 60% coverage is expressed as a percentage of total lot coverage.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Small Solar Facilities (less than 50 megawatts). Under section C.3.h (Maintenance), it states: 'Small Solar Facilities shall be maintained in good working order at all times. The owner of the property and owner of the Small Solar Facilities shall, within thirty (30) days of permanently ceasing operation of a Small Solar Facility, provide written notice of abandonment to the Zoning Inspector. An unused Small Solar Facility may stand no longer than ninety (90) days following abandonment. All costs associated with the dismantling/demolition of the Small Solar Facility and associated equipment shall be the responsibility of the property owner. A Small Solar Facility is considered abandoned when it ceases transmission of electricity for thirty (30) consecutive days. Removal includes removal of all apparatuses, supports, and or other hardware associated with the existing Small Solar Facility. The property shall be returned to a graded, seeded and/or landscaped state similar to its condition prior to construction/installation.' Additionally, section E.2.d requires 'A maintenance schedule as well as a dismantling plan that outlines how the Small Solar Facility including all equipment and components thereof will be dismantled at the end of their use and/or upon abandonment' as part of the certificate of zoning compliance application. Other solar energy system types addressed include Integrated Solar Energy Systems, Rooftop Solar Energy Systems, and Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems, each with their own height, coverage, and maintenance requirements, but the decommissioning requirements specifically apply to Small Solar Facilities as described.

Small Solar Facilities are defined as systems with an aggregate capacity of less than fifty (50) megawatts. They may be permitted as a conditional use on parcels five (5) acres and larger in the M-1 Limited Industrial District. The ordinance includes specific fencing requirements: "Any fencing and/or screening installed in connection with the Small Solar Facility shall be harmonious and compatible with the surrounding properties and uses. Fencing shall be always maintained in good repair." Additional requirements include height limits (maximum ten (10’) feet), visual buffers of natural vegetation, plantings, and/or fencing to reduce view and noise, setbacks from residential dwellings, property lines, and public rights-of-way, underground electrical lines, lighting restrictions, maintenance, abandonment procedures, and compliance with all applicable laws. Other solar energy system types mentioned are Integrated Solar Energy Systems, Rooftop Solar Energy Systems, and Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems, each with their own regulations and conditions.

The ordinance defines a Small Solar Facility as "a Solar Energy System and associated facilities with a single interconnection to the electrical grid and designed for, or capable of, operation at an aggregate capacity of less than fifty (50) megawatts." Small Solar Facilities are permitted as a conditional use on parcels five (5) acres and larger in the M-1 Limited Industrial District. The ordinance includes specific glare restrictions: "Solar panels shall be placed or arranged in a manner so as not to reflect unreasonable glare onto adjacent buildings, properties, or roadways." Other relevant restrictions include height limits ("The maximum height of Small Solar Facilities at any point shall not exceed ten (10’) feet"), visual buffers, lighting requirements, setbacks, and maintenance obligations. The ordinance also covers Integrated Solar Energy Systems, Rooftop Solar Energy Systems, and Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems, each with their own conditions and zoning permissions.

The maximum height of Small Solar Facilities at any point shall not exceed ten (10) feet in height from grade. This is stated explicitly in Section 1925.C.3.a and reiterated in Section 1925.D.b.iv. Other height limits mentioned include 8 feet for Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems and height restrictions for Integrated or Rooftop Solar Energy Systems that must not exceed the maximum height applicable to principal structures in the zoning district or the highest point of the roof to which it is attached. However, for Small Solar Facilities (less than 50 megawatts), the most restrictive maximum height is 10 feet, measured from grade.

A Small Solar Facility is defined as a Solar Energy System and associated facilities with a single interconnection to the electrical grid and designed for, or capable of, operation at an aggregate capacity of less than fifty (50) megawatts. Larger solar facilities of fifty (50) megawatts or more must submit an application with the Ohio Power Siting Board (OPSB) and meet OPSB regulations. The ordinance restricts Small Solar Facilities to parcels five (5) acres and larger in the M-1 Limited Industrial District. The maximum height for Small Solar Facilities is ten (10) feet. The megawatt size and generating capacity in megawatts must be specified in the zoning compliance application. The unit for the maximum project size is megawatts (MW).

Small Solar Facilities may be permitted as a conditional use on parcels five (5) acres and larger in the M-1 Limited Industrial District. Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems are permitted on parcels greater than one (1) acre in size. Both minimum parcel sizes are expressed in acres.

No Small Solar Facility (other than components located entirely underground) shall be located within fifty (50’) feet of any property line. Other setback options include: no part of the Small Solar Facility shall be located within one hundred (100’) feet of an existing residential dwelling when adjacent to or near residentially zoned property, and no part shall be within one hundred (100’) feet of a public right-of-way or shared-use driveway.
section: D. CRITERIA FOR CONDITIONAL USES, b. Where identified as a conditionally permitted use, v. Buffers and Setbacks

summary: No Small Solar Facility (other than components located entirely underground) shall be located within one hundred (100’) feet of a public right-of-way or shared-use driveway. Other setback options include: no part of the Small Solar Facility shall be within fifty (50’) feet of any property line, and if adjacent to residential use, no part shall be within one hundred (100’) feet of an existing residential dwelling.

Small Solar Facilities shall have a visual buffer of natural vegetation, plantings, and/or fencing that provides reasonable visual screening to reduce view of and noise from the Small Solar Facilities on adjacent lots and from any public right-of-way. Small Solar Facilities located on corner lots shall comply with the applicable requirements (including, but not limited to, those for yards, buffering, and screening) for lots in the zoning district where located. The Small Solar Energy System shall not be located in a landscape buffer. Additionally, any fencing and/or screening installed in connection with the Small Solar Facility shall be harmonious and compatible with the surrounding properties and uses and shall be always maintained in good repair. The visual buffer must enhance the view from any existing residential dwelling and from any public right-of-way; be in harmony with the existing vegetation in the area; and provide reasonable visual screening to minimize view of and noise from the Small Solar Facilities to adjacent lots and from any public right-of-way. Other options for solar energy systems include Integrated Solar Energy Systems, Rooftop Solar Energy Systems, and Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems, each with their own specific regulations. Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems also require a visual buffer of natural vegetation, plantings, and/or fencing that provides reasonable visual screening to minimize view of and noise from the Small Solar Facilities on adjacent lots and from any public right-of-way.

Small Solar Facilities and the property where located shall not be used for the display of advertising. For the purposes of this section, reasonable and customary identification (name, insignia, logo, and/or similar) of the manufacturer or operator of the system that is incorporated into or manufactured on the equipment itself shall not be considered advertising. Other options for solar energy systems include Integrated Solar Energy Systems, Rooftop Solar Energy Systems, and Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems, each with their own regulations and conditions.

Where a Small Solar Facility is located on property adjacent to or in close proximity to property zoned for residential use (as determined by the Zoning Inspector), no part of the Small Solar Facility (other than components located entirely underground) shall be located within one hundred (100’) feet of an existing residential dwelling. Other setback requirements include no part of the Small Solar Facility (other than underground components) within fifty (50’) feet of any property line and within one hundred (100’) feet of a public right-of-way or shared-use driveway, but these do not pertain to occupied dwellings.

Small Solar Facilities shall have a visual buffer of natural vegetation, plantings, and/or fencing designed to (1) enhance the view from any existing residential dwelling and from any public right-of-way; (2) be in harmony with the existing vegetation in the area; and (3) provide reasonable visual screening to minimize view of and noise from the Small Solar Facilities to adjacent lots and from any public right-of-way. A site drawing showing the location of the Small Solar Facility including all equipment and components thereof in relation to (and measurements of distances from) all existing structures on the property, roads and other public rights-of-way, and neighboring property lines must be provided when applying for a certificate of zoning compliance. Other options for solar energy systems include Integrated Solar Energy Systems, Rooftop Solar Energy Systems, and Ground Mounted Solar Energy Systems, each with their own height, coverage, and component requirements, but the visual buffer and related visual impact assessment requirements are specifically detailed for Small Solar Facilities as conditional uses in the M-1 Limited Industrial District on parcels five acres and larger.

Freestanding solar or photovoltaic systems "shall not be positioned so as to reflect sunlight onto neighboring property, public streets or sidewalks, including on any neighboring structures." Freestanding systems are conditionally permitted pursuant to Chapter 1153, Conditional Zoning Certificates, in all zoning districts and their maximum height in non-residential districts is determined on a case by case basis. Roof mounted systems must be flush mounted unless good cause is shown, located in the most inconspicuous location on the roof, and not extend higher than the peak of a sloped roof or five feet from a flat roof. The ordinance applies to solar panels or solar collection systems that contribute significantly to a structure's energy supply and includes provisions for systems connected to the local utility power grid through net metering.

Freestanding solar or photovoltaic systems shall not extend more than ten (10) feet above the existing grade in residential districts. In all other districts, the maximum height will be determined on a case by case basis upon plan review under Chapter 1153, Conditional Zoning Certificates. This applies to freestanding systems, which could include utility-scale solar energy systems.

Freestanding solar or photovoltaic systems "be landscaped at the base and the back of the panel structure if structure is visible from neighboring property" (Section (d)(3)(E)). Other requirements include: systems "not extend more than ten (10) feet above the existing grade in residential districts"; "not be located in the front yard"; "not be located in any required side or rear yard setback areas for accessory uses"; and "not be positioned so as to reflect sunlight onto neighboring property, public streets or sidewalks, including on any neighboring structures." Freestanding systems are subject to conditional use review pursuant to Chapter 1153. Roof-mounted systems have separate mounting and height restrictions.

Freestanding solar panels or solar collectors, which would typically include utility-scale solar energy systems, "shall be considered an accessory structure and shall be subject to the requirements for such, together with all other applicable building codes and ordinances, through a conditional use review process." Additionally, "Solar panels or solar collection systems which are freestanding, mounted on poles or other structures excluding the roof of a building, shall be conditionally permitted pursuant to Chapter 1153, Conditional Zoning Certificates, in all zoning districts." Structurally attached solar panels are permitted as accessory uses with administrative approval, and roof-mounted panels are permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts without conditional use review.

If the Small Solar Energy Farm is no longer being operated or utilized (unless due to documented maintenance or electrical grid issues and written notice has been provided to the township), the Small Solar Energy Farm shall be removed within 180 days after the Use has been discontinued. The Owner/operator shall remove all towers within the system, all transmission equipment, buildings and fences, and restore the site to its original condition prior to the location of such system on said property.

In no case shall any solar panel within a Small Solar Energy Farm be located closer than 250 feet from any public right-of-way, any adjacent property line that abuts an existing one- or two-unit residential structure, or any zoning district that permits one or two unit residential structures. New residential structures shall not be permitted within this setback area.

In no case shall any solar panel within a Small Solar Energy Farm be located closer than 250 feet from any public right-of-way. Other setback conditions include adjacent property lines abutting residential structures or zoning districts permitting one or two unit residential structures, but the 250 feet applies specifically to public rights-of-way (roads).
section: Section 26.03 Solar Energy Systems, B. Small Solar Energy Farm

summary: No signage shall be permitted within any portion of a Small Solar Energy Farm except for a Sign, not to exceed six (6) square feet, containing emergency contact information and no trespassing language. Other conditions for Small Solar Energy Farms include setbacks of at least 250 feet from public rights-of-way and certain residential properties, compliance with ANSI and UL standards, certification by a Licensed Ohio Professional Engineer, conformance to electrical codes, one point of access from a public road, noise level restrictions, no lighting except as required by Federal regulations, annual operation notice submission, and site restoration upon discontinuation.

For Small Solar Energy Farms, 'In no case shall any solar panel within a Small Solar Energy Farm be located closer than 250 feet from any adjacent property line that abuts an existing one- or two-unit residential structure, or any zoning district that permits one or two unit residential structures. New residential structures shall not be permitted within this setback area.' This setback is measured from adjacent property lines abutting residential structures or zoning districts permitting such residences, not directly from the structures themselves.

The ground mounted solar energy system(s) shall not exceed in the aggregate 25% of the total area of the lot or tract if the zoning district does not have a restriction limiting the ground area permitted to be occupied by buildings, structures, parking areas, sidewalks, or other impervious surfaces. This is the maximum land coverage allowed for large solar facilities as defined (50 MW or more). The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the total lot or tract area.

Section (e)(2)(D) states: 'Any solar energy system shall be placed or arranged in a manner so as not to reflect unreasonable glare onto adjacent buildings, properties, or roadways.' The ordinance defines 'large solar facility' as a solar facility of 50 or more megawatts required to submit an application with the Ohio Power Siting Board (OPSB). The glare restriction applies to all solar energy systems, including large solar facilities. Other relevant conditions include height limits, coverage, location, setbacks, and maintenance requirements for solar energy systems as detailed in section (e).

The ordinance defines a 'Large solar facility' as a solar facility of 50 or more megawatts which is required to submit an application with the Ohio Power Siting Board (OPSB). It also defines a 'Small solar facility' as a solar energy system designed for, or capable of, operation at an aggregate capacity of less than 50 megawatts. The ordinance prohibits the use of solar energy systems for commercial generation of power for sale or use off the property, except for incidental excess power sold to the power company, effectively restricting large solar facilities (50 MW or more) from being constructed or sited in the city. The units for the size threshold are explicitly stated as megawatts.

The ordinance states that the construction, erection, or siting of any solar energy system, including any large solar facility, that does not meet the requirements to be a permitted use as defined in division (b) is prohibited in all zoning districts in the city. Permitted solar energy systems are allowed in all zoning districts except residential districts only if the system is sized and used to provide electric power solely for uses on the property and not for commercial generation or offsite sale, except for occasional incidental excess power sold to the power company. Off-premises connections may be permitted under specific conditions including common ownership and city approval. Therefore, large solar facilities intended for commercial generation or offsite sale/use are unconditionally prohibited citywide, across all zoning districts without exception or specific district names given.

Section (16) requires that "Solar energy systems and all solar energy equipment that are no longer functioning shall be completely removed from the property within six (6) months from the date they are no longer producing electricity, become damaged, discontinued or broken." Additionally, "Any earth disturbance as a result of the removal of the ground mounted solar energy system shall be graded and reseeded within thirty (30) days of removal." This decommissioning requirement applies explicitly to Principal Solar Energy Production Facilities. Other relevant provisions include a required "end-of-life decommissioning plan" as part of the application materials in (19)(j), but the specific removal and site restoration requirements are detailed in (16).

All mechanical equipment of solar energy systems including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum seven (7) foot high fence with a self-locking gate. Screening shall be established in accordance with the provisions of the Warren County Rural Zoning Code and may be supplemented by fencing or walls, but shall not be the primary method. Fencing shall incorporate gaps or spaces of at least six (6) inches by six (6) inches to allow passage of small mammals.

All principal solar energy production facilities shall meet the following requirements: Solar energy systems shall be designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare towards any inhabited building on adjacent properties as well as adjacent street right-of-way. Applicants must complete and provide the results of the Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT), or an equivalent report, for neighboring lots and right-of-way.

For Principal Solar Energy Production Facility, roof mounted systems shall not exceed 10 feet above roof height. Other height limits include ground/pole mounted systems no taller than 15 feet, and building mounted/other structure mounted/integrated systems no taller than the primary mounting structure, except parking lot solar canopies which shall be no taller than 35 feet. Units are feet.

The proposed principal solar energy production facility must be located on a lot of at least twelve (12) acres in size. This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for Principal Solar Energy Production Facility. The unit is acres, a standard measure of land area. No other minimum lot size values are provided for this category.

Setback requirements for solar energy equipment not housed in a building shall be: (a) Non-Participating Parcels: 1. One-hundred and fifty (150) feet from lot lines. Other options include: 2. Three-hundred (300) feet from any dwelling (not applicable as dwellings are not equivalent to property lines). 3. One-hundred and fifty (150) feet from the edge of any adjacent road right-of way (excluded per instructions). For Participating Parcels, setbacks for all other buildings and structures comply with the applicable zoning setback standards.

Buffering shall be established in accordance with the provisions of the Warren County Rural Zoning Code. In addition to any other buffering requirements of the Warren County Rural Zoning Code, the following standards shall apply: (a) A one-hundred and twenty (120) foot setback along stream boundaries (including ephemeral and intermittent streams). (b) A one-hundred and twenty (120) foot setback from Category 1 and 2 wetland boundaries. (c) A three-hundred (300) foot setback from Category 3 wetland boundaries. (Note: a, b, and c above are all subject to an environmental assessment by Warren County Soil and Water.)

Setback requirements for solar energy equipment not housed in a building shall be: Non-Participating Parcels: 3. One-hundred and fifty (150) feet from the edge of any adjacent road right-of way. Other related provisions include screening from ground-level view from any adjacent road right-of-way, prevention of reflective glare towards adjacent street right-of-way, and requirements for a Road Use Maintenance Agreement to protect roadways and rights-of-way used in connection with the Principal Solar Energy Production Facility.
section: 3.102.10 Solar: (B) Principal Solar Energy Production Facility

summary: All principal solar energy production facilities shall meet the following requirements: Screening shall be established in accordance with the provisions of the Warren County Rural Zoning Code, be maintained in good condition, and free of all advertising or other signs. Screening shall consist of vegetation, mounding, natural landforms, or any combination thereof. Screening may be supplemented by fencing or walls, but shall not be the primary method. Fencing shall incorporate gaps or spaces of at least six (6) inches by six (6) inches to allow passage of small mammals. Screening shall be a minimum of six (6) feet in height. Mounding shall be seeded and planted with trees. The base of the mound shall not be graded at an angle greater than forty-five degrees (45°). Screening shall be clustered around groups of solar energy equipment and buildings and not the entirety of the lot to allow for  "wildlife corridors"  where wildlife can traverse the lot. Buffering shall be established in accordance with the provisions of the Warren County Rural Zoning Code. In addition to any other buffering requirements of the Warren County Rural Zoning Code, the following standards shall apply: (a) A one-hundred and twenty (120) foot setback along stream boundaries (including ephemeral and intermittent streams). (b) A one-hundred and twenty (120) foot setback from Category 1 and 2 wetland boundaries. (c) A three-hundred (300) foot setback from Category 3 wetland boundaries. (Note: a, b, and c above are all subject to an environmental assessment by Warren County Soil and Water.)

The ordinance requires that new access drives within the Principal Solar Energy Production Facility "shall be designed to minimize the extent of soil disturbance, water runoff, and soil compaction on the premises." It permits "the use of geotextile fabrics and gravel placed on the surface of the existing soil for temporary roadways during construction," provided they are removed once the facility is in operation. Areas not devoted to active use "shall be landscaped with vegetation in such a manner as to prevent soil erosion by wind or rain or the spreading of invasive species and noxious weeds," following "the standards set forth in the Ohio Department of Natural Resources (ODNR) Guidance for Proposed Solar Energy Facilities in Ohio." Upon removal of non-functioning ground-mounted solar energy systems, "any earth disturbance as a result of the removal... shall be graded and reseeded within thirty (30) days of removal." The application must include "a drainage plan, including any methods of stormwater management," and proof of notice and/or compliance with "County-level stormwater and sediment control regulations."

Setback requirements for solar energy equipment not housed in a building shall be: (a) Non-Participating Parcels: 2. Three-hundred (300) feet from any dwelling. Other options include: 1. One-hundred and fifty (150) feet from lot lines; 3. One-hundred and fifty (150) feet from the edge of any adjacent road right-of way. For Participating Parcels, setbacks for all other buildings and structures comply with the applicable zoning setback standards.

All principal solar energy production facilities shall meet the following requirements: Screening shall be established in accordance with the provisions of the Warren County Rural Zoning Code, be maintained in good condition, and free of all advertising or other signs. Screening shall consist of vegetation, mounding, natural landforms, or any combination thereof, supplemented by fencing or walls but not primarily fencing. Screening shall be a minimum of six (6) feet in height and clustered around groups of solar energy equipment and buildings to allow for wildlife corridors. Other categories include Accessory Uses, Small-Scale Solar Power Generation Facilities (non-commercial, up to 150% of expected annual energy need), and Commercial Solar Power Generation Facilities (power used on the same parcel or tract). Utility-Scale facilities require a Conditional Use Permit and compliance with Type III procedures.

The ordinance also details site plan requirements including showing right-of-way and public roads, and use of public roads for construction and maintenance must be identified and managed. No multiplier based on structure height is mentioned for setbacks from roads.

Major Energy Systems "Shall provide a fifty (50') foot planted buffer/screen along all property lines" and "Shall conceal solar collector's supporting structures fixtures and piping where applicable." These requirements are found under the subsection for Major Energy Systems in (5) Setbacks, Restrictions, and Easements. The ordinance distinguishes Major Energy Systems as "a Solar System that is not a minor energy system, such as, but not limited to a solar farm," and treats them as "Special Exception Use" in certain zoning districts. Minor Energy Systems have different requirements, such as being considered an accessory use and having to "conceal solar collector's structures, fixtures and piping where applicable," but the 50-foot planted buffer/screen is specific to Major Energy Systems.

Each Major Energy System shall have a minimum one sign, not to exceed two (2) square feet in area, posted on the security fence if applicable. The sign shall contain at least the following: Warning high voltage; Manufacturer and owner/operator's name; Emergency contact numbers (list more than one number).

summary: Section (14) Soil Erosion and Sedimentation Control: Stormwater Management states: "If applicable, all earth disturbances shall comply with the soil erosion and sedimentation control requirements of the Luzerne Conservation District and the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection; and no approval shall be granted under this Ordinance until Applicant provides a copy of the approved soil erosion and sedimentation control plan and any required permits. A stormwater management plan and stormwater management facilities shall be provided for all major energy systems in accord with the Township's current Stormwater Management Requirements. There are no impervious area exemptions to relieve the requirement of submitting a storm water management plan for Major Energy Systems." This explicitly applies to Major Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance. Other related provisions include requirements for decommissioning, site plan submissions, and compliance with other regulations, but these do not specifically address soil, erosion, or sediment control.

summary: Major Energy Systems "shall be considered a 'Special Exception Use' in all C-1, I-1, B-1, and A-1 zoning districts." They must meet conditions including setbacks, buffers, and easements, and variances may be granted by the Zoning Hearing Board. Minor Energy Systems are permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts and reviewed by the Zoning Officer. The ordinance also specifies minimum lot size for Major Energy Systems as fifty (50) acres.

Major Energy Systems must be a minimum of one thousand (1,000') feet from any property line of existing residential, public, or quasi-public use. This setback directly pertains to occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, and/or residences. Other setback distances mentioned include 500 feet from a public or private road right-of-way and 100 feet from all other property lines, but these do not specifically relate to occupied dwellings or residences.

Except for Minor Energy Systems, no Major Energy System shall be located less than one thousand (1000') feet from any Important Bird Area or migration corridor, National Wetland Inventory Wetland, Historic Site or lake, dam, ponds or public water supply sources.

The ordinance requires that "The facility owner and operator shall, at their expense, complete decommissioning of the solar electric energy facility or individual solar electric system within 12 months after the end of the useful life of such facility or system." Decommissioning includes "removal of all solar electric energy systems, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations and any other associated facilities." Disturbed earth must be "graded and reseeded, unless the Township explicitly approves a landowner's written request that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored." Financial security must be provided "at the time of issuance of the permit" and updated every five years with an estimate including an administrative and inflation factor of 25%, minus a resale credit of 80% of salvage value. The facility owner and operator may be required to enter into a decommissioning agreement with the Township prior to permit approval. These requirements apply to solar electric energy facilities of two acres or more, which are not for on-site residential or commercial use.

Section 329-7(D) states: 'A solar electric energy facility shall be enclosed by a fence, barrier or other appropriate means to prevent or restrict unauthorized persons or vehicles from entering the property.' It also requires that 'Clearly visible warning signs shall be placed on the fence, barrier or solar electric energy facility perimeter to inform individuals of potential voltage hazards.' The ordinance applies to solar electric energy facilities defined as facilities with the main purpose of generating and supplying electricity and not for on-site residential or commercial use (§ 329-3).

All solar electric energy systems shall be located 50 feet from all property lines where the system is located. These distances shall be measured from the closest edge of the solar electric energy system to the property line.

§ 329-7 D requires that "clearly visible warning signs shall be placed on the fence, barrier or solar electric energy facility perimeter to inform individuals of potential voltage hazards." This applies to solar electric energy facilities as defined as facilities "that have a main purpose of generating and supplying electricity" and "shall not include solar electric energy systems meant for on-site residential or commercial use." No other signage requirements are explicitly stated.

All AEF land development plans shall contain a Decommissioning Plan meeting the following minimum requirements: The Facility Owner or Operator shall, at its expense, complete decommissioning of the facility within 12 months after the end of the useful life of the facility. The facility will be presumed to be at the end of its useful life if no electricity is generated for a continuous period of 12 months. Decommissioning shall include removal of Solar Collectors, panels, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations to a depth of 36 inches and any other associated facilities. Disturbed earth shall be graded and reseeded. Soil samples shall be collected and analyzed. Ground water samples shall be collected and analyzed at the site and on all adjacent properties within 1,000 feet of the site boundaries. Results of the ground and water sample tests shall be submitted to the Township. Results of the water sample test shall also be provided to the adjacent property owners. The Facility Owner or Operator shall retain an independent and licensed professional engineer to calculate the estimated cost of the complete decommissioning of the facility without regard to salvage value of the equipment. This value shall be known as 'the decommissioning cost.' This cost shall also consider any soil or ground water remediation necessary or anticipated. The estimates shall be submitted to the Township prior to the start of construction and updated every fifth (5) year on the anniversary of the facility’s startup date. The Facility Owner or Operator shall post and maintain with the Township decommissioning funds in an amount equal to the value of 100% of the decommissioning cost, as determined by the Township engineer, before construction begins on the facility. The decommissioning cost escrow shall be provided by a bonding company or financial institution, authorized to conduct such business within the Commonwealth and approved by the Township, and held by the Township in escrow. Decommissioning funds may be in the form of a performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit, corporate guarantee or other form of financial guarantee as may be acceptable to the Township. If neither the Facility Owner nor Operator complete decommissioning within the prescribed period, then the Township may take such measures as necessary to complete decommissioning at the cost of the Facility Owner, Operator or property owner. The Facility Owner or Operator shall maintain and update the surety bond/financial guarantee until such time as the bond/guarantee is released by the Board of Supervisors. The Decommissioning Plan shall identify all state and local public roads to be used to transport equipment and parts during decommissioning activity. The Facility Owner or Operator may be required to bond state and/or local public roads prior to the start of decommissioning activity.

summary: The ordinance defines a Solar Farm as "An installation of a solar array, and all related structures and equipment, typically designed as the primary land use of a parcel and including multiple solar energy collectors on mounting systems, from which the energy generated is sold for use on an energy grid system rather than being consumed on site." It requires a decommissioning plan "including provisions for the removal of all structures and foundations and the restoration of soil and vegetation." The decommissioning must be completed "within six (6) months after the end of the useful Life of the facility," which is presumed if "no electricity is generated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months." Decommissioning includes "removal of solar arrays, support equipment, buildings, electrical components and lines, roads, foundations to a depth of 36 inches, and any other associated facilities." Disturbed earth must be "graded and re-seeded," unless the landowner requests otherwise and the supervisors approve. The facility owner or operator must submit an estimate of decommissioning costs and maintain financial assurance (Decommissioning Funds) equal to the net decommissioning costs, with a minimum of 25% of total costs. If the owner/operator fails to decommission, the landowner must complete it within six months, and if neither completes it, the Township may take necessary measures and use escrow funds to cover costs. The ordinance also states that the land will be restored to a condition where productive agricultural use can be resumed if the prior use was agricultural.

Solar farms are subject to the following conditions: Solar farms shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing at a height of six (6) feet to restrict unauthorized access. Fencing shall be permitted within the front, rear and side yards of a lot and shall be set back a minimum of fifteen (15) feet from all property lines or five (5) feet from any street right of way line.

Section 110-74.3(A)(6) states: 'All individual solar energy collectors, storage cells and connecting equipment in a solar array shall be subject to the setback requirements for a principal structure in that district and shall have a maximum height of fifteen (15) feet, except that any overhead power lines necessary for connection to the local electrical grid may be up to a height of fifty (50) feet.' The maximum height for solar farm structures is 15 feet, with overhead power lines allowed up to 50 feet.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'The minimum net lot area required to install a solar farm shall be five (5) acres.' This applies to solar farms defined as installations where energy generated is sold for use on an energy grid system. The unit for this minimum lot size is acres.

Solar farms shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing at a height of six (6) feet to restrict unauthorized access. Fencing shall be permitted within the front, rear and side yards of a lot and shall be set back a minimum of fifteen (15) feet from all property lines or five (5) feet from any street right of way line.

Solar farms shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing at a height of six (6) feet to restrict unauthorized access. Fencing shall be permitted within the front, rear and side yards of a lot and shall be set back a minimum of fifteen (15) feet from all property lines or five (5) feet from any street right of way line.

Section 110-74.3.A.4 requires that the solar farm "shall be screened from the property line view of (i) any residential structures on adjacent lots existing at the time the solar farm is established and located within three hundred (300) feet of the nearest solar array on the solar farm and (ii) any pedestrian or vehicular traffic on any street directly adjacent to the solar farm." The screening requirement can be adjusted by the Township Planning Commission where topographic conditions of the property make total compliance unreasonably difficult to achieve.

Section 110-74.3(A)(5) requires that "Earth disturbance and grading activities must be minimized and natural vegetal cover must be preserved and/or restored." Vegetative cover must have "90% or better uniform coverage" with a "meadow condition preferable, particularly for slopes between 5 and 10%." Individual PV panels must be arranged to allow runoff passage; if spacing is inadequate (width exceeds 3 feet), then BMPs such as "infiltration trenches (min. 12" wide by 12" deep) or infiltration berms must be installed downgradient between each row." Panels must allow vegetation growth beneath and between arrays. Ground-mounted panels must occupy a maximum of 5% of the total project area. Panels must be situated on mild slopes (max 10%); if slopes exceed 10%, BMPs like infiltration trenches or berms are required. The Township Engineer may require greater stormwater management where pre-existing deficiencies exist, considering guidelines to establish a "Meadow" runoff cover condition, infiltrate at least ½ inch of rainfall, and reduce pass-through flow rate to 80% of inflow. These requirements apply to solar farms defined as installations where energy is sold to an energy grid system, typically the primary land use of a parcel.

Utility-scale solar energy systems, referred to as 'Solar Farms,' are permitted as special exceptions in the Agricultural-2 (AG-2) District and the Light-Industrial (LI) District, as stated in Sections 110-19.B.2.u and 110-25.B.2.f respectively. Both uses are 'subject to § 110-74.3,' which details conditions such as minimum lot area of five acres, fencing, screening, setback and height requirements, and maintenance obligations. The ordinance specifies that 'Solar farms may be proposed as the principal use of a property, or in addition to an existing use already on a property,' and includes provisions for agrivoltaics and continuation of existing agricultural uses. The text does not include solar overlay districts as primary use in this context.

summary: The solar farm shall be screened from the property line view of (i) any residential structures on adjacent lots existing at the time the solar farm is established and located within three hundred (300) feet of the nearest solar array on the solar farm. Additionally, all individual solar energy collectors, storage cells and connecting equipment in a solar array shall be subject to the setback requirements for a principal structure in that district. No fixed numeric setback distance solely for solar farms from residences is specified.

Section 860.2(A)(10) Decommissioning: "The SEF owner is required to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The SEF shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of six (6) continuous months. The SEF owner shall then have twelve (12) months in which to dismantle and remove the SEF including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations, solar facility connections and other associated facilities in accordance with agreements with landowners and good industry practice. To the extent possible the materials shall be re-sold or salvaged. Materials that cannot be re-sold or salvaged shall be disposed of at facility authorized to dispose of such materials by federal or state law. Any soil exposed during the removal shall be stabilized in accordance with applicable erosion and sediment control standards. Any access drive paved aprons from public roads shall remain for future use unless directed otherwise by the landowner. The SEF site area shall be restored to its pre-existing condition, suitable for its prior use, except the landowner may authorize, in writing, any buffer landscaping or access roads installed to accommodate the SEF to remain. Any necessary permits, such as Erosion and Sedimentation and NPDES permits, shall be obtained prior to decommissioning activities. The SEF owner shall provide financial security in the form and amount acceptable to the Township, in favor of the Township, to secure its obligations under this Subsection (h). The SEF Developer shall, at the time of submitting the Subdivision and Land Development (SALDO) application, provide the Township with an estimate of the cost of performing the decommissioning activities required herein. The Township shall obtain an independent review of the estimate of the cost of performing the decommissioning activities. The Township shall establish the cost of performing the decommissioning activities based upon this review. The SEF Developer/Owner shall be responsible for administrative, legal, and engineering costs incurred by the Township for such review. As a condition of Zoning approval, no later than at the time of review of the SALDO plans by the Township, the SEF Developer shall enter into a Decommissioning Agreement with the Township outlining the responsibility of the parties under this Ordinance as to the Decommissioning of the SEF. The SEF Developer shall, upon receipt of SALDO approval, and not later than the start of any construction activities, provide the Township the decommissioning security. The decommissioning security may be in the form of a surety bond guaranteed by a company listed in U.S. Treasury Circular 570, or a cash account or an irrevocable letter of credit on deposit with, or issued by a Federal or Commonwealth chartered lending institution which is insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) in the amount of 110% of the total proposed decommission cost estimate and, in a form satisfactory to the Supervisors and the Township Solicitor. On every 5th anniversary of the date of providing the decommissioning financial security, the SEF Owner shall provide an updated decommission cost estimate, utilizing the formula set forth above with adjustments for inflation and cost and value changes. The Township shall obtain an independent review of the estimate. The Township shall establish the cost of performing the decommissioning activities based upon this review. If the decommissioning security amount increases, the SEF Owner shall remit the increased financial security to the Township within 30 days of the approval of the updated decommissioning security estimate by the Township. If the decommissioning security amount decreases by greater than 10%, the Township shall release from security any amounts held in excess of 110% of the updated decommission cost estimate. The SEF Developer/Owner shall be responsible for administrative, legal, and engineering costs incurred by the Township for such review." Other options and conditions: For Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), Section 860.1(A)(5) requires removal within twelve (12) months of discontinuation or abandonment, presumed if no electricity is generated for twelve (12) continuous months, but these apply to smaller or on-site systems, not SEFs. The ordinance distinguishes SEFs as systems supplying power primarily for off-site use and subject to these detailed decommissioning requirements.

Section 860.2.B.8(a) requires that "All ground-mounted SEFs shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate as deemed appropriate by the Supervisors at Conditional Use approval." Additionally, a "clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence on the surrounding the SEF informing individuals of potential voltage hazards." This fencing requirement applies specifically to Solar Energy Facilities (SEF), defined as systems "principally to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy power and supply electrical power primarily for off-site use." Other related provisions include vegetative buffering requirements around the fence and access road requirements, but the explicit fencing mandate is the eight-foot high fence with a self-locking gate.

Section 860.2.A.(8) of the ordinance states: "All SEF shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures or roadways. Exterior surfaces shall have a non-reflective finish." It further requires that "The applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation." This applies explicitly to Solar Energy Facilities (SEF), defined as systems "principally to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy power and supply electrical power primarily for off-site use." Other related options include Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES) with similar glare restrictions in Section 860.1.A.(4), but those apply to smaller or on-site systems, not SEFs.

The ordinance states: 'All ground mounted solar panels shall comply with a maximum twelve (12) foot height requirement.' (Section 860.2.B.4(a)). Other SEF components should comply with the underlying district maximum height requirement but may exceed it if the applicant demonstrates necessity and benefit at Conditional Use approval. There are no maximum height restrictions for structures that support Solar Facility Connections and Solar Project Connections. For roof and wall mounted principal SEFs, the total height of a building with the system shall not exceed more than 3 feet above the maximum building height specified for principal or accessory buildings within the applicable zoning district. The units for the maximum height are feet.

During operation of the SEF, audible sound shall not exceed a maximum of 60 dBA during daytime hours and 45 dBA during nighttime hours as measured at the property line on a non-participating landowner’s property. The most restrictive value is 45 dBA at night. Units are dBA, a standard noise measurement unit.
section: 860.2. SOLAR ENERGY FACILITY (SEF), A. Criteria Applicable to All SEFs, 7) Noise Management

summary: The fence as required by Paragraph 9 below shall be considered a principal structure for purposes of setbacks. Minimum setbacks shall be in accordance with the District Requirements for a principal structure. Where the minimum setbacks in accordance with the District Requirements is less than fifty (50) feet a setback of fifty (50) feet shall be required. No lot line setback will be required where there is a grouping of two or more Solar Energy Facilities which are held by a common owner or leased to a common lessee and which are part of a single Solar Energy Project, where each landowner has provided a written waiver of the lot line setback.

The ordinance requires a minimum of a 25’ buffer along either side of any regulated stream or regulatory wetland. Solar Arrays shall not be located in regulated natural and man-made drainage corridors, extending twenty-five (25) feet from the centerline of any such drainage feature unless the Supervisors at Conditional Use approval determines a lesser setback would create less impacts to the overall project. Other locations where Solar Arrays shall not be located include floodways, wetlands and their buffers (also 25 feet), slopes in excess of 15%, and wooded areas with mature trees over 2 acres, all subject to possible Conditional Use approval for lesser setbacks.

Section 860.2(6) requires that "Ground mounted SEF shall be screened and buffered from adjacent property that is residentially zoned or used for residential purposes. The screen shall consist of plant materials which provide a visual screen." Vegetative buffering "shall be installed at the perimeter of the SEF installation, except where the Supervisors determine that the existing vegetation and trees constitutes the required vegetative buffer or where the Supervisors determine that the solar panels cannot be viewed from an occupied residential building." The buffering "shall be installed along the exterior side of the fencing" and "all required vegetative buffering shall be located within fifty (50) feet of the required fencing." The buffering "should be designed to emulate the mix of native species and appearance of existing tree lines, hedge rows, and wooded areas already in existence within the landscape where the SEF is proposed," and "Arborvitae may be used as vegetative buffering." At least "20% of vegetative buffering plantings shall be pollinator friendly species." The buffering "shall be selected to provide year-round buffering and shall be of sufficient height, density, and maturity to screen the facility from visibility, as set forth herein within thirty-six months of the installation of the SEF." A combination of natural topography and vegetation can serve as a buffer, but "Earthen berms may not be created to serve as a buffer." A "screening plan shall be required with the Conditional Use Application that limits the visibility of the SEF from public roads, public parks or existing residences on surrounding properties." The buffering requirements "shall supersede the provisions of the Briar Creek Township Zoning Ordinance and Columbia County Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance as they may pertain to SEFs." The SEF owner "shall be required to maintain vegetative buffering throughout the life of the project. Dead and or diseased planting shall be removed and replace in accordance with this section."

Section 860.2.A.(6) states: 'No portion of the SEF shall contain or be used to display advertising. The manufacturer's name and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of the SEF provided they comply with the prevailing sign regulations.' Section 860.2.B.(8)(b) requires: 'A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence on the surrounding the SEF informing individuals of potential voltage hazards.' These are the explicit signage requirements for Solar Energy Facilities (SEF) in the ordinance.

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Solar Energy Facilities (SEF). Section 860.2.B.5 on Stormwater Management requires that "stormwater runoff from an ASES [Accessory Solar Energy System] shall be managed in accordance with the requirements of 25 Pa. Code § 102, and specifically the most recent guidance published by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) related to Chapter 102 Permitting for Solar Panel Farms." It further states that "Where there is a discrepancy between this guidance and the provisions of this section of the Zoning Ordinance, the DEP guidance shall be followed." Conditions for vegetation cover include: "a minimum uniform 70% perennial vegetative cover with a density capable of resisting accelerated erosion and sedimentation," and "vegetated areas shall not be subject to chemical fertilization or herbicide/pesticides application, except for those applications necessary to establish the vegetative cover or to prevent invasive species and in accordance with an approved Erosion and Sediment Control Plan." Agrivoltaics are allowed with conditions including "a written erosion and sediment control plan must be developed for agricultural plowing or tilling activities or a portion of the overall farm conservation plan must identify BMPs used." Areas not meeting these conditions are treated as impervious for runoff analysis. summary: The ordinance explicitly requires that "Ground mounted PSES shall be screened from any adjacent property that is a residence. The screen shall consist of plant materials which provide a visual screen. In lieu of a planting screen, a decorative fence may be used." It applies to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) which are defined as systems "principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use." The ordinance exempts PSES "which do not encompass greater than two (2.0) acres in size" from these terms and conditions. Other options for screening include a decorative fence instead of plant materials. The screening requirement is part of the regulations applicable to all PSES, specifically under "Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems."

Section 4.B.2.b requires that the applicant shall submit a Stormwater Management Plan that demonstrates compliance by the ground-mounted PSES with any applicable municipal stormwater management regulations. Section 4.B.5 states that ground-mounted PSES shall not be placed within any storm water conveyance system or in any other manner that would alter or impede storm water runoff from collecting in a constructed storm water conveyance system. Section 4.A.2 exempts PSES constructed prior to the effective date of this Ordinance or which do not encompass greater than two (2.0) acres in size from meeting the terms and conditions of this Ordinance. Any physical modification to an existing PSES that materially alters the PSES requires approval under this Ordinance. Routine maintenance or like-kind replacements do not require a permit.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Solar Farms defined as a Principal Use on a minimum 40-acre lot. Key provisions include: "The Solar Farm owner is required to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation," with abandonment presumed if "no electricity is generated by the system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months." The owner "shall have twelve (12) months in which to dismantle and remove the Solar Farm including all solar related equipment or appurtenances," and "to the extent possible, the materials shall be re-sold or salvaged." Materials that cannot be salvaged "shall be disposed of at a facility authorized to dispose of such materials by federal or state law," with notification to the Municipality. "Any soil exposed during the removal shall be stabilized in accordance with applicable erosion and sediment control standards." The site "shall be restored to its pre-existing condition, suitable for its prior use," except that the landowner may authorize certain buffers or access roads to remain. "Any necessary permits, such as Erosion and Sedimentation and NPDES permits, shall be obtained prior to decommissioning activities." Financial security is required at permit issuance to secure decommissioning obligations, with an initial estimate including an administrative and inflation factor of 25%, salvage credit of 80%, and a minimum security amount of $500,000. The security must be updated annually and approved by the Township, with the developer responsible for review costs. The security may be in cash, letter of credit, or investment grade corporate guarantee. The developer must enter into a Decommissioning Agreement with the Township prior to plan or permit approval. These requirements are found under the Solar Farm provisions and do not apply to Accessory Solar Energy Systems, which have separate decommissioning rules.

All ground-mounted Solar Farms shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate. A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the Solar Farm informing individuals of potential voltage hazards. This fencing requirement applies specifically to Solar Farms as defined in this Ordinance, which are not considered Accessory Uses but may operate as a Principal Use on a Lot with other Principal Uses, with a minimum lot size of 40 acres. The ordinance distinguishes Solar Farms from Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), which have different standards and fencing provisions. For example, ground mounted solar arrays (ASES) must be enclosed by an eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate, but these are accessory systems with output size not greater than 10kw and intended primarily for on-site use, whereas Solar Farms are larger scale, principal uses intended for offsite electricity generation or sale.

The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Solar Farms under Section 1401.SS. It requires that "All Solar Farms shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures or roadways. Exterior surfaces shall have a non-reflective finish." The applicant "has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation." Additionally, "Solar panels shall have a surface that minimizes glare and shall be shielded, buffered, and directed so that glare will not become a nuisance to adjoining properties, adjoining districts, and Streets." These restrictions apply to Solar Farms defined as a principal use on a minimum 40-acre lot. Other related provisions include fencing, setbacks, height limits, stormwater management, buffering, security, access, and decommissioning requirements, but glare restrictions are specifically detailed in this section.

All ground mounted Solar Farms shall comply with a ten (10) foot maximum height requirement. Solar Arrays shall not exceed ten (10) feet in height. For fixed solar arrays, height shall be measured at the highest point of the solar array above ground level. For solar arrays designed to rotate, height shall be measured with the solar array oriented at maximum tilt.

Section 437.12 states: 'If a ground-mounted solar system is ever removed, any earth disturbance as a result of the removal of the ground-mounted solar energy system shall be graded and reseeded to the satisfaction of the Borough.' The applicant must submit a signed statement certifying that "the proposed system shall not produce glare or reflect concentrated solar radiation visible beyond the property lines... such that the nuisance situation is created." If glare occurs post-installation causing a nuisance or safety hazard, "the Borough may at its discretion require mitigation action or may require the removal of the system or portion thereof generating the glare or reflected solar radiation." Failure to comply with mitigation or removal within six months (or immediately if a safety hazard) allows the Borough to act and place a lien for costs. This obligation continues for the life of the system and subsequent owners must be notified. Other options or conditions include mitigation or removal actions by the Borough if glare becomes a nuisance or hazard, with cost recovery provisions. These glare restrictions apply specifically to Large Solar Energy Systems as defined in Section 437, which are "installed on large parcels of land for the purpose of generating revenue."

Section 437.1 states: 'The minimum lot size or any large solar energy system shall be five acres.' This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for Large Solar Energy Systems. Large solar energy systems shall be set back a minimum of 100 feet from any public right-of-way, any lot line, and/or any residential use.
