The applicant must provide technical documentation acceptable to the Borough indicating that the noise standard will be achieved at all times, in the form of a sound study completed for another installation by a certified sound consultant.

The ordinance states: 'Solar Energy Systems shall only be permitted in the Agricultural Zone, provided that all provisions are met.' This implies that utility-scale solar energy systems are prohibited in all other zoning districts, although no other district names or abbreviations are explicitly mentioned. The text adds a conditional use for Alternative Energy Facilities in the Agricultural Zone and sets a minimum lot size of ten (10) acres for Principal Solar Energy Systems.

PSES shall be set back from the side yard property lines a minimum of one hundred (100) feet, from the rear yard property line a minimum of 100 feet, and from the front yard edge of road Right-of-way a minimum of 100 feet. PSES shall be set back from all perennial streams, runs, and/or creeks a minimum of 100 feet. (Note: Only the side and rear yard property line setbacks apply directly to property lines; the front yard setback references road right-of-way.)

PSES shall be set back from the front yard edge of road Right-of-way a minimum of 100 feet. Other setbacks include 100 feet from side yard property lines and rear yard property lines, but only the road right-of-way setback is relevant here.

The ordinance defines Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) as systems designed to supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use. It requires that "PSES shall be screened from any adjacent property that is residentially zoned or used for residential purposes." The screening "shall consist of plants, evergreens, arborvitae, trees, or similar plants and shrubs which provide an effective visual screen." Additional requirements include setbacks of 100 feet from property lines and water bodies, a maximum height of 20 feet for ground-mounted systems, underground placement of transmission lines to the extent feasible, safety signage, prohibition of advertising, glare mitigation, noise limits, security fencing, lighting restrictions, and access road specifications. Decommissioning requirements are also detailed but do not pertain to screening.

Section 1210.A.6 requires "appropriate safety/warning signage concerning live voltage shall be placed on or within 3 feet of any ground mounted electrical devices, equipment, and/or structures." This applies to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), defined as "a system designed to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power, and supply said electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use." No other signage requirements are explicitly stated for PSES. Other conditions for PSES include setbacks, height limits, noise limits, screening, fencing, lighting, access roads, public hearings, and decommissioning requirements, but these do not pertain to signage.

The ordinance requires that "Prior to the installation of any Principal Solar Energy System facilities, any company proposing said installation shall collect and analyze background soil samples in the area where the facilities are to be installed for pH, lead, selenium, cadmium, arsenic, chromium, and copper. Results shall be submitted to the Borough." Additionally, for decommissioning, "Disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded. Soil samples shall be collected and analyzed for the elements listed above respectively for a Principal Solar Facility or Wind Energy Facility. Results shall be submitted to the Borough. Any soil remediation work needed shall be included in decommissioning costs." These requirements apply to Principal Solar Energy Systems, defined as systems "designed to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power, and supply said electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use." No other soil, erosion, or sediment control requirements are explicitly stated.

A Principal Solar Energy System, or PSES, is permitted only in the Agricultural Zone, listed under conditional uses: 'Solar Energy Systems shall only be permitted in the Agricultural Zone, provided that all provisions are met.' It is added as a conditional use in section 802(3)(G) and further detailed in section 27-1210, which requires compliance with provisions to minimize impacts and a minimum lot size of ten (10) acres.

Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) shall be set back from all perennial streams, runs, and/or creeks a minimum of 100 feet. Other setbacks include 100 feet from side yard property lines, rear yard property lines, and front yard edge of road Right-of-way, but only the 100 feet setback from perennial streams, runs, and/or creeks pertains to water bodies.

Commercial solar energy systems are permitted by conditional use in the Industrial District (I) and Local Commercial District (LC), subject to requirements including: location on lots of at least five (5) acres; compliance with principal use setback and height requirements; design, installation, and maintenance in accordance with applicable local, state, and federal codes and regulations; no glare or reflectivity posing safety hazards; screening from view from adjacent residential properties to the extent practicable; and removal within six (6) months of ceasing to be operational. Other solar energy systems include accessory solar energy systems permitted in all zoning districts with conditions such as building-mounted or ground-mounted limits, setback and height requirements, and removal within six (6) months of ceasing operation. Roof-mounted and ground-mounted solar collectors have additional specific standards. The decommissioning requirement explicitly applies to commercial solar energy systems as stated: 'Commercial solar energy systems shall be removed within six (6) months of ceasing to be operational.'

Commercial solar energy systems are permitted by conditional use in the Industrial District (I) and Local Commercial District (LC), subject to requirements including: "Commercial solar energy systems shall not create glare or reflectivity that poses a safety hazard to motorists or adjacent properties." Other requirements include location on lots of at least five (5) acres, compliance with principal use setback and height requirements, design and maintenance in accordance with applicable codes, screening from view from adjacent residential properties to the extent practicable, and removal within six (6) months of ceasing to be operational. For comparison, accessory solar energy systems (non-commercial) have similar glare restrictions but are permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts with additional height and setback limitations.

Commercial solar energy systems shall be located on lots of at least five (5) acres. This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for commercial solar energy systems, as stated in the ordinance. The unit 'acres' is used to specify the area. Other related requirements include compliance with principal use setback and height requirements, design and maintenance standards, glare control, screening from adjacent residential properties, and removal within six months of ceasing operation.

Commercial solar energy systems are permitted by conditional use in the Industrial District (I) and Local Commercial District (LC), subject to requirements including: "Commercial solar energy systems shall be screened from view from adjacent residential properties to the extent practicable." Other requirements include location on lots of at least five (5) acres, compliance with principal use setback and height requirements, design and maintenance per applicable codes, no glare or reflectivity hazards, and removal within six (6) months of ceasing operation. For non-commercial solar energy systems, screening is also required but under accessory use provisions. Ground mounted solar collectors may use "fences or vegetative screens... to prevent glare from impacting adjoining properties or street rights-of-way," but this applies to accessory systems, not explicitly commercial systems.

The ordinance states: 'The maximum lot coverage shall be 75% and the area of the solar collectors shall be included in the calculation of lot coverage.' This applies to commercial solar power generation facilities, which are typically utility-scale systems. The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the lot area, not as a specific area value.

The solar power facility owner and operator shall, at its own expense, complete decommissioning of the solar power facility, or individual components, within 12 months after the end of the useful life of the solar power facility or individual components. The solar power facility or individual components shall be presumed to be at the end of its useful life if no electricity is generated for a continuous period of 12 months. Decommissioning shall include removal of collectors, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations to a depth of 36 inches, and any other associated facilities. Disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded, unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored. An independent and certified professional engineer shall be retained to estimate the total cost of decommissioning and net decommissioning costs, with estimates submitted after the first year of operation and every fifth year thereafter. Prior to issuance of a zoning permit, the owner or operator must provide a financial security bond with the Township as payee, not less than $50,000, to insure decommissioning within 180 days of license expiration or cessation of use. The bond shall remain in place as long as the facilities exist. Decommissioning funds may be in the form of a performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit, corporate guarantee, or other acceptable financial assurance. If the owner or operator fails to complete decommissioning within the prescribed time, the landowner has 180 days to complete it. If neither completes decommissioning, the Township may take necessary measures to complete it. The escrow agent shall release decommissioning funds when the owner/operator demonstrates satisfactory completion or upon Township approval to implement the plan.

Section C(8) states: 'Glare. The applicant shall provide details about anticipated glare from the facility, including the time of day, time of year and direction of peak glare periods and document how potential nuisances to area properties and on public roads shall be controlled.' This applies to commercial solar power generation facilities, which are permitted only in certain districts and require a permit. Other relevant conditions include setbacks, height limits, fencing, landscaping, and compliance with state and federal regulations, but these do not specifically address glare.
The setback for solar collectors, all structures, equipment containers and any associated mechanical facilities shall be 100 feet from property lines.

Landscaping may be required to screen as much of the solar power facility ground features as possible, the fence surrounding the support structure, and any other ground-level features (such as a building), and in general buffer the solar power facility ground features from neighboring properties. The Township may permit any combination of existing vegetation, topography, walls, decorative fences or other features instead of landscaping, if the same achieves the same degree of screening as the required landscaping.

Section C(13) requires "a clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations." Section C(14) states "No advertising material or signs other than warning, manufacturer and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of structures." These signage requirements apply to commercial solar power generation facilities.

Section 11. Decommissioning: The Facility Owner is required to notify Covington Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the use. The SEF shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by the system for a continuous period of twelve (12) months. The Facility Owner shall then have six (6) months in which to dismantle and remove the SEF, including all solar-related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, as well as all buildings, cabling, electrical components, transmission and plumbing lines, roads, foundations, and other associated facilities from the property. The Facility Owner shall also restore the land to its original pre-construction condition. If the SEF owner fails to dismantle and/or remove the SEF and restore the land within the six (6) month period, Covington Township may, but shall not be required to, complete the decommissioning and land restoration at the owner’s expense. At the time of issuance of the permit for the construction of the SEF, the Facility Owner shall provide proof of liability insurance and a financial security to Covington Township to secure the expense of dismantling and removing the SEF and restoration of the land to its original condition. The financial security shall be in the amount of 110% of the costs of decommissioning. The decommissioning funds shall be posted and maintained during the life of the project in the form of a performance bond, irrevocable letter of credit, or other financial form of security acceptable to the Covington Township Board of Supervisors. An independent and registered professional engineer shall be retained by Covington Township at the Facility Owner’s cost to estimate the total cost of decommissioning without regard to salvage value of the equipment, and the cost of decommissioning net salvage value of the equipment. Thereafter, the Facility Owner shall retain an engineer to provide Covington Township with cost estimates of decommissioning after the first (1st) year of operation and every fifth (5th) year thereafter. Said estimate is subject to the review and approval of Covington Township’s engineer. During the operation of the SEF, the Facility Owner shall maintain financial security in the amount of 110% of the estimate of the cost of decommissioning. The Financial Security may be in any one of the forms set forth in section 7 herein.

§ 27-2403 Decommission and Removal of a PSES requires that "A PSES and/or property owner shall notify the Township immediately upon cessation of operation of or abandonment of a PSES." A PSES is presumed abandoned if "no electricity has been generated by the system for a period of six consecutive months." Upon cessation or abandonment, the owner must "immediately begin to dismantle and remove from the property the PSES and all solar-related equipment and appurtenances thereto... and the property restored to its original condition, within six months." Failure to comply allows the Township to "complete the dismantling, removal, and/or restoration process at the PSES and/or property owner's expense." Additionally, "At the time of issuance of the permit for construction of a PSES, the property owner shall provide financial security to the Township... to secure the dismantling and/or removal of the PSES, and any necessary restoration of the land to its original condition." The financial security must be "in an amount equal to 125% of the written cost estimate" for dismantling and removal, with periodic adjustments and possible increases as deemed necessary by the Township.
section: § 27-2403  Decommission and Removal of a PSES

summary: Section 7, subsection D states: "A SEF shall be enclosed by a fence, barrier or other appropriate means to prevent or restrict unauthorized persons or vehicles from entering the property." It also requires "Clearly visible warning signs shall be placed on the fence, barrier or SEF perimeter to inform individuals of potential voltage hazards." This fencing requirement applies explicitly to Large-Scale Solar Electric Energy Facilities (SEFs) as defined in the ordinance, which are facilities "whose main purpose is to generate and supply electricity and consists of one or more Solar Electric Systems and other accessory structures and buildings... primarily for off-site use."
section: Section 7. Design, Construction, Financial Security, Maintenance and Insurance

summary: The ordinance requires that every ground-mounted Principal Solar Energy System (PSES) "shall be completely enclosed by fencing at least eight feet high with a locking gate." Additionally, "a clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations, and on the fence surrounding the PSES, to inform individuals of potential voltage hazards." The fencing requirement applies specifically to ground-mounted PSES, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. Other options for screening include plant material or a fence that provides a visual screen for PSES adjacent to residentially zoned or used properties, but the explicit fencing requirement with height and locking gate applies to full enclosure of the PSES.

The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Large-Scale Solar Electric Energy Facilities (SEFs). It states: 'All SEFs shall be situated in such a way that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby properties, structures or roadways.' This applies to SEFs as defined in the ordinance, which are facilities whose main purpose is to generate and supply electricity primarily for off-site use and consist of one or more Solar Electric Systems and accessory structures. The ordinance applies to any SEF of two (2) acres or more proposed to be constructed after the effective date. Other relevant conditions include design safety certification, visual appearance, warnings, site inspections, financial security, noise limits, setbacks, emergency services, and decommissioning requirements.

Each PSES shall be situated to eliminate glare onto nearby structures and roadways. This is found in § 27-2402, Standards and Requirements, subsection 1, item H. The ordinance applies to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), which are utility-scale solar energy systems. Other relevant standards include compliance with industry standards, underground placement of utility lines, screening from residential properties, fencing requirements, and dismantling and removal obligations, but these do not pertain to glare restrictions.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'Noise from a SEF shall not exceed 55 dBa, as measured at the property line.' This applies directly to Large-Scale Solar Electric Energy Facilities (SEFs) as defined in the ordinance, which are facilities whose main purpose is to generate and supply electricity primarily for off-site use. No other noise level values or conditions are provided for SEFs in the text. The unit 'dBA' is the standard unit for noise level measurement.
Ground-mounted SEFs shall have a minimum setback at all property lines of 150 feet. These distances shall be measured from the closest edge of the SEF to the property line.

The ordinance requires that "The PSES shall be screened from any adjacent property that is residentially zoned or used for residential purposes. The screen shall consist of either plant material or a fence that provides a visual screen." This applies to every ground-mounted Principal Solar Energy System (PSES).

The ordinance explicitly enacts signage requirements for Large-Scale Solar Electric Energy Facilities (SEFs). Section 8.D.2 requires that "clearly visible warning signs shall be placed on the fence, barrier or SEF perimeter to inform individuals of potential voltage hazards." Additionally, Section 9 mandates that "a sign shall be posted providing the name of the operator and a phone number to be used in case of an on-site emergency at the primary entrance of the SEF," and that "reflective signs shall be posted providing the name of the operator and a phone to be used in case of an on-site emergency along the perimeter of the SEF at intervals of 250 feet." These signage requirements apply to SEFs as defined in the ordinance, which are large-scale facilities whose principal purpose is to generate and supply electricity primarily for off-site use.
section: Section 8.D. Warnings and Section 9. Emergency Services and Safety

summary: Signage shall comply with all applicable sign regulations. A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations, and on the fence surrounding the PSES, to inform individuals of potential voltage hazards. Such signs shall be kept free from vegetation and other obstructions so they are clearly visible at all times.

Ground-mounted SEFs shall have a prepared stormwater management plan in accordance with Township Ordinances and Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection ( "Pa DEP" ) Best Management Practices. This shall include the use of low maintenance and low growing vegetative surfaces that support native pollinators under the SEF. This plan is subject to approval by the Lackawanna County Soil Conservation District. Ground-mounted SEFs shall have a prepared grading plan that minimizes to the best extent possible the disturbance or alteration of the existing topography on the site. This plan is subject to approval by the Lackawanna County Soil Conservation District.

The maximum impervious lot coverage of a solar energy facility is 40%. The following components of a solar energy facility shall be considered impervious coverage and calculated as part of the impervious coverage limitations: surface area of the arrays, regardless of the mounted angle of any panels; all structures ancillary to the arrays, including structures for solar related equipment or transmission; gravel or paved access roads servicing the solar energy facility. This applies specifically to Solar Energy Facility (Principal Use). For smaller or accessory solar energy systems, different coverage limits apply, such as ground-mounted solar energy systems in residential zones not exceeding 5% of the lot area, but these do not apply to principal use facilities.

Section 27-705.55 N. Decommissioning requires that "The solar energy facility owner is required to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The solar energy facility shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months." The owner then has "twelve (12) months in which to dismantle and remove the solar energy facility including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations and other associated facilities from the property." If the owner fails to do so, "the municipality may complete the decommissioning at the owner's expense." Additionally, "At the time of issuance of the permit for the construction of the solar energy facility, the owner shall provide financial security in the form and amount acceptable to the Township to secure the expense of dismantling and removing said solar energy facility and restoration of the land to its original condition, including forestry plantings of the same type/variety and density as the original." These requirements apply explicitly to Solar Energy Facility (Principal Use), defined as facilities "principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use."

Secure perimeter fencing, that is a minimum of 8 feet high, shall be installed around the solar energy facility. The fencing shall not be constructed within any required landscape buffer or setback. The fencing shall be chain link construction with rubberized coating in neutral earth tone colors such as black or brown. All components of solar energy facilities, including the security fencing, shall be no closer than 100 feet to any property line, unless the proposed solar energy facility is adjacent to a residential use or lot, in which case all components of the solar energy facility, including the security fencing, shall be no closer than 150 feet to the property line with the residential use or lot.

Section 27-705.55 (Solar Energy Facility, Principal Use) includes explicit glare restrictions: 'All solar energy facilities shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures or roadways.' The applicant 'has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation.' These requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities defined as principal uses supplying power primarily for off-site use. No other specific glare restriction options or conditions are provided in the ordinance text.

The arrays of Solar energy facilities shall not exceed a maximum height of 10 feet measured from ground level to the tallest point on the system. Any ancillary structures of the facility shall comply with principal maximum height regulations. This applies specifically to Solar Energy Facility (Principal Use) as defined in the ordinance. The unit 'feet' is explicitly stated in the text.

The minimum lot size required for a solar energy facility shall be 20 acres. This applies specifically to Solar Energy Facility (Principal Use) as defined in the ordinance: 'The minimum lot size required for a solar energy facility shall be 20 acres.' The unit 'acres' is explicitly stated as the area measurement for this minimum lot size.

Noise from any facility shall not exceed 50 decibels at the lot line adjacent to any lot in a nonresidential zoning district and 15 decibels at the lot line adjacent to any lot in a residential zoning district. The most restrictive value is 15 decibels at the lot line adjacent to residential zoning. The units for noise levels are assumed to be dBA, the standard unit for noise measurement.

All components of solar energy facilities, including the security fencing, shall be no closer than 100 feet to any property line, unless the proposed solar energy facility is adjacent to a residential use or lot, in which case all components of the solar energy facility, including the security fencing, shall be no closer than 150 feet to the property line with the residential use or lot.

Section 27-705.55.L Landscaping requires that "All solar energy facilities shall be screened and buffered in accordance with the following standards: Landscape buffering, to the extent practical, shall be installed around the entire perimeter of the solar energy facility installation, except where Township staff determines that the retention of existing trees within the vegetative buffering area may constitute the required vegetative buffer or where the Township determines that the solar array cannot be viewed from a public roadway or residential building. Landscape buffering shall be installed along the exterior side of the fencing. All buffering shall be installed in accordance with Chapter 22 Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance. Required landscape buffering may be modified so that tall tree species may be replaced with lower-growing tree species where the required tree species may interfere with the functioning of the solar energy facility, only where the required landscape buffer is adjacent to property where nonresidential uses are permitted." Additionally, Section 27-705.55.M requires "Secure perimeter fencing, that is a minimum of 8 feet high, shall be installed around the solar energy facility. The fencing shall not be constructed within any required landscape buffer or setback. The fencing shall be chain link construction with rubberized coating in neutral earth tone colors such as black or brown." These requirements apply explicitly to Solar Energy Facility (Principal Use).

Section 27-705.55 Solar Energy Facility (Principal Use) states: 'A solar energy facility shall be considered a land development and is subject to the requirements of Chapter 22 Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance in addition to all applicable zoning requirements outlined in this chapter.' It requires 'a soil analysis report of the proposed solar energy facility site, prepared by a certified engineer.' Additionally, 'All stormwater runoff associated with a solar energy facility shall be managed in accordance with applicable local and state requirements.' These provisions explicitly apply to Solar Energy Facilities (Principal Use), defined as facilities 'principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use.'

The ordinance states in Section 27-705.55 that a Solar Energy Facility (Principal Use) requires the applicant to "demonstrate through project planning and proposed mitigation that a proposed facility's visual impacts will be minimized" and that "a solar energy facility shall be considered a land development and is subject to the requirements of Chapter 22 Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance in addition to all applicable zoning requirements." It further requires submission of detailed project information, compliance with local, state, and federal regulations, and adherence to setback, height, landscaping, fencing, and decommissioning standards. The Table of Authorized Principal Uses (Chapter 27, Attachment 2) shows Solar Energy Facility (Principal Use) is permitted (marked 'R') in multiple districts including R-1, R-2, R-3, RMU, C-1, C-2, C-3, SU-1, SP-1, BPK, I-L, PIC, TLI, and MU. The ordinance does not explicitly label any district as permitting Solar Energy Facility (Principal Use) solely as a special use or conditional use by a zoning appeals board, but the detailed application and mitigation requirements imply that approval is conditional and involves a formal permitting process in all districts where permitted. No solar overlay districts are included in this analysis.

All components of solar energy facilities, including the security fencing, shall be no closer than 100 feet to any property line, unless the proposed solar energy facility is adjacent to a residential use or lot, in which case all components of the solar energy facility, including the security fencing, shall be no closer than 150 feet to the property line with the residential use or lot.

Section 27-705.55.A requires the applicant to "demonstrate through project planning and proposed mitigation that a proposed facility's visual impacts will be minimized for surrounding properties and the community. This may include, but not be limited to, information regarding site selection, system design or appearance, buffering, and screening of ground-mounted electrical and control equipment." Section 27-705.55.J.6 requires "A viewshed impact analysis illustrating views of the proposed facility from multiple angles." These provisions explicitly establish visual impact assessment requirements for Solar Energy Facility (Principal Use).

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Solar Energy Facilities (SEFs), defined as systems supplying electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use or on-site use if output size is greater than 10kw. Under Section 3, Part 2, subsection 7 'Decommissioning': 'The SEF owner is required to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The SEF shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months.' The SEF owner then has twelve (12) months to dismantle and remove the SEF including all solar related equipment or appurtenances. The site must be restored to its pre-existing condition except for authorized buffer landscaping or access roads. Financial security must be provided at permit issuance, with a minimum amount of $500,000, updated every 5 years, and may be in the form of cash, letter of credit, or investment grade corporate guarantee. A Decommissioning Agreement must be entered into prior to permit approval. Other solar energy systems defined include Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), which have separate decommissioning requirements, and Ground Mounted Accessory Solar Energy Systems, which are limited to output size not greater than 10kw and have their own decommissioning rules. The decommissioning requirements described here apply specifically to SEFs, including Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems, which have additional criteria such as minimum lot size of 100 acres, setbacks, height limits, and buffering requirements.

A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the SEF informing individuals of potential voltage hazards.

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Solar Energy Facilities (SEF), which are defined as systems supplying electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use or with output size greater than 10kw. Specifically, under Section 3, 2. SOLAR ENERGY FACILITY (SEF), item 5) Glare states: 'All SEF shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures or roadways. Exterior surfaces shall have a non-reflective finish.' Additionally, 'The applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation.' This applies to Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Facilities as defined. Other solar energy systems mentioned include Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), which are primarily for on-site use and have output size not greater than 10kw, and have separate glare restrictions under item 4) Glare, but these do not apply to principal SEFs. The ordinance also distinguishes between ground mounted and roof/wall mounted systems, with specific criteria for each.
section: SECTION 3: Chapter 27, Part 16 the Township of Cumberland Code of Ordinances, entitled Supplementary Uses, Section 1606, Solar Energy Systems

summary: The ordinance states: 'All ground mounted SEF shall comply with a fifteen (15) foot height requirement.' This applies specifically to Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Facilities (SEF). Other height restrictions mentioned include a 15-foot height limit for ground mounted Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES) and a 3-foot height limit above maximum building height for roof and wall mounted systems, but these apply to different categories. The unit for the SEF height restriction is feet.
section: SECTION 3: Chapter 27, Part 16 the Township of Cumberland Code of Ordinances, entitled Supplementary Uses, Section 1606, Solar Energy Systems, Part 2, B, 5) Height

summary: The ordinance explicitly states a minimum lot size of 100 acres for Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems (SEF) in Section 3, Part 2, subsection B, item 1: 'Minimum lot size — 100 acres.' This is the only minimum lot size value provided for SEFs. The unit 'acres' is a standard measure of land area.
section: SECTION 3: Chapter 27, Part 16 the Township of Cumberland Code of Ordinances, entitled Supplementary Uses, Section 1606, Solar Energy Systems, 2. SOLAR ENERGY FACILITY (SEF), B. Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems

summary: SEF shall be set back a minimum of two hundred (200) feet from any lot line. This applies to Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance. Other setback-related provisions include buffering around the entire perimeter of the SEF installation and restrictions on placement within legal easements or rights-of-way, but the fixed setback distance from lot lines is 200 feet.

Ground mounted SEF shall be screened and buffered in accordance with the following standards: Vegetative buffering shall be installed around the entire perimeter of the SEF installation, except where the Zoning Officer determines that the retention of existing trees within the vegetative buffering area may constitute the required vegetative buffer. Existing Natural Buffers shall be retained in accordance with Chapter 27, Section 1201 (6). The vegetative buffering shall be installed along the exterior side of the fencing. All required vegetative buffering shall be located within fifty (50) feet of the required fencing. Vegetative buffering shall be designed to emulate the mix of species and appearance of existing tree lines, hedge rows, and wooded areas already in existence within the landscape where the SEF is proposed. The applicant shall assess the species mix and characteristics found in existing tree lines, hedge rows, and wooded areas surrounding the SEF and document that the vegetative buffering is designed to emulate these characteristics. Vegetative buffering shall be selected to provide year round buffering and shall be of sufficient height, density, and maturity to screen the facility from visibility, as set forth herein within thirty-six months of the installation of the SEF. The primary use of evergreen trees shall not be permitted, and a monotonous straight row of the same species, particularly evergreen trees, is specifically prohibited. A combination of Natural topography and vegetation can serve as a buffer provided that the SEF will not be visible from public roads, public parks, the Gettysburg National Military Park or existing residences on surrounding properties. Earthen berms may not be created to serve as a buffer. Visibility of SEF shall be determined as visible in a photograph taken at a point with a digital camera with an APS-C Sensor and a 35 mm focal length lens. A SEF shall be considered to not be visible provided that no more than 5% of the SEF shall be visible in accordance with the measure of visibility set forth above. The buffering requirements of this section shall supersede the provisions of Part 12 of Chapter 27 as they pertain to SEFs.

summary: The ordinance requires that "a clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the SEF informing individuals of potential voltage hazards." It also states that "No portion of the SEF shall contain or be used to display advertising. The manufacturer's name and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of the SEF provided they comply with the prevailing sign regulations." These requirements apply to Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Facilities (SEF).
section: SECTION 3: Chapter 27, Part 16 the Township of Cumberland Code of Ordinances, entitled Supplementary Uses, Section 1606, Solar Energy Systems, Part 2, SOLAR ENERGY FACILITY (SEF), subsection 9) Security

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Facilities (SEFs). Stormwater runoff from an SEF shall be managed in accordance with the requirements of the Cumberland Township Stormwater Management Ordinance. The horizontal area of the panel may be considered a Disconnected Impervious Area ("DIA") and therefore, will have no increase from the pre-development to post-development runoff coefficient only if: natural vegetative cover is preserved and/or restored utilizing low impact construction techniques; the vegetative cover has a minimum uniform 90% perennial vegetative cover with a density capable of resisting accelerated erosion and sedimentation; panels on slopes 0 to 5% maintain a minimum 4" height of vegetative cover; panels on slopes 5% to 10% maintain a meadow condition; panels on slopes 10% to 15% cannot be considered DIA; solar panels on slopes over 15% are not permitted; vegetated areas shall not be subject to chemical fertilization or herbicide/pesticides except as necessary to establish vegetative cover or prevent invasive species and in accordance with an approved Erosion and Sediment Control Plan; agrivoltaics may be used provided a written erosion and sediment control plan is developed for agricultural plowing or tilling activities or a portion of the overall farm conservation plan identifies BMPs used, among other conditions. The horizontal area of any solar panel or array that cannot meet all DIA conditions shall be treated as impervious area and included in runoff analysis for Post Construction Stormwater Management (PCSM) Best Management Practices. Use of gravel is permissible but disqualifies the area from DIA consideration. Ground mounted SEFs shall not be placed within any storm water conveyance system unless it can be demonstrated that the SEF will not impede stormwater management. Decommissioning requires that any soil exposed during removal be stabilized in accordance with applicable erosion and sediment control standards, and any necessary permits, such as Erosion and Sedimentation and NPDES permits, shall be obtained prior to decommissioning activities.

summary: Section 852.2(A)(18) requires that "A private utility system, and all materials, structures, and accessory equipment installed with that system, that has not been in use for commercial generation purposes for six (6) months, shall be removed completely within ninety (90) days of the issuance of an enforcement action." The site must be "cleaned, restored and re-vegetated to blend with the existing surrounding vegetation, and to prevent soil erosion and down gradient sedimentation." The owner must "post a bond or other financial security in a form acceptable to the Township at the time of zoning approval to cover the cost of equipment removal and site restoration," which "shall be increased every five (5) years at the amount ten percent (10%) from the previous bond amount." Additional costs beyond the bond are the responsibility of the owner. Section 852.3(D) states that if a commercial energy system "is designated as a public utility by the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission, but not entirely exempt from municipal zoning requirements, then the requirements of 852.2 should apply to the proposed public utility use, in addition to those outlined in Section 852.3, as deemed legally applicable." Other options include community utilities subject to Section 852.1 and private utilities subject to Section 852.2, with community utilities serving multiple existing uses considered private utilities and thus subject to Section 852.2 requirements (Section 852.1(C) and (D)).

All mechanical equipment of Commercial Solar Energy Systems, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate, and provided with screening provisions of the Code of Ordinances of the Township of Cumru. Commercial Solar Energy Systems, as defined under Article 2 of this Zoning Ordinance, will be considered a community utility, private utility, or public utility, and therefore, subject to the requirements of Sections 852.1, 852.2, or 852.3, respectively, as applicable. Other types include community utilities subject to Section 852.1, private utilities subject to Section 852.2, and public utilities subject to Section 852.3, with specific conditions outlined for each. For example, private utilities must comply with removal and bonding requirements (Section 852.2(A)(18)), and public utilities designated by the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission must comply with both Section 852.2 and 852.3 as applicable.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems shall be located on a lot or parcel in a manner that avoids directing concentrated solar radiation or glare onto any adjacent property or public way. Commercial Solar Energy Systems, as defined under Article 2 of this Zoning Ordinance, will be considered a community utility, private utility, or public utility, and therefore, subject to the requirements of Sections 852.1, 852.2, or 852.3, respectively, as applicable. Other options include community utilities subject to Section 852.1, private utilities subject to Section 852.2, and public utilities subject to Section 852.3, with additional conditions depending on designation by the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission.

No part of a Ground-Mounted Commercial Solar Energy System or its support structures shall exceed a height of twenty (20) feet. This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems that serve as the principal use of any parcel and provide power primarily for off-site use by multiple users, and are considered community, private, or public utilities. Other categories such as Accessory Solar Energy Systems have different height limits (e.g., 15 feet for ground-mounted accessory systems), but these do not apply to Public Utility Solar Energy Systems.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems, as defined under Article 202, are considered a community utility, private utility, or public utility, and are subject to the requirements of Sections 852.1, 852.2, or 852.3, respectively. Section 721(A)(21) requires that "a clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations." No display advertising is permitted except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer of the system. Other options include community utilities subject to Section 852.1, private utilities subject to Section 852.2, and public utilities subject to Section 852.3. Section 852.3(D) states that if a commercial energy system is designated as a public utility by the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission but not entirely exempt from municipal zoning requirements, then the requirements of 852.2 apply in addition to those in 852.3, as legally applicable.

Section 852.2:(A) includes the GI Zoning District location restriction and the requirement of special exception approval for private utility systems, which by extension applies to public utility solar systems as well per Sections 852.2 and 852.3. Specifically, it states: 'With the exceptions of the GI Zoning District location restriction (Section 852.2:(A)), the requirement of special exception approval (Section 852.2:(A)), and the minimum lot size requirement of 25 acres (Section 852.2:(A)(1)), all of the requirements provided in under Section 852.2 shall apply to all community utility uses.' Section 721(A) clarifies that Commercial Solar Energy Systems are considered community, private, or public utilities and are subject to Sections 852.1, 852.2, or 852.3 respectively. Other options include community utilities subject to Section 852.1, private utilities subject to Section 852.2, and public utilities subject to Section 852.3, with additional conditions such as bonding, emergency services coordination, and utility company approval for grid connection. No other districts are explicitly named for special use or similar approval for public utility solar systems.

The ordinance states: 'The surface area of the arrays of a ground mounted PSES, regardless of the mounted angle of any solar panels, shall be considered impervious and calculated in the lot coverage of the lot on which the system is located. The PSES shall not exceed the maximum lot coverage requirements of the underlying zoning district 60% I1.' This means the maximum land coverage allowed for a Principal Solar Energy System is 60 percent of the lot area in the I-1 Industrial zoning district. No other maximum land coverage values for PSES are provided.

Section II.H.12 Decommissioning requires that "The PSES owner is required to notify Curwensville Borough immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation." Abandonment is defined as "no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months." The owner "shall then have twelve (12) months in which to dismantle and remove the PSES including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto... The owner shall also restore the land to its original condition, including forestry plantings of the same type/variety and density as the original." If the owner fails, "Curwensville Borough may complete the decommissioning and land restoration at the owner’s expense." Additionally, "At the time of issuance of the permit for the construction of the PSES, the owner shall provide financial security... to secure the expense of dismantling and removing said PSES and restoration of the land." The financial security must be maintained at no less than 100% of decommissioning costs and may be in the form of bonds, letters of credit, or other acceptable forms. The Borough may take necessary measures to complete decommissioning if the owner fails to do so within the prescribed period. Other sections address permit requirements, design, installation, and enforcement but do not provide additional decommissioning specifics.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "PSES shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high-security fence." This fencing requirement applies to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), which are defined as systems "principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use." The fencing requirement is part of the design and installation standards, which also include setbacks, height restrictions, screening, and lighting controls. Other conditions for PSES include lot size minimums, setbacks of not less than 100 feet to any property line, height limits of 20 feet for ground-mounted systems, and maintenance access roads. The ordinance distinguishes PSES from Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES) and Small Solar Energy Facilities, which have different regulations and do not have this fencing requirement explicitly stated.

The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). It states: 'All PSES shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures or roadways.' The applicant 'has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have a significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation.' Additionally, 'Glare from the Solar Facility determined by Curwensville Borough to be a nuisance to adjacent properties or roadways shall be prohibited. The Solar facility owners shall remediate any nuisance glare claims within six (6) months of being notified.' These glare restrictions apply specifically to PSES, which are defined as systems 'principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use.' Other options mentioned in the ordinance include Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), which are primarily for on-site use and are not subject to these glare restrictions, and Small Solar Energy Facilities, which are accessory to principal uses and have separate conditions but no explicit glare restrictions stated.

Under section G.3. Height Restrictions, the ordinance states: 'Ground mounted PSES shall not exceed 20 feet in height.' It also states that 'A Solar Energy system mounted on a roof shall conform to the height of the Zone where the Solar Energy system is installed.' The 20 feet limit applies explicitly to ground-mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems. The units are feet.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'Lot Size: A PSES shall require a lot size of not less than ten (10) acres.' This is a minimum lot size requirement specifically for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), which are defined as systems primarily used to supply power off-site. The unit 'acres' is the standard area measurement used here.

Noise from a PSES shall not exceed 55dBA, as measured at the property line. This is explicitly stated in section II.H.7: 'Noise from a PSES shall not exceed 55dBA, as measured at the property line.' The unit dBA is the standard unit for noise level measurement.

Section 318.5 provides decommissioning requirements for Principal Use Solar Energy Systems (PSES). It states: 'No construction of the PSES shall be undertaken until the owner shall have provided the Township with a Bond or other financial security... to secure the estimated expense of dismantling and removing said PSES, and restoration of the land for agricultural or other reasonable use...'; 'an affidavit... affirming a lease agreement with a decommissioning clause... that shall apply to Successors and Assigns'; 'a new engineer’s estimate of cost for decommissioning... shall be submitted every ten (10) years'; 'The PSES owner is required to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation'; 'If the PSES owner fails to dismantle and/or remove the PSES within eighteen (18) months of cessation or abandonment, the Township may complete the decommissioning and recover the costs by use of the Bond or other security or by other legal remedies permitted by law'; and 'If a ground mounted PSES is removed, any earth disturbance... must be returned to an environmentally stable condition.'

summary: For Ground-mounted Solar Energy Systems exceeding 35 kW output (which includes Solar Energy System (Large)), system components and earth disturbance shall not be closer than fifty (50) feet from any environmentally sensitive areas, including but not limited to wetlands, ponds and streams, so long as it can be shown that the project is in compliance with the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) regulations if applicable. The ordinance does not explicitly specify setbacks from public conservation lands, natural resource protection areas, or preservation areas by those exact terms, but 'environmentally sensitive areas' may encompass such areas. Other setback options include: for systems not exceeding 35 kW, a 50-foot setback from environmentally sensitive areas; and setbacks from property lines (30 feet for small systems, 100 feet for systems exceeding 35 kW), which are outside the scope of this request.
section: 433.6. Setback Requirements for Solar Energy Systems.

summary: Section 433.8.B states: 'Ground-mounted Solar Energy Systems (Medium & Large): The Board of Supervisors may impose screening requirements for systems in locations that would create a negative visual impact.' Section 433.12.A requires: 'In addition, vegetative screening shall be installed as determined by the Board of Supervisors' for all Solar Energy Systems that exceed 35 kW output. Screening is not required for building-mounted or roof-mounted systems (433.8.A). The ordinance distinguishes between systems not exceeding 35 kW (permitted as accessory uses) and those exceeding 35 kW (conditional uses) in Rural Residential and Industrial Districts, with the latter subject to these screening and vegetative buffer requirements.

Said information shall be depicted within an area no more than thirty-six (36) square inches in size. No display shall be artificially lighted.' This applies to all Solar Energy Systems, including those defined as Solar Energy System (Large) with rated capacity greater than two hundred (200) kilowatts per hour.

Ground-mounted Solar Energy Systems exceeding 35 kW output shall be permitted in the Rural Residential and Industrial Zoning Districts as a Conditional Use on any property. The text states: 'B. summary: Section 490.G requires the applicant to remove the wind and/or solar farm, or individual wind turbines and solar panels, within twelve (12) months after the end of the useful life, presumed if no electricity is generated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months. Removal includes elimination of wind turbines and solar panels, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations to a depth of 36 inches, and any other associated facilities. Disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored. An independent and certified Professional Engineer shall estimate the total cost of removal and net removal costs, with estimates submitted after the first year of operation and every fifth year thereafter. The applicant shall post and maintain removal funds equal to net removal costs, with a minimum of twenty-five percent (25%) of removal costs, in the form of a performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit, corporate guarantee, or other financial assurance acceptable to the Township. If the applicant fails to complete removal within the prescribed period, the landowner has six (6) months to complete removal. If neither completes removal, the Township may take necessary measures to complete removal using the removal funds. The escrow agent releases funds when removal is satisfactorily completed or upon written municipal approval to implement the removal plan.

Section 404.P.1 requires that "Solar energy panels shall be designed and located in order to minimize reflective glare towards any adjoining use and/or road." This applies to alternate energy systems, which include solar energy systems. Section 490 governs Wind and/or Solar Farms as conditional uses and requires compliance with all applicable regulations in the Ordinance, including Section 404.P. Therefore, solar farms must abide by the glare restriction to minimize reflective glare. Other related requirements in Section 404.P include installation by certified installers, limits on advertising, size and height restrictions for storage buildings, roof-mounted and ground-mounted solar system requirements, and vegetative screening to serve as a barrier to visibility and glare when located within the front yard behind the building setback line.

Section 404.E.2 states: 'ground-mounted solar panels shall not exceed a height of 20 feet at the highest point of the structure.' This is the most restrictive maximum height explicitly provided for solar panels within the context of Solar Farms under Section 490. Other height limits include 50 feet for wind turbines (Section 404.E.3 and 490.D.15), but since the question focuses on Solar Farms and solar panels, the 20 feet limit applies. Units are feet as specified in the ordinance.

Section 490.D.18 states: 'Audible sound from a wind and/or solar farm shall not exceed fifty (55) dBA, as measured at the following minimum distances...'. This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for Solar Farms under Section 490. The measurement standard referenced is AWEA Standard 2.1 - 1989. No other numerical noise limits are provided for Solar Farms in this section.

Wind turbines shall be setback the following distances as measured from the center of the wind turbine base to the nearest point of the respective feature listed below: Adjoining road right-of-way: 1.5 times turbine height. Other setback distances include: Occupied building on site: Turbine height plus ten feet; Above ground utility line right-of-way: Turbine height plus ten feet; Adjoining property: 1.5 times turbine height.

Section 404.P.7.d. requires that "Unless no other suitable location exists upon a property, a solar energy system, or part thereof, may be located within the front yard provided it is located behind the required building setback line and vegetative screening is provided to serve as a barrier to visibility and glare, subject to the following standards: i. All vegetative materials shall reach a minimum height of six feet above finished grade within two years of planting. However, all vegetative materials used for screening of an industrial use shall be six feet at initial planting. ii. The vegetative screen shall be permanently maintained in order to ensure effective screening and replaced when necessary. iii. The vegetative screen must be comprised of plant material that will provide a minimum opacity of 80% year-round. One of the following arrangements shall be utilized: [a] Screen planting shall contain three staggered rows of vegetative material. This screen planting shall consist of one row of fast-growing needled evergreens spaced not more than 12 feet on center and two rows of deciduous trees, with a minimum height potential of 20 feet, spaced not more than 25 feet on center. [b] Screen planting shall contain two staggered rows of vegetative material. Seventy-five percent shall be fast-growing needled evergreens planted 10 feet on center and staggered for effective screening. The remaining 25% shall be deciduous trees planted in staggered clusters with 25 feet being the maximum spacing between trees. [c] Screen planting shall contain two staggered rows of vegetative material. Seventy-five percent shall be fast-growing needled evergreens planted 10 feet on center and staggered for effective screening. Fifteen percent shall be deciduous trees planted in staggered clusters 25 feet on center. The remaining 10% shall be staggered shrub masses used as understory plants and in combination with deciduous tree clusters. The maximum spacing for shrubs shall be four feet on center. The deciduous trees and shrubs are suggested to break up the straight-line planting of one type of plant material. iv. Prior to issuance of a zoning permit, a sketch plan showing the proposed arrangement, placement, species and size of all screen planting material shall be submitted for approval to the Dickinson Township Zoning Officer. Only those specific plant arrangements listed above in Section 404.O.7.D.3.a.-c. of this Ordinance may be used for vegetative screening. All such plant materials shall comply with Section 321 of this Ordinance." Section 490 (Wind and/or Solar Farms) references compliance with all applicable regulations in the Ordinance but does not itself explicitly enact vegetative buffer or screening requirements.

Section 490.D requires that "a clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all at-grade transformers and substations." Additionally, "visible, reflective, colored objects, such as flags, reflectors, or tape shall be placed on the anchor points of each guy wire and along each guy wire up to a height of ten feet from the ground." These requirements apply specifically to wind and/or solar farms as part of the conditional use standards. No other explicit signage requirements for Solar Farms are stated in Section 490.

Solar farms are permitted by conditional use in the Conservation Zone (C) and Mixed Use Zone (MU), subject to the requirements of Section 490 of this Ordinance and the review procedures of Section 805. Specifically, Section 200.D.5 states: 'Wind and solar farms, subject to the requirements of Section 490 of this Ordinance.' Section 203.D.8 states: 'Solar farms (specifically excluding wind farms), subject to the requirements of Section 490 of this Ordinance.' Section 490.A and 490.B confirm that within the (C) and (MU) Zones, solar farms are permitted by conditional use, requiring the applicant to meet all applicable regulations and burden of proof. Other zones such as Agricultural (A), Low Density Residential (LDR), and Light Industrial (LI) only mention alternative or accessory energy systems permitted by right, not utility-scale solar farms. No solar overlay districts are included in this determination.
section: SECTION 200 – CONSERVATION ZONE (C); SECTION 203 – MIXED USE ZONE (MU); Section 490 – Wind and/or Solar Farms

summary: Wind turbines shall be setback the following distances as measured from the center of the wind turbine base to the nearest point of the respective feature listed below: Above ground utility line right-of-way: Turbine height plus ten feet. Note: This setback is explicitly stated for wind turbines within wind and/or solar farms. Additionally, on-site electrical transmission and power lines connected to or associated with the alternate energy system that are not contained within a building shall be located underground, effectively eliminating overhead line setbacks for those lines.

Section 490.C requires the applicant to prepare and submit a narrative and mapping describing the proposed wind and/or solar farm including: "1. an overview of the project; 2. the project location; 3. the approximate generating capacity of the wind and/or solar farm; 4. the approximate number, representative types and height or range of heights of wind turbines and/or solar panels to be constructed, including their generating capacity, dimensions and respective manufacturers; 5. a description of accessory facilities; 6. an affidavit or similar evidence of agreement between the property owner(s) and the applicant demonstrating that the applicant has the permission of the property owner(s) to apply for necessary permits for construction and operation of the wind and/or solar farm; 7. a listing and map of the properties on which the proposed wind and/or solar farm will be located, and the properties adjacent to where the wind and/or solar farm will be located; 8. a site plan showing the planned location of each wind turbine, solar panel, property lines, setback lines, access road and turnout locations, substation(s), electrical cabling from the wind and/or solar farm to the substation(s), ancillary equipment, buildings, and structures, including permanent meteorological towers, associated transmission lines, and layout of all structures within the geographical boundaries of any applicable setback." These requirements apply to solar farms as defined in Section 490, which are permitted by conditional use in the (C) and (MU) zones. No other sections explicitly require visual impact assessment for solar farms of this scale. Section 404 applies to alternate energy systems as accessory uses and does not impose such narrative or mapping requirements for commercial solar farms. Glare restrictions are excluded from consideration per instructions.

The ordinance requires that "mechanical equipment associated with and necessary for the operation of the solar energy system shall be screened from any adjacent property that is residentially zoned or used for residential purposes" using "shrubbery, trees, or other plant materials that provide a visual screen." Additionally, "the design of solar energy systems shall, to the extent reasonably possible, use materials, colors, textures, screening, and landscaping that will blend the facility into the natural setting and existing environment." These requirements apply to solar energy systems "not the primary use of the property" and include ground-mounted systems. Other requirements include conforming to zoning district area and dimensional regulations, prohibiting ground-mounted systems in front yards, and restrictions on roof-mounted solar panels' placement and height.

Section 949 requires that "The applicant shall submit a plan for the removal of the principal solar energy systems when it becomes functionally obsolete or is no longer in use." It further states that "The principal solar energy system owner is required to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation." The owner "shall be responsible for the removal of the facility within twelve (12) months from the date the applicant ceases use of the facility or the facility becomes obsolete." This applies to principal solar energy systems, which are solar energy systems utilized as a principal use, consistent with utility-scale solar energy systems. Other provisions in Section 949 include design, installation, lot coverage, fencing, signage, and glare prevention requirements, but these do not pertain to decommissioning. Section 602.4.E addresses accessory alternative energy systems, which are not the focus here.

Section 949 states that "All mechanical equipment of principal solar energy systems including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self‐locking gate, and provided with screening in accordance with Section 607.5 of this Chapter." This fencing requirement applies to principal solar energy systems, which are solar energy systems utilized as a principal use. Other conditions in Section 949 include compliance with industry standards, lot coverage considerations, underground placement of utility lines where feasible, prevention of reflective glare, height regulations for roof-mounted systems, visible warning signs on transformers or fences, and a removal plan for obsolete systems.

Section 949 applies to principal solar energy systems and includes the glare restriction: 'all principal solar energy systems shall be designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare toward any inhabited buildings on adjacent properties as well as adjacent street rights-of-way.' Other conditions in Section 949 include compliance with industry standards, lot coverage considerations, fencing and screening requirements, warning signs, and removal plans. Section 602.4.E addresses accessory alternative energy systems and states: 'Glare from solar voltaic installations are to be minimized with the use of anodized or similar finishes.'

Where ground mounted systems are permitted, all equipment shall be setback two (2) feet for every one (1) foot in height of panel height in addition to the prescribed setback for accessory structures in the identified zoning district. No other multiplier values are given. The prescribed setback for accessory structures is an additional static distance that must be added to the multiplied value. This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems as ground-mounted photovoltaic systems permitted in non-residential zoning districts. Screening requirements apply when installed adjacent to residential uses or property lines unless the installation is more than 500 feet from the nearest residential use or property line. No ground mounted systems shall be installed in a front yard.

summary: Section 23050.F (Decommissioning) requires that "The landowner or facility operator shall complete decommissioning of the alternative energy facility within (12) twelve months after the end of its useful life," defined as "no energy is generated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months." It further requires that "The removal of the above-ground alternative energy facility components shall be completed within twelve (12) months of decommissioning" and that "All disturbed earth shall be restored, graded and re-seeded." If the landowner or operator fails to complete decommissioning, "the Township may take such measures as necessary to complete decommissioning." Section 23050.2 applies to "Alternative energy facilities as a principal use, which may include geothermal heat pumps, solar energy systems, wind turbines and/or wind energy facilities" and states they "are permitted by conditional use within the AG, I-1, I-2 and BP Zoning Districts, subject to the provisions specified under Section 23050.2." It also requires compliance with all applicable regulations, including "landscaping, lighting, noise standards, off-street parking, off-street loading and signage," and that such facilities "shall be located, designed and operated to serve other uses within a regional service area, which is supplied by an energy service provider regulated by the Public Utility Commission and Public Utility Code."

The required setback distance shall be measured from the closest part of the alternative energy facility and/or any appurtenant structures and/or facilities associated with their operation to the property line and street right-of-way line. This applies to alternative energy facilities as a principal use, which may include solar energy systems intended for offsite electricity generation or sale. Other setback provisions, such as a multiplier of 1.1 times the system height from roads, apply only to accessory solar energy systems and not to principal use facilities.

Other requirements for principal use facilities include compliance with "all applicable regulations of this Zoning Ordinance and other ordinance adopted by East Lampeter Township, including but not limited to, the requirements for landscaping, lighting, noise standards, off-street parking, off-street loading and signage" (Section 23050.2.B.3).

All such principal uses shall be permitted by conditional use, subject to Sections 23050.2 and 25080 of this Zoning Ordinance." Accessory uses are generally permitted by right in many districts, and local service area facilities are permitted by right in I-1, I-2, and BP districts. Other uses such as manure digesters require conditional use in AG, I-1, and I-2. The relevant conditional use provisions are found in Sections 23050.2 and 25080.
