summary: Section 1904. 8 Screening and Visibility requires that 'Ground -mounted Systems shall be screened from adjoining residential uses or zones according to the standards found in Part 1901 of this chapter.' There is an exception: 'Screening from residential uses shall not be required in the A- 1 Agricultural, PRO Professional Office, O -A Office - Apartment, C -L Commercial Limited, C -G Commercial General, CPL Commercial Park Limited and IP Industrial Park districts.' Building-mounted systems on a sloped roof are not required to be screened.

Section 1904. 11 Signage states: 'No signage or graphic content may be displayed on the solar photovoltaic system except the manufacturer's badge, safety information and equipment specification information. Said information shall be depicted within an area no more than thirty-six ( 36) square inches in size.' This applies to solar photovoltaic systems up to 3,000 kilowatts at non-residential locations as defined in the ordinance.

Section 1904.9 Impervious Lot Coverage states that "the surface area of any ground-mounted system, regardless of the mounted angle of any portion of the system, is considered impervious surface and shall be calculated as part of the property lot coverage limitations for the zoning district," except where the system is mounted above existing impervious surface. Ground-mounted systems complying with all of the following conditions shall not be considered impervious lot coverage: (1) Projects where earth disturbance and grading activities are minimized and where natural vegetative cover is preserved and/or restored; (2) Utilization of low impact construction techniques must be used, referring to BMP 5.6.1, 5.6.2, and 5.6.3 from the PA Stormwater Best Management Practices Manual; (3) Vegetative cover must have a minimum uniform 90% perennial vegetative cover with a density capable of resisting accelerated erosion and sedimentation; (4) The individual photovoltaic panels within an "array" are arranged to allow passage of runoff and growth of vegetation beneath; (5) Ground mounted solar panels supported with structures/foundations require little earth disturbance, assumed to disturb 5% of the total project area; (6) Solar panels must be situated on slopes of 10% or less; (7) The lowest vertical clearance of the solar "array" should be 10 feet or less from the ground surface but must be adequate to promote vegetative growth below the array, limiting potential for accelerated erosion along the drip line. Alternate designs may be proposed for review and approval by the Zoning Officer and Township Engineer, with final approval by the Board of Commissioners. These provisions explicitly address soil disturbance, erosion control, and sedimentation prevention for ground-mounted solar photovoltaic systems up to 3,000 kW.

Principal Solar Energy Facilities (PSEF) are permitted as accessory or similar uses in the Mixed-Use (MU) and Commercial (C) districts where they may be mounted on building rooftops or constructed within parking lots. Specifically, Section 1001.1.KK and 1001.3.F for MU, and Section 1201.1.BB and 1201.3.N for C, allow PSEFs in these forms "in accordance with the provisions of Section 1827 - Accessory Solar Energy Facilities, with the exception that the power generation limits of Section 1827.8 shall not apply." Outside these districts, PSEFs are permitted only as principal uses by conditional use in the Industrial (I) and Utility (U) districts, with a minimum lot size of twenty (20) acres, as stated in Section 1301.3.1 and 1306.7. The ordinance clarifies that "PSEF shall be considered as principal use structures and the generation of energy as a principal use unless all provisions for an Accessory Solar Energy Facility are met."

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Principal Solar Energy Facilities (PSEF). It requires the PSEF owner to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of operation, with abandonment presumed if no electricity is generated for twelve (12) continuous months. The owner then has twelve (12) months to dismantle and remove the PSEF including all solar related equipment or appurtenances. If the owner fails, the municipality may complete decommissioning at the owner's expense. A Decommissioning Agreement must be executed and approved by the Township before final plan release. Decommissioning includes removal of all structures, equipment, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations to a depth of 36 inches, and restoration of disturbed earth unless waived by the landowner. An independent Pennsylvania certified Professional Engineer must estimate total decommissioning costs plus ten percent (10%), with estimates submitted after the first year of operation and every fifth year thereafter. The Facility Owner or Operator must post and maintain Decommissioning Funds in an approved form such as a performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit, or corporate guarantee. If neither the Facility Owner or Operator nor the landowner complete decommissioning within prescribed periods, the Township may take necessary measures to complete it. The escrow agent releases funds only when decommissioning is satisfactorily completed or upon written municipal approval. These requirements apply specifically to PSEFs as defined in the ordinance and do not apply to smaller or accessory solar energy systems.

Applicants shall provide a glare analysis report prepared and sealed by an engineer licensed in the Commonwealth of PA demonstrating that glare shall not be projected onto any public street or any building on a property other than the one whereupon the system is located, or all solar panels shall be equipped with anti-reflective coatings.
section: Article XIII, Section 1306.7 - Conditional Use performance regulations for Principal Solar Energy Facilities

summary: The minimum lot size for a Principal Solar Energy Facility (PSEF) shall be twenty (20) acres. This is explicitly stated in Section 1306.7: 'Lot Size: The minimum lot size for a PSEF shall be twenty (20) acres.' The unit 'acres' is the standard area measurement used. This minimum lot size applies specifically to PSEFs as defined in the ordinance, which are solar energy systems principally used to capture solar energy and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use. No other minimum lot size values for PSEFs are provided in the text.

All components of a PSEF shall be set back 75 feet from all property lines. This is stated explicitly in Section 1306.7: 'Setbacks: All components of a PSEF shall be set back 75 feet from all property lines.' No other setback distances or multipliers based on height or other factors are provided for PSEFs. Other solar energy systems such as Accessory Solar Energy Facilities (ASEF) have setback requirements tied to zoning district side and rear yard setbacks but these apply only to smaller, non-commercial systems and are not relevant to PSEFs.

Section 1306.7 states: 'Screening and landscaping shall be provided for all uses as established in Section 1709, Landscaping, Screening and Buffering, of the Township Zoning Ordinance.' It further provides that 'No trees or other landscaping otherwise required by the municipal ordinances or attached as a condition of approval of any plan, application, or permit may be removed for the installation or operation of a PSEF, unless authorized as part of the Conditional Use Decision.' This applies to Principal Solar Energy Facilities (PSEF), which are defined as 'An area of land or other area used for a solar collection system principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power, and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use.' PSEFs are permitted by Conditional Use in the Industrial (I) District and Utility (U) District. Other options for PSEFs include rooftop-mounted and parking lot-constructed facilities in Mixed-Use (MU) and Commercial (C) Districts, which follow provisions of Section 1827 (Accessory Solar Energy Facilities) but without the 50 kW power generation limit. However, explicit screening or vegetative buffer requirements are only detailed for PSEFs under Section 1306.7 in the Industrial and Utility Districts.

All Conditional Use applications for a Principal Solar Energy Facility (PSEF) shall meet the following standards and criteria, including that a PSEF "shall be considered a Land Development and is subject to the requirements of the East Pikeland Township Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance. In addition, all requirements of Township Code Chapter 22 — Grading Erosion and Sediment Control and Stormwater Management Ordinance shall be met." This explicitly imposes soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements on PSEF developers. Other relevant provisions include setbacks, screening, design and installation standards, submission requirements, certifications, inspections, decommissioning, and use of public roads, but these do not pertain to soil, erosion, or sediment control.

Conditional Use: Principal Solar Energy Facilities (PSEF), which are facilities used for principal use solar energy generation except as provided in the Mixed Use (MU) and Commercial (C) Zoning districts, shall be permitted only in the Industrial (I) District and Utility (U) District by Conditional Use in accordance with this Section and Article XX Conditional Use Process. In the MU District, a Principal Solar Energy Facility Constructed Within a Parking Lot requires Conditional Use approval (Section 1001.3.F). In the C District, a Principal Solar Energy Facility Constructed Within a Parking Lot also requires Conditional Use approval (Section 1201.3.N). Rooftop PSEFs in MU and C districts are permitted uses with exceptions to power generation limits. The minimum lot size for a PSEF in the I and U Districts is twenty (20) acres.
section: Section VI and Section VII (Article XIII of the East Pikeland Township Zoning Ordinance)

summary: Section (13) Vacation, abandonment and/or decommissioning requires that "a solar PV system including its solar PV related equipment must be removed within 12 months of the date of discontinuation and/or abandonment or upon termination of the useful life of the solar PV system." Discontinuation/abandonment is presumed if the system "has been disconnected from the net metering grid for a period of six continuous months without being connected to a battery system or has not produced electricity for a period of six months." Removal includes "removal of all structural and electrical parts of the ground or building-mounted system and any associated facilities or equipment and removal of all net metering equipment." If the owner fails to remove or repair the system within six months, the Borough may remove it and charge the owner, with unpaid costs constituting a lien on the property. This applies to both ground-mounted and building-mounted systems. Other relevant provisions include permit requirements before construction (Section 14) and performance requirements (Section 12).

Ground-mounted systems may not exceed 10 feet in height, measured from the tallest part of the structure when installed. This is stated in section (7)(b)[2] under Height restrictions. Other height restrictions include: building-mounted systems on sloped roofs must not exceed the highest point of the roof; building-mounted systems on flat roofs may not exceed six feet above the roof; and building-mounted systems on sloped roofs facing the front yard must be installed at the same angle as the roof with a maximum distance of 18 inches perpendicular to the roof. The 10 feet limit applies notwithstanding the height limitations of the zoning district and is the most restrictive numerical value for ground-mounted systems, which would typically include utility-scale solar energy systems. The units for this restriction are feet.

No signage or graphic content may be displayed on the solar PV system except the manufacturer's badge, safety information and equipment specification information. Said information shall be depicted within an area no more than 36 square inches in size.

Ground-mounted systems are subject to the accessory use or structure yard requirements in the zoning district, with required yards measured from the lot line to the nearest part of the system; no part of the system shall extend into the required yard due to tracking or adjustments. Setback requirements shall not apply to ground-mounted, freestanding photovoltaic arrays, but a clear, brush-free area of 10 feet (3,048 millimeters) shall be required for ground-mounted photovoltaic arrays.

Ground mounted systems shall provide a buffer yard in accordance with § 130-41. Ground-mounted systems are permitted only in the rear yard and are subject to the accessory use or structure yard requirements in the zoning district. Setback requirements shall not apply to ground-mounted, freestanding photovoltaic arrays. A clear, brush-free area of 10 feet (3,048 millimeters) shall be required for ground-mounted photovoltaic arrays.

Solar energy systems shall be designed and installed to minimize glare or reflection onto adjacent properties, public streets, and rights-of-way. The applicant shall provide documentation demonstrating that the proposed solar energy system will not create excessive glare or reflection. This applies to solar energy systems permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts, including ground-mounted systems that shall not exceed 20 feet in height in nonresidential districts. The systems must comply with all applicable Borough, State, and Federal laws, codes, and regulations, and be maintained in good working order.

The ordinance states that "A solar energy system is permitted in all zoning districts as an accessory to a residential or a commercial use" (§ 1325(A)). However, it also specifies that a solar energy system "shall not be used for the generation of power for the sale of energy to others," except for the occasional sale of excess power to the local utility company (§ 1325(C)). This effectively prohibits utility-scale solar energy systems intended for offsite electricity generation or sale in all districts. Other provisions allow solar energy systems to be roof-mounted and/or ground-mounted (§ 1325(B)) and treat solar collectors as exempt from height regulations (§ 1308).

Ground-mounted solar energy systems "shall be screened from adjacent residential properties and public streets by landscaping, fencing, or other screening methods approved by the Zoning Officer." Mechanical equipment associated with solar energy systems "shall be screened from any adjacent property that is residentially zoned or used for residential dwelling purposes" by "shrubbery, trees, or other plant materials which provide a visual screen." A decorative fence is also an option that "shall meet the requirements of this Section."

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). It requires "an affidavit, or similar evidence, signed by the property owner and the PSES facility owner affirming a lease agreement with a decommissioning clause (or similar) and a successors and assignees clause." The decommissioning clause must provide "sufficient financial security: including a cash deposit, surety bond, irrevocable letter of credit, cashier’s check, or escrow account from a federal or Commonwealth chartered lending institute naming both the property owner and Township as holders to dismantle and remove the PSES, including all solar-related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, electrical components, roads and other associated facilities from the property." The successors and assignees clause must bind successors and assigns to the lease agreement. The PSES owner must notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of operation, with abandonment presumed if no electricity is generated for twelve (12) continuous months without remedial action. If the owner fails to dismantle and/or remove the PSES within eighteen (18) months of cessation or abandonment, the Township may complete decommissioning at the property owner's expense. The PSES owner must post a bond when applying, "in an amount determined by the Township's Engineer, to ensure the proper decommissioning." During operation, a new engineer's estimate of decommissioning costs must be submitted every 10 years, and a revised surety provided to the Township in the amount of 150% of the new estimate. These requirements are specific to PSES and do not apply to Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES).

All ground-mounted PSES shall be completely enclosed by fencing with a locking gate. Current NEC code requires a minimum six-foot-high fence with barbed wire or a seven-foot-high fence. A perimeter fence shall be placed between the buffer screening and solar panels. Street buffer screening shall consist of slat fencing or shrubs, six feet to eight feet high when mature, planted every fifteen (15) feet of property abutting a public right-of-way. Residential buffer screening may be slat fencing or a row of evergreen conifers or broadleaf evergreens spaced to achieve a continuous visual barrier reaching six (6) feet to eight (8) feet in height within two years of planting. Screening may be a combination of plantings and/or structures with prior approval by the Township. Reasonable modifications to these requirements may be requested through Article 8C, Modifications.

summary: Article 7 A (12) states: "All PSES shall be situated to eliminate concentrated glare onto nearby structures or roadways." This glare restriction applies explicitly to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), which are defined in Article 4 as "an area of land or other area used for a solar collection system principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use." No other specific glare restrictions for PSES are mentioned. For comparison, Article 6 A (6) states that "All ASES shall be situated to eliminate concentrated glare onto nearby structures or roadways," but this applies only to Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), which are typically smaller or residential systems.

Ground-mounted PSES solar panels shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet in height. Roof-mounted PSES shall be subject to the maximum height regulations specified for buildings within the applicable zoning district. The ordinance explicitly states: 'Ground-mounted PSES solar panels shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet in height.' and 'PSES mounted on roofs of any building shall be subject to the maximum height regulations specified for buildings within the applicable zoning district.' The unit for the height restriction is feet.

Ancillary and support buildings/facilities "shall be located at the center of the solar energy system so as to minimize noise (noise levels shall be kept below 85 dBA at the source) and visual impacts to adjacent properties." This is the only explicit maximum noise level restriction for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) in the ordinance. The unit dBA refers to A-weighted decibels, a standard measure of noise level.

PSES shall comply with the following setback requirements: Building setbacks of the applicable zoning districts, except adjacent to any residential district (R-1, R-2, R-3) or parcel with an existing residential structure, the solar panels must follow a minimum fifty (50) - foot setback while the fencing shall comply with the setbacks of the underlying zoning district. If the PSES occupies two or more adjacent properties, setbacks between the adjacent properties shall be waived along the shared property boundaries so that the PSES may be installed continuously and make the most efficient use of the project area.

summary: Section 305.54(d) states: 'The total coverage of a lot with freestanding solar panels cannot exceed the greater of 50% lot coverage or the maximum allowable coverage for the district in which they are located.' This sets a maximum land coverage limit for utility-scale solar energy systems such as Urban Solar Farms. The coverage is expressed as a percentage of lot coverage, not an absolute area value.

Urban Solar Farms shall be permitted in M-1, M-2, and 1-P Districts, and in W-M as a conditional use, in accordance with the following regulations: (f) The following requirements shall be met for decommissioning: 1. Solar farms which have not been in active and continuous service for a period of one (1) year shall be removed at the owners or operators expense. 2. The site shall be restored to as natural condition as possible within six (6) months of the removal.

Urban Solar Farms shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access at a height of eight and a half (8.5) feet. Additional requirements include posting manufacturers' or installers' identification and appropriate warning signage, placing on-site power lines underground to the maximum extent practicable, and adhering to setback, height, and coverage requirements of the district. Permit applications must include a descriptive plot plan, evidence of utility notification, property owner permission, and any other relevant studies or approvals. Decommissioning requires removal of inactive solar farms within one year and site restoration within six months.

Freestanding solar panels located on the ground or attached to a framework located on the ground shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in height above the ground (305.54 b). Urban Solar Farms shall adhere to the height requirements of the district in which they are located (305.55 d). The 20 feet limit is the explicit maximum height given for freestanding solar panels, which applies to utility-scale systems such as Urban Solar Farms permitted in M-1, M-2, and W-M districts.

summary: Section 305.55 URBAN SOLAR FARM requires that "the manufacturers' or installers' identification and appropriate warning signage shall be posted at the site in a clearly visible manner." Urban Solar Farms are permitted in M-1, M-2, and 1-P Districts, and conditionally in W-M. Other requirements include perimeter fencing at 8.5 feet, underground placement of on-site power lines to the maximum extent practicable, adherence to setback, height, and coverage requirements of the district, and various permit application and decommissioning conditions.

Urban Solar Farms are permitted uses in M-1 LIGHT MANUFACTURING DISTRICT, M-2 HEAVY MANUFACTURING DISTRICT, and Industrial Park (IP) Districts, but are CONDITIONAL USES in the W-M WATERFRONT MANUFACTURING DISTRICT. The ordinance further details permitting requirements for Urban Solar Farms under section 305.55. No solar overlay districts are included in this analysis.

Commercial solar power generation facilities (utility-scale solar energy systems) are permitted as conditional uses in the RUR Rural District. Additionally, a solar power facility shall be permitted on a property with an existing use as a second principal use, subject to compliance with minimum lot area, setbacks, height, and other land development standards. Accessory structures housing equipment necessary for the operation of the solar power facility are allowed, but other ancillary uses (including business offices greater than 1,000 sq. ft.) are prohibited unless otherwise permitted in the zoning district. The text states: 'solar power generation, commercial' is added as a conditional use in the RUR Rural District, and 'A solar power facility shall be permitted on a property with an existing use subject to the following land development standards...' The ordinance also requires permits for every solar power facility installed in the Borough.

The solar power facility owner and operator shall, at its own expense, complete decommissioning of the solar power facility, or individual components, within (12) twelve months after the end of the useful life of the solar power facility or individual components. The solar power facility or individual components shall be presumed to be at the end of its useful life if no electricity is generated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months. Decommissioning shall include removal of collectors, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations to a depth of thirty-six (36) inches, and any other associated facilities. Disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded, unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored. An independent and certified Professional Engineer shall be retained to estimate the total cost of decommissioning (decommissioning costs) without regard to salvage value of the equipment, and the cost of decommissioning net salvage value of the equipment (net decommissioning costs). Said estimates shall be submitted to the Borough after the first year of operation and every fifth year thereafter. The solar power facility owner or operator, prior to the issuance of a zoning permit, shall provide a financial security bond with the Borough as payee in an amount approved by the Borough Council, but not less than $50,000, from a company and in a form and content acceptable to the Borough Council, to insure the decommissioning within one hundred eighty (180) days of the expiration of the license or lease and/or cessation of use. The bond shall remain in place for as long as the facilities exist at the site. Decommissioning funds may be in the form of a performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit, corporate guarantee or other form of financial assurance as may be acceptable to the Borough. If the solar power facility owner or operator fails to complete decommissioning within the prescribed time period, then the landowner shall have eighty (180) days to complete decommissioning. If neither the solar power facility owner or operator, nor the landowner complete decommissioning within the prescribed periods, then the Borough may take such measures as necessary to complete decommissioning. The escrow agent shall release the decommissioning funds when the solar power facility owner or operator has demonstrated and the Borough concurs that decommissioning has been satisfactorily completed, or upon written approval of the Borough in order to implement the decommissioning plan.

Section 847.3.H states: 'The applicant shall provide details about anticipated glare from the facility, including the time of day, time of year and direction of peak glare periods and document how potential nuisances to area properties and on public roads will be controlled.' This applies to commercial solar power generation facilities, which are permitted only in certain districts and require a permit. The ordinance includes other standards such as height limits, setbacks, fencing, landscaping, and compliance with industry standards, but the explicit glare restriction is limited to the requirement for glare details and nuisance control documentation.

Landscaping may be required to screen as much of the solar power facility ground features as possible, the fence surrounding the support structure, and any other ground level features (such as a building), and in general buffer the solar power facility ground features from neighboring properties. The Borough may permit any combination of existing vegetation, topography, walls, decorative fences or other features instead of landscaping, if the same achieves the same degree of screening as the required landscaping.

Section 847.3 M requires "A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations." It also requires "Visible, reflective, colored objects, such as flags, reflectors, or tape shall be placed on the anchor points of guy wires and along the guy wires up to a height of ten (10) feet from the ground." Section 847.3 N states "No advertising material or signs other than warning, manufacturer and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of structures."

In the RUR Rural District, 'solar power generation, commercial' is added as a conditional use. The ordinance states: 'solar power generation, commercial' shall be permitted only in the districts as provided by the Schedule of Uses. A permit shall be required for every solar power facility installed in the Borough. The text specifies that commercial solar power generation facilities are permitted as conditional uses in the RUR district, implying approval through a permitting process or similar. No other districts or solar overlay districts are mentioned in the provided text.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Solar Energy Facilities (SEFs). It states: 'The SEF owner is required to notify Fairfield Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The SEF shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months.' The SEF owner then has 'eighteen (18) months in which to dismantle and remove the SEF including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations, solar facility connections and other associated facilities in accordance with agreements with landowners and good industry practice.' Materials should be 're-sold or salvaged' where possible, and 'disposed of at facility authorized to dispose of such materials by federal or state law' if not. The site must be restored to its 'pre-existing condition, suitable for its prior use,' unless the landowner authorizes otherwise. Necessary permits must be obtained prior to decommissioning. Financial security is required at the time of SALDO approval, with the SEF Developer providing an estimate of decommissioning costs and posting security of 110% of that estimate. The estimate is updated every three years, with adjustments for inflation and cost changes. The security may be in the form of cash deposit, surety bond, irrevocable letter of credit, cashier's check, or escrow account. A Decommissioning Agreement must be entered into prior to final SALDO approval. These requirements apply specifically to SEFs, which are defined as systems supplying power primarily for off-site use, including ground-mounted principal solar energy systems. The ordinance also separately addresses decommissioning for Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), which must be removed within twelve months of discontinuation or abandonment, but these apply to smaller, primarily on-site use systems.

summary: Solar Arrays shall not be located within fifty (50) feet of Floodways, as identified in the FEMA FIRM mapping. Solar Arrays shall not be located within twenty-five (25) feet from the top of the bank of regulated natural and man-made drainage corridors unless the Township at SALDO approval determines a lesser setback would create less impacts. summary: Section 3, Article 12, subsection 2.B.(6) requires that "Ground mounted SEF shall be screened and buffered in accordance with the following standards." Vegetative buffering "shall be installed around the entire perimeter of the SEF installation, except where Fairfield Township determines that the retention of existing trees within the vegetative buffering area may constitute the required vegetative buffer or where Fairfield Township determines that the solar panels cannot be viewed from a public roadway or residential building." The buffering "shall be selected to provide year-round buffering and shall be of sufficient height, density, and maturity to screen the facility from visibility, as set forth herein within thirty-six months of the installation of the SEF." A combination of "Natural topography and vegetation can serve as a buffer provided that the SEP will not be visible from public roads, public parks or existing residences on surrounding properties." "Earthen berms may not be created to serve as a buffer." Visibility is measured by a photograph standard, and the buffering requirements "shall supersede the provisions of the Fairfield Township Zoning Ordinance and Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance as they may pertain to SEFs."

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Facilities (SEFs). Stormwater runoff from an SEF "shall be managed in accordance with the requirements of the Fairfield Township Stormwater Management Ordinance." The horizontal area of solar panels may be considered a Disconnected Impervious Area ("DIA") only if: "natural vegetative cover is preserved and/or restored utilizing low impact construction techniques from the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection Stormwater Best Management Practices Manual," including "minimizing the total disturbed area, minimizing soil compaction in disturbed areas, and re-vegetating and re-foresting disturbed areas using native species;" and "the vegetative cover has a minimum uniform 70% perennial vegetative cover with a density capable of resisting accelerated erosion and sedimentation." Vegetated areas "shall not be subject to chemical fertilization or herbicide/pesticides application, except for those applications necessary to establish the vegetative cover or to prevent invasive species and in accordance with an approved Erosion and Sediment Control Plan." Agrivoltaics may be used provided that a "written erosion and sediment control plan must be developed for agricultural plowing or tilling activities or a portion of the overall farm conservation plan must identify BMPs used." Additionally, "Any soil exposed during the removal [decommissioning] shall be stabilized in accordance with applicable erosion and sediment control standards," and "Any necessary permits, such as Erosion and Sedimentation and NPDES permits, shall be obtained prior to decommissioning activities." These requirements apply specifically to Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance.

Disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded unless the landowner requests otherwise. An independent and certified Professional Engineer must estimate the total cost of decommissioning and net decommissioning costs, with estimates submitted after the first year of operation and every fifth year thereafter. Prior to permit issuance, the owner/operator must provide a financial security bond of not less than $50,000 to insure decommissioning within one hundred eighty (180) days of license expiration or cessation of use. If the owner/operator fails to decommission, the landowner has 180 days to complete it, and if neither completes decommissioning, the Township may take necessary measures. The escrow agent releases funds when decommissioning is satisfactorily completed or upon Township approval. These requirements apply to commercial solar power generation facilities, which are permitted as conditional uses in RA (Rural Agricultural) and I (Industrial) districts. Accessory solar collectors, which are sized and intended to generate electricity for the principal structure and not for sale, have separate provisions and do not have explicit decommissioning requirements in the provided text.

Section 847.3.C states: 'A fence may be required around the facility or portions of the facility for safety reasons.' This applies to commercial solar power generation facilities, which are defined as facilities 'used for the generation of electricity which is sold on the open market.' The ordinance also includes other related provisions such as setback requirements, landscaping, and access, but the explicit fencing requirement is that a fence may be required for safety reasons. This fencing requirement is part of the standards and design regulations for commercial solar power generation facilities.

Section 847.3.H states: 'The applicant shall provide details about anticipated glare from the facility, including the time of day, time of year and direction of peak glare periods and document how potential nuisances to area properties and on public roads will be controlled.' This applies to commercial solar power generation facilities, which are defined as 'A facility where one (1) or more solar collectors and/or other accessory structures and buildings... are located and are used for the generation of electricity which is sold on the open market.' The ordinance also includes other standards for commercial solar power generation facilities such as height limits, setbacks, fencing, landscaping, and compliance with industry standards, but glare restrictions are specifically detailed in 847.3.H.

Section 847.3.D states: 'Landscaping may be required to screen as much of the solar power facility ground features as possible, the fence surrounding the support structure, and any other ground level features (such as a building), and in general buffer the solar power facility ground features from neighboring properties.' The Township may permit 'any combination of existing vegetation, topography, walls, decorative fences or other features instead of landscaping, if the same achieves the same degree of screening as the required landscaping.'

Section 2, item 13 states: 'Secure perimeter fencing shall be installed around the solar-energy facility. The fencing shall be chain link construction with rubberized coating in neutral earth tone colors such as black or brown and a minimum of six (6) feet in height.' The ordinance defines a solar-energy facility as 'An electric generating facility, with the purpose of electricity supply, consisting of one or more solar panels and other ancillary associated buildings and structures, including substations, meteorological towers, electrical infrastructure, transmission lines, and other appurtenant structures and facilities.' Other conditions for solar-energy facilities include visual impact minimization, noise limits, FAA compliance, underground or out-of-sight transmission lines, and a maximum height of 15 feet.

The ordinance defines a 'Solar-Energy Facility' as an electric generating facility for electricity supply and explicitly states in Section 2, item 10: 'Solar-energy facilities shall not exceed a maximum height of 15 feet, measured from ground level to the tallest point on the facility.' This height restriction applies to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined by the text. No other maximum height values are provided.

Noise from any facility shall not exceed 50 decibels at the lot line adjacent to any lot in a nonresidential zoning district and 30 decibels at the lot line adjacent to any lot in a residential zoning district, unless the adjacent property owner shall have executed a nondisturbance easement, covenant, or consent. The decibel measurement shall be taken at the exterior of any occupied structure on any property other than that occupied by the facility. The units are standard decibels (dBA).

The ordinance requires that solar-energy facilities minimize visual impacts through project planning and proposed mitigation, which may include "buffering, and screening of ground-mounted electrical and control equipment." It also mandates compliance with all zoning provisions including "buffering and landscaping." These requirements apply to solar-energy facilities defined as "an electric generating facility, with the purpose of electricity supply." Additionally, secure perimeter fencing of chain link construction with rubberized coating and a minimum height of six feet is required around the facility.

Solar-Energy Facility shall be permitted as a CONDITIONAL USE only in the AG, MXU, BPK, LI and HI Zoning Districts, provided the following conditions are met. The TABLE OF PRINCIPAL USES reflects these zoning changes, indicating Solar-Energy Facility as a conditional use (Cc) in these districts.

The ordinance requires that for every proposed solar-energy facility, "a viewshed impact analysis illustrating views of the proposed facility from multiple angles" must be submitted to the Township. This is part of the conditions for conditional use approval in the AG, MXU, BPK, LI, and HI Zoning Districts. Additional project information required includes a project narrative, affidavit of permission, property identification, site plan, and design certification. The ordinance defines a Solar-Energy Facility as "an electric generating facility, with the purpose of electricity supply," which includes solar panels and ancillary structures. Other conditions include noise limits, FAA compliance, underground transmission lines, height limits, fencing, and compliance with zoning setbacks and landscaping.

Section 3.1.11 Decommissioning requires the PSES owner to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation, with abandonment presumed if no electricity is generated for twelve (12) continuous months. The owner then has twelve (12) months to dismantle and remove the PSES including all solar related equipment or appurtenances, including buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations and other associated facilities. If the owner fails to dismantle and/or remove the PSES within the established timeframes, the municipality may complete the decommissioning at the owner’s expense. At the time of issuance of the permit for the construction of the PSES, the owner must provide evidence of financial security in the form of a bond, irrevocable letter of credit, or other financial security acceptable to the Township to secure the expense of dismantling and removing the PSES and restoration of the land to its original condition, in the amount of 110% of the estimated decommission cost minus salvageable value. Every 5 years a new engineer’s estimate of probable cost of decommission shall be submitted for approval, and the financial security shall be adjusted accordingly.

Section 3.2.7 Security requires that "All ground-mounted PSES shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate." Additionally, a "clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad mounted transformers and substations and on the fence on the surrounding the PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards."

summary: § 16-105 Decommissioning Alternative Energy Facilities requires that the facility owner or operator shall, at its expense, complete decommissioning of the facility within 12 months after the end of the useful life of the facility. Decommissioning includes removal of solar panels or collectors, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations to a depth of 36 inches, and any other associated facilities. Disturbed earth shall be graded and reseeded. Soil samples shall be collected and analyzed for specified elements, with results submitted to the Township. An independent licensed professional engineer must calculate the estimated cost of complete decommissioning, which shall be submitted after the first year of operation and every fifth year thereafter. The owner/operator must post and maintain decommissioning funds equal to 100% of the decommissioning cost, provided by an approved bonding company or financial institution and held in escrow by the Township. If decommissioning is not completed within the prescribed period, the Township may take necessary measures at the cost of the owner/operator or property owner. The escrow agent releases funds upon satisfactory completion or Township approval.
PSES shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight-foot-high security fence.

All PSES shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures or roadways. The applicant has the burden of proving, either through demonstration or mitigation, that any glare produced does not have a significant adverse impact or cause safety concerns for neighboring properties, neighboring property uses, or vehicular traffic. Of particular concern is lessening the impacts on those surrounding properties where an individual or individuals with sensory processing disorder may reside or visit.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'Ground-mounted PSES shall not exceed 20 feet in height.' This is the maximum structure height allowed for Principal Solar Energy Systems and Facilities (PSES). No other height restrictions for PSES are provided. The unit of measurement is feet.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'The minimum lot size shall be 15 acres.' This applies to Principal Solar Energy Systems and Facilities (PSES), which are defined as systems designed to supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use, including supplying it to a nearby electric utility's grid. The unit for the minimum lot size is acres, a standard area measurement.

Noise from a PSES shall not exceed 55 dBA at the nearest property line measured at a height of both six feet above the ground surface and also 15 feet above the ground surface. The applicant shall provide technical documentation acceptable to the Township indicating the noise standard will always be achieved. This documentation shall be in the form of a sound study completed for another installation by a certified sound consultant.

PSES shall be setback from the side yard property lines a minimum of 75 feet, the rear yard property line 100 feet, and the front yard edge of road right-of-way 250 feet. These setbacks apply to Principal Solar Energy Systems and Facilities designed primarily for off-site use.

PSES shall be setback from the front yard edge of road right-of-way 250 feet. Other setbacks include 75 feet from side yard property lines and 100 feet from rear yard property lines, but only the 250 feet setback applies to roads.

Section 16-103, item 10 requires that "PSES shall be screened from any adjacent property that is residentially zoned or used for residential purposes." The screen "shall consist of plants, evergreens, arborvitae, trees, or similar plants and shrubs which provide an effective visual screen."

§ 16-103, item 6 requires that "appropriate safety/warning signage concerning live voltage shall be placed on or within three feet of any ground-mounted electrical devices, equipment, and/or structures." Additionally, item 7 states "No portion of the PSES shall contain or be used to display advertising." These are the explicit signage-related requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems and Facilities (PSES).

PSES shall be set back from all perennial streams, runs, and/or creeks a minimum of 250 feet. The ordinance does not specify setbacks from lakes, reservoirs, or wetlands. Other setbacks mentioned include 75 feet from side yard property lines, 100 feet from rear yard property lines, and 250 feet from the front yard edge of road right-of-way, but these do not pertain to lakes, reservoirs, streams, rivers, or wetlands.

The owner or operator of a major energy system or the owner(s)/operator(s)/landowner(s) of the land on which the major energy system is located shall complete decommissioning within 12 months after the end of the useful life. Decommissioning shall include the removal of panels, buildings, electrical components, and roads to a depth of 60 inches, as well as any other associated facilities. Foundations shall be removed to a minimum depth of 60 inches below grade or to bedrock if less. The site and any disturbed earth shall be stabilized, graded, and cleared of debris. If the owner(s)/operator(s)/landowner(s) fail to complete decommissioning within the prescribed period, the Township may designate a contractor to complete decommissioning with expenses charged to the violator and/or become a lien against the premises. A bond must be provided to the Township for the cost of decommissioning if the system is not owned by the landowner(s). An independent certified professional engineer shall estimate total decommissioning costs and net decommissioning costs, with possible annual escalators. The owner(s)/operator(s)/landowner(s) shall post and maintain decommissioning funds in an amount equal to or greater than net decommissioning costs, with a performance bond made out to Foster Township. Failure to keep the bond in effect is a violation and may result in ceasing operation until reposted. The escrow agent shall release funds when decommissioning is satisfactorily completed or upon written approval of the Township. The Township may take necessary measures to complete decommissioning if the owner(s)/operator(s)/landowner(s) fail to do so. The entry into and submission of evidence of a participating landowner agreement constitutes consent for the Township to take such action.

Additionally, 'A stormwater management plan and stormwater management facilities shall be provided for all major energy systems in accord with the Township's current stormwater management requirements.'
