summary: Section 1103.05, subsection 9 "Decommissioning" requires the PSES owner to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The PSES shall be presumed abandoned if no electricity is generated for twelve (12) continuous months or if solar production falls below Thirty Percent (30%) of its total engineered production within a two (2) year period, unless the owner can provide evidence of repair. Upon decommissioning, the owner has twelve (12) months to dismantle and remove the PSES including all solar related equipment, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations, and other associated facilities. If the owner fails, the Township may complete the decommissioning and bill the owner. Additionally, subsection 8 "Financial Security" requires the owner to provide financial security of $1,000 per acre at the time of permit issuance to secure dismantling, removal, and land restoration costs. These requirements apply explicitly to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES).

All ground-mounted PSES shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fences with a self-locking gate. Additionally, a clearly visible sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards. The ground-mounted PSES shall not be artificially lighted except to the extent required for safety or applicable federal, state, or local authority.

Section 1103.05.C.5 states that "Ground-mounted PSES shall be screened from adjacent residential Zoning Districts or uses according to applicable standards in the underlying Zoning District." Additionally, Section 1103.05.C.4 encourages PSES owners to "use low-maintenance and low growing vegetative surfaces under the system as a best management practice for stormwater management," but this is not mandatory. No other explicit vegetative buffer or screening requirements for PSES are provided.

Section 1103.05.C.8 requires that "a clearly visible sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence on the surrounding of the PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards." Section 1103.05.A.6 states "No portion of the PSES shall contain or be used to display advertising. The manufacturer's name and equipment information shall be permitted on the PSES." These are the explicit signage requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES).

The District Use Table (Section 505 amendment) states that Principal Solar Energy Systems ("PSES") are permitted as a Special Exception (SE) in Agricultural, Residential, B-1 Business, and B-2 Business districts, requiring approval by the Zoning Hearing Board. The table uses the key: P=Permitted Use (approved by Zoning Administrator), SE=Special Exception (approved by Zoning Hearing Board). Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES) are permitted or special exception as outlined in Section 505. Section 1103.05 details that PSES require a zoning permit and must comply with various conditions including design standards, underground utilities, financial security, decommissioning, and maintenance. Roof-mounted and ground-mounted PSES must comply with height, setback, and screening requirements of the applicable zoning district. Routine maintenance or like-kind replacements do not require a permit. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this determination.
section: Section 505 and Section 1103.05 Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES)

summary: A principal solar energy system shall be a conditional use in any the Industrial (I) zoning district and subject to specific criteria as set forth in Subsection D below. If a facility is classified and defined as a 'principal solar energy production facility,' it shall be deemed a principal use.

The ordinance requires that "The PSES owner is required to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation." It further states that "The PSES shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of six (6) continuous months." The owner "shall then have six (6) months in which to dismantle and remove the PSES including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations and other associated facilities from the property." If the owner fails to remove the system within this timeframe, "the municipality may complete the decommissioning at the owner’s expense." Additionally, "The PSES owner shall, at the time of the issuance of the permit for the construction of the PSES, provide to Township with an estimate of the cost of performing the decommissioning activities required herein" and "provide financial security of 110% of the estimated cost of decommissioning." This estimate is subject to updates every 5 years and review by the Township. The financial security may be in the form of cash deposit, surety bond, irrevocable letter of credit, cashier's check, or escrow account. Prior to final permit approval, "the PSES owner shall enter into a Decommissioning Agreement with the Township outlining the responsibility of the parties under this Agreement as to the Decommissioning of the PSES." The ordinance also includes decommissioning provisions for Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), but those apply only to smaller or non-commercial systems and are not relevant to Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES).

section: F. Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES)

summary: Ground-mounted PSES shall not be placed within any legal easement or right-of-way location, or be placed within any storm water conveyance system or in any other manner that would alter or impede storm water runoff from collecting in a constructed storm water conveyance system. If a ground mounted PSES is removed, any earth disturbance resulting from the removal must be graded and reseeded. Additionally, no more than twenty-five (25) percent of the entire area for development in the Agriculture Zoning District shall consist of Class I and Class II prime agricultural soils. The following components of a PSES shall be considered impervious coverage and calculated as part of the impervious coverage limitations for the underlying zoning district: foundation systems, mechanical equipment including structures for batteries or storage cells, and gravel or paved access roads servicing the PSES.
section: F. Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES)

summary: Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) "shall be permitted by conditional use in the Agricultural Zoning District." (Section 612.D.1). In the Agricultural (A) district, PSES are listed as a conditional use (Section 301.C.7). Other districts such as Commercial (C), Industrial (I), Rural Residential (RR), and Village Center (VC) only list Accessory Solar Energy Systems as permitted uses. The ordinance also details specific regulations for PSES including setbacks, height restrictions, and security measures, but only the Agricultural district explicitly permits PSES as a conditional use.

In the Agricultural District, 'No more than 50% of the parcel may be used for development of the PSES.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). The unit is expressed as a percentage of the parcel area. Other related restrictions include minimum lot size of 25 acres, setbacks, and slope limitations, but these do not specify maximum land coverage.

§ 1703 7. Decommissioning requires the solar energy system owner to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment, presumed if no electricity is generated for 12 continuous months, and to dismantle and remove the system within six months or the Township may do so at the owner's expense. § 1704 1.E. Decommissioning for PSES requires financial security at permit issuance to secure obligations, including an independent engineer's cost estimate, posting and maintaining funds equal to net decommissioning costs (not less than 50% of total costs), updating estimates every five years, and entering into a decommissioning agreement with the Township. Other options include forms of financial security permitted by the Township Land Development Ordinance and administrative, legal, and engineering costs borne by the PSES developer/owner.

All ground-mounted PSES shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate. The fence shall meet setback requirements for the use. Additionally, a clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards.

All solar energy systems shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures or roadways. Exterior surfaces shall have a nonreflective finish. The applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation. (Section § 1703, All Solar Energy Systems, item 5, Glare). These glare restrictions apply to all solar energy systems, including Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES).

The ordinance states under § 1704, Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), subsection F, Dimensional Requirements: 'Maximum Height: 20 feet at maximum tilt.' This applies to ground-mounted PSES. For roof- and wall-mounted PSES, the height 'shall be subject to the maximum height regulations of the underlying zoning district.' The explicit numerical maximum height given is 20 feet, and the unit is feet.

The property upon which the PSES will be developed shall be a minimum of 25 acres in size. Additionally, under Dimensional Requirements, the Minimum Lot Size is listed as 25 acres. This minimum lot size applies specifically to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) in the Agricultural District. Other conditions include that no more than 50% of the parcel may be used for development of the PSES, and the minimum lot size is expressed in acres.

PSES are permitted in the Industrial zoning district. PSES are permitted in the Agricultural District with the following restrictions: minimum 25-acre property size, no more than 50% of the parcel used for PSES development, 150-foot setback from nearest occupied residential building on nonparticipating property, slope not greater than 15%, and no development within 50 feet of certain environmental features unless an encroachment permit is obtained. Dimensional requirements include minimum lot size of 25 acres, minimum setbacks of 50 feet, and maximum height of 20 feet at maximum tilt. Roof- and wall-mounted PSES must comply with building codes and height regulations of the underlying zoning district. Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES) are permitted in all districts but are not considered PSES. No solar overlay districts are mentioned in the text.

The ordinance states under § 1704, section 1.F 'Dimensional Requirements' that the minimum setbacks for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) are '50 feet (front, rear and side)'. Other related provisions include a minimum lot size of 25 acres and that no more than 50% of the parcel may be used for development of the PSES. The fence enclosing the PSES must also meet setback requirements for the use. The ordinance also mentions a 150-foot setback from the nearest occupied residential building on a nonparticipating landowner's property, but this setback is from a structure, not a property line or parcel boundary, and thus not included here.
Ground-mounted PSES shall be screened from adjoining residential uses or zones according to the standards found in Chapter 27, Part 10, § 1015.

A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards. This signage requirement is found under Security for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). No other explicit signage requirements for PSES are provided in the ordinance.

Stormwater for a PSES shall be designed in accordance with Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection's (PADEP) Chapter 102 guidelines on permitting for solar panel farms. This is found in § 1704  Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), subsection 1.C. Other relevant conditions for PSES include: PSES are permitted in the Industrial zoning district and Agricultural District with restrictions such as minimum 25 acres property size, no more than 50% parcel use, setbacks from residential buildings, slope limitations, and restrictions near streams or wetlands unless a DEP encroachment permit is obtained. PSES must comply with municipal subdivision and land development ordinance requirements, maintain good repair, and provide financial security for decommissioning. Additional requirements cover setbacks, height, screening, fencing, access roads, and emergency plans.

The ordinance states: 'PSES are permitted in the Industrial zoning district.' and 'PSES are permitted in the Agricultural District with the following restrictions...' including minimum lot size, setbacks, slope limitations, and environmental protections. There is no mention of PSES being permitted as a special use or requiring approval by the zoning appeals board or a similar process. Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES) are permitted as a use by right in all zoning districts, but this does not apply to PSES. No other districts or special use conditions for PSES are mentioned.

Solar panels shall be set back from the nearest occupied residential building located on a nonparticipating landowners property, a distance of not less than 150 feet measured from the outer edge of the solar panel nearest to the occupied building to the nearest point on the foundation of the occupied building. Other dimensional requirements include a minimum setback of 50 feet (front, rear and side) for PSES, but the 150 feet setback from occupied residential buildings on nonparticipating properties is the more specific and restrictive requirement.

The PSES cannot be developed within 50 feet of the top of bank of any stream, river, drainage corridor, FEMA delineated floodway or delineated wetland unless an encroachment permit is obtained through DEP.

The ordinance requires that the facility owner or operator "shall, at its expense, complete decommissioning of the solar farm within 6 months after the end of the useful life of the facility." The end of useful life is presumed if "no electricity is generated for a continuous period of 12 months." Decommissioning includes "removal of solar arrays, support equipment, buildings, electrical components and lines, roads, foundations to a depth of 36 inches, and any other associated facilities," and "disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded, unless the landowner requests in writing and the supervisors approve that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored." An estimate of decommissioning costs must be submitted and updated periodically, and the facility owner or operator "shall post and maintain Decommissioning Funds" with specified minimum amounts and acceptable financial assurance forms. If the owner/operator fails to decommission, the landowner must complete it within 6 months, and if neither completes it, the Township may take necessary measures and use escrow funds to cover costs. These requirements apply to "Solar Farms" defined as utility-scale systems with a minimum net lot area of 5 acres and other specified criteria.
Solar farms shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing at a height of 8 feet to restrict unauthorized access.

The ordinance states: 'All individual solar energy collectors and connecting equipment in a solar array... shall have a maximum height of 15 feet.' This applies to Solar Farms, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit of measurement is feet as explicitly mentioned in the text.

The minimum net lot area required to install a solar farm shall be 5 acres. This applies specifically to Solar Farms as defined in the ordinance, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. The text states: 'The minimum net lot area required to install a solar farm shall be 5 acres.'

The solar farm shall be screened from the view of persons on any adjacent land which is currently used for residential purposes. Solar farms are subject to the following criteria: minimum net lot area of 5 acres, enclosed by perimeter fencing at a height of 8 feet, underground electric lines to the maximum extent practicable, adherence to yard dimension, impervious coverage, building coverage and height requirements, setbacks for solar arrays, maximum height of 15 feet for solar energy collectors, and other operational and decommissioning requirements.
Solar Farms are subject to the following criteria: Warning signs shall be placed at the base of any pad-mounted transformers or electrical conducting apparatus on the site.

Section 377 Solar Farm includes decommissioning requirements: 'Should any solar farm cease to be used, the owner or operator or the then owner of the land on which the solar farm is located shall remove all elements of the solar farm within one (1) year from cessation of operation. Failure to effect such removal shall constitute an authorization for the township to remove all elements of the solar farm from the property and assess the cost of removal to the owner of the land on which the solar farm is located. Upon the failure of the owner to pay costs of removal within thirty days of notice thereof, the township may file a municipal lien against such land to recover the costs of removal, together with reasonable attorney fees.' The ordinance also includes other conditions for solar farms such as location, fencing, setbacks, screening, permits, underground utilities, signage, and annual payments to a Township Energy Fund based on capacity.

All solar related facilities must be enclosed with six (6) feet high fence unless otherwise secured. All mechanical equipment of the solar farm, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum of eight (8) feet high fence with a self-locking gate and shall include vegetative screening around the fence.

Section 377 Solar Farm permits solar farms as a principal use in certain districts, subject to conditions including: (i) "All solar panels shall be situated in such a manner as to prevent concentrated solar radiation or glare from being directed onto adjacent properties, roads or public gathering places." Other conditions include setbacks, fencing, screening, underground utilities, and payment to a Township Energy Fund based on capacity.

The ordinance explicitly permits 'Solar Farm' as a principal permitted use in the Agricultural, Conservation, Commercial and Industrial Districts. Each district's use regulations list 'Solar Farm (see Section 377)' under Principal Uses. Section 377 states: 'This use is permitted as a principal permitted use in the Agricultural, Conservation, Commercial and Industrial Districts subject to the following' and then lists regulatory requirements such as location on low-quality agricultural land (for Agricultural and Conservation Districts), setbacks, fencing, screening, building permits, and payment obligations. These requirements are conditions for operation but do not constitute special approvals or discretionary permits. No other districts are mentioned as permitting utility-scale solar energy systems as a principal use. The text does not mention any solar overlay districts, but by assumption, such overlay districts would also be considered primary use districts.

Section 377 Solar Farm requires: 'a security fence with a hedge planting on the outside of the fence must be erected to screen the solar farm from adjacent residential uses. Plant materials used in the screen plantings shall be at least two (2) feet in height when planted. The screen planting shall be maintained permanently and any plant material which does not live shall be replanted within one (1) year.' It also requires that 'No part of the solar farm may be located between the front of a principal building and the front lot line ... unless such facilities are completely screened from the street.' Additionally, 'All mechanical equipment of the solar farm, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum of eight (8) feet high fence with a self-locking gate and shall include vegetative screening around the fence.'

Section 377(k) states: 'Signage or text on solar energy systems may be used to identify the manufacturer, equipment information, warranty or ownership but shall not be used to display any commercial advertising message or anchor any streamers, balloons, flags, banners, ribbons or other materials to attract attention.' This applies to solar farms, which are permitted as principal uses in various districts and are subject to multiple conditions including fencing, setbacks, screening, and removal upon cessation of use.

Utility-scale solar energy systems, referred to as 'Solar Farm,' are permitted as a principal permitted use in the Agricultural, Conservation, Commercial, and Industrial Districts, subject to conditions such as setbacks, fencing, screening, and permitting requirements including a Building Permit and Use Certificate. The ordinance states: 'This use is permitted as a principal permitted use in the Agricultural, Conservation, Commercial and Industrial Districts subject to the following...' and lists detailed conditions (a through n). There is no mention of these systems being permitted only as special uses or requiring approval by a zoning appeals board or similar entity. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this determination.

All facilities and equipment used in connection with the solar farm must be located at least one hundred (100) feet from any dwelling, other than a dwelling owned by the owner of the land on which the solar farm is located.

Section 9.34.A.8 Decommissioning: The owner is required to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The Commercial Solar Energy System shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months. The owner shall then have twelve (12) months in which to dismantle and remove the Commercial Solar Energy System including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations and other associated facilities from the property. If the owner fails to dismantle and/or remove the system within the established timeframes, the municipality may complete the decommissioning at the owners expense. The system owner or operator shall post and maintain decommissioning funds in an amount 100% of the identified decommissioning costs, as adjusted over time. The decommissioning funds shall be posted and maintained with a bonding company or lending institution chosen by the system owner or operator and participating land owner posting the financial security, provided that the bonding company or lending institution is authorized to conduct business within the Commonwealth and is approved by Lower Frankford Township.

All ground-mounted systems shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate. A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the system informing individuals of potential voltage hazards. This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems used to capture solar energy and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use. Other requirements for Commercial Solar Energy Systems include compliance with industry standards, setbacks, height limits (not to exceed twenty (20) feet), and screening from adjoining residential uses.

Section 9.34.A.6 states: 'All Solar Energy Systems shall be placed such that concentrated glare does not project onto nearby structures or roadways. The applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have an adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation.' This glare restriction applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems 'principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use.'

Under section 9.34.A.12.c, the ordinance states: 'Height - Systems shall not exceed twenty (20) feet in height.' This applies specifically to ground-mounted Commercial Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems used principally to capture solar energy and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use. The unit of measurement is feet. No other maximum height values for utility-scale systems are provided.

Section 9.34.A.12.e states: 'Ground mounted systems shall be adequately screened from adjoining residential uses.' This applies to Commercial Solar Energy Systems, defined as systems 'principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use.' Other related requirements include setbacks, height limits, fencing, and stormwater management, but only the screening requirement explicitly mandates screening from adjoining residential uses.

No portion of the Commercial Solar Energy System shall contain or be used to display advertising. The manufacturer’s name, equipment information or ownership shall be allowed provided it complies with the sign regulations. All ground-mounted systems shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate. A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the system informing individuals of potential voltage hazards.

Commercial Solar Energy Systems are permitted by conditional use within the (A) and (AR) zones, subject to approval by the Board of Supervisors after a public hearing and recommendation by the Planning Commission, as stated in '4.04 Conditional Uses' and '5.04 Conditional Uses' referencing Section 9.34. Section 9.34 specifies: 'Within the (A) and (AR) zones Commercial Solar Energy Systems are permitted by conditional use subject to the following criteria.'

If a principal alternative energy system remains unused (ceasing active and continuous operation) for a period of twelve (12) consecutive months, the owner or operator shall either: file a certificate of intent to continue the use; or dismantle and remove the principal alternative energy system within six (6) months of the expiration of the twelve (12) month period. The failure of a landowner to file with the municipality the certificate of intent to continue the use shall serve as prima facie evidence that the landowner does not intend to continue the use. The certificate shall include the date that the use discontinued, the date that the use will recommence, a description of the extent of the use, and the reason for discontinuing the use. A notation describing this requirement shall appear on the land development plans for the facility (or, to the extent that it is determined that a land development plan is not required, shall appear on the plans submitted to the municipal engineer for consideration and shall be a condition for any permit issued hereunder).

The site of the principal alternative energy system shall be secured by a locked chain-link fence and gate with a minimum height of eight (8) feet to limit accessibility by the general public or other unauthorized persons. The gate shall provide automatic access to emergency personnel. (Section 531(a)(5))

Section 531(b)(1) states: "All principal solar energy systems shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby properties, structures or roadways. The applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation." This applies to principal alternative energy systems, defined as systems "whose purpose is to supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use." For accessory solar energy systems, Section 503(5)(c)(2) similarly requires: "All accessory solar energy systems shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby properties, buildings or roadways. The applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation." The ordinance distinguishes principal systems (typically larger, off-site supply) from accessory systems (primarily for on-site consumption), with separate but similar glare restrictions for each category.
section: Section 531 ("Alternative Energy System, Principal") and Section 503(5)(c)(2)

summary: Section 531(a)(2) states: 'Principal Alternative Energy Systems (Solar and Wind) are only permitted on lots with a minimum of two (2) acres in area.' This is the explicit minimum lot size for Ground Mounted Principal Alternative Energy Systems (Solar). No other minimum lot size values for principal systems are provided. The unit 'acres' is explicitly used in the text.

Principal Alternative Energy Systems (Solar and Wind) shall only be permitted in the A-1, A-2, C-2, C-3, C-4, I-1 or I-2 Zoning Districts. They require a minimum lot area of two (2) acres and must comply with setback requirements: for C-2, C-3, C-4, I-1, or I-2 districts, a minimum of 120 feet from existing principal residential uses and residential or agricultural zoning boundaries; for A-1 or A-2 districts, a minimum of 500 feet from adjoining property lines, with systems located on the least productive soils to preserve prime agricultural land. Accessory Alternative Energy Systems (solar and wind) are permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts but are not principal uses. No solar overlay districts are mentioned in the text, but by assumption, such overlay districts would also be considered primary use districts for utility-scale solar energy systems.
section: Section 531 ("Alternative Energy System, Principal"), Article V ("General Regulations")

summary: Principal Alternative Energy Systems (Solar and Wind) "shall only be permitted in the A-1, A-2, C-2, C-3, C-4, I-1 or I-2 Zoning Districts." By stating this, the ordinance effectively prohibits such systems in all other zoning districts not listed. Accessory Alternative Energy Systems (solar and wind) are permitted as accessory uses and structures in all Zoning Districts, subject to requirements. Additional conditions include minimum lot area of two acres, setback requirements depending on district, and restrictions to preserve prime agricultural land in A-1 and A-2 districts.

Principal alternative energy systems in the A-I or A-2 Zoning Districts shall be setback a minimum of five hundred (500) feet from adjoining property lines. Other options include a minimum setback of one hundred and twenty (120) feet from the lot line of an existing principal residential use and the boundary of any residential or agricultural Zoning District in the C-2, C-3, C-4, I-1 or I-2 Zoning Districts, and compliance with the setback and yard requirements for principal structures for the zoning district within which it is located.

Section 531(b)(4) states: 'Screening. Any ground mounted principal solar energy system located on a property which directly abuts any existing residential use shall provide buffer yards and planting screens in accordance with the provisions of Section 506(4)(c).' This is an explicit vegetative buffer and/or screening requirement for principal alternative energy systems (solar). Other relevant provisions include setback requirements, fencing, noise compliance, signage, and maintenance, but these do not pertain to vegetative buffer or screening. Accessory solar energy systems have separate screening requirements under Section 503(5)(c)(4)(v), but those apply only to accessory systems, not principal systems.

Signage on principal alternative energy systems (other than warning signs) shall be limited to a single sign located at the main entrance to the facility. Such sign shall have a total area of no greater than twelve (12) square feet and shall display only the name of the facility and the contact phone number. No advertising signs shall be permitted. All signage shall comply with Section 516. A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed on the protective fence and/or at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations. Visible, reflective, colored objects, such as flags, reflectors, or tape shall be placed on the anchor points of guy wires located outside of the fenced area and along the guy wires up to a height of ten feet from the ground.

The ordinance states that "Principal Alternative Energy Systems (Solar and Wind) shall only be permitted in the A-1, A-2, C-2, C-3, C-4, I-1 or I-2 Zoning Districts" and sets conditions such as a minimum lot area of two acres and specific setback requirements. There is no mention that these systems require special use approval or zoning appeals board approval; rather, they are permitted principal uses subject to compliance with the listed requirements. Accessory Alternative Energy Systems are permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts. No districts are identified where utility-scale solar energy systems are permitted only as special use or similar conditional approvals.

Section 531(a)(3)(c) states that principal alternative energy systems in the A-I or A-2 Zoning Districts shall be setback a minimum of five hundred (500) feet from adjoining property lines. Additionally, Section 531(a)(3)(b) requires a minimum setback of one hundred and twenty (120) feet from the lot line of an existing principal residential use in C-2, C-3, C-4, 1-1 or 1-2 Zoning Districts. Section 531(a)(3)(a) requires compliance with the setback and yard requirements for principal structures in the zoning district. The most restrictive setback directly pertaining to occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, and/or residences is 500 feet in agricultural zoning districts (A-I, A-2).

The entire facility comprising a principal alternative or renewable energy system and its appurtenant and accessory structure(s) and equipment shall be enclosed by a fence or barrier to prevent or restrict unauthorized persons or vehicles from entering the facility. Clearly visible warning signs shall be placed on the fence, barrier or at the perimeter of the facility to inform individuals of potential voltage hazards. All mechanical equipment associated with the facility shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight feet high fence with a self-locking gate.
section: § 27-1207 Principal Alternative or Renewable Energy Systems

summary: Section K (Glare) states: 'Solar collectors shall be installed so as to prevent glare or concentrated solar radiation as may otherwise be directed onto other properties or onto roadways such that a nuisance situation is created. Anti-reflective surface materials or coatings shall be used to preclude glare.' It further requires: '(2) The applicant or the installer or manufacturer of any solar energy system shall submit with the application for permit or conditional use approval, as applicable, a signed statement... including: (a) Certification that the proposed system shall not produce glare or reflect concentrated solar radiation visible beyond the property lines... such that a nuisance situation is created; (b) Acknowledgement that... should any glare or concentrated solar radiation produced prove to be visible beyond the property lines... such that... a nuisance situation or safety hazard arises... the Township may... require mitigative action or removal; (c) Acknowledgement that... failure to comply may result in Township mitigation or removal with costs reimbursed or lien placed; (d) Acknowledgement that these obligations continue so long as the system remains in operation.' These glare restrictions apply to all solar energy systems permitted as principal uses, including those selling power directly to the grid (utility-scale).

summary: Principal alternative or renewable energy systems shall be permitted subject to conditional use approval in the I - Industrial District only. Solar energy systems as a principal use, whether providing power to multiple users or properties, or selling power directly to the grid, are permitted only pursuant to the provisions set forth in Part 10 and § 27-1207. Other setback provisions include a 200 feet setback from certain scenic byways (§ 27-1207 B) and compliance with zoning district setbacks for accessory or principal structures (§ 27-1204 O.(1)). The 100 feet setback from lot lines is the most direct fixed distance value for utility-scale solar energy systems.
section: § 27-1207 Principal Alternative or Renewable Energy Systems

summary: Principal alternative or renewable energy systems shall be set back a minimum of 100 feet from any public right-of-way. Except where greater setbacks apply, they shall be set back a minimum of 200 feet and shall be screened from view from the right-of-way of any road designated as part of the Delaware River Valley Scenic Byway.
section: § 27-1207 Principal Alternative or Renewable Energy Systems

summary: Any application for conditional use approval for a principal solar energy system shall include submission of a visual analysis demonstrating that the system is designed and located to meet the objectives stated above. The applicant shall provide a buffer yard around the perimeter of any facility comprising a principal solar energy system... providing a continuous visual screen between such facility and any adjacent property, public right-of-way or historic structure as viewed by a person standing at ground level.

Solar energy systems and appurtenant or accessory structures shall not display any advertising, except for identification of the panel or other equipment manufacturer, and the facility owner, on a sign not to exceed two square feet in area (§ 27-1204 I). For principal alternative or renewable energy systems, the entire facility and its appurtenant and accessory structures shall be enclosed by a fence or barrier with clearly visible warning signs placed on the fence, barrier or at the perimeter of the facility to inform individuals of potential voltage hazards (§ 27-1207 C).

summary: Principal alternative or renewable energy systems shall be permitted subject to conditional use approval in the I - Industrial District only (§ 27-1207). Solar energy systems may be permitted as a principal use, whether providing power to multiple users or properties, or selling power directly to the grid, pursuant to the provisions set forth in Part 10 and § 27-1207 (§ 27-1204). section: § 27-1207 Principal Alternative or Renewable Energy Systems

summary: Any application for conditional use approval for a principal solar energy system shall include submission of a visual analysis demonstrating that the system is designed and located to meet the objectives stated above, including that the solar installation will not unduly impact other property owners or the travelling public or that potential impacts are mitigated by design of the system or structure(s) upon which it is mounted, by distance from points of visibility, by the presence of intervening topography, vegetation or structures, or will be mitigated through introduction of landscaping consistent with the standards set forth in § 27-1408. Additionally, the applicant shall provide a buffer yard around the perimeter of any facility comprising a principal solar energy system, providing a continuous visual screen between such facility and any adjacent property, public right-of-way or historic structure as viewed by a person standing at ground level.

The lot coverage within the Agricultural District shall be limited to 20% total lot coverage for access drives and equipment, and an additional 40% coverage for solar panels. The coverage is expressed as a percentage of total lot coverage, not as a specific area value.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Solar Energy Facilities (SEFs), defined as "an area of land five acres or more, used for a solar collection system, principally to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use." The requirements include: (a) "The SEF owner is required to notify the municipality immediately upon permanent cessation or abandonment of the operation." (b) "The SEF shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of 12 continuous months." (c) "The SEF owner shall have 18 months in which to dismantle and remove the SEF, including all solar-related equipment or appurtenances related thereto... in accordance with agreements with landowners and good industry practice." (d) "To the extent possible, all materials shall be resold or salvaged." (e) "Any soil exposed during the removal shall be stabilized in accordance with applicable erosion and sediment control standards." (f) "The SEF site area shall be restored to its preexisting condition, suitable for its prior use, except the landowner may authorize... any buffer landscaping or access roads installed to accommodate the SEF to remain." (g) "Any necessary federal, state and local permits... shall be obtained prior to decommissioning activities." (h) "Prior to any issuance of a zoning or building permit for the SEF, the owner shall provide financial security... to secure its obligations under this section." The financial security must be "in the amount of 110% of the total proposed decommissioning costs" and updated every five years with adjustments for inflation and cost changes. The developer must provide a decommissioning cost estimate and enter into a decommissioning agreement with the municipality. These provisions apply specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance.

All ground-mounted SEFs shall be completely enclosed by fencing that consists of a minimum eight-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate. This fencing may consist of agricultural-style fence or "game" fence so long as the fencing meets all applicable regulations. (§ 360-3(B)(8)(a))

SEFs shall be located to minimize concentrated glare on adjacent properties or streets. The Township may require reasonable corrective actions after installation of the SEF to eliminate glare to adjacent properties or streets which causes a risk to public health or safety. The Township may require a glare study to be completed and submitted with the final land development plan and then again six months after operation of the SEF.

The ordinance explicitly states in § 360-3, subsection B(5) that 'Ground-mounted SEFs shall not exceed 25 feet in height.' This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems defined as Solar Energy Facilities (SEFs) of five acres or more used principally for off-site electricity generation. No other maximum height values for SEFs are provided, and the unit is feet.

The ordinance defines a Solar Energy Facility (SEF) as "an area of land five acres or more, used for a solar collection system, principally to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use." Additionally, it states that "The SEF shall meet the lot size requirements of the applicable zoning district." The minimum lot size is thus explicitly set at five acres or more, with units in acres.
section: § 360-2 Definitions and word usage; § 360-3 Solar energy facility regulations

summary: Noise from a SEF, as measured at the property lines, shall not exceed 45 dBA or otherwise create excessive noise which constitutes a nuisance as determined by the Township. The applicant will install mitigation measures acceptable to the Township to mitigate any noise exceedance identified by the study. This applies specifically to Solar Energy Facilities (SEFs), defined as areas of land five acres or more used for solar collection systems principally to capture solar energy and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use.

Ground-mounted SEFs shall be set back a minimum of 50 feet from all property lines and street rights-of-way. Additionally, buffer yards shall be 50 feet wide and installed around the entire perimeter of the SEF installation. No side or rear setback will be required where a solar energy project spans across lot lines, provided each landowner has signed a written waiver of the lot line setback. Other setback mentioned is 150 feet from all occupied residential structures, but this does not pertain to property lines or parcels.

summary: Ground-mounted SEFs shall be set back a minimum of 50 feet from all property lines and street rights-of-way and 150 feet from all occupied residential structures.
section: § 360-3 Solar energy facility regulations, B. Ground-mounted SEF, (4) Setbacks

summary: The ordinance requires that ground-mounted SEFs be screened and buffered with a "minimum 25 feet wide" vegetative screening "around the entire perimeter of the SEF installation," except where existing trees may constitute the required screen or where screening is not feasible. The vegetative screening "shall be installed along the exterior side of the fencing" and "within 50 feet of the required fencing." It must "emulate the mix of native species and appearance of existing tree lines, hedge rows, and wooded areas," be designed by a licensed professional, include "no less than 20% of vegetative screen plantings" that are "pollinator-friendly species," exclude invasive species, and provide "year-round buffering" with sufficient height, density, and maturity "within 36 months of the installation." A combination of natural topography and vegetation can serve as a screen if the SEF is not visible from public roads, parks, or residences, but "earthen berms alone may not be used." Buffer yards must be "50 feet wide" and installed around the entire perimeter. An "operation and maintenance agreement shall be submitted which includes a plan to control invasive species." These screening requirements "shall supersede the provisions of the Zoning Ordinance or Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance as they may pertain to SEFs."

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for utility-scale solar energy facilities (SEFs) defined as "an area of land five acres or more, used for a solar collection system, principally to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use." Relevant provisions include: "Any soil exposed during the removal shall be stabilized in accordance with applicable erosion and sediment control standards" (§360-3(A)(16)(e)); "Any necessary federal, state and local permits, such as erosion and sediment pollution control and NPDES permits, shall be obtained prior to decommissioning activities" (§360-3(A)(16)(h)); "A written erosion and sediment control plan shall be developed for agricultural plowing or tilling activities, or a portion of the overall farm conservation plan identifies BMPs used" (§360-3(B)(6)(c)); "Stormwater runoff from a ground-mounted SEF shall be managed in accordance with the requirements of the Lower Windsor Township Stormwater Management Ordinance" (§360-3(B)(6)(a)); and "Vegetative cover is required to be maintained under all panels" (§360-3(B)(6)(b)). These requirements apply to SEFs meeting the utility-scale definition and impose explicit obligations on developers regarding soil stabilization, erosion, sediment control, and stormwater management.

Ground-mounted SEFs shall be set back a minimum of 150 feet from all occupied residential structures. (See § 360-3.B.(4)(a)) Other setback requirements include 50 feet from all property lines and street rights-of-way, but these do not pertain to occupied dwellings.

Solar-related equipment shall not be located in wetlands. Riparian buffers extending 25 feet from any wetland or the top of bank of any body of water. This establishes a minimum 25-foot setback from wetlands and from the top of bank of any body of water for utility-scale solar energy systems. Other setback requirements mentioned in the ordinance relate to property lines, occupied residential structures, and street rights-of-way, but these do not pertain to lakes, reservoirs, streams, rivers, or wetlands.

summary: Section 10. Decommissioning requires the Facility Owner to notify Madison Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the SEF, which is presumed if no electricity is generated for twelve (12) months. The Facility Owner has six (6) months to dismantle and remove the SEF, including all solar-related equipment, buildings, cabling, electrical components, transmission and plumbing lines, roads, foundations, and other associated facilities, and restore the land to its original pre-construction condition. If the owner fails to do so, Madison Township may complete the decommissioning and land restoration at the owner's expense. At permit issuance, the Facility Owner must provide proof of liability insurance and financial security in the amount of 110% of the decommissioning costs, maintained during the life of the project. An independent registered professional engineer retained by Madison Township at the Facility Owner's cost will estimate decommissioning costs initially and every five years thereafter, subject to Madison Township's engineer's review and approval. Financial security may be in the form of a performance bond, irrevocable letter of credit, or other acceptable financial security as set forth in section 7.

Section 7.D states: 'A SEF shall be enclosed by a fence, barrier or other appropriate means to prevent or restrict unauthorized persons or vehicles from entering the property.' It also requires 'Clearly visible warning signs shall be placed on the fence, barrier or SEF perimeter to inform individuals of potential voltage hazards.' This fencing requirement applies to Large-Scale Solar Electric Energy Facilities (SEFs) whose main purpose is to generate and supply electricity primarily for off-site use, as defined in Section 3.F. No other fencing options or conditions are provided in the ordinance.
section: Section 7. Design, Construction, Financial Security, Maintenance and Insurance

The solar panels shall also be coated with an anti-reflective film.' This glare restriction applies to Large-Scale Solar Electric Energy Facilities (SEFs) as defined in the ordinance, which are intended to generate and supply electricity primarily for off-site use. No other specific glare restrictions or alternative conditions are provided in the ordinance text.
section: Section 7. Design, Construction, Financial Security, Maintenance and Insurance

summary: The ordinance states: 'Noise from a SEF shall not exceed 55 dBa, as measured at the property line.' This applies to Large-Scale Solar Electric Energy Facilities (SEFs) whose main purpose is to generate and supply electricity primarily for off-site use. No other maximum noise levels are provided in the text for utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit 'dBA' is the standard unit for noise level measurement.
section: Section 7. Design, Construction, Financial Security, Maintenance and Insurance

summary: Ground-mounted SEFs shall have a minimum setback at all property lines of 150 feet. These distances shall be measured from the closest edge of the SEF to the property line.

Section 7.D requires that "Clearly visible warning signs shall be placed on the fence, barrier or SEF perimeter to inform individuals of potential voltage hazards." Section 9.E states "A sign shall be posted providing the name of the operator and a phone number to be used in case of an on-site emergency at the primary entrance of the SEF. Additionally, reflective signs shall be posted providing the name of the operator and a phone to be used in case of an on-site emergency along the perimeter of the SEF at intervals of 250 feet." These signage requirements apply to Large-Scale Solar Electric Energy Facilities (SEFs), defined as facilities "whose principal purpose is to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use."
section: Section 7. Design, Construction, Financial Security, Maintenance and Insurance and Section 9. Emergency Services and Safety

summary: Ground-mounted SEFs shall have a prepared stormwater management plan in accordance with Township Ordinances and Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (Pa DEP) Best Management Practices. This plan is subject to approval by the Lackawanna County Soil Conservation District and the Madison Township engineer. Additionally, ground-mounted SEFs shall have a prepared grading plan that minimizes to the best extent possible the disturbance or alteration of the existing topography on the site. This plan is also subject to approval by the Lackawanna County Soil Conservation District.

Section 7, subsection EK (Decommissioning) requires the applicant to present a decommission bond in sufficient form, subject to approval of Township Engineer and licensed surety, prior to issuance of building permit. An independent and certified Professional Engineer must estimate the total cost of decommissioning/removal/remediation of the site, incorporating estimated salvage values. The solar energy farm owner must notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of operation. Abandonment is presumed if no electricity is generated for twelve (12) continuous months. The owner then has twelve (12) months to dismantle and remove all solar related equipment or appurtenances, including buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations, and other associated facilities. If the owner fails to do so, the municipality will complete the decommissioning at the applicant’s expense. Other conditions for Solar Energy Farms include minimum lot size of five (5) acres, permitted by conditional use in specified zoning districts, operations agreement, host municipality fee, transportation plan, telecommunications interference documentation, financial security for dismantling and land restoration, public inquiries/complaints contact, required certifications/licenses/permits, environmental impact compliance, lighting plans, power purchase/sale agreements, and security fencing and signage.

Section 7, subsection S states: "All ground-mounted solar energy farms shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a locking gate." This fencing requirement applies to Solar Energy Farms defined as systems primarily to generate energy for sale back into the energy grid, located on properties with a minimum lot size of five (5) acres, and permitted exclusively by conditional use within specified zoning districts. Other conditions for Solar Energy Farms include requirements for screening, operations agreement, compliance with zoning provisions, host municipality fee, transportation plan, telecommunications interference documentation, decommissioning bond, financial security, public inquiries/complaints contact, certifications/licenses/permits, environmental impact reports, lighting plans, power purchase/sale agreements, permitting, design compliance with UCC and NEC, noise limits, signage, access roads, and options for zoning or UCC appeals if permits are denied.

Section 7 states: 'Solar farms shall be located on properties with a minimum lot size of five (5) acres' and this minimum lot size applies specifically to Solar Energy Farms, which are defined as systems primarily to generate energy for sale back into the grid. The unit 'acres' is explicitly used in the ordinance.

Section 7, item Q states: 'No solar energy farm facilities shall exceed sixty-five (65) dBA as measured at the property line.' This applies specifically to Solar Energy Farms, defined as systems primarily to generate energy for sale back into the energy grid system. The unit 'dBA' is the standard unit for noise level measurement.

Section 7.A requires the Applicant to "demonstrate appropriate screening for the operation and demonstrate compliance with general requirements for non-residential uses within the zoning ordinance, including but not limited to environmental considerations." Section 5.E.1 states that "Mechanical equipment shall be screened from any adjacent property that is residentially zoned or used for residential purposes. The screen shall consist of shrubbery, trees, or other plant materials which provides a visual screen." These provisions explicitly impose vegetative buffer and/or other screening requirements for Solar Energy Farms. Other conditions for Solar Energy Farms include minimum lot size of five (5) acres, conditional use permit, operations agreement, host municipality fee, transportation plan, telecommunications interference documentation, decommissioning bond, financial security, lighting plans, signage, security fencing, access roads, and compliance with various permits and codes.

Section 7, Signage— Appropriate safety/warning signage concerning voltage shall be placed at ground mounted electrical devices, equipment, and structures. All electrical control devices associated with the solar energy farm shall be locked to prevent unauthorized access or entry. A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad mounted-transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the solar energy farm informing individuals of potential voltage hazards.

Solar farms shall be located on properties with a minimum lot size of five (5) acres and shall be permitted within the CM - Conservation Mining or I - Manufacturing Districts. Solar Farms shall be permitted exclusively by conditional use. "Solar Energy Farms are to be added as conditional uses by creation of the following within the Mahanoy Township Zoning Ordinance: 408.2 Conditional uses in the CM District and Section 407.3 Conditional uses in the I District." The CR - Conservation Residential District is mentioned initially but not included in the final conditional use designation. Smaller or accessory Solar Energy Systems are permitted in other districts without Planning Commission or Zoning Board review.

Photovoltaic Power Station (PPS), also known as a solar park, solar farm or solar power plant are permitted in the Marion Township Industrial District and not to exceed 75% of total lot coverage. This 75% is expressed as a percentage of total lot coverage. PPS proposed outside the Industrial District require a Conditional Use Permit. Other lot coverage minimums for conditional uses in various zones are listed but do not apply as maximums for PPS.

If the solar energy system is abandoned or is in a state of disrepair it shall be the responsibility of the property owner to repair and maintain the solar energy system or to remove the solar energy system. Any solar energy system which is in a state of disrepair and has not been active and in continuous service for a period of one (1) year shall be removed from the property to a place of safe and legal disposal. All structures and enclosures accessory to the solar energy system shall also be completely removed from the property to a place of safe and legal disposal. The property owner (or the solar system owner on behalf of the property owner) shall post and maintain 'Decommissioning Funds' in an amount equal to the cost of removing the solar energy system and disposing of it in a safe manner that is in accordance with all federal, state, and local laws and regulations. The Decommissioning Funds shall be posted and maintained with a bonding company or Federal or Commonwealth chartered lending institution chosen or approved by the property owner, provided that the bonding company or lending institution is authorized to conduct such business within the Commonwealth and is approved by the Township. Decommissioning Funds may be in the form of a performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit, corporate guarantee or other form of financial assurance as may be acceptable to the Township.

The ordinance states: 'Solar panels shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways.' This applies generally to solar panels, including Photovoltaic Power Stations (PPS), which are defined as 'large-scale photovoltaic system (PV system) designed for the supply of merchant power into the electricity grid.' The ordinance also includes other conditions for PPS such as requiring a Conditional Use permit outside the Industrial District, limiting lot coverage to 75%, and requiring written authorization from the local utility for grid connection.

Photovoltaic Power Station (PPS), also known as a solar park, solar farm or solar power plant are permitted in the Marion Township Industrial District and not to exceed 75% of total lot coverage. Photovoltaic Power Station (PPS) proposed for construction anywhere except the Marion Township Industrial District must first obtain a Conditional Use Permit. All Ground based Solar Systems require a Conditional Use permit, unless located in the Industrial Zone. Building-Mounted/Building-Integrated roof mounted small-scale solar energy systems are permitted in all zoning districts as an accessory use.

Conditional Use Solar System Set Backs and Minimum Lot Coverages specify minimum setbacks from property lines for Photovoltaic Power Stations (PPS) as follows: Min Front Setback ranges from 75 to 150 feet depending on zoning district, with the most restrictive being 150 feet in A-1, R-1, and CN zones. Min Side Setback ranges from 25 to 100 feet, with the most restrictive being 100 feet in A-1, R-1, and CN zones. Min Rear Setback ranges from 40 to 100 feet, with the most restrictive being 100 feet in A-1, R-1, and CN zones. Lot coverage limits also vary by zone. The ordinance states: 'Zone Min Front Setback Min Side Setback Min Rear Setback Lot Coverage Feet Feet Feet Percent % A-1 150 100 100 40% R-1 150 100 100 25% CN 150 100 100 40% B-1 100 75 75 50% B-2 100 75 75 60% LD 75 25 40 75%'. These setbacks apply to PPS as conditional uses outside the Industrial District.

summary: All mechanical equipment associated with and necessary for the operation of the solar energy system shall comply with the following: a) Mechanical equipment shall be screened from any adjacent property. The screen shall consist of shrubbery, trees, or other plant materials which provides a visual screen. Minimum screen height will be the same height as mechanical equipment but no less than 6 feet high. In lieu of a planting screen a decorative screening fence may be used.

Photovoltaic Power Station (PPS), also known as a solar park, solar farm, or solar power plant are permitted in the Marion Township Industrial District without a Conditional Use Permit, subject to not exceeding 75% of total lot coverage. section: Article Ill General Requirements. Solar Energy Systems

summary: If a solar energy facility remains nonfunctional or inoperative for a continuous period of one year, the facility shall be deemed to be abandoned and shall constitute a public nuisance, unless the owner demonstrates a good-faith intent to sell the facility. Within six months of abandonment, the owner shall remove the system, after a demolition permit has been obtained, in accordance with the following: (a) Any aboveground mechanical equipment, wiring, and structural components shall be removed. (b) Underground wiring and structural components shall be removed and the resulting void space filled. When a solar energy facility is removed, any disturbed earth as a result of the removal of the system shall be restored, graded and reseeded.
All equipment for solar energy facilities, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum of eight-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate.

Solar panels shall be positioned to prevent solar glare upon any neighboring properties or any public or private street and to prevent additional heat load upon neighboring properties. This applies specifically to solar energy facilities, which are permitted as a conditional use on parcels over 10 acres. The relevant provision is found in § 275-206 B(5).

Solar energy facilities are permitted as a conditional use on parcels over 10 acres (§ 275-206). This is the explicit minimum lot size requirement for Solar Energy Facilities, which are defined as facilities with the primary intention of generating electricity or converting solar energy for primarily commercial or off-site use. No other minimum lot size values are provided for Solar Energy Facilities in the text. The unit 'acres' is used to specify the area.

Solar energy facilities shall not be used to display advertising or decoration, including signage, streamers, pennants, spinners, reflectors, ribbons, tinsel, balloons, flags, banners, lights or similar items. Manufacturers and equipment information, safety warnings, and ownership information may be displayed on solar energy facility equipment, provided such information complies with applicable sign regulations.

Solar energy facilities "shall be installed in compliance with all applicable building and construction codes, including regulations with respect to floodplain management and stormwater management." The applicant must provide "a stormwater management plan for the facility that will minimize the impact of stormwater leaving the site through the use of stormwater BMPs." Upon removal, "any disturbed earth as a result of the removal of the system shall be restored, graded and reseeded." These requirements apply to solar energy facilities as defined: "An alternative energy facility... with the primary intention of generating electricity or otherwise converting solar energy to a different form of energy for primarily commercial or other off-site use."

Solar energy facilities are permitted as a conditional use on parcels over 10 acres (§ 275-206). The conditional use regulations apply in addition to those of the underlying zoning district, but the text does not specify particular district names or abbreviations. Alternative energy facilities are permitted as a conditional use in all nonresidential zoning districts (§ 275-204 B). Solar energy systems (smaller or accessory systems) are permitted as an accessory use in all zoning districts (§ 275-205).

Section 1001.7(c) requires the Applicant to "demonstrate the manner of abandonment and removal of the solar arrays that comprise the field." It mandates "An abandonment decommissioning plan, agreement and decommissioning escrow shall be provided and updated every five (5) years." The ordinance defines Solar Energy Fields as "systems which exist solely to generate energy for sale back into the energy grid system, rather than being consumed on site." Other relevant provisions include requirements for screening, operations agreements, and compliance with land development and stormwater management ordinances, but these do not pertain directly to decommissioning.

Section 1001.7(a) states that solar panels "must be comprised of antiglare/reflection coating material." This applies to Solar Energy Fields, defined in Section 1001.3(c) as "systems which exist solely to generate energy for sale back into the energy grid system." Additional requirements include minimum lot size, screening, setbacks from residential dwellings, and compliance with other zoning and land development regulations, but these do not pertain to glare restrictions.

The ordinance states: 'Solar fields shall be located on properties with a minimum lot size of five (5) acres... and not exceed ten (10) acres of Lot Area (Net).' This sets a maximum lot size of 10 acres for Solar Energy Fields, which are defined as systems that generate energy for sale back into the energy grid system.

Section 1001.7 states: 'Solar fields shall be located on properties with a minimum lot size of five (5) acres in the appropriate Zoning District as set forth in Article V of this Ordinance and not exceed ten (10) acres of Lot Area (Net).' The minimum lot size is explicitly given as five acres, which is an area measurement. This applies to Solar Energy Fields defined as systems which exist solely to generate energy for sale back into the energy grid system.

Section 1001.7(a) requires that "Solar panels and equipment must be fully screened and placed a minimum of one hundred feet (100') from the property line of an existing residential dwelling." This applies to Solar Energy Fields, defined in Section 1001.3(c) as "systems which exist solely to generate energy for sale back into the energy grid system." The ordinance also states that the applicant "shall demonstrate appropriate screening for the operation and demonstrate compliance with general requirements for non-residential uses within the zoning ordinance, including but not limited to environmental considerations."
section: Article X, Section 1001.7, entitled  "Solar Energy Fields"

summary: Solar panels and equipment must be fully screened and placed a minimum of one hundred feet (100') from the property line of an existing residential dwelling. (Section 1001.7(a)) The ordinance defines Solar Energy Fields as systems which exist solely to generate energy for sale back into the energy grid system, rather than being consumed on site (Section 1001.3(c)), indicating applicability to utility-scale solar energy systems. No other setback distances or multipliers based on structure height are provided for setbacks from occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, or residences.

The ordinance explicitly requires for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) an affidavit or similar evidence signed by the property owner and the PSES facility owner affirming a lease agreement with a decommissioning clause that "must provide sufficient funds to dismantle and remove the PSES, including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, electrical components, roads and other associated facilities from the property." Relevant soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements include: "Stormwater requirements" where only certain components are considered impervious coverage, and solar modules must be arranged to "allow passage of runoff between each module, minimizing the creation of runoff" and "shall not exceed four (4) feet in width to allow for adequate vegetative cover to be established and maintained." Additionally, "the owner of a PSES shall plant ground cover at the PSES site that includes native and naturalized perennial vegetation beneficial to native species and pollinators," with ground cover designed to provide a mixture of perennial grasses and wildflowers, and "No less than 20% of ground cover plantings shall be pollinator-friendly species." These requirements explicitly apply to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined by the ordinance. Other provisions include setbacks from wetlands, floodplains, and historic structures, fencing and security, glare mitigation, and decommissioning, but these do not pertain directly to soil, erosion, or sediment control.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) in Section 468.9 under 'Decommissioning.' It states: 'The PSES owner is required to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The PSES shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months.' Further, 'The PSES owner shall then have twelve (12) months in which to dismantle and remove the PSES including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including, but not limited to, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations, and other associated facilities from the property.' If the owner fails to dismantle and/or remove the PSES within the established timeframes, 'the municipality may complete the decommissioning at the owners expense.' Other relevant provisions include requirements for underground placement of on-site transmission and plumbing lines, notification to the public utility company, and maintenance obligations during the permit term. The ordinance distinguishes PSES from Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), which have different thresholds and requirements, such as power rating limits (e.g., ASES with a maximum power rating of not more than 15kW are permitted by right, while those above 15kW must comply with Section 468.2 for PSES).

All ground-mounted PSES shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate. A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards. This fencing requirement is found under Section 468.11 Security for Principal Solar Energy Systems. Other related requirements include setbacks, height restrictions, screening from adjoining residential uses, access road and cartway widths, and lighting restrictions, but these do not pertain to fencing.

The solar power facility owner and operator shall, at its own expense, complete decommissioning of the solar power facility, or individual components, within twelve (12) months after the end of the useful life of the solar power facility or individual components. The solar power facility or individual components shall be presumed to be at the end of its useful life if no electricity is generated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months. Decommissioning shall include removal of collectors, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations to a depth of thirty-six (36) inches, and any other associated facilities. Disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded, unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored. An independent and certified Professional Engineer shall be retained to estimate the total cost of decommissioning (decommissioning costs) without regard to salvage value of the equipment, and the cost of decommissioning net salvage value of the equipment (net decommissioning costs), with estimates submitted after the first year of operation and every fifth year thereafter. The owner or operator must provide a financial security bond with the Borough as payee in an amount approved by the Borough Council, but not less than $50,000, prior to issuance of a zoning permit, to insure decommissioning within 180 days of license or lease expiration and/or cessation of use. The bond remains in place as long as the facilities exist. Decommissioning funds may be in the form of a performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit, corporate guarantee, or other acceptable financial assurance. If the owner or operator fails to complete decommissioning within the prescribed time, the landowner has 180 days to complete it. If neither completes decommissioning, the Borough may take necessary measures. The escrow agent releases funds when decommissioning is satisfactorily completed or upon Borough approval to implement the plan.

Other related standards include height limits, setbacks, fencing, landscaping, and compliance with various codes and regulations, but the explicit glare restriction is specifically in item (8) of section C.

Landscaping may be required to screen as much of the solar power facility ground features as possible, the fence surrounding the support structure, and any other ground level features (such as a building), and in general buffer the solar power facility ground features from neighboring properties. The Borough may permit any combination of existing vegetation, topography, walls, decorative fences or other features instead of landscaping, if the same achieves the same degree of screening as the required landscaping.

Ground-mounted solar photovoltaic systems "shall be screened from adjacent properties and streets by landscaping or 100% opaque fencing." The applicant shall submit a plan for the removal of the principal solar energy system when it becomes functionally obsolete or is no longer in use. The principal solar energy system owner is required to notify the Borough immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The owner shall be responsible for the removal of the facility within six (6) months from the date the applicant ceases use of the facility or the facility becomes obsolete. At the time of issuance of the permit for the construction of the principal solar energy system, the owner shall provide financial security in form and amount acceptable to the Borough to secure the expense of dismantling and removing said structure. Other options and conditions related to accessory solar energy systems include decommissioning requirements if the system remains nonfunctional or inoperative for a continuous period of one year, where the system shall be deemed abandoned and must be removed at the owner's expense after obtaining a demolition permit.

All mechanical equipment of principal solar energy systems including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum of eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate, and provided with screening in accordance with the screening and landscaping requirements of this chapter (see § 270-113).

All principal solar energy production facilities shall be designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare toward any inhabited buildings on adjacent properties as well as adjacent street right-of-ways. This applies to Principal Solar Energy Systems as defined in section RR. Other options include Accessory Solar Energy Systems, which are roof-mounted, provide power only for the principal use on-site, and have glare minimized through the use of non-reflective finishes, but these do not apply to Principal Solar Energy Systems.

Section 37, subsection N states: 'Secure perimeter fencing shall be installed around the solar energy facility. The fencing shall not be constructed within any required landscape buffer or setback.
