The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Solar Energy Facilities (SEF). It states: 'The SEF owner is required to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The SEF shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months.' The SEF owner then has twelve (12) months to dismantle and remove the SEF including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations, solar facility connections and other associated facilities. The site must be restored to its pre-existing condition, except the landowner may authorize any buffer landscaping or access roads to remain. Necessary permits must be obtained prior to decommissioning activities. Financial security must be provided at the time of permit issuance, with a minimum amount of $500,000. The security may be in the form of cash, letter of credit, or an investment grade corporate guarantee. The SEF Developer must provide an estimate of decommissioning costs including an administrative and inflation factor of 25%, less a salvage and resale credit of 80%. This estimate must be updated every 5 years. The SEF Developer must enter into a Decommissioning Agreement with the Township prior to approval of any plan or permit. These requirements apply specifically to SEFs, defined as solar collection systems primarily for off-site use or on-site use if output size is greater than 10kw, with a minimum lot size of 100 acres.

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Solar Energy Facilities (SEF). It requires that "Stormwater runoff from a SEF shall be managed in accordance with the requirements of the Mount Pleasant Stormwater Management Ordinance." The horizontal area of solar panels may be considered a Disconnected Impervious Area ("DIA") only if conditions such as "natural vegetative cover is preserved and/or restored utilizing low impact construction techniques," "vegetative cover has a minimum uniform 90% perennial vegetative cover with a density capable of resisting accelerated erosion and sedimentation," and slope restrictions (e.g., "Panels located on slopes over 15% are not permitted"). Vegetated areas "shall not be subject to chemical fertilization or herbicide/pesticides application, except for those applications necessary to establish the vegetative cover or to prevent invasive species and in accordance with an approved Erosion and Sediment Control Plan." Agrivoltaics require "a written erosion and sediment control plan" for agricultural activities. Upon decommissioning, "Any soil exposed during the removal shall be stabilized in accordance with applicable erosion and sediment control standards." Also, "Any necessary permits, such as Erosion and Sedimentation and NPDES permits, shall be obtained prior to decommissioning activities." These requirements apply specifically to SEFs, defined as systems "principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use or for use on-site if the output size is greater than 10kw."
section: SECTION 5: Article 4 of Ordinance No. 2-07, Section 402, thereof entitled  "ADDITIONAL REQUIREMENTS FOR SPECIFIC PRINCIPAL USES"

summary: The ordinance text permits Solar Energy Facility (SEF) as a principal use only in the AP District with a 100 acre minimum lot area (Section 4). There is no explicit mention of SEF being permitted as a special use or requiring approval by a zoning appeals board or similar process in any district. Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES) are permitted by right in all zoning districts (Section 3), but this does not apply to SEFs. The ordinance sets criteria for SEFs including minimum lot size, setbacks, and height restrictions (Section 5), but these appear as conditions rather than indications of special use status. No other districts or special use provisions for SEFs are mentioned.
section: SECTION 4: Article 3 of Ordinance No. 2-07, Section 306.B.1.f; SECTION 5: Article 4 of Ordinance No. 2-07, Section 402.A.51

summary: The ordinance requires a 50-foot Wetlands Buffer extending from any wetland as part of the Constrained Area where Solar Energy Facilities (SEFs) cannot be sited. Additionally, there is a 25-foot buffer extending from the centerline of natural and man-made drainage corridors (streams, rivers). Solar Arrays shall only be placed outside these constrained areas. No explicit setback distances are provided for lakes or reservoirs. Other constrained areas include floodplains, slopes over 15%, wooded areas, road rights-of-way, and setback areas defined in the underlying zoning district.

The ordinance defines 'Solar glare' as 'The effect produced by light reflecting from a solar panel with an intensity sufficient to cause annoyance, discomfort, or loss in visual performance and visibility.' It states that 'Solar panels shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare shall not be directed onto nearby properties or roadways.' However, the ordinance applies only to 'accessory solar energy systems' defined as systems 'installed to reduce the on-site consumption of utility supplied energy' and 'shall not be used for the generation of power for the sale of energy to other users, although this provision shall not be interpreted to prohibit the sale of excess power generated from time to time to the local utility company.' Therefore, the glare restriction applies only to accessory solar energy systems and not to utility-scale solar energy systems intended for offsite electricity generation or sale.

Mechanical equipment associated with and necessary for the operation of the system shall be screened from any adjacent property that is residentially zoned or used for residential purposes. The screen shall consist of shrubbery, trees, or other non-invasive plant species which provides a visual screen. In lieu of a planting screen, a decorative fence or an accessory structure meeting the requirements of the Zoning Ordinance may be used.

Section E.(7) states: 'No more than twenty (20%) percent of a lot may be covered with a ground mounted Solar Energy System and total lot coverage must not exceed the maximum permitted within the underlying zoning district.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for ground mounted solar energy systems, which can include utility-scale systems. No other more restrictive maximum land coverage values are provided for utility-scale solar energy systems in the text.

The ordinance states: 'The height of a ground mounted Solar Energy System shall not exceed six (6) feet.' This is the most restrictive maximum height explicitly provided that would apply to utility-scale solar energy systems, which are allowed as a principal use only in the Extractive Industrial Zoning District. Other height limits include roof-mounted systems not exceeding the roof line or three (3) feet above a flat roof, but these apply to smaller or accessory systems. The unit for the height restriction is feet.

value: ['All zoning districts except the Extractive Industrial Zoning District']
summary: Solar Energy Commercial Systems are prohibited as a principal use in all zoning districts except in the Extractive Industrial Zoning District. Solar Energy Systems shall be a permitted use in all zoning districts as an accessory to a residential or non-residential use.

All mechanical equipment associated with and necessary for the operation of the Solar Energy System shall be screened from any adjacent property. The screen shall consist of shrubbery, trees, or other plant materials which provide a visual screen. In lieu of a planting screen, a decorative fence, meeting the requirements of the Zoning Ordinance, may be used.

The ordinance states: 'Solar Energy Commercial Systems are prohibited as a principal use in all zoning districts except in the Extractive Industrial Zoning District.' It does not mention any districts where utility-scale solar energy systems are permitted as a special use or require approval by a zoning appeals board or a permitting process. Solar Energy Systems are permitted as an accessory use in all zoning districts, but this applies to smaller or non-commercial systems, not utility-scale systems.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for commercial solar power generation facilities, defined as "Solar Power Generation, Commercial". Key provisions include: "The solar power facility owner and operator shall, at its own expense, complete decommissioning of the solar power facility, or individual components, within (12) twelve months after the end of the useful life of the solar power facility or individual components." Decommissioning must include "removal of collectors, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations to a depth of thirty-six (36) inches, and any other associated facilities." Disturbed earth "shall be graded and re-seeded, unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored." A "financial security bond with the Township as payee in an amount approved by the Board of Supervisors, but not less than $50,000" must be provided prior to permit issuance to insure decommissioning. If the owner/operator fails to decommission, the landowner has 180 days to complete it, after which the Township may take necessary measures. The bond remains in place as long as the facilities exist. These requirements are found under section 847.5 Decommissioning. Other related sections include 847.1 Purposes, 847.2 Permits; Use Regulations, 847.3 Standards and Design, 847.4 Public Inquiries and Complaints, and 847.6 Review Fees, but these do not contain decommissioning requirements.

Section 847.3.C states: "Fencing - A fence may be required around the facility or portions of the facility for safety reasons." This applies to commercial solar power generation facilities, defined as "a facility where one (1) or more solar collectors and/or other accessory structures and buildings... are located and are used for the generation of electricity which is sold on the open market." The ordinance does not mandate fencing but allows that a fence may be required for safety. No other explicit fencing requirements or conditions are provided.

Section 847.3.H states: 'The applicant shall provide details about anticipated glare from the facility, including the time of day, time of year and direction of peak glare periods and document how potential nuisances to area properties and on public roads will be controlled.' This applies to 'Solar power generation, commercial' facilities, which are defined as 'A facility where one (1) or more solar collectors and/or other accessory structures and buildings... are located and are used for the generation of electricity which is sold on the open market.' The ordinance distinguishes these commercial solar power generation facilities from 'Solar collectors, accessory' systems, which are intended to generate electricity for the principal structure and are not for sale of energy. The glare restriction applies explicitly to the commercial solar power generation facilities, not to accessory solar collectors.

Section 847.3.D states: "Landscaping may be required to screen as much of the solar power facility ground features as possible, the fence surrounding the support structure, and any other ground level features (such as a building), and in general buffer the solar power facility ground features from neighboring properties." The Township may permit "any combination of existing vegetation, topography, walls, decorative fences or other features instead of landscaping, if the same achieves the same degree of screening as the required landscaping."

Section 847.3.N states: 'No advertising material or signs other than warning, manufacturer and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment or structures.' Section 847.3.M requires 'a clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations.' These signage requirements apply to commercial solar power generation facilities, defined as 'A facility where one (1) or more solar collectors and/or other accessory structures and buildings... are used for the generation of electricity which is sold on the open market.'

The ordinance lists 'Solar power generation, commercial' under SPECIAL EXCEPTIONS requiring approval by the Planning Commission / Zoning Hearing Board in the Agricultural District. Accessory solar collectors are permitted in all districts but are limited to providing power for the principal use and not for sale, thus not applying to utility-scale systems. No other districts explicitly mention utility-scale solar energy systems as special use or similar.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). The PSES owner is required to notify the Township within thirty (30) days following permanent cessation or abandonment of the operation. The PSES shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months and the owner has evidenced its intent to permanently discontinue operation. The owner shall then have twelve (12) months in which to dismantle and remove the PSES, including all solar-related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, except to the extent the owner agrees that roads and foundations may remain in place. If the owner fails to dismantle and remove the PSES within the established time frames, the Township may complete the decommissioning at the owner's expense, with costs and a penalty of ten (10%) percent charged as a municipal lien or recovered through legal action. Prior to permit issuance, the owner must provide financial security in the form of cash, a letter of credit, or bond, acceptable to the Township, in the amount of eighty-five percent (85%) of the estimated net cost of decommissioning based on an estimate by a professional engineer, accounting for salvage value. This estimate must be updated every five (5) years at the owner's expense and the financial security adjusted accordingly. Other options or conditions include that roads and foundations may remain if agreed by the property owner, and the financial security must be at least $25,000 if the estimate is lower. These requirements apply specifically to PSES and not to Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), which have separate decommissioning provisions.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "All ground mounted PSES (excluding transmission lines) shall be completely enclosed by a minimum seven foot (7’) high fence." Additionally, a "clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence on the surrounding PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards." For screening, "Any areas of a ground mounted PSES that are directly adjacent to a parcel containing an occupied residence and are within the line of sight from the residential structure... shall provide a suitable landscaping buffer area at least ten (10) feet in width of evergreen-type plants... In lieu of a vegetative screen, a decorative fence meeting the Zoning Ordinance requirements may be used."

Noise from the operation of a PSES shall not exceed 50 dBA, as measured at the property line of the nearest property that is not participating (by means of a lease, easement, solar easement or other agreement) in the development and/or operation of the PSES. This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) in the ordinance.

Ground mounted PSES shall not be placed within any legal easement or right-of-way location if such placement would violate the terms and conditions of such easement or right-of-way. A minimum twenty (20) foot wide access road, from a public roadway, shall be provided to the site.

Any areas of a ground mounted PSES that are directly adjacent to a parcel containing an occupied residence and are within the line of sight from the residential structure (other than a residence of the owner participating in the PSES) shall provide a suitable landscaping buffer area at least ten (10) feet in width of evergreen-type plants that shall be of a kind, or used in such a manner, so as to provide a continuous opaque screen within 36 months of commencement of operations in such line-of-sight area to be screened. In lieu of a vegetative screen, a decorative fence meeting the Zoning Ordinance requirements may be used.

The ordinance explicitly enacts signage requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). It states: 'No portion of the PSES shall contain or be used to display advertising. The manufacturer’s name and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be permitted on any equipment of the PSES provided they comply with all existing sign regulations.' Additionally, for ground mounted PSES, 'A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence on the surrounding PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards.' These are the explicit signage requirements for PSES. Other signage-related provisions include that no advertising is allowed except for manufacturer identification, and signage must comply with existing sign regulations.

Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) shall be permitted as a Conditional Use in the "Agricultural/Conservation and Industrial" zoning districts. Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES) are permitted as a use by right in all zoning districts. The text distinguishes PSES from ASES, indicating that larger or utility-scale systems (PSES) require conditional use approval, while smaller or accessory systems (ASES) do not.

Any areas of a ground mounted PSES that are directly adjacent to a parcel containing an occupied residence and are within the line of sight from the residential structure (other than a residence of the owner participating In the PSES) shall provide a suitable landscaping buffer area at least ten (10) feet in width of evergreen-type plants that shall be of a kind, or used In such a manner, so as to provide a continuous opaque screen within 36 months of commencement of operations In such line-of-sight area to be screened. In lieu of a vegetative screen, a decorative fence meeting the Zoning Ordinance requirements may be used.
section: SECTION 3: PRINCIPAL SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS (PSES), B, Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems

summary: The surface area of a ground-mounted solar energy system shall not exceed thirty (30) percent of maximum lot coverage of the lot. This is stated in section 18.D: 'The surface area of a ground-mounted solar energy system... shall not exceed thirty (30) percent of maximum lot coverage of the lot.' No other explicit maximum land coverage limits for wind turbines or the entire wind and/or solar farm are stated. The units are expressed as a percentage of the lot's maximum allowable coverage, not an absolute area measurement.

The applicant shall be responsible for the decommissioning of the wind and/or solar farm in accordance with the following requirements: 1. The applicant shall, at his/her expense, complete decommissioning of the wind and/or solar farm, or individual wind turbines, within (12) twelve months after the end of the useful life of the wind and/or solar farm or individual wind turbines or solar panels. The wind and/or solar farm or individual wind turbines or solar panels will presume to be at the end of its useful life if no electricity is generated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months. 2. Decommissioning shall include removal of wind turbines and solar panels, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations to a depth of 36 inches, and any other associated facilities. 3. Disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded, unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored. 4. An independent and certified Professional Engineer shall be retained to estimate the total cost of decommissioning ('Decommissioning Costs') without regard to salvage value of the equipment, and the cost of decommissioning net salvage value of the equipment ('Net Decommissioning Costs'). Said estimates shall be submitted to the Township after the first year of operation and every fifth year thereafter at the applicant’s and/or any successor’s expense. 5. The applicant shall post and maintain decommissioning funds in an amount equal to net decommissioning costs; provided, that at no point shall decommissioning funds be less than twenty-five (25) percent of decommissioning costs. The decommissioning funds shall be posted and maintained with a bonding company or Federal or Commonwealth chartered lending institution chosen by the Facility Owner or Operator and participating landowner posting the financial security, provided that the bonding company or lending institution is authorized to conduct such business within the Commonwealth and is approved by the Township. 6. Decommissioning funds may be in the form of a performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit, corporate guarantee or other form of financial assurance as may be acceptable to the Township. 7. If the applicant fails to complete decommissioning within the period prescribed, then the landowner shall have six (6) months to complete decommissioning. 8. If neither the applicant, nor the landowner complete decommissioning within the periods prescribed, then the Township may take such measures as necessary to complete decommissioning. 9. The escrow agent shall release the decommissioning funds when the applicant has demonstrated and the municipality concurs that decommissioning has been satisfactorily completed, or upon written approval of the municipality in order to implement the decommissioning plan.

Solar energy panels shall be designed and located in order to minimize reflective glare towards any adjoining use and/or road. This applies to alternate energy production facilities generally (item 10) and is reiterated under Power Generation Facilities (item S). For wind and/or solar farms specifically, the ordinance requires detailed project descriptions and compliance with various standards but does not exempt glare restrictions. The ordinance also sets maximum energy generation limits based on the principal use type, such as 1.5 times annual energy needs for residential use, 2.0 times for commercial use, up to 5.0 times for municipal use, and includes structural height, lot coverage, and setback requirements.

Audible sound from a wind and/or solar farm shall not exceed fifty-five (55) dbA, as measured at specified minimum distances. Methods for measuring and reporting acoustic emissions shall meet or exceed AWEA Standard 2.1 - 1989 titled Procedures for the Measurement and Reporting of Acoustic Emissions from Wind Turbine Generation Systems Volume I: First Tier. The measurement distances include not less than fifty (50) feet or 1.1 times the wind turbine height, whichever is greater, from the nearest principal building of a consenting property owner, adjoining property line, and right-of-way of any street. The unit 'dbA' is clarified as 'dBA' in standard noise measurement terms.

Wind turbines shall be setback the following distances as measured from the center of the wind turbine base to the nearest point of the respective feature listed in Table 4.5: Adjoining property - 1.5 times turbine height. Another value mentioned is a minimum distance of 1.1 times the wind turbine height or 50 feet, whichever is greater, from the adjoining property line, but this applies to audible sound measurement, not siting setbacks. No static distance value is added to the multiplier for setbacks from property lines. No explicit multiplier or numeric setback is provided for solar panels or solar farms from property lines.

Wind turbines shall be setback the following distances as measured from the center of the wind turbine base to the nearest point of the respective feature listed in Table 4.5: Adjoining road right-of-way 1.5 times turbine height. Additionally, audible sound from a wind and/or solar farm shall not exceed fifty-five (55) dbA, as measured at a distance of not less than fifty (50) feet or 1.1 times the wind turbine height, whichever is greater, from the right-of-way of any street. Other options include a minimum distance of 50 feet or 1.1 times the turbine height, whichever is greater, from the right-of-way of any street for sound measurement purposes.

The ordinance states that 'Wind and/or Solar Farms' are listed under 'USES PERMITTED BY CONDITIONAL USE,' requiring approval by the Board of Supervisors and compliance with specific use standards found in Article 4, Section 402. It also notes that 'Alternative Energy Production Facilities' are permitted in the Agricultural District (200.B) and as accessory uses, but the conditional use status specifically applies to 'Wind and/or Solar Farms.' The text specifies: 'In addition to the general criteria listed in Article 4, Section 401.B of this Ordinance, specific use standards can be found in Article 4, Section 402. These standards must be satisfied prior to approval of any application for a conditional use by the Board of Supervisors.' Solar overlay districts are excluded from this analysis.

The minimum setback distance from the nearest principal building of a property owner who has agreed to locate the proposed wind and/or solar farm upon his/her property is a distance of not less than fifty (50) feet or 1.1 times the wind turbine height, whichever is greater. There is no static distance value added to the multiplier; the fifty feet is a standalone minimum distance. Other setback distances mentioned in the ordinance apply to adjoining property lines, roads, and other features, but are not relevant to participating occupied dwellings.

Wind turbines shall be setback the following distances as measured from the center of the wind turbine base to the nearest point of the respective feature listed in Table 4.5: Above ground utility line right-of-way - Turbine height plus ten feet. Other setbacks listed in Table 4.5 include: Occupied building on site - Turbine height plus ten feet; Adjoining property - 1.5 times turbine height; Adjoining road right-of-way - 1.5 times turbine height.

Section 18.A requires the applicant to "prepare and submit a narrative and mapping describing the proposed wind and/or solar farm, including: 1. An overview of the project. 2. The project location. 3. The approximate generating capacity of the wind and/or solar farm. 4. The approximate number, representative types and height or range of heights of wind turbines and/or solar panels to be constructed, including their generating capacity, dimensions and respective manufacturers. 5. A description of accessory facilities. 6. An affidavit or similar evidence of agreement between the property owner(s) and the applicant demonstrating that the applicant has the permission of the property owner(s) to apply for necessary permits for construction and operation of the wind and/or solar farm. 7. A listing and map of the properties on which the proposed wind and solar farm will be located, and the properties adjacent to where the wind and/or solar farm will be located. 8. A site plan showing the planned location of each wind turbine and/or solar panel, property lines, setback lines, access road and turnout locations, substation(s), electrical cabling from the wind and/or solar farm to the substation(s), ancillary equipment, buildings, and structures, including permanent meteorological towers, associated transmission lines, and layout of all structures within the geographical boundaries of any applicable setback." These requirements apply to wind and/or solar farms and constitute explicit visual impact assessment requirements. Other provisions in section 18 address design, safety, setbacks, maintenance, decommissioning, and insurance but do not specifically impose additional visual impact assessment requirements.

§ 27-1307 Maintenance and Protection Assurances states: 'A disconnected or abandoned energy system shall be removed from the property within 60 days of such abandonment.' This decommissioning requirement applies to energy systems, which includes commercial solar farms as defined in § 27-1306. § 27-1306 Solar Farms; Commercial Solar Energy Systems; Wind Energy Conversion Systems permits commercial solar farms only in the I-1 Industrial Zoning District as a conditional use, requires a minimum lot size of 50 acres, and mandates a minimum setback of 100 feet from any property line and/or road right-of-way line.

The minimum lot size for the establishment of any solar farm or other commercial solar energy system or wind energy conversion system shall be 50 acres. (§ 27-1306(2)) This applies to solar farms and other solar energy systems installed for commercial production, distribution, or sale of energy or off-site distribution. The unit 'acres' is explicitly stated as the measure of area for this minimum lot size.
section: § 27-1306 Solar Farms; Commercial Solar Energy Systems; Wind Energy Conversion Systems

summary: Commercial solar farms and other solar energy systems installed for commercial production, distribution, or sale or off-site distribution shall be permitted only in the I-1 Industrial Zoning District as a conditional use (§ 27-1306.1). The minimum lot size for such systems is 50 acres (§ 27-1306.2). By implication, commercial solar farms are not permitted in any other zoning districts, although no other districts are specifically named or abbreviated as prohibiting these uses unconditionally. Smaller or non-commercial solar energy systems are permitted in any zoning district (§ 27-1305.1), but these provisions apply only to systems installed for the benefit of the property owner and not for commercial distribution (§ 27-1305.2).
section: § 27-1306 Solar Farms; Commercial Solar Energy Systems; Wind Energy Conversion Systems.

summary: The solar panels, wind rotors, and/or other associated structures of the solar farm or other commercial solar energy system or wind energy conversion system shall be set back a minimum of 100 feet from any property line and/or road right-of-way line. Other setback provisions apply only to smaller or non-commercial systems, such as solar panels with a combined glazing area of 65 square feet or less which must be a minimum of three feet from any property line, or solar panels attached to principal or accessory structures which must comply with zoning setbacks for those structures.
section: § 27-1306 Solar Farms; Commercial Solar Energy Systems; Wind Energy Conversion Systems.

summary: The solar panels, wind rotors, and/or other associated structures of the solar farm or other commercial solar energy system or wind energy conversion system shall be set back a minimum of 100 feet from any property line and/or road right-of-way line.
section: § 27-1306 Solar Farms; Commercial Solar Energy Systems; Wind Energy Conversion Systems.

summary: Commercial solar farms and other solar energy systems or wind energy conversion systems installed for the commercial production, distribution, or sale of energy or other off-site distribution shall be permitted only in the I-1 Industrial Zoning District as a conditional use. The minimum lot size for the establishment of any solar farm or other commercial solar energy system or wind energy conversion system shall be 50 acres. The solar panels, wind rotors, and/or other associated structures shall be set back a minimum of 100 feet from any property line and/or road right-of-way line. Other solar, wind and alternate energy systems installed for the benefit of the property owner and used on-site are permitted within any zoning district under § 27-1305, but these do not apply to commercial solar farms.

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Solar Energy Facilities (SEFs). It states: 'The SEF owner is required to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The SEF shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months.' The SEF owner then has twelve (12) months to 'dismantle and remove in its entirety the SEF, including all surface and subsurface solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, fencing, foundations, solar facility connections and other associated facilities in accordance with agreements with the property owners and good industry practice.' The materials shall be re-sold or salvaged to the extent possible, and any soil exposed during removal shall be stabilized. The SEF site must be restored to its pre-existing condition unless the landowner authorizes otherwise. Necessary permits must be obtained prior to decommissioning. Financial security in the amount of 110% of the estimated decommissioning cost must be provided at the time of SALDO approval and updated every five years. A Decommissioning Agreement must be entered into with the Township outlining responsibilities. These requirements apply specifically to SEFs, which are defined as systems supplying power primarily for off-site use and include large-scale facilities with associated infrastructure.

All ground-mounted SEF shall be completely enclosed by a minimum six (6) foot high fence and a self-locking gate. A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the SEF, informing individuals of potential voltage hazards. The security fencing required around the perimeter of the SEF shall be located on the interior side of the buffer yard. Screen Plantings shall be provided in the buffer yard in areas where adjacent or neighboring properties contain residential uses. The Screen Plantings shall be installed along the exterior side of the security fencing required, except where existing vegetation already screens the view, access points or utility easements preclude planting, or the SEF is not visible from adjacent residential properties.

The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Solar Energy Facilities (SEF) under §515.3: "(7) Glare (a) All SEF shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures or roadways. Exterior surfaces shall have a non-reflective finish. (b) The applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation." This applies specifically to SEFs, which are defined as systems "principally to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use." The ordinance also includes glare restrictions for Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), but those apply to smaller, primarily on-site systems and are not the focus here.

All ground mounted solar panels shall comply with a maximum fifteen (15) foot height requirement. All other SEF components should comply with the underlying district maximum height requirement. SEF components may be in excess of the maximum height requirement where the Applicant can demonstrate in the subdivision and land development process the necessity and benefit. For roof and wall mounted principal Solar Energy Facilities, the total height of a building with the system shall not exceed by more than 3 feet above the maximum building height specified for principal or accessory buildings within the applicable zoning district.

The ordinance explicitly states under Noise Management (§515.3, item 7(a)) that 'Noise from a SEF shall not exceed 50dBA, as measured at the property line.' This is the only maximum noise level restriction provided for Solar Energy Facilities (SEF), which are defined as systems primarily for off-site electricity generation or sale. The unit 'dBA' refers to A-weighted decibels, a standard unit for measuring noise levels.

In addition to property line setbacks, ground mounted SEF shall be buffered from uses on adjacent or neighboring properties by a buffer yard with a minimum width shall be 20 ft. The security fencing required around the perimeter of the SEF shall be located on the interior side of the buffer yard. ... Minimum yard setbacks shall be as defined in the underlying zoning district. No lot line setback will be required where there is a grouping of two or more Solar Energy Facilities which are held by a common owner or leased to a common lessee and which are part of a single solar energy production development project, where each landowner has provided a written waiver of the lot line setback. A minimum of a 25’ setback shall be maintained along either side of any regulated stream or regulatory wetland.
section: §515.3 Solar Energy Facility (SEF) - Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems - Setbacks

summary: A minimum of a 25’ setback shall be maintained along either side of any regulated stream or regulatory wetland. Solar Arrays shall not be located in wetlands or within a 50-foot buffer from any wetland, unless a jurisdictional determination has been made by the Army Corps of Engineers. Solar Arrays shall not be located in floodplains, regulated natural and man-made drainage corridors (with a 25-foot buffer), slopes over 25%, wooded areas requiring removal of more than 50% of mature trees, road rights-of-way, or setback areas defined in the underlying zoning district.

Ground mounted SEF shall be screened and buffered in accordance with the standards set forth below providing that: (a) In addition to property line setbacks, ground mounted SEF shall be buffered from uses on adjacent or neighboring properties by a buffer yard with a minimum width shall be 20 ft. The security fencing required around the perimeter of the SEF shall be located on the interior side of the buffer yard. Screen Plantings shall be provided in the buffer yard in the areas where adjacent or neighboring properties contain residential uses. (b) The Screen Plantings shall be installed along the exterior side of the security fencing required in Paragraph 8 below, around the perimeter of the SEF, except where: Existing vegetation already screens the view of the SEF from the residential uses; Access points or utility easements preclude the planting of vegetation; or, The SEF is not visible from any adjacent or neighboring properties containing residential uses. (c) The Screen Plantings shall be made in three rows of staggered plant material with a mix of evergreen trees (not less than 70%), deciduous trees, flowering trees, and shrubs. Separation distances between the plant material shall achieve the density necessary to fully screen the view of the SEF from the residential uses. Trees shall be a minimum of 6 ft. in height from grade at the time of planting. Screen Plantings shall be permanently maintained, and shall be replaced as necessary to continuously screen, year-round, the SEF from visibility.

The ordinance requires that a clearly visible warning sign be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the Solar Energy Facility (SEF), informing individuals of potential voltage hazards. The manufacturer's name and equipment information or indication of ownership is allowed on any equipment of the SEF provided they comply with the prevailing sign regulations. Additionally, an emergency contact number and responsible person's name must be posted at the main access point to the SEF as well as at intervals around the perimeter of the SEF to facilitate an immediate response in case of emergency. summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). Key provisions include: "If a PSES remains nonfunctional or inoperative for a continuous period of six months, the facility shall be deemed to be abandoned and shall constitute a public nuisance... Within six months of abandonment, the facility operator shall remove the system, after a demolition permit has been obtained..." Removal includes "Any aboveground mechanical equipment, wiring, and structural components" and "Underground wiring and structural components" which "shall be removed and disposed of in accordance with all legal requirements." The PSES owner must "secure the property pursuant to the applicable provisions... until the PSES is completely decommissioned or returned to another allowed use." Disturbed earth "shall be restored, graded and reseeded, or immediately returned to another allowed use." The owner must submit "an estimate for the total cost of decommissioning... and also an estimate of the cost of decommissioning net of the salvage value..." prior to building permit and update it every five years. Financial security must be posted at "110% of the net decommissioning costs, provided that at no point shall the financial security be less than 50% of the gross decommissioning costs." (Section 8(D)) The most restrictive setback from property lines or lot lines is 75 feet from side yard property lines.
section: SECTION 8. ADDITIONAL REQUIREMENTS FOR SOLAR ENERGY FACILITIES (SEF)

summary: All SEF buildings and equipment shall be setback a minimum of 250 feet from the front yard edge of road right-of-way. This applies to commercial Solar Energy Facilities (SEFs) designed to supply electrical power primarily for off-site use. Other setbacks mentioned include 75 feet from side yard property lines, 100 feet from rear yard property line, 300 feet from perennial streams and occupied buildings, but these do not pertain to roads.
section: SECTION 8. ADDITIONAL REQUIREMENTS FOR SOLAR ENERGY FACILITIES (SEF)

summary: The ordinance requires screening at the perimeter of the Alternative Energy Facility property in the form of "privacy fencing or native evergreen plant species or some combination thereof" (Section 5(H)). Additional vegetative cover may be required at the discretion of the Township along with security fencing (Section 5(F)). For Solar Energy Facilities specifically, "the SEF shall be screened from any adjacent residential or agricultural property" using "plants, evergreens, arborvitae, trees or similar plants and shrubs which provide an effective visual screen" (Section 8(K)). Also, the SEF "shall be completely enclosed with a minimum eight-foot-high security fence with additional deterrents attached to the top. Additional vegetative cover may be required at the discretion of the Township" (Section 8(L)). These requirements apply to commercial Alternative Energy Facilities, including Solar Energy Facilities designed to supply electrical power primarily for off-site use, and do not apply to individual residential or farm uses.
section: SECTION 5. AEF DESIGN, INSTALLATION AND MAINTENANCE REQUIREMENTS and SECTION 8. ADDITIONAL REQUIREMENTS FOR SOLAR ENERGY FACILITIES (SEF)

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts signage requirements for commercial Alternative Energy Facilities, including Solar Energy Facilities designed primarily for off-site use. It requires "appropriate safety/warning signage concerning live voltage shall be placed on or within three (3) feet of any ground-mounted electrical devices, equipment and structures" (Section 5(I)). It also mandates that "signs with the current emergency contact name and phone number and site name" be posted "at each gate entry point to the facility during installation and operations" (Section 6(D)). Additionally, "a valid physical address for the site from the Township" must be "posted clearly near the road at the entrance to the facility at all times" (Section 6(A)). These requirements apply to commercial-scale facilities and are not limited to smaller or residential systems.
section: SECTION 5. AEF DESIGN, INSTALLATION AND MAINTENANCE REQUIREMENTS and SECTION 6. AEF EMERGENCY RESPONSE PLAN AND EMERGENCY SERVICES ON-SITE TRAINING

summary: The ordinance requires that during decommissioning, "Disturbed earth shall be graded and reseeded. Soil samples shall be collected and analyzed. Ground water samples shall be collected and analyzed at the site and on all adjacent properties within 1,000 feet of the site boundaries. Results of the ground and water sample tests shall be submitted to the Township. Results of the water sample test shall also be provided to the adjacent property owners." Additionally, prior to construction, the Developer shall "collect and analyze background soil samples in the area where the facilities are to be installed for pH, oil, grease, lead, benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene (BTEX), cadmium, chromium and zinc" and "collect and analyze ground water samples at the site and on all adjacent properties within 1,000 feet of the site boundaries." The Operator shall repeat soil and water sampling every five years on the anniversary of the facility’s startup date, with all results submitted to the Township (and adjacent property owners for groundwater). These requirements apply to commercial Solar Energy Facilities designed to supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use.

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires that "The facility owner and/or operator of a ground array solar energy system shall, at its expense, complete decommissioning of the facility within six (6) months after the facility is abandoned or at the end of its useful life." Decommissioning includes "the removal of the ground array solar energy system and any other associated facilities and the cleaning and restoration of the site." If not completed within six months, the Township will notify the owner to complete decommissioning within thirty days, after which the Township may perform the decommissioning and charge the owner. The decommissioning process "shall be subject to a Decommissioning Agreement prepared by or approved by the Township Solicitor and the Township Engineer and shall require that financial security be posted in an amount necessary to facilitate the removal of all aspects of the Solar Array Field." Additionally, "The Applicant shall provide a decommissioning plan (acceptable to the Township Engineer) and sufficient financial security to cover the costs to Decommission the Ground array solar energy system according to all applicable state and federal regulations." These requirements apply to Grid-Scale Solar Energy Systems, defined as systems with "a rated capacity of more than thirty (30) kilowatts or that has a lot coverage collector area of more than one thousand five hundred (1,500) square feet."

Section 8, subsection 6.C.iii states: 'All ground arrays shall be enclosed with fencing in order to provide for the security and safety of the solar energy system and the public.' This fencing requirement applies to Grid-Scale Solar Energy Systems, defined as systems with 'a rated capacity of more than thirty (30) kilowatts or that has a lot coverage collector area of more than one thousand five hundred (1,500) square feet.' Other related requirements include height limits, setbacks, emergency lighting provisions, screening from residential properties, and decommissioning plans.

Section 8.D.i states: 'Any glare from a solar panel shall be directed away from an adjoining property; in addition the solar panel system shall not project glare onto the adjoining roadways.' Section 8.D.ii requires: 'Solar panels shall be covered with anti-reflective surface materials or coatings. If there is a concern about glare for a specific location, the developer shall prepare a glint and glare study.' These requirements apply to Grid-Scale Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems with a rated capacity of more than thirty (30) kilowatts or a lot coverage collector area of more than one thousand five hundred (1,500) square feet, and are treated as principal uses subject to special exception use criteria in the Farm & Forest Zoning District and other zoning districts as specified.

For roof-mounted Grid-Scale Solar Energy Systems, solar panels shall not exceed the height of the roofline on pitched roofs, and on flat roofs, panels shall be angled so they are not more than three (3) feet above the roofline, also not exceeding the height requirements for the zoning district. For ground array Grid-Scale Solar Energy Systems, ground arrays shall not exceed a height of fifteen (15) feet above the ground. The most restrictive maximum height is three (3) feet above the roofline for flat roofs.

Ground arrays are subject to a setback distance of no less than 100 feet from the front, rear or side yards or from the set back distance prescribed for any structure for the zoning district in which the ground array is to be constructed, whichever is greater.

summary: Section 8, subsection 6.C.vi requires that "All ground mounted solar energy mechanical equipment shall be screened from any adjacent property that is used for residential purposes. The screen shall consist of shrubbery, trees or other non-invasive plant species as set forth in Section 27-404.4. to provide a visual screen from any adjacent property that is zoned or used for residential and/or commercial purposes." It further specifies that "If the panels are fixed screening shall be to the base of the panel for the side facing the sun. The remaining sides shall be fully screened. If the panels rotate with the sun the panels shall be screened to the base of the panel in all rotational directions. The other sides shall be fully screened." This screening shall not be located in the utility easement area. No advertising display is allowed except for reasonable identification of equipment manufacturers. This applies to Grid-Scale Solar Energy Systems defined as systems with rated capacity of more than thirty (30) kilowatts or lot coverage collector area of more than one thousand five hundred (1,500) square feet. Other related requirements include fencing for security, setback distances, height limits, and decommissioning plans, but these do not pertain to vegetative buffer or screening.

Grid-Scale Solar Energy Systems shall be a special exception use in the Farm & Forest Zoning District as set forth in Section 27-305 of the Plainfield Township Zoning Ordinance. Section 7 states: 'Grid-Scale Solar Energy Systems shall be added to the Farm & Forest Zoning District as a special exception use.' Section 8 further clarifies: 'A Grid-Scale Solar Energy System shall be a special exception use in the Farm & Forest Zoning District and is subject to the specific criteria as set forth in Subsection 6 below.' Accessory Solar Energy Systems are permitted as accessory uses in all zoning districts but are not grid-scale or primary use. No other districts are mentioned as permitting Grid-Scale Solar Energy Systems as a special exception or similar use. Solar overlay districts are excluded per instructions.

summary: Ground arrays are subject to a setback distance of no less than 100 feet from the front, rear or side yards or from the set back distance prescribed for any structure for the zoning district in which the ground array is to be constructed, whichever is greater.

Subsection 6.C.vi requires: 'All ground mounted solar energy mechanical equipment shall be screened from any adjacent property that is used for residential purposes. The screen shall consist of shrubbery, trees or other non-invasive plant species as set forth in Section 27-404.4. to provide a visual screen from any adjacent property that is zoned or used for residential and/or commercial purposes. The screening shall be placed within the line of sight distance from adjacent properties.' Section 9 requires submission of a Land Development Plan containing detailed site plans and 'Other relevant studies, reports, certifications and approvals as may be provided by the Applicant or required by the Township to ensure compliance with this Ordinance.' These provisions explicitly enact visual impact assessment requirements for Grid-Scale Solar Energy Systems. Other conditions include setback distances, height limits, fencing, decommissioning plans, and compliance with construction codes, but these do not pertain directly to visual impact assessment requirements.

The ordinance states in Section 3.16(D)(2) that 'The PSES shall not exceed twenty-five (25%) percent of the total area of the lot in the Agricultural District.' The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the total lot area, not as a specific area value.
section: SECTION 3.16 Ground Mounted Principal Solar Systems

summary: Section 3.14 Decommissioning states: (A) Each PSES and all solar related equipment shall be removed within twelve (12) months of the date when the use has been discontinued or abandoned by system owner and/or operator, or upon termination of the useful life of same. (B) The PSES owner is required to notify Porter Township, Clinton County, Pennsylvania, immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The PSES shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months. (C) The PSES owner shall then have twelve (12) months in which to dismantle and remove the PSES including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations and other associated facilities from the property. The owner shall also restore the land to its original condition, including forestry plantings of the same type/variety and density as the original, as set forth in the silviculture study mentioned above, without re-introduction of invasive species. If the owner fails to dismantle and/or remove the PSES and restore the land within the established time frames, Porter Township, Clinton County, Pennsylvania, may complete the decommissioning and land restoration at the owner’s expense to include Court costs and reasonable attorney’s fees. (D) At the time of issuance of the permit for the construction of the PSES, the owner shall provide financial security in the form and amount acceptable to Porter Township, Clinton County, Pennsylvania, to secure the expense of dismantling and removing said PSES and restoration of the land to its original condition, including forestry plantings of the same type/variety and density as the original. (E) The PSES owner shall, at the request of Porter Township, Clinton County, Pennsylvania, provide information concerning the amount of energy generated by the PSES in the last 12 months.

Ground mounted PSES shall be screened from adjoining residential uses or zones by placement of a fence, at least eight (8) feet in height, that is sufficiently opaque to prohibit a person at ground level from seeing through it. All ground-mounted PSES shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate. A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards.
section: Sec. 3.16 Ground Mounted Principal Solar Systems

summary: Section 3.9 Glare: (A) All PSES shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures or roadways. (B) The applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation.

Section 3.16(E) states: 'Ground mounted PSES shall be screened from adjoining residential uses or zones by placement of a fence, at least eight (8) feet in height, that is sufficiently opaque to prohibit a person at ground level from seeing through it.' The ordinance does not explicitly require vegetative buffers for PSES but encourages 'low maintenance and low growing vegetative surfaces under the system as a best management practice for storm water management' (Section 3.16(D)(4)). No other explicit vegetative buffer or screening requirements for PSES are provided.

Section 3.8 Signage: "No portion of the PSES shall contain or be used to display signage, except that the manufacturer’s name and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of the PSES provided they comply with the prevailing sign regulations." This applies specifically to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), which are defined as systems "principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use." Other signage provisions in the ordinance apply only to Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), such as Sec. 2.6 which states: "Signage is prohibited except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer of the system."

PSES shall be permitted as a conditional use in the Agricultural and Commercial Industrial Districts. Sections I, III, and IV amend various Articles to add 'Solar Energy Systems' under conditional uses. ASES shall be permitted as an accessory use in all zoning districts, but this applies to smaller or accessory systems and is not relevant to utility-scale systems.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for commercial solar power generation facilities. Key provisions include: the owner/operator must complete decommissioning within twelve (12) months after the end of the useful life or if no electricity is generated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months; decommissioning shall include removal of collectors, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations to a depth of thirty‐six (36) inches, and any other associated facilities; disturbed earth shall be graded and re‐seeded unless the landowner requests otherwise in writing; an independent and certified Professional Engineer shall estimate decommissioning costs and net decommissioning costs, with estimates submitted after the first year of operation and every fifth year thereafter; the owner/operator must provide financial security to the Borough, not less than $50,000, to insure decommissioning within one hundred eighty (180) days of license expiration or cessation of use; decommissioning funds may be in the form of a performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit, corporate guarantee, or other acceptable financial assurance; if the owner/operator fails to decommission, the landowner has one hundred eighty (180) days to complete decommissioning; if neither completes decommissioning, the Borough may take necessary measures; and decommissioning funds shall be released upon satisfactory completion or written Borough approval to implement the plan.

Section C.3 states: 'A fence may be required around the facility or portions of the facility for safety reasons.' This applies to commercial solar power generation facilities, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. The ordinance does not mandate fencing in all cases but allows the Borough to require it based on safety considerations.

Section C.8 states: 'The applicant shall provide details about anticipated glare from the facility, including the time of day, time of year and direction of peak glare periods and document how potential nuisances to area properties and on public roads shall be controlled.' This applies to commercial solar power generation facilities, which are permitted only in specified districts and require permits. The ordinance includes other standards such as height limits, setbacks, fencing, landscaping, and more, but only C.8 explicitly addresses glare restrictions.

Section C.4 Landscaping states: 'Landscaping may be required to screen as much of the solar power facility ground features as possible, the fence surrounding the support structure, and any other ground level features (such as a building), and in general buffer the solar power facility ground features from neighboring properties.' The Borough may permit 'any combination of existing vegetation, topography, walls, decorative fences or other features instead of landscaping, if the same achieves the same degree of screening as the required landscaping.'

Section C.13 requires "A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad‐mounted transformers and substations." It also requires "Visible, reflective, colored objects, such as flags, reflectors, or tape shall be placed on the anchor points of guy wires and along the guy wires up to a height of ten (10) feet from the ground." Section C.14 states "No advertising material or signs other than warning, manufacturer and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment or structures." These signage requirements apply to commercial solar power generation facilities.

The applicant shall submit a plan for the removal of the principal solar energy systems when it becomes functionally obsolete or is no longer in use. The principal solar energy system owner is required to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The owner shall be responsible for the removal of the facility within six (6) months from the date the applicant ceases use of the facility or the facility becomes obsolete. At the time of issuance of the permit for the construction of the principal solar energy system, the owner shall provide financial security in form and amount acceptable to the Township to secure the expense of dismantling and removing said structures.

Section 404.5.9 states: 'All mechanical equipment of principal solar energy systems including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate, and provided with screening in accordance with Screening and Landscaping requirements of this Ordinance (see Section 320).' This fencing requirement applies specifically to Principal Solar Energy Systems. Other related provisions include that principal solar energy systems must conform to industry standards (404.5.1), be designed to prevent reflective glare (404.5.7), have underground utility lines where feasible (404.5.6), and submit a removal plan when obsolete (404.5.10).

Section 404.5.7 states: 'All principal solar energy systems shall be designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare toward any inhabited buildings on adjacent properties as well as adjacent street rights-of-way.' Principal Solar Energy Systems are permitted by special exception in the Industrial Zone subject to regulations including compliance with industry standards, lot coverage considerations, underground utility placement, fencing and screening requirements, and removal plans. Other options mentioned include Accessory Solar Energy Systems (Section 404.3), which have their own glare restriction: 'Accessory solar energy systems shall be designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare toward any inhabited structure on adjacent properties as well as adjacent street rights-of-way.' However, these apply to accessory systems, not principal systems.

Section 404.5.9 states: 'All mechanical equipment of principal solar energy systems including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate, and provided with screening in accordance with Screening and Landscaping requirements of this Ordinance (see Section 320).' There is no explicit mention of vegetative buffer requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems in the provided text.

Section 404.5.9 requires that "A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations or fence" for Principal Solar Energy Systems. Additionally, all mechanical equipment must be enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate and screening per Section 320. The owner must submit a removal plan and provide financial security for dismantling. Other related requirements include design standards, underground utility lines, glare prevention, height regulations, and impervious surface considerations, but these do not pertain to signage. No other signage requirements are explicitly stated for Principal Solar Energy Systems.

Principal Solar Energy Systems are permitted by special exception in the Industrial Zone subject to the following regulations: '404.5 Principal Solar Energy Systems are permitted by special exception in the Industrial Zone subject to the following regulations.' Accessory Solar Energy Systems are permitted as accessory uses in all zones but are limited to on-site use and smaller scale. No other districts are listed as permitting principal solar energy systems as a special use or similar. The Land Use Table confirms: 'Alternative energy production facilities (Principal Solar Energy Systems and Principal Wind Energy Systems), subject to the requirements of Section 404.' are special exceptions (SE) in the Industrial Zone.

The ordinance defines a 'Principal Solar Energy Facility' as a utility-scale facility used to supply electrical or thermal power for off-site use. It requires a decommissioning plan including: anticipated life, conditions for decommissioning (e.g., expiration of land lease, intent to abandon), manner of disposal of structures and hazardous waste, restoration of property to pre-development conditions, estimated decommissioning cost without regard to salvage value, identification of responsible entity with notice requirements, and proposed amount and form of performance security. The plan must be recorded with the Recorder of Deeds. Upon cessation or abandonment (presumed if no power is generated for six months), the facility must be decommissioned within one year, meaning removal of solar panels, related equipment, and transmission lines (except those buried more than 42"  below grade) and site restoration. Performance security of $100,000 per megawatt is required, subject to reduction by 80% of salvage value and periodic updates every five years. The security must be submitted no later than the application for building or electric permit or 30 days prior to development start. The ordinance also requires written notice to the Township 60 days in advance of ownership changes and immediate notification upon cessation or abandonment.

The ordinance defines a principal solar energy facility as "a utility-scale facility consisting of one or more freestanding ground or roof mounted solar panels... and used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power, and supply electrical or thermal power for off-site use(s)." It explicitly requires that "The solar energy facility shall be enclosed with a fence not exceeding eight feet in height with a self-locking gate. The fence shall maintain a minimum ground clearance of six inches. The required perimeter fence shall be placed on the inside of the required buffer."

The ordinance defines a Principal Solar Energy Facility as "a utility-scale facility ... used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power, and supply electrical or thermal power for off-site use(s)." It requires that the zoning permit application include a "Glare analysis demonstrating, through components design, siting or mitigation measures, that any glare produced by the solar energy facility will not have an adverse impact on adjacent uses and roadways." Additionally, "Solar energy panels and support structures shall be constructed of non-reflective materials."

The ordinance defines a principal solar energy facility as a utility-scale facility and explicitly states: 'Ground-mounted solar panels shall not exceed a height of 12 feet at the highest point of the structure.' This is the maximum structure height allowed for utility-scale solar energy systems. No other height limits for such systems are provided. The unit of measurement is feet.

The ordinance states: 'Noise generated from the activities at the use shall not exceed 60 dBA measured at the lot line, but in no event shall exceed the ambient noise level, measured at the lot line and made a part of the application, by more than 10 dBA.' This applies specifically to principal solar energy facilities defined as utility-scale systems supplying off-site power. The units for noise level are dBA, a standard unit for measuring sound levels.

The solar energy facility shall be no closer than 200 feet from the lot line of an adjacent lot improved with a dwelling or an unimproved lot in a residential zoning district; provided that the setback shall not apply to a shared property line of properties hosting a single solar energy facility. Additionally, a buffer no less than 30 feet in depth shall be required along any lot line adjacent to a lot improved with a dwelling or an unimproved lot in a residential zoning district, provided that the buffer along a lot line shall not apply to lots hosting a single solar energy facility.

A buffer no less than 30 feet in depth shall be required along (i) any public road frontage ... Where the siting of the solar energy facility requires the buffer to be sited in the immediate proximity of a public road, the required buffer shall be measured from the existing right-of-way or from the minimum future right-of-way, whichever is larger. Additionally, the solar energy facility use developed area shall exclude road rights-of-way.

The ordinance explicitly requires a buffer no less than 30 feet in depth along (i) any public road frontage and (ii) any lot line adjacent to a lot improved with a dwelling or an unimproved lot in a residential zoning district, provided that the buffer along a lot line shall not apply to lots hosting a single solar energy facility. The buffer shall be planted to establish a visual screen designed to provide a natural looking visual element, including a mix of species and spacing, primarily of species native to Pennsylvania, resistant to disease, road salt and air pollution, and capable of producing within 3 years a mostly solid year-round visual screen at least 6 feet in height. The planted visual screen shall be continuous except for vehicle or pedestrian ingress and egress sited perpendicular to the buffer and other necessary openings. Required buffers shall be planted before installation of solar panels. Additional requirements include preservation of healthy existing trees within the buffer to the maximum extent feasible, minimum shrub height of 36 inches at planting, and proper protection of plantings against damage from vehicles. These requirements apply to principal solar energy facilities defined as utility-scale facilities used to supply electrical or thermal power for off-site use(s).

The ordinance defines a principal solar energy facility as "a utility-scale facility consisting of one or more freestanding ground or roof mounted solar panels... and used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power, and supply electrical or thermal power for off-site use(s)." It explicitly states that "The solar energy facility shall not be used for displaying advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer and ownership of the facility. In no case shall such identification exceed 864 square inches." Furthermore, "The owner and operator of the solar energy facility shall post in a prominent location current information identifying the owner and operator of the facility, the person to contact with inquiries or complaints and his/her toll-free telephone number." This identification sign must be updated "No later than the change in owner and/or operator." These signage requirements apply specifically to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined. No other signage options or conditions are provided.

A principal solar energy facility use shall be permitted as a special exception in the Commercial/Industrial District (I/C District) and shall comply with the following definitions, requirements and standards. section: Section 3. Proposed Amendments to Zoning Ordinance

summary: The solar energy facility shall be no closer than 200 feet from the lot line of an adjacent lot improved with a dwelling or an unimproved lot in a residential zoning district; provided that the setback shall not apply to a shared property line of properties hosting a single solar energy facility. Additionally, a buffer no less than 30 feet in depth shall be required along any lot line adjacent to a lot improved with a dwelling or an unimproved lot in a residential zoning district, with the same exception for lots hosting a single solar energy facility.

The ordinance requires that the application for a principal solar energy facility include a site plan "depicting the facility and its principal components including, but not limited to, related ancillary facilities and structures." It also mandates a buffer "planted to establish a visual screen meeting the following requirements," including natural looking visual elements, species mix, spacing, and a mostly solid year-round visual screen at least 6 feet in height within 3 years. The buffer is required along public road frontage and adjacent to residential lots, with exceptions for lots hosting a single solar energy facility. These requirements explicitly constitute visual impact assessment and mitigation standards for utility-scale solar energy facilities, defined as "a utility-scale facility consisting of one or more freestanding ground or roof mounted solar panels... used to capture solar energy... and supply electrical or thermal power for off-site use(s)."

The solar energy facility use developed area shall exclude: a. floodplains and wetlands, except to extent permitted to be developed under federal or state law; b. area within 25’ of the center-line of a natural or man-made drainage corridor; c. area within 50’ from a designated wetlands, except to extent permitted to be developed under federal or state law; d. area within a riparian buffer required by federal or state law. The most restrictive fixed setback distance directly stated is 25 feet from the center-line of a natural or man-made drainage corridor. Other setbacks include 50 feet from designated wetlands and exclusion from floodplains and riparian buffers as required by law.
section: §27-1317 Principal Solar Energy Facility Use, Subsection B. Supplemental Standards

summary: Section 9. Decommissioning requires that "The Facility Owner and Operator shall, at their expense complete decommissioning of the Solar Electric Energy Facility or individual Solar Electric System within twelve (12) months after the end of the useful life of such Facility or System." It further states that "A Solar Electric Energy Facility or System will be presumed to be at the end of its useful life if no electricity is generated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months." Decommissioning includes "removal of all Solar Electric Energy Systems, buildings, cabling, solar panels, electrical components, roads, foundations, and any other associated facilities." Disturbed earth "shall be graded and re-seeded unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored." Financial Security must be provided "at the time of approval of the Subdivision and Land Development Plan (if applicable) and permit for the Facility" to secure decommissioning obligations, with detailed requirements for cost estimates, annual updates, and adjustments. The ordinance applies to any Solar Electric Energy Facility in excess of fifteen (15) acres as per Section 4.A. Other sections referenced include definitions of Facility Owner, Solar Electric Energy Facility, and Financial Security in Section 3, and applicability in Section 4.

Section 7.D.1 states: 'A Solar Electric Energy Facility shall be enclosed by a fence, barrier or other appropriate means to prevent or restrict unauthorized persons or vehicles from entering the property.' This applies to any Solar Electric Energy Facility in excess of Fifteen (15) Acres as per Section 4.A: 'This Ordinance applies to any Solar Electric Energy Facility in excess of Fifteen (15) Acres proposed to be developed or constructed after the effective date of the Ordinance.'

Section 8.C states: 'All solar panels must be arranged so as to not create glare onto adjoining properties.' This glare restriction applies to Solar Electric Energy Facilities as defined in Section 4.A, which applies to any Solar Electric Energy Facility in excess of fifteen (15) acres. Therefore, developers of such facilities must ensure their solar panels do not create glare onto neighboring properties.

Section 8.A states: 'All Solar Electric Energy Systems shall be located on a contiguous tract of land being not less than Fifteen (15) Acres in size.' This sets a minimum lot size of 15 acres for Solar Electric Energy Facilities greater than 15 acres, which are commercial-scale installations generating electricity for commercial applications. The unit is explicitly given as acres.

Setback distances shall be measured from the closest edge of any part or portion of the Solar Electric Energy System to the nearest property line. All structures including solar panels comprising any part or portion of the Solar Electric Energy System shall be located no less than One Hundred Fifty (150) Feet from the nearest property line. For any portion of the Solar Electric Energy System located within Two Hundred (200) Feet of the nearest property line, visual screening shall be included as part of the required fence or barrier limiting access to the property.
