The solar power facility owner and operator shall, at its own expense, complete decommissioning of the solar power facility, or individual components, within twelve (12) months after the end of the useful life of the solar power facility or individual components. The solar power facility or individual components shall be presumed to be at the end of its useful life if no electricity is generated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months. Decommissioning shall include removal of collectors, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations to a depth of thirty‐six (36) inches, and any other associated facilities. Disturbed earth shall be graded and re‐seeded, unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored. An independent and certified Professional Engineer shall be retained to estimate the total cost of decommissioning (decommissioning costs) without regard to salvage value of the equipment, and the cost of decommissioning net salvage value of the equipment (net decommissioning costs). Said estimates shall be submitted to the Township after the first year of operation and every fifth year thereafter. The solar power facility owner or operator, prior to the issuance of a zoning permit, shall provide a financial security bond with the Township as payee in an amount approved by the Township Supervisors, but not less than $50,000, from a company and in a form and content acceptable to the Township Supervisors, to insure the decommissioning within one hundred eighty (180) days of the expiration of the license or lease and/or cessation of use. The bond shall remain in place for as long as the facilities exist at the site. Decommissioning funds may be in the form of a performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit, corporate guarantee or other form of financial assurance as may be acceptable to the Township. If the solar power facility owner or operator fails to complete the decommissioning within the prescribed time period, then the landowner shall have one hundred eighty (180) days to complete decommissioning. If neither the solar power facility owner or operator, nor the landowner complete decommissioning within the prescribed periods, then the Township may take such measures as necessary to complete decommissioning. The entry into the record and submission of evidence of a participating landowner agreement to the Township shall constitute agreement and consent of the parties to the agreement, their respective heirs, successors and assigns that the Township may take such action as necessary to implement the decommissioning plan. The escrow agent shall release the decommissioning funds when the solar power facility owner or operator has demonstrated and the Township concurs that decommissioning has been satisfactorily completed, or upon written approval of the Township in order to implement the decommissioning plan.

summary: Section 21. Decommissioning requires the Facility Owner or Operator to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the use, defined as no electricity generated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months. The Facility Owner or Operator shall have six (6) months to dismantle and remove the system including all solar related equipment or appurtenances, and restore the land to its original pre-construction condition. If the Facility Owner or Operator fails to do so, the Township may complete the decommissioning at the Owner's expense. At permit issuance, the Facility Owner or Operator must provide financial security in the amount of one hundred ten (110%) percent of the cost of decommissioning, maintained during the life of the project. An independent certified professional engineer retained by the Township will estimate decommissioning costs, and the Facility Owner or Operator must update cost estimates and financial security every five (5) years. No other options or conditions for decommissioning are provided in the ordinance.

Section 7(d)(i) states: 'A Solar Electric Energy Facility shall be enclosed by a minimum eight (8’) foot fence with a self-locking gate fence to prevent or restrict unauthorized persons or vehicles from entering the property.' This fencing requirement applies explicitly to Large-scale Solar Electric Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance. Additionally, Section 7(d)(ii) requires 'Clearly visible warning signs shall be placed on the fence, barrier or Solar Electric Energy Facility perimeter to inform individuals of potential voltage hazards.'

Section 13. Glare states: 'The Solar Electric Energy Facility shall be placed such that solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby properties, structures, buildings, roadways.' The Applicant 'has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have an adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation.' A 'Glare Study shall be submitted by the Applicant to show compliance with this subsection at the time of the Application.' Additionally, the Applicant 'shall undertake timely corrective actions in the event of any complaints.' The Board of Supervisors determines the time frame for corrective actions. These requirements apply to large-scale Solar Electric Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance, which are intended to generate and supply electricity primarily for off-site use and exclude systems meant primarily for residential or commercial onsite use.

Section 9 states: 'All ground mounted solar panels shall comply with a maximum of twelve (12) feet in height.' This is the explicit maximum structure height allowed for Large-scale Solar Electric Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance. No other height restrictions are provided for these facilities. The unit of measurement is feet.

Section 14 states: 'Noise from the system may not exceed 45 dBA as measured at the lot line of the property where the system is located. This requirement shall be a maximum noise level using a Lmax standard, and not based upon an average.' The noise study must be performed by an independent expert and paid for by the applicant. Applicant shall undertake timely corrective actions in the event of any complaints. The Board of Supervisors determines the time frame for corrective actions.

The Solar Electric Energy Facility shall be located at least 100 feet from all adjoining properties. Notwithstanding the same, the Solar Electric Energy Facility shall be located no closer than two hundred (200’) feet from all residential or occupied structures located on adjoining properties. These distances shall be measured from the closest edge of the Solar Electric Energy Facility including the fence to the property line. The setbacks above may be waived in the case of adjoining tracts within a single Solar Electric Energy Facility, with the landowner’s written consent.

Section 11 states: 'A Solar Electric Energy Facility shall be screened from all residential or occupied structures located on adjoining properties. The same may be waived in writing by adjoining residential use written consent. The screening shall consist of a minimum of a double row of evergreens (not deciduous) with a beginning height of six (6’) feet. The Applicant shall replace any dead or deceased trees in the buffer. All screening shall be properly maintained throughout the life of the project.'

Section 7.d.ii requires 'clearly visible warning signs shall be placed on the fence, barrier or Solar Electric Energy Facility perimeter to inform individuals of potential voltage hazards.' Section 16 states 'The Facility Owner or Operator shall provide current contact information to the Township which includes a phone number and identifies the responsible person for the Township or public to contact regarding emergencies, inquires and complaints for the duration of the project. The contact information shall be conspicuously posted on the lot where the system is located so that a person will not believe they were trespassing while viewing it.' These signage requirements apply to Large-scale Solar Electric Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance.

summary: Section 19 requires the Applicant to provide satisfactory proof to the Township that it has received approvals under: 1) the Northumberland County Stormwater Ordinance; 2) Erosion and Sedimentation (E&S) Control; and 3) the National Pollution Discharge Elimination Systems (NPDES) Program and any other applicable local, state, or federal rules or regulations. Facility Owners shall also follow the current PA DEP guidelines for solar collectors as best management practices for stormwater management.

The Solar Electric Energy Facility shall be located no closer than two hundred (200’) feet from all residential or occupied structures located on adjoining properties. These distances shall be measured from the closest edge of the Solar Electric Energy Facility including the fence to the property line. (Section 8(a)) The ordinance also mentions a 100 feet setback from all adjoining properties generally, but the 200 feet setback from residential or occupied structures is more restrictive. Additionally, setbacks may be waived in the case of adjoining tracts within a single Solar Electric Energy Facility with the landowner’s written consent.

The PSES owner is required to notify the Township within thirty (30) days following permanent cessation or abandonment of the operation. The PSES shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months and the owner of the PSES has evidenced its intent to permanently discontinue operation of the PSES. The PSES owner shall then have twelve (12) months in which to dismantle and remove the PSES, including all solar-related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including, but not limited to, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations and other associated facilities, from the property, except to the extent the owner of the property agrees that roads and foundations may remain in place. If the owner fails to dismantle and remove the PSES to the extent required by this paragraph within the established time frames, the Township may complete the decommissioning at the owner's expense. The costs of such decommissioning together with a penalty of ten (10%) percent to be charged upon the land upon which the PSES exists as a municipal lien, or alternatively to recover such costs and penalty together with reasonable attorney fees incurred by the Township, in a suit at law against the owner or owners, but, failing to recover same, the judgment therefore shall be charged upon the land as a lien; and, this subsection is separate from and in addition to the fine, penalty, and costs which may be imposed by any other subsection of this Ordinance. Prior to the issuance of a permit by the Township, the owner shall provide financial security in the form of cash, a letter of credit or bond, acceptable to the Township, in the amount of eighty-five percent (85%) of the estimated cost of decommissioning based on an estimate provided by a professional engineer registered in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania to secure the expense of dismantling and removing the PSES and stabilizing the land for storm water management purposes. The decommissioning cost estimate shall be updated by a professional engineer registered in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania at the developer/owner’s expense every five (5) years thereafter and the financial security shall be adjusted accordingly.

All ground mounted PSES (excluding transmission lines) shall be completely enclosed by a minimum seven foot (7’) high fence. A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence on the surrounding PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards. In lieu of a vegetative screen, a decorative fence meeting the Zoning Ordinance requirements may be used for screening areas adjacent to residential parcels within line of sight. Other fencing or screening options include a suitable landscaping buffer area at least ten (10) feet in width of evergreen-type plants providing a continuous opaque screen within thirty-six (36) months of commencement of operations.

Under section 1303.97 Principal Solar Energy System (PSES), the ordinance explicitly states: 'All PSES shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto adjacent structures or roadways or adjoining property owners.' This is a direct glare restriction applicable to PSES. Other relevant provisions include requirements for layout, design, installation, maintenance to conform to industry standards; underground placement of transmission and plumbing lines; prohibition of advertising except for manufacturer's name and equipment information; noise limits; preservation of landscaping; decommissioning requirements; solar easements; permit requirements; and specific area, setback, screening, security, and access standards for ground mounted and roof/wall mounted PSES. However, none of these other provisions explicitly address glare restrictions beyond the quoted statement.

For ground mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), the maximum height is explicitly limited to 15 feet, with the exception that substation improvements, poles, and wires are not subject to this height limitation. For roof and wall mounted PSES, the systems "shall be subject to the maximum height restrictions of the underlying Zoning District." Thus, the most restrictive explicit numerical height limit given is 15 feet for ground mounted PSES.

The ordinance specifies a minimum lot area of 32,000 square feet for Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). This is explicitly stated as 'Minimum Lot Area (square feet) 32,000' in the dimensional requirements for PSES. Other dimensional requirements include minimum lot width of 150 ft., front setback of 20 ft., side yard setback of 15 ft., rear yard setback of 15 ft., and maximum height of 15 ft. The minimum lot size is expressed in square feet, which is a standard area measurement.

Noise from the operation of a PSES shall not exceed 50dbA, as measured at the property line of the nearest property that is not participating (by means of a lease, easement, solar easement or other agreement) in the development and/or operation of the PSES. The unit 'dBA' refers to A-weighted decibels, a standard measure of noise level.

Section 604.01 K states: 'substations and inverters shall be setback a minimum distance so the noise levels from such substations or inverter shall not exceed forty (40) DBA when measured at the exterior lot line.' This is the explicit maximum noise level allowed for utility-scale solar energy system equipment such as substations and inverters. No other maximum noise levels for utility-scale solar energy systems are provided.

summary: The ordinance explicitly prohibits solar energy systems that "shall not be used solely for the generation of power for the sale of energy to other users" (Section 631, 1.c). This prohibition applies broadly and unconditionally to all solar energy systems within the jurisdiction and is not limited by geographic area, permit status, or other conditions. The ordinance is presented as an active regulation with no indication that it is merely proposed or pending adoption, and it does not include any expiration date or time limit for the prohibition. Other provisions in the ordinance address design, installation, setbacks, height restrictions, and permit requirements but do not modify or condition the prohibition on utility-scale solar energy systems intended for offsite electricity generation or sale.

A solar farm installed to supply electricity other than for the needs of the principal use on that lot requires a permit. "Should any solar farm or solar farm cease to be used, the owner or operator or then owner of the land on which the solar farm or solar farm is located, shall be required to remove the same within one (1) year from the abandonment of use." Failure to remove authorizes the Township to remove the facility and assess the cost to the parties, including filing a municipal lien to recover costs and attorney's fees.

A fence in compliance with Section 1507 shall be required around solar farms and other equipment. Solar farms are defined as systems installed to supply electricity other than for the needs of the principal use on that lot. Additional requirements include setbacks, landscaping, buffering, screening, and site plan submissions. The fencing requirement is explicitly stated in item 4.d of the Solar Farm standards. Other conditions include setbacks from property lines and residential structures, landscaping and buffering in compliance with Section 1506 and the Township’s Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance, and removal of abandoned solar farms within one year.

No solar farm shall be located closer to any property line than its height plus the normal setback for the district. The 'normal setback for the district' is a static distance value added to the height-based setback, but the exact numeric value is not specified in the provided text. Additionally, the setback for equipment containers, other accessory structures and safety items shall be a minimum of thirty (30) feet. If the land is leased or used by license or easement, setbacks of at least thirty (30) feet apply from the lease, license or easement line, and the property line setback remains height plus normal district setback.

Screening and buffering, sufficient to screen the use from any location in a residential district and from any existing dwelling in any district, shall be provided in accordance to the Township’s Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance. Landscaping, buffering, and screening in compliance with Section 1506 of this Ordinance and the Township’s Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance shall be required to screen as much of the solar farm ground features as possible, the fence surrounding the support structure, and any other ground level features (such as a building), and in general buffer the solar farm ground features from neighboring properties. The Township may permit any combination of existing vegetation, topography, walls, decorative fences or other features instead of landscaping, if the same achieves the same degree of screening as the required landscaping.

Utility-scale solar energy systems, referred to as 'electric generating facility,' 'solar farm,' or 'solar and wind farms,' are permitted as special exceptions by the Zoning Hearing Board in the following districts: Agricultural District (A) - 'electric generation facility (solar and wind farms only)'; Commercial District (C) - 'electric generating facility (wind or solar only)'; Interchange District (I) - 'electric generating facilities, including solar and wind farms'; Industrial District (I) - 'electrical generating facility, includes solar and wind farms.' Accessory alternative energy systems designed for private use are permitted as accessory uses in several districts but are distinct from these commercial-scale facilities. The ordinance requires screening and buffering for these facilities to shield residential districts and dwellings.

No solar farm shall be located less than one hundred (100) feet from any principal residential structure existing prior to the erection of the solar farm. Other setback requirements include setbacks from property lines based on height plus normal district setback, and a minimum 30 feet setback for equipment containers and accessory structures, but these do not apply to occupied dwellings.

Section 4(A)(13) Decommissioning. Unless satisfactory evidence is furnished to the Township that the PSES owner and/or operator has included in a lease agreement or other agreement with the landowner a provision for sufficient financial security to cover the costs of decommissioning all improvements or common amenities including, but not limited to, the solar panels and any base and footing, storm water detention and/or retention basins and other related drainage facilities, and electrical apparatus and restoration of the land to its original condition including forestry plantings of the same type and density as the original, which provision is at least as stringent as the requirements set forth below, and unless satisfactory evidence has been furnished to the Township that such security has, in fact, been provided, the following requirements must be met: a. Before a permit may be approved and/or issued to a PSES owner and/or operator, the said owner and/or operator must submit to the Township financial security (which shall be in addition to any other financial security required pursuant to any applicable subdivision and land development ordinance) which shall be deposited with the Township in an amount sufficient to cover the costs of decommissioning all improvements or common amenities including, but not limited to, the solar panels and any base and footing, storm water detention and/or retention basins and other related drainage facilities, and electrical apparatus and restoration of the land to its original condition including forestry plantings of the same type and density as the original. b. Such financial security shall be in the form of cash, an irrevocable letter of credit, or a bond, satisfactory in form to the Township Solicitor whose review of same shall be reimbursed to the Township by the owner and/or operator, and posted with a bonding company chosen by the party posting the financial security, provided that said bonding company is authorized to conduct such business with the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. The bond shall provide for and secure to the Township the decommissioning of the improvements. The amount of the bond to be posted for the decommissioning of any improvements shall be equal to one hundred ten (110%) percent of the estimated cost thereof. The Township may adjust the required amount of the bond by Resolution every three (3) years. Subsequent to said adjustment, the Township may require the PSES owner and/or operator to post additional security in the form of an increased bond in order to assure that the financial security equals said one hundred ten (110%) percent. The amount of financial security required shall be based upon an estimate of the cost of decommissioning of any improvements, submitted by the PSES owner and/or operator and prepared by a professional engineer licensed as such in this Commonwealth and certified by such engineer to be a fair and reasonable estimate of such cost. The Township, upon the recommendation of the municipal engineer, may refuse to accept such estimate for good cause shown. If the PSES owner and/or operator and the Township are unable to agree upon an estimate, then the estimate shall be recalculated and recertified by another professional engineer licensed as such in this Commonwealth and chosen mutually by the Township and the PSES owner and/or operator. The estimate certified by the third engineer shall be presumed fair and reasonable and shall be the final estimate. As the work of decommissioning of any improvements proceeds, the party posting the bond may request the governing body to release, or authorize the release, from time to time, such portions of the bond(s) necessary for payment to the contractor or contractors performing the work. The owner of any participating property which is subject to decommissioning shall be given the option to keep the road(s) created on such owner's property by or in connection with construction of any PSES. When the PSES owner and/or operator has completed the decommissioning of all improvements, such owner and/or operator shall notify the Board of Supervisors, in writing, by certified or registered mail, of the completion of the aforesaid decommissioning of all improvements and shall send a copy thereof to the municipal engineer. The Board of Supervisors shall direct and authorize the municipal engineer to inspect the site. The municipal engineer shall indicate to the Township approval or rejection of said decommissioning of all improvements, either in whole or in part, and if said improvements, or any portion thereof, shall not be approved or shall be rejected by the municipal engineer, said report shall contain a statement of reasons for such non-approval or rejection. The Board of Supervisors shall notify the PSES Owner and/or Operator as to the municipal engineer's acceptance or rejection of the decommissioning. If the decommissioning is acceptable, the Township shall release the bond. If the decommissioning is not acceptable, the PSES owner and/or operator shall, within thirty (30) days of notice by the Township of the deficiencies, correct the same and in the event the said deficiencies are not so corrected within the said time period, the Township may utilize the bond to accomplish the same as set forth herein. All disposal of PSES components shall be in accordance with all applicable federal, state, and local laws, rules, and regulations. c. In the event that any required decommissioning of improvements has not been completed as provided in this Ordinance, the Board of Supervisors of the Township is hereby granted the power to enforce any corporate bond or otherwise leverage the financial security required hereunder. If proceeds of such financial security are insufficient to pay the cost of decommissioning of improvements covered by said security, the Board of Supervisors of the Township may, at its option, proceed with the decommissioning of all improvements and may institute appropriate legal or equitable action to recover the monies necessary to complete the remainder of the improvements, including but not limited to the placement of a municipal lien. d. The PSES owner and/or operator shall reimburse the Township for the reasonable and necessary expenses incurred for the inspection of decommissioning of improvements, including review of any plans, documents, or materials by the municipal engineer and/or Solicitor in connection therewith, as well as view of the site, if necessary. Such expense shall be reasonable and in accordance with the ordinary and customary fees charged by the municipal engineer or Solicitor for work performed for similar services performed for the Township. e. As used herein, the  "municipal engineer"  shall be a duly registered professional engineer appointed by the Township or one engaged by the Township as a consultant. f. Each PSES and all solar related equipment shall be removed by the owner and/or operator within twelve (12) months of the date that the use of the same has been discontinued or abandoned or upon expiration of the useful life of the same. g. The PSES shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such PSES for a period of twelve (12) continuous months or if no electricity is generated by such PSES for a nonconsecutive period of 365 days over an eighteen (18)-month period. h. The PSES owner shall, at the request of the Township, provide documentation to the Township sufficient to show the daily amounts of energy generated by the PSES over the immediately preceding twenty-four (24) months.

The PSES owner is required to notify the Township within 30 days following permanent cessation or abandonment of the operation. The PSES shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of 12 continuous months. The PSES owner shall then have 12 months in which to dismantle and remove the PSES, including all solar-related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including, but not limited to, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations, and other associated facilities, from the property, except to the extent the owner of the property agrees that roads and foundations may remain in place. If the owner fails to dismantle and remove the PSES within the established time frames, the Township may complete the decommissioning at the owner’s expense, with costs and a 10 percent penalty charged as a municipal lien or recovered through legal action. Prior to permit issuance, the owner must provide financial security in the amount of 85 percent of the estimated cost of decommissioning, based on an estimate by a professional engineer, updated every five years. When a ground mounted PSES is removed, any earth disturbance resulting from the removal shall be graded and re-seeded.

Section 10 (Decommissioning) requires that "The Facility Owner and Operator shall, at their expense, complete decommissioning of the Solar Energy Facility, or individual solar panels, within twelve (12) months after the end of the useful life of such Facility or solar panels." summary: The maximum lot coverage for commercial solar power generation facilities is seventy-five (75) percent, and the area of the solar collectors shall be included in the calculation of lot coverage. This is explicitly stated in section c.i.(c) under Conditional Uses for Solar Power Generation, Commercial (§603a.12). No other maximum land coverage values for commercial solar power generation are provided in the text.

The ordinance requires that "the solar power facility owner and operator shall, at its own expense, complete decommissioning of the solar power facility, or individual components, within twelve (12) months after the end of the useful life of the solar power facility or individual components." Decommissioning includes "removal of collectors, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations, and any other associated facilities." Disturbed earth "shall be graded and re-seeded, unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored." An independent Professional Engineer must estimate "the total cost of decommissioning (decommissioning costs) without regard to salvage value of the equipment, and the cost of decommissioning net salvage value of the equipment (net decommissioning costs)," with estimates submitted after the first year of operation and every fifth year thereafter. Prior to permit issuance, the owner/operator must provide "a financial security bond with the Borough as payee in an amount approved by the Borough Council, but not less than $50,000," to insure decommissioning within 180 days of license expiration or cessation of use. The bond remains in place as long as the facilities exist. Decommissioning funds may take various forms including "performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit, corporate guarantee or other form of financial assurance." If the owner/operator fails to decommission timely, the landowner has 180 days to complete it. If neither completes decommissioning, the Borough may intervene and take necessary measures. Release of funds occurs when decommissioning is satisfactorily completed or upon Borough approval to implement the plan.

summary: Section 603a.12.c.iii states: 'A chain link fence not less than six (6) feet in height shall be installed around the perimeter of the facilities to restrict access.' The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for commercial solar power generation facilities under Conditional Uses §603a.12. It requires the applicant to provide details about anticipated glare from the facility, including the time of day, time of year and direction of peak glare periods, and document how potential nuisances to area properties and on public roads shall be controlled. This is found in item viii under Standards and Design. Other conditions include requirements for parcel size, setbacks, lot coverage, height limits, fencing, landscaping, licenses, access, communications interference, historic structure setbacks, design standards, construction codes, electrical components, warnings, signs, transmission lines, stray voltage/EMF, emergency services, site plans, public inquiries and complaints, and decommissioning procedures.

The ordinance states: 'Solar collectors shall not exceed the principal structure height limitations for the underlying zoning district.' Other districts have maximum building heights of 36 or 40 feet. Therefore, the most restrictive maximum height applicable to commercial solar power generation is 30 feet. The units for these height limits are feet.

The minimum lot area for the I-1 Industrial District, where commercial solar power generation is a conditional use, is 15,000 square feet as listed in the 'Table 1 SCHEDULE OF DISTRICT DIMENSIONAL REGULATIONS'. The ordinance states: 'The minimum lot area required by this Ordinance for the solar power facility shall apply,' indicating that the minimum lot size in the underlying zoning district (I-1) applies to commercial solar power generation. Other district minimum lot areas are: R-1 Residential District - 8,800 sq ft; C-1 Commercial Downtown District - 5,000 sq ft; C-2 Commercial Highway District - 10,000 sq ft; S-1 District - 40,000 sq ft. The units for minimum lot size are explicitly given as square feet.

summary: The setback for solar collectors, all structures, equipment containers and any associated mechanical facilities shall be forty (40) feet front, thirty (30) feet sides and thirty (30) feet rear. These setbacks apply to commercial solar power generation facilities as specified under Conditional Uses §603a.12.c.i.(b).

Landscaping may be required to screen as much of the solar power facility ground features as possible, the fence surrounding the support structure, and any other ground level features (such as a building), and in general buffer the solar power facility ground features from neighboring properties. The Borough may permit any combination of existing vegetation, topography, walls, decorative fences or other features instead of landscaping, if the same achieves the same degree of screening as the required landscaping.

Section 12.c.xiii requires "A clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations." The ordinance lists 'Solar power generation, commercial' as a conditional use under the I-1 Industrial District (section 504, item 5 under Conditional Uses). Other districts such as R-1 Residential, C-1 Commercial Downtown, C-2 Commercial Highway, and I-1 Industrial list 'Solar collector, accessory' as accessory uses, which do not apply to commercial-scale solar power generation. No other districts explicitly mention commercial solar power generation as a permitted or conditional use.

The setback for solar collectors, all structures, equipment containers and any associated mechanical facilities shall be forty (40) feet front, thirty (30) feet sides and thirty (30) feet rear. These setbacks apply to commercial solar power generation facilities as specified under Conditional Uses, section 12.c.i.(b).

The ordinance requires landscaping to screen as much of the solar power facility ground features as possible, including fencing and other ground level features, to buffer the facility from neighboring properties. The Borough may permit existing vegetation, topography, walls, decorative fences or other features instead of landscaping if they achieve the same degree of screening. A full site plan is required for all solar power facility sites, showing the solar power facility, fencing, screening, buffers, access, and all other items required by this Ordinance. These requirements apply to 'Solar power generation, commercial' as a conditional use. Other related standards include setbacks, height limits, fencing, and signage, but these do not explicitly constitute visual impact assessment requirements.

Section 857.3, subsection R states: 'The area of the solar panels shall be included in the calculation of lot coverage which shall not exceed seventy-five (75) percent.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for Solar Power Generation, Commercial. The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the total lot area. No other maximum land coverage values for commercial solar power generation are provided in the text.

The solar power facility owner and operator shall, at its own expense, complete decommissioning of the solar power facility, or individual components, within twelve (12) months after the end of the useful life of the solar power facility or individual components. The solar power facility or individual components shall be presumed to be at the end of its useful life if no electricity is generated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months. Decommissioning shall include removal of collectors, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations to a depth of thirty-six (36) inches, and any other associated facilities. Disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded, unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored. An independent and certified Professional Engineer shall be retained to estimate the total cost of decommissioning (decommissioning costs) without regard to salvage value of the equipment, and the cost of decommissioning net salvage value of the equipment (net decommissioning costs). Said estimates shall be submitted to the Township after the first year of operation and every fifth year thereafter. The solar power facility owner or operator, prior to the issuance of a zoning permit, shall provide a financial security bond with the Township as payee in an amount approved by the Board of Supervisors, but not less than $50,000, from a company and in a form and content acceptable to the Board of Supervisors, to insure the decommissioning within one hundred eighty (180) days of the expiration of the license or lease and/or cessation of use. The bond shall remain in place for as long as the facilities exist at the site. Decommissioning funds may be in the form of a performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit, corporate guarantee or other form of financial assurance as may be acceptable to the Township. If the solar power facility owner or operator fails to complete decommissioning within the prescribed time period, then the landowner shall have one hundred eighty (180) days to complete decommissioning. If neither the solar power facility owner or operator, nor the landowner complete decommissioning within the prescribed periods, then the Township may take such measures as necessary to complete decommissioning. The escrow agent shall release the decommissioning funds when the solar power facility owner or operator has demonstrated and the Township concurs that decommissioning has been satisfactorily completed, or upon written approval of the Township in order to implement the decommissioning plan.

Section 857.3 Standards and Design, subsection C states: "Fencing - A fence may be required around the facility or portions of the facility for safety reasons." This indicates that fencing is not always mandatory but may be required for safety. Additionally, landscaping and screening requirements are mentioned to buffer the facility from neighboring properties. The ordinance also allows for a combination of existing vegetation, topography, walls, decorative fences or other features instead of landscaping if they achieve the same degree of screening. No other explicit fencing requirements or specifications are provided.

Section 857.3 Standards and Design, subsection H states: 'The applicant shall provide details about anticipated glare from the facility, including the time of day, time of year and direction of peak glare periods and document how potential nuisances to area properties and on public roads shall be controlled.' This glare restriction applies specifically to commercial solar power generation facilities as defined: 'Solar Power Generation, Commercial: A facility where one (1) or more solar collectors and/or other accessory structures and buildings... are located and are used for the generation of electricity which is sold on the open market.'

Section 857.3.D Landscaping states: "Landscaping may be required to screen as much of the solar power facility ground features as possible, the fence surrounding the support structure, and any other ground level features (such as a building), and in general buffer the solar power facility ground features from neighboring properties." The Township may permit "any combination of existing vegetation, topography, walls, decorative fences or other features instead of landscaping, if the same achieves the same degree of screening as the required landscaping."

Section 857.3 Standards and Design includes signage requirements for Solar Power Generation, Commercial: 'No advertising material or signs other than warning, manufacturer and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of structures.' Additionally, subsection M requires 'a clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations.' These are the explicit signage requirements that a commercial solar power developer must abide by.

The ordinance lists 'Solar power generation, commercial' as permitted with conditions ('C') in the C-1 General Commercial District and the I Industrial District, while it is not permitted ('N') in R-1, R-2, OS-W, and C-2 districts. The text states: 'Solar power generation, commercial       857      N     N          C       N       C        N' indicating conditional use in C-1 and I. Accessory solar collectors are permitted in all districts but are limited to generating power for the principal structure and not for sale, thus not covering utility-scale systems.

A Large-Scale Solar Energy System facility, including solar panels, equipment, accessory structures and their appurtenances, shall occupy no more than 50% of the total of any existing agriculturally used land on a parcel, whether in active production or fallow, as well as any additional land on a parcel that would be classified as farmland by the criteria within Section 12-405.E (or 12-505.E in another section). summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). The PSES owner must notify the municipality immediately upon cessation or abandonment of operation. The PSES shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated for twelve (12) continuous months. If permanently ceased or abandoned, the PSES owner shall have eighteen (18) months to dismantle and remove the PSES including all solar related equipment or appurtenances, restore the site to its pre-existing condition, and obtain any necessary permits. Financial security in favor of the municipality must be provided at the time of approval, including an estimate of decommissioning costs and updates every 5 years. The security may be in the form of cash deposit, surety bond, irrevocable letter of credit, cashier’s check, or escrow amount. A decommissioning agreement with the municipality is required prior to final plan approval. These requirements apply specifically to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES) also have decommissioning requirements but are distinct and apply to smaller or on-site systems.

Section 1102.05(C)(8)(c) states that "Ground mounted solar energy systems shall be enclosed by a fence, barrier or other appropriate means to prevent or restrict unauthorized persons or vehicles from entering the property." This fencing requirement applies to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). Other related provisions include setbacks, height limits, stormwater management, buffer and screening requirements, access roads, and public safety measures, but fencing is specifically mandated as a security measure for ground mounted PSES.

Section 1102.05(A)(7) states: 'All PSES shall be situated to prevent concentrated glare onto nearby structures or roadways. Exterior surfaces shall have a non-reflective finish.' Additionally, 'The applicant and/or operator has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have a significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation.' These glare restrictions apply specifically to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). Other options include Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), which have similar but separate glare provisions under Section 1102.04(A)(7), and exemptions for ASES with an aggregate collection area of 100 square feet or less. The ordinance distinguishes PSES as systems primarily for off-site use and subject to special exception in industrial districts.

Ground mounted solar related equipment shall not exceed 25 feet in height above the ground elevation surrounding the systems, except that there shall be no maximum height restrictions for structures that support the electric conveyance lines which connect the solar energy system to the high-voltage electric interconnection grid. Roof and wall mounted PSES shall be subject to the maximum height regulations of the underlying zoning district. (Section 1102.05.C.7 and 1102.05.B.1)

Noise generating equipment, including but not limited to electricity storage equipment, inverters and transformers shall be located a minimum of 100 feet from all road rights-of-way and property lines of a non-participating landowner’s property; and a minimum of 150 feet from any occupied building located on a non-participating landowner’s property. Property owners of non-participating properties may waive these setback requirement by signing a waiver that sets forth the applicable setback provision(s) and the proposed changes. However, in no case shall setbacks from the non-participating property lines be less than the required setbacks for a principal structure within the underlying zoning district. Additionally, solar arrays and other solar related equipment shall be setback a minimum of twenty (20) feet from the inside perimeter fencing to allow for maintenance and emergency vehicles. PSES shall comply with the setbacks of the underlying zoning district for principal structures, unless specified otherwise.

Noise generating equipment, including but not limited to electricity storage equipment, inverters and transformers shall be located a minimum of 100 feet from all road rights-of-way and property lines of a non-participating landowner’s property; and a minimum of 150 feet from any occupied building located on a non-participating landowner’s property. Property owners of non-participating properties may waive these setback requirement by signing a waiver that sets forth the applicable setback provision(s) and the proposed changes. However, in no case shall setbacks from the non-participating property lines be less than the required setbacks for a principal structure within the underlying zoning district.

Section 1102.05(C) Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems states: "Buffer and Screening Requirements: Ground mounted PSES shall comply with all applicable requirements of Section 702, Buffer Yard and Screening Requirements." This explicitly enacts vegetative buffer and/or other screening requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). The ordinance defines PSES as systems "principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use." No other specific buffer or screening requirements for PSES are detailed in the provided text. Other options or conditions related to accessory solar energy systems (ASES) include screening for ground mounted ASES: "Ground mounted ASES shall be screened from any adjacent property that is residentially zoned or used for residential purposes. The screen shall consist of plant materials which provide a visual screen. In lieu of a planting screen, a decorative fence meeting requirements of the zoning ordinance may be used." However, this applies only to ASES, not PSES.

The ordinance requires that "a clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards" (Section 1102.05.C.8.d). It also states that "No portion of the PSES shall contain or be used to display advertising. The manufacturer’s name and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of the PSES provided they comply with the prevailing sign regulations" (Section 1102.05.A.7). These are the explicit signage requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) that an energy system developer must abide by.

The ordinance requires that "any soil exposed during the removal shall be stabilized in accordance with applicable erosion and sediment control standards." It also mandates that "any necessary permits, such as Erosion and Sedimentation and NPDES permits, shall be obtained prior to decommissioning activities." Additionally, "the applicant shall submit a stormwater management plan that demonstrates compliance with the Union City Borough Stormwater Management Ordinance." These requirements apply specifically to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES).

Article 5, Section 505, District Use Table, is hereby amended to add  "Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) to the list of non-residential uses. The use shall be permitted uses a special exception  "SE"  in the I-1, Industrial District. The text states: 'Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) (1102.05) | SE' in the I-1 district. This indicates that PSES require approval as a special exception in this district. Other districts are not mentioned for PSES special use. Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES) are permitted in all zoning districts, but that is not applicable to PSES. The ordinance also includes detailed setback, height, and other conditions for PSES, such as minimum lot size, setbacks from residential districts, and height limits.

Noise generating equipment, including but not limited to electricity storage equipment, inverters and transformers shall be located a minimum of 150 feet from any occupied building located on a non-participating landowner’s property. Property owners of non-participating properties may waive these setback requirement by signing a waiver that sets forth the applicable setback provision(s) and the proposed changes. However, in no case shall setbacks from the non-participating property lines be less than the required setbacks for a principal structure within the underlying zoning district. Other setback options include a minimum of 20 feet from adjacent residential districts or structures, and 100 feet from all road rights-of-way and property lines of a non-participating landowner’s property (for noise generating equipment).
section: 1102.05 Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), C. Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems, 2. Setbacks

summary: The ordinance requires Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) applicants to submit a land development plan that includes "a narrative describing the proposed PSES," "a site plan showing the planned location of solar related equipment, property lines, setback lines, access road and turnout locations, substation(s), electrical cabling," and "other relevant studies, reports, certifications and approvals as may be reasonably requested by the municipality to ensure compliance with this ordinance." Ground mounted PSES must comply with "all applicable requirements of Section 702, Buffer Yard and Screening Requirements." Screening is required to "provide a visual screen" from adjacent residential properties. These requirements serve as visual impact assessment measures. Roof mounted PSES are exempt from submitting a land development plan. The ordinance also requires written confirmation of utility connection approval and includes other criteria such as setbacks, height limits, and decommissioning plans. Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES) have separate, less stringent requirements and exemptions, such as exemption for systems with an aggregate collection area of 100 square feet or less, and do not require the same level of plan submission or screening. PSES are permitted by special exception in the I-1 Industrial District.

Decommissioning of the principal system shall be subject to the following: The principal system owner is required to notify Union Dale Borough immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The principal system shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months. The principal system owner shall then have nine (9) months in which to dismantle and remove the principal system including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations and other associated facilities from the property. If the principal system owner fails to dismantle and/or remove the principal system within the established timeframes, the Borough may complete the decommissioning at the principal system owner’s expense. Upon application for permit for the purpose of installation of a solar energy system, the principal system owner hereby agrees to be liable for all costs of decommissioning pursuant to this system, together with all court costs and attorneys’ fees incurred by the Borough in collection of any such funds. At the time of issuance of the approval for the construction of the principal system, the principal system owner shall provide financial security in the form and amount acceptable to Union Dale Borough to secure the expense of dismantling and removing said system, regrading as necessary and revegetation/seeding of any disturbed areas to provide erosion control. Specifically, owner shall post a bond for decommissioning in an amount necessary to cover the expense to dismantle and remove the principal system including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations and other associated facilities from the property, as security if owner fails to comply with the above decommissioning requirements. In lieu of the bond, owner may deliver other security acceptable to Union Dale Borough. The amount of financial security required shall be updated every five (5) years utilizing decommissioning costs estimated by the principal system owner and validated by Union Dale Borough, and/or its employees and/or engineers. Failure to update the amount of financial security shall be cause to order the immediate dismantling of the principal system using existing security, which shall not be released until replaced with the approval of the Borough.

All principal systems shall be completely enclosed by a minimum seven (7) foot high fence with a self-locking gate. Security fencing should nonetheless be of the height that makes it non-climbable with additional deterrents attached to the top. The subject fence shall be considered a part of the principal system and shall meet the setback requirements of this Ordinance. This fencing requirement applies to principal solar energy systems, which are defined as systems used to capture solar energy and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use, including substations, electrical infrastructure, transmission lines, and other appurtenant structures.

The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Principal Solar Energy Systems. It states: 'All principal systems shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures or roadways. The applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation.' This applies specifically to Principal Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems 'principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use.' The ordinance also includes similar glare restrictions for Accessory Solar Energy Systems, but those apply to smaller, primarily on-site use systems and are not the focus here.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'The system height of a principal system shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet.' This applies directly to principal solar energy systems, which are defined as systems primarily used to supply electrical or thermal power off-site. The unit 'feet' is used consistently in the ordinance for height measurements. Other height restrictions mentioned apply only to accessory (smaller, on-site) systems, which also have a 15 feet maximum height but are distinct from principal systems.

Noise from a principal system shall not exceed fifty (50) dBA, as measured at the property line. The applicant and/or operator shall be responsible for establishing and certifying to the Borough the required decibel level prior to approval of the solar energy facility. This work shall be done by a professional engineer.

The principal system shall not be less than one hundred (100) feet from any property line and/or any road. Battery storage systems shall be located a minimum of two hundred (200) feet from any property line and be placed on concrete pads. Upon request, the Borough may grant partial waivers of setback requirements hereunder where it has determined that literal enforcement will exact undue hardship because of peculiar conditions pertaining to the land in question and provided that such waiver will not be contrary to the public interest.

The principal system shall not be less than one hundred (100) feet from any property line and/or any road. Principal systems shall not be placed within any legal easement or right-of-way location. A minimum twenty-five foot (25’) wide paved access road must be provided from a State or Borough roadway into the site. (Section 4.17.1, 4.17.6, 4.17.10)

Principal systems shall be screened from adjoining occupied buildings within two hundred (200) feet of any part of a system and/or occupied buildings on opposite side of any road and visible from the proposed solar development. The screen shall consist of two rows of evergreen trees on fifteen feet (15) staggered centers to provide a visual screen. Evergreens shall be a minimum of three feet (3') tall when planted. Immediate replacement of dead trees shall be required, and all buffers shall be in keeping with the character of the area. Additionally, all principal systems shall be completely enclosed by a minimum seven (7) foot high fence with a self-locking gate. Security fencing should nonetheless be of the height that makes it non-climbable with additional deterrents attached to the top.

The ordinance explicitly enacts signage requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems. It states: 'No portion of the principal system shall obtain or be used to display advertising. The manufacturer’s name and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of the principal system.' Additionally, 'A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the system informing individuals of potential voltage hazards.' These requirements apply to principal systems, which are defined as systems 'principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use.'

The ordinance requires that "The applicant shall submit a Stormwater Management Plan that demonstrates compliance with Union Dale Borough stormwater management regulations" (4.17.3). It also mandates that "the principal system owner shall provide financial security in the form and amount acceptable to Union Dale Borough to secure the expense of dismantling and removing said system, regrading as necessary and revegetation/seeding of any disturbed areas to provide erosion control" (4.14.3). This financial security must be updated every five years and may be a bond or other acceptable security. These requirements apply specifically to Principal Solar Energy Systems, defined as systems "principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use" (Definitions).

The ordinance requires that principal solar energy systems must obtain approval under the ordinance if materially altered (4.1), comply with the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code and other applicable requirements (4.2), and submit manufacturer specifications as part of the application. Prior to construction, a land development approval is required (4.14, 4.15), and a $5,000 application fee must be paid (4.18.1). The Borough may grant partial waivers of setback requirements upon request (4.17.2). The ordinance does not explicitly list any zoning districts or abbreviations where principal solar energy systems are permitted as a special use or similar, nor does it mention approval by a zoning appeals board. The text focuses on permitting, operational, and decommissioning requirements for principal solar energy systems generally, without specifying district-based use permissions.

The principal system shall not be less than one hundred (100) feet from any occupied building. This setback applies specifically to Principal Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as systems primarily used to supply power off-site and include large-scale installations with associated infrastructure. Other setback options mentioned in the ordinance include setbacks from property lines and roads, battery storage setbacks, and screening requirements, but these do not pertain to occupied buildings. The ordinance also states that no multiplier of system height applies to principal systems for setbacks from occupied buildings.

The ordinance requires that "The PSES owner is required to notify the municipality immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation." The PSES is "presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months." If permanently ceased or abandoned, "the PSES owner shall then have eighteen (18) months in which to dismantle and remove the PSES including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations and other associated facilities from the property." Materials "shall be re-sold or salvaged" if possible, otherwise disposed of properly. "Any soil exposed during the removal shall be stabilized in accordance with applicable erosion and sediment control standards." The site "shall be restored to its pre-existing condition, suitable for its prior use, except the landowner may authorize, in writing, any buffer landscaping or access roads installed to accommodate the PSES to remain." Necessary permits "shall be obtained prior to decommissioning activities." Financial security is required at the time of construction approval, with the PSES developer providing "an estimate of the cost of performing the decommissioning activities" and posting "financial security of 110% of the estimated cost of decommissioning." The estimate may include salvage value discounted by 10%. The security must be updated every 5 years, subject to municipal review, and may be in forms such as cash deposit, surety bond, irrevocable letter of credit, cashier’s check, or escrow. Prior to final plan approval, the PSES developer must enter into a decommissioning agreement with the municipality outlining responsibilities. These requirements apply specifically to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES).

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). Key provisions include: "The PSES owner is required to notify the Township immediately upon permanent cessation or abandonment of the operation." The system "shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months" and "shall constitute a public nuisance after six (6) months of being inoperative, unless the facility operator demonstrates a good faith intent to sell." Upon permanent cessation or abandonment, "the PSES owner shall have eighteen (18) months in which to dismantle and remove the PSES, including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto... Underground wiring/equipment must be removed and graded, restored, and reseeded with 90% perennial." The site "shall be restored to its pre-existing condition, suitable for its prior use, except the landowner may authorize, in writing, any buffer landscaping or access roads installed to accommodate the PSES to remain." The owner must provide financial security in an amount acceptable to the Township, with a schedule increasing from 10% to 110% of the decommissioning cost over 30 years, subject to review every 5 years. If the developer defaults, escrow funds revert to the Township and a lien may be filed on the land. A decommissioning agreement must be entered into prior to final plan approval. These requirements apply specifically to PSES, defined as systems "principally to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use" and typically producing "in excess of 3 MW of power."

summary: Ground mounted solar energy facilities shall be buffered and screened from adjacent residential zoning districts, residential uses on surrounding properties, platted residential lots, and public roads in accordance with the following requirements: (a) Vegetative buffering shall be installed to screen and buffer adjacent residential zoning districts, residential uses on surrounding properties, platted residential lots, and public roads from the PSES.
