summary: Section 104-25.C requires that any solar farm not in active and continuous service for one year "shall be removed from the property and all structures and panels associated with same shall be disposed of at a disposal site approved by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania for those purposes." The property must be "restored to as close as possible to its pre-use condition." The Applicant must submit a "recycling, reuse, disposal and decommissioning plan" detailing disposal of damaged panels, responsible parties for decommissioning, and disposal of removed materials. The facility and property owner are "jointly and severally responsible for the decommissioning, recycling and removal of the solar farm within 12 months of the end of the useful life of the facility." Financial security must be provided "in an amount equal to the cost of decommissioning and removal of the Solar Farm initially and as updated thereafter." The "end of useful life" is defined as "any point in time where no electricity is generated from the Site for a period of 12 consecutive months." These requirements apply to solar farms with a minimum lot size of 25 acres and designed for commercial utility-scale applications as per Section 118-23.A.43. Other conditions include underground placement of transmission lines unless modified, buffering mechanical equipment from residential properties, and operation and maintenance agreements with the Township. The ordinance excludes solar farms regulated by the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission.

The ordinance requires that all solar farms with a minimum lot size of 25 acres, designed for commercial utility-scale solar applications, must have the 'Coverage Area' fenced with a fence not less than 8' in height, topped with barbed wire and gated to prohibit access by persons and animals. This is stated in Section 118-23.A.44(j). Other conditions include compliance with federal and commonwealth laws, minimum setbacks of 250-400 feet from adjoining lot lines, submission of detailed scaled drawings, and obtaining special exception use approval. Additional requirements cover underground placement of transmission lines, buffering mechanical equipment, removal of inactive solar farms, submission of decommissioning plans, insurance maintenance, noise limits, and operation and maintenance agreements as detailed in Section 104-25.C. The ordinance also clarifies that solar panels intended primarily to supply electricity to on-site buildings with de minimus excess power returned to the grid are not considered a principal use and have different placement restrictions.

Section 118-23.A.44(d) states: 'All solar panels must be arranged so as not to create glare onto adjoining properties.' This applies to solar farms with a minimum lot size of 25 acres and 'principally designed and used to generate electricity for commercial utility-scale solar applications.' Other relevant conditions include minimum lot size requirements (at least 25 acres), setback distances (no structure or equipment less than 250-400 feet from any adjoining lot line), and compliance with federal and commonwealth laws. Additional requirements cover fencing, special exception use approval, land development plan approval, and operational and decommissioning plans. The ordinance also clarifies that solar panels whose principal purpose is to provide electricity to an existing building may only be placed on rooftops, not on the ground.

Section 118-23.A.43(a) states that any solar farm must be conducted on property within the Conservation Zoning District having a minimum lot size of at least 25 acres. Subsection (b) clarifies that the solar farm must be principally designed and used to generate electricity for commercial utility-scale solar applications. The minimum lot size is explicitly given as an area value in acres.

Section 104-25.C.7 states: 'Sounds from permanent equipment used in the operation of the solar farm shall not exceed 45 decibels at any property line.' This applies specifically to solar farms on properties of at least 25 acres designed for commercial utility-scale solar applications. The unit for noise level is conventionally expressed as dBA.

No structure or equipment used in the operation of any solar farm shall be located less than 250 4-00 feet from any adjoining lot line. (The text shows both 250 and 400 feet, but 400 feet appears to be the intended setback.) This setback applies to solar farms designed and used for commercial utility-scale solar applications on properties of at least 25 acres. No other fixed setback distances from property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, parcels, or subdivisions are explicitly stated for such solar farms in the provided text.

Section 104-25.C.2 requires that "Mechanical equipment associated with, and necessary for, the operation of the solar farm shall be located entirely within the Operating Area of the Solar Farm and buffered from any adjacent property that is residentially zoned or used for residential purposes. The buffering shall consist of shrubbery, trees, or other plant materials which provide a visually intrusive screen and shall be installed in addition to any landscaping required under the Township's Zoning or Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance." This applies to solar farms with a minimum lot size of at least 25 acres and designed for commercial utility-scale applications as per Section 118-23.A.43.a and b. Other requirements include fencing the coverage area with an 8' high fence topped with barbed wire (Section 118-23.A.43.j), setbacks of 250-400 feet from adjoining lot lines (Section 118-23.A.43.e), and compliance with various permitting and operational conditions, but these do not pertain to vegetative buffer or screening.

Commercial Utility-Scale Solar Farms are authorized as a "special exception use" in the C - Conservation Zoning District, requiring special exception use approval from the Zoning Hearing Board and compliance with specific requirements such as minimum lot size (at least 25 acres), setbacks (no less than 250-400 feet from adjoining lot lines), fencing, and submission of detailed scaled drawings and certifications. The applicant must also obtain land development plan approval from the Board of Supervisors and comply with applicable ordinances. Additional operational and decommissioning requirements are outlined in Section 104-25.C, including underground transmission lines, buffering from residential properties, removal of inactive farms, submission of decommissioning plans, insurance requirements, noise limits, and an Operation and Maintenance Agreement with the Township. No other zoning districts are mentioned as permitting such solar farms as special use or similar.

Section P states that "A commercial solar energy system, and all materials, structures and accessory equipment installed with that system, that has not been in use for commercial generation purposes for six months shall be removed completely within 90 days of the issuance of an enforcement action." It further requires that "Upon removal, the site shall be cleaned, restored and revegetated to blend with the existing surrounding vegetation, and to prevent soil erosion and downgradient sedimentation." Additionally, if the system remains nonfunctional for one year and has not been removed, "the system may be deemed to be abandoned, and may constitute a public nuisance as determined by the Township Zoning Officer." Section Q requires that "A commercial solar energy system owner shall post a bond or other financial security in a form acceptable to the Township at the time of zoning approval to cover the cost of equipment removal." Any additional or unanticipated costs beyond the bond are the responsibility of the owner.

All mechanical equipment of commercial solar energy systems, including any structure for batteries or storage cells, shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate, and provided with screening in accordance with the landscaping and screening provisions of the Code of the Township of Upper Frederick.
Commercial solar energy systems shall be located on a building, lot or parcel in a manner that does not direct concentrated solar radiation or glare onto any neighboring property or public way.

Section E states: 'No part of a ground-mounted commercial solar energy system or its support structures shall exceed a height of 20 feet.' This applies explicitly to commercial solar energy systems, which are utility-scale systems intended for offsite electricity generation or sale. The unit of measurement is feet. Other height-related provisions include roof-mounted systems subject to maximum height regulations of the underlying zoning district (Sections H, I, and L), but these do not specify numerical height limits. The 20 feet limit is the most restrictive explicit maximum height for ground-mounted commercial solar energy systems.

The ordinance states: 'Such use shall have a minimum lot size of five acres, and a maximum of 20 acres.' This sets a maximum lot size of 20 acres for commercial solar energy systems, which would typically include utility-scale solar energy systems. The units are explicitly given as acres, a standard measure of land area.

The ordinance states: 'Such use shall have a minimum lot size of five acres, and a maximum of 20 acres.' This minimum lot size applies to commercial solar energy systems, which would typically include utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit of measurement is acres, a standard area unit.

Section K requires 'a clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage' at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations. Section O states that commercial solar energy systems 'shall not be used to display advertising of any type, and may only display signage when consistent with this chapter and when said signage identifies the manufacturer and/or installer, or provides warning statements.'

Section 483.E states: 'The surface area of a ground-mounted solar energy system ... shall not exceed thirty percent (30%) of maximum lot coverage of the lot.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for Wind and/or Solar Farms in the I-1 & Q Zones. The unit is a percentage of the maximum lot coverage allowed by the zoning district. No other more restrictive maximum land coverage values for Wind and/or Solar Farms in these zones are provided.

Section 483.I states: 'The applicant shall be responsible for the decommissioning of the wind and/or solar farm in accordance with the following requirements: 1. The applicant shall, at his/her expense, complete decommissioning of the wind and/or solar farm, or individual wind turbines, within (12) twelve months after the end of the useful life of the wind and/or solar farm or individual wind turbines or solar panels. The wind and/or solar farm or individual wind turbines or solar panels will presume to be at the end of its useful life if no electricity is generated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months. 2. Decommissioning shall include removal of wind turbines and solar panels, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations to a depth of 36 inches, and any other associated facilities. 3. Disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded, unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored. 4. An independent and certified Professional Engineer shall be retained to estimate the total cost of decommissioning ('Decommissioning Costs') without regard to salvage value of the equipment, and the cost of decommissioning net salvage value of the equipment ('Net Decommissioning Costs'). Said estimates shall be submitted to the Township after the first year of operation and every fifth year thereafter at the applicant’s and/or any successor’s expense. 5. The applicant shall post and maintain decommissioning funds in an amount equal to net decommissioning costs; provided, that at no point shall decommissioning funds be less than twenty five percent (25%) of decommissioning costs. The decommissioning funds shall be posted and maintained with a bonding company or Federal or Commonwealth chartered lending institution chosen by the Facility Owner or Operator and participating landowner posting the financial security, provided that the bonding company or lending institution is authorized to conduct such business within the Commonwealth and is approved by the Township. 6. Decommissioning funds may be in the form of a performance bond, surety bond, letter of credit, corporate guarantee or other form of financial assurance as may be acceptable to the Township. 7. If the applicant fails to complete decommissioning within the period prescribed by §483.I.1. of this Ordinance, then the landowner shall have six (6) months to complete decommissioning. 8. If neither the applicant, nor the landowner complete decommissioning within the periods prescribed by §483.I.1.or §483.I.7. of this Ordinance, then the Township may take such measures as necessary to complete decommissioning. The entry into and submission of evidence of a participating landowner agreement to the Township in accordance with §483.B.8. of this Ordinance shall constitute agreement and consent of the parties to the agreement, their respective heirs, successors and assigns that the Township may take such action as necessary to implement the decommissioning plan. 9. The escrow agent shall release the decommissioning funds when the applicant has demonstrated and the municipality concurs that decommissioning has been satisfactorily completed, or upon written approval of the municipality in order to implement the decommissioning plan.' These requirements apply specifically to wind and/or solar farms as conditional uses in the I-1 and Q zones.

Section 483.B.6 requires "a completed glare study ensuring that reflective glare is not directed towards nor upon any adjacent properties as well as any adjacent street rights-of-way." The glare study shall include: "A. the angle of the solar collector system panels, arrays, cells, etc. at the location; B. a diagram showing the maximum and minimum angles of reflective glare from the solar collector system panels, arrays, cells, etc. at the location and the relationship of that glare to adjacent properties, structures and rights-of-way; and, C. a mitigation plan that limits or eliminates reflective glare on adjacent properties, structures, and rights-of-way." Section 483.C.22 states that "solar energy panels shall be designed and located in order to minimize reflective glare and/or heat towards any adjoining use and/or road."

Section 405.R.D requires that "In those instances when the solar energy system is proposed as a freestanding installation within the front yard, the applicant must provide vegetative screening to serve as a barrier to visibility and glare, in accordance with §322 of this Ordinance. Prior to issuance of a zoning permit, a site plan showing the proposed arrangement, placement, species and size of all screen planting material shall be submitted for approval to the Zoning Officer." Section 483.B.6 requires "a completed glare study ensuring that reflective glare is not directed towards nor upon any adjacent properties as well as any adjacent street rights-of-way" including "a mitigation plan that limits or eliminates reflective glare on adjacent properties, structures, and rights-of-way." These provisions explicitly enact vegetative screening and glare mitigation requirements for wind and/or solar farms as conditional uses in the I-1 and Q Zones. Other relevant requirements include minimizing reflective glare and heat towards adjoining uses and roads (§483.C.22), and that solar panels shall be designed and located to minimize reflective glare (§467.W).

Section 483.C.15 requires "a clearly visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all at-grade transformers and substations." Section 483.C.16 requires "visible, reflective, colored objects, such as flags, reflectors, or tape shall be placed on the anchor points of each guy wire and along each guy wire up to a height of ten feet from the ground." Section 483.C.18 requires "all access doors to wind turbines and/or solar panels and electrical equipment shall be locked or fenced, as appropriate, to prevent entry by non-authorized persons." These are explicit signage and safety marking requirements for wind and/or solar farms in the I-1 & Q Zones. Other related requirements include non-advertising identification insignia not exceeding 200 square inches (§483.C.13), and no artificial lighting except as required by FAA (§483.C.7), but these are not signage requirements per se.

Section 483.I.3 requires that upon decommissioning of a wind and/or solar farm, "Disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded, unless the landowner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored." This is a direct soil restoration and erosion control requirement. The decommissioning process also includes removal of equipment and grading to a depth of 36 inches (483.I.2), and financial assurance for decommissioning costs (483.I.4-6). No other explicit soil, erosion, or sediment control requirements are stated for wind and/or solar farms in the provided text.

Utility-scale solar energy systems, referred to as 'wind and/or solar farms,' are permitted by conditional use in the Quarry Zone (221.C.2) and the Light Industrial Zone (220.C.18), subject to the review procedures of Section 905 of this Ordinance and the requirements of Section 483. Section 483 states that within the (I-1 & Q) Zones, wind and/or solar farms are permitted by conditional use provided the applicant meets all applicable regulations including general criteria in Section 905.B. Other zones list 'Alternative energy systems' as accessory uses permitted by right but subject to Section 405, which does not explicitly address utility-scale or commercial solar farms.
section: SECTION 200 - AGRICULTURAL ZONE (A), Section 220 - I-1: LIGHT INDUSTRIAL ZONE, Section 221 - QUARRY ZONE, SECTION 483 - WIND AND/OR SOLAR FARMS

summary: Section 483.B requires the applicant to "prepare and submit a narrative and mapping describing the proposed wind and/or solar farm, including: an overview of the project; the project location; the approximate generating capacity; the approximate number, representative types and height or range of heights of wind turbines and/or solar panels; wind turbine system specifications; a description of accessory facilities; an affidavit or similar evidence of agreement between the property owner(s) and the applicant; a listing and map of the properties on which the proposed wind and solar farm will be located and adjacent properties; and a site plan showing the planned location of each wind turbine and/or solar panel, property lines, setback lines, access road and turnout locations, substation(s), electrical cabling, ancillary equipment, buildings, and structures." This submission constitutes a visual impact assessment requirement for wind and/or solar farms as conditional uses in the I-1 and Q Zones. The glare study requirement in 483.B.6 is excluded from consideration per instructions. No other visual impact assessment options or conditions are provided in the text.

Section 4.A.11 Decommissioning requires that "The PSES owner is required to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The PSES shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months." The owner then "shall have twelve (12) months in which to dismantle and remove the PSES including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations and other associated facilities from the property." If the owner fails to do so, "the municipality may complete the decommissioning at the owners expense." Additionally, "At the time of issuance of the permit for the construction of the PSES, the owner shall provide financial security in the form and amount acceptable to the Township to secure the expense of dismantling and removing said PSES and restoration of the land to its original condition, including forestry plantings of the same type/variety and density as the original." The financial security must be "not less than the total actual or fair market value cost, whichever is greater, of the system and its installation."

Section 4 - PRINCIPAL SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS (PSES) states: 'All ground-mounted PSES shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate.' Additionally, a 'clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence on the surrounding the PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards.' This fencing requirement applies specifically to ground-mounted PSES. No other fencing options or conditions are provided for PSES in the ordinance.

Section 4, subsection A, item 8 states: 'Glare a. All PSES shall be placed such that glare does not project onto nearby structures or roadways. b. The applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation.' This is a clear and specific glare restriction that applies to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), which are defined as systems 'principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use.'

The ordinance sets maximum height limits for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES): 'Ground mounted PSES shall not exceed 15 feet in height.' and 'PSES mounted on the roof or wall of any building shall not extend higher than 5’ above the current height of the building.' The most restrictive maximum height is 5 feet above the building height for roof or wall mounted PSES. Units are feet.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "Ground mounted PSES shall be screened from adjoining residential uses or zones according to the standards found in The Upper Mifflin Township Land Development and Subdivision Ordinance Article IX Mobile Home Park Regulations." No explicit vegetative buffer requirements are detailed for PSES, but this screening mandate applies. Other related provisions include that "PSES owners are encouraged to use low maintenance and low growing vegetative surfaces under the system as a best management practice for storm water management," which is a recommendation rather than a requirement. The ordinance also includes various other regulations for PSES such as setbacks, height limits, impervious coverage, underground placement of transmission lines, and decommissioning requirements, but these do not pertain to vegetative buffer or screening requirements.

Section 4.A.7 states: 'No portion of the PSES shall contain or be used to display advertising. The manufacturer’s name and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of the PSES but shall not exceed a maximum of one square foot in area.' Section 4.B.8.a requires: 'All ground-mounted PSES shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate.' Section 4.B.8.b mandates: 'A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence on the surrounding the PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards.' These are explicit signage requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) that an energy system developer must abide by.

The ordinance requires PSES applicants to submit a Stormwater Management Plan that demonstrates compliance with the Township Stormwater Management Regulations. Ground-mounted PSES shall not be placed within any storm water conveyance system or in any other manner that would alter or impede storm water runoff from collecting in a constructed storm water conveyance system. If a ground mounted PSES is removed, any earth disturbance resulting from the removal must be graded and reseeded. These requirements are found under 'Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems' and address soil disturbance, erosion, and sediment control. Other related provisions include impervious coverage calculations and screening requirements, but these do not explicitly address soil, erosion, or sediment control.

If a solar energy system remains nonfunctional or inoperative for a continuous period of one year, the system may be deemed to be abandoned and may constitute a public nuisance as determined by the Township Zoning Officer, with the exception of BIPV systems. If deemed abandoned or a public nuisance, the owner shall remove the system within six months of abandonment after a demolition permit has been obtained. Removal requirements include: (a) Any aboveground mechanical equipment, wiring, and structural components shall be removed; (b) Underground wiring and structural components shall be removed and the resulting void space filled; (c) When a ground-mounted or freestanding system is removed, any disturbed earth as a result of the removal of the system shall be restored, graded and reseeded. This applies to solar energy facilities, which are permitted as a conditional use on parcels over 10 acres in the Industrial Zoning District. Additional removal provisions include that removal requires a demolition permit and disposal must comply with Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection or Federal Environmental Protection Agency regulations, not municipal trash stream.

All equipment for solar energy facilities including any structure for batteries or storage cells shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight-foot-high fence with a self-locking gate. This fencing requirement is explicitly stated in § 350-225.E.(7). Other related regulations include setbacks, height limits, design and installation standards, and removal requirements, but these do not pertain to fencing. For example, setbacks must meet applicable primary use setbacks and not encroach on easements; height limits vary by roof type and ground-mounted systems; design must conform to industry codes; and removal requires a demolition permit and restoration of disturbed earth.

Solar modules shall be positioned to prevent solar glare upon any neighboring properties or any public or private street, and to prevent additional heat load upon neighboring properties. This requirement is found in the design and installation section for solar energy facilities. Other related regulations include setbacks, height limits, fencing, stormwater management, and decommissioning requirements, but these do not specifically address glare. The relevant glare restriction is explicitly stated in § 350-225.E.(6).

Solar energy facilities are permitted as a conditional use on parcels over 10 acres in the Industrial Zoning District (§ 350-225 A). This is the explicit minimum parcel size requirement for Solar Energy Facilities. The unit 'acres' is used to specify the area.

Solar energy facilities shall not be used to display advertising or decoration, including signage, streamers, pennants, spinners, reflectors, ribbons, tinsel, balloons, flags, banners, lights, or similar items. Manufacturers and equipment information, safety warnings, and ownership information may be displayed on solar energy system equipment, provided such information complies with applicable sign regulations.

Solar energy facilities shall be installed in compliance with all applicable state and federal building, construction and fire codes, including regulations with respect to stormwater management (§ 350-225.B.(1)). The applicant will provide a stormwater management plan for the facility that will minimize the impact of stormwater leaving the site, and promote infiltration of stormwater on-site, through the use of stormwater BMPs (§ 350-225.E.(8)). When a ground-mounted or freestanding system is removed, any disturbed earth as a result of the removal of the system shall be restored, graded and reseeded (§ 350-225.F.(3)(c)).

Solar energy facilities are permitted as a conditional use on parcels over 10 acres in the Industrial Zoning District. The conditional use regulations, requirements and restrictions set forth below in this article shall apply to solar energy facilities in addition to the conditional use requirements of § 350-204 and those regulations, requirements and restrictions of the underlying zoning district. Solar energy systems, as defined by this article, are a permitted accessory use in all zoning districts.

Section 3 – Decommission of Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) requires: (1) An affidavit or similar evidence signed by the property owner and PSES facility owner affirming a lease agreement with a decommissioning clause and successors and assigns clause; (2) The PSES owner must notify the Municipality immediately upon cessation or abandonment of operation, with abandonment presumed if no electricity is generated for 12 continuous months and no remedial actions are initiated; (3) The PSES owner must dismantle and remove the system within 18 months of cessation or abandonment or the Municipality may complete decommissioning at the owner's expense; (4) The PSES owner must post a bond or financial security equal to 125% of the estimated decommissioning cost when applying for a permit, with the estimate subject to Municipality approval and updated every five years; (5) The Municipality may use the financial security to pay for repair, dismantling, removal, or restoration costs and charge an administrative fee of 10%; (6) The landowner and developer must execute an agreement authorizing the Municipality to enter the property for inspections, repairs, dismantling, or removal, including a release of liability and indemnification. These requirements apply specifically to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), defined as systems principally used to supply power off-site.

This is the explicit maximum height restriction for Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), which are defined as systems primarily used for off-site electricity generation or sale. Principal solar energy systems (PSES) are a conditional use in Agricultural (A) and Industrial (I) Zoning Districts. Accessory solar energy systems are a permitted use in all zoning districts.

Ground mounted PSES shall be screened from any adjacent property that is residentially zoned or used for residential purposes. The screen shall consist of plant materials which provide an effective visual screen. Street screening shall consist of shrubs, six feet to eight feet high when mature, that shall be planted every 15 feet of property abutting a public right-of-way in a manner to provide an effective visual screen. The exact type and placement type of vegetation shall be approved by the Township. Shrubs shall be planted adjacent to or outside of the road right-of-way. Solar perimeter fence shall be placed between shrubs and solar panels. Perimeter fence shall be placed between shrubs and solar panels.

The ordinance explicitly enacts signage requirements for Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). It states: 'No portion of the PSES shall contain or be used to display advertising. The manufacturing name and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of the PSES provided they comply with the prevailing sign regulations.' summary: The ordinance requires that for Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES): the applicant shall submit a storm water management plan demonstrating stormwater infiltration at a rate equal to pre-installation conditions; PSES shall not be placed within any storm water conveyance system or in any manner that would alter or impede storm water runoff from collecting in a constructed stormwater conveyance system; if a ground mounted PSES is removed, any earth disturbance must be graded and re-seeded; excavation or grading shall be limited to that required for footers, posts, etc., within Class 1 and Class 2 prime agricultural soils, and grading that alters existing contour, elevation, stormwater drainage, or soil profiles beyond this exception is not permitted. Additionally, widespread use of herbicides to control ground cover growth is prohibited, and solar grazing with sheep is encouraged as a best management practice for vegetation control. These requirements are explicitly applicable to PSES as defined in the ordinance. section: Section 3 - SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS, 2. Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), B. Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems

summary: Principal solar energy systems (PSES) are a conditional use in Agricultural (A) and Industrial (I) Zoning Districts. "2. Principal solar energy systems (PSES) are a conditional use in Agricultural (A) and Industrial (I) Zoning Districts." Other relevant conditions include: "No PSES construction can be developed in lands that are enrolled in the Agricultural Preservation program." and "Agricultural and PSES uses are permitted on the same lot and are considered as dual primary uses as prescribed by the zoning code." Ground mounted PSES must meet lot size and setback requirements of the applicable zoning district, and have a maximum height of fifteen (15) feet. Additional requirements include screening, security fencing, stormwater management, noise study, and maintenance obligations.

The ordinance requires that "All PSES shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures, roadways or beyond the boundaries of the land upon which it is located." The applicant "has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses." The Municipality "may, in its sole and absolute determination, require applicant to provide the Municipality with a glare report/study" which "shall be subject to review and approval by the Municipality." Additionally, ground mounted PSES must be screened from any adjacent property that is residentially zoned or used for residential purposes with plant materials providing an effective visual screen, and street screening shall consist of shrubs "six feet to eight feet high when mature, that shall be planted every 15 feet of property abutting a public right-of-way in a manner to provide an effective visual screen." The exact type and placement of vegetation shall be approved by the Township. These requirements apply to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) which are defined as systems "principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use."

The ordinance states: 'Solar arrays shall not exceed 20% coverage on otherwise unoccupied property area.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage limit for ground-mounted solar arrays, which would typically include utility-scale solar energy systems. The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the property area, not as an absolute area value.

Systems shall use reduced or antiglare coatings. Glare from solar arrays shall not impinge on any road or public motorway, or otherwise create a nuisance situation. If glare creates a safety hazard or a nuisance situation, the Township may at its discretion require the system owner or the property owner to take appropriate mitigation measures at their own expense or to require the removal of the system or portion thereof generating the hazard or nuisance.

The maximum height of a ground-mounted solar array shall be 15 feet to its highest point. This applies to ground-mounted systems, which are typically utility-scale solar energy systems. Rooftop solar arrays have a different limit of 15 inches above the roof surface, but this applies to smaller, non-utility-scale systems. The 15 feet limit is the most restrictive height for utility-scale solar arrays mentioned.

Solar energy systems, wind energy systems and geothermal energy systems shall be allowed as an accessory use in all zoning districts unless otherwise provided. Solar and wind energy systems are specifically prohibited in the following areas: (1) All areas designated as public open space, whether general public or homeowners' association owned open space, or as specified in the Comprehensive Plan, or in third-party conservation or agricultural preservation easements; (2) Wastewater reclamation areas; (3) Greenways, as designated in the Comprehensive Plan; (4) Riparian buffer areas.

Ground-mounted solar arrays must be located no less than 15 feet from the property line. (§ 77-6 E.(1)) The text states: 'all portions of the solar array shall be within the side and rear yard building setbacks applicable to accessory structures but no less than 15 feet from the property line.' No other setback distances from property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, parcels, or subdivisions are specified for utility-scale solar energy systems.

Ground-mounted assemblies must be screened in accordance with § 200-77 of Chapter 200, Zoning, but not to an extent which precludes adequate and efficient operations (§ 77-6 E (4)). The maximum height of a ground-mounted solar array shall be 15 feet to its highest point, and all portions of the solar array shall be within the side and rear yard building setbacks applicable to accessory structures but no less than 15 feet from the property line (§ 77-6 E (1)).

The maximum height of a ground-mounted solar panel array shall be 15 feet to its highest point and all portions of the solar panels shall be within the side and rear yard building setbacks but in no case less than 15 feet from a property line.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) in section 12 titled 'Decommissioning.' It requires the PSES facility owner and/or Applicant to provide the Township with an irrevocable bond in the amount of fifty (50%) of the projected cost of the project, subject to a final audit of actual costs, to secure the expense of dismantling and removing the PSES and restoration of the land to its original condition based on the baseline analysis performed during the application process. The bond will be reviewed every eighteen (18) months for valuation purposes and adjusted as needed. The PSES owner must notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of operation. The PSES is presumed abandoned if no electricity is generated for six (6) continuous months without remedial action. If the PSES owner fails to dismantle and/or remove the system within twelve (12) months of cessation or abandonment, the Township may complete decommissioning at the property owner's expense. Disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded unless the property owner requests otherwise in writing. These requirements apply specifically to PSES as defined in the ordinance as systems 'principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use.'

The ordinance explicitly requires that "all ground mounted PSES shall be completely enclosed by seven (7) foot high fencing with locking gate in accordance with NEC code requirements." It also mandates that "locked access gates shall be at all road entrances" and that "solar panels that will be adjacent to residential areas will need to have an additional fifty (50) foot wide 'natural' buffer on the outside of the chain-linked fence," which can be a natural mound-buffer, planted earth berms, decorative fencing, or two rows of native evergreen trees providing year-round coverage. Furthermore, fencing, visual buffers, and emergency access roads may be located within setback areas. These fencing requirements apply specifically to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) as defined in the ordinance.

The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). Section (C)3.c.xiii states: 'All PSES shall be designed and installed to prevent and eliminate glare onto nearby structures and roadways, and to prevent and eliminate glare from having a substantial adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses.' Additionally, section (C)5.c states: 'All PSES shall be situated to eliminate concentrated glare onto nearby structures or roadways.' These provisions impose clear glare restrictions that a PSES developer must abide by. Other related options include glare restrictions for Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), which must be 'situated to eliminate concentrated glare onto nearby structures or roadways' per (B)1.h, but this applies only to ASES, not PSES.

The ordinance explicitly states that 'Ground-mounted PSES solar panels shall not exceed 15 feet in height' (section (C)6.c) and similarly 'Ground-mounted PSES shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet in height' (section (C)3.g.iii). Roof-mounted PSES are subject to the maximum height regulations specified for buildings within the applicable zoning districts (section (C)9.b). The unit for the height restriction is feet.

The total land for use as a PSES in the Township will be Five Hundred (500) aggregate acres. For purposes of this section,  "Aggregate acres"  of land for PSES use includes all land leased by the PSES facility owner to include both useable and non-usable land. (Section (C)5)

Principal Solar Energy Systems are a Conditional Use in the A-1 and I-1 Zoning Districts only. A PSES cannot be used as an accessory use for commercial or industrial activity on another property. By implication, PSES are prohibited in all other districts, including R-1 and R-2. Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems must follow setbacks and height limits but are only conditionally permitted in A-1 and I-1.

PSES shall be setback (a) a minimum of three hundred feet (300’) from any property line of an adjoining parcel on which a residential building is located, and (b) a minimum of three hundred feet (300’) from any right of way or public road and (d) a minimum of one hundred feet (100’) from any other property line. Fencing, visual buffers and emergency access roads may be located within the setback areas. If the PSES occupies two or more adjacent properties, setbacks between the adjacent properties shall be waived along the shared property boundaries so that the PSES may be installed continuously and make the most efficient use of the project area. Also, all PSES solar panels adjacent to any right-of-way or public road and PSES adjacent to any residential district (R-1; R-2) or parcel with an existing residential structure must follow a 300-foot setback.

The ordinance requires that Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) "shall be setback (b) a minimum of three hundred feet (300’) from any right of way or public road." Additionally, "All PSES solar panels adjacent to any right-of-way or public road ... must follow a 300-foot setback." Other setback options include 300 feet from property lines adjoining residential buildings and 100 feet from other property lines, but these do not pertain to roads. Fencing, visual buffers, and emergency access roads may be located within the setback areas. If the PSES occupies two or more adjacent properties, setbacks between the adjacent properties shall be waived along shared boundaries to allow continuous installation.

Section (C)6.d of the ordinance specifies screening and vegetation requirements for ground mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES): "Street screening shall consist of slat fencing or shrubs, a minimum of 6’ high when planted and 10’ high when mature, shall be planted every 15 feet along property abutting a public right-of-way. Shrubs shall be planted adjacent to or outside of the road right-of-way. Solar perimeter fence shall be placed between shrubs and solar panels. Reasonable modifications to these requirements may be requested." For residential buffer screening: "an additional fifty (50) foot wide  "natural"  buffer on the outside of the chain-linked fence. This can be a natural mound-buffer of native vegetation planted earth berms and or decorative fencing that provides a reasonable visual and lighting screen to reduce the view of the PSES from residential dwellings, or in lieu of the mound buffer can be 2 alternative rows of native  "evergreen"  trees of a minimum height of ten (10) foot that will provide year-round coverage of the facility behind the fencing. Reasonable modifications to these requirements may be requested." The perimeter fence must be placed between shrubs and solar panels. These requirements apply explicitly to PSES as defined in the ordinance, which are systems "principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use."

Section (C)7.b requires a clearly visible warning sign placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards. Section (C)5.b states that no portion of the PSES shall contain or be used to display advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer of the system. The manufacturer's name and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of the PSES provided they comply with prevailing sign regulations.

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). It requires a Stormwater Management Plan (C)3.a, prohibits placing PSES within stormwater conveyance systems or in any manner that would alter or impede stormwater runoff (C)2.b and (C)6.e, and encourages use of low maintenance and low growing vegetative surfaces under the system as a best management practice for stormwater management (C)6.f. Soil samples must be collected for baseline conditions and ongoing monitoring to detect contamination or disturbance (C)3.d. Upon removal or decommissioning, "disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded unless the property owner requests in writing that the access roads or other land surface areas not be restored" (C)12.c, and restoration includes "soil remediation, forestry planting, grasses, and vegetation of the original type" (C)12.a). These requirements apply specifically to PSES, which are defined as systems "principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use."

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). It states: 'The PSES owner is required to notify the Borough immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The PSES shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated by such system for a period of twelve (12) continuous months.' The owner then has 'twelve (12) months in which to dismantle and remove the PSES including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations, solar energy system connections and other associated facilities.' Materials should be resold or salvaged if possible, and disposed of properly if not. The site must be restored to its pre-existing condition, except that the landowner may authorize buffer landscaping or access roads to remain. Necessary permits must be obtained prior to decommissioning. Additionally, 'At the time of issuance of the permit for the construction of the PSES, the owner shall provide financial security in the form and amount acceptable to the Borough to secure its obligations under this Section,' with detailed requirements for cost estimates, updates every 5 years, minimum amounts, and acceptable forms of security. These requirements are found under the subsection titled 'Decommissioning' within the Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) standards. The ordinance also includes decommissioning provisions for Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), but those apply only to smaller or on-site use systems and are not relevant here.

The ordinance explicitly requires that all ground-mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) "shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate." Additionally, a clearly visible warning sign must be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards. This fencing requirement is found under Section 295-58, Part B, subsection 2(a)(1). Other related requirements for PSES include underground placement of on-site transmission lines to the extent feasible, setbacks of no less than 200 feet from residential district boundaries and residential dwellings (measured to the fence enclosing a ground-mounted PSES), and plant screening installed along the exterior side of the fencing within 50 feet. The ordinance also details decommissioning, permit requirements, access roads, height limits, glare mitigation, and stormwater management for PSES.

Section 295-58.B.1.e states: 'All PSES shall be placed such that concentrated solar radiation or glare does not project onto nearby structures or roadways.' Additionally, 'The applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced does not have significant adverse impact on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or mitigation.' This glare restriction applies explicitly to Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES), which are defined as systems 'principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use or for use on-site if the output size is greater than 10kw.'

The ordinance explicitly states: 'Ground mounted PSES shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet in height above the ground elevation surrounding the systems.' This is found under Section 295-58, Part B, subsection 2(c). No other maximum height limits for PSES are mentioned. The unit 'feet' is used consistently in the text for height restrictions.

All PSES shall be setback no less than two hundred (200) feet from a Residential (R) District Boundary; and all PSES shall be setback no less than two hundred (200) feet from the lot line of a lot on which a residential dwelling is located. The enhanced setback set forth above shall be measured from the district boundary to the fence enclosing a ground mounted PSES or to the structure on which a roof or wall mounted PSES is attached. Except as specifically altered herein, a PSES shall meet the setback requirements of the underlying zoning district.

All ground mounted PSES shall be screened and buffered in accordance with the following standards: Plant screening shall be installed around the perimeter of the PSES. Existing trees within the required screening and buffer area should be incorporated. The plant screening shall be installed along the exterior side of the fencing required by Section B.(2)(a)[1] above and located within fifty (50) feet of the required fencing. Plant screening shall be depicted in accordance with the Landscape Plan required by the SALDO. Plant screening shall be designed in accordance with the following standards: materials shall reach a minimum height of six feet above finished grade within two years; planting materials shall be permanently maintained and replaced when necessary; vegetative screen must provide a minimum opacity of 80% in winter and summer; designed to emulate the mix of species and appearance of existing tree lines, hedge rows, and wooded areas; primary use of evergreen trees is not permitted and monotonous straight rows of the same species, particularly evergreen trees, are prohibited; earth berms may be intermixed with the plant screening to enhance screening while retaining topographic characteristics.

The ordinance explicitly enacts signage requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). It states: 'No portion of the PSES shall contain or be used to display advertising. The manufacturer’s name and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of the PSES provided they comply with the prevailing sign regulations.' Additionally, 'A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards.' Furthermore, 'The PSES owner and/or operator shall maintain a phone number and identify a person responsible for the public to contact with inquiries and complaints throughout the life of the project on any and all entrances to the facility.' These are the explicit signage requirements for PSES. Other options or conditions related to signage include prohibition of advertising on the system, allowance of manufacturer and ownership information if compliant with sign regulations, and mandatory safety/warning signage at electrical equipment and facility entrances.

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). It requires that "Any soil exposed during the removal shall be stabilized in accordance with applicable erosion and sediment control standards." It also mandates that "Any necessary permits, such as Erosion and Sedimentation and NPDES permits, shall be obtained prior to decommissioning activities." Stormwater runoff from a PSES "shall be managed in accordance with the requirements of the Borough of Waynesboro Stormwater Management Ordinance." For vegetative cover beneath solar panels, conditions include: "Where natural vegetative cover is preserved and/or restored utilizing low impact construction techniques from the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection Stormwater Best Management Practices Manual," with specific requirements on vegetative cover density and slope limitations. Agrivoltaics are allowed with conditions including "A written erosion and sediment control plan must be developed for agricultural plowing or tilling activities or a portion of the overall farm conservation plan must identify BMPs used." The ordinance also details when solar panel areas can be considered Disconnected Impervious Areas (DIA) to manage runoff and erosion, with various conditions on panel arrangement, vegetative growth, and slope. These requirements apply specifically to PSES, defined as systems "principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use or for use on-site if the output size is greater than 10kw."

The ordinance text specifies that Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) are permitted as a use by right in the Institutional District (Section 295-21(B)(1)(n)). There is no explicit mention of any zoning districts where Ground Mounted Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) are permitted only as a special use or require approval by a zoning appeals board or similar conditional use process. The text includes detailed criteria for PSES such as setbacks, fencing, access roads, and height limits, but does not designate any districts for special use permitting. Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES) are permitted as a use by right in all zoning districts, but these are distinct from PSES. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this analysis as per instructions.

If a principal alternative energy system remains unused (ceasing active and continuous operation) for a period of twelve (12) consecutive months, the owner or operator shall either: file a certificate of intent to continue the use; or dismantle and remove the principal alternative energy system within six (6) months of the expiration of the twelve (12) month period. A notation describing this requirement shall appear on the land development plans for the facility (or, to the extent that it is determined that a land development plan is not required, shall appear on the plans submitted to the municipal engineer for consideration and shall be a condition for any permit issued hereunder).

The gate shall provide automatic access to emergency personnel. (Section 531(a)(5))

Section 531(a)(2) states: 'Principal Alternative Energy Systems (Solar and Wind) are only permitted on lots with a minimum of two (2) acres in area.' Principal Alternative Energy Systems (Solar and Wind) "shall only be permitted in the A-1, A-2, C-2, C-3, C-4, I-1 or I-2 Zoning Districts." They are permitted as primary uses with a minimum lot area of two (2) acres. Accessory Alternative Energy Systems (solar and wind) are permitted as accessory uses and structures in all Zoning Districts, subject to requirements. No mention of special conditions or approvals is made for principal systems in the listed districts. By assumption, solar overlay districts would also be considered primary use districts.

The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Solar Energy Facilities (SEF) in Section 210-162(A)(63)(18). It requires the SEF owner/operator to notify the Township immediately upon permanent cessation or abandonment of the SEF, which is presumed if no commercial production occurs for twelve (12) continuous months. The SEF owner/operator has eighteen (18) months to dismantle and remove the SEF, including all solar-related equipment and appurtenances. The owner/operator is encouraged to resell or salvage materials, dispose of non-salvageable materials according to law, stabilize exposed soil, and maintain paved access drives unless directed otherwise. Necessary permits must be obtained prior to decommissioning. Prior to construction, a decommissioning plan with estimated costs must be submitted and financial security of 110% of the decommissioning cost posted, subject to periodic updates every five (5) years. The Township may use the financial security to remove the SEF and restore the property if the owner/operator fails to comply. These requirements apply specifically to SEFs, defined as systems primarily for off-site use and typically producing in excess of 3 MW of power.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "All Ground-Mounted SEFs shall be completely enclosed by fencing with a self-locking gate." A fencing detail including "location, height, type, gate location and details, and footing details" must be submitted to the Township for review. Additionally, "A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the SEF informing individuals of potential voltage hazards." The entry gate "shall be accessible 24 hours a day by emergency personnel and vehicles, whether by key, or access code, which shall be provided to the Township upon completion but before the SEF begins operation." An emergency shut-off device (ESD) "shall be installed near to the entry gate and also at the ancillary structures installed near the center of facility." These fencing and security requirements apply specifically to Solar Energy Facilities (SEF), which are defined as systems "principally to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use" and typically produce "in excess of 3 MW (megawatts) of power."

The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Solar Energy Facilities (SEF). It states: "The Applicant has the burden of proving that any glare produced by the SEF does not have adverse impacts on neighboring or adjacent uses either through siting or through mitigation." The Applicant "shall provide a completed Glare Study ensuring that glare created by the SEF does not fall into the 'red category' of glare as used in Sandia’s Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT) or similar commercially available glare analysis tool as approved by the Township with a one-minute interval over the course of an entire year." "All adjacent roads and non-participating property owners’ residences within 1,000 feet must be included in the Glare Study." Additionally, under screening and buffering requirements, "Buffering shall be sufficient to manage glare on roads adjacent to the SEF so that the glare is not hazardous to drivers." These glare restrictions apply specifically to SEFs, which are defined as systems "principally to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use" and typically produce "in excess of 3 MW (megawatts) of power." The ordinance also includes glare prevention provisions for Accessory Solar Energy Systems (ASES), but those apply to smaller, on-site use systems and are not relevant to SEFs. Other related provisions include requirements for emergency shut-off devices, setbacks, buffering, and maintenance, but these do not specifically address glare.

The ordinance explicitly requires vegetative buffering for Ground-Mounted Solar Energy Facilities (SEF) "in a manner which will to the greatest extent feasible based upon the topography of the land, prevent the SEF from being seen from roadways adjacent to the SEF and/or non-participating owner’s residential structures on adjacent properties." The buffering "shall be installed along the exterior side of the fencing" and "should be designed to emulate the mix of non-invasive native species and appearance of existing tree lines, hedge rows, and wooded areas already in existence within the landscape where the SEF is proposed." Trees "shall be of such a height when planted as to provide immediate screening and shall be a minimum of eight feet (8’) in height." At least "20% of vegetative buffering plantings shall be pollinator friendly species." The buffering "shall be selected to provide year-round buffering and shall be of sufficient height, density, and maturity to screen the facility from visibility, as set forth herein within thirty-six (36) months of the installation of the SEF." The SEF Owner/Operator "is required to maintain (and if necessary replace) all vegetative buffering plantings during the life of the development." Buffering must also be "sufficient to manage glare on roads adjacent to the SEF so that the glare is not hazardous to drivers." The Applicant "shall submit a View Shed Analysis and Landscaping Plan with its application to show compliance with the above-listed screening and buffering provisions." These requirements apply to SEFs as conditional uses in the Rural Estate District, defined as systems "principally to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use" and typically producing "in excess of 3 MW (megawatts) of power."

However, "A small sign at the SEF vehicular entrance gate is required to state the owner of the SEF, emergency contact information including a current operating phone number that is answered 24 hours/day, 7 days/week, and address information." During construction, "the name and contact information for the general contractor shall also be posted at the entrance gate." Additionally, "The manufacturer's name and equipment information or indication of ownership shall be allowed on any equipment of the SEF provided that such signage complies with the applicable Township sign regulations." Safety signage is also mandated: "A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the SEF informing individuals of potential voltage hazards." These signage requirements apply to Solar Energy Facilities (SEF) defined as systems primarily for off-site use and typically producing in excess of 3 MW.

summary: Ground-mounted solar energy systems shall be permitted as an accessory use to all uses in all zoning districts by special exception subject to compliance with all applicable requirements in this § 84-57.17 and upon the issuance of a zoning permit pursuant to this chapter and a grading permit pursuant to Chapter 69 of the West Goshen Township Code (§ 84-57.17.A(2)). Roof-mounted solar energy systems in all zoning districts and ground-mounted solar energy systems on properties with single family dwellings are permitted as an accessory use by right (§ 84-57.17.A(1)). Ground-mounted solar energy systems built as an accessory use to a commercial use require land development approval (§ 84-57.17.A(3)). Solar energy systems as a principal use are permitted in specific districts (Commercial and Industrial Districts, Planned Office Park District, Multipurpose District, M-S Medical Services District, and MCX Municipal Complex District) by conditional use (§ 84-57.17.B(1)).

The ordinance includes decommissioning requirements under section B(4) 'Abandonment' which states: '(a) A solar energy system that is out of service for a continuous twelve-month period will be deemed to have been abandoned. (b) The Zoning Officer may issue a notice of abandonment... The owner shall have the right to appeal... (c) Any abandoned system shall be removed at the owner's sole expense within six months after the owner receives a notice of abandonment... (d) In granting a conditional use for a solar energy system, the Board may impose a requirement that the property owner post financial security with the Township in an amount sufficient to cover the cost of removal of the solar energy system in the event of abandonment.' These requirements apply to solar energy systems permitted as a principal use, which includes ground-mounted solar energy systems in Commercial and Industrial Districts and other specified districts by conditional use. Other options for solar energy systems include accessory uses such as roof-mounted or ground-mounted systems on single-family dwellings or commercial uses, which have different permitting and design standards but do not explicitly include decommissioning requirements.

Section B(2) states: 'The solar energy system shall be enclosed by a fence, barrier or other appropriate means to prevent or restrict unauthorized persons or vehicles from entering the property. The specifications and details of the fence or barrier shall be approved by the Board as part of the conditional use approval.' This fencing requirement applies to ground-mounted solar energy systems as a principal use in specified commercial and industrial districts. Other options include accessory use systems, which have no explicit fencing requirements mentioned, and screening requirements in B(3) which allow fencing or landscaping or a combination thereof for visual screening. The ordinance also includes safety signage requirements on the fence or barrier.

The ordinance requires that "the applicant shall demonstrate that the solar energy system shall be designed and located in order to prevent reflective glare from reaching adjacent properties or streets." This applies to "all rooftop-mounted and ground-mounted solar arrays" including those permitted as principal uses in commercial and industrial districts by conditional use. Other relevant provisions include that ground-mounted solar energy systems as a principal use are permitted in various commercial and industrial districts by conditional use, subject to compliance with all applicable regulations, and that ground-mounted solar arrays "shall not exceed a height of 12 feet" and must be screened from view from adjacent streets and properties, though the screening is not required to cover the solar panels themselves.

The ordinance explicitly states in § 84-57.17.A(6)(c) that 'Ground arrays shall not exceed a height of 12 feet.' This applies to ground-mounted solar energy systems, which would include utility-scale solar energy systems built as a principal use or accessory use to commercial uses. Other height limits mentioned include rooftop-mounted solar panels not exceeding 3 feet above the roof and not extending above the ridge line, but these apply to smaller or accessory systems. The 12 feet limit is the most restrictive for utility-scale systems. The units are feet as explicitly stated.

The ordinance requires that ground-mounted solar arrays built as an accessory use be screened from view from adjacent streets and properties, with screening covering supporting infrastructure but not the solar panels themselves (Section 84-57.17.A.6.d). For solar energy systems as a principal use, "Each solar energy system shall be screened by a buffer yard to create a continuous visual screen between the facility and a person standing at ground level on an adjacent lot. Such buffer yard shall be comprised of fencing or landscaping or some combination thereof and shall comply with the provisions in § 84-55A" (Section 84-57.17.B.3). Ground-mounted solar energy systems as a principal use are permitted in Commercial and Industrial Districts and other specified districts by conditional use. summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). Key provisions include: "The PSES owner shall provide an annual report by January 31 of each year showing the energy generated of the PSES for the preceding calendar year." If a PSES "remains nonfunctional or inoperative for a continuous period of six months, the facility shall be deemed to be abandoned and shall constitute a public nuisance," and "within six months of abandonment, the facility operator shall remove the system, after a demolition permit has been obtained," including removal and disposal of aboveground and underground components. The owner must secure the property until complete decommissioning or reuse, and "any disturbed earth as a result of the removal of the equipment shall be restored, graded and reseeded, or immediately returned to another allowed use." The PSES owner must submit "an estimate for the total cost of decommissioning without regard to salvage value of the equipment (gross decommissioning cost), and also an estimate of the cost of decommissioning net of the salvage value of the equipment (net decommissioning cost)" prior to building permit approval, with updates every five years. Financial security in the form of a bank-issued auto-renewed letter of credit must be posted and maintained at 110% of net decommissioning costs, but never less than 50% of gross costs. If the owner fails to decommission, the landowner must complete decommissioning within six months, and if neither completes it, the Township may do so and recover costs, including municipal liens and penalties. Upon satisfactory completion, remaining financial security is released to the owner.

The SEF owner and/or operator is required to notify the Township immediately upon cessation or abandonment of the operation. The SEF shall be presumed to be discontinued or abandoned if no electricity is generated from the solar panels for a period of twelve (12) continuous months. The SEF owner and/or operator shall then have eighteen (18) months in which to dismantle and remove the SEF including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations, solar facility connections and other associated facilities in accordance with agreements with landowners and good industry practice. To the extent possible, the materials shall be re-sold or salvaged. Materials that cannot be re-sold or salvaged shall be disposed of at a facility authorized to dispose of such materials by federal or state law. Any soil exposed during the removal shall be stabilized in accordance with applicable erosion and sediment control standards and requirements. Any access drive paved aprons from public roads shall remain for future use unless directed otherwise by the landowner. The SEF site area shall be restored to its pre-existing condition, suitable for its prior use. The landowner may authorize in writing that any buffer landscaping or access roads installed to accommodate the SEF will remain. Any necessary permits, such as Erosion & Sedimentation and NPDES permits, shall be obtained prior to decommissioning activities. The developer shall, at the time of zoning application, provide the County or municipality with an estimate of the cost of performing the decommissioning activities required herein. The solar project Owner shall provide financial security of 110% of the estimated cost of decommissioning, which will be reviewed by Lycoming County’s consulting engineer. The estimate may include an estimated salvage and re-sale value, discounted by a factor of 10%. The decommissioning cost estimate formula shall be: Gross Cost of Decommissioning Activities - 90% credit of salvage and re-sale value = the Decommissioning Cost Estimate. On every 5th anniversary of the date providing the decommissioning financial security, the SEF Owner shall provide an updated decommission cost estimate, utilizing the formula set forth above with adjustments for inflation and cost & value changes. If the decommissioning security amount decreases by greater than 10%, the Municipality shall release from security any amounts held in excess of 110% of the updated decommission cost estimate. The decommissioning security may be in the form of cash deposit, surety bond, irrevocable letter of credit, cashier’s check, or escrow account from a federal or Commonwealth chartered lending institution in the amount of 110% of the total proposed decommission cost estimate and in a form satisfactory to the Municipality’s Zoning administrator and Solicitor. The ordinance explicitly requires that "all major and medium solar installations shall be removed in accordance with their approved decommissioning plan." The property owner and the owner/operators are "jointly and severally responsible for removing all obsolete, abandoned or unused equipment within 12 months after a solar installation has ceased operations." Removal includes "physical removal of all systems, structures, equipment, wiring and security from the site both above and below ground," recycling of components "whenever feasible," proper disposal of waste, and "stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion." The owner/operator must notify the Building Official by certified mail before decommissioning. A solar installation is "considered abandoned when it has been nonoperational for more than one year," and if not removed within 150 days of abandonment, the Town may remove it at the owner's expense. Applicants must provide "a form of surety, either through escrow account, bond or otherwise, to cover the cost of removal." This surety amount is determined by the Planning Commission with input from Town officials and includes inflation adjustments and salvage value. Surety is not required for municipally or state-owned installations. These requirements apply specifically to major and medium solar installations, defined as ground-mounted systems occupying 40,000 square feet or more (major) or more than 1,750 but less than 40,000 square feet (medium), designed primarily to generate and sell electricity to a utility company. Minor solar installations and roof-mounted systems are not subject to these decommissioning requirements.

Buffers may be incorporated into the required setback area. Other options include a reduced ten-foot hybrid buffer (vegetated buffer plus fencing) in industrial, commercial, and business zones, extended to 20 feet where abutting a residential zone. summary: All medium and major solar installations shall maintain a vegetated buffer between the installation and all property boundaries to screen the solar installation from view from abutting properties and roads. Medium and major solar installations in industrial, commercial and business zones may request permission from the Zoning Board (through a special use permit) to use a reduced ten-foot hybrid buffer that combines a vegetated buffer with solid or slatted security fencing to both secure and obscure view of the panels.
