These requirements apply to all ground-mounted solar installations, including Major Solar Installations, which are defined as 'A ground-mounted solar installation designed primarily to generate and sell electricity to a utility company for resale to consumers that occupies an area of 40,000 square feet or more.' Major solar installations require 'major land development approval from the Planning Commission pursuant to Article V of the Coventry Subdivision and Land Development Regulations' and a special use permit. Other categories include Medium Solar Installations (more than 1,750 sq ft but less than 40,000 sq ft) and Minor Solar Installations (1,750 sq ft or less, designed primarily to service the property on which located).

All major solar installations require the issuance of a special use permit from the Zoning Board of Review pursuant to Article IV of this chapter and major land development approval from the Planning Commission pursuant to Article V of the Coventry Subdivision and Land Development Regulations (§ 255-2140 C(1)). Medium solar installations are permitted or permitted by special use permit in all zoning districts (§ 255-2140 B(1)). Ground-mounted solar installations proposed on lots of record that are nonconforming by area require a special use permit (§ 255-2140 D(3)). Medium and major solar installations in industrial, commercial and business zones may request permission from the Zoning Board (through a special use permit) to use a reduced ten-foot hybrid buffer (§ 255-2140 E(3)(e)). The text references broad zone categories such as residential, industrial, commercial, and business zones but does not specify formal district names or abbreviations where major solar installations are permitted as special use.

For major solar installations, defined as ground-mounted solar installations designed primarily to generate and sell electricity to a utility company for resale to consumers that occupy an area of 40,000 square feet or more, the ordinance requires a special use permit and major land development approval. As part of the development plan review, the application must include a "viewscape analysis demonstrating that the reasonable steps have been taken in the siting of the proposed solar installation to reduce negative impacts on rural and forested viewscapes." This is explicitly stated under § 255-2140.E.(1)(l). Other requirements for major and medium solar installations include a shading analysis, landscape plan, buffer requirements, and various operational and safety plans. Medium solar installations cover more than 1,750 but less than 40,000 square feet and have similar but slightly different requirements, including minor land development approval if over 20,000 square feet. Minor solar installations are those 1,750 square feet or less and primarily service the property on which they are located, with fewer requirements.

The Solar Lot Coverage of all ground-mounted SES’s are as follows: Principal SES in M-1 & M-2 zones is 60%, in C-4 & C-5 zones is 85%, and N/A in EI & G zones. The most restrictive maximum land coverage allowed for Principal Solar Energy System is 20% in C-4 & C-5 zones. Solar Lot Coverage is defined as the amount of Upland Area allowed to be occupied by ground-mounted solar panels and associated equipment, exclusive of fencing but inclusive of inter-row and panel spacing. Solar Lot Coverage applies to all Major Accessory and Principal SES’s and does not apply to Minor Accessory SES’s.
section: F. GENERAL REQUIREMENTS. 4. Solar Lot Coverage.

summary: Any SES shall be removed within 180 days from the date of discontinued operations. Decommissioning and restoration shall consist of: a. Physical removal and recycling of all solar energy facility structure, equipment, security barriers, fencing and overhead and underground electrical lines from the site. b. Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with all federal, state and local laws, regulations and ordinances. c. Disposal of all components, wiring, and/or foundations in accordance with the provisions of the City’s solid waste regulations. d. Stabilization and re-vegetation of the site in compliance with all state and local laws, regulations, and ordinances necessary to minimize erosion. The site shall be inspected by the Zoning Inspector and/or his/her designee in coordination with the Planning Director. A decommission/restoration plan including an itemized cost estimate for the decommissioning and restoration of the site is required at the Preliminary Plan stage for Major Accessory and Principal SES. Prior to the issuance of a building permit for a Major Accessory or Principal SES, a cash bond, escrow agreement or escrow fund to cover 125% of the cost of decommissioning, as approved by the Approving Body, shall be posted with the City of Cranston.

Section F.8 (Fencing) states: "This section shall apply to all Major Accessory and Principal SES’s. This section shall not apply Minor Accessory SES’s." It requires "a minimum of an 8-foot fence around the perimeter of all ground-mounted SES’s." The Planning Board may waive the fencing requirements "where the applicant can show that the surrounding area and site do not require fencing for protection or trespass, or to allow agricultural production within the array area." It prohibits "Barbed wire, razor or anything similar" and requires that "Where chain-link fencing is allowed, it must be black vinyl-coated."

Section 17.24.020.F.46 states: "All SES’s shall be designed and located to prevent reflective glare toward any inhabited buildings or adjacent properties. Glare generated from solar panels shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard. Racks shall have a matt finish to reduce glare and glimmer." This glare restriction applies to all Solar Energy Systems, including Principal Solar Energy Systems, as no exemption is provided. Principal Solar Energy Systems are defined as "A ground-mounted SES that is not a Minor or Major Accessory Solar Energy System."

The ordinance states: 'No individual panel within a ground-mounted SES shall exceed 12 feet in height.' This applies to Principal Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as ground-mounted SES that are not Minor or Major Accessory SES. Other height-related provisions include: roof-mounted and building-integrated SES’s are exempt from building height regulations; no Solar Canopy shall exceed the height limitation of the zoning district on which it is located. The 12 feet height limit is the explicit maximum for ground-mounted panels, including Principal SES.

Applicants for a building permit to construct a SES must submit a noise study as part of their application. The noise study assesses the potential impacts at any off-site noise receptors (e.g. residences) due to sound emitted by the SES’s electrical equipment including, but not limited to, inverters and transformers. The noise study is required to demonstrate that the facility, as designed, does not exceed a forty (40) decibel noise level (approximately the noise level experienced in a quiet office or library). The city's review engineer will assess the noise study to determine acceptable distance from the SES to any off-site receptor. The units for noise level are standard decibels, expressed as dBA.

The ordinance explicitly enacts vegetative buffer and other screening requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems. Under section F.7 "Visual Screening / buffering," it states: "Applicability. This section applies to Major Accessory and Principal SES’s. This section shall not apply to Minor Accessory SES’s." It requires that "Required visual screening shall be maintained for the life of the SES" and that "The property owner and/or facility owner shall be required to replant any section of the buffer/screening found not to meet the requirements of this section as determined by the City Zoning Official." For M-1 and M-2 zones, "no additional visual screening will be required unless the project abuts an incompatible use or a residential zone." Where it does abut such uses, "the applicant shall use an Inclusive Approach with the abutters within 400’ of the project site to develop an effective visual screening plan." Buffer depth requirements are flexible based on site conditions but must achieve effective visual screening. "Where appropriate, stockade fencing shall be used to satisfy the screening where the existing screening is insufficient," but "A stockade fence alone will not suffice for visual screening, from the right-of way or abutting properties. Plantings shall be required in between the project fencing and the property lines as determined during the Inclusive Approach." The Plan Commission may require an independent review of the visual screening/buffering plan by a Rhode Island registered Landscape Architect. These requirements apply specifically to Major Accessory and Principal SES’s, which includes Principal Solar Energy Systems as defined in the ordinance.

Section F.9 'Stormwater Management and Erosion and Sediment Control' applies to all SES’s in all zones, requiring site alterations to conform to the most recent edition of the RIDEM Stormwater Design and Installation Standards Manual and the RI Soil Erosion and Sediment Control handbook, as well as applicable City regulations. 'All applicable erosion and sediment controls must be in place prior to construction, including site work, begins.' Additionally, Section F.4.d requires 'Stabilization and re-vegetation of the site in compliance with all state and local laws, regulations, and ordinances necessary to minimize erosion' after decommissioning, with inspection by the Zoning Inspector and/or designee. These requirements apply to Principal Solar Energy Systems as defined as 'A ground-mounted SES that is not a Minor or Major Accessory Solar Energy System.'

The ordinance's Schedule of Uses in Sec. 17.20.030 shows Principal SES as either 'Y' (use allowed by right) or 'N' (use not allowed) in various districts, with no 'S' (special use permit) designation for Principal SES. Specifically, Principal SES are allowed by right in M-1 and M-2 zones and not allowed in other zones. The permit requirements section states that Principal SES in M-1 and M-2 zones require Development Plan Review Committee approval and building permits but do not require a special use permit. Special use permits are only required for ground-mounted Minor Accessory SES in certain zones, not for Principal SES. Therefore, no districts are identified where Principal SES are permitted solely as a special use or similar conditional approval.

The maximum height of a ground-mounted solar energy system shall be 12 feet, with the exception of solar covered parking structures which shall have a maximum height of 18 feet from the ground. This applies to systems structurally mounted to the ground, which may be of any size including major scale.

Major solar system installations require Major Land Development approval from the Planning Board and must include a decommission plan. It is the responsibility of the parcel owner to remove all obsolete or unused systems within six months of cessation of operations. Reusable components are to be recycled whenever feasible. Physical removal of solar energy systems, structures and equipment shall include stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion. The Planning Board may require a financial security instrument covering the entire solar energy system from commencement of operations through decommissioning. Such instrument may be cash held in escrow or a surety bond or other form acceptable to the Town. The security must be sufficient to cover the complete cost of removal and disposal of the system. The applicant shall submit a fully inclusive estimate of the costs associated with removal, at the end of the useful life of the facility, prepared by a qualified engineer licensed in the State of Rhode Island. Major and minor system installations must also adhere to other requirements including design standards, setbacks and height, code compliance, electrical requirements, security fencing, emergency access, signage, lighting, and operations and maintenance plans.

For major and minor solar system installations, a fence shall surround the perimeter of any installation unless adequate property perimeter fencing already exists to the satisfaction of the Planning Board. Said fencing shall be no less than seven feet in height nor greater than 10 feet in height. This fencing requirement is found under § 260-123 B(3)(f). Major solar system installations are defined as any ground-mounted solar energy system installation with an output exceeding 25kW or with lot coverage that exceeds 40% of the net buildable area. Minor solar system installations are those that do not qualify as major but meet criteria such as being designed primarily to sell electricity to a utility supplier, having a footprint exceeding 5,000 square feet, or lot coverage exceeding 20% but not exceeding 40% of the net buildable area.

summary: Major and minor system installations shall be allowed in the CH, M/LI-O, PD, and MUPD Zones. Such installations shall not be permitted in any other zones (§ 260-123B). Accessory system installations are permitted in all other zones except where prohibited pursuant to § 260-122A(1) (Downtown East Greenwich Historic District Overlay Zone prohibits all ground-mounted system installations). Building-mounted or building-integrated systems are allowed by right in all zones, subject to Historic District Commission approval in Historic District Overlay Zones (§ 260-122A and § 260-123C).

Any major and minor solar system installations must meet all height, lot coverage, and minimum front, side, and rear yard requirements in the applicable zone, and must additionally maintain a twenty-foot vegetated buffer from all adjacent properties and roadways.

Any major and minor solar system installations must meet all height, lot coverage, and minimum front, side, and rear yard requirements in the applicable zone, and must additionally maintain a twenty-foot vegetated buffer from all adjacent properties and roadways.

All major and minor system installations shall adhere to the following: (c) Setbacks and height. Any major and minor solar system installations must meet all height, lot coverage, and minimum front, side, and rear yard requirements in the applicable zone, and must additionally maintain a twenty-foot vegetated buffer from all adjacent properties and roadways.

For major solar system installations, signage on the security perimeter fencing is limited to a sign displaying the installation name, address and emergency contact information, and trespassing/warning/danger signs to ensure safety. No sign shall exceed four square feet in area. This is specified in § 260-123 B(3)(h). Other signage is not allowed on the fencing. This applies to major and minor solar system installations, which require Major Land Development approval and must meet various design, setback, code, electrical, security, emergency access, lighting, abandonment, operations and maintenance, and financial security requirements.

Major and minor system installations shall be allowed in the CH, M/LI-O, PD, and MUPD Zones. Such installations shall not be permitted in any other zones and shall be subject to the following: (1) Minor solar system installations shall require Minor Land Development approval. (2) Major solar system installations shall require Major Land Development approval from the Planning Board. Accessory system installations are permitted in all other zones with conditions, and building-mounted or building-integrated systems are allowed by right in all zones with Historic District Commission review where applicable.

Any major and minor solar system installations must meet all height, lot coverage, and minimum front, side, and rear yard requirements in the applicable zone, and must additionally maintain a twenty-foot vegetated buffer from all adjacent properties and roadways. The ordinance does not specify a fixed setback distance solely from occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, or residences, nor does it provide a multiplier based on structure height. The setback is therefore based on applicable zoning yard requirements plus a 20-foot vegetated buffer from adjacent properties.
Applicants proposing to develop large-scale ground-mounted solar photovoltaic projects shall provide a form of surety, either through escrow account, related to abandonment and decommissioning.
The maximum height of a ground-mounted solar energy panels shall be 15 feet. The height of a ground-mounted solar energy system shall be measured from the ground level.

summary: In the A-4, A-3 and R-2 zone, the solar land coverage plus any additional or existing structures on the lot shall not exceed 15% of the land suitable for development of the lot. Other zones have different limits: B-1 and B-2 zones allow up to 25%, and the I zone allows up to 30%. These percentages represent maximum land coverage limits for medium-scale solar energy systems as defined by the ordinance.

Subsection J(18) states: 'Any solar energy system which has reached the end of its useful life shall be removed within 180 days from the date of discontinued operations. A decommissioning estimate, prepared by a RI licensed engineer, must be approved by the Planning Board during the preliminary plan review. Each element of the decommissioning cost estimate must include a verifiable source with contact information. Decommissioning shall consist of: (a) Physical removal and recycling of all solar energy system structures, equipment, security barriers, fencing and transmission lines from the site. (b) Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with all federal, state and local laws, regulations and ordinances. (c) Stabilization and revegetation of the site necessary to minimize erosion and in compliance with all state and local laws, regulations, and ordinances, approved by the Glocester Zoning Official or his/her designee.' Subsection J(19) provides that if the owner/operator fails to remove the system, the Town may remove it and charge the cost to the owner/operator and/or landowner. Subsection J(20) requires 'Prior to the issuance of any building permit for a medium-, large-, or utility-scale ground-mounted or solar canopy solar energy system, an escrow agreement or escrow funds to cover 125% of the cost of decommissioning as approved by the Planning Board, shall be posted with the Town of Glocester. This surety shall be automatically renewed annually for a minimum of 20 years or for the anticipated life of the solar energy system.' These requirements apply explicitly to medium-scale solar energy systems as defined as 'a solar energy system that has a solar land coverage of more than 1,750 square feet but less than 40,000 square feet.'

Subsection J(9) Security fencing requires that "a minimum six-foot security fence shall surround the perimeter of the solar energy system." It prohibits barbed wire fencing, mandates the fence be "at least eight inches off the ground to allow small animals to pass underneath," and requires new fences to be flagged for at least six months. "Solar canopies are exempt from this requirement." These fencing requirements apply to medium-, large-, and utility-scale solar energy systems. Additionally, medium-scale solar energy systems must meet all performance standards listed in Subsection J, which includes these fencing requirements.

All solar energy systems shall be designed and located to prevent reflective glare toward any inhabited building or adjacent properties. Glare generated from solar panels shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard. This applies to medium-scale solar energy systems as they are included in the general solar energy system provisions. Additionally, medium-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems require major land development approval from the Planning Board and must meet all performance standards listed in Subsection J. Other relevant performance standards include height limits (not exceeding 12 feet), setbacks (e.g., 300-foot undisturbed setback in certain zones), solar land coverage limits, screening requirements, lighting, noise, security fencing, and operation and maintenance plans. Solar canopies and other scale systems have specific conditions and exemptions, but glare restrictions are explicitly stated for all solar energy systems.

Subsection J(1)(a) states that 'Ground-mounted solar energy systems shall not exceed 12 feet in height.' Medium-scale solar energy systems are ground-mounted and thus subject to this height limit. Other height limits include solar canopies not exceeding 20 feet and roof-mounted systems not exceeding the maximum height for the applicable zoning district. The 12 feet height limit applies explicitly to medium-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems. Units are feet.

Utility-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems are not permitted. (§350-46 I: "Utility-scale ground-mounted solar energy system is not permitted."). This prohibition applies universally across all zones. Other scale solar systems have different rules: medium-scale systems are permitted in all zones except the Village Overlay District and Village Overlay Center District; solar canopies are permitted only in B-1, B-2, and I zones; large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems are also not permitted (§350-46 H). Setback and land coverage requirements vary by zone (A-4, A-3, R-2, B-1, B-2, I).

All medium- and large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems in the A-4, A-3, and R-2 zone shall maintain a 300-foot undisturbed setback from any roadway or property line. In the B-2, B-1 and I zones, solar energy systems shall meet the setbacks of the applicable zoning district unless the parcel abuts property zoned A-4, A-3, or R-2, then the 300-foot undisturbed setback shall be required along the property line abutting the A-4, A-3, or R-2 zoned property. Additionally, all medium-, large- and utility-scale solar energy systems shall maintain a minimum fifty-foot vegetated buffer from all adjacent properties and roadways with a minimum height of eight feet at planting. The Planning Board may allow encroachment into the setback area for ground-mounted solar energy systems where panels will cross the property lines of one or more properties if it leads to a seamless installation, minimizes clearing, and maximizes screening.

All medium- and large-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems in the A-4, A-3, and R-2 zone shall maintain a 300-foot undisturbed setback from any roadway or property line. Additionally, all medium-, large- and utility-scale solar energy systems shall maintain a minimum fifty-foot vegetated buffer from all adjacent properties and roadways with a minimum height of eight feet at planting. Other setback options include: utility-scale systems in A-4 or A-3 zones require a 500-foot undisturbed setback from any roadway; solar energy systems in B-2, B-1 and I zones must meet applicable zoning district setbacks unless abutting A-4, A-3, or R-2 zones, then the 300-foot setback applies along that property line. The Planning Board may allow encroachment into setback areas under certain conditions.

All medium-, large-, and utility-scale solar energy systems shall maintain a minimum fifty-foot vegetated buffer from all adjacent properties and roadways with a minimum height of eight feet at planting. A vegetated buffer plan prepared by a RI licensed landscape architect shall be required at the preliminary plan review stage to verify that the vegetated buffer is adequate to thoroughly screen the solar energy system year round, using plants from the RI Native Plant database or plants used for agricultural purposes. The Planning Board may alter this width dependent on unique site characteristics. The required screening shall be maintained for the life of the solar energy system, and the property owner shall be required to replant any section of the buffer found to not meet the requirements. Additionally, while not subject to the setbacks, the driveway accessing a solar energy system shall require the same buffer when within 100 feet of a property line. Solar canopies are exempt from these screening requirements.

Subsection J(11) of the ordinance states: 'No signage is permitted on solar energy system fencing except for a sign displaying the facility name, address and emergency contact information.' It also allows: 'Signs such as no trespassing, warning or danger signs are allowed as needed to ensure the safety of individuals who may come in contact with the system.' Additionally, 'Temporary signage as outlined in § 350-26 is permitted.' These signage requirements apply to all solar energy systems, including medium-scale solar energy systems as defined in the ordinance.

Subsection J(14) requires that "site alterations must conform to the most recent edition of the RI Stormwater Design and Installation Standards Manual and the RI Soil Erosion and Sediment Control handbook, as well as applicable town regulations." It also mandates that "all applicable erosion and sediment controls must be in place before construction, including site work, begins." Additionally, Subsection J(7) states "No removal of topsoil or unnecessary disturbance of the ground or grading is permitted as part of the installation or maintenance of a solar energy system. Any topsoil that must be removed shall be stored and stabilized on-site for future use. In no case shall soil be exported from the site." Subsection J(8) requires minimizing clearing of natural vegetation and maintaining vegetative cover to prevent soil erosion, with a preference for pollinator-friendly seed mixes and native plants. These requirements apply to medium-scale solar energy systems, which are defined as systems with solar land coverage of more than 1,750 square feet but less than 40,000 square feet, and are subject to major land development approval and performance standards listed in Subsection J. Other scale categories include small-scale (1,750 square feet or less), large-scale (40,000 to 200,000 square feet), and utility-scale (more than 200,000 square feet, prohibited if over 20 acres).

The ordinance states: 'I. Utility-scale solar energy system. A utility-scale ground-mounted solar energy system is not permitted.' There is no mention of utility-scale solar energy systems being permitted as a special use or with approval in any zoning district. Medium-scale solar energy systems require 'major land development approval from the Planning Board' in all zones except the Village Overlay District and Village Overlay Center District, but this does not apply to utility-scale systems. Large-scale solar energy systems are also not permitted. Rooftop solar systems are permitted by right in all zones, and small-scale solar systems are permitted as accessory structures in all zones. Solar canopies are permitted in B-1, B-2, and I zones with conditions, but large- and utility-scale solar canopies are not permitted.

Sec. 82-1204.4.C.4. Abandonment or Decommissioning: "Any solar energy system that has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned shall be removed by the licensee. The owner/operator shall physically remove the system no more than 150 days after the date of discontinued operations. The applicant shall notify the Zoning Officer by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Decommissioning shall consist of: physical removal of all structures, equipment, security barriers, and transmission lines from the site; disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations; stabilization or re-vegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion. The Zoning Officer may allow the owner to leave landscaping or designated below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and disruption. Abandonment is defined as failure to operate for more than one year without written consent of the Zoning Officer. If removal is not completed within 150 days of notice, the Town may remove the facility. Financial surety is required from applicants for major solar energy systems to cover removal costs, not exceeding 125 percent of estimated costs, except for municipally or state-owned facilities. The applicant must submit a fully inclusive removal cost estimate prepared by a qualified engineer, including inflation adjustments.

Sec. 82-1204.4.C.3.e states: "A fence shall surround the perimeter of any ground-mounted installation unless adequate property perimeter fencing already exists to the satisfaction of the Zoning Officer. Said fencing shall be no less than seven feet in height nor greater than 10 feet in height, shall be secured from unauthorized entry, shall be located behind any vegetated buffer required by this section, and, as feasible, shall not obscure scenic views and shall incorporate wildlife passage features for small mammals and birds in its design and installation." This fencing requirement applies to Major Solar Energy Systems. Other related requirements include setbacks, height, vegetated buffers, underground utility connections, emergency access, signage, lighting, operations and maintenance plans, and decommissioning plans. A Special Use Permit and Formal Development Plan Review are required where allowed, with exceptions for municipally-owned property or agricultural land under certain conditions.

Sec. 82-1204.4.A.1 states: "All solar energy systems shall be designed and located to prevent reflective glare toward any inhabited buildings on adjacent properties. Glare generated from solar panels shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard." This applies to "all solar energy systems, including accessory and major solar energy systems," thus explicitly including Major Solar Energy Systems. Other relevant provisions include that major solar energy systems require a Special Use Permit where allowed, must meet setbacks, height, and vegetated buffer requirements, and must adhere to various operational, safety, and maintenance standards as detailed in Sec. 82-1204.4.C.

Major solar energy systems are prohibited in Jamestown, as indicated in Table 6-1. Table 6-1 shows Major Solar Energy System use as 'N' (Not permitted) in all districts except 'P' where it is 'S' (Permitted by Special Use Permit). Sec. 82-1204.3.A states: 'Major solar energy systems are prohibited in Jamestown, as indicated in Table 6-1.' Additionally, Sec. 82-1204.3.C outlines that where allowed, major solar energy systems require a Special Use Permit, except on municipally-owned property or agricultural/farming use property of five acres or greater with systems not exceeding 20% of net buildable area. When exceeding 40% of net buildable area, major land development approval and a Special Use Permit are required. Accessory solar energy systems are permitted in all zones. The district 'P' is the only district permitting Major Solar Energy Systems with a Special Use Permit.
section: Sec. 82-601. Uses and districts; Sec. 82-1204.3. General requirements

summary: Any major solar energy system, including any solar canopies that may be part of the system, must meet all height, lot coverage, and minimum front, side, and rear yard requirements in the applicable zone, unless otherwise specified herein, and must additionally maintain a twenty-foot vegetated buffer from all adjacent properties and roadways.

Any major solar energy system, including any solar canopies that may be part of the system, must meet all height, lot coverage, and minimum front, side, and rear yard requirements in the applicable zone, unless otherwise specified herein, and must additionally maintain a twenty-foot vegetated buffer from all adjacent properties and roadways.

Major solar energy systems "must additionally maintain a twenty-foot vegetated buffer from all adjacent properties and roadways" (Sec. 82-1204.4.C.3.c). Fencing requirements include a perimeter fence "located behind any vegetated buffer required by this section" (Sec. 82-1204.4.C.3.e). On prime farmland, "required vegetative buffers are composed of plant materials listed in the University of Rhode Island’s native plant database, with a preference for pollinator-friendly materials" (Sec. 82-1204.4.A.7.d). The Planning Commission may require "additional landscaping beyond the minimum requirements of this section" to mitigate impacts (Sec. 82-1204.4.C.5.b). Major solar energy systems require a Special Use Permit and Formal Development Plan Review unless on municipally-owned property or agricultural land over five acres with system size not exceeding 20% of net buildable area (Sec. 82-1204.4.C.1). If the system exceeds 40% of net buildable area, major land development approval and Special Use Permit are required (Sec. 82-1204.4.C.2).

For Major Solar Energy Systems, "no signs are allowed on the security perimeter fencing except for a sign displaying the installation name, address and emergency contact information, and trespassing/warning/danger signs to ensure the safety of individuals who may come in contact with the installation." Additionally, "No sign shall exceed four square feet in area." These requirements are found in Sec. 82-1204.4.C.3.g. Other conditions for Major Solar Energy Systems include requirements for Special Use Permits, building permits, setbacks, fencing, emergency access, lighting, operations and maintenance plans, decommissioning, and surety, but these do not pertain to signage.

Sec. 82-1204.4.A.2 requires that "On-site drainage management and erosion and sedimentation control shall conform to the latest Rhode Island Stormwater Design and Installation Standards Manual, and the RI Soil Erosion and Sediment Control Handbook, as well as all applicable Town regulations." This applies to all solar energy systems, including major solar energy systems. Additionally, Sec. 82-1204.4.A.3 states "Clearing of natural vegetation shall be strictly limited to what is necessary for the construction, operation, and maintenance of the solar energy system or as otherwise prescribed by applicable laws and regulations. Excavation and filling of project sites shall be limited to what is necessary to stabilize the installation area." These requirements are part of the development standards that major solar energy systems must follow.

Major solar energy systems are permitted only by Special Use Permit ('S') in the P district and not permitted ('N') in all other listed districts (OS-I, OS-II, RR-200, RR-80, R-40, R-20, R-8, CL, CD, CWe, CWw, DC) as per Table 6-1 in Sec. 82-601. "Where allowed, major solar energy systems require a Special Use Permit from the Planning Commission and Formal Development Plan Review per Article 10 and the Town’s Subdivision and Land Development Regulations and Unified Development Review per section 82-210." Specifically, "When a major solar energy system exceeds 40% of the net buildable area of the lot on which it is located, then such major solar energy system shall require major land development approval from the Planning Commission (per the Town’s Subdivision and Land Development Regulations) and a Special Use Permit through Unified Development Review." Agricultural or farming use property with 5 acres or more and systems not exceeding 20% of net buildable area are exempt from the Special Use Permit requirement. Accessory solar energy systems are permitted as accessory uses in all districts but are not relevant here.

Owners of all ground-mounted principal solar energy systems which have not been used for their intended purpose for a period of one year or more shall provide notice to the Town of this lack of use and be considered abandoned and shall be dismantled, removed and the site shall be restored at the owner's expense. The owner shall remove, or cause to be removed, the solar energy system within 120 days of receipt of notice from the Building Official. The applicant for a ground-mounted principal solar energy system shall post a bond or cash security with the Town sufficient to cover the cost of removal and restoration of the site prior to the issuance of a building permit for the solar energy system. The amount of said bond or security shall be determined jointly by the Building Official and the Planning Board as part of the major plan review.

All solar energy systems shall be designed and located to minimize reflective glare toward any inhabited building or roadway. This applies to Principal solar energy systems, which are defined as any solar array/solar energy system, interconnected with a public utility electrical distribution system that is the primary use of a lot or lots, designed for commercial generation of power that is sold. Principal solar energy systems require a special use permit (§ 14-9.5) and major plan review by the Planning Board. Other options include accessory solar energy systems with varying size thresholds and permit requirements: ground-mounted accessory solar systems ≤ 1,000 sq ft are permitted by right; > 1,000 sq ft but < 2,000 sq ft require a special use permit; > 2,000 sq ft require both a special use permit and development plan review. Accessory-principal agricultural solar energy systems require a special use permit and development plan review. Principal solar energy systems are prohibited in the Residential Zone.

A ground-mounted solar energy system shall not exceed 12 feet in height, as measured from the natural grade to its highest point, including the top of any support structure or panel when adjusted to its highest seasonal position. This applies generally to ground-mounted solar energy systems, which includes principal solar energy systems as defined. Other height-related provisions include roof-mounted solar panels which may not extend above the highest point of the roof by more than one foot and must not be higher than four feet above the plane of the roof, but these apply to accessory systems. The 12 feet limit is the most restrictive explicit maximum height for principal solar energy systems. Units are feet.

Principal solar energy systems are prohibited in the Residential Zone. All principal solar energy systems require a special use permit (§ 14-9.5) and major plan review by the Planning Board. Accessory solar energy systems have different conditions based on size and location, such as being permitted by right if ground-mounted and 1,000 square feet or less, or requiring special use permits and plan reviews for larger sizes. Additionally, solar energy systems within historically critical areas like within 1,500 feet radius of Pikes Peak or the Business Zoning District of Adamsville require special use permits and major plan review. Ground-mounted solar energy systems are also prohibited on land under conservation easement or within 100 feet of freshwater or coastal wetlands unless specifically allowed by legal documents.

The ordinance requires that "The solar energy system design shall incorporate appropriate landscaping and design elements to visually screen the installation from view of public roads and abutting properties." Vegetative buffers must be composed of plant materials listed in the University of Rhode Island's native plant database, with a preference for pollinator-friendly materials to the maximum extent practicable. This applies to all solar energy systems, including Principal solar energy systems, which are defined as "Any solar array/solar energy system, interconnected with a public utility electrical distribution system that is the primary use of a lot or lots, designed for commercial generation of power that is sold." Principal solar energy systems require a special use permit and major plan review by the Planning Board. Other options include accessory solar energy systems with various size thresholds and permit requirements: ground-mounted accessory solar systems ≤1,000 sq ft are permitted by right; >1,000 sq ft but <2,000 sq ft require a special use permit; >2,000 sq ft require a special use permit and development plan review. Accessory-principal agricultural solar energy systems require a special use permit and development plan review. Principal solar energy systems are prohibited in the Residential Zone.

On-site drainage management and erosion and sedimentation control shall conform to the latest Rhode Island Stormwater Design and Installation Standards manual, and the Rhode Island Soil Erosion and Sediment Control Handbook, as well as applicable Town regulations. Clearing of natural vegetation shall be strictly limited to what is necessary for the construction, operation and maintenance of the solar energy system. No more than 20% of the area covered by solar panels shall be cleared woodland, and total cleared woodland shall not exceed 20,000 square feet. Upon abandonment, the site shall be restored at the owner's expense, with stabilization and revegetation to prevent erosion and/or reestablish original habitat. The applicant must post a bond or cash security sufficient to cover removal and restoration costs prior to permit issuance. Other options for solar systems include accessory solar energy systems with varying size thresholds and permit requirements, and accessory-principal agricultural solar energy systems, all with different review procedures and dimensional standards.

summary: All principal solar energy systems require a special use permit (§ 14-9.5) and major plan review by the Planning Board. Any solar energy system located within the Business Zoning District of Adamsville requires a special use permit (§ 14-9.5) and major plan review by the Planning Board. Principal solar energy systems are prohibited in the Residential Zone. Other accessory solar energy systems have different conditions based on size, such as requiring special use permits or development plan review.

Ground-mounted solar energy systems and any associated equipment or structures shall not be located within 100 feet of any freshwater or coastal wetland as defined by the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management and/or the Coastal Resources Management Council. This applies to principal solar energy systems as defined: 'Any solar array/solar energy system, interconnected with a public utility electrical distribution system that is the primary use of a lot or lots, designed for commercial generation of power that is sold.' Other options and conditions mentioned in the ordinance relate to accessory solar systems or other zoning considerations but do not specify different setbacks from lakes, reservoirs, streams, rivers, or wetlands for principal systems.

The dimensional table in section (B)(1) sets maximum lot coverage limits: 50% of developable land for general ground-mounted solar energy systems (except solar carport or canopy), 25% in residential districts for such systems, and 10% for solar carports or canopies in residential districts. The most restrictive applicable maximum land coverage for large solar energy systems is 25%. Lot coverage includes land within the fenced area of the installation as well as land used for access roads and utilities exclusively serving the installation.

All ground-mounted solar energy systems shall be decommissioned and removed after they cease to generate electricity, as follows: (1) A decommissioning plan must be submitted as part of the application package for a special use permit, including the responsible party, conditions triggering decommissioning, removal plan, recycling plan, restoration plan, and timeline. (2) Decommissioning shall begin no later than six months after cessation of electricity generation. (3) Within six months of beginning decommissioning, the system and all associated structures shall be removed and the property restored to its prior condition or another condition appropriate for the land use. (4) If the owner fails to remove the installation, the town may remove it and recover costs via a lien on the property.

The ordinance requires that a ground-mounted solar energy system installation be surrounded by visual screening, consisting of fencing, dense vegetation, or a combination of both, that is a minimum of six feet in height at the time of installation (§ 725 (C)(3)(b)). Additionally, the system shall be designed to prevent unauthorized access to panels and equipment, such as by use of protective fencing, locked equipment shelters, and other means as appropriate (§ 725 (C)(4)(b)). Where the development parcel includes or is adjacent to wetlands, fencing must provide a minimum of six inches of ground clearance to allow for wildlife movement (§ 725 (C)(4)(c)). These requirements apply to large solar energy systems subject to development plan review (§ 725 (C)(2)(a)).

The ordinance specifies a maximum height of 12 feet for ground-mounted solar energy systems, except solar carports or canopies. Height is measured from pre-development lot grade at the location of the panel. For solar carports or canopies, the height is as per accessory building height in § 603 or § 604. In residential districts, the maximum height for ground-mounted solar energy systems (except carports or canopies) is also 12 feet, while solar carports or canopies must comply with accessory building height in § 603 or § 604.

The ordinance requires that "the site design shall incorporate landscaping and design elements to visually screen the installation from view from public roads and adjoining properties to the greatest practical extent." It mandates that "the installation shall be surrounded by visual screening, consisting of fencing, dense vegetation, or a combination of both, that is a minimum of six feet in height at the time of installation." The "required vegetated buffer/screening shall be maintained for the life of the solar energy system," and the property or facility owner must "replant any section of the buffer/screening found not to meet the requirements." These requirements apply to large solar energy systems, which are subject to development plan review and must submit utility feasibility or impact studies. Other options for screening include fencing alone or dense vegetation alone, but the minimum height and maintenance requirements apply to all. Vegetation planted under solar panels must include native wildflower or grass seed mix.

The ordinance includes soil preservation requirements for large ground-mounted solar energy systems: '(a) Except for carport or canopy installations, no removal of topsoil or unnecessary disturbance of the ground or grading is permitted as part of the installation or maintenance. Any topsoil that must be moved shall be stored and stabilized onsite for future use.' and '(b) Except for carport or canopy installations, siting of the facility and individual panels shall maintain the existing contours of the land, and only pile driven or ballast block footing are to be used, so as to minimize the disturbance of soils during installation.' The exception applies only to carport or canopy installations, which are treated differently in these soil preservation requirements.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "Prior to the issuance of a permit under this chapter, the applicant shall deposit in the form of cash with the municipality the full estimated cost of dismantling and removal of the solar photovoltaic system, including the cost necessary to return the property to its pre-siting condition," held in an interest-bearing escrow account. A system "that is not generating electricity for six consecutive months shall be deemed discontinued," and must be removed within 120 days of notice unless appealed. Decommissioning must be overseen and certified by the Town's peer review engineer. The cost per megawatt for decommissioning is determined by the Town's peer review engineer. Additionally, as a condition of approval for nonaccessory ground-mounted solar photovoltaic systems, "the landowner shall grant a municipal lien for all costs necessary to remove the entire solar array including all appurtenance structures along with costs related to landscaping to preexisting conditions," and the landowner and developer are responsible for removal and restoration. For utility-scale systems defined as "For the purpose of selling energy and energy credits to an electric utility company, a municipality, or any other third-party consumers of energy, which area size exceeds six acres and 30% of the gross lot area," decommissioning "shall require approval by the Town Council as part of the preliminary plan application to the Planning Board." Surety may be in the form of "a combination of bond, cash, and/or property liens, to ensure adequate financial protection exists to support dismantling of an abandoned system." The Planning Board may waive requirements as requested.

In Rhode Island, developers of ground-mounted solar energy facilities must submit decommissioning plans with cost estimates when applying for municipal permits, including removal of all installations, proper waste disposal, and site stabilization or revegetation, and municipalities may require a performance bond. Senate Bill S0499 would further require applicants to demonstrate in writing that sufficient resources are available to cover decommissioning and recycling of photovoltaic panels at the end of their useful life.

Ground-mounted solar facilities allowed pursuant to this section shall have a solar land coverage of no more than 30% of the parcel on which they are located, including existing structures. The Plan Commission may waive this requirement if it finds that the parcel and/or circumstances of the facility are unique and/or would serve a public benefit and/or the potential abutting impacts have been adequately mitigated to allow a higher percentage of solar land coverage. Conversely, the Plan Commission may require a reduction in solar land coverage if it finds that the parcel or the circumstances of the facility are unique with regards to environmental considerations, potential impact to abutters, consistency with the Comprehensive Plan or other such circumstance in which the Plan Commission determines a reduction is warranted. For nonresidential zones (BL, BG and M), the maximum solar land coverage is 60%. The unit 'percent' refers to the percentage of the total parcel area.

Any solar energy facility which has reached the end of its useful life, sustained casualty loss, or other significant damage, is not repaired or used or has reached a point of obsolescence, or is not being properly maintained shall be removed within 180 days of the precipitating event from the date of discontinued operations. A decommissioning estimate prepared by a RI licensed engineer must be approved by the Plan Commission during the preliminary phase of review. Decommissioning shall consist of physical removal and recycling of all solar energy facility structure, equipment, security barriers, fencing and transmission lines from the site; disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with all federal, state and local laws, regulations and ordinances; and stabilization and revegetation of the site. Prior to the issuance of a building permit for a medium-, large- or utility-scale ground-mounted or solar canopy solar energy facility, an escrow agreement, bond, letter of credit or escrow fund by an A-rated or above institution to cover 125% of the cost of decommissioning, as approved by the Plan Commission, is required. This surety shall be automatically renewed annually for a minimum of 20 years or for the anticipated life of the solar energy facility and must be updated at least every five years to account for inflation.

The applicant shall be required to install a minimum of a six-foot fence around the perimeter of the solar energy facility. Barbed-wire fencing is prohibited. The fence shall be installed a minimum of eight inches off the ground to allow small animals to pass underneath. Newly installed fences shall be flagged for at least six months to protect both fencing and wildlife. Solar canopies are exempt from this requirement.

All solar energy facilities shall be designed and located to prevent glare toward any inhabited buildings or adjacent properties. Glare generated from solar panels shall not interfere with traffic or create a nuisance or safety hazard. This requirement is found in subsection (a)(3)(xix) and applies to all solar energy facilities, including utility-scale solar energy facilities, which are defined as systems occupying more than 220,000 square feet of area. The ordinance also includes other general requirements for solar energy facilities such as height limits, fencing, decommissioning, landscaping, and lighting, but the explicit glare restriction is stated only in subsection (a)(3)(xix).

No individual panel within a ground-mounted solar energy facility shall exceed 12 feet in height. Solar canopies are exempted from this requirement. Utility-scale solar energy facilities are ground-mounted systems occupying more than 220,000 square feet, so this 12-foot maximum panel height applies to them. No other explicit maximum height restrictions for utility-scale solar energy facilities are provided.

Solar installations shall maintain a 200-foot undisturbed vegetated setback from all abutting/adjoining or adjacent properties and roadways. As part of the major land development or development plan review process the Plan Commission may increase or decrease the 200-foot setback requirement or require additional screening elements dependent on site characteristics such as slope, wetland area and existing buffering.

Solar installations shall maintain a 200-foot undisturbed vegetated setback from all abutting/adjoining or adjacent properties and roadways. The Plan Commission may increase or decrease the 200-foot setback requirement or require additional screening elements dependent on site characteristics such as slope, wetland area and existing buffering.

The ordinance requires that utility-scale solar energy facilities be "sited and screened to minimize the aesthetic effect of solar facilities on viewsheds for abutting/adjoining property owners and within the community." It mandates that the design "incorporate landscaping and design elements to visually screen the installation from view of public roads and abutting/adjoining properties to the maximum extent practicable." A "200-foot undisturbed vegetated setback from all abutting/adjoining or adjacent properties and roadways" must be maintained, and if natural screening is lacking, plantings "shall be a minimum of six feet in height at the time of installation." The Plan Commission may adjust the 200-foot setback or require additional screening based on site characteristics. Verification by a Rhode Island licensed landscape architect is required to confirm that the "landscape buffer and visual screening are adequate to thoroughly screen the solar energy facility year-round," and the buffer must be maintained for the life of the facility, with replanting required as determined by the Zoning Enforcement Officer. The landscape plan must include "pre" and "post" viewshed analysis, use only native vegetation for screening, and additional landscaping may be required by the Plan Commission. Building-mounted solar energy facilities and solar canopies are exempt from the landscape requirement. Other options include adjustments to location and additional landscaping as required by the Plan Commission to mitigate negative impacts. These requirements apply to utility-scale solar energy facilities, defined as systems occupying more than 220,000 square feet.

Subsection (a)(3)(xiv) requires that "site alterations must conform to the most recent edition of the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management Stormwater Design and Installation Standards Manual and the Rhode Island Soil Erosion Control Handbook, as well as all applicable Town regulations." It further mandates that "all applicable erosion and sediment controls must be in place prior to the start of construction, including site work." Additionally, subsection (a)(3)(vi) states that "proposed site regrading shall not be excessive and shall be kept to a minimum amount necessary. No removal of topsoil or unnecessary disturbance of the ground or grading is permitted as part of the installation or maintenance. Any topsoil that must be removed shall be stored and stabilized on-site for future use." These requirements apply to all solar energy facilities, including utility-scale solar energy facilities defined as "a solar energy system that occupies more than 220,000 square feet of area, inclusive of inter-row and panel/collector spacing."

Ground-mounted solar facilities in residential zones require Plan Commission approval to waive or reduce solar land coverage limits based on unique circumstances or public benefit: "The Plan Commission may waive this requirement if it finds that the parcel and/or circumstances of the facility are unique and/or would serve a public benefit... Conversely, the Plan Commission may require a reduction in solar land coverage..." In nonresidential zoning districts (BL, BG and M), ground-mounted solar facilities have a solar land coverage limit of no more than 60% of the parcel and must meet applicable zone requirements, implying a permitting or approval process. The text references compliance with Article II, § 75-2.1(k) (Section 11) for location of solar energy facilities, which may include additional zoning conditions. Other options include building-mounted solar energy facilities permitted in all districts and solar canopies subject to zone requirements, but these are not utility-scale systems.

Solar installations shall maintain a 200-foot undisturbed vegetated setback from all abutting/adjoining or adjacent properties and roadways. This setback is intended to minimize the aesthetic effect of solar facilities on viewsheds for abutting/adjoining property owners and within the community. The Plan Commission may increase or decrease the 200-foot setback requirement or require additional screening elements dependent on site characteristics. summary: A limited solar energy system shall cover no greater than 50% of a lot or contiguous lots in common ownership. The lot coverage calculation shall include inter-row and panel/collector spacing, meaning that the entire area of the installation shall be counted as lot coverage.

Applicants proposing to develop limited solar energy systems shall be required to provide a form of surety, either through escrow account, bond or otherwise, to cover the cost of removal in the event the Town must remove the facility and restore the landscape, in an amount and form determined to be reasonable by the Board (and subject to the review of the Town Solicitor), and/or as agreed to and detailed in the site lease agreements. The applicant shall submit a fully inclusive estimate of the costs associated with removal, including a mechanism for calculating increased removal costs due to inflation and any expected salvage or resale value. Such surety will not be required for municipally or state-owned facilities. The applicant shall submit the financial guarantee before any local permits are issued. Any solar energy system that has reached the end of its useful life or has been abandoned shall be removed. The applicant shall submit a decommissioning plan to the Zoning Board and/or Planning Board with the application for project review and approval. The owner or operator shall physically remove the facility no more than 180 days after the date of discontinued operations and notify the Board by certified mail no later than 90 days before the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Decommissioning shall consist of physical removal of all ground-mounted solar energy systems, structures, equipment and security from the site; disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations; and stabilization or revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion. The Board may allow the owner or operator to leave landscaping or designated below-grade foundations to minimize erosion and disruption to vegetation. Absent notice of a proposed date of decommissioning or written notice of extenuating circumstances, the solar energy system shall be considered abandoned when it fails to operate for more than one year without the written consent of the Town Council and Planning Board. If the owner or operator fails to remove the facility within 150 days of abandonment or the proposed date of decommissioning, the Town may physically remove the facility without further notice and may place a lien on the property for any costs incurred over and above the bond amount, with statutory interest.

The lot coverage calculation includes inter-row and panel/collector spacing. Also, "a limited solar energy system that is located on more than one contiguous parcel of land shall be considered a single system and shall not exceed the land area/capacity threshold specified in § 400-204." The units for the maximum lot size are acres.

A solar energy system that has a rated nameplate capacity of no more than 1 MW AC and occupies no more than four acres of surface area, including inter-row and panel/collector spacing (§ 400-204 Definitions). The most restrictive numerical value for maximum project size is 1 MW AC (megawatts alternating current).

A limited solar energy system shall have a setback requirement of 200 feet from adjacent residential zoning districts and from the front yard line. Where the subject property borders a nonresidential zoning district, the setback shall be 50 feet.

Applicants proposing ground-mounted solar energy systems shall propose an appropriate buffer that adequately mitigates visual impacts on surrounding properties and the neighborhood in general. Selection of the proposed buffer should be based on the context and characteristics of the specific site, and shall be done in consultation with a landscape designer. Choices include, but are not limited to: 1) wooded buffer; or 2) full landscape screen. The Board shall determine the appropriate buffer based on site conditions. If a full landscape screen is utilized, the applicant shall post a bond for the maintenance of that landscape screen during the expected life of the system. The required buffer shall be delineated with permanent markers. If a 200-foot setback is required, the first 150 feet of that setback distance shall be a no-cut zone, and the only allowable trimming of buffer vegetation shall be growth (branches/limbs) that overhang the buffer zone.

Drainage and erosion and sedimentation control shall conform to the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management Stormwater Design Manual and all applicable regulations, local and state. Clearing of natural vegetation shall be limited to what is necessary for the construction, operation, and maintenance of the solar energy system or otherwise prescribed by applicable laws, regulations, and bylaws/ordinances. The disturbance of topsoil shall be limited to those areas that are required for the installation of the proposed solar energy system. Topsoil shall be stockpiled for re-use, restoration, and stabilization of the site after.

Following "a continuous six month period in which no electricity is generated, the permit holder will have six months to complete decommissioning of the solar farm," which includes "removal of solar panels, buildings, cabling, electrical components, and other associated facilities above and below grade as described in the decommissioning plan." Prior to issuance of Zoning Compliance, the applicant must provide "a performance guarantee in the form of a surety or performance bond, certified check, or irrevocable letter of credit in the amount of 125% of the estimated decommissioning cost minus the salvage value of equipment on the site." Construction approval varies by district: in FA districts, approval is by the Planning Commission, which "may approve as presented, approve with specified modifications, or disapprove" (with written reasons for disapproval); in RDD, GC, LI, and BI districts, approval is by the Zoning Administrator. summary: Section 11, Decommissioning, requires the applicant to provide a decommissioning plan signed by the responsible party and landowner that describes the anticipated life of the solar farm, estimated decommissioning costs in current dollars, the method for ensuring funds will be available, and the anticipated timeline and manner for decommissioning and site restoration. Decommissioning is required following a continuous period of twelve (12) months in which no electricity is generated other than for mechanical, repair, replacement and/or maintenance purposes. The permit holder has twelve (12) months to complete decommissioning, which includes removal of solar panels, foundations, structures, cabling, electrical components, conduit, and any other associated facilities. Prior to issuance of the Development Permit, the applicant must provide a performance guarantee in the form of a bond, irrevocable letter of credit, or other financial security acceptable to the County in the amount of 125% of the estimated decommission cost minus salvageable value, or $50,000, whichever is greater. Every five (5) years, a new engineer’s estimate of probable cost must be submitted and the financial security adjusted accordingly. Proof that the decommissioning plan has been recorded with the Colleton County Register of Deeds is also required.

A security fence shall be required at least six feet (6’) in height to secure the solar equipment unless a taller fence is needed in order to obscure the solar equipment from exterior view. A chain link fence shall not be allowed unless it is screened from exterior view from adjoining property owners and public right of ways; screening may include plantings to create a  "living fence" , or to obscure the view of the fence. Breaks in fencing may be allowed or required by Council to facilitate wildlife needs where natural features provide appropriate barriers to access by humans for security and safety purposes. Additionally, access to the site must be controlled by a six foot (6’) wooden fence or gate if the fencing is visible from the exterior of the property. If the fencing/gate is within the interior 25% of the buffer, or is not visible from the exterior of the property, chain link gate and fencing may be used.

The ordinance applies to Solar Farm Floating Zone (SFFZ) systems of a minimum of five (5) acres intended for electricity generation. It requires solar collectors to be "designed with anti-reflective coating to minimize glare," prohibits mirrors, and mandates that solar collection devices "are to be designed and located to avoid directing glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard." These glare restrictions are part of the General Requirements (Section 9) for solar farms. Other development standards include buffers, landscaping and screening, setbacks, fencing, height limits, underground electrical interconnections, lighting controls, noise limits, and decommissioning plans.

The Solar Energy System shall not exceed ten feet (10’) in height, as measured from the ground to the foremost/tip end of the solar collector, provided there is a demonstration that the screening prevents the system from being visible from the exterior of the property. Ancillary non solar collector structures, such as inverters, transformers, etc., may be taller than ten feet (10’) in height, provided that such are not visible from the exterior of the property.

The ordinance states that 'The solar farm consists of a minimum of five (5) acres' as a condition for utilizing the Solar Farm Floating Zone (SFFZ). This minimum lot size applies to solar farms intended for electricity generation and sale. The unit is explicitly given as acres. No other minimum lot size values are provided for utility-scale solar energy systems in the text.

Section 9.g states: 'Adequate provisions to reduce average/constant noise levels at the property boundary not to exceed 50dBA at the property line, except during construction.' This applies to solar farms defined as systems consisting of a minimum of five (5) acres and intended for electricity generation. The unit 'dBA' is the standard unit for noise level measurement.

The Solar Farm Floating Zone (SFFZ) is intended to promote the use of solar energy as a source of electricity and facilitate the construction, installation, and operation of Solar Energy Systems (SES) in Colleton County. The SFFZ "may be utilized in any zoning district except for the Resource Conservation District," provided certain conditions are met, including a minimum size of five acres and proximity to electrical transmission lines. It requires a zoning map amendment and a recommendation from the Planning Commission to County Council. The SFFZ adds an extra layer of land use regulation over the underlying zoning and is considered a primary use district for utility-scale solar energy systems. Other options or conditions include adherence to development standards such as buffers, landscaping, setbacks, fencing, height limits, and general requirements. The text does not mention any other districts or zones where utility-scale solar energy systems are permitted as a primary use without special conditions or approval.

The ordinance sets bufferyard requirements measured from the property line for solar farms, with buffers ranging from 25 feet to 200 feet depending on the existing use of adjacent properties. The most restrictive buffer is 200 feet for 'Single Family Dwelling and All Other Residential Use' buffers, which may be increased or reduced at the Council’s discretion with approved berms or landscaping. Additionally, setbacks for solar equipment must be 25 feet larger than the applicable bufferyard to allow for an access road around the perimeter of the property. Other buffer distances include 50 feet for Agricultural and Residential Uses, 25 feet for Commercial/Non Effluent Industry and Effluent Producing Industry, and 100 feet for Street buffers (which may be reduced to 50 feet with approved screening).

The ordinance requires a bufferyard for solar farms with specific widths depending on the existing use of adjacent properties, e.g., 50’ for agricultural, 200’ for single family dwelling and all other residential uses (which may be adjusted by Council with an approved berm and/or landscaping and screening plan). The buffer is measured from the property line and only certain activities are permitted within it, including landscaping and fencing. Landscaping and screening requirements mandate providing landscape within the buffer to achieve a minimum height of ten feet (10’) within three (3) years to obscure solar equipment from exterior view. A visually opaque screen is required for adjacent properties zoned Residential, with existing residential use, or zoned Rural Development subdivided to 5 acres or less, composed of walls, fences, landscaping, berms, or combinations thereof. Natural vegetated areas may also be used if sufficient. Fencing must be at least six feet (6’) in height, and chain link fences are not allowed unless screened from exterior view. These requirements apply to solar farms of at least five (5) acres under the Solar Farm Floating Zone (SFFZ).

Section 9.c. requires that "a warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the main gate that states the address of the site, the name of the solar farm operator, and a local phone number for the solar farm operator in the case of an emergency." This signage requirement applies to solar farms under the Solar Farm Floating Zone (SFFZ) regulations, which cover solar farms consisting of a minimum of five (5) acres and intended for electricity generation. Other related provisions include buffers where signage is permitted within landscaped buffers (section 4), and fencing requirements that may include signage (section 7).

Section 10 Site Restoration/Stabilization requires the applicant to submit a ten percent (10%) Site Restoration/Stabilization Guarantee in the form of a bond, irrevocable letter of credit and agreement, or other financial security acceptable to the County prior to issuance of the Development Permit. The Guarantee shall insure satisfactory grading, seeding, and stabilization of the site in case of default by the applicant and/or if the applicant does not install the required site improvements in a timely fashion as determined by the Director, including the costs of landscaping, screening, and or fencing for the site or such portion thereof being permitted. The Developer shall provide the County with an itemized engineer’s estimate of the approved site improvements in conformity with Article 1.8 of the Colleton County Land Development Regulations for approval and calculation of the bond amount. The Site Restoration Guarantee may be refunded upon issuance of a Certificate of Project Close-Out for the site stabilization and improvements.

The Solar Farm Floating Zone (SFFZ) requires a zoning map amendment and a recommendation from the Planning Commission to County Council. The County Council may require a development agreement and may impose additional conditions. No other districts or special use processes for utility-scale solar energy systems are mentioned in the text.

The ordinance sets a 200-foot bufferyard from single-family dwellings and other residential uses, plus an additional 25-foot setback for solar equipment to allow for an access road around the perimeter of the property, resulting in a total setback of 225 feet. summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for utility-scale solar energy facilities. It requires the applicant to submit a decommissioning plan to be reviewed and approved by County Staff, County Attorney, and the Planning Commission, with updates every three to five years by a certified independent utility-scale solar facility engineer. The estimated cost of decommissioning must be guaranteed by depositing funds equal to 125% of the estimated cost in an escrow account or alternative security approved by the County. The plan must include the anticipated life of the project, estimated decommissioning cost, method of ensuring funds availability, and the manner of decommissioning and site restoration. When the facility ceases operation, the owner/operator must return the land to its original natural state, removing all surface and sub-surface materials. Decommissioning must be enforced if the facility is non-operational for twelve months unless the owner is actively rectifying issues. If not removed timely, the County may remove the facility at the owner's expense. Hazardous materials must be disposed of through viable recycling methods outside Edgefield County. All decommissioning activities must be completed within twelve months after notice of inactivity. The ordinance also references compliance with regulations formulated by SCDHEC as mandated by the South Carolina Legislature.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "The perimeter of the facility shall be secured through the use of security fencing of at least eight (8) feet in height." The fencing "shall not be topped with razor/barbed wire" and "shall be installed at the limits of the constructed solar field and not include the buffer." Additionally, "For every one-hundred linear feet of fencing, the buffer shall contain a minimum four (4) native evergreen tree specimens with a minimum DBH of two (2) inches at the time of planting, a mature height of 30-40 feet and an expected longevity of thirty (30) years." The trees and shrubs must be "species native to the Carolina Piedmont." This fencing requirement applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy facilities as defined in the ordinance as "any solar facility designed to produce electricity for sale" and excludes residential or commercial property. No alternative fencing options or conditions are provided.

No aspect of the facility shall exceed twenty (20) feet in height, as measured from grade at the base of the structure to its highest point (excluding power lines). This restriction applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy facilities as defined in the ordinance.

The percent of acreage coverage for a utility-scale solar facility shall not exceed 65% of the total solar facility site or a maximum of 200 acres (308 gross acres) of solar panels and support structures. An approved utility-scale solar facility must maintain a minimum 1000 feet distance from any other utility-scale solar facility. This is explicitly stated under section (h) Location/Setbacks, item 6. The units are feet as indicated in the text.

Utility-scale solar energy facilities are permitted as a conditional use exclusively in Industrial Manufacturing zones. Conditionally, a utility-scale solar facility may be permitted on lands defined as pastures, open, and former farmland which has not been clear-cut or logged in the last five years.'
