The ordinance requires a minimum 300 feet setback (buffer) from all abutting residential properties and a 1000 feet minimum distance between any two utility-scale solar facilities on separate parcels. Specifically, section (h) Location/Setbacks, item 2 states: 'The 300 feet setback is from all abutting residential properties.' Item 6 states: 'An approved utility-scale solar facility must maintain a minimum 1000 feet distance from any other utility-scale solar facility.' Additionally, section (j) Landscaping/Appearance, item 7 requires 'A minimum 300 foot vegetative buffer shall be installed and maintained around the entire circumference of the facility and its components.' The 300 feet setback is the most restrictive fixed distance directly pertaining to setbacks from property lines or parcels. Other distances mentioned include 100 feet from public roadways and 200 feet from historic sites, but these do not pertain to property lines or parcels.

The ordinance requires a setback of 100 feet from all public roadways for utility-scale solar energy facilities. This setback is in addition to a 300 feet setback from abutting residential properties. The relevant text states: 'The 300 feet setback is from all abutting residential properties and 100 feet from all public roadways.'

The ordinance explicitly requires vegetative buffer and screening for utility-scale solar energy facilities. Section (e)(4) mandates the site plan to include 'the location and nature of proposed buffers and screening elements, including vegetative and constructed buffers.' Section (h)(4) requires that 'for every one-hundred linear feet of fencing, the buffer shall contain a minimum four (4) native evergreen tree specimens with a minimum DBH of two (2) inches at the time of planting, a mature height of 30-40 feet and an expected longevity of thirty (30) years,' with all trees and shrubs being native to the Carolina Piedmont and prohibits clear-cutting the buffer. Section (j)(7) requires 'a minimum 300 foot vegetative buffer shall be installed and maintained around the entire circumference of the facility and its components to reduce the visual impact on the surrounding property owners.' In areas lacking a native timber buffer of at least 300 feet, 'a bufferyard type 5 as described in section 24-107 shall be followed.' The applicant must replace any dead or diseased trees within 180 days, and all landscaping must be approved by the County.

Construction of utility-scale solar facilities "shall be subject to erosion and sedimentation ordinances which include but are not limited to: extent of grading and grading phases, runoff information, management of runoff and pollution both during construction and throughout the lifetime of the project." An "approved Stormwater Plan by the South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control (SCDHEC) shall be obtained prior to the commencement of any construction to include land clearing (e.g. timbering)." Additionally, construction "shall be subject to any relevant erosion and sedimentation ordinances which include but are not limited to: extent of grading and grading phases, runoff information, management of runoff and pollution both during construction and throughout the lifetime of the project." These requirements apply explicitly to utility-scale solar facilities as defined in the ordinance.

Conditionally, a utility-scale solar facility may be permitted on lands defined as pastures, open, and former farmland which has not been clear-cut or logged in the last five years. These regulations require a special use permit binding on any successors, assignees, current or future lessee or owner of the facility and is granted solely for the construction and operation of a utility-scale solar energy facility.

The ordinance requires a minimum 300 feet setback from all abutting residential properties for utility-scale solar energy facilities. A berm is a vegetated earthen wall at least five feet in height." Additionally, for solar layouts larger than a quarter of an acre, "shall be screened by vegetative landscaping on sides adjacent residential properties per section 30-121, Table VI." Screening is not required along properties adjacent to non-residential uses. Other options for screening include landscaping and/or berm, with berm defined as a vegetated earthen wall at least five feet in height.

section: Sec. 30-114.8. - Solar energy system permitted use.

summary: Section 375.3 states that a 'Solar Farm,' synonymous with a commercial scale solar facility, must be located on a site larger than three (3) acres, which is described as the minimum zoning district requirement. This sets a clear minimum lot size for commercial scale solar energy systems.

Section 8:7.6 Decommissioning requires the applicant to provide a decommissioning plan signed by the responsible party and landowner, describing the anticipated life, estimated costs, funding method, and timeline for decommissioning and site restoration. Decommissioning is required after a continuous period of 12 months with no electricity generation other than for mechanical, repair, replacement and/or maintenance purposes. The permit holder has 12 months to complete decommissioning, which includes removal of solar panels, foundations, structures, cabling, electrical components, conduit, and any other associated facilities. Prior to permit issuance, a performance guarantee in the form of a bond, irrevocable letter of credit, or other financial security must be provided in the amount of 125 percent of the estimated decommission cost minus salvageable value, or $50,000, whichever is greater. Every five years, a new engineer's estimate must be submitted and the financial security adjusted accordingly. Proof that the decommissioning plan has been recorded with the Jasper County Register of Deeds is also required.

A security fence shall be required at least six feet in height to secure the solar equipment unless a taller fence is needed in order to obscure the solar equipment from exterior view; a chain link fence shall not be allowed unless it is screened from exterior view from adjoining property owners and public right of ways. Breaks in fencing may be allowed or required by council to facilitate wildlife needs where natural features provide appropriate barriers to access by humans for security and safety purposes. Access to the site must be controlled by a six foot wooden fence or gate if the fencing is visible from the exterior of the property. If the fencing/gate is within the interior 25 percent of the buffer, or is not visible from the exterior of the property, chain link gate and fencing may be used.

Section 8:7.4 General requirements includes glare restrictions for solar farms: 'Solar collectors shall be designed with anti-reflective coating to minimize glare. Mirrors are prohibited.' Additionally, 'A solar collection device or combination of devices are to be designed and located to avoid directing glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and adjacent roadways and shall not interfere with traffic or create a safety hazard.' These requirements apply to solar farms consisting of a minimum of five acres within the Solar Farm Floating Zone (SFFZ).

The solar energy system shall not exceed ten feet in height, as measured from the ground to the foremost/tip end of the solar collector, provided there is a demonstration that the screening prevents the system from being visible from the exterior of the property. Ancillary non solar collector structures, such as inverters, transformers, etc., may be taller than ten feet in height, provided that such are not visible from the exterior of the property. (Section 8:7.3-5 Height)

The Solar Farm Floating Zone (SFFZ) requires that 'The solar farm consists of a minimum of five acres;' this is the explicit minimum lot size for utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit is acres, which is an area measurement. This minimum size applies to solar farms intended for electricity generation and sale. No other minimum lot size values are provided for utility-scale systems in the text.

Section 8:7.4 General requirements, item 7 states: 'Adequate provisions to reduce average/constant noise levels at the property boundary not to exceed 50 dBA at the property line, except during construction.' This applies to solar farms in the Solar Farm Floating Zone (SFFZ), which are utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit for noise level is dBA, a standard unit for measuring sound levels.

The setbacks for solar equipment associated with the solar energy system shall be 25 feet larger than the applicable bufferyard to allow for an access road around the perimeter of the property. Bufferyard requirements vary by existing use of adjacent properties as follows: 50 feet for agricultural use, 200 feet for single-family residential and all other residential uses, 200 feet for commercial/office/institutional, 50 feet for effluent producing industry, 25 feet for non-effluent producing industry, and 100 feet for street. The buffer is measured from the property line. Thus, the most restrictive setback is 200 feet (bufferyard) plus 25 feet, totaling 225 feet.

The ordinance requires a 100-foot street buffer measured from the property line for solar farms, which may be reduced to 50 feet at the council's discretion with an approved berm and/or landscaping and screening plan (§8:7.3-1 Bufferyard, Table 8:7-1). Additionally, setbacks for solar equipment shall be 25 feet larger than the applicable bufferyard to allow for an access road around the perimeter of the property (§8:7.3-3 Setbacks). Thus, the effective setback from roads is generally 125 feet, or 75 feet if the buffer is reduced to 50 feet with screening.

The ordinance requires a bufferyard for solar farms with specific widths depending on the existing use of adjacent properties, measured from the property line (Table 8:7-1). Buffers range from 25' to 200', with possible adjustments by the council with an approved berm and/or landscaping and screening plan. Only certain activities are permitted within the landscaped buffer, including vehicular access drives, landscaping, lighting, fencing, signage, utility lines, and drainage. Additionally, landscaping/screening is required to achieve a minimum height of ten feet within three years to obscure solar equipment from exterior view. A visually opaque screen must be provided for adjacent properties zoned Residential, with existing residential use, or zoned Rural Preservation subdivided to five acres or less. The opaque screen may be a wall, fence, building, landscaping, landscaped berm, or combination thereof. Natural vegetated areas on the property may also be used to meet screening requirements. Fencing must be at least six feet in height and secure the solar equipment, with chain link fences only allowed if screened from exterior view. The solar energy system height shall not exceed ten feet unless screening prevents visibility. These requirements apply to solar farms of at least five acres intended for electricity generation under the Solar Farm Floating Zone (SFFZ).

Section 8:7.4 General requirements, item 3 states: 'A warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the main gate that states the address of the site, the name of the solar farm operator, and a local phone number for the solar farm operator in the case of an emergency.' Additionally, signage is permitted within the landscaped buffer as listed in 8:7.3-1, which includes 'Signage' among other activities such as vehicular access drives, landscaping, lighting, fencing, and utility lines. No other specific signage requirements or options are detailed in the ordinance.

Section 8:7.5 Site restoration/stabilization requires the applicant to submit a ten percent site restoration/stabilization guarantee in the form of a bond, irrevocable letter of credit and agreement, or other financial security acceptable to the county prior to issuance of the development permit. The guarantee shall insure satisfactory grading, seeding, and stabilization of the site in case of default by the applicant and/or if the applicant does not install the required site improvements in a timely fashion as determined by the DSR, including the costs of landscaping, screening, and or fencing for the site or such portion thereof being permitted. The developer must provide an itemized engineer's estimate of the approved site improvements for approval and calculation of the bond amount. The site restoration guarantee may be refunded upon issuance of a certificate of project close-out for the site stabilization and improvements.

The Solar Farm Floating Zone (SFFZ) may be utilized in any zoning district except for the Resource Conservation District, provided: 1. The solar farm consists of a minimum of five acres; 2. Any portion of the solar farm property boundary is within two miles of an existing electrical transmission line; 3. A conceptual plan which illustrates that the solar farm can meet the design and development standards set forth in article 8:7; 4. Jasper County Council may require, at its sole discretion, a development agreement between the county and developers for properties developed as a SFFZ as a prerequisite to development plan approval. Property within the SFFZ shall be required to adhere to all provisions of the Jasper County Zoning Ordinance and Land Development Regulations otherwise applicable within the underlying zoning district, including all subdivision plats and development plan applications.

Table 8:7-1 requires a 200-foot bufferyard from single-family dwellings and all other residential uses, which may be adjusted by the council with approved berm and/or landscaping and screening plans. Section 8:7.3-3 states that setbacks for solar equipment shall be 25 feet larger than the applicable bufferyard to allow for an access road around the perimeter of the property. Therefore, the typical setback is 225 feet. Other bufferyard values in Table 8:7-1 include 50 feet for agricultural dwellings, 50 feet for commercial/industry, 25 feet for effluent producing industry, and 100 feet for street buffers, but these are less restrictive or apply to different adjacent uses.

Buffers are required along street frontages in all districts. All screening shall be vegetative screening. This applies to Solar Energy Systems defined as ground mounted solar collector panels within an area for the generation of power or energy (commonly referred to as a solar farm).

It is the responsibility of the company managing and/or owning the solar energy system or wind farm, whether land is owned or leased, to submit during the initial planning phase and maintain throughout operation an updated facility decommission plan. The latest facility decommission plan shall be recorded in the County's Building Code Department. An applicant must include a decommissioning plan that describes the anticipated life of the solar energy system or wind farm; the estimated decommissioning cost in current dollars; the method for ensuring that funds will be available for decommissioning and restoration; and the anticipated manner in which the project will be decommissioned, and the site restored. Following a continuous six (6) month period in which no electricity is generated, the permit holder will have six (6) months to complete decommissioning of the solar energy system or wind farm. Decommissioning includes removal of solar panels, turbines, buildings, cabling, electrical components, and any other associated facilities below grade as described in the decommissioning plan. Decommissioning Plan must be passed by conveyance to successive owner(s).

Section 2, item 11 states: 'Security fence will surround the perimeter of the solar energy system or wind farm with a 6-foot-high woven or barbed wire fence from the ground up.' Section 2, item 1(f) requires site plans to include 'equipment location, fencing.' Section 4 states: 'The fence must be located on the inside of the vegetative buffer.' The ordinance defines a solar energy system as 'A series of ground mounted solar collectors placed in an area for generating photovoltaic (PV) power as a commercial enterprise' with a minimum size of one acre and maximum output of 75 megawatts. Other fencing-related requirements include that no signage is allowed on the fencing except for facility identification and warning signs (Section 2, item 13).

The ordinance states: 'Solar energy systems, equipment, and structures shall not exceed 25 feet in height when ground mounted.' This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems as defined by the ordinance (minimum size one acre, maximum output 75 MW). Roof mounted solar energy systems have a different height limit: 'shall not exceed the maximum height for the applicable zoning district.' The 25 feet limit is the most restrictive explicit maximum height for ground mounted utility-scale solar energy systems.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'The maximum megawatt output of a solar energy system is 75.' This is found in the definition of Solar Energy System, which is described as a commercial enterprise with a minimum size of one acre. No other maximum project size or total installation limits in MW or number of systems/panels are provided. The 75 megawatt limit applies to utility-scale solar energy systems and cannot be bypassed by permit.

The ordinance defines a Solar Energy System as a commercial enterprise solar farm with a minimum size of one acre. This is explicitly stated in Section 1: Definitions: 'The minimum size for a solar energy system is one acre.' The unit 'acre' is an area measurement. No other minimum lot, parcel, or tract size values are provided for utility-scale solar energy systems.

Solar Energy Systems must be set back the greater of 100 feet from an adjoining property line OR 400 feet from the nearest dwelling. Ground mounted solar energy systems shall meet the minimum zoning setback requirements of the applicable zoning district in which it is located.

Section 4: Screenings requires "A continuous vegetative buffer shall be installed around the perimeter of the solar energy system or wind farm. This buffer shall be 36"  to 48"  in height at planting and must reach 100 percent of the solar panel height within three (3) years of planting. The vegetation must be planted in two staggered rows at a spacing interval between 8’ to 10’ on center. The fence must be located on the inside of the vegetative buffer. Screening is not required along properties adjacent to non-residential uses or along roadways." Additionally, "Development shall maintain a 50-foot vegetated buffer from any body of water (i.e., lakes, streams, ponds, and rivers) to preserve the county's water quality and prevent any adverse stormwater effects." These requirements apply to commercial solar energy systems defined as "A series of ground mounted solar collectors placed in an area for generating photovoltaic (PV) power as a commercial enterprise" with a minimum size of one acre and up to 75 megawatts output. Other related conditions include security fencing inside the buffer and setback requirements, but only the vegetative buffer and screening requirements are detailed here.

Section 2, item 13 states: 'No signage is allowed on the solar energy system fencing except for: a) Assign, not to exceed 32 square feet, displaying the facility name, address, and emergency contact information. b) Warning signage.' This applies to solar energy systems defined as 'A series of ground mounted solar collectors placed in an area for generating photovoltaic (PV) power as a commercial enterprise' with a minimum size of one acre and maximum output of 75 megawatts. No other signage options or conditions are provided.

Solar energy systems and wind farms may be permitted by the Planning and Zoning Committee as a conditional use in Marlboro County. "Solar energy systems and wind farms should be approved provided all the following conditions are met." The ordinance does not specify particular district names or abbreviations where this conditional use applies. There is also a provision that the ordinance shall not apply to renewable energy systems approved by the Marlboro County Planning & Zoning Commission within the last year prior to the effective date, unless modified or expanded after that date.
Solar Energy Systems must be set back the greater of 100 feet from an adjoining property line OR 400 feet from the nearest dwelling.

Development shall maintain a 50-foot vegetated buffer from any body of water (i.e., lakes, streams, ponds, and rivers) to preserve the county's water quality and prevent any adverse stormwater effects. Site plans must show bodies of water with minimum 50-foot buffer shown.

The ordinance requires a decommissioning plan signed by the responsible party and landowner that "describes the anticipated life of the solar farm, the estimated decommissioning costs in current dollars, the method for ensuring that funds will be available for decommissioning and restoration, and the anticipated manner in which the solar farm project will be decommissioned and the site restored to its condition prior to the development of the solar farm." Decommissioning is required "following a continuous 6 month period in which no electricity is generated by the facility." The permit holder has "12 months to complete decommissioning of the solar farm," which includes removal of "solar panels, foundations, structures, cabling, electrical components, conduit, and any other associated facilities as described in the decommissioning plan." Prior to issuance of the zoning permit and annually thereafter, the applicant must provide a performance guarantee "in the form of an irrevocable letter of credit in the amount of 125% of the estimated decommission cost minus the salvageable value or $50,000, whichever is greater." Estimates must be determined by an engineer licensed to practice in South Carolina.

A security fence at least six feet in height shall be provided around the perimeter of the solar farm facility and shall meet the requirements of § 153.033 - Fences and walls, however the security fence may be chain link for this use.

Solar collection equipment shall be installed so that no reflected glare is visible at the property line or right-of-way as required by § 153.034 - Light and Glare. This applies to new solar farms or solar farms proposed to be expanded by more than 10% of original footprint, which must meet various requirements including site plan, setbacks, buffers, screening, height limits, fencing, preservation of existing vegetation, and decommissioning plans.

Section (E) states: 'Systems, equipment, and structures shall not exceed 20 feet in height, with the exclusion of associated electric transmission lines and utility poles.' This applies to solar farms, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. No other maximum height values are provided for these systems.

A minimum setback of 125 feet is required from all road rights-of-way and all adjacent property lines (§ 153.156(B)). Additionally, a buffer of at least 100 feet is required from all road rights-of-way and all adjacent property lines (§ 153.156(C)). A security fence at least six feet in height shall be provided around the perimeter of the solar farm facility (§ 153.156(F)).

A minimum setback of 125 feet is required from all road rights-of-way and all adjacent property lines. Additionally, a buffer of at least 100 feet shall be required from all road rights-of-way and all adjacent property lines, per the requirements of § 153.182 - Buffers. Site design shall ensure safe, predictable vehicular access and movement onto and off of the site and shall accommodate safe access to the property by emergency vehicles.

The ordinance requires a buffer of at least 100 feet from all road rights-of-way and adjacent property lines (§ 153.156(C)), screening per § 153.183 for any adjacent property with existing residential use or residential zoning (§ 153.156(D)), and a planting plan demonstrating sufficient plantings to screen solar panels from view from any adjacent right of way (§ 153.156(A)(10)). It also mandates preservation of existing vegetation in buffer and setback areas to provide natural screening where possible (§ 153.156(G)). These requirements apply to new solar farms or expansions over 10% of the original footprint.

The ordinance requires a decommissioning plan for the anticipated service life of the facility or in the event that the facility is abandoned or has reached its life expectancy (Sec. 343.05.k.(3)). All obsolete or unused systems, defined as any structure or equipment not operated for a continuous period of one year, shall be removed and decommissioned per the approved decommission plan (Sec. 343.05.l.(1)). The site shall be restored to as natural a condition as possible within six (6) months of the removal (Sec. 343.05.l.(2)).

Access gates and equipment cabinets must be locked when not in use. Signs shall be installed on all gates, and every 50 feet of the security fencing stating,  "DO NOT ENTER – SOLAR POWER GENERATING FARM."
section: Sec. 343.05. Solar energy farm installation and construction

summary: Solar energy system components "shall be designed with an antireflective coating or at least shall not produce glare that would constitute a nuisance to occupants of neighboring properties, aircraft, or persons traveling adjacent or nearby roads." This applies generally to solar energy systems, including solar energy farms defined as installations on 10 or more acres. Other relevant conditions for solar energy farms include: installation as a Special Use in Agricultural zoning or allowed by right in Industrial zoning; minimum 50 feet setbacks from property lines and 100 feet from residences; maximum height of 25 feet for freestanding panels; full screening from adjoining properties and roads; and security fencing requirements. These are found in Sec. 343.03(d) and Secs. 343.04 and 343.05.
section: Sec. 343 Utility substations and solar energy systems

summary: Freestanding solar panels or solar arrays shall not exceed 25 feet in height as measured from the grade at the base of the structure to the highest point. (Sec. 343.05.e.(1)) This applies specifically to solar energy farms (solar farms) defined as installations on 10 or more acres. Another height limit mentioned is for mounted solar panels or solar arrays, which shall not exceed eight feet above the apex of the structure on which it is mounted, but this applies to different mounting conditions. The 25 feet limit is the most restrictive for freestanding solar arrays in solar farms. Units are explicitly stated as feet.
section: Sec. 343.05. Solar energy farm installation and construction

summary: The ordinance explicitly states: 'A solar farm installation shall be located on 10 or more acres.' This is the minimum lot size requirement for solar energy farms, which are defined as solar energy facilities typically with multiple solar arrays designed for electric energy generation. No other minimum lot size values are provided for solar farms in the text.

Inverter noise shall not exceed 40dBA, measured at the property line. Mitigation noise barriers may be approved on an individual basis by the Development Review Committee. This applies specifically to solar energy farms as detailed in the section on solar energy farm installation and construction.
section: Sec. 343.05. Solar energy farm installation and construction

summary: The installation and construction of solar energy farms shall be subject to the following: a solar farm installation shall be permitted as a Special Use in the Agricultural (AG) zoning district, and allowed by right in the Industrial (I) zoning district. A solar farm installation shall be located on 10 or more acres. The text does not explicitly list any districts where solar energy farms on 10 or more acres are unconditionally prohibited, but by implication, such farms are not allowed outside the AG and I districts.

A solar energy farm and its accessories and structures shall be set back a minimum of 50 feet from all property lines and 100 feet from any residence. The 50 feet setback from property lines is the relevant fixed distance for setbacks from property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, parcels, and/or subdivisions for Solar Energy Farms (10 or more acres).
section: Sec. 343.05. Solar energy farm installation and construction

summary: Sec. 343.05(d) requires that a solar energy farm "shall be fully screened from adjoining properties and adjacent roads using the natural topography or by installation of an evergreen buffer capable of reaching a height of 6 feet within three years of planting, with at least 75% opacity at the time of planting." This applies to solar energy farms defined as facilities typically with multiple solar arrays and located on 10 or more acres. Other related requirements include setbacks (50 feet from property lines and 100 feet from residences), height limits (not to exceed 25 feet), security fencing, and maintenance of buffer screening in compliance with approved plans.

Additionally, a solar energy system shall not be used to display advertising, including signage, but manufacturers’ or installers’ identification and appropriate warning signage shall be posted at the site in a clearly visible manner.
section: Sec. 343.05. Solar energy farm installation and construction.

A solar energy farm and its accessories and structures shall be set back a minimum of 100 feet from any residence. Other setback requirements include a minimum of 50 feet from all property lines, but only the 100 feet from residences directly pertains to occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, and/or residences for solar energy farms of 10 or more acres.

summary: Section 3 titled "DECOMMISSIONING AND ABANDONMENT" requires a performance guarantee "in the amount of 125% of the estimated decommissioning cost minus the salvageable value, or $50,000, whichever is greater". The decommissioning plan must be "recorded in the Williamsburg County Register of Deeds prior to the issuance of a building permit" and include: "anticipated life of the solar energy facility", "restoration plan" with removal of all panels, buildings, foundations, and debris, "conditions upon which decommissioning will be initiated" (e.g., "end of land lease, no power production for twelve (12) months, abandonment"), "time for completion of decommissioning activities" ("six (6) months for projects under five hundred (500) acres and one year for projects over five hundred (500) acres"), "identification of the party currently responsible for decommissioning", and "estimated cost of site restoration". Abandonment is defined as "cease to produce energy on a continuous basis for twelve (12) months" unless evidence of intent to repair is provided. Upon abandonment, the responsible party must remove the facility and restore the site per the decommissioning plan within six months of notice or face legal actions. These requirements apply to "any new solar energy facilities to be constructed or installed within the unincorporated area of Williamsburg County" and are tied to permitting and site plan approval.

Section 2(C)(1)(d) requires that a permanent solar energy facility "shall surround the facility, not including stormwater facilities" with "a minimum six (6') foot tall fence or wall." Acceptable fences include "chain link and durable galvanized wire or welded wire fences." This fencing is part of the buffering and screening requirements that also include a vegetative buffer with a minimum depth of fifty (50') feet, a row of evergreens at least six (6') feet tall at planting spaced no more than eight feet apart, and a separate row of dense, low-lying shrubs. Additional buffering is not required if there is existing vegetation of sufficient depth and height, topographical features, water features, or if a berm is constructed in lieu of the fence or wall, provided it limits visibility to a height of 5' at the adjacent property line. These requirements apply to solar energy facilities defined as "a series of at least three (3) solar panels placed on a parcel of property for the purpose of generating electricity for resale purposes and/or an area principally used to convert solar energy to electricity."

Section 2(D) Glare standards: "All Solar Panels shall have anti-reflective coating. Solar energy facility equipment is to be designed and located in a way to avoid directing glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and roadways and shall not interfere with vehicle traffic or create a safety hazard (no after image shall occur from the glare)." This applies to solar energy facilities defined as "a series of at least three (3) solar panels placed on a parcel of property for the purpose of generating electricity for resale purposes and/or an area principally used to convert solar energy to electricity."

Section 2(B) states: 'The maximum height of solar panels shall not exceed Twenty (20’) feet above grade.' This applies to solar energy facilities defined as systems generating electricity for resale and/or converting solar energy to electricity, which fits the typical definition of utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit is explicitly given as feet.

Noise levels shall not exceed sixty-five (65) decibels (dba) as measured at the adjacent property line once the facility becomes fully operational. Maintenance work shall be exempt from these requirements. This requirement may be reduced or waived if agreed to in writing by the owner of the adjacent property or residence.
section: Section 2. DESIGN AND OPERATION STANDARDS. (F) Noise.

summary: All buildings, structures, fencing, equipment, and parking areas related to the solar energy facility, but not including stormwater facilities, shall be setback at least one hundred (100) feet from all public rights-of-way and the property lines around the perimeter of the solar facility when it is adjacent to property not owned by the same property owner as that on which the solar facility is located at the time of submission. This requirement may be reduced or waived if agreed to, in writing, by the owner of the adjacent property or residence. Roads to the facility as well as utility easements are exempt from this requirement. Additionally, a 300-foot setback from the nearest residence or church is required, but residences are not equivalent to property lines. The 100-foot setback from property lines is the relevant fixed distance for setbacks from property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, and parcels.

All buildings, structures, fencing, equipment, and parking areas related to the solar energy facility, but not including stormwater facilities, shall be setback at least one hundred (100') feet from all public rights-of-way. This requirement may be reduced or waived if agreed to, in writing, by the owner of the adjacent property or residence. Roads to the facility as well as utility easements are exempt from this requirement. Other setback distances mentioned include three hundred (300') feet from the nearest residence or church, and buffering/screening requirements within five hundred (500') feet of public road rights-of-way, but these do not pertain directly to the setback from roads.

Section 2(C) "Buffering and screening" requires that "Permanent solar energy facilities must be screened from public road rights-of-way, residences or churches within five hundred (500') feet of the solar facility with a vegetative buffer and fence or wall per the following specifications: (a) A vegetative buffer with a minimum depth of Fifty (50') feet shall be installed and replanted should the plantings die; (b) The vegetative buffer shall include a row of evergreens which are a minimum of six (6') feet in height at the time of planting and are spaced not more than eight feet apart which at maturity will form an intermittent visual barrier to a minimum height of fifteen (15') feet. Evergreens shall be a species or genus native to South Carolina as included in Appendix A: Approved Native Vegetative Species List; (c) A separate row of shrubs that are dense, low-lying, continuous, and planted and maintained so as to visually fill in the low-lying gaps between the trunks of the evergreens. Shrubs shall also be a species native to South Carolina to the extent possible and shall be replanted should the plantings die; and (d) A minimum six (6') foot tall fence or wall shall surround the facility, not including stormwater facilities. Chain link and durable galvanized wire or welded wire fences are acceptable." Additional buffering is not required when: (a) existing vegetation of at least fifty (50') feet in depth and greater than fifteen (15') feet in height or will grow to fifteen (15') feet in height at maturity of equivalent or greater density exists and is healthy; (b) topographical features reduce visual impact at the property line at a height of six (6') feet; (c) water features would be adversely impacted by buffer and screening requirements; or (d) the applicant constructs a berm in lieu of the fence or wall, provided the berm limits visibility at a height of 5' at the adjacent property line. This buffering and screening requirement may be reduced or waived if agreed to in writing by the owner of the adjacent property or residence. Roads to facilities as well as utility easements are exempt from this requirement.

Section 2(H)(1) states: 'A sign shall be fixed and maintained at the entrance(s) to the facility that lists the name and phone number of the operator. Access roads are to be marked with identifying signage. The manufacturers’ or installers’ identification and appropriate warning signage shall be posted on or near the panels in a clearly visible manner. The signage must identify the owner and provide a 24-hour emergency contact phone number.' This applies to solar energy facilities defined as 'a series of at least three (3) solar panels placed on a parcel of property for the purpose of generating electricity for resale purposes and/or an area principally used to convert solar energy to electricity.'

All buildings, structures, fencing, equipment, and parking areas related to the solar energy facility ... three hundred (300) feet from the nearest residence or church in existence at the time of submission to the solar facility shall be maintained. This requirement may be reduced or waived if agreed to, in writing, by the owner of the adjacent property or residence.

summary: The ordinance requires a performance guarantee "in the amount of 125% of the estimated decommission cost minus the salvageable value, or $50,000, whichever is greater" prior to issuance of a building permit. The decommissioning plan must be "recorded in the York County Register of Deeds prior to the issuance of a building permit" and include: "type of panels, storage facilities, and materials to be installed; restoration plan; removal of solar panels, buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, and any other associated facilities; defined conditions upon which decommissioning will be initiated (e.g. end of land lease, no power production for 12 months, abandonment); timeframe for completion (maximum six months); description of any agreement with landowner regarding decommissioning; identification of the party responsible for decommissioning; estimated cost of site restoration; plans for periodically updating the decommissioning plan."

Solar energy facilities must be screened from adjacent properties and rights-of-way with a vegetative buffer and opaque fence or wall per the following specifications: a vegetative buffer with a minimum depth of 75 feet; a row of evergreens a minimum of six feet in height at planting spaced not more than eight feet apart, reaching a minimum height of ten feet within three years; a separate row of dense, low-lying native shrubs; and a minimum six foot tall fence or wall constructed of durable materials with a completely opaque surface, with the finished side facing outward. Chain link fences are permitted only to secure equipment internal to the solar energy facility and must be screened from rights-of-way and adjacent properties. The Zoning Administrator determines fence placement relative to the vegetative buffer. The Board of Zoning Appeals may modify height specifications where topography prevents meeting the intent. Alternative compliance by special exception may be granted if existing vegetation, topographical features, water features, or berms meet the intent of the screening requirements.

The ordinance in § 155.503(G) Glare standards states: '(1) The design and construction of solar energy facilities shall not produce light emissions, either direct or indirect (reflective), that would interfere with pilot vision and/or traffic control operations of airports located within five nautical miles of the proposed solar energy facility. (2) Solar energy facilities equipment is to be designed and located in a way to avoid directing glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and roadways, and shall not interfere with vehicle traffic or create a safety hazard.' These glare restrictions apply to solar energy facilities defined as 'an energy generating facility or area principally used to convert solar energy to electricity,' excluding only roof-mounted systems on buildings not primarily for commercial solar production. The ordinance also includes related aviation notification requirements in § 155.503(J) involving use of the Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT) for airports within five nautical miles. No other alternative options or conditions for glare restrictions are provided.

The maximum height of all equipment shall not exceed 20 feet above the average site grade. This applies to solar energy facilities as defined in the ordinance, which are energy generating facilities principally used to convert solar energy to electricity and exclude rooftop systems where the primary purpose is not commercial production of solar energy.

All buildings, structures, equipment, and parking areas related to the solar energy facility shall be setback at least 125 feet from all property lines; other setback distances include 125 feet from all public rights-of-way and 500 feet from public rights-of-way along a designated South Carolina Scenic Byway.

All buildings, structures, equipment, and parking areas related to the solar energy facility shall be setback at least: 125 feet from all public rights-of-way; and 500 feet from all public rights-of-way along a designated South Carolina Scenic Byway.

Section (F) Bufferyards and screening requires that solar energy facilities "must be screened from adjacent properties and rights-of-way with a vegetative buffer and opaque fence or wall" including: "a vegetative buffer with a minimum depth of 75 feet" complying with Type D bufferyard standards; "a row of evergreens which are a minimum of six feet in height at the time of planting" spaced not more than eight feet apart and reaching a minimum height of ten feet within three years to form an intermittent visual barrier to a height of 15 feet; "a separate row of shrubs that are dense, low-lying, continuous, and planted so as to visually fill in the low-lying gaps between the trunks of the evergreens"; and "a minimum six foot tall fence or wall that is constructed in a durable fashion" with an opaque surface. Alternative compliance by special exception may be granted if: (a) existing vegetated areas on the property meet the intent; (b) topographical features reduce visual impact; (c) water features would be adversely impacted by buffers; or (d) a berm is proposed in lieu of the fence or wall, meeting the intent of the section.

An attached sign meeting the dimensional standards of this chapter shall be posted and maintained at the entrance(s), which lists the name and phone number of the operator. Freestanding signs are prohibited.

Section 5.35.06 Decommissioning/Restoration/Abandonment requires the owner or operator of a SES to be responsible for all costs associated with decommissioning. Prior to construction, a decommissioning plan including an acceptable financial assurance plan must be filed for Board of Adjustment approval. Financial assurance may include a performance bond, surety bond, escrow account, letter of credit, corporate guarantee, or other acceptable forms. Funding of the decommissioning account is at a rate of $2,500 per megawatt of installed DC capacity per year for the first 30 years or until sufficient funds are accumulated. The decommissioning must begin within eight months of permit expiration or earlier termination and be completed within eighteen months. The permittees must dismantle and remove all solar collectors, components, foundations, and ancillary equipment to a depth of four feet and restore the site to pre-project conditions unless otherwise agreed with the landowner. If the SES owner/operator fails to decommission, the Board of Adjustment may take necessary action including forfeiture of financial assurances. Additionally, if the South Dakota Public Utilities Commission requires a Decommissioning Plan with a financial instrument, the county may waive its own financial instrument requirement.

Section 5.35.05 (6) Safety Fencing/Gates and Locks requires that "All SES shall be fenced around the exterior of the SES with a fence at least six (6) feet in height." The fencing and gates must "substantially lessen the likelihood of entry into a SES by unauthorized individuals." All gates must be "equipped with locks or other means to provide restricted access, and shall always remain locked or otherwise restrict access except for those times when the owner and/or operator, or their respective agents is/are using the gate for ingress and/or egress or is/are otherwise present and monitoring the SES." The fencing and gates "shall be maintained in serviceable condition" and these requirements "shall continue notwithstanding the fact that a SES is no longer operational and/or falls into disuse unless and until the SES is properly decommissioned."

summary: Section 1643.05(1) requires that "a minimum thirty (30) foot managed vegetative buffer shall always be present and maintained around the perimeter of the site" for ground-mount solar energy systems designed for off-site uses or export to the wholesale market. Section 1643.05(7) states that "All solar energy systems shall minimize glare from affecting adjacent or nearby properties" with measures including "screening on the north side of the solar array". These requirements apply to Solar Energy Systems (SES) as defined: "A commercial facility that converts sunlight into electricity... for the primary purpose of wholesale sales of generated electricity."
section: Section 1643.05. General Provisions for Solar Energy Systems

summary: An emergency contact name and phone number must be posted at the point of access on all SES sites. This is the only explicit signage requirement stated. Other requirements include fencing and gates around the SES perimeter, safety measures, setbacks, site plans, decommissioning plans, and compliance with state and federal regulations, but these do not pertain to signage.

The ordinance requires that applications for SES Conditional Use Permits include a 'storm water pollution and prevention plan' (Section 1643.03(2)(g)). All SES are subject to 'State of South Dakota Storm Water Management regulations, erosion and sediment control provisions if adopted and National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit requirements, if applicable' (Section 1643.04(1)). Ground-mount systems must maintain topsoils and be planted with perennial vegetation 'to prevent erosion, manage run off and build soil' and maintain a 'minimum thirty (30) foot managed vegetative buffer' around the site perimeter (Section 1643.05(1)). Additionally, 'reasonable measures and practices of construction to control dust' must be utilized (Section 1643.05(13)(d)). These requirements apply to SES defined as 'a commercial facility that converts sunlight into electricity... for the primary purpose of wholesale sales of generated electricity' (definition of Solar Energy System (SES)).

Solar panels will be kept at least five hundred (500) feet from a residence. Exception: The Board of Adjustment may allow setback/separation distances to be less than the established distance identified, if the applicant obtains waivers from all dwellings and owners of property within the separation distance. If approved, such agreement is to be recorded and filed with the County Register of Deeds. Said agreement shall be binding upon the heirs, successors, and assigns of the title holder and shall pass with the land. Additionally, every SES shall observe a minimum rear and side yard setback of thirty (30) feet and meet the minimum front yard setback of the applicable zoning district.
section: Section 1643.05. General Provisions for Solar Energy Systems

summary: Every SES shall be setback at least one hundred (100) feet from the highwater mark of any lake, stream or river. Other setbacks include solar panels kept at least five hundred (500) feet from a residence, with possible waivers, and minimum rear and side yard setbacks of thirty (30) feet, and front yard setbacks as per zoning district. However, only the 100 feet setback applies specifically to lakes, reservoirs, streams, and rivers.
section: Section 1643.05. General Provisions for Solar Energy Systems

summary: Applications for solar energy facilities in South Dakota must include a decommissioning plan detailing cost estimates, expected site conditions after removal, land committed to energy conversion, and any required financial security controlled by the Public Utilities Commission.

Solar farms, subject to site plan review, must be enclosed by fencing (8.5 feet), adhere to setback, height, and coverage requirements, be on lots no less than 40 acres, and not create increased noise or nuisance glare. Electrical lines must be underground. Solar farms inactive for over one year must be removed at the owner's expense, including dismantling all equipment and restoring the site within 18 months. A decommissioning plan must be submitted describing decommissioning methods and financial capability, with possible bonding or escrow accounts to guarantee performance. Financial provisions must not make the solar farm unfeasible.

Solar farms shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access at a height of eight and a half (8.5) feet. Additional conditions include site plan review by the Board of Zoning Appeals, adherence to setback, height, and coverage requirements, a minimum lot size of 40 acres, noise and glare restrictions, underground electrical lines, removal of inactive solar farms within 18 months, and submission of a decommissioning plan with financial assurances.

Solar farms must not produce glare that would constitute a nuisance to occupants of neighboring properties or persons traveling neighboring roads. Other conditions for solar farms include: enclosure by perimeter fencing at 8.5 feet height; adherence to setback, height, and coverage requirements; minimum 100 feet setback from residentially zoned properties and structures; location on lots no less than 40 acres; no increased noise levels discernible to nearby residential uses; all electrical interconnection and distribution lines underground; removal of inactive solar farms exceeding one year with site restoration; and submission of a decommissioning plan with financial assurance provisions.

The ordinance states that 'Solar farms must be located on lots of no less than 40 acres in size.' This is a minimum lot size requirement specifically for solar farms, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. Other conditions for solar farms include perimeter fencing, setback requirements, noise and glare restrictions, underground electrical lines, and decommissioning plans, but these do not specify different minimum lot sizes.

Solar farm structures must be setback a minimum of 100 feet from residentially zoned properties (FAR, R-1, and R-2) and residentially used structures. This applies to solar farms, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. Other conditions include enclosure by perimeter fencing at 8.5 feet height, adherence to district setback, height, and coverage requirements, minimum lot size of 40 acres, noise and glare restrictions, underground electrical lines, and decommissioning requirements.

Section 7(b) requires that if the solar farm is no longer operational for a period of twelve consecutive months and the lessee or landowner does not commence a good faith effort to make the solar farm operational within that period, the solar farm shall be deconstructed within twelve months thereafter, and the land returned to the owner in substantially the same condition as prior to development. Section 7(c) states that the property owner is ultimately responsible for the removal of the solar farm array.

All solar farms shall be enclosed with a fence measuring a minimum of six (6) feet in height that is topped with at least three strands of barbed wire that shall be maintained in good condition to the satisfaction of the Enforcing Officer. Buffer zones shall be a minimum of fifty feet in width as measured from the exterior of the fence surrounding a solar farm and maintained as green space except for necessary intrusions for vehicular or power access, fencing, or drainage structures. Solar farm buffer strips shall be located outside required fencing, planted with evergreen shrubs and/or trees at least six feet in height at planting, staggered ten feet on center, and maintained even if the solar farm is no longer operational unless dismantled. Buffer strips are required where fencing would be visible off-site or where lease lines overlay exterior property lines, but not required within the interior of a solar farm development where areas leased from different property owners abut one another. Setbacks require a minimum of fifty feet from lease/property lines and three hundred feet from residential dwellings. The Enforcing Officer approves buffer strip design and maintenance responsibilities.

Setback requirements to the lease/property line for any building or solar array shall be a minimum of fifty feet. The setback from any Residential Dwelling existing at the time of approval of the solar panel farm shall be three hundred (300) feet from the corner of the residential dwelling to the closest solar array. Residential Dwelling shall mean a permanent, not temporary, improvement used for residential purposes.
section: S. Solar panel farms, provided: 3. Setbacks.

summary: Buffer Zones shall be a minimum of fifty feet in width as measured from the exterior of the fence surrounding a solar farm; maintained as green space for the entire width of the buffer zone; used to preserve, where possible and practical, existing trees. Solar Farm Buffer Strips shall be located outside required fencing; planted with evergreen shrubs and/or trees at a minimum of six feet in height at the time of planting and staggered ten feet on center; may be waived if existing vegetation meets standards; maintained even if the solar farm is no longer operational; required where the solar farm fencing would be visible off-site; required where lease lines overlay exterior property lines (except not required within the interior where leased areas abut); and must be shown on plans approved by the Enforcing Officer who approves design, width, height, opacity, growing period, installation schedule, and maintenance responsibility.

Section 5, Land Development requires: (a) Pre-development drainage patterns shall be maintained so that post development surface water run-off does not exceed pre-development surface water run-off for a 25 year storm event. (b) Soil shall be retained on-site through the appropriate use of silt fencing, straw bales, or other effective manner. (c) The area of the solar farm located to the interior of the buffer zone shall be maintained in a grassed condition, with the exception of access driveways, building pads, utility facilities and necessary equipment supports. (d) Grassed areas within the solar array shall be maintained in accordance with established and recommended procedures for maintaining hay crop and pasture weed management as recommended by the University of Tennessee Extension Service.

The setback from any Residential Dwelling existing at the time of approval of the solar panel farm shall be three hundred (300) feet from the corner of the residential dwelling to the closest solar array. Residential Dwelling shall mean a permanent, not temporary, improvement used for residential purposes. Other setback requirements include a minimum of fifty feet to the lease/property line for any building or solar array.

Any commercial solar plant with a nameplate output rating between 101KW-10MW shall be decommissioned in accordance to the regulation specifications of TCA 66-9-207, however, no bond or financial assurance is required. Decommissioning shall be by developer, operator, lease, management or landowner and removed from the property as in the timeframe stated herein. Any solar plant that has been deemed  "inactive"  for one (1) year; shall immediately begin decommissioning. Decommissioning shall be complete within eighteen (18) months from date of inactivity.  "Inactive"  shall be defined as: no longer in use or use has been reduced to less than 30% of original nameplate and permitted output rating or by any termination of any power purchase agreement (ppa) with any public utility.

All solar panels "shall use anti-reflective coatings on all panels to mediate glare to prevent public hazard and nuisance." This applies to Power Plant-Solar facilities with a nameplate output rating between 101KW-10MW. Other provisions include maximum height limits, setback requirements, access to sunlight design responsibility, compliance with National Electric Code, wiring depth, decommissioning requirements, and building code compliance for accessory buildings.

Maximum height of any part of an array, accessory, or associated supporting structure shall not exceed 15’-0"  at maximum vertical tilt or free-standing height. (Section 14.02(D)(1)(a)(iv)(A)(1)) The unit is feet as indicated by the notation '15’-0" '. There is an exemption for utility poles or structures from height requirements.

The ordinance states that all power plants generating 1MW or more, including solar power plants, "shall meet all provisions for a 'use permitted on appeal' of 14.02(a-o)." This indicates that commercial solar plants between 101 kW and 10 MW require approval through a special use or appeal process. The text includes detailed conditions such as environmental assessments, setback requirements, decommissioning under TCA 66-9-207, and compliance with state and federal regulations. However, the text does not explicitly list or name any specific zoning districts or abbreviations where these uses are permitted as special use or similar. Other options or conditions mentioned include exemptions for facilities solely owned or operated by public or private utilities, and distinctions for smaller solar systems under 100 kW which are not considered commercial enterprises.

Solar farms that become inactive for a period exceeding one (1) year shall be removed at the owners or operators’ expense and the site shall be returned to its natural state. This includes the obligation to dismantle and remove from the site all electrical generating equipment, cables, panels, foundations, buildings, and ancillary equipment. The restoration activities must be complete within 18 months from the date the Building Official declares in writing to the solar farm operator the solar farm inactive. The applicant shall submit to the board a decommissioning plan describing the way the applicant anticipates decommissioning the project, including a description of the way the applicant will ensure that it has the financial capability to carry out the restoration requirements. The BZA may require financial assurances such as bonding or escrow accounts to guarantee decommissioning performance. If the solar farm operation involves more than one property owner, a surety is required for each landowner. Financial provisions shall not be so difficult as to make the solar farm unfeasible.

Solar farm operations equipment enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access. Adequate screening for solar farm operations that will be located on arterial status roads deemed a scenic highway by the State of Tennessee. This can be achieved by vegetative screening being placed beyond the perimeter fence to a density and height that adequately buffers the solar farm from any nearby uses. Screening along the side and rear of solar farm operations located on all other roads. This may be achieved by vegetative screening being placed beyond the perimeter fence to a density and height that adequately buffers the solar farm from any nearby uses. However, this requirement may be waived at the discretion of the Board of Zoning Appeals when the proposed solar farm operation is in an area in which the surrounding properties are primarily vacant.

Solar farm operations must not produce glare that would constitute a nuisance to occupants of neighboring properties or persons traveling neighboring roads. Additionally, lighting shall use fixtures to minimize off-site glare and shall be the minimum necessary for safety and security purposes. Other conditions include site plan review by the Board of Zoning Appeals, acreage limits, fencing, screening, setback requirements, FAA standards compliance, structural integrity, decommissioning plans, and financial assurances.

Solar farm operations must be located on a site not less than 150 acres. This is a minimum lot size requirement for solar farms, which are utility-scale solar energy systems. The unit 'acres' is a standard measure of land area.

Solar farm operations shall have a front-yard setback requirement of 100 feet on Arterial Status Roads. Solar farm operations shall have a front yard setback of requirement of 60 feet on all other roads.

Solar Farms, subject to site plan review by the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA) and the following conditions: 'Adequate screening for solar farm operations that will be located on arterial status roads deemed a scenic highway by the State of Tennessee. This can be achieved by vegetative screening being placed beyond the perimeter fence to a density and height that adequately buffers the solar farm from any nearby uses.' Screening is also required 'along the side and rear of solar farm operations located on all other roads,' which 'may be achieved by vegetative screening being placed beyond the perimeter fence to a density and height that adequately buffers the solar farm from any nearby uses.' This screening requirement 'may be waived at the discretion of the Board of Zoning Appeals when the proposed solar farm operation is in an area in which the surrounding properties are primarily vacant.' The ordinance applies to solar farms with a minimum site size of 150 acres, indicating utility-scale solar energy systems.

Solar Farms are subject to site plan review by the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA) and must meet conditions including acreage limits in FAR, I-1, and I-2 districts (not exceeding 3% of total acreage), perimeter fencing, screening, setback requirements, minimum site size of 150 acres, and compliance with FAA and building codes. The BZA reviews and approves the site plan and may require financial assurances for decommissioning. The text does not mention other districts or overlay districts for utility-scale solar energy systems.
section: H. Solar Farms, subject to site plan review by the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA)

summary: Solar farm operation structures must be setback a minimum of 500 feet from residential structures. Other setback requirements include front-yard setbacks of 100 feet on Arterial Status Roads and 60 feet on all other roads, but these relate to roads, not residences.

Solar panels shall be set back from front property lines a minimum of thirty (30) feet and twenty-five (25) feet from side and rear property lines. These requirements apply to solar energy systems as a principal use (i.e., systems where electricity generated is primarily sold or used off site). The most restrictive setback distance is 25 feet from side and rear property lines. Associated buildings and appurtenances must meet the minimum setback requirements for the district in which they are located. Solar energy systems producing electricity solely for on-site use are considered accessory and must meet district setback requirements.
section: 7.9 Development Standards for Solar Energy Systems

summary: Utility-scale solar energy systems, defined as solar energy systems where electricity generated is primarily sold or used off site and considered a principal use of land, are explicitly permitted as a principal use only in the Agricultural-Forestry District, A-1, "provided they respectively meet the requirements of subsections 7.9. and 7.10." In all other districts listed (R-1, R-2, C-1, C-2, I-1, I-2), solar energy systems are only allowed as accessory uses, not principal uses. There is no mention of utility-scale solar energy systems being permitted as a special use or requiring approval by a zoning appeals board or similar conditional use process in any district. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this analysis per instructions.
