summary: Requires a decommissioning plan that mandates safe removal of facility components (except deeply buried lines), land restoration, a decommissioning plan, and grid disconnection at the end of the facility™s life. It also requires grantees to provide escalating financial assurance" starting at 5% of decommissioning costs at commercial operation, 50% by year ten, and 100% by year fifteen" through approved instruments such as bonds, letters of credit, or guarantees, with landowners allowed to extend the initial delivery deadline to year fifteen.

The ordinance defines Wind and Solar Farms as large-scale systems supplying power into any electrical grid and located on lots of no less than fifty (50) acres. It requires the applicant to submit a decommissioning plan describing how the project will be decommissioned and ensuring financial capability. Any wind or solar farm not in operation for thirty (30) continuous months is considered abandoned, and the parcel owner must remove all systems within ninety (90) days of notice. A performance bond of $1,000 per acre must be submitted to ensure removal and disposal of all systems, including dismantling all electrical generating equipment, cables, panels, foundations, buildings, and ancillary equipment. The operator must restore and reclaim the site to its pre-project topography and topsoil quality within eighteen (18) months from the date the farm becomes inactive. The bond is released after removal and site restoration are completed. Any agreement for lesser removal must be approved by the Planning Commission.

All wind and solar farms shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access at a height of at least eight feet (subject to Subsection 4.230). Adequate screening shall be provided. This can be accomplished by either the required perimeter fencing being constructed as a board-to-board privacy fence or by vegetative buffer (as required in Subsection 3.110) being placed beyond the perimeter fence. All solar and wind farms shall be located on lots of no less than fifty (50) acres in size.

The ordinance states: 'All solar and wind farms shall be located on lots of no less than fifty (50) acres in size.' This minimum lot size applies explicitly to wind and solar farms, which are defined as large-scale systems designed for utility-scale power supply. The unit of measurement for this minimum lot size is acres.

All wind and solar farms shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access at a height of at least eight feet (subject to Subsection 4.230). Adequate screening shall be provided. This can be accomplished by either the required perimeter fencing being constructed as a board-to-board privacy fence or by vegetative buffer (as required in Subsection 3.110) being placed beyond the perimeter fence. All solar and wind farms shall be located on lots of no less than fifty (50) acres in size.

Wind and Solar Farms, as defined in Article II, Section 2.020, are considered as Uses Permitted as Special Exceptions in the I-1, Industrial Zoning District, and shall meet the following requirements: perimeter fencing at least eight feet high, adequate screening, minimum setbacks including 500 feet from any residential structure, location on lots no less than fifty (50) acres in size, underground electrical lines, building permit based on 4% of construction cost, submission of a decommissioning plan, and performance bond. Approval requires review by the Board of Zoning Appeals and site plan approval by the Planning Commission (Section 5.058 C). Other districts permit solar energy devices generally but do not specifically address large-scale solar farms or require special exception approval for them. For example, solar energy devices are permitted uses in FAR, R-1, R-3, C-1, C-2, and C-3 districts, sometimes subject to site plan approval, but wind and solar farms (minimum 50-acre lots) are only listed as special exceptions in the I-1 district.

Solar and wind farms shall adhere to the minimum setback requirements, except that farms shall be setback a minimum of five hundred (500) feet from any residential structure. All solar and wind farms shall be located on lots of no less than fifty (50) acres in size.

Section 15-6-187 titled "Discontinuance" requires that if all legally approved use of a solar energy system supporting structure or solar energy related equipment has been discontinued for a period of 180 days, the Director of Planning & Development Services and/or designee may make a preliminary determination of discontinuance and provide written notice by certified mail. Failure to respond within 90 days or adequately demonstrate that the structure is not discontinued will lead to a declaration of discontinuance. Within 120 days of this declaration, the property owner must either (a) Reactivate the use of the structure or transfer ownership to another who will use it, or (b) Dismantle and remove the facility. If the facility remains discontinued after 120 days, the property is declared a nuisance and the City may remove the facility at the owner's expense.

Section 15-6-186(A)(3) states: 'Shall be of a type which provides a low glare or anti-reflective layer applied to the solar panel to reduce the reflection or glare of the system.' This glare restriction applies to all Solar Energy Systems, which includes Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) as defined in the ordinance. The ordinance defines PSES as systems 'principally used to capture solar energy, convert it to electrical energy or thermal power, and supply electrical or thermal power primarily for off-site use.'

Section 15-6-185(A)(1) states: 'Properties containing solar energy systems as principal uses shall contain a minimum of one acre.' This minimum lot size applies to ground-mounted solar energy systems permitted as principal uses, which are defined as systems primarily used to supply power off-site. No other minimum lot size values for Principal Solar Energy Systems are provided.
section: Sec. 15-6-185. Solar Energy Systems As Principal Uses

summary: The front yard setback for principal use SES shall be twenty feet. All SES permitted as principal uses shall comply with the side-yard and rear yard setbacks for accessory structures within the applicable zoning district.
section: Sec. 15-6-185. Solar Energy Systems As Principal Uses

summary: Ground mounted solar energy systems are permitted as principal uses by right in the I-1 and I-2 zoning districts, subject to conditions such as minimum one acre property size, setback requirements, no residential use on the property, and providing energy to off-site locations other than the property owner. Accessory solar energy systems (ASES) are permitted as a use by right in all zoning districts. There is no mention of any districts where utility-scale solar energy systems require special use permits, approval by a zoning appeals board, or a special permitting process. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this consideration.
section: Sec. 15-6-185. Solar Energy Systems As Principal Uses

summary: The front yard setback for principal use solar energy systems (PSES) shall be twenty feet. All SES permitted as principal uses shall comply with the side-yard and rear yard setbacks for accessory structures within the applicable zoning district. No residential use or structure shall exist on the property. (Sec. 15-6-185)
section: Sec. 15-6-185. Solar Energy Systems As Principal Uses

summary: Section 41.10.C.3 states: 'Ground- or pole-mounted solar systems shall not exceed fifteen feet (15') in height when oriented at maximum tilt.' This is the explicit maximum height restriction applicable to ground- or pole-mounted solar energy systems, which are typically utility-scale. Other height-related provisions include roof-mounted systems not exceeding the maximum allowed height in the applicable zoning district (41.10.C.2), but no specific numerical value is given there. The 15 feet limit is the most restrictive explicit numerical height limit provided for these systems.

The ordinance requires that 'Wall-mounted and ground-mounted solar collectors shall be screened from public view.' It applies to ground-mounted solar energy systems, which can include utility-scale systems. Other relevant provisions include height limits for ground- or pole-mounted solar systems (not to exceed fifteen feet), setback requirements, and design guidelines such as blending into the architecture and color consistency. However, no explicit vegetative buffer requirements are stated.

Ground or pole-mounted Solar Energy Systems are allowed in all zoning districts, but only with a Specific Use Permit (SUP), and are allowed as an accessory use to a building or structure requiring energy. Roof-top mounted Solar Energy Systems are allowed in all zoning districts as an accessory use without mention of special permits.

Section 7.02 b) 2) states: 'No more than one and a half percent (1.5%) of the gross site area shall be occupied by enclosed buildings and structures.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage restriction applicable to commercial solar farms with a minimum power output of twenty-five (25) megawatts AC. The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the gross site area.

The ordinance applies to commercial solar farms with a minimum power output of twenty-five (25) megawatts AC. Under Termination of Use, the right to use and develop the property for a solar farm expires if a certificate of occupancy is not granted within three years or if the property ceases operation for 360 consecutive days (except in cases of fire or windstorm damage, where operation must recommence within eighteen months). The owner must remove all solar farm equipment, appurtenances, signage, and security fences not later than one hundred eighty (180) days after discontinuation of use.

Section 7.02(b)(10) requires "An eight (8) feet tall chainlink security fence with up to three (3) strands of barbed wire" along the "thirty-foot (30') required setback for the property developed as a solar farm." This applies to commercial solar farms with a minimum power output of twenty-five (25) megawatts of alternating current (AC) power as defined in Section 7.02(a) and (b)(1).

The maximum height of a solar panel array shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet. The maximum height for structures located in a switchyard and/or utility company substation area(s) shall not exceed thirty-five (35) feet. The height of any solar panel array, structure, poles, wiring systems, and other components of the system may exceed these maximum heights if approved as part of the Specific Use Permit authorizing development of the solar farm. Units are expressed in feet.

A thirty-foot setback shall be required along the perimeter of the property on which the solar farm is located. An eight (8) feet tall chainlink security fence with up to three (3) strands of barbed wire shall be required along thirty-foot (30') required setback for the property developed as a solar farm. When the property on which the solar farm is located abuts a public street and/or a property zoned or developed for residential uses, a twenty (20) foot wide landscape buffer shall be installed along the property line(s) adjacent to (i) the abutting residentially zoned or developed property and, (ii) except in areas required for driveways and sidewalks, the public street. Required landscape buffer may be located within the 30-foot setback on the property.

Section 7.02(b)(5) Landscaping and Screening requires: "a twenty (20) foot wide landscape buffer shall be installed along the property line(s) adjacent to (i) the abutting residentially zoned or developed property and, (ii) except in areas required for driveways and sidewalks, the public street." The buffer "shall consist of a mixture of trees, shrubs, grass, and other plants selected from the lists of approved plant species set forth in Section 4.5404." Additionally, "One (1) overstory/large tree shall be planted within the required landscape buffers on centers of not greater than forty (40) linear feet," with specified minimum trunk diameter and height. The buffer "may be located within the 30-foot setback on the property." Exceptions to these requirements "may be approved as part of a landscape plan set forth in the Specific Use Permit authorizing development of the solar farm."

Section 7.02(b)(8) Signs and Lighting: "At each entrance gate to the solar farm, a permanent sign shall be affixed to the entry gate providing contact information for the owner and/or operator of the solar farm, including one or more emergency contact telephone numbers. Such sign shall be no larger than four (4) feet by five (5) feet." "Pole signs, monument/ground signs, and all electronic message centers/electronic signs are prohibited." "Except as provided in this Section 7.02 or as set forth in the ordinance granting the Specific Use Permit for development and use of property for a solar farm, all signs installed on the property shall be in compliance with the sign regulations applicable to the zoning district in which the property is located."

Distributed Generation (DG) is defined as an electrical generating facility located at a customer's point of delivery of ten (10) megawatts (MW) or less. The City has established a DG size threshold at 50 kW AC for certain policies, with systems larger than 50 kW AC subject to additional engineering studies and potentially additional terms in the DG Agreement. Section 8 references compliance with SB398 for DG systems with capacity of 250 kW up to ≤10 MW. The manual explicitly limits DG systems to a maximum size of 10 MW AC. Other size thresholds mentioned include 20 kW AC and 50 kW AC for engineering review and study requirements, but the maximum project size is 10 MW AC.

The DG System shall not have a generation capacity greater than 10 MW. Distributed Generation is defined, for the purposes of this Rider, as an electrical generating facility located at Customer’s point of delivery that is 10 MW or less and connected to the City of Seguin distribution system. This 10 MW limit is a firm cap stated in the Agreement and the Rate Rider, with no mention of bypass by permit or alternative installation size limits such as number of systems or solar panels.
section: AGREEMENT FOR THE INTERCONNECTION AND PARALLEL OPERATION OF DISTRIBUTED GENERATION IN THE CITY ELECTRIC SYSTEM

summary: Solar power facility agreements to ensure the grantee is responsible for removing all solar equipment, foundations, cables, and lines, and restoring the land to its prior condition, including soil refilling, reseeding, and optional road or rock removal if requested by the landowner within 180 days of decommissioning. Section 302.0005 mandates that grantees provide financial assurance, such as a guaranty, letter of credit, or bond, sufficient to cover removal and land restoration costs (net of salvage value), with costs and estimates verified by independent engineers and updated regularly to ensure adequacy.

An appropriate security/livestock fence (height and material to be established through the Conditional Use Permit process) shall be placed around the perimeter of the solar power plant. Knox boxes and keys shall be provided at locked entrances for emergency personnel access. Appropriate warning signage, including emergency contact information, shall be placed at the entrance and along the perimeter of the solar power plant project. This fencing requirement applies to all solar power plants, including utility-scale commercial facilities using concentrating solar thermal devices (CST) for wholesale or retail electricity sales, as defined under "Solar Power Plant."

The ordinance explicitly enacts glare restrictions for Concentrated Solar Thermal Power Plants. It states: 'No solar power plant shall produce glare that would constitute a nuisance to occupants of neighboring properties or persons traveling neighboring roads.' Additionally, projects with reflective components or taller structures must provide 'a viewshed analysis of the project, including visual simulations of the planned structures and analysis of potential glare impacts.' The ordinance applies to utility-scale commercial facilities using concentrating solar thermal devices (CST) for electricity generation and sale. Other relevant conditions include minimum lot size (no concentrated solar thermal power plant on less than forty acres), maximum height established through Conditional Use Permit, setbacks to mitigate noise and glare impacts, and requirements for visual appearance and lighting to mitigate visual impacts.

The maximum height for all structures shall be established through the Conditional Use Permit process, provided a structure height of thirty feet or less shall always be permitted. This applies to solar power plants, including concentrated solar thermal power plants. The ordinance states: 'Maximum Height. The maximum height for all structures shall be established through the Conditional Use Permit process, provided a structure height of thirty feet or less shall always be permitted.'

The ordinance states: 'No concentrated solar thermal power plant shall be erected on any lot less than forty acres in size.' For comparison, it also specifies that 'No photovoltaic solar power plant shall be erected on any lot less than five acres in size.' The minimum lot size for concentrated solar thermal power plants is therefore 40 acres, with 'acres' being the unit of measurement.

No operating solar power plant shall produce noise that exceeds any of the following limitations: (a) Fifty dBA, as measured at the property line of any neighboring residence; (b) Forty-five dBA, as measured at any existing neighboring residence between the hours of nine p.m. and seven a.m.; (c) Sixty dBA, as measured at the property lines of the project boundary, unless the owner of the affected property and the Planning Commission agree to a higher noise level. The most restrictive limit is 45 dBA during nighttime hours at neighboring residences. The units for noise levels are dBA.

Solar power plant structures shall be set back from all property lines and public road rights-of-way at least thirty feet, or one and one-half times the height of the structure, whichever is greater. Additional setbacks may be required to mitigate noise and glare impacts or to provide for designated corridors. The ordinance provides two alternative minimum setback distances: a static minimum of thirty feet or a multiplier of 1.5 times the structure height, with the greater of the two to be applied.

Solar power plant structures shall be set back from public road rights-of-way at least thirty feet, or one and one-half times the height of the structure, whichever is greater. This setback applies to utility-scale commercial facilities including Concentrated Solar Thermal Power Plants. There is no requirement to add these distances; the setback is the greater of the two values.

The ordinance requires that "Appropriate landscaping and/or screening materials may be required to help screen the solar power plant and accessory structures from major roads and neighboring residences." This applies to all solar power plants, including Concentrated Solar Thermal Power Plants, defined as "a utility-scale commercial facility that converts sunlight into electricity... for the primary purpose of wholesale or retail sales of generated electricity." The ordinance also includes other design standards such as minimum lot size ("No concentrated solar thermal power plant shall be erected on any lot less than forty acres in size."), maximum height limits, setbacks, safety fencing, noise limitations, visual appearance standards, underground electrical interconnections, fire protection, and requirements for permits and agreements. Visual impact analysis is required for projects with structures taller than thirty feet or those in sensitive viewsheds, including visual simulations and possibly a Zone of Theoretical Visibility/Zone of Visual Impact (ZVI) Analysis. Screening is part of the visual appearance standards to mitigate visual impacts.

All solar power plants shall comply with the following minimum regulations and design standards. The Planning Commission may also require a "Zone of Theoretical Visibility/Zone of Visual Impact (ZVI) Analysis," which is "a three hundred sixty degree computer analysis to map the lands within a defined radius of a location that would likely be able to see an object." The full estimated decommissioning cost "shall be guaranteed by escrow at a federally insured financial institution, irrevocable letter of credit, or surety bond before a building permit is issued." The cost estimate "shall be recalculated every three years" with adjustments to the guarantee. Systems "which have reached the end of their useful life or have not been in active service for a period of one year shall be removed at the facility owner/operator's expense," with possible extension by the Zoning Administrator. The owner/operator must "notify the Zoning Administrator by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal" and has "12 months to complete decommissioning." Decommissioning includes removal of all components and restoration of agricultural ground unless the landowner requests otherwise, and disposal of hazardous materials in accordance with law. summary: Generally, all solar energy facilities shall be located a minimum of 500 feet to 1,000 feet from adjoining property lines and public rights-of-way. Article X. — Surety for decommissioning of a utility-scale solar generation facility requires that a site plan for a utility-scale solar generation facility include a detailed decommissioning plan with procedures for removal of all parts of the facility at the end of its useful life or if deemed abandoned. The plan must include the anticipated life, estimated cost, methodology for cost estimate, and manner of decommissioning, updated at least every five years. The disposal of panels and equipment must meet all local, state, and federal regulations. The owner must work with County staff to ensure recycling through best practices. As a condition of site plan approval, the responsible party must enter a written agreement with the county ensuring decommissioning if the facility ceases generating electricity for more than twelve consecutive months, allowing the county to enter the property to decommission if the responsible party defaults. Financial assurance must be provided in the form of certified funds, cash escrow, bond, letter of credit, or parent guarantee, based on a professional engineer's estimate approved by the county, including projected costs, net salvage value, administrative costs, and inflation. Other sections in the ordinance address development standards, application requirements, community meetings, and special exceptions for utility-scale solar generation facilities but do not explicitly enact decommissioning requirements.

The buffer "should be made up of plant materials at least three (3) feet tall at the time of planting and that are reasonably expected to grow to a minimum height of eight (8) feet within three (3) years." It must use "Non-invasive plant species and pollinator-friendly and wildlife-friendly native plants, shrubs, trees, grasses, forbs and wildflowers." Fencing "must be installed on the interior of the buffer" and the buffer "must be maintained for the life of the facility." Section 923.04(4)(g) requires "A landscaping and screening plan that addresses the vegetative buffering required, including the use of existing and newly installed vegetation to screen the facility." The plan must also address "the use of pollinator-friendly and wildlife-friendly native plants, shrubs, trees, grasses, forbs, and wildflowers in the project area and in the setbacks and vegetative buffering." summary: The ordinance requires a decommissioning plan for utility-scale solar generation facilities that includes 'reasonable restoration of the real property, including (i) soil stabilization and (ii) revegetation of the ground cover of the real property disturbed by the installation of such equipment, facilities, or devices.' The project area must be 'seeded promptly following completion of construction in such a manner as to reduce invasive weed growth and sediment in the project area.' These requirements apply specifically to utility-scale solar generation facilities. The decommissioning plan must also include procedures for removal of all parts of the facility and an estimate of decommissioning costs. Financial assurance for decommissioning is required as a condition of site plan approval. Other development standards include vegetative buffering with native plants and maintenance of the buffer for the life of the facility, but these focus more on visual impact and habitat preservation rather than explicit soil, erosion, or sediment control. The zoning administrator may waive some requirements for smaller facilities under 1.5 MW or less than 4 acres, but the final decision lies with the board of supervisors.

summary: Section 923.04(4)(j) requires "photo or other realistic simulations or modeling of the proposed solar energy project from potentially sensitive locations as deemed necessary by the zoning administrator to assess the visual impact of the project." Section 923.05 requires "A vegetative buffer sufficient to mitigate the visual impact of the facility" with specific landscaping and screening plans. The board of supervisors "may impose conditions requiring that through project siting and proposed mitigation the solar project minimizes impacts on viewsheds, including from residential areas and areas of scenic, historical, cultural, archeological, and recreational significance." Section 923.06 lists considerations including "The proximity of the site to, observability from, and impact on urban and residential areas," "areas of historical, cultural, and archaeological significance," "areas of scenic significance," and "public rights-of-way." The zoning administrator may require additional information "such as a scaled elevation view and other supporting drawings, photographs of the proposed site" to assess visual impact. The ordinance also allows the zoning administrator to waive some requirements for smaller facilities under certain conditions. Other relevant provisions include requirements for public meetings and application materials that support visual impact assessment.

The ordinance requires a detailed decommissioning plan that "provides procedures and requirements for removal of all parts of the solar energy generation facility and its various structures at the end of the useful life of the facility or if it is deemed abandoned or unsafe." The plan must include "the anticipated life of the facility, the estimated overall cost of decommissioning the facility in current dollars, the methodology for determining such estimate, and the manner in which the project will be decommissioned." The decommissioning plan and cost estimates must be updated every five years, with a maximum of twice every 10 years. Prior to receiving a certificate of occupancy, the applicant must provide security equal to the estimated decommissioning cost, which may be a "cash escrow, a performance surety bond, or an irrevocable letter of credit." This security must remain valid until decommissioning obligations are met and may be adjusted by the county. If the facility is unsafe, abandoned, or not operated for 12 months, the county may require repairs or commencement of decommissioning in accordance with the approved plan. The county may pursue legal action to remove the facility at the owner's expense and may use the decommissioning security to cover removal costs. Other options for security include cash escrow, performance surety bond, or irrevocable letter of credit, and the security must be renewed or replaced as needed based on updated cost estimates.

The ordinance explicitly requires decommissioning for utility scale solar installations as a condition of site plan approval. The responsible party must notify the zoning administrator within ten (10) days of knowledge of abandonment or discontinuation and physically remove the system and restore the site no more than twelve (12) months after discontinued operations. Decommissioning includes physical removal of all solar panels and above-ground appurtenant structures, reasonable restoration of the real property including soil stabilization and revegetation, and proper disposal of all solid and hazardous waste. The system is considered abandoned if it fails to operate for more than one (1) year without written consent. The county may remove the system at the owner's expense if not timely decommissioned. The owner must provide updated decommissioning cost estimates every five years and provide financial assurance in the form of certified funds, cash escrow, bond, irrevocable letter of credit, or parent guarantee. The surety must cover estimated costs plus ten (10) percent for administrative costs, inflation, and potential damage, and remains in effect until the county verifies decommissioning. This surety is binding on subsequent owners. A building and zoning permit is required prior to decommissioning. Other solar types include small-scale solar installations, which have separate height and setback requirements but no explicit decommissioning requirements stated here, and solar agricultural generators, which have decommissioning requirements including removal within twelve (12) months and restoration, but are limited to 1.5 MW and accessory to agricultural use.

section: Utility Scale Solar Installation: Performance Standards

summary: Utility scale solar installations require a vegetative buffer "sufficient to mitigate the visual impact of the facility" consisting of "a landscaping strip at least one hundred fifty (150) feet wide, located within the required setbacks and shall run around the entire perimeter of the project area." The buffer must have "sufficient existing vegetation and trees to create an opaque visual barrier to screen the project area from view." If no such barrier exists, the applicant must establish "two (2) rows of staggered evergreens ten (10) feet apart and on fifteen (15) foot centers," with trees "at least three (3) feet tall at the time of planting and expected to grow to a minimum height of twenty (20) feet within ten (10) years." The buffer must use "non-invasive plant species and pollinator-friendly and wildlife-friendly native plants, shrubs, trees, grasses, forbs, or wildflowers." Existing trees and vegetation in the buffer "shall be maintained for the life of the facility," and "trees removed from the buffer shall be replaced by planting a similar tree in the buffer at least five (5) feet in height at the time of planting." Security fencing "must be installed on the interior of the vegetative buffer required so that it is screened from the ground level view of adjacent property owners." The planning commission and board of supervisors may "impose alternative conditions having the effect of waiving or altering the vegetative screening and/or buffer requirements when the applicant proposes to preserve existing wetlands or woodlands to serve as a buffer." These requirements apply solely to utility scale solar installations allowed by conditional use permit in the M-1 district. Other solar types such as small-scale solar installations and solar agricultural generators have different buffer and screening requirements, e.g., small-scale installations require a vegetative screen "at least equal to the height of the installation" and a minimum distance of 30 feet from adjoining structures, while solar agricultural generators require a minimum 75-foot buffer from adjoining properties and a 30-foot vegetative screen at least equal to the height of the installation.

The ordinance explicitly requires erosion and sediment control for utility scale solar installations: "Site clearing shall not exceed one hundred (100) acres for each phase of development. Sediment control features shall receive county approval on each phase before beginning any land disturbance or construction activities. Applicants to obtain a written report from an independent engineer determining the stabilization of each phase of construction. Once this determination is made another phase of land disturbance activities can begin." Additionally, decommissioning must include "reasonable restoration of the real property, including soil stabilization and revegetation of the ground cover of the real property disturbed by the installation of such equipment, facilities, or devices." These requirements apply specifically to utility scale solar installations, which are defined as projects "designed to interconnect with the electrical grid and/or serve facilities that are not adjacent or under common use, ownership, or control." Other solar types such as small-scale solar installations and solar agricultural generators have different conditions and limitations, but the explicit soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements are detailed for utility scale solar installations and solar agricultural generators (the latter requiring a "proposed erosion and sediment control plan for minimizing water quality impacts from the use for the lifetime of the project").

Utility scale solar installations shall be allowed solely by conditional use permit in the M-1 district. A solar agricultural generator shall be allowed solely by conditional use permit in the A-1 district. Small-scale solar installations are permitted by right in all zoning districts with certain restrictions, but these do not apply to utility scale systems.

Utility scale solar installations shall be allowed solely by conditional use permit in the M-1 district. The application must include a project narrative and a concept plan with detailed information such as property lines, setbacks, an area map within a five-mile radius, existing and proposed buildings and structures, access roads, fencing, vegetative buffering areas, wetlands, woodlands, and soil types. A generalized landscaping and screening plan addressing vegetative buffering is required, including the use of pollinator-friendly and wildlife-friendly native plants. Performance standards require a vegetative buffer sufficient to mitigate the visual impact of the facility, consisting of a landscaping strip at least one hundred fifty (150) feet wide, creating an opaque visual barrier. The board of supervisors may impose conditions to minimize impacts on viewsheds, including from residential areas and areas of scenic, historical, cultural, archeological, and recreational significance. Other requirements include setbacks, anti-glare technology, erosion control, security fencing, height limits, FAA compliance, and decommissioning plans. Small-scale solar installations and solar agricultural generators have separate requirements and are not the focus here.

The ordinance requires the applicant to provide a decommissioning plan, updated every three (3) years, to ensure (i) that the real property will be returned to its original condition upon closure of any facility, or at the end of its useful life, and (ii) that decommissioned equipment and panels are disposed of appropriately and in an environmentally sound manner. Decommissioning shall be guaranteed by cash, commercial surety, letter of credit, performance bond, etc., subject to approval by the County Attorney. Final reporting at the conclusion of decommissioning is required before any guarantee is released. Decommissioning surety must be in place and adequate from project onset until decommissioning. Upon inactivity for more than two consecutive years, the facility must be decommissioned, including removal of all surface and subsurface features, filling trenches, and maintaining wetland protections, natural vegetation, erosion control, and stormwater features. The applicant must notify the Zoning Administrator within 30 days of inactivity. If inactive for more than twelve (12) consecutive months, the permit may be revoked unless restoration efforts are ongoing. Decommissioning activities must be completed within nine (9) months of notice of inactivity. If not removed timely, the County may remove the facility at the owner's expense. Components removed must be handled and disposed of in compliance with all applicable laws, with emphasis on recycling and reuse. No hardware or parts shall be disposed of in local landfills. A surety agreement for decommissioning must be submitted prior to construction permits, reviewed every three years, and may hold the landowner responsible if the applicant fails to perform. These requirements apply to utility scale solar facilities up to 300 acres, as defined by the policy and conditional use permit provisions.

summary: No signage of any type may be placed on the facility other than notices, warnings, and identification information required by law. During construction only, limited signage may be permitted to identify the companies performing the construction and to provide notice to the general public.

The ordinance explicitly requires an erosion and sediment control plan prior to land disturbance permits that must "adhere to the Virginia Erosion and Sedimentation Control Regulations and the Virginia Erosion and Sedimentation Control Handbook (a/k/a the 'Green Book')." It mandates that "no topsoil will be removed from the Facility but instead will be used on site to establish ground cover," and requires "riparian buffers of at least 50 feet from the top-of-bank of all stream segments." The plan must include "a protocol... that specifies the phased construction of designated units of land so that the total area of disturbed land at any one time is appropriately limited," with a limit that "no land disturbing activity associated with any phase of the project shall disturb more than 50 acres at a time." The applicant must provide "sufficient surety to guarantee that funding is available to implement and maintain all required erosion and sediment control measures" and fund "a third-party erosion and sediment control inspector." Additionally, prior to construction, the applicant must obtain a "Virginia Stormwater Management Program Permit ('VSMP Permit'), including a proposed Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan ('SWPPP')." Vegetation management plans must emphasize "native grasses and associated low-growing species," control invasive species, limit herbicide use, and use "biodegradable soap and water" for panel cleaning. Soil protection measures include prompt reporting of hazardous spills, soil sampling before disturbance and during operation, and proper disposal of damaged panels. Mass grading is limited to fifty (50) acres at a time. These requirements apply to utility scale solar facilities up to 300 acres, as defined by the ordinance. Other related conditions include bonding requirements such as an "Erosion and Sediment Control Bond," stormwater management bonds, and decommissioning plans to restore soil conditions post-operation.

Utility scale solar energy generation facilities in the A-1 (Agricultural) and RA (Rural Area) Zoning Districts require a conditional use permit pursuant to Article 17 of the Culpeper County Zoning Ordinance. The permit is subject to conditions including nontransferability, permit duration tied to commercial operation, reconstruction limitations, and the requirement to obtain zoning and building permits within 24 months of the conditional use permit. Facilities that adversely affect health, safety, public welfare, or conflict with the Comprehensive Plan will not be approved. Final conditions are at the sole discretion of the Culpeper County Board of Supervisors.

The policy requires a preliminary decommissioning plan with financial assurance in the form of a bond not less than the estimated cost of decommissioning, calculated by a third party hired by the applicant. A final decommissioning plan must be updated and submitted prior to the issuance of the land disturbance permit, with possible third-party review at the applicant's expense. The decommissioning plan is to be reviewed every 5 years for potential changes, including cost increases, technology changes, and project size/scope. The project must be decommissioned within twelve (12) months of cessation of operations, which begins if (i) the facility is inactive or substantially discontinuing electricity delivery for a continuous twelve (12) month period; (ii) the project is declared unsafe and not repaired or removed; or (iii) at a time selected by the applicant, owner, or operator if neither (i) nor (ii) apply. The plan shall identify the anticipated life of the facility, estimated overall cost in current dollars, methodology for the estimate, and execution manner.

Fencing for the solar energy facility complies with the latest version of the National Electric Code as of the effective date of the amendatory act that added this section or any applicable successor standard approved by the County. Solar panels must be enclosed by a security fence with a minimum height of six (6) feet. Fencing shall be installed on the interior of the vegetative buffer and must be screened from ground level view of non-participating properties. All fencing must be properly maintained while the facility is in operation. Fencing shall be removed at decommissioning.
section: Development Standards for Energy (Solar or Solar Plus Energy Storage) Facilities

summary: The ordinance requires that a "glint and glare study shall be conducted and provided by a qualified firm that demonstrates that the panels will be sited, designed, and installed to eliminate glint and glare effects on nearby residences, vehicular traffic, commercial areas, and other sensitive viewing locations." Additionally, "Solar panels shall be non-reflective type" and "All panels will use anti reflective coatings. Exterior surfaces of the collectors and related equipment shall have a non-reflective finish and solar panels shall be designed and installed to limit glare to a degree that no after image would occur." These requirements apply to large scale solar energy facilities, defined as those producing more than 5 megawatts and intended for sale or use offsite. Other development standards include setbacks, landscaping and buffering, fencing, height limits, sound limits, lighting, construction, signage, wildlife corridors, vegetation management, erosion and sediment control, wind resistance, panel standards, access, and insurance requirements.
section: Development Standards for Energy (Solar or Solar Plus Energy Storage) Facilities

summary: Under the 'Development Standards for Energy (Solar or Solar Plus Energy Storage) Facilities,' subsection D states: 'Solar panel components do not exceed a maximum height of 15 feet above ground when the arrays are at full tilt.' This is the explicit maximum height limit applicable to large scale solar energy facilities as defined in the policy. No other maximum height values are provided for large scale energy facilities.
section: Development Standards for Energy (Solar or Solar Plus Energy Storage) Facilities

summary: The solar energy facility does not generate a maximum sound in excess of 50 average hourly decibels as modeled at the nearest adjacent nonparticipating property. Decibel modeling shall use the A-weighted scale as designed by the American National Standards Institute and will be monitored and reported back to the County for the first 2 years of operation.
section: Development Standards for Energy (Solar or Solar Plus Energy Storage) Facilities

summary: Large scale utility solar projects will not be considered if proposed to be located within 1 aerial miles of a previously approved large scale energy project unless an existing approved project is considering expansion. Energy projects of any size will not be considered if proposed to be located within 1 aerial mile of an identified village within the County’s Comprehensive Plan.
section: Development Standards for Energy (Solar or Solar Plus Energy Storage) Facilities

summary: A minimum of a one hundred (100) foot setback from fencing around the energy producing equipment to the property line and any public rights of way shall be provided around the perimeter of the project where it is adjacent to non-participating property owners at the time of approval. Other setback distances mentioned include a 500-foot setback from the fence line to adjoining or adjacent residential dwellings, but residences are not equivalent to property lines unless explicitly stated. Additionally, large scale utility solar projects will not be considered if proposed within 1 aerial mile of a previously approved large scale energy project or within 1 aerial mile of an identified village, which relates to distance separation but not direct setbacks from property lines.
section: Development Standards for Energy (Solar or Solar Plus Energy Storage) Facilities

summary: A minimum of a one hundred (100) foot setback from fencing around the energy producing equipment to the property line and any public rights of way shall be provided around the perimeter of the project where it is adjacent to non-participating property owners at the time of approval. Along existing public right of way where there is existing timber, there shall be a fifty (50) foot buffer maintained.
section: Development Standards for Energy (Solar or Solar Plus Energy Storage) Facilities

summary: The ordinance requires under 'Development Standards for Energy (Solar or Solar Plus Energy Storage) Facilities' that within the one hundred (100) foot setback, there shall be maintained at least a fifty (50) foot buffer of vegetation and timber, preferably existing, with the intent to obscure from view the project. All buffer areas will be properly maintained including appropriate thinning, trimming, seeding or other modifications. Along existing public right of way where there is existing timber, there shall be a fifty (50) foot buffer maintained. A performance bond reflecting the estimated costs of anticipated landscaping maintenance shall be posted prior to construction to ensure buffer landscaping is adequately maintained for the life of the project. Additionally, fencing shall be installed on the interior of the vegetative buffer and must be screened from ground level view of non-participating properties. These requirements apply to energy generating facilities that require a conditional use permit, which includes large scale energy facilities defined as those producing more than 5 megawatts.
section: Development Standards for Energy (Solar or Solar Plus Energy Storage) Facilities

summary: No signage shall be allowed on the fencing, structures, or buildings of the facility except for one 32 square foot sign at the main ingress/egress area which shall list the required warnings, facility name, address and relevant contact information. Any signage required by state or federal agencies, any industrial code or standard, or any commercial insurance or safety standards shall be exempt from this requirement.
section: Development Standards for Energy (Solar or Solar Plus Energy Storage) Facilities, subsection J

summary: Section N under Development Standards for Energy (Solar or Solar Plus Energy Storage) Facilities requires an Erosion and Sediment (E&S) plan to be submitted and approved by the Soil and Water Conservation District for projects 5 MW or less and by DEQ for projects more than 5 MW. The plan must be prepared in accordance with the Virginia Erosion and Sediment Control Handbook. During construction, the applicant must ensure all E&S facilities are inspected by a qualified third-party inspector at least every four calendar days and within 24 hours following any runoff producing storm event, with corrective actions taken as needed. A Stormwater Management Plan must be submitted to and approved by DEQ prior to any land disturbance, including approval of a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP). The applicant and contractors must implement SWPPP measures and make the active SWPPP publicly available at least once per month upon request. These requirements apply explicitly to large scale energy facilities, defined as energy producing facilities that total more than 5 megawatts.
section: N. Erosion and Sediment Control and Stormwater Management

summary: A minimum five hundred (500) foot setback shall be maintained from the fence line to any adjoining or adjacent residential dwellings that exist at the time of approval. Additionally, a minimum of a one hundred (100) foot setback from fencing around the energy producing equipment to the property line and any public rights of way shall be provided around the perimeter of the project where it is adjacent to non-participating property owners at the time of approval.
section: Development Standards for Energy (Solar or Solar Plus Energy Storage) Facilities

summary: The ordinance requires a site plan for an energy facility to include '(i) the location and a description of the energy facility; (ii) a description of the anticipated effects of the energy facility on the environment, natural resources,' and additional information requested by Cumberland County. The application must include 'a description of the energy facility, including a site plan,' 'the expected direct impacts of the proposed energy facility on the environment and natural resources and how the applicant intends to address and mitigate these impacts,' and 'a summary of the community outreach and education efforts.' Development standards include maintaining 'at least a fifty (50) foot buffer of vegetation and timber, preferably existing with the intent to obscure from view the project,' and fencing 'must be screened from ground level view of non-participating properties.' These requirements apply to large scale energy facilities defined as those producing more than 5 megawatts and intended for sale or offsite use. Other considerations include setbacks, landscaping, and consultation with relevant agencies. The policy also mandates public notice, consultation, and a conditional use permit process with evaluation of impacts on local land use and environment.

A one hundred (100) foot setback shall be maintained from energy generating equipment to the edge of all perennial streams and connected wetland within the project area. Other setbacks include 100 feet from fencing to property line and 500 feet from fence line to residential dwellings, but these do not pertain to lakes, reservoirs, streams, rivers, or wetlands.
section: Development Standards for Energy (Solar or Solar Plus Energy Storage) Facilities

summary: The owner or operator of a solar farm shall completely decommission the solar farm within twelve (12) months if the solar farm ceases to generate electricity for a continuous period of twelve (12) months. This period may be extended by the Board of Supervisors if the owner or operator provides evidence that the failure to generate electricity is due to circumstances beyond the owner's or operator's reasonable control and the solar farm has not been abandoned. Decommissioning shall include the removal of all solar collectors, cabling, electrical components, fencing, and any other associated equipment, facilities and structures to a depth of at least 36 inches. Disturbed earth shall be graded and re-seeded. To ensure the full completion of decommissioning requirements, Dinwiddie County requires financial assurance of decommissioning, in the form of certified funds, cash escrow, bond, letter of credit, or parent guarantee, in a form acceptable to the County Attorney, and in accordance with Va. Code §15.2-2241.2. The placement of a surety/performance bond or certified check meeting certain terms and in certain amounts as determined by the Dinwiddie County Planning Department is required to ensure that such decommissioning or removal is completed expeditiously, and at no cost to the landowner.

All solar farms shall be fenced at a minimum around the exterior of the solar collector areas with a fence which shall be at least 6 feet in height. The planning director may require fencing to be placed on the solar energy farm in a manner as to allow wildlife corridors through and around the project site. All fencing shall be constructed so as to substantially lessen the likelihood of entry into a solar farm by unauthorized individuals. The fencing required hereunder shall be maintained in good condition. Failure to maintain the fencing required hereunder shall constitute a violation of this ordinance. The fencing requirements specified hereunder shall continue notwithstanding the fact that a solar farm is no longer operational and/or falls into disuse unless and until the solar farm is dismantled and removed from the parcel or parcels of land upon which it was constructed.

The maximum height for all solar collector equipment shall be eighteen (18) feet. This applies to utility scale solar energy projects as defined in the ordinance. The relevant text is from Sec. 22-234.64 – Height. Other height restrictions mentioned, such as a 15 feet maximum for ground-mounted solar collectors, apply only to solar collectors not associated with a solar energy project (i.e., smaller or non-commercial systems) and are therefore not applicable here.

A continuous vegetative buffer shall be present and maintained at all times around the perimeter of the exterior of the fencing and gates which are required around the perimeter of the solar farms. The buffer shall be composed of trees or shrubs a minimum of 4 feet in height at planting and maintained at not less than 6 feet in height at maturity, spaced no more than ten feet apart, and shall shield screen the project site from surrounding properties during all seasons. Existing vegetation may be used if adequate and supplemented as needed. The buffer shall be depicted on the Site Plan and maintained in good condition. Failure to maintain the buffer constitutes a violation. These requirements continue even if the solar farm is no longer operational until dismantled and removed. Additionally, the site plan must include vegetative buffers and setbacks, and the layout shall preserve existing views from public thoroughfares by setbacks and vegetative buffering. These requirements apply to utility scale solar energy projects as defined in the ordinance.

Warning signage shall be placed on solar equipment to the extent appropriate or legally required. Solar equipment shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the solar energy project. All signs, flags, streamers or similar items, both temporary and permanent, are prohibited on solar equipment except as follows: (a) manufacturer's or installer's identification; (b) appropriate warning signs and placards; (c) signs that may be required by a federal agency; (d) signs that provide a 24-hour emergency contact phone number and warn of any danger. Educational signs providing information about the project and benefits of renewable energy may be allowed as provided in the local sign ordinance.

Sec. 22-234.70 B states: 'A Solar energy project with a disturbance zone in excess of five acres, requires a conditional use permit. The applicant may offer and the county may accept conditions reasonably related to the project in accordance with Va. Code § 15.2-2288.8.' The text does not specify any particular zoning districts where this applies. Other uses such as 'Solar collectors not associated with a solar energy project' are permitted in any zoning district provided they meet certain standards outlined in Sec. 22-234.69 and Sec. 22-234.70 A.
section: Sec. 22-234.70 – Allowable Zoning Districts, Conditional Use Permits, Comprehensive Plan, Revenue Share, Siting Agreements, Applicable Codes and Inspections

summary: Sec. 22-234.53(6) requires the site plan to include a Community Impact Assessment and may require "photo or other realistic simulations or modeling of the proposed solar energy project from potentially sensitive locations as deemed necessary by the planning director to assess the visual impact of the project." Sec. 22-234.59 states: "The applicant shall demonstrate through project siting and proposed mitigation, if necessary, that the solar project minimizes impacts on the visual character of features including but not limited to schools, churches, structures with documented historic significance, a scenic landscape, State scenic river, State rural historic district, scenic vista, or scenic corridor as identified in the comprehensive plan."

Section 5-2003, item 4 states: 'Solar panels shall not cover more than 80% of the project area.' This is the explicit maximum land coverage allowed for Utility Scale Solar projects. Other related restrictions include a maximum project size of 1,000 acres (item 1) and limits on the percentage of land in a 2.5 mile radius that can be used for new projects (item 2), but these do not specify maximum land coverage as a fraction or percentage of the project area. The unit 'percent' refers to the proportion of the project area covered by solar panels.
section: 5-2003 Additional Standards for Utility Scale Solar Projects

summary: The owner or operator of a Utility Scale Solar facility shall completely decommission a facility within 12 months if the facility ceases to generate electricity for a continuous period of 12 months. The Board of Supervisors may extend this period if the owner or operator provides evidence that the failure to generate electricity is due to circumstances beyond their control and the facility has not been abandoned. A decommissioning plan shall be submitted with the Site Plan application. Decommissioning shall include the removal of all solar collectors, cabling, electrical components, fencing and any other associated equipment, facilities and structures to a depth of at least 36 inches and stabilization of the site. The plan shall include the anticipated life of the project; the estimated decommissioning cost in current dollars; how said estimate was determined; and the manner in which the project will be decommissioned. The full estimate of decommissioning shall be guaranteed by escrow at a federally insured financial institution, irrevocable letter of credit or surety bond prior to a building permit being issued. The decommissioning cost guarantee shall remain valid until the solar energy facility has been fully decommissioned. The cost estimate shall be recalculated every five (5) years and the surety increased when the recalculated estimate exceeds the guarantee amount by 10%. The facility owner/operator shall notify the Zoning Administrator by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal.
section: 5-2003 Additional Standards for Utility Scale Solar Projects

summary: All property containing panels shall be enclosed with chain link fencing not less than six (6) feet in height, topped with an appropriate anti-climbing device, and secured with gates. Fencing shall be installed on the interior of any buffer.
section: 5-2003 Additional Standards for Utility Scale Solar Projects

summary: A glint and glare study is required that demonstrates either that the panels will be sited, designed, and installed to eliminate glint and glare effects on roadway users, nearby residences, commercial areas, and other sensitive viewing locations, or that the applicant will use all reasonably available mitigation techniques to reduce glint and glare to the lowest achievable levels. Additionally, solar panel components shall have a UL listing and shall be designed with an anti-reflective coating. Individual arrays/panels shall be designed and installed in order to prevent glare toward buildings on adjacent properties and vehicular traffic.
section: 3. A Special Exception application for a Utility Scale Solar project

summary: Solar panels shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet in height measured from existing grade below the panel and the lowest surface of the panel shall be a minimum of eighteen (18) inches above grade.
section: 5-2003 Additional Standards for Utility Scale Solar Projects

summary: The maximum project size for individual Utility Scale Solar projects shall not exceed one thousand (1,000) acres. Projects consisting of multiple parcels shall be contiguous in order to be considered part of the project. This is the explicit maximum lot, parcel, or tract size allowed for Utility Scale Solar projects. Other related restrictions include that no more than eight percent of the land in a two and one-half mile radius of the project area of any existing utility scale solar project shall be approved for use as the project area for a new utility scale solar project, but this is not a direct maximum size limit. The unit for the maximum size is acres.
section: 5-2003 Additional Standards for Utility Scale Solar Projects

summary: Solar equipment shall not be placed within the minimum setback required by the district within projects that consist of multiple parcels. The following additional minimum setbacks shall apply from all solar equipment: a. 100’ setback to the project boundary. Additionally, a vegetated buffer shall be required that consists of a landscaped strip at least 50 feet wide measured from each boundary line of the project around the entire perimeter. The 100-foot setback to the project boundary is the most restrictive fixed distance setback directly pertaining to property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, or parcels.
section: 5-2003 Additional Standards for Utility Scale Solar Projects

summary: Solar equipment and panels shall be set back a distance of 1,000 feet from a right-of-way line of a street identified as a Corridor of Statewide Significance. The setback may be modified by the Board of Supervisors upon demonstration the panels will not impact the viewshed from the identified corridor with the Special Exception application. Other setbacks include a 100-foot setback to the project boundary, but the 1,000-foot setback is the most restrictive distance directly pertaining to roads.
section: 5-2003 Additional Standards for Utility Scale Solar Projects

summary: Section 5-2003.13 requires "a vegetated buffer ... at least 50 feet wide measured from each boundary line of the project around the entire perimeter" with "a buffer of plant materials that are mature enough to effectively screen the view, to eight feet above ground level, of the solar panels from adjacent properties all year around." Screening "shall be fully established within five years and effectively maintained for the life of the project." The plants used shall be "Non-invasive plant species, pollinator–friendly and wildlife-friendly native plants, shrubs and trees." Section 5-2003.12 requires "All property containing panels shall be enclosed with chain link fencing not less than six (6) feet in height, topped with an appropriate anti-climbing device, and secured with gates. Fencing shall be installed on the interior of any buffer." Section 5-2003.15 states that "When a buffer is not required based on the results of a viewshed analysis, buffer requirements may be waived or modified when the adjoining property is subject to an active agricultural use and the adjoining property owner(s) agree that no buffer is necessary or a reduced buffer is acceptable."
section: 5-2003 Additional Standards for Utility Scale Solar Projects

summary: The ordinance states: 'The following additional minimum setbacks shall apply from all solar equipment: ... b. 150’ setback to any existing residential dwelling.' This setback applies to Utility Scale Solar projects and is a fixed distance. Other setbacks mentioned include a 100’ setback to the project boundary and a 1,000 feet setback from a right-of-way line of a street identified as a Corridor of Statewide Significance, but these do not pertain to occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, or residences.
section: 5-2003 Additional Standards for Utility Scale Solar Projects

summary: A viewshed analysis utilizing a scaled elevation view and other supporting drawings and photographs of the proposed site, or other realistic simulation or modeling of the proposed solar energy project to assess the visual impact of the project is required (Section 3.C). Additionally, when a buffer is not required based on the results of a viewshed analysis, buffer requirements may be waived or modified when the adjoining property is subject to an active agricultural use and the adjoining property owner(s) agree that no buffer is necessary or a reduced buffer is acceptable (Section 5-2003.15).
