summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Utility-Scale Solar Generation Facilities. Section 25-147(d) states that the Site Development plan shall include a detailed decommissioning plan providing: procedures and requirements for removal of all solar energy infrastructure, equipment, facilities, or devices at the end of the useful life or if deemed abandoned; provisions for restoration and regeneration of soil and vegetation; the anticipated life of the facility; the estimated overall cost of decommissioning and methodology; and the plan for disposal of each component material type. Financial assurance of decommissioning is required unless the facility is owned by a public utility, including surety posted prior to operation and updated cost estimates every five years. The applicant or successor must decommission within six months after cessation of use, or the property owner must do so using bonded resources. The County may commence decommissioning if the applicant, successor, and property owner fail to do so, with rights to access property and surety funds. All physical improvements and equipment must be removed within 90 days of decommissioning. A Reclamation Plan is required as part of site plan approval, including removal and recycling of infrastructure, final land surface conditions, restoration of soil and vegetation, final contours and grades, and disposal plans. Partial decommissioning obligations also apply. Other sections address application requirements, environmental and cultural resource reports, landscaping, fencing, setbacks, and performance standards, but these do not replace or negate the decommissioning requirements.

Section 25-147(a)(5)(d) states: 'The facility area shall be enclosed by security fencing not less than eight feet in height and equipped with appropriate anticlimbing device such as strands of barbed wire on top of the fence. The height and/or location of the fence may be altered in the conditions for a particular permit. Fencing must be installed on the interior of the vegetative buffer required so that it is screened from the ground level view of adjacent property owners. The fencing shall always be maintained while the facility is in operation and posted with appropriate safety messaging. Fencing height and design shall be coordinated with the Department of Wildlife Resources regarding wildlife fencing that would allow ingress and egress.' This fencing requirement applies explicitly to Utility Scale Solar Generation Facilities as defined in the ordinance. Other related requirements include vegetative buffers, setbacks, landscaping, and security lighting, but fencing is specifically detailed as above.

Section 25-147(a)(5)(a) requires that the solar facility "shall utilize only panels that employ anti-glare technology, antireflective coatings, and other available mitigation techniques, all that meet or exceed industry standards, to reduce glint and glare." Additionally, subsection (i) mandates that "the applicant must also provide a glint and glare study that demonstrates that the panels will be sited, designed, and installed to eliminate glint and glare effects on airport operations" for facilities located within one mile of an airport. These provisions explicitly regulate glare for Utility Scale Solar Generation Facilities.

The ordinance states: 'Ground-mounted solar energy generation facilities shall not exceed a height of 15 feet, which shall be measured from the highest natural grade below each solar panel.' This height limit applies specifically to Utility-Scale Solar Generation Facilities. The limit does not apply to utility poles and the interconnection to the overhead electric utility grid that meet State Corporation Commission requirements.

The facility area shall be set back a distance of at least a minimum 150 feet from all property lines and public rights of way. Increased setbacks over 150 feet and additional buffering may be included in the conditions for a permit as required to reduce the visual impact of the facility.

The facility area shall be set back a distance of at least a minimum 150 feet from all property lines and public rights of way. Increased setbacks over 150 feet and additional buffering may be included in the conditions for a permit as required to reduce the visual impact of the facility.

Section 25-147(a)(3) requires the applicant to submit a landscaping and screening plan with the location, size, and type of planting yards including the use of existing and newly installed vegetation to screen the facility. Section 25-147(a)(5)(e) mandates "A vegetative buffer sufficient to mitigate the visual impact of the facility as approved by the Zoning Administrator is required. The buffer shall consist of a landscaping strip at least 30 feet wide, shall be located within the setbacks required under subsection (3) above, and shall run around the entirety of the area proposed for development. The buffer shall consist of existing vegetation and as needed, an installed landscaped strip consisting of multiple rows of staggered trees and other vegetation. This buffer should include vegetation a minimum of 6 feet high at planting and reasonably expected to grow to full maturity within three years." The ordinance further requires use of "Non-invasive plant species and pollinator-friendly and wildlife-friendly native plants, shrubs, trees, grasses, forbs and wildflowers must be used in the vegetative buffer following Virginia Pollinator-Smart Program best practices." Screening and/or buffer creation requirements may be waived or altered for alternative designs such as landscaped berms, existing wetlands or woodlands, if the berms, wetlands or woodlands are permanently protected and maintained for use as a buffer. Fencing must be installed on the interior of the vegetative buffer so that it is screened from ground level view of adjacent property owners. The vegetative buffer shall be maintained for the life of the facility.

The ordinance requires that Utility-Scale Solar Generation Facilities obtain approval of Erosion and Sedimentation Control plans prior to any grading, permitting, or construction (Sec. 25-147(b)(4)(a)). An Environmental Impact Report must address soil including erosion, siltation, toxicity, productivity, and suitability for agriculture (Sec. 25-147(d)(4)(c)(i)). The decommissioning and reclamation plans must include provisions for the restoration and regeneration of soil and vegetation with descriptions of pre-construction and desired post-construction conditions including productivity goals for agricultural viability (Sec. 25-147(d)(6)(c)). These requirements apply specifically to Utility-Scale Solar Generation Facilities, defined as projects designed to interconnect with the electrical grid and/or serve facilities not adjacent or under common ownership. The ordinance also includes requirements for landscaping, vegetative buffers, and maintenance of site features, but these are not explicitly soil, erosion, or sediment control requirements. Small Solar Generation Facilities have separate provisions that do not include explicit soil, erosion, or sediment control requirements.

Utility-Scale Solar Generation Facility may be allowed in Franklin County by issuance of a Special Use Permit by the Board of Supervisors in the A-1, M-1, M-2, PCD, and REP districts. Small Solar Generation Facilities are a permitted accessory use in all zoning districts where structures of any sort are allowed, subject to certain requirements. The text distinguishes between 'Solar Generation Facility, Small' (allowed by right with supplemental regulations) and 'Facility, Utility-Scale' (requiring a Special Use Permit).

The ordinance requires that applications for Utility-Scale Solar Generation Facilities include 'photo or other realistic simulations or modeling of the proposed solar energy facility from potentially sensitive locations as deemed necessary by the zoning administrator to assess the visual impact of the facility' (Sec. 25-147(a)(2)(k)). It mandates that 'the solar facility shall minimize impacts on viewsheds, including from residential areas and areas of scenic, historical, cultural, archeological, and recreational significance' (Sec. 25-147(a)(5)(a)). Applicants must submit a 'Generalized Landscaping and screening plan' and a 'vegetative buffer sufficient to mitigate the visual impact of the facility as approved by the Zoning Administrator' (Sec. 25-147(a)(3) and (a)(5)(e)). The zoning administrator may require 'scaled elevation view and other supporting drawings, photographs of the proposed site, photo or other realistic simulations or modeling' and other information to assess visual impact (Sec. 25-147(a)(2)(k)). These requirements apply specifically to Utility-Scale Solar Generation Facilities, defined as projects designed to interconnect with the electrical grid and/or serve facilities not adjacent or under common ownership. The ordinance distinguishes these from Small Solar Generation Facilities, which have separate, less detailed visual impact provisions. Other options include the requirement for a Special Use Permit, community meetings, and environmental and cultural resource reports, but these are not exclusively about visual impact assessment.

Section 716.05 Decommissioning requires that the site development plan for a solar energy system include a detailed decommissioning plan with: (1) Procedures and requirements for removal of all solar energy infrastructure, equipment, facilities, or devices at the end of the useful life or if deemed abandoned; (2) Provisions for restoration and regeneration of soil and vegetation with description of pre-construction and desired post-construction conditions including productivity goals for agricultural viability; (3) The anticipated life of the facility; (4) The estimated overall cost of decommissioning in current dollars and methodology for determining such estimate; (5) The way the facility will be decommissioned including disposal plans; and (6) Updates to the plan and cost estimate every five years. Financial assurance in the form of certified funds, cash escrow, bond, letter of credit, or parent guarantee is required unless owned by a public utility. Decommissioning must commence within six months after cessation of use and be completed within twelve months. The County may undertake decommissioning using surety funds if the owner fails to do so, with excess costs becoming a tax lien. All physical improvements must be removed within ninety days of decommissioning. A reclamation plan is required as part of site plan approval, including removal and recycling of infrastructure, final land surface conditions, soil and vegetation restoration, final contours and grades, and disposal plans. Partial decommissioning is also addressed and must comply with the plan. These requirements apply to community and utility scale solar energy systems as defined in Section 716.01-3 (utility scale defined as ground mounted solar energy system with capacity over five megawatts).

The ordinance requires that "The facility area containing equipment, panels, and/or supporting accessory structures shall be enclosed by security fencing not less than eight (8) feet in height." The fencing "must be installed on the interior of the vegetative buffer required so that it is screened from the ground level view of adjacent property owners." The fencing "shall always be maintained while the facility is in operation and posted with appropriate safety messaging." This applies to solar energy system, utility scale, defined as "A ground mounted solar energy system that connects to a distribution network which has the capacity to produce more than five megawatts." Other requirements for community and utility scale solar energy systems include setbacks, vegetative buffers, anti-glare technology, lighting, safety standards, and decommissioning plans, but fencing is specifically detailed in subsection (f) under 716.03-1 Requirements for Solar Energy System, Community and Utility Scale.
section: 716.03 REQUIREMENTS FOR SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEM, COMMUNITY AND UTILITY SCALE

summary: Section 716.03-1(E)(1)(a) requires that solar facilities located within one (1) mile of an airport must submit a glint and glare study demonstrating that the panels will be operated, sited, designed, and installed to eliminate glint and glare effects on airport operations. Section 716.03-1(E)(1)(d)(i) mandates that the facility shall utilize only panels that employ anti-glare technology, anti-reflective coatings, and other available mitigation techniques, all that meet or exceed industry standards, to reduce glint and glare. These requirements apply to solar energy system, community and utility scale as defined in Sections 716.01-2 and 716.01-3, which include ground mounted solar energy systems with capacity to produce five or less megawatts (community scale) and more than five megawatts (utility scale).

Ground-mounted solar energy panels shall not exceed a height of fifteen (15) feet, which shall be measured from the highest natural grade below each solar panel to the highest point of the panel at its tallest position. This limit shall not apply to utility poles and the interconnection to the overhead electric utility grid that meet existing state and federal requirements.
section: 716.03 REQUIREMENTS FOR SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEM, COMMUNITY AND UTILITY SCALE

summary: The ordinance defines a 'solar energy system, community scale' as a ground mounted solar energy system that connects to a distribution network which has the capacity to produce five or less megawatts, and a 'solar energy system, utility scale' as one that connects to a distribution network which has the capacity to produce more than five megawatts (Section 716.01-2 and 716.01-3). Additionally, Section 302.147 restricts commercial solar farms exceeding 1 megawatt under the Public Utilities section, but the main zoning provisions for utility scale systems apply to those over 5 megawatts. The units for these size limits are megawatts (MW). No maximum number of systems or solar panels is specified.

Solar energy system, utility scale as defined in Section 716.01-3 are permitted as a conditional use in all zones except for R-1, R-2, MH-1 and FH-1. Solar Energy System, Accessory Use is deemed to be an accessory use in all zones. Solar energy system, community scale and utility scale are permitted as a conditional use in all zones except the four listed.

The facilities photovoltaic panels, equipment, and accessory structures shall be set back a distance of at least a minimum one hundred (100) feet from all property lines and public rights of way. Increased setbacks over one hundred (100) feet may be included in the conditions for a permit as required to reduce the visual impact of the facility to adjacent residential districts, agriculture and conservation districts, lands under a conservation easement, or historic districts registered through the National Register of Historic Places or the Virginia Landmarks Register or to mitigate other impacts.
section: 716.03 REQUIREMENTS FOR SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEM, COMMUNITY AND UTILITY SCALE

summary: A vegetative buffer sufficient to mitigate the visual impact of the facility as approved by the zoning administrator is required. The buffer shall, at minimum, consist of a landscaping strip at least 30 feet wide, located within the setbacks required. The buffer shall consist of existing vegetation and as needed, an installed landscaped strip consisting of multiple rows of staggered trees and other vegetation, with vegetation a minimum of three (3) feet high at planting and reasonably expected to grow to a minimum of 15 feet at full maturity. The planning commission or board of supervisors may require additional or taller vegetative buffering in certain situations, such as proximity to residential districts, conservation districts, or historic districts. Non-invasive plant species and pollinator-friendly and wildlife-friendly native plants must be used following Virginia Pollinator-Smart Program best practices. Screening and/or buffer creation requirements may be waived or altered for alternative designs such as landscaped berms, existing wetlands, or woodlands, if these are permanently protected and maintained for use as a buffer. Existing trees and vegetation must be maintained within buffer areas except where dead, diseased, or necessary for development or healthy growth, and may supplement or satisfy landscaping requirements. If disturbed, new plantings shall be provided at least three (3) feet tall at planting. The vegetative buffer shall be maintained for the life of the facility. Additionally, a landscaping and screening plan must be submitted with the application, including location, size, and general type of plantings, with a detailed plan required at site plan review. Fencing must be installed on the interior of the vegetative buffer so it is screened from ground level view. These requirements apply to solar energy system, community and utility scale, with utility scale defined as ground mounted solar energy systems with capacity to produce more than five megawatts.

Section 716.04-3(2)(a) requires approval of a site development plan and erosion and sediment control plans as defined by the County Code prior to any construction. All solar generation facilities shall require a site development plan and all other documentation and approvals required by law, including those provided for any conditional use permit. Erosion and sediment control plans and stormwater maintenance plans shall be submitted to the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality for review and approval. Additionally, Section 716.05 requires a decommissioning plan that includes provisions for the restoration and regeneration of soil and vegetation with a description of pre-construction and desired post-construction conditions including productivity goals for agricultural viability. These requirements apply to solar energy system, utility scale, defined as ground mounted solar energy systems that connect to a distribution network with capacity to produce more than five megawatts.

summary: Solar energy system, utility scale (defined as a ground mounted solar energy system with capacity to produce more than five megawatts) are permitted as a conditional use in all zones except for R-1, R-2, MH-1 and FH-1. Conditional use implies approval by a zoning appeals board or meeting certain conditions like completing a permitting process. Solar energy system, accessory use is permitted as an accessory use in all zones with approval procedures required for accessory uses. Solar energy system, community scale (capacity five megawatts or less) is also permitted as a conditional use in the same zones as utility scale.

Section 716.03-1.B.(10) requires "photo or other realistic simulations or modeling of the proposed solar energy facility from adjoining properties, and potentially sensitive locations" to assess visual impact. Section 716.03-1.B.(11) allows the zoning administrator to require "additional information... to assess the visual impact of the facility." A "generalized landscaping and screening plan" must be submitted (716.03-1.C), and a vegetative buffer "sufficient to mitigate the visual impact of the facility as approved by the zoning administrator is required" (716.03-1.E.(e)). Section 716.04-3.(e)(iii)(7) requires submission of a report addressing "Visual" impacts as part of environmental and cultural resources reports. Section 716.04-4 lists criteria for evaluation including "The proximity of the site to, observability from, and impact on urban and residential areas," "areas of scenic significance," "public rights-of-way," and other sensitive areas. These requirements apply to solar energy system, utility scale, defined as systems with capacity to produce more than five megawatts connected to a distribution network. Other requirements include a project narrative, concept plan, environmental and cultural resources identification, and performance standards related to setbacks, height, fencing, and lighting, but these are not specifically visual impact assessment requirements.

A decommissioning plan shall be submitted for review and approval with the initial plan of development. The plan must include contact information for the party responsible for decommissioning, a timeline and written description of decommissioning procedures including removal of all facility-related equipment and restoration of the land to a natural condition or other approved state, a detailed cost estimate prepared by a licensed engineer, and a surety payable to the county equal to the estimated costs. The plan must be updated every three years. The director of community development must be notified 30 days prior to decommissioning. Decommissioning must be completed within 1 year of notice or abandonment. If the owner/operator fails to comply, the county may remove the facility using the surety and seek to recover costs. "Natural condition" means stabilization of soil to a minimum depth of 3 feet and restoration of site vegetation and topography to pre-existing condition, subject to plan of development review. Recycling or disposal of solar panels in Goochland County is not permitted. Additional conditions include maintenance of a dry-waste container for damaged panels and notification requirements for changes in ownership. These requirements apply specifically to Solar Energy Facility, Principal (SEFP) as defined in the ordinance.

summary: Section 3-14.3.6.10 Decommissioning and Reclamation requires that solar facilities which have reached the end of their useful life or have not been in active and continuous service for a period of 6 months shall be removed at the owner’s or operator’s expense, except if the project is being repowered or a force majeure event has or is occurring requiring longer repairs. The owner or operator shall notify the Zoning Administrator by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal. Decommissioning shall be performed in compliance with an approved Decommissioning Plan, which must be submitted for approval by the Board of Supervisors prior to the issuance of a Zoning Permit. Decommissioning includes removal of all electric systems, buildings, cabling, electrical components, security barriers, roads, foundations, pilings, and any other associated facilities, so that any agricultural ground upon which the facility was located is again tillable and suitable for agricultural uses. The site shall be graded and re-seeded to restore it to as natural a condition as possible within 12 months of removal of facilities. Hazardous material shall be disposed of in accordance with federal and state law. The estimated cost of decommissioning shall be guaranteed by the deposit of funds in an escrow account equal to the estimated cost plus 10%, with provisions for recalculation every five years and possible alternative securities such as performance bonds or letters of credit. If the owner or operator fails to remove the installation as required, the County may collect the surety and remove the installation. These requirements apply to utility-scale solar facilities, defined as those with rated capacity over 100 kW and specifically as Large-Scale Solar Energy Facilities.

For large-scale solar facilities, such facilities shall be enclosed by security fencing on the interior of the buffer area (not to be seen by other properties) at a minimum of 7 feet in height and topped with razor/barbed wire, as appropriate. The height and/or location of the fence may be altered in the conditions for any particular special use permit. Fencing must be installed on the interior of the vegetative buffer. Fencing shall be placed around sections of the infrastructure (not the entire site) to provide access corridors for wildlife to navigate through the facility. All fencing shall be constructed so as to substantially lessen the likelihood of entry into a solar facility by unauthorized individuals. A performance bond reflecting the costs of anticipated fence maintenance shall be posted and maintained. Failure to maintain the security fencing shall result in revocation of the discretionary-use Permit and the facility’s decommissioning.

Section 3-14.3.4.10 Lighting: For large-scale solar facilities, proposed lighting fixtures as approved by the County to minimize off-site glare and shall be the minimum necessary for safety and/or security purposes. No facility shall produce glare that would constitute a nuisance to the public. Any exceptions shall be enumerated on the Concept Plan and approved by the Zoning Administrator. Lighting on the site shall comply with any Dark Skies Ordinance the Board of Supervisors may adopt or, from time to time, amend.

Section 3-14.3.4.4 states: 'For accessory, small-, and large-scale solar facilities, the maximum height of the lowest edge of photovoltaic panels shall be 10 feet as measured from the finished grade. The maximum height of panels, buildings, structures and other components of a solar facility shall be 15 feet, which shall be measured from the highest natural grade below each element.' This limit does not apply to utility poles, substations, or the interconnection to the overhead electric utility grid. The Board of Supervisors may approve a greater height based upon the demonstration of a significant need where the impacts of increased height are mitigated. The units for height are feet. The ordinance applies this height restriction explicitly to large-scale solar facilities, defined as ground-mounted solar facilities with rated capacity of one megawatt (MW) alternating current or greater.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'The maximum project area of a solar facility shall be 500 acres.' This applies to Large-Scale Solar Energy Facilities, defined as ground-mounted solar facilities with rated capacity of one megawatt (MW) or greater. Additional related restrictions include that solar panel coverage may not exceed 65 percent of the total acreage, and other location and setback requirements, but the maximum lot size is specifically limited to 500 acres.

Section 3-14.3.6.1 Noise/Sound states: 'Audible sound from solar facilities shall not exceed sixty (60) decibels, as measured from any adjacent non-participating landowners' property line.' This applies to solar facilities subject to a Special Use Permit, which includes utility-scale solar power facilities (defined as those with rated capacity over 100 kW, thus encompassing Large-Scale Solar Energy Facilities). The unit for noise level is assumed to be dBA as standard for noise measurements.

The ordinance explicitly states: 'No solar facility shall be located within 2 miles of another existing or permitted large-scale solar facility.' This minimum separation distance applies to Large-Scale Solar Energy Facilities, defined as ground-mounted solar facilities with rated capacity of one megawatt (MW) alternating current or greater. Other related location standards include setbacks from town or city boundaries and certain zoning districts, but the 2-mile distance between large-scale solar facilities is the explicit minimum separation distance with other existing or planned solar energy conversion systems. The unit 'miles' is used as stated in the text.

The minimum setback of structures and uses associated with the facility, including fencing, PV panels, parking areas, and outdoor storage, but not including landscaping and berming, shall be: 150 feet from adjacent property lines. The Planning Commission may recommend and the Board of Supervisors may require increased setbacks up to 300 feet in situations where the height of structures or the topography affects the visual impact of the facility. These setback requirements shall not apply to the internal property lines of those parcels on which a solar facility is located. Access, erosion and stormwater structures, and interconnection to the electrical grid may be made through setback areas provided that such are generally perpendicular to the property line.

The minimum setback of structures and uses associated with the facility, including fencing, PV panels, parking areas, and outdoor storage, but not including landscaping and berming, shall be 150 feet from all public rights-of-way. The Planning Commission may recommend and the Board of Supervisors may require increased setbacks up to 300 feet in situations where the height of structures or the topography affects the visual impact of the facility. These setback requirements shall not apply to the internal property lines of those parcels on which a solar facility is located.

For large-scale solar facilities, such facilities, including security fencing that is not ornamental, shall be screened from the ground-level view of adjacent properties and public streets by a buffer zone at least 100’ in width. The buffer shall be located within the setbacks required under this Section and shall run around the entire perimeter of the property. The buffer shall be maintained for the life of the facility. Screening may also be required in other locations to screen specific uses or structures. A recommendation that the screening and/or buffer creation requirements be waived or altered may be made by the Planning Commission when the applicant proposes to use existing wetlands or woodlands to satisfy the screening requirement. The wetlands or woodlands shall be permanently protected as a designated buffer and the overall buffer shall measure at least 75 feet. Screening methods may include: (a) Existing Screening: Existing vegetation, topography, buildings, open space, or other elements located on the site may be considered as part of the required screening. (b) Vegetative Screening: In the event existing vegetation or landforms providing the screening are inadequate or disturbed, new plantings shall be provided in a landscaped strip at least 50 feet wide. Landscaping intended for screening shall consist of a combination of non-invasive species, pollinator species, and native plants, shrubs, trees, grasses, forbs, and wildflowers. Trees intended for screening shall consist of a combination of evergreen and deciduous trees that are 5-6 ft. in height at time of planting. A triple row of trees shall be placed on average at 15 feet on center. (c) Berming: Berms shall generally be constructed with a 3:1 side slope to rise ratio, 4-6 ft. above the adjacent grade, with a 3 ft. wide top with appropriate pollinator-friendly native plants, shrubs, trees, forbs, and wildflowers. The outside edges of the berm shall be sculpted such that there are vertical and horizontal undulations to give variations in appearance. (d) Opaque Architectural Fencing: Fencing intended for screening shall be at least 50 percent visually solid as viewed on any line perpendicular to the fence from adjacent property or a public street. Such fencing may be used in combination with other screening methods but shall not be the primary method. A typical example is the use of wood privacy fencing and landscaping to screen structures such as substations. Depending on the location, ornamental features may be required on the fence. Fencing material shall not include plastic slats.

Section 3-14.3.4.11 Signage: For all solar facilities, no signage of any type may be placed on the facility other than notices, warnings, and identification information required by law. Warning signage shall be placed on solar equipment to the extent appropriate or legally required. Solar equipment shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the solar energy project. All signs, flags, streamers, or similar items, both temporary and permanent, are prohibited on solar equipment except as follows: a. manufacturer's or installer's identification; b. appropriate warning signs and placards; c. signs that may be required by a federal or state agency; and d. signs that provide a 24-hour emergency contact phone number and warn of any danger. Educational signs providing information about the project and benefits of renewable energy may be allowed as provided in the local sign ordinance.

The ordinance explicitly requires a draft grading plan for Large-Scale Solar Energy Facilities that "limits grading to the greatest extent practicable" and includes: "existing and proposed contours; locations and amount of topsoil to be stripped and stockpiled onsite (if any); percent of the site to be graded; an earthwork balance achieved on-site with no import or export of soil; and indication of natural flow patterns in drainage design and amount of impervious surface." Additionally, for large-scale solar facilities, "ground cover on the site shall be native vegetation and maintained in accordance with the landscaping plan in accordance with established performance measures." The operator must post a performance bond for maintenance costs, and failure to maintain ground cover may result in revocation of the Special Use Permit and decommissioning. The County reserves the right to request soil and water testing. These requirements apply to "Large-Scale Solar Energy Facility: A ground-mounted solar facility that generates electricity from sunlight on an area adequate to support a rated capacity of one megawatt (MW) alternating current or greater."

Utility scale solar power facilities will require a Special Use Permit. For the purpose of this Ordinance Utility Scale Solar are those systems with rated capacity of over 100 KW of electricity. By adding  "Large-Scale Solar Energy Facilities in accordance with Section 3.14"  in the lists of Special Uses Permitted for the Rural Farm District (RF) and Industrial (I) District (IND) zoning districts. Solar facilities are permitted either by-right or subject to a Special Use Permit as specified within the applicable zoning districts in Article 4. Solar photovoltaic and solar thermal systems with rated capacity of under 100KW or the equivalent is allowed in all zone districts.

The minimum setback of structures and uses associated with the facility, including fencing, PV panels, parking areas, and outdoor storage, but not including landscaping and berming, shall be: 250 feet from a dwelling. The Planning Commission may recommend and the Board of Supervisors may require increased setbacks up to 300 feet in situations where the height of structures or the topography affects the visual impact of the facility. Other setback requirements include 150 feet from adjacent property lines and 150 feet from all public rights-of-way, but these do not pertain to dwellings.

Section 3-14.3.3.5 Visual Impact Analysis requires "an analysis demonstrating project siting and proposed mitigation, if necessary, so that the proposed facility minimizes impacts on the visual character, viewsheds, and/or vistas of the County." The analysis must include "accurate, to scale, photographic simulations showing the relationship of the facility and its associated equipment and development to its surroundings" from locations such as property lines, roadways, and/or scenic viewsheds/vistas as deemed necessary by the County. The number of simulations and perspectives are established by the Zoning Administrator after the pre-application meeting. Visual representations must be in color and include "actual pre-construction photographs and accurate post-construction simulations of the height and breadth of the facility," including existing and proposed buildings and tree coverage. This requirement applies to all solar facilities requiring a Special Use Permit, which includes utility scale solar power facilities defined as those with rated capacity over 100 KW. Other application requirements include a Project Narrative, Concept Plan, Grading Plan, Landscape Plan, Community Impact Assessment, Environmental Impact Assessment, Traffic and Transportation Assessment, and Decommissioning and Reclamation Plan. The ordinance defines Large-Scale Solar Energy Facility as "a ground-mounted solar facility that generates electricity from sunlight on an area adequate to support a rated capacity of one megawatt (MW) alternating current or greater." Utility scale solar power facilities require a Special Use Permit. The ordinance also includes procedural requirements such as a pre-application meeting, neighborhood meeting, Comprehensive Plan Review, and potential third-party review. The Board of Supervisors may waive certain requirements such as the siting agreement. The ordinance explicitly excludes glare restrictions from visual impact assessment requirements.

Decommissioning of utility-scale solar generation facilities requires the project to be "deconstructed and removed within 12 months after the project sites are permanently decommissioned." "Deconstructed and removed" means removal of all project facilities and appurtenances including permanent foundations (except structural members three feet or more in the ground that break off), filling and compacting trenches or excavations, removal of debris, and providing a phase II environmental site assessment report to the county. Disposal of solar panels in county landfills is prohibited. County staff will review the decommissioning report for approval or denial, and properties must be restored to be "ready for agricultural or forestal use, preserving and protecting the county's rural and agricultural character." A site development plan for a utility-scale solar generation facility must include a detailed decommissioning plan with procedures for removal, estimated costs, and methodology. The responsible party must enter a written project development agreement with the county, including provisions that if the facility ceases generating electricity for more than 12 months, it will be decommissioned; the county may enter the property to decommission if the responsible party defaults; financial assurance covering 100% of estimated decommissioning costs must be provided; and salvage value of materials shall not offset decommissioning costs. All references to "construction" also mean "deconstruction" and "decommissioning."

For Utility-Scale Solar Energy Generation Facilities defined as "A solar energy conversion system producing a minimum of one MW or more electricity to a utility provider" and sited on 1/2 acre or more, the ordinance requires "Security fencing. Such fencing shall enclose the project area at least six feet in height and be equipped with appropriate anticlimbing devices, such as strands of barbed wire on top of the fence." The fencing "shall go on the interior of the required vegetative buffer to screen it from the ground-level view of adjacent property owners" and "Continual maintenance of the fencing shall occur while the facility is in operation." Other related requirements include vegetative buffers, setbacks, lighting, and decommissioning plans, but these do not pertain to fencing specifically.

The ordinance requires that Utility-Scale Solar Energy Generation Facilities "shall utilize only panels that employ anti-glare technology, anti-reflective coatings, and other available mitigation techniques, all of which meet or exceed industry standards, to reduce glint and glare." The applicant must provide "written certification from a qualified expert acceptable to the county that the facility's panels incorporate and utilize anti-glare technology and anti-reflective coatings, reduce glint and glare to levels that meet or exceed industry standards, and National standards." These requirements apply to solar energy conversion systems producing a minimum of one MW or more electricity to a utility provider, sited on 1/2 acre or more, and interconnected with an existing electrical grid serving other facilities not adjacent or under everyday use, ownership or control. Other related performance standards include setbacks, security fencing, vegetative buffers, height limits, lighting restrictions, and decommissioning plans, but these do not specifically address glare. Smaller or accessory solar systems such as rooftop or ground-mounted small-scale solar generation facilities have different requirements and are not subject to these glare restrictions.

Ground-mounted solar energy generation facilities shall not exceed a height of 12 feet, measured from the highest natural grade below each solar panel. This limit shall not apply to utility poles and the interconnection to the overhead electric utility grid that meet state corporation commission requirements. This restriction applies to utility-scale solar energy generation facilities defined as producing a minimum of one MW or more electricity to a utility provider and sited on 1/2 acre or more. The text distinguishes this from smaller or accessory solar systems, which have separate provisions.

The ordinance defines Solar Energy Generation Facilities as "a solar energy conversion system producing a minimum of one MW or more electricity to a utility provider" and states that "a power generating plant that is sited on 1/2 acre or more in size" qualifies as such a facility. This sets a minimum site size of one-half acre for utility-scale solar facilities. The unit for this minimum lot size is explicitly given as acres.

The project area shall be set back at least 300 feet from all abutting public rights-of-way and main buildings on adjoining parcels, and from adjacent property lines. Exceptions to this distance are possible for adjoining parcels owned or leased by the applicant. Increased setbacks over 300 feet and additional buffering may be included in the conditions for a particular permit. The buffer shall consist of a landscaping strip at least 300 feet wide, located within the setbacks required, and shall circle the entire perimeter of the property. The planning commission or board of supervisors may require increased setbacks and additional or vegetative buffering in situations where the height of structures or topography affects the visual impact of the facility.

section: Solar Energy Generation Facilities - Performance requirements, subsection (f) Setbacks

summary: The ordinance requires for Utility-Scale Solar Energy Generation Facilities (defined as producing a minimum of one MW or more electricity to a utility provider and sited on 1/2 acre or more) an opaque vegetative buffer "consisting of a landscaping strip at least 300 feet wide, shall be located within the setbacks required, and shall circle the entire perimeter of the property." The buffer must have "sufficient existing vegetation and trees to create an opaque visual barrier to screen the project area from view" or, if none exists, "four rows of staggered evergreens, ten feet apart and on 15-foot centers," with trees "at least five feet tall at the time of planting and expected to grow to a minimum height of 20 feet within ten years." Security fencing "shall go on the interior of the required vegetative buffer to screen it from the ground-level view of adjacent property owners." The planning commission or board of supervisors may require "increased setbacks and additional or vegetative buffering" based on height or topography. Maintenance of the buffer is required for the life of the facility, including replacing dead or diseased trees.
