Section 7-7-10 (K) requires "A buffer shall be located within the setbacks required under this Section and shall run around the entire perimeter of the property." This buffer "shall be maintained for the life of the facility" and "Forest resources shall be preserved by maintaining natural buffers." Section 7-7-10 (AA) mandates a Landscaping Plan "prepared by a certified landscape architect or other qualified, licensed person" that "shall indicate all ground cover, screening and buffering materials, landscaping, and elevations" and that "All landscaping, screening, and buffering shall be in accordance with Article VIII, Community Design Standards of this Ordinance." Section 7-7-10 (N) requires maintenance of "the buffer areas, and landscaping." Additionally, Section 7-7-10 (J)(1) requires that "tie lines shall be located and buffered to block visibility from public roads or other right-of-way." These provisions explicitly impose vegetative buffer and screening requirements for utility-scale solar energy facilities (minimum generation of 5 MW). Other scale categories such as medium-scale (500 KW to 5 MW) and small-scale (up to 500 KW) solar energy facilities also have landscaping and screening requirements (Sections 7-7-8 (I) and 7-7-9 (H)), but the focus here is on utility-scale systems as defined in Section 7-7-10.

Section 7-7-10 (Solar Energy, Utility-Scale), subsection (R) Signage states: "No signage of any type may be placed on the facility other than notices, warnings, and identification information required by law." Signage "shall not exceed 40 sq. ft. displaying the facility name, address, and emergency contact information, unless additional signage is required by National Electric Safety Code." Warning signage "shall be placed on solar equipment to the extent appropriate or legally required." Solar equipment "shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the solar energy project." All signs, flags, streamers, or similar items, both temporary and permanent, are prohibited on solar equipment except for: (i) Manufacturer's or installer's identification; (ii) Appropriate warning signs and placards; (iii) Signs that may be required by a federal agency; and (iv) Signs that provide a 24-hour emergency contact phone number and warn of any danger. Other sections (7-7-8 Medium-Scale and 7-7-9 Small-Scale) do not explicitly enact signage requirements for utility-scale solar energy facilities.

Section 7-7-10 (E) Land Disturbance states: 'The clearing, grading, and overall site disturbance is limited to only that which is necessary; superfluous clearing and grading is not permitted, in order to retain existing trees and other groundcover.' Section 7-7-10 (Z) Grading Plan requires: 'A Grading Plan that limits grading to the greatest practicable extent by avoiding steep slopes and laying out arrays parallel to landforms,' including details such as 'existing and proposed contours,' 'locations and amount of topsoil to be stripped and stockpiled onsite (if any),' 'percent of the site to be graded,' 'an earthwork balance achieved on-site with no import or export of soil,' and 'indication of natural flow patterns in drainage design and amount of impervious surface.' Section 7-7-10 (DD) Decommission and Reclamation Plan mandates: 'The site shall be graded and re-seeded or replanted within 12 months of removal of solar facilities to restore it to as natural a pre-development condition as possible.' These requirements explicitly regulate soil disturbance, erosion control, and sediment management for utility-scale solar energy facilities (minimum generation of 5 megawatts). Other solar energy facility categories include medium-scale (500 KW to 5 MW) and small-scale (up to 500 KW), which have similar but separate provisions. The utility-scale section applies to facilities with minimum generation of 5 MW and includes additional requirements such as buffers, setbacks, and environmental impact assessments.

Section 7-7-10(I)(1)(ii) states: 'All structures - including fences, panels, and all ancillary equipment/buildings – shall be at least 200 ft. from any residential district, planned development district, or dwelling.' Other setback distances mentioned include no minimum setbacks for interior or abutting lot lines and 100 ft. from agricultural, commercial, or industrial districts, but these do not pertain to occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, or residences.

Section 7-7-10 (W)(6) Visual Impact Analysis requires that "The applicant shall provide accurate, to scale, photographic simulations showing the relationship of the facility and its associated amenities and development to its surroundings." These simulations "shall show such views of solar structures from locations such as property lines and roadways, as deemed necessary by the municipality to assess the visual impact of the facility." The "total number of simulations and the perspectives from which they are prepared shall be established by the Administrator after the pre-application meeting." This applies specifically to utility-scale solar energy facilities with a minimum generation of 5 megawatts (5 MW). Other related requirements include a Community Impact Assessment, Environmental Impact Assessment, and various plans (Grading, Landscaping, Herbicide Land Application), but these do not explicitly address visual impact assessment. The ordinance distinguishes utility-scale (5 MW+), medium-scale (500 KW to 5 MW), and small-scale (up to 500 KW) solar energy facilities, but only the utility-scale section explicitly mandates a visual impact assessment.

All applications for Solar facilities shall be accompanied by a comprehensive decommissioning plan, as required by the King William County Solar and Energy Storage Policy. The decommission plan must include provisions addressing the removal of all materials and equipment including, but not limited to, cabling and wiring, both above and below ground; the restoration of the property to its predevelopment condition including soil remediation and reforestation; an estimate of the gross cost for the complete removal of the solar facility and all associated infrastructure; the means by which the solar provider shall reimburse the County for an independent review and analysis of the cost estimate; financial surety to King William County in an amount sufficient to undertake decommissioning activities should the owner default; updating the decommissioning cost estimate every five years and adjusting for inflation; and that decommissioning shall commence within six months after the facility ceases to produce any electricity for the distribution system to which it was connected. Utility-scale solar facilities exceeding 21 megawatts (MW) may be installed with a conditional use permit in the agricultural conservation district to provide electricity for use off-site. Medium-scale solar facilities may be installed in industrial districts to provide electricity for use on-site for commercial and industrial applications. Small-scale solar facilities may be installed by-right in all zoning districts to provide electricity to individual structures. Utility scale facilities may be no greater than one thousand (1,000) acres.

Section 86-383 requires that "Security fencing and gates shall be provided and shall be designed and located in accordance with the following: a. All security fencing shall be located on the inner edge of the buffer (the edge furthest from the property line) when possible. b. Maximum height for fencing shall be eight (8) feet. c. Fencing shall include wildlife friendly design features, where the Director of Planning deems them appropriate." Additionally, height limitations specify that "Security fencing shall be limited to eight (8) feet in height." These requirements apply to principal solar energy facilities, which include utility-scale solar facilities exceeding 21 megawatts (MW) installed with a conditional use permit in the agricultural conservation district to provide electricity for use off-site. Other types of solar facilities mentioned include medium-scale solar facilities (for on-site commercial/industrial use) and small-scale solar facilities (for individual structures), but fencing requirements are explicitly detailed only for principal (utility-scale) solar energy facilities.

Section 86-383, item 5 states: 'No building, structures, solar panel arrays or other equipment utilized on site may exceed twenty (20) feet in height above finished grade.' This height limitation applies to principal solar energy facilities, which include utility-scale solar facilities. The restriction does not apply to electric utility poles. Security fencing is limited to eight (8) feet in height.

Utility scale facilities may be no greater than one thousand (1,000) acres. This is stated explicitly in Section 86-383, item 13.a. The text also includes a project area limit stating no more than three percent of the County’s land mass shall be approved for large scale solar energy facilities, but this does not specify a maximum lot size and excludes local industries producing electricity for their own consumption. The maximum lot size is therefore 1,000 acres, with units explicitly given as acres.

No medium scale, or utility scale solar facilities shall be permitted in the Transportation Corridor Overlay District (Sec. 86-136(d)(13)). Utility-scale solar facilities exceeding 21 megawatts may be installed with a conditional use permit in the agricultural conservation district to provide electricity for use off-site (Sec. 86-382(c)). Utility-scale solar facilities are listed as conditional use (C) in the use matrix without specific district prohibitions except for overlay restrictions (Sec. 86-140). Small-scale and medium-scale solar facilities have different permissions and conditions, but only the Transportation Corridor Overlay District is explicitly stated as prohibiting medium or utility scale solar facilities unconditionally.

For photovoltaic panels, substations, and other equipment associated with the production and distribution of electricity (other than poles and wires) the following minimum buffers are required: a. One hundred fifty (150) feet from any property line or road. No panels, cabinets, or other associated equipment, exclusive of utility poles, wires, cables, access roads, fencing, and stormwater outfalls, shall be located closer than twenty-five (25) feet from the buffer. Fencing is to placed on the outside perimeter of the panel.

For photovoltaic panels, substations, and other equipment associated with the production and distribution of electricity (other than poles and wires) the following minimum buffers are required: One hundred (100) feet from RPA wetlands, rivers, streams or other environmentally sensitive features and fifty (50) feet from any wetland not associated with an RPA. No panels, cabinets, or other associated equipment; exclusive of utility poles, wires, cables, and access roads, shall be located closer than ten (10) feet from the buffer. Fencing is placed on the outside perimeter of the panel array and may conflict with the additional 10’ buffer setback.

For photovoltaic panels, substations, and other equipment associated with the production and distribution of electricity (other than poles and wires) the following minimum buffers are required: One hundred fifty (150) feet from any property line or road. No panels, cabinets, or other associated equipment, exclusive of utility poles, wires, cables, access roads, fencing, and stormwater outfalls, shall be located closer than twenty-five (25) feet from the buffer.

Section 86-383 requires buffers for photovoltaic panels, substations, and other equipment associated with electricity production and distribution: a minimum of 150 feet from any property line or road, and 100 feet from RPA wetlands, rivers, streams or other environmentally sensitive features. No panels or equipment shall be located closer than 25 feet from the buffer (except utility poles, wires, cables, access roads, fencing, and stormwater outfalls). Buffers must be landscaped according to specified standards, maximizing preservation of existing healthy vegetation, with detailed planting requirements for forested buffers and supplemental plantings if needed. Fencing is to be placed on the outside perimeter of the panel array and on the inner edge of the buffer. Surety for landscaping and a landscape maintenance schedule are required. The ordinance applies to utility-scale solar facilities exceeding 21 MW installed with a conditional use permit in the agricultural conservation district to provide electricity for use off-site. Other solar facility types include medium-scale solar facilities (conditional use in industrial districts for on-site commercial/industrial use) and small-scale solar facilities (by-right in all districts for individual structures).

Section 86-383 requires site stabilization: "Pollinator and other ecologically friendly and beneficial ground covers that promote wildlife habitats and forage are required to be planted and maintained within the facility including, but not limited to, the ground below and surrounding the solar arrays." It also mandates a decommissioning plan that includes "soil remediation, including de-compaction, to ensure agricultural soils are able to support crops or pastureland." These requirements apply to utility-scale solar facilities exceeding 21 megawatts (MW) installed with a conditional use permit in the agricultural conservation district to provide electricity for use off-site. Other scale options include small-scale solar facilities installed by-right in all zoning districts to provide electricity to individual structures, and medium-scale solar facilities installed in industrial districts to provide electricity for on-site commercial and industrial use, both requiring site plan review and approval.

Utility-scale solar facilities exceeding 21 megawatts (MW) may be installed with a conditional use permit in the agricultural conservation district to provide electricity for use off-site; provided all federal, state and local regulations have been followed (Sec. 86-382(c)). The use matrix indicates utility-scale solar facilities require a conditional use permit ("C"), but specific districts beyond AC are not fully listed. Medium-scale solar facilities require conditional use permits in some districts, and small-scale solar facilities are permitted by-right in all districts with conditions. The Transportation Corridor Overlay District prohibits medium and utility scale solar facilities (Sec. 86-136(d)(13)).

For photovoltaic panels, substations, and other equipment associated with the production and distribution of electricity (other than poles and wires) the following minimum buffers are required: One hundred (100) feet from RPA wetlands, rivers, streams or other environmentally sensitive features and fifty (50) feet from any wetland not associated with an RPA. No panels, cabinets, or other associated equipment; exclusive of utility poles, wires, cables, and access roads, shall be located closer than ten (10) feet from the buffer.

The ordinance requires that Utility Scale Solar Facilities must include a detailed decommission plan with the Site Plan submission, which "provides procedures and requirements for removal of all components of the solar facility at the end of the useful life of the solar facility or if the solar facility is deemed abandoned by the Zoning Administrator." The plan must include "the anticipated life of the solar facility," "the estimated overall cost of decommissioning the solar facility in current dollars and the methodology used for determining such estimate," and "the manner in which the solar facility will be decommissioned." The decommission plan must be approved by the Zoning Administrator prior to Site Plan approval and updated every 5 to 10 years upon request. Security in the form of "a cash escrow, a performance surety bond, an irrevocable letter of credit, or other security acceptable to the Zoning Administrator" must be provided in the amount of the approved estimated cost of decommissioning and maintained until all obligations are met. If the facility is unsafe, the owner must either "promptly repair the solar facility to meet federal, state, and local safety standards" or "remove the solar facility in accordance with the solar facility’s approved decommission plan." If the facility is abandoned (not operated for 12 continuous months), the owner must respond to the Zoning Administrator and either correct the issue or remove the facility per the approved decommission plan within 365 days, subject to possible extension. The County may pursue legal action and use the security to remove or repair the facility if the owner fails to comply. These requirements apply specifically to Utility Scale Solar Facilities permitted in the GI district.

Section 4.07.06.B.3.b states: 'The facility must use only panels that employ anti-glare technology, anti-reflective coatings, and other available mitigation techniques, all that meet or exceed industry standards to reduce glint and glare.' This applies to Utility Scale Solar Facilities that are a permitted use in the GI zoning district. Other relevant conditions include size, height, setbacks, and decommissioning requirements detailed throughout Section 4.07.06.B.

Ground-mounted solar panels must not exceed 20 feet in height as measured from the highest natural grade below each such solar panel to the top of the solar panel or its support structure, whichever is higher. This height limit does not apply to electric utility poles that are connected or interconnected with such solar panels. (Section 4.07.06.B.3.c.1)

The minimum lot size must be 20 acres (Section 4.07.06.B.3.a.2). Other minimum sizes mentioned include 500 acres for the primary parcel and 250 acres for abutting lots (Section 4.07.06.B.1.b.1 and 4.07.06.B.1.b.2), but the most restrictive (smallest) minimum lot size is 20 acres. All units are expressed in acres.

All components of the solar facility must be set back a distance of at least 25 feet from property lines, or the applicable yards and setbacks of the underlying Zoning District, Section 7.04, or Section 5.08, whichever is greatest. Other options include setbacks from public roads and buildings (75 feet), but these do not pertain to property lines or lot lines.

All components of the solar facility must be set back a distance of at least 75 feet from all public roads and buildings and at least 25 feet from property lines, or the applicable yards and setbacks of the underlying Zoning District, Section 7.04, or Section 5.08, whichever is greatest.

Utility Scale Solar Facilities that are a permitted use in the GI zoning district "must meet Section 7.04" for Landscaping/Buffering/Screening as stated in 4.07.06.B.3.e. This requirement applies to solar facilities with a nameplate capacity rating exceeding 5,000 kilowatts and minimum lot size of 20 acres. The text also references other requirements such as height limits, setbacks, visual impact mitigation, access, decommissioning plans, and security, but the explicit vegetative buffer and screening requirement is to comply with Section 7.04.

Utility Scale Solar Facilities that meet all of the following standards are a permitted use in the GI zoning district (Section 4.07.06.B.1). Unless listed as a permitted use under Section 4.07.06.B.1, Utility Scale Solar Facilities are a Special Exception use in the GI and MR-HI Zoning Districts and are subject to Section 4.07.06.B.3 (Section 4.07.06.B.2).

All components of the solar facility must be set back a distance of at least 75 feet from all buildings. This setback applies to Utility Scale Solar Facilities permitted in the GI district. The ordinance states: 'All components of the solar facility must be set back a distance of at least 75 feet from all public roads and buildings and at least 25 feet from property lines, or the applicable yards and setbacks of the underlying Zoning District, Section 7.04, or Section 5.08, whichever is greatest.' The 75 feet setback from buildings is the relevant and most restrictive setback distance from occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, and/or residences. Other setbacks mentioned (e.g., 25 feet from property lines, setbacks from public roads) are not directly related to occupied dwellings or structures.

Section 8. Decommissioning; Unsafe or abandoned projects explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for large-scale solar energy facilities. It requires that prior to operation, the applicant shall provide a final decommissioning and reclamation plan for review and approval and must provide security in the amount of the estimated cost of the decommissioning, which may include a cash escrow, performance surety bond, certified check, or other security acceptable to the County. The decommissioning cost estimate may not be reduced by estimated salvage values and must be updated every five years. If a facility is unsafe or abandoned, the owner/operator must repair or remove it within specified timeframes, with removal to be completed within 365 days of abandonment unless extended by the Board of Supervisors. The site must be restored to as natural a pre-development condition as possible, including removal of all solar electric systems, buildings, cabling, electrical components, security barriers, roads, foundations, pilings, and any other associated facilities. Hazardous materials must be disposed of in accordance with federal and state law. If the owner/operator fails to remove or repair the facility after notice, the County may pursue legal action and use the decommissioning security to remove the facility. These requirements apply specifically to medium-scale and large-scale solar energy facilities, including those defined as large-scale (5 MW or greater).
section: Section 8. Decommissioning; Unsafe or abandoned projects

summary: The project area shall be enclosed by security fencing not less than six feet in height and equipped with an appropriate anticlimbing device such as strands of barbed wire on top of the fence. The height and/or location of the fence may be altered in the conditions for a particular conditional use permit. Fencing must be installed on the interior of the vegetative buffer. Fencing shall be placed around sections of the infrastructure (not the entire site) to provide access corridors for wildlife to navigate through the facility. The fencing shall be maintained while the facility is in operation.
section: Section 5. Location, appearance, and operational requirements, A. Requirements that apply to all solar energy facilities, 6. Fencing

summary: Section 5.D.4 requires that large-scale solar energy facilities "shall utilize only panels that employ anti-glare technology, anti-reflective coatings, and other available mitigation techniques, all that meet or exceed industry standards, to reduce glint and glare." The applicant must provide "written certification from a qualified expert, acceptable to the county, that the facility's panels incorporate and utilize anti-glare technology and anti-reflective coatings and reduce glint and glare to levels that meet or exceed industry standards." Additionally, Section 4.k.7 mandates a "glint and glare study that demonstrates either that the panels will be sited, designed, and installed to eliminate glint and glare effects on roadway users, nearby residences, commercial areas, and other sensitive viewing locations, or that the applicant will use available mitigation techniques to reduce glint and glare to the lowest achievable levels." This study must assess and quantify potential glint and glare effects and address health, safety, and visual impacts, and be conducted by qualified individuals using appropriate software and procedures at the time of building permit application. These explicit glare restrictions apply to Solar Energy Facility, Large-Scale, defined as ground-mounted solar facilities with rated capacity of five megawatts (5 MW) alternating current or greater.
section: Section 5. Location, appearance, and operational requirements

summary: The maximum height of the lowest edge of photovoltaic panels shall be ten feet as measured from the finished grade. Solar energy generation facilities shall not exceed a height of 15 feet, which shall be measured from the highest natural grade below each solar panel. This limit shall not apply to utility poles and the interconnection to the overhead electric utility grid. The Board of Supervisors may approve a greater height based upon the demonstration of a significant need where the impacts of increased height are mitigated.
section: Section 5. Location, appearance, and operational requirements

summary: Setbacks are measured from the outermost structure including the security fence, substation, and inverters but not including the driveways and power poles. The project area shall be set back a distance of at least 250 feet from adjacent property lines. Setbacks may be increased by a reasonable amount, not to exceed 500 feet, and additional buffering may be included in the conditions for a particular conditional use permit. Solar energy facilities also shall meet all setback requirements for primary structures for the zoning district in which the facility is located, in addition to the requirements set forth above. In the case of the facility location incorporating multiple zoning districts, the more restrictive requirements shall apply. Access, erosion and stormwater structures, and interconnection to the electrical grid may be made through setback areas provided that such are generally perpendicular to the property line. Exceptions may be made for adjoining parcels that are owned by the applicant.
section: Section 5. Location, appearance, and operational requirements, D. The following requirements also apply to large-scale solar energy facilities, 5. Setbacks

summary: The project area shall be set back a distance of at least 275 feet from the centerline of all adjoining or abutting public rights-of-way. Setbacks are measured from the outermost structure including the security fence, substation, and inverters but not including the driveways and power poles. Setbacks may be increased by a reasonable amount, not to exceed 500 feet, and additional buffering may be included in the conditions for a particular conditional use permit. Solar energy facilities also shall meet all setback requirements for primary structures for the zoning district in which the facility is located, in addition to the requirements set forth above. In the case of the facility location incorporating multiple zoning districts, the more restrictive requirements shall apply. Access, erosion and stormwater structures, and interconnection to the electrical grid may be made through setback areas provided that such are generally perpendicular to the property line. County approved permanent, buffered setback easements with non-solar facility landowners may be utilized to meet these setback requirements so long as solar facility setbacks from public rights of way are maintained.
section: Section 5. Location, appearance, and operational requirements. D. The following requirements also apply to large-scale solar energy facilities: 5. Setbacks.

summary: Section 5.D.6 requires for large-scale solar energy facilities a vegetated buffer sufficient to mitigate the visual impact of the facility. The buffer "shall consist of a landscaped strip at least 50 feet wide, shall be located within the setbacks required under this Section, and shall run around the entire perimeter of the property." Existing vegetation is preferred, but if necessary, "an installed landscaped strip consisting of multiple rows of staggered trees and other vegetation" must be provided. The buffer plants "should be made up of plant materials at least three feet tall, at the time of planting, and that are expected to grow to a minimum height of eight feet within three years." Landscaping must consist of "plants, shrubs, trees, grasses, forbs, and wildflowers native to the County," with non-invasive plants allowed if native plants are insufficient. The Planning Commission or Board of Supervisors may require "increased setbacks and additional or taller vegetative buffering" depending on height or topography. The buffer "shall be maintained for the life of the facility." An earthen berm may also be used to "screen or mitigate the visual impact of the solar facilities from public view." These requirements apply specifically to large-scale solar energy facilities, defined as "a ground-mounted solar facility that generates electricity from sunlight on an area adequate to support a rated capacity of five megawatts (5 MW) alternating current or greater."
section: Section 5. Location, appearance, and operational requirements

summary: The ordinance requires a Draft grading plan as part of the application for solar energy facilities, which "shall identify: Areas of steep slopes; Locations of topsoil to be removed and preserved, noting that no topsoil will be removed from Lunenburg County, Virginia; Locations of stormwater drainage and erosion and sediment control features." It further states that "no panels will be placed on steep slopes and that no grading or land disturbance will occur that will create a slope greater than 8%." Additionally, for large-scale solar energy facilities, "Access, erosion and stormwater structures, and interconnection to the electrical grid may be made through setback areas provided that such are generally perpendicular to the property line." These requirements apply to large-scale solar energy facilities defined as "A ground-mounted solar facility that generates electricity from sunlight on an area adequate to support a rated capacity of five megawatts (5 MW) alternating current or greater."
section: Section 4. Applications and procedures for solar energy facilities

summary: For large-scale solar energy facilities, the project area shall be set back a distance of at least 450 feet from residential structures on non-project parcels. Exceptions may be made for adjoining parcels that are owned by the applicant. Setbacks may be increased by a reasonable amount, not to exceed 500 feet, and additional buffering may be included in the conditions for a particular conditional use permit. Setbacks are measured from the outermost structure including the security fence, substation, and inverters but not including the driveways and power poles. Solar energy facilities also shall meet all setback requirements for primary structures for the zoning district in which the facility is located, in addition to the requirements set forth above. In the case of the facility location incorporating multiple zoning districts, the more restrictive requirements shall apply.

Section 5.D.4 requires that "The applicant shall demonstrate through project siting and proposed mitigation, that the solar project minimizes impacts on public viewsheds, including from residential areas and areas of scenic, historical, cultural, archaeological, and recreational significance." It also requires "photo or other realistic simulations or modeling of the proposed solar energy project from potentially sensitive locations as deemed necessary by the Planning Office to assess the visual impact of the project" (Section 4.3.e.12). The Planning Commission or Board of Supervisors "may require other relevant information deemed to be necessary to evaluate the application." Section 7 states that "to preserve the intent and goals of the Comprehensive Plan, protect County viewsheds and resources... the following non-exhaustive list of additional criteria may be considered" including "The proximity of the site to, observability from, and impact on areas of scenic, historical, and archaeological significance" and "The proposed use of available technology, coatings, and other measures for mitigating adverse impacts of the facility."
section: Section 5. Location, appearance, and operational requirements

summary: Section 20.8 DECOMMISSIONING requires that "Solar facilities which have reached the end of their useful life or have not been in active and continuous service for a period of one (1) year shall be removed at the owner’s or operator’s expense." The owner must "notify the Zoning Administrator by certified mail of the proposed date of discontinued operations and plans for removal." Decommissioning includes "removal of all solar electric systems, buildings, cabling, electrical components, security barriers, roads, foundations, pilings, and any other associated facilities," and the site "shall be graded and re-seeded to restore it to as natural a condition as possible." The decommissioning must be "performed in compliance with the approved decommissioning plan," which includes a detailed cost estimate, updated every five years, and financial assurance through escrow or other security. If the owner fails to remove the installation, "the County may collect the surety and the County or hired third party may enter the property to physically remove the installation." These requirements apply to utility-scale solar facilities as defined in 20.3(l) as "a facility that generates electricity from sunlight which will be used to provide electricity to a utility provider" with "capacity in excess of one megawatt (1 MW)" and generally over two acres. Other solar facility types mentioned include small-scale and medium-scale, with different definitions and conditions, but the decommissioning requirements described are explicitly stated for solar facilities generally and apply to utility-scale facilities as part of the ordinance.

The ordinance explicitly requires that utility-scale solar facilities "shall be enclosed by security fencing on the interior of the buffer area (not to be seen by other properties) not less than seven (7) feet in height and topped with razor/barbed wire, as appropriate." It also mandates that "a performance bond reflecting the costs of anticipated fence maintenance shall be posted and maintained." Failure to maintain the security fencing "shall result in revocation of the SEP and the facility’s decommissioning." Additionally, the fencing is part of the minimum development standards for utility-scale solar facilities, which include other requirements such as setbacks, height limits, and screening buffers. The ordinance distinguishes between small-scale, medium-scale, and utility-scale solar facilities, with this fencing requirement applying specifically to utility-scale facilities defined as those "which will be used to provide electricity to a utility provider" with sites generally over two acres and capacity in excess of one megawatt (1 MW).

The Maximum height of primary structures and accessory buildings shall be 15 feet as measured from the finished grade at the base of the structure to its highest point, including appurtenances. The Board of Supervisors may approve a greater height based upon the demonstration of a significant need where the impacts of increased height are mitigated. This restriction applies specifically to utility-scale solar facilities as stated in section 20.7(d).

Section 20.11(2) states: 'The area, within which all construction, material storage, grading and related activities for the utility-scale solar facility occurs, will be no more than a total of five (500) acres.' Additionally, section 20.14 sets a cumulative maximum acreage cap of 2,325 acres within Mecklenburg County for all solar projects combined, including Utility-Scale Solar Facilities. The units for these maximum lot sizes are acres.

The minimum area of a utility-scale solar facility shall be two (2) acres. Utility-scale solar facilities are defined as facilities that generate electricity from sunlight which will be used to provide electricity to a utility provider, generally over two acres and with capacity in excess of one megawatt (1 MW). This minimum size is explicitly stated in section 20.7(a)(1). Other scale categories include small-scale (less than 15 kW or disturbance zone equal to or less than an acre) and medium-scale (sites between one to three acres with a maximum capacity of 999 kW), but these do not apply to utility-scale facilities. The unit for the minimum lot size is acres.

Section 20.11(3) states: 'A utility-scale solar facility will not be located within two (2) miles of another approved or constructed Utility-Scale, Small-Scale, or Community-Scale Solar facility to mitigate the impacts related to the scale of the use.' This is the explicit minimum required separation distance for utility-scale solar facilities from other existing or planned solar energy conversion systems. Other scale categories (small-scale and community-scale) have the same 2-mile separation requirement from other solar facilities. The unit 'miles' is used as stated in the text.

The minimum setback to all property lines shall be 150 feet for utility-scale solar facilities. Additionally, a buffer zone at least 100 feet wide extending from the property line shall be landscaped for screening purposes. These requirements apply specifically to utility-scale solar facilities, defined as facilities with sites generally over two acres and capacity in excess of one megawatt (1 MW).

Section 20.7(e) requires that utility-scale solar facilities "shall be significantly screened from the ground-level view of adjacent properties by a buffer zone at least 100 feet wide extending from the property line that shall be landscaped with plant materials consisting of an evergreen and deciduous mix (as approved by County staff), except to the extent that existing vegetation or natural land forms on the site provide such screening as determined by the Zoning Administrator." Opaque architectural fencing may supplement but not be the primary screening method. Additionally, section 20.7(f) requires security fencing on the interior of the buffer area, at least seven feet in height and topped with razor/barbed wire as appropriate. The buffer and screening requirements apply specifically to utility-scale solar facilities, defined as facilities generating electricity for utility providers, generally over two acres and with capacity over 1 MW.

The ordinance explicitly requires that the Special Exception Permit (SEP) "may require the applicant to submit an erosion and sediment control plan for review by the County or by a qualified third party," and that the applicant "shall construct, maintain, and operate the solar facility in compliance with the approved plan." This applies to utility-scale solar facilities, which require a SEP as per section 20.4(a). Additionally, the SEP "may require the applicant to submit a stormwater management plan for review by the County or by a qualified third party," with compliance required. The applicant must also pay a supplemental application fee for third party review of these plans. These requirements are found under conditions that the Board of Supervisors may impose on solar facilities.

summary: The ordinance requires that applicants for Solar Energy Facilities provide "a detailed decommissioning plan that provides procedures and requirements for removal of all parts of the Solar Facility... at the end of the useful life of the Solar Energy Facility or if it is deemed abandoned pursuant to section 4-19-9." The plan must include "the anticipated life of the Solar Energy Facility; the estimated overall cost of decommissioning...; the methodology for providing security for the determined cost of decommissioning, which shall be either cash escrow, performance surety bond(s), certified check(s), irrevocable letter(s) of credit, or other surety acceptable to the County." Section 4-19-9 further details that if a facility is "not operated for a continuous period of twelve (12) months," it may be declared abandoned and must be removed "at the Facility Owner’s, Site Owner’s or operator’s expense in compliance with decommissioning plan established for such facility." Removal must be completed "within 365 days of the date of abandonment," including "removal of all solar electric systems, buildings, cabling, electrical components, security barriers, roads, foundations, pilings, and any other associated facilities," and the site must be restored "to as natural a pre-development condition as possible or replanted with pine seedlings." Financial assurance must be provided "in a form and amount approved by the Board of Supervisors and shall remain in full effect until all decommissioning activities are completed." The County may call upon the decommissioning security to complete removal if the responsible parties fail to do so. These requirements apply explicitly to Solar Energy Facilities defined as having a project area four acres or greater.

summary: The Project Area shall be enclosed by security fencing not less than six (6) feet in height and equipped with an appropriate anticlimbing device such as strands of barbed wire on top of the fence. The height and/or location of the fence may be altered in the approved special exception permit conditions for a particular permit. The fencing shall be properly maintained at all times while the Solar Facility is in operation.

summary: The ordinance requires that Solar Energy Facilities shall utilize only panels that employ anti-glare technology, anti-reflective coatings, and other available mitigation techniques, all that meet or exceed industry standards, to reduce glint and glare. The applicant must provide written certification from a qualified expert acceptable to the County that the facility's panels incorporate and utilize anti-glare technology and anti-reflective coatings and reduce glint and glare to levels that meet or exceed industry standards. Additionally, a glint and glare study is required that demonstrates either that the panels will be sited, designed, and installed to eliminate glint and glare effects on roadway users, nearby residences, commercial areas, and other sensitive viewing locations, or that the applicant will use all reasonably available mitigation techniques to reduce glint and glare to the lowest achievable levels. The study must assess and quantify potential glint and glare effects and address the potential health, safety, and visual impacts associated with glint and glare, and must be conducted by qualified individuals using appropriate and commonly accepted software and procedures.

summary: The ordinance explicitly requires vegetative buffering and screening for Solar Energy Facilities (4 acres or greater). Applicants must submit a landscaping and screening plan that addresses "the vegetative buffering required in this article, including the use of existing and newly installed vegetation to screen the facility," and the use of "pollinator-friendly and wildlife-friendly native plants, shrubs, trees, grasses, forbs, and wildflowers in the project area and in the setbacks and vegetative buffering." The Project Area must be enclosed by security fencing "installed on the interior of the vegetative buffer required in this section so that it is screened from the ground-level view of adjacent property owners." Vegetative buffer requirements include: use of native or adaptive plant materials; retention of existing healthy vegetation; plant sizes and standards conforming to the American Standard for Nursery Stock 2014 and Nottoway County planting standards; buffer location within mandated setbacks on the property it serves; and specific buffer types such as "Agricultural Buffer Opaque" (existing natural vegetative woodland with minimum 12' height) and "Agricultural Constructed Buffer Opaque" (minimum 30' width, 80% opacity, with specified numbers and types of trees and shrubs). The ordinance also requires maintenance responsibility for the buffer during the life of the facility. Fencing must be at least six feet tall with anti-climbing devices and located inside the vegetative buffer. Additional requirements include a surface water buffer of at least 250 feet on either side of any perennial stream within the project area. Pollinator habitats must be seeded promptly following construction. These requirements apply as part of the special exception permit application and approval process for Solar Energy Facilities as defined (4 acres or greater).

summary: The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Industrial/Utility-scale solar facilities, defined as "A facility that generates electricity from sunlight primarily for sale to a utility provider" and "occupying more than two (2) acres of total land area." Key provisions include: "A decommissioning plan shall be developed by the applicant, owner or operator and included as part of the special use permit"; a facility is "deemed abandoned" if it ceases operation or construction for specified periods; "Within six (6) months of a utility scale solar facility being declared abandoned... the owner or operator shall, at its sole cost and expense, complete the decommissioning... in accordance with the decommissioning plan approved by the County"; the County may decommission if the owner fails to do so, using surety funds; and financial assurance is required via escrow or bonds with periodic reassessment. Decommissioning includes "removal of all solar electric systems, buildings, cabling, electrical components, security barriers, roads, foundations, pilings, and any other associated facilities" and site restoration. Partial decommissioning is also addressed. Other solar facility scales (small-scale and medium-scale) have separate decommissioning provisions with different timelines and requirements.

summary: Utility-scale solar facilities shall be enclosed by security fencing on the interior of the buffer area (not to be seen by other properties) not less than nine (9) feet in height. The fence shall not be topped with razor/barbed wire. A performance bond reflecting the costs of anticipated fence maintenance shall be posted and maintained. Failure to maintain the security fencing shall result in revocation of the SUP and the facility’s decommissioning.

The maximum height of the lowest edge of the photovoltaic panels shall be 10 feet as measured from the finished grade. The maximum height of photovoltaic panels, primary structures, battery storage systems and accessory buildings shall be 15 feet as measured from the finished grade at the base of the structure to its highest point, including appurtenances. The Board of Supervisors may approve a greater height based upon the demonstration of a significant need where the impacts of increased height are mitigated. Units are feet.

No more than thirty (30) acres of acreage coverage may be approved for an individual utility-scale solar facility. This shall be measured by total acreage coverage as defined herein, not accessory structures necessary for the operation of the solar energy facility. Additionally, there is an aggregate cap of three hundred (300) acres of acreage coverage in total for utility-scale solar facilities. The minimum area of a utility-scale solar facility shall be two (2) acres. The units for these size limits are acres.

The minimum area of a utility-scale solar facility shall be two (2) acres. This is explicitly stated in § 134-7, item 10.b: 'The minimum area of a utility-scale solar facility shall be two (2) acres.' Additionally, the definition in § 134-3 states that an industrial/utility scale solar facility occupies more than two (2) acres of total land area. The units are acres, a standard area measurement.

Industrial/utility scale solar facilities shall not be located within two (2) miles of another existing or permitted industrial/utility scale solar facility, unless the combined acreage coverage is thirty (30) acres or less (§ 134-7.12.c). This is the explicit minimum required separation distance with other existing or planned solar energy conversion systems for Industrial/Utility-scale solar facilities. The unit of measurement is miles.

summary: Utility-scale solar facilities shall be permitted in industrial and agricultural zoning districts by Special Use Permit (SUP) only. Industrial/Utility scale solar facilities shall not be permitted in any other zoning district. Small-scale solar facilities may be installed by-right in all zoning districts to provide electricity to individual structures. Medium-scale solar facilities may be installed by-right in agricultural, commercial, woodland/conservation and industrial zoning districts to provide electricity to individual structures.

Setbacks for a utility-scale solar facility shall be: (a) All above-ground infrastructure, equipment, improvements or structures, including security fencing, shall be no less than three hundred (300) feet from property lines with existing dwellings. (d) Transformers shall be set back six hundred (600) feet from property lines. (f) When located adjacent to a residential zoned property, then all setbacks shall be six hundred (600) feet from the residential zoned property lines, notwithstanding of any other provisions set forth herein. Other setback distances include 300 feet from property lines with existing dwellings, and some setback distances from other property lines are left blank. Setbacks are not required among and between participating landowners’ parcels. The Board of Supervisors may determine additional minimum setbacks as part of the special use permit process.

Industrial/utility scale solar facilities shall not be located in or within three hundred (300) feet of historic and cultural resources as defined in the Comprehensive Plan (§134-7.12.g). Other natural resource protection areas such as forested areas must be avoided but no fixed numeric setback is specified (§134-7.12.f). Wildlife corridors must be at least 25 feet wide (§134-7.22.b). The Board of Supervisors may impose more restrictive buffer zones and setbacks during the special use permit process (§134-10.3, §134-10.6).

Utility-scale solar facilities, including fencing, shall be significantly screened from the ground-level view of adjacent properties by a buffer zone at least 100 feet wide that shall be landscaped with native and non-invasive plant materials consisting of an evergreen and deciduous mix (as approved by County staff). Trees shall be a minimum of 6 feet in height at time of planting and in staggered rows of ten (10) foot on center. In the event existing vegetation or landforms providing the screening are disturbed, new plantings shall be provided which accomplish the same. The effectiveness of screening shall be maintained as the plant materials mature. Unhealthy and dead plants shall be replaced within one (1) year of being provided written notice by the County of the violation. The special use permit application site plan shall include the location and nature of proposed buffers and screening elements, including vegetative and constructed buffers. These requirements apply to utility-scale solar facilities defined as facilities primarily for sale to a utility provider occupying more than two (2) acres of total land area.

The ordinance explicitly requires soil, erosion, and sediment control measures for industrial/utility-scale solar facilities. Key requirements include: submission of a proposed grading plan with the special use permit application (§134-6(4)); an environmental site assessment and impact study including an Erosion and Sediment Control Plan prepared by a Virginia certified engineer experienced in karst landscapes (§134-6(7)(d)); facilities on karst topography must have a site assessment and an Erosion & Sediment Control Plan confirming no adverse groundwater impact (§134-7(16)); inspections by county-approved qualified third parties as required by Virginia Erosion & Sediment Control Regulations and Virginia Stormwater Management Program Regulations (§134-7(31)); and adherence to all local, state, and federal requirements for land disturbance activities during decommissioning (§134-8(10)). These requirements apply specifically to utility-scale solar facilities defined as "A facility that generates electricity from sunlight primarily for sale to a utility provider... occupying more than two (2) acres of total land area."

summary: Utility-scale solar facilities shall be permitted in industrial and agricultural zoning districts by Special Use Permit (SUP) only. Industrial/Utility scale solar facilities shall not be permitted in any other zoning district. Small-scale solar facilities may be installed by-right in all zoning districts to provide electricity to individual structures; provided a site plan (as applicable) has been submitted to Page County for review and approval; all Federal, State and Local regulations have been followed; and the system is located upon the property or structure being served. Medium-scale solar facilities may be installed by-right (roof-mounted or ground-mounted) in agricultural, commercial, woodland/conservation and industrial zoning districts to provide electricity to individual structures; provided a site plan (as applicable) has been submitted to Page County for review and approval; all Federal, State and Local regulations have been followed; and the system is located upon the property or structure being served.

Setbacks for a utility-scale solar facility shall be: (a) All above-ground infrastructure, equipment, improvements or structures, including security fencing, shall be no less than three hundred (300) feet from property lines with existing dwellings. (f) When located adjacent to a residential zoned property, then all setbacks shall be six hundred (600) feet from the residential zoned property lines, notwithstanding of any other provisions set forth herein. The 600 feet setback from residential zoned property lines is the most restrictive setback directly pertaining to occupied dwellings or residences for Industrial/Utility-scale solar facilities.

Applications for a utility-scale solar facility shall include "a visual impact analysis demonstrating project siting and proposed mitigation, if necessary, so that the solar facility minimizes impact on the visual character of the County." The impact analysis "shall include, but not necessarily be limited to: Accurate, to scale, photographic simulations showing the relationship of the solar facility and its associated amenities and development to its surroundings, including projected vegetative growth." The number and perspectives of simulations "shall be established by Page County after the pre-application meeting." Additional information may be required, such as "a scaled elevation view of the property and other supporting drawings, photographs of the proposed site, photo or other realistic simulations or modeling of the proposed project from potentially sensitive locations as deemed necessary by Page County to assess the visual impact of the project, landscaping and screening plan, coverage map, and additional information that may be necessary for a technical review of the proposal." These requirements apply to utility-scale solar facilities defined as "a facility that generates electricity from sunlight primarily for sale to a utility provider" and occupying more than two (2) acres of total land area. Smaller scale solar facilities have different requirements and are not subject to these visual impact assessment mandates.

summary: The Patrick County Board of Supervisors "does hereby adopt amendments to the Patrick County Comprehensive Plan" that state "utility-scale solar facilities are not considered to be an appropriate land use in the County and should therefore be prohibited." Proposed utility-scale solar facilities "shall be deemed as not being substantially in accord with the Comprehensive Plan" under § 15.2-2232 of the Code of Virginia. The prohibition applies broadly across the County without conditions or geographic limitations, except that it "is not applicable to facilities other than utility-scale solar facilities, for instance, accessory solar facilities associated with an agricultural, residential, commercial, or industrial use where generated electricity is principally utilized on-site and/or net-metered to off-set on-site electricity use." There is no expiration date or moratorium period specified; the prohibition is effective as of the adoption date, April 28, 2025.

A decommissioning plan shall be developed by the applicant, owner or operator prior to the approval of a site plan being issued for a solar energy facility. The plan specifies the procedure to remove the solar energy facility after the end of its useful life and restore the property. If the facility is inactive or substantially discontinuing delivery of electricity for a continuous 6-month period, it is considered abandoned. Decommissioning shall commence within six (6) months of notice. Unless owned by a public utility, the gross costs of decommissioning shall be secured by an adequate surety posted within 30 days of receiving the certificate of completion. The surety amount must be updated every five years. The applicant or successor must decommission within six months after cessation of use; if they fail, the property owners must commence decommissioning. If both fail, the County may commence decommissioning using the surety funds and has rights to the equipment. All physical improvements, materials, and equipment shall be removed unless otherwise approved. Access roads will be removed unless the landowner requests otherwise. Partial decommissioning applies if only a portion of the facility is discontinued. The decommissioning plan must include: anticipated life, estimated cost by a State licensed professional engineer, method of estimate, manner of decommissioning, and responsible party. The applicant and property owners must grant the County rights to access and equipment for decommissioning upon default.

The ordinance requires that "the applicant shall install temporary security fencing prior to the commencement of construction activities occurring on the solar energy facility" (Section 9.a.iv). Additionally, "the applicant shall install a permanent security fence, consisting of chain link, 2-inch square mesh, (or comparable fencing) a minimum of 6 feet in height around the Solar Facility prior to the commencement of operations of the Solar Energy Facility" (Section 10.a). The permanent fence must "contain all required buffers, screening and plantings, and shall comply with the same setback requirements that are applicable to solar panels, structures and equipment associated with the solar energy facilities land use." These requirements apply to solar energy facilities permitted by special exception in the M-3 zoning district, which are utility-scale systems as defined in the policy.

All solar energy facility structures, racks and associated facilities shall have a non-reflective finish or appearance. Silicon based panels shall be used; cadmium-based panels are prohibited. The solar collectors shall be designed to maximize absorption and minimize glare outward toward adjoining properties and upward toward military and general aviation aircraft or other similar aircraft. Vehicles travelling on adjoining interstate and state-maintained roads shall also be protected from potential glare, including elevated tractor trailer cabs.

Solar Energy Facility structures shall not exceed 15 feet; however, towers constructed for electrical lines may exceed the maximum permitted height as provided in the zoning district regulations, provided that no structure shall exceed the height of 25 feet above ground level, unless required by applicable code to interconnect into existing electric infrastructure or necessitated by applicable code to cross certain structures.

The minimum aggregate parcel size for a solar energy facility is seventy (70) contiguous acres. This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems as described in the policy for large-scale solar energy facilities in the M-3 zoning district. The text states: 'e. The minimum aggregate parcel size for a solar energy facility is seventy (70) contiguous acres.'

Daytime noise generated by the facility post-construction will be under an average 67 dBA per day, measured at the property line, throughout the day with no noise emissions at night; provided, however the operator may seek temporary waivers from the Planning Department for specific repair or maintenance needs. The unit of measurement is dBA, a standard noise level unit.

The Board of Supervisors has proposed that any new solar energy facilities should only be permitted in the M-3 Zoning District with a special exception. Prince George County desires that no additional acreage (0 additional acres) should be dedicated to solar energy facility land uses outside of the M-3 zoning district, except for accessory uses which are permitted by-right. The already-approved facilities in R-A or A-1 zoning districts should not be expanded beyond their existing approved acreages. New facilities may still be permitted if the land is zoned or rezoned to M-3 Heavy Industrial zoning district, with special exception approval by the Board of Supervisors.

summary: The ordinance requires that the solar energy facility be constructed, maintained, and operated in accordance with the approved County Grading and Erosion and Sediment (E&S) Control Plans, with an E&S bond or letter of credit posted for construction. The grading plan must: (i) clearly show existing and proposed contours; (ii) note locations and estimated amount of topsoil to be removed and percent of site to be graded; (iii) limit grading by avoiding steep slopes and laying out arrays parallel to landforms; (iv) require an earthwork balance on-site with no import or export of soil unless it reduces clearing and grading; and (v) require topsoil stripping from areas to be gravelled or cut and stockpiling for later use. Additionally, groundcover should be expeditiously established following construction to minimize erosion and loss of soil, and synthetic herbicides are prohibited for groundcover maintenance. These requirements apply to large-scale solar energy facilities as indicated by references to special exception approvals, minimum parcel size of seventy (70) contiguous acres, and location in the M-3 zoning district.

The M-3 zoning district continues to be the desired location for any new Solar Energy Facilities. The Board of Supervisors has proposed that any new facilities should only be permitted in the M-3 Zoning District with a special exception. Five solar energy facilities have been approved by special exception in Prince George County, zoned R-A or A-1. The County does not wish to approve any additional facilities outside of the M-3 zoning district, except for accessory uses which are permitted by-right. New facilities may still be permitted in the County on a case-by-case basis if the land is zoned or is rezoned to M-3 Heavy Industrial zoning district, with special exception approval by the Board of Supervisors.

Applicants for a new solar energy facility must provide "photographic simulations illustrating the relationship of the proposed solar energy facility use in relation to the surrounding properties and uses, and additional simulations showing the relationship of any new or modified service road or utility corridors to be constructed or modified to serve the proposed solar energy facility use or other nearby infrastructure." Additionally, applicants must submit "buffering, screening, fencing and landscaping schematics with sufficient details to facilitate review for compliance with policy." These requirements apply as part of a complete Special Exception Application for utility-scale solar energy facilities, which must be located in the M-3 zoning district and meet minimum size criteria such as "The minimum aggregate parcel size for a solar energy facility is seventy (70) contiguous acres." The review process includes a "Substantial Accord" review for compliance with the Comprehensive Plan and requires community meetings and various plans and documentation. Other requirements include compliance with zoning ordinance standards, local, state, and federal codes, and any additional conditions imposed with special exception approval.

Section 9.10 Decommissioning requires the applicant to submit a Decommissioning Plan at the time of applying for the large-scale solar project, including: anticipated life expectancy, estimated decommissioning cost, methodology for cost estimate, funding assurance, biennial updates, and site restoration methods. The plan must be sealed by a professional engineer. If a large solar energy facility is abandoned or discontinued, the owner must notify the Planning and Zoning Administrator 30 days prior and complete removal and site restoration within 365 days, subject to extension by the Board of Supervisors. Unsafe facilities must be repaired or removed within allowed timeframes. Equipment must be disposed of per federal, state, and local requirements, with all equipment removed except internal paths, roads, and landscaping at the site owner's discretion. Failure to comply allows the County to remove the facility at the owner's expense and use decommissioning bonding/security. Section 9.12 Bonding requires submission of an itemized cost estimate plus 25% for removal and restoration, excluding salvage value, and a bond or surety in the approved amount. The bond must secure removal costs, include CPI adjustments, and remain until the site is inspected and restored, after which it will be released. These requirements apply to Large Scale Solar Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance.

Section 9.8 Site Plan, subsection F states: "Fencing shall be shown in detailed illustration on the site plan. The project area shall be enclosed by security fencing no less than 8 feet in height and equipped with an appropriate anticlimbing device. Fencing must be installed on the interior of the required vegetative buffer as referenced in this ordinance." This fencing requirement applies to Large Scale Solar Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance.

Section 9.9 J) requires a Glint and Glare study that "shall be provided that demonstrates that the panels will be sited, designed and installed to eliminate glint and glare effects on roadways users, adjacent residents, commercial areas, and other sensitive viewing locations." The study "will assess and quantify potential glint and glare effects and address the potential health safety or welfare." Section 9.9 N) requires "written confirmation from a qualified expert that the projects panels incorporate and utilize anti-glare technologies and anti-reflective coatings to reduce glint and glare to levels that meet industry standards." These requirements apply to Large Scale Solar Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance, which are subject to a Special Use Permit and other regulatory provisions.

Ground mounted solar energy generation panels and facilities shall not exceed 30 feet in height. This shall be measured from the highest natural grade below each solar panel. This height limit shall not apply to overhead electric, utility poles and interconnection to the grid.

The project area shall be setback a distance of at least 50 from any adjacent property lines. Exceptions may be made for adjoining parcels that are owned by the applicant. Increased setbacks up to 100 feet and additional buffering may be included in the conditions for a certain permit. Solar energy facilities also must meet all setback requirements for primary structures within the current zone district standards in addition to the requirements set forth above.

The project area shall be setback a distance of at least 75 feet from all public right of ways. Exceptions include increased setbacks up to 100 feet and additional buffering which may be included in the conditions for a certain permit. This applies to Large Scale Solar Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance.

Section 9.8 Site Plan, subsection G) Vegetative Buffer requires "a sufficient vegetative buffer shall be installed to mitigate the visual impacts of the solar energy facility." The buffer "shall consist of at least a 50’ wide strip of landscape buffer located within the setbacks" and "shall run around the entirety of the proposed area of development." It "may consist of existing vegetation and as needed, installed noninvasive species consisting of multiple rows of staggered trees and other vegetation." Vegetation "should include at least 6’ in height at the time of planting and be reasonably expected to grow to full maturity within three years." If existing vegetation is disturbed, "new plantings shall be provided for the buffer at least 6’ feet tall at planting." The buffer must use "non-invasive plant species and pollinator-friendly and wildlife friendly native plants, trees, shrubs, grasses, forbs and wild flowers" following Virginia Pollinator-Smart Programs best practices. The buffer "shall be maintained for the entirety of the life of the facility." The Planning Commission or Board of Supervisors "may require increased setbacks and additional or taller vegetative buffering in situations where the height of structures or topography affects the visual impacts of the facility." Additionally, fencing "must be installed on the interior of the required vegetative buffer as referenced in this ordinance." These requirements apply to Large Scale Solar Energy Facilities as defined in the ordinance and are part of the special use permit and site plan requirements.

The table indicates that 'Solar Farm' uses are permitted as a Special Use Permit (SUP) in districts C, A, RC, CM, and LI. The ordinance requires that "The applicant shall provide a detailed decommissioning plan that provides procedures and requirements for removal of all parts of the solar energy generation facility and its various structures at the end of the useful life of the facility or if it is deemed abandoned pursuant to section (E)." The plan must include "the anticipated life of the facility, the estimated overall cost of decommissioning the facility in current dollars, the methodology for determining such estimate, and the manner in which the project will be decommissioned." Prior to operation, "the applicant must provide security in the amount of the estimated cost of the decommissioning" through options such as "a cash escrow, a performance surety bond, a certified check, an irrevocable letter of credit, or other security acceptable to the county." The security must remain valid until decommissioning obligations are met and may be adjusted based on updated cost estimates. Section (E) addresses unsafe or abandoned projects, requiring repair or removal within specified timeframes, notification to the zoning administrator upon scheduled abandonment, and removal within 365 days of abandonment in compliance with the decommissioning plan. All equipment must be removed, with internal paths and landscaping left at the site owner's discretion. summary: The ordinance explicitly requires a vegetative buffer for Utility-Scale Solar Generation Facilities: "A vegetative buffer sufficient to mitigate the visual impact of the facility is required. The buffer shall consist of a landscaped strip at least 15 feet wide, shall be located within the setbacks required under subsection (3) above, and shall run around the entire perimeter of the property." The buffer must include "existing vegetation and, if deemed necessary for the issuance of a special use permit, an installed landscaped strip consisting of multiple rows of staggered trees and other vegetation." Plants must be "at least three feet tall at the time of planting and that are reasonably expected to grow to a minimum height of eight feet within three years." The ordinance also requires "non-invasive plant species and pollinator-friendly and wildlife-friendly native plants, shrubs, trees, grasses, forbs, and wildflowers" in the buffer. Until the buffer fully screens the facility, "the owner and/or operator shall use green privacy slats in the required fencing." Fencing must be "installed on the interior of the vegetative buffer required in this section so that it is screened from the ground level view of adjacent property owners." The buffer "shall be maintained for the life of the facility." The landscaping and screening plan is a required part of the application for Utility-Scale facilities. Other related requirements include the use of pollinator-friendly native plants in the project area and setbacks, and the possibility of increased setbacks and additional or taller vegetative buffering as conditions for a permit. The Planning Commission or Board of Supervisors may waive or alter screening and buffer requirements if existing wetlands or woodlands are permanently protected for use as a buffer. The ordinance also allows for increased setbacks up to 300 feet and additional buffering in certain situations. These requirements are found in the application and location, appearance, and operational requirements for Utility-Scale Solar Generation Facilities.

Applications for Utility-Scale Solar Generation Facilities shall include an erosion and sediment control plan approved by the Erosion and Sediment Control plan reviewer prior to any land disturbing activity equal to or over 10,000 square feet. Additionally, a stormwater management plan must be approved prior to any land disturbing activity equal to or over one acre. These requirements are part of the application and procedural standards for Utility-Scale Solar Generation Facilities. The ordinance also includes other application requirements such as project narrative, site plan, decommissioning plan, liability insurance, landscaping and screening plan, and various reports and studies. Exemptions may apply for facilities smaller than four acres with a rated capacity equal to or less than one megawatt (MW) from some of these requirements.

summary: Applications for Utility-Scale Solar Generation Facilities shall include "photo or other realistic simulations or modeling of the proposed solar energy project from potentially sensitive locations as deemed necessary by the zoning administrator to assess the visual impact of the project." A "landscaping and screening plan that addresses the vegetative buffering required in these standards" must be submitted, and a "vegetative buffer sufficient to mitigate the visual impact of the facility is required." The buffer shall be "a landscaped strip at least 15 feet wide" around the property perimeter, with specific planting requirements. The Planning Commission or Board of Supervisors may require increased setbacks and additional or taller vegetative buffering based on visual impact. Additional criteria for permit conditions include proximity and impact on various sensitive areas and viewsheds. The ordinance also allows the Planning Commission or Board of Supervisors to require other relevant information to evaluate the application.

Section § 165-173E requires a completed decommissioning plan to be submitted and approved prior to, or along with, site plan approval, detailing: (1) removal of structures, materials, buildings, roads (unless retrofitted within two years), cabling, electrical components, large-scale operational equipment, and other associated facilities; (2) site restoration including soil stabilization and revegetation; (3) anticipated life of the large-scale solar facility; (4) estimated decommissioning cost in current dollars and projected costs for three separate decades following; (5) how estimates were determined; and (6) impacts on surrounding lots when decommissioned. Section § 165-174E requires posting and maintaining a bond prior to construction, reassessed every two years based on estimated decommissioning costs. Sections § 165-174F-H require the owner/operator to notify the County if the facility becomes abandoned, complete decommissioning within 183 days or six months if requested by the Board of Supervisors (extendable upon approval), and authorize the County to decommission and recover costs from the bond if the owner/operator fails to act.
