summary: Clean Footprint or its successors agree to be responsible for all decommissioning costs and agree that any future buyer or successor of the project will assume the same decommissioning responsibilities. Upon removal, the project site shall be restored to pre-construction conditions as is reasonably practical, including removal of structures, foundation, and restoration of soil and vegetation. The system will be dismantled and removed using minimal impact construction equipment and materials will be safely recycled or disposed of. Appropriate temporary construction-related erosion and sediment control best management practices (BMP) will be used during the decommissioning of the project. Decommissioning will occur 20-30 years after the system becomes operational or if the array is not used for twelve consecutive months. The decommissioning party shall: obtain any permits required; remove and dispose of all equipment and components; remove hazardous materials; perform grading and re-vegetation as appropriate; preserve and reclaim soils; remove non-biodegradable electrical conduits and backfill trenches. Equipment removal proceeds in reverse order of installation, including disconnection from the grid, removal and recycling of PV modules, support racking, electrical devices, concrete pads, and fencing. Clean Footprint will hire an engineer to develop a decommissioning plan prior to construction and will submit a financial guarantee to comply with county or state requirements.

The solar array will be contained within an area protected by a seven-foot 'deer style' chain link fence with wooden posts and anti-climbing device such as strands of barbed wire on the top of the fence. There will be signage along the fence, including utility hazard, company information, and contact information on the fence.

The installation will not exceed a maximum height of ten feet above grade. The panels are mounted on a steel and aluminum racking structure that generally averages approximately seven feet above grade. This maximum height applies to the 10 MW AC ground mounted photovoltaic solar facility described in the text.

The text explicitly states a maximum system size for the utility-scale solar energy system proposed: a 10 MW AC ground-mounted photovoltaic solar facility with a DC system size of 13.456 MWp. This is a clear specification of the total installation size for the project, which an energy system developer would have to abide by as part of the special use permit application. The project size is specifically provided as a system size in megawatts: 10 MW AC and 13.456 MW DC. Additionally, the installation size is detailed by the number of solar panels, which is 30,240 PV modules. The units for the maximum project size are megawatts (MW).

The ordinance specifies a '150' SETBACK FROM PROPERTY LINE' and also mentions a 'PARCEL BOUNDARY: 100FT' setback. The 150 feet setback from property line is the most restrictive value directly pertaining to the utility-scale solar energy system described (10 MW AC ground mounted photovoltaic facility).
The 10 MW AC ground mounted photovoltaic local community solar facility will have signage along the fence, including utility hazard, company information, and contact information on the fence.

Clean Footprint will use appropriate temporary (construction-related) erosion and sediment control best management practices through construction and decommissioning. Stormwater management measures include an analysis of the existing topography, the use of erosion control logs and silt fences where necessary, and establishment of a germinated pollinator friendly vegetative base underneath the project site before construction begins to prevent erosion. Compliance with all county and state guidelines is required.

Sec. 18-624 states: 'The total land area devoted to utility scale solar projects shall be no more than one (1) percent of the area of Southampton County, approximately 3,850 acres.' This is the maximum lot size allowed for Utility Scale Solar Energy Projects (20 MW to 100 MW). The ordinance also specifies the minimum and maximum rated nameplate capacity as 20 MW and 100 MW respectively, but the maximum land area is explicitly limited to approximately 3,850 acres.

Sec. 18-631 explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Utility Scale Solar Energy Projects (20 MW to 100 MW). It requires "a decommissioning plan signed by the project owner and binding upon their successors and assigns," including "the anticipated life of the project," "an equipment and materials analysis," "the estimated decommissioning costs in current dollars," "the method for ensuring that funds will be available for decommissioning and restoration," and "the anticipated timeline and manner in which the project will be decommissioned and the site restored to agricultural ready." Decommissioning must occur "following a continuous period of twelve (12) months of the cessation of use for the electrical power generation or revocation of the special exception permit," with completion within twelve (12) months. It mandates removal of all solar panels, footers, foundations, structures, cabling, electrical components, conduit, and other associated facilities. Non-utility improvements like fences and access roads must be removed unless an agreement allows them to remain. Prior to site plan approval, a performance guarantee covering "one-hundred (100) percent of the estimated decommissioning cost, with no allowance for salvage value" must be provided. The bond must be reviewed and adjusted every five (5) years. The plan must be recorded with the Clerk of the Circuit Court. The County may enter the property up to three (3) times per year for unannounced inspections and has enforcement rights. Any changes in ownership require updated plans and surety. These requirements apply specifically to utility scale solar projects as defined in the ordinance, which have a minimum rated capacity of 20 MW and a maximum of 100 MW.

Fencing shall be as required by the National Electric Code. It shall be screened from exterior view from occupied adjacent properties and public rights-of-way. Screening may include plantings to mitigate the view of the fence. Breaks in fencing shall be provided to facilitate wildlife movement corridors where necessary. Fencing abutting public rights-of-way requires a landscape plan providing an intermittent screen reflecting the agricultural nature of the surrounding countryside, including four (4) foot tall landscaped berms planted with grass as necessary. Fencing not abutting public rights-of-way, but abutting residential uses, cemeteries, schools, historic structures, places of worship, or State Scenic rivers, requires an opaque screen to a height of eight (8) feet within three (3) years of installation, with a four (4) foot tall landscaped berm planted with grass if abutting residential use. Plantings shall be native or locally adapted vegetation to the greatest extent possible. The landscape plan must ensure long-term viability and include pest management plans. A $50,000 landscape bond shall remain in effect for the life of the project to cover landscaping replacement, damaged fencing, and maintenance. Annual inspections by a licensed Landscape Architect are required.

All solar collection devices shall be located to avoid directing glare or reflection onto adjacent properties and roadways so as to not create a traffic or safety hazard or nuisance to adjacent properties. In the event that glare is identified as an issue after construction, the owner of the solar energy facility, or its assigns, shall prepare and implement a corrective plan of action that is acceptable to the County sixty (60) days after notification of the issue to the owner by the County. The required landscape bond may be utilized by the County to abate the condition should the operator fail to do so.

Sec. 18-629(6) states: 'Solar Energy Arrays shall not exceed eighteen (18) feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt, as measured from the ground, and shall be screened to meet the visual buffering requirements at the time of site plan approval. Ancillary non-solar collector equipment and/or structures, including, but not limited to inverters and transformers, may exceed the height limitation of eighteen (18) feet, provided such equipment or structures are not visible from the exterior of the property.' This height restriction applies explicitly to Utility Scale Solar Energy Projects with rated capacity between 20 MW and 100 MW as defined in the ordinance.

Sec. 18-624 states: 'The minimum rated nameplate capacity of any utility scale solar energy project shall be at least twenty (20) megawatts (MW). The maximum rated nameplate capacity of any utility scale solar energy project shall be no more than one hundred (100) megawatts (MW).' Additionally, 'The total land area devoted to utility scale solar projects shall be no more than one (1) percent of the area of Southampton County, approximately 3,850 acres.' The units for the maximum project size are megawatts (MW), referring to rated nameplate capacity. The 100 MW maximum is the most restrictive numerical limit for project size.

Sec. 18-630(8) states: 'No utility scale solar energy project shall be located within five (5) miles of another major solar energy project permitted under this section as measured at the nearest exterior boundary of each project.' This minimum separation distance applies to entire utility scale solar energy projects (20 MW to 100 MW), not individual components or smaller systems. The unit of measurement is miles.

Within the required exterior setbacks, a minimum of one-half the setback shall provide a buffer area on all sides of the project, including areas around any new substation or connector station, to any adjacent parcel or public right-of-way. If the adjacent parcel includes a residence, a place of worship, a structure with documented historical significance, a cemetery, or a school, the minimum buffer width shall instead be one hundred (100) feet. Utility scale solar energy projects shall meet the front, side, and rear setbacks of the M-1, Limited Industrial district for the exterior parcel boundaries of the project unless specified otherwise elsewhere in these regulations. Buildings and equipment may cross property lines interior to the utility scale solar project, however, subsequent to development, should properties be removed from the project, perimeter setbacks must be installed on properties remaining within the project.

New substations or connector stations shall be set back at least five hundred (500) feet, and inverters and transformers set back at least two hundred and fifty (250) feet, from existing dwellings, schools, places of worship, State Scenic rivers, and rights-of-ways. Utility scale solar energy projects shall meet the front, side, and rear setbacks of the M-1, Limited Industrial district for the exterior parcel boundaries of the project unless specified otherwise elsewhere in these regulations. The Board of Supervisors may modify the setbacks as it deems necessary to ensure adequate buffer yards and screening to mitigate visibility from public rights-of-way. Additionally, within the required exterior setbacks, a minimum of one-half the setback shall provide a buffer area on all sides of the project, including areas around any new substation or connector station, to any adjacent parcel or public right-of-way. If the adjacent parcel includes certain sensitive uses, the minimum buffer width shall be one hundred (100) feet. Landscaping and fencing abutting public rights-of-way must provide an intermittent screen with four (4) foot tall landscaped berms planted with grass as necessary.

Section 18-629 requires an exterior buffer area within setbacks, with a minimum buffer width of 100 feet adjacent to residences, places of worship, schools, cemeteries, or historic structures. The buffer must screen the project from view from the exterior of the property and may include "any combination of landscaping, fencing, berms, or natural areas." Landscaping and buffering standards include: a landscape plan for fencing abutting public rights-of-way providing an intermittent screen; plantings at intersections to reduce visual impacts; four (4) foot tall landscaped berms planted with grass as necessary abutting public rights-of-way; opaque screening to a height of eight (8) feet within three (3) years where fencing abuts residential uses, cemeteries, schools, historic structures, places of worship, or State Scenic rivers; use of native and pollinator species; and a $50,000 landscape bond to remain in effect for the life of the project. Fencing must be screened from exterior view, potentially with plantings. The Board of Supervisors may modify buffer and screening requirements as necessary to ensure adequate screening. These requirements apply to Utility Scale Solar Energy Projects with a minimum rated capacity of 20 MW and maximum of 100 MW, requiring a Conditional Use Permit in the M-1 zoning district.

Signage shall be limited to a notification sign placed at each site entrance and at locations along the exterior fence that states (a) the rated nameplate capacity, (b) the name of the project owner, and operator (if different from the owner), (c) the street address of the site, and (d) a 24-hour emergency contact phone number for the operator. Signage is prohibited on solar equipment except as follows: (a) appropriate warning signs and placards; (b) signs required by a federal or state agency; (c) signs that provide a 24-hour emergency contact phone number, and (d) panel manufacturer information and/or other identifier. If the contact information changes, new signage with up-to-date contact information is required.

The ordinance explicitly enacts soil, erosion, and sediment control requirements for Utility Scale Solar Energy Projects (20 MW to 100 MW). It requires a construction management plan including dust mitigation (Sec. 18-628). Within buffer areas, "erosion and sediment control/stormwater management measures" are permitted (Sec. 18-629(1)(g)). Grading restrictions include: "Clear-cutting and grading of the development zone shall be prohibited, except in areas where panels, internal paths, and equipment are to be installed." The ordinance mandates adherence to "Southampton County Code Ch. 6, Erosion and Sediment Control," use of existing contours "to the extent practical," and prohibits disturbance of slopes exceeding 15% or critical slopes per the Virginia Erosion and Sediment Control Handbook. Site development must be phased so that "not more than fifty (50) percent of the land disturbance areas reflected on the site plan shall be disturbed without stabilization at any time." Topsoil removal is prohibited. If forested land is included, "the requirements of the Virginia Department of Forestry BMP standards shall be included." Additionally, all construction within floodplain areas must comply with the erosion and sediment control chapter of the Southampton County Code (Sec. 18-632(1)(2)). The ordinance applies to projects with a minimum rated capacity of 20 MW and maximum of 100 MW (Sec. 18-624).

New substations or connector stations shall be set back at least five hundred (500) feet, and inverters and transformers set back at least two hundred and fifty (250) feet, from existing dwellings, schools, places of worship, State Scenic rivers, and rights-of-ways. Additionally, within the required exterior setbacks, a minimum buffer width of one hundred (100) feet is required if the adjacent parcel includes a residence. Utility scale solar energy projects shall meet the front, side, and rear setbacks of the M-1, Limited Industrial district for the exterior parcel boundaries of the project unless specified otherwise.

The ordinance requires a visual impact assessment for Utility Scale Solar Energy Projects (20 MW to 100 MW) as part of the Conditional Use Permit application. Specifically, Sec. 18-628(4)(i) mandates "A general landscape and buffering plan that demonstrates that the application meets the buffering requirements of Sec. 18-629." Sec. 18-628(4)(j) requires "Demonstration through project siting and proposed mitigation, if necessary, that the project mitigates impacts on the visual character of adjacent properties, designated scenic roads or rivers, or historic properties as designated in the Comprehensive Plan or the Virginia/National Register of Historic Places." Sec. 18-629 details design and development standards including "Exterior Buffer Area," "Landscaping and Buffering," "Fencing," "Grading," and "Signage" to mitigate visual impacts. Sec. 18-630(1) requires "Site access shall be designed to mitigate site visibility from the public road, residences, schools, places of worship, properties on a historic register or listing, and state scenic rivers." Additionally, Sec. 18-632(2) requires a "Community impact assessment" analyzing the probable impact of the project on the vicinity and community, which includes visual character considerations. The Board of Supervisors may modify these provisions if they find the amended provisions protect public health, safety, and welfare.

The ordinance states: 'Solar panels shall cover no more than eighty percent (80%) of the total land area of the solar project site.' This applies to commercial solar facilities designed to convert sunlight to electricity for storage and/or distribution, fitting the definition of utility-scale solar energy systems. The coverage is expressed as a percentage of the total land area, not as a specific area value.

The ordinance defines a 'solar facility' as a commercial facility designed to convert sunlight to electricity for storage and/or distribution from one property to other properties through a utility grid, excluding residential or non-residential properties generating electricity for on-site use only. It requires that 'a proposed decommissioning agreement shall be submitted as part of the conditional use permit application.' Decommissioning includes 'the removal of all solar panels, collectors, cabling, electrical components, fencing and all other associated equipment, facilities and structures to a depth of at least thirty-six (36) inches from the ground surface of the property with site rehabilitation establishing preconstruction conditions of the solar project site.' The agreement must include: a description of any agreement with landowners regarding decommissioning; identification of the party responsible; types of panels and material specifications; standard removal and rehabilitation procedures; an estimate of all removal and disposal costs; and a deadline for completion. Additionally, the zoning administrator must be notified within thirty (30) days of abandonment or discontinuance of the solar facility use.

The ordinance requires that "The solar project site shall be enclosed with chain link fencing not less than six (6) feet in height, include an appropriate anti-climbing device, and shall be secured with gates." The fencing "shall be installed on the interior of the buffer required in subsection (z)(8) below." The buffer is "a vegetated buffer... at least fifty (50) feet wide measured from each boundary line of the solar project site around the entire perimeter" with specific landscaping requirements. These requirements apply to solar facilities defined as "a commercial facility primarily consisting of activities, applications or devices designed to convert sunlight to electricity for storage and/or distribution from one property to other properties through a utility grid."

Sec. 28-39(z)(6) requires that "Solar panel components shall have a UL listing and shall be designed with an anti-reflective coating. Individual arrays/solar panels shall be designed and installed in order to prevent glare toward buildings on adjacent properties and nearby vehicular traffic." This applies to commercial solar facilities defined as "a commercial facility primarily consisting of activities, applications or devices designed to convert sunlight to electricity for storage and/or distribution from one property to other properties through a utility grid."

All equipment shall be placed at least one hundred (100) feet from any property line or habitable structure located on adjacent properties unless such modification is approved by the board of supervisors. Additionally, a vegetated buffer shall be required around the solar project site consisting of a landscaped strip at least fifty (50) feet wide measured from each boundary line of the solar project site around the entire perimeter. The 100 feet setback from property lines is the most restrictive fixed distance directly pertaining to setbacks from property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, parcels, and/or subdivisions for utility-scale solar energy systems.

The ordinance requires that "The zoning administrator shall be notified in writing at least one hundred eighty (180) days in advance of any intent to repower the facility." The ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for large-scale solar energy facilities. In Washington, developers of solar energy facilities must submit a site restoration plan with their Site Certificate application addressing environmental impacts, decommissioning measures, and financial assurances, while solar PV manufacturers must finance the takeback and recycling of modules at no cost to the facility owner.

Subsection (8) Abandonment and Decommissioning requires that SPPFs which have not generated electricity sold for commercial use over any 18-month period shall be deemed abandoned and removed at the SPPF owner’s/operator’s expense. The applicant must provide a detailed decommissioning plan with procedures and requirements for removal of all parts of the solar energy generation facility and its structures at the end of the useful life or if deemed abandoned. The site shall be restored within six (6) months of removal, including dismantling all photovoltaic solar power generation facilities and accessory structures, restoring private off-site access roads unless the landowner directs otherwise, grading the area to original or agriculturally advantageous contours, and re-vegetation consistent with noxious weed control measures. The SPPF owner/operator must provide removal, restoration, and decommissioning assurances to Yakima County in the form of a surety bond or escrow account covering 125% of the estimated cost, prepared by a qualified Washington State licensed engineer, with reevaluation every five years. Failure to provide adjusted guarantees may result in the County declaring the SPPF abandoned and triggering removal and decommissioning. Perimeter fencing for the site shall not include barbed wire or woven wire designs, and shall preferably use wildlife-friendly fencing standards. Alternative fencing can be used if deemed necessary to accommodate the specific agrivoltaic use on site.

Solar Power Production Facilities (SPPF) are allowed only in agriculturally zoned areas outside of an established irrigation district, as stated in the Allowable Land Use Table 19.14-1. The ordinance requires Solar Power Production Facilities (SPPF) to submit a screening plan that "identifies the type and extent of screening" and states that "Screening shall not be required along property lines within the same zoning district, except where the adjoining lot has an existing residential use within 150 feet." Additionally, the agrivoltaic plan must include "all proposed measures and improvements intended to create a buffer between the proposed solar facility and adjacent agricultural operations (detailed information must be shown on Site Plan) and provide factual/technical data supporting the effectiveness of said proposed buffering measures." Section 19.18.435(6)(n) Signage requires that solar equipment shall not be used for displaying any advertising except for reasonable identification of the manufacturer or operator of the solar energy project. Warning signs shall be placed on solar equipment to the extent appropriate. All signs, flags, streamers, or similar items, both temporary and permanent, are prohibited on solar equipment except as follows: (a) manufacturer's or installer's identification; (b) appropriate warning signs and placards; (c) signs that may be required by a federal agency; and (d) signs that provide a twenty-four-hour emergency contact phone number and warn of any danger.

A Noxious Weed Management Plan outlining methods, maintenance schedules, and potential soil viability impacts is required. A Stormwater Management Plan must be prepared in accordance with YCC 12.10 including mitigation measures for ground disturbance to contain storm water runoff. The Buffalo County Solar Ordinance explicitly enacts decommissioning requirements for Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES). The PSES owner is required to notify the Zoning Department within 30 days upon cessation or abandonment of the operation, with abandonment presumed if output falls below 25% of designed output for 12 continuous months. A permit from the Zoning Department is required for all decommissioning and demolition. The owner has twelve (12) months to dismantle and remove the PSES including all solar related equipment or appurtenances related thereto, including but not limited to buildings, cabling, electrical components, roads, foundations, and other associated facilities from the property. If the owner fails to dismantle and/or remove the PSES within the established timeframes, Buffalo County may complete the decommissioning at the owner’s expense. At the time of issuance of the permit for the construction of the PSES, the owner shall provide financial security in the form and amount acceptable to the County to secure the expense of dismantling and removing said PSES and restoration of the land to its original condition. This financial security shall be the average of at least 2 qualifying bids of removal and disposal, reviewed every 5 years and updated, with staged amounts: 25% prior to the start of construction, 50% after two years, and 100% at the conclusion of 5 years of operation.

PSES shall be effectively fenced around the perimeter with a minimum of eight (8) foot fencing made of steel wire. The wire shall not be of barbed wire or woven wire designs. The fencing shall preferably use wildlife friendly fencing standards that includes passage of small animals such as rabbits and raccoons. Such fencing shall effectively keep large animals such as deer out of the enclosure. It shall be upon the operator to see that entrapped animals are immediately released. If wild animals such as deer have entered the enclosure, those animals shall be removed within 24 hours or they shall fall under captive wildlife regulations under WI Stats 169.04 and must be reported immediately to Local wildlife authorities. The fencing shall not cross navigable waters. All ground mounted PSES shall be completely enclosed by a minimum eight (8) foot high fence with a self-locking gate. A clearly visible warning sign shall be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations and on the fence surrounding the PSES informing individuals of potential voltage hazards.

summary: Decommissioning of the system must occur within one year from either the end of the system's serviceable life or from the time that the energy generation from the system becomes a discontinued use. Energy generation from the system shall be considered a discontinued use after one year without energy production, unless a plan is developed and timely submitted to the Town of Pacific outlining the steps and schedule for returning the system to service. Decommissioning shall consist of the following: (1) The removal of the system's equipment and the removal of the system's foundation to a depth of at least three feet, with possible exemption if removal increases erosion or disrupts vegetation; (2) Disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with local, state, and federal waste disposal regulations; (3) The restoration of the surface grade, and soil, the stabilization of soils and revegetation of the site as necessary to minimize erosion, including measures to restore farmland to productive agricultural use. A cost estimate for full decommissioning must be provided and approved by the Town Engineer prior to commencement. Before beginning decommissioning, a performance bond assuring funds to restore the site must be submitted and approved. Decommissioning must follow the approved decommissioning plan or any amendments approved by the Town.

Reflecting solar energy systems shall be designed and operated to prevent the misdirection of reflected solar radiation onto adjacent or nearby property, public roads, or other areas open to the public. The chapter applies to all solar energy systems except small solar energy systems, as defined in Chapter 414 of the Town Code. System standards mandate that "systems shall be designed to reduce land disturbance and provide for such measures as may be reasonably necessary so that farmland can be returned to productive agricultural use" and that "systems that result in the creation of one or more acres of impervious surface must also provide plans that comply with the WONR NR 216 and NR 151 construction stormwater permit requirements prior to final stormwater and erosion control permitting at the Town" (§ 415-6 System standards). These requirements apply to large-scale solar energy systems defined as those with a total panel size of more than 600 square feet (§ 415-9 Definitions).

Power inverters and any sound-producing equipment shall be at least 150 feet from any residential dwelling(s) adjacent to the parcel covered by the application. summary: Section 12.40(h)(6)(t) requires the Solar Farm Owner to implement the Decommissioning Plan attached as Exhibit F upon permanent cessation of the commercial operation of the Solar Farm, defined as cessation for 12 consecutive months for reasons other than force majeure. The plan must include: 1) Notify the Department when permanent cessation has been determined; 2) Remove, at its expense, all Solar Farm components including but not limited to solar collectors and associated facilities to a depth of 4 feet and properly dismantle all components disposed of at a licensed solid waste disposal facility and/or consistent with federal, state, and local regulations; 3) Restore the land to a condition reasonably similar to pre-existing conditions, including de-compacting areas where solar Farm access roads were installed; 4) Prior to issuance of a zoning permit, post a commercially reasonable financial assurance (bond, letter of credit) equal to the difference between estimated decommissioning costs and salvage value, reviewed and updated approximately every 5 years; 5) All solar equipment shall be decommissioned and disposed of in accordance with State, Federal and local regulations. These requirements apply to Solar Farms less than 100 MW, which are defined as "a solar energy system that generates electricity to serve many customers by wholesale or retail sale and not primarily for consumption on the property on which the system is located and is on-grid" and require conditional use approval. Other SES categories include SES equal to or greater than 100 MW, which must follow PSC requirements and enter into an MOU with the County and Town, and Individual Use SES which are smaller and accessory to the principal use of the property.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "other than the fencing directly surrounding the Solar Farm substation, O&M and BESS the Solar Farm’s perimeter fencing shall consist of 'deer fencing' (wire mesh), which can be described in greater detail as a six (6) to ten (10) foot in height woven wire partition with posts." Fences must be set within/inside property lines or rights-of-way edges unless otherwise requested by the landowner. Installed fencing "shall be adequately maintained at all times during the Solar Farm operation," with fence posts installed per prudent engineering practice and impairments remedied within two weeks of written notification. "Leaning" of the fence shall not exceed plus or minus 10 degrees of perpendicular and must be corrected within two weeks of notice. This fencing requirement applies to Solar Farms, defined as commercial, on-grid systems generating electricity for wholesale or retail sale and requiring conditional use approval. Section 12.27.060(h) states: "All SES using a reflector to enhance solar production shall minimize reflected light from the reflector affecting adjacent or nearby properties. Measures to minimize reflected light include selective placement of the system, screening on the north side of the solar collector, modifying the orientation of the system, reducing use of the reflector system, or other remedies that limit reflected light." Additionally, Section 12.27.050(s) requires: "For Solar Farms located within 1,000 feet of an airport or within approach zones of an airport or landing strip, the applicant must complete and provide the results of the Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT) for the Airport Traffic Control Tower cab and final approach paths." These provisions apply to Solar Farms less than 100 MW, which are defined as "a solar energy system that generates electricity to serve many customers by wholesale or retail sale and not primarily for consumption on the property on which the system is located and is on-grid" and are subject to conditional use permit processes. Section 12.40 CONDITIONAL USE, subsection (c) states: 'Maximum height for solar collectors: 15 feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt.' Sec. 115-614(c)(3) states: "All solar energy systems using a reflector to enhance solar production shall minimize reflected light from the reflector affecting adjacent or nearby properties. Measures to minimize reflected light include selective placement of the system, screening on the north side of the solar array, modifying the orientation of the system, reducing use of the reflector system, or other remedies that limit reflected light." Sec. 115-615(b)(8) requires: "For solar farms located within 1,000 feet of an airport or within approach zones of an airport, the applicant must complete and provide the results of the Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT) for the Airport Traffic Control Tower cab and final approach paths, consistent with the Interim Policy, FAA Review of Solar Energy Projects on Federally Obligated Airports, or most recent version adopted by the FAA."

summary: Solar farms must meet ground cover and buffer area standards, including: discouragement of large-scale removal of mature trees; soils planted and maintained in perennial vegetation to prevent erosion, manage runoff, and improve soil; seed mixes including grasses and wildflowers native to the region; blooming shrubs in buffer areas for visual screening; and a financial guarantee equal to 125 percent of the costs to meet these standards. These requirements are in addition to NFPA provisions and may be supplemented by Multifamily Residential and Commercial Design Standards. The financial guarantee remains until vegetation is established. (Sec. 115-615(b)(3)) Other standards for solar farms include conditional use permits in certain districts, stormwater and erosion control, foundation certification, compliance with codes, undergrounding power lines, site plan submission, aviation and agricultural protections, and decommissioning plans.

Solar farms are subject to all City of La Crosse's stormwater management and erosion control provisions requirements. Ground cover and buffer area standards include: discouraging large-scale removal of mature trees; top soils shall not be removed during development unless part of remediation; soils shall be planted and maintained in perennial vegetation to prevent erosion, manage runoff, and improve soil; seed mixes should include native grasses and wildflowers; seed mixes and maintenance practices should follow recommendations from qualified natural resource professionals; plant material must not be treated with systemic insecticides; and a financial guarantee equal to 125 percent of the costs to meet ground cover and buffer area standards must be submitted and remain until vegetation is established. These requirements apply to solar farms defined as ground-mount solar energy arrays that are the primary use on the lot, designed for providing energy to off-site uses or export to the wholesale market.

Ground-mount solar energy arrays that are the primary use on the lot, designed for providing energy to off-site uses or export to the wholesale market, are conditional uses in Light Industrial, Heavy Industrial, and Agricultural districts. "Solar farms are conditional uses in Light Industrial, Heavy Industrial, and Agricultural districts." Other related uses include: solar gardens, where rooftop community systems are permitted in all districts; ground-mount community solar energy systems less than six acres are conditional uses in all districts; and ground-mount solar developments covering more than six acres are considered solar farms. Solar farms must meet various standards including stormwater management, ground cover and buffer areas, foundation certification, compliance with codes, undergrounding power lines, site plan submission, aviation and agricultural protections, and decommissioning plans.

Section 1.6 Abandonment and Decommissioning states: "A schedule with details for abandonment and decommission of a solar energy system may be established during the conditional use process. Upon termination of solar rights, in the absence of an approved schedule, and/or after a solar system is no longer in operation, the owner shall have 90 days to remove the system and restore the site unless weather prohibits such efforts." The procedure requires the owner to "remove all solar energy system and outdoor storage; remove all hazardous material from the property and dispose of the hazardous material in accordance with Federal and State law." If the owner fails to remove the system and reclaim the site, "the County may remove or cause the removal of the solar system and the reclamation of the site" and recover costs from financial assurance or place a lien on the property. This applies to solar energy systems designed for nominal operation at a capacity of less than 100 megawatts, as the ordinance states it "only applies to SES which are designed for nominal operation at a capacity of less than 100 megawatts."

Section 1.3 Performance standards, subsection A.2 states: "Glare and light: Collector surfaces shall minimize glare and reflected light." This applies to all solar energy systems permitted under the ordinance, which applies to systems designed for nominal operation at a capacity of less than 100 megawatts (Section 1.1.C). Other relevant conditions include that ground mounted/pole mounted solar systems not exceeding 12.5 kilowatt in rated capacity total for a parcel, and no more than 21 feet in height, may be exempt from the conditional use process but still require a zoning permit (Section 1.3.A.4). Building-mounted solar systems have separate exemptions and conditions (Section 1.3.A.5).

All solar energy systems that require conditional use approval shall be located at least 100 feet from all property lines. The Committee may modify the 100-foot setback from side and rear property lines shared by parcels supporting the same solar energy system. Other setback distances mentioned include 63 feet from township road centerlines, 75 feet from county highway centerlines, and 110 feet from state highway centerlines, but these relate to roads and are not applicable here.

Any new or altered solar energy systems shall not be located within 63 feet from the centerline of any township road or recorded access easement, 75 feet from the centerline of any county highway and 110 feet from the centerline of any state highway.

The ordinance states that "A solar energy system shall be permitted in all upland zoning classifications where buildings are permitted. If the system fails to meet the following standards, a conditional use review and approval in accordance with Section 4 of Chapter 6-1 shall be required." Specifically, "Ground mounted/pole mounted solar systems that do not exceed 12.5 kilowatt in rated capacity total for a parcel, are no more than 21 feet in height, and meet the total accessory structure limitations provided within Chapter 6-1 may be exempt from the conditional use process, but are required to obtain a zoning permit." Larger systems exceeding these thresholds require conditional use approval. The conditional use permit process involves application to the Manager, review by a Committee, and compliance with setback requirements such as being "at least 100 feet from all property lines and 150 feet from the ordinary high-water mark," and other conditions including agreements with owners of adjacent habitable structures within 500 feet. The ordinance does not specify particular zoning district names or abbreviations where these conditional uses are permitted. It also excludes solar overlay districts from this consideration.

summary: Any new solar energy system shall not be located within 500 feet of any adjacent habitable structure existing at the time of application that is not owned by the applicant unless an agreement is signed and recorded. This applies to systems requiring conditional use approval, which typically includes ground-mounted solar energy systems under 100 megawatts. Other setback distances mentioned include 100 feet from all property lines and 150 feet from the ordinary high-water mark, but these do not pertain to setbacks from occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, or residences.
All solar energy systems that require conditional use approval shall be located at least 150 feet from the ordinary high-water mark.

The ordinance specifies a 25 ft. property line setback for principal and conditional use structures, which include utility-scale solar energy systems listed as conditional uses in districts such as Exclusive Agricultural (EA), General Agricultural (GA), Large Estate Residential (LE), Small Estate Residential (SE), Rural Residential (RR), and Industrial (ID). Accessory structures have a 10 ft. setback. For example, in the EA district: '25 ft. property line setback for principal and conditional use structures' and '10 ft. property line setback for accessory structures.' Similar setbacks are repeated in other districts. No height-based multiplier is mentioned; setbacks are fixed distances.

Utility-scale solar energy systems, referred to as 'solar energy facilities,' are listed as conditional uses in the Exclusive Agricultural (EA) district: 'Conditional Uses - ... solar energy facilities ...'. Similarly, in the General Agricultural (GA) district, 'solar energy facilities' are included under compatible infrastructure uses. The Industrial (ID) district also permits 'solar energy facilities' as compatible infrastructure uses. Other districts such as Large Estate Residential (LE), Small Estate Residential (SE), Rural Residential (RR), High Density Residential (HD), and Lake Residential (LR) mention only 'solar energy systems' or 'small wind energy systems,' which likely refer to smaller or non-commercial systems and are not included here. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this summary as per instructions.

A decommissioning plan shall be required to ensure that facilities are properly removed after their useful life. Decommissioning of solar panels must occur in the event they are not in use for 12 consecutive months. The plan shall include provisions for removal of all structures and foundations, restoration of soil and vegetation, and a plan ensuring financial resources will be available to fully decommission the site. Structures and/or foundations shall be disposed of at a licensed solid waste disposal facility and/or otherwise in a manner consistent with federal, state, and local regulations. Marathon County Conservation, Planning, and Zoning Department may require the posting of a bond, letter of credit or the establishment of an escrow account to ensure proper decommissioning.

summary: Section 17.408.03.A.3 requires that for Commercial Use Solar Energy Systems, "Large-scale removal of mature trees on the site is discouraged" and "Marathon County may set additional restrictions on tree clearing, or require mitigation for cleared trees." It mandates that "soils shall be planted and maintained for the duration of operation in perennial vegetation to prevent erosion, manage run off, and improve soil." Seed mixes should include "a mix of grasses and wildflowers, exclusively native to the region of the project site" and "Blooming shrubs may be used in buffer areas as appropriate for visual screening." Seed mixes and maintenance practices must be consistent with recommendations by the department and/or Wisconsin DNR. Plant material must not be treated with systemic insecticides. A financial guarantee must be submitted to ensure vegetation establishment. Additionally, Section 17.408.03.A.7 requires a site plan showing "screening features" among other site characteristics. These requirements apply to commercial use SES designed for providing energy to off-site uses and/or export to the wholesale market, subject to conditional use permit approval.
section: Section 17.408.03 COMMERCIAL USE: PERMIT, APPLICATION, AND FILING REQUIREMENTS

summary: Commercial Use SES are subject to the Wisconsin DNR stormwater management, erosion, sediment control provisions as well as NPDES permit requirements. Ground cover and buffer areas provisions include: discouragement of large-scale removal of mature trees; top soil shall not be removed during development unless part of remediation; soils shall be planted and maintained in perennial vegetation to prevent erosion, manage runoff, and improve soil; seed mixes should include native grasses and wildflowers resulting in a short stature prairie; seed mixes and maintenance practices shall be consistent with recommendations by the department and/or Wisconsin DNR; plant material must not be treated with systemic insecticides; and a financial guarantee equal to 125% of the costs to meet ground cover and buffer area standards must be submitted and remain until vegetation is established. These requirements apply to ground-mounted solar energy systems designed for providing energy to off-site uses and/or export to the wholesale market, which require a conditional use permit in designated districts.

summary: Section 17.408.03(A)(1) states: 'Commercial use SES require a conditional use permit in all designated districts seen in Table 2 of this ordinance.' The Farmland Preservation District is explicitly mentioned where 'No conditional use permit for a commercial use SES shall be approved by the Board of Adjustment within the Farmland Preservation Zoning District unless such application proposal also meets the standards and conditions identified in Wis. Stats., 91.46(4)(a-e) also listed in Section 17.301.09 of this ordinance.' Section 17.408.04(A)(2) confirms that 'All Commercial Use SES are subject to administrative and Board of Adjustment review and approval as a conditional Use in all zoning districts designated in Table 2.' Other districts are referenced but not named in the provided text. Solar overlay districts are excluded from this analysis as per instructions.

When decommissioning of a SES is required, all equipment, whether above the ground surface or below, shall be completely removed and properly recycled or disposed of, and the property restored as set forth in section 70.32(E)(4)(g)(4), as determined by the Zoning Administrator. A bond, letter of credit, or an escrow account is required for all SES with a nameplate rating of 1MW or greater to ensure proper decommissioning, in an amount determined by the Zoning Administrator. A decommissioning plan must be included in the SES Special Exception application, outlining the anticipated means and cost of removing the SES at the end of its useful life. Decommissioning must occur if the SES is not in use for 12 consecutive months unless otherwise approved by the Board of Adjustment. Decommissioning shall consist of removal of the SES structures and subsurface foundations and equipment, disposal of all solid and hazardous waste in accordance with all applicable waste disposal regulations, and stabilization of soils and/or revegetation of the site as necessary to prevent erosion and to restore the property to a safe condition. The plan shall provide that decommissioning will begin within 180 days from the end of the SES useful life or if the SES is not in use for 12 consecutive months and be completed within 9 months from the start of decommissioning activities. Other options and conditions include: Large Scale SES must be approved by the Wisconsin Public Service Commission and are allowed only in certain districts; Mid-Scale SES are subject to a Special Exception permit; Small Scale SES are considered a permitted accessory use in all districts and require a county zoning permit.

This glare restriction applies to Mid-Scale Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as facilities with an electrical generation capability of less than 100 MW but greater than 30 KW (Section 70.35 KKKK). Mid-Scale SES are subject to a Special Exception permit (Section 70.32(E)(3)(b)) and must comply with additional requirements including setbacks, noise limits, installation by certified installers, buffering, underground power lines, and decommissioning plans. Other types of SES include Large Scale SES (100 MW or more) requiring Wisconsin Public Service Commission approval and allowed only in certain districts, and Small Scale SES (30 KW or less) considered permitted accessory uses requiring only a county zoning permit.

Section 70.32(E)(4)(e) requires that "A SES shall be appropriately buffered and screened from public view by the system owner or representative." This applies to Mid-Scale Solar Energy Systems, which are defined as facilities with an electrical generation capability of less than 100 MW but greater than 30 KW (Section 70.35 KKKK). Mid-Scale SES are subject to a Special Exception permit (Section 70.32(E)(3)(b)). Other types include Large Scale SES, which must be approved by the Wisconsin Public Service Commission and are allowed only in certain districts, and Small Scale SES, which are permitted accessory uses requiring only a county zoning permit.

summary: Section 70.32(E)(3)(a) states that Large Scale SES "Must be approved by the Wisconsin Public Service Commission" and "are allowed only in AG-1, AG-2, AO, CM-B and CM-I Districts." The County may require a developer’s agreement. The text does not explicitly state that Large Scale SES require a special exception permit or special use approval by the zoning appeals board. In contrast, Mid-Scale SES "are subject to a Special Exception permit," and Small Scale SES "are considered a permitted accessory use in all districts and require a county zoning permit." Therefore, while Large Scale SES require regulatory approval and possibly developer agreements, the ordinance does not explicitly list any districts where Large Scale SES are permitted as a special use or similar within the zoning ordinance itself.

All above ground equipment and structures shall be set back at least 100 yards from the boundary with adjacent parcels if the adjacent parcel contains a dwelling within 100 yards of the boundary. This applies to Mid-Scale Solar Energy Systems as defined in Section 70.35 (KKKK) and subject to a Special Exception permit per Section 70.32(E). Other requirements include glare control, noise limits, installation by certified installers, buffering, underground lines, and decommissioning plans.
section: 70.32 Various Land Uses, E. Solar Energy Systems (SES), 4. Requirements for Mid-Scale SES

summary: The ordinance defines Large Solar Energy Systems (Large SES) as equipment intended for off-site consumption (§ 240-4.D.(3)(a)[2]). Under the standards for SES (§ 240-4.D.(3)(b)), it requires that "The SES shall be positioned so that the glare does not create any unsafe conditions" (§ 240-4.D.(3)(b)[3]). Other standards include setbacks, height restrictions, installer qualifications, code compliance, utility notification, structural integrity, and orderly development. Large SES require a conditional use permit prior to construction (§ 240-4.D.(3)(c)[2]).
A SES shall not exceed 35 feet in height. Building-mounted SES may extend up to eight feet above the allowable building height. Exemptions may be granted by the Land Management Committee.

Large SES shall require a conditional use permit, prior to construction, and may be permitted in all zoning districts, except the Shoreland Wetland District, and subject to the regulations and requirements of this section. Small SES may be permitted in all zoning districts, except the Shoreland Wetland District. The Shoreland Wetland District is explicitly excluded from permitting for both small and large solar energy systems.

Any portion of the Large Solar Energy System (SES) shall not encroach within 10 feet of any property line. (§ 240-6 D(3)(b)[1]) This setback applies explicitly to Large SES, defined as equipment intended for off-site consumption. No other setback distances from property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, parcels, or subdivisions are mentioned for Large SES in the provided text.

Any portion of the Large Solar Energy System (Large SES) shall not encroach within 10 feet of any property line or road right-of-way. Large SES are defined as equipment intended for off-site consumption. This setback is a fixed distance and does not vary with system height or other factors.

Large SES shall require a conditional use permit, prior to construction, and may be permitted in all zoning districts, except the Shoreland Wetland District, and subject to the regulations and requirements of this section. The Table of Uses shows Large Solar Energy System (§240-41 D) as a conditional use ('c') in the districts EA, PA, GR, GRF, AR, RR-8, RR-12, RR-20, C, Ll, I, and f-11. Small SES require a land use permit and may be permitted in all zoning districts except the Shoreland Wetland District. The Shoreland Wetland District (S-W) is excluded for Large SES.

Small Solar Energy Systems with an installed name plate capacity of less than 100 megawatts "shall require a conditional use permit prior to construction" and must submit "a decommissioning and site restoration plan providing reasonable financial assurance the large SES under 100 megawatts will be removed at the end of its useful life." Upon permanent cessation of commercial operation (defined as cessation for 12 consecutive months), the SES owner "shall implement the Decommission Plan" which includes: (a) notifying the Department; (b) removing all SES components to a depth of 4 feet and disposing of them properly; (c) restoring the land to a condition reasonably similar to pre-existing conditions; (d) posting a commercially reasonable financial assurance prior to permit issuance, reviewed and updated every 5 years; and (e) decommissioning and disposal in accordance with Federal, State, and Local laws. Other options include Accessory Solar Energy Systems, which require a land use permit but not necessarily a conditional use permit, and Large Solar Energy Systems (100 megawatts or greater), which are reviewed by the Public Service Commission and require a certificate of public necessity.

Section 5(a) states: 'Fencing. Other than fencing directly surrounding the large SES, the SES perimeter fencing shall consist of a six (6) to ten (10) foot in height woven wire partition with posts. Fences shall meet the provisions of s. 7.102.' This fencing requirement applies to Large Solar Energy Systems under 100 megawatts, which are considered Small Solar Energy Systems in this context. Other options or conditions for fencing are not provided in the text.

The ordinance states that for Small Solar Energy Systems (SES) with an installed name plate capacity of less than 100 megawatts, a conditional use permit is required (Section 2b). Regarding glare, it explicitly requires that "The SES shall be positioned so glare does not create any unsafe conditions on adjacent properties or roadways" (Section 3c). Additionally, the application requirements for large SES under 100 megawatts include a "Glare analysis study" (Section 4g8). Other options and conditions include accessory solar energy systems which require a land use permit but no permit for roof-mounted systems if provisions are met (Section 2a), and large solar energy systems of 100 megawatts or greater which are reviewed by the Public Service Commission (Section 2c). The ordinance also allows for additional conditions or restrictions consistent with Wis. Stats. § 66.0401(1m) on a case-by-case basis for accessory and small SES (Section 2d).

A SES shall not exceed the following: (1) A roof mounted SES shall not exceed the maximum allowed height for the base zoning district unless the system extends less than one foot from the surface from which it is directly attached or if the roof pitch is 2/12 or less, then the system shall not extend more than six (6) feet. (2) A ground mounted SES shall not exceed fifteen (15) feet in height when oriented at maximum tilt. The units for these height restrictions are feet.

The ordinance states that for Small Solar Energy Systems with an installed name plate capacity of less than 100 megawatts, "The Department may require visual vegetative buffers between the SES development and adjacent residential land uses. The SES owner shall install a vegetative buffer in accordance with Section 7.104 of this Ordinance." This is found under additional standards for large solar energy systems, specifically section 5(d)(7). Other related provisions include ground cover requirements such as planting and maintaining perennial vegetation to prevent erosion and improve soil, with seed mixes consistent with Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources recommendations. The ordinance also allows for case-by-case consideration of conditions consistent with Wis. Stats. § 66.0401(1m), including conditions to preserve public health and safety, not significantly increase cost or decrease efficiency, or allow alternatives of comparable cost and efficiency.

Section 5(c) states: 'The SES owner shall ensure compliance with Chapter 51 Erosion Control and Stormwater Ordinance for Sauk County. The SES owner shall also comply with any stormwater and erosion control requirements imposed by the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources.' Section 5(d) provides ground cover requirements: '(1) Large scale removal of mature trees on the site is discouraged. (2) To the greatest extent possible, the topsoil shall not be removed during development, unless part of a remediation effort. (3) Soils shall be planted and maintained for the duration of the operation in perennial vegetation to prevent erosion, manage run-off, and improve soil. (4) Seeds should include a mix of grasses and wildflowers (pollinator habitat), exclusively native to the region of the SES site, which will result in short stature prairie with a diversity of forbs and flowering plants that bloom throughout the growing season. (5) Seed mixes and maintenance practices shall be consistent with the recommendations of the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources. (6) The applicant shall submit a financial guarantee in the form of a letter of credit, cash deposit, or bond in favor of the county equal to 125% of the costs to meet the ground cover standard. The financial guarantee shall remain in effect until vegetation is 75% established. (7) The Department may require visual vegetative buffers between the SES development and adjacent residential land uses.' These requirements apply to large SES under 100 megawatts, which the ordinance defines as Small Solar Energy Systems requiring a conditional use permit.

Small Solar Energy Systems with an installed name plate capacity of less than 100 megawatts shall require a conditional use permit prior to construction (Section 2.b). The application must include a "visual analysis study" among other requirements (Section 4.g.(9)). This visual analysis study is an explicit visual impact assessment requirement. Other application requirements include a glare analysis study, market impact analysis, decommissioning and site restoration plan, and various environmental and engineering reports (Section 4.g.(1)-(14)). The ordinance also references compliance with Wis. Stats. § 66.0401(1m) for additional conditions or restrictions applied on a case-by-case basis (Section 2.d).

Sawyer County has enacted a nine-month moratorium on the acceptance of any application to operate a solar energy system or battery energy storage system and on the consideration and/or issuance of zoning permits, building permits, conditional use permits and zoning approvals for such systems. This moratorium is declared in Sec.1 and is intended to allow time to research and draft appropriate regulations. The moratorium shall be in effect for nine (9) months following the effective date of this ordinance or until an amendment to the Sawyer County Ordinances relating to solar energy systems and battery energy storage systems is adopted and takes effect, whichever is earlier. The moratorium applies broadly without conditional exceptions or geographic limitations. The ordinance text does not specify the effective date, so it is not possible to determine if the moratorium has expired as of December 13, 2025.

Upon cessation of the operation of the solar, wind energy facility or turbine, the individual panels, facility or turbine and other related improvements to the property shall be removed. The applicant shall furnish sureties which will enable the county to remove such improvements if the applicant/owner fails to do so. The amount of such sureties shall be determined by the zoning administrator. The form and type of such sureties shall be approved by the corporation counsel. Such fiscal surety shall be for a period not to exceed five years and will be renewed thereafter upon a favorable review of the operation and maintenance of such facility or turbine by the zoning committee and corporation counsel and updated cost estimates furnished by the applicant. All local units of government within the county shall be exempted from having to furnish fiscal sureties.

Solar panels and any associated structures shall, at a minimum, maintain a 50’ perimeter setback and/or all roadway setbacks for principal structures within each respective zoning district as permitted herein. This 50-foot perimeter setback applies to utility-scale solar energy systems. No multipliers based on structure height are specified for solar facilities; multipliers mentioned apply only to wind turbines.

Solar panels and any associated structures shall, at a minimum, maintain a 50’ perimeter setback and/or all roadway setbacks for principal structures within each respective zoning district as permitted herein.

Solar facilities shall maintain a continuous vegetative buff when located adjacent to the following zoning districts: A-R, RS-10, RS-20, R-M, RS-P, RM-P and/or existing properties that have been developed for residential uses. Overall design shall be incorporated into the development plans and as approved by the Waushara County Land Conservation Department and Planning & Zoning Committee.

The ordinance requires that "Appropriate warning signage shall be placed on solar substation facilities, wind turbine towers, electrical equipment, and wind energy facility entrances." This applies to solar facilities with substations and associated electrical equipment, which are indicative of utility-scale solar energy systems. Other requirements include setbacks, security measures, and design standards, but these do not pertain to signage. The ordinance also references compliance with Wisconsin Administrative Codes Ch. SPS 66.0401 and 66.0403.

Sec. 58-236 lists solar and wind energy facilities as conditional uses with minimum standards for location and operation. Sec. 58-454 states: 'Conditional uses in the A-G-* zone are as follows: (29) Solar or Wind wind energy facility.' This indicates that utility-scale solar energy systems require conditional use approval in the A-G-* zone. Other districts such as A-R, RS-10, RS-20, R-M, RS-P, and RM-P are mentioned only in relation to setback and buffering requirements, not as districts permitting these systems as conditional uses.
section: Sec. 58-236. – Selected conditional Uses; Sec. 58-454. - Conditional uses.

summary: Solar panels and any associated structures shall, at a minimum, maintain a 50’ perimeter setback and/or all roadway setbacks for principal structures within each respective zoning district as permitted herein. This applies to utility-scale solar energy systems as indicated by references to large scale Solar Farms/Facilities and inquiries from utility companies. Other setback options mentioned include roadway setbacks for principal structures, but the fixed 50-foot perimeter setback is the clear minimum. Wind turbines have different setback requirements, including multipliers based on blade tip height, but these do not apply to solar energy systems.

Solar panels and any associated structures shall, at a minimum, maintain a 50’ perimeter setback and/or all roadway setbacks for principal structures within each respective zoning district as permitted herein. No specific fixed distance setback from overhead electrical transmission lines, overhead utility lines, utility easements, utility lines, power lines, electrical lines, and/or transmission lines is provided for utility-scale solar energy systems. The only multiplier setback (1.1 times total height) applies exclusively to wind turbines from above ground public overhead communication or electric transmission lines, other than lines serving individual homes or outbuildings.

Solar energy facilities in West Virginia must submit a decommissioning plan and financial assurance to the DEP within one year of commercial operation, including removal of panels, diagrams of structural and electrical components, cost estimates, and any alternative agreements with landowners or local authorities approved by the DEP.

Applicants must provide a site and facility reclamation and decommissioning plan which "indicates the planned life of the ... solar energy facility and the means by which the facility and its site will be decommissioned and reclaimed at the end of the facility’s life" and "certifies that any property owner within the ... solar energy facility and its site who is not the applicant has been consulted in development of the reclamation and decommissioning plan." The plan "shall comply with all requirements adopted by the industrial siting council under §§35-12-105 (d)." The plan "shall be updated every five (5) years until site reclamation and decommissioning is complete." All applications for a Solar Energy Facility Permit "shall meet the requirements adopted pursuant to §§35-12-105 (d) and (e) regardless of whether the facility is referred to the industrial siting council pursuant to §§18-5-509 or is otherwise subject to the industrial siting act." Albany County will request that the Wyoming Industrial Siting Council include Albany County as an entity that can access the financial assurance provided for decommissioning and reclamation to ensure proper decommissioning and reclamation occurs at the end of the project’s life.

The sign shall state the property is being proposed for development and shall give contact information for the Planning Department. The sign(s) shall be posted at least fourteen (14) days prior to consideration of a development proposal before the Planning and Zoning Commission and the Board of County Commissioners. section: Section 12. Commercial Wind and Solar Energy Siting Regulations and Permitting

summary: Section 12, subsection F.4(f)(v) requires that "soil disturbance on the site will be minimized and that appropriate measures will be taken to restore disturbed areas to its former state." Subsection G.10 'Sediment Control' mandates that Owners or Operators shall: (a) minimize disturbance and construction on erodible slopes; (b) minimize the number of new roads and construction staging areas; (c) minimize the grading width of roads; and (d) reclaim areas disturbed by construction activities with native vegetation as areas of the solar energy facility complete construction. Subsection G.11 requires that "all phases of construction shall be routinely inspected by a professional licensed in the State of Wyoming" to ensure "potential erosion impacts are mitigated and disturbed areas are revegetated with native grasses." These requirements apply to commercial solar energy facilities defined as having a rated power capacity of more than one-half (0.5) megawatt of electricity and not for personal use, as per the definition of Solar Energy Facility. No alternative options or conditions for soil, erosion, or sediment control are provided in the text.
section: Section 12. Commercial Wind and Solar Energy Siting Regulations and Permitting

summary: Solar energy facilities shall be setback three hundred (300) feet of an occupied structure or residence unless waived in writing by the owner of the structure or residence; other setbacks include one hundred (100) feet from any outer boundary of the facility and two hundred (200) feet from any public road right-of-way.

summary: The ordinance requires that the permit application for Solar Energy Facilities greater than 0.5 MW include a "site and facility reclamation and decommissioning plan which indicates the planned life of the facility and the means by which the facility and its site will be decommissioned and reclaimed at the end of the facility’s life," and that the plan "shall comply with all requirements adopted by the industrial siting council under W.S. 35-12-105(d)." The plan "shall be updated every five (5) years until site reclamation and decommissioning is complete." Bonding "may be required for facility reclamation and decommissioning for facilities not meeting W.S. 35-12-102." These requirements also apply to addendum applications for additions to the facility. The ordinance applies to facilities "with gross generation of more than 0.5 megawatts."
section: APPLICATION FOR WIND AND/OR SOLAR ENERGY FACILITY PERMIT

summary: For solar energy facilities (W.S. 18-5-504): b. Would locate solar panels within one hundred (100) feet of any outer boundary of the facility; Additionally, other setback options include: a. Would locate the facility within three hundred (300) feet of an occupied structure or residence unless waived in writing by the owner of the structure or residence; c. Would locate the facility on unzoned land less than two hundred (200) feet from any public road right-of-way or on other land less than one hundred (100) feet from any public road right-of-way. Only the 100 feet from the outer boundary of the facility applies to non-participating property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, parcels, and/or subdivisions.

The ordinance explicitly requires that "Any addition to a previously permitted wind and/or solar energy facility must receive separate approval and an Addendum application for each addition must be submitted for approval." The addendum application must include: "Certification that the proposed addition to the facility will comply with all the standards required by W.S. 18-5-504," "an updated written emergency management plan," "an updated waste management plan," "evidence sufficient for the Board of County Commissioners to determine if construction and operation of the proposed addition has adequate legal access," and "a reclamation and decommissioning plan which indicates the planned life of the addition in the facility." The Board "shall not issue an addendum to a permit for a facility if that facility does not comply with standards properly adopted by the Board of County Commissioners." The addendum process also requires public notice, hearings, and compliance with bonding and industrial siting council requirements if applicable. The application fee for an addendum is "25% of the facility permit fee or $5,000, whichever is greater." These requirements apply to facilities with gross generation of more than 0.5 megawatts. No other options or exceptions for repowering or additions are provided in the text.
section: WIND AND/OR SOLAR ENERGY PERMIT ADDENDUM

summary: For solar energy facilities (W.S. 18-5-504): c. Would locate the facility on unzoned land less than two hundred (200) feet from any public road right-of-way or on other land less than one hundred (100) feet from any public road right-of-way.

The regulations require Commercial Scale Wind and Solar Energy Facilities to submit a site and facility reclamation and decommissioning plan specifying triggering events for decommissioning upon 18 months of continuous non-operation, removal of structures, debris, and cabling down to 36 inches below soil surface, restoration of soil and vegetation, and a certified estimate of decommissioning costs updated every five years. Financial assurance must be secured by the Developer/Owner(s) in an amount equal to the certified estimate, with acceptable forms including a self bond, surety bond, federally insured certificate of deposit, government-backed securities, or cash. section: CHAPTER III, PERMIT AND DESIGN REQUIREMENTS, COMMERCIAL SCALE WIND AND SOLAR PROJECTS, 5. Minimum Design Requirements, IV. Reclamation, Decommissioning and Financial Assurance Responsibility and V. Reclamation, Decommissioning and Financial Assurance Requirements

If glare is predicted, the Applicant/Developer "shall provide mitigation measures to address the impacts of solar glare." Mitigation measures "may include and are not limited to textured glass, anti-reflective coatings, screening, and angling of solar PV modules in a manner that reduces glare to surrounding land uses." This applies to Commercial Scale Solar Energy Facilities as defined as "a wind or solar facility with a rated capacity of 25 KW or greater."
section: CHAPTER III PERMIT AND DESIGN REQUIREMENTS COMMERCIAL SCALE WIND AND SOLAR PROJECTS

summary: Solar Energy Facilities shall not be located less than two hundred (200) feet from any public road right-of-way or on other land less than one hundred (100) feet from any public road right-of-way. section: CHAPTER III PERMIT AND DESIGN REQUIREMENTS COMMERCIAL SCALE WIND AND SOLAR PROJECTS, C. Solar Energy Facilities

summary: The Fremont County Wind and Solar Energy Facility Siting Regulations explicitly require Commercial Scale Solar Energy Facilities (defined as 25 KW or greater) to submit detailed site plans including construction site plans showing all components necessary during construction (Chapter III, Section 4.A.1). Applicants must provide a report by a Wyoming Licensed Professional Engineer detailing "produced water quality, supply, demand, disposal of water during the construction and maintenance of the Wind or Solar Facility Area, and the Project’s effect on water quality and supply" including a water impact mitigation plan if significant adverse impacts are identified (Chapter III, Section 3.B.k). An inventory of wetlands and riparian areas and any anticipated impacts with appropriate mitigation plans must also be submitted (Chapter III, Section 3.B.l). The Applicant/Developer must present tentative proposals regarding "storm drainage and use of County infrastructure; natural hazard areas including flood zones, environmental problems, irrigation ditch and drainage issues, wildlife and fisheries considerations, erosion controls, vegetative cover and grading proposals, soils problems" during the pre-application conference (Chapter IV, Section 1.B.I.b and c). Additionally, reclamation and decommissioning plans must include "provisions for the restoration of the soil and vegetation" and removal of structures and debris down to 36 inches below soil surface (Chapter III, Section 5.V.A.iii). These requirements apply specifically to Commercial Scale facilities and are conditions for permit approval.
section: CHAPTER III PERMIT AND DESIGN REQUIREMENTS COMMERCIAL SCALE WIND AND SOLAR PROJECTS
