section: CHAPTER III, PERMIT AND DESIGN REQUIREMENTS, C. Solar Energy Facilities, I.

summary: Prior to receiving siting approval under these regulations, Goshen County and the applicant or facility owner must formulate a decommissioning and recycling plan to ensure that the SECS Project is properly deactivated, shut down and removed as stated in WS §§ 18-5-503 (x). The recycling and decommissioning plan shall include: provisions for decommissioning and recycling the SECS facility when no electrical energy is generated for a continuous period of six (6) months; provisions for the removal of structures, debris and cabling, including those below the soil surface down to forty-eight (48) inches from original grade; no damaged or decommissioned solar panels will be disposed of in Goshen County, WY; the recycling and decommissioning plan will clearly state the location and company name contracted to accept the damaged and decommissioned panels; provisions for the restoration of the soil and vegetation; an estimate of the decommissioning costs certified by a professional engineer to be updated yearly and submitted to the Commissioners; financial assurance secured by the applicant, facility owner or operator, in an amount equal to the professional engineer's certified most recent estimate of the decommissioning and recycling costs; identification of and procedures for access by Goshen County officials to the financial assurances; binding terms on the facility owner and operator and any successors, assigns or heirs; County access to the site to effect or complete decommissioning; County Commissioners' right to review and reconsider the plan at decommissioning; financial assurance may be provided by letter of credit, self-bond, surety bond, federally insured certificate of deposit(s), government-backed securities, or cash; a conservation fund assessed at a rate of ½ % of the project's monthly power generation/sales may be required; the County Commissioners may reject proposed forms of financial assurance if inadequate; bond or financial assurance forfeiture proceedings may occur after notice and decision by the Commissioners. These requirements apply to SECS Projects as defined, which exclude only those with generating capacity of 30 MW or less located solely on owner's property, thus applying to projects greater than 30 MW or involving multiple properties.

SECS Facilities shall be designed so that there is not a glare at an adjacent property unless waived in writing and recorded against the property by the landowner in the Goshen County Clerk's office. This applies to SECS Projects as defined, which exclude SECS with a generating capacity of 30 Mega Watts or less located solely on owner's property.
section: IV. Application Process for SECS Use Permit, B. Supplemental Information, 6. Significant Glare

summary: All SECS Project structures shall be located such that the base of any array is at a distance of not less than 1/4 mile from any property line contiguous or adjacent to the facility, unless waived in writing by the owner of every property which would be located closer than the minimum distance. All SECS Project structures shall be constructed such that any array or other structure, other than underground installations, transmission lines, roadways and structures appurtenant to roadways, is at a distance of not less than 1 mile from any platted subdivision unless this restriction is waived in writing by the owners of all lands included within the distance specified. Setback distances may be modified at the discretion of the County Commissioners upon: a) affected adjacent property owner(s) providing a waiver to the setback requirement, including such recordation at the Office of the Clerk; b) the determination by the Commissioners that a significant degradation of the visual character of the area will occur; or c) the determination by the Commissioners that health, safety or welfare of the public will require a different setback. Any waiver of any of the above setback requirements shall run with the land and be recorded as part of the chain of title in the deed of the subject property.
section: V. DESIGN AND INSTALLATION, D. SETBACKS

summary: Section IV.B.7 states: 'SECS Facility structures shall be located to make maximum use of existing terrain, vegetation and structures for the purposes of maintaining viewshed.' Section IV.B.8 requires that 'outdoor storage is not permitted within the project boundary except at locations that are screened.' These requirements apply to SECS Projects as defined, which exclude SECS with a generating capacity of 30 Mega Watts or less located solely on owner's property. Thus, these vegetative buffer and screening requirements explicitly apply to SECS Projects greater than 30 megawatts or involving multiple properties.
section: IV. Application Process for SECS Use Permit

summary: There shall be no advertising or promotional lettering of any type allowed on any SECS Facility structures beyond the manufacturer's or applicant's logo. A reasonably visible warning sign concerning voltage must be placed at the base of all pad-mounted transformers and substations. Directional signage may be permitted by Goshen County on an individual basis for accessory uses such as visitor centers where the public may be permitted to view a facility and obtain information about the specific facility and solar farms in general.

All SECS Project structures shall be located such that the base of any array is at a distance of not less than 1 mile from an occupied structure, unless waived in writing by the person holding title to the residential dwelling or occupied structure. Other setback options include 1/4 mile from any property line (unless waived), 1 mile from any platted subdivision (unless waived), and 1 mile from the limits of any city or town. Setback distances may be modified at the discretion of the County Commissioners upon waiver by affected adjacent property owners, or if significant degradation of visual character or public health, safety, or welfare concerns arise.
section: V. DESIGN AND INSTALLATION, D. SETBACKS

summary: Utility scale solar systems which have not been in active and continuous service for a period of one (1) year shall be removed at the owner's or operator's expense. The site shall be restored in accordance with the approved reclamation plan within six (6) months of the removal. Unless exempt by the Public Service Commission, proof of financial assurance for complete decommissioning and site reclamation shall be provided in accordance with WECS regulations.

Utility scale solar system shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access. (4.10.12 B.1) This fencing requirement applies specifically to Utility Scale Solar Systems, defined as commercial facilities whose primary purpose is to supply electricity and consist of one or more solar arrays and accessory structures. Additional related standards include compliance with Natrona County adopted codes and Wyoming Department of Fire Prevention and Electrical Safety (4.10.12 B.2). For accessory solar generators, fencing requirements differ: all solar panels and equipment (excluding fencing, poles, and wires necessary to connect to facilities of the electric utility) shall be enclosed by a fence at least six (6) feet high, with wildlife fencing styles encouraged (4.10.13 D).

No utility scale solar system shall be placed such that concentrated solar glare projects onto adjacent properties or roadways within 1-1/4 mile of the project site. Additional setback may be required to mitigate noise and glare impacts. The applicant shall provide an analysis from solar glare hazard analysis software for PV systems that provide a quantified assessment of when and where glare will occur throughout the year onto nearby properties and public roadways. If glare is predicted, the applicant shall provide mitigation measures to address the impacts of solar glare, which may include textured glass, antireflective coatings, screening, and angling of solar PV modules in a manner that reduces glare to surrounding land uses.

Section 4.10.12 B.3 states: 'All utility scale solar systems shall not exceed twenty-five (25) feet in height.' This is the explicit maximum structure height allowed for Utility Scale Solar Systems. The units are feet. Other height limits mentioned, such as for accessory solar generators, also specify 25 feet but apply only to smaller, non-commercial systems and are therefore not relevant here.

Utility scale solar system structures shall be setback from all property lines and public rights-of-way at least fifty (50) feet. Additional setback may be required to mitigate noise and glare impacts, or to provide for designated road or utility corridors, as identified through the review process.

Utility scale solar system structures shall be setback from all property lines and public rights-of-way at least fifty (50) feet. Additional setback may be required to mitigate noise and glare impacts, or to provide for designated road or utility corridors, as identified through the review process.

Utility scale solar systems shall incorporate screening requirements as "Appropriate landscaping and/or screening material may be required to help screen the project area." Additionally, utility scale solar systems "shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access." Other related standards include height limits (not to exceed twenty-five (25) feet), setbacks, and visual impact mitigation measures such as limiting lighting and preventing solar glare onto adjacent properties or roadways. These requirements are explicitly applicable to Utility Scale Solar Systems as defined as commercial facilities supplying electricity with one or more solar arrays and accessory structures.

Section 4.10.12 D. Site Management requires that "Drainage from the site shall not adversely affect upstream and downstream properties," and that the project "Shall avoid soil erosion, controlled runoff, disturbance and construction on the erodible soils and slopes." It also mandates "Dust control within all phases of the project is mandatory by means acceptable to Natrona County and WDEQ. A wind erosion bond may also be required." Additionally, section 5.09 A.8 requires a "Drainage, Erosion, Dust Control, Grading and Vegetation Removal Plan prepared by a Wyoming licensed engineer" including "Erosion mitigation and runoff control" and a "Dust control plan." These requirements apply explicitly to Utility Scale Solar Systems, defined as "a commercial facility whose primary purpose is to supply electricity and consists of one (1) or more solar arrays and other accessory structures, equipment, including substations, switchyards, battery storage, electrical infrastructure, generators, transmission lines, communications infrastructure, and other appurtenant structures and/or facilities."

Solar panels shall be kept at least five hundred (500) feet from a residential zoning district and at least five-hundred (500) feet from existing residences that are not within a residential zoning district. (Section 4.10.12 F.2) Other setback mentioned is fifty (50) feet from property lines and public rights-of-way, but that does not pertain to occupied dwellings, buildings, structures, or residences.

Section 5.09.A.12 requires that projects within scenic viewsheds or utilizing reflective components provide a viewshed analysis of the project, including visual simulations from no less than ten vantage points that together provide a view from all sides of the project. The County may require analysis from significantly more vantage points, such as different distances and sensitive locations. This is a clear visual impact assessment requirement for Utility Scale Solar Systems. Other related provisions include 4.10.12.E on Visual Appearance, which states that "Appropriate landscaping and/or screening material may be required to help screen the project area" and lighting "may be required when determined necessary to mitigate visual impacts," but these do not explicitly mandate a visual impact assessment. Glare is addressed separately and is not considered part of the visual impact assessment requirements.

Section 3.a.(12)(h) Decommissioning requires that "Solar energy facilities which have not been in active and continuous service for a period of one (1) year shall be removed at the owner's or operator's expense." Additionally, "The site shall be restored in accordance with the approved reclamation plan within six (6) months of the removal." Furthermore, "proof of financial assurance for complete decommissioning and site reclamation shall be provided as part of a complete application in compliance with W.S. § 35-12-105(d) and (e)" unless exempt by the Public Service Commission.

Solar energy facilities shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access. This fencing requirement is part of the Design Standards for solar energy facilities, which also include height limits (not to exceed twenty-five (25) feet), signage restrictions, screening materials, glare prevention, airport interference considerations, and lighting limitations. These requirements apply to solar energy facilities that must obtain a Special Use Permit and comply with other application and operational standards outlined in the ordinance.

The ordinance requires that "No solar energy facilities shall be placed such that concentrated solar glare projects onto adjacent properties or roadways within 1-1/4 mile of the project site." This glare restriction applies to solar energy facilities defined as major utility uses requiring a Special Use Permit. Other related standards include height limits ("shall not exceed twenty-five (25) feet in height"), FAA approval for placement near airports, and lighting restrictions to mitigate visual impacts. The ordinance also mandates compliance with Wyoming Department of Fire Prevention and Electrical Safety standards and includes requirements for public notice, application review, and decommissioning plans.

The ordinance states: 'All solar energy facilities shall not exceed twenty-five (25) feet in height.' This applies to solar energy facilities requiring a Special Use Permit and subject to industrial siting approval, indicating utility-scale systems. The unit is explicitly given as feet.

Section 3.a.(12)(f)(iv) states: 'Appropriate screening material may be required to help screen the project area.' Additionally, solar energy facilities 'shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access' (f)(ii), and lighting 'shall be limited to the minimum necessary and full cut-off lighting may be required when determined necessary to mitigate visual impacts' (f)(vii). These requirements apply to solar energy facilities subject to a Special Use Permit, indicating utility-scale systems. No explicit vegetative buffer is mandated, but screening material is allowed. Other design standards include height limits (25 feet), signage restrictions, glare control, and FAA approval for airport proximity.

No sign shall be installed on any part of a solar facility except for signs related to safety, warning, emergency contact, and manufacturer’s name or logo. This applies to all solar energy facilities which require a Special Use Permit and include detailed application requirements such as a project narrative, site plans, and compliance with various standards. Other related provisions include perimeter fencing, height limits (not to exceed twenty-five (25) feet), screening requirements, glare restrictions, FAA approval for airport vicinity, and lighting limitations to mitigate visual impacts.

Under Section 3.a.(12)(e)(iv), the ordinance explicitly requires that "Dust and erosion control is required in compliance with DEQ regulations" for solar energy facilities. These facilities are defined as major utility uses requiring a Special Use Permit and include requirements such as a project narrative, site and facility reclamation and decommissioning plan, and compliance with Wyoming Department of Fire Prevention and Electrical Safety standards. Other related requirements include controlling noxious weeds and invasive species until decommissioning is complete, drainage not adversely affecting upstream and downstream properties, and compliance with setback requirements per W.S. § 18-5-504. Industrial Siting Council approval is required for solar energy facilities meeting industrial facility standards under W.S. § 35-12-102.

Section 13.15.060 requires a Site and Facility Reclamation and Decommissioning Plan as part of the Solar Energy Facility Permit application, including: "a description of the plan to remove the solar energy facility equipment and to restore the land to its previous use upon the end of the facility’s life," "provisions for the removal of structures, debris, and associated equipment on the surface and to a level of not less than five (5) feet below the surface," "provisions for the restoration of the soil and vegetation," "an estimate of the decommissioning costs in future dollars at the time of filing certified by a Wyoming Licensed Engineer," "a written financial plan approved to ensure that funds will be available for decommissioning and land restoration," and that "the facility owner/operator shall provide Platte County with Financial Assurance to cover the estimated costs of decommissioning and that the County shall have access to the facility and to the funds to effect or complete decommissioning one (1) year after cessation of operations." The applicant must provide a new estimate of decommissioning costs every five years. Section 13.15.070 N further requires the decommissioning plan and financial assurance, stating the Board of Commissioners "shall set an amount to be held in bond, escrow, or other acceptable form of funds" and that the county shall have access to these funds after cessation of operations. These requirements apply explicitly to Solar Power Facilities defined as utility-scale commercial facilities for wholesale or retail sales of electricity.

Section 13.15.050 D. Safety/Access requires that "An appropriate security/livestock fence (height and material to be established through the Solar Energy Facility Permit process) shall be placed around the perimeter of the solar energy facility." This fencing requirement applies to all solar energy facilities, which includes utility-scale commercial facilities as defined in Section 13.15.030 F. Other related safety measures include appropriate warning signage at entrances and perimeter, and locked entrances must have visible  "High Voltage"  signs, contact information for the electric utility provider and site operator, the facility’s 911 address and GPS coordinates, and Knox boxes and keys for emergency personnel access.

summary: Section 13.15.050 F.e states: 'No solar energy facility shall produce glare that would constitute a nuisance to occupants of neighboring properties or persons traveling neighboring roads.' Additionally, Section 13.15.060 K requires that for solar energy facilities located within five hundred (500) feet of an airport or within approach zones of an airport, applicants shall complete and provide the results of the Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool (SGHAT) for the Airport Traffic Control Tower cab and final approach paths, consistent with the Interim Policy, FAA Review of Solar Energy Projects on Federal Obligated Airports, or most recent version adopted by the FAA.
section: Section 13.15.050 - Regulations and Design Standards—Solar Energy Facilities

The maximum height for all structures shall be established through the Solar Energy Facility Permit process, provided a structure height of thirty feet, or less shall always be permitted.' This means 30 feet is the default maximum height always allowed, with the possibility of other heights set through the permit process. The units are feet.
section: Section 13.15.050 - Regulations and Design Standards—Solar Energy Facilities

summary: Section 13.15.050 B.a states: 'No concentrated solar energy facility shall be erected on any lot less than forty acres in size. No photovoltaic solar energy facility shall be erected on any lot less than five acres in size.' The most restrictive minimum lot size applicable to Solar Power Facility (Utility-Scale Commercial Facility) is five acres for photovoltaic solar energy facilities. The units are acres.
section: Section 13.15.050 - Regulations and Design Standards—Solar Energy Facilities

summary: No operating solar energy facility shall produce noise that exceeds any of the following limitations: (a) Fifty (50) dBA, as measured at the property line of any neighboring residentially zoned lot; (b) Forty-five (45) dBA, as measured at any existing neighboring residence between the hours of nine p.m. and seven a.m.; (c) Sixty (60) dBA, as measured at the property lines of the project boundary, unless the owner of the affected property and the planning commission agree to a higher noise level. The most restrictive limit is 45 dBA during nighttime hours. Units are dBA as explicitly stated in the text.
section: Section 13.15.050 - Regulations and Design Standards—Solar Energy Facilities

summary: Solar energy facility structures shall be set back from all property lines at least one hundred (100) feet. Additional setbacks include 200 feet from public road rights-of-way within an Agriculture District and 100 feet within Commercial and Industrial Districts, and 300 feet from all residentially zoned lots and existing residences and/or occupied structures. Additional setbacks may be required to mitigate noise and glare impacts, or to provide for designated road or utility corridors, as identified through the review process.
section: Section 13.15.050 - Regulations and Design Standards—Solar Energy Facilities

summary: Solar energy facility structures shall be set back from public road rights-of-way at least two hundred (200) feet within an Agriculture District and one hundred (100) feet within Commercial and Industrial Districts. The 200 feet setback in Agriculture Districts is the most restrictive value. Additional setbacks may be required to mitigate noise and glare impacts, or to provide for designated road or utility corridors, as identified through the review process.
section: Section 13.15.050 - Regulations and Design Standards—Solar Energy Facilities

summary: Section 13.15.050 F.b states: "Appropriate landscaping and/or screening materials may be required to help screen the solar energy facility and accessory structures from major roads and neighboring residences." This indicates that screening requirements, including vegetative buffers or other materials, may be imposed to mitigate visual impacts of utility-scale solar power facilities. No other explicit vegetative buffer or screening requirements are detailed in the provided text.
section: Section 13.15.050 - Regulations and Design Standards—Solar Energy Facilities

summary: Section 13.15.050 D (Safety/Access) requires that "appropriate warning signage shall be placed at the entrance and perimeter of the solar energy facility project." At all locked entrances, the following must be provided: "i. A visible 'High Voltage' warning sign. ii. Name(s) and contact number(s) for the electric utility provider. iii. Name(s) and contact number(s) for the site operator. iv. The facility’s 911 address and GPS coordinates. v. Knox boxes and keys shall be provided at locked entrances for emergency personnel access." These signage requirements apply to solar energy facilities as defined in the chapter, which includes utility-scale commercial solar power facilities. No other signage options or conditions are specified.
section: Section 13.15.050 - Regulations and Design Standards—Solar Energy Facilities

summary: Section 13.15.050 C requires a "Drainage, Erosion, Dust Control, Grading and Vegetation Removal Plan prepared by a Wyoming Licensed Engineer based on a 25-year storm event unless the location, terrain and topography dictate a higher amount." Section 13.15.060 J further specifies that the application must include a Drainage, Erosion, Dust Control, Grading and Vegetation Removal Plan to include: "a. Existing and proposed contours. b. Existing wetlands and floodways. c. Water management structures. d. Drainage flow direction. e. Effects on downstream and upstream properties. f. Effects on irrigation. g. Erosion mitigation and runoff control. h. Dust control plan." These requirements apply to all solar energy facilities as defined, which includes utility-scale commercial facilities for wholesale or retail sales of electricity.
section: Section 13.15.050 - Regulations and Design Standards—Solar Energy Facilities and Section 13.15.060 - Permit Applications

summary: Solar Power Facilities (Solar Energy Facilities) require a Solar Energy Facility Permit from the Board of County Commissioners before locating, erecting, constructing, or enlarging such a facility (Section 13.15.040). summary: Section 13.15.070 F requires that "projects that are within a sensitive viewshed, utilize reflective components (e.g., exposed mirrors), or that propose structures taller than thirty (30) feet must provide a viewshed analysis of the project, including visual simulations of the planned structures and analysis of potential glare impacts." The visual simulations must be from "no less than four (4) vantage points that together provide a view from all sides of the project." More visually sensitive proposals "may require analysis from significantly more vantage points, such as different distances and sensitive locations." Additionally, the planning commission may require a "Zone of Theoretical Visibility/Zone of Visual Impact (ZVI) Analysis," which is a "three hundred sixty-degree (360°) computer analysis to map the lands within a defined radius of a location that would likely be able to see an object." It also states that "Significant visual impacts that cannot be adequately mitigated are grounds for denial."

summary: The ordinance requires a "site and facility reclamation and decommissioning plan which indicates the planned life of the facility and the means by which the facility and its site will be decommissioned and reclaimed at the end of the facility's life". This plan "shall comply with all requirements adopted by the industrial siting council under W.S. 35-12-105(d)" and "shall be updated every five (5) years until site reclamation and decommissioning is complete." This requirement applies to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities defined as those "with a rated power capacity of more than one-half (0.5) megawatt of electricity from solar power". The plan must be submitted as part of the permit application and the applicant must certify that "any owner of land within the facility and its site who is not the applicant has been consulted in development of the reclamation and decommissioning plan."

Section 6(b) states: "No facility shall be placed such that solar glare casts on to adjacent properties or public roads." Section 4(c)(xvi) requires "A Solar Glare Hazard Analysis utilizing software for Photovoltaic (PV) systems that provide an assessment of when and where glare will occur throughout the year. If solar glare is predicted, the applicant shall provide mitigation measures to address the impacts of solar glare. Mitigation measures may include and are not limited to textured glass, anti-reflective coatings, screening, distance, and angling of Solar PV modules in a manner that reduces glare to surrounding land uses of non-participating property owners." These requirements apply to commercial solar energy facilities defined as having a rated power capacity of more than one-half (0.5) megawatt of electricity from solar power.

Section 6(c)(i) states: 'No solar array shall exceed fifteen (15) feet in height above adjacent grade.' On-site poles, interconnection, or safety system equipment are not limited in height. The unit is feet.

summary: Commercial Solar Energy Facilities shall only be located in the Agricultural, Heavy Industrial and Light Industrial zoning districts.

The ordinance requires a setback of one hundred (100) feet from any outer boundary of the facility. Additional setback distances include two hundred (200) feet from any public road right-of-way in the Agricultural district or one hundred (100) feet in other zoning districts, but these relate to roads rather than property lines. The key setback from non-participating property lines, lot lines, facility perimeters, or parcels is the 100 feet from the facility outer boundary as stated in Section 6(a)(ii) and Wyoming Statute 18-5-504(a)(vii)(B): 'Would locate the facility within one hundred (100) feet of any outer boundary of the facility.'

Setback distances from public road rights-of-way for Commercial Solar Energy Facilities are: "In the Agricultural district, two hundred (200) feet from any public road right-of-way, or in any other zoning district, one hundred (100) feet from any public road right-of-way." The Board may increase setbacks beyond these values to accommodate wildlife and reduce vehicle-animal collisions. For lands within incorporated municipalities, setbacks shall follow municipal governing body recommendations. The 200 feet setback in agricultural zones is the most restrictive fixed distance value. Other options include 100 feet in other zoning districts and possible increases for wildlife considerations.

Section 6(e) states: 'No advertising or promotional lettering shall be displayed on any facility beyond the non-illuminated manufacturer’s or applicant’s logo.' It also permits 'Safety, warning, regulatory, emergency contact, directional and identification signs.' The application requirements in Section 4(c)(iv) require a site plan showing 'types of signage and location.' These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities defined as having 'a rated power capacity of more than one-half (0.5) megawatt of electricity from solar power.'

The ordinance requires a drainage study quantifying stormwater runoff and identifying necessary drainage improvements that will result in no net increase from historic runoff rates (Section 4(c)(xv), application checklist item 13). It mandates that drainage improvements be installed to ensure no net increase above historic runoff rates and prohibits placing facilities in regulatory Special Flood Hazard Areas (Section 6(d)). These requirements apply to Commercial Solar Energy Facilities defined as having a rated power capacity of more than one-half (0.5) megawatt of electricity from solar power. No other soil, erosion, or sediment control options or conditions are explicitly provided in the text.

summary: Section 9.a.(14) Decommissioning: (a) Solar Energy Facility which has not been in active and continuous service for a period of one year shall be removed at the owner’s or operator’s expense. (b) The site shall be restored in accordance with the approved reclamation plan within six months of the removal. (c) Unless exempt by the Public Service Commission, proof of financial assurance for complete decommissioning and site reclamation shall be provided in accordance with WECS regulations. Additionally, Section 9.b.(15) requires a site and facility reclamation and decommissioning plan which indicates the planned life of the facility and the means by which the facility and its site will be decommissioned and reclaimed at the end of the facility's life and which certifies that any owner of land within the facility and its site who is not the applicant has been consulted in development of the reclamation and decommissioning plan. Such plan shall comply with all requirements adopted by the industrial siting council under W.S. 35-12-105(d). If the permit is granted, the plan shall be updated every five (5) years until site reclamation and decommissioning is complete.

Solar Energy Facilities shall be enclosed by perimeter fencing to restrict unauthorized access. (Section 9.a.(1)) Other requirements for Solar Energy Facilities include potable water and sanitary sewer for permanent occupied buildings, compliance with National Electrical Code and Wyoming Department of Fire Prevention and Electrical Safety standards, height not exceeding twenty five feet, minimum lot size of 40 acres, underground on-site power lines, setbacks from property lines and public rights-of-way, visual appearance standards, noise limitations, decommissioning plans, and various application requirements including fencing detail in drawings.

No Solar Energy Facility shall be placed such that concentrated solar glare projects onto adjacent properties or roadways within 1-1/4 mile of the project site. Solar panels shall not be placed in the vicinity of any airport in a manner that would interfere with airport flight patterns. Acknowledgement of approval from the Federal Aviation Administration will be necessary. The applicant shall provide an analysis from solar glare hazard analysis software for PV systems that provide a quantified assessment of when and where glare will occur throughout the year on to nearby properties and public roadways. If glare is predicted, the applicant shall provide mitigation measures to address the impacts of solar glare. Mitigation measures may include and are not limited to textured glass, anti-reflective coatings, screening, and angling of solar PV modules in a manner that reduces glare to surrounding land uses.

Section 9.a.(4) states: 'All Solar Energy Facilities structures shall not exceed twenty five feet in height.' This is the explicit maximum height restriction for Solar Energy Facilities, which are distinguished from smaller on-site systems. Other height limits mentioned apply only to on-site solar energy systems, such as ground or pole-mounted on-site systems not exceeding 15 feet in height, but these do not apply to Solar Energy Facilities as defined here. The unit for the height restriction is feet.

The ordinance states: 'No Solar Energy Facility shall be constructed on any parcel less than 40 acres in size.' This is the explicit minimum parcel size requirement for Solar Energy Facilities, which are defined as systems intended for offsite electricity generation or sale. The unit of measurement is acres, a standard area unit.

No operating Solar Energy Facility shall produce noise that exceeds the following limitations: 50 decibels on the dB(A) scale during the hours between 7 AM and 7 PM MDT as measured at the property line of any neighboring residentially zoned lot, and 45 decibels on the dB(A) scale during the hours between 7 PM and 7 AM MDT as measured at the property line of any neighboring residentially zoned lot. The most restrictive value is 45 dBA during nighttime hours.

Solar Energy Facility structures shall be setback from all property lines at least fifty feet. All Solar Energy Facility structures shall be setback not less than two hundred feet from public rights-of-way for properties zoned agriculture and one hundred feet on all other lands allowed by this Resolution, or one and one-half times the height of the Solar Energy Facility structure, whichever is greater. Solar Energy Facilities shall also be setback a minimum of one hundred (100) feet from any outer boundary of the facility. Additional setback may be required to mitigate noise and glare impacts, to accommodate known big game animal migrations and frequent local wildlife movements and to reduce the risk of motor vehicle from any big game animal collisions, or to provide for designated road or utility corridors, as identified through the review process. Solar Energy Facility structures shall be setback a minimum of 1.25 miles from any residentially zoned properties or residence.

Solar Energy Facility structures shall be setback not less than two hundred feet from public rights-of-way for properties zoned agriculture and one hundred feet on all other lands allowed by this Resolution, or one and one-half times the height of the Solar Energy Facility structure, whichever is greater. Additional setback may be required to mitigate noise and glare impacts, to accommodate known big game animal migrations and frequent local wildlife movements and to reduce the risk of motor vehicle from any big game animal collisions, or to provide for designated road or utility corridors, as identified through the review process.

Section 9.a.(11)(b) states: 'Appropriate landscaping and/or screening materials may be required to help screen the Solar Energy Facility.' This applies to Solar Energy Facilities, which are subject to conditional use permits and have specific design standards including fencing, setbacks, and visual appearance requirements. Other related provisions include visual appearance requirements such as blending materials and colors (9.a.(11)(a)), restrictions on solar glare (9.a.(11)(c)), and lighting limitations (9.a.(11)(e)).

Solar Energy Facilities shall avoid soil erosion and controlled runoff. Disturbance and construction on erodible soils and slopes shall be avoided. A Drainage, Erosion, Dust Control, Grading and Vegetation Removal Plan prepared by a Wyoming Licensed Engineer is required, including erosion mitigation and runoff control. Dust control within all phases of the Solar Energy Facility is mandatory by means acceptable to Sweetwater County and WDEQ. Disturbed areas shall be reseeded in accordance with WDEQ regulations and the reclamation plan approved by the Board. These requirements apply specifically to Solar Energy Facilities, which are subject to conditional use permits and have additional standards such as fencing, setbacks, height limits, and decommissioning plans.

Solar Energy Facility structures shall be setback a minimum of 1.25 miles from any residentially zoned properties or residence. Other setback requirements include 50 feet from all property lines, 200 feet from public rights-of-way for properties zoned agriculture, and 100 feet on all other lands or one and one-half times the height of the Solar Energy Facility structure, whichever is greater, but these do not pertain to occupied dwellings or residences.

Section 9.b.(17) requires that projects that are within a sensitive viewshed or utilize reflective components (e.g., exposed mirrors) "shall provide a viewshed analysis of the project, including visual simulations of the planned structures." The number of visual simulations "shall be sufficient to provide adequate analysis of the visual impacts of the proposal, which shall be from no less than ten vantage points that together provide a view from all sides of the project." The County may require analysis from significantly more vantage points, such as different distances and sensitive locations.

Owners of solar facilities in Wyoming with capacities greater than 500 kW must submit a decommissioning plan to the county prior to construction that outlines the planned life of the facility, methods for site reclamation, and financial assurances to ensure proper decommissioning, with updates required every five years.
